experiences.title: Avoid task-restatement rubrics for import normalization fixes
experiences.description: Retrieve when a trajectory is fixing author-name or metadata normalization in an import/query-building pipeline and has found multiple plausible matching/import modules. Be wary of rubrics that only ask for a helper plus exception list without verifying the exact pipeline boundary and regression risks.
experiences.context: This applies in Python legacy import codebases where imported records are converted into saved/query objects through functions such as query builders, entity lookup, and matching utilities. The misleading pattern is a rubric that says the agent should strip leading honorifics case-insensitively with exceptions during import, which largely repeats the task and can overvalue patches that add a broad helper, mutate author dictionaries at the wrong layer, edit unrelated matching code, or omit proof that cleaned names flow through the query-building path. The original idea is still appropriate as a high-level acceptance criterion once a concrete patch exists, but it should be narrowed with visible evidence about the exact call site, mutation boundaries, existing name-order behavior, and targeted tests. During early exploration with no edits, absence of implementation should not be judged as a specific code flaw; at final-review stage, generic evidence of a `strip_honorifics` function is not enough.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often generated a broad positive criterion: implement case-insensitive honorific stripping with an exception list during import/query building. That criterion is directionally correct but too permissive for this task because many visible trajectories satisfied the surface shape while still being risky or wrong: they placed normalization only in lower-level matching/import helpers instead of the query-building author loop, mutated shared input records in place, expanded unrelated title/matching modules, introduced overly broad honorific lists and arbitrary exception lists, or attempted to normalize both sides of matching to compensate for regressions. A better rubric should focus on the integration contract: imported author dictionaries should be normalized at the point they are added to the query/edition author list before subsequent resolution, without rewriting unrelated matching behavior, without breaking existing comma-name/date matching, and with small targeted tests for representative honorifics and canonical exceptions. Avoid the tempting criterion “has a configured honorific list and exception handling” by itself; prioritize visible evidence of the call site, preservation of existing import semantics, bounded prefix matching, exact/case-insensitive exception preservation, and regression tests around existing author matching.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that address honorific stripping only at the surface level while failing to demonstrate safe integration with the import query-building path. This flaw is present when the visible plan or patch merely adds a generic `strip_honorifics` helper/list or modifies matching utilities/import lookup in isolation, but lacks evidence that author dicts are cleaned at the query-building boundary before author resolution and saved candidate creation, or introduces broad/unrelated changes that can alter existing name-order/date matching behavior.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Surface-only honorific normalization

evidence_to_check: normalization call site relative to query-building author loop
whether author dictionaries are copied or mutated in a way that affects existing matching tests
whether unrelated matching modules or comparison logic are rewritten
whether honorific detection is bounded to leading prefixes with delimiter/longest-match handling
whether canonical exception names are preserved case-insensitively
whether tests cover task examples and existing author matching behavior
metadata.applies_when: the task asks to normalize imported author names during query building/import resolution, especially in a codebase with separate query-building, entity lookup, and matching modules

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory targets the query-building/import boundary, preserves existing matching semantics, uses bounded honorific/exception logic, and adds or plans focused tests.
scale.2: Minor concern: the trajectory has the right integration point but leaves small uncertainty about copying/mutation, longest-prefix handling, or regression coverage.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory adds plausible stripping and exceptions but the visible evidence is ambiguous about whether cleaned names flow through the actual query-building path or whether existing matching behavior is preserved.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory mainly adds a helper/list or modifies lower-level matching/import lookup while missing the requested query-building boundary, mutating inputs unsafely, or broadening unrelated matching/title behavior.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory rewrites unrelated import/matching code, uses an overbroad honorific/exception scheme, breaks or ignores existing author name/date matching behavior, and lacks targeted tests proving the import pipeline contract.

experiences.title: Append-slash redirects must preserve query placement
experiences.description: Use when a Django/admin redirect bug concerns APPEND_SLASH dropping query strings and the trajectory is inspecting or changing redirect URL construction.
experiences.context: Applies in Django-style codebases when the task explicitly involves a slash-appending redirect that currently uses a path-only value and loses `QUERY_STRING`, especially in `AdminSite.catch_all_view()` or analogous final catch-all routing. This is most useful once the trajectory has located the redirect line or proposed an edit, because the visible evidence can show whether the constructed `Location` is `/path/?a=b` rather than `/path/` or `/path?a=b/`. It may be premature during pure repository exploration. It should not be generalized to unrelated redirect tasks where query preservation is not part of the contract, and it should not require one exact helper implementation if the visible code constructs the same URL semantics correctly.
experiences.experience: The useful criterion in these cases was not merely “uses `get_full_path()`” or “preserves the query string.” The discriminative boundary is that the redirect must append the slash to the path component before the `?` and keep the original query component intact. A patch that changes `request.path` to `request.get_full_path()` but then formats `"%s/"` around it can appear to preserve parameters while producing `/foo?id=123/`, which is wrong; the rubric should explicitly catch this ordering bug. Conversely, a manual construction from the existing path plus `?` + `QUERY_STRING` can satisfy the task even if it does not use Django’s idiomatic helper, so avoid making the helper name the sole pass condition. Also avoid adding speculative requirements such as SCRIPT_NAME or deployment-prefix handling unless the task or trajectory specifically investigates them; those can make the rubric too strict for the visible issue. Prioritize visible evidence from the edit or tests: the redirect target for a slashless URL with `id=123` becomes `/.../?id=123`, no-query redirects still become `/.../`, and unresolved or no-append cases retain existing 404/routing behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show that the slash-appending redirect constructs a Location whose path has the missing trailing slash inserted before any query string, while preserving the original query string and leaving the surrounding redirect/404 conditions unchanged. Strong evidence includes replacing a path-only redirect with an API or construction that explicitly supports appending the slash before `?`, or tests/verification demonstrating a URL like `/admin/auth/foo?id=123` redirects to `/admin/auth/foo/?id=123` rather than dropping the query or appending the slash after the query.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Correct query-preserving append-slash redirect

observable_evidence: The edited redirect no longer uses only a path value that omits `QUERY_STRING`.
The slash is inserted into the path component before the query separator.
The original query string is retained without moving the slash after query parameters.
Existing conditions for whether to redirect versus raise 404 are not broadened or removed.
avoid_overfitting_to: Requiring a specific helper name when equivalent URL construction is visible.
Accepting any query-preserving change that produces `/path?query/`.
Adding unrelated deployment-prefix or routing requirements not raised by the task or trajectory.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the redirect preserves query strings or fixes the slash placement.
scale.2: Recognizes that query strings are involved but proposes or leaves code that likely drops them, appends the slash after the query, or changes unrelated redirect conditions.
scale.3: Shows partial progress toward preserving the query string, but the slash/query ordering or preservation of existing no-query/404 behavior remains ambiguous.
scale.4: Clearly updates the redirect so query strings are preserved and the slash is placed before the query, with little or no evidence of unrelated routing changes.
scale.5: Provides decisive code and/or focused verification showing `/path?query` redirects to `/path/?query`, no-query redirects remain correct, and existing redirect eligibility/404 behavior is preserved.

experiences.title: Avoid checklist rubrics that over-credit superficial archival refactors
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating an Open Library coverstore archival trajectory that has broad task bullets about DB state, validation, locking, zero-padded paths, and legacy tar/zip behavior.
experiences.context: This applies in Python/web.py coverstore work where the task spans archival packaging, archive.org upload/serving, SQL state, legacy tar compatibility, and documentation. A misleading rubric in this setting praises general understanding of all requirements, adding an archive_batch table, adding lock/status columns, or enforcing zero-padded names, even when the visible trajectory has not connected those changes to the actual end-to-end archive flow. Those ideas can still be appropriate if the trajectory shows concrete integration with packaging, upload validation, DB finalization, retrieval redirects, and legacy behavior. They are weak or misleading when the agent is only doing reconnaissance, copying task bullets into a plan, making broad schema rewrites, adding local-only validation, changing tests to fit the patch, or producing code with visible compatibility/placement issues.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked for broad “system understanding,” “requirements fulfillment,” “validation/batch tracking,” or “zero-padded schema enforcement.” These criteria are not inherently wrong, but they became misleading because they rewarded visible buzzwords and partial infrastructure rather than the high-risk semantic contract: archived covers must be packaged and served from the correct archive.org layout while preserving legacy tar-index behavior. A future rubric should not treat the presence of status fields, locks, batch tables, zero-padding helpers, or a validation function as strong evidence by itself. Instead, prioritize visible evidence that the implementation connects all layers: creates the intended archive package format for new batches, computes item/batch/filename paths consistently from cover IDs and sizes, verifies actual uploaded package completeness rather than only local file existence, updates cover rows only when archival/upload/finalization succeeds, redirects served covers to the correct direct archive.org URL, documents the historic ID-range boundaries, and preserves existing tar/index APIs and tests. Avoid tempting criteria that merely ask whether the agent decomposed the five task bullets or added validation/concurrency/status concepts. Replacement criteria should look for end-to-end behavior and compatibility evidence, especially tests or inspections that exercise archive creation, database updates, retrieval URL construction, and legacy ranges without modifying tests to mask breakage.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear to address cover archival by adding broad schema/status/locking/zero-padding scaffolding but do not visibly implement or preserve the end-to-end archival contract: correct package format and archive.org layout, upload completeness validation, authoritative DB finalization, serving redirects, documented ID-range boundaries, and legacy tar-index compatibility. This flaw is especially important when the agent performs wholesale rewrites, validates only local files, changes existing tests, or leaves retrieval code inconsistent with the new archive metadata.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial archival-state scaffolding without end-to-end serving compatibility

metadata.environment: Open Library coverstore, Python/web.py, SQL schema, archive.org-backed cover archival
misleading_positive_cues_to_discount: validation functions that check only local tar/index files
tests altered to fit the patch rather than preserving legacy behavior
preferred_visible_evidence: package creation uses the intended remote-friendly archive layout for new batches
ID and size mapping are consistently used in archive creation, DB filenames/state, and serving URLs
upload validation checks actual archive.org package completeness or equivalent remote state
DB updates distinguish archived/uploaded/failed only after the corresponding operation succeeds
legacy tar-index paths and historic ID ranges remain compatible
documentation explains current archive locations and boundaries
existing coverstore tests or targeted behavioral checks pass without weakening assertions

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory ties any schema/status/locking changes to concrete package creation, upload validation, DB updates, serving redirects, and legacy compatibility, or it is still explicitly investigating without overclaiming implementation completeness.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory mentions or begins adding scaffolding, but also shows awareness of the need to integrate it with packaging, retrieval, and legacy behavior.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory adds some status/lock/path helpers or broad requirements coverage, but integration with upload validation, serving URLs, or legacy tar behavior remains unclear.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory makes substantial schema/status/locking/zero-padding changes while validation is local-only, retrieval integration is incomplete, or compatibility with existing tar/index behavior is visibly at risk.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory performs a broad rewrite or test modification that overfits the task checklist while leaving core archive packaging/remote retrieval/DB finalization inconsistent, broken, or unvalidated.

experiences.title: Robust Topic-Link Extraction for Backlink Features
experiences.description: Retrieve when a NodeBB-like forum task implements reverse topic backlinks by parsing post content for topic URLs, especially after the trajectory shows regex-based extraction or custom backlink storage.
experiences.context: Applies in Node.js/NodeBB-style forum codebases when the feature depends on detecting links from one post/topic to another and the visible trajectory has moved beyond exploration into a concrete parser/regex or hook-based implementation. It is most useful when the agent has inspected topic route formats, post creation/edit flows, or post parsing, and has added or is about to add backlink extraction logic. It is less useful if no extraction strategy has been chosen yet, if the implementation delegates URL recognition to a trusted existing router/parser with clear tests, or if the visible evidence is dominated by unrelated catastrophic corruption where a broader preservation/compilation criterion would be more decisive.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics focused on whether backlink detection handled NodeBB topic URL formats. That focus is useful because a backlink feature is only semantically correct if it recognizes the actual links users can place in posts. In these trajectories, visible regexes often matched only one narrow representation, such as rendered HTML href attributes or only `/topic/<number>` with a trailing slash. That is risky because the post lifecycle may expose raw markdown/plain content rather than sanitized HTML, and NodeBB topic links may be relative or absolute, include a slug, post index, query string, or fragment, and should be restricted to same-site topic references while ignoring self-links and false positives. A better rubric should not merely say “use a regex”; it should evaluate whether the extraction logic is aligned with the content representation at the hook point and the route formats already observed in the codebase. Avoid the tempting but too-narrow criterion of checking only that some `/topic/(\d+)` regex exists. Also avoid treating URL extraction as the only success condition when the trajectory visibly corrupts templates, overwrites core files, misses exports, or fails to render anything. Prioritize evidence such as inspected route patterns, whether extraction runs on raw or parsed post content, support for relative and absolute same-site URLs, handling of slugs/post-index suffixes/query/fragment, deduplication, topic existence checks, and exclusion of self/external links.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Actual Topic URL Extraction Coverage
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that backlink creation parses post content in the same representation available at the chosen post lifecycle hook and reliably extracts referenced topic IDs from the forum's real topic URL forms. Strong evidence includes support for same-site relative and absolute topic links, topic URLs with slugs and optional post-position/query/fragment suffixes, deduplication of repeated references, exclusion of self-links, avoidance of external or malformed false positives, and validation that referenced topics exist before recording backlinks.

metadata.environment: Node.js / NodeBB-like forum
evidence_to_check: observed topic route or canonical URL patterns
post lifecycle hook where extraction runs
whether content at that hook is raw markdown/plain text or rendered HTML
regex/parser implementation and supported URL variants
self-link, external-link, duplicate, and nonexistent-topic handling
do_not_overweight: presence of any regex alone
manual examples that cover only one URL form
template/admin/localization work unrelated to whether references are detected

scale.1: No concrete backlink extraction logic is visible, or the visible logic cannot plausibly parse the post content representation used at its hook point.
scale.2: Extraction exists but handles only a very narrow form, such as a single HTML href or bare `/topic/<id>` pattern, with no evidence it matches actual user-authored or canonical topic links.
scale.3: Extraction covers the basic same-site topic ID pattern and avoids the most obvious self-link case, but evidence is incomplete for raw-versus-rendered content, absolute URLs, slugs, suffixes, duplicates, or invalid targets.
scale.4: Extraction is clearly aligned with observed route formats and content representation, supports common relative/absolute topic URLs with slugs or suffixes, and includes most safeguards such as deduplication, self-link filtering, and topic existence checks.
scale.5: The trajectory provides strong, validated evidence that topic-link extraction is comprehensive for the forum's actual URL/content formats, avoids false positives, handles duplicates and edits consistently, validates targets, and is tested or otherwise checked against representative URL examples.

experiences.title: Restore ModelForm M2M Semantics in Custom Save Overrides
experiences.description: Use this when a Django task concerns a ModelForm subclass whose custom save() bypasses normal many-to-many persistence, especially when the trajectory has inspected both the subclass save() and BaseModelForm.save().
experiences.context: Applies in a Django repository when the reported bug is that a form subclass manually calls super().save(commit=False), mutates the instance, then saves it directly, causing ManyToManyField-backed form data to be dropped. It is most useful once the trajectory has localized the relevant save() override or has begun editing/testing it. It is less useful as a sole criterion during very early repository exploration before the agent has inspected the save path, and it should not be narrowed to an exact spelling of the fix if the visible code preserves the same ModelForm contract.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the real semantic contract: after a valid form has populated cleaned_data and the instance is saved, many-to-many form data must be persisted using Django’s save_m2m/_save_m2m mechanism, while password hashing, return behavior, and commit=False deferred-save behavior remain intact. This aligned well because the decisive visible evidence was not generic test activity, dependency installation, or ad hoc script success; it was whether the trajectory identified that the custom save() bypassed BaseModelForm.save(commit=True) and restored the missing m2m step after instance.save(). A better rubric should accept equivalent implementations that call the public save_m2m hook or the underlying _save_m2m at the correct time, and should optionally reward preserving or exposing deferred save_m2m for commit=False. Avoid a tempting but overly brittle criterion requiring an exact call shape, exact test command, or official regression test before judging implementation quality. Also avoid giving high credit merely because the agent reproduced the bug with a temporary script; reproduction is useful but incomplete unless the trajectory has applied or is clearly about to apply the localized save semantics fix.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should restore Django ModelForm many-to-many save semantics in the custom user-creation form save path: keep creating the instance with commit=False so the password can be hashed before saving; when commit=True, save the user instance first and then persist cleaned many-to-many/private relation data through the form’s save_m2m/_save_m2m mechanism; when commit=False, preserve the standard deferred workflow so callers can save the instance and then call save_m2m. Judge from visible code inspection, edits, and validation output, while accepting semantically equivalent implementations rather than requiring one exact method spelling.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: ModelForm-Compatible M2M Persistence

primary_visible_evidence: The trajectory identifies that the custom save() override calls the parent with commit=False and therefore bypasses BaseModelForm.save(commit=True).
The implementation saves many-to-many data only after the model instance has been saved and has a primary key.
Password hashing via set_password and the returned user instance behavior are preserved.
The commit=False path is not broken and preferably exposes or preserves deferred save_m2m behavior.
acceptable_fix_variants: Call the public save_m2m hook after saving the instance when it is available.
Call the underlying _save_m2m after saving the instance, with deferred save_m2m assignment for commit=False.
Use another local implementation only if it clearly delegates to the same cleaned_data relation-saving behavior.
non_decisive_evidence: Installing dependencies or repeatedly adjusting standalone Django settings.
Running unrelated test suites without inspecting the actual save semantics.
Reproducing that m2m data is missing but not applying the save-path fix.

scale.1: The trajectory has not identified the overridden save() as the cause and shows no concrete plan or edit for many-to-many persistence.
scale.2: The trajectory notices a many-to-many/save_m2m issue but only reproduces it or discusses it, with no correct localized implementation yet.
scale.3: The trajectory is comparable to the parent state: it has localized the save() override and understands that ModelForm save semantics are missing, but the visible implementation is incomplete, unverified, or risks breaking commit=False/password behavior.
scale.4: The trajectory applies a mostly correct fix that saves m2m data after the user is saved and preserves password hashing, with only minor uncertainty around deferred commit=False behavior or validation coverage.
scale.5: The trajectory clearly implements ModelForm-compatible semantics for both commit=True and commit=False, preserves password hashing and return behavior, and provides focused validation or tests demonstrating immediate and deferred many-to-many persistence.

experiences.title: Do not let playlist JSON support hide SQL membership contract gaps
experiences.description: Retrieve when a criteria/filter task requires both JSON operator persistence and SQL translation for relational membership, especially in Go/Squirrel criteria engines where the trajectory has already added JSON cases but SQL semantics remain uncertain.
experiences.context: Applies to Go codebases with a criteria engine whose expressions implement Squirrel-style ToSql methods and JSON rules use dedicated operator keys. The misleading pattern is generating a rubric focused mainly on recognizing/marshalling new JSON keys after the trajectory has visibly added those cases, while the task also requires a relational predicate against a referenced public playlist. JSON round-trip criteria are still appropriate when no JSON dispatch/marshal support exists yet, or when the only remaining uncertainty is persistence shape. They are not sufficient as the main discriminator once the trajectory already has inPlaylist/notInPlaylist-style keys and operator types but shows uncertain SQL construction, playlist-id extraction, public-playlist filtering, or validation.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics rewarded playlist-membership JSON recognition and round-trip preservation. That criterion is necessary but misleading in this cluster because many trajectories visibly added JSON switch cases and MarshalJSON methods, yet still left acceptance-critical defects: extracting an arbitrary first map value instead of a well-defined playlist reference field, using an unverified payload key, omitting or incorrectly expressing the public-playlist constraint, building subqueries in ways that produce wrong placeholders/args, or testing only JSON while SQL semantics were incomplete. A better rubric should focus on the end-to-end operator contract: the new expression must parse the intended playlist id from the JSON payload, generate parameterized include/exclude predicates over media_file membership in playlist_tracks, enforce that the referenced playlist is public via the playlist table/flag, and be validated by project-native SQL/arg and JSON tests. Avoid the tempting criterion that says dedicated JSON keys and round-trip behavior are enough evidence of progress; prioritize visible ToSql implementation details, schema-verified table/column/public-flag usage, placeholder/argument behavior, and tests that exercise both include and exclude SQL.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory appears to satisfy playlist-membership JSON recognition but leaves the relational SQL contract under-specified or wrong: the new operators do not reliably extract the expected playlist identifier from the operator payload, do not generate parameterized IN/NOT IN or equivalent EXISTS/NOT EXISTS predicates comparing media_file.id to playlist_tracks.media_file_id for the referenced playlist, do not enforce that the referenced playlist is public through the playlist table/public flag, or only validate JSON round-trip without SQL/args coverage for both inclusion and exclusion.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: JSON-only playlist operator implementation masks SQL contract defects

required_visible_evidence: Task requires playlist membership criteria operators with JSON persistence and SQL translation
Trajectory adds or plans dedicated playlist operator JSON keys
Trajectory includes or discusses ToSql/subquery implementation against playlist membership tables
Judge should inspect playlist-id payload handling, public-playlist filtering, parameterized SQL, and tests
metadata.environment: Go criteria package using Squirrel Sqlizer expressions and custom JSON operator dispatch

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory visibly handles JSON keys and also implements or plans schema-verified, parameterized SQL membership predicates with public-playlist filtering and meaningful SQL/JSON tests.
scale.2: Minor evidence: JSON support is present and SQL direction is mostly correct, but one detail such as payload-key validation, explicit public filtering, or SQL test coverage is only weakly evidenced.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory balances JSON and SQL but leaves important uncertainty, such as using an unverified playlist id key or not clearly validating generated SQL/args for both include and exclude operators.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory emphasizes JSON round-trip and adds operator types, but the visible SQL omits public-playlist enforcement, extracts arbitrary map values, uses questionable Squirrel/subquery construction, or lacks SQL-focused tests.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory treats JSON recognition as success while the visible ToSql implementation is absent, non-parameterized, malformed, ignores the referenced public playlist requirement, or cannot correctly compare media_file.id to playlist membership.

experiences.title: AnsiballZ-aware module respawn viability
experiences.description: Use when an Ansible-core trajectory is addressing interpreter compatibility for modules with system Python bindings, especially after it has begun designing or editing a respawn mechanism.
experiences.context: Applies to Ansible module-runtime tasks where modules such as package managers or fact collectors fail because the current remote Python lacks distro-specific bindings, and the requested fix is a module-side respawn under a compatible interpreter. It is most useful once the trajectory has inspected or edited module_utils, module_common/AnsiballZ execution, action execution, or affected modules’ import-failure paths. It is less useful as a standalone positive signal during very early reconnaissance: merely finding import guards, grepping for existing respawn support, or naming interpreter discovery files should not be treated as strong progress unless the trajectory also shows a concrete plan or implementation that can execute the packaged module correctly. It should also not replace separate criteria for SELinux compatibility work except where SELinux is being used as another missing-binding trigger.
experiences.experience:
The recurring useful criterion in these cases is not whether the agent understands that respawn is needed, nor whether it adds calls named respawn_module. The discriminative question is whether the trajectory is converging on a real module-runtime mechanism that works with Ansible’s packaged module execution model. Previous rubrics that required preserving arguments, avoiding loops, probing interpreters for required imports, and integrating with AnsiballZ/action execution identified the central risk: naive subprocess re-exec of sys.argv[0], hardcoded interpreter lists, action-plugin recursion without a guard, or broad edits to basic.py do not satisfy the feature even if they look plausible. Rubrics that only rewarded 'architecture understanding' or 'correct feature scope' were too generous during exploration and can overvalue repeated greps and file inspection.

A better rubric should require visible evidence of a robust respawn contract: a reusable module_utils API; a way to detect whether the module has already respawned; probing candidate interpreters for the actual missing import before switching; recreating or invoking the same packaged module payload with the original JSON arguments/module_utils environment; returning the respawned module’s JSON result to the original caller; and preserving each module’s existing fallback behavior when no compatible interpreter exists. Module integrations should be targeted at existing missing-binding branches and guarded so they do not respawn forever or skip existing auto-install/fail behavior. Avoid rewarding superficial proxies such as touching all mentioned modules, adding a method to AnsibleModule, using controller-side ansible_python_interpreter assignment, or hardcoding common Python paths without import probing and payload preservation.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show concrete progress toward a working Ansible module respawn mechanism for missing system Python bindings. Strong evidence includes a reusable module-runtime helper rather than ad hoc per-module subprocess calls; explicit prevention of repeated respawns; probing candidate interpreters for the required binding before respawning; execution of the same packaged module payload with the original JSON arguments and module_utils context; correct propagation of stdout/stderr/JSON result and cleanup behavior; and targeted integration into affected modules’ existing import-failure paths while preserving their original install/fail behavior when no compatible interpreter is found.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Working packaged-module respawn contract

metadata.environment: Ansible core module runtime using AnsiballZ-style packaging, module_utils helpers, and modules with distro-specific Python bindings
prioritize_evidence: shared respawn API or helper in module_utils/runtime support
has-respawned guard or equivalent recursion prevention
candidate interpreter probing for specific imports
payload/module arguments preserved across interpreter switch
respawned module result returned through normal Ansible JSON handling
affected modules call respawn only at missing-binding decision points and keep fallback errors/auto-install paths
do_not_overreward: hardcoded interpreter list without import probing
adding respawn_module calls without implementation viability
direct sys.argv subprocess re-exec that ignores packaged payload and JSON args

scale.1: No concrete respawn design or implementation is visible, or the trajectory only inspects files/searches for existing support.
scale.2: Recognizes missing-binding respawn as needed or identifies likely files, but has no viable mechanism for preserving packaged execution, arguments, and results.
scale.3: Adds or plans a respawn API and some module call sites, but key runtime requirements such as import probing, recursion guard, or argument/payload preservation are incomplete or unclear.
scale.4: Implements a mostly coherent respawn flow with guarded interpreter probing and targeted module integrations, but some edge cases in result propagation, fallback behavior, or AnsiballZ/module_utils packaging remain uncertain.
scale.5: Provides a robust, reusable, AnsiballZ-aware respawn mechanism with guarded interpreter probing, preserved module payload and JSON arguments, correct result propagation, cleanup behavior, and targeted integrations that preserve existing fallback semantics.

experiences.title: ROC Artificial Threshold as Infinite Sentinel
experiences.description: Use when evaluating a scikit-learn `roc_curve` fix centered on the prepended threshold used to create the initial `(fpr=0, tpr=0)` ROC point.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/scikit-learn trajectories where the task and investigation have localized the issue to `sklearn.metrics.roc_curve` prepending `thresholds[0] + 1` after `_binary_clf_curve`, especially when the agent has inspected `sklearn/metrics/_ranking.py`, compared local code with newer installed behavior, or discussed probability scores in `[0, 1]`. This is most useful once the agent is choosing or reviewing the implementation, not during very early repository exploration. It may be irrelevant for unrelated threshold-producing metrics, for fixes in `_binary_clf_curve`, or for tasks that explicitly require all returned thresholds including sentinels to be finite probability values.
experiences.experience: The useful criterion should not merely ask whether the agent detects probability scores and clips the prepended threshold to `1.0`. That proxy is tempting because the issue statement mentions probability estimates and a possible clipping workaround, but it misses the deeper API contract: the first returned threshold is artificial and represents a classifier predicting no positives, not an actual probability cutoff. A strong rubric should focus on replacing the finite `max(y_score) + 1` sentinel with a semantically explicit non-finite sentinel such as `np.inf`, while preserving the prepended zero `fps`/`tps` alignment, descending threshold order, and behavior for arbitrary decision scores. It should also give credit for updating docstrings/examples/tests to describe the new sentinel. Prioritize visible evidence such as the agent identifying the artificial threshold block, recognizing that `_binary_clf_curve` returns real score thresholds, noticing newer sklearn behavior uses `inf`, editing the repository source rather than installed packages, and updating documentation/examples. Penalize range-detection heuristics like `if thresholds[0] <= 1: extra_threshold = 1`, `np.all(y_score <= 1)`, or clipping, because they create ambiguous behavior at score exactly `1.0`, treat the artificial point as a real probability threshold, and leave documentation/API semantics inconsistent. Also avoid a rubric that literally requires every threshold to be `<= 1`, since the intended sentinel may be `np.inf`; the better criterion is that no inappropriate finite artificial threshold above the probability range is introduced.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Infinite ROC Sentinel Semantics
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should move `roc_curve` away from a finite `max(y_score) + 1` artificial first threshold and toward an explicit sentinel such as `np.inf` for the prepended `(fpr=0, tpr=0)` point, while preserving `fps`/`tps` alignment, threshold ordering, arbitrary decision-score behavior, and public documentation/examples for the returned thresholds.

prioritize_evidence: identifies that the problematic threshold is artificial and added after real thresholds are computed
uses a non-finite sentinel such as np.inf rather than probability-range clipping
keeps prepended fps/tps zeros aligned with the first threshold
updates docstring or examples that previously described max(y_score) + 1
distinguishes local repository source from installed sklearn behavior
avoid_proxy_criteria: requiring all returned thresholds to be <= 1 including the sentinel
using y_score or threshold range detection to choose 1.0
patching installed site-packages instead of repository files

scale.1: No meaningful progress on the `roc_curve` artificial threshold, or changes are made in unrelated files/functions.
scale.2: Recognizes the threshold issue but only proposes or applies a probability-detection/clipping heuristic without addressing the sentinel semantics or docs.
scale.3: Modifies the prepended threshold area and preserves basic ROC alignment, but the solution remains a finite `1.0`/range-based workaround or lacks consideration of boundary and decision-score behavior.
scale.4: Clearly identifies the artificial first threshold as a sentinel and replaces `max(y_score) + 1` with a non-finite sentinel while preserving ROC alignment; documentation or tests may be incomplete.
scale.5: Implements an explicit `np.inf`-style sentinel for the first threshold, preserves `fps`/`tps` and ordering semantics, avoids probability-clipping heuristics, and updates public documentation/examples or regression coverage to match the sentinel contract.

experiences.title: Django lookup resolver must preserve list-vs-tuple containers
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django ORM task concerns `Query.resolve_lookup_value()` changing list lookup values into tuples, especially after expression-resolution changes for iterable lookup RHS values.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django source tree when the task or trajectory explicitly identifies `django/db/models/sql/query.py` and the `Query.resolve_lookup_value()` branch that handles `list` and `tuple` lookup values. It is most useful once the agent has inspected or edited that branch, or has reproduced that list inputs are returned as tuples. The criterion is less relevant for unrelated ORM lookup bugs, for broad iterable-normalization work, or for stages where the agent has not yet found the resolver code. It should also not be reduced to a test-runner/setup criterion: test execution evidence is helpful, but the decisive semantic evidence is the handling of list/tuple reconstruction while preserving expression resolution.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the exact behavioral contract from the issue: resolving lookup RHS containers must not coerce a `list` into a `tuple`; a tuple should remain a tuple; and the expression handling introduced for iterable lookup values must still work. This aligns with visible trajectory evidence such as the agent locating `Query.resolve_lookup_value()`, identifying an unconditional `tuple(resolved_values)` reconstruction, replacing it with same-type reconstruction or an equivalent list-vs-tuple branch, and validating both list and tuple inputs. A stronger rubric should explicitly include preservation of nested/expression element resolution, preferably by requiring recursive resolution of elements rather than only checking the top-level container type. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as “run Django tests successfully,” “install missing dependencies,” “use PickledField specifically,” or “convert all iterables using `type(value)`”; those are proxies and can miss the core compatibility boundary. The best judgeable criterion should prioritize code/validation evidence that the existing `list`/`tuple` branch returns the same concrete container type it received, while continuing to call the resolver or expression-resolution path for contained expressions and leaving non-container lookup values unchanged.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the Django ORM lookup-value resolver fixes the list-to-tuple regression at the source: in the `list`/`tuple` handling path of `Query.resolve_lookup_value()`, resolved lookup values are reconstructed as the same concrete container type supplied by the caller, while contained expression values are still resolved with the appropriate resolver semantics and non-list/tuple values keep their existing behavior.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Preserve lookup iterable container type without regressing expression resolution

key_positive_evidence: identifies unconditional tuple reconstruction as the cause of list coercion
changes reconstruction so list inputs return lists and tuple inputs return tuples
keeps expression elements inside list/tuple values resolved rather than bypassed
does not broaden behavior to unrelated arbitrary iterables without justification
uses reproduction or validation comparing input and output concrete types
metadata.important_boundary: Container type preservation is necessary but strongest evidence also preserves recursive or nested expression-resolution behavior introduced for iterable lookup values.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory found or addressed the `resolve_lookup_value()` list/tuple coercion behavior.
scale.2: Recognizes the list-to-tuple symptom but does not show a concrete source change in the resolver, or proposes a change that risks bypassing existing expression resolution.
scale.3: Makes a plausible top-level fix so list inputs remain lists and tuple inputs remain tuples, but provides limited evidence about contained expressions, nested values, or unchanged non-container behavior.
scale.4: Clearly fixes same-type reconstruction for the resolver's list/tuple branch and preserves existing expression-element handling, with some validation for list and tuple behavior.
scale.5: Provides strong source and validation evidence that list, tuple, empty, and expression-containing iterable lookup values preserve their concrete container type while all contained values continue through the correct resolution path and unrelated lookup values are not changed.

experiences.title: Do not let metadata exposure stand in for full routing/deprecation behavior
experiences.description: Retrieve when an Ansible plugin-loader task asks for consistent handling of redirects, tombstones/removals, deprecations, and contextual messages, but the candidate rubric is tempted to focus mainly on exposing PluginLoadContext-style metadata.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Ansible-style plugin loader work where resolution context already exists and the trajectory discusses or edits loader.get(), find_plugin_with_context(), Jinja2 filter/test loading, collection plugin_routing, tombstones, deprecation warnings, or plugin error classes. The misleading pattern is treating attachment of resolution fields to returned plugin objects, a metadata dict, or a get_with_context-like helper as the central success signal for a task that also demands standardized user-facing warnings/errors and consistent behavior for removed/deprecated/redirected plugins. Metadata exposure can still be an appropriate rubric when the task or subtask is explicitly limited to preserving caller access to resolution context, or during early exploration as one piece of progress. It should not dominate final-review rubrics when the visible task requires end-to-end handling across routing metadata, removed-plugin exceptions, deprecation formatting, Jinja2/template consumers, and backward-compatible loader APIs.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster generated a positive criterion like “Plugin Resolution Metadata Exposure,” rewarding trajectories for recognizing that PluginLoadContext contains fields such as deprecation state, redirect chains, removal dates/versions, and exit reasons. That criterion is partly correct: a robust fix should preserve structured resolution context and avoid breaking existing get() callers. However, it becomes misleading when it overpredicts trajectories that only add object attributes, a metadata dictionary, or a new tuple-returning helper, while leaving removed/tombstoned plugins as None, duplicating warning text, missing contextual exception propagation, ignoring Jinja2/template paths, or even making broad brittle edits without relevant behavioral validation. For broad plugin-routing/deprecation tasks, generate rubrics that treat metadata exposure as necessary but insufficient. Prefer criteria that look for visible evidence of: backward-compatible context access; centralized deprecation/removal message construction; plugin-specific errors that carry the resolution context; callers that catch and render those errors consistently; special handling for Jinja2 filters/tests and template/action consumers; and tests or smoke checks for routed redirect, deprecated plugin, removed/tombstone plugin, and normal plugin loading. Avoid the tempting criterion “metadata is exposed on returned plugin instances” as a standalone high-value signal unless the current task is explicitly only about API introspection.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Metadata-only plugin routing fix
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for a broad plugin redirection/deprecation/removal task when the visible approach mainly exposes resolution metadata, such as by adding attributes, a metadata dictionary, or a helper returning context, but does not also address standardized contextual warnings/errors, tombstone/removal propagation, special plugin-loader consumers, and backward compatibility. This flaw is especially important when the task text asks for consistent error/warning formatting and centralized handling, not merely caller introspection.

metadata.environment: Python Ansible-style plugin loader with collection routing metadata and Jinja2 filter/test loaders
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: Presence of metadata fields on returned plugin objects or a get-with-context helper
required_visible_evidence: Resolution context remains accessible without changing existing get() semantics for normal callers
Removed or tombstoned plugins produce contextual plugin errors instead of silent None or ad hoc text
Deprecation/removal message formatting is centralized and reused by display/error paths
Redirect, deprecation, and tombstone metadata from collection routing is preserved through resolution
Special consumers such as template/Jinja2/action paths are considered, not only the base loader
Validation covers normal plugin loading plus routed redirect, deprecated plugin, and removed/tombstone cases
metadata.stage_boundary: Use this as a final-review or implementation-quality criterion; during early exploration, absence of all pieces may be acceptable if the trajectory has not yet proposed a patch.

scale.1: No evidence of the metadata-only flaw: the trajectory treats metadata exposure as one component and visibly addresses contextual errors/warnings, central formatting, compatibility, and relevant consumers.
scale.2: Minor evidence of overfocus on metadata, but the trajectory also plans or implements substantial behavior for removed/deprecated/redirected plugins and does not appear to break existing APIs.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory exposes context and mentions broader behavior, but visible edits or tests are concentrated in the base loader and leave important message/consumer/removal paths uncertain.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the implementation or plan primarily adds metadata attributes/dicts/helper returns and lacks convincing centralized message handling, tombstone error propagation, Jinja2/template/action coverage, or compatibility validation.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory equates metadata exposure with the fix, changes public return semantics or makes brittle/wrong-scope edits, ignores removed/deprecated user-facing behavior, or validates only unrelated/basic loading paths.

experiences.title: Preserve Behavior Flags Without Re-entering `syms` Reordering
experiences.description: Use this when a trajectory is fixing order-dependent `diophantine(..., syms=..., permute=True)` behavior caused by an internal recursive solve that normalizes symbol order.
experiences.context: Applies in a SymPy-like Python codebase when the visible task and trajectory involve a public solver option such as `permute=True` being lost only when an explicit `syms` order differs from the internally sorted variable order. The decisive situation is a reordering branch that calls the same public solver recursively to solve in canonical order, then remaps tuple positions back to the requested symbol order. This guidance is most useful once the agent has located that branch, reproduced the mismatch between two `syms` orders, or is proposing a patch there. It is not a generic rule to forward every argument through every recursive helper call: forwarding `syms` back into the same reordering branch can cause repeated re-entry, and unrelated recursive calls that solve numerator/denominator or internal subproblems may have different semantics.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric should focus narrowly on preserving the caller's behavioral flag through the symbol-normalization recursive solve while intentionally not forwarding the non-default `syms` argument into that same recursive entry path. Earlier broad rubrics about recursive parameter propagation captured the right root cause only when they emphasized `permute`; they become misleading if phrased as forwarding all user-supplied parameters, because the visible trajectory may try to pass `syms` as well and trigger infinite recursion. A better criterion asks whether the trajectory recognizes that the recursive call should solve with default/internal symbol order, keep `permute=True` active so sign/value permutations are generated, and then use the existing index mapping to return tuples in the requested `syms` order. The criterion should prioritize visible evidence such as: reproduction showing `syms` order changes result completeness; identification of the `syms != var` branch; discovery of a recursive call that omits `permute`; a patch or plan that passes only the behavior flag into that recursive solve; and validation that both `syms` orders produce complete permuted solutions while ordinary tuple ordering remains coherent. Avoid tempting but overbroad criteria that require propagating every option to every recursive call, adding broad algorithm changes, or judging success solely by running the whole test file when unrelated existing failures are present.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should identify the symbol-order normalization branch as the source of the order-dependent incomplete results and ensure that the internal recursive solve preserves the `permute` behavior flag without re-passing the non-default `syms` ordering into the same branch. Strong evidence includes reproducing the mismatch for reversed `syms`, locating the recursive self-call used before tuple remapping, explaining why `permute` must be forwarded to generate all sign/value variants, avoiding forwarding `syms` in a way that re-enters the reorder branch, and validating that results are complete and returned in the requested tuple order for multiple `syms` orders.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Selective Option Preservation in Symbol Reordering

required_visible_evidence: task involves incomplete or order-dependent solver results only when `syms` and `permute=True` interact
trajectory locates code that compares requested symbols with internal sorted variables and remaps result tuples
trajectory notices a recursive public solver call in that branch drops the permutation option
trajectory distinguishes forwarding the behavior flag from re-forwarding the non-default symbol order
boundary_conditions: do not apply as a blanket requirement to all recursive calls in the module
do not reward patches that pass `syms` back into the same normalization branch and risk infinite recursion
do not require changing unrelated denominator or helper recursive solves unless visible evidence shows they affect the reported behavior

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory connects the order-dependent incompleteness to the `syms` reordering recursive solve or to preserving `permute`.
scale.2: The trajectory suspects generic recursive parameter loss but has not clearly tied the issue to the `syms != internal order` branch or may propose forwarding all arguments indiscriminately.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies that `permute` is lost in the recursive solve used for symbol reordering, but its plan or validation is incomplete or ambiguous about avoiding re-passing `syms`.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly proposes or applies preserving `permute` in the symbol-normalization recursive call while leaving `syms` out of that recursive entry path, with targeted reproduction showing improved completeness.
scale.5: The trajectory fully demonstrates the selective fix: it locates the exact reordering mechanism, preserves `permute` through the recursive solve, avoids recursive `syms` re-entry, confirms both requested symbol orders return complete permuted solutions in the correct tuple convention, and avoids unnecessary unrelated recursive-call changes.

experiences.title: Require End-to-End Watcher Metrics, Not Buffer-Only Progress
experiences.description: Use when a Go observability task explicitly combines a missing circular float64 buffer with watcher event metrics and UI/reporting visibility, especially after the trajectory has only searched or has found existing watcher queue metrics but no event-rate instrumentation.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go repository with Prometheus-style metrics and a monitoring/top-style reporting surface, where the requested behavior includes watcher events-per-second, bytes-per-second, top resources, and a reusable fixed-size float64 rolling buffer. It is most useful once the trajectory has inspected utilities, watcher/event fan-out or watch stream code, metric registration, and monitoring/reporting code enough to distinguish the existing event buffer/queue-size metrics from the missing numeric rolling buffer and event observability. It may be premature during the first few exploratory steps before any relevant paths are known, and it should be narrowed to a standalone utility criterion only if the task is solely to fix a utility build symbol rather than to expose watcher observability.
experiences.experience: The earlier rubrics often asked for a circular float64 buffer, which was a useful minimum check when the visible trajectory had made no edits and was stuck repeating searches: there was no evidence of the named utility dependency being implemented, and that absence was strongly diagnostic. However, for this task family a buffer-only criterion is too weak as the main rubric because a standalone utility buffer does not deliver watcher event volume, byte throughput, per-resource frequency, or monitoring visibility. A better rubric should explicitly require the trajectory to connect three visible threads: a reusable fixed-size float64 buffer with focused tests; instrumentation at the actual watcher event emission/serialization path that records event counts/sizes with resource labels using existing metric conventions; and reporting/UI changes that compute and display rolling events/sec, bytes/sec, and top resources. Avoid rewarding repeated greps, successful builds that do not exercise the requested behavior, changes to unrelated byte/event buffers, or isolated utility tests as sufficient progress. Prioritize concrete evidence from the trajectory: relevant file edits or a precise implementation plan spanning utility, metrics registration, watcher event observation, report generation, and validation commands.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Watcher Event Observability
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show substantive progress toward the full observability feature: implementing or clearly designing the missing fixed-size float64 rolling buffer, adding tests or validation for its circular overwrite/window behavior, instrumenting the real watcher event emission path to record event size/count with resource identity, registering metric names/collectors through the existing Prometheus conventions, and extending the monitoring/top report path to compute and expose rolling events-per-second, bytes-per-second, and top resources. Evidence should go beyond broad searches or existing queue-size metrics and should not treat a standalone buffer as complete unless it is integrated into the watcher metrics flow.

required_evidence: utility_buffer_added_or_precisely_specified
buffer_tests_or_validation_for_fixed_capacity_window_behavior
watcher_event_emission_path_identified_and_instrumented
event_size_count_and_resource_labels_recorded
metrics_registered_using_existing_project_conventions
monitoring_or_top_report_computes_rates_and_top_resources
build_or_targeted_tests_run_after_changes
anti_evidence: repeated_duplicate_searches_without_new findings
only existing watcher queue-size metrics discussed
only unrelated byte buffer or backend event buffer modified
standalone float64 buffer added with no watcher metrics integration
build success used as substitute for implementing requested observability

scale.1: No substantive progress beyond repository exploration or repeated searches; no implementation plan or edits for either the rolling buffer or watcher metrics.
scale.2: Identifies the missing utility or existing watcher metric gaps, but only at a high level; may propose a buffer without locating the event emission, metric registration, or reporting integration points.
scale.3: Makes moderate progress on one major part, such as a plausible fixed-size float64 buffer or locating watcher/metrics/reporting paths, but lacks clear end-to-end integration for event rate, byte rate, and top-resource observability.
scale.4: Shows strong progress across most required areas: buffer behavior, watcher event instrumentation, metrics registration, and reporting/rate calculation are implemented or concretely planned, with only minor validation or polish gaps.
scale.5: Demonstrates complete end-to-end progress visible in the trajectory: the rolling buffer is implemented and tested, watcher event sizes/counts are recorded with resource labels at the correct emission point, metrics are registered consistently, monitoring/top reporting computes and displays rolling rates and top resources, and relevant builds/tests pass.

experiences.title: Do not score tracing config tasks by internal fields alone
experiences.description: Retrieve this when generating rubrics for Go/OpenTelemetry configuration tasks where an agent adds sampling or propagator settings. A rubric that only checks for new config fields, defaults, and validation can overvalue incomplete or broken trajectories.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go service using Viper/mapstructure configuration, OpenTelemetry tracer provider setup, global text-map propagators, and public CUE/JSON schema files. The misleading pattern is a trajectory that appears to add SamplingRatio/Propagators and some validation/defaults, but visible evidence shows unresolved build/test failures, corrupted server wiring, missing public schema updates, mismatched config key naming, unsupported or inconsistently mapped propagator names, or invalid values being silently coerced instead of rejected. The original idea is still appropriate when the visible trajectory is at a final-review stage and shows a coherent end-to-end path: config load accepts documented keys, defaults preserve existing runtime behavior, validation rejects bad inputs through the normal load path, runtime OpenTelemetry sampler/propagator setup uses those values, accepted propagators are backed by actual dependencies, and relevant builds/tests pass. During early exploration, absence of implementation should be judged as research/progress rather than by a completion checklist.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often restated the task as: add sampling_ratio and propagators to TracingConfig, validate them, set defaults, and wire them into tracing.go/grpc.go. That criterion is too broad and can mislead because superficial internal changes are not enough for a user-facing configuration feature. In these trajectories, the more predictive visible evidence was whether the implementation maintained an end-to-end contract: public schema and config naming conventions were updated consistently; the loader’s actual defaulting/validation path was exercised rather than ad hoc direct calls to unexported methods; accepted propagator strings matched both schema validation and constructible OpenTelemetry propagators/dependencies; invalid sampling ratios were rejected with errors rather than silently reset; and the server startup code remained syntactically valid and tested. Avoid the tempting criterion that simply rewards the presence of fields named sampling_ratio/propagators or validation snippets, and avoid prematurely narrowing supported propagators solely because the current core package lacks optional propagators unless the trajectory also makes a deliberate, documented support-boundary decision. A better rubric should prioritize visible consistency across schema, defaults, validation, dependency support, runtime wiring, and passing targeted build/config tests.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Internal-only or inconsistent tracing configuration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for a configurable tracing feature when the visible work only adds internal config fields or validation snippets but does not establish a reliable user-facing configuration contract. Evidence of this flaw includes missing or inconsistent public schema/default documentation, config key names that do not match repository conventions, validation that is not registered or not exercised through the normal load path, accepted propagator names that differ between schema/validation/runtime mapping or lack required dependencies, invalid sampling ratios being silently coerced instead of rejected, loss of the existing default behavior of full sampling and TraceContext+Baggage propagation, or unresolved build/test failures caused by the tracing changes.

metadata.environment: Go service with Viper/mapstructure config loading and OpenTelemetry tracing
evidence_priorities: public schema/default config updates use the same key names as loaded config
normal config load path applies defaults and rejects invalid values
runtime sampler and text-map propagator use loaded values
propagator options are consistently supported by dependencies and mapping code
targeted config/tracing/server builds or tests pass after edits
metadata.avoid_proxy: Do not treat the mere presence of SamplingRatio/Propagators fields or a validate method as sufficient evidence of correctness.

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory shows consistent schema/config/load validation/runtime wiring and relevant build or test confirmation.
scale.2: Minor evidence: one peripheral artifact such as documentation or a narrow test is missing, but naming, validation, runtime support, and builds appear coherent.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: internal fields/defaults/runtime wiring are present, but at least one important contract boundary is unclear or incomplete, such as public schema updates, load-path validation tests, or accepted propagator support.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory has partial internal implementation while visible tests/builds fail, schema or key naming is inconsistent, invalid values may be silently accepted, or propagator validation/runtime mapping disagree.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the work is syntactically broken or corrupted, lacks a coherent end-to-end config path, and relies mainly on superficial field additions despite unresolved build failures or incompatible propagator choices.

experiences.title: Snapshot Mutable Iterator Outputs at Every Yield
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task asks to stop an iterator/generator from reusing mutable output objects, especially after the trajectory has found an internal mutable accumulator and multiple yield forms.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python codebase when the reported bug is that materializing an iterator, such as with list(...), stores aliases to the same mutable dictionary/list and later mutations make earlier results appear wrong. The useful stage is after the trajectory has localized the target generator, identified the mutable working object, and can inspect all yield paths, including optional tuple-wrapped modes such as a size flag. It is less useful during broad repository search before the target generator is found, and it should not be applied to iterators that intentionally document in-place reuse as required API behavior or to immutable yielded values. Edge-case yields that already create fresh literals are lower priority than reused accumulator yields, though they should not be broken.
experiences.experience: The generated rubrics were useful because they targeted the semantic contract requested by the task: each emitted partition object must be an independent snapshot, not the same mutable accumulator returned repeatedly. The strongest versions explicitly required covering both the normal yield and the tuple form used by an option like size=True, while preserving partition contents, order, and metadata. This aligned with visible evidence such as `yield ms` / `yield sum(...), ms`, edits to `ms.copy()` at each accumulator yield, and smoke tests showing materialized results have correct contents and distinct identities. A weaker or misleading criterion would focus only on updating the docstring, only on making `list(partitions(...))` display the right values, or only on adding tests; those can miss aliasing in tuple-wrapped outputs or accidentally reward documentation-only changes. Another tempting overfit is to require copying every literal dictionary yield: fresh literals are not the aliasing source, so the rubric should prioritize all yields of the reused mutable accumulator while ensuring edge cases remain behaviorally unchanged. For similar tasks, generate a rubric that judges whether the trajectory found every mutable yield path, returns shallow snapshots where sufficient, keeps the generator algorithm and output semantics intact, and validates both equality/content and object independence.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Independent snapshots from mutable generator outputs
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the target generator no longer exposes the same mutable working object across iterations: every yield path that returns the internal mutable accumulator should instead yield a snapshot, including any option that wraps the object in a tuple, while preserving the generated values, ordering, and accompanying metadata. Visible evidence can include locating direct accumulator yields, replacing them with shallow copies or equivalent snapshots, leaving the generation algorithm otherwise unchanged, and validating with materialized multi-result cases plus object-identity or mutation-independence checks.

required_evidence: identifies the internal mutable accumulator that is reused between iterations
covers all public yield forms that expose that accumulator, including tuple-wrapped modes
preserves output contents, ordering, and metadata such as size/count fields
uses identity or mutation-independence validation, not only equality checks
lower_priority_evidence: docstring cleanup to remove stale warnings about reuse
copying edge-case literal dictionaries that are already freshly allocated
anti_patterns: documentation-only change with accumulator still yielded directly
fixing only the normal output mode while missing the option that yields tuples
rewriting the partition generation algorithm unnecessarily
testing only printed contents without checking object independence

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory identifies or addresses mutable output aliasing; it may only inspect files or discuss documentation.
scale.2: Recognizes the aliasing problem or reproduces it, but has not located all accumulator yield paths or proposes an incomplete/documentation-only fix.
scale.3: Shows parent-level progress: localizes the generator and the reused mutable object, with a plausible plan or partial edit for snapshotting, but coverage of all modes or validation remains uncertain.
scale.4: Strong evidence of a correct fix: accumulator yields are changed to snapshots in the main output path and likely in wrapped modes, with content-preservation checks or relevant tests.
scale.5: Complete evidence: every accumulator-exposing yield path, including tuple-wrapped option modes, returns an independent snapshot; outputs and metadata are preserved; materialized multi-result and mutation/identity tests confirm independence, with no unnecessary algorithm rewrite.

experiences.title: Property Descriptor Docstring Inheritance Without Descriptor Scope Creep
experiences.description: Use when a Python metaclass or class-creation hook copies inherited docstrings and the reported bug is that overridden properties are skipped because the code only recognizes functions.
experiences.context: Applies in Python repositories, especially older Astropy-like code, where a metaclass iterates over class body attributes and fills missing subclass docstrings from base-class members. Retrieve this when the visible task specifically names properties/descriptors and the trajectory has found that `inspect.isfunction` is false for `property` while regular methods already work. The criterion is most useful once the agent has inspected the relevant inheritance loop or begun proposing edits. It is less useful for unrelated doc generation systems, for tasks whose requested behavior is broad descriptor support rather than properties, or very early exploration before the agent has identified the docstring-copying mechanism.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic contract: an overriding public `property` with no docstring should inherit the first applicable base property docstring, while existing normal-method behavior, explicit child docstrings, public/private filtering, and MRO precedence remain intact. This aligned well because the visible trajectory often contained decisive evidence: probes showing `inspect.isfunction(property_obj) == False`, properties exposing assignable `__doc__`, and the existing metaclass already copying `val.__doc__` from base members for functions. A better rubric should reward a narrow, compatibility-preserving extension of the eligibility predicate to include property-like descriptors and should require validation of property-level `__doc__`, not just the getter function docstring. It should also check that the agent does not accidentally change the inheritance lookup semantics, skip inherited base members, overwrite explicit docs, or broaden the task into classmethod/staticmethod support without need. A tempting but weaker criterion is “handle all descriptors/classmethods/staticmethods”; that can distract the agent into risky descriptor-protocol rewrites and may mask regressions even when the property bug is solved. Prioritize visible evidence that the patch keeps the original loop’s filtering and base-search behavior, adds property eligibility, and tests representative cases: regular method still inherits, property now inherits, explicit property docstring is preserved, private members remain skipped, and multiple-inheritance/first-base behavior is not disturbed.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Scoped Property Docstring Inheritance
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate or implement a narrowly scoped fix to the docstring-inheritance metaclass so that public overriding `property` attributes whose property-level `__doc__` is missing inherit the appropriate base attribute docstring, while preserving the pre-existing behavior for ordinary methods, explicit subclass docstrings, public/private filtering, and MRO/first-applicable-base lookup. The strongest evidence is a proposed or applied change that treats properties as eligible alongside functions without unnecessary descriptor-protocol rewrites, plus validation that checks `Derived.prop.__doc__` rather than only `Derived.prop.fget.__doc__`.

required_visible_evidence: Agent identifies that the existing function-only predicate excludes property objects.
Agent inspects or reasons about property `__doc__` storage and assignment.
Agent preserves ordinary method docstring inheritance and explicit subclass docstrings.
Agent preserves original member visibility and base-class lookup semantics.
Agent avoids making broad classmethod/staticmethod or raw-descriptor changes unless separately justified and validated.
metadata.task_boundary: Property docstring inheritance is the core requested behavior; broader descriptor support is not required and should not be used as a substitute for preserving the existing contract.

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward property docstring inheritance, or the trajectory remains at repository search without identifying the function-only predicate.
scale.2: Recognizes that properties are skipped but proposes an incomplete or incorrect direction, such as changing only the getter docstring or broadly rewriting descriptor handling without preserving existing behavior.
scale.3: Comparable to the parent trajectory: identifies the property predicate issue and sketches a plausible fix, but validation or preservation of MRO/public/explicit-doc behavior is incomplete.
scale.4: Strong evidence of a correct property-focused fix that includes properties in the inheritance path, checks property-level `__doc__`, and preserves ordinary method behavior, with some targeted validation.
scale.5: Complete, well-scoped evidence: the trajectory implements or clearly plans property docstring inheritance while retaining original filtering and base lookup semantics, validates property, method, explicit-doc, private-member, and MRO cases, and avoids unnecessary risky descriptor expansion.

experiences.title: Do not overvalue ad hoc pre-load type checks when a validation framework owns the field
experiences.description: Retrieve this when an Ansible/core-style bug occurs in a convenience path before schema validation, and the trajectory is tempted to fix the immediate traceback by adding local type checks around the crashing operation.
experiences.context: This applies in Python repositories with an existing object/field validation lifecycle, such as Ansible playbook loading, where malformed user input crashes in an early helper that derives display/name data from a raw field. The misleading case is a trajectory that reproduces the crash and adds checks around the string join or downstream inventory use, then manually verifies several invalid and valid examples. That behavioral progress is relevant, but it is not sufficient when the codebase already declares field types and validation hooks for the same attribute. The original idea remains appropriate as a baseline behavioral criterion when the trajectory has not yet found any framework-level validation mechanism, or when the surrounding code truly has no schema hook. Once the trajectory has visible evidence of field attributes, post-validation, or validate-method conventions, the rubric should shift from only rejecting the bad value before the crash to requiring integration at the semantic validation boundary.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster correctly emphasized that invalid host values should produce a user-facing parser error and that valid string/list hosts should keep working. They became misleading because they treated any early `hosts` type check before `join()` or inventory lookup as strong evidence of a correct fix. In this codebase, such patches can still be incomplete or non-idiomatic: they validate raw data only in some branches, duplicate framework responsibilities, use narrow `list` checks instead of the repository's sequence/string conventions, mutate the raw play data to synthesize names before validation, and miss the intended validation lifecycle for named plays or future callers. A better rubric should ask whether the agent recognizes the existing field-validation mechanism and moves host validation/name derivation to the appropriate object-level boundary, so all paths see the same checks. Avoid the tempting criterion: 'the fix checks every list element before `join()`.'
