Prefer evidence that the trajectory inspects the field declaration and validation order, adds or plans a validator tied to the host field, defers display-name generation until after validated data is available, and tests named and unnamed plays plus valid strings, valid host sequences, empty/null values, mappings, and non-string entries.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that frame the fix as local guarding of the immediate raw-data crash site, rather than integrating malformed field handling with the existing play/object validation lifecycle. This flaw is present when the visible trajectory has found or should reasonably find field declarations, post-validation, or validate-hook conventions, but the implementation or plan still centers on ad hoc checks around name derivation or downstream use. The concern is strongest if the approach mutates raw input to synthesize a name before validation, handles only concrete lists instead of the repository's accepted sequence/string abstractions, or only covers branches without an explicit play name.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Ad hoc pre-validation guard instead of schema-level validation

metadata.environment: Python Ansible/core-style playbook loading with existing field attributes and parser-error conventions
visible_evidence_to_prioritize: inspection of field declarations or validation hooks for the affected attribute
understanding of load order: raw data processing versus object validation
whether validation applies to named and unnamed plays alike
whether accepted sequence and string types follow repository utilities rather than narrow built-in type checks
whether display/name generation is deferred until after validated host data is available
tempting_but_insufficient_evidence: manual reproduction no longer crashes for one malformed list case
a local loop checks list elements immediately before a string join
valid scalar and list examples still run in manual CLI tests

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory explicitly investigates and uses the repository's field-validation lifecycle, and treats the crash site as a symptom rather than the sole fix location.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory mentions framework validation but still leaves some emphasis on local guards, with a plausible plan to reconcile the approach with validation hooks.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory fixes both named and unnamed behavioral cases, but the visible approach remains mostly ad hoc around raw loader data and does not clearly align with the existing validation abstraction.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory has inspected validation-related code yet implements or plans local raw-data checks around name generation/downstream use, with narrow list/type handling or duplicated validation logic.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory treats checking before `join()` as the complete solution despite visible validation infrastructure, leaves validation branch-dependent or raw-data-mutating, and does not address how all callers will receive consistent parser errors.

experiences.title: Repository-Origin Propagation for Vendor Extra Advisories
experiences.description: Use when a vulnerability scanner task asks to support a distro/vendor extra repository whose advisories differ by package repository origin, especially after the trajectory has inspected package repository metadata and OVAL/advisory matching paths.
experiences.context: Applies in Go vulnerability-scanner codebases with RedHat-like/Amazon-like package scanning, yum/repoquery/rpm collection, package models that can store repository names, and OVAL or vendor advisory matching. The task should be about correct advisories for packages sourced from an extra/non-core repository, not merely allowing a config option. This guidance is most useful once the trajectory has visible evidence about both scan-time package collection and advisory matching. It is less applicable during very early broad exploration with no package/advisory flow identified, or for tasks where repositories only affect which updates are queried and advisory definitions do not distinguish affected repositories.
experiences.experience: For this kind of feature, rubrics that only check whether the agent permits or auto-enables an extras repository name are too narrow and can reward an incomplete fix. The decisive behavior is whether the implementation preserves repository origin for installed packages and uses that origin when deciding which vendor advisory applies. A better rubric should look for an end-to-end flow: collect repository metadata for installed Amazon Linux 2 packages when possible, normalize fallback/core repository names, store it on the package model, pass it into OVAL/advisory requests, and filter advisory definitions by affected repository so core and extras packages are not conflated. Avoid the tempting proxy of validating `enablerepo` strings or adding `--enablerepo=amzn2extra*` alone; that may affect update queries but does not solve incorrect advisory matching for already installed packages. Prioritize visible evidence such as investigation or edits around repoquery/rpm installed-package collection, parsing repository fields into package metadata, request structs or advisory matching code carrying repository, and tests or reasoning that distinguish core repository packages from extra-repository packages.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Repository-Aware Advisory Matching
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should recognize and implement Amazon Linux 2 Extra Repository support as an end-to-end repository-origin problem: installed package scanning must capture the package's source repository, preserve that repository on the package model, and advisory/OVAL matching must compare the package repository with the advisory's affected repository so extra-repository and core-repository advisories are selected correctly. Merely allowing or auto-enabling an extras repository configuration value is insufficient unless accompanied by repository-aware installed-package collection and advisory filtering.

expected_visible_evidence: Identifies that update-query repository metadata alone is not enough; installed packages need repository origin for advisory matching.
Uses a package collection mechanism capable of reporting the repository that installed packages came from, with fallback behavior for core packages when repository output is generic.
Parses and stores repository origin in the package data structure used later by vulnerability detection.
Carries repository information into OVAL or vendor advisory lookup requests.
Filters or matches advisory definitions using affected repository metadata so extra and core repositories are not conflated.
Keeps the behavior scoped to the relevant distro/version and avoids breaking existing RedHat-like distribution behavior.
insufficient_proxies: Only changing TOML/config validation to accept extras repository names.
Only appending an extras repo to enabled repositories during OS detection.
Only documenting extras support or changing comments/changelog.
Only querying updatable packages from extras without preserving installed package repository origin.
Guessing repository names without verifying how package and advisory metadata represent them.
metadata.environment: Go vulnerability scanner with RedHat-family scanner code, Amazon Linux support, yum/repoquery/rpm package collection, package repository fields, and OVAL/vendor advisory matching.

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory considers repository origin beyond generic Amazon Linux or broad distro/advisory exploration.
scale.2: Mentions Amazon Linux extras or enablerepo/config handling, but treats the issue mainly as enabling or validating repository names.
scale.3: Identifies both package repository metadata and advisory matching as relevant, but has not connected installed-package repository origin through to advisory filtering.
scale.4: Shows strong evidence of implementing or planning repository-origin propagation from package scan results into advisory lookup, with awareness that extras and core advisories must be distinguished.
scale.5: Provides complete visible evidence of a repository-aware flow: installed package repo collection/parsing, model propagation, advisory request/matching by affected repository, scoped Amazon Linux 2 behavior, and validation/tests covering core versus extra repository cases.

experiences.title: Do not reward non-reproduction as progress when the visual autoscale path remains unexamined
experiences.description: Retrieve this when a plotting/autoscale bug is not reproduced in ad hoc runs and the agent is tempted to conclude the bug is fixed, version-specific, or nonexistent without validating the target checkout and tracing generic artist data-limit/autoscale code.
experiences.context: Applies in Matplotlib-like Python plotting repositories where the report concerns a displayed axis limit/autoscale failure for a specific artist style, while returned numerical data may still be correct. The misleading pattern is an agent repeatedly testing synthetic/random inputs, often against a pip-installed or otherwise non-target package, seeing matching returned values or y-limits, then focusing rubrics on reproduction persistence, git-history searches, environment awareness, or a correct 'bug does not exist' conclusion. Those ideas can be appropriate only when the trajectory visibly verifies the imported source/version, tests the reporter's conditions or a deterministic equivalent, and either finds a concrete prior fix or exhaustively traces the relevant rendering/autoscale pipeline. They are not sufficient when the visible evidence still leaves the main failure mode unexplored: how a step-like polygon contributes vertices/extrema to generic patch data limits and autoscaling.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded broad bug reproduction verification, version-aware debugging, git-history investigation, or concluding the bug was already fixed. In this setting that guidance is misleading because the agent's visible evidence mostly showed that histogram density values matched and that simple random reproductions did not fail; it did not establish that the target checkout and reported scenario were exercised, nor did it address the lower-level autoscale mechanism that can omit plotted step vertices from data limits. A better rubric should judge whether the trajectory moves from 'density values are correct' to the visual rendering/autoscale contract: inspect the artist path used for the step histogram, how patch limits are computed from paths, whether path simplification or vertex extraction can drop extrema, and whether a regression assertion checks axis limits/data limits against the actual step path. Avoid the tempting criterion that non-reproduction plus git log searching is itself positive evidence of correctness. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence of target-source validation, deterministic autoscale checks, and investigation of generic patch data-limit/path processing rather than only the hist-specific density computation or sticky-edge baseline.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat failure to reproduce a plotting autoscale bug as evidence that no code change is needed, while the visible work has not reliably exercised the target checkout and has not traced the generic artist path-to-data-limit/autoscale pipeline. This is especially severe when the agent only compares returned histogram values or simple y-limits in an installed package, repeats broad git-history searches, or proposes/focuses on hist-branch sticky-edge/autoscale calls without investigating whether the step polygon's path vertices/extrema are being preserved when patch limits are computed.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Premature non-reproduction conclusion for visual autoscale bug

misleading_positive_evidence: synthetic random reproductions show matching returned density arrays
bar and step y-limits match in a non-target or unverified import
git history searches do not reveal an obvious prior fix
required_visible_focus: verify the code under test is the repository checkout or target version
test autoscale/data limits rather than only returned numeric histogram values
trace step-like polygon artist paths through generic patch limit calculation
consider whether path simplification or vertex extraction can remove extrema needed for autoscale
avoid_rewarding: declaring the report fixed or nonexistent from non-reproduction alone
repeated grep/git-log searches without new evidence
patching only hist-specific sticky edges or requesting autoscale without explaining missing data limits

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory verifies the target source/version, distinguishes returned data from visual autoscale, and investigates the generic patch/path data-limit path or creates an autoscale-focused regression check.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: some non-reproduction or environment discussion appears, but the agent also begins tracing artist data limits or acknowledges that matching numeric densities do not resolve the visual bug.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory balances reproduction attempts and source inspection but remains mostly in the hist-specific branch or environment/history checks, with only shallow attention to generic patch limit computation.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the agent repeatedly relies on non-reproduction, installed-package behavior, or git-history absence, and focuses on density/sticky-edge explanations without a credible check of path-to-data-limit autoscaling.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the agent explicitly concludes the bug is fixed/nonexistent or no patch is needed based on unverified/simple reproductions, despite the task requiring a visual autoscale fix and with no meaningful investigation of generic patch path limit handling.

experiences.title: Entry-point task: prefer exact dialog/flag contract over full feature build
experiences.description: Retrieve when a React/TypeScript UI task asks to add a feature-flagged button that opens a named dialog with a specific prop, especially when the dialog/flag is missing and the task is framed as setup or entry-point work.
experiences.context: Applies in a React/TypeScript frontend codebase with settings/labs feature flags, reusable button components, and modal dialogs opened through an existing Modal.createDialog-style API. The matching situation is a task whose acceptance contract is: add a RoomSummaryCard action, gate it on an experimental flag, open a PollHistoryDialog, and pass the current roomId. This guidance is strongest after the trajectory has visibly found the relevant card, feature-flag patterns, dialog-opening patterns, and absence of the named dialog/flag. It is less applicable if the task explicitly requires implementing the full poll-history data UI, if an existing PollHistoryDialog API clearly expects a whole Room object instead of roomId, or if the trajectory has not yet inspected enough code to know the expected modal prop shape.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics tended to require creating a PollHistoryDialog that fetches and displays real poll history using SDK poll APIs. That is an over-scoped criterion for this kind of setup/entry-point task: visible trajectory evidence repeatedly showed the task wording centered on a button, a labs flag, and opening a dialog with roomId, while attempts to build a full poll-history UI led agents toward private or unavailable poll APIs, extra props, and TypeScript risk. A better rubric should focus on the exact integration contract: register the experimental feature flag in the project’s settings pattern; render the “Polls history” RoomSummaryCard button only when that flag is enabled; open the dialog through the existing modal pattern; pass `{ roomId: room.roomId }` rather than the whole room or unrelated client objects; and, if the dialog is absent, create only a lightweight project-pattern dialog accepting roomId/onFinished so the entry point compiles. Avoid the tempting proxy “must display poll history from room.polls” unless the problem statement explicitly asks for data rendering. Prioritize visible evidence such as the agent noting the required roomId prop, correcting any `{ room }` modal call, avoiding private SDK fields or speculative poll fetching, and keeping the dialog implementation minimal and type-safe.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Exact Feature-Flagged Dialog Entry Point
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should converge on the narrow entry-point contract rather than an overbuilt poll-history feature: add/register the experimental `feature_poll_history` setting using the repository’s feature/labs settings pattern; add a `RoomSummaryCard` button labeled “Polls history” that is hidden unless `useFeatureEnabled("feature_poll_history")` is true and follows existing non-video-room/action-button conventions where applicable; open `PollHistoryDialog` via the existing modal dialog mechanism; pass the current room identifier exactly as a `roomId` prop; and, if no dialog exists, create a lightweight dialog component following existing BaseDialog/IDialogProps patterns that accepts `roomId` without relying on speculative poll data APIs or private SDK fields.

prioritize_evidence: Agent has identified existing RoomSummaryCard button and Modal.createDialog patterns
Agent has identified feature flag definitions and useFeatureEnabled usage
Planned or edited modal props use roomId, not a Room object
Any newly created dialog is minimal, typed around roomId/onFinished, and compile-oriented
Agent avoids or removes full poll-history fetching/display code unless explicitly required
red_flags: Modal.createDialog receives { room } or matrix client props despite the task requiring roomId
Rubric or implementation requires rendering poll history from room.polls as an acceptance criterion
Use of private/uncertain SDK fields or nonexistent poll APIs
Button is not gated by the experimental flag or is visible unconditionally

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of the entry-point contract: the trajectory does not identify the correct card/flag/dialog pattern, or focuses almost entirely on unrelated poll data implementation.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory has found some relevant files or mentions the button/dialog, but omits key contract pieces such as the feature flag, modal integration, or required roomId prop.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory is on the right path with a gated button and dialog creation/opening plan, but still has ambiguity or mistakes such as passing the whole room, overbuilding poll data UI, or not clearly registering the flag.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory plans or edits the flag, gated button, modal call, and dialog component mostly correctly, with only minor naming/style/i18n/icon uncertainties.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory clearly implements or plans a minimal, type-safe entry point matching existing patterns, including the experimental flag, conditional “Polls history” button, `Modal.createDialog(PollHistoryDialog, { roomId: room.roomId })`, and a lightweight roomId-accepting dialog if absent, while explicitly avoiding unnecessary poll-history data fetching.

experiences.title: End-to-End YAML Config Runtime Wiring
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go/Viper-style YAML configuration bug requires a newly supported nested config section to be both decoded and used by runtime initialization, especially when current code has an empty method config and a bootstrap path that generates values internally.
experiences.context: Applies in Go services where YAML is decoded into tagged config structs, schemas restrict accepted keys, and runtime initialization separately consumes the config. It is especially relevant after the trajectory has identified both the config definition and the runtime bootstrap/create path. It is less useful during very early repository exploration before the call chain is known, or for tasks that only ask to document schema without changing runtime behavior. The criterion should be stricter when the visible task says user-provided values must be applied, not merely accepted.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the full propagation chain for the new bootstrap settings: YAML/schema recognition, config struct fields with mapstructure tags, call-site plumbing into bootstrap, and actual use when creating the initial authentication. This was discriminative because many trajectories made partial progress—adding a config field or JSON schema, passing a config pointer, or setting only expiration—while still leaving the configured static token unused because the storage layer continued generating tokens or the token was merely placed in metadata. A better rubric should explicitly require evidence that both token and expiration flow from decoded config into the creation request and that every storage implementation that hashes/persists tokens honors an optional caller-supplied token while preserving random generation when absent. It should also check for the repository’s authoritative schema source when visible, and for preserving existing config methods/interfaces. Avoid tempting but weak criteria such as compile success, schema-only support, adding tests only for YAML parsing, or comments claiming the store cannot set the token. Prioritize visible evidence from inspected diffs/commands: tagged nested config fields, schema entries for the new YAML keys, the runtime auth setup passing those values, bootstrap constructing expiration timestamps and client-token requests conditionally, and store create implementations using supplied tokens consistently.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Bootstrap Config Application
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a complete, working path for token-auth bootstrap configuration: the new YAML bootstrap section is accepted by the relevant schema/source schema, decoded into the token method config with correct tags while preserving required config interfaces/default methods, passed from auth initialization into the bootstrap routine, and used to create the initial token authentication with the configured static token and optional expiration. The implementation must also update the storage creation path so caller-supplied client tokens are hashed and persisted consistently across backends, while retaining generated-token behavior when no bootstrap token is configured.

required_visible_evidence: Nested bootstrap config fields for token and expiration exist on the token method config and have YAML/mapstructure-compatible tags.
Schema or schema source accepts the bootstrap object and both token and duration/integer expiration forms expected by the config loader.
Runtime auth setup passes decoded bootstrap values to the bootstrap creation path only when token auth is enabled.
Bootstrap logic conditionally applies configured token and expiration to the authentication create request, and preserves no-existing-token short-circuit behavior.
Storage create implementations honor an optional supplied client token before hashing/persisting, falling back to generated tokens when absent.
Existing config interface methods and unrelated auth registration behavior remain intact.
common_failure_signals: Only schema or config structs are changed, with no runtime bootstrap consumption.
Only expiration is wired; the configured static token is ignored, stored as metadata, or overwritten by generated-token logic.
Only one storage backend supports supplied tokens.
Generated schema is edited while an authoritative schema source remains stale.
Broad text edits corrupt surrounding config methods or auth registration blocks.

scale.1: No substantive evidence that bootstrap YAML values are decoded or used; changes are absent, corrupt, or limited to unrelated exploration.
scale.2: Partial config or schema support is visible, but runtime bootstrap still ignores one or both values, or edits break required config/auth structure.
scale.3: Comparable progress to the current parent trajectory: some chain elements are present, but important gaps remain such as missing schema source updates, no storage support for supplied tokens, only expiration support, or inconsistent call-site wiring.
scale.4: Strong end-to-end implementation evidence for decoding, wiring, and using both token and expiration, with only minor validation/test/schema-source uncertainty.
scale.5: Complete evidence that both bootstrap token and expiration are accepted, decoded, passed through initialization, applied in bootstrap creation, persisted consistently across backends, covered by appropriate config/runtime tests, and default behavior is preserved.

experiences.title: Do not equate dialog accessibility with a generic polyfill or role attribute
experiences.description: Retrieve when a React/Jest/JSDOM task involves native elements with incomplete JSDOM support, especially `<dialog>`, and the trajectory is considering `role`, `open`, external polyfills, global DOM monkeypatches, or replacing the production element.
experiences.context: Applies in a TypeScript React component library using Jest, JSDOM, and Testing Library where the user wants role-based queries to find children rendered inside an open native `<dialog>`. The misleading pattern is to generate a rubric that requires or rewards a broad “dialog polyfill/workaround” without distinguishing whether the fix is targeted to the test environment and whether production browser semantics are preserved. Adding `role="dialog"`, `open`, or `aria-modal` can be useful for accessibility but is not enough evidence that JSDOM can traverse children. Importing an external polyfill or monkeypatching `HTMLDialogElement.showModal`, `document.createElement`, or global visibility behavior may create unrelated modal regressions or dependency churn. Replacing the production `<dialog>` with a `<div role="dialog">` may satisfy a narrow JSDOM query but changes real-browser semantics. A polyfill-oriented rubric may still be appropriate if the repository already has an established dialog polyfill dependency and the trajectory shows it is correctly registered, scoped, and regression-tested. During early exploration, absence of a workaround is not yet a meaningful flaw; focus rubrics on reproduction quality and whether the planned fix respects the test-vs-production boundary.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often said the fix should “integrate a dialog polyfill” or generally “make `<dialog>` children discoverable via `getByRole`.” That wording is too broad or too implementation-specific. It can under-credit trajectories that are still reproducing the issue, and it can over-credit superficial changes such as adding `role`, adding `open`, importing `dialog-polyfill`, or globally monkeypatching dialog methods. It can also miss the important design boundary: the safest solution for this kind of JSDOM incompatibility is usually a targeted test-environment shim or wrapper that leaves production rendering as the native element while allowing Jest/JSDOM to render an accessible, traversable substitute. A better rubric should prioritize visible evidence that the agent: reproduces the role-query failure with Testing Library; avoids unverified new dependencies and lockfile churn; avoids global DOM/prototype patches that alter visibility or modal lifecycle for unrelated tests; preserves the production component API and native browser semantics; and validates both the focused role-query scenario and existing modal/consumer behavior. Avoid generating a criterion that treats “uses a polyfill,” “adds `role="dialog"`,” or “switches to `<div role="dialog">` everywhere” as sufficient on its own.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that address JSDOM `<dialog>` accessibility by relying on superficial or overly global changes instead of a targeted test-environment compatibility layer that preserves production native-dialog behavior. This flaw is present when the visible trajectory or planned patch only adds ARIA/open attributes, imports or installs an unproven dialog polyfill, monkeypatches global dialog methods or element creation, or replaces the production native dialog with a generic element without evidence that real-browser semantics and existing modal consumers remain intact.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial or Global Dialog Workaround

metadata.environment: React component library with Jest/JSDOM and Testing Library role queries
metadata.problem_signal: children inside an open native dialog are not discoverable by role queries in JSDOM
better_evidence: focused reproduction using role/name query for an interactive child
test-scoped shim or wrapper rather than production semantic downgrade
production rendering still uses native dialog semantics
no unverified dependency or lockfile churn
existing modal and representative consumer tests remain passing
risky_evidence: imports dialog-polyfill without proving availability and effect
production replacement of native dialog with div
ignores visible regressions in other modal tests

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory is still investigating/reproducing, or the proposed fix is clearly scoped to JSDOM tests while preserving production native-dialog behavior.
scale.2: Minor risk: the agent mentions role attributes or a polyfill as possibilities but has not committed to them and is still gathering evidence.
scale.3: Moderate risk: the trajectory implements or favors a workaround that may make the focused role query pass, but visible evidence is insufficient that it preserves production semantics or avoids broader modal regressions.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory adds role/open attributes, a global dialog monkeypatch, an external polyfill, or a production element replacement without adequate verification against existing modal behavior.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory commits an unscoped or dependency-heavy workaround, ignores failed/regressing modal tests, or changes production native-dialog semantics solely to satisfy JSDOM role queries.

experiences.title: Metaclass descendant semantics for default primary key validation
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django task reports that a configured default primary-key field is rejected because it subclasses an auto-field variant through a compatibility metaclass rather than direct inheritance.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django/Python repository when the visible task or trajectory connects DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD or AppConfig.default_auto_field validation to a metaclass-based AutoField compatibility check, especially where exact-class recognition of BigAutoField/SmallAutoField works but user-defined descendants are rejected. It is most useful once the trajectory has inspected the subclass-checking hook or the default-primary-key validation path, or has begun editing that path. It is less useful for unrelated default-field import errors, app registry setup mistakes, database backend issues, or tasks about explicit primary keys rather than automatic primary key class validation. At very early exploration stages, the criterion should judge whether the agent has identified the correct semantic target, not assume correctness merely from reproducing dependency/setup failures.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic contract: the canonical subclass check must treat descendants of the recognized auto-field variants as AutoField-compatible while continuing to reject unrelated field classes and preserving direct AutoField behavior. This was discriminative because the successful trajectories visibly identified the exact compatibility boundary: default primary-key validation calls a subclass check against AutoField, and the existing metaclass logic only accepted exact variant classes. A good rubric should therefore look for evidence that the agent either edits or plans to edit the metaclass subclass hook to use real subclass relationships over the registered variant classes, plus optional validation with custom BigAutoField and SmallAutoField descendants and unrelated non-auto fields. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as merely changing DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD import resolution, weakening validation in the model options layer to accept any field, only testing the direct BigAutoField class, or giving high credit for installing dependencies/reproducing setup errors without a visible semantic fix. Also avoid over-specifying the exact implementation form: iterating with issubclass() and passing the variant tuple directly are equivalent if they preserve the same acceptance/rejection boundary.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly converge on the canonical subclass-checking change so that default automatic primary-key validation accepts user-defined descendants of the recognized large and small auto-field variants, including transitive descendants, while preserving existing AutoField compatibility and continuing to reject unrelated field subclasses. Prioritize visible evidence from inspected validation flow, edits to the metaclass subclass hook rather than broad validation bypasses, and targeted checks demonstrating both acceptance and rejection boundaries.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Preserve AutoField compatibility boundary for variant descendants

metadata.required_semantic_target: metaclass subclass compatibility hook used by default automatic primary-key validation
positive_acceptance_cases: custom subclass of the large auto-field variant
custom subclass of the small auto-field variant
negative_boundary_cases: ordinary non-auto field subclasses remain rejected
validation is not bypassed or moved to accept arbitrary fields
strong_evidence: code change replaces exact-class membership with subclass relationship checking
trajectory confirms the default primary-key validation path uses the subclass hook
manual or suite tests exercise custom variant subclasses and unrelated fields

scale.1: No visible evidence that the trajectory identified the metaclass subclass semantics; work is limited to repository exploration, dependency installation, or unrelated setup errors.
scale.2: The trajectory mentions AutoField/default-primary-key validation but only proposes a vague or potentially broad change, or tests only existing direct classes without addressing descendants of the variant classes.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies the correct compatibility hook and intended descendant acceptance, but has not yet shown a clean edit or has not addressed preservation of unrelated-field rejection.
scale.4: The trajectory makes a plausible subclass-relationship change in the canonical hook and preserves the existing validation path, with some evidence that custom variant subclasses are accepted.
scale.5: The trajectory cleanly implements the subclass-relationship check in the canonical hook, avoids validation weakening, and validates both custom large/small auto-field descendants and rejection of unrelated field subclasses.

experiences.title: DDL Reference Helper Table-Type Semantics
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django schema-editor task concerns deferred DDL `Statement.references_column()` behavior and the trajectory is inspecting or editing how unique/index SQL wires `Table`, `Columns`, or `_index_columns()` reference helpers.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django codebase, especially during investigation or review of schema-editor DDL construction where SQL statement parts are represented by reference helper objects. The key matching evidence is that a statement builder creates a `Table` wrapper for SQL rendering but also passes that wrapper into a column-reference helper that compares against raw table-name strings. This guidance is useful once the trajectory has either identified the `Table` versus table-name mismatch from the task statement or inspected the relevant helper constructors/call sites. It is less useful for unrelated SQL rendering bugs, for issues where `references_column()` is not part of the contract, for changes inside the reference-helper classes without evidence of a bad call-site type, or for very early exploration before the trajectory has located the statement builder and column-reference path.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic boundary between SQL-rendering references and dependency-tracking identity. They judged whether the trajectory made the unique-statement construction pass a raw model database table-name string into `Columns` or the helper that creates it, while preserving a `Table` reference object for the `Statement` table placeholder. This aligned well because the visible evidence repeatedly showed the bug was not malformed SQL text but failed reference comparison: `Columns`/`TableColumns` stores a table value and `references_column(table, column)` compares it to a caller-provided string. A `Table` object can still stringify correctly, so judging only rendered SQL or generic test execution is a weak proxy. A better rubric should prioritize visible evidence such as comparing the unique SQL builder with the index SQL builder, inspecting `TableColumns.references_column()`, confirming `_index_columns()` returns `Columns(...)`, and validating with a direct `Statement.references_column(raw_table, column)` check. Avoid tempting but less discriminative criteria such as requiring full test-suite success despite environment setup failures, penalizing harmless local variable refactors, or suggesting broad changes to `Statement`/`Columns` semantics when the call site can pass the correct type. Also avoid over-demanding an exact patch shape; equivalent implementations are acceptable if column references receive the raw table identity and statement table rendering remains wrapped appropriately.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluate whether the trajectory correctly preserves the distinction between table-name identity for column-reference tracking and `Table` objects for SQL rendering in the unique-DDL statement path. Strong evidence includes identifying that the column-reference helper stores and compares raw table-name strings, changing or planning the unique-statement construction so `Columns`/`_index_columns()` receives the raw model database table name, keeping the `Statement` table part as a `Table` reference or equivalent rendering wrapper, and validating the behavior with direct `references_column(raw_table_name, referenced_column)` checks rather than relying only on rendered SQL.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Reference Helper Table-Type Correctness

applies_when: The task or trajectory concerns Django deferred DDL `Statement` reference detection.
The relevant code path builds unique constraint or unique index SQL using `Table`, `Columns`, `TableColumns`, `Expressions`, `IndexName`, or `_index_columns()`-style helpers.
Visible evidence indicates a mismatch between a wrapper object used for SQL interpolation and a raw table-name string expected for column-reference comparison.
prioritize_evidence: Inspection of the column-reference helper showing table equality is checked against a raw table-name argument.
Comparison with a nearby working index/constraint builder that passes a table-name string to column helpers and a `Table` wrapper to the statement table placeholder.
A code edit or explicit plan that sends the raw database table name into `Columns`/`_index_columns()` in the unique-statement path.
Direct reproduction or validation where `Statement.references_column(table_name, column_name)` returns true for affected unique columns and false for unrelated columns.
do_not_overweight: Rendered SQL looking correct, because the bug can persist despite correct stringification.
Generic schema test attempts that fail due to local dependency or settings setup rather than product behavior.
Large rewrites of reference helper classes when the visible problem is a call-site type mismatch.
Exact variable names or an exact diff shape, as long as the semantic type boundary is preserved.

scale.1: No visible evidence that the trajectory understands the table wrapper versus raw table-name distinction; it focuses on unrelated SQL text, test setup, or broad helper rewrites without addressing the column-reference type mismatch.
scale.2: The trajectory notices `references_column()` or the relevant unique-statement path but does not clearly connect the failure to passing a `Table` wrapper into `Columns`/the column-reference helper, or proposes an ambiguous fix that may leave the mismatch intact.
scale.3: The trajectory has parent-level understanding: it identifies the likely `Table` versus string mismatch in the unique-statement column path, but has not yet made or verified a clearly correct call-site change.
scale.4: The trajectory strongly addresses the issue by editing or planning the unique-statement construction so the raw table name is used for column references while the statement table remains renderable as a `Table` reference; validation may be partial or indirect.
scale.5: The trajectory provides the strongest evidence: it inspects the helper semantics, aligns the unique-statement path with the established index-statement pattern, implements an equivalent correct call-site fix without broad semantic rewrites, and directly verifies `references_column()` behavior for referenced and unrelated columns.

experiences.title: Version-Gated Compound Setting Semantics
experiences.description: Use when a task exposes a new backend/version-specific toggle through an existing config value because the new toggle is only meaningful as a refinement of an existing mode.
experiences.context: Applies in qutebrowser/Python settings-plumbing tasks where the task text and investigation show: a version-specific QtWebEngine/Chromium feature, existing per-version dark-mode Variant definitions, an existing user-facing option such as image policy, and a stated need to avoid affecting older Qt versions. It is especially relevant once the trajectory has found the mapping layer that converts config values into Chromium key/value tuples and the configdata/help definitions. It is less useful as a standalone criterion during very early repository search before the agent has inspected the mapping semantics, and it should not be reduced to generic version gating when the central risk is mapping the new value to the wrong Chromium setting or creating an unintended separate config option.
experiences.experience: The earlier rubrics correctly noticed that adding a QtWebEngine 6.6 variant and gating behavior behind it is necessary, but that criterion alone is too broad. Several trajectories can add a qt_66 branch while still implementing the feature incorrectly by inventing a new ImagePolicy enum value, naming the value merely `simple`, adding a separate `policy.images.classifier` option, or copying the old variant without adding the classifier setting. For this task shape, the discriminative rubric should focus on the compound semantics: the new user-facing value remains part of the existing image-policy option, behaves like smart image policy for the existing ImagePolicy switch, and only on the supporting backend/version emits an additional classifier-policy setting. The rubric should also look for plumbing that can intentionally omit a switch for values where the classifier setting is irrelevant, because the task explicitly calls out that the current mapped-value path always emits a switch. Avoid a tempting proxy rubric that only checks for `Variant.qt_66` or a version comparison; prioritize visible evidence that the agent understands the old and new Chromium keys are distinct, older variants keep their previous output, always/never do not emit classifier choices, config/help document the same existing option value, and tests or planned tests assert both Qt 6.6 and pre-6.6 output.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Compound Smart Image Classifier Mapping
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly plan the new classifier as a version-gated refinement of the existing image-policy setting, not as a generic new image policy enum or unrelated separate option. Strong evidence includes adding a QtWebEngine 6.6-specific variant before broader Qt 6.4+ detection, keeping the new user-facing value under the existing image-policy config, mapping that value to the existing smart image policy for the old ImagePolicy key, adding a separate classifier-policy key only for the supporting variant, allowing mapped values to intentionally emit no classifier switch when not applicable, preserving older Qt behavior, and updating docs/tests to reflect both supported and unsupported version behavior.

prioritize_visible_evidence: version-specific variant/detection ordered before broader version branches
new value is represented under the existing image-policy option because it refines smart mode
implementation distinguishes existing image policy key from new classifier-policy key
mapping/plumbing supports omitting a switch for values where the new classifier does not apply
older variants continue to emit only their previous image-policy settings
tests or validation cover Qt 6.6 and pre-6.6 outputs plus always/never/smart-derived values
configdata/help/changelog describe the new value and version constraint consistently
avoid_overcrediting: only adding a Qt 6.6 Variant enum member and _variant branch
inventing a new ImagePolicy enum value for the simple classifier
adding a separate user-facing classifier config option despite the task requesting an additional image-policy value
documenting the value without changing switch-generation semantics

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of version-gated classifier semantics; trajectory is still repeating searches or makes unrelated/documentation-only changes.
scale.2: Recognizes Qt 6.6 gating or adds a new config value, but treats the feature as a simple new image-policy enum, a separate option, or otherwise misses the compound smart-policy-plus-classifier behavior.
scale.3: Adds or plans Qt 6.6 detection and mentions the existing image-policy option, but the switch mapping, suppression behavior, or older-version behavior remains ambiguous or incomplete.
scale.4: Clearly implements or plans the existing-option value with separate classifier-policy emission for Qt 6.6+ and preserves older variants, with only minor gaps such as incomplete docs or limited tests.
scale.5: Fully demonstrates the compound mapping: correct version branch, existing image-policy value semantics, separate classifier key only where supported, intentional switch omission for irrelevant values, unchanged older outputs, and synchronized tests and user-facing documentation.

experiences.title: Close the DI Constructor Migration, Not Just the Obvious Test Calls
experiences.description: Use when a Go constructor gains a new dependency-injected parameter and the trajectory has evidence of same-package tests, generated Wire code, or singleton-to-DI behavior that must be kept consistent.
experiences.context: Applies to Go repositories where a router/service constructor signature changed to accept a new dependency, especially when Google Wire or other generated DI code constructs the object and tests are in the same package so calls may appear as bare `New(...)` rather than `pkg.New(...)`. This criterion is most useful once the trajectory has inspected the constructor signature, found call sites, or started editing production/test wiring. It is less appropriate for very early exploration before any signature or call-site evidence is visible, and it should be narrowed for simple non-DI constructor changes with no generated code, singleton behavior, or runtime use of the new dependency.
experiences.experience: The earlier rubrics often focused on identifying and updating Subsonic router test instantiations, which is useful when the visible flaw is that same-package tests still call the old signature. However, that criterion becomes misleading when the trajectory has already expanded into production DI changes or when generated Wire code and singleton usage are visible: merely finding test calls, or adding a parameter to the constructor, does not show the migration is closed. A better rubric should check observable closure across the constructor contract: the new dependency type and argument order are confirmed from source; all actual call forms are updated, including unqualified same-package tests and generated/regenerated DI construction; production providers match the dependency factory signature; runtime code uses the injected dependency rather than continuing to fetch the singleton directly; and validation output or follow-up fixes address any compile/Wire errors. Avoid rewarding a trajectory just for grepping `subsonic.New`, hand-editing generated files, or adding optional/variadic parameters to preserve old call sites, since those are tempting shortcuts that can leave tests compiling against the wrong contract or production wiring inconsistent. Also avoid requiring elaborate mocks in tests that do not exercise the new dependency; a nil placeholder can be acceptable when the constructor only stores the dependency and the tested paths do not dereference it. Prioritize visible evidence such as post-edit grep results for both `pkg.New` and bare `New(`, exact constructor signature snippets, diffs showing all call sites and behavior sites updated consistently, Wire regeneration or equivalent generated-code updates, and compiler/Wire outputs showing no stale old-signature calls remain.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates a complete and consistent dependency-injection constructor migration: it confirms the new constructor parameter type and position, updates every visible constructor call site including unqualified same-package test calls and generated or DI-managed production calls, supplies appropriate arguments for tests and production wiring, replaces any runtime singleton lookup that the new injected dependency is meant to supersede, and validates or responds to build/Wire/test feedback showing no stale old-signature calls or provider mismatches remain.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete DI Constructor Migration Closure

metadata.di_system: Google Wire or similar generated dependency injection
call_site_patterns_to_check: qualified constructor calls such as pkg.New
unqualified same-package test calls such as New(
runtime singleton usages superseded by the new dependency
metadata.acceptable_test_argument: nil or a lightweight stub is acceptable only when the exercised test paths do not use the new dependency
validation_evidence: Wire regeneration or equivalent generated-code consistency
go test/go test package output or concrete compile errors fixed

scale.1: No reliable evidence that the new constructor contract was understood or applied; the trajectory only explores unrelated files, misses same-package test calls, or makes unrelated/broken edits.
scale.2: Shows weak progress such as locating the constructor or one call site, but does not update all visible old-signature calls or does not confirm the new dependency type/order.
scale.3: Equivalent partial behavior: identifies the important test and production call-site categories and may update some of them, but leaves uncertainty about generated DI, singleton replacement, provider signatures, or validation.
scale.4: Strong evidence of a consistent migration across constructor definition, most/all visible call sites, and DI providers, with sensible test arguments; minor validation gaps or unresolved nonblocking checks may remain.
scale.5: Complete evidence: all visible qualified and unqualified call sites are updated in the correct order, DI/generated code and provider signatures are consistent, runtime code uses the injected dependency where intended, and build/Wire/test feedback is run or concretely addressed with no stale old-signature usages remaining.

experiences.title: Do not over-credit superficial webhook contract coverage during unstable integration
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go service task adds a new config-driven HTTP/webhook sink and the trajectory is mid-implementation or repair-heavy, especially with broad file rewrites, sed/heredoc edits, truncated observations, failing or absent tests, or unresolved config/schema/test integration.
experiences.context: This warning applies in a Go backend repository where a new audit sink must be added end-to-end: config structs/defaults/validation, generated or checked config schemas, production sink package, server wiring, interface propagation, existing sink compatibility, tests, gofmt, and build/test validation. The misleading pattern is a trajectory that mentions or partially creates HMAC signing, JSON POSTs, retry/backoff, and context propagation, causing a broad webhook-requirements rubric to look satisfied, while visible evidence still shows unstable integration: malformed grpc wiring attempts, overwritten large files, old interface implementations in tests, config expected-value mismatches, missing schema updates, or no successful relevant validation. A webhook security/retry rubric can still be appropriate when the trajectory has already reached final review of an actual production webhook implementation and integration artifacts are visibly stable; it is not the right primary criterion while the agent is still repairing compile/test/config fallout.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics asked whether all webhook-specific behavior was present, such as HMAC-SHA256 signing, x-flipt-webhook-signature, JSON POSTs, exponential backoff, context cancellation, and multi-sink support. Those are real requirements, but as a trajectory-quality criterion they became misleading when judged from superficial evidence like imports, function names, or a summary claiming a webhook sink exists. In these cases the more predictive visible signal was repository integration risk: repeated destructive sed/heredoc edits, grpc.go block corruption and reverts, tests still failing after interface changes, config defaults not reflected in Default()/config tests/schema files, or the new production package not clearly present and compiled. A better rubric should first check whether the implementation is coherent and validated across the whole codebase before rewarding detailed webhook behavior. Avoid the tempting broad criterion 'all webhook requirements are implemented' unless the visible trajectory includes inspected production code and successful relevant validation. Replacement criteria should prioritize concrete evidence: production webhook files under the intended package, server wiring that appends rather than replaces sinks, all SendAudits implementers and test doubles updated consistently, config defaults/validation/schema/testdata aligned, no accidental unrelated file corruption, gofmt/build/tests run successfully, and retry/signing behavior verified by code or tests rather than inferred from symbol names.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for a config-driven webhook/audit-sink task when visible evidence shows the agent is treating feature-level webhook behavior as complete while repository-wide integration remains unproven or unstable. This includes missing or unverified production webhook package files, imports or wiring that may not compile, old SendAudits signatures in implementations or test doubles after adding context.Context, config defaults or validation not reflected in Default()/schema/config tests, repeated broad sed/heredoc edits that corrupted Go blocks or tests, or lack of successful gofmt/build/relevant test output after these cross-cutting changes. Do not apply this penalty merely because webhook unit tests are not yet written during early exploration; apply it when the trajectory is near implementation/finalization or claims readiness despite visible integration gaps.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Unstable end-to-end webhook sink integration

metadata.task_type: new config-driven HTTP/webhook sink
high_risk_evidence: broad sed or heredoc rewrites of Go/config/test files
grpc/server wiring block corruption or repeated reverts
interface signature changed without all implementers/tests updated
production webhook package existence or compile status not visibly confirmed
build/tests absent or still failing after cross-cutting edits
replacement_focus: production package and server wiring coherence
config/default/schema/test alignment
context interface propagation across all implementers
successful gofmt/build/relevant tests
absence of accidental unrelated file corruption

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory shows coherent production webhook files, stable server wiring, aligned config artifacts, updated interfaces/tests, and successful relevant validation.
scale.2: Minor risk only: most integration artifacts are visibly coherent, with at most small unvalidated areas such as missing dedicated webhook unit tests while build/config consistency appears addressed.
scale.3: Moderate risk: the feature behavior is partially implemented, but some integration evidence is missing or uncertain, such as uninspected overwritten files, incomplete schema/config-test updates, or validation not yet rerun after changes.
scale.4: Clear flaw: visible trajectory shows compile/test/config failures, corrupted wiring attempts, stale interface implementers, or missing validation while still proceeding as though the webhook sink is substantially complete.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory strongly suggests the patch is structurally incoherent, such as importing a production webhook package without clear production implementation, placing implementation code in the wrong file, repeatedly corrupting core wiring/tests, or ending with unresolved build/test failures.

experiences.title: Missing-Credential Auth Shortcut Before Lookup
experiences.description: Use when a Django/Python authentication backend task asks to avoid database work for absent credentials while preserving configured username-field fallback and normal authentication behavior.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories working on an authentication backend method that accepts username/password plus arbitrary credential kwargs, where the reported bug is unnecessary database lookup or password hashing when this backend has no usable credentials. It is most useful after the agent has inspected or edited the target method, because the decisive evidence is the ordering of credential normalization, early return, lookup, and dummy password hashing. Do not apply as a primary criterion when the task is only about test coverage, when no implementation location has been reached yet, or when the backend intentionally treats missing credentials as a valid lookup value. In Django-like environments, account for multiple authentication backends and custom user models where the username may be supplied through the configured username field rather than the explicit username parameter.
experiences.experience: For this cluster, rubrics requiring an in-repository regression test were often less predictive than rubrics judging the implementation contract itself: a compact code-only change can fully satisfy the requested behavior even without adding a project-native test. The better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory preserves the existing username resolution from credential kwargs, then short-circuits if the resolved username or password is still missing, before any user lookup or password hashing side effect. It should also check that normal supplied-credential behavior remains intact, including the dummy hasher/timing mitigation for nonexistent users when both credentials are present. Avoid the tempting but over-strict criterion that success requires adding assertNumQueries tests; tests are valuable supporting evidence, but lack of a committed test should not dominate when visible code and manual query-count validation already show the semantic fix. Prioritize visible evidence such as the edited control-flow order, references to configured username-field compatibility, manual or official test output showing zero queries for missing credentials, and verification that valid or nonexistent username/password attempts still use the normal path.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement the authentication backend so it first resolves the username from the configured username-field kwargs when the explicit username argument is absent, then returns None if the resolved username or password is None before performing any user lookup or dummy password hashing. It should preserve the existing behavior for complete username/password attempts, including normal user lookup, password checking, user eligibility checks, and the timing-mitigation hasher path for nonexistent users with supplied credentials.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Resolved-Credential Short-Circuit Contract

required_evidence: Username fallback from configured credential kwargs remains before the missing-credential guard.
The guard covers both missing resolved username and missing password.
The guard is placed before database lookup and before dummy password hashing.
Normal supplied-credential authentication path is left intact.
supporting_evidence: Manual or project-native query-count checks show zero queries for missing-credential calls.
Tests or scripts show valid credentials still authenticate and nonexistent users with complete credentials still follow the existing lookup path.
avoid_overweighting: Do not make committed regression-test presence the sole or primary correctness signal when the implementation evidence is decisive.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that missing credentials are short-circuited before lookup/hash, or the trajectory edits an unrelated area.
scale.2: Attempts an early return for missing credentials but omits an important condition, places it before required username-field fallback, or otherwise risks breaking valid credential forms.
scale.3: Comparable to the parent trajectory: recognizes the correct target and partial contract, but evidence is incomplete about ordering, side effects, or preservation of normal authentication.
scale.4: Strong evidence of the correct guard after username fallback and before lookup/hash, with some validation or reasoning that normal authentication remains intact.
scale.5: Decisive evidence of the full contract: correct ordering after configured username fallback, no lookup/hash for missing username or password, preserved complete-credential behavior including timing mitigation, and relevant validation through tests or query-count checks.

experiences.title: Exact Cached-Method Invalidation in clear_cache
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python/Django-style task reports that a documented cache-clearing/reset method misses a specific functools-cached method, and the trajectory has identified both the cached method and the reset method.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django/Python repository when the task is narrowly about a registry or manager reset method whose documentation says it clears internal caches, and the visible trajectory shows a specific method decorated with functools.cache/lru_cache whose cache is not cleared by the reset path. It is especially applicable once the agent has inspected the relevant class and either added or is about to add a cache_clear() call for that exact cached method. It is less applicable for broad performance-cache audits, tasks that explicitly require test-only work, or early exploration before the trajectory has connected the reported cached method to the reset method.
experiences.experience: For this pattern, the most useful rubric should focus on the concrete invalidation contract: the reset/clear method must explicitly call cache_clear() on the reported cached lookup while preserving the existing cache-clearing behavior. Rubrics that targeted this exact implementation evidence aligned well because the task itself named the missing cache and the trajectory visibly found the @functools.cache decorator, found the existing clear_cache() implementation, and inserted the missing cache_clear() alongside the existing cache reset. A broader version such as “all cached methods in the class must be cleared” can be acceptable only when the trajectory has enumerated those methods and the class scope is small; otherwise prefer the named missing cache from the issue. Avoid making a project-native regression test the primary criterion unless the task or repository standards make tests mandatory at this stage: in these trajectories, requiring an added official test was too strict because the decisive correctness evidence was the source change and cache-info reproduction. The judge should prioritize visible evidence that the agent identified the cached method, updated the documented cache-clearing path, did not alter lookup semantics or unrelated registry behavior, and optionally verified that a post-clear call is a cache miss or that cache_info/currsize resets.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should ensure that the documented app-registry cache clearing method explicitly clears the functools cache for the swappable-settings-name lookup, in addition to preserving the existing model cache clearing and model metadata expiration behavior. Strong evidence includes inspecting the cached lookup decorator, locating the existing clear_cache implementation, adding the missing cache_clear() call for that lookup, and verifying that calling clear_cache() resets the lookup cache without changing returned swappable-model results.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Clear the Missing Swappable Lookup Cache

metadata.required_cached_lookup: get_swappable_settings_name or the task-named functools-cached lookup
metadata.required_clear_path: Apps.clear_cache or the documented registry cache reset method
key_positive_evidence: trajectory observes the lookup is decorated with functools.cache/lru_cache
trajectory observes the reset method already clears other internal caches
trajectory adds an explicit cache_clear() call for the missing cached lookup
trajectory preserves existing cache clearing and lookup semantics
non_required_evidence: adding a formal project-native regression test is beneficial but should not be the sole pass/fail criterion unless explicitly required

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory connects the reported cached lookup to the cache-clearing method, or it changes unrelated behavior without addressing the missing cache.
scale.2: The trajectory identifies a cache issue but only discusses or tests it, or proposes a vague cache invalidation change without showing the specific cached lookup will be cleared.
scale.3: The trajectory reaches behavior roughly equivalent to the parent: it recognizes the cached lookup and reset method but has incomplete, uncertain, or unverified implementation evidence.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly updates the reset method to clear the specific cached lookup while retaining existing cache-clearing behavior, with little evidence of unrelated semantic changes.
scale.5: The trajectory conclusively identifies the functools-cached lookup, adds the exact missing cache_clear() call in the documented reset path, preserves existing behavior, and verifies through cache state or repeated-call evidence that the cache is reset after clear_cache().

experiences.title: Do not treat direct Qt QFlags copying as a complete fix for direction-toggle state bugs
experiences.description: Retrieve when a qutebrowser/PyQt WebEngine search task involves `FindFlags`, reverse/forward search toggling, and PyQt type errors from temporary flag mutation.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Qt browser code where persistent search state is stored as Qt `QFlags`/enum wrappers and navigation temporarily flips a direction bit before calling Qt APIs. The misleading pattern is to generate a rubric that rewards only replacing `QWebEnginePage.FindFlags(int(self._flags))` with `QWebEnginePage.FindFlags(self._flags)` or similar direct copy-constructor usage. That can be a useful local practice when the task is strictly about avoiding an unnecessary integer cast and the existing Qt wrapper storage model is known to be safe. It is not sufficient when the problem statement emphasizes repeated `n`/`N` direction switching, preserving original search direction, PyQt binding type fragility, and consistent behavior across temporary mutations.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster over-focused on preserving the Qt flag wrapper type during a local copy. That criterion is tempting because the visible code contains an `int(self._flags)` copy in `prev_result()`, and the task mentions PyQt5 type loss. However, for this class of bug, a one-line constructor-copy replacement can still leave the implementation dependent on mutable/fragile Qt flag wrappers for persistent logical state, and it may not address the broader invariant: direction and case-sensitivity should be stored as ordinary logical state, temporary opposite-direction navigation should derive a separate logical copy, and conversion to Qt flags should happen only at the boundary where `findText()` is called. A better rubric should look for evidence that the agent separates stored search semantics from Qt API flags, updates both initial search and duplicate-search flag storage, computes `prev_result`/`next_result` direction from logical state rather than bitwise tests on Qt wrappers, and preserves logging/API behavior via an explicit conversion/string representation. Avoid a misleading criterion that says direct `QFlags(self._flags)` copying is the required or sufficient fix. Prioritize visible evidence of a binding-agnostic flag representation, temporary inversion without mutating stored state, and conversion to valid Qt flags only for the Qt call.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a PyQt/qutebrowser WebEngine search-direction bug where persistent search flags are stored as Qt `QFlags` and temporary navigation flips a direction bit, penalize trajectories that only plan or implement a local replacement of integer coercion with direct `QFlags` copy construction while leaving persistent search state represented and manipulated as Qt flag wrappers. This flaw is especially clear if the trajectory does not propose a binding-agnostic logical representation for direction/case state, does not update the search and duplicate-search paths that store flags, and continues deriving `prev_result`/`next_result` behavior through bitwise operations on stored Qt wrappers.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Local QFlags Copy Is Too Narrow

metadata.environment: Python qutebrowser-style QtWebEngine search implementation using PyQt Qt enum/QFlags wrappers
observable_bad_evidence: The proposed fix is limited to changing `QFlags(int(stored_flags))` to `QFlags(stored_flags)` or `type(stored_flags)(stored_flags)`
Stored search flags remain Qt wrapper objects used as application state
Temporary direction changes still rely on bitwise mutation/testing of Qt wrappers
No explicit conversion boundary from logical state to Qt flags is introduced
observable_good_boundary: A direct Qt flag copy may be acceptable only when the task and investigation show the storage model is safe and the bug is solely the cast itself
For repeated direction-toggle bugs, stronger evidence is needed: ordinary logical state for direction/case, non-mutating temporary inversion, and Qt conversion only at API call time

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory separates logical search state from Qt flags or otherwise clearly addresses binding-agnostic state, non-mutating temporary direction inversion, and API-boundary conversion.
scale.2: Minor evidence of narrowness: the trajectory mentions direct Qt flag copying but also investigates or plans broader stored-state and conversion-boundary changes.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies the integer coercion and stored-state concerns, but the visible plan or edits mostly center on a local direct-copy replacement without fully addressing all flag storage paths.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory implements or strongly commits to only replacing `int(stored_flags)` with direct Qt flag copy while leaving persistent Qt-wrapper state and bitwise direction logic unchanged.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory treats the direct Qt copy-constructor change as definitively sufficient, possibly adds unrelated edits/tests, and shows no awareness that persistent logical search state should be decoupled from Qt flag wrappers for repeated direction toggling.

experiences.title: Flag Must Reach the Enrichment Path Before API Lookups
experiences.description: Retrieve when a CLI flag is requested to skip inactive WordPress-like components and the codebase separates inventory collection from later vulnerability/API enrichment.
experiences.context: Applies in Go CLI vulnerability scanners or similar tools where one phase detects installed components and another phase/report integration performs external vulnerability lookups. The visible trajectory should show that component records already include status/type metadata, and that the expensive behavior occurs in a later enrichment/report path rather than merely during inventory scanning. This guidance is most useful once the agent has inspected the command flag definitions, config plumbing, the integration option/caller, and the loop that performs external API requests. It is premature during early repository exploration before the active command path is known. It may not apply if the project performs vulnerability API calls directly during the scan command, if the task only asks to hide inactive results after lookup, or if inactive status is not available before the lookup.
experiences.experience: The earlier rubrics correctly emphasized the semantic core: inactive plugins/themes should be skipped only when the new option is enabled, while core, active components, must-use components, and default no-flag behavior remain intact. That criterion is useful because visible evidence often shows whether the agent is filtering before the WPVulnDB/API loop or merely filtering results afterward. However, for split scan/report architectures it is not enough to ask for filtering inside the lookup loop. A stronger rubric must also verify that the flag is exposed on the command path that actually performs vulnerability enrichment and is propagated into the lookup logic. In these trajectories, adding a flag only to the inventory scan command or proving only that scan help lists the flag is a tempting but misleading proxy, because the API calls happen later in the report/enrichment integration. Likewise, filtering detected inventory during scan, relying on an existing post-processing result filter, or binding a flag to a non-addressable/per-server map entry should not be credited as satisfying the efficiency requirement. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent has identified the real API-calling phase, registered the flag where users invoke that phase, stored it in an addressable config/option, passed it through the integration option or equivalent call chain, and applies the inactive-status check before each plugin/theme API request without mutating unrelated inventory or suppressing core/must-use components.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Effective Inactive-Component Skip on the API-Enrichment Path
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the new ignore-inactive flag is wired through the command/config path that actually performs WordPress vulnerability enrichment, and that the enrichment logic skips external vulnerability lookups for inactive plugin/theme packages before making requests. Strong evidence includes recognizing the split between inventory detection and later vulnerability filling, exposing the option on the enrichment/report command or otherwise ensuring it is available at that phase, passing the option through the integration/caller into the lookup loop, and preserving default behavior plus core, active, and must-use component scanning.

metadata.applicability: Use for CLI feature requests that aim to reduce external vulnerability API calls by skipping inactive WordPress-like plugins/themes in a split scan/report architecture.
prioritize_evidence: agent identifies which command or phase invokes external vulnerability lookup
flag/config is registered on or available to that effective enrichment command path
option is propagated through integration/caller state into the API lookup function
inactive check occurs before plugin/theme API requests
default no-flag behavior and core/active/must-use behavior are preserved
do_not_credit_as_sufficient: flag appears only on an unrelated inventory-scan command when enrichment is run elsewhere
post-processing result filtering after API calls
removing inactive packages from stored inventory instead of skipping lookup
binding CLI flag directly to an unsafe per-server map entry
help output for the wrong command without propagation to the lookup path

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the flag reaches the vulnerability API/enrichment path, or the trajectory is focused on unrelated exploration or leaves broken command/config edits.
scale.2: Some pieces exist, such as adding a flag or noting package status, but the flag is on the wrong command/path, not stored safely, or not connected to the API lookup logic.
scale.3: Partial implementation comparable to the parent trajectory: the agent may add filtering in the lookup loop or add some option plumbing, but important routing is missing or ambiguous, such as only exposing the flag on the inventory scan path or relying on post-fetch filtering.
scale.4: Strong evidence that the flag is available to the enrichment phase and inactive plugin/theme lookups are skipped before API requests, with only minor uncertainty around validation, naming consistency, or edge cases.
scale.5: Complete visible evidence that the effective user-facing enrichment command accepts the flag, config/option plumbing reaches the API lookup function, inactive plugin/theme requests are skipped before network calls, core/active/must-use and default behavior are preserved, and the changes are syntactically validated or otherwise carefully checked.

experiences.title: First-Class Wire-Compatible Database Backend Contract
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go SQL application is adding a new database backend that is wire-compatible with an existing backend but must still be recognized as a distinct protocol, migration target, and documented deployment option.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories for backend-support feature work in a Go repository with centralized database configuration, URL/driver parsing, command-level store selection, migration orchestration, and Docker Compose or example documentation. It is especially relevant when the requested backend can reuse an existing SQL driver/store path, but the task explicitly asks for first-class protocol and migration support. Use this at implementation or review stages where the trajectory has inspected or edited protocol maps, SQL driver maps, migrator code, migration assets, command store switches, and examples.
