It is less useful for very early exploration with no edits except as a planning target, and it should not be applied to tasks that only ask users to use an existing compatible URL scheme without distinct backend recognition.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric pattern is to evaluate the complete backend contract, not just whether the agent mentioned the new database or got the project to build. Previous rubrics in this cluster were useful when they checked the key semantic boundary: the new backend should be first-class at user-facing/configuration and migration-selection boundaries, while reusing the existing compatible SQL/store behavior where appropriate. The most discriminative visible evidence is concrete inspection or diff output showing symmetric protocol mappings, URL/driver parsing for the new scheme, all runtime and CLI store-selection switches wired without malformed cases, migration orchestration using the backend-specific golang-migrate driver rather than silently treating it as the compatible existing backend, migration files/source paths for the new backend, and a working documented Compose example using the repository's real configuration environment variables. A better rubric should require these surfaces together and should also watch for regressions caused by broad rewrites or brittle sed edits, such as broken switch bodies, missing imports, copied whole files with syntax errors, root example files overwritten incorrectly, or validations that do not cover the new backend. Avoid tempting but wrong criteria: do not reward creating a separate duplicated store package if routing to the existing compatible store is the intended design; do not accept a postgres URL or postgres migration driver as sufficient when the task asks for a distinct CockroachDB backend; do not treat successful generic build/tests as proof unless the trajectory also shows the new protocol and migration paths are actually present; and do not let documentation-only or copied migrations substitute for config/parser/migrator wiring.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete First-Class Compatible Backend Integration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates, through visible file inspection, diffs, commands, or validation output, that the new wire-compatible database backend is integrated as a distinct supported backend across the full application contract: configuration accepts and serializes the new protocol string symmetrically; SQL URL/driver parsing recognizes the new scheme and opens it through the compatible existing SQL driver behavior where appropriate; every application entrypoint that chooses a concrete store handles the new driver without breaking existing SQLite/Postgres/MySQL cases; migration setup imports and selects the backend-specific golang-migrate driver and uses a backend-specific migration source/path with compatible migration assets; dependency/module changes needed for that migration driver are present; documentation or a Docker Compose example is placed in the repository's example/docs pattern and uses the correct runtime configuration variables and connection URL; and the agent validates with formatting, build/tests, and diff review sufficient to catch syntax, import, switch-placement, and accidental rewrite regressions.

required_visible_evidence: distinct protocol enum/string mapping or equivalent config parser support
SQL driver/url mapping for the new scheme
store-selection handling in all relevant server and CLI entrypoints
backend-specific golang-migrate driver selection rather than only compatible-backend migration selection
migration assets/source path for the new backend
working deployment example or documentation using correct environment variables
validation or diff review that checks modified Go files and examples
common_false_positives_to_penalize: only copying migration files or adding documentation
using the compatible existing backend name everywhere instead of a distinct protocol
using the compatible existing migration driver when the task asks for a backend-specific migration driver
creating duplicated store code when the existing compatible store should be reused
malformed switch cases or missing imports caused by automated text insertion
build success without evidence that the new backend paths are wired

scale.1: No concrete implementation evidence beyond exploration or generic mentions; the new backend is not visibly accepted as a distinct protocol and no migration/runtime/doc wiring is shown.
scale.2: Some isolated surface is addressed, such as documentation, copied migrations, or a config string, but major required integration points such as SQL parsing, store selection, or migration driver selection are absent or visibly flawed.
scale.3: Partial backend support is visible across several surfaces, but the trajectory still relies on broad claims or compatible-backend shortcuts, misses at least one important entrypoint, lacks the backend-specific migration driver, or has unvalidated risky edits.
scale.4: Most required surfaces are wired with good visible evidence and existing compatible SQL behavior is reused appropriately, but there are minor gaps in validation, documentation placement, dependency evidence, or review of accidental regressions.
scale.5: The trajectory provides strong, concrete evidence for the full first-class backend contract across config, SQL parsing/opening, all store-selection entrypoints, backend-specific migrations, examples/docs, dependencies, and validation, while avoiding unnecessary duplication and preserving existing backend behavior.

experiences.title: Private Naming for Autogenerated pytest xUnit Fixtures
experiences.description: Retrieve when a pytest issue concerns internally generated xUnit/unittest fixtures appearing in `--fixtures` output and the trajectory is inspecting or editing generated fixture `name=` values.
experiences.context: Applies in the pytest codebase or similar fixture systems where fixture listing visibility is controlled by a naming convention, especially when the task text says generated unittest or xUnit setup/teardown fixtures should be hidden unless verbose. The trajectory should have visible evidence such as locating the autogenerated fixture creation path, observing a generated public name, reading documentation or listing code that hides leading-underscore fixtures, or testing `--fixtures` versus `--fixtures -v`. This is most useful after the agent has moved beyond generic repository exploration into the fixture-generation/display path; early exploration can be judged only on whether it is converging on that path. It is less applicable when the issue is about fixture execution order, user-defined public fixtures, missing fixture docstrings, or general changes to fixture-list filtering rather than the privacy of generated internal fixtures.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic contract: autogenerated unittest/xUnit fixtures are implementation details and must receive private leading-underscore fixture names so normal `--fixtures` hides them while verbose output can still show them. This aligned well because the visible trajectory repeatedly exposed the decisive evidence: the task explicitly identifies the missing underscore as the regression, the code creates an autouse fixture with an explicit generated `name=...`, comments/docs say the fixture is intended to be hidden and leading `_` controls privacy, and the agent either patches that generated name or validates the non-verbose/verbose listing behavior. A better rubric should not merely ask whether the agent found `unittest.py` or ran tests; it should judge whether the trajectory preserves the generated fixture’s autouse behavior, scope, and uniqueness while changing only the privacy-relevant display name. It should also give credit for recognizing related generated xUnit naming paths if the trajectory surfaces them, but should not require broad refactors unless the task/trajectory indicates those paths are in scope. Avoid tempting wrong criteria such as adding docstrings to internal fixtures, changing global `--fixtures` filtering, removing generated fixture names, relying only on normal test execution, or treating a globally installed pytest smoke test as decisive without evidence it exercised the checkout. Prioritize visible evidence of the exact privacy mechanism, the generated fixture naming site, preservation of execution semantics, and validation comparing hidden default output with verbose visibility.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should identify that internally generated pytest xUnit/unittest fixtures are exposed because their explicit generated fixture names lack the private leading-underscore prefix, and should move toward or implement a fix that prefixes those generated names while preserving autouse registration, scope, cleanup/setup behavior, and uniqueness. Strong evidence includes connecting the task’s `--fixtures` complaint to the fixture display convention for leading underscores, locating the generated `name=` construction rather than the wrapper function name, avoiding global display-filter changes, and validating or planning validation that normal `--fixtures` hides the internal fixture while verbose mode can still show it.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Autogenerated Fixture Privacy Contract

task_cues: generated pytest/unittest/xUnit fixture appears in non-verbose fixture listing
expected behavior depends on leading underscore privacy
fixture is internal and undocumented
trajectory_cues: locates dynamic fixture creation with explicit generated fixture name
connects fixture listing behavior to leading-underscore filtering
preserves autouse, scope, lifecycle, and unique naming semantics
checks or plans both non-verbose and verbose fixture listing behavior
avoid: global changes to fixture listing filters
adding documentation to internal generated fixtures as the main fix
removing unique generated names or altering lifecycle execution
validating only ordinary test pass/fail without fixture-list visibility

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory connects the issue to generated fixture names or the leading-underscore privacy convention.
scale.2: Some evidence of inspecting unittest/xUnit fixture code or fixture listing output, but the trajectory remains focused on generic exploration, installation issues, docstrings, or unrelated fixture behavior.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies the generated fixture naming site and the likely need for a leading underscore, but has not clearly preserved execution semantics or has limited validation/planning.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly targets the generated fixture `name=` privacy issue, preserves autouse/scope/unique behavior, and avoids broad or unrelated changes, with reasonable validation strategy or partial checks.
scale.5: The trajectory fully demonstrates the privacy contract: it changes or plans to change only the generated internal fixture names to leading-underscore private names, preserves lifecycle behavior and uniqueness, and verifies or convincingly reasons about hidden default `--fixtures` output plus verbose visibility.

experiences.title: Do not reward stripping XQuartz DISPLAY to the pre-colon path
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for Go X11 forwarding fixes involving macOS/XQuartz DISPLAY values that look like absolute filesystem paths followed by :display[.screen].
experiences.context: Applies in a Go/Teleport-style X11 forwarding implementation where DISPLAY parsing separates a host/path portion from display and screen numbers, and socket resolution decides between Unix-domain sockets and TCP. The misleading rubric pattern is to require only that the trajectory detect an absolute path such as /private/tmp/.../org.xquartz:0, extract the path before the colon, and use that path directly. Recognizing that the pre-colon component is not a TCP hostname is useful, but it is not sufficient for XQuartz because the actual Unix socket name may include the display number suffix, and sometimes the screen suffix, as part of the filesystem path. The original idea may still be appropriate for environments where the DISPLAY value truly contains a bare socket pathname with no X11 display suffix, but for X11 DISPLAY syntax the rubric must distinguish parsing the display number from resolving the actual socket filename.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics over-focused on the broad idea of 'handle XQuartz absolute Unix socket paths' and often specified an incorrect implementation: store or use the pre-colon path directly. That criterion can overvalue trajectories that add a UnixSocketPath field or accept any absolute HostName but then dial /private/tmp/.../org.xquartz instead of the real socket path /private/tmp/.../org.xquartz:0 or /private/tmp/.../org.xquartz:0.0. A better rubric should require evidence that the trajectory preserves standard hostname/unix/:display behavior while resolving XQuartz paths by checking the actual filesystem socket candidates derived from the full DISPLAY string, including display and optional screen suffixes, before treating the value as valid. Avoid rubrics that make 'extract socket path and use it directly' the success condition. Prioritize visible evidence such as: the resolver reattaches or preserves the display suffix when building the Unix address; it handles both with-screen and without-screen socket names; it verifies the candidate socket exists or otherwise avoids silently accepting arbitrary absolute host paths; and tests cover the resolved Unix address, not just that parsing returns a new field.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat macOS/XQuartz DISPLAY support as complete merely by detecting an absolute path and using the substring before the final colon as the Unix socket address. In this task family, the important behavior is resolving the actual X11 socket filename represented by an absolute-path DISPLAY, which may include the display number and possibly screen number suffix. A trajectory shows this flaw when it proposes or implements direct use of the pre-colon path, adds parsing-only storage for that path without preserving the suffix in socket resolution, or changes tests to expect the stripped path as the socket address. Do not penalize early investigation that has only identified the likely area and has not yet chosen an implementation.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Stripped XQuartz socket path false positive

metadata.environment: Go X11 forwarding/display parsing code
trigger_evidence: DISPLAY examples are absolute filesystem paths followed by :display or :display.screen
trajectory discusses Unix socket resolution, display parsing, or macOS/XQuartz forwarding
candidate fix uses absolute path detection or a new socket-path field
preferred_evidence: socket resolution tries full DISPLAY-derived candidates including display and optional screen suffix
candidate socket path is validated or not blindly accepted as the stripped host portion
standard TCP and conventional Unix DISPLAY formats remain covered by tests
avoid_as_success_proxy: tests expect the pre-colon substring as the Unix address

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory either has not implemented the XQuartz handling yet, or clearly plans to resolve the full DISPLAY-derived socket path including display/screen suffixes while preserving existing formats.
scale.2: Minor concern: the trajectory recognizes absolute XQuartz paths but remains ambiguous about whether socket resolution will use the full DISPLAY-derived pathname or the stripped pre-colon component.
scale.3: Moderate flaw: the trajectory focuses on parsing/storing the absolute path and only weakly addresses how the actual Unix socket address will be derived, leaving a real risk that the display suffix is dropped.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory explicitly proposes using the pre-colon absolute path directly as the Unix socket address or tests that behavior as expected.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory implements or strongly commits to stripped-path resolution, treats arbitrary absolute host components as valid Unix sockets, and lacks tests for suffix-preserving XQuartz socket candidates or existing format compatibility.

experiences.title: Minimal Serialization Hook for Autocomplete Results
experiences.description: Use this when a Django admin autocomplete task asks for a low-risk refactor that exposes per-result JSON serialization as an overridable hook while preserving the existing response contract.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django source-tree trajectory where the task specifically requests refactoring an admin autocomplete JSON view so subclasses can add extra fields without overriding the full request-handling method. It is most useful once the trajectory has visible evidence from an implementation summary, inspected diff, or source output showing changes to the autocomplete view class. The criterion is less useful during very early exploration before any implementation exists, and it should not be replaced by a test-only criterion unless the task or repository instructions explicitly require new regression tests. It may also be irrelevant for broader autocomplete behavior changes involving permissions, query construction, widget wiring, or response schema redesign rather than extracting the existing per-object result mapping.
experiences.experience: For this task family, the most predictive rubric focuses on the exact extension-point refactor: the view should gain an overridable per-object serialization method, and the existing response-building method should call that hook for each object in the results list. This is useful because the requested change is intentionally small: preserving all request processing, permission checks, queryset/context construction, pagination, and the default Select2-compatible JSON shape matters more than adding unrelated behavior. Prior rubrics that checked for the serialization hook were well targeted when visible trajectory evidence showed `get()` delegating result creation to the new method and the method returning the original `id`/`text` mapping. A tempting but weaker rubric is to require a new subclass customization test as the main criterion; such tests are helpful supporting evidence, but absence of a new test is not decisive when the implementation evidence already shows the minimal hook and existing tests are run or considered. Prioritize visible code/diff evidence that the hook has the intended signature, is invoked inside the `results` list comprehension, preserves string conversion for `id` and `text`, and leaves pagination plus permission/query flow untouched.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement the requested autocomplete result serialization extension point as a minimal behavior-preserving refactor: add an overridable per-result method on the autocomplete JSON view with the expected object and target-field arguments, have the existing response method call that hook for every object in the results list, preserve the default item mapping of stringified object identifier and display text, and avoid changing pagination, permission checks, request processing, queryset construction, or the top-level JSON response shape.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Behavior-Preserving Result Serialization Hook

metadata.environment: Django admin autocomplete JSON view refactor
primary_evidence: visible source or diff of the autocomplete view class
response construction delegates each result object to an overridable serialization method
default serialization still returns only the original id and text fields with the same string conversion semantics
pagination and request/permission/query flow remain unchanged
secondary_evidence: ad hoc or official validation showing subclass override can add an extra field
existing admin autocomplete tests or broader admin tests run without relevant failures
avoid_as_primary: requiring a new regression test as the main proof when implementation evidence is decisive
crediting unrelated test-runner troubleshooting as task progress
accepting changes that customize results by overriding or rewriting the whole response method

scale.1: No visible implementation of a per-result serialization hook, or the trajectory remains only in exploration/test-runner setup without code evidence for the requested refactor.
scale.2: Mentions or partially adds a serialization helper, but the response method does not clearly use it for each result, or the default output semantics are incomplete or uncertain.
scale.3: Adds a plausible hook and uses it in result construction, but visible evidence leaves some preservation details unclear, such as exact string conversion, response shape, or whether unrelated request/pagination logic was changed.
scale.4: Clearly adds the overridable hook, calls it for each result, preserves the original id/text mapping and pagination shape, with only minor uncertainty such as documentation wording or incomplete validation.
scale.5: Provides decisive visible code/diff evidence of the minimal hook extraction, exact default id/text semantics, unchanged permissions/query/pagination/response structure, and optionally supporting validation that subclass overrides can add extra fields.

experiences.title: Do not let OLID fallback alone stand in for the full autocomplete refactor
experiences.description: Retrieve this when evaluating an Open Library autocomplete refactor where the trajectory mentions embedded OLID detection/fallback, but the task also requires a shared autocomplete base, generic key conversion, consistent Solr query defaults, edition exclusion, and response normalization.
experiences.context: In the Open Library Python/web.py worksearch plugin, `/works/_autocomplete`, `/authors/_autocomplete`, and `/subjects_autocomplete` are Solr-backed endpoints with work/author primary-source fallback via model records. A rubric that only checks whether work/author OLIDs are detected and fetched from the database can be useful when the change is narrowly about fallback behavior. It becomes misleading for this broader task when visible evidence shows only per-endpoint `find_work_olid_in_string`/`find_author_olid_in_string` use, hard-coded key prefixes, or superficial `as_fake_solr_record()` fallback, while the trajectory has not demonstrated a truly shared autocomplete implementation with generic OLID-to-key conversion, consistent query fields, edition exclusion, subject integration through the base, and stable output shape.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics emphasized embedded OLID resolution and primary-source fallback. That criterion is semantically relevant but too narrow here: many trajectories can appear strong on fallback by preserving or rewrapping the existing work/author logic, yet still fail the main refactor contract by keeping endpoint-specific parsing, omitting a general OLID/key utility, searching only title for works or only name for authors/subjects instead of applying the shared default query, using fragile key-suffix filters instead of excluding editions consistently, or giving subjects a separate duplicated GET path. Avoid generating a standalone positive criterion that treats `key_prefix + embedded_olid` plus `web.ctx.site.get(...).as_fake_solr_record()` as sufficient progress. A better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory visibly unifies the autocomplete contract end-to-end: one base path for common GET/Solr/limit/fallback/doc wrapping behavior, resource-specific configuration only where necessary, a generic embedded OLID extractor and OLID-to-entity-key conversion, default exact and starts-with matching over title/name, `-type:edition` or equivalent edition exclusion, subject type filtering without duplicating the whole flow, and response normalization that preserves expected fields.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial OLID fallback without unified autocomplete semantics
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear to address embedded OLID fallback but do not visibly implement the broader shared autocomplete contract. This applies when the patch or plan relies on per-resource OLID helpers, hard-coded key prefixes, endpoint-specific GET implementations, or ad hoc subject/key behavior while lacking a generic OLID-to-key conversion layer and common base logic for query construction, filtering, limits, fallback, and document wrapping.

metadata.environment: Open Library Python worksearch autocomplete endpoints using web.py delegate pages and Solr
visible_evidence_to_check: whether work/author OLID extraction is generalized rather than left as separate endpoint-only helpers
whether OLIDs are converted to canonical entity keys through shared logic
whether works/authors/subjects share one common GET/Solr flow instead of duplicated endpoint bodies
whether default queries include exact and starts-with matching on title/name as required
whether edition records are excluded consistently
whether fallback records are passed through the same response normalization as Solr docs
whether subject type filtering is integrated as a specialization rather than a full duplicate implementation

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory clearly implements a shared autocomplete base plus generic OLID extraction/key conversion, consistent query/filter/limit handling, fallback, and response normalization.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: most common behavior is unified, but one small resource-specific detail remains less clearly centralized while the main OLID/key/query/filter contract is visible.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory has a base class and some fallback behavior, but still depends on per-resource OLID parsing or leaves important query/filter/doc-wrapping behavior split across endpoints.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory mainly preserves or rewraps existing work/author fallback with hard-coded key prefixes and duplicated subject or author/work logic, without a convincing generic OLID-to-key utility or consistent shared defaults.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory treats `as_fake_solr_record()` fallback as the solution while missing or breaking the unified base contract, edition exclusion, title/name exact-prefix search, canonical key conversion, or expected response shapes.

experiences.title: Upgrade-Level Changelog Requires State-Derived Version Classification
experiences.description: Use when a qutebrowser trajectory is changing changelog-on-upgrade behavior from a boolean gate to configurable major/minor/patch filtering.
experiences.context: Applies in the qutebrowser Python codebase when the task is to stop showing the changelog for every upgrade and the trajectory has found or edited the startup changelog gate, the YAML config setting, and the state/version-change code. It is especially relevant once the agent is implementing or reviewing logic that compares previous and current application versions. It is less useful for unrelated changelog rendering/documentation tasks, for codebases without persisted previous-version state, or at a very early search-only stage before the agent has identified how upgrade detection works. Boundary condition: merely adding a string/enum setting is not enough evidence; the important question is whether the implementation can reliably classify the actual stored upgrade as major, minor, patch, equal, downgrade, or unknown before the stored version is overwritten.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics were useful because they judged the core semantic contract rather than superficial edits: the new setting must control changelog display by upgrade significance, patch upgrades should be suppressed by the meaningful-upgrade default, users must still be able to choose all-upgrades or never, and the decision must be based on a reliable previous-versus-current version comparison. In these trajectories, a recurring visible flaw was that agents tried to read the old version from the state general/version entry inside the app startup changelog block, even though the state initialization flow had already read the previous version and then stored the current version back into that entry. Another recurring flaw was leaving upgrade detection as a boolean, which cannot distinguish patch/minor/major, or inventing config values/defaults that preserve all-upgrades behavior by default despite the requested behavior. A better rubric should explicitly require the state layer to expose or store a classified version change before overwriting the persisted version, and the app layer to use that classification against the configured threshold. Avoid the tempting but weaker criterion of rewarding any enum/string config or any ad-hoc version split in the app; those can look plausible while still comparing the current version to itself, mishandling downgrades/unknown versions, or failing to suppress patch releases by default. Prioritize visible evidence such as: old version captured during state loading, parsed with the repository’s version utility, converted into a durable change category; a threshold/matching helper mapping major/minor/patch/never semantics; the changelog gate using that helper; default set to meaningful upgrades; and config/docs reflecting all supported modes.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Reliable Upgrade-Threshold Changelog Policy
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement changelog display as a configurable upgrade-threshold policy backed by reliable state-derived version classification. An excellent trajectory captures the previous persisted application version during state initialization before it is overwritten, parses previous and current versions with the repository’s version utility, classifies the change into meaningful categories such as equal, patch, minor, major, downgrade, or unknown, and exposes a helper or durable value that the startup changelog gate can match against the user setting. The setting should default to showing only meaningful minor-or-major upgrades, should allow major-only, all patch/minor/major upgrades, and never/disabled behavior, and the existing changelog anchor/opening workflow should remain intact. Visible implementation evidence should show valid config schema and documentation consistent with the runtime values, plus validation that avoids relying on known-unrelated import failures or corrupted broad YAML edits.

metadata.environment: qutebrowser Python application with YAML-driven settings, typed config values, persistent state file, and startup changelog opening logic
required_visible_evidence: previous persisted version is captured during state loading before current version is written back
upgrade category is derived from parsed previous and current versions rather than a boolean changed flag alone
configured threshold maps correctly to major-only, minor-or-major, patch/all, and never behavior
default suppresses patch-only changelog prompts while showing meaningful upgrades
startup changelog logic uses the state-derived category and preserves existing changelog anchor/resource handling
common_flaws_to_penalize: reading the old version from state after initialization when it may already contain the current version
changing only the config type without implementing version-category filtering
using truthiness of a non-empty string setting so disabled values still show the changelog
defaulting to all upgrades when the requested behavior is to avoid patch-level interruptions
broad scripted edits corrupting unrelated settings

scale.1: No meaningful implementation evidence beyond searching or superficial edits; changelog behavior remains controlled by a boolean or always-on version-change gate.
scale.2: Adds a configurable-looking setting or partial app checks, but does not reliably obtain the previous version or cannot actually distinguish patch, minor, and major upgrades.
scale.3: Implements some threshold logic and config values, but with important gaps such as reading a possibly overwritten state version, ambiguous defaults, missing all/never behavior, or fragile ad-hoc parsing.
scale.4: Mostly implements correct configurable filtering with a sensible default and previous/current version comparison, with only minor concerns around validation, edge cases, naming consistency, or documentation.
scale.5: Fully implements a robust state-derived upgrade classification and clean threshold matching, with valid config/docs, correct default behavior, disabled/all/major/minor semantics, preserved changelog opening flow, and evidence of targeted validation.

experiences.title: End-to-End Protobuf Option Follow-Through
experiences.description: Use when a Go/gRPC service task adds a new request option that changes server behavior, especially when the trajectory has edited the .proto file or generated code and is trying to honor the option in request handling.
experiences.context: Applies in Go projects with checked-in protobuf/gRPC/gateway/OpenAPI outputs where the requested fix introduces a new boolean request field that controls conditional error handling in a batch/server path. It is most useful after the agent has identified the protobuf request message and the server loop, or after it has attempted generation/manual generated-file edits. It is less useful for purely internal behavior changes with no API schema evolution, for repositories that do not check in generated protobuf artifacts, or very early exploration before the agent has found whether the API contract is protobuf-backed. If generation tooling is unavailable and the agent hand-edits generated files, this criterion becomes more important, not less, because hand-added struct fields/getters may compile while protobuf reflection, JSON/gateway, and documentation remain inconsistent.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful judgment is that adding the visible option name to the source proto or manually adding a Go struct field is not enough. A strong rubric for these trajectories should evaluate end-to-end follow-through: the API schema must expose the new field with a backward-compatible default, generated artifacts must be regenerated or consistently updated, server-side batch logic must use the new field to skip only typed not-found errors while preserving existing fail-fast behavior when false, and tests must cover both enabled and disabled behavior. Previous narrow rubrics that focused only on the batch loop were useful when the trajectory had not yet touched core logic, but they became too lenient once the agent added plausible server code while leaving generated protobuf/gateway/swagger state incomplete or unverified. Conversely, a rubric focused only on protobuf regeneration can miss an implementation that exposes the field but never honors it. Avoid tempting proxies such as: the proto contains `exclude_not_found`; a getter exists in generated Go; `go build` or an existing batch test passes; or the agent tried `make proto` but failed due missing tooling. Prioritize visible evidence of a clean generated-code path or comprehensive equivalent updates, typed not-found discrimination rather than string/new-error comparison or swallowing all errors, unchanged default behavior for omitted/false options, preservation of existing response request ID and timing behavior, and new regression tests for mixed existing/missing requests.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete API Option Contract and Semantics
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a complete implementation of a new protobuf-backed batch request option: the source request schema adds a backward-compatible boolean field; generated API artifacts are regenerated or consistently updated without corrupt manual edits; the server batch loop reads the generated option and, only when true, skips individual requests that fail with the project’s typed not-found error while returning all other errors and preserving the default fail-fast behavior when false; existing response identifier and timing behavior remains intact; and regression tests or a clear test plan cover mixed existing/missing requests with the option enabled, missing requests with it disabled, and non-not-found errors.

metadata.environment: Go service using protobuf/gRPC with checked-in generated request types and gateway/documentation artifacts
required_visible_evidence: protobuf request message contains a new optional/default-false boolean field with a fresh tag and appropriate JSON/Go naming
generated code or equivalent artifacts are updated consistently, not merely a hand-added field/getter with stale descriptors or gateway/docs
batch request handler reads the generated option field
not-found detection uses the repository's typed error mechanism, such as errors.As or an established helper, rather than comparing to a newly constructed error or matching strings
when the option is false or omitted, the first not-found error still fails the batch
when the option is true, only not-found subrequests are omitted and successful responses retain existing request identifier and timing conventions
tests or planned tests exercise enabled partial success, disabled fail-fast behavior, and non-not-found error propagation
common_negative_cues: protoc or generation failed and the trajectory proceeds with partial manual generated-file edits
only the .proto file or Go struct/getter is changed
generated descriptor, gateway, or documentation consistency is not considered in a repository that checks those in
server logic skips all errors or uses brittle error equality/string checks

scale.1: No meaningful end-to-end progress: the option is absent from the API contract or the trajectory is still only exploring without a concrete schema and server plan.
scale.2: Weak progress: the source schema or generated struct is partially edited, but generated artifacts are incomplete/unverified or server behavior is not implemented.
scale.3: Moderate progress: the option is exposed and some batch-loop logic exists, but there are gaps such as stale generated metadata, no gateway/documentation consistency, weak error typing, or missing tests.
scale.4: Strong progress: schema, generated types, and server semantics are mostly correct, with typed not-found handling and default fail-fast behavior preserved, but validation or one generated/test surface remains incomplete.
scale.5: Strongest progress: the trajectory shows a coherent generated API update, correct conditional server semantics for only not-found subrequests, preserved identifiers/timing, and targeted regression coverage for enabled, disabled, and non-not-found cases.

experiences.title: Do not treat local cookie sanitizers as complete config-domain fixes
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go OIDC/session task says a configured session domain may include scheme/port or localhost, and the trajectory focuses on patching cookie call sites or callback URL joining without showing config-level normalization or preservation of existing OIDC server behavior.
experiences.context: This applies in Go authentication/OIDC code where `authentication.session.domain` is a configuration value consumed by HTTP cookie creation, and the reported bug includes both cookie Domain compliance and callback URL slash joining. A criterion that only asks whether cookies are assigned a hostname-only Domain or callback URLs avoid `//` is relevant but can be misleading if the visible trajectory implements an ad hoc helper inside the OIDC HTTP/server package while leaving the configuration value itself unnormalized, or if it rewrites unrelated OIDC server APIs while chasing the fix. The original cookie/callback criterion is still appropriate when the task is explicitly limited to Set-Cookie header generation and the configuration layer is guaranteed already normalized, or when the trajectory has not reached implementation and the rubric is only measuring investigation progress. At final-review stages, visible evidence should include where the configured domain is normalized, how localhost is handled at cookie emission, and whether the callback join is a narrow change.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often rewarded visible edits such as adding `cookieDomain`/`extractHostname` around `http.Cookie.Domain`, using `strings.TrimSuffix` in the callback builder, or running tests. Those are semantically related but not enough for this task because the user-facing contract is about `authentication.session.domain` accepting URL-like values and being made safe for session use. If an agent only sanitizes at two OIDC cookie call sites, the stored config may still contain a scheme/port for other session consumers, tests may miss config-loading behavior, and local helpers may mishandle bare host:port or introduce broad server rewrites. A better rubric should check for a cohesive, minimal fix: normalize the session domain during config validation/loading or otherwise before all session consumers see it; surface invalid parse errors rather than silently returning unsafe input; omit the cookie Domain attribute for localhost at the actual cookie creation point; and fix callback URL construction by trimming/joining slashes without stripping scheme/port from the redirect base. Avoid the tempting criterion “cookie Domain is sanitized wherever cookies are set” as a standalone success signal. Prefer visible evidence such as edits to authentication config validation/defaulting, focused testdata or tests covering `http://localhost:8080` and `localhost`, preservation of the existing OIDC server constructor/registration shape, and a narrowly scoped callback change.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that address the OIDC session-domain bug only by adding ad hoc cookie-domain helpers at OIDC HTTP cookie call sites, while leaving the configured session domain unnormalized at configuration validation/loading and/or making broad unrelated OIDC server API rewrites. This flaw is especially important when the task text says `authentication.session.domain` itself may contain a scheme/port and should be accepted as configuration. Judge from visible evidence: whether `internal/config` or the equivalent config-validation path is updated or explicitly ruled out; whether tests/config fixtures cover URL-like session domains; whether localhost omission is applied where cookies are emitted; and whether callback URL handling is a narrow trailing-slash fix rather than a rewrite that changes redirect semantics.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Local cookie-only sanitization misses session config contract

primary_evidence: Task states the configured session domain may include scheme/port
Trajectory edits only OIDC HTTP/server cookie assignment helpers
No visible config validation/loading normalization or config fixture/test for URL-like session domain
Possible unrelated OIDC server constructor, registration, or response handling rewrites
metadata.acceptable_boundary: Do not apply this negative rubric when the trajectory explicitly implements or justifies normalization before all session consumers, or when the task is limited to direct Set-Cookie behavior with config already guaranteed host-only.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory normalizes the session-domain configuration before downstream use or gives a clear, code-supported reason why config-level normalization is unnecessary, while keeping cookie and callback changes narrow.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: cookie call sites are patched and config normalization is only partially addressed, but the trajectory includes tests or analysis showing URL-like config values flow safely to all relevant session consumers.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory has correct-looking cookie and callback edits but config-level normalization is absent or merely discussed, with no focused tests proving the configured URL-like domain is handled at load/validation time.
scale.4: Clear flaw: implementation is limited to OIDC-local cookie helper usage and callback trimming, with no config validation/loading change despite the task framing the bad value as `authentication.session.domain` input.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory both misses config-level normalization and introduces broad unrelated OIDC server API/response rewrites or fragile parsing behavior, making the visible fix likely to regress existing flow even if cookie Domain strings look sanitized.

experiences.title: Defensive Optional-Kwarg Removal in Deconstruction Normalizers
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django migration/autodetector task traces a crash to code that removes an expected deconstructed relation kwarg, and the reported valid custom field may omit that kwarg.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django codebase when the task and trajectory make the failure boundary explicit: migration autodetection or similar model-state comparison deconstructs fields, then normalizes relation metadata for rename/comparison purposes, but crashes because a custom relational field hardcodes its target and omits the serialized target kwarg. This guidance is most useful once the trajectory has inspected the crashing normalization code, reproduced the missing-key scenario, or proposed a source edit. It can still guide early-stage rubrics if the task itself provides the traceback and minimal suggested fix. Do not apply to unrelated migration execution failures, database backend issues, general test-runner setup problems, or cases where the desired behavior is to require custom fields to serialize the kwarg. Also avoid making checked-in test integration the primary correctness criterion unless the task explicitly requires a regression test or the source behavior remains ambiguous.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged the semantic contract: relation targets should still be ignored when present for rename/model comparison, but the normalizer must not assume every relational field deconstruction includes the target kwarg. That aligns with visible evidence such as the traceback into relation-agnostic field comparison, the user’s custom ForeignKey-style field deleting the target from deconstruct() kwargs, and an agent edit that changes unconditional key deletion into a tolerant optional removal or equivalent guard. Less useful rubrics over-focused on adding a project-native regression test; such a test is valuable engineering hygiene, but in this narrow task the decisive evidence is the source behavior, and a correct minimal patch can exist without a checked-in test. A better rubric should prioritize: identifying the exact unsafe assumption, applying the fix in the normalization/comparison path rather than changing the custom field or broad migration logic, preserving existing behavior for ordinary relational fields that do include the target, and validating with the supplied reproduction plus, when available, normal relation/autodetector tests. Avoid broad criteria like “handle custom fields” without naming the missing optional relation kwarg, and avoid rewarding changes that swallow arbitrary errors, stop ignoring relation targets, or alter field deconstruction semantics globally.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should make the deconstructed relation-target normalization defensive: when a relational field has runtime relation metadata but its deconstruct() kwargs omit the serialized target, migration autodetection/model-state comparison should not raise a missing-key error; when the target is present, it should still be removed/ignored so existing rename-detection semantics are preserved. Judge using visible evidence from the task and trajectory, including inspected traceback code, proposed source edits, reproduction results, and validation against normal relational fields.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Tolerant Relation Target Normalization

metadata.bug_signature: custom relational field hardcodes its target and omits the target kwarg from deconstruct() output; comparison code unconditionally removes that kwarg
metadata.desired_behavior: optional removal of the relation-target kwarg during relation-agnostic comparison, without changing normal field deconstruction or disabling target-agnostic rename detection
high_priority_evidence: agent locates the deconstruction-normalization path reached by the traceback
agent recognizes the target kwarg may be legitimately absent
source change uses an optional removal or presence check in that path
normal relational fields with the target kwarg continue to be normalized the same way
provided reproduction no longer raises the missing-key error
low_priority_or_nondecisive_evidence: temporary ad hoc scripts without source behavior changes
checked-in regression test presence when the source fix is already clear
avoid_rewarding: changing the custom field contract to force serialization of the target
removing relation-target normalization entirely
catching broad exceptions around autodetection
modifying unrelated migration execution or database setup code

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory understands or addresses the missing deconstructed relation-target kwarg; work is unrelated or limited to environment/test-runner setup.
scale.2: Some investigation of migrations or field deconstruction is visible, but the proposed direction is vague, targets the wrong layer, or risks changing custom field/global deconstruction behavior rather than the relation-agnostic comparison path.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies the unsafe assumption and may reproduce the missing-key failure, but has not yet shown a clear source change that both tolerates absence and preserves target removal when present.
scale.4: The trajectory applies a plausible defensive removal/presence-check fix in the correct normalization path and shows the supplied missing-key scenario no longer crashes, with limited evidence about normal relational-field behavior.
scale.5: The trajectory applies a minimal correct defensive normalization fix, explicitly preserves ordinary relation target ignoring, validates the supplied custom-field reproduction, and checks normal relational/autodetector behavior through focused scripts or project tests.

experiences.title: Server-Side Authorized Namespace Discovery
experiences.description: Use when a React/RTK UI becomes unusable because the namespace-list API returns 403 for users lacking access to a default namespace, and the expected behavior requires discovering, displaying, and redirecting to only authorized namespaces.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go backend plus React/TypeScript frontend system where namespace selection is bootstrapped by a list-namespaces API call, authorization is enforced before handlers run, and the user can have access to non-default namespaces while being denied access to the default namespace. This guidance is most useful once the trajectory has found the failing namespace-list request, default-namespace fallback assumptions, UI layout/dropdown initialization, or backend authorization mapping for list endpoints. It is less applicable if the backend already returns a filtered authorized namespace list and the remaining defect is purely frontend route selection, or during very early repository exploration before the namespace-list/authz relationship is visible.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster focused on the semantic contract rather than on a narrow UI symptom: a valid fix must let authenticated users discover the namespaces they are allowed to view without requiring access to the default namespace, must filter the namespace list to authorized namespaces, and must let initial routing/dropdown selection choose an authorized namespace. This is discriminative because patches that only render through a 403, show an error notification, fabricate a placeholder namespace, return an empty list, redirect to login, or globally swallow 403 responses do not provide any trustworthy source of authorized namespaces and often preserve the unusable dropdown/navigation problem. A better rubric should prioritize visible evidence that the agent is addressing the authorization/listing contract at the source: investigating or changing backend authorization for namespace-list requests, adding a way for policy/authz evaluation to compute viewable namespaces, filtering the server response before it reaches the UI, and then using that filtered result for dropdown population and initial redirect. Avoid the tempting criterion that merely rewards `isError` handling in the layout, changes to `selectCurrentNamespace`, or base-query hacks; those are at best ancillary unless paired with a secure authorized discovery mechanism. When judging a trajectory, give strongest credit to evidence that the agent has moved beyond UI error masking into backend/API semantics and has preserved strict authorization by returning only permitted namespaces.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Authorized Namespace Discovery Contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should identify and implement, or clearly progress toward implementing, a secure namespace discovery flow in which the namespace-list operation succeeds for users who lack default-namespace access but have access to other namespaces, returns only namespaces authorized by policy, and enables the UI to populate the namespace dropdown and redirect or initialize to an authorized namespace without masking real authorization failures.

required_visible_evidence: Recognition that a 403 from the namespace-list API cannot be solved solely by UI rendering or generic error handling
Investigation of backend/API authorization semantics for namespace-list requests or equivalent server-side access-control path
A mechanism to derive or evaluate the authenticated user's viewable namespaces under policy
Filtering of namespace-list results to only authorized namespaces before the UI consumes them
Frontend routing/dropdown behavior that consumes the authorized list rather than fabricating placeholders or swallowing failures
common_insufficient_evidence: Only adding layout isError handling or an error toast
Returning an empty namespace list on 403
Using the current URL/local storage namespace as proof of authorization
Globally suppressing 403 responses in a shared base query
Redirecting to login or showing access denied when the user may have access to another namespace
metadata.environment: Go backend authorization with React/TypeScript RTK Query namespace bootstrap

scale.1: The trajectory treats the issue as a generic frontend loading/error problem, or makes no meaningful connection between namespace listing, default access, and authorized namespace discovery.
scale.2: The trajectory notices the namespace-list 403 and default fallback symptoms but proposes or edits only UI error handling, placeholder selection, empty-list behavior, or broad 403 suppression without a trustworthy authorized namespace source.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies that namespace discovery must avoid default-namespace dependence and begins inspecting backend/API authorization or list semantics, but has not yet established a concrete secure mechanism for returning only authorized namespaces.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly targets backend/API authorization for namespace listing and designs or partially implements policy-based authorized namespace derivation plus filtered results, with frontend redirect/dropdown behavior considered as a consumer of that filtered list.
scale.5: The trajectory provides strong visible evidence of an end-to-end secure bootstrap: namespace-list authorization no longer requires default access for users with other namespace permissions, the server/API returns only policy-authorized namespaces, real unauthorized access remains denied, and the UI uses that filtered list to populate the dropdown and redirect or initialize to an authorized namespace.

experiences.title: Delegate Return Aggregation Contract
experiences.description: Use when a Django ORM task asks a wrapper/bulk API to return the same matched-row count semantics as an underlying `update()`-style delegate that it already calls repeatedly.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django codebase when the visible trajectory has identified a bulk/wrapper method that batches work and calls a lower-level method whose return value already represents the desired count. It is most useful once the agent has located the target method or is editing/reviewing its implementation. It is less useful for early repository exploration with no code evidence, for tasks about changing update SQL generation rather than return propagation, or for unrelated changes in neighboring bulk APIs unless the task explicitly covers them.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases checked the semantic contract, not merely whether the agent found the right file or ran tests: the wrapper must initialize a numeric accumulator, add each batched delegate call's returned row count, return the total after all batches, and return zero when there are no batches/objects. The criterion should also require preserving existing validation order, batching construction, transaction scope, and method metadata/attributes, because a patch can appear to implement counting while accidentally deleting a method attribute or changing unrelated neighboring behavior. A tempting but weaker criterion is to reward any manual script that prints a count, or any diff that mentions a counter, without checking the empty-input path and preservation of surrounding method structure. Prioritize visible evidence such as an early empty-input branch returning `0`, the original delegate call being replaced by `accumulator += delegate_update(...)`, the final return being placed after the transaction block at the same method indentation, and no removal of existing method attributes or unrelated API semantics.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement the bulk wrapper's return contract by summing the matched-row counts returned by each internal batched update call, returning that integer total after all batches, returning `0` when the object list is empty, and leaving the existing validation, batching, transaction handling, method metadata, and unrelated APIs unchanged.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Matched-Row Count Aggregation Without Structural Regression

required_visible_evidence: The target bulk method's empty-input branch returns a numeric zero rather than `None`.
A row-count accumulator is initialized before executing batch updates.
Each internal batched update call contributes its return value to the accumulator.
The accumulator is returned after the batch update loop, not inside the loop in a way that skips later batches.
Existing transaction boundaries, validations, batching expression construction, and method-level attributes remain intact.
The patch does not introduce unrelated behavioral changes in neighboring bulk methods.
metadata.common_false_positive: A patch that accumulates counts for non-empty batches but leaves empty input returning `None`, removes method metadata, misindents the return so later batches or attributes are skipped, or changes unrelated bulk API behavior.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the target bulk method will return matched-row counts; the trajectory is only exploring or changes unrelated code.
scale.2: Some intent to use the internal update return value is visible, but the implementation is incomplete, unverified, or misses major cases such as empty input or multiple batches.
scale.3: The trajectory is roughly comparable to the parent: it identifies the right delegate-return aggregation approach but still has uncertain placement, incomplete edge-case handling, or limited evidence that existing structure is preserved.
scale.4: Strong evidence of a correct localized implementation: counts are accumulated across batches and returned, with most existing behavior preserved; only minor validation/test/documentation uncertainty remains.
scale.5: Complete visible evidence of the intended contract: empty input returns `0`, every batch update return is summed, the total is returned at the correct method scope, transaction/validation/method metadata are preserved, and no unrelated behavioral changes are introduced.

experiences.title: Do not reward “already fixed” conclusions from non-representative reproductions
experiences.description: Retrieve when an agent says a reported bug appears fixed because the MVCE passes locally, but the trajectory shows dependency/version drift, temporary compatibility edits, checkout switching, or no task-specific patch/regression test.
experiences.context: This applies in Python scientific-library tasks where behavior can depend on library versions, especially pandas/numpy-backed dtype or index materialization behavior. The misleading case is an agent repeatedly running the MVCE successfully in a checkout/runtime that differs from the report, sometimes after unrelated environment workarounds, then focusing on git-history searches or declaring a pre-existing fix without modifying the relevant user-visible behavior or adding a regression test. A rubric about recognizing an already-fixed bug can still be appropriate when the agent has verified the exact target baseline and dependency range, identified a credible in-repo fix or existing regression coverage, and either adds the requested regression test or gives a well-supported no-op rationale. It should not apply merely because current local execution passes under newer/different dependencies or after unrelated compatibility edits.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics rewarded “Verification of Pre-Existing Fix,” “Historical Bug Verification,” or “Codebase History Investigation.” That criterion is tempting because the agent’s local MVCE output showed the expected result and git history hinted at prior index work. It is misleading when visible evidence shows the reproduction environment does not match the report, the agent installed unconstrained newer dependencies, made unrelated compatibility edits just to import the package, or stayed in investigation mode with no focused patch/test. In such situations, a passing MVCE is weak evidence: the actual defect may be in a version-sensitive adapter/materialization path that only appears under the reported dependency behavior, and the task still needs a targeted fix or regression coverage for the user-visible contract. A better rubric should penalize premature “already fixed” conclusions and prioritize evidence that the agent isolates the dtype-preservation path for stacked MultiIndex level coordinates, avoids committing unrelated environment hacks, tests the user-visible coordinate dtype after stack, and either adds a regression test or changes the adapter/index materialization logic so stored coordinate dtype metadata is honored when values are converted to arrays. Avoid generating a positive rubric that rewards repeated git-log searches or broad historical speculation as if it were task progress.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that prematurely conclude a reported version-sensitive dtype/index bug is already fixed based mainly on a passing local MVCE in a non-representative environment, without adding a targeted regression test or addressing the code path that materializes the user-visible stacked level coordinate dtype. This is especially applicable when the trajectory shows unconstrained dependency installation, mismatch with the report's library versions, temporary unrelated compatibility edits, checkout switching, or repeated git-history searches instead of a focused fix.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Premature already-fixed conclusion from mismatched environment

visible_evidence_to_check: The task report specifies particular dependency/version behavior or an old release, while the agent validates under different installed versions or a different checkout.
The agent's local MVCE passes but the trajectory records environment drift, import workarounds, or unrelated compatibility edits.
No task-specific source change or regression test is added for the reported user-visible behavior.
The agent relies on git-history searches or broad statements about an existing architecture rather than verifying the relevant adapter/index materialization path.
replacement_focus: User-visible coordinate dtype after stacking, not internal MultiIndex code dtype or unrelated import compatibility.
Evidence that original coordinate dtype metadata is honored when level coordinate values are converted/materialized.
A focused regression test matching the reported MVCE or a minimal code change in the relevant dtype-preservation path.
boundaries: Do not apply if the agent has matched the reported dependency/runtime conditions or otherwise demonstrated the issue is genuinely obsolete with existing regression coverage.
Do not penalize early exploratory reproduction by itself; the flaw is treating non-reproduction as sufficient final resolution.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the agent either works under representative conditions or, despite non-reproduction, still adds/targets an appropriate regression or fix and avoids unrelated changes.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the agent notes local non-reproduction in a possibly different environment but continues toward a focused test or relevant code path and does not present history as sufficient.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent relies significantly on local passing behavior or history-search results, but still identifies the correct user-visible dtype contract and possible implementation path.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the agent repeatedly treats local non-reproduction or broad historical clues as proof the bug is fixed, with no focused patch/test and with visible environment mismatch or workaround contamination.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory ends with no task-specific fix or regression, possibly only unrelated compatibility edits, while explicitly or implicitly concluding the issue is already fixed based on non-representative local runs and repeated history searches.

experiences.title: Do not over-credit superficial timeOffset propagation across the wrong surfaces
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for a Go media-streaming task that adds a start-offset parameter through HTTP handlers, core streaming/transcoding interfaces, cache jobs, mocks/tests, and FFmpeg command templates.
experiences.context: This warning applies when a trajectory is adding a new streaming offset parameter in a Go server with several stream-like paths: user playback endpoints, public/share token streams, download/archive flows, core media streamer interfaces, FFmpeg command construction, and mocks/tests. A propagation rubric is useful only if it distinguishes the real offset source from legacy/internal callers that should preserve full-file behavior with offset 0. It is misleading when it blindly requires every endpoint or token path to parse/pass a user-provided offset, mandates a particular FFmpeg -ss position despite template-placeholder semantics, or treats broad call-chain plumbing as sufficient while the trajectory shows wholesale rewrites, compile errors, missing default command-template updates, or unrelated archive/share/download regressions. Early exploration may not yet show all call sites, but once implementation begins, visible evidence such as grep results, diffs, build/test output, and whether original handler/archive behavior was preserved should drive the rubric.
experiences.experience: The flawed rubrics in this cluster rewarded broad criteria such as “timeOffset flows from endpoints through MediaStreamer to FFmpeg” or “FFmpeg uses -ss before -i.” That idea is partly valid, but too broad here: agents often appeared to propagate the parameter while also parsing it in public/share or download flows that should default to 0, rewriting archive/share logic, dropping headers or logging, inventing nonexistent fields/methods, and missing the configuration/templates that define the actual default transcoding commands. A better rubric should not ask for maximal endpoint coverage or a fixed -ss placement. It should focus on scoped compatibility: the playback endpoint that actually accepts the offset parses the documented parameter and defaults to 0; non-playback or token-based legacy callers pass 0 unless an explicit input source exists; the core stream job/cache key includes the offset only for transcoded output identity; FFmpeg command generation honors an offset placeholder and preserves existing commands when offset is 0; default transcoding template definitions and any advertised protocol capability are updated consistently; mocks/tests compile without unrelated rewrites. Avoid tempting criteria that reward touching public tokens, downloads, archives, raw-stream seeking, or mandatory input-seek placement unless the visible task/repository evidence explicitly requires those behaviors. Prioritize visible evidence from precise diffs, repository-wide call-site searches, successful build/tests, and absence of unrelated changes over the mere presence of a new parameter in many signatures.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that implement a streaming time-offset feature by superficially threading a new parameter through many layers while failing to preserve scoped API behavior and existing code contracts. This flaw is present when visible evidence shows any combination of: user offset parsing added to legacy/public-share/download/archive paths without a clear request source; internal callers not defaulting to 0; FFmpeg command handling that ignores template placeholders or leaves default transcoding templates unable to receive the offset; required feature/capability metadata not considered when the protocol has discoverable extensions; cache identity not accounting for offset when transcoded bytes differ; mocks/tests or call sites left with inconsistent signatures; or broad file rewrites causing compile errors, removed headers/logging, invented fields/methods, or unrelated archive/share behavior changes. Do not mark the flaw solely because early exploration has not yet edited all files; apply it when the trajectory has begun implementation and the visible plan or diffs indicate overbroad, incompatible, or incomplete offset plumbing.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Scoped Offset Compatibility Regression

metadata.task_type: Go media streaming/transcoding offset support
evidence_to_check: handler parameter parsing and defaulting
legacy/public/download/archive callers
core streamer and transcoder signatures
transcoding cache key identity
FFmpeg command placeholder or appended offset behavior
default command template/configuration source
protocol feature-discovery metadata if present
mocks/tests and build output
unrelated diffs or compile errors from wholesale rewrites
avoid_rewarding: parameter appearing in many signatures without scoped semantics
mandatory -ss-before-input placement when templates control placement
public/share token or download offset parsing without explicit source
passing builds in only a narrow package while visible diffs show unrelated regressions

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: implementation or plan is scoped, preserves legacy callers with offset 0, honors command templates/default behavior, updates relevant call sites/mocks/tests, and avoids unrelated rewrites.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: one questionable endpoint/defaulting choice or missing validation remains, but the trajectory mostly preserves existing behavior and is actively checking call sites/builds.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: offset is threaded through core pieces, but the trajectory is ambiguous or incomplete on endpoint scope, command templates, cache identity, or tests, with some signs of risky broad edits.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory adds offset handling to inappropriate surfaces or misses key template/configuration/protocol pieces while also showing compile errors, stale signatures, or unrelated behavior changes.
scale.5: Severe evidence: broad rewrites or sed/cat replacements corrupt existing streaming/archive/share/download logic, invent nonexistent APIs, leave build-breaking errors, and the offset propagation is mostly superficial or semantically mis-scoped.

experiences.title: CLI Flag Must Reach the Vulnerability-Enrichment Path
experiences.description: Use when a task adds a CLI flag intended to skip external vulnerability lookups or other expensive enrichment, and the trajectory has evidence that detection/scan and reporting/enrichment are separate phases.
experiences.context: Applies in Go CLI repositories where the requested feature is a flag such as `-wp-ignore-inactive`, model data already records component status, and the agent has traced that installed components are detected in one phase but external vulnerability API calls are made later in a reporting/enrichment path. Especially relevant when the trajectory shows existing per-target configuration for the behavior, a wrapper option object around the enrichment call, or an existing post-processing filter that would not reduce API calls. Do not apply this as the main criterion when the agent has not yet identified the enrichment call path, when the feature is purely output filtering, or when the expensive work truly occurs during initial detection rather than report/enrichment.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged whether the new flag was wired through the configuration path that actually controls WordPress vulnerability lookups, not merely whether a flag string was added somewhere. This was predictive because several trajectories added a scan-command flag, invented a separate global setting, bound to an invalid dummy server/map entry, or passed only an existing per-server setting while leaving the newly parsed CLI value unused. A better rubric should focus on end-to-end observability: the flag is registered on the command that triggers vulnerability enrichment, stored in a project-consistent configuration field, combined or propagated without conflicting with existing per-target configuration, and read at the point where plugin/theme API requests are selected. It should also require the skip decision to occur before external lookups for inactive plugins/themes, while preserving core and non-inactive packages. Avoid the tempting proxy of rewarding any `-wp-ignore-inactive` registration or any post-result filtering; those can compile or hide output while failing the efficiency goal. Prioritize visible evidence such as: the agent has identified which command owns report-time enrichment, has avoided address-taking through map entries or empty server keys, has not introduced an unused duplicate config field, has updated all enrichment call sites consistently, and has placed inactive checks before HTTP/API requests rather than after vulnerabilities are already fetched.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly move toward a project-consistent `-wp-ignore-inactive` wiring in which the parsed CLI value reaches the WordPress vulnerability-enrichment code that chooses plugin/theme API calls. Strong evidence includes registering the flag on the command path that performs report/enrichment, storing it in an appropriate global or per-target configuration field without duplicating/conflicting with existing WordPress ignore-inactive config, passing or reading that setting at the enrichment option/function boundary, and skipping packages whose status is inactive before external plugin/theme vulnerability requests are made. The implementation should preserve default behavior when the flag is absent, continue scanning WordPress core, and avoid invalid map-field bindings, dummy server entries, or post-fetch-only filtering as the sole behavior.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Enrichment-Path Flag Propagation

metadata.task_type: CLI feature flag for skipping inactive WordPress plugin/theme vulnerability lookups
key_evidence: flag is exposed on the command path responsible for vulnerability enrichment/reporting, not only unrelated detection flow
parsed flag value is stored in a configuration location actually read later
existing per-target WordPress ignore-inactive setting is reused or cleanly combined rather than shadowed
enrichment wrapper/call site/function receives the effective ignore-inactive value
inactive plugin/theme filtering happens before external vulnerability API requests
core and non-inactive packages remain included
common_failure_modes: adding a scan-only flag whose value is never read by report/enrichment
introducing a duplicate global config field that is not propagated
binding a flag to an unaddressable map entry or dummy empty server
only filtering reported results after API calls have already happened
changing function signatures without updating all call sites

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the flag value reaches WordPress vulnerability lookup selection; the trajectory only explores files or adds unrelated/broken pieces.
scale.2: Some flag or config work is visible, but it is on the wrong command path, stored in an unused duplicate field, or not connected to the enrichment call that performs API requests.
scale.3: The trajectory is roughly equivalent to the parent state: it has identified relevant config and enrichment code but has not yet shown reliable propagation of the parsed flag to the lookup decision.
scale.4: Strong evidence that the flag/config is propagated into the WordPress enrichment path and used to skip inactive plugin/theme lookups, with only minor uncertainty about command placement, config interaction, or validation.
scale.5: Complete, coherent evidence of end-to-end behavior: correct command exposure, valid config storage/combination with existing settings, updated enrichment boundary, pre-request filtering of inactive plugins/themes only, preserved defaults/core behavior, and no invalid or unused wiring.

experiences.title: Do not reduce required Subs grouping to precedence-only parentheses
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating SymPy LaTeX printer work for `Subs`/evaluation-bar notation where the requested output explicitly shows the substituted body enclosed as `\left(...\right)` before the substitution bar.
experiences.context: This applies in SymPy/Python printer tasks involving `LatexPrinter` output for `Subs(expr, variables, points)`, especially when the visible trajectory proposes or implements `parenthesize(expr, PRECEDENCE["Mul"], strict=True)` and frames the goal as only parenthesizing low-precedence inner expressions. The original precedence-aware idea is still appropriate for ordinary infix contexts or tasks that explicitly ask to avoid superfluous parentheses based on operator precedence. It is misleading here because the desired evaluation-bar notation structurally groups the body of the substitution; passing the motivating additive example is not enough evidence if the implementation leaves equal/higher-precedence bodies unwrapped or changes global precedence behavior.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics rewarded 'precedence-aware parenthesization' and even required avoiding parentheses for atoms, products, powers, functions, and fractions.
