That criterion can over-credit a trajectory that replaces direct body printing with a conditional precedence helper: it fixes `-x + y` in the shown product example, but treats the grouping as an outer multiplication-precedence problem rather than as part of the `Subs` LaTeX construct. A better rubric should focus on visible evidence that the `Subs` printer wraps the already-rendered body inside explicit LaTeX parentheses immediately before the substitution bar while preserving the existing variable/value substack formatting. Avoid the tempting criterion that high-precedence inner expressions should remain unparenthesized unless the task explicitly asks for minimal parentheses. Prefer evidence from the changed return format or exact regression expectations for the full `\left. \left(...\right) \right|_{\substack{ ... }}` shape, and be cautious about global `Subs` precedence edits or tests that only validate the additive motivating case.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Precedence-only Subs body grouping
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for this SymPy LaTeX `Subs` issue when they treat the required grouping as conditional precedence parenthesization of the inner expression, for example by relying only on a `parenthesize(..., PRECEDENCE["Mul"], strict=True)`-style helper or by explicitly preserving unwrapped products/atoms/powers as a desired property. The concerning evidence is stronger when the trajectory validates only the shown additive example or existing `Subs` tests while not showing that the evaluation-bar form itself encloses the rendered body in explicit parentheses. Do not apply this penalty merely because an early investigation mentions precedence helpers as a possibility before the agent has selected or implemented an approach.

metadata.environment: SymPy Python repository, LaTeX printer behavior for Subs/evaluation-bar notation
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: Passing the additive example or using a precedence helper as proof of the correct structural formatting
preferred_visible_evidence: The Subs-specific LaTeX output construction explicitly places \left( and \right) around the printed body before the substitution bar
The substitution variable/value substack formatting is preserved
No unjustified global precedence change is used to solve a local printer-formatting issue
Regression expectations check the full evaluation-bar string shape, not only that an Add in a product happens to be parenthesized

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory either remains in investigation without committing to precedence-only behavior, or it focuses on explicit structural wrapping of the Subs body while preserving the substitution bar formatting.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory discusses precedence helpers as one possible mechanism, but also recognizes the exact evaluation-bar grouping requirement and has not implemented or locked in conditional behavior.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory frames the problem mainly as low-precedence/additive parenthesization and lacks visible evidence that all Subs bodies will be structurally wrapped, but the final implementation direction is still not fully clear.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory implements or strongly plans a conditional precedence-helper replacement for the Subs body and validates the motivating additive output without demonstrating the required structural wrapper in the returned evaluation-bar form.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory both implements conditional precedence-only grouping and explicitly treats unwrapped products/atoms/powers or global Subs precedence changes as desirable, thereby cementing behavior that conflicts with the structural grouping required by the task.

experiences.title: Classify FormSet non-form ErrorLists at construction sites
experiences.description: Use this when a Django forms/formsets task asks for a CSS class on FormSet-level non-form errors analogous to Form non-field errors.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django repository when the task concerns `formset.non_form_errors()` rendering or custom `ErrorList` classification, and the visible trajectory has inspected or is editing `django/forms/formsets.py`, `django/forms/forms.py`, or `django/forms/utils.py`. It is most useful after the agent has found that `ErrorList` accepts an `error_class` argument and that Forms use `error_class='nonfield'` for non-field errors. It is less useful for generic documentation-only work, unrelated form rendering changes, or very early exploration before the agent has located how `_non_form_errors` is created. Do not apply it to tasks that require changing global `ErrorList` rendering or ordinary field/form non-field error behavior.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged whether the agent covered the actual semantic contract: FormSet-level non-form `ErrorList` instances must carry the additional `nonform` class everywhere they are created or replaced, while preserving the existing `self.error_class` hook and error contents. This aligned well because visible evidence showed two decisive construction paths in `BaseFormSet.full_clean()`: the initial `_non_form_errors = self.error_class(...)` list, which also receives appended management-form errors, and the `ValidationError` handler that replaces `_non_form_errors` from formset-wide validation such as `clean()`, min/max checks, or similar non-form errors. A better rubric should focus on that complete construction-path coverage and on preserving the analogy to Forms’ `nonfield` implementation. Avoid the tempting but overly narrow criterion “modify `non_form_errors()` only”; at early stages the agent may not yet know whether the correct hook is the accessor or the population sites, and an accessor-only patch may obscure whether the stored container, custom `ErrorList`, and replacement paths are handled cleanly. Also avoid rewarding global changes to `ErrorList`, template rendering hacks, or adding `nonform` to ordinary per-form field errors. Prioritize observable evidence such as grepping all `_non_form_errors` assignments, comparing with `forms.py` `nonfield` call sites, passing `error_class='nonform'` to the configured `self.error_class`, checking management-form and custom-clean/min-max paths, and verifying that ordinary field errors retain their existing classes.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that FormSet-level non-form errors are classified by passing `error_class='nonform'` to the configured `ErrorList` class at every relevant `_non_form_errors` construction or replacement point, mirroring the existing Form non-field error mechanism. Strong evidence includes identifying all `_non_form_errors` assignment sites, updating the initial empty/non-form list and the `ValidationError`-derived replacement list, recognizing that appended management-form errors inherit the initialized list’s class, preserving custom `error_class` subclasses and existing error contents, and not applying `nonform` to ordinary form field or form non-field errors.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete non-form ErrorList classification

key_evidence: uses Form `nonfield` handling as precedent
checks all `_non_form_errors` creation or assignment sites
passes `error_class='nonform'` through `self.error_class`
covers empty, appended management-form, and validation-raised non-form errors
preserves ordinary form field/non-field error behavior
avoid: accessor-only criteria when construction sites are visible

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent has identified the FormSet non-form `ErrorList` construction mechanism or the `nonfield` precedent.
scale.2: The agent recognizes the desired `nonform` class or inspects relevant files, but only proposes a vague rendering change, global `ErrorList` change, or a single unverified path.
scale.3: The agent mirrors the `nonfield` mechanism for one FormSet non-form path or has located multiple paths but has not clearly covered both initialized/appended and `ValidationError` replacement cases.
scale.4: The agent updates or plans to update the relevant FormSet non-form `ErrorList` construction paths with `error_class='nonform'` and avoids changing ordinary form errors, with minor gaps in validation, docs, or explicit custom `ErrorList` reasoning.
scale.5: The agent clearly identifies all relevant `_non_form_errors` construction/replacement sites, applies `error_class='nonform'` via `self.error_class`, explains coverage of empty, management-form, min/max/custom-clean validation paths, preserves custom `ErrorList` and existing error contents, and validates or plans targeted tests without unrelated rendering changes.

experiences.title: Do not equate UI gating with an independent device-level notification toggle
experiences.description: Retrieve when a React/TypeScript settings task asks for a missing independent current-device notification toggle, especially where existing account-level and session/desktop notification switches already exist.
experiences.context: Applies in Element/Matrix-style notification settings code where settings are split across account-level push rules, device/session-local settings, SettingsStore metadata, notification controllers, and UI components. The misleading pattern is generating a rubric that rewards only finding the Notifications UI, relabeling an existing desktop/session switch, or conditionally hiding body/audio options. That UI behavior is relevant, but it is not enough when the task says the device-level control is missing or independent and the existing visible controls are account/session-level. The original idea may still be appropriate for a purely presentational bug where a known master toggle already exists and only needs to reveal dependent options. It should not be the main criterion when the trajectory has not established a separate per-device state/persistence contract or compatibility behavior for the current device.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics focused on adding or recognizing a device-level toggle in the notification settings UI and gating related session options. This over-rewards patches that only rename the existing `notificationsEnabled` desktop/session switch or wrap body/audio switches in a conditional. In this task family, visible UI hierarchy is only one layer: a correct trajectory should also investigate whether the existing setting is truly an independent current-device master, whether a separate setting/account-data event is needed, how the current device advertises or initializes its notification state, and how legacy/session-local notification settings are migrated or interpreted. Avoid the tempting criterion: “dependent settings are hidden when the toggle is off” as the core success measure. A better rubric should prioritize visible evidence that the agent distinguishes account-level push rules, session-local notification options, and independent current-device notification state; wires the new toggle to the correct storage/persistence path; initializes or migrates per-device notification state on startup/login; and only then updates the UI to show/hide dependent options.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat the missing independent device-level notification toggle as a UI-only relabeling or conditional-rendering problem without establishing a separate current-device notification state and persistence/initialization contract. This flaw is present when the agent reuses an existing desktop/session notification setting as the supposed device master, changes labels, or hides body/audio options, but shows no investigation or implementation of how the current device's notification enabled/silenced state is stored, created, migrated from existing local settings, and kept distinct from account-level push rules and subordinate session options.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: UI-only device toggle conflation

failure_signals: Agent claims existing desktop/session notification setting is sufficient for the independent device toggle without validating independence
Implementation or plan only changes labels or conditional rendering in the notification settings component
No visible work on settings metadata, per-device persistence/account-data, startup initialization, or migration/backwards compatibility
No separation between account-level master push rule, device-level master toggle, and dependent body/audio session options
acceptable_boundaries: Early exploration may receive a low severity if the agent has not yet committed to a UI-only approach
UI gating is positive only when paired with evidence of correct independent device-state storage and initialization
For tasks explicitly limited to presentation of an already-correct master setting, this negative criterion should not apply

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory distinguishes account, device, and session notification layers and investigates or implements appropriate per-device persistence/initialization before UI changes.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory mentions UI gating or relabeling, but also shows active investigation into whether the existing setting is truly independent and how per-device state is persisted.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies the UI component and existing device/session setting but is ambiguous about whether a separate independent device state or initialization path is needed.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory settles on relabeling an existing session/desktop toggle and hiding dependent options as the main fix, with little or no persistence/model investigation.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory implements or repeatedly defends a UI-only fix, ignores failed or missing validation, or leaves the code broken while still focusing on the conditional visibility criterion.

experiences.title: Do not reduce zero-residue nthroot fixes to a prime-only early return
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a SymPy/modular-arithmetic trajectory for `nthroot_mod` or similar root-finding bugs where `a % modulus == 0`, especially if the visible API/docstring says the modulus is a positive integer while the implementation currently contains a prime-only guard.
experiences.context: This warning applies in Python/SymPy number-theory tasks where the reported zero-residue bug is visible in a public function that has both prime-specific helper algorithms and broader-looking public semantics. A rubric that only checks whether the agent adds `if a % p == 0: return 0/[0]` for prime `p` can be misleading when the trajectory has evidence that the public function is documented for positive integer moduli, the solvability predicate already handles composite or prime-power cases, or the implementation raises `NotImplementedError` for composites after partial validation. The simpler prime-only zero-root criterion may still be appropriate when the task statement, function documentation, and inspected implementation all clearly restrict the API to prime moduli, or when the cutoff is still early exploration and the rubric is explicitly framed as a provisional hypothesis rather than a sufficiency condition.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics focused on the mathematically true fact that, over a prime field, `x**n == 0` implies `x == 0`, and they rewarded a local early return avoiding discrete-log code. That criterion is useful but too narrow here: it can overvalue patches that merely bypass `_nthroot_mod1` for prime zero residues while leaving the broader public contract, composite-modulus path, or existing validation order unexamined. A better rubric should ask whether the trajectory reconciles the zero-residue fix with the documented modulus domain and existing helper behavior, and whether it avoids unrelated API changes such as ad hoc `n == 0` semantics or altered no-solution return conventions. Avoid the tempting criterion “prime zero residue returns `0`/`[0]`” as the main success proxy when visible evidence shows the function advertises or partially supports non-prime moduli. Prioritize evidence that the agent inspected the public docstring, the primality guard, solvability helpers, existing tests, and failure paths, then planned or implemented a fix that handles zero residues consistently across the supported modulus domain without disturbing unrelated cases.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for zero-residue modular root bugs that settle on a prime-only early return or helper-local patch without addressing visible evidence that the public API may support general positive integer moduli. This flaw is present when the agent has inspected, or reasonably should inspect, a docstring/API contract that does not restrict the modulus to primes, a solvability predicate or related helpers that handle composite/prime-power moduli, and an implementation guard that currently raises for composites, yet the proposed fix preserves that gap and treats prime zero-root behavior as sufficient. The flaw is stronger if the trajectory also makes unrelated behavioral changes instead of adding regression coverage for the documented zero-residue contract.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Narrow prime-only zero-residue fix despite broader modulus contract

metadata.applicable_environment: Python SymPy number-theory modular root functions such as nthroot_mod
key_visible_evidence: public function documentation describes a positive integer modulus rather than explicitly prime-only
implementation contains prime-specific algorithms plus a separate primality guard or composite rejection
solvability or square-root helpers show composite or prime-power handling
task asks for zero-residue root behavior rather than explicitly limiting the fix to prime fields
metadata.avoid_using_as_success_proxy: only checking that a % p == 0 returns 0 or [0] before a prime-field discrete-log algorithm

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory explicitly reconciles zero-residue handling with the documented modulus domain, inspects composite/prime-power behavior, and avoids unrelated API changes.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory focuses mostly on prime zero residues but mentions the public modulus contract or composite guard and leaves room to verify it before finalizing.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory implements or plans a prime zero-residue early return and preserves existing composite rejection without discussing whether that matches the public API.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory treats the prime-only early return as complete despite visible documentation/helper behavior suggesting broader modulus support, and does not add tests for non-prime zero-residue cases.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory confidently finalizes a narrow prime-only zero-residue patch, ignores the broader modulus contract and composite guard, and introduces unrelated special-case behavior or return-contract changes.

experiences.title: Concise Date Offset Completeness Depends on Boundary Labels
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a Matplotlib ConciseDateFormatter trajectory that is modifying level/offset logic for same-year, sub-year date ranges, especially where January may or may not appear among ticks.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Matplotlib codebase when the task concerns concise date tick labels and the visible trajectory has reached the formatter’s batch tick-formatting logic, offset-string decisions, or tests for month-spanning ranges. It is most relevant once the agent is proposing or validating a fix involving level selection, offset suppression, zero/boundary formats, or January/month-start behavior. It is less useful during initial repository search, for unrelated date locator bugs, or when the trajectory has only produced environment/import troubleshooting without inspecting how tick labels and offset text share date context. Do not apply it as a generic demand that every sub-year plot have a non-empty offset; the key boundary is whether the year is already made visible by a boundary tick label such as January.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often asked for the original reported plot to show the year in the offset and to preserve general concise formatting. That is directionally useful, but it can be too weak: a trajectory can make the reported case appear to contain a year while still missing the precise ConciseDateFormatter contract, or can accept misleading outputs caused by timezone/DST hour variation, manual scalar formatter calls, or testing against an installed package rather than the edited source. A better rubric should focus on the semantic completeness rule: when month labels vary within one year and no tick label will itself show the year, the formatter must put the common year in the offset; when a boundary tick such as January already causes the year to be shown in the tick labels, the formatter should not add redundant or stale offset text. The criterion should reward visible reasoning about the interaction between level selection, offset suppression, and boundary/zero formats, not merely a one-line broad condition change or an assertion that the offset is non-empty in the original reproduction. Prioritize evidence that the agent inspects tick component uniqueness, recognizes January/month value as the year-bearing boundary case, validates both no-January and January-present ranges, and avoids replacing meaningful month/day labels with hour labels due to lower-level timezone artifacts.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a precise ConciseDateFormatter fix or plan in which date context is complete but not redundant: for same-year ranges where the visible tick labels vary by month and do not include a year-bearing boundary tick, the common year is shown once in the offset; for ranges where a boundary tick label already displays the year, offset suppression/clearing behavior is preserved. The judgment should be based on visible reasoning, code changes, or tests that connect level selection, boundary/zero-format labels, and offset text, rather than on a single reproduction output or misleading scalar formatting calls.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Boundary-Aware Year Offset Contract

required_visible_evidence: Identifies that concise formatter completeness depends on whether the year appears in either tick labels or offset text
Distinguishes month-spanning same-year ranges without January from ranges containing January or year-changing ticks
Accounts for boundary/zero-format behavior where January can make the year visible in a tick label
Validates or proposes tests for both no-January and January-present cases
Avoids relying solely on manual scalar formatter calls, unrelated installed-package behavior, or DST-induced hour labels as proof of correctness
common_false_positives: Only checks that the original reproduction has some offset containing the year
Changes offset suppression broadly without considering whether a tick label already contains the year
Forces coarser month labeling in a way that may override legitimate day/hour/minute granularity
Treats timezone/DST lower-level variation as the main semantic fix instead of preserving the formatter’s context-sharing contract

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory understands the year must appear exactly somewhere across tick labels and offset, or it remains focused on unrelated setup/import issues.
scale.2: Recognizes the missing-year symptom or locates formatter offset logic, but only proposes a broad non-empty-offset fix or validates the original case without considering January/boundary-label behavior.
scale.3: Shows moderate understanding of month-level offset suppression and the need to preserve concise labels, but lacks clear evidence that January or other year-bearing boundary labels are handled separately.
scale.4: Clearly reasons that no-January same-year month ranges need the year in the offset while January-present ranges may already display the year in tick labels, and proposes corresponding validation.
scale.5: Provides strong, boundary-aware evidence through implementation reasoning and/or tests covering no-January, January-present, year-changing, and finer-granularity cases, while explicitly avoiding misleading scalar-call or timezone-artifact validation.

experiences.title: Scoped Permission-Gated Calendar Settings Controls
experiences.description: Use when a React/TypeScript calendar settings task is about enforcing canEdit/canShare-style user permissions across UI controls while preserving read-only visibility and access-reduction actions.
experiences.context: Applies in a Proton-style monorepo or similar React settings UI where the task explicitly says restricted calendar users must not edit event defaults, member permissions, or create new shares, but should still see existing settings and retain member removal/revocation ability. This criterion is most useful once the trajectory has found or started editing the shared calendar settings components, permission helpers, parent settings page, member rows, event default controls, and public/private sharing sections. It can also be used to identify a stalled trajectory that is repeatedly searching without reaching these components. Do not apply it broadly to unrelated calendar event editing, backend authorization, invitation acceptance flows, or tasks where deletion/removal is meant to be blocked. Be cautious with early reconnaissance: lack of implementation is only decisive if the trajectory has spent substantial steps without locating the shared settings implementation or is making edits in the wrong layer.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster focused on the behavioral contract rather than just whether some permission flag was introduced: permission-sensitive controls must be disabled everywhere they can escalate access or mutate settings, while current values remain visible and removal actions remain available. This aligns well when visible trajectory evidence shows whether the agent has found the parent calendar settings component, derived permission booleans from the calendar permission model, and propagated them into event-default controls, member permission rows, private sharing buttons, and public link creation. A better rubric should require scoped completeness: edit/default controls use the edit permission; sharing/member-management controls use the share/member-management permission; member deletion or invitation revocation is not disabled merely because sharing is restricted. It should also check that the implementation remains type-safe after prop plumbing, because broad rewrites and unresolved TypeScript errors can make an otherwise plausible permission plan unusable. Avoid tempting but wrong criteria such as “disable all sharing-related actions,” which may incorrectly block access reduction, or “modify the share modal only,” which misses the settings page controls called out by the task. Also avoid over-specifying controls not required by the visible task, such as forcing deletion of public links to be disabled when the requirement emphasizes preserving removal/reduction. Prioritize observable evidence: located shared settings components rather than only app sidebar wrappers; permission booleans are computed from existing calendar permission data; props/interfaces/call sites are consistently updated; disabled attributes are applied to selectors/buttons that create shares or change permissions/defaults; member removal/revoke buttons remain enabled; and validation output does not show unresolved compile errors from the changes.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Scoped permission gating across calendar settings UI
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly progress toward a type-safe, scoped permission-gating solution for calendar settings: derive edit/share capability from the existing calendar permission model in the settings parent, propagate those capabilities through the relevant settings sections, disable controls that edit calendar metadata/default event settings/notifications, change member permissions, or create new private/public shares when the user lacks the corresponding capability, while preserving read-only display of current settings and leaving member/invitation removal or revocation actions available for access reduction. The evidence should show consistent prop/interface updates at call sites and no unresolved TypeScript or JSX errors caused by the permission plumbing.

metadata.environment: React TypeScript monorepo with shared calendar settings components and permission bit helpers
task_signals: calendar settings access restrictions
canEdit or canShare false
permission dropdowns, event defaults, notification settings, share buttons
read-only access must remain
member removal remains enabled
positive_evidence: permission booleans derived from existing calendar permission data in a parent settings context
edit permission applied to calendar metadata/header and event default or notification controls
share/member-management permission applied to member permission selectors and new-share/create-link controls
existing settings and member lists remain rendered when controls are disabled
member deletion or invitation revocation is not disabled solely due to lack of share/edit permission
prop plumbing is complete across interfaces, call sites, tests, and validation
negative_evidence: only app-level sidebar or modal entry points are changed while shared settings controls remain unrestricted
all sharing actions are disabled indiscriminately, including access-reduction removal
new permission helpers use unsupported or semantically wrong permission bits without justification
sections are hidden instead of shown read-only
large rewrites introduce unresolved TypeScript, unused imports, bad hook usage, or broken modal state handling

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward scoped permission gating: the trajectory is stuck searching, edits unrelated components, or leaves the key settings controls unrestricted.
scale.2: Weak progress: identifies some relevant controls or adds a permission flag in one area, but misses major settings sections, derives permissions unreliably, or does not preserve read-only/removal behavior.
scale.3: Moderate progress: gates several important controls and shows the right high-level design, but has incomplete propagation, ambiguous edit/share separation, missing call-site updates, or unresolved validation issues.
scale.4: Strong progress: consistently derives and propagates edit/share permissions to nearly all relevant controls, preserves member removal and read-only display, with only minor omissions or validation concerns.
scale.5: Complete progress: all permission-sensitive calendar settings controls are scoped to the correct capability, access-reduction actions remain enabled, current settings remain visible, and the resulting React/TypeScript implementation is coherent and validation-clean.

experiences.title: CASE WHEN full-result predicate must render as explicit truth
experiences.description: Use when a Django ORM trajectory involves `Case`/`When` conditions built from `Q` objects or empty `__in` lookups where a predicate may simplify to match-all/empty SQL in a context that still requires a boolean expression.
experiences.context: Applies in Django ORM SQL-generation tasks where the reported or observed failure is malformed searched `CASE` SQL such as an empty `WHEN ... THEN` condition, especially after investigation shows that a non-empty predicate like negated empty `IN` resolves to a where-clause node whose SQL fragment is `''` because it represents a full result set. It is strongest once the trajectory has reproduced the invalid `CASE WHEN  THEN` SQL or traced `Q(pk__in=[])` versus its negation through expression resolution. It may be premature for unrelated `Q` bugs, normal top-level filtering behavior, backend quoting issues, or cases where the condition raises/skips as empty-result rather than compiling to a full-result empty fragment.
experiences.experience: The useful criterion in these cases was not merely “avoid SQL syntax errors”; it captured the semantic boundary that empty SQL can be a valid match-all sentinel in a WHERE context but is invalid inside a `CASE WHEN` predicate slot. A good rubric should reward trajectories that identify the distinction between non-negated empty `IN` as an empty-result condition and negated empty `IN` as an always-true/full-result condition, then require the conditional-expression renderer to emit an explicit truth predicate or equivalent while preserving existing empty-result and ordinary predicate behavior. Visible evidence to prioritize includes: reproduction of `CASE WHEN  THEN`, resolving raw `Q` conditions before compilation, observing the resolved condition compile to `''` with no params for the always-true case, observing the non-negated case raise or skip as false, and choosing a localized expression-context fix rather than altering global where-clause simplification. Avoid a tempting but weaker criterion that only asks for “valid SQL” or accepts shortcuts that return the `then` result directly from a `When`/`Case`; those can satisfy the single example while risking incorrect composition with multiple branches, nested expressions, defaults, ordering, or backend boolean handling.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that a condition which simplifies to a full-result predicate, such as the negation of an empty `IN` lookup, cannot be left as an empty SQL fragment inside a searched `CASE WHEN` clause. It should favor a localized fix in conditional-expression SQL rendering that converts the empty full-result condition into an explicit always-true SQL predicate or backend-compiled boolean value, while preserving the existing behavior that the non-negated empty `IN` condition is treated as empty-result and ordinary `Q`/lookup conditions compile normally.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Explicit truth rendering for full-result CASE conditions

prioritize_visible_evidence: reported or reproduced SQL contains an empty condition in a searched CASE WHEN clause
trajectory traces a negated empty IN Q object through resolution into a where-like condition
compiled full-result condition is observed as an empty SQL string with no parameters
non-negated empty IN remains an empty-result/false condition rather than becoming true
proposed change is localized to expression-context predicate rendering and does not globally change where-clause match-all semantics
avoid_overrewarding: generic claims that the SQL should be valid without explaining the full-result sentinel
changing Q negation or empty-IN lookup behavior globally
short-circuiting a When or Case to return only the result expression instead of rendering a valid WHEN predicate
judging unresolved raw Q compilation failures as the production bug

scale.1: The trajectory does not recognize the empty full-result condition or focuses on unrelated causes such as ordering, quoting, backend syntax, or raw unresolved Q compilation.
scale.2: The trajectory notices the malformed CASE WHEN SQL but only proposes a generic syntax fix, without distinguishing always-true empty SQL from empty-result behavior.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies that the conditional expression receives an empty condition for the negated empty IN case, but has not clearly preserved non-negated empty-result semantics or localized the fix.
scale.4: The trajectory shows strong evidence that the negated empty IN compiles to an empty match-all fragment and proposes rendering an explicit true predicate in the CASE WHEN context while keeping ordinary and false conditions intact.
scale.5: The trajectory fully establishes the context-sensitive sentinel semantics, implements or plans a localized expression-rendering fix using backend-appropriate truth SQL, and validates the reported case plus non-negated empty IN and normal predicate behavior.

experiences.title: Django filterable is an expression protocol, not an RHS value attribute
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django ORM trajectory investigates `Query.check_filterable()` rejecting a filter RHS because an ordinary model/value has a user-defined `filterable=False` attribute, and the patch must preserve rejection of non-filterable ORM expressions.
experiences.context: Applies in Django ORM query-construction tasks where `QuerySet.filter()` reaches `django/db/models/sql/query.py::Query.check_filterable()` on a RHS value, and visible evidence shows a collision between Django's internal expression `filterable` flag and a normal model field/attribute named `filterable`. It is most useful once the trajectory has inspected `build_filter()`, `resolve_lookup_value()`, expression classes such as `BaseExpression`/`Window`, or reproduced that a ForeignKey model instance with `filterable=False` is rejected. It is less useful for unrelated queryset errors, for tasks about documenting reserved model field names, or before there is evidence that the failing object is an ordinary RHS value rather than an ORM expression. At final-review stage, the criterion should distinguish a robust expression-protocol guard from narrower fixes that merely skip model instances.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases focused on the semantic boundary: `filterable=False` is meaningful for ORM expressions participating in SQL WHERE construction, not for arbitrary Python/model RHS values. This aligned well because the observable trajectory often contained decisive evidence: `build_filter()` calls `check_filterable(value)` on the raw RHS; model instances expose user fields as normal attributes; expression objects expose `resolve_expression()`/source-expression APIs; and `Window` is a genuine non-filterable expression that must still raise `NotSupportedError`. A better rubric should therefore reward trajectories that either implement or clearly aim for guarding the `filterable` check behind expression-like behavior, preferably the expression protocol such as `hasattr(obj, 'resolve_expression')`, while still recursing through source expressions and preserving `NotSupportedError` for nested non-filterable expressions. Do not over-focus on broad proxies such as 'adds lots of tests', 'skips objects with `_meta`', or 'uses `BaseExpression` only': those can fix the reported model-instance case but may miss expression-like objects outside that exact class hierarchy or fail to state the protocol boundary. Prioritize visible evidence of the agent understanding the namespace collision, validating both sides of the behavior with a `filterable=False` model-instance RHS and a true non-filterable expression, and modifying `check_filterable()` or its call site narrowly rather than removing the check entirely.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Expression-protocol-gated filterable check
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that Django's `filterable` restriction is applied only to ORM expression-like objects, not arbitrary RHS values or model instances with user-defined `filterable` attributes, while preserving recursive rejection of genuine non-filterable expressions in filter/WHERE clauses.

expected_visible_evidence: Identifies `Query.check_filterable()` and its RHS call from `build_filter()` as the failure point.
Recognizes that model instances can legally expose a normal field/attribute named `filterable` and should remain valid RHS values for relation lookups.
Recognizes that actual ORM expressions are identified by expression protocol behavior such as `resolve_expression()` and/or source-expression traversal.
Preserves `NotSupportedError` for real non-filterable expressions such as window expressions, including nested source expressions.
Avoids removing filterability validation entirely or treating every object with a `filterable` attribute as an expression.
metadata.preferred_fix_shape: Guard the `filterable` attribute check so it is honored only for expression-like objects, ideally objects with `resolve_expression`, while keeping source-expression recursion.
metadata.common_insufficient_fix: Only bypassing `_meta`/model instances or checking only `BaseExpression` may solve the reported example but is a narrower proxy than the expression-protocol boundary.

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory distinguishes user RHS attributes from ORM expression flags; it may remove the check, document the field name as reserved, or keep blindly reading `filterable` from arbitrary values.
scale.2: Weak evidence of the collision, but the planned or applied fix is broad or incomplete, such as only avoiding the immediate model instance without preserving non-filterable expression behavior.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies `check_filterable()` and allows the reported model-instance RHS while making some effort to keep expression checks, but the discriminator is a narrow proxy or validation of nested/non-filterable expressions is unclear.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory clearly separates ordinary RHS values from expression-like objects, preserves `NotSupportedError` for real non-filterable expressions, and validates both the reported model-instance case and an expression negative control.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory implements or converges on an expression-protocol-gated `filterable` check, maintains recursive source-expression validation, adds/targets an in-suite regression for a `filterable=False` RHS model instance, and confirms genuine non-filterable expressions still fail.

experiences.title: Do not reward KeyStore method-name coverage without semantic contract evidence
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for a Go/Teleport-style task that asks for a new cryptographic KeyStore abstraction and raw PEM backend, especially when the visible trajectory is either still exploring CertAuthority key types or has just added an interface with similarly named methods.
experiences.context: This warning applies in a Go codebase where certificate authority key material is represented by existing SSH/TLS/JWT keypair structs and active key sets, and the requested work is to add a server-side key backend abstraction for raw PEM keys. The misleading pattern is a rubric that says the KeyStore interface is complete if it contains operations for RSA generation, signer retrieval, and TLS/SSH/JWT CertAuthority selection; such a rubric can overvalue code that merely has those words in method names while using incompatible signatures, invented storage APIs, wrong signer types, wrong key formats, missing raw-key filtering, or failing tests. The same idea can still be useful after implementation is visible, but it must be phrased as semantic compatibility with existing keypair behavior, not as broad checklist coverage. If the trajectory is only repository exploration with no edits, a final-interface-completeness rubric is premature; focus instead on whether the agent has found the exact existing keypair structs, key generation helpers, and signer parsing behavior. Conversely, do not require auth-server wiring unless the task or visible plan explicitly expands beyond adding the abstraction and initial raw implementation.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics mostly generated broad criteria such as “KeyStore Interface Completeness” or “KeyStore Interface Design,” requiring methods for RSA, TLS, SSH, JWT, and CertAuthority selection. That criterion is only partially right: the task does require those capabilities. It becomes misleading when it treats superficial API coverage as correctness. In these trajectories, agents often invented extra factories, context parameters, memory backends, key IDs as strings, public-key verifiers, Close-only cleanup, TLS certificate creation, or direct storage/list APIs, while missing the key semantic contract: raw PEM keys should be used as key identifiers for the raw backend, signer retrieval should parse raw private key bytes, TLS selection should return the active raw TLS certificate together with a crypto.Signer and tolerate cert-only cases where appropriate, SSH selection should return an ssh.Signer wrapped with the existing signing algorithm behavior, JWT selection should return a crypto.Signer from the active raw JWT private key, and raw-vs-non-raw private key types should be respected. A better rubric should prioritize visible evidence that the implementation preserves existing Teleport key representations and parser/signing behavior, compiles, and does not broaden the task into unrelated storage systems or mandatory auth-server integration. Avoid tempting criteria like “defines all named operations, no more/no less” or “is wired into auth server initialization” unless the trajectory already shows a final-review implementation where those exact concerns are central and supported by the task. Replacement criteria should inspect concrete method signatures, return types, use of existing CertAuthority active key sets, raw key type filtering, parser helpers, SSH algorithm wrapping, TLS cert-plus-signer handling, no-op deletion semantics for raw keys, and validation/build evidence.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial KeyStore Contract Compatibility
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear to satisfy the KeyStore task by naming RSA/TLS/SSH/JWT methods but diverge from the existing raw PEM CertAuthority contract. This applies once the trajectory contains a proposed interface or raw backend implementation. Evidence of the flaw includes using incompatible signatures or types, inventing unrelated storage/listing/memory backends, returning parsed certificates or public verifiers instead of the requested signer/keypair behavior, failing to select from active CertAuthority SSH/TLS/JWT key sets, failing to filter raw private key types, omitting existing SSH signing-algorithm wrapping, parsing the wrong PEM fields, treating missing CA keys as successful nil returns where existing behavior expects errors, or leaving visible compile/test failures unresolved. Do not apply this as a failure to pure exploration-only trajectories; for those, judge whether the agent has discovered the relevant existing types and helper behavior instead.

metadata.environment: Go Teleport-style repository with api/types CertAuthority key sets and lib/auth/lib/services cryptographic helper code
metadata.stage_condition: Apply when a KeyStore interface or rawKeyStore implementation is visible; use exploration-focused criteria before edits exist
evidence_to_prioritize: method signatures and return types
raw PEM key identifier and signer parsing semantics
active SSH/TLS/JWT CertAuthority key selection
raw private key type filtering
SSH signer algorithm wrapping with existing helper behavior
TLS cert plus crypto.Signer behavior
JWT private key parsing to crypto.Signer
compile or test output when available
avoid_overweighting: mere presence of method names containing RSA, TLS, SSH, JWT, or CertAuthority
unrequested storage backends or CRUD/list APIs
mandatory auth-server wiring unless explicitly in scope
passing no-op test discovery as behavioral validation

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the visible implementation or plan preserves the existing raw PEM CertAuthority semantics, uses compatible signer/keypair return types, respects raw key types, and has no unresolved build/test evidence.
scale.2: Minor evidence of drift: mostly compatible contract, but with small naming, error-message, or helper-choice inconsistencies that do not obscure raw PEM signer/keypair behavior.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory covers the required operation names but has ambiguous or partially incompatible signatures, limited raw-type handling, incomplete TLS/SSH/JWT selection semantics, or weak validation.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the implementation relies on method-name coverage while using wrong return types, invented storage or config concepts, missing raw-key filtering, missing SSH algorithm wrapping, or unresolved compile/test failures.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the proposed KeyStore/raw backend is architecturally incompatible with existing CertAuthority raw PEM behavior, largely implements unrelated storage/key generation APIs, cannot compile or pass its own visible tests, or omits core signer selection semantics despite having superficially named methods.

experiences.title: End-to-End BookWorm Staging Contract Over Parser-Only Google Books Work
experiences.description: Use when an Open Library task adds a new metadata provider for fallback/staging imports, especially when the trajectory has found vendor parsing code plus import queue/staged-source and promise/API import paths.
experiences.context: Applies in the Open Library codebase when the requested feature is not merely a standalone Google Books lookup but adding a source that BookWorm can stage and later use to supplement incomplete promise or /api/import records. It is most useful once the trajectory has enough evidence about the existing import queue, staged source prefixes, affiliate/BookWorm lookup flow, promise batch imports, or import API supplementation. It is premature during very early repository search if the agent has not yet located the staging path. It is also too narrow for tasks that only ask for a generic external API client, a UI metadata display, or a one-off edition creation endpoint.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics that demanded complete Google Books integration were useful because the common failure mode was superficial provider code: adding a Google Books fetch/parser and sometimes adding the source name, but not preserving the existing BookWorm staging contract that makes metadata available to promise items and /api/import. A parser-focused rubric can be misleading: a trajectory may map volumeInfo fields reasonably well yet still fail the task if metadata is never staged, source-prefixed, discovered by staged-source queries, or merged into incomplete import records. A better rubric should focus on end-to-end source behavior: ISBN-13 should be used as the preferred lookup identifier for incomplete records, the new source prefix should be recognized by staged import lookup, Google Books results should be staged through the same import-item/affiliate-server path as existing metadata rather than only returned from a vendor helper, and the import API should be able to supplement missing title/authors/publish_date-style fields from the staged record. It should still check parsing edge cases, but as part of the staging contract rather than as the sole criterion. Avoid tempting proxies such as adding an API key config, wiring Google Books into a price endpoint, directly creating editions from model methods, modifying unrelated sponsorship/model code, or accepting the first Google Books result when multiple matches are reported. Prioritize visible evidence that the trajectory has identified and modified the actual staging pipeline, source identifiers, promise import fallback behavior, and mock-based tests for zero/multiple/missing-field responses.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate an end-to-end Google Books BookWorm staging integration, not just a standalone API parser. Strong evidence includes recognizing the existing staged import source filtering, adding the new source prefix consistently, making incomplete promise/import records request staging using ISBN-13-first identifiers through the existing BookWorm/affiliate staging path, ensuring staged Google Books records can later supplement missing import fields, and adding mock-based tests for single-match parsing plus no-result behavior for zero, multiple, or unusable responses.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: BookWorm Staging Pipeline Integration

required_visible_evidence: New metadata source is registered wherever staged import queries restrict accepted source prefixes.
Promise or import fallback logic uses ISBN-13 when available and does not rely solely on Amazon ISBN-10/ASIN paths.
Google Books results are represented with a consistent source record/prefix so import-item lookup and supplementation can find them.
Implementation connects to the existing staging/import-item flow rather than only returning metadata to a direct API endpoint or model helper.
Tests or planned tests use mocked Google Books responses and cover field mapping, missing optional fields, no ISBN-13/unusable records, zero matches, and multiple matches.
anti_patterns: Only adding a Google Books parser/client in the vendor module.
Adding the source to a constant but never staging or consuming records from that source.
Using Google Books only in unrelated price, sponsorship, or direct edition-creation flows.
Requiring a new API key when the discovered configuration and task do not establish that requirement.
Taking the first result on ambiguous Google Books responses.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of Google Books integration with the staged import pipeline; work is only exploratory or unrelated.
scale.2: Adds or plans a standalone Google Books lookup/parser, but little or no evidence that staged imports, source prefixes, or promise/API fallback paths will use it.
scale.3: Roughly preserves parent-level behavior: identifies some relevant staging pieces such as source registration or promise fallback, but integration is incomplete or unvalidated.
scale.4: Strong evidence of a coherent staged-source integration, including source-prefix registration, ISBN-13 fallback staging, and normalized metadata that import supplementation can consume, with only minor gaps.
scale.5: Complete visible contract: Google Books is wired through the existing BookWorm/affiliate/import-item staging path, source records and staged-source queries are consistent, incomplete promise/API imports can be supplemented from staged records, ambiguous/no-match responses return no result, and mock-based tests cover required mappings and edge cases.

experiences.title: Canonical Config Rename Compatibility
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task requires introducing a new user-facing configuration option while keeping an old option name working through the project’s existing rename/migration mechanism.
experiences.context: Applies in qutebrowser/Python-style projects with a data-driven config schema and backend code that derives config lookup keys from per-setting option suffixes. The task should explicitly require both a new public option name and backward compatibility for an old option name, especially when a backend API key also changed by dependency version. This guidance is most useful after the trajectory has located the config schema/rename mechanism and the backend option lookup path, or has started editing them. It is premature during initial file discovery, and it is less relevant when the task is backend-only, when old and new options are intentionally meant to remain separate public settings, or when no migration/renamed-option support exists in the codebase.
experiences.experience: Rubrics in this pattern checked whether the new foreground threshold option was exposed while old text-threshold configs still worked. That criterion was useful because the trajectory often showed decisive evidence: the agent either found the existing `renamed:` migration convention and aligned backend lookups to the new option, or instead added duplicate option blocks, left the old full option active, used an ad-hoc runtime fallback, or changed only the backend key. However, a broad rubric saying merely “preserve legacy compatibility” is too weak: it can give partial credit to patches that add both names or mutate runtime config but do not use the project’s canonical migration path and still leave lookup/version behavior inconsistent. A better rubric should require the supported rename/alias mechanism, correct new-option metadata, and alignment between the backend `_Setting.option`/config lookup and the new canonical option. Avoid the tempting proxy of rewarding a new config block plus a comment saying the old option is deprecated. Prioritize visible evidence that the old key is represented as a rename to the new key, the new key carries the original integer bounds/default/restart/backend semantics, backend settings read the canonical new suffix for all relevant versions, and the dependency-version-specific backend key selection remains separate from the user-facing rename.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Canonical Config Rename and Backend Lookup Alignment
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show that the new user-facing configuration option is added as the canonical option with the same type, range, default, restart, and backend metadata as the old option, while the old option name is handled through the repository’s supported rename/migration mechanism rather than by leaving two independent public options or adding an ad-hoc runtime fallback. The backend mapping should look up the new canonical option suffix and only vary the backend API key by dependency version, so old configurations resolve to the same effective value through the config system.

required_visible_evidence: The config schema contains the new canonical option with integer threshold metadata matching the old option.
The old option name is represented as a rename/migration/alias using the project’s established config mechanism.
The backend setting lookup uses the new canonical option suffix rather than continuing to depend on the old suffix.
The dependency-version branch changes only the backend key emitted for the same logical foreground threshold option.
Documentation or generated setting references no longer present the old option as an independent current setting.
common_flaws_to_penalize: Adding both old and new option blocks as separate active settings.
Adding a deprecation note without a real rename/migration.
Using runtime config mutation or one-off fallback code instead of the existing config rename mechanism.
Changing only the backend key while the public option remains the old name.
Making the new option work only for the newest dependency version while older supported versions still look up the old option directly.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of a canonical new option or backward-compatible rename; the trajectory is still searching or only changes unrelated backend strings.
scale.2: Weak evidence: a new option or old-option compatibility is mentioned, but implementation details are missing or rely on comments/deprecation without visible migration support.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: both the new option and some compatibility handling are present, but the old option remains a duplicate active setting, the backend lookup is not clearly aligned to the new canonical name, or the fallback is ad-hoc.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the new option has correct metadata and the old name is mostly handled via the established rename mechanism, with backend lookup largely using the new option, though documentation/tests or one variant-specific detail may still be incomplete.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory cleanly makes the new option canonical, maps the old option through the project’s supported rename/migration path, aligns backend option lookup to the new name across versions, and keeps version-specific backend key selection separate and validated.

experiences.title: Deterministic Deduplication for Generated Location Lists
experiences.description: Use when a Python documentation/i18n/gettext-style builder is being patched to remove duplicate source-location entries from generated output.
experiences.context: Apply when the task reports repeated location/comment entries in generated catalog or build artifacts, and the trajectory has identified an aggregation path where repeated `(source, line)`-like pairs are stored or passed into a message/output object. This is most useful once the agent has started editing the relevant storage or iteration code, because the visible patch can reveal whether deduplication is deterministic and scoped to locations only. It is less useful during very early repository exploration, for unrelated duplicate-message bugs, or when the problem is about preserving duplicate semantic occurrences rather than suppressing redundant identical locations.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster did not merely ask whether duplicates were removed; they checked the important boundary that generated output must remain stable and must keep all distinct locations. A patch that uses an unordered set-to-list conversion is a tempting proxy because it eliminates repeated tuples in a toy check, but it can reorder location comments unpredictably and can create nondeterministic generated files. A better rubric should focus on observable evidence that the trajectory deduplicates identical location pairs at the point where output locations are constructed or stored, uses a deterministic method such as sorting or ordered first-seen filtering, leaves message text and unrelated metadata handling intact, and verifies the modified section is not corrupted by broad scripted edits. Avoid making the criterion only about running tests or only about matching the user's suggested `set()` approach; the discriminating evidence is the actual deduplication semantics and output-order stability visible in the edited code and validation.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement deterministic deduplication of generated message/source-location entries so each identical location appears once, all distinct locations remain present, generated output order is stable, and unrelated message fields or catalog metadata are not changed.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Stable Location Deduplication Semantics

prioritize_visible_evidence: deduplication targets identical source-location pairs rather than message text or unrelated metadata
implementation avoids unordered set-to-list output unless followed by deterministic ordering
distinct locations are retained
message identifiers and auxiliary metadata handling remain unchanged
the edited class/function region is syntactically intact after any scripted edits
avoid_overweighting: a toy assertion that only counts unique entries without checking order
blindly following the user's sample unordered set conversion
generic test-running effort when the visible code still has nondeterministic deduplication

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of location deduplication, or the trajectory is still only exploring files without a relevant implementation.
scale.2: Attempts to remove duplicates but does so with an unordered conversion, corrupts the edited region, or risks dropping distinct locations or unrelated metadata.
scale.3: Removes duplicate location pairs in roughly the right area but has incomplete evidence about deterministic output ordering or preservation of adjacent message metadata.
scale.4: Clearly deduplicates identical locations with stable ordering or sorting, preserves distinct locations and unrelated fields, and the edited code appears intact.
scale.5: Implements a narrow deterministic deduplication at the construction/output boundary, explicitly preserves all distinct locations and unrelated metadata, and validates with a targeted check or relevant tests that generated location lists contain no repeats and remain stable.

experiences.title: Non-native logical XOR must be judged by n-ary parity semantics
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django/ORM task concerns chained logical XOR query predicates on databases without native XOR support, especially when the trajectory is inspecting or modifying fallback SQL generation.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python Django ORM environment where query predicate XOR is represented correctly at the object/tree level but compiled through a backend-dependent SQL fallback when the database lacks native logical XOR. The useful stage is after the task statement or trajectory exposes the semantic distinction between “exactly one operand is true” and “an odd number of operands are true,” or after the agent has found the fallback path that counts truthy child predicates. The criterion is less useful for unrelated bitwise XOR expression operators, native-XOR-only behavior, pure Q-object construction/deconstruction work, or trajectories that have not yet identified whether the bug is in SQL rendering versus predicate construction. It should not be reduced to checking for a particular import or test command; the decisive boundary is the fallback’s logical semantics for three or more operands.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the invariant that non-native logical XOR fallback SQL must implement odd parity across all child predicates, not exactly-one semantics. This aligned well because the visible trajectory repeatedly showed the key evidence: the agent found the backend feature gate for non-native XOR, observed a fallback that turns boolean children into numeric indicators and compares their sum directly to 1, reproduced the bad 1,0,0,0,0 behavior for repeated true predicates, and then moved toward a modulo-2 parity check that produces 1,0,1,0,1. A better rubric should evaluate whether the trajectory is fixing the backend fallback path so n-ary XOR is true for any odd count of true operands while preserving ordinary one-/two-operand behavior and avoiding changes to native-XOR backends. It should prioritize visible evidence such as locating the SQL fallback branch, replacing or proposing replacement of the direct sum-equals-one check with an odd-count check, using backend-agnostic ORM expressions rather than raw backend-specific SQL, and validating with three-or-more operand query behavior. Avoid tempting but weak criteria: merely touching Q.__xor__ or tree combination code, testing only binary XOR, checking only that a Mod symbol appears, confusing logical XOR with bitwise XOR, or requiring an exact patch shape when several parity-equivalent implementations are acceptable.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Backend fallback implements n-ary XOR parity
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the non-native logical XOR SQL fallback is being evaluated and corrected so chained query predicates are true when an odd number of operands are true, rather than only when exactly one operand is true. Strong evidence includes identifying the fallback branch guarded by lack of native logical XOR support, recognizing the existing truth-count comparison as the exactly-one bug, implementing or clearly planning an odd-parity check such as count modulo 2 equals 1 using portable ORM expressions, preserving native-XOR and binary XOR behavior, and validating with three-or-more operand cases such as repeated true predicates that alternate true/false by arity.

metadata.task_family: Django ORM logical XOR fallback SQL
metadata.primary_semantic_boundary: odd parity for n-ary logical XOR versus exactly-one truth count
high_value_visible_evidence: fallback path for databases without native logical XOR is identified
truthy child predicates are counted via conditional expressions
direct count == 1 comparison is recognized as the bug for more than two operands
patch or plan uses an odd-count/parity condition, e.g. modulo 2 equals 1
manual or targeted tests cover three and five operands, not only two
common_false_proxies: modifying logical XOR object construction rather than SQL fallback
testing only two-operand XOR
checking for a Mod import without confirming it is applied to the truth count
confusing logical query XOR with bitwise expression XOR
changing native-XOR backend behavior unnecessarily

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory has identified the non-native logical XOR fallback or the exactly-one versus parity distinction.
scale.2: The trajectory mentions XOR or Q-object behavior but focuses on construction, native behavior, or binary cases without addressing the fallback truth-count semantics.
scale.3: The trajectory locates the relevant fallback and recognizes that sum equals one is suspicious, but the fix or validation is partial, speculative, or does not clearly cover more than two operands.
scale.4: The trajectory implements or clearly specifies an odd-parity fallback for non-native logical XOR and shows evidence that three-or-more operand behavior is corrected, with limited but relevant validation.
scale.5: The trajectory robustly corrects the non-native fallback to odd parity using portable ORM expressions, preserves native and one-/two-operand behavior, avoids unrelated XOR paths, and validates representative n-ary cases including repeated true predicates.

experiences.title: Feature-gated runtime setting migration with legacy startup path
experiences.description: Use when a qutebrowser/QtWebEngine task asks to make a previously restart-only, global setting dynamic and URL-pattern-aware via a newly available QWebEngineSettings attribute while preserving older command-line/startup behavior.
experiences.context: Applies in Python QtWebEngine/qutebrowser trajectories involving config metadata in YAML, WebEngineSettings-style attribute mapping, AbstractSettings/update_for_url pattern plumbing, and an existing legacy startup-argument implementation. It is especially relevant when the setting has one newly dynamic enable/toggle flag but related subsettings still remain startup-only. Retrieve this after the agent has identified or edited the runtime settings bridge, config metadata, or legacy startup dark-mode/argument code. For early pure investigation with no edits, judge only whether the agent has found the correct mechanisms and boundaries; do not expect completed implementation. Do not apply this criterion to tasks with no legacy startup path, no version/feature-gated API, or settings whose entire option family is known to be dynamically supported.
experiences.experience: The earlier rubrics correctly noticed that simply adding a QWebEngineSettings ForceDarkMode-style attribute is central, because visible evidence such as an _ATTRIBUTES entry plus supports_pattern metadata is a real prerequisite for runtime and per-URL updates. However, broad rubrics that only ask for “runtime toggling via ForceDarkMode” are not discriminative enough: several trajectories looked good by that proxy while still leaving subtle but decisive flaws. A better rubric should require a coordinated migration of only the enable/toggle setting: the runtime mapping must use the existing settings bridge rather than ad-hoc profile setters; config metadata must expose URL patterns and remove unconditional restart semantics only for the supported toggle, with documentation explaining the older-version caveat; the legacy command-line path must stop passing the enable flag only when the new API is actually available, while preserving other dark-mode startup arguments and older-version behavior. The criterion should prioritize visible evidence of actual feature detection of the enum/API, not just QtWebEngine version numbers, because PyQt bindings can be missing the enum even when version checks appear favorable. It should also penalize overbroad changes such as making all related dark-mode options pattern-capable, adding new conditional config parser semantics without need, custom duplicate setters that bypass existing AbstractSettings plumbing, or repeated API probing without implementation progress. Avoid a tempting but wrong criterion that rewards any mention of ForceDarkMode or any removal of restart: correctness depends on the interaction among feature gating, config metadata, URL-pattern application, startup-argument compatibility, and limiting the scope to the single enabled setting.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Coordinated feature-gated runtime migration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show a coherent implementation plan or patch that makes only the target enable/toggle setting dynamic and URL-pattern-aware through the existing WebEngine settings infrastructure, while preserving legacy startup behavior for unsupported environments and related restart-only options. Strong evidence includes: mapping the setting to the new QWebEngineSettings WebAttribute through the generic attribute bridge with try/except or hasattr-based feature detection; config metadata that removes the unconditional restart requirement and enables URL patterns for the target setting with an older-version caveat; legacy startup argument logic that omits the enable flag only when the runtime API is truly available but keeps other dark-mode arguments and old-version behavior; and validation/diff review focused on these compatibility boundaries.

prioritize_evidence: existing settings bridge is used rather than a parallel custom update path
actual enum/API availability is checked, not only a version number
URL pattern support is connected to existing config metadata and update_for_url plumbing
only the enable/toggle option is made dynamic; related startup-only options remain compatible
legacy command-line/startup handling is adjusted only for supported runtime environments
penalize_evidence: unconditional reference to a new enum that may be absent
pure QtWebEngine version gating without binding/API feature detection
making the whole dark-mode option family non-restart or pattern-capable
new conditional config parser machinery when a local metadata/documentation change would suffice
repeated exploratory greps/probes with no concrete integration progress

scale.1: No concrete progress toward the runtime settings bridge or URL-pattern metadata, or the trajectory is stuck in repetitive probing without identifying the existing config/update mechanisms.
scale.2: Identifies the new runtime WebAttribute or the config metadata issue, but lacks a credible integration path through existing settings updates or ignores URL-pattern plumbing and compatibility boundaries.
scale.3: Implements or plans a plausible runtime mapping and metadata change, but leaves important risks visible, such as incomplete feature detection, no adjustment of conflicting startup enable flags, or unclear preservation of older behavior.
scale.4: Shows strong coordinated changes across runtime mapping, config metadata, URL-pattern support, and legacy startup handling, with only minor missing validation or documentation details.
scale.5: Provides a tightly scoped, validated migration: the target setting is mapped via the existing settings bridge with robust API/enum gating, URL-pattern metadata and documentation are correct, startup enable flags are suppressed only when the runtime API is available, other dark-mode options and older environments remain compatible, and targeted checks or tests support the behavior.

experiences.title: Do not treat a normalized table as enough when user scope must be transparent
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go persistence task asks to move user-specific global properties into a dedicated table and expose a user-scoped repository through a context-based DataStore abstraction.
experiences.context: In this repository style, repositories are created from `DataStore` methods that receive `context.Context`, and authenticated user information is available from request context. A rubric that only checks for a `user_props` table, CRUD methods, and removal of string prefix concatenation can be misleading: an implementation may still require every caller to pass `userID` into repository methods, may update only the local storage helper while leaving higher-level Last.fm authorization/scrobbling call paths using explicit user IDs, or may damage unrelated datastore wiring while adding the new method. The original schema/repository idea is still appropriate as a subcheck when the task only requests a normalized `(user_id, key)` data model, or during early exploration when no implementation exists yet. It should not be the main success criterion once visible edits show a context-scoped repository pattern and task wording promises a transparent user-scoped repository.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded visible creation of a `user_props` table and a `UserPropsRepository` with methods like `Put(userID, key, value)` plus changing Last.fm from `Property(prefix+uid)` to `UserProps(uid, key)`. That criterion is too superficial for tasks asking for transparent user-scoped access: passing `userID` through every repository operation merely moves the manual user scoping from a concatenated key into an API parameter, and it can miss call-site behavior where the authenticated user should come from context. A better rubric should prioritize whether the new repository owns user scoping by deriving the user from its construction context, rejects unauthenticated use consistently, exposes methods keyed only by property name/value, and forces Last.fm session-key helpers and their callers to operate from a context that contains the intended user. It should also watch for unrelated regressions in central datastore wiring, because broad file rewrites often remove existing Resource cases. Avoid generating a criterion that says the patch is good merely because a composite primary key and no string prefix are visible; instead, look for evidence that callers no longer need to know how user scope is represented, that all session-key consumers were updated coherently, and that existing non-user repository behavior remains intact.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize implementations of a user-specific properties repository that expose user identity as a required argument to every CRUD operation or only replace string key-prefixing with explicit userID parameters, rather than making the repository transparently scoped to the authenticated user/context. Also penalize visible incomplete call-site migration where Last.fm session-key helpers or higher-level authorization/scrobbling/link-status/unlink/callback paths still require user IDs for storage lookup instead of relying on a context carrying the active user, or where datastore edits remove unrelated existing repository routing cases while adding the new repository.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Leaky User Scope and Incomplete Session-Key Integration

metadata.expected_environment: Go codebase with model.DataStore repository factories taking context.Context, request-context user lookup, SQL persistence repositories, and Last.fm session-key storage currently backed by global properties.
failure_signals: UserPropsRepository methods are declared as Put/Get/Delete(userID, key, ...) rather than property-key methods on a context-scoped repository
Last.fm code calls UserProps(ctx).Get(uid, key) or Put(uid, key, value), preserving caller-managed user identity
Only auth_router/session helper storage lines are changed while other Last.fm methods still pass user IDs for session-key retrieval in a way inconsistent with the new abstraction
Callback or unauthenticated route code stores a user property without first ensuring the target user is present in context
persistence.DataStore Resource switch or other central repository routing loses pre-existing model cases unrelated to user props
acceptable_boundaries: A `(user_id, key)` table and SQL predicates on user_id are still expected internally
Explicit userID parameters may be acceptable only if the task or surrounding architecture defines repositories as non-context-scoped services rather than user-scoped DataStore factories
