During pre-edit exploration, absence of the context-scoped API is not yet a flaw unless the trajectory commits to an incompatible design

scale.1: No evidence of leaky user scope or integration regression: repository API is context/user-scoped, callers use property-key methods, all relevant Last.fm session-key paths are coherently migrated, and unrelated datastore routing remains intact.
scale.2: Minor concerns only, such as naming ambiguity, but visible design mostly keeps user scope inside the repository and does not damage existing datastore behavior.
scale.3: Mixed design: some code suggests context/user-scoped behavior, but visible callers or interfaces still pass user IDs in enough places that transparency is uncertain.
scale.4: Clear flaw: repository CRUD requires userID arguments or Last.fm storage helpers still manage user identity explicitly, even though string key-prefixing was removed.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the implementation mainly performs a superficial table/API rename from prefixed global properties to explicit userID parameters, misses important Last.fm call paths or context setup, and/or corrupts unrelated central datastore repository routing.

experiences.title: Do not reward calendar folder reshuffling without module-resolution safety
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for a TypeScript monorepo refactor that moves shared calendar modules into domain folders and the visible trajectory shows bulk `mv`/`sed` path rewrites, barrel exports, stale-import searches, or unresolved typecheck/module errors.
experiences.context: This applies to structural calendar-module refactors in a JS/TS monorepo where shared code is imported through deep paths such as package aliases and relative imports. The misleading pattern is a trajectory that appears to satisfy the user-facing separation-of-concerns goal by creating folders like alarms, crypto, recurrence, mail, ICS, models, utils, etc., but has not demonstrated that old consumers, internal relative imports, and TypeScript resolution still work. It is especially risky when the agent uses broad scripts or repeated `sed` replacements, creates `index.ts` barrels, requires that no files remain at the calendar root, or is still investigating unresolved `Cannot find module` errors. A domain-organization criterion can still be useful when paired with evidence of preserved imports/build validity, or at an early planning stage as an intent/progress signal; it should not be treated as a strong final-quality predictor merely because files have been moved into named folders.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster emphasized domain-specific directory grouping, no files left in the old flat structure, and barrel exports. That idea matches the task at a high level, but it became misleading because visible trajectories often had broken or unverified module resolution: old deep imports were still present, internal relative imports pointed to the wrong depth/domain, generated barrels did not preserve direct-file consumers, broad scripts produced nonsensical paths, and typecheck errors remained. Future rubric generation should not make “all files grouped by domain” or “root calendar directory emptied” the decisive criterion for this kind of refactor. Instead, focus on whether the agent maintains a conservative old-path-to-new-path mapping, updates or preserves every deep import that consumers actually use, fixes internal imports based on original intent rather than blanket text replacement, avoids over-broad domain moves that collapse unrelated modules, and validates with a relevant TypeScript/build/test command after the path updates. Avoid the tempting criterion that more folders, more moved files, or more barrel exports means a better patch; prioritize visible evidence from searches for stale imports, inspection of moved files’ imports, compatibility shims or systematic consumer rewrites, and successful or improving typecheck output.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a calendar-module separation refactor in a TypeScript monorepo, penalize trajectories that rely on bulk directory moves, `sed`/scripted import rewrites, or newly added barrel exports while leaving module resolution unproven or visibly broken. This flaw is present when the agent has moved shared calendar files into domain folders but has not completed a reliable old-path-to-new-path migration, has unresolved or newly introduced import/typecheck errors, uses root or subdirectory `index.ts` files as a substitute for preserving direct deep imports, or requires an overly broad condition such as no calendar files remaining at the old root without evidence that consumers still compile.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Unvalidated path-breaking structural refactor

metadata.environment: TypeScript/React monorepo with shared calendar modules and deep package-alias imports
evidence_to_check: visible unresolved TS2307/Cannot find module/typecheck errors after moves
bulk mv/sed/import rewrite scripts without complete validation
old deep imports or internal relative imports still under investigation
barrel exports added but direct-file consumers not updated or shimmed
over-broad folder moves such as emptying root or merging domains without checking collisions/original import intent
not_a_flaw_when: trajectory is only in early exploration/planning and has not claimed completion
moves are accompanied by exact compatibility shims or comprehensive consumer rewrites
internal imports are inspected and corrected per original source intent
relevant typecheck/build/tests pass or remaining errors are unrelated and documented

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory either remains exploratory or shows conservative domain moves plus verified import preservation and passing relevant checks.
scale.2: Minor evidence: some moves or barrels are present before validation, but the agent is actively inventorying old paths and has not treated grouping as sufficient.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: many files have been moved and some imports rewritten, but validation is incomplete or stale-import/internal-import auditing is only partial.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory shows broken or unresolved imports/typecheck errors after broad moves, or assumes barrel exports/new folders solve deep-import compatibility.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the agent aggressively empties/restructures the shared calendar tree with broad scripts, introduces nonsensical or unresolved paths, ignores compile failures, or judges completion primarily from folder names rather than resolvable imports.

experiences.title: Do not let redirect-only progress stand in for a full collection module_utils resolver fix
experiences.description: Retrieve this when an Ansible/module_common task combines collection module_utils redirects with package __init__.py relative imports, namespace-style missing __init__.py directories, payload bundling, and diagnostics, especially when the trajectory only investigates or partially patches redirect metadata/shims.
experiences.context: Applies in Ansible 2.10-era module_common / collection loader work where the visible issue is multi-symptom dependency discovery: collection metadata redirects, cross-collection or core redirects, relative imports from module_utils package initializers, nested collection module_utils directories without parent __init__.py, payload zip contents, and missing-import error clarity. A redirect-resolution rubric is still appropriate as one subcriterion when the task or trajectory is specifically about plugin_routing/import_redirection behavior, or when the stage is early exploration and the rubric only asks whether the agent has identified the redirect hypothesis. It becomes misleading at implementation/final-review stages if it treats checking collection metadata, converting plugin_routing to import_redirection, or generating a sys.modules shim as sufficient evidence of correctness without integrated recursive dependency and packaging behavior.
experiences.experience: The recurring misleading rubrics focused on "Collection Module Utils Redirect Resolution" and credited source-collection metadata lookup, cross-collection redirects, import_redirection conversion, or shim generation. That concern is real, but in this task it is only one failure mode. The visible trajectories often showed repeated inspection, no code changes, or narrow ad-hoc patches that could still pass superficial import smoke tests while leaving core requirements unaddressed: redirected target files may not be recursively parsed and bundled, relative imports inside package __init__.py may be resolved against the wrong module FQN, namespace-style parent directories may lack usable package entries, metadata keys may use the wrong collection-name shape, and diagnostic messages may remain generic. Future rubric generation should avoid a tempting criterion that rewards merely "checks plugin_routing.module_utils" or "creates a redirect shim" as an outcome-level signal. A better criterion should require visible evidence that the resolver handles the complete module_utils dependency graph: correct metadata lookup for the imported collection and redirect target, payload inclusion of original shim and target source as needed, recursive scanning with correct package context for __init__.py, behavior when collection directories exist without physical __init__.py files, and targeted tests or manual payload inspections covering both import styles and error paths. If the cutoff is exploration-only, generate a stage-appropriate rubric about validating the hypothesis and identifying required tests rather than an implementation-completeness rubric.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a multi-symptom Ansible collection module_utils resolution task, this flaw is present when the trajectory narrows the solution or evaluation to redirect metadata/shim handling without visible evidence that the full payload dependency resolver is correct. Judge from the trajectory: look for whether redirect handling is integrated with recursive module_utils discovery, whether redirected targets are loaded and recursively scanned, whether package __init__.py relative imports are resolved using the current dependency's package context, whether nested collection module_utils directories without parent __init__.py are handled, whether missing-module errors report useful lookup context, and whether tests or manual checks exercise these behaviors. Do not credit repeated inspection, an import smoke test, or a standalone metadata/shim patch as sufficient for this broader task.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Redirect-only module_utils fix misses resolver/package semantics

metadata.environment: Ansible module_common and collection loader; Python module_utils dependency discovery and AnsiballZ-style payload bundling
metadata.avoid_proxy: Do not use mere mention of plugin_routing.module_utils, import_redirection conversion, source collection metadata lookup, or sys.modules shim generation as a sufficient proxy for correctness.
prioritize_visible_evidence: targeted code changes connect redirect lookup to recursive module_utils discovery and payload inclusion
redirected target source is included and scanned for further dependencies
relative imports in package initializer files are resolved relative to the initializer's package
existing collection directories without __init__.py are treated compatibly with namespace package behavior
diagnostics distinguish missing source, redirect failure, collection lookup failure, and bad relative import context
tests or manual payload inspections cover both import forms, cross-collection/core redirects, package initializer imports, missing parent __init__.py, and error messages
metadata.stage_boundary: At early exploration, absence of implementation is not itself this flaw; at patch/final-review stage, narrow redirect-only changes without the above evidence should be treated as a serious flaw.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory treats redirects as one part of an integrated module_utils resolver fix and shows concrete evidence for payload recursion, package initializer context, namespace-style directories, diagnostics, and relevant tests.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory emphasizes redirects but also explicitly plans or partially validates the other resolver requirements, with no conflicting implementation visible.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory mainly works on redirect metadata or shims and only acknowledges other requirements at a high level, with little concrete evidence that recursive payload/package semantics are handled.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory implements or proposes a redirect-only patch, metadata conversion, or shim generation while leaving relative __init__.py imports, missing parent __init__.py behavior, payload inclusion, or diagnostics untested or unaddressed.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory treats superficial redirect handling, repeated inspection, or an import smoke test as completing the task despite visible unresolved metadata-shape errors, no integrated resolver validation, or no meaningful patch.

experiences.title: Do not over-credit generic source splitting when constructor API naming is part of the refactor
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a Python refactor that splits an overloaded factory/constructor by version-information source, especially in qutebrowser/PyQtWebEngine-style version detection code.
experiences.context: This applies when the visible task asks to replace an overloaded source-parameter factory with separate source-specific methods and the trajectory shows the agent adding three constructors with correct labels and fallback order. The misleading pattern is to judge the patch as complete merely because there are separate methods for importlib, PyQt, and Qt/qVersion paths. In this setting, the maintainability goal also depends on the new public/internal API being named with enough domain context to distinguish PyQtWebEngine package metadata from a generic importlib mechanism, and on not preserving the old source-parameter overload as the core design. The original broad criterion may still be appropriate when the task explicitly says method names are arbitrary or when the repository already uses generic constructor names consistently; it is insufficient when the old API name and the source provenance are central to readability.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics rewarded trajectories for creating any three source-specific constructors with correct source strings and fallback order. That was too broad: agents could satisfy it with a generic importlib-named constructor or by keeping a backward-compatible `source` switch inside the old PyQt constructor, while still missing the refactor’s API clarity goal. For this cluster, a better rubric should inspect the visible diff for the public/classmethod surface, not only behavior. It should prefer a source-specific importlib constructor whose name and docstring retain the PyQtWebEngine/PyQt package context, a PyQt constructor that no longer needs a caller-supplied source value, and a Qt fallback constructor used directly by the fallback branch. Avoid the tempting criterion “there are separate methods and the labels are importlib/PyQt/Qt,” because that over-credits generic or partially overloaded designs. Prioritize evidence from method signatures, method names, docstrings describing the actual provenance, and call sites in the detection flow.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize a PyQtWebEngine version-detection refactor that appears source-split but leaves the new constructor API ambiguous or still centered on the old source-parameter overload. This includes using an overly generic importlib constructor name that does not identify the PyQtWebEngine/PyQt package provenance, keeping `from_pyqt(..., source=...)` as an active dispatch mechanism for importlib or Qt fallback paths, or updating call sites to generic methods without preserving domain-specific readability. The acceptable trajectory evidence is a domain-specific importlib/PyQtWebEngine metadata constructor, a PyQt metadata constructor with a fixed PyQt source label, a Qt/qVersion fallback constructor with a fixed Qt source label, and detection-flow call sites that invoke those constructors directly in the intended fallback order.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Ambiguous or still-overloaded source-specific constructor API

evidence_to_check: constructor method names and signatures
whether the old source parameter remains part of core dispatch
docstrings explaining PyQtWebEngine-Qt importlib metadata versus PyQt metadata versus Qt fallback
call sites in the version-detection fallback chain

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: constructors are source-specific, domain-aware, fixed-label, and used directly by the fallback flow.
scale.2: Minor evidence: source-specific methods exist and are used directly, but naming or documentation is only slightly less clear while not reintroducing overload dispatch.
scale.3: Moderate issue: behavior and labels are mostly correct, but the importlib constructor/API is generic enough to obscure the PyQtWebEngine package provenance.
scale.4: Clear issue: the patch both uses ambiguous constructor naming/documentation and partially retains the old source-parameter pathway or compatibility dispatch.
scale.5: Severe issue: the refactor is mostly cosmetic; the old overloaded source-parameter design remains the main mechanism or the new methods do not clearly represent the three provenance-specific sources.

experiences.title: Do not reward generic cookie parsing when transport metadata and bypass identity are underspecified
experiences.description: Use this when evaluating a Go gRPC/grpc-gateway authentication middleware task where the trajectory claims cookie-token support and auth bypass by adding config fields, path/method/server-name matching, or manual Cookie parsing.
experiences.context: Applies in Flipt-like Go services where authentication is enforced by a gRPC unary interceptor using metadata from grpc-gateway. The misleading pattern is a trajectory that appears to satisfy the surface requirements by parsing a metadata key like `cookie` or `Cookie`, adding `AuthenticationConfig.ExcludedServers/ExcludedPaths/ExcludedMethods`, wiring that config through `cmd/flipt/main.go`, and writing tests around those invented strings. That evidence is not enough when the codebase has a specific gateway metadata convention and the bypass is intended to be tied to actual registered server instances, not arbitrary config path strings. A generic cookie-extraction criterion may still be appropriate in a simpler HTTP middleware task, or when visible exploration confirms that raw `Cookie` metadata is the accepted transport contract and path-based exclusions are the existing project convention.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics over-rewarded trajectories for merely extracting `flipt_client_token` from a Cookie header and adding a configurable excluded list. In this codebase that criterion is too broad: agents can pass it while using the wrong metadata key for grpc-gateway cookies, hand-rolling incomplete cookie parsing, inventing new config fields that destabilize config tests, or bypassing by `FullMethod`/service-name strings instead of the server identity available on `grpc.UnaryServerInfo`. A better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory verifies and follows the existing transport and interceptor extension contracts: cookie data should be read from the metadata key actually populated by grpc-gateway for cookies and parsed with HTTP cookie semantics, Bearer behavior should remain unchanged, and skip-auth should be implemented as an interceptor option or equivalent server-instance registration mechanism rather than broad config-driven path matching unless the repository already exposes such config. Avoid a tempting criterion that says 'implements cookie extraction and configurable excluded paths/servers' without checking the concrete metadata key, cookie parser, and bypass identity evidence visible in the trajectory.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that implement the surface feature using invented metadata/config/path conventions rather than the repository's actual gRPC gateway and interceptor contracts. This flaw is present when the visible work reads cookies from generic `cookie`/`Cookie` metadata without confirming the gateway-populated cookie metadata key, manually splits cookie strings instead of using HTTP cookie parsing semantics, or adds authentication config fields and matches `FullMethod`/service names/paths for bypass when the available design should register server instances/options for skip-auth. The criterion is especially important if the agent is already editing `internal/server/auth/middleware.go`, `cmd/flipt/main.go`, or `internal/config/authentication.go` and tests only cover the invented conventions.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Wrong transport or bypass contract

metadata.environment: Go gRPC unary interceptor with grpc-gateway metadata
bad_cookie_evidence: metadata key hard-coded as `cookie` or `Cookie` without gateway-contract verification
manual semicolon splitting of Cookie headers
new gateway metadata forwarding invented solely to match middleware
bad_bypass_evidence: new AuthenticationConfig fields for excluded paths/methods/servers without existing config precedent
bypass matched by `FullMethod` prefix, path, or bare service-name strings
production wiring changed to pass config slices into auth interceptor
better_evidence: uses the repository's actual grpc-gateway cookie metadata key
parses cookie values through HTTP cookie semantics
preserves Authorization Bearer behavior
implements skip-auth using interceptor options or server-instance identity from `UnaryServerInfo.Server` when that is the available contract

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory investigates and follows the actual metadata key and server-skip contract, or has not yet chosen an implementation approach.
scale.2: Minor risk only: the trajectory mentions generic Cookie parsing or excluded paths, but also shows active investigation of gateway metadata and server identity before committing.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory implements cookie fallback or bypass tests, but visible evidence is ambiguous about the metadata key or bypass identity and no validation of repository conventions is shown.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory hard-codes generic cookie metadata/manual parsing or adds config-based path/server exclusions despite little evidence these match the codebase contracts.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory rewires production/config/tests around invented cookie metadata and config-driven method/server matching, and treats passing self-authored tests as sufficient while ignoring the actual grpc-gateway metadata and server-instance skip semantics.

experiences.title: Active dimension-system equivalence for unit additions
experiences.description: Retrieve when a SymPy units task or trajectory concerns addition of quantities whose dimensions are physically equivalent but represented differently, especially when `_collect_factor_and_dimension` rejects addends like derived-vs-composite dimensions.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/SymPy units subsystem setting where the visible problem is an addition failing because dimensions such as velocity and acceleration*time are not syntactically equal even though their dimensional dependencies match. The criterion is most useful once the trajectory has inspected the units dimension collection logic, the Add branch, or the dimension-system APIs; it can also be prompted by an explicit reproducer showing a false incompatibility error for equivalent dimensions. It is less applicable to unrelated unit conversion bugs, scale-factor registration problems, dimensionless exponent handling, generic dependency-install failures, or trajectories that have not yet narrowed the issue beyond initial repository exploration. It should not be broadened into accepting arbitrary additions or changing global Dimension equality semantics.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases evaluated the semantic boundary that matters: addition should require dimensional compatibility under the active dimension system, not raw object or expression equality. This aligned with visible evidence because the agent repeatedly found that the Add branch compared dimensions directly, found an existing equivalence API based on dimensional dependencies, and either planned or applied a localized replacement while leaving factor summation and incompatibility errors intact. A better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory recognizes and uses the unit system’s own equivalence relation for addend dimension checks, and whether it preserves rejection of genuinely incompatible dimensions. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as merely reproducing the error, installing missing test dependencies, asserting a particular returned dimension spelling, changing Quantity setup, normalizing all dimensions globally, or modifying Dimension equality. Prioritize visible evidence including: inspection of the Add-handling code path, identification of direct inequality as the false-negative source, discovery or use of `equivalent_dims`/dimensional dependency comparison through the active system, validation with equivalent derived/composite dimensions, and validation that incompatible dimensions still raise.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Dimension-system equivalence in addition checks
reference_golden_rubrics.description: For unit-expression addition, the trajectory should show that addend dimensions are compared using the active dimension system's equivalence semantics, so differently represented but dependency-equivalent dimensions are accepted, while truly incompatible dimensions still raise and existing factor collection behavior is preserved.

metadata.environment: Python SymPy units subsystem
metadata.target_behavior: addition accepts physically equivalent dimensions represented differently
key_positive_evidence: locates the addition branch in dimension/factor collection logic
identifies direct dimension inequality or structural equality as the cause of false rejection
uses or plans to use active dimension-system equivalence based on dimensional dependencies
keeps summing scale factors only after compatibility is established
checks that incompatible dimensions are still rejected
key_negative_evidence: treats any non-identical dimensions as incompatible
accepts all additions without compatibility checks
changes global dimension equality instead of using system-specific equivalence
focuses only on dependency installation or reproduction without a semantic fix
alters unrelated scale-factor or quantity registration behavior

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory understands the equivalent-dimension addition issue; it remains at repository exploration, dependency setup, or unrelated unit behavior.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory reproduces the failure or notices a dimension mismatch, but does not identify that structural/direct comparison is the wrong compatibility test.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies that equivalent dimensions should be accepted and points to the addition compatibility check, but has not clearly tied the fix to the active dimension system's equivalence/dependency API or has not addressed incompatible-dimension preservation.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory identifies the direct comparison flaw and proposes or implements a localized active-system equivalence check for addend dimensions while preserving factor summation and error behavior.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory applies the localized equivalence check through the active dimension system, verifies the reported equivalent-dimension addition, and also verifies representative compatible and incompatible edge cases without broad or unrelated semantic changes.

experiences.title: Do not reward confirming an already-passing narrow contract when the task evidence points elsewhere
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Solr/Open Library-style task states author redirect/update behavior, but the visible trajectory finds that the named author code paths and existing tests already satisfy those behaviors.
experiences.context: Applies in Python repository trajectories involving Solr request generation/configuration where the issue text is internally contradictory or says current behavior matches expected behavior, and the agent has run or inspected tests showing redirected authors already return delete requests and no-work author updates already return update requests. In that situation, a rubric centered on merely locating or understanding `update_author` can overvalue unproductive investigation and unsupported patches. The original author-contract rubric is still appropriate when there is visible evidence that the redirect/no-work author behavior is actually failing, untested, or being changed in a way that risks regression; it is not sufficient once the agent has demonstrated that those exact behaviors already pass.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics rewarded trajectories for verifying the explicit author redirect/update contract, and sometimes added unsupported requirements such as transitive redirect deletion or graceful handling of missing authors. This was misleading because the visible trajectory repeatedly showed that the stated author behaviors already existed and tests passed, while the agent kept patching unrelated author edge cases. For similar cases, generate a rubric that distinguishes preserving the stated author contract from solving the real integration problem. The better criterion should penalize stopping at `update_author` after passing tests and should prioritize evidence that the agent broadened investigation to how Solr requests are constructed and sent: configuration keys, base URL vs host handling, select/update endpoint formation, callers in search/readlink/indexer code, and whether valid request objects actually reach the intended Solr endpoint. Avoid tempting criteria that require transitive redirects, missing-author no-ops, or extra delete requests unless the task text, a failing test, or runtime reproduction specifically establishes those as required.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Overfitting to Already-Passing Author Request Logic
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that, after observing that the named author redirect and no-work update behaviors already pass or are implemented, continue to treat `update_author` edge-case changes as the main solution without investigating the broader Solr integration path that determines whether valid requests are formed and sent to the correct endpoint. This includes unsupported additions such as transitive redirect deletion, missing-author behavior changes, or work-level author redirect deletion when no visible failing evidence requires them.

applies_when: Task concerns Solr integration and author redirect/update behavior
Visible tests or exploratory scripts show redirected authors already produce DeleteRequest objects
Visible tests or exploratory scripts show valid authors with zero Solr works already produce an UpdateRequest
No failing reproduction has been found in the author request object logic
replacement_focus: Solr base URL or host configuration
select/update URL construction
request sending path and endpoint compatibility
cross-module callers that consume Solr configuration
regression tests that expose the integration boundary rather than duplicating already-passing author unit tests
avoid_requiring_without_evidence: extra deletes for authors referenced by works
patches whose only effect is changing already-passing author edge cases

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory recognizes the author contract is already satisfied and either preserves it while investigating broader Solr integration or finds a concrete failing reproduction outside the already-passing author unit path.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory spends some time on existing author behavior but notes passing evidence and begins checking request transport/configuration or other Solr integration boundaries.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory verifies the author contract and remains mostly focused on it, with limited or inconclusive exploration of broader Solr request construction despite no author failure.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory runs or inspects passing author tests but still proposes or pursues unsupported edits to `update_author` or nearby author-only logic as the likely fix.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory explicitly demonstrates that the stated author behaviors already work, then makes or plans author edge-case changes unrelated to any visible failing reproduction while ignoring Solr endpoint/configuration/request-sending paths.

experiences.title: Release/Update Decoupling Metadata Contract
experiences.description: Use when a Go startup task combines a prerelease classification bug with an explicit requirement to decouple release/update logic and expose update metadata for UX/logging/telemetry decisions.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go application where startup code currently performs release classification, latest-release lookup, update-availability comparison, logging/console messaging, metadata construction, and telemetry gating inline. The task must explicitly require more than recognizing prerelease identifiers: it should also ask for reusable/testable release-update logic and startup-visible metadata such as current version, latest version, update availability, and a latest-version URL. This criterion is most useful once the trajectory has inspected or begun editing the startup/version flow, especially when visible work is gravitating toward a narrow `isRelease` or suffix/semver-only fix. It is less applicable when the task only asks for a local release-classification bug fix, when no update metadata or telemetry contract is involved, or during very early repository exploration before the agent has located the relevant startup flow.
experiences.experience: The generated rubrics in these cases were useful because they judged the broader startup release/update contract rather than only whether `-rc` became non-release. The visible trajectories repeatedly showed agents discovering semver prerelease detection and then patching only the local release predicate in the startup file; some also validated builds or scratch scripts, but they did not extract reusable/testable version-update logic, did not fully model latest-release URL as part of a structured update result, and left most update-check behavior coupled to startup. That observable gap aligned with poor final patch quality because the task required decoupling and a complete metadata/telemetry contract, not just a classification tweak. A better rubric for similar situations should reward evidence that the agent creates or plans a reusable release/update evaluation boundary, passes version strings and latest-release fetching through testable interfaces or helpers, returns structured metadata for current/latest/update/URL, wires that structure into startup logging/UX and telemetry gating, and adds targeted tests for prerelease and update cases. Avoid the tempting but too-narrow criterion of “uses semver or checks `len(Pre)==0` for prereleases”; that can fix the reproduction while missing the requested architecture and metadata behavior. Prioritize visible evidence such as new or refactored non-startup release/update code, parameterized helpers instead of global state, dependency-injected latest-release checks, explicit propagation of latest-version URL only when an update is available, startup using the reusable result instead of duplicating comparison logic, and tests covering `dev`, `snapshot`, `rc`, normal releases, and update/no-update outcomes.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate progress toward a complete release/update startup contract: prerelease builds are not treated as proper releases; release/update decision logic is separated from startup orchestration into a reusable and testable boundary; latest-release lookup and version comparison produce structured metadata containing current version, latest version, update availability, and latest-version URL when applicable; startup logging/UX and exposed info consume that metadata; and telemetry/update checks remain disabled for non-release builds. Judge from visible investigation, plans, edits, and validation, not from hidden final results.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Decoupled Release Update Metadata Contract

metadata.environment: Go application with startup code currently mixing version parsing, update checks, UX/logging, metadata exposure, and telemetry gating
required_visible_evidence: release classification excludes prerelease identifiers such as dev, snapshot, and rc
version/update logic is moved or designed behind a reusable helper/component rather than remaining entirely inline in startup
latest-release fetching/comparison is testable, for example by accepting a version string and injectable checker/client
structured update info includes current version, latest version, update availability, and latest-version URL only when applicable
startup logging/UX/info construction and telemetry gating use the reusable release/update result
targeted tests or planned tests cover prerelease strings and update/no-update behavior
anti_patterns: only changing a local suffix or semver check in the release predicate
leaving all update comparison and GitHub lookup logic embedded in startup
adding an ad hoc URL field without a reusable update-info contract
validating only with scratch scripts while adding no maintainable tests

scale.1: No visible progress on the broader contract; work either has not reached version/update logic or only mentions the prerelease symptom without addressing metadata, telemetry, or decoupling.
scale.2: Weak progress: identifies or patches prerelease classification, but visible work remains a local startup predicate change with no reusable/testable release-update boundary and no complete metadata/URL handling.
scale.3: Moderate progress: fixes or plans prerelease classification and recognizes telemetry/update metadata implications, but extraction is incomplete, update URL/current/latest/update fields are only partially wired, or tests are missing.
scale.4: Strong progress: introduces or clearly designs a reusable release/update component, wires most metadata and telemetry behavior through it, and validates key prerelease cases, with only minor gaps in URL handling, test coverage, or startup cleanup.
scale.5: Strongest progress: fully separates release/update evaluation from startup, provides structured current/latest/update/URL metadata consumed by logging/UX/info and telemetry gating, and includes maintainable tests for prerelease, release, update-available, no-update, and error cases.

experiences.title: Gate no-op signal registration on configured dependent fields
experiences.description: Use when a Django trajectory is addressing performance overhead from an `ImageField` `post_init` receiver that does no work unless width/height dimension fields are configured.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django model-field task where the visible issue is signal-dispatch overhead, the trajectory has identified that the image dimension update receiver exits immediately when no dimension fields are configured, and the agent is editing or validating the model-field class wiring. The criterion is most useful once the trajectory has enough evidence about both sides of the behavior: plain image fields should avoid receiver registration, while image fields with either width or height metadata must keep their initialization-time dimension update path. It is premature during repository search before the signal hookup and no-op condition are known, and it is not the right criterion for unrelated image upload/form validation, storage behavior, or dimension calculation bugs where signal registration overhead is not the defect.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic boundary that predicts correctness: the fix must suppress the unnecessary `post_init` connection only for dimensionless image fields, not remove or weaken dimension maintenance globally. A strong rubric should ask whether the trajectory preserves the existing abstract-model guard and adds a dependency-field guard at registration time, with either width or height field being sufficient to retain the receiver. This is better than a broad 'ImageField tests pass' criterion because skipped or misconfigured tests can hide the behavior, and better than focusing on optimizing the receiver body because the reported cost is dispatching a no-op receiver during model initialization. Avoid rewarding patches that remove the signal entirely, require both width and height fields instead of either one, drop the concrete/abstract distinction, or rely only on fragile receiver introspection without interpreting sender-specific bound-method receivers correctly. Prioritize visible evidence such as code that gates the signal connection on configured dimension metadata, validation showing no receiver for a plain image field and a receiver for width-only/height-only cases, and checks that assignment-time or database-load dimension behavior remains intact.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the image model field's initialization signal receiver is registered only when dimension metadata is actually configured: no `post_init` receiver is added for a concrete model with a plain image field, but the receiver is still registered when either a width field or a height field is configured, while preserving the existing exclusion for abstract models and existing dimension-update behavior.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Conditional dimension-dependent signal wiring

primary_visible_evidence: signal hookup is changed at field/model contribution time rather than merely adding work inside the receiver
condition treats width-only and height-only configurations as requiring the receiver
existing concrete-vs-abstract model behavior is preserved
validation distinguishes absence of a receiver for dimensionless fields from presence of a receiver for configured dimension fields

removing the initialization signal for all image fields
requiring both width and height metadata before registering
judging receiver identity from raw signal internals without resolving sender-specific bound methods

scale.2: Recognizes the no-op receiver overhead but only changes the receiver body or proposes broad cleanup without proving that dimensionless fields avoid signal registration.
scale.3: Adds or plans a conditional signal guard, but evidence is incomplete or ambiguous about width-only/height-only cases, abstract models, or preservation of dimension updates.
scale.4: Clearly gates registration on the presence of configured dimension metadata and preserves the prior abstract-model guard, with some validation for plain versus configured image fields.
scale.5: Provides decisive visible evidence that plain image fields add no `post_init` receiver, width-only and height-only configurations still register and update dimensions correctly, abstract-model behavior is unchanged, and validation is run through an appropriate Django setup or carefully interpreted signal checks.

experiences.title: Disambiguate Non-Unique Composite Index Deletion
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django schema/migration task involves deleting a legacy composite index that shares columns with a unique constraint, especially when introspection can report unique constraints as indexes.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django repository, around schema editor or migration operations, when the reported failure is that removing an `index_together` entry on fields also present in `unique_together` causes constraint lookup to find more than one database object. This is most useful once the trajectory has inspected or modified the schema deletion path, backend constraint introspection, or has reproduced the duplicate match. It is less useful for unrelated index creation, migration autodetector-only changes, generic test-runner setup work, or tasks whose main requirement is avoiding index recreation when moving declarations to `Meta.indexes` rather than fixing the crash during deletion.
experiences.experience: For this cluster, the useful rubric focused on the semantic boundary between deleting an ordinary composite index and deleting a unique constraint. The important observable evidence is that the agent recognizes a unique constraint may also satisfy `index=True` in database introspection, so an `index_together` deletion lookup using only `index=True` can match both the non-unique index and the unique constraint on the same columns. A good rubric should reward trajectories that narrow the index deletion predicate to target non-unique indexes, preserve the existing unique-constraint deletion path, and validate that removing `index_together` leaves `unique_together` intact. It should not overfit to generated suffix names such as `_idx` or `_uniq`, require an exact call-site-only patch shape, or broaden the task into solving all declaration-refactor/recreation behavior unless the trajectory explicitly addresses that separate requirement. Also avoid judging only on successful test commands: in these cases test-runner setup was often noisy, while direct introspection evidence and focused schema-editor reproduction were more decisive.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that deleting a legacy composite index targets only the non-unique index when a unique constraint exists on the same columns. Strong evidence includes identifying the schema editor deletion path, explaining that unique constraints may also be reported as indexes by introspection, adding or proposing a constraint filter that distinguishes `index=True` and `unique=False` for ordinary index deletion, and checking that unique constraint deletion and preservation behavior remain correct.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Non-Unique Index Deletion Disambiguation

recognizes unique constraints can have index metadata
narrows index deletion to non-unique constraints/indexes
preserves unique_together deletion semantics
validates that removing the ordinary index leaves the unique constraint intact
avoid_as_primary_evidence: relying only on generated constraint name suffixes
generic migration autodetector changes without schema deletion disambiguation
test-runner success or failure unrelated to the constraint lookup behavior
treating declaration move/recreation optimization as required for the crash fix

scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory locates relevant schema or migration code and mentions duplicate constraints, but does not identify that a unique constraint can also match an index lookup or does not propose a type-specific filter.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory understands that the same columns have both a unique and non-unique database object and considers filtering by constraint type, but the implementation or validation is incomplete or could still affect unique constraint deletion.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory implements or clearly plans a fix that excludes unique constraints when deleting ordinary composite indexes and checks at least one relevant reproduction or existing test path.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory directly targets the `index_together` deletion lookup with a non-unique index predicate, explains the introspection reason, verifies that the ordinary index is removed while the unique constraint remains, and also confirms unique constraint deletion or other composed-index cases are not regressed.

experiences.title: Do not reward overbroad dotted-name matching for type-comment import fixes
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for Pylint unused-import false positives involving assignment type comments or annotation-only import usage, especially when the trajectory is inspecting astroid Attribute nodes and `_type_annotation_names`-style bookkeeping.
experiences.context: In this Pylint/astroid setting, the reported behavior is a narrow false positive: an import such as `import abc` is used as the receiver of a qualified type comment like `# type: abc.ABC`, while direct imported names like `ABC` may already be handled. A tempting rubric is to reward any trajectory that makes type comments suppress `unused-import`, including full dotted paths and nested imports. That becomes misleading when the visible trajectory starts adding prefix/root matching, `split('.')` checks, full `as_string()` annotation storage, or broad import-check changes, because those can mask genuinely unused imports and drift away from the checker’s existing exact-name annotation contract. The original idea of checking that type comments count as import usage is still appropriate when evaluating high-level diagnosis or reproduction; it should not be expanded into a requirement for arbitrary nested dotted import matching unless the task explicitly asks for that compatibility boundary and the trajectory shows tests proving it is safe.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded trajectories for recognizing imports in assignment type comments and often praised support for nested or full dotted names. That criterion was too broad: agents could satisfy the visible `abc.ABC` sample by ad hoc string matching or by broadening unused-import suppression, while introducing unsafe behavior for unrelated dotted imports. For this kind of issue, generate a rubric that focuses on preserving the existing annotation-name accounting design: an `Attribute` annotation should be integrated by recording the name(s) used by its receiver through the same collector used for other annotations, and the final unused-import decision should not be loosened with prefix/root/full-string matching unless there is explicit task evidence requiring it. Avoid the tempting criterion “handle full dotted paths such as nested modules” as a general success signal. Prefer visible evidence such as astroid node-shape inspection, a minimal localized change to annotation collection, no broad changes to import warning suppression, and validation that truly unused imports still warn.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a Pylint unused-import fix involving imports referenced from assignment type comments, penalize trajectories that broaden the unused-import suppression logic by matching annotation strings, dotted prefixes, or root-module splits against import names instead of minimally integrating qualified annotation receivers into the existing annotation-name collection path. This applies when the visible trajectory proposes or implements changes such as storing full `abc.ABC`/`collections.abc.Iterable` strings as used imports, adding `startswith` or `split('.')` matching in the unused-import check, or treating nested dotted import support as required without explicit task evidence. It does not apply to early investigation that merely inspects dotted astroid Attribute shapes, nor to a task that explicitly requires safe handling of dotted-module imports with corresponding regression coverage.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Overbroad dotted type-comment import suppression

risky_evidence: prefix or startswith matching between annotation names and import names
splitting imported dotted names to match only their root
storing full annotation strings or class-qualified paths as import usage
modifying the final unused-import emission condition instead of only annotation collection
safer_evidence: localized handling of astroid Attribute annotations through existing annotation-name collection
preservation of exact imported-name or alias checks
tests for the reported qualified type comment and for genuinely unused imports

scale.1: No evidence of overbroad dotted-name or prefix/root matching; the trajectory stays within the existing annotation collection contract or is only investigating.
scale.2: Minor speculative discussion of nested/full dotted handling, but no concrete change to unused-import suppression or annotation storage that would broaden matching.
scale.3: Moderate risk: the trajectory considers or partially drafts full dotted-name storage or root-name extraction, but the final visible direction is not clearly an overbroad import-suppression change.
scale.4: Clear evidence of an implemented or planned broadening, such as root-module matching, full annotation-string storage, or prefix matching, with limited validation of unused-import preservation.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory changes the final unused-import decision to match prefixes/roots or arbitrary dotted annotation paths and treats nested dotted import suppression as a success criterion without explicit task need or robust regression coverage.

experiences.title: End-to-End Nullable DB Field Semantics
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go application bug involves SQL scan errors from upgraded data with NULL database columns mapped into non-nullable model fields, and the agent is identifying nullable columns or converting model/caller code.
experiences.context: Applies in Go repositories with struct-tagged persistence models, SQL migrations, and runtime scan errors such as NULL-to-string or NULL-to-time failures after an upgrade. It is most useful once the trajectory has visible evidence of column-to-model mapping, migration nullability, or edits converting fields to pointers/null-safe representations. It should not be used as a generic timestamp-cleanup rubric, should not reward converting every nullable-looking field without task/schema evidence, and is premature if the agent has only listed files without mapping the reported columns to models and usage sites. At final-review stages, the criterion should require implementation completeness and validation rather than mere exploration.
experiences.experience: Rubrics in this cluster were useful when they emphasized the actual nullability contract: identify the reported nullable database-backed fields, represent absent values safely, and preserve behavior at all call sites. The discriminative evidence was visible in trajectories: grep results mapping columns such as nullable metadata timestamps, share expiration, and logged image-file paths to model fields; migrations showing absence of NOT NULL/defaults; model edits to pointer/null-safe types; downstream usages with IsZero, Before, time.Since, address-taking, assignments, API response mapping, token generation, scanner writes, and artwork readers; and build/grep results showing remaining type errors or nil-dereference risks. A better rubric should focus on end-to-end correctness: exact field coverage, safe model/DB representation for legacy NULL rows, nil/zero equivalence where prior business logic expected zero values, pointer-safe assignments using real computed timestamps, no pointer-to-pointer or unconditional dereference, and validation via build/tests or an explicit NULL-load scenario. Avoid tempting but weak criteria such as rewarding broad pre-fix exploration, model-only pointer conversions, converting all nullable timestamps indiscriminately, or passing compilation alone. Also avoid penalizing/crediting unrelated nullable fields unless the trajectory shows they are part of the failure path or persistence contract.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete Nullable Persistence Contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate an end-to-end fix plan or implementation for upgraded rows containing NULL database values: it maps each implicated nullable column from the task/logs and migrations to its persistence model field, chooses a scan-safe representation or DB normalization strategy, updates all consumers to preserve prior zero/unset behavior without nil panics or type mismatches, avoids unrelated schema/API churn, and validates the result with build/tests or a targeted NULL-row loading check.

metadata.environment: Go application with SQL migrations, struct-tagged persistence models, and DB scan errors after upgrade
prioritize_visible_evidence: grep or inspection linking reported column names to model fields and nullable migration definitions
handling of both timestamp and non-timestamp NULL scan paths mentioned by the issue/logs
model or database changes that make legacy NULL values scan safely
nil/zero-safe updates at all observed usages: comparisons, time arithmetic, assignments, API serialization, token/expiry logic, scanner writes, and artwork/file path logic
validation output from build/tests or an explicit scenario with NULL database values
risk_indicators: only changing model field types without auditing callers
using nil where prior behavior required zero-time semantics, or zero-time where absence should be omitted
over-converting unrelated nullable fields without task evidence
repeated command loops or sed-corrupted files without diff/build recovery

scale.1: No meaningful mapping from the scan error to nullable database/model fields, or the trajectory is stuck in unrelated/repeated exploration with no fix direction.
scale.2: Identifies one or two nullable fields or changes model types, but misses reported nullable columns, ignores migration/schema evidence, or leaves most caller semantics unaudited.
scale.3: Covers the main nullable model fields and some caller updates, comparable to the parent trajectory, but visible evidence still shows incomplete usage coverage, questionable nil/zero semantics, unvalidated edits, or possible unrelated conversions.
scale.4: Shows strong end-to-end coverage of implicated nullable fields with schema-backed reasoning, mostly correct pointer/null-safe caller updates, preservation of behavior for set and unset values, and active build/grep/test validation with only minor unresolved uncertainty.
scale.5: Demonstrates a complete, validated nullable persistence contract: every implicated NULL scan path is handled, legacy rows are safe, all downstream semantics are preserved, no unrelated API/schema churn is introduced, and validation confirms the application can load and use rows with absent values without internal errors.

experiences.title: Guard Optional Max-Length Validator Construction
experiences.description: Use when a framework field constructor creates a max-length validator even though internal callers may instantiate the field with no max length, and the trajectory has evidence that the intended fix is conditional validator creation rather than changing the caller.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django-style ORM codebase when the task concerns an internal expression/output-field path that constructs a string-like model field without a max length, causing an unusable max-length validator with a null limit and avoidable instantiation overhead. The trajectory should have visible evidence such as: inspection of the relevant model field constructor, discovery that it unconditionally appends a max-length validator, confirmation that an analogous field already guards validator creation on a non-null max length, and/or a small reproduction showing a no-max-length field has the bad validator and may fail validation. This guidance is most useful once the agent has identified the constructor-level cause or is about to patch it. It is less applicable for unrelated performance work, form-field validators, cases where the field must always require a max length at construction time, or trajectories that have not yet distinguished between fixing the field constructor and special-casing the expression caller.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic invariant: only create a max-length validator when there is an actual max length, while preserving validation for explicitly bounded fields. That criterion aligned well because the visible trajectory repeatedly showed the exact causal chain: an internal string output-field path constructs a bare model field; the constructor unconditionally appends a validator with a null limit; an analogous field already uses the conditional pattern; reproductions show the bare field’s validators list becomes empty after the fix while bounded fields still retain a validator. A better rubric should explicitly judge both sides of the boundary: no validator for the no-max-length/internal-output-field case, and unchanged validator behavior for fields with a real max length. It should also prefer a localized constructor change and avoid rewarding broad proxies such as merely improving timing, modifying the expression resolver to pass a fake max length, stripping validators after construction, removing max-length validators globally, or making sweeping text substitutions that alter already-correct analogous fields. Prioritize visible evidence of scoped implementation, preservation checks, and targeted reproduction over noisy full-suite test failures caused by local test configuration.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement the task-specific Django behavior in the model CharField constructor: append MaxLengthValidator(self.max_length) only when self.max_length is not None. Strong evidence includes a scoped edit in django/db/models/fields/__init__.py within CharField.__init__, no changes to Value._resolve_output_field() that fake or special-case string lengths, no removal of max-length validation for CharField(max_length=N), and validation or inspection showing Value('string')._resolve_output_field() or CharField() has no MaxLengthValidator while CharField(max_length=N) still has one.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Conditional MaxLengthValidator for Optional Length

metadata.required_behavior_without_max_length: No MaxLengthValidator is appended when max_length is None
metadata.required_behavior_with_max_length: MaxLengthValidator is still appended for explicit numeric max_length
metadata.preferred_scope: Localized constructor guard matching existing optional-max-length field precedent
anti_patterns: Changing the expression resolver instead of constructor semantics
Passing an arbitrary max_length for string values
Removing all max-length validators
Accidentally modifying analogous fields that already have the correct guard

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory identifies or addresses the invalid MaxLengthValidator(None) behavior.
scale.2: Recognizes the no-max-length validator problem but proposes or pursues an indirect or risky approach, such as changing the expression resolver or broadly removing validators.
scale.3: Identifies the constructor-level fix but has only partial or unverified progress, or does not clearly preserve bounded-field validation.
scale.4: Shows a scoped change or clear plan to guard validator creation on non-None max_length and includes evidence that the no-max-length case no longer gets the invalid validator.
scale.5: Fully demonstrates the localized conditional guard, verifies the internal string output-field/no-max-length case has no MaxLengthValidator, and verifies explicit max_length fields still receive and enforce the validator without unintended related-field changes.

experiences.title: Do not treat the issue sketch as sufficient for Astropy ITRS-observed correctness
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating an Astropy coordinate-transform trajectory that adds direct ITRS↔AltAz/HADec edges and appears to satisfy the basic topocentric subtract/rotate/add recipe.
experiences.context: This applies in Astropy coordinate-frame tasks where a direct ITRS-to-observed transform is requested to improve nearby Earth-fixed or topocentric objects. A rubric that rewards only raw observer-location subtraction/addition, left-handed rotation matrices, registration, and avoiding ITRS obstime synchronization can be misleading at implementation-review stages: those cues match the motivating sketch but do not prove integration with Astropy’s frame-attribute model, atmospheric observed-frame behavior, or existing transform graph expectations. The basic topocentric recipe may still be an appropriate early-exploration or smoke-test criterion, especially before the agent has inspected existing CIRS/ICRS observed transforms, but it should not be the main correctness rubric once code changes are visible or route regressions have been observed.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics over-rewarded implementations that copied the direct-transform sketch: create a new module, register ITRS↔AltAz/HADec, subtract `location.get_itrs().cartesian`, rotate with minus_x/minus_y matrices, and add the observer back on inverse transforms. That criterion is too narrow for this codebase. In Astropy, a correct direct observed transform must fit the coordinate frame semantics: ITRS may need a location-aware representation rather than being treated only as geocentric Cartesian data; intermediate rotation transforms may need to preserve location attributes; direct observed transforms must choose the correct path when input/output obstime or location differ; AltAz/HADec behavior with pressure/refraction must not silently bypass existing observed-frame semantics; and adding lower-cost graph edges must not break existing GCRS/ICRS/CIRS route-consistency tests. Avoid the tempting criterion that says “never perform any ITRS transform across obstimes” or that raw subtract/add topocentric math is enough. A better rubric should prioritize visible evidence that the agent inspected and integrated with existing frame attributes and transform graph behavior, handled atmospheric/refraction or explicitly preserved existing behavior, and ran targeted regression tests including different obstimes, different locations, pressure/nonzero atmosphere, existing observed-route comparisons, and finite-distance nearby objects.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Issue-sketch-only ITRS observed transform
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that implement only the simple topocentric subtract/rotate/add ITRS↔AltAz/HADec recipe without visible integration with Astropy’s broader coordinate-frame semantics. This flaw is present when the trajectory’s evidence shows a new direct transform module and registration, but little or no handling of ITRS location frame attributes, intermediate transform propagation, atmospheric/refraction behavior for observed frames, transform graph route regressions, or tests beyond basic finite-distance round trips.

metadata.environment: Astropy coordinates builtin frame transforms

Inverse path adds observer EarthLocation Cartesian coordinates
Rotation matrices use apparent left-handed AltAz/HADec sign flips
Manual round-trip tests pass for simple Cartesian nearby objects

Existing intermediate transforms preserve or respect location when needed
Direct observed transforms account for pressure/refraction or explicitly preserve existing observed-frame behavior
Transform graph changes are checked against existing GCRS/ICRS/CIRS observed-route tests
Tests include different locations, different obstimes, atmospheric settings, and nontrivial existing regression cases

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory goes beyond the sketch and visibly addresses frame attributes, route compatibility, observed-frame atmospheric behavior, and relevant regressions.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the direct recipe is central, but the trajectory has begun inspecting or testing frame-attribute integration and existing observed-route behavior.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the implementation mostly follows subtract/rotate/add and has basic round-trip tests, with only partial or uncertain attention to location/obstime attributes, refraction, or graph-route regressions.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory treats the sketch as essentially complete, registers direct edges, and relies on simple manual tests while missing important integration points or observing unresolved route/regression failures.
scale.5: Most severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory only adds raw direct transforms and registration, lacks meaningful regression testing, ignores existing transform semantics, and may add ad hoc handling for edge cases without understanding frame-model compatibility.

experiences.title: Overflow-safe metric formula with count dtype boundary
experiences.description: Retrieve when a scientific Python task reports integer overflow in a metric/statistical formula involving large count aggregates, and the trajectory has located the exact computation or is about to patch it.
experiences.context: Applies in repositories like scikit-learn/NumPy/SciPy where a function computes a mathematically defined score from contingency/count totals and the issue identifies overflow from multiplying or squaring large integer intermediates. It is most useful once the agent has found the relevant function and variables, even if local package builds/tests are failing. It is less applicable during pure repository exploration before the formula is identified, or for bugs about API behavior, model logic, or ordinary floating-point precision where no large integer intermediate is implicated.
experiences.experience: For this cluster, the useful rubrics judged whether the trajectory preserved the Fowlkes-Mallows semantics while eliminating the overflowing integer multiplication. That focus is good because the decisive visible evidence is the agent locating the return expression, recognizing that `pk * qk` overflows before `sqrt`, and planning a mathematically equivalent decomposition that keeps the `tk == 0` branch. However, a stronger rubric should not stop at abstract mathematical equivalence: it should also check that all large count intermediates in the actual implementation are evaluated in a sufficiently wide numeric type, since overflow can occur before the final denominator as counts are squared/dotted or when sparse contingency data has platform-dependent integer width. Avoid generating a criterion that only rewards adding a regression test or only asks for generic numerical stability; those can be premature or too broad when the visible trajectory is still blocked by build issues. Also avoid judging tests run against an installed newer package as decisive evidence for the local patch. Prioritize evidence that the agent patches the actual target function, removes the overflowing product or safely promotes it, preserves zero-case behavior and ordinary-input equivalence, and considers dtype promotion for count-based intermediates.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should move toward a patch in the actual metric implementation that prevents integer overflow in large-count Fowlkes-Mallows-style computations while preserving the defined score. Strong evidence includes identifying the overflowing count expression, replacing or safely promoting the large denominator multiplication so `pk` and `qk` are not multiplied in a narrow integer type, preserving the explicit zero-numerator behavior, maintaining mathematical equivalence for ordinary valid inputs, and ensuring contingency/count data or other squared/dotted intermediates use a sufficiently wide numeric dtype before aggregation. Evidence from standalone algebra checks can support the reasoning, but should not substitute for patching the repository function.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Overflow-safe count-score implementation

target_evidence: actual target function is located and patched
large integer multiplication in denominator is avoided or safely promoted
count/intermediate dtype width is considered for platform-dependent overflow
avoid_as_primary_evidence: tests run only against an installed external package
generic numerical-stability claims without addressing integer overflow
test-only work without an implementation path

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses the overflowing count computation in the target implementation.
scale.2: The trajectory recognizes a numerical issue or writes exploratory tests, but does not clearly identify or patch the actual overflowing formula or preserve the metric contract.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies the correct function and proposes an algebraically equivalent overflow-avoiding denominator change, but gives little evidence about edge behavior, actual patch application, or count dtype/intermediate overflow.
scale.4: The trajectory patches or clearly plans to patch the actual function to avoid the overflowing denominator multiplication, preserves the zero case and ordinary equivalence, and provides some reasoning or validation for large inputs.
scale.5: The trajectory directly patches the target implementation with an overflow-safe formula, preserves all documented edge behavior and ordinary results, and explicitly handles or verifies sufficiently wide dtype promotion for large count intermediates as well as the final denominator.

experiences.title: Direct Environment Lookup Replacement
experiences.description: Use when an Ansible task asks to remove obsolete `ansible.utils.py3compat.environ` usage for environment-variable retrieval, especially in the env lookup plugin.
experiences.context: Applies in an Ansible/Python codebase when the task explicitly identifies a compatibility environment wrapper as obsolete and expects direct `os.environ.get()` behavior while preserving existing lookup semantics. It is most useful once the trajectory has inspected or edited the target lookup/config code and visible evidence includes imports and the retrieval line. Do not apply as a primary rubric when the current stage is only test discovery, when the issue is about unrelated environment configuration precedence, or when the task is specifically a repository-wide py3compat deprecation requiring many call sites; in those broader cases, add separate criteria for all affected call sites and compatibility-module behavior.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases should focus on the semantic replacement: the code path that retrieves environment variables must stop using the obsolete compatibility shim and instead call the standard library environment mapping directly. Strong evidence is a visible diff or file read showing `os` imported, `ansible.utils.py3compat` no longer imported in the target file, and the existing loop still using the requested variable name and default value while changing only the lookup expression to `os.environ.get(var, d)`. The criterion should also check that the surrounding behavior is preserved: requested terms are appended in order, the configured default still flows through, and `Undefined` still raises the same lookup error. Avoid making repository-native test updates the central criterion unless the task explicitly asks for tests; existing tests may mock the old shim and can fail for reasons unrelated to the implementation. Also avoid a vague UTF-8-only criterion: UTF-8 handling matters, but the observable implementation cue is direct use of `os.environ` without added conversion layers.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement the requested environment lookup modernization by replacing obsolete compatibility-wrapper access with direct standard-library environment access in the relevant Ansible lookup path, while preserving the plugin's existing ordering, default, and undefined-variable behavior. Judge from visible trajectory evidence such as inspected source, diffs, or file contents: the target code should import/use `os`, remove the obsolete compatibility import from that target, call `os.environ.get()` with the same variable name and default value used before, and avoid introducing custom encoding conversions or altered term parsing.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Modern Direct Environment Retrieval

metadata.target_behavior: Environment variables are read directly from the standard library environment mapping.
required_visible_evidence: The obsolete compatibility environment import or reference is removed from the target lookup implementation.
The replacement retrieval expression uses `os.environ.get()` with the existing variable and default arguments.
The surrounding loop still appends one result per requested term in order.
Existing default and Undefined/error handling are preserved.
No new text/byte conversion layer is added around environment values.
secondary_evidence: Focused validation may include actual environment variables, UTF-8 values, defaults, or existing lookup tests, but tests are not a substitute for the source-level replacement.
avoid_as_primary: Requiring test rewrites when the task only asks for implementation behavior.
Judging only on UTF-8 examples without checking removal of the obsolete shim.
Rewarding broad unrelated config or plugin-system exploration over the concrete retrieval-path change.

scale.1: No visible evidence that the obsolete compatibility environment access has been identified or changed in the relevant lookup path.
scale.2: The trajectory recognizes the obsolete shim or discusses `os.environ`, but the visible code change is missing, incomplete, or risks altering defaults/order/error behavior.
scale.3: The trajectory makes a partial or plausible replacement, but evidence is ambiguous about import cleanup, exact `os.environ.get()` arguments, or preservation of surrounding semantics.
scale.4: The visible code clearly uses `os.environ.get()` in the relevant retrieval path and largely preserves existing behavior, with only minor uncertainty such as limited validation or incomplete cleanup evidence.
scale.5: The visible trajectory conclusively shows the obsolete target import/reference removed, `os.environ.get(var, default)` used in the existing loop, ordered result/default/Undefined behavior preserved, and no extra conversion or unrelated behavioral changes introduced.

experiences.title: Do not over-scope TLS trust tasks into mTLS completeness
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for a Go/config-backed Redis TLS fix where the requested behavior is custom server trust configuration, inline CA data, and optional verification skipping, especially if the trajectory is still editing config structs, schema, or startup wiring.
experiences.context: This applies to tasks like a Flipt Go service Redis cache backend failing against TLS Redis with self-signed or non-standard CA certificates. A misleading rubric in this setting treats success as providing every possible TLS feature, especially client certificate/key or mutual-TLS support, and may give too much credit to patches that add many TLS fields while leaving config naming, schema generation, validation, formatting, syntax, or tests broken. The original idea of checking TLS option completeness is still appropriate when the task explicitly asks for mutual TLS/client authentication or when the trajectory already has a compiling, convention-compliant implementation and the remaining question is whether all requested trust options are wired into the Redis client.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics asked for custom CA, inline client certificate/key, and skip-verify support as the core criterion.
