Avoid generating a criterion that is satisfied merely by chaining `res.status(code).json(...)`; instead require proof from the trajectory/diff that all relevant shared admin upload validation callers are handled consistently through the established error path or that a local direct response has been explicitly verified to preserve the expected JSON contract.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that frame or implement the admin upload fix as only adding an explicit HTTP status to the local JSON response from the shared upload validator, or that allow 400 for the reported upload failures, without visible evidence that the invalid-file-type path is routed through the project’s existing admin/API error handling or otherwise verified to preserve the required HTTP 500 JSON error contract across shared upload callers.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Status-only upload error fix bypasses established error pipeline

metadata.environment: Node.js/Express admin upload controllers with route-level async error wrapper or central error middleware
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: presence of res.status(...).json(...) on the direct validation-error response
better_visible_evidence: shared upload validator no longer directly sends a successful-response-style JSON error without using established error handling
invalid upload type is thrown or passed to next(err), or a local response is explicitly verified to match the required HTTP 500 JSON contract
all callers of the shared validator remain covered
temporary uploaded files are still deleted on validation failure
the task-specific status expectation remains HTTP 500 rather than substituting 400
global API error formatting is not changed in a way that breaks existing admin response shape

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory clearly routes invalid admin upload validation failures through the existing error mechanism or verifies an equivalent local HTTP 500 JSON contract across shared callers.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory mentions status-code chaining but also investigates the existing error path and keeps the required HTTP 500/message contract mostly intact.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory focuses on adding status codes and only partially considers central error handling, shared callers, or response shape.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the proposed or applied fix is mainly a direct `res.status(...).json({ error })` change, permits 400 despite the task’s 500 requirement, or lacks evidence that all admin upload validation paths follow the expected contract.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory both relies on a status-only local response and introduces broader error-handler/response-format changes or repeated unverified searches that obscure whether admin uploads still return the required HTTP 500 JSON error message.

experiences.title: End-to-End Per-Item Annotation Contract
experiences.description: Use when a web-app task adds optional notes/metadata to individual list or collection entries while some entry types must remain unannotated.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/web template codebase where collection items are stored in heterogeneous seed-like representations, such as object references for real entities and string/pseudo-key entries for subjects or categories. Retrieve this experience once the trajectory has identified the data model, input normalization, edit form, list view rendering, or API/export paths for the collection. It is especially relevant when the task explicitly requires per-item public Markdown notes, safe rendering, editability, persistence, backward compatibility with existing entries, and exclusion of one seed subtype. It is less useful for very early repository exploration before the agent has located the relevant model/template/request paths, and it should not be applied to tasks where all collection items share one uniform representation or where the annotation is only a display-only UI decoration.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics were useful because they judged the feature as an end-to-end data contract rather than as a single UI or type change. In these trajectories, the agent often found the right files and added visible pieces such as a note field, a textarea, or a render block, but the observable work still showed major risks: notes were made required instead of optional, metadata was lost when a stored reference was resolved into an object, subject/string seeds sometimes received or preserved notes, duplicate/removal logic was not consistently by item identity, form parsing/API normalization was only partially handled, and Markdown rendering was sometimes concatenated into HTML without a clear sanitization boundary. A better rubric should therefore focus on whether the agent has preserved the per-item note through the whole lifecycle: request/form/API input, normalization, stored representation, model wrapping/load/save, list editing UI, list rendering, exports/API output, and tests for old entries and excluded seed types. Avoid the tempting but weak criterion of only checking whether a `note` field or textarea was added; that can look like progress while still failing persistence, safety, or subtype constraints. Prioritize visible evidence such as explicit handling of heterogeneous seed shapes, optional/backward-compatible typing or validation, subject-seed note rejection/drop behavior, safe Markdown formatting with existing sanitization helpers, updates to both edit and view paths, and targeted tests or inspection of failing tests around existing seed behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Annotated Item Lifecycle
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show that optional public Markdown notes for individual collection items are implemented as a complete lifecycle contract for real entity items only. Strong evidence includes: preserving notes in the stored item representation without making existing item keys or legacy items invalid; normalizing form/API input so notes are accepted only for real entity items and are dropped or rejected for subject/string items; carrying note metadata through model load/wrapping without losing it when resolving item references; keeping duplicate detection, removal, and membership checks based on item identity rather than note content; exposing editable note fields only where appropriate in the edit UI; rendering notes beneath the corresponding item using the project's safe Markdown/sanitization conventions; and validating compatibility with existing lists, APIs, exports, or tests. The criterion should not give high credit for isolated additions of a note field, textarea, or render block unless the trajectory also addresses persistence, safety, subtype exclusion, and backward compatibility.

metadata.common_false_positive: A patch that only adds a note key to an item dict/type, a textarea in the edit page, or a display block in the view without proving the note survives normalization/load/save and without excluding subject/string items.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that per-item notes are handled beyond unrelated exploration or cosmetic changes.
scale.2: Weak partial evidence, such as adding a note field, textarea, or render block, but with no clear persistence path, no subtype boundary, or no safe rendering/backward-compatibility handling.
scale.3: Moderate progress comparable to the parent trajectory: several layers are touched, but important lifecycle gaps remain, such as incomplete API/form parsing, metadata loss during model resolution, subject/string seeds still accepting notes, or unvalidated template/model changes.
scale.4: Strong evidence that notes are handled across most of storage, normalization, model wrapping, edit UI, and view rendering, with mostly clear subject exclusion and safe Markdown behavior, though some secondary paths or validation may still be missing.
scale.5: Complete visible evidence of an end-to-end, backward-compatible implementation: optional notes persist with real entity items through form/API input, save/load/model wrappers, edit UI, safe rendered list views, exports/API output as applicable, identity-based add/remove behavior, subject/string exclusion, and targeted tests or validation.

experiences.title: Named Target Discovery Under Repository Mismatch
experiences.description: Use when a task names specific components to refactor, but the visible trajectory shows the agent cannot find those named components and the repository appears to be for a different domain.
experiences.context: Applies in Go repository trajectories, especially early or mid-investigation, where the user asks for encapsulation/refactoring of explicitly named clients or packages, but searches over the checkout find none of the named services, no matching directories, no matching imports, and no expected public boundary packages. It is most useful when the agent is at risk of substituting generic exported Client types or analogous internal clients from an unrelated codebase. It should not be used once the named targets have actually been located, when the task intentionally allows broad refactoring of all clients, or during final review of a patch that clearly operates on the intended named components; in those cases, generate rubrics about preserving APIs, compile correctness, and behavior instead.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster focused on target-code discovery and task-codebase alignment: before any encapsulation work, the agent must locate the exact named clients and their call sites, or explicitly recognize that the checkout does not contain them. This is discriminative because the visible evidence repeatedly shows a repository whose module/domain and file tree do not match the requested LastFM, ListenBrainz, and Spotify client architecture, while later attempts drift toward unrelated exported Client-like types. A better rubric should reward systematic confirmation of the named targets or a clear mismatch diagnosis, and penalize proceeding with unrelated refactors merely because some exported Client structs, interfaces, or constructors exist. Avoid the tempting but wrong criterion of 'make any exported client unexported' or 'adapt to actual internal clients present' unless the task text supports that broader scope; this can encourage breaking public package boundaries in unrelated code. Prioritize visible evidence such as case-insensitive searches for the exact service names returning no results, module metadata indicating a different project, empty or missing integration/agent directories, searches showing only unrelated client types, and whether the agent stops to validate repository/branch/submodule state instead of editing analogous packages.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate task-specific target discovery before refactoring: it must search for and attempt to locate the exact named client packages/types/methods and expected public boundary packages from the task, interpret repeated absence of those symbols as a possible repository/branch/submodule mismatch, and avoid modifying unrelated exported Client-like types solely by analogy. Strong evidence includes checking module/project identity, searching exact and case-insensitive service names across source and relevant metadata, inspecting likely integration or agent locations, identifying that found Client symbols belong to unrelated domains, and choosing to verify scope rather than perform speculative encapsulation edits.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Task-Specific Target Discovery Before Refactoring

metadata.environment: Go repository with package-level exported/unexported identifiers
required_visible_evidence: searches for the explicitly named task components and service names
inspection of repository/module identity and likely integration or agent directories
distinction between named targets and unrelated generic Client-like symbols
decision not to refactor unrelated packages when named targets are absent
anti_evidence: editing unrelated exported clients because they share a generic name
unexporting constructors or interfaces used across packages without confirming they are internal
continuing repeated blind greps without recognizing a likely task-codebase mismatch

scale.1: No meaningful attempt to locate the named task components; the agent jumps directly into unrelated code or generic Client symbols.
scale.2: Performs a few superficial searches for the named components but does not interpret their absence and starts considering unrelated packages as targets.
scale.3: Searches for the named components and notes difficulty finding them, but remains ambiguous about whether analogous clients should be edited.
scale.4: Systematically searches likely locations and metadata, recognizes that found Client-like symbols are unrelated, and delays/refuses speculative refactoring pending scope verification.
scale.5: Clearly establishes from multiple visible sources that the named task components are absent or the checkout is likely mismatched, documents the mismatch, checks plausible repository/branch/submodule explanations, and avoids unrelated code changes.

experiences.title: Do not judge sqf fixes by the grouping example alone
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for SymPy sqf/sqf_list trajectories where the agent has already identified that same-multiplicity factors should be combined, especially after manual repros or partial patches.
experiences.context: This applies in the SymPy polynomial factoring environment, particularly tasks involving public expression-level `sqf`/`sqf_list` behavior in `sympy/polys/polytools.py`. A misleading rubric in this setting praises the abstract mathematical requirement that `(x-a)^n*(x-b)^n` be reported as one square-free factor with multiplicity `n`. That requirement is necessary, but after the trajectory already knows it, it is too weak to distinguish a correct patch from a patch that only fixes the sample, changes the wrong layer, drops denominators, changes Poly/expression return conventions, or relies on broad expansion. The mathematical-combination rubric is still useful early, before the agent has understood the square-free vs irreducible-factorization distinction, or as a small subcriterion. It should not be the main final-review criterion once implementation strategy and regression risks are visible.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster mostly said that square-free decomposition must combine same-multiplicity factors. That statement is correct in isolation, but it overemphasizes the easiest visible part of the task. Agents often demonstrated the sample output or added a helper that groups factors, while the visible trajectory showed unresolved risks: edits in low-level sqfree algorithms despite evidence they already worked, whole-expression expansion that bypassed symbolic numerator/denominator handling, empty or unsubmitted diffs after manual experiments, failing existing tests, repeated probing without code, or confusion over Poly vs Expr output. A better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory is converging on a robust public symbolic-path fix: conditional sqf-only aggregation in the expression factoring path, with factor_list semantics unaffected and with evidence from tests/manual checks covering the reported factored input, the already-correct polynomial example, `sqf` product reconstruction, Poly input and `polys=True` behavior, rational denominators/frac handling, constants, and nontrivial multivariate expressions if those are part of the visible risk. Avoid a tempting criterion that treats the original grouped output or a mathematical explanation as sufficient progress. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible implementation boundaries, regression-test coverage, and whether the agent noticed and resolved API regressions exposed by test failures.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat the sqf/sqf_list task as solved merely because the reported sample now groups same-multiplicity factors, while visible evidence shows the implementation is incomplete, in the wrong layer, or unvalidated against public API regressions. This includes broad whole-expression expansion without preserving numerator/denominator behavior, low-level sqfree rewrites despite evidence the low-level algorithm already works, post-hoc grouping that changes unrelated factorization semantics, loss of Poly-vs-Expr return conventions, unresolved failing tests, or no actual patch after manual confirmation.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Sample-only sqf grouping masks API regressions

key_visible_evidence: public sqf_list/sqf path vs Poly/low-level path distinction
patch location and scope
handling of factor_list separately from sqf_list
rational denominator and frac behavior
Poly input and polys flag behavior
manual or pytest evidence beyond the original reproducer
presence of unresolved test failures or empty diff
metadata.avoid_as_primary_signal: The reported expression alone returns a combined same-multiplicity factor

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory either has not reached implementation judgment yet, or it clearly targets the public sqf path and validates relevant API boundaries beyond the sample.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the agent focuses heavily on the sample but also shows some awareness of preserving surrounding behavior and has not introduced visible broad or risky changes.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the sample is fixed or explained, but validation is narrow and important boundaries such as sqf vs factor_list, Poly output, or fractions remain unchecked.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the patch or plan uses a broad expansion, low-level rewrite, or post-processing helper while visible tests/manual checks expose unresolved regressions or missing API coverage.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory claims success based on the sample despite an empty/incomplete patch, repeated non-progress probing, unresolved failing tests, or visible regressions in rational, Poly, factor_list, or other public behavior.

experiences.title: Readable enum support via Rego-layer compatibility helper
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go authorization policy task asks for readable identifiers for protobuf enum-backed fields used in OPA/Rego policies, and the trajectory has found that policy input currently carries the raw/internal enum value.
experiences.context: Applies in Go services using OPA/Rego authorization where authentication data is passed as generic policy input and an enum field is currently compared by internal numeric values. The useful stage is after the trajectory has identified the enum definition, the middleware or verifier boundary that passes authentication into policy evaluation, and the Rego/bundle engine paths. It is especially relevant when existing policies or tests imply numeric/internal enum comparisons should continue to work. Do not apply as-is if the product requirement explicitly says the existing input field must become a string, if the policy engine is not extensible with builtins/helpers, or if the trajectory has not yet found enough architecture to distinguish input-shape changes from policy-language extensions.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics correctly noticed that the agent needed a stable mapping from auth method enum values to readable labels such as token, jwt, and kubernetes, and that visible investigation should connect the protobuf enum to the policy evaluation path. However, they were too likely to reward a middleware/input-conversion patch that replaces or augments input.authentication.method with strings. In this code shape, that is a tempting but risky proxy: it changes the policy input contract, may break existing numeric comparisons, may only affect the gRPC middleware path, and does not necessarily cover every Rego engine implementation. A better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory is moving toward a Rego/OPA-level compatibility mechanism: a registered policy helper/builtin that accepts readable labels, maps them to internal enum numbers, compares against the existing input.authentication.method, and is registered for all authorization engine variants. The criterion should prioritize visible evidence that the agent has identified both engine implementations, the unchanged EvalInput boundary, the existing enum numeric representation, and the need to preserve current policy semantics while adding readable policy syntax. Avoid making the rubric require a bidirectional mapping or direct `input.authentication.method == "token"` conversion unless the visible task/context explicitly demands that exact field shape.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Rego-level readable auth method helper preserving input compatibility
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should favor adding a policy-language helper or OPA/Rego builtin for readable authentication method checks, mapping documented lowercase identifiers to the existing internal enum numbers and registering that helper across all authorization engine implementations, rather than replacing the existing authentication.method input field with a string. Strong evidence includes recognizing that the middleware currently passes authentication through, the Rego engine evaluates the provided input without normalization, existing policies may rely on numeric/internal method values, and both local Rego and bundle-style engines need the same extension available.

prioritize_evidence: Identifies the enum-backed authentication method field and its numeric/internal representation in policy input
Identifies that policy evaluation is performed by OPA/Rego over a generic input map
Recognizes compatibility risk of changing input.authentication.method from numeric/internal value to readable string
Plans or implements a Rego-accessible helper/builtin that maps readable labels to enum values
Ensures the helper is registered for every authz engine path used by the application
Tests readable method policies without removing existing metadata/role behavior
avoid_rewarding_as_complete: Only adding a string field in gRPC middleware
Replacing authentication.method with a lowercase string and assuming all policies still work
Using protobuf enum names such as METHOD_JWT as the user-facing readable identifiers
Adding mappings without connecting them to actual Rego policy evaluation

scale.1: No meaningful connection is made between readable identifiers, the enum-backed authentication method, and Rego policy evaluation.
scale.2: The trajectory finds the enum or authz input path but only suggests generic string conversion without considering existing policy compatibility or all engine paths.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies the enum, the policy input boundary, and the need for readable labels, but remains ambiguous between changing input shape and adding a Rego-level compatibility mechanism.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly favors a Rego-accessible helper/builtin or equivalent compatibility layer that maps readable labels to existing enum values, with some attention to preserving current input semantics.
scale.5: The trajectory provides a complete, compatibility-preserving plan or implementation: readable-label-to-enum mapping in a Rego helper/builtin, registration in every authorization engine path, coverage for documented labels and aliases where appropriate, and tests demonstrating readable method policies while preserving existing authorization behavior.

experiences.title: Do not reward broad ImageSet∩Reals math awareness without solution-set and singularity handling
experiences.description: Retrieve when a SymPy trajectory is fixing `ImageSet` intersection with `Reals` and has already identified that real outputs require the lambda imaginary part to vanish, especially if it is editing parameter-root filtering logic.
experiences.context: Applies in SymPy/computer-algebra set-operation tasks where an integer-parametrized complex `ImageSet` is intersected with `Reals`. The misleading rubric pattern is a broad criterion like “the fix must implement the mathematical semantics of set intersection by keeping only imaginary-zero values.” That idea is useful during early exploration, before the agent has localized the handler. Once the trajectory shows concrete edits or debugging around roots of the imaginary part, finite solution sets, complements, or denominator exclusions, the broad criterion becomes too weak: an agent can satisfy it verbally and pass the reported example while still mishandling how roots are combined or how singular parameter values are excluded. The original broad criterion may still be appropriate for a very early stage where the agent has not yet reproduced or localized the issue, but it should be replaced by a more discriminating criterion at partial-implementation or review stages.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster correctly named the high-level mathematical requirement for `ImageSet ∩ Reals`, but they were misleading because they did not distinguish three different parameter-set operations: retaining the union of values where the imaginary part is zero, expanding/representing multiple roots as separate set elements or condition sets, and subtracting values where the original expression is undefined. This caused over-optimistic judgments when the trajectory found the inversion bug or fixed the displayed tuple issue, but then applied the same operation to denominator handling or failed to build a union of all valid roots. A better rubric should focus on visible evidence that the proposed patch constructs the valid base parameter set as: original base restricted to the solution set of the numerator/imaginary-zero condition, with denominator-zero solutions excluded afterward, preserving fallback behavior for unsolved factors. Avoid the tempting criterion that merely asks whether the agent “keeps imaginary-zero values” or “returns the correct reported finite set”; that is not enough when the code has separate branches for realness and singularities. Prioritize evidence from debug output, code edits, and tests showing that realness filters and singularity filters are handled with opposite set operations and that multiple roots/condition sets are represented as a union rather than as a tuple or a single arbitrary condition.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Conflates realness roots with singularity exclusions
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that edit or propose the `ImageSet`-with-`Reals` intersection logic but only address the visible complement/finite-set symptom, without correctly separating the parameter set for real outputs from the parameter values where the expression is undefined. This flaw is present when the trajectory intersects with denominator roots instead of subtracting them, subtracts imaginary-zero roots instead of retaining their union, wraps a tuple of roots as one finite-set element, drops the original base-domain restriction, or replaces unsolved factors with a single imprecise condition rather than a union/fallback solution set.

metadata.environment: SymPy set intersection / computer algebra
visible_evidence: trajectory is in or beyond implementation/debugging of ImageSet intersected with Reals
edits or planned edits manipulate base parameter sets using roots of an imaginary part
there is denominator or singularity handling in the same code path, or no evidence that such handling was considered
tests focus only on the reported polynomial example and do not exercise undefined parameter values or fallback conditions
metadata.better_focus: Check whether the agent builds a valid parameter set by intersecting the original base domain with the union of imaginary-zero solutions, then subtracting denominator-zero solutions, preserving multiple roots and condition-set fallbacks.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory clearly distinguishes imaginary-zero filtering from denominator exclusion and preserves correct union/fallback behavior.
scale.2: Minor risk only: the trajectory states the right separation but has not yet fully validated singularities or fallback cases.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory fixes the reported example but visible evidence is incomplete about denominator-zero values, multiple roots, or condition-set handling.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory applies the same set operation to realness roots and denominator roots, or constructs finite roots in a way that can collapse multiple roots into one tuple element.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory explicitly inverts one of the required set operations, drops base-domain restrictions, or replaces robust solution-set construction with a change that only makes the reported example appear correct.

experiences.title: Do not over-credit signal formatting when SIGTERM still follows the error path
experiences.description: Use this when a qutebrowser/Qt guiprocess task asks to improve signal-termination messages and the trajectory is focused on mapping signal numbers or formatting strings, especially before there is visible evidence that controlled termination changes message severity and verbosity behavior.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/qutebrowser code using Qt QProcess, where signal-ended child processes arrive as a crash exit status with an exit code that may be the signal number. The misleading rubric pattern is to require or reward broad signal-name mapping and crash-vs-termination classification lists as if that alone solves the task. That can be insufficient or misleading when the visible trajectory only edits outcome string/state helpers, is still in exploration, repeats greps, or assumes shell-style 128+signal codes without verifying QProcess behavior. The original idea of checking signal-name formatting is still useful once there is concrete implementation evidence, but it should be secondary to whether the user-facing finish path treats controlled termination, especially SIGTERM, as neutral and respects verbose/non-verbose messaging.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked for mapping SIGSEGV/SIGTERM and many other signals, classifying crash versus termination, and formatting messages with status and signal names. That criterion is partly relevant, but it led judgments toward over-optimism because several trajectories either had no applied patch or only changed ProcessOutcome.__str__/state_str while leaving the finished-message path to emit error notifications for SIGTERM. Some rubrics also tempted the agent to implement broad signal taxonomies or 128+signal exit-code logic, even though the task evidence and expected examples hinge on QProcess’s delivered code and on SIGTERM’s neutral handling. A better rubric should focus on visible evidence that the patch connects signal-aware outcome formatting to the actual finish notification path: SIGSEGV remains an error/crash with status and signal name, while SIGTERM is considered a non-error termination, suppresses the error notification when not verbose, uses an informational message when verbose, and does not regress existing successful/unsuccessful exits. Avoid making “handles many signal categories” or “adds a signal-name helper” the central success proxy unless the trajectory also shows the severity/verbosity path has been updated and the exit-code convention is consistent with observed QProcess behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Signal formatting without neutral SIGTERM finish handling
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear to solve signal termination mainly by adding signal-name lookup or crash/termination string formatting, but do not show evidence that the actual process-finished notification path treats SIGTERM as a neutral/non-error termination while preserving crash behavior for genuine crashes. This includes patches or plans that leave SIGTERM routed through error-message/logging behavior, ignore verbose versus non-verbose notification differences, assume an unverified 128+signal exit-code convention for QProcess, or classify many signals broadly without addressing the specific controlled-termination contract.

metadata.environment: Python qutebrowser code using Qt/QProcess for GUI-managed subprocesses
primary_visible_evidence: Outcome string/state logic for signal exits
Finished-process message severity and verbosity handling
Whether SIGTERM is explicitly treated as neutral/non-error
Whether signal names are derived from the actual QProcess exit code convention visible or tested in the trajectory
metadata.boundary: Do not penalize merely for not handling every possible signal if the trajectory correctly handles the task-critical SIGSEGV and SIGTERM semantics and preserves existing normal-exit behavior.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the visible trajectory updates or plans both signal-aware formatting and the actual finish notification path so SIGTERM is neutral/non-error with correct verbose behavior, while crash signals still produce error/crash messages.
scale.2: Minor concern: the trajectory covers SIGTERM neutrality and finish-path behavior but leaves small uncertainties such as limited tests or minor formatting gaps.
scale.3: Mixed evidence: the trajectory recognizes SIGTERM should differ from crashes and may update state/string logic, but evidence is incomplete that the user-facing finish path and verbosity/error severity are handled.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory mainly implements signal-name mapping or state/string changes while leaving controlled terminations likely to be reported through the existing error path or without respecting verbosity.
scale.5: Severe flaw: there is no applied relevant implementation, or the trajectory is based on an incorrect exit-code convention/broad signal taxonomy and lacks evidence for the required SIGTERM non-error behavior.

experiences.title: Do not treat EC2 instance-ID validation as sufficient when the patch bypasses the existing IMDS client abstraction
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for Go/cloud-metadata tasks where the requested fix is to validate EC2 metadata content, but the codebase already has an IMDS/AWS SDK wrapper, metadata read helper, timeout/error handling, or mockable client abstraction.
experiences.context: In this Teleport Go codebase, the task asks for EC2 availability detection to reject captive-portal HTML by validating metadata content as an EC2 instance ID. A rubric that only checks whether the trajectory queries an instance-id endpoint and matches an EC2 ID format is tempting and partly relevant. However, it becomes misleading when the visible trajectory edits the availability probe by adding a separate hard-coded HTTP request to the metadata IP/URL, manual body reading, and an ad hoc regex, while an existing IMDS client wrapper and metadata helper already handle metadata paths, AWS SDK behavior, bounded reads, parsed metadata errors, and can be made mockable for tests. The original content-validation idea remains appropriate as a behavioral requirement, especially if no cloud metadata abstraction exists or the task explicitly requires a raw HTTP probe. But in a codebase with an established IMDS client abstraction, the stronger criterion should also evaluate whether the fix preserves that abstraction and its compatibility/testability boundaries.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics rewarded trajectories for validating that EC2 metadata content looks like an instance ID and rejecting arbitrary HTTP 200 responses. That criterion is necessary for this bug, but it is too broad and over-optimistic: a patch can satisfy it by hard-coding the EC2 metadata URL and using raw net/http while bypassing the existing IMDS client, configured SDK behavior, shared metadata read limits/error parsing, and opportunities for deterministic tests. For similar tasks, generate a rubric that keeps content validation as one requirement but does not make it the sole success proxy. The better rubric should focus on visible evidence that the agent uses the repository’s existing metadata access path or cleanly extends it, applies a short context timeout, validates the instance-id response, preserves existing helpers and interfaces, and enables mocking or testing of valid/invalid metadata responses. Avoid a tempting criterion like “fetch /latest/meta-data/instance-id and regex-match it” if it would rate a direct hard-coded probe as complete despite bypassing established client configuration and error handling.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Bypasses existing IMDS abstraction with ad hoc HTTP probe
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that fix EC2 availability by adding a separate hard-coded HTTP request to the metadata URL/IP and manual response parsing, instead of using or cleanly extending the repository's existing IMDS/AWS SDK metadata client path with bounded timeout, shared read/error handling, and testable client injection. This flaw applies even if the new code queries an instance-id endpoint and validates an EC2 instance ID, because it may ignore configured IMDS behavior, duplicate metadata access logic, and make regression testing captive-portal responses difficult.

metadata.repository_type: Go service using an EC2 IMDS client abstraction
visible_evidence: Existing metadata client/wrapper or getMetadata helper is present
Patch constructs hard-coded metadata URL or uses raw net/http for availability
Patch does not use existing metadata helper/client for instance-id retrieval
Patch lacks or avoids mockable client injection/testing path
metadata.boundary: Do not apply this penalty when no metadata abstraction exists, or when task/code comments explicitly require a raw HTTP probe and the patch preserves timeout, bounded reads, compatibility, and testability.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory uses the existing metadata client/helper or cleanly extends it with timeout and validation, without duplicating raw metadata access.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory briefly considers or prototypes raw HTTP but final visible direction preserves the existing client abstraction and shared behavior.
scale.3: Mixed evidence: the trajectory validates instance-id content but only partially integrates with the existing abstraction, leaving uncertainty about timeout/error handling or mockability.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory implements availability through a hard-coded raw HTTP request while an existing IMDS client/helper is available, though it still validates the instance-id body.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory duplicates metadata access with hard-coded URL/raw HTTP, ad hoc regex/body handling, no testable client injection, and ignores existing SDK/helper behavior while presenting this as the complete fix.

experiences.title: Status UI Must Be Backed by Authoritative Confirmation State
experiences.description: Retrieve when an email-validation bug involves expired confirmation keys, stale “sent” markers, or UI/status indicators for pending versus expired validation. Use it to avoid rewarding cosmetic status labels that are not derived from the real confirmation lifecycle.
experiences.context: Applies in Node.js/NodeBB-like user email confirmation flows where confirmation codes are stored in expiring database keys, a separate per-user “validation sent” marker or throttle key exists, and the task asks for admin/user-facing tools to distinguish confirmed, pending, expired, or missing email validation states. It is especially relevant once the trajectory has traced both the email backend and the UI/status consumer, or when the agent begins editing templates/controllers to add status labels. It is less useful for purely cosmetic UI tasks, for unrelated email delivery bugs, or at a very early exploration stage before the trajectory has identified how pending confirmation state is stored and expired.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics often asked whether the ACP UI displayed validated/pending/expired/missing email states. That criterion was useful only when the visible trajectory showed no implementation or obvious lack of any backend status source. It became misleading when an agent added template icons, controller fields, or ad hoc status strings: superficial UI progress did not imply correctness because the underlying bug was stale or non-authoritative pending-confirmation state after confirmation-code expiry. A better rubric should require the status indicator and resend/validation logic to be backed by the same authoritative lifecycle: create or maintain a durable per-user pointer to the active confirmation attempt, verify pending state against the still-existing confirmation object and matching email, clear both the pointer and confirmation object when a new validation is sent or when validation/reset/email-change completes, and update status consumers to use that centralized helper instead of reading a stale sent/throttle marker. Avoid rewarding a tempting proxy such as “four UI labels exist,” “email history fallback was added,” or “the admin template changed.” Prioritize visible evidence that the agent replaced direct stale-marker checks with a central pending-validation helper, prevents old confirmation attempts from lingering, and derives any UI/status display from that helper rather than guessing expired or pending states.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should establish an authoritative email-validation pending-state lifecycle and ensure any admin/user-facing email status is derived from it. Strong evidence includes a central backend helper that determines whether validation is actually pending by following a per-user active-confirmation reference to a live confirmation object and, when relevant, matching the intended email; send/resend logic that expires or replaces previous validation attempts before creating a new one; confirmation, reset, and email-change paths that clear pending-validation state consistently; and UI/status consumers that call the helper instead of directly checking a stale sent/throttle marker. Cosmetic status labels or controller fields alone should not count as strong progress unless they are connected to this backend source of truth.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Authoritative Email Validation State

prioritize_evidence: central backend helper for pending validation state
pending status tied to live confirmation data rather than stale sent marker
cleanup/replacement of old confirmation attempts on resend, confirm, reset, or email change
status/UI consumers use the centralized helper
avoid_rewarding_alone: template icons or translated labels for multiple statuses
ad hoc expired/pending guesses based only on a sent/throttle key
email-history fallback without confirmation-state lifecycle cleanup

scale.1: No visible progress toward authoritative validation state; trajectory is stuck in exploration or only repeats searches.
scale.2: Weak progress such as identifying stale confirmation keys or adding superficial UI/status labels, but no central backend source of truth.
scale.3: Moderate progress: some backend status helper or cleanup idea appears, but it still relies on stale sent markers, guesses expiry, or is not wired through all relevant consumers.
scale.4: Strong progress: pending validation is mostly centralized around live confirmation data, with resend or confirmation cleanup handled, though one related lifecycle consumer may still be missing or unverified.
scale.5: Strongest progress: the trajectory clearly implements or plans a coherent lifecycle where pending status, resend, confirmation, reset/email-change cleanup, and UI/status consumers all use the same authoritative validation-state mechanism.

experiences.title: Complete Protobuf Schema Evolution Before Trusting Feature Logic
experiences.description: Retrieve when a trajectory adds or modifies a protobuf field in a Go project with committed generated protobuf code, especially when the agent cannot run the normal generator and begins manually editing generated artifacts.
experiences.context: Applies to Go repositories where protobuf definitions and generated Go files are both part of the source tree, and the task requires adding an additive field while preserving an existing legacy field. It is most useful once the agent has edited the .proto file, attempted regeneration, or touched generated .pb.go code. The criterion is less useful before any schema/API change is chosen, or for tasks where protobuf code is generated only in CI and generated artifacts are not committed. It should be combined with separate feature-behavior criteria when the trajectory has already demonstrated complete generated-code synchronization and is instead at the CLI/server behavior stage.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster focused on protobuf schema evolution completeness: adding a new field to the source .proto is not enough, and manually adding only a struct field/getter is especially risky. In the observed trajectories, agents often encountered missing protoc/Docker/build tooling, then used broad sed or string replacements that corrupted generated Go, inserted new-field handling into unrelated messages, or omitted serialization/deserialization/size/descriptor updates. These visible signs strongly indicate that downstream producers and consumers may compile inconsistently or silently drop the new field over the wire. A better rubric should check for a coherent schema-evolution contract: new field uses a safe new tag, legacy field remains, generated artifacts are regenerated or manually updated across all required generated-code surfaces, manual edits are narrowly scoped to the intended message, and the agent validates with a package/module build or focused tests. Avoid a tempting but weaker criterion that only checks whether CLI parsing splits comma-separated values or whether server code reads the new field; those can look correct while the protobuf transport still loses the data. Also avoid demanding successful local regeneration unconditionally when the visible environment lacks protoc/Docker; instead judge whether the agent either used the canonical generator successfully or explicitly compensated with complete, validated, mechanically consistent manual updates.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a task that adds a protobuf field used by client/server code, the trajectory should demonstrate complete protobuf schema evolution: the source .proto adds the field with a non-conflicting tag while preserving compatibility fields; generated Go artifacts are regenerated with the project workflow or manually updated in all required places for the intended message only; serialization, deserialization, sizing, getters, registration/descriptor metadata where applicable, and struct tags remain consistent; and the agent validates the result with a meaningful build or focused tests. If generation tooling is unavailable, the trajectory should document the constraint and compensate with precise, reviewed, scoped manual edits rather than broad sed/regex replacements.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Protobuf Schema and Generated Artifact Consistency

required_visible_evidence: source protobuf definition changed with a safe new field number
legacy field retained when compatibility is required
generated code updated beyond just struct/getter, including wire encoding/decoding and size logic where applicable
manual generated-code edits are scoped to the intended message and inspected for corruption
validation command run or credible explanation of blocked validation
warning_signs: protoc or make generation fails and the agent proceeds with partial manual edits
only .proto or only generated struct/getter is updated
broad sed/range replacements over generated code
build errors mentioning the new field on unrelated protobuf message types
repeated environment/path inspection instead of addressing generated-code inconsistency

scale.1: No meaningful protobuf synchronization evidence: the .proto is changed without generated artifacts, generated code is corrupted, or the agent ignores failed generation/build errors.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the new field appears in the .proto and perhaps the generated struct/getter, but serialization/deserialization/size/descriptor surfaces are missing or unverified, or manual edits are visibly fragile.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: most necessary generated-code surfaces appear updated for the intended message, but regeneration was not canonical, descriptor/reflection consistency or validation is incomplete, or manual edits have not been strongly scoped and tested.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the schema and generated artifacts are coherently updated, compatibility fields are preserved, manual edits if any are precise and inspected, and relevant packages build or focused tests pass.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the project’s canonical protobuf generation succeeds or a fully equivalent manual update is demonstrably complete; all generated-code surfaces and descriptors are consistent; compatibility behavior is preserved; and focused tests/builds verify the new field is transmitted and consumed correctly.

experiences.title: Buildable End-to-End Go Shadowing Fix for Cache Middleware Wiring
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go server task explicitly involves cache middleware failing to initialize because a short declaration shadows an outer cacher used later in startup wiring.
experiences.context: Applies to Go backend/server initialization trajectories where the agent has found or is close to finding a pattern like an outer cache/middleware dependency variable declared before a conditional, an inner multi-value `:=` assignment that may shadow it, and a later middleware/interceptor registration or nil check that depends on the outer variable. This is most useful after the startup wiring site and downstream consumer have been inspected, or during final review of a proposed patch. It is less useful during very early repository exploration before producer/consumer scope relationships are visible, and it should not be applied to unrelated cache-key, serialization, TTL, or middleware-behavior bugs unless the trajectory shows a concrete Go shadowing issue in initialization code.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics often rewarded identifying the obvious `:=` shadowing and changing it to `=`, which is necessary but too weak once the trajectory has reached patching. In these cases, agents could correctly identify the outer cacher being left nil yet still produce incomplete or non-buildable patches: replacing `:=` can leave another returned value undeclared, adding declarations can accidentally redeclare an existing `err`, and fixing only one server initialization path can leave other cache-enabled entrypoints unwired. A better rubric should judge the whole visible initialization contract: the agent must connect the cache factory result to the same variable later passed to middleware, declare only the newly needed left-hand variables in the correct outer scope, preserve shutdown/error handling, verify the code builds, and audit analogous cache middleware setup paths when the repository has more than one server transport. Avoid the tempting criterion “found the Go shadowing bug” as a final-review rubric; it overvalues diagnosis and a one-line edit. Prioritize visible evidence such as the exact producer/consumer scope relationship, the final assignment/declaration shape, build output, and searches showing all middleware registration sites were considered.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should deliver a complete, buildable Go shadowing fix for cache middleware initialization. It should identify the outer cache dependency variable that is later used for middleware registration, identify the inner short declaration that prevents that outer variable from receiving the initialized cache instance, and patch the assignment so the initialized instance flows to the middleware. The patch must also handle all variables in the multi-value assignment correctly: declare only genuinely new values in the appropriate outer scope, avoid redeclaring an already existing error variable, preserve shutdown registration and storage/cache wrapping, and confirm compilation or targeted tests. If the codebase has multiple cache-enabled server startup paths or transports, the trajectory should inspect them and either fix equivalent shadowing there or justify why they are unaffected.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete Cache Initialization Wiring

required_visible_evidence: outer cache dependency variable is traced to a later middleware/interceptor registration or nil check
inner short declaration causing shadowing is identified at the cache factory call
assignment/declaration patch is buildable and preserves error and shutdown handling
analogous cache startup paths are searched or reviewed when present
Go build or relevant tests are run, or unresolved compile errors are explicitly addressed
common_failure_modes: only changing `:=` to `=` while leaving another left-hand variable undefined
adding a second declaration for an error variable already declared in the same function scope
fixing only one middleware path without checking other server transports
modifying cache middleware behavior without proving initialization wiring is fixed

scale.1: No concrete cache initialization shadowing site is identified, or the work focuses on unrelated cache internals without tracing the middleware wiring.
scale.2: The trajectory suspects Go shadowing and may inspect cache middleware, but has not clearly connected the cache factory assignment to the later middleware registration or proposed a safe patch.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies the correct shadowing relationship and proposes or applies a basic `:=` to `=` change, but has not fully resolved multi-variable declaration scope, build validation, or analogous startup paths.
scale.4: The trajectory applies a buildable scope fix for the identified cache initialization path, correctly handles returned variables and shutdown/error handling, and validates with a build or targeted test, but only lightly checks for equivalent paths.
scale.5: The trajectory provides a buildable, validated fix that assigns the initialized cache instance to the variable used by middleware, declares only necessary companion variables, preserves shutdown/storage behavior, and audits all relevant cache-enabled server startup paths for the same initialization contract.

experiences.title: Central Wrapper Deprecation Boundary
experiences.description: Use when a task asks to deprecate a low-level wrapper/proxy in favor of a public wrapping API and the trajectory has inspected both direct call sites and the central wrapping implementation.
experiences.context: Applies in Python codebases like Ansible where unsafe/tainted value marking is centralized in a helper module, with runtime paths such as task execution and templating calling either a deprecated constructor/proxy or a preferred public wrapper. This experience is most relevant once the trajectory has searched for direct constructor use and inspected the public wrapper’s implementation. It is less useful if the task is only import cleanup, if the preferred wrapper is already known not to delegate to the deprecated API, or if the trajectory is still at repository discovery with no evidence about the central helper’s semantics.
experiences.experience: For this cluster, rubrics that only checked whether direct `UnsafeProxy(...)` call sites were replaced with `wrap_var(...)` were too shallow: visible trajectories often did that while leaving the central `wrap_var` implementation delegating to the deprecated proxy, or while adding warnings in a way that made normal `wrap_var` usage noisy. The better criterion should focus on the deprecation boundary and canonical wrapping semantics: direct use of the deprecated proxy should produce the project’s deprecation signal and remain backward-compatible, but the approved public wrapper should implement wrapping itself using the intended unsafe text/bytes classes, recursively handle collections, preserve `None`, and return already unsafe values unchanged. The criterion should also value removal of stale direct imports/comments after callsite migration, but not make import cleanup the main signal. Avoid the tempting proxy criterion of counting only grep results for direct callsites or accepting a private internal flag that suppresses warnings while still routing the blessed API through the deprecated constructor. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent inspected the central helper, recognized the wrapper-delegates-to-deprecated-proxy problem, changed or planned changes to text/bytes/already-unsafe handling, and validated that direct proxy use warns while normal wrapper calls do not.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Deprecation Boundary and Canonical Unsafe Wrapping
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the preferred public unsafe-wrapping API, not the deprecated proxy, is the canonical implementation path. Strong evidence includes migrating direct runtime call sites to the public wrapper, making direct deprecated-proxy construction emit the project-standard deprecation signal while staying compatible, refactoring the public wrapper so ordinary wrapper calls do not trigger deprecated-proxy behavior, preserving already unsafe values, and wrapping text, bytes, and collections with the intended unsafe marker classes and recursive semantics.

required_visible_evidence: Search or inspection distinguishes direct deprecated-proxy call sites from the central wrapper implementation.
The trajectory addresses runtime call sites that wrap loop/template/result-like values directly through the deprecated proxy.
The central wrapper’s behavior for already unsafe values, text, bytes, collections, and None is considered.
Deprecation behavior is scoped to direct deprecated-proxy use rather than normal public-wrapper use.
Validation or planned validation checks both direct deprecated use and normal wrapper behavior.
avoid_overweighting: Replacing only direct call sites while leaving the public wrapper dependent on the deprecated proxy.
Adding a warning inside the deprecated constructor without checking whether the public wrapper now emits noisy warnings.
Using a private internal flag merely to hide warnings from the public wrapper instead of making the wrapper canonical.
Treating stale imports or comments as sufficient evidence of semantic correctness.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory inspected or addressed the central wrapping implementation or direct deprecated-proxy usage.
scale.2: Finds or edits some direct deprecated-proxy call sites, but does not address deprecation behavior or the public wrapper’s scalar/type semantics.
scale.3: Migrates direct call sites and attempts deprecation signaling, but leaves the public wrapper delegating to the deprecated proxy, risks noisy wrapper calls, or omits already-unsafe/text/bytes/collection semantics.
scale.4: Addresses both callsite migration and most central wrapper semantics, including scoped deprecation and preservation of already unsafe values, with only minor cleanup or validation gaps.
scale.5: Fully establishes the public wrapper as the canonical path: direct deprecated use warns compatibly, normal wrapper calls avoid deprecated behavior, text/bytes/collections/None/already-unsafe cases are handled consistently, runtime call sites are migrated, stale imports/comments are cleaned, and relevant behavior is validated.

experiences.title: Avoid 880-only rubrics when MARC author extraction is a contract refactor
experiences.description: Use this when evaluating Open Library MARC parsing trajectories where alternate-script 880 linkage is only one part of a broader author JSON contract change involving 1xx/7xx aggregation, legacy contributions, roles, and personal_name cleanup.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Open Library MARC parser tasks where the problem statement asks for consistent structured authors from MARC 1xx and 7xx fields and also mentions 880 alternate-script linkage. A misleading rubric in this setting focuses mainly on demonstrating 880 subfield-6 linkage across field types, especially when the visible trajectory also shows legacy 7xx-to-contributions behavior, merge/overwrite risks in edition construction, role punctuation, and redundant personal_name requirements. The original 880-linkage idea remains appropriate as a subcriterion when the trajectory has already addressed the author aggregation contract and is specifically working on linked multilingual names. It should not be the dominant or sole criterion during early investigation or final review if the visible evidence shows unresolved structured-author aggregation or continued legacy contributions behavior.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics overemphasized whether the agent understood or implemented 880 alternate-script linkage across 100/110/111/700/710/711/720 fields. That criterion is relevant but too narrow here: patches can add alternate_names for linked fields while still leaving 7xx creators in legacy plain-text contributions, merging 7xx authors through an overwrite-prone path, preserving the old asymmetric JSON contract, or choosing the wrong primary/alternate name semantics. In this task family, the stronger predictor is whether the trajectory creates one coherent author aggregation path that emits people, organizations, and events from both main and added MARC entries as structured authors, eliminates or bypasses legacy contributions for creator entities, preserves role punctuation only for role subfields, removes redundant personal_name, and handles 880 linkages as part of that same entity-building path. Avoid generating a rubric that rewards broad claims like 'handles 880 across all field types' unless the visible code/test evidence also shows the author array contract is fixed. Prefer a rubric that penalizes superficial linkage work or fixture-updating when the implementation still routes 7xx through legacy contributions, keeps incompatible return shapes, appends dict keys instead of author objects, overwrites existing authors, or leaves name/alternate_names direction inconsistent with the stated contract.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial 880 linkage without unified structured author contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that focus on adding or demonstrating MARC 880 subfield-6 alternate-script linkage while failing to visibly establish a single structured authors array for creator entities from both 1xx and 7xx MARC fields. This flaw is present when the trajectory leaves 7xx people, organizations, or events routed to legacy plain-text contributions; merges 7xx authors by overwriting or otherwise corrupting existing 1xx authors; keeps inconsistent helper return shapes between dicts and lists; updates expectations to match local output without resolving contract mismatches; or attaches alternate_names while retaining the old asymmetric author/contribution behavior. The flaw is more severe if role punctuation or redundant personal_name handling is also ignored, or if the name versus alternate_names choice for linked 880 fields contradicts the task's stated entity contract.

metadata.environment: Python Open Library MARC-to-edition parser
visible_evidence_to_check: whether 7xx fields are emitted as structured author dicts even when 1xx fields exist
whether legacy contributions are removed or bypassed for creator entities
whether author aggregation preserves existing 1xx authors instead of overwriting them
whether people, organizations, and events share a coherent aggregation strategy
whether 880 linkage is integrated into entity construction rather than patched as a standalone feature
whether role subfield punctuation and redundant personal_name cleanup are addressed
avoid_overvaluing: claims of 880 linkage coverage without author-contract evidence
tests or scripts that only inspect alternate_names
fixture rewrites that mask remaining parser contract problems

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory visibly prioritizes and implements a unified structured authors contract, with 880 linkage handled as part of entity construction and no legacy 7xx contributions path for creators.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory discusses 880 linkage prominently, but also shows credible code or tests for unified 1xx/7xx author aggregation and correct merge semantics.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory partially promotes 7xx fields but still relies on fragile merge paths, unclear helper return shapes, or incomplete handling of roles/personal_name while giving 880 linkage disproportionate attention.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory mainly adds alternate_names or 880 lookup logic while leaving legacy contributions, overwrite risks, or inconsistent author aggregation unresolved.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory treats 880 linkage as the main success condition, rewrites tests or expectations around that output, and visibly preserves or introduces broken author JSON contract behavior such as lost 1xx authors, continued plain-text creator contributions, or incompatible return shapes.

experiences.title: Sentinel fallback for duplicated estimator parameters
experiences.description: Use this when a task reports a constructor parameter being shadowed by a method argument and asks for backward-compatible precedence semantics rather than API removal.
experiences.context: Applies in Python library maintenance, especially estimator-style APIs, when the visible task and trajectory identify the same option accepted at object construction and again in a fitting/execution method. The method default currently masks the constructor setting, and the requested compatible behavior is a sentinel default where an omitted method argument falls back to the instance attribute while an explicitly supplied method value overrides it. This is most useful once the trajectory has inspected the relevant method body or started editing it, because the decisive evidence is whether the effective value is resolved before all copy/mutation-sensitive call sites. It is less applicable during pure repository exploration with no implementation plan, when the task explicitly permits removing the method argument, or when the parameter is not used by multiple downstream operations with different precedence sources.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic contract, not just the surface signature: the method argument should become a sentinel, the constructor value should be used only when the method argument is omitted, explicit method arguments must remain supported, and the resolved value must be propagated consistently to every internal operation affected by the option. This criterion correctly distinguishes strong trajectories that change the default, add fallback logic, and replace direct uses of the instance attribute in copy-sensitive calls from weaker trajectories that only change the signature, remove the method argument and break compatibility, or insert the fallback after an earlier operation has already used the wrong source. A tempting but insufficient rubric is to check only whether the method signature says `None` or whether the docstring mentions the constructor fallback; those are easy to satisfy while still leaving mixed behavior. Another tempting proxy is to reward broad grepping of similar estimators, but that only supports diagnosis and does not prove the local precedence contract is implemented. Future rubrics should prioritize visible evidence in the trajectory: the agent identifies the constructor/method shadowing, preserves the public method keyword, resolves a single effective value from sentinel versus explicit argument, and uses that effective value at all relevant downstream call sites before any copy/mutation-sensitive use.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement the duplicated-parameter fix by preserving the method-level keyword with a sentinel default, resolving one effective option value from the explicit method argument or the constructor-stored value, and passing that effective value consistently to every internal operation whose behavior depends on the option. Strong evidence includes edits or a concrete plan showing that an omitted method argument respects the constructor setting, an explicitly supplied method argument remains a backward-compatible override, and no earlier copy- or mutation-sensitive call still uses the stale constructor attribute or stale method default directly.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Effective parameter precedence and propagation

required_visible_evidence: method argument default changed or planned as a sentinel rather than a fixed behavioral value
fallback logic distinguishes omitted method argument from explicit true/false method values
public method keyword is retained for compatibility unless the task explicitly allows removal
the resolved effective value is used at all downstream call sites affected by the parameter
docstring or comments, if changed, describe override/fallback semantics without being the sole evidence
common_failure_modes: signature-only change with no fallback resolution
method argument removed despite compatibility concerns
fallback added after an affected operation has already used the wrong value
some downstream calls use the resolved value while others still use the constructor attribute or stale local default

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory addresses the constructor-versus-method precedence issue, or it moves toward removing/ignoring the method argument without preserving the requested override behavior.
scale.2: Recognizes the duplicated parameter or changes documentation/signature, but does not add clear fallback logic or leaves the effective value ambiguous.
scale.3: Adds a sentinel default and some fallback behavior, but visible evidence suggests propagation is incomplete, occurs after at least one affected use, or does not clearly preserve explicit method-level overrides.
scale.4: Clearly implements or plans sentinel fallback and preserves explicit overrides, with most affected internal uses switched to the resolved value; only minor uncertainty remains about exhaustive propagation or validation.
scale.5: Decisively implements the full precedence contract: omitted method argument uses the constructor value, explicit method argument overrides it, the public keyword remains compatible, and the same resolved value is used before all relevant copy/mutation-sensitive operations.

experiences.title: Do not treat a startup timing tweak as sufficient for multi-path metrics/auth bugs
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go web-service task combines delayed startup metrics with custom Bearer-header authentication, especially when the trajectory finds both a metrics startup call/delay and a middleware that copies a custom auth header.
experiences.context: This warning applies in a Navidrome-like Go repository where metrics have more than one path, such as Prometheus gauge initialization and a separate periodic insights collector, and authentication uses jwtauth plus a custom UI authorization header. The misleading rubric pattern is to judge mainly whether an initial delay was removed or whether a metrics write call was moved earlier. That idea can be appropriate only after the trajectory has clearly established that the delayed collector is the sole reported metric mechanism and the authentication issue is already correctly handled. It is not appropriate when the visible task explicitly contains a second Bearer-token parsing requirement, or when the trajectory has not distinguished Prometheus initialization, scanner/post-scan metrics, and insights collection.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics often rewarded evidence like removing an initial sleep before a collector starts, making WriteInitialMetrics unconditional, or moving a metrics write before background goroutines. These are tempting but can be misleading: in this task shape, a localized timing edit may leave the actual metrics subsystem inconsistent, duplicate or remove initialization calls, fail to preserve handler/collector behavior, or ignore the custom Bearer-token contract. A better rubric should require visible progress on both independent requirements and should check the semantic boundary between header copying/normalizing and token extraction/validation. Avoid a criterion that says the trajectory is good simply because a delay is removed or a startup metrics call exists. Prefer evidence that the agent identified the relevant metrics implementation, updated the startup/handler/scanner integration coherently, preserved build-tag-aware compilation, and replaced blind custom-header forwarding with a parser/extractor that accepts only a valid Bearer scheme and passes the token to JWT verification without relying on an obsolete mapper.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for this multi-issue Go service task when they focus on a superficial startup metrics timing change while leaving either the broader metrics integration or the custom Bearer-token parsing contract unresolved. The flaw is present if visible evidence shows the agent only removes a collector delay, only moves/adds/deletes a startup metrics call, or only normalizes a header string, without verifying the correct metrics subsystem and without replacing blind custom-header copying with validation and token extraction for JWT verification.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial metrics timing fix misses multi-subsystem contract

metadata.task_type: Go web service bug fix
visible_cues: task mentions both startup metrics and custom authorization header Bearer handling
repository contains separate metrics paths such as startup/Prometheus metrics and periodic collector or scan metrics
auth middleware copies or rewrites a custom authorization header into Authorization
trajectory proposes removing a delay, moving WriteInitialMetrics, or adding Bearer prefix without validating the scheme and extracting the token
better_evidence: agent distinguishes which metrics path is responsible for startup-visible system metrics
agent keeps metrics initialization, handler exposure, and later metric updates on a coherent instance or abstraction
agent implements a custom-header token extractor that validates Bearer syntax and returns only the token
agent removes or bypasses obsolete blind mapping middleware when JWT verification can read the custom header directly
agent runs the repository-appropriate Go build/tests, including required build tags when applicable

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory clearly addresses both startup metrics integration and custom Bearer-token extraction/validation, and validates the affected Go packages.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory has mostly correct coverage of both issues but leaves small uncertainty about tests, formatting, or exact startup placement.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory makes a plausible localized metrics timing change or a plausible auth normalization change, but only partially establishes that both task requirements are semantically satisfied.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory emphasizes removing a delay or moving a metrics call while leaving auth as header copying/prefixing, or implements auth superficially while metrics integration remains ambiguous or duplicated.
scale.5: Most severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory produces or plans changes that delete required metrics calls/imports, duplicate startup logic, corrupt files, or entirely ignore one of the two stated requirements while being judged primarily on a superficial timing cue.

experiences.title: Do not reward indiscriminate key-sorting in export streams
experiences.description: Use this when generating rubrics for Go/Cobra export or declarative serialization tasks that add an opt-in sort-by-key flag and the exporter has both backend-enumerated resources and user-specified selection order.
experiences.context: This applies in a Go CLI/export pipeline where a new flag such as `--sort-by-key` is propagated from a command layer into an exporter that builds YAML/JSON documents from backend list APIs. The misleading pattern is a rubric that simply rewards sorting namespaces, flags, segments, and variants by key everywhere. That criterion is only safe for collections whose order comes from backend listing, such as all-namespaces enumeration, flags within a namespace, segments within a namespace, and variants within a flag. It is not safe when namespaces are explicitly requested by the user in a comma-separated order, because the output document stream may need to preserve that user-specified order even when nested resources are sorted. It is also not safe to extend the sorting requirement to semantic/ranked collections such as rules or rollouts unless the task explicitly names them.
experiences.experience: The earlier rubrics generated broad criteria like “stable, case-sensitive sorting by key for namespaces, flags, segments, and variants using slices.SortStableFunc with strings.Compare.” That is partly useful, but it can over-reward trajectories that implement the visible sorting calls while breaking important export semantics. In this task shape, a better rubric should distinguish backend-derived ordering from caller-specified ordering: sort all namespaces only when they are enumerated from the backend, preserve the order of explicitly selected namespaces, sort flags and segments after each full paginated collection is accumulated, and sort variants inside each flag after variants are copied. The rubric should also verify the feature remains opt-in, default output ordering is preserved, and no unrelated rank/semantic ordering such as rules or rollouts is sorted or changed. Avoid tempting criteria that demand unconditional namespace sorting or mention rollouts as a required sorted entity. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence in the trajectory: how namespace keys are obtained (`all` listing versus explicit requested list), where sorting occurs relative to pagination and encoding, whether the flag is threaded without changing default behavior, whether existing conversion logic for rules/rollouts/segments is preserved, and whether validation uses the actual export tests rather than only a compile or help-output check.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for treating the sort-by-key feature as an indiscriminate sort of every exported slice. This flaw is present when the visible implementation or plan sorts explicitly requested namespace documents instead of preserving the request order, sorts only within individual pages before the full collection is accumulated, extends sorting to semantic/ranked entities such as rules or rollouts without task support, or changes default export ordering when the flag is not enabled. The criterion should be applied only when the task and code expose separate paths for backend enumeration versus user-selected resources and an opt-in deterministic export flag.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Overbroad export ordering changes

metadata.environment: Go CLI/exporter producing YAML or JSON declarative documents from backend list APIs
