It should not require successful full-package imports if the environment blocks them, and it should not reward removing unrelated absolute values from FFT-result magnitude or phase logic.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete Signed Window Normalization

prioritize_visible_evidence: agent located the spectral helper normalization block
agent identified `np.abs(window).sum()` as wrong for negative-valued windows
agent considered all coherent-gain normalization paths, not only the initially reported line
agent preserved or correctly reformulated power/density scaling
agent used mathematical or reference-formula validation when full package import was blocked
avoid_overbroad_penalties: do not penalize touching magnitude or complex mode when they share the same window-sum denominator
do not treat failed local imports caused by missing compiled/runtime dependencies as disproving the fix
do not require changing algebraically equivalent real-window squared-power normalization if the main coherent-gain bug is fixed
avoid_false_positive: do not reward indiscriminate removal of `np.abs` from FFT result magnitude, PSD construction, angle, or phase operations

scale.1: No visible progress toward the signed-window normalization issue, or the trajectory edits/tests unrelated `np.abs` usages without identifying the window-sum bug.
scale.2: Recognizes that a reported `np.abs(window)` expression is suspicious, but only inspects or edits a narrow line without evidence of understanding signed coherent gain or negative-window behavior.
scale.3: Matches parent-level progress: identifies the main `np.abs(window).sum()**2` discrepancy for a negative-valued window and begins applying the signed-sum fix, but has incomplete coverage of related coherent-gain paths or limited validation.
scale.4: Strongly addresses the issue by using signed window sums for the main spectrum/PSD normalization, checking other `np.abs(window)` occurrences, and preserving unrelated spectral semantics, with mathematical or reference-based validation.
scale.5: Fully demonstrates the bug with a negative-valued window, compares against the intended reference formulas, updates every coherent-gain normalization path to use the raw window sum, handles density/power scaling correctly, and avoids unrelated `np.abs` changes despite any environment import limitations.

experiences.title: Do not reward a generic early init call when the task requires an earlyinit information pipeline
experiences.description: Retrieve for qutebrowser/Python startup tasks involving Qt wrapper selection, missing-wrapper errors, SelectionInfo formatting, and early initialization, especially when a trajectory only moves/catches machinery.init or edits machinery.py without proving integration through earlyinit.py.
experiences.context: The misleading pattern is a rubric that says wrapper selection must happen early or machinery.init must be called before Qt use. In this repository, the visible baseline may already call machinery.init(args) before earlyinit.early_init(args), so merely preserving or wrapping that call is not enough evidence of solving the task. The important boundary is whether the agent routes the constructed SelectionInfo through the early initialization checks and user-facing fatal error path. A generic early-call criterion can still be useful if the baseline truly lacks any pre-Qt selection or if the trajectory is only at a high-level planning stage. At implementation/final-review stages for qutebrowser, it becomes misleading unless it distinguishes: startup entry point ordering, earlyinit.py ownership of dependency/fatal error reporting, machinery.py no-wrapper semantics, implicit init behavior, and debug/log visibility.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics overemphasized “early initialization integration” as if any early machinery.init call or catch in qutebrowser.py predicted correctness. That led to overly favorable judgments for trajectories that edited only machinery.py, caught no-wrapper errors in the main entry point, added GUI/tkinter handling in the wrong layer, rewrote large startup files, or changed default/autoselection behavior while leaving earlyinit.check_pyqt/check_libraries dependent on global INFO. The better rubric should focus on the information path visible in the trajectory: machinery._autoselect_wrapper should collect per-wrapper import outcomes and return SelectionInfo on total failure; init(args) should return the INFO object and raise the dedicated no-wrapper error only for implicit initialization when no wrapper is available; explicit early startup should be able to receive an INFO with wrapper=None so earlyinit can render the fatal message; earlyinit should import machinery safely, call init(args) near the start of early_init after faulthandler setup, pass the returned info into a renamed/updated Qt-availability check, append SelectionInfo to module import failures, and log the SelectionInfo after logging starts; the main startup should not duplicate initialization after moving it into earlyinit. Avoid the tempting criterion “machinery.init is called before earlyinit” or “qutebrowser.py catches the new error,” because in this task those can be irrelevant or actively wrong. Replacement criteria should prioritize concrete file/function evidence in earlyinit.py and machinery.py, preservation of existing parser/startup behavior, and validation/tests around no-wrapper, explicit wrapper, implicit init, and SelectionInfo string output.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial or misplaced early Qt wrapper initialization
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat early initialization as merely adding, preserving, moving, or catching machinery.init in the startup entry point, without establishing the required earlyinit-owned SelectionInfo/error-reporting pipeline. This flaw is present when visible edits or plans do not show earlyinit receiving the returned SelectionInfo, handling wrapper=None before QtCore/QtWidgets checks, appending SelectionInfo to fatal Qt availability messages, and avoiding duplicate explicit initialization in the main startup flow. Also penalize attempts that add unrelated GUI/toolkit dependencies or broad rewrites of startup/parser files to handle no-wrapper errors instead of reusing the repository's existing early fatal-error path.

visible_evidence_to_check: earlyinit.early_init calls machinery.init(args) near the beginning and stores the returned SelectionInfo
earlyinit Qt availability check accepts SelectionInfo rather than reading only machinery.INFO.wrapper
wrapper=None is handled by earlyinit's fatal error path with the SelectionInfo included
init_log/debug output includes SelectionInfo after logging initialization
qutebrowser.py no longer performs a duplicate explicit machinery.init(args) after earlyinit owns the call
machinery.init returns INFO and distinguishes explicit startup from implicit no-arg initialization
avoid_rewarding: only adding a dedicated error class in machinery.py
only catching no-wrapper errors in qutebrowser.py
only asserting machinery.init is before earlyinit when that was already true
rewriting parser/startup/error-display code without preserving existing behavior

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory explicitly connects machinery SelectionInfo to earlyinit's Qt availability/error path, preserves startup/parser behavior, and avoids duplicate or misplaced initialization.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory mostly integrates through earlyinit but leaves a small ambiguity, such as not yet showing the debug log addition or not fully validating duplicate initialization removal.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory improves machinery error/SelectionInfo behavior and mentions early initialization, but visible edits do not clearly update earlyinit to own the returned info and fatal Qt availability checks.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory focuses on qutebrowser.py or machinery.py only, catches/prints no-wrapper errors outside earlyinit, or rewards the existing early call while earlyinit still depends on global INFO.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory performs broad or unrelated startup/earlyinit rewrites, adds inappropriate dependencies or duplicate initialization, breaks parser/startup structure, and still lacks the earlyinit SelectionInfo/error-reporting pipeline.

experiences.title: Display-only normalization for documented CLI host shorthands
experiences.description: Retrieve when a web framework CLI accepts a documented shorthand host/address but prints an unusable startup URL, especially when the trajectory has found the command parser and banner formatting code.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django-like source tree where the task is specifically about the text of a development-server startup banner for an address shorthand such as `0:PORT`, not a general networking failure. The useful evidence appears once the trajectory has inspected the management command implementation, identified how addr/port parsing stores the host token, and located the banner formatting that prints the URL. It is most relevant during implementation or final-review stages. It is less useful during very early repository exploration before the agent has found the runserver command, or for tasks whose requested behavior is changing actual socket binding, validating hostnames, or rewriting address parsing semantics broadly.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics were useful when they evaluated the core behavioral contract: `runserver 0:PORT` must print `0.0.0.0:PORT` in the startup URL while not disturbing ordinary IPv4, hostname, port-only default, or IPv6 bracket behavior. The strongest formulation focuses on the displayed startup address, because the reported bug is that the browser link says `http://0:PORT/`; merely proving the regex parses `0` as a hostname or changing unrelated server code is not enough. A better rubric should reward visible evidence that the agent found the banner construction, understands `0` is a special documented shorthand, and either implements or plans a narrow normalization used by the banner. It should also check compatibility boundaries such as preserving `_raw_ipv6` bracket formatting and normal address/port parsing. Avoid making the criterion primarily about running a full server, broad regex rewrites, or adding tests only. Also avoid over-penalizing solely because the agent normalizes earlier in parsing rather than with a separate display variable unless the visible trajectory shows this causes a real regression; the observable task requirement is the startup URL, with bind semantics as an important preservation check rather than the only success condition.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a narrow fix for the development server startup URL so a documented host shorthand of `0` in `0:PORT` is rendered as `0.0.0.0:PORT` in the printed banner, while preserving existing behavior for explicit IPv4 addresses, hostnames/FQDNs, port-only defaults, and raw IPv6 bracket display. Strong evidence includes locating the runserver management command, recognizing that `0` is parsed/stored as a literal host token, modifying or planning the banner address formatting or equivalent narrow normalization, and validating the affected case plus representative non-affected address forms.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Startup URL shorthand expansion without address regressions

metadata.target_behavior: Printed development-server URL expands host token `0` to `0.0.0.0` for the same port.
primary_evidence: Inspection or modification of the runserver command's startup banner formatting.
Recognition that the parsed address for `0:PORT` is the literal string `0`.
A code change or explicit plan that uses `0.0.0.0` for display when the stored address is `0`.
compatibility_evidence: Raw IPv6 display keeps bracket handling.
avoid_as_primary_proxy: Only testing the regex without addressing the banner.
Only running or attempting to run a full server.
Broad address parser rewrites not tied to the printed URL.
Requiring a specific patch location when equivalent visible behavior is preserved.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory has identified the startup URL formatting or the special `0` shorthand behavior.
scale.2: The trajectory has found runserver-related code or reproduced that `0:PORT` parses as `0`, but has not connected this to a concrete banner-display fix.
scale.3: The trajectory proposes or partially implements normalization of `0` to `0.0.0.0`, but evidence is incomplete about whether it affects the startup banner or preserves other address forms.
scale.4: The trajectory implements or clearly plans a narrow startup URL normalization for `0:PORT` and checks several ordinary IPv4/hostname/default cases, with no visible major regression.
scale.5: The trajectory cleanly implements the banner display expansion for `0:PORT`, preserves or explicitly reasons about bind behavior and IPv6 bracket formatting, and validates the affected output plus representative unaffected address forms with targeted tests or reliable simulations.

experiences.title: Scoped Disabled Default for Read-Only Password Hash Fields
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django auth-form task asks to make a read-only password hash field use Field.disabled semantics so submitted password data is ignored in favor of initial data.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django repository when the visible task and trajectory concern `django.contrib.auth.forms.ReadOnlyPasswordHashField`, `UserChangeForm`, and the framework-level `forms.Field(disabled=True)` contract. It is most useful once the agent has located or edited the auth forms code, inspected disabled-field behavior, or is validating password tamper preservation. It is less applicable for unrelated form fields, purely rendering-only disabled attributes, tasks that do not involve server-side initial-data preservation, or very early exploration before the relevant field and form-cleaning path are identified. Treat cleanup of redundant `clean_password()`, `bound_data()`, documentation examples, or tests as secondary unless the trajectory explicitly changes them or the task wording/test evidence makes that cleanup central.
experiences.experience: For this task family, the discriminative evidence is not merely that some form is disabled or that a widget has a disabled HTML attribute. The useful rubric should check the field-level contract: `ReadOnlyPasswordHashField.__init__()` defaults `disabled=True` using a default-preserving pattern such as `kwargs.setdefault`, keeps existing behavior like `required=False`, and leaves callers able to pass `disabled=False`. It should also look for evidence that the agent understands the server-side effect: disabled fields are cleaned from initial data, so tampered submitted password hashes do not replace the stored/initial password, including in custom forms that use this field without their own password cleaner. Prior generated rubrics were useful when they focused on this scoped default and tamper-preservation behavior. Rubrics became less reliable when they overemphasized broader cleanup such as requiring removal of `UserChangeForm.clean_password()` or removal of existing `bound_data()`/`has_changed()` methods as mandatory, because the core observable fix can be correct without completing every redundant-code cleanup. Another important failure mode is broad textual edits that insert `disabled` into unrelated auth form constructors; a good rubric should penalize evidence that field-only kwargs are passed to `ModelForm` constructors or other forms. Prioritize visible diff snippets, constructor placement, override checks, form-cleaning inspection, and targeted validation over generic claims that tests were attempted.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluate whether the trajectory implements and validates the scoped disabled-field contract for a read-only password hash field: the field class itself should default to `disabled=True` in its initializer without clobbering explicit caller choices or existing defaults, and the agent should preserve the server-side guarantee that submitted password values are ignored in favor of initial data. Strong evidence includes a localized edit to the read-only field initializer, use of `setdefault` or equivalent override-preserving logic, no leakage of `disabled` into unrelated form constructors, and validation or reasoning that tampered POST data cannot replace the initial password hash. Cleanup of now-redundant password-cleaning helpers is a bonus but should not be treated as the sole indicator of correctness.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Scoped disabled-field password preservation contract

primary_code_evidence: Localized change in the read-only password hash field initializer
Default `disabled=True` applied before or during superclass field initialization
behavioral_evidence: Agent inspects or explains disabled field cleaning uses initial data
Agent validates or reasons about tampered submitted password values being ignored
Agent considers forms using the field without a custom password cleaner
regression_evidence_to_penalize: Broad edits add `disabled` kwargs to unrelated `ModelForm` or auth form constructors
Patch only changes widget/rendering without field cleaning semantics
Patch removes password protection logic without establishing disabled initial-data behavior
Patch breaks existing read-only field behavior or required/default settings
secondary_evidence: Targeted tests or smoke checks for default disabled state and override behavior
Targeted tests or reasoning for `UserChangeForm` password preservation
Optional cleanup of redundant password cleaner or read-only helper methods when done safely

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the read-only password hash field itself defaults to disabled, or the work targets only unrelated rendering/forms behavior.
scale.2: Some awareness of disabled fields or password preservation, but the edit is missing, placed on the wrong object, or risks passing field-only kwargs into unrelated form constructors.
scale.3: Comparable progress to the parent: the trajectory identifies the right field and likely adds a disabled default, but evidence for override preservation, scoping, or tamper-to-initial behavior is incomplete.
scale.4: Strong evidence of a localized override-preserving disabled default on the read-only field, with existing defaults preserved and no obvious constructor leakage; includes reasoning or partial validation of initial-data preservation.
scale.5: Complete evidence of the scoped contract: localized `disabled=True` default with override support, existing read-only/required behavior preserved, no unrelated form regressions, and targeted validation or clear reasoning that tampered submitted password values are ignored in favor of initial data for forms using the field.

experiences.title: Do not reward kube proxy fixes that only prefer one address field or blindly rewrite every source
experiences.description: Use when a Go/Teleport-style task fixes kubeconfig server address selection for `tctl auth sign --format=kubernetes`, especially where generic proxy `public_addr` may carry the web proxy port and there are multiple proxy address sources.
experiences.context: This warning applies to trajectories investigating or patching Kubernetes-format identity/kubeconfig generation in a Go CLI where a selected proxy address is passed through to kubeconfig output. The misleading pattern is a rubric that only asks whether the agent uses the Kubernetes-specific port or `Proxy.Kube.PublicAddrs`, which can overvalue partial fixes that still fall back to generic `PublicAddrs` unchanged, omit `https://`, ignore kube listen/default-port fallback, mishandle registered proxy discovery, or rewrite explicit user-provided `--proxy` values. A general 'use the Kubernetes proxy endpoint rather than the generic web proxy endpoint' criterion is still appropriate, but only if it is framed as a complete source-selection contract rather than as a single-field preference or unconditional port substitution.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster correctly noticed the core bug: kubeconfig generation must not use a generic proxy public address with the web proxy port. However, they were often too broad or too shallow. They encouraged judging success from visible evidence that the agent found `checkProxyAddr`, found `KubeProxyListenPort`, or inserted a priority check for `Proxy.Kube.PublicAddrs`. That is not enough in this code path: a robust fix must distinguish explicit user input from auto-detection, handle local proxy configuration when Kubernetes service is enabled, construct a Kubernetes endpoint with the correct scheme/host/port even when no kube public address is configured, and repair the registered-proxy fallback by parsing the generic public address host and using the Kubernetes proxy port. Avoid generating a criterion that says to intercept all sources including user-provided `--proxy`, because that can break the documented override behavior. Also avoid a criterion that treats `Proxy.Kube.PublicAddrs` preference alone as sufficient; it misses the reported configuration where only generic `public_addr` exists and must be converted to the kube port. A better rubric should prioritize visible evidence that the trajectory has mapped every address source in the command flow and either implements or plans a helper/centralized derivation that preserves explicit overrides while producing an `https://host:kube-port` endpoint for auto-discovered addresses.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that frame or implement the Kubernetes kubeconfig address fix as only preferring a Kubernetes public-address field, only replacing a port in one branch, or blindly rewriting all proxy address sources, without demonstrating the full source-selection contract for the CLI path. The flaw is present when visible evidence shows the agent would leave generic `PublicAddrs` or registered proxy `GetPublicAddr()` values unchanged for Kubernetes format, would omit the HTTPS server URL construction, would ignore the kube listen/default port fallback when Kubernetes proxy is enabled but no kube public address is configured, or would override an explicit user-supplied proxy address.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Incomplete Kubernetes proxy address source handling

metadata.environment: Go CLI generating Kubernetes kubeconfig server addresses from proxy configuration or registered proxy records
visible_signals: patch or plan touches only the local kube public-address priority branch
fallback still assigns generic proxy public address directly
registered proxy discovery still returns `GetPublicAddr()` unchanged
explicit `--proxy` is rewritten instead of respected
address construction lacks scheme or default/listen-port handling
safer_replacement_focus: trace the selected cluster address from command validation into kubeconfig writing
derive local kube endpoint from kube-enabled config, kube public address if present, otherwise host plus kube listen/default port
convert discovered generic proxy public address host to Kubernetes proxy port
parse invalid discovered addresses defensively rather than accepting malformed values

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory explicitly preserves user-provided proxy overrides and handles local kube config, missing kube public address fallback, registered proxy fallback, scheme, and kube port derivation.
scale.2: Minor evidence of incompleteness: the trajectory identifies most source cases but leaves one secondary concern ambiguous, such as exact invalid-address handling or scheme formatting.
scale.3: Mixed evidence: the trajectory recognizes the generic-versus-Kubernetes port issue and at least one correct source, but does not clearly cover all automatic address sources or override behavior.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory proposes or applies a partial fix such as preferring `Proxy.Kube.PublicAddrs` while leaving generic public-address fallbacks unchanged, or rewrites ports without respecting documented override semantics.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory treats any mention of port 3026 or a single field substitution as a complete fix, ignores the command's address-source flow, and would still generate kubeconfigs pointing at a generic proxy endpoint in common configurations.

experiences.title: Conservative required-field projection for ORM cascade deletion
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django-like ORM delete task involves cascade collection SELECTs fetching unneeded columns, especially where the agent is inspecting or patching the deletion collector and related-object querysets.
experiences.context: Apply in Django/Python ORM maintenance tasks where QuerySet.delete() or an equivalent cascade collector materializes related objects and the problem is excessive SELECT column projection, not the final DELETE SQL or database-driver decoding policy. This is most useful once the trajectory has located the cascade collection path or is proposing an only()/defer()/projection change. It is premature during generic repo exploration, and it is not the right criterion for fixes that only change MySQL/client Unicode handling, raw delete SQL, or application-level cleanup. Boundaries matter: a criterion that merely rewards selecting primary keys or the current foreign key is too weak when the collector exposes instances to delete signals, supports custom/select_related querysets, or must traverse further relationships.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics were useful because they aimed at the semantic core: related-object queries during cascade delete should avoid loading unrelated text/blob fields while preserving deletion behavior. They aligned with visible trajectories that either made no progress, repeatedly searched metadata without editing, or implemented naive `.only(pk)`/`.only(pk, current_fk)` patches. However, future rubrics should be more discriminating than a broad 'load only pk/FK' statement. A strong rubric should require evidence that the agent understands where evaluation happens in the non-fast cascade path, restricts fields only when safe, includes all relationship fields needed for further cascade traversal, and avoids deferring fields when user-visible instances may be observed by delete signal listeners or when an existing related queryset uses select_related/custom loading. Avoid the tempting wrong criterion that any `.only()` added to related_objects() is sufficient, or that passing a narrow delete test suite proves correctness. Prioritize visible evidence such as: locating the collector's related-object queryset before truthiness/on_delete evaluation; preserving base-manager filtering and fast-delete decisions; computing required referenced relation fields from model metadata rather than hard-coding only the current relation; guarding against signal-listener and select_related cases; and adding regression validation that generated SELECTs omit nonessential data columns while cascades, signal behavior, protected/null relations, and fast deletes still work.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly converge on a conservative required-field projection in the ORM cascade deletion collection path: related-object SELECTs should defer non-referenced data columns, but only after preserving all fields needed for recursive cascade traversal and only in cases where deferred instances won't be exposed incompatibly through delete signals or custom/select_related querysets. The work should target the collector-side related-object evaluation that causes full-row materialization, not database-driver Unicode behavior or final DELETE SQL, and should include validation that unnecessary text/blob columns are absent from deletion SELECTs while normal delete semantics remain intact.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Safe cascade-delete field projection

metadata.environment: Django-like ORM deletion collector using QuerySet.delete(), cascade on_delete handlers, fast-delete optimization, model instances, and query projection APIs such as only()/defer().
key_visible_evidence: Identifies cascade collection related-object queryset evaluation as the source of excessive SELECT columns.
Restricts non-fast related-object querysets before they are evaluated for on_delete/cascade handling.
Keeps required primary and relationship/referenced fields for further cascade traversal rather than blindly loading only the primary key.
Avoids or guards field deferral when delete signal listeners, select_related/custom related querysets, or user-visible instance behavior require full instances.
Preserves fast-delete eligibility, base-manager semantics, protected/null/on_delete behavior, parent links, and generic/private relation handling.
Validates both behavior and SQL projection, including tests or inspection showing unrelated text/blob columns are not selected.
metadata.common_false_positive: A patch that simply appends only(pk) or only(pk, current_fk) to the related queryset, or changes unrelated generic/backend code, without handling signals, select_related/custom querysets, or fields needed by deeper cascades.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of targeting the cascade collection projection problem; focuses on driver decoding, final DELETE SQL, repeated metadata searches, or unrelated files.
scale.2: Identifies the related-object collection path and projection idea, but proposes only primary-key loading or remains at investigation without a safe implementation plan.
scale.3: Adds or plans a narrow only()/defer() optimization for primary key and perhaps the immediate foreign key, with some delete validation, but misses important safety boundaries such as signal listeners, select_related/custom querysets, or deeper referenced relation fields.
scale.4: Implements or clearly designs projection in the correct non-fast cascade path, preserves fast-delete/base-manager semantics, includes all referenced relationship fields needed for recursive deletion, and guards against signal/select_related cases, with targeted deletion tests.
scale.5: Provides a robust, minimal, well-tested collector-side solution that defers only non-referenced data columns under safe conditions, proves generated deletion SELECTs exclude unnecessary problematic fields, and validates cascades, signals, protected/null relations, parent links, generic/private relations, and fast-delete behavior.

experiences.title: End-to-End Upgrade Semantics for CLI-Driven Dependency Features
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task adds a user-facing install/upgrade option whose correctness depends on plumbing the flag through CLI code into installer and dependency-resolution candidate selection, especially when installed artifacts are currently treated as preferred/no-op candidates.
experiences.context: Applies in Python CLI/package-management style codebases where the trajectory has identified or edited multiple layers: command-line option parsing, command execution argument propagation, install orchestration, and dependency resolver/provider logic. It is most useful once the agent has moved beyond pure repository exploration or has enough visible evidence about existing installed-candidate filtering/preference behavior. It is less useful as a sole criterion during the first few exploratory commands, for tasks that are only about exposing a flag without behavioral changes, or when upgrade behavior is implemented in a single self-contained function rather than through resolver candidate ordering.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics were useful because the task was not satisfied by adding a CLI switch or passing a boolean through one call. The decisive observable issue was whether the trajectory recognized and changed the existing semantics that skip already-installed satisfying requirements and prefer installed candidates ahead of newer compatible remote candidates. A strong rubric for similar cases should require evidence of complete flag plumbing plus semantic integration with dependency resolution: normal installs still prefer/skip installed collections, upgrade mode can select newer compatible versions, already-latest installed versions remain no-ops, dependencies are upgraded only when constraints require it, and pre-release handling continues to be controlled by the existing pre-release flag. It should avoid tempting proxies such as “the flag exists,” “the installer accepts an upgrade parameter,” “all preferred candidates are cleared,” or “messages/docs mention upgrade.” Clearing all installed preferences may be a flaw if it causes unnecessary dependency upgrades; conversely, leaving installed candidates always first may prevent upgrades. Prioritize visible evidence from diffs, inspected code, and agent reasoning showing the option is connected through every layer and that candidate ordering/filtering changes are conditional and compatibility-aware.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete Upgrade-Aware Resolver Integration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate an end-to-end implementation plan or code changes for a collection install upgrade option: the option is added only to the relevant collection install CLI, read safely from parsed arguments, passed through installer entry points, and used by dependency resolution so installed candidates are retained only when they satisfy constraints and are already at least as new as the latest compatible candidate. Upgrade mode should not behave like force reinstall: it should avoid reinstalling already up-to-date artifacts, preserve normal non-upgrade behavior, upgrade dependencies only as required by resolved constraints or explicit dependency-upgrade semantics, and continue to rely on the existing pre-release flag for including pre-release versions.

evidence_to_check: CLI flag is scoped to the collection install command and is not accidentally added to unrelated role/download/build commands.
The parsed upgrade value is propagated from command execution into the collection installer and then into the resolver/provider layer.
Existing skip/no-op logic for installed requirements is conditional on upgrade mode rather than unconditionally treating any satisfying installed version as terminal.

Resolver candidate ordering compares installed/preferred candidates against the available compatible candidates and only keeps an installed candidate first when it should prevent unnecessary reinstall.
Dependency behavior and pre-release behavior are bounded by existing no-deps/pre-release controls instead of globally upgrading everything or including pre-releases by default.
The agent verifies syntax/structure after edits when modifying sensitive parser or function-signature code.
anti_patterns: Only adding a CLI option and passing a boolean to the installer.
Changing user messages without changing resolver candidate selection.
Dropping all installed/preferred candidates in upgrade mode, causing unnecessary transitive upgrades.
Leaving installed candidates always preferred, preventing newer compatible versions from being selected.
Breaking parser branches, function signatures, or existing pre-release/force options while inserting the new flag.

scale.1: No meaningful implementation evidence beyond exploration, or edits are structurally broken and do not establish the upgrade flag behavior.
scale.2: Only superficial CLI or parameter plumbing is present, with no credible change to installed-candidate skip/preference behavior.
scale.3: Some installer-level upgrade handling is attempted, but resolver integration, idempotency, dependency selectivity, or pre-release boundaries remain missing or ambiguous.
scale.4: Strong end-to-end plumbing and resolver-aware candidate-selection changes are visible, with mostly correct preservation of normal install behavior and compatibility constraints.
scale.5: Complete, well-scoped upgrade implementation is visible across CLI, installer, and resolver/provider layers, including conditional installed-candidate preference, latest-compatible selection, dependency/pre-release boundaries, idempotency, and basic validation of edited code.

experiences.title: DynamoDB Native Map Event-Field Migration Completeness
experiences.description: Use this when a Go/AWS DynamoDB audit-log task changes event metadata from an opaque JSON string attribute to a native DynamoDB map attribute and the trajectory has located or edited the event item model, emit paths, read paths, or migration code.
experiences.context: Applies in Go repositories using AWS SDK DynamoDB marshalling, especially when an internal event/item struct is persisted with dynamodbattribute.MarshalMap and existing rows store metadata as a JSON string. The useful stage is after the trajectory has identified the relevant storage struct and at least some write/read/migration paths, or is actively editing them. It is less useful during very early repository exploration before the DynamoDB event backend is located, and it should not be applied to unrelated backends or tasks that only add client-side filtering without changing storage format. Do not require one exact compatibility shape: preserving the old string field, dual-writing during transition, or replacing it can all be acceptable only if old rows remain readable/queryable through fallback or a safe migration.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful rubric in these cases was a migration-completeness criterion for converting event metadata from JSON string storage to a native DynamoDB map. It aligned with visible trajectory quality because incomplete or broken trajectories typically only added a FieldsMap field or one write-site assignment, repeatedly grepped for missing functions, corrupted Go function boundaries, used the wrong Go type, or failed to connect the change to all read and migration paths. A better rubric should judge the end-to-end storage contract: the internal item model must expose a Go map/EventFields-like field that dynamodbattribute will encode as a DynamoDB M attribute; every event emission path that persists audit events must populate it from the authoritative event fields; read/search/session paths must consume the map when present and still handle legacy string rows until migration is complete; existing rows must be backfilled or otherwise handled by an idempotent migration integrated with the repository’s locking/flag conventions; and the trajectory should validate with build/tests or focused test updates. Avoid tempting but weak proxies: merely adding a struct field, adding a non-key map attribute to DynamoDB AttributeDefinitions, manually storing map[string]*dynamodb.AttributeValue inside the persisted struct without understanding MarshalMap semantics, or asserting that query expressions use the new field before the storage/migration contract exists. Prioritize visible evidence in the trajectory: inspected emit/read/migration functions, careful per-path edits rather than broad sed substitutions, correct conversion of typed audit events versus legacy EventFields, old-row compatibility, migration locking/idempotence, and compile/test feedback.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Native Map Storage Migration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate an end-to-end, backward-compatible DynamoDB storage migration for audit event fields: define the persisted event metadata as a DynamoDB-native map via an appropriate Go map/EventFields type; populate it in all event write paths from the correct field representation; update all event read/search/session reconstruction paths to prefer the map while handling legacy JSON-string rows until migration is complete; provide or integrate an idempotent backfill/migration strategy for existing rows using the project’s concurrency/lock/flag patterns; avoid invalid DynamoDB schema changes for non-key map attributes; and validate the implementation with build/tests or targeted test updates.

evidence_to_prioritize: internal DynamoDB item struct/type change uses a MarshalMap-compatible Go map or EventFields type for the native map attribute
all persistent emit paths are covered, including modern typed events, legacy event fields, and batch/session slice writes when present
typed audit events are converted through an appropriate event-field conversion rather than blindly assigning an interface or ignoring conversion errors
read and search paths reconstruct events from the native map when available and tolerate legacy JSON string rows until migration is complete
migration/backfill is idempotent, resumable, integrated with existing startup/lock/flag conventions, and converts old JSON string fields to native map attributes
tests or validation inspect DynamoDB-marshaled attributes or old/new row behavior and the code is kept syntactically/build correct
pitfalls_to_penalize: only adding FieldsMap to the struct or one write path
adding a non-key map attribute to DynamoDB AttributeDefinitions as if it were required for storage
using map[string]*dynamodb.AttributeValue as the persisted struct field without a coherent MarshalMap/UnmarshalMap design
dropping legacy compatibility without a migration/fallback
corrupting large Go files with broad text substitutions or leaving missing functions/braces/compile errors
claiming field-level query support without actually storing existing and new event fields as native DynamoDB maps
metadata.applicability_stage: Most discriminative once the trajectory has identified the event storage struct and at least one write/read/migration path; premature during initial repository search.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of a native DynamoDB map migration, or the trajectory is stuck in unrelated exploration/broken repeated searches with no coherent storage plan.
scale.2: Weak evidence such as adding a map field or touching one emit path, but missing most write paths, read compatibility, migration/backfill, or using visibly wrong types/conversions.
scale.3: Moderate progress comparable to a partial parent trajectory: some correct struct/write/read changes are visible, but important paths, migration integration, validation, or compile integrity remain unresolved.
scale.4: Strong evidence covering the item model, most or all write paths, read fallback, and sensible conversion/testing, with only minor gaps such as incomplete migration orchestration or limited validation.
scale.5: Complete evidence of an end-to-end native map storage migration: correct MarshalMap-compatible type, all emit/read/search/session paths covered, safe legacy-row migration/backfill with project locking/flags, avoidance of invalid DynamoDB schema assumptions, and successful focused validation.

experiences.title: Do not equate any defensive copy with a correct coordinate snapshot
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task involves mutable coordinate/position inputs in a plotting or public API object, especially when the trajectory proposes `np.asarray(...).copy()` or `np.array(..., copy=True)` as a generic defensive-copy fix.
experiences.context: Applies in Python plotting/library code where a two-element coordinate argument is stored for later rendering and may be exposed as a public attribute or reused by helper transforms. The misleading case is a rubric that rewards generic defensive copying of mutable inputs even when the chosen copy mechanism changes API-visible representation, coerces unit-aware or non-numeric coordinate components, weakens shape validation, or fixes only one aliasing storage site. The original defensive-copy idea is still appropriate when the code truly owns a private mutable container and conversion to the chosen representation is already part of the API contract. It is not enough when the coordinate is a public two-value sequence whose component types and tuple-like semantics are expected to be preserved.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics correctly identified the broad aliasing pattern, but they were too permissive: they treated any copy of `xy` as sufficient. In this setting, a robust fix should snapshot the two coordinate values without unnecessarily converting the public coordinate representation to a NumPy array, and should check all delayed-rendering storage paths that can retain the caller's mutable array. A better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory preserves annotation coordinate semantics while breaking aliasing: unpack the coordinate into `x, y` and store an immutable/value snapshot such as a tuple, allow normal unpacking to validate shape, and inspect helper objects that store reference coordinates for offset transforms or arrow positioning. Avoid the tempting criterion "uses a defensive copy for mutable inputs" by itself, because it can over-credit patches that use NumPy conversion, pass narrow manual tests, or validate against an installed package instead of the working tree. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence of API-compatible value snapshotting, coverage of all stored coordinate references used during rendering, and trustworthy local regression checks that mutate the original array after annotation creation.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Coordinate snapshot changes public semantics or misses aliasing paths
reference_golden_rubrics.description: For mutable coordinate-input bugs in annotation/rendering code, penalize trajectories that stop at a generic defensive-copy patch when visible evidence shows the coordinate is a public two-element value or is reused by helper transforms. The flaw is present if the proposed fix converts coordinates wholesale to a NumPy array, otherwise changes tuple/list/component semantics, or only snapshots the main annotation coordinate while leaving another stored reference coordinate used during delayed rendering. The trajectory should instead demonstrate an API-compatible value snapshot of each relevant two-coordinate input, preferably by unpacking into components and storing a tuple-like value, with validation that later mutation of the caller's array cannot affect the rendered position.

evidence_to_check: storage of coordinate arguments for later drawing or transform computation
patch mechanism used to break aliasing
whether public coordinate attributes keep tuple-like/component-preserving behavior
whether helper/reference coordinate storage sites are also considered
whether validation runs against the local checkout rather than an unrelated installed package
metadata.misleading_positive_proxy: presence of np.asarray(...).copy(), np.array(..., copy=True), or generic defensive-copy reasoning alone
metadata.better_proxy: component-preserving snapshot of every delayed-use coordinate reference plus a regression check mutating the original coordinate object

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory explicitly preserves coordinate semantics while snapshotting all relevant delayed-use coordinate references, and validation targets the local code.
scale.2: Minor concern only: the trajectory identifies public/API compatibility and multiple coordinate storage paths, but implementation or tests are not yet complete.
scale.3: Mixed evidence: the trajectory addresses the main mutable coordinate alias but does not clearly justify representation preservation or investigate helper reference coordinates.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory proposes a generic array copy or similar conversion for the main coordinate without considering public semantics, unit-aware components, shape validation, or other stored references.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory repeatedly relies on the generic defensive-copy idea or unreliable validation, changes coordinate representation wholesale, and ignores visible evidence of additional delayed-rendering reference coordinates.

experiences.title: Canonical Config Option With Versioned Backend Key
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task involves a user-facing configuration option renamed for compatibility while the backend/API key changes only for newer dependency versions.
experiences.context: Applies in Python projects like qutebrowser where configuration schema is declared separately from runtime backend argument generation, and the trajectory has identified both the config schema and the version-specific mapping layer. This is most useful once the agent has inspected or begun editing the mapping definitions, variant/version dispatch, and config rename/migration mechanism. It is premature during very early repository exploration, and it may be irrelevant for tasks that only change an internal backend key without renaming the public option or preserving old user configs. It should not be reduced to merely checking for a new version branch or the new backend key; the boundary is whether the same new canonical public option is usable across old and new dependency versions, with the old option handled by the project’s compatibility mechanism.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics correctly noticed the central requirement: a dependency-version split must map the foreground threshold to the old backend key before the API rename and to the new backend key after it. However, as a standalone criterion this was too broad and could overvalue patches that only add a Qt 6.4 variant or only emit the new Chromium key. The better rubric should focus on the distinction between the public config option name and the backend key: the new public option must become the canonical option read by the runtime mapping for all relevant versions, while only the backend key changes at the version boundary. Existing old-option configs should be supported through the repository’s established rename/migration/alias mechanism, not by ad-hoc mutation of config state or by leaving older variants to read only the deprecated option. Also require all version-indexed companion mappings needed by the variant system to be updated and implemented with valid helper APIs. Avoid the tempting proxy of rewarding any appearance of the new backend key, any added version enum, or documentation-only changes. Prioritize visible evidence from the trajectory: mapping entries showing option suffix versus backend key, version dispatch ordering, config schema entries showing a canonical new option and old-name rename, absence of broken/invented helper calls, and tests or inspections that demonstrate both pre-boundary and post-boundary mappings.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a coherent compatibility design where the new public configuration option is the canonical option used by the runtime mapping across dependency versions, while the emitted backend/API key changes at the documented version boundary. Strong evidence includes: the old config name is represented as a rename/alias to the new config name using the project’s existing config migration mechanism; pre-boundary variants read the new option and emit the old backend key; post-boundary variants read the same new option and emit the new backend key; version dispatch selects the post-boundary variant before broader older-version checks; all variant-indexed companion mappings are updated; and the implementation uses valid existing helpers or adds well-formed helpers rather than ad-hoc runtime config mutation. The criterion should distinguish this from partial fixes that only add a new backend key, only expose a new config option, or leave the deprecated option as the runtime source for older versions.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Canonical Option, Versioned Backend

evidence_to_check: runtime mapping separates config option suffix from backend/API key
same new canonical option suffix is used for old and new dependency variants
backend/API key differs only at the specified version boundary
old option name is handled by established rename/alias migration
version dispatch and companion variant mappings include the new version without breaking older variants
visible validation or inspection covers both sides of the version boundary
common_false_positives: new backend key appears only in the newest variant while older variants still read the deprecated public option
new config option is added but not read by runtime mapping for all required versions
old option compatibility is attempted by mutating runtime config state instead of using the config migration mechanism
variant is added without updating every variant-indexed mapping
helper methods are called without being defined or verified

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory handles the public option rename and backend key split; it may only explore files or mention the new backend key.
scale.2: Weak evidence of the version boundary or new backend key, but the public config option, old-name compatibility, or runtime mapping relationship is mostly missing.
scale.3: Moderate progress: the trajectory adds or plans a version-specific backend mapping and exposes the new option, but leaves important ambiguity about older-version use of the new option, rename migration, helper validity, or companion variant mappings.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory mostly implements the new canonical option, old-name rename, version-specific backend keys, and variant dispatch, with only minor validation or documentation gaps.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory clearly shows a valid implementation where the canonical new option works on both sides of the version boundary, the old option is migrated/aliased through existing mechanisms, all variant mappings are complete, and targeted checks confirm the generated backend keys for both old and new dependency versions.

experiences.title: Django grouped queryset default-ordering suppression
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django ORM task concerns `QuerySet.ordered` disagreeing with generated SQL for annotated/aggregate `GROUP BY` queries on models with `Meta.ordering`.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django source tree when the visible task and trajectory involve the `QuerySet.ordered` property, aggregate annotations or `values().annotate()` causing `query.group_by`, and the distinction between model default ordering and explicit `order_by()`. The criterion is most useful after the agent has at least located `QuerySet.ordered` or investigated SQL compiler/query ordering behavior; it can still flag early trajectories that are only repeating searches without understanding the semantic boundary. Do not apply broadly to unrelated ordering bugs, to SQL generation changes where the desired fix is to preserve `ORDER BY`, or to cases where ordering is explicit via `order_by()`/`extra_order_by` rather than coming only from `Meta.ordering`.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster focused on the specific semantic contract: grouped aggregate querysets should not be considered ordered solely because `query.default_ordering` and model `Meta.ordering` are true, since Django’s compiler suppresses default/meta ordering when emitting `GROUP BY`; however explicit ordering must still make the queryset ordered. This criterion aligned well because visible trajectories that inspected compiler behavior, reproduced `group_by` with no SQL `ORDER BY`, or patched the default-ordering branch of `QuerySet.ordered` had decisive evidence of likely correctness, while trajectories stuck repeating greps lacked such evidence. A better rubric should not merely reward finding `default_ordering` or `group_by` strings; it should require recognizing the interaction among `query.group_by`, default `Meta.ordering`, and explicit ordering preservation. Avoid tempting but wrong criteria such as “all annotated queries are unordered,” “set `default_ordering` to false during annotation,” or “tests passed” without checking the behavioral boundary. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent compared `.ordered` with actual SQL, identified that compiler suppression applies only to meta/default ordering, and implemented or planned a minimal change in the introspection property rather than altering unrelated SQL generation.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Rewards trajectories that correctly handle Django grouped queryset ordering introspection: `QuerySet.ordered` should return false when a queryset has `GROUP BY` from aggregate annotation/values grouping and its only possible ordering is model `Meta.ordering`, because the compiled SQL omits that default `ORDER BY`; explicit `order_by()` or `extra_order_by`, non-grouped default-ordered querysets, and empty querysets should retain their existing ordered behavior.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Default meta ordering suppressed by GROUP BY

metadata.environment: Django ORM source tree
key_state: query.group_by is truthy for aggregate/grouped querysets
query.default_ordering can remain true despite SQL lacking ORDER BY
query.order_by or query.extra_order_by indicates explicit ordering that should remain ordered
preferred_visible_evidence: inspection of QuerySet.ordered default-ordering branch
inspection or reproduction showing compiler drops Meta.ordering for GROUP BY SQL
manual or formal checks comparing .ordered and generated SQL
patch or plan that adds a not-grouped condition only to the default Meta.ordering path
boundaries: do not mark explicit order_by grouped querysets unordered
do not require changing SQL compilation to add ORDER BY
do not treat repeated grep output as sufficient understanding

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory understands or addresses the grouped-query/default-ordering mismatch; it may only repeat searches or discuss ordering generically.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory locates `QuerySet.ordered`, `default_ordering`, or `group_by`, but does not connect grouped aggregate queries to suppression of default `Meta.ordering` in emitted SQL.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies that aggregate annotations create `GROUP BY` and that `.ordered` can disagree with SQL, but the proposed fix or investigation is incomplete or risks treating explicit ordering/default ordering incorrectly.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory clearly distinguishes default `Meta.ordering` from explicit ordering and proposes or applies a targeted `QuerySet.ordered` change so grouped queries relying only on defaults are unordered.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory demonstrates the compiler/introspection mismatch with SQL or tests, applies a minimal fix in the default-ordering branch, preserves explicit and non-grouped ordering behavior, and validates relevant regression cases.

experiences.title: DB alias on temporary natural-key instances
experiences.description: Use this when a Django deserialization/loaddata task involves natural primary keys whose `natural_key()` method may traverse foreign keys while loading into a non-default database.
experiences.context: Applies in the Django codebase, especially `django/core/serializers/base.py::build_instance()` and the Python/JSON deserialization flow, when the reported failure differs between the default database and a specified database alias and the traceback shows `Model(**data).natural_key()` leading to a related-object lookup. The criterion is most useful once the trajectory has inspected or reasoned about temporary unsaved model instances, FK descriptors, `_state.db`, `using`/`db` aliases, or the distinction between natural FK field resolution and natural primary-key lookup. It may be premature during initial repository exploration, and it is not the right focus for unrelated natural-key bugs, plain natural keys with no relation access, generic fixture ordering/forward-reference issues, or code paths where the explicit manager lookup already has the alias and no temporary instance relation traversal occurs.
experiences.experience:
For this cluster, the useful rubrics focused on propagating the target database alias into the temporary model instance used to compute a natural key during deserialization. That focus is discriminative because the visible failure mechanism is not the final `get_by_natural_key()` call, which already uses a database-aware manager, but the earlier call to user-defined `natural_key()` on a freshly constructed instance. If that method accesses a foreign key, the related descriptor can query the default database unless the temporary instance carries the target alias in its state.

A strong rubric should therefore ask whether the trajectory identifies and fixes the database context for relation access during `natural_key()` computation, typically by creating the temporary instance, setting its DB state to the deserialization alias, and only then calling `natural_key()`. It should prioritize visible evidence such as: tracing `PythonDeserializer(..., using)` into `build_instance(Model, data, db)`; recognizing that natural FK field deserialization already uses the alias; observing that `Model(**data)` has no DB state; connecting FK descriptor/router behavior to wrong default-database queries; and validating with a non-default load where the default DB lacks the related row.

Avoid weaker or misleading criteria that only require catching `DoesNotExist`, changing `deserialize_fk_value()`, changing user managers, broadening forward-reference handling, or proving success when the default database is populated. Also avoid over-specifying that the returned deserialized instance must have `_state.db` set unless the visible task specifically requires post-build relation access; the essential bug is the temporary instance used for natural-key computation.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should correctly identify and address the need to give the temporary model instance used for natural-primary-key computation the target deserialization database context before invoking `natural_key()`, so that any foreign-key traversal inside `natural_key()` queries the requested database alias rather than the default database. Strong evidence includes distinguishing this from natural foreign-key field resolution, preserving the existing database-aware manager lookup, and validating or planning validation with a non-default database where the default database lacks the related object.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Target DB context for FK-dependent natural-key computation

metadata.environment: Django serializers/deserialization/loaddata with multiple database aliases
metadata.key_code_path: format deserializer -> Python deserializer -> build_instance(Model, data, using/db) -> temporary instance natural_key()
critical_evidence: The trajectory recognizes that `Model(**data).natural_key()` is called on an unsaved temporary instance.
The trajectory connects FK access inside `natural_key()` to related descriptor database routing.
The trajectory uses or proposes the deserialization alias for the temporary instance before calling `natural_key()`.
The trajectory does not misattribute the bug solely to the explicit `get_by_natural_key()` lookup or to natural FK field deserialization.
metadata.validation_boundary: Best validation loads a fixture into a non-default database while the default database lacks the related natural-key row.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory understands the non-default database alias problem during natural-key deserialization; it focuses on unrelated fixture loading, generic exceptions, or repository setup only.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory notices natural keys or non-default databases but misplaces the fix on broad manager behavior, exception swallowing, forward references, or natural FK field conversion without addressing relation access during `natural_key()`.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies `build_instance()` and the `Model(**data).natural_key()` call as relevant, but has not clearly connected temporary instance DB state to FK descriptor routing or has not proposed a concrete alias propagation mechanism.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory explains that a temporary instance lacks the target DB alias and proposes or implements setting its DB state before calling `natural_key()`, while preserving the existing alias-aware manager lookup.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: in addition to the correct temporary-instance DB-context fix, the trajectory distinguishes this path from already-correct natural FK deserialization, avoids masking by default-DB data, and validates or designs validation for loading into a non-default database with the default database empty.

experiences.title: Provider Localization Before Device-Name Fixes
experiences.description: Use when a monorepo task names a specific listing provider or cache API, and the trajectory is still trying to find where the behavior is implemented.
experiences.context: Applies in early discovery or pre-implementation stages for TypeScript/React monorepos where the bug statement gives concrete behavioral identifiers such as a device loader, cached device state, share-id lookup, empty device names, and root-link metadata fetching. The criterion is most useful when the agent has not yet shown reliable evidence of finding the actual provider/test area, or is searching a plausible but wrong product domain. It is less useful after the trajectory has already opened the relevant provider and adjacent tests/actions; at that later stage, rubrics should evaluate the semantic implementation of empty-name resolution and cache preservation instead of localization.
experiences.experience: For this pattern, the useful rubric is a discovery-quality criterion: require the trajectory to localize the actual device listing provider and nearby tests by searching for task-specific identifiers across the repository, then pivoting away from wrong domains when searches come up empty. The previous rubrics were directionally useful because trajectories that only browsed top-level packages, stayed in unrelated share/pass code, or searched generated/cache artifacts lacked the evidence needed to make a correct fix. A better rubric should focus on observable localization evidence: exact identifier searches, broadening from an initially plausible package to the application/source area suggested by device/link terminology, finding the provider that owns loading and cached lookup behavior, and identifying the link-fetching API/hook used by that provider. Avoid a tempting but weaker criterion such as rewarding any exploration of share APIs, any mention of `getLink`, or adding tests before proving the provider was found. Also avoid making the criterion require the full fix too early; at this stage, the discriminative signal is whether the agent has found the right owner of the behavior, not whether it has already implemented every edge case.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Concrete device provider localization
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the agent has found, or is very close to finding, the source-owned device listing provider responsible for loading devices, maintaining cached devices, and looking up devices by share id. Strong evidence includes searching for the task's concrete identifiers across both packages and applications, recognizing when an initially plausible domain has no matching device/link code, avoiding generated cache artifacts as editable source, and opening the provider or adjacent tests/API hooks where empty device names would be resolved from root-link metadata.

prioritize_evidence: Exact or near-exact searches for the loader, cache, share-id lookup, empty-name flag, device fields, and root-link fetching terminology
Search scope broadens beyond an initially wrong package when no matching identifiers are found
The agent identifies source files under the relevant application/device-store area rather than generated build caches or unrelated API types
The agent connects the provider's load path with the link metadata retrieval mechanism needed to resolve empty names
deprioritize_evidence: Only listing directories without identifier searches
Continuing to inspect unrelated pass/share/vault code after repeated no-match searches
Treating generated webpack/cache output as an implementation target
Editing tests or low-level API helpers before locating the provider that owns cached device state

scale.1: No meaningful localization evidence: the trajectory only lists broad directories or remains in an unrelated domain without searching task-specific identifiers.
scale.2: Weak localization evidence: the trajectory performs a few relevant searches but keeps investigating areas that visibly lack the device listing/provider/link behavior.
scale.3: Moderate localization evidence: the trajectory uses task-specific searches and has indications of the correct product/source area, but has not yet opened the provider or adjacent tests that own device loading and cached lookup behavior.
scale.4: Strong localization evidence: the trajectory has pivoted to the likely source area, found relevant device/link modules or tests, and can explain how they relate to loading devices and resolving empty names.
scale.5: Strongest localization evidence: the trajectory has opened the actual provider or immediately adjacent owner code, identified the load/cache/share-id lookup path, and identified the link metadata fetch mechanism needed for empty-name resolution while avoiding unrelated domains and generated artifacts.

experiences.title: Do not treat canonical username substitution as a complete stable-identity fix
experiences.description: Retrieve when a bug involves case-insensitive authentication but downstream registration/association still keys records by username in a Go web service with request context, model, repository, and persistence layers.
experiences.context: This applies when the task asks registration or association to stop depending on case-sensitive username matching and preferably use a stable user identifier, while the visible trajectory shows player/client records are stored, matched, or permission-filtered by username. In this setting, using the authenticated user object is a useful clue, but using only its canonical username at one middleware or service call site is not enough if the data model and repository still persist and query username as the association key. The original idea may be appropriate only for a narrower bug where the schema intentionally remains username-keyed and the task explicitly asks for canonicalization rather than stable identity. At early investigation stages, a rubric can reward discovering raw request username flow, but at implementation/final-review stages it should not mark the trajectory strong unless it addresses the identity key across persistence, lookup, creation, and downstream player-state access.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often said the trajectory should use the authenticated user's canonical username or a stable user ID instead of the raw request username. That wording is too permissive: it lets a superficial patch that swaps request username for canonical username appear correct even though the durable requirement is to stop using username casing as the persisted association key. For tasks framed around stable identity, generate criteria that distinguish canonicalization from true identifier migration. The better rubric should focus on whether the agent recognizes and updates all places where player records are associated, found, saved, filtered, and read by user identity, including schema/model/repository compatibility and regression coverage for mixed-case login. Avoid the tempting criterion that merely asks for `UserFrom(ctx).UserName` or a case-insensitive comparison at the request boundary. Prioritize visible evidence that the trajectory inspected the player data model/repository, found username-based matching or authorization restrictions, planned or made a consistent move to authenticated user ID, considered migration/backward compatibility for existing records, and verified player-state-dependent behavior such as scrobbling/preferences after registration.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that resolve a mixed-case username registration bug only by replacing the raw request username with the authenticated user's canonical username at a middleware or service boundary, while leaving the player association model and persistence layer keyed by username. This flaw is especially important when visible evidence shows player lookup, creation, REST restrictions, or permissions compare a username string, and the task calls for a stable user identifier so player state remains attached to the correct account regardless of username casing or future username changes.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial canonical-username fix instead of stable identity

applicable_when: Authentication succeeds with mixed-case username input
Downstream player/client registration or association uses username from request context
The authenticated user object exposes a durable ID or equivalent stable identifier
Player records or repository filters visibly store, query, or authorize by username
evidence_to_prioritize: Whether the trajectory updates the association key used for player lookup and creation from username to stable user identity
Whether persistence/model/schema or migration/backward-compatibility concerns are addressed for existing player records
Whether all username-based repository restrictions or permission checks for player state are considered
Whether tests cover mixed-case login leading to correct player association and usable player state
metadata.misleading_positive_signal: The trajectory only changes one call site to use the authenticated user's canonical username and passes existing tests that do not exercise mixed-case registration or persistence identity semantics.

scale.1: No evidence of the superficial-fix flaw: the trajectory either has not implemented yet, or it explicitly recognizes username-keyed persistence as insufficient and works toward stable identity across the model/repository flow.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory mentions canonical username as a possible quick fix but also investigates stable IDs, schema, repository matching, or migration implications.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory updates or plans to update a boundary to use canonical username and only partially considers deeper username-keyed persistence or player-state restrictions.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory implements or strongly commits to canonical username substitution while leaving visible username-based lookup/creation/authorization paths unaddressed.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory declares the issue solved after a one-site canonical-username change, ignores visible username-keyed persistence/model constraints, and relies on generic build/test success without a mixed-case identity regression test.

experiences.title: Matrix Column-Insertion Source-Index Invariant
experiences.description: Retrieve when a SymPy-style matrix insertion bug involves columns after an inserted block being copied from the wrong original columns or appearing in wrong rows.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/SymPy repository trajectories for a reported `Matrix.col_insert(pos, other)` regression where the visible symptom is that entries to the right of inserted columns are displaced, especially when inserting multiple columns at a nonzero position. The criterion is most useful once the trajectory has inspected or reasoned about the coordinate-mapping callback/evaluator for column insertion, or has reproduced output showing the post-insertion block is read from the wrong part of the original matrix. It can still be useful during early exploration if the agent has found the relevant implementation and articulated the splice invariant. It is less applicable when the issue is only about dependency setup, test runner availability, shape validation, sparse-only behavior, row insertion, or unrelated Python compatibility edits; in those stages, this criterion should not be replaced by generic environment-progress or broad off-by-one checks.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the exact splice semantics for column insertion: original columns before the insertion point remain unchanged, inserted columns come from the inserted matrix, and original columns at or after the insertion point are shifted right by only the inserted width while preserving their original row coordinates. This was discriminative because the visible bad output and inspected implementation both pointed to a post-insertion source-column formula that over-subtracted the insertion position, causing the right-hand portion of the original matrix to be read from the wrong columns. A better rubric should therefore ask whether the trajectory identifies and corrects the post-insertion coordinate mapping, not merely whether it finds `col_insert`, installs dependencies, runs tests, or describes the symptom as a row shift. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as “fix an off-by-one,” “handle Python 3.10 collection imports,” or “add any regression test”; those may correlate with effort but do not verify the semantic invariant. Prioritize visible evidence such as: inspection of the insertion evaluator’s three-way branch, explanation that result columns after the inserted block map back by subtracting only the inserted matrix width, reproduction showing the right-side identity/block is preserved in the original rows after the change, and avoidance of unrelated compatibility changes in the intended patch.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates the correct column-insertion source-index invariant: for a matrix column insertion at position `pos`, entries before `pos` are copied unchanged from the original matrix, entries in the inserted interval are copied from the inserted matrix, and entries after the inserted interval are copied from the original matrix with the source column shifted left by exactly the number of inserted columns, preserving all original row positions. Strong evidence includes identifying the shared column-insertion evaluator or equivalent coordinate-mapping logic, explaining why subtracting the insertion position again is wrong, and validating with a nonzero insertion position and multi-column inserted matrix.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Post-Insertion Column Mapping Preserves Rows

observable_evidence: agent inspects the coordinate mapping for column insertion
agent distinguishes left segment, inserted segment, and right segment semantics
agent states that right-side original columns shift only by inserted width
agent recognizes that the reported misplaced block comes from wrong source-column indexing rather than row mutation
agent validates or plans validation using a multi-column insertion at a nonzero position
avoid_as_primary_evidence: dependency installation or Python-version compatibility edits
generic off-by-one language without the column-source mapping invariant
test discovery alone without semantic reasoning
changes to unrelated matrix operations

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory understands or targets the column-insertion mapping; focus is on unrelated setup, file browsing, or generic debugging only.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory finds `col_insert` or mentions misplaced columns, but does not articulate how columns after the inserted block should map back to the original matrix.
