scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies the insertion evaluator and describes preserving original columns/rows, but the exact right-side source-column offset is incomplete, ambiguous, or not yet connected to the reported failure.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory clearly states that right-side result columns should map to original columns shifted by only the inserted width and identifies an over-shift/extra-position subtraction as the likely bug.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory both applies or proposes the exact corrected mapping for the post-insertion branch and validates it against a nonzero-position, multi-column insertion case showing the right-side original block remains in its original rows.

experiences.title: Value-wrapper hash/equality contract for unhashable dict/set failures
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python object used as a transparent wrapper for a primitive value fails in dict/set membership because it defines value-based equality but lacks a compatible hash implementation.
experiences.context: Applies in Python codebases, especially framework code, when the task reports `TypeError: unhashable type` during hash-based container operations such as dict membership, dict lookup, set insertion, or set membership, while equality/list membership still works. The trajectory should have visible evidence that the problematic class wraps an underlying prepared/raw value, implements `__eq__` by comparing that underlying value to either another wrapper or a raw value, and currently has no suitable `__hash__`. This guidance is most useful once the agent has inspected the class or reproduced the hash failure; it can be premature during broad repository exploration before equality semantics are known. Do not apply it when the object’s equality is identity-based, when the desired behavior is to make a mutable/unhashable wrapped value hashable anyway, when the failure is better solved by changing caller-side coercion, or when the task concerns list/array membership only.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic contract between equality and hashing rather than merely requiring that an error disappear. They were aligned because the decisive visible evidence was: a wrapper object compared equal to its underlying primitive value and to other wrappers with the same underlying value, but Python made it unhashable because `__eq__` existed without `__hash__`. A strong rubric should therefore ask whether the trajectory makes the wrapper hashable using the same basis as equality, so hash-based containers can find primitive-keyed entries and equal wrappers have equal hashes. It should also preserve the existing string/equality behavior and avoid unrelated widget-level or membership-call-site rewrites. A tempting but wrong criterion is to reward any hash implementation, such as identity hashing, hashing the associated model/object instance, or converting the wrapper to a string in callers; those approaches can either violate the Python hash/equality invariant or narrow the fix to one caller. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent inspected `__eq__`, identified the missing `__hash__`, selected the underlying value as the hash basis, and validated dict/set behavior plus equality/hash consistency. Formatting or exact insertion location is secondary unless the edit corrupts the class structure.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should fix the unhashable wrapper by implementing hashability consistently with its existing value-based equality semantics. The best evidence is that the agent recognizes the class defines equality against both another wrapper and the wrapped raw/prepared value, adds or plans a `__hash__` based on that same wrapped value, and validates that dict/set membership or lookup works without changing the wrapper’s comparison or string behavior. The criterion should distinguish this from identity-based hashing, hashing unrelated associated objects, caller-side coercion, or list-membership-only tests.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Consistent hash for value-based wrapper equality

required_visible_evidence: problem involves a Python object failing in hash-based containers with an unhashable-type error
trajectory identifies a wrapper class or value object with custom value-based equality
trajectory recognizes that equality compares using the wrapped/raw/prepared value
proposed or applied fix makes the object hashable using the same equality basis
validation or reasoning covers dict/set membership or lookup, not only list membership
avoid_credit_for: identity-based hash when equality is value-based
hashing an associated instance/object ignored by equality
rewriting only a widget/caller to coerce values
changing equality or string behavior unnecessarily
tests that only demonstrate list membership or equality

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory identifies the hash/equality contract; it treats the issue generically or works only around one caller without addressing the unhashable wrapper.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory notices hashability or adds a hash-like change, but does not clearly connect the hash basis to existing equality semantics or risks hashing identity/unrelated state.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory understands the missing-hash cause and proposes making the wrapper hashable, but validation or reasoning about equality with raw values and equal wrappers is incomplete.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory implements or clearly plans a hash based on the wrapped value, preserving existing equality behavior, and checks dict/set behavior for the reported failure mode.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory explicitly preserves the Python invariant that equal wrappers/raw values have compatible hashes, avoids identity or instance-based hashing, and validates dict/set lookup plus equality/hash consistency without unrelated behavioral changes.

experiences.title: Do Not Treat a Missing Permanent Regression Test as Proof of an Incorrect Fix
experiences.description: Use when a rubric generator is about to make the presence of a repository-native regression test the decisive criterion during an intermediate implementation trajectory.
experiences.context: In framework maintenance tasks, an agent may first use focused reproductions or scratch tests while locating and correcting the behavioral defect. The absence of a committed test at such a cutoff is weak evidence about implementation correctness. A test-integration criterion becomes appropriate near claimed completion when tests are explicitly required or when no behavior-level validation exists at all.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics over-weighted a very specific permanent multi-database test artifact, so useful diagnosis and implementation evidence looked poor simply because test integration had not happened yet. A better criterion should inspect whether the agent is validating database routing and natural-key behavior against the reported boundary. Avoid using exact test placement as a proxy for patch correctness; penalize only claimed completion with no meaningful behavioral validation or with a still-reproducing defect.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Claimed Completion Without Database-Routing Validation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize a trajectory only when it presents the fixture/deserialization fix as complete while visible checks do not exercise the target database routing and natural-key dependency, or when those checks still reproduce lookup against the wrong database. Do not penalize an intermediate trajectory merely because validation is currently ad hoc rather than committed to the repository test suite.

observable_evidence: trajectory stage and completion claims
target-database fixture or reproduction commands
observed lookup database and test outcome
correction after failed validation

scale.1: No visible evidence of an unresolved database-routing defect being presented as complete; the available implementation and validation evidence is consistent with the required behavior.
scale.2: A minor or early-stage concern about an unresolved database-routing defect being presented as complete is visible, but it is not confirmed and the trajectory is still actively resolving it.
scale.3: Evidence about an unresolved database-routing defect being presented as complete is mixed or incomplete; the concern remains plausible but is not yet decisive.
scale.4: Clear visible evidence indicates an unresolved database-routing defect being presented as complete, with no convincing correction or validation yet.
scale.5: The trajectory directly reproduces or validates an unresolved database-routing defect being presented as complete, or claims completion while the contradiction remains unresolved.

experiences.title: Do not equate exact parameter-wiring shape with effective user opt-out
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for an Ansible/Python fix that adds a boolean authentication option through shared URL helpers, especially when the module builds its options from a shared argument spec and delegates to helper functions.
experiences.context: This applies in Ansible-style module code where a user-facing module such as `uri` delegates request handling to shared utilities like `url_argument_spec()`, `fetch_url()`, `open_url()`, and a `Request.open()` method. A tempting rubric is to require a specific checklist such as declaring the option directly in the module's local `argument_spec`, adding it to every wrapper signature, and updating every consumer of the shared utility. That checklist can be misleading when the module already imports a shared argument spec, when `fetch_url()` reads values from `module.params`, or when the visible trajectory is still early exploration. The original idea remains useful at final-review stage if the task explicitly requires a public option and there is visible code showing incomplete or incompatible propagation; it should not be used as a rigid proxy for correctness when alternative plumbing makes the option available and effective.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often rewarded or penalized trajectories based on whether `use_netrc` appeared at named call-chain locations or was declared directly in the `uri` module. That can understate good trajectories because adding the option to the shared URL argument spec may already expose it to the module, and passing `module.params['use_netrc']` directly to `fetch_url()` can be sufficient without changing an intermediate helper signature. It can also overstate bad trajectories because superficial appearances of threading do not guarantee that `use_netrc: false` actually reaches the `.netrc` lookup; for example, a gate that checks an object default instead of the resolved per-call value leaves the opt-out ineffective. A better rubric should focus on semantic evidence: the user can set the option through the module's effective argument spec, the value read from `module.params` or an explicit argument reaches the request-opening logic, the `.netrc` lookup and Basic `Authorization` overwrite are skipped only when the option is false, and the default continues to preserve existing behavior. Avoid making “declared directly in the module-local `argument_spec`” or “all shared utility consumers were updated” mandatory unless visible repository structure or task text makes those exact integration points necessary.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial netrc opt-out wiring without effective behavior
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear to add a `use_netrc` or equivalent boolean but leave visible evidence that setting it false from the user-facing module would not actually prevent the `.netrc` fallback from assigning a Basic `Authorization` header. This includes gating the netrc block on an unchanging constructor default instead of the resolved per-call value, adding a helper parameter without reading the module's effective params, passing `None` in a way that re-enables the default unexpectedly, or exposing documentation without an effective argument spec. Do not penalize merely because the option is supplied by a shared argument spec rather than repeated directly in the module, or because the implementation uses a different but semantically equivalent path to pass the flag.

metadata.environment: Ansible/Python module and shared URL helper stack
primary_evidence: effective user-facing option source, including shared argument spec usage
module params or explicit arguments flow into request helper
netrc lookup and Authorization overwrite are guarded by the resolved option
default behavior remains enabled when option is unspecified
avoid_as_required_proxy: direct local argument_spec declaration when shared url_argument_spec is used
exact signature placement or exact number of call-chain layers
updates to unrelated shared-utility consumers unless task scope makes them necessary

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the visible trajectory shows or plans an effective option source, value propagation, and a netrc guard based on the resolved false value while preserving the default.
scale.2: Minor risk only: the trajectory has mostly effective propagation, with small uncertainty about docs or exact helper placement but no visible reason the false value would be ignored.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory adds the option in some places but visible evidence is incomplete about whether the user-facing value reaches the netrc lookup.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory shows a likely ineffective path, such as reading a default instead of `module.params`, gating on `self.use_netrc` after passing a per-call value, or omitting the effective argument source.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the patch is mostly cosmetic or structurally broken, with visible code indicating `use_netrc: false` cannot stop `.netrc` credentials from overwriting `Authorization` or the modified request path is likely unusable.

experiences.title: Effective Email as Stable Token Hash State
experiences.description: Use when a Django auth task asks for password reset tokens to become invalid after a user email change, especially when the trajectory has found `PasswordResetTokenGenerator._make_hash_value()` and `AbstractBaseUser.get_email_field_name()`.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django source repository when the visible task and trajectory concern the stateless password reset token hash and the required behavioral boundary is: old tokens must be rejected after the user's relevant email changes, while unchanged users and newly generated tokens remain valid. This is most useful once the agent has inspected or edited the token generator and user email-field APIs. It is less useful for unrelated password reset form lookup bugs, session-auth hashing changes, timeout-only token issues, or very early exploration where the agent has not yet identified token hash construction. Do not apply as a generic requirement to normalize email values unless the task or codebase explicitly makes normalization part of token semantics.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful rubric focused on whether the token hash incorporates the user's current effective email. However, the best version must be narrower than simply 'append user.email': the task explicitly warns that `AbstractBaseUser` does not guarantee a normal email field. A discriminative criterion should require using the model's configured email-field hook, retrieving that attribute defensively, and treating missing or `None` email values as a stable empty value so token generation/checking does not crash or concatenate non-strings. It should also check the behavior contract: a token generated before an email change is rejected, while the same token remains valid if relevant user state is unchanged and a new token after the change is valid. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as only verifying a manual script for the default `User.email`, only adding a documentation bullet, hardcoding `.email`, or requiring email normalization without visible support. Prioritize visible evidence from the trajectory: inspection of `_make_hash_value()`, use of `get_email_field_name()` or equivalent configured-field access, defensive `getattr(..., '')` plus `or ''`/string-safe handling, and tests or scripts that cover email-change invalidation plus empty/missing/custom email compatibility.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement password reset token hashing so the current configured user email value contributes to `PasswordResetTokenGenerator._make_hash_value()`, making tokens generated before an email change invalid while preserving token validity for unchanged state and compatibility with users whose effective email field is missing, empty, custom-named, or `None`.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Configured Email in Token Hash with Defensive Empty Handling

required_visible_evidence: The agent identifies the password reset token hash construction as the place where token validity is determined.
The proposed or applied change obtains the email field through the user model's configured email-field API rather than assuming only a literal `email` attribute.
The email value is retrieved defensively and converted to a stable empty/string-safe value for missing or `None` cases.
The intended behavior distinguishes old-token invalidation after email change from unchanged-token validity and new-token validity.
avoid_as_primary_evidence: Only adding comments or documentation about email changes.
Only testing the default user model without considering custom or absent email fields.
Hardcoding direct `user.email` access when the codebase exposes a configured email-field hook.
Requiring email normalization unless it is explicitly part of the visible task or existing token contract.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the token hash will depend on the user's email, or changes are confined to unrelated password reset code.
scale.2: Recognizes email should affect password reset tokens but only proposes a vague or hardcoded default-email approach with no compatibility handling.
scale.3: Adds or plans to add an email value to the token hash for the default user and likely invalidates old tokens after a simple email change, but evidence is incomplete for configured email fields or empty/`None` handling.
scale.4: Uses the configured email-field mechanism and defensive attribute access, and visible reasoning or tests cover email-change invalidation plus unchanged/new-token behavior, with only minor gaps in edge-case validation.
scale.5: Clearly implements or specifies configured-field email inclusion in `_make_hash_value()` with stable handling for missing, empty, custom, and `None` email values, and validates that old tokens are rejected after email changes while unchanged and newly generated tokens remain valid.

experiences.title: Do not reward parent-link preference while ordinary OneToOne fields still enter MTI parent maps
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for Django multi-table inheritance bugs involving multiple OneToOneField relations to a parent model and order-dependent parent_link selection.
experiences.context: Applies in Django ORM/model metaclass work where a trajectory investigates ModelBase.__new__ parent_links collection and Options._prepare() primary-key promotion. A tempting rubric is to require only that an explicit parent_link=True OneToOneField wins over another OneToOneField to the same parent in both declaration orders. That is relevant but too narrow when the implementation still records ordinary OneToOneField relations as candidate inheritance links or treats absence of parent_link=True as an expected configuration error. The original idea remains appropriate as one subcondition when the visible trajectory is still in early reproduction or when the task only asks to compare two same-target fields and there is no evidence about non-parent relations. At patch-review stage, however, visible edits/tests must distinguish explicit inheritance links from ordinary relations and account for downstream primary-key setup behavior.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster mostly rewarded trajectories for making the explicit parent_link=True field take precedence regardless of declaration order, sometimes even requiring preservation of an ImproperlyConfigured error when no explicit parent_link exists. This can be misleading: a patch that merely prefers parent_link=True on key collisions can pass the reported two-order reproducer while still allowing ordinary OneToOneFields to be stored in the MTI parent_links map when no explicit parent link has been seen. That preserves the same flawed semantic model: non-parent relations are still candidates for inheritance setup, and Options._prepare() can still raise an error because a normal relation was selected as if it were a parent link. Better rubrics should focus on the discriminator used when building inheritance metadata: only fields explicitly marked as parent links should be collected as MTI parent links; ordinary OneToOne relations to a parent must remain ordinary relations and must not be used as fallback parent-link candidates. A replacement criterion should prioritize visible evidence such as code filtering on the parent_link marker before inserting into the parent-link map, tests/assertions that _meta.parents contains the true inheritance link while unrelated OneToOne fields are not treated as parents, and review of downstream primary-key setup so it does not rely on rejecting non-parent links after the wrong field has already been selected. Avoid generating a criterion that says the fix must preserve a failure when no explicit parent_link is declared unless the task or inspected Django behavior explicitly establishes that as the intended contract.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: At patch-review stage for a Django MTI parent-link bug, the trajectory is flawed if it only makes parent_link=True win over another same-target OneToOneField on dictionary collisions but still permits ordinary OneToOneFields to be inserted into the MTI parent-link map or relies on Options._prepare() to reject non-parent links after selection. Judge using visible evidence from code edits, tests, and stated reasoning: the fix should collect only explicitly marked inheritance links as parent-link candidates and should not treat a normal OneToOne relation to the parent as an expected fallback/error path for MTI primary-key setup.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Ordinary OneToOne Still Treated as MTI Parent Candidate

metadata.environment: Django ORM multi-table inheritance model construction
visible_evidence: ModelBase.__new__ parent_links collection logic
Options._prepare() primary-key promotion/error path
regression tests or manual assertions involving _meta.parents and ordinary OneToOne relations
metadata.avoid_proxy: Do not judge correctness solely from both declaration orders of explicit parent_link=True versus ordinary OneToOne passing.

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the visible trajectory filters MTI parent-link candidates by the explicit parent_link marker before registration and accounts for downstream primary-key setup so ordinary OneToOne relations are not selected or rejected as parent links.
scale.2: Minor risk only: the trajectory mainly targets explicit parent_link selection and has limited downstream discussion, but visible edits/tests suggest ordinary OneToOne fields are not inserted as MTI parent candidates.
scale.3: Equivalent/uncertain: the trajectory demonstrates both field orders but visible evidence is insufficient to tell whether ordinary OneToOne fields remain in parent-link discovery or whether downstream setup still treats them as parent links.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the visible patch uses a collision-preference rule that keeps or inserts non-parent OneToOne fields as parent-link candidates when no parent_link=True field is already stored, or the rubric/test plan explicitly requires preserving the old error for no explicit parent_link cases.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory strongly validates only order-independence with ad hoc tests while implementing or defending logic that treats ordinary OneToOne relations to the parent as MTI parent links and leaves downstream primary-key setup dependent on rejecting those ordinary relations.

experiences.title: Do not treat loop cache usage as the fix when ownership of delegation evaluation is the issue
experiences.description: Retrieve this when an Ansible TaskExecutor task involves duplicate evaluation of loop items and delegate_to, and the trajectory fixates on _ansible_loop_cache as the success signal.
experiences.context: Applies in the Ansible Python execution pipeline when a task combines loop handling with delegate_to resolution and the visible code shows delegated-variable gathering evaluating loop expressions before TaskExecutor later evaluates loops. The misleading case is a trajectory that correctly discovers _ansible_loop_cache but then rewards merely setting, propagating, or consuming that cache. That can overvalue a workaround and miss the deeper ownership problem: loop and delegation evaluation should not be split across variable gathering and task execution in a way that still duplicates or freezes evaluation at the wrong stage. The original cache-focused idea may still be appropriate for early investigation, or for a narrowly scoped bug where the intended architecture is explicitly to preserve a precomputed cache and only propagation is broken. It is not appropriate as the main final-correctness rubric when the task statement emphasizes single calculation within TaskExecutor and the codebase contains duplicated loop-evaluation logic in variable management.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked judges to reward identifying _ansible_loop_cache, verifying that VariableManager sets it, and ensuring TaskExecutor consumes it. That is useful exploration evidence, but it becomes misleading as a final criterion: agents can satisfy it by broadening the cache condition or changing comments while leaving the architecture that caused duplicate loop/delegate_to evaluation intact. A better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory recognizes and addresses evaluation ownership: delegated host resolution should be performed in the executor at the point where task variables, templating context, and loop items are controlled, while variable gathering should avoid eagerly evaluating loops just to compute delegated vars. Avoid the tempting criterion that the patch “properly uses _ansible_loop_cache” unless the visible task specifically asks to repair that cache mechanism. Prioritize visible evidence such as tracing the strategy/worker/task-variable path, recognizing that copied loop-evaluation code in variable management is a smell, planning or implementing a change that centralizes delegate_to resolution in TaskExecutor, and validating behavior with loop+delegate_to cases that would expose repeated templating or inconsistent delegated hosts.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that make _ansible_loop_cache the central correctness mechanism for a loop+delegate_to double-evaluation bug while failing to address that delegated-variable gathering and task execution both participate in loop/delegation templating. This flaw is especially clear when the agent only changes cache conditions, cache comments, or cache propagation checks, and shows no plan to move or centralize delegate_to calculation into the executor-side task execution flow.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Cache-workaround tunnel vision

metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: Treating presence or broader use of _ansible_loop_cache as sufficient evidence that loop and delegate_to are calculated exactly once
metadata.preferred_evidence: The trajectory distinguishes cache workaround behavior from evaluation ownership and aims to avoid duplicate evaluation by centralizing delegate_to handling in the executor-side flow

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory treats the cache as at most a diagnostic clue and focuses on eliminating split loop/delegate_to evaluation ownership.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory discusses the cache heavily during exploration but also investigates whether variable gathering should be removed from the evaluation path.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies both VariableManager and TaskExecutor involvement but leaves the final direction ambiguous between cache repair and architectural ownership.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory proposes or implements only cache-condition/cache-propagation changes while still leaving delegated-variable gathering responsible for loop evaluation.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory explicitly defines success as always setting or consuming _ansible_loop_cache and ignores executor-side delegate_to ownership, despite visible duplicated loop-evaluation logic.

experiences.title: Multi-Issue NodeBB Cache/Slug Tasks Need Cache-Coverage Rubrics
experiences.description: Retrieve when a NodeBB-like bug report combines `Meta.slugTaken` array handling with inconsistent post-cache behavior across admin, socket, and post-processing modules, especially when the trajectory is drifting toward only the slug fix or an unsupported cache theory.
experiences.context: Applies in JavaScript/NodeBB CommonJS repositories where the visible task names two separable defects: a utility method must support scalar and array inputs, and a post/cache module must behave consistently across admin controllers, socket handlers, parsing, and plugin/cache invalidation paths. This is most useful after the agent has inspected relevant cache call sites or has begun editing, because there is enough visible evidence to judge whether both reported bugs are being addressed. It is less useful during very early repository discovery before cache usages are known, and it should not be replaced by a narrow criterion about adding a generic cache factory or reacting to config-update events unless the trajectory has concrete evidence that those are the actual cache inconsistency mechanism.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster focused on whether the trajectory covered the cache half of a two-part bug report, not merely whether `slugTaken` gained array support. This aligned with final patch quality because many trajectories visibly inspected `Meta.slugTaken`, added per-element slug logic, created ad hoc tests, and then either ignored the post-cache issue or proposed unrelated cache changes. A better rubric should explicitly judge whether the agent investigates and patches the post-cache access contract across all named consumers: the admin cache controller, socket admin cache handlers, post parsing, and plugin/cache reset paths should all use the same shared post-cache interface and preserve consistent reset/toggle/dump behavior. The rubric should also reward recognizing that repeated CommonJS `require` calls alone do not prove multiple instances, and should penalize speculative fixes such as adding a generic `create` method to the local cache module, changing default cache sizes, or rebuilding on config updates without evidence. Visible evidence to prioritize includes grep results for all post-cache imports, inspection of the post-cache export shape, whether the implementation updates each consumer consistently, and whether slug-array work preserves scalar boolean behavior while returning per-input results for arrays. Avoid a generic 'complete bug coverage' rubric when a more concrete cache-consistency criterion can be judged from the trajectory.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Consistent Post-Cache Access Across Consumers
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show that the agent treats the post-cache inconsistency as a first-class part of the task, not as incidental exploration. Strong progress means the agent identifies every relevant consumer of the post cache in admin cache views/dumps, socket cache clear/toggle handlers, post parsing, and plugin/cache invalidation paths; understands the current export/import semantics of the post-cache module; and proposes or implements a single shared access contract so all consumers operate on the same cache instance and compatible API. The trajectory should preserve existing cache operations such as clear/reset, enabled toggling, dump/peek/stat display, and post parsing reads/writes, while also keeping the separate slug-array fix compatible with existing scalar callers. It should not rely on unsupported proxies such as assuming repeated `require` calls are the bug, adding a factory to an unrelated local cache, changing cache defaults, or listening for config updates unless the inspected code directly supports that as the cause.

metadata.environment: Node.js/CommonJS NodeBB-style repository
task_signals: Bug report names both post-cache inconsistency and slug array handling
Affected areas include admin cache controller, socket admin cache handlers, post parsing, and meta utility code
prioritized_visible_evidence: Search results or inspections covering all post-cache import/use sites
Inspection of the post-cache module export shape and cache object API
Patch or plan updates all relevant cache consumers to a common shared interface
Slug handling remains additive: scalar input returns a boolean, array input returns aligned per-slug booleans
avoid_as_primary_evidence: Only editing the slug utility
Standalone tests that do not run in the project environment
Speculative cache factory/config-reactivity changes without call-site coverage

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the post-cache inconsistency is investigated or addressed; the trajectory focuses only on slug handling or unrelated setup.
scale.2: Mentions the cache issue or inspects one cache file, but does not map the relevant admin/socket/post-processing consumers or propose a coherent shared-cache fix.
scale.3: Identifies some relevant cache call sites and recognizes the need for consistency, but the plan or edits remain partial, speculative, or omit important consumers such as socket handlers, admin dump/get paths, parsing, or reset/invalidation paths.
scale.4: Clearly investigates the post-cache module and most consumers, and proposes or begins a coherent shared-access change while preserving existing cache operations; minor gaps or unvalidated details may remain.
scale.5: Comprehensively covers the post-cache inconsistency across all named consumers with a consistent shared interface and compatible API semantics, while also preserving scalar slug behavior and adding array slug behavior in a way supported by the inspected helper methods.

experiences.title: Avoid broad Qt-version rubrics when the issue is structured key-flow
experiences.description: Retrieve when a qutebrowser/keyutils task combines Qt5/Qt6 `QKeyCombination` compatibility with a request to replace raw integer key handling using `KeyInfo` or another structured key abstraction.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/qutebrowser key input code where the visible evidence includes `KeyInfo`, `KeySequence`, `QKeySequence`, a Qt5-only local environment, a Qt6-only `QKeyCombination` import fallback, and multiple methods still flattening or mutating key combinations as integers. A Qt-version compatibility criterion is still useful as a small sub-check when the trajectory is only deciding how to avoid an undefined `QKeyCombination` name. It becomes misleading when used as the main rubric for a type-safety migration, especially if it requires a particular mechanism such as `machinery.IS_QT6` or `TYPE_CHECKING` rather than judging whether structured key information is preserved through the public and internal `KeySequence` operations.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics mostly asked whether the trajectory identified or implemented Qt5/Qt6 conditional handling for `QKeyCombination`, sometimes naming `machinery.IS_QT6`, conditional imports, or runtime availability checks. That criterion is not wrong as a compatibility subgoal, but it over-emphasizes the import/version branch and can approve patches that merely bind `QKeyCombination = None`, add a dummy class, or convert `KeyInfo` immediately back to ints while leaving the raw-int design intact. For this task family, the better rubric should focus on the representation boundary: `KeyInfo` should be the structured unit used by `KeySequence` construction, slicing, appending, stripping modifiers, and mappings; conversion to `int` or `QKeyCombination` should be encapsulated at the Qt `QKeySequence` boundary; iteration from Qt should round-trip through `KeyInfo.from_qt`; and the unavailable Qt6 type should have a safe sentinel/import strategy without inventing a fake runtime type. Avoid making `machinery.IS_QT6`, `TYPE_CHECKING`, or generic 'Qt6 strategy identified' the decisive criterion. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent has found and plans/edits all raw-int manipulation paths (`_iter_keys`, constructor conversion, `__getitem__`, `append_event`, `strip_modifiers`, `with_mappings`) and has added conversion helpers such as structured-to-Qt and modifier-stripping helpers on the key-info abstraction.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial Qt branch leaves raw-int key flow
reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a key-sequence type-safety and Qt6 compatibility task, penalize trajectories or patches that mainly fix the `QKeyCombination` import/version check while leaving `KeySequence` operations centered on raw integer combinations. This flaw is present when the constructor still accepts or normalizes to ints as the primary internal representation, helper methods such as slicing, appending events, stripping modifiers, or applying mappings still call a raw `_iter_keys()` and perform bitwise integer operations, or `KeyInfo` is only accepted as a wrapper that is immediately converted to `int` rather than becoming the structured representation passed through the class. Also penalize fake fallback classes or broad `hasattr` checks for a Qt6-only type, because they obscure the compatibility boundary instead of using a clear absence sentinel and conversion helper.

metadata.task_family: qutebrowser KeySequence type-safety and Qt5/Qt6 QKeyCombination compatibility
evidence_to_check: QKeyCombination import fallback
KeyInfo.from_qt and structured-to-Qt conversion helper
KeySequence.__init__ argument type and conversion boundary
remaining uses of _iter_keys or raw integer bit operations
append_event, strip_modifiers, with_mappings, and slicing behavior
not_decisive_alone: adding Union[int, KeyInfo] while immediately converting KeyInfo to int

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory clearly preserves structured key information across `KeySequence` operations and confines int/QKeyCombination conversion to Qt API boundaries with a safe unavailable-type sentinel.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: import handling is safe and most key-flow operations are structured, but one secondary path or type hint still exposes raw Qt integer combinations without clear justification.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory handles the undefined `QKeyCombination` problem and recognizes `KeyInfo`, but only partially migrates operations, leaving some core methods or new constructors primarily int-based.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory adds Qt version/import checks or accepts `KeyInfo`, but most `KeySequence` manipulation still relies on `_iter_keys()` and integer bit operations, so type safety is largely superficial.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory treats Qt compatibility as solved by a dummy fallback class, `hasattr` checks, or version branching alone, while leaving the raw-int constructor/manipulation design essentially unchanged or making the Qt6 type boundary less precise.

experiences.title: Don’t let a TOTP behavior checklist hide duplicate-component integration risk
experiences.description: Retrieve when a React/TypeScript auth-code input task has an existing shared TOTP/code input and known consumers, and the trajectory is creating a new OTP component or stories/tests around it instead of clearly upgrading the existing component contract.
experiences.context: This applies in a monorepo UI package with shared React components, Storybook, SCSS conventions, and existing authentication flows. The misleading pattern is a rubric that only checks whether a newly written component renders per-character boxes, handles focus/backspace/paste/validation, has labels, is responsive, and has stories. That checklist is task-relevant, but it becomes insufficient when the trajectory has already discovered an existing shared TOTP input and existing account/authentication consumers: a parallel component can satisfy the checklist while leaving the public API, actual flow integration, style/story placement, or recovery-code behavior incompatible. The original checklist is still useful as a secondary functional review once the implementation is demonstrably in the right shared component or the trajectory has shown there is no suitable existing component. During early exploration, absence of the full behavior set should not be treated as failure; the more important signal is whether the agent is tracing existing component usage and planning an in-place, compatible change.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster generated broad “TOTP component completeness” criteria: render N inputs, auto-advance, backspace, paste, validation modes, separator, accessibility, responsiveness, and Storybook. Those criteria are correct requirements, but they led judgment toward over-optimism because visible trajectories often created new components such as alternative TOTP/code-input names, added separate exports/stories/tests, or moved into legacy/component-local locations after discovering an existing shared TOTP input. The better rubric should first ask whether the agent is preserving and upgrading the existing shared component and its consumers: compatible props such as value/onValue, length, validation type names used by the codebase, disabled/loading behavior, autocomplete/inputMode, error handling through the existing field wrapper, Storybook location consistent with repository conventions, and actual integration in the authentication flow without accidentally changing recovery-code behavior. Avoid making “all UX behaviors are present somewhere in a new component” the main criterion when there is visible evidence of an existing component/API. A replacement criterion should prioritize visible evidence that the agent modifies or intentionally migrates the existing TOTP component, keeps public imports and consumer usage coherent, avoids duplicate unreferenced components, and validates type/tests after integration.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Parallel OTP component instead of compatible shared-component upgrade
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for a TOTP/code-input feature when they have discovered an existing shared TOTP input and its authentication-flow consumers, but proceed to build a separate or inconsistently named component without clearly upgrading the existing component API and wiring it into the actual flow. Judge from visible evidence such as new duplicate component files/exports, stories or tests targeting only the duplicate, incompatible prop or validation-mode names, styling/story placement that does not match repository conventions, partial consumer migration, or unintended changes to recovery-code handling. Do not apply this flaw when the trajectory has not yet found an existing component, is still in early exploration, or explicitly documents and executes a coherent migration plan that preserves consumer contracts.

visible_evidence: Existing shared TOTP/code input and consumers were inspected
Agent creates a new alternative component rather than modifying or intentionally migrating the existing one
New component uses different API/validation names or styling/story conventions from the existing component family
Authentication-flow integration is missing, partial, or changes recovery-code behavior without justification
metadata.task_type: React TypeScript shared UI component for authentication code entry
metadata.stage_boundary: Use after the trajectory has enough repository knowledge to know whether an existing shared component/consumer exists; use behavior checklist only after integration-contract risk is addressed

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory upgrades the existing shared TOTP/code input or gives a clear compatible migration plan, preserves consumer contracts, and uses repository story/style conventions.
scale.2: Minor concern: the trajectory creates helper code or a temporary new component but clearly plans to fold it into the existing shared component and has not yet introduced incompatible exports or consumers.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory implements many required UX behaviors but leaves uncertainty about whether the existing shared component, public API, Storybook location, or actual authentication consumers will be updated coherently.
scale.4: Clear flaw: after finding the existing shared component/consumers, the trajectory builds and documents a parallel component with different naming/API or inconsistent conventions, with only partial or questionable integration.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory finalizes a duplicate or wrong-location component that may satisfy the UX checklist in isolation but fails to preserve the existing shared component contract, leaves key consumers on the old implementation or broken, or changes recovery-code behavior without justification.

experiences.title: Scoped manager swap for Django ForeignKey validation
experiences.description: Use when a Django ORM task specifically requires ForeignKey validation to ignore filters from a related model’s default manager while preserving unrelated form/queryset behavior.
experiences.context: Applies in Django source trajectories where the issue is that `ForeignKey.validate()` rejects an existing related row because the related model’s default manager filters it out, while the base manager can see it. This is most useful once the agent has inspected or edited the related-field validation code and there is visible evidence about whether the manager change is localized. It should not be applied broadly to tasks about default form field querysets, many-to-many form behavior, admin choice lists, or changing a model’s default manager. It is also less useful as a primary criterion when the trajectory is only doing initial repository exploration and has not yet identified manager usages or the validation path.
experiences.experience: The reliable rubric in these cases is not simply “the agent should add a test” or “the agent should replace default manager with base manager everywhere.” Standalone or in-tree tests are helpful, but the decisive visible evidence is whether the agent changes the existence check inside `ForeignKey.validate()` to use the related model’s base manager while leaving unrelated default-queryset construction alone. Several trajectories found multiple `_default_manager` occurrences in the same Django file; broad `sed` replacements changed `ForeignKey.formfield()` and `ManyToManyField.formfield()` too, which altered default form choice semantics beyond the requested validation fix. Better rubrics should reward recognizing the boundary between model-field validation/existence checks and UI/form default querysets. They should also check that the existing validation contract is preserved: database routing via `.using(using)`, lookup by the remote target field, `limit_choices_to` filtering, null handling, and existing error behavior. Avoid using “added a project-native regression test” as the main predictor when the implementation change is already visible and simple; such a test criterion may under-rate a correct minimal code patch. Prioritize evidence such as grep results showing multiple manager usages, comments or edits distinguishing validation from formfield paths, and the final inspected diff or snippet showing only the validation manager was swapped.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement the requested Django ORM behavior by updating the `ForeignKey.validate()` related-object existence query to use the remote model’s `_base_manager` instead of `_default_manager`, while preserving the rest of the validation logic and avoiding unrelated manager changes in formfield or many-to-many queryset construction.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Localized base-manager validation fix

metadata.target_behavior: ForeignKey validation accepts existing related rows hidden by a filtered default manager but visible through the base manager.
required_visible_evidence: The agent identifies the ForeignKey validation existence query as the relevant path.
The validation query uses the remote model's base manager.
Database routing, target-field filtering, limit_choices_to handling, null handling, and existing validation errors are not rewritten unnecessarily.
Other default-manager usages for default formfield or many-to-many querysets are left unchanged unless the task explicitly asks for those behaviors.
excluded_false_proxies: Adding only a standalone reproduction script without the scoped code change.
Replacing every default-manager occurrence in the related-field module.
Changing the related model's default manager or global form choice behavior to mask the validation bug.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory targets ForeignKey validation, or it focuses on unrelated managers/form querysets without addressing the validation existence check.
scale.2: Recognizes that default-manager filtering is involved but either has not made the validation change or proposes a broad/global manager change with no clear scoping.
scale.3: Shows parent-equivalent progress: identifies `ForeignKey.validate()` and the base-manager idea, but visible evidence is incomplete about whether routing, target-field lookup, limit_choices_to, or unrelated manager usages are preserved.
scale.4: Clearly changes the ForeignKey validation existence query to use the base manager and preserves the surrounding validation structure, with little or no evidence of unrelated manager changes.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory localizes the manager swap exactly to ForeignKey validation, explicitly distinguishes validation from formfield/many-to-many default querysets, preserves routing and existing filters/error semantics, and validates the filtered-default-manager scenario.

experiences.title: Centralized secure default for atomic file creation
experiences.description: Use when an Ansible-style file utility bug concerns atomically-created new files becoming world-readable because a shared default permission is masked by umask.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Ansible trajectories where the task is a security bug about files created through a shared atomic move helper receiving permissions like 0644 from a 0666 default and common umask. The useful stage is after the agent has either located the helper's new-destination chmod path or edited the shared/default permission used by that path. It remains relevant during validation if the trajectory shows tests or reproductions checking resulting mode bits. It is less applicable for tasks about existing-file replacement semantics, symbolic mode parsing, ownership/SELinux behavior, documentation-only changes, or module-specific file creation that does not go through the shared atomic move path. If the agent is still in very early repository exploration and has not found the permission calculation, score this criterion as investigatory progress rather than demanding a completed patch.
experiences.experience: The rubrics in these cases were useful because final correctness was driven by one observable semantic requirement: newly-created destinations through the shared atomic move path must not grant world/other read permission under common umasks. The best evidence is not broad module churn or adding a new API parameter; it is tracing the central chmod expression from the atomic move helper to the shared default permission constant, then changing or otherwise constraining that default so the creation branch computes a restrictive mode such as 0600. A good rubric should also mention preserving the boundary between new destinations and existing destinations: replacing an existing file should continue to preserve/copy its metadata where the helper already does so, while explicit mode/file-attribute handling by callers should still work after the move. Avoid making warnings, changelog, porting-guide text, or adding a mode argument mandatory unless the visible task/trajectory specifically makes those the remaining acceptance blocker; in these trajectories, the decisive observable fix was the secure default. Also avoid overvaluing tests that only assert `DEFAULT_PERM & ~umask` symbolically, because they may pass without proving the literal security regression; stronger validation controls umask or inspects final mode bits and confirms no world-read bit. Prioritize visible evidence such as locating `DEFAULT_PERM & ~umask`, tracing the default from a common file utility, changing it away from a permissive 0666 value, verifying 0022 no longer yields 0644, and checking relevant atomic-move/caller tests without treating unrelated broad-suite failures as decisive.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should address the shared atomic-move new-file permission path by ensuring newly created destination files receive restrictive default permissions that do not include world/other read access under common or permissive umasks, while preserving existing-destination metadata behavior and later explicit mode/file-attribute handling by callers. Strong evidence includes locating the new-destination chmod calculation, tracing its shared default permission source, changing or constraining that default to a secure value such as 0600, and validating the resulting mode bits rather than only relying on symbolic test expectations.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Secure shared atomic creation permissions

expected_visible_evidence: identifies the atomic move helper's new-destination creation branch
identifies a default permission masked by umask as the source of world-readable modes
changes the shared default or equivalent central logic so new files are not other-readable
does not replace existing-destination metadata preservation with a blanket chmod
validates with a controlled umask or final mode-bit check when possible
avoid_as_primary_requirements: adding a mode parameter to the atomic helper without fixing the unsafe default
requiring warnings or documentation as the core correctness criterion
counting tests that merely follow the changed constant as proof of the security behavior

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent found or addressed the atomic new-file permission calculation; work is unrelated or only inspects generic file modes.
scale.2: The agent recognizes that atomic file creation can be world-readable but has not traced the central default-permission/umask path or proposes only module-specific or documentation-only changes.
scale.3: The agent locates the shared atomic move chmod/default-permission path and reasons correctly about 0666 with umask producing 0644, but has not yet made a secure central change or has not considered preservation of existing-file and explicit-mode behavior.
scale.4: The agent makes a central change that causes newly created atomic-move destinations to be restrictive, and shows some relevant validation or compatibility reasoning, though regression testing or mode-bit proof may be incomplete.
scale.5: The agent clearly traces the root cause, implements a centralized secure default or equivalent logic preventing other-read access for new destinations, preserves existing-destination and explicit-mode semantics, and validates with relevant tests or controlled umask/final-mode checks.

experiences.title: Guard the Specific Empty Culling Threshold Fetch
experiences.description: Use this when a Django database cache task centers on `_cull()` crashing because the culling-threshold query can return no row before `fetchone()[0]` is used.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django repository when the visible task/trajectory identifies `django/core/cache/backends/db.py` database cache culling, the traceback or diagnosis points to `cursor.fetchone()[0]` after `connection.ops.cache_key_culling_sql()`, and inspection shows backend culling SQL using OFFSET/LIMIT or equivalent that may legitimately return zero rows. It is most useful once the agent has inspected or modified `_cull()` or is at final-review stage where a diff can be judged. It is premature during generic repository exploration before the target query is identified, and it should not be generalized to every cursor fetch in the codebase or to unrelated count queries unless the task independently establishes those as part of the bug.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the exact semantic contract: after executing the culling-threshold SQL, the agent should store the `fetchone()` result, check that a row exists before subscripting it, skip the threshold DELETE when no row exists, and preserve the existing DELETE behavior when a threshold key is returned. This aligns with the observable cause because the inspected backend SQL selects one cache key at an OFFSET, so an empty result is a valid outcome, especially under races or stale counts. A better rubric should prioritize visible evidence such as: the trajectory locates the `_cull()` threshold `fetchone()[0]`, explains why `cache_key_culling_sql()` can return no row, applies a localized guard around that particular result, avoids fabricating a fallback key or clearing the cache, and verifies both the empty-result and normal-row paths if tests are attempted. Avoid the tempting broader criterion “defensively null-check all cursor fetches”; it can reward unrelated changes like guarding `SELECT COUNT(*)` in `_base_set()` or `_cull()` even when the reported failure is the threshold query. Also avoid rewarding test-runner exploration alone unless the patch evidence shows the specific guard and preserved behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a localized fix for the database cache culling threshold path: after the backend-specific culling key query is executed, the result of `fetchone()` is captured and checked before indexing; if no row is returned, the threshold DELETE is skipped without raising; if a row is returned, the existing deletion by cache key threshold is still performed. Strong evidence includes inspecting the OFFSET-based culling SQL, keeping the change focused on `_cull()`, and validating or reasoning about both empty-result and normal-result behavior.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Localized Empty Threshold Row Handling

required_evidence: identifies the unchecked fetch after the culling-threshold query
guards the fetched threshold row before using element 0
skips only the threshold delete when no row exists
preserves normal threshold deletion when a row exists
keeps changes localized rather than broadly rewriting cursor handling
anti_patterns: only guarding unrelated count queries
clearing the cache or inventing a fallback threshold when no row is returned
making broad defensive cursor changes without addressing the culling-threshold fetch
leaving malformed or duplicated code from line-based edits

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory addresses the culling-threshold `fetchone()` result; it may only explore files, change unrelated code, or leave the direct indexing in place.
scale.2: Recognizes that a cursor result can be empty but applies an incomplete, misplaced, or overly broad change that does not clearly protect the threshold DELETE path.
scale.3: Identifies the correct `_cull()` threshold query and proposes or partially applies a guard, but visible evidence is uncertain, malformed, unverified, or does not clearly preserve normal deletion behavior.
scale.4: Applies a clean guard around the culling-threshold `fetchone()` and preserves deletion when a row is returned, with mostly localized changes; validation may be limited or incomplete.
scale.5: Clearly diagnoses the OFFSET-based empty-row possibility, applies a minimal localized guard that skips only the threshold DELETE on no row and preserves the normal row path, verifies the diff, and tests or convincingly reasons through both empty and non-empty result cases.

experiences.title: Dynamic Galaxy Server Config Registration for ansible-config
experiences.description: Use when evaluating Ansible ansible-config work for Galaxy servers where per-server sections are derived from a configured server list rather than from static base options or normal plugin loaders.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories for an Ansible-style configuration CLI task where `[galaxy] server_list` / `GALAXY_SERVER_LIST` names dynamic `[galaxy_server.<name>]` sections, and `ansible-config dump --type base` or `--type all` must display those per-server settings with values, origins, required markers, and default fallbacks. It is most useful once the trajectory has inspected the config manager, the ansible-config dump flow, and the Galaxy CLI/runtime code that creates per-server definitions, or once it has begun implementing in those areas. It is less useful as a strict success criterion during the first few repository-discovery steps, and it should not be applied to ordinary static config keys or real plugin types that already have loader-backed configuration discovery.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in this cluster is not merely “find galaxy_server sections”; it should check whether the trajectory understands the semantic integration point: Galaxy servers are dynamic, named configuration definitions derived from `GALAXY_SERVER_LIST`, and ansible-config must initialize/register those definitions before dumping them. A strong trajectory should mirror or refactor the existing Galaxy CLI definition construction, use the configuration manager’s value-and-origin resolution, and explicitly include a `GALAXY_SERVERS` structure in both base and all dumps. It should also preserve the required-option contract and timeout fallback behavior rather than formatting raw INI values by hand. Avoid a tempting but weak criterion that rewards adding `galaxy_server` to a generic configurable-plugin list or searching for a nonexistent loader; Galaxy servers are plugin-like internally but not a normal loader-backed plugin category. Also avoid over-crediting repeated greps of `base.yml` or `manager.py` unless they lead to the dynamic definition-registration insight. Visible evidence to prioritize: recognition that per-server option definitions are absent from static base config, discovery of existing Galaxy runtime code that builds definitions from the server list, a plan or edits that register those definitions in the config manager before ansible-config dump/list/validate paths, and handling of base/all output plus required/default origin semantics.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Dynamic Galaxy Server Definition Integration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates and acts on the need for ansible-config to construct or reuse dynamic per-Galaxy-server configuration definitions from the configured server list, register them with the configuration system before dumping, and render them in base/all output while preserving value origins, required-option markers, and fallback defaults such as server timeout. It should treat Galaxy servers as a special dynamic config family, not as an ordinary loader-backed plugin type.

required_visible_evidence: Identifies that `[galaxy_server.<name>]` sections are named by `GALAXY_SERVER_LIST` / `[galaxy] server_list` and are not present as static base definitions.
Finds or describes existing Galaxy runtime logic that creates per-server option definitions and registers them with the configuration manager.
Plans or implements ansible-config-side initialization of those definitions before dump/list/validation reads them.
Ensures dump output for both base and all includes a `GALAXY_SERVERS`-style grouping with per-server options.
Uses configuration resolution that retains origins and handles missing required options and timeout defaults.
anti_patterns: Only adding `galaxy_server` to a generic configurable-plugin list without addressing the lack of a plugin loader.
Parsing raw INI sections directly in a way that bypasses normal value/origin/default/type handling.
Limiting changes to plugin dump paths while the task requires base dump output too.
Repeating searches for static `galaxy_server` definitions without progressing to dynamic registration.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of the dynamic per-server configuration model; the trajectory only performs generic exploration or unrelated searches.
scale.2: Notices Galaxy server list or `[galaxy_server.<name>]` sections but treats them mostly as static config entries or has no concrete registration/dump plan.
scale.3: Understands that Galaxy server settings are dynamic and omitted from ansible-config, but the plan is incomplete, overbroad, or still risks normal plugin-loader handling or missing base/all output semantics.
scale.4: Clearly identifies the need to initialize/register per-server definitions from the server list before ansible-config dump and plans to use existing config resolution, with only minor uncertainty around required/default formatting.
scale.5: Provides or implements a coherent integration: dynamic definitions are constructed from the server list, registered before ansible-config operations, included under a Galaxy servers grouping for base and all dumps, and resolved through the configuration manager so origins, required markers, types, and timeout fallbacks are preserved.

experiences.title: Gettext Catalog Override Precedence
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Sphinx/gettext localization bug involves project-configured catalogs being built but ignored because bundled translations for the same domain and msgids take priority.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Sphinx trajectories where the task describes `locale_dirs`, `gettext_auto_build`, project `locale/<language>/LC_MESSAGES/<domain>.po` or `.mo` files, and bundled Sphinx translations for the same `sphinx` catalog entries. It is especially useful once the trajectory has inspected `sphinx.application` i18n setup, `sphinx.locale.init()`, `CatalogRepository`, or gettext fallback behavior. It may be premature if the agent has not yet established that the project catalog exists and contains the target msgids. It is less relevant for bugs about missing `.mo` compilation, wrong `locale_dirs` path configuration, extension-only message catalogs, or untranslated messages that have no conflicting bundled translation.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on catalog precedence: project/user locale directories must be ordered before the bundled Sphinx locale directory for the same gettext domain, because gettext fallback chains use the first catalog that contains a msgid and only consult fallbacks for missing messages. This criterion aligned well because the visible trajectory repeatedly found that `.mo` generation worked, the project and bundled catalogs both contained entries such as figure/listing labels, and direct `locale.init()` or gettext tests showed old order returned bundled strings while project-first order returned custom strings. A better rubric should reward evidence that the agent understands and changes the search/fallback order, keeps bundled translations available as fallback for messages not supplied by the project, and validates the exact translation path either through direct translation calls or a Sphinx build that actually renders numbered figure/code-block labels. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as merely checking that `.mo` files are created, grepping HTML from a document that does not enable the relevant caption numbering, treating unrelated dependency/test failures as decisive, or requiring unrelated broad i18n rewrites. Also avoid making the criterion about exact syntactic shape or type-only edits; the semantic evidence is whether configured project catalogs precede packaged catalogs without dropping fallback behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should identify and address gettext catalog precedence for Sphinx's core `sphinx` domain: configured project locale directories should be loaded before the packaged Sphinx locale directory so project translations override bundled translations for duplicate msgids, while existing system/default lookup behavior and bundled catalogs remain available as fallbacks for messages not provided by the project. Strong evidence includes inspecting the locale initialization call site and `locale.init()` fallback semantics, confirming the project `.mo` contains the target messages, and validating with direct translation calls or a correctly configured Sphinx build that exercises the translated labels.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Project Catalog Before Bundled Fallback

key_visible_files_or_concepts: application-level construction of locale directory list
priority_evidence: project catalog exists and contains duplicate msgids with desired translations
agent recognizes earlier gettext catalogs take precedence over later fallbacks
configured project locale dirs are placed before bundled locale dir
bundled/default translations are retained as fallback rather than removed
validation uses direct translation output or rendered labels with the necessary Sphinx settings
avoid_as_primary_evidence: presence of an auto-built .mo file alone
HTML grep from a document that does not trigger numbered captions/listings
unrelated environment dependency failures
exact formatting of the code change without semantic precedence analysis

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory understands or changes catalog precedence; it focuses only on compilation, paths, or unrelated rendering/test issues.
scale.2: Some recognition that locale loading order might matter, but no clear evidence that project catalogs should precede bundled catalogs or that fallback behavior should be preserved.
scale.3: Moderate progress: the trajectory locates Sphinx locale initialization and proposes or reasons about reordering, but validation is incomplete or the fallback/system behavior is ambiguous.
scale.4: Strong progress: the trajectory clearly explains gettext first-catalog precedence, changes or plans to change the locale directory order so project dirs precede bundled dirs, and preserves bundled fallback in intent.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: in addition to the correct precedence and fallback design, the trajectory verifies project override behavior with direct translation checks or a Sphinx build that actually exercises the affected translated labels, and avoids relying on misleading `.mo` existence or irrelevant test failures.

experiences.title: Don’t reward language-normalization intent without production-code and test-isolation evidence
experiences.description: Retrieve when an Open Library/Python task already explicitly requires accepting multiple language identifier formats, especially if the trajectory is early exploration, has failing targeted tests, or starts changing pytest/mock-site fixtures to make language tests pass.
experiences.context: This applies in a Python web application where an import-language normalizer is supposed to map language keys, MARC-style codes, ISO two-letter codes, English names, and localized names to canonical language references while handling duplicates, empty values, and invalid or ambiguous inputs. The misleading pattern is a rubric that simply restates the requested multi-format normalization contract and then gives credit for comments, ad-hoc probes, helper discovery, or claimed coverage even when the visible trajectory still has failing tests, no actual production implementation, or broad fixture/mock changes that mask a request-context dependency. The original multi-format coverage idea is still appropriate at implementation or final-review stage, but only when coupled to visible evidence that the production path performs the normalization and that tests pass without globally altering the test environment.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked whether the implementation accepts MARC codes, ISO codes, English names, translated names, mixed case, duplicates, empty values, and invalid or ambiguous identifiers. That is a real requirement, but as a standalone criterion it becomes misleading: it can over-credit trajectories that only discovered relevant helpers or wrote docstrings/ad-hoc scripts while targeted tests still fail, and it can miss risky fixes that make shared mock fixtures autouse or seed global test language data instead of fixing the normalizer. It can also under-credit early investigation where the agent has not yet implemented anything but is gathering the right evidence. For similar tasks, generate a stage-aware criterion focused on visible production-code behavior and test isolation: look for actual normalization logic in the import path, reuse of existing language/catalog helpers where appropriate, preservation of canonical key/code behavior, explicit invalid/ambiguous handling, order-preserving deduplication, and targeted tests that pass without broad fixture changes. Avoid the tempting criterion “mentions or intends to support all language formats”; prioritize concrete diff evidence, failure outputs, and whether the agent is masking the original request-context dependency rather than removing or properly encapsulating it.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear to satisfy multi-format language normalization only through intent, ad-hoc scripts, docstrings, or test-harness manipulation while the production import normalizer remains unproven or still brittle. Evidence of this flaw includes targeted language tests still failing, no visible production-code change after exploration, reliance on global/autouse mock-site fixtures, adding default language data to shared mocks solely to make isolated tests pass, or keeping validation tied to request context in a way that rejects known-valid code/name inputs outside a seeded catalog. Do not penalize merely because the trajectory is early and exploratory; the flaw is present when the trajectory claims progress, edits tests/fixtures, or leaves failing evidence unaddressed without a credible production fix.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Fixture-masked or unverified language normalization

metadata.repo_environment: Python web application using request-context site/catalog objects and pytest fixtures
misleading_proxies_to_ignore: docstring lists supported formats but code evidence is absent
ad-hoc script output without targeted test confirmation
discovery of a language mapping helper without integrating it into the production path
passing tests achieved by broad global mock-site or fixture changes
preferred_visible_evidence: production normalizer maps full language keys, three-letter codes, two-letter codes, English names, and catalog-backed translated names to canonical references
invalid and ambiguous identifiers are converted to the expected domain error
duplicates and empty inputs are handled deliberately
targeted tests pass without unsafe shared fixture or global mock mutations
existing canonical-code behavior is preserved
metadata.stage_boundary: At early exploration, absence of implementation is neutral unless the trajectory makes unsupported success claims or applies masking fixture changes; at implementation/final-review stage, require concrete code and test evidence.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the visible work either remains honest early exploration or shows production-code normalization with appropriate targeted tests and no broad fixture masking.
scale.2: Minor concern: the trajectory mostly investigates or prototypes correctly but relies on ad-hoc checks or incomplete tests, without unsafe global fixture changes or unresolved targeted failures.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory has some production normalization evidence but also ambiguous test coverage, unresolved request-context assumptions, or unclear handling of invalid/ambiguous inputs.
scale.4: Clear flaw: targeted tests are failing, or the implementation still depends on seeded request-context catalog state for basic valid inputs, or the agent starts modifying test fixtures to make the behavior appear valid.
scale.5: Severe flaw: there is no credible production implementation despite claimed coverage, or the trajectory broadly changes global/autouse fixtures/shared mocks to mask the original dependency while leaving the real normalization contract unverified.

experiences.title: AlterField relation dependencies in migration autodetection
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django migration-autodetector task concerns an existing scalar/concrete field being altered into a ForeignKey or other remote relation and the generated migration is missing a dependency on the related model/app.
experiences.context: Applies in the Django source/test environment when the task and trajectory point to migration autodetection, especially a change that stays on the AlterField path rather than an AddField path: an existing non-relational field becomes a ForeignKey to a model in another app, and visible evidence includes inspection or reproduction of missing migration dependencies/auto-dependencies. This criterion is most useful after the agent has located the autodetector’s altered-field logic or reproduced the missing dependency; it can still be used early as a task-derived target, but lack of implementation evidence should be judged cautiously. Do not apply it to unrelated database backend behavior, migration application/executor bugs, plain added ForeignKey fields already handled by added-field dependency logic, pure non-relational field attribute changes, or cases where the operation is intentionally decomposed into remove/add and dependency handling belongs to the add-field path.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic contract that changing an existing field into a relation must attach the related model dependency to the AlterField operation. This was discriminative because the visible trajectories repeatedly showed the key codebase asymmetry: newly added relational fields already collect dependencies through an existing helper and pass them into operation addition, while altered fields emitted AlterField without those auto-dependencies, causing migrations to depend only on the local app. A better rubric should therefore evaluate whether the trajectory identifies the altered-field code path, uses the new relational field’s remote target to compute dependencies via the existing helper, and passes those dependencies into the operation-registration mechanism so the final migration can order the target app/model first.
