Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as requiring a RemoveField/AddField rewrite, treating the issue as PostgreSQL-specific, merely checking that an AlterField operation exists, or broadly mentioning ManyToMany without confirming the relevant AlterField/remote-field dependency path. Prioritize visible evidence such as: reproduction output showing missing target-app dependency or empty auto-dependencies; inspection of the added-field dependency pattern; recognition that UUIDField-to-ForeignKey remains an AlterField because both are non-M2M concrete fields; a code edit or planned edit that attaches dependency metadata to AlterField; and, at stronger levels, a regression test or generated-migration check asserting the target app/model dependency.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluate whether the trajectory is making the correct migration-autodetector fix for an existing field altered into a remote relation: it should recognize that the AlterField operation, not only added fields, must carry auto-dependency metadata for the new related target, preferably by reusing the existing relation-dependency helper and passing the resulting dependencies into the operation-addition mechanism so generated migrations depend on the referenced app/model.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Altered relational field carries target dependency

priority_evidence: trajectory identifies the altered-field path as distinct from added-field handling
trajectory observes or explains that added relational fields already compute dependencies
trajectory checks the new field's remote relation target rather than the old scalar field
trajectory uses existing dependency helper/auto-dependency mechanism instead of hand-rolled migration ordering
trajectory verifies generated migration dependencies or adds a focused autodetector regression test
avoid_as_primary_evidence: database backend-specific reasoning
only confirming an AlterField operation is generated
rewriting all such changes as RemoveField/AddField without justification

scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory mentions ForeignKey dependencies or searches migration code, but does not identify that the existing-field AlterField path needs dependency metadata distinct from the AddField path.

experiences.title: Polylog Fixes Need Evaluation-Boundary and Coverage Rubrics
experiences.description: Retrieve when a SymPy special-function task asks for exact polylog evaluation/expand_func behavior, especially Li_2 special values and removing exp_polar from Li_1 expansion.
experiences.context: Applies in an old SymPy codebase where `polylog` is implemented as a `Function` with `eval`, `fdiff`, `_eval_rewrite_as_lerchphi`, and `_eval_expand_func`, and the trajectory has reached implementation or final-review stage in the special zeta/polylog module. It is especially relevant when the task gives one exact value example such as `polylog(2, Rational(1, 2))` plus a branch/expansion complaint about `polylog(1, z)` producing `exp_polar`. It is less useful during initial repository exploration before the agent has inspected or edited the implementation, and should not be generalized to unrelated numerical-evaluation tasks where there is no symbolic expand/eval contract or branch-semantics discussion.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics correctly identified two visible requirements: `Li_2(1/2)` should become `pi**2/12 - log(2)**2/2`, and `expand_func(polylog(1, z))` should become `-log(1 - z)` without `exp_polar`. However, rubrics that only check those examples are too permissive: trajectories can add a one-off identity and remove `exp_polar` while still failing the broader special-function contract. A stronger rubric should judge whether the agent implements the identities in the canonical polylog code without damaging the surrounding class, preserves existing `z == 0`, `z == 1`, `z == -1`, derivative, and rewrite behavior, keeps `Li_1(z)` as an expansion rule rather than eagerly evaluating all `polylog(1, z)` constructions, and treats `s == 2` special-value evaluation as a coherent exact-evaluation branch rather than an isolated smoke-test hardcode. The criterion should prioritize visible evidence such as edits to `polylog.eval` and `_eval_expand_func`, preservation/restoration of `fdiff` and exports, exact symbolic tests for both requested behavior and existing regressions, and absence of broad unrelated sed damage or environment-only compatibility changes in the intended patch. Avoid the tempting but weak criterion of merely observing that a smoke script prints the two requested outputs; also avoid rewarding local Python-version compatibility edits as part of the solution.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Canonical Polylog Evaluation and Expansion Contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement the polylog fix as a robust symbolic special-function change: add exact order-2 special-value evaluation in the canonical `polylog` implementation, make functional expansion of order 1 return `-log(1 - z)` without `exp_polar`, preserve existing polylog class methods and special cases, and validate both new and existing behavior. Strong evidence includes a coherent `s == 2` exact-value branch rather than only an ad hoc single-output workaround, `Li_1` handled through `_eval_expand_func` rather than eager construction-time evaluation for symbolic `z`, retained `fdiff`/rewrite/export behavior, and regression tests covering the exact half-value, nonpolar expansion, and preexisting `z`/nonpositive-order behavior.

metadata.environment: SymPy special functions; polylog implemented as a Function in the zeta/special-functions module
observable_evidence: edits are localized to canonical polylog implementation and relevant tests
exact symbolic `Li_2(1/2)` value is implemented
`expand_func(polylog(1, z))` no longer contains `exp_polar`
`polylog.fdiff`, rewrite behavior, and existing special cases are preserved
tests or smoke checks include both new behavior and existing regressions
avoid_counting_as_solution: environment compatibility edits made only to import old SymPy
one-off smoke-test hardcodes without preserving the surrounding polylog contract
eagerly evaluating symbolic `polylog(1, z)` in `eval` when only expansion was requested

scale.1: No meaningful polylog implementation progress, or the trajectory damages/removes the polylog class or exports while attempting the fix.
scale.2: Only exploratory work or environment setup, or a narrow edit/test addresses one visible symptom while leaving the other requested behavior untouched.
scale.3: Implements the two headline outputs but with weak evidence of contract preservation, limited tests, or risky placement such as ad hoc hardcoding or unclear eval/expand boundaries.
scale.4: Implements the requested exact value and nonpolar expansion in the appropriate polylog methods, preserves existing special cases and derivative/rewrite behavior, and updates relevant regression tests.
scale.5: Provides a robust canonical fix: coherent exact `s == 2` special-value evaluation coverage, `Li_1` handled only as functional expansion, preserved class invariants and exports, cleanup of obsolete imports/docs, and tests for new identities plus existing polylog regressions.

experiences.title: Verified Device API Contract for New Network Modules
experiences.description: Use when an agent is adding a new Ansible/F5 BIG-IP module for a resource with no existing in-repository implementation, especially after searches only reveal unrelated references and the agent must infer a REST endpoint and schema.
experiences.context: Applies in an Ansible core-style repository with modules under `lib/ansible/modules/network/f5/`, shared F5 utilities under `lib/ansible/module_utils/network/f5/`, and unit tests under `test/units/modules/network/f5/`. The key matching situation is a feature request for a new BIG-IP resource module where local grep/find exploration confirms no existing module, tests, docs, or fixtures for that resource. This criterion is most useful once the agent has begun deciding endpoint names, argument specs, payload fields, or CRUD behavior. It is less useful for the very first repository-orientation steps before any API/schema decision is expected, and it should not be replaced by generic checks that the module follows Ansible structure, compiles, or has mocked tests.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics were useful when they asked whether the agent had discovered the correct BIG-IP REST API endpoint and data model before implementing the module: repeated visible evidence showed only repository searches returning no route-specific references, followed by guessed endpoints and guessed fields such as a generic `addresses` list. That is predictive because a new device module can be structurally well-formed but still unusable if the resource path, subtype path, version support, or field mapping is wrong. However, a broad rubric like “API contract correctness” can become misleading if it gives credit merely for plausible-looking code, syntax success, or self-authored unit tests; visible trajectory evidence must show that the exact external/device contract was verified or faithfully encoded. A better rubric should focus on the observable boundary between using existing F5 modules as style templates and independently confirming the message-routing route API schema. It should prioritize evidence such as: the agent identifies the subtype-specific message-routing route endpoint rather than inventing a generic path; maps module parameters to the device’s actual route fields, including source/destination address concepts, peer selection mode, peers formatting, partition/name handling, and default/wildcard behavior; accounts for platform/version support; and implements idempotent read/create/update/delete around those confirmed fields. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria about repository exploration, docs presence, Python syntax, or unit tests alone, because those can pass while the module still targets the wrong API contract.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a new BIG-IP message-routing route module with no in-repository precedent, the trajectory should visibly establish and implement the exact device API contract rather than guess from naming conventions. Strong evidence includes confirming the subtype-specific REST resource path and CRUD methods, using the device’s actual route fields and object formats, exposing an argument spec that matches that contract, preserving F5 module conventions for partition/name transformation and idempotent read/compare/update/delete, and handling version or feature-support boundaries for message routing. Repository templates such as static-route modules may be used for structure, but they should not substitute for API/schema verification.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Confirmed Resource API Schema

metadata.environment: Ansible core-style F5 BIG-IP network module
evidence_to_prioritize: verified or explicitly justified REST path for the concrete resource/subtype
argument spec and payload fields matching the device schema
correct handling of peers/object references and source/destination route matching fields
idempotent read-current, compare, create, update, delete flow over those fields
feature or TMOS version gating when the resource is unavailable on older devices
evidence_not_sufficient: grep searches only showing no local implementation
mocked unit tests that mirror guessed behavior
a plausible but unverified endpoint string

scale.1: No meaningful API-contract discovery is visible; the agent is only exploring the repository or repeating searches, with no confirmed endpoint, schema, or implementation decisions.
scale.2: The agent has identified relevant F5 module patterns and absence of an existing resource module, but endpoint and payload schema remain speculative or are based only on naming guesses.
scale.3: The trajectory implements or plans a plausible REST-backed module using existing F5 conventions, but visible evidence does not confirm the exact resource path, subtype, field names, object formats, or version boundaries.
scale.4: The trajectory shows strong alignment with the device contract: a plausible confirmed endpoint, correct major fields, idempotent CRUD flow, and F5 conventions are present, with only minor uncertainty or omissions.
scale.5: The trajectory clearly verifies and implements the exact BIG-IP message-routing route API contract, including subtype path, schema fields, peer formatting, defaults/wildcards, partition/name handling, version support, and idempotent CRUD semantics.

experiences.title: Do not equate caught date overflow with safe invalid-date fallback
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django form widget or similar validation path catches `OverflowError` from user-controlled date construction and returns a string for downstream field validation.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Django form validation tasks where a widget recombines user-controlled year/month/day values, catches exceptions around `datetime.date(int(...))`, and returns a pseudo-date string that will later be parsed by a form field. The misleading pattern is judging success merely because `OverflowError` is added to an existing `ValueError` handler and the immediate widget call no longer crashes. That may still be wrong if the fallback preserves the oversized numeric component, because downstream validation may parse that returned string and encounter the same overflow. The original idea of broadening an exception handler can still be appropriate when the returned fallback is guaranteed not to be reparsed into overflowing integers, or when the project contract explicitly says to preserve raw invalid components. In this Django `SelectDateWidget`-style environment, the safer contract is to convert overflow cases to a bounded invalid sentinel while leaving ordinary invalid-but-representable dates on the existing path.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics rewarded trajectories for making `SelectDateWidget.value_from_datadict()` catch `OverflowError` "like `ValueError`" and preserve existing pseudo-ISO invalid-date return semantics. That criterion is too optimistic: visible manual tests returning values such as a huge year joined with month/day show that the crash was only moved from the widget constructor to potential downstream field parsing. A better rubric should distinguish ordinary `ValueError` invalid dates from numeric overflow. It should require a scoped fix that catches `OverflowError` from the date construction path and returns a bounded invalid placeholder that cannot itself overflow when later parsed, while valid dates and normal incomplete/invalid dates keep their established behavior. Avoid the tempting criterion "oversized values are treated like other invalid date parts" unless the trajectory demonstrates that the returned representation is safe for the full form validation path. Prioritize visible evidence from diffs and tests: whether overflow has a separate/safe return value, whether form-level `is_valid()` or downstream parsing is exercised, whether manual output still contains giant numeric components, and whether broad search-and-replace modified unrelated exception handlers.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For tasks fixing user-controlled date-component overflow in a Django-style widget, penalize trajectories that only add `OverflowError` to the existing invalid-date `ValueError` fallback when that fallback returns the original oversized year/month/day text. This is a flaw because the returned pseudo-date may be parsed later by form validation and can still trigger overflow. The trajectory should instead show a scoped overflow-specific handling path that returns a bounded invalid value or otherwise proves downstream validation cannot overflow.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Unsafe raw overflow fallback

metadata.environment: Python/Django form widget validation
metadata.risk_signal: manual widget tests return huge numeric components after catching OverflowError
metadata.safe_evidence: overflow path returns bounded invalid sentinel or form-level validation is shown not to crash
metadata.scope_signal: change is limited to the relevant widget conversion path and does not rely on broad unrelated exception-handler edits

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: overflow handling is scoped and returns a bounded invalid value, or full form validation is shown safe without preserving oversized components.
scale.2: Minor concern: overflow is caught and most evidence suggests downstream safety, but the trajectory does not clearly prove the returned value cannot be reparsed into overflow.
scale.3: Equivalent/mixed behavior: the trajectory catches overflow but provides only widget-level testing and leaves downstream safety unclear.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory catches overflow by sharing the existing `ValueError` fallback and visible tests show oversized components are returned as pseudo-date strings.
scale.5: Most severe flaw: the patch broadly changes exception handlers and explicitly validates success by showing huge returned date strings, with no form-level test demonstrating that validation no longer crashes.

experiences.title: Do not let the easy cache-map fix eclipse inactive-package filtering
experiences.description: Retrieve when a WordPress scanning task has both a cache pointer-indirection requirement and an inactive plugin/theme filtering requirement, but the trajectory evidence mostly addresses `searchCache`/map signatures.
experiences.context: In Go WordPress vulnerability scanning code, changing `*map[string]string` to `map[string]string` in cache lookup/update paths is a real and useful sub-fix. However, it is misleading as the primary or sole rubric when the task also asks for accuracy changes around ignoring inactive plugins/themes based on a package `Status` field. This warning applies especially when the visible trajectory shows many edits to `searchCache`, `FillWordPress`, callers, and tests, but little or no demonstrated work on how `WpIgnoreInactive` is applied throughout theme/plugin selection and later vulnerability matching. The cache criterion may still be appropriate as one sub-rubric if the trajectory has already inspected and corrected inactive filtering, or if the task is explicitly only about cache indirection.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics rewarded direct WordPress cache map access: removing `*map[string]string`, indexing the map directly, and updating callers/tests. That criterion is technically sound but too narrow for this task shape, so it can overstate trajectories that fix the performance cleanup while leaving the accuracy bug untouched. A better rubric should prioritize visible evidence that inactive packages are excluded based on `Status == "inactive"` when the ignore-inactive option is enabled, and that later fix-status/version matching cannot reintroduce inactive packages by searching the unfiltered package inventory. Avoid the tempting criterion that treats successful cache signature changes, passing tests for `searchCache`, or preserved cache writes as sufficient progress. Replacement criteria should look for: use of the configured ignore-inactive setting in the WordPress scan path, filtering of both plugins and themes by the `Status` field, retention of active packages, and tests or reasoning covering active versus inactive package cases.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a WordPress vulnerability scanning task that includes both cache pointer removal and inactive package filtering, penalize trajectories that only or mainly update cache map signatures/lookups while failing to show that inactive plugins/themes are excluded by package `Status` whenever the ignore-inactive setting is enabled. This includes cases where the initial package list is filtered but later vulnerability matching searches the original unfiltered package collection, or where tests cover cache hits/misses but not active versus inactive package behavior.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Missing status-based inactive package exclusion

metadata.visible_requirement: ignore inactive plugins/themes based on package Status when configured
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: direct map access in searchCache as the sole success indicator
evidence_to_prioritize: configuration flag for ignoring inactive WordPress packages is consulted in the scan path
theme and plugin package lists exclude Status="inactive" entries when enabled
active packages remain eligible for scanning
vulnerability/fix matching uses the filtered package set or otherwise prevents inactive packages from being reintroduced
tests or explicit checks cover inactive and active Status cases

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory visibly handles the ignore-inactive setting, filters by Status for relevant WordPress packages, and avoids reintroducing inactive packages during later matching.
scale.2: Minor concern: inactive filtering is mentioned or partially tested, but one edge of the scan path or test coverage remains unclear.
scale.3: Mixed evidence: cache indirection is addressed and some inactive filtering is inspected, but the trajectory does not convincingly prove that both plugins and themes are filtered by Status throughout the vulnerability matching flow.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory primarily changes cache map usage and leaves the ignore-inactive behavior unmodified or only superficially inspected.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory treats cache pointer removal as the complete fix, ignores the Status-based filtering requirement, or makes broad unrelated edits that risk package matching behavior without validating inactive package exclusion.

experiences.title: DataArray merge-method parity via canonical coercion
experiences.description: Retrieve when an xarray-like task reports that a top-level merge API accepts DataArray inputs but the Dataset instance merge method treats them like mappings and fails.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/xarray codebase when the visible task or trajectory contrasts `xr.merge([dataset, dataarray])` with `dataset.merge(dataarray)`, and the traceback or investigation shows a raw DataArray reaching merge internals that expect Dataset-like or mapping-like objects. It is most useful once the agent has inspected the public merge path, the Dataset method path, or the coercion layer, or has begun implementing a fix. It should not be used for unrelated merge conflicts, alignment bugs, formatting/dependency failures, or cases where the input is already a Dataset/mapping and no DataArray acceptance boundary is involved. Do not require a specific source file location for the fix; the important boundary is that DataArray normalization occurs before mapping assumptions such as `.items()` or overwrite splitting.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases judged whether the trajectory preserves semantic parity between the Dataset method and the top-level merge API for named DataArray inputs. This was discriminative because successful trajectories visibly identified that the top-level API converts DataArray objects with `to_dataset()` before calling lower-level merge machinery, then added equivalent normalization before the Dataset method path reaches mapping-only logic. The better criterion should reward evidence that `dataset.merge(named_dataarray)` produces the same variables and values as the top-level merge, that unnamed DataArray errors remain delegated to existing conversion behavior, and that existing Dataset/dict inputs plus options such as `overwrite_vars`, `compat`, `join`, and `fill_value` are not broken. Avoid a tempting but weaker criterion that merely fixes the immediate AttributeError by changing low-level coercion or by making DataArray look mapping-like; that risks expanding internals beyond their contract. Also avoid overfitting to the exact patch location, since normalizing in the public method or its backend can both satisfy the behavior. Prioritize visible evidence such as source inspection comparing the two API paths, conversion before `.items()` or overwrite handling, structural equality checks against `xr.merge`, and clean recovery from any accidental edit corruption rather than dependency/repr-related noise.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should make the Dataset instance merge method accept a named DataArray using the same canonical input-normalization semantics as the top-level merge API: convert the DataArray to a Dataset before lower-level merge code treats inputs as mappings, produce an equivalent merged Dataset containing both the original dataset variables and the DataArray variable, preserve existing Dataset and mapping behavior, preserve merge options including overwrite handling, and retain the existing error behavior for unnamed DataArrays.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Canonical DataArray coercion parity

required_visible_evidence: Identifies that the top-level merge path accepts DataArray inputs and normalizes them before calling lower-level merge internals
Identifies that the Dataset method path was passing a raw DataArray into mapping-oriented logic such as `.items()`
Implements or plans a DataArray-to-Dataset conversion before mapping assumptions or overwrite splitting
Validates behavior by comparing `dataset.merge(dataarray)` against the top-level merge behavior using structural checks rather than only absence of an exception
acceptable_fix_locations: public Dataset merge method before delegating
Dataset merge backend before mapping-based processing
anti_patterns: Changing low-level coercion to treat arbitrary DataArray inputs as mappings
Only suppressing the AttributeError without matching top-level merge semantics
Breaking unnamed DataArray, Dataset input, dict input, or overwrite behavior

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory recognizes the DataArray-vs-mapping boundary or the top-level merge parity requirement.
scale.2: Some recognition that DataArray lacks `.items()` or that the method path fails, but no clear use of the top-level merge coercion semantics and no preservation plan for existing merge behavior.
scale.3: Equivalent parent-child behavior: identifies that a DataArray should be converted before merge internals, but validation or compatibility coverage is partial, or the fix location/implementation details remain uncertain.
scale.4: Strong evidence of a correct parity fix: converts named DataArray inputs before mapping assumptions, preserves Dataset/mapping paths and key options, and validates the reported case against top-level merge behavior.
scale.5: Complete evidence of robust semantic parity: implements clean canonical normalization, explicitly checks named and unnamed DataArray behavior, verifies overwrite/options and existing inputs are preserved, and avoids unrelated dependency or formatting noise in validation.

experiences.title: Alpine source-origin mapping requires verified metadata and matcher wiring
experiences.description: Retrieve when an Alpine Linux vulnerability-scanning task concerns missed CVEs because installed binary packages are not associated with source/origin packages.
experiences.context: Applies in Go vulnerability scanner trajectories where the visible investigation shows Alpine package scanning currently records only binary package names/versions, while the model or detector architecture already has a source-package mapping concept. It is most useful after the agent has inspected the Alpine scanner and shared vulnerability lookup enough to know where packages and source packages flow. It is less useful for unrelated distro/package-manager issues, pure version-comparison bugs, or very early exploration before the agent has identified whether source-package support exists in the architecture. Be careful when the trajectory only speculates about apk flags without verified output; such speculation should not be treated as sufficient progress.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics correctly noticed the central requirement: the fix must produce Alpine binary-to-source package associations and feed them into vulnerability detection. They aligned with trajectory quality because the visible work repeatedly showed no implementation, no verified Alpine metadata source, and sometimes speculative use of apk commands. However, rubrics that require a specific unverified command such as `apk info -s` or `apk info -o` are too narrow and can reward an incorrect patch. A better rubric should focus on the semantic contract: obtain source/origin package names from a reliable Alpine package metadata source, parse both binary package identity and origin/source fields robustly, populate the existing source-package mapping with all derived binary names, wire that mapping into scan results and offline/manual parsing paths, and ensure Alpine vulnerability matching evaluates source-package requests rather than treating every binary package name as independently advisory-keyed. Avoid tempting proxies such as merely changing the installed package parser, adding a new parser with guessed output, or copying Debian parsing details. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent has verified or encoded the actual Alpine output format, preserved hyphenated package/version handling, grouped multiple binaries under one source package, propagated source packages through the scanner result, and considered the Alpine-specific matching boundary.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Verified Alpine source-origin association and source-aware detection
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate concrete progress toward a complete Alpine source-vs-binary fix: it must identify a reliable Alpine metadata format that exposes each installed binary package's source/origin package, parse it into existing package and source-package models without guessing an unsupported command format, preserve correct binary package name/version handling, populate source packages with all associated binary names, propagate those source packages into scan results including non-live parsing paths, and adjust or confirm vulnerability matching so Alpine advisories keyed by source package are evaluated through source-package requests rather than only installed binary names.

required_visible_evidence: Inspection or use of Alpine package metadata that includes an origin/source field, not only binary package-version lines
Use of the repository's existing source-package model with binary-name associations
Scanner result wiring that stores both binary packages and source packages for Alpine
Consideration of Alpine-specific vulnerability matching behavior for source-package requests
Tests or fixtures representing binaries whose source/origin package name differs from the binary name
insufficient_evidence: Repeated grep/search with no new findings
Speculative reliance on an apk flag without verified output or fixture coverage
Only changing version parsing or binary package collection
Populating source packages as one-to-one copies of binary packages
Ignoring the detector/matching path after scanner changes

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward Alpine source-package handling; the trajectory only repeats searches or inspects binary package parsing.
scale.2: Recognizes that Alpine source-package mapping is missing, but provides no reliable metadata source, no implementation plan beyond speculation, or no detector/scanner wiring evidence.
scale.3: Identifies the need to populate existing source-package models and has a plausible direction, but the metadata format or matching behavior remains unverified or incomplete.
scale.4: Shows strong progress by using a credible Alpine metadata source, mapping binaries to source/origin packages, and wiring source packages into scan results, with some attention to tests and matching behavior.
scale.5: Demonstrates a complete, verified approach: robust Alpine metadata parsing, correct grouping of multiple binaries under source packages, propagation through scanner/manual parse paths, source-aware Alpine vulnerability matching, and representative tests for binary/source mismatch cases.

experiences.title: Do not equate a large token utility module with a correct integration
experiences.description: Retrieve this when a Node.js/NodeBB-style API-token task asks for centralized lifecycle utilities and the trajectory has created or planned a broad token module while also refactoring users/auth/admin/middleware call sites.
experiences.context: In this environment, API-token behavior is spread across user API methods, auth verification, admin settings last-seen rendering, and middleware usage logging. A rubric that only asks whether a cohesive module implements list/get/create/update/delete/log/verify is misleading when the trajectory shows brittle line-number edits, whole-file rewrites, damaged neighboring functions, unverified imports, mismatched utility names, or altered authentication/route/controller contracts. A feature-completeness rubric can still be useful after the files are syntactically stable and the visible code demonstrates that the new utility surface matches existing call sites and preserves current behavior. Before that point, the most important evidence is not the count of exported token methods, but whether the refactor is safe, compatible, and actually wired through the existing integration points.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded trajectories for creating a centralized token-management module with many lifecycle operations. That criterion was too broad: agents often had visible evidence of serious regressions while still satisfying the superficial checklist, such as corrupted JavaScript after blind sed deletions, missing adjacent auth helpers, imports inserted before 'use strict', rewritten route/controller files with unrelated changes, newly added public routes not required by an internal-utility task, call sites invoking functions whose return shape did not match their callers, or authentication semantics changed from the existing uid/master-token behavior. For similar tasks, avoid generating a rubric that simply asks whether all named operations exist in one module. Prefer a criterion that checks whether centralization preserves the repository’s established storage contract, return values, authorization boundaries, auth verification behavior, last-seen tracking, and existing call-site compatibility while avoiding collateral edits. Visible replacement evidence should prioritize clean diffs to the existing token utility/integration points, successful syntax checks after risky edits, preserved wrappers for existing generate/delete/log/getLastSeen callers, and no unresolved file corruption or unrelated route/controller rewrites.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Unsafe or incompatible token centralization
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that centralize API-token lifecycle code in name only while visibly risking regressions in existing token workflows. This applies when the agent creates a new token module or broad lifecycle API but the visible trajectory shows broken or unvalidated integration: brittle line-range edits leave stray braces or partial functions, adjacent authentication or login-strategy functions are removed, imports or require paths are inconsistent with the repository, existing generate/delete authorization and return semantics are not clearly preserved, bearer-token verification may no longer return the expected user/master result, last-seen logging/admin display call sites are not consistently updated, or unrelated routes/controllers are rewritten or expanded beyond the internal-utility requirement. Do not treat the mere presence of list/get/create/update/delete/log/verify exports as sufficient progress if these compatibility and safety signals are missing.

metadata.environment: Node.js CommonJS application with existing API-token storage, user API wrappers, bearer authentication, middleware usage logging, and admin last-seen rendering
visible_evidence_to_check: new token utility surface matches names and return shapes used by modified call sites
existing privilege and same-user checks remain in public API wrappers or are equivalently preserved
auth verification still distinguishes user tokens from master tokens and calls the bearer callback correctly
usage logging and last-seen reads continue to use the same sorted-set contract or are fully and compatibly migrated
modified files pass syntax checks after mechanical edits
diff avoids unrelated route/controller rewrites or damaged neighboring functions

scale.1: No evidence of unsafe centralization: changes are narrow, syntactically validated, and visibly preserve existing token call-site contracts while adding the internal utility surface.
scale.2: Minor concerns only, such as style inconsistencies or incomplete validation, but existing generate/delete/auth/logging/admin paths appear structurally intact and compatible.
scale.3: Mixed evidence: a utility module exists and some wrappers are updated, but visible call-site compatibility, return shapes, or validation of modified files is uncertain.
scale.4: Clear unsafe centralization: the trajectory shows broken or mismatched integration, risky sed/whole-file edits, missing compatibility wrappers, or likely changes to existing auth/last-seen/permission behavior.
scale.5: Severe regression risk: visible syntax corruption, removed neighboring functions, unrelated route/controller rewrites, or call sites invoking nonexistent/mismatched token utilities despite the presence of a broad lifecycle module.

experiences.title: Galaxy response cache must be wired end-to-end, not just sketched
experiences.description: Retrieve this when an Ansible `ansible-galaxy collection install/download` task asks for persistent Galaxy API response caching with disable/clear controls, safe cache storage, and update detection.
experiences.context: Applies in the Ansible codebase when the trajectory is implementing or reviewing caching for Galaxy collection API metadata/version requests. The useful evidence is whether the agent has moved beyond exploration into an end-to-end design: cache persistence in the Galaxy API request path, collection install/download CLI controls, safe cache file handling, and freshness/update invalidation. It is most discriminative after the agent has identified the Galaxy API client, collection version/metadata calls, and Galaxy CLI parser/constructor flow, or after it has produced a partial patch. It is premature as a harsh correctness criterion during the first few exploratory commands, and it should not be applied to unrelated fact/inventory cache plugin work, collection artifact tarball downloads, or tasks that explicitly require a different HTTP-cache protocol.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics were useful when they checked for concrete cache integration rather than generic cache intentions: a trajectory that only greps for config constants, adds standalone helper methods, or drafts config without wiring cache reads/writes into the Galaxy request flow is visibly unlikely to satisfy this task. A better rubric should prioritize observable end-to-end evidence: cacheable collection metadata/version API calls go through persistent cache logic; cache keys distinguish request identity; cache data is safely loaded/written and unsafe files are rejected; install/download expose disable and clear controls; those controls are passed into every Galaxy API client used by the command; and a fresh request can invalidate stale version-list data when a collection changes. Avoid over-specific or tempting proxies: do not require ETag/If-None-Match, a TTL-only strategy, Ansible’s generic cache plugin system, `--cache-dir` flags, or unconditional caching of all GETs unless the task or trajectory establishes those as required. Also avoid giving credit for cache helper functions or CLI flags in isolation if there is no visible propagation into the actual API client and no cache read/write around the request path.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-end Galaxy API response cache integration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: For an Ansible Galaxy collection install/download caching task, the trajectory should demonstrate a coherent persistent response cache integrated with the actual Galaxy collection metadata/version request path. Strong evidence includes: cache storage in a dedicated user cache location or equivalent config-backed location; safe cache creation/loading that avoids trusting group/world-writable or otherwise unsafe cache files and writes atomically or with restrictive permissions; cache lookup and update on the API calls used to resolve collection versions and version metadata, including paginated version-list requests; request identity included in cache keys; a freshness mechanism that allows newly published collection versions to be detected when a fresh request is made, such as invalidating cached version lists from collection modified metadata; explicit CLI controls to disable cache use and clear existing cached responses on collection install/download; and propagation of those CLI options into all Galaxy API client instances used by the selected command.

metadata.task_family: Ansible Galaxy collection API response caching

CLI install/download options include disable-cache and clear-cache controls
CLI option values are passed into Galaxy API client construction before command execution
cache storage has safety checks for file or directory permissions
fresh request/update detection invalidates stale collection version data
avoid_as_required: ETag or If-None-Match support unless explicitly requested
TTL-only cache freshness as the sole update-detection mechanism
standalone cache helper methods without request-flow integration
artifact tarball caching instead of API response caching

scale.1: No meaningful cache implementation is visible, or the trajectory is still only exploring/searching without edits or a concrete integration plan.
scale.2: Some cache-related constants, helper methods, or plans are present, but they are not wired into the Galaxy API request path or the collection install/download CLI flow.
scale.3: Partial parent-equivalent progress: cache logic or CLI controls exist, but important integration is missing, such as option propagation, clear-cache behavior, safe file checks, or update invalidation.
scale.4: Strong implementation evidence: persistent cache is wired into the relevant Galaxy API calls and CLI disable/clear controls are propagated, with only minor uncertainty around edge cases such as pagination, auth-sensitive keys, or cache safety.
scale.5: Complete end-to-end evidence: cache is safely persisted and read/written for the relevant collection metadata/version requests including pagination, CLI disable and clear controls are scoped to install/download and propagated to all API clients, unsafe cache files are avoided, and fresh requests can invalidate stale version data when collections change.

experiences.title: Do not let enum/string cleanup overshadow state-machine compatibility
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a migration from legacy integer state constants to public enum-like types in behavior-sensitive iterator/strategy code, especially when the task also requires backward compatibility and unchanged execution flow.
experiences.context: This applies in an Ansible-like Python codebase where `PlayIterator`/`HostState` state constants drive task scheduling, rescue/always handling, and third-party strategy-plugin compatibility. A rubric that only checks public enum exposure or readable `HostState.__str__` output is misleading when the visible trajectory shows partial edits, wholesale rewrites of iterator or strategy files, unresolved deprecation/class-vs-instance access issues, failing or absent iterator-flow tests, or repeated debugging of task-order regressions. The enum/string requirement is still a valid secondary criterion when the trajectory already preserves original state-machine behavior and demonstrates legacy compatibility; it should not be the main predictor while task advancement, bit-flag behavior, or old API access remains unproven.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this situation focused on narrow subrequirements such as creating public enum types or making `HostState.__str__` print readable names. Those are correct requirements, but they overvalue superficial migration progress: an implementation can expose enums and print names while breaking task iteration order, changing `_get_next_task_from_state` semantics, using an enum type that does not preserve bitwise failure flags, failing to warn on class-level legacy access, or producing warning spam from internal legacy references. For this class of task, generate a rubric that prioritizes preservation of the existing state machine and the migration contract. The judgeable evidence should include whether the agent keeps iterator control flow minimally changed, uses integer-compatible run and failure state types, updates core strategy references to the new public names, verifies both `PlayIterator.CONST` and `iterator.CONST` legacy access with deprecation behavior, and runs targeted iterator/strategy tests or investigates failures. Avoid a standalone high-confidence criterion that treats readable string output or `__all__` exposure as sufficient progress unless the trajectory also shows behavior and compatibility validation.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory is likely deficient if it emphasizes public enum creation or human-readable state strings while leaving unresolved evidence that the iterator state machine, failure-flag semantics, or legacy class/instance access may have changed. Apply this when visible steps show large rewrites of iterator/strategy files, failing or absent task-iteration tests, deprecation warnings not firing for class or instance legacy constants, direct class attributes bypassing compatibility hooks, failure states implemented without flag-safe behavior, or internal code still relying on deprecated aliases in a way that could emit warnings during normal execution.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: State migration preserves behavior and compatibility

metadata.task_type: public state constant migration in behavior-sensitive iterator code
primary_visible_evidence: targeted tests or manual checks of task advancement/order and completion
legacy constant access verified through both class and instance paths
failure states preserve bitwise OR/AND semantics
core strategy code uses new public state names without relying on deprecated aliases
iterator control-flow methods are minimally changed or explicitly compared against prior behavior
misleading_proxy_to_avoid: enum classes exist
state types are exported
HostState.__str__ prints names
import smoke tests pass

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory preserves or validates iterator flow, bitwise failure behavior, old class and instance access with deprecation, and updates strategy usages while treating readable strings as only one subrequirement.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: enum/string work is prominent, but there is at least some targeted validation of iteration behavior and compatibility with no unresolved failures.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory implements public types or string output and performs only import/smoke checks, with limited evidence about task-order preservation, deprecation behavior, or failure-flag semantics.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: visible steps show unresolved deprecation or compatibility issues, broad rewrites of iterator/strategy logic, missing behavioral tests, or reliance on deprecated internal aliases despite successful enum/string checks.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory has failing iterator/task-order tests, known state-advancement regressions, broken class or instance legacy access, incorrect failure-flag handling, or abandons/overwrites behavior-sensitive files while still treating enum exposure or readable strings as sufficient progress.

experiences.title: Do not turn player MaxBitRate precedence into a global bitrate-cap rubric
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go/Navidrome streaming task concerns Player.MaxBitRate versus Transcoding.DefaultBitRate and the trajectory is inspecting or editing bitrate selection across request context, core media streaming, or Subsonic handlers.
experiences.context: The misleading pattern is to generate a broad criterion saying Player.MaxBitRate must override or cap DefaultBitRate in all transcoding scenarios, including explicit format requests, explicit client bitrates, Stream and Download handlers, or any later repository lookup. In this codebase, visible evidence usually points to a narrower core selection problem: request context carries a player and possibly a player-associated transcoding, while core/media_streamer.go resolves raw passthrough, requested format/bitrate, context transcoding defaults, and repository transcoding defaults. The original idea remains appropriate only if the task or inspected tests explicitly establish MaxBitRate as a universal cap across every explicit request and download path. Otherwise, the rubric should distinguish player-associated default transcoding from client-supplied bitrate and raw passthrough behavior.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked for MaxBitRate to take precedence over DefaultBitRate in all code paths or as an upper bound. That is tempting but misleading: it can reward handler-level fallbacks, post-resolution clamping, broad test expectation changes, or single-condition edits that do not preserve the existing source-of-truth ordering. A better rubric should focus on whether the agent has found and preserved the core bitrate decision contract: raw requests stay raw, explicit client bitrates are not silently capped unless specified, a player-associated transcoding default is replaced by the player's configured MaxBitRate when no explicit bitrate is supplied, and later transcoding lookup must not reintroduce the default bitrate. Avoid criteria requiring changes to Stream and Download simply because those parse bitrate parameters, and avoid requiring MaxBitRate for every explicit format request unless the visible task/tests demonstrate that behavior. Replacement criteria should prioritize inspected evidence in core selection functions, request.PlayerFrom/request.TranscodingFrom usage, cmp.Or/default fallback behavior, and focused tests that distinguish requested bitrate, requested format, default player transcoding, and raw passthrough cases.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat Player.MaxBitRate as a universal global cap or handler-level fallback instead of fixing the core bitrate-source precedence. This flaw is present when the trajectory edits only request handlers, changes expectations so explicit client format/bitrate paths always use the player bitrate, adds a post-transcoding clamp that can override explicit requests, or merely removes a less-than comparison without verifying that the selected player-associated transcoding default is replaced and not later overwritten by a repository DefaultBitRate. The criterion applies when visible code shows request context carries Player and Transcoding and core media streaming resolves bitrate through default/requested/raw branches.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Overgeneralized MaxBitRate precedence

metadata.environment: Go Navidrome media streaming/transcoding code
relevant_evidence: core bitrate selection functions are inspected or edited
Transcoding.DefaultBitRate may be used as a fallback
explicit request bitrate and raw passthrough cases exist
avoid_as_success_evidence: global MaxBitRate clamp after transcoding lookup
test changes requiring player bitrate for every explicit format request
single comparison change without checking fallback reapplication

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory clearly separates explicit client bitrate, raw passthrough, player-associated transcoding defaults, and repository defaults, and focuses the fix/tests on the core selection contract.
scale.2: Minor evidence of overgeneralization, but the trajectory still mostly preserves explicit request and raw behavior while investigating the core default-bitrate path.
scale.3: Mixed behavior: the trajectory identifies core MaxBitRate/DefaultBitRate precedence but uses vague language or partial edits that may conflate a player default override with a global cap.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory proposes or implements MaxBitRate as an all-scenarios cap/override, changes explicit format or requested bitrate expectations, or focuses on Stream/Download parameter fallbacks without ensuring core default resolution is fixed.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory relies almost entirely on a handler-level or post-resolution global clamp, ignores explicit bitrate/raw passthrough preservation, and treats every transcoding DefaultBitRate as subject to Player.MaxBitRate regardless of how the bitrate was chosen.

experiences.title: Do not treat minimal JWT size removal as full public-image correctness
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go HTTP service task asks to decouple public image/artwork JWT identity from presentation size, especially when the trajectory has found token generation, a public image handler, URL builders, and image resizing behavior.
experiences.context: Misleading rubrics in this cluster rewarded the obvious three-part refactor: remove `size` from public artwork JWT claims, stop requiring it in JWT validation, and read `size` from a query parameter. That criterion is necessary, but it becomes too weak at implementation or final-review stages in a Navidrome-like Go codebase where public image URLs are emitted by Subsonic response helpers, absolute URL construction may need query-aware handling, artwork IDs need typed parsing/validation, and image resizing behavior changes once size is externally supplied by callers. The simpler JWT/query rubric may still be appropriate during early exploration or as one subcriterion if the visible trajectory has not yet reached URL consumers or resizing code. It should not be the main success criterion once the trajectory has already identified the public route, token helper, public URL generator, and artwork reader/resizer path.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics mostly asked whether public artwork JWTs contain only the ID and whether size is moved to the HTTP query string. That over-credits trajectories that make a narrow local edit and pass compilation while leaving end-to-end public image behavior incomplete. A better rubric should require evidence that the agent followed the whole public image contract: the ID token is encoded and decoded/validated through a clear artwork-ID boundary; invalid token IDs and malformed size query values are handled deliberately; all public artist/image URL producers are updated, not just the one helper initially found; query parameters are attached through URL-aware construction rather than fragile string concatenation when absolute/base URLs are involved; and resized-image behavior is checked for externally supplied sizes, including no-upscale or small-image edge cases if the codebase has such a reader. Avoid the tempting criterion that a patch is likely correct simply because grep shows no `size` JWT claim and a handler calls `Atoi` or a param helper. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence of broad call-site inspection, query-safe URL generation, typed artwork ID parsing, explicit invalid-query behavior, and tests or reasoning that cover generated public URLs and resizing boundaries.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Over-narrow public image JWT/query refactor
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that stop at the local JWT-claim decoupling and do not demonstrate end-to-end public image behavior. This flaw is present when the visible work removes `size` from token creation/validation and reads a query parameter, but lacks evidence of comprehensive public URL producer updates, query-safe absolute URL construction, central typed artwork-ID decode/validation, deliberate malformed-size handling, or review of image resizing behavior affected by externally supplied sizes.

metadata.environment: Go HTTP service using JWT-authenticated public image routes, typed artwork IDs, Subsonic-style response URL builders, and artwork resizing readers
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: No size claim in JWT plus one handler reading size from query
better_visible_evidence: Token encode/decode boundary validates required ID claim, claim type, and typed artwork ID parsing
Public image handler obtains size from request query with explicit invalid-value behavior
All response paths that emit public image URLs are updated, including search/detail variants rather than only the first helper found
URL generation uses query-aware construction or an absolute URL helper that preserves base paths and encodes query parameters
Resizing code and tests/reasoning cover externally supplied sizes, zero/default size, and small-image/no-upscale behavior

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory treats JWT size removal as one part of a broader end-to-end public image refactor and visibly checks ID validation, URL consumers, query construction, and resizing/query edge cases.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory mainly implements the JWT/query move but also inspects most URL producers and validates ID and size behavior, with only small uncertainty about edge-case coverage.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory completes the obvious token-generation, token-validation, and handler-query changes, but only partially checks generated public URLs or leaves query construction and some public image consumers unreviewed.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory relies on the minimal decoupling as sufficient, updates only the first discovered URL helper, uses ad hoc query concatenation or weak size parsing, and shows little evidence of typed ID decode/validation or broader public URL coverage.
scale.5: Most severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory repeatedly asserts the task is complete after removing the `size` claim and adding a query read, while visibly ignoring or failing to inspect known public URL producers, absolute URL/query handling, malformed size behavior, and resizing implications.

experiences.title: Do not overvalue superficial API unification in cross-cutting UI sizing migrations
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for a React/TypeScript UI component refactor that replaces scattered boolean sizing props with a standardized size API and CSS-variable mapping across many wrappers and consumers.
experiences.context: Applies in monorepo UI tasks where a shared component such as a dropdown exposes legacy sizing flags and the requested change is a standardized size prop with predictable CSS variables. The misleading pattern is a trajectory that can show visible evidence like defining a size type, adding CSS size classes, removing legacy prop names by grep, or keeping old flags for compatibility, while also showing signs of incomplete consumer coverage, unsafe wholesale rewrites, unrelated diffs, or unverified semantic mappings. The original idea is still useful when the trajectory is at an implementation-review stage and the rubric is framed as one requirement among several: a size prop and CSS-variable translation are necessary. It is not sufficient by itself, especially after broad edits. In early exploration, absence of implementation should not be scored as failure; focus instead on whether the agent has identified all relevant dropdown wrappers, direct consumers, style files, and old-prop semantics. Legacy-prop removal should apply only to dropdown-owned API props, not unrelated identifiers with similar names in payments/modals or other non-dropdown sizing contexts.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded criteria such as “all noMaxWidth/noMaxHeight/noMaxSize instances are removed,” “CSS variables exist for each size,” “the size prop coexists with booleans,” or the generic “replace booleans with a unified size prop.” Those criteria are partly aligned with the task but become misleading when used as the main predictor: a grep can pass after destructive rewrites, a CSS class table can exist while breaking existing SCSS behavior, and backward compatibility can mask that the old scattered API was not actually migrated. A better rubric should require evidence of a behavior-preserving, scoped migration: explicit mapping from each old dropdown flag to the new size semantics; propagation through wrapper components and application-level consumers that actually use dropdown sizing; preservation of special cases such as same-anchor width, auto height, max-height/max-width unsetting, popper available-size variables, caret/adaptive touch styles, and custom sizing classes; exclusion of unrelated non-dropdown noMaxWidth props; and diff/type/test validation after broad edits. Avoid tempting criteria that treat name removal, size-type creation, or CSS variable presence as sufficient. Prioritize visible evidence such as reviewed diffs with minimal unrelated churn, searches across both packages and applications, targeted call-site migrations, validation output, and comments or code showing why each old behavior maps to a new size value.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial or unsafe dropdown size migration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for a dropdown sizing standardization task when they appear to satisfy the surface API change but visible evidence shows the migration is not behavior-preserving or safely scoped: relying mainly on grep-based removal of legacy prop names; adding size variants or CSS variables without mapping each old dropdown behavior to equivalent width, height, max-width, and max-height semantics; retaining legacy booleans as a parallel public API without a clear migration purpose; rewriting large files or SCSS wholesale with unrelated deletions/formatting/lockfile churn; migrating unrelated non-dropdown props with similar names; failing to propagate the new size prop through wrappers and real application consumers; or stopping after repeated searches without diff review, typecheck, or relevant tests.

metadata.environment: React/TypeScript monorepo with shared UI components and SCSS/CSS-variable styling
visible_evidence_to_check: diff scope and unrelated churn
legacy prop search results scoped to dropdown consumers
explicit mapping from old dropdown flags to new size values or CSS variables
wrapper and application-level consumer propagation
preservation of existing popper, custom sizing, adaptive/touch, caret, and auto-height behavior
typecheck/test/diff review after broad edits
avoid_as_primary_proxy: no remaining legacy prop names by grep
presence of a DropdownSize type alone
presence of CSS size classes alone

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory scopes the migration to dropdown sizing, maps old behaviors explicitly, updates wrappers/consumers broadly and carefully, avoids unrelated churn, and validates the diff.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: mostly behavior-preserving migration with small gaps such as limited test coverage or a few consumers still needing review, but no broad unsafe rewrites or misleading grep-only reasoning.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory implements a size prop and some CSS/consumer updates, but relies partly on superficial indicators and leaves unclear whether old no-max-width/height/size semantics are preserved across wrappers and consumers.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory emphasizes removed names, added CSS classes, or compatibility while visible diffs/searches show incomplete coverage, unrelated edits, questionable old-to-new mappings, or missing validation.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory performs broad/destructive rewrites or unrelated migrations, repeatedly relies on grep/no-op checks, breaks or ignores existing sizing/style behavior, and lacks meaningful diff/type/test validation despite claiming the sizing standardization is complete.

experiences.title: Worksearch Identifier Response Propagation
experiences.description: Use when an Open Library task concerns an `id_*` identifier existing in Solr/index metadata but being missing from work-search output; the key judgment is whether the trajectory wires the identifier through the user-facing worksearch fetch/serialization path with the established list-shaped contract.
experiences.context: Applies in the Open Library Python codebase, especially trajectories investigating Solr work documents, edition identifiers, and the worksearch plugin. Retrieve this experience when visible evidence shows or strongly suggests generic Solr identifier generation/dynamic `id_*` schema already handles the identifier, while explicit worksearch default-field selection or result-object construction may omit it. It is most useful after the agent has located neighboring external identifier fields or is making final implementation choices. It is less applicable during very early repository exploration with no worksearch-layer evidence, when the raw indexing path is actually broken, or when the task is primarily about book-provider UI/acquisition behavior rather than search-result document exposure.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in this cluster should not merely ask whether the agent found identifier indexing code. The discriminative evidence is whether the agent propagates the new identifier through the worksearch response contract: the field should be available to the search result builder and explicitly emitted in the returned document using the same list-valued/default-empty shape as analogous provider identifiers. Prior rubrics that said “fetch and expose `id_project_runeberg` with list shape” were directionally right because successful trajectories edited the response serialization path and often the default fetched-field allowlist, while failed partial trajectories commonly added only the default fetched-field entry and left the result object unable to expose the field. A better rubric should therefore distinguish complete response exposure from a single allowlist edit: adding only a search/default field list is weak evidence; adding the result serialization with `doc.get(..., [])`-style behavior is stronger; checking both explicit worksearch locations and updating a focused output test is strongest. Avoid tempting but misleading criteria that demand Solr schema changes, special-casing the generic Solr updater, adding the field to a broad `all_fields` set used for search syntax, treating the value as a scalar, or expanding into unrelated provider/template work. Prioritize visible greps/edits around neighboring identifier fields, confirmation that raw Solr already has the dynamic `id_*` field, and tests or manual checks that absent identifiers default to an empty list while present identifiers remain list-valued.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Identifier Response Contract Completion
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should complete the worksearch response contract for the missing Project Runeberg identifier by ensuring the field is available to default work-search results and is emitted by the result normalization/serialization path with the same list-valued shape and empty-list default used by neighboring external identifier fields. Strong evidence includes comparing analogous `id_*` fields, recognizing that generic Solr indexing already supports the field, avoiding unnecessary schema/updater special-casing, and validating the user-facing output layer rather than only the raw Solr builder.

scale.2: Recognizes the identifier or generic Solr `id_*` handling but focuses mainly on indexing, schema, or search-field parsing; there is little or no concrete worksearch response propagation and no clear list-shape contract.
scale.3: Finds the worksearch layer and modifies or proposes one relevant hook, such as a default fetched-field allowlist or response mapping, but leaves another explicit output path unchecked or provides only partial evidence that returned documents will include the field consistently.

experiences.title: Preserve Validation While Allowing Overlapping Cycle Inputs
experiences.description: Use when a permutation/cycle constructor task asks for non-disjoint cycle lists to be accepted and composed, and the trajectory has found a duplicate-element validation gate before existing cycle-composition logic.
experiences.context: Applies in Python library maintenance trajectories, especially mathematical/combinatorics code, where the reported bug is that list-of-cycles constructor input is rejected because elements repeat across cycles. The criterion is most useful once the agent has inspected the constructor path enough to distinguish cyclic-form input from array-form input and has found existing machinery that can compose cycles in sequence. It is less useful during very early repository exploration, for unrelated permutation operations, or when the proposed fix replaces composition logic without clear evidence about order semantics. It should also not be reduced to simply 'remove duplicate checks,' because array-form permutations and malformed single cycles may still need duplicate validation.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic contract: overlapping cycle lists must no longer be rejected, must be composed in the specified input order, and must still yield a valid permutation. The recurring decisive evidence was not just that the agent found the raised error, but that the trajectory identified the duplicate-check gate as applying too broadly and recognized that cyclic-form inputs should be allowed to continue into existing sequential cycle composition. A better rubric should check for this boundary explicitly: repeated elements across separate cycles are allowed, repeated elements in array-form input remain invalid, and validation/tests include both the reported duplicate-transposition identity and at least one nontrivial overlapping-cycle composition to expose order mistakes. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as 'uses the Cycle class' or 'removes the ValueError,' since those can miss order semantics or accidentally permit invalid array forms. Also avoid over-penalizing harmless cleanup differences if the visible code still preserves the behavioral boundary. Prioritize visible evidence from the trajectory: inspected constructor branching, proposed or applied guard conditioned on cyclic-form vs array-form input, acknowledgement of left-to-right application, and concrete validation outputs rather than environment-import workarounds.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the constructor fix narrowly permits repeated elements across separate cycle-list inputs while preserving duplicate rejection for array-form permutations, and should rely on or implement cycle composition in the task-specified input order. Strong evidence includes identifying the over-broad duplicate validation before cycle conversion, changing or planning to change that validation only for cyclic-form input, and validating both the duplicate-transposition identity case and a nontrivial overlapping-cycle case that would reveal reversed composition order.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Cyclic-Form Duplicate Boundary and Composition Order

required_visible_evidence: distinguishes cyclic-form list-of-lists input from array-form input
allows repeated elements across different cycles without raising the prior duplicate-elements error
preserves duplicate validation for non-cycle array-form inputs
checks or reasons about left-to-right composition using representative overlapping-cycle examples
common_false_proxies_to_avoid: only removing all duplicate checks
only confirming the reported example no longer raises
assuming any existing cycle helper has the correct order without verification
treating environment compatibility edits as the substantive fix

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses non-disjoint cyclic-form input or composition semantics.
scale.2: Recognizes the duplicate-cycle failure but proposes a broad or vague fix without preserving array-form validation or checking order semantics.
scale.3: Identifies the constructor duplicate check and intends to allow cyclic-form duplicates, but evidence about preserved validation or composition order is incomplete.
scale.4: Shows a targeted cyclic-form-only duplicate allowance and preserves array-form duplicate rejection, with some validation of the reported case or composition behavior.
scale.5: Clearly implements or plans the narrow validation boundary, preserves invalid array-form behavior, and validates both the reported identity case and a nontrivial overlapping-cycle case demonstrating correct input-order composition.

experiences.title: Forked Worker Stdio Requires FD-Level Child Isolation
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python multiprocessing/fork worker task is about preventing inherited terminal stdin/stdout/stderr while preserving queue-based logging or IPC.
experiences.context: Applies in Python codebases where long-lived or forked worker processes execute task/plugin code and the task explicitly concerns inherited standard I/O, terminal leakage, hangs, or process isolation. It is most useful after the trajectory has identified the worker lifecycle entrypoint or has begun editing the worker startup path. It is less useful during very early repository exploration before the process model is known, and should not be reduced to a generic testing rubric unless the trajectory is specifically adding a regression test for inherited file descriptors.
experiences.experience: The useful criterion in these cases was not merely whether the agent redirected output somewhere. The discriminating issue was whether the proposed fix actually detaches inherited OS file descriptors 0/1/2 early in the child worker lifecycle, before task or plugin code can read/write them, while keeping intended result/display communication on controlled queues. Several trajectories made tempting but insufficient edits such as reassigning only Python sys.stdout/sys.stderr, omitting stdin, changing streams rather than the underlying descriptors, doing it late in the run wrapper, or relying on broad executor tests that do not prove terminal detachment. A better rubric should explicitly check for all three standard descriptors, fd-level detachment or an equivalent robust abstraction, correct placement in the child startup path, compatibility with existing queue/display/result channels, and any required process/session-group semantics. Avoid rewarding superficial `/dev/null` reassignment, comments, or passing unrelated unit tests as sufficient evidence.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete Worker I/O Isolation Semantics
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a robust implementation plan or code change that prevents forked worker children from inheriting usable terminal stdin, stdout, and stderr at the OS descriptor level before any task/plugin execution; handles descriptor lifecycle safely; preserves intended queue/IPC/display logging paths; and accounts for worker process-group/session isolation and termination behavior when the task or codebase requires it.

required_evidence: identifies the actual worker child entrypoint or startup lifecycle rather than unrelated manager code
covers stdin, stdout, and stderr, not only output streams
detaches or replaces fd 0, fd 1, and fd 2 themselves, or uses an equivalent mechanism that prevents C-level/subprocess/direct-fd terminal access
places isolation before task/plugin/user code can run
keeps controlled result, display, logging, or IPC channels functional
does not rely solely on unrelated passing tests or Python-level stream reassignment

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward worker stdio isolation; only repository exploration or unrelated tests/edits.
scale.2: Recognizes the relevant worker area but proposes or applies a superficial change, such as redirecting only stdout/stderr or reassigning Python stream objects without addressing inherited descriptors.
scale.3: Implements partial child-side redirection in a plausible lifecycle location but misses important requirements such as stdin, fd-level semantics, process-group/session behavior, or preservation of controlled channels.
scale.4: Strongly addresses fd-level detachment for all standard descriptors early in worker execution and considers display/IPC preservation, with only minor uncertainty around cleanup, validation, or process-group details.
scale.5: Fully addresses worker isolation: all standard descriptors are robustly detached before task/plugin code, descriptor ownership/cleanup is safe, controlled display/result channels remain intact, process-group/session and termination behavior are handled as required, and validation directly exercises inherited-stdio behavior.

experiences.title: Refactor Acceptance Requires Tests Plus Provider Integration
experiences.description: Use when a frontend refactor task explicitly asks to move a small business rule out of a provider/component into a reusable onboarding/checklist module and add isolated tests for named user-plan scenarios.
experiences.context: Applies in a TypeScript/React monorepo where the task is not just to change behavior, but to extract an inline eligibility rule from a UI provider into a reusable/testable unit under the same feature directory. The trajectory should be far enough along to show edits or a concrete implementation plan; during pure discovery, the criterion can be premature except as a checklist of required next steps. It is most relevant when the acceptance criteria name both the extracted rule and required scenario tests, and when preserving provider behavior is critical. It is less useful for unrelated onboarding UI changes, broad subscription-helper changes, or tasks where tests are not required and no extracted module is expected.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics were useful when they noticed that this task has an explicit, observable contract: create a separate module for the checklist-marking eligibility rule and add unit tests covering free, paid-mail, and paid-VPN/get-started cases with checklist settings. In trajectories with no test file or no provider consumption, that missing evidence strongly indicated an incomplete solution. However, a test-only criterion is too narrow: several partial attempts created a helper or tests but still left broken integration, wrong argument ordering/types, shadowed imports, no provider update, or accidental provider control-flow changes. The better rubric should combine three visible requirements: the business rule is removed from the provider and consumed through a clean imported helper/hook; the extracted unit preserves the exact original boolean semantics by using existing subscription helpers and checklist IDs rather than reimplementing plan logic; and a dedicated unit test suite covers the required user-plan/settings combinations and failure cases.
