Avoid rewarding broad rewrites, mocked tests that do not match real provider usage, or passing helper tests while existing provider tests/type checks are failing. Prioritize evidence from the diff and command output: old inline subscription-helper expression gone from the provider, no unused direct subscription/user-settings hooks left there unless still needed, imported module/hook called with the same data shape/order it expects, no naming/import-path errors, new focused tests for all specified scenarios, and validation of both the new tests and existing provider behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete Testable Extraction With Behavior Preservation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a complete refactor of the checklist item-marking eligibility rule into a standalone reusable unit within the feature directory, with the original provider consuming that unit and retaining the same side-effect gating behavior. The extracted unit should preserve the original rule by delegating to existing subscription eligibility helpers and checking the appropriate checklist settings for paid-mail and VPN/get-started users, while allowing free users as before. A dedicated unit test suite should cover free users, paid-mail users with and without the paid checklist setting, paid-VPN/get-started users with and without the get-started checklist setting, and negative cases where helper results or settings do not match. The visible trajectory should also show validation or a credible plan to run the new tests and existing provider tests/type checks, with no evidence of import-path errors, name shadowing, wrong argument order, type mismatches, or unrelated provider control-flow rewrites.

required_evidence: inline eligibility expression no longer lives in the provider/component
provider imports and uses the extracted helper or hook without changing unrelated checklist display/update logic
extracted unit uses existing subscription eligibility helpers and checklist settings rather than duplicating plan-name logic
unit tests cover free, paid-mail, paid-VPN/get-started, matching settings, missing settings, and nonmatching helper results
validation includes new unit tests and, when changes have been made, existing provider tests or type checking
failure_signals: only creates a helper with no tests
only creates tests but provider still contains or does not consume the rule
helper signature and provider call disagree
import is shadowed by a local variable or points to the wrong path
provider behavior is broadly rewritten beyond the extraction
tests pass only because subscription helpers are over-mocked while integration remains broken

scale.1: No meaningful extraction or tests are visible; the provider still owns the business rule or the trajectory remains at generic discovery with no concrete implementation evidence.
scale.2: Some extraction work is visible, such as a new helper or provider import, but required scenario tests are absent or the provider does not clearly consume the helper correctly.
scale.3: The trajectory roughly matches the parent state: partial extraction or partial tests exist, but there are unresolved integration risks such as wrong argument order, type issues, missing provider validation, incomplete scenario coverage, or unrelated provider changes.
scale.4: Strong evidence of a correct extraction and provider integration is present, with focused tests covering most required scenarios and no obvious behavior-changing rewrites, though validation may be incomplete or one edge case may be missing.
scale.5: The rule is cleanly removed from the provider, consumed through the new reusable unit with matching types/signature and unchanged provider control flow, comprehensive tests cover all required user-plan/settings combinations and negative cases, and relevant tests/type checks have been run successfully.

experiences.title: Django Enum migrations must emit bracketed member-name lookup
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django migration serialization task involves standard Python Enum members being written to migrations by value, especially where enum values may be translated or otherwise unstable.
experiences.context: Applies in Django repository trajectories focused on migration value serialization for ordinary `enum.Enum` members used as model field defaults. It is most useful once the agent has located or is editing the migration serializer/serializer registry, or has reproduced output like `EnumClass('value')`. The criterion should be scoped to plain Python enums, because Django `models.Choices`/`TextChoices`/`IntegerChoices` have a separate serializer path and database-value semantics. It may be premature for broad migration/autodetector exploration before enum serialization has been connected to the issue, and it should not be applied to unrelated enum display, model field deconstruction, or choices-label behavior.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases checked the semantic contract that migration code must recreate an enum member by its stable member name, not by its stored value. This aligned well when visible trajectory evidence showed the agent changing the enum serializer from `.value` plus constructor syntax to an expression like `module.EnumClass['NAME']`, and validating serialized output such as `Status['GOOD']`. A better rubric should be stricter than merely saying “use the enum name”: `EnumClass('GOOD')` still calls the Enum constructor by value and is wrong when the enum’s value is not `'GOOD'`; changing only `.value` to `.name` without changing `()` to `[]` should be treated as incomplete. Likewise, broad changes to the Django Choices serializer or test expectations for Choices are suspect unless the task explicitly asks for them. Avoid overcrediting trajectories that update tests to match constructor-with-name or mutate Choices behavior. Prioritize visible source/output evidence: the plain Enum serializer should build an importable enum-class expression using bracket subscription with the quoted member name, should not serialize or import anything derived from the enum member value, should preserve the enum module import, and should leave separately registered Choices serialization alone unless separately justified.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For Django migration serialization of ordinary Python Enum members, the trajectory should implement or clearly converge on emitting an importable enum-class subscription by member name, such as `module.Status['GOOD']`, rather than constructing the enum from a serialized value or from the name as a constructor argument. Strong evidence includes editing the enum-specific serializer to use `self.value.name`, formatting with `[...]` rather than `(...)`, preserving the enum module import, validating exact serialized output, and avoiding unnecessary changes to the separate Django Choices serializer.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Bracketed Enum Member-Name Serialization

metadata.target_behavior: plain enum.Enum migration values serialize as module.EnumClass['MEMBER_NAME']
anti_patterns: continuing to serialize self.value.value
using EnumClass('MEMBER_NAME') constructor syntax
serializing as raw name/value without the enum class import
changing models.Choices serialization without task-specific justification
priority_evidence: source code in the enum-specific migration serializer
exact serializer output from a reproduction script or migration writer test
import set includes the enum module
separate Choices/TextChoices behavior remains value-based unless explicitly in scope

scale.1: No visible progress toward the enum-specific migration serializer behavior, or the trajectory remains focused on unrelated migration/model code.
scale.2: Identifies enum value serialization as relevant but proposes only vague name-based handling, with no clear expression form or import preservation.
scale.3: Partially changes or plans to change serialization to use the enum member name, but still risks constructor syntax, raw-name output, broken imports, or unintended Choices behavior.
scale.4: Clearly implements or validates plain Enum serialization as `module.EnumClass['NAME']` with correct imports, with only minor gaps such as limited official test coverage.
scale.5: Fully demonstrates the intended bracketed member-name serialization for ordinary Enum defaults, preserves import behavior, avoids unrelated Choices changes, and includes or updates focused migration serialization tests/reproductions covering string/binary/integer or translated-value cases.

experiences.title: Do not let ident round-trip evidence hide missing integration and error-contract work
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for Ansible/password-lookup style fixes where a parser must read serialized encryption metadata such as salt and ident, especially if the trajectory shows manual round-trip checks or test updates but the task also mentions conflict handling, controlled errors, or full lookup integration.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Ansible codebases where a lookup/plugin reads a stored single-line file format and passes parsed metadata into encryption. A rubric about parsing `ident` separately from `salt` is useful when the visible work is specifically evaluating the core parser/serializer inverse relationship. It becomes misleading when used as the main or sole criterion at final-review time, because a trajectory can demonstrate `_parse_content('password salt=X ident=Y')` returning separate pieces while still leaving other required behavior unresolved: all call sites may not be updated safely, new-file branches may not initialize parsed variables, stored-vs-explicit ident conflicts may be silently overwritten, hashing failures may still escape as raw library exceptions, lock cleanup may not be protected if new errors are introduced, or the actual repository code/import path may not be the code being tested. Conversely, during early exploration, absence of tests or complete precedence/error handling should not be treated as decisive if the agent is still diagnosing the parser bug.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often rewarded or penalized broad outcomes like “ident round-trip preservation,” “ident parsing consistency,” or “test coverage for API changes.” Those are only partial signals. They correctly identify the root parser issue, but they over-credit trajectories that stop after manual parser checks or ad hoc bcrypt checks and under-credit early trajectories that have not yet reached test updates. A better rubric should ask whether the visible trajectory is converging on a complete integrated fix: the serialized file format is parsed and formatted symmetrically; the parsed ident is actually used by the lookup on existing files; explicit user ident is handled according to the task’s inconsistency/conflict contract rather than silently overriding stored metadata; variables are initialized across both existing-file and new-file paths; encryption/hash failures are converted into the project’s expected error type; and any lock acquired before these checks is released on errors. Avoid making “unit tests updated for the new return signature” the decisive correctness criterion unless the trajectory is at the test-maintenance stage or visible test failures are the primary remaining blocker. Replacement criteria should prioritize concrete evidence from inspected code, diffs, and focused repros that exercise the full read-parse-precedence-encrypt-error path, not just isolated parser output or passing ad hoc scripts.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat parsing saved `ident` as complete while visible evidence leaves the full lookup contract incomplete: the parser may split `salt` and `ident`, but the run path does not safely propagate it through all branches, does not handle stored-vs-explicit ident inconsistencies as a controlled error, does not wrap hashing/library `ValueError` failures in the project error type, or introduces cleanup/initialization regressions around the locked file read/write flow.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Parsing-only ident fix masks missing lookup contract

metadata.environment: Python Ansible lookup plugin with single-line password file metadata and encryption via passlib/crypt helpers
required_visible_evidence: Parser/formatter round-trip keeps password, salt, and ident distinct
Existing-file and new-file branches initialize and propagate ident safely
Explicit ident and stored ident precedence/conflict behavior is visibly addressed
Hashing failures are converted to the plugin/framework error type
Lock/file cleanup remains safe if parsing or conflict checks raise
avoid_overweighting: Ad hoc parser output alone
Manual bcrypt success alone
Test return-arity updates alone
Pytest/import-path investigations without confirming the actual patched code path

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the visible work addresses both ident parsing and the integrated lookup/error-handling contract, or the trajectory is clearly still in early diagnosis without claiming completion.
scale.2: Minor evidence: parser and main flow are mostly integrated, but one secondary contract such as targeted test coverage or cleanup verification remains weak.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the parser handles ident, but visible work only partially addresses propagation, branch initialization, or explicit-vs-stored ident behavior.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory relies mainly on parser/manual round-trip checks while leaving important run-path behavior, conflict handling, or controlled hashing errors unimplemented or unverified.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory presents the fix as complete despite code or tests showing uninitialized variables, stale call sites, silent metadata conflicts, raw encryption exceptions, or unsafe lock release paths.

experiences.title: Require Consumed Backend Cap, Not Just Matching Literals
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task asks to keep an infrastructure limit, such as Solr boolean clauses in Docker Compose, aligned with an application/backend cap for large generated queries.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python web application with Docker Compose/Solr configuration when the trajectory has visible evidence that a runtime config flag must match a backend cap used by reading-log or similar large-filter search code. It is especially relevant after the agent has inspected the named config file and backend module, found the Solr option missing, or is repeatedly searching for cap names without connecting the cap to the query path. It is less useful for very early exploration before either side of the alignment has been inspected, or for tasks that only require a standalone config default without any application-level query cap or consumption site.
experiences.experience: The earlier rubrics correctly emphasized that the agent must find both the Solr setting and the backend reading-log cap; this was useful when trajectories visibly got stuck in repeated greps or only noticed one side of the alignment. However, the stronger rubric should not reward merely adding the string `30000` to two files or inventing an unused class constant. For this kind of task, final correctness depends on a semantic contract: the backend cap must be defined in the appropriate backend scope, the code path that builds or executes large reading-log/Solr filters must actually use that cap, and Docker Compose must pass the same limit to Solr while preserving existing options. A tempting but weak criterion is 'does the trajectory put `-Dsolr.max.booleanClauses=30000` in `SOLR_OPTS` and add any constant in `bookshelves.py`?' That proxy misses patches where the constant is dead and large queries remain uncapped or unvalidated. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent inspected the reading-log-to-Solr query path, distinguished SQL pagination limits from boolean-clause limits, avoided endless repeated searches after establishing absence, and planned or implemented a linked alignment/validation rather than unrelated literals.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Consumed Backend Limit Aligned With Solr Runtime Limit
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the agent is aligning the Solr boolean-clause runtime setting with the actual backend cap that governs large reading-log/Solr filter queries. Strong evidence includes preserving existing Solr `SOLR_OPTS` while adding the requested boolean-clause property, defining or locating the backend cap in the named backend module, connecting that cap to the code path that constructs or executes large OR/filter queries, and adding or identifying validation so the two values do not drift. Merely adding a matching numeric literal in an unused location is not sufficient.

metadata.environment: Python web application using Docker Compose and Solr
metadata.required_config_evidence: Solr service `SOLR_OPTS` is inspected and updated or planned to include the boolean-clause property while keeping existing JVM/system properties
metadata.required_backend_evidence: Backend cap is found or introduced in the reading-log/backend module in a reusable scope rather than as an arbitrary unused class attribute
metadata.required_consumption_evidence: Trajectory connects the cap to the reading-log search/filter or Solr query-building path that can create many boolean clauses
anti_patterns: Repeatedly running the same unsuccessful grep without changing strategy
Confusing SQL LIMIT or pagination batch size with the Solr boolean-clause cap
Adding the same numeric literal in two files without showing the backend value is used
Modifying only a secondary compose/config file when the task names the root runtime compose file

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward alignment; the trajectory repeats broad searches, fails to identify the Solr runtime setting or backend cap, and does not inspect the relevant query path.
scale.2: Identifies only one side of the contract, such as the missing Solr option or an unrelated backend limit, but does not establish where the application cap is defined or consumed.
scale.3: Recognizes that both Solr configuration and a backend cap must match, and may plan or add matching literals, but lacks evidence that the backend cap is placed in the right scope or used by the large-query code path.
scale.4: Shows strong alignment work: preserves existing Solr options, defines or locates a plausible backend cap, and investigates the reading-log/Solr filter path, but validation or actual consumption of the cap is incomplete or not clearly demonstrated.
scale.5: Fully demonstrates the semantic alignment: Solr receives the requested boolean-clause limit, the backend cap is defined in the appropriate reusable location, the large reading-log/Solr query path enforces or consumes that cap, and the trajectory includes a concrete check, test, or maintainability mechanism preventing future drift.

experiences.title: Protobuf API Field Contract Propagation
experiences.description: Use this when a task adds a field to a protobuf/gRPC response payload in a Go service and the trajectory is editing the `.proto`, generated bindings, OpenAPI/swagger output, and server logic that constructs the response.
experiences.context: Applies to Go repositories where API payloads are defined in protobuf files and generated artifacts are committed, especially when the new field is meant for client-visible diagnostics such as an evaluation reason. It is most useful after the agent has located the protobuf source or started modifying it, and remains relevant through final review. It may be premature during initial repository exploration before the schema/build workflow is known. It should be narrowed or skipped for purely internal structs, projects that do not commit generated files, or APIs without an HTTP/OpenAPI gateway; in those cases, adapt the propagation targets to the visible generation workflow.
experiences.experience: A strong rubric for this situation should not only ask whether the evaluator assigns some human-readable reason strings. Prior rubrics that focused on populating messages in many branch paths could over-reward patches that add ad hoc strings while leaving the public protobuf contract incomplete, generated code stale, swagger output missing, or error/not-found cases unhandled. Conversely, a rubric that only asks whether the `.proto` file was edited is too weak because clients consume generated bindings and gateway schemas. The better criterion should focus on end-to-end API contract propagation: the source protobuf adds the field compatibly, any categorical reason type is represented consistently with generated constants rather than scattered literals, generated Go and HTTP/OpenAPI artifacts are regenerated through the project’s canonical tooling or convincingly synchronized, and the server sets the field on the meaningful response-producing paths including disabled/not-found/error and successful match outcomes. Avoid demanding overly granular constraint-by-constraint explanations unless the visible task or existing API design requires that granularity; prioritize observable evidence of schema consistency, generated artifacts, public documentation, and branch-specific but stable reason values.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Protobuf Response Reason Contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a protobuf-defined client response field such as an evaluation reason, the trajectory should preserve the public API contract end to end: update the authoritative `.proto` using a backward-compatible new field number and an appropriate stable type for the reason, regenerate or consistently update all committed generated artifacts consumed by clients such as Go protobuf bindings and HTTP/OpenAPI/swagger output, and wire the server-side response construction to set reason values on meaningful evaluation outcomes and error paths using generated types/constants where applicable. Evidence should include use of the repository's canonical generation workflow when available, verification that generated accessors/descriptors and public schema expose the field, and review of evaluator return points rather than only a proto edit or scattered string assignments.

metadata.environment: Go service with protobuf/gRPC API definitions, committed generated Go bindings, and swagger/OpenAPI gateway output
primary_evidence: authoritative protobuf response message changed with a new compatible tag
generated protobuf bindings updated consistently, including struct field, getter, descriptors, and enum metadata if a categorical type is used
public HTTP/OpenAPI/swagger schema updated to expose the new response field/type
server evaluation logic assigns reason values on disabled, not-found/error, and successful match response paths
canonical generation/build tooling is used or the trajectory explains why manual synchronization was necessary
avoid_as_sole_evidence: manual partial edits to generated code without descriptor/schema consistency
only adding human-readable strings in evaluator branches
demanding excessively detailed constraint-level reasons when the visible API contract only establishes stable outcome categories

scale.1: No substantive evidence that the protobuf API contract was updated beyond exploration, or the trajectory edits irrelevant code without locating the authoritative response schema.
scale.2: A partial change is visible, such as adding a field only to the `.proto` or only assigning reason strings in server logic, but generated client-facing artifacts or response construction are largely missing.
scale.3: The trajectory has behavior comparable to the parent: it recognizes the protobuf source, the need for generation, and some evaluator wiring, but still lacks clear evidence that all public artifacts and important outcome/error paths are synchronized.
scale.4: Strong evidence shows the `.proto`, generated bindings, and most evaluator response paths are handled, with only minor uncertainty around public gateway documentation, exact reason typing, or verification.
scale.5: Complete evidence shows a compatible protobuf field/type, regenerated Go and public OpenAPI/swagger artifacts, stable generated reason constants or otherwise consistent reason representation, evaluator assignments for meaningful success/failure/error outcomes, and build or generation verification.

experiences.title: Do not score context plumbing without call-site and build evidence
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go task fixes lost cancellation by changing a configuration-loading API to accept context.Context and thread it through helpers.
experiences.context: This applies to Go repositories where the agent finds a top-level configuration loader hardcoding context.Background() while a lower helper already accepts context and uses it for remote/blob/file access, often with Cobra command contexts available at the CLI boundary. A misleading rubric only asks whether context flows from Load to getConfigFile/blob access; that can look satisfied while the repository is still broken because the API signature change leaves buildConfig/getStore/tests/other commands calling the old signature, or because production callers still use a background-context compatibility wrapper. The original context-propagation idea remains appropriate when the trajectory is at final-review stage and there is visible evidence that all relevant call sites and tests were updated and validated. During early exploration, absence of call-site edits should not be treated as failure yet; during implementation/review, unresolved compile errors or incomplete caller updates should dominate the assessment.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster correctly noticed the semantic target: accept a caller context, remove context.Background() from the configuration-loading path, and pass the context to the helper that performs cancelable storage access. The misleading part was treating that core edit as sufficient and sometimes demanding vague propagation through “parsing” or local file operations that may not have context-aware APIs. A better rubric for this situation should prioritize visible end-to-end API integration: the caller’s context is sourced from the real command/request boundary, every intermediate helper signature and invocation is updated, tests are updated or a compatibility layer is proven not to hide the old background-context path, and package builds/tests no longer report old-signature errors. Avoid generating a criterion that rewards merely adding LoadContext or changing getConfigFile if existing production paths still call a wrapper using context.Background(), and avoid requiring context support in libraries such as Viper or os.Open unless the trajectory shows an actual context-aware alternative. Replacement criteria should look for grep/build evidence, remaining context.Background() uses in the relevant loader path, and unresolved compiler diagnostics after signature changes.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that make or plan a context.Context signature change for configuration loading but do not visibly complete the mechanical integration across all callers and validation points. This includes leaving buildConfig/getStore/command handlers/tests on the old signature, introducing a context-aware wrapper while production callers still use a background-context wrapper, failing to search for remaining internal config Load invocations, or leaving compiler/build output showing old-signature call errors. Judge this only after the trajectory has begun implementation or final review; early investigation that has not yet edited code should not be treated as having this flaw.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Incomplete API fallout after context propagation

metadata.task_type: context propagation through configuration loading
key_visible_evidence: changed loader signature to accept context.Context
remaining old-signature call sites or compiler diagnostics
call-site grep/build/test output
production caller source of context such as Cobra cmd.Context
absence or presence of context.Background in the relevant loader path
do_not_require: context-aware parsing when the parser API does not accept context
context-aware local os.Open unless an actual alternative is present

scale.1: No evidence of incomplete API integration: all visible relevant callers/tests are updated or compatibility is clearly safe, no relevant context.Background path remains, and validation does not show old-signature errors.
scale.2: Minor risk only: most call sites are updated and no clear build error is visible, but the trajectory has not shown a comprehensive final grep or validation.
scale.3: Mixed evidence: the core loader-to-helper context path is changed, but some call-site/test coverage or validation remains uncertain at the current stage.
scale.4: Clear flaw: visible compiler output, grep results, or inspected files show old-signature calls or production paths not yet updated after the API change.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the patch mainly changes the core loader or adds a wrapper but leaves multiple production callers/tests broken or still using context.Background, with no credible plan or validation to resolve it.

experiences.title: Pinned-list reorder must preserve real drag semantics, not just rewrite scores
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Node.js/forum-style task involves reordering pinned or sticky items stored in a sorted set, and the trajectory has located both the client drag payload and the server/socket reorder path.
experiences.context: Applies in a NodeBB-like JavaScript application where pinned category topics are stored in a per-category sorted set, display order is read through sorted-set range/reverse-range APIs, and reordering is triggered by a browser drag event over a socket endpoint. This is most useful once the trajectory has visible evidence about the storage key, score direction, socket payload shape, permission helper, and existing tests. It is less useful during very early exploration before the agent has found the reorder implementation, and it should not be used as a generic sorted-set rubric for unrelated ranking features. It is also insufficient by itself if the task is only about authorization or only about ignoring unpinned items; in those cases generate narrower criteria for those contracts.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics that asked whether multiple pinned topics maintain correct relative order were directionally useful because the task’s decisive behavioral bug is not merely accepting a reorder call: the displayed pinned list must change to the intended order after a drag, under the repository’s sorted-set score semantics. They aligned especially when the trajectory showed repeated searching or no implementation progress, or when a patch assigned scores in a way that contradicted the API used to read display order. However, a tempting but wrong version of this criterion is to require that every pinned topic in the category be blindly reassigned sequential scores, or that unmentioned topics be appended after explicitly ordered topics. That can reward patches that mutate the pinned set during an unpinned-topic no-op request, preserve the old array payload contract even when the UI actually supplies a single moved item and visual index, or misunderstand whether higher or lower scores appear first. A better rubric should focus on the end-to-end reorder contract visible from the trajectory: the client drag handler should send enough information about the moved pinned topic and target visual position; the socket/backend should validate the payload and category permissions; the backend should first confirm the tid is already pinned and return without changing the pinned list if not; then it should move that existing pinned tid within the current pinned list and write scores consistent with the repository’s range/reverse-range display semantics. Prioritize evidence from observed frontend payload construction, socket validation, sorted-set read direction, existing tests that share state between no-op and reorder cases, and any actual patch/diff. Avoid judging only by isolated targeted tests or by comments claiming scores were normalized.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates that the agent is fixing pinned-topic reordering as an end-to-end move operation over the existing pinned list: it uses the client drag position or equivalent target index, validates a single concrete moved topic/order payload at the socket/tool boundary, enforces category admin/mod permissions, no-ops without mutating the sorted set when the requested topic is not currently pinned, and rewrites sorted-set scores so the repository’s display-range API returns the intended visual order after moving one pinned topic among multiple pinned topics. The evidence should come from inspected code, planned or applied changes, and relevant tests covering unauthorized users, unpinned no-op behavior, and multi-pinned relative order.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-end pinned reorder move semantics

prioritize_evidence: client drag payload includes moved topic identity and target visual position or an equivalent unambiguous ordering contract
socket/backend validation rejects malformed payloads before mutation
category admin/mod privilege is checked server-side
backend checks membership in the category pinned sorted set before writing scores
unpinned reorder attempts leave the pinned sorted set unchanged
multi-pinned reorder moves the existing pinned topic within the full current pinned list
score assignment matches the sorted-set range direction used for display
tests or reasoning account for shared state between no-op and successful reorder cases
avoid_as_primary_evidence: repeatedly searching for endpoints after the only entrypoint has been found
only updating requested array entries without considering current pinned-list order
blindly assigning sequential scores to all pinned topics in response to any request
passing an isolated reorder test while preceding no-op tests would mutate state
client-only UI permission gating without server-side validation

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses pinned-list reorder semantics; it mostly searches, loops, or focuses on unrelated endpoints without using the discovered storage and display-order facts.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory mentions sorted-set score updates or relative order, but does not connect client payload, server validation, pinned membership, no-op behavior, and display range direction.
scale.3: Moderate evidence equivalent to the parent trajectory: it identifies the reorder path and some ordering concerns, but the approach may still rely on incomplete array score updates, isolated tests, or an ambiguous score direction.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory plans or implements server-side permission checks, pinned-membership no-op behavior, and score updates consistent with display ordering, though one part of the client/socket contract or comprehensive validation may remain uncertain.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory clearly implements or verifies the complete end-to-end move contract from drag payload through socket validation to backend pinned-list mutation, with tests or reasoning for unauthorized users, unpinned no-op preservation, and correct multi-pinned visual order under the repository’s sorted-set semantics.

experiences.title: Version-aware reconciliation for contradictory historical fixes
experiences.description: Retrieve when a bug report names a specific release or historical implementation detail, while the trajectory has discovered that the checked-out workspace already contains or contradicts a known related fix.
experiences.context: Applies in repositories with meaningful git history, release tags, or backports, especially desktop/native bugs where the reported version, current checkout, and visible implementation disagree. The useful signal is not merely that the agent found a relevant historical commit, but that it has evidence such as the current commit identity, the reported release baseline, a contradictory implementation detail, and a comparison showing which codebase is actually being patched. This criterion is most useful after the agent has begun inspecting history or noticed a version mismatch. It is premature during initial code search before any version evidence exists, and it is less relevant for tasks without a named release, backport context, or conflicting current-code observation.
experiences.experience: In these cases, rubrics about validating a historical fix were useful only insofar as they penalized trajectories that kept exploring or patched peripheral symptoms without resolving the baseline mismatch. The better rubric should focus on whether the agent establishes the correct version context and patch direction before editing: does the visible trajectory reconcile the bug report’s release and implementation hint with the actual checked-out code, compare the suspected old/new native download behavior, and decide whether the target is the release baseline, a reverted fix, or a newer refactor? A tempting but weaker criterion is generic hypothesis-driven debugging or simply rewarding discovery of a commit whose title matches the bug. Another tempting wrong criterion is to require blindly restoring/adopting the named historical fix; in these trajectories the visible workspace sometimes already contained the apparently relevant change, so that proxy did not prove correctness. Prioritize observable evidence: git status/log or tag checks, direct inspection of the disputed native download implementation, comparison between reported release and current checkout, and a clear plan that ties the eventual patch to the actual failing open path rather than unrelated cleanup, UI dialog handling, or delete-file plumbing.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should explicitly reconcile the reported release/version and implementation hint with the actual workspace before committing to a fix. Strong evidence includes identifying whether the checkout already contains a related historical change, comparing the current native attachment download/open behavior against the reported release or relevant history, resolving contradictory observations such as a supposedly removed network call still being present, and using that conclusion to choose the correct patch target and direction. The rubric should reward version-aware reasoning that prevents patches to the wrong codebase or peripheral symptoms.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Version-context reconciliation

required_visible_evidence: current checkout or branch/commit/tag inspection
comparison against the bug-reported release or relevant historical implementation
direct inspection of the disputed native download/open path
explicit conclusion about which baseline is actually being fixed
do_not_reward_as_sufficient: only finding a historical commit title
generic code reading without resolving the version mismatch
patching UI error messages or cleanup paths without tying them to the reported native open failure
assuming the historical change direction is correct without checking the current workspace

scale.1: No meaningful version or baseline check; the trajectory treats the visible code as unquestionably correct for the report and explores or edits unrelated areas.
scale.2: Mentions history or a relevant release only superficially, but does not compare it with the current checkout or resolve contradictory implementation evidence.
scale.3: Identifies some version/history mismatch and inspects the disputed download/open path, but leaves the patch target or direction ambiguous.
scale.4: Clearly compares the reported release, current checkout, and relevant historical implementation, and narrows the fix to the native download/open behavior with a plausible patch direction.
scale.5: Fully resolves the baseline mismatch with concrete git/code evidence, explains why a specific implementation variant is the correct target, and uses that conclusion to avoid peripheral or wrong-direction changes.

experiences.title: Do not over-credit release-only Trivy parser edits
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go/Vuls task asks to parse OS version from Trivy results for downstream CVE detection, and the trajectory is focusing on `Metadata.OS.Name` to `ScanResult.Release` mapping.
experiences.context: Applies in the Vuls `trivy-to-vuls` Go integration, especially after the agent has found the Trivy schema-v2 parser and existing tests showing report-level OS metadata. The misleading pattern is a rubric that treats the task as satisfied by merely assigning the Trivy OS name/version field into the model's `Release` field and adding fixture expectations. That idea is useful during early exploration or as one subcriterion, but it is not sufficient at implementation/final-review stages when the task explicitly mentions downstream OVAL/GOST behavior and the visible code has legacy metadata logic based on result targets or detector gates that may still skip Trivy scans.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics correctly identified an important subtask: the parser must read Trivy's structured OS metadata and populate the existing release/version field. They were misleading because they made that narrow mapping the main success criterion, so trajectories that only added `Release = Metadata.OS.Name` looked strong even when they did not verify Trivy type semantics, did not update tests for all OS-bearing cases, did not reconsider family/server-name metadata source, and did not inspect downstream detector eligibility paths that the feature request says should become active. For similar tasks, generate a rubric that evaluates end-to-end OS metadata enablement: parser metadata should consistently come from report-level OS/artifact metadata, library-only reports should still behave as pseudo/library scans, unsupported/empty reports should still error appropriately, and downstream package CVE detection should no longer be skipped solely because Trivy scan metadata was incomplete. Avoid a tempting criterion that only says 'extract `Metadata.OS.Name` into `Release` while preserving existing behavior'; the existing behavior may itself be the compatibility problem. Prioritize visible evidence such as inspection of detector skip conditions, parser metadata construction, fixture coverage for OS-only, OS+library, and library-only reports, compile/test feedback or type verification, and minimal changes that preserve non-OS scans.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Release-only Trivy fix ignores end-to-end detector enablement
reference_golden_rubrics.description: At implementation or final-review stage for a Trivy OS-version parsing feature, penalize trajectories that stop at setting the scan result release/version from Trivy OS metadata without visible evidence that they checked the surrounding metadata and downstream detection contract. This flaw is present when the trajectory only edits the parser to assign the release field and possibly adjusts expected parser fixtures, but does not inspect or update package-CVE detector gating/reuse logic, does not verify whether report-level artifact/OS metadata should replace legacy result-target-derived family/server naming, and does not preserve behavior for library-only or unsupported reports. Do not apply this harshly during initial repository exploration before the parser and detector paths have been located.

metadata.repo_context: Go project with Vuls Trivy integration under a contrib parser using Trivy schema-v2 reports and a ScanResult model consumed by downstream CVE detectors.
metadata.stage_condition: Use mainly when the agent has already found the Trivy parser or is making/finalizing code edits.
primary_evidence_to_check: Parser maps structured OS metadata into both family and release consistently when OS metadata exists.
Artifact/server identity handling is considered rather than blindly preserving result-target strings.
Library-only reports without OS metadata remain pseudo/library scans and do not get bogus releases.
Unsupported or empty reports still produce the intended error behavior.
Downstream package detector eligibility no longer skips valid Trivy OS package scans because of incomplete metadata.
Tests or static checks cover OS-only, OS+library, and no-OS/library scenarios.
External Trivy type pointer/value assumptions are verified by compilation, module source inspection, or careful evidence.
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: Presence of a single assignment from Trivy OS name/version to the release field.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory treats release parsing as part of a broader metadata and detector-flow change, with clear attention to OS, library-only, unsupported, and downstream detection behavior.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory emphasizes the release mapping but also inspects some surrounding metadata or detector behavior and has a plausible plan to validate the broader contract.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory implements or plans the release mapping and tests basic parser output, but only partially checks missing-OS behavior, server/family metadata, or downstream detector gating.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory mainly adds the release assignment and fixture expectations while leaving legacy metadata construction and detector skip conditions unexamined.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory finalizes a release-only parser patch, relies on unverified type assumptions or uncompiled code, and provides no visible consideration of downstream detector activation or non-OS scan compatibility.

experiences.title: Vendor-Accurate Static Windows KB Tables
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go task requires updating hard-coded Windows cumulative update mappings for specific OS builds and preserving composite literal style so kernel-version KB detection remains correct.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories in a Go codebase where Windows update applicability is driven by static nested release/build tables containing revision-to-KB pairs, and the task explicitly names modern Windows builds whose KB data must be refreshed. It is most useful once the agent has located or begun editing the Windows release table, or when a long trajectory has spent time on adjacent EOL/config work while leaving the required Windows data untouched. Do not apply as the primary rubric for tasks that only change OS EOL dates, change runtime parsing logic without static KB data, or are still in very early repository discovery with no reasonable opportunity to address the required Windows mapping. Also do not treat a successful build alone as sufficient, because stale or fabricated KB tables can compile while still violating the task.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster focused on the task-critical Windows KB mapping requirement rather than the easier adjacent EOL edits. They correctly treated trajectories that only inspected files, repeatedly grepped for struct literal issues, or updated Fedora/macOS/SUSE data without adding credible Windows KB rows as lacking a core requirement. A stronger version should also check data authenticity: adding many named-field rows is not enough if the revision numbers and KB IDs look synthetic, arithmetic, placeholder-like, or unsupported by the existing vendor-update-history pattern. The better criterion should ask whether each requested build key has chronological, vendor-plausible revision/KB entries in the static table, uses the existing named-field literal style consistently, and preserves the behavior of kernel-version-based applied/unapplied KB calculation. Avoid tempting proxies such as rewarding any large KB list, passing compilation, adding tests alone, or searching for mixed literals without actually updating stale data. Prioritize visible evidence such as changed table sections for the requested builds, actual-looking Microsoft KB article IDs paired with matching build revisions, chronological insertion after the previous tail entries, no positional literals mixed into named slices, and optional focused validation showing modern kernel versions classify newly added KBs correctly.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a credible update to the static Windows KB release mapping for every build named in the task. Excellent evidence includes locating the correct release/build keys, appending or updating chronological revision-to-KB pairs that match real vendor update history rather than fabricated sequences, preserving the existing named-field composite literal style for all new release entries, and considering or validating the downstream kernel-version applied/unapplied KB behavior. This criterion should not award high credit for compile success, EOL-only changes, repeated literal-style searches, or bulk-generated placeholder KB data.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Vendor-Verified Windows KB Mapping Completeness

required_evidence: static Windows release table sections for all task-specified builds are edited or explicitly verified current
new revision and KB pairs are chronological and vendor-plausible
new composite literals use the same named-field style as surrounding entries
kernel-version KB detection impact is considered through tests, examples, or reasoned inspection
red_flags: no changes to the Windows KB table after substantial work
only OS EOL/config data is updated
reliance on build success as proof of mapping correctness
search loops for mixed literals without adding current KB data

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of updating the required Windows KB mapping; the trajectory only explores files, performs unrelated EOL edits, or repeats searches/compilation checks.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the agent has identified relevant build sections or mentions intended KB updates, but has not added credible mapping data, or only checks struct literal style.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: some Windows KB table edits are present, but coverage of the required builds is incomplete, vendor accuracy is unclear, ordering is questionable, or downstream detection is not considered.
scale.4: Strong evidence: all required build sections receive plausible chronological revision/KB updates using consistent named-field literals, with some inspection or validation of kernel-version detection.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: all required builds are updated with vendor-verified revision/KB pairs, no synthetic or placeholder entries, literal style is consistently preserved, and focused validation confirms applied/unapplied KB behavior for representative modern kernel versions.

experiences.title: Targeted HTTP Body Read Coverage
experiences.description: Use when a Go security/resource-exhaustion task asks for a bounded read helper and the trajectory is auditing or replacing unbounded HTTP request/response body reads.
experiences.context: Applies in Go repositories where the issue is unbounded `ReadAll` on HTTP `Request.Body` or `Response.Body`, especially after the agent has visible grep results or identified call sites such as JSON request helpers, auth handlers, external API response readers, or HTTP error-response readers. It is most useful during implementation or final-review stages when there is enough visible evidence to judge whether the agent is covering the relevant HTTP body sites. It is less useful before any repository-wide search has been done, and it should not be applied as a generic requirement to replace every `ReadAll`: file reads, config reads, SSH stderr reads, decompression reads, event stream internals, and test helpers may be unrelated or harmful to change. Coverage also should not be treated as sufficient if the helper only truncates without detecting an exceeded limit or if edits introduce syntax/import corruption; those need separate criteria.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics correctly emphasized that the task is not satisfied by adding `ReadAtMost` or changing only the most obvious JSON helper: the agent must find and update the actual internal HTTP request/response body reads that can grow due to remote input. This was discriminative when the visible trajectory showed only one call site changed, repeated failed edits, or many identified body reads still pending. However, a broad 'complete coverage' rubric can be misleading if it rewards indiscriminate replacements: some trajectories replaced non-HTTP reads or used one request-size constant for response bodies while leaving semantic problems in `ReadAtMost`. A better rubric should focus on targeted coverage: the agent should use grep/search evidence to enumerate relevant HTTP `r.Body`, `resp.Body`, `response.Body`, or equivalent response-body reads; replace those with the bounded helper and appropriate request/response limits; preserve existing error wrapping, parsing, and body-close behavior; and explicitly leave unrelated `ReadAll` usages alone unless justified. Avoid the tempting proxy of counting many `ReadAll` replacements or package builds as success. Prioritize visible evidence such as narrowed grep commands, inspection of each candidate context, concrete updates to central HTTP JSON helpers and external response readers, removal of remaining unbounded HTTP body reads, and notes explaining why non-HTTP candidates were excluded.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Targeted Coverage of Unbounded HTTP Body Reads
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a targeted audit and remediation of all relevant internal HTTP request/response body reads that were previously unbounded. Strong evidence includes repository searches for `ReadAll` on HTTP bodies, inspection of each candidate to distinguish request/response bodies from unrelated readers, conversion of the relevant body reads to the new bounded helper with appropriate fixed request/response limits, preservation of existing body closing, parsing, and error-wrapping behavior, and avoidance of unrelated file/config/SSH/event-stream replacements unless explicitly justified.

preferred_visible_evidence: grep or equivalent search for non-test `ReadAll` usages involving `r.Body`, `req.Body`, `resp.Body`, `response.Body`, or equivalent HTTP response variables
updates to central HTTP JSON/body parsing helpers as well as scattered direct HTTP response/request body readers
remaining `ReadAll` hits are inspected and classified as non-HTTP or otherwise out of scope
call sites use a fixed maximum size appropriate to request versus response bodies
existing `defer Body.Close`, status handling, unmarshalling, and trace/error wrapping semantics are preserved
boundaries: Do not reward replacing every `ReadAll` blindly
Do not count unrelated file, config, SSH stderr, decompression, event stream, or test reads as required coverage
Do not treat call-site coverage as sufficient if the bounded helper silently truncates oversized input or the code is syntactically broken

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of auditing or updating HTTP request/response body reads; the trajectory only adds a helper, edits unrelated code, or remains stuck before identifying body-read call sites.
scale.2: Updates one obvious HTTP body read but leaves other identified relevant HTTP request/response body reads pending, or performs only a shallow search without classifying candidates.
scale.3: Comparable to the parent trajectory: some relevant HTTP body call sites are identified and partially converted, but coverage is incomplete, uncertain, or mixed with unreviewed candidates.
scale.4: Strong targeted coverage: most relevant HTTP body reads found by search are converted to the bounded helper, with visible inspection of remaining candidates and preservation of existing call-site behavior; only minor omissions or uncertainties remain.
scale.5: Comprehensive and well-scoped coverage: all visibly relevant internal HTTP request/response body reads are audited and converted with appropriate fixed limits, unrelated `ReadAll` usages are explicitly excluded with reasons, and existing parsing, closing, and error semantics are preserved.

experiences.title: Audit Sinks Must Be Driven by Runtime Event Emission
experiences.description: Retrieve when an audit logging task asks for pluggable/configurable sinks or OTEL-based audit export, and the trajectory is adding sink/config/manager infrastructure. The key rubric should test whether audit events are actually emitted from request-handling or security-relevant code paths, not merely whether sinks are initialized.
experiences.context: Applies in Go service/backend repositories where the task is to implement or refactor audit logging so external sinks can receive security-relevant or mutation events. It is especially relevant after the agent has created audit packages, Sink interfaces, file/OTEL sinks, config sections, manager/lifecycle code, or server constructor plumbing, but visible evidence shows little or no wiring into RPC/HTTP middleware, auth handlers, or resource mutation handlers. It is less useful before any implementation exists beyond exploration, when the task is explicitly limited to a standalone sink library, or when the trajectory already shows concrete middleware/handler emission code; in those cases, the rubric should shift toward event coverage, config validation, OTEL correctness, or build/test health.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on runtime audit event source integration. They were discriminative because a configurable Sink interface, file sink, OTEL sink, and startup manager can all compile in isolation while still producing no audit log records if nothing calls them during real requests. A better rubric should ask for observable code paths that convert relevant API activity into audit events and send them through the configured pipeline: for example, a gRPC/HTTP interceptor or equivalent handler hooks for authentication/security actions and mutating operations such as create/update/delete of flags, namespaces, segments, rules, constraints, variants, or distributions. Prioritize visible evidence such as middleware added to the server interceptor chain, switch/type handling over mutating request types, calls that add audit events to the current OTEL span or export them to sinks, propagation of author/IP/request metadata, and tests or build output exercising the emission path. Do not treat mere existence of config structs, default YAML, manager construction, context storage, server accessors, or Close hooks as sufficient. Also avoid overfitting to a requirement for before/after state capture unless the task explicitly demands it; the core boundary is that configured sinks must receive events generated from real request processing.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The implementation connects the audit sink infrastructure to actual runtime event generation. Strong evidence includes a request middleware/interceptor or equivalent service-handler hooks that identify security-relevant and mutating operations, construct structured audit events with relevant metadata, and route those events through the configured sink/OTEL pipeline. This criterion should not be satisfied by standalone sink implementations, config wiring, or lifecycle initialization unless there is also visible evidence that real API operations emit audit records.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Runtime Audit Event Emission

required_visible_evidence: audit emission code in request middleware, interceptors, or operation handlers
coverage of security-relevant or mutating API actions rather than only startup/shutdown
calls that send constructed audit events to configured sinks or add them to the OTEL processing path
audit metadata derived from request context or request payload, such as action/resource/author/IP where available
insufficient_evidence: only defining Sink/Event interfaces
only adding file or OTEL sink implementations
only adding audit config/defaults/schema
only constructing an audit manager at startup or storing it in context/server fields
only adding Close/shutdown hooks
metadata.applicable_stage: mid-to-late implementation or review stage after sink/config scaffolding is visible

scale.1: No visible runtime emission path; the work only explores or defines standalone audit/config/sink scaffolding.
scale.2: A manager or sink is initialized and perhaps passed through startup/server structs, but no concrete request or handler path is shown calling it for real operations.
scale.3: Some emission hook exists, but coverage is narrow, ad hoc, or disconnected from the configured/OTEL sink pipeline.
scale.4: Clear request-processing integration emits audit events for important mutating or security-relevant operations through the configured pipeline, with reasonable metadata.
scale.5: Comprehensive, centralized emission integration covers the expected operation classes, preserves extensible sink semantics, uses the OTEL-backed processing path correctly, and includes validation or tests demonstrating events reach configured sinks.

experiences.title: Path-Branch Exclusivity for Format Identifiers
experiences.description: Retrieve when an Astropy-style IO registry identifier crashes after a non-matching filepath falls through to optional positional-object detection.
experiences.context: Applies in Python library bug-fix trajectories where the reported failure is an IO registry format-identification call, the traceback points into a registered identifier, and visible source inspection shows the identifier first checks a file object or filepath and then unconditionally inspects optional positional arguments. It is especially relevant once the agent has confirmed that the public registry call can pass an empty args list and has located the identifier’s filepath-extension branch. Do not apply this criterion to unrelated registry dispatch bugs, to cases where the identifier is only meant to classify in-memory objects with no filepath semantics, or before the trajectory has enough evidence to distinguish filepath handling from positional object handling.
experiences.experience: The repeated rubrics in these cases focused on making the FITS identifier return False instead of raising IndexError when called with a non-FITS filepath and no positional data object. That was useful because the visible traceback, reproducer, and source all showed an unsafe args[0] access after a non-matching filepath. However, a rubric that only asks for an empty-args guard is too broad: it can accept a patch that merely wraps args[0] while still allowing a supplied non-FITS filepath to fall through into object-based detection when args is non-empty. The better criterion should capture the semantic boundary visible in the issue text: a supplied filepath should be decided by the filepath branch itself, returning True only for matching FITS-like extensions and False for non-matching filenames; positional HDU-like object detection should only be reached when there is no filepath/file object to decide from. Prioritize evidence such as source diffs or tests showing the public identify_format reproducer no longer raises, non-FITS path strings are treated as non-matches, FITS extensions and file-object signature checks remain intact, and HDU-like object detection is preserved only for the no-filepath case. Avoid tempting proxies such as simply searching for an if args guard, adding broad changes to other identifiers without task evidence, or relying on hand-written mock tests that pass arguments in a shape different from the registry call contract.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should restore the identifier’s filepath-branch contract: when a filepath is provided, the identifier must return the result of the extension check directly, so non-matching path strings do not fall through to positional args indexing or object detection. It should also preserve existing behavior for matching FITS-like extensions, file-object signature detection, and HDU-like positional inputs when no filepath is available. Evidence may include code inspection, a targeted public-registry reproducer, or focused tests covering non-FITS paths, FITS paths, file objects, and no-filepath HDU-like inputs.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Exclusive filepath decision in format identifier

prioritize_visible_evidence: traceback or source shows non-matching filepath reaches optional args indexing
registry call contract shows args can be empty
patch makes filepath branch return a boolean match result rather than falling through
validation covers reported public API reproducer and preserves positive FITS/file-object/no-filepath object cases
avoid_overcrediting: a guard around args[0] that still lets non-matching filepaths consult positional objects
unnecessary edits to unrelated identifiers without task-specific evidence
tests that do not exercise the registry-style argument passing

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory identifies the unsafe fallthrough from filepath handling to positional args, or it changes unrelated registry behavior without addressing the reported identifier.
scale.2: Recognizes the args[0] crash but only proposes a generic empty-args guard, with little or no attention to the intended filepath-branch semantics.
scale.3: Matches the parent-level behavior: prevents the reported empty-args crash and preserves obvious positive FITS extension detection, but does not clearly establish that non-matching filepaths are decided before positional object detection.
scale.4: Strong evidence that the fix treats non-matching filepaths as non-matches without indexing empty args, preserves FITS path/file-object behavior, and validates the public reproducer.
scale.5: Fully demonstrates the correct branch contract: filepath presence causes an immediate extension-based boolean result, positional HDU-like detection remains available only when no filepath/file object decides the format, and targeted validation covers the reported call plus relevant positive and negative edge cases.

experiences.title: Do not let prerelease parsing alone stand in for a coupled startup/update refactor
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go startup task combines release classification fixes with requirements to decouple update-check logic and expose version/update metadata for UX, logging, API, or telemetry.
experiences.context: This warning applies when the problem statement is not merely “classify prerelease versions correctly,” but also says startup currently blends release/update checks, asks for improved testability or reuse, and requires current version, latest version, update availability, and latest-release URL to be available to startup logging/UX while release status controls telemetry. In such cases, a trajectory that only edits an inline `isRelease`-style helper, manually validates `-rc`/`dev`/`snapshot`, and runs a build has addressed only one subproblem. The original prerelease-detection idea remains appropriate as a supporting criterion when the task is solely about release classification semantics, or as one component of a broader rubric; it is misleading as the main or only criterion when the visible task includes update-info propagation and separation of release logic from startup flow.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster emphasized correct SemVer prerelease detection, often rewarding use of `Version.Pre` or lists of prerelease identifiers. That criterion is technically useful, but in this task shape it over-focuses on the easiest local bug and misses the broader contract: release/update checking should be reusable/testable rather than embedded in startup, and startup-visible info should include current/latest versions, update availability, and the latest-version URL when applicable. A better rubric should ask whether the trajectory is moving release classification and update-check computation into a testable abstraction and whether startup consumes a structured result to populate logging/UX/info/telemetry consistently. Avoid generating a standalone “pre-release classification correctness” rubric as the decisive signal when the trajectory evidence shows only changes to the inline classification helper. Prioritize visible evidence such as creation or planned creation of a release/update checking component, dependency-injected or mockable latest-release lookup, structured release info containing current version, latest version, update flag, and URL, startup code using that structured info, and tests covering both classification and update-info behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a Go startup task that explicitly combines prerelease release-detection fixes with decoupling release/update checks and exposing startup version/update metadata, penalize trajectories that treat the task as complete after only changing an inline release-classification helper. This flaw is present when visible evidence shows the agent mainly edits a local `isRelease`-style function or string/SemVer predicate, validates prerelease examples manually, and perhaps removes an unused import, but does not introduce or plan a reusable/testable release/update-check abstraction, does not propagate a structured latest-release URL alongside current/latest versions and update availability, and leaves startup responsible for intertwined parsing, remote lookup, comparison, logging, info construction, and telemetry decisions.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Classification-only fix misses release/update information contract

task_cues: problem statement mentions startup blending release/update checks
problem statement asks for testability or reuse
expected behavior includes current version, latest version, update availability, and latest-version URL
telemetry behavior depends on proper release classification
flaw_evidence: trajectory only modifies inline release classification
manual tests focus only on prerelease strings
no reusable release/update checker or mockable latest-release lookup is introduced or planned
startup still owns parsing, latest-release fetch, comparison, messaging, info population, and telemetry gating
latest-version URL or structured release info is absent or added ad hoc without decoupling
acceptable_evidence: trajectory creates or plans a separate release/update checking abstraction
latest-release lookup is injectable or otherwise testable
structured result carries current version, latest version, update flag, and URL
startup consumes that result for logging/UX/info/telemetry
tests cover prerelease classification and update-info behavior

scale.1: No evidence of the classification-only flaw: the trajectory addresses prerelease classification as part of a broader reusable release/update-check design and structured metadata propagation.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: prerelease classification is emphasized, but the trajectory also shows concrete work toward decoupled update logic or structured current/latest/update/URL info.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory recognizes broader startup/update requirements but implementation work remains mostly focused on the release predicate, with only partial or speculative metadata propagation.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory patches and validates only the inline release predicate while leaving update lookup, comparison, logging, info construction, and URL handling coupled in startup.
scale.5: Most severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory explicitly concludes the task is complete based on prerelease classification tests/build success despite no reusable update-check abstraction and no reliable structured propagation of latest-version URL and update metadata.

experiences.title: Require Evidence of a Compatibility Break, Not an Idealized Polyfill Checklist
experiences.description: Use when generated criteria demand exhaustive specification fidelity, exact version boundaries, injection wiring, and permanent tests before the visible compatibility fix has reached final validation.
experiences.context: Browser compatibility work often progresses from locating the injection path to implementing a guarded shim and then validating affected runtimes. At an early or middle cutoff, missing one final integration detail is not equivalent to an incorrect final patch. Strong criticism is appropriate once visible code uses a contradicted runtime boundary, cannot reach the page context, overwrites native behavior, or fails representative indexing checks.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics bundled every ideal property of the final solution and therefore under-valued trajectories that were converging on a working guarded quirk. Generate a criterion around observable incompatibility: unsupported runtime coverage, ineffective injection, native-method replacement, or demonstrated indexing errors. Do not require the exact final version predicate or complete language-spec coverage unless the task or visible investigation establishes those as necessary.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Unresolved Runtime or Injection Incompatibility
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize visible polyfill work when its runtime gate excludes a demonstrated affected engine, its registration cannot inject before affected page code, it overwrites an existing native method, or representative index behavior visibly fails. Treat unverified but still-investigated boundaries as uncertainty rather than a confirmed defect.

observable_evidence: runtime/version investigation
quirk registration and injection timing
native-method guard
representative positive, negative, and out-of-range checks

scale.1: No visible evidence of a demonstrated runtime, injection, or indexing incompatibility remaining in the proposed shim; the available implementation and validation evidence is consistent with the required behavior.
scale.2: A minor or early-stage concern about a demonstrated runtime, injection, or indexing incompatibility remaining in the proposed shim is visible, but it is not confirmed and the trajectory is still actively resolving it.
scale.3: Evidence about a demonstrated runtime, injection, or indexing incompatibility remaining in the proposed shim is mixed or incomplete; the concern remains plausible but is not yet decisive.
scale.4: Clear visible evidence indicates a demonstrated runtime, injection, or indexing incompatibility remaining in the proposed shim, with no convincing correction or validation yet.
scale.5: The trajectory directly reproduces or validates a demonstrated runtime, injection, or indexing incompatibility remaining in the proposed shim, or claims completion while the contradiction remains unresolved.

experiences.title: Do not treat collecting overload lines as sufficient for autodoc signature fixes
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating or generating rubrics for Sphinx autodoc changes that add support for multiple SWIG-style docstring signatures, especially when the trajectory focuses on parsing consecutive lines from `_find_signature()`.
experiences.context: Applies in the Sphinx `sphinx.ext.autodoc` environment where `autodoc_docstring_signature` extracts callable/class signatures from prepared docstring lines and downstream formatting uses `Documenter.format_signature()`, `autodoc-process-signature`, and directive-header newline splitting. The misleading case is a trajectory that correctly discovers that the regex can match multiple leading signature lines and modifies parsing to collect them, but represents them as a changed return type, newline-joined raw args, a single shared return annotation, direct formatted return strings, or ad-hoc delimiters. The original idea of checking for multiple leading signature extraction is still useful, but only as one part of the criterion; it is not enough if the implementation bypasses the normal signature formatting pipeline, breaks single-signature behavior, leaves extra signatures in the docstring body, scans non-leading prose, or mishandles per-overload return annotations.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often rewarded trajectories for 'collecting all consecutive signature lines' or 'combining them with newlines.' That criterion is too broad for this task because many plausible patches collect the right text but produce invalid autodoc output: base formatting may wrap an already-parenthesized multiline string, a single `retann` may be appended to all overloads, the `autodoc-process-signature` hook may be skipped, or stripped-signature mixins may receive an incompatible return shape. A better rubric should focus on compatibility with the existing autodoc data contract: preserve the normal first-signature `(args, retann)` path, store or append additional overload signatures in a way that becomes separate directive signatures, preserve per-overload return annotations, remove exactly the consumed signature lines from rendered docstrings, and keep existing single-signature/config-disabled/explicit-signature behavior intact. Avoid tempting criteria that praise returning a list from `_find_signature()`, joining raw args with `\n`, using the last return annotation, returning preformatted strings directly from `format_signature()`, or scanning the whole docstring for matching-looking lines. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence such as inspection of `Documenter.format_signature()` wrapping behavior, `add_directive_header()` newline behavior, tests or failures showing exact directive output for single and multiple signatures, and explicit handling of remaining docstring content.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Incompatible overload signature representation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that add multiple docstring-signature extraction for Sphinx autodoc but represent or format the extracted overloads in a way that is incompatible with the existing signature pipeline. This flaw is present when visible code or plans change `_find_signature()` to return a list consumed inconsistently, join only raw argument strings while keeping one shared return annotation, preformat signatures and bypass `Documenter.format_signature()`/signature events without accounting for existing behavior, introduce ad-hoc delimiters, leave additional overload signatures in the docstring body, or scan beyond the leading signature block. The issue is especially severe if existing single-signature output would gain extra parentheses, lose return annotations, skip configured processing hooks, or if tests already show exact-output failures that the trajectory has not resolved.

metadata.environment: Sphinx autodoc, `autodoc_docstring_signature`, docstring-derived callable/class signatures
visible_evidence_to_check: How `_find_signature()` return values are represented and consumed
Whether `Documenter.format_signature()` wrapping and `autodoc-process-signature` behavior are preserved
Whether each overload keeps its own return annotation
Whether all consumed signature lines, and only those lines, are stripped from the docstring body
Whether existing single-signature and config-disabled tests still pass or failures are explained as baseline
metadata.misleading_positive_proxy_to_avoid: The patch merely loops over consecutive regex matches or produces a newline-containing string
