scale.1: No evidence of an incompatible representation; the trajectory explicitly preserves the existing formatting pipeline while adding overload support.
scale.2: Minor uncertainty about formatting details, but the trajectory recognizes the wrapping/return-annotation/docstring-stripping contracts and avoids obvious incompatible representations.
scale.3: Mixed evidence: the trajectory collects multiple signatures but only partially accounts for how they flow through existing formatting, return annotations, or docstring stripping.
scale.4: Clear evidence of an incompatible approach, such as newline-joining raw args with one return annotation, returning preformatted signatures directly, or changing `_find_signature()` return shape without updating all consumers safely.
scale.5: Severe incompatible implementation: it breaks existing single-signature output or hooks, uses ad-hoc delimiters or shared return annotations, leaves/duplicates signature lines in docs, scans non-leading content, or ignores failing exact-output tests caused by the change.

experiences.title: Empty path entries must be filtered before path normalization
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django/template autoreload-style bug is caused by empty string configuration paths being converted by pathlib into the current/project directory.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Django code where a configured list of filesystem directories is normalized with pathlib.Path or a helper wrapping pathlib, and the task explains that an empty string entry such as [''] is accidentally treated as the current working directory. This is most useful once the trajectory has inspected the directory-collection logic or path-normalization helper, or has reproduced that Path('') joined to cwd equals the project root. It is less applicable for unrelated autoreload failures, generic test-running problems, broad settings validation refactors, or tasks where empty strings are not the regression trigger. Do not require whitespace-only handling unless the task or visible investigation makes it part of the expected contract.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic fix: empty directory entries must be skipped before pathlib normalization so autoreload does not watch the whole project as a template directory, while valid relative/absolute template directories and existing framework-path exclusions remain intact. This aligned well because visible trajectory evidence repeatedly showed the agent identifying `Path('')`/cwd behavior and editing the collection point rather than changing unrelated template engine semantics. A better rubric should check both configured backend directories and loader-provided directories, since either source can feed the autoreload directory set. It should also check preservation: non-empty paths still get normalized and included, existing Django/internal path filtering is not removed, and the later `template_changed()` behavior remains scoped to real template directories. Avoid the tempting criterion that success requires a project-native regression test or perfect test-runner setup; in this setting, ad hoc validation and failed pytest setup are weaker evidence than whether the implementation targets the empty-string normalization boundary correctly. Also avoid overbroad criteria such as changing global path conversion helpers, rejecting invalid settings everywhere, or treating whitespace-only strings as mandatory unless explicitly supported by the task.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the fix prevents empty string directory entries from being converted into the current/project directory during template autoreload directory collection, while preserving valid configured and loader-provided template directories and existing framework path filtering.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Filter empty directory entries before normalization

metadata.environment: Python Django-style template autoreload using pathlib-based directory normalization
key_observable_evidence: Agent recognizes that an empty string normalized with pathlib represents the current directory
Agent targets the autoreload/template-directory collection path rather than unrelated global settings behavior
Implementation or plan skips falsy empty directory entries before path conversion for configured template dirs
Implementation or plan also considers loader-returned directories if they feed the same watched directory set
Valid non-empty relative and absolute template directories remain included
Existing internal/framework path exclusion logic remains in place
avoid_as_primary_evidence: Merely installing missing dependencies
Requiring a native regression test as the main correctness signal
Broadly changing global path conversion or template engine configuration parsing without need
Mandating whitespace-only filtering when the visible task only requires empty strings

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses empty string paths becoming the current/project directory.
scale.2: Recognizes the empty string/pathlib issue but has not clearly targeted the directory collection logic or risks breaking valid directory handling.
scale.3: Targets empty configured template directory entries before normalization, but evidence is incomplete for loader-provided directories or preservation of existing filtering.
scale.4: Clearly filters empty entries in the relevant autoreload directory collection path and preserves valid template directories, with only minor uncertainty about edge sources or validation.
scale.5: Fully addresses empty entries from both configured and loader-provided directory sources before normalization, preserves valid paths and existing internal-path filtering, and has visible reasoning or validation showing the project root is no longer watched accidentally.

experiences.title: Native reST typed-param right-split boundary
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Sphinx task involves malformed rendering of native `:param <type> <name>:` fields where the type contains whitespace, commas, or delimiters.
experiences.context: Applies in the Sphinx codebase or similar documentation systems after the trajectory shows the reported input is native reStructuredText/Sphinx field-list syntax, such as `:param dict(str, str) opc_meta:`, rather than a Google/NumPy-style Napoleon parameter section. It is especially useful once the agent has inspected the generic docfield/Python-domain field transformation path or has reproduced that the field argument becomes a single string like `<type> <name>`. It is less useful during very early repository exploration before the parser path is known, and it should not be applied to tasks about function signatures, autodoc type-hint injection, or Napoleon-only `name (type)` parsing.
experiences.experience:
The useful rubric should not merely say “handle nested type annotations.” In these trajectories, the decisive issue is the grammar boundary for native typed parameter fields: the parameter name is the final whitespace-delimited token, while the type expression before it may itself contain spaces, for example after commas in `dict(str, str)`. A good criterion rewards evidence that the agent has identified the generic docfield transformation path for native `:param type name:` fields and is changing the type/name split to preserve the whole type while assigning the final token as the parameter name. It should also reward validation using the exact field-argument shape, e.g. showing old behavior parses `dict(str, str) opc_meta` as a truncated type and wrong name, while the proposed behavior yields type `dict(str, str)` and name `opc_meta`.

Avoid tempting but weaker criteria that focus on autodoc generally, Python signature parsing, or Napoleon’s Google-style regex; raw `:param ...:` lines are not transformed by Napoleon in this scenario. Also avoid requiring an elaborate nested-delimiter parser when the visible grammar only requires splitting the compact typed field from the right. At final-review stages, the rubric should penalize unrelated environment compatibility edits and broad rendering changes, because the localized parsing boundary is enough and safer.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates that the reported syntax is a native Sphinx/reST typed parameter field, identifies the generic docfield/Python-domain transformation that supports `:param <type> <name>:`, and proposes or applies a localized fix that separates the parameter name from the type at the final whitespace boundary so type strings containing spaces, commas, or delimiters are preserved. Strong evidence includes inspecting the typed-field transformation code, recognizing that Napoleon/Google-style parsing is not the relevant path for raw `:param` fields, and testing or reasoning over `dict(str, str) opc_meta` to confirm the rendered output would use parameter name `opc_meta` and full type `dict(str, str)` without unrelated compatibility or rendering changes.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Correct native typed-field split

metadata.critical_boundary: parameter name is the final token; preceding text is the type and may contain whitespace
preferred_evidence: locates generic docfield/Python-domain typed field handling
shows first-whitespace splitting truncates `dict(str, str)`
uses rightmost whitespace or equivalent logic to preserve full type
does not rely on Napoleon-only parsing for the raw field syntax
avoid_evidence: changes broad rendering behavior instead of the type/name split
keeps unrelated local environment compatibility workarounds

scale.1: The trajectory does not connect the bug to native typed parameter field parsing, or focuses only on unrelated areas such as signatures, generic autodoc lookup, or Napoleon regexes without evidence they affect raw `:param` fields.
scale.2: The trajectory recognizes complex type strings are involved but remains at a broad parsing/rendering level, with little evidence of the native docfield path or the final-token name boundary.
scale.3: The trajectory has behavior roughly comparable to the parent: it suspects the type/name split problem or inspects relevant docfield/Python-domain code, but the evidence is incomplete, mixed with wrong-parser investigation, or not yet tied to a concrete localized fix.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly identifies native typed-field handling and the unsafe first-whitespace split, and proposes a rightmost-whitespace or equivalent split that preserves `dict(str, str)` while keeping the parameter name separate.
scale.5: The trajectory provides strong, localized evidence: it traces raw `:param type name:` through the generic typed-field transformer, explicitly rules out Napoleon for this input style, demonstrates old vs new parsing on `dict(str, str) opc_meta`, preserves normal simple/untyped cases, and avoids unrelated changes.

experiences.title: Context-overlap grouping for consecutive search hits
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Matrix/Element-style TypeScript React room-search task asks to combine consecutive matching messages and the trajectory has found that each search hit is rendered independently from an EventContext-like timeline.
experiences.context: Applies to search-result UI work where results are objects containing a matched event plus surrounding context events, and the visible trajectory has identified the one-result-per-tile rendering path or the tile's single matched-event rendering model. It is most useful once the agent is planning or editing grouping/rendering logic, not during very early repository navigation. Do not apply as-is to unrelated search backend ranking, query parsing, global search indexing, or tasks where result objects do not expose context timelines. Be cautious if the trajectory only discusses timestamps, sender continuity, or pagination tokens without showing how those prove adjacency or preserve multiple matched events.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases is not simply 'did the agent mention grouping search results?' but whether the agent is moving toward a concrete UI/data transformation that merges adjacent or overlapping result contexts while preserving every matched message as a match. Earlier rubrics that asked for consecutive-result grouping were directionally right because the decisive visible evidence is the render loop producing one tile per search result and the tile treating only one context index as non-contextual. However, a broader criterion can over-credit flawed approaches: grouping by timestamp windows, same sender, or arbitrary recency order is only a proxy and does not establish that there are no intervening messages; constructing a synthetic single SearchResult can also drop highlighting/contextual status for all but one matched event. A better rubric should focus on observable implementation choices: comparing neighboring result context timelines by room and overlapping/adjacent event IDs, deduplicating merged context events in chronological/display order, carrying a list or equivalent representation of all matched event indexes into rendering, and leaving non-consecutive hits separate. It should also watch for regressions where the agent changes unrelated error handling, thread processing, pagination, or room headers while trying to implement grouping. Prioritize evidence from inspected code or edits showing the render loop, context timeline APIs, matched-event index handling, and preservation of highlights over evidence that merely locates search files or repeatedly searches for nonexistent timeline-index helpers.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Robust context-preserving grouping of consecutive search hits
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show a concrete plan or implementation for combining consecutive room-search hits by using the existing per-result context timelines rather than weak proxies. Strong evidence includes detecting adjacent/overlapping contexts for neighboring results in the same room via event IDs, merging timelines without duplicate context events, preserving chronological/display order, and rendering all matching messages in the combined entry as non-contextual/highlighted matches. The criterion should not give high credit for timestamp-only or same-sender grouping, repeated API exploration with no implementation path, or merging into a representation that can only mark one event as the matched result.

metadata.environment: TypeScript React Matrix-style room search UI with SearchResult/EventContext-like objects
key_visible_evidence: A one-result-per-tile render path has been identified or edited
Each result context exposes a timeline and a matched-event index
The proposed grouping compares neighboring context timelines by event identity or overlap
The rendering model can represent multiple matched indexes in one grouped entry
anti_patterns: Using only timestamp distance, sender continuity, or pagination tokens as proof of consecutiveness
Creating a merged result that preserves only one matched-event index
Changing unrelated search error handling, threading, pagination, or room header behavior
Continuing repetitive exploration after relevant context/timeline APIs are already known

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward grouping; the trajectory is still generic navigation or repeats irrelevant searches without identifying the result rendering/context model.
scale.2: Identifies search UI or result structures but only states that grouping is needed, with no viable method for detecting adjacency or preserving multiple matched events.
scale.3: Proposes or begins grouping neighboring results, but relies on weak proxies such as timestamps/sender/order or risks losing highlights because the rendering still supports only one matched index.
scale.4: Implements or clearly plans grouping based on context timeline overlap/adjacent event IDs, deduplicates context, and mostly preserves display order and non-consecutive separation, with minor uncertainties or incomplete validation.
scale.5: Provides a robust context-overlap grouping design or implementation that keeps all matched event indexes highlighted in one grouped entry, avoids duplicate context events, respects room/order boundaries, and does not disturb unrelated search behavior.

experiences.title: Conditional legacy write-format compatibility
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django session-transition task says a compatibility setting such as sha1 is insufficient because the session data format changed, and the trajectory has located the session encode/decode path or legacy decode logic.
experiences.context: Applies in Django/Python maintenance tasks involving rolling-upgrade compatibility for persisted session data, especially when the task explicitly distinguishes digest algorithm compatibility from wire-format compatibility and suggests using legacy encoding under a transitional setting. It is most useful once the trajectory has inspected or modified the session encoding path, observed the existing legacy decode fallback, or produced tests showing the encoded string shape under sha1 versus the default algorithm. It is premature during generic repository exploration unless the task statement itself already provides the needed behavior. It should not be used for unrelated signing changes, pure hashing-algorithm validation, signed-cookie-only behavior, or cases where compatibility depends on decoding old data only rather than controlling the format of newly written data.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases focused on the exact compatibility boundary: when the transitional hashing setting is sha1, newly written sessions must use the pre-transition legacy envelope, while normal/default settings must continue to use the new signing-based envelope. This aligned well because the decisive visible evidence was not merely that sessions round-trip, or that sha1 is selected, but that the agent recognized the issue as a data-format mismatch and either planned or implemented a conditional legacy write path mirroring the existing legacy decode format. A better rubric should ask whether the trajectory preserves the new format outside the compatibility setting, reuses the configured serializer and legacy hash/checking path, and leaves existing decode fallback intact. Avoid tempting but weak criteria such as “uses sha1 in signing,” “changes the hashing algorithm,” “all encode/decode round-trips pass,” or “modifies the signing module,” because those can miss that older instances cannot parse the new signing envelope. Prioritize observable evidence such as inspection of legacy decode, comparison of legacy base64 hash-plus-serialized payloads with new signed timestamped payloads, conditional branching on the transitional setting in the session write path, and tests or manual checks that distinguish sha1 legacy-format output from default new-format output.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the compatibility fix is about the session data envelope written during a rolling upgrade: under the transitional sha1 setting, the session encoder emits the legacy base64-encoded hash-and-serialized payload that older instances can read, while non-sha1/default behavior continues to emit the new signing-based format and existing legacy decode support is preserved.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Legacy write-format gated by transition setting

required_visible_evidence: Recognition that the problem is a session wire-format/envelope mismatch, not only a digest algorithm mismatch.
A planned or implemented conditional path in the session encoding/write logic for the sha1 transitional setting.
Legacy-format construction mirrors the existing legacy decode contract using the configured serializer and legacy hash comparison expectations.
Default or non-sha1 settings continue to use the new signing-based encoding path.
Decode compatibility for both existing legacy data and new-format data is not removed or bypassed.
anti_patterns: Only changing DEFAULT_HASHING_ALGORITHM handling in signing or HMAC code.
Testing only same-version round trips without checking encoded format shape.
Applying the legacy format unconditionally and thereby regressing default/new-format behavior.
Focusing on unrelated session backends when the shared base session write path is the compatibility boundary.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses the session write-format compatibility issue; it treats the task as generic exploration, pure hashing configuration, or unrelated signing behavior.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory identifies sessions or sha1 but does not distinguish the legacy session envelope from the new signing format, or proposes only algorithm-level changes.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory recognizes that sha1 alone is insufficient and points toward the session encoder, but has not clearly preserved default new-format behavior or mirrored the legacy decode contract.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory plans or implements a sha1-gated legacy session encoding path using the existing serializer/hash behavior, while leaving non-sha1 signing-based encoding and decode fallback intact.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: in addition to the correct conditional legacy write path and preserved default behavior, the trajectory validates or reasons from visible encoded-format differences and legacy decode compatibility across the transition scenario.

experiences.title: PostgreSQL dbshell TLS via libpq environment
experiences.description: Use when a Django/PostgreSQL dbshell task requires passing DATABASES OPTIONS for mutual TLS from connection parameters into the psql subprocess.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django-like repository where the agent has identified the PostgreSQL backend dbshell implementation, especially a runshell_db-style method that builds psql arguments and a subprocess environment from connection parameters. The task text or trajectory should explicitly involve PostgreSQL SSL/mutual TLS options such as sslmode, sslrootcert, sslcert, and sslkey. This guidance is most useful once the agent is reasoning about or editing the PostgreSQL client invocation; it may be premature during pure repository exploration, and it should not be applied to non-PostgreSQL database shells or tasks where SSL settings are consumed by a different client mechanism.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster judged whether the agent propagated the actual PostgreSQL SSL connection options from Django connection parameters to psql using libpq-recognized environment variables. This was discriminative because successful trajectories mapped sslmode, sslrootcert, sslcert, and sslkey to PGSSLMODE, PGSSLROOTCERT, PGSSLCERT, and PGSSLKEY in the subprocess environment while leaving the existing user, host, port, database, password, and signal-handling behavior intact. A better rubric should focus on the exact end-to-end contract: OPTIONS are already available in connection parameters, and dbshell must expose them to psql through the subprocess environment only when present. Avoid the tempting but wrong criterion that rewards adding --ssl-mode, --ssl-cert, --ssl-key, or --ssl-rootcert command-line flags, and avoid a partial criterion that checks only client cert/key while omitting sslmode or sslrootcert. Visible evidence to prioritize includes locating the PostgreSQL client shell code, recognizing get_connection_params carries OPTIONS through, adding the four PGSSL* environment assignments alongside existing PGPASSWORD handling, and tests/mocks that inspect the subprocess environment rather than expecting new psql flags.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly converge on PostgreSQL dbshell support that reads sslmode, sslrootcert, sslcert, and sslkey from the PostgreSQL connection parameters and passes them to the psql subprocess via the standard libpq environment variables PGSSLMODE, PGSSLROOTCERT, PGSSLCERT, and PGSSLKEY. It should preserve existing dbshell argument construction and environment behavior, including PGPASSWORD and user/host/port/database handling, and should not replace this with unsupported or unverified psql-specific SSL command-line flags.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete libpq SSL environment propagation

metadata.target_behavior: Set each environment variable from the corresponding connection option only when the option is present, using the copied subprocess environment passed to psql.
avoid: expecting --ssl-mode/--ssl-cert/--ssl-key/--ssl-rootcert psql flags as the primary solution
changing how connection parameters are produced when OPTIONS are already included

scale.1: No evidence that PostgreSQL SSL dbshell options will be propagated to psql, or the trajectory is focused on unrelated files/backends.
scale.2: Recognizes the need for PostgreSQL SSL dbshell support but has not identified the correct propagation point or mechanism.
scale.3: Identifies the PostgreSQL client invocation and connection parameters, but proposes an incomplete or ambiguous mapping, such as only some SSL options or unclear psql delivery mechanism.
scale.4: Strong evidence of mapping the relevant SSL options to PGSSL* environment variables, with only minor uncertainty such as missing tests or minor type/conditional handling details.
scale.5: Clearly propagates all four SSL options to the correct PGSSL* environment variables in the psql subprocess environment, preserves existing dbshell behavior, and validates the environment-based behavior with suitable tests or inspection.

experiences.title: End-to-End QtWebEngine Locale Workaround Criterion
experiences.description: Retrieve when a qutebrowser/PyQt5 task requires an opt-in workaround for QtWebEngine locale .pak resolution, especially when the trajectory is searching for or partially implementing locale fallback behavior.
experiences.context: Applies to Python/qutebrowser trajectories involving QtWebEngine startup behavior where QLocale-derived locale names may not match Chromium locale .pak filenames. It is most useful after the agent has either found that no existing locale workaround exists, added the new config option, or started implementing fallback logic. The criterion should be narrower than generic locale support: it does not apply to HTTP Accept-Language headers, spellcheck dictionary language selection, UI translations, devtools resource .pak files, or generic environment-variable cleanup. If the trajectory is still in very early reconnaissance with no design choice, the rubric can judge lack of progress, but should not reward repeated grep searches as implementation progress.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric pattern is to require an end-to-end, startup-time QtWebEngine locale override, not merely discovery or a standalone fallback helper. Earlier rubrics correctly emphasized the task’s discriminating conditions: the new opt-in setting, strict Linux plus exact QtWebEngine-version gating, checking actual QtWebEngine locale .pak files before overriding, Chromium-compatible fallback mapping, and en-US as a last resort. However, a too-narrow rubric that only checks whether a helper returns plausible fallback strings can be misleading: visible code may compute a fallback while applying it too late, via the wrong API, or in a way Chromium will not consume. A better rubric should prioritize visible evidence that the resolved locale is fed into QtWebEngine/Chromium during early startup argument/environment assembly, before profiles or subprocesses are initialized. It should also check that the implementation distinguishes Chromium resource locale selection from Accept-Language, spellcheck dictionaries, QLocale.setDefault after profile creation, temporary symlink directories, or nonexistent/private QtWebEngine locale APIs. Reward concrete implementation and validation evidence over repeated searches: a correct trajectory should show a config schema entry for qt.workarounds.locale, a resolver using QLocale/Qt library translation paths and filesystem existence checks, exact platform/version/config guards, Chromium-style fallback rules, no override when the original .pak exists or locale directory is absent, and integration into early QtWebEngine startup so the chosen locale is actually used.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Startup-Time Chromium Locale Workaround Completeness
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement the QtWebEngine locale workaround as a complete opt-in startup mechanism: define the qt.workarounds.locale setting with the correct default and backend scope; when enabled, and only on Linux with exactly the affected QtWebEngine version, derive the current QLocale Chromium-style locale name, locate the QtWebEngine locale .pak directory through Qt library translation/resource APIs, skip overriding when the original .pak exists or the locale directory is unavailable, otherwise compute a Chromium-compatible mapped fallback and verify its .pak exists, fall back to en-US when no mapped .pak exists, and pass the resolved locale to QtWebEngine/Chromium early enough for subprocess/resource locale selection. The trajectory should avoid treating Accept-Language, spellcheck dictionaries, QLocale.setDefault during profile initialization, or ad hoc locale directory copying as sufficient.

required_visible_evidence: A new Bool setting named qt.workarounds.locale, defaulting disabled and scoped to QtWebEngine where the config system supports that.
Strict guards for the opt-in setting, Linux platform, and exact affected QtWebEngine version rather than broad Qt/runtime/version checks.
Use of QLocale-derived Chromium/BCP47-style locale names and Qt library translation/resource paths to find qtwebengine locale .pak files.
Filesystem checks that preserve the original locale when its .pak exists and avoid overriding when the locale directory itself is absent.
Chromium-compatible fallback mapping for major locale families plus en-US as the final fallback.
Integration through early QtWebEngine/Chromium startup argument or environment handling, before WebEngine profiles/subprocesses initialize.
Tests or direct validation covering disabled setting, wrong platform/version, original .pak present, mapped fallback present, and final en-US fallback.
common_false_positives_to_penalize: Only adding the config option without runtime locale override logic.
Only writing a fallback helper that is never used by QtWebEngine startup.
Applying QLocale.setDefault or profile settings after WebEngine initialization.
Confusing HTTP Accept-Language or spellcheck language settings with Chromium locale .pak selection.
Using broad language-prefix guesses without Chromium-specific fallback behavior or without checking .pak existence.

scale.1: No meaningful implementation evidence: the trajectory is still repeating searches or only notes that no existing locale code exists.
scale.2: Very weak progress: adds or discusses the config setting or possible hook points, but lacks guarded .pak-based fallback logic and startup integration.
scale.3: Partial equivalent progress: implements some locale fallback checks or mapping, but misses important guards, .pak existence semantics, config/backend details, or has unclear/late integration.
scale.4: Strong progress: implements most guards and fallback rules with real .pak checks and a plausible early startup hook, with only minor omissions such as documentation or limited validation.
scale.5: Complete evidence: an opt-in, Linux/exact-version-gated resolver checks original and fallback .pak files, uses Chromium-compatible fallback behavior with en-US final fallback, integrates via early QtWebEngine/Chromium startup configuration, avoids unrelated locale mechanisms, and includes targeted validation.

experiences.title: Teaser escaping as preservation evidence, not the main fix
experiences.description: Use when a mixed chat/users API task includes recent-chat teaser escaping, but the visible trajectory suggests teaser escaping may already exist and the active repair is mostly input validation.
experiences.context: Applies in Node.js chat/user API trajectories where the task combines fail-fast invalid-data handling with a requirement that recent-chat teasers escape markup. Retrieve this when the agent has inspected the recent-chat teaser pipeline or tests and found existing escaping, or when a generated rubric is tempted to focus on XSS/teaser output. It is most useful at mid-to-late review stages, after the trajectory has enough evidence about whether teaser formatting was touched. Do not apply as the primary criterion when the reported bug is mainly a teaser/XSS regression, when the agent has actually modified teaser generation, or when no visible evidence exists about the teaser path yet; in those cases a direct escaping criterion may be premature or should be paired with validation-focused criteria.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics emphasized that recent chats must return escaped teaser content. That can be weakly useful because a trajectory that neither verifies nor preserves teaser behavior has unresolved acceptance risk. However, in this pattern the visible code investigation often already shows an existing escape/strip/decode step in the teaser construction path, while the real implementation risk is malformed input validation at chat/user API boundaries. A better rubric should not demand new teaser-escaping edits just because the task mentions markup. It should judge whether the agent recognized teaser escaping as existing behavior, preserved it, and—if using it as evidence—verified it with the relevant recent-chat flow. Avoid the tempting proxy of rewarding any work on XSS or documentation; unnecessary changes to the teaser pipeline can be harmful, and a passing-looking teaser observation does not compensate for missing fail-fast validation. Prioritize visible evidence such as explicit inspection of the teaser formatter, a targeted test or assertion involving markup in recent chats, absence of changes that return raw message content as teasers, and a clear decision to keep focus on required API validation once escaping is confirmed.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should treat recent-chat teaser escaping as a preservation and verification concern when visible investigation shows the escaping pipeline already exists. Excellent evidence includes identifying the existing markup-sanitization/escaping step used for recent-chat teasers, avoiding unnecessary changes that could weaken or bypass it, and, when practical, validating the posted-markup-to-recent-chat flow with a targeted test or clear reasoning. The criterion should not require adding a new escaping implementation unless the trajectory has concrete evidence that the existing teaser path is missing or broken.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Preserves and verifies existing teaser escaping

expected_visible_evidence: inspection of the recent-chat teaser construction path
recognition that markup is already escaped or sanitized before teaser output
no raw-content pass-through or unnecessary rewrite of teaser formatting
optional targeted validation using a markup-containing chat message and recent-chat response
avoid_as_proxy_for: new escaping code when existing behavior is already adequate
broad XSS commentary without checking the actual recent-chat teaser flow
metadata.stage_boundary: Best used after the agent has inspected teaser-related code/tests; weak or premature during initial file discovery.

scale.1: No visible evidence that the trajectory inspected, preserved, or verified recent-chat teaser escaping; it may ignore the requirement or risk returning raw markup.
scale.2: Mentions teaser escaping or XSS only at a high level, without checking the actual recent-chat teaser path or confirming existing behavior.
scale.3: Inspects or identifies the existing teaser escaping path but provides only moderate evidence of preservation, with no targeted validation and no clear integration into the repair plan.
scale.4: Clearly recognizes existing teaser escaping, avoids unnecessary changes to it, and keeps the main repair focused elsewhere while providing reasonable reasoning or partial validation that teaser output remains escaped.
scale.5: Strongly confirms the full markup-message-to-recent-chat-teaser flow remains escaped through targeted testing or equivalent concrete evidence, while preserving the existing escaping pipeline and avoiding irrelevant rewrites.

experiences.title: Do not reward cross-platform path changes without no-config control-flow semantics
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go/Cobra application task combines platform-specific default config paths with optional startup fallback through internal defaults, especially when config loading uses Viper and a caller currently passes a single path string into Load.
experiences.context: This applies to Flipt-like Go services where startup chooses a config path in a CLI entrypoint, then calls a Viper-based config loader that previously failed on ReadInConfig errors. The misleading case is generating a rubric that primarily rewards replacing a hardcoded Linux path with build tags, runtime OS checks, or os.UserConfigDir, while the trajectory has not shown a safe way to distinguish an explicitly supplied config path, an existing discovered user config file, a Linux packaged default path, and the absence of any config file. The original cross-platform-path idea is still useful as a subcriterion when the trajectory already preserves the config-loading contract and only the OS-specific default path remains to be fixed. It is not sufficient as a standalone criterion for this task, and it should not imply that non-Linux needs another implicit default file in the user config directory if the code already checks that user config path before falling back.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked whether the default config path was made platform-specific, often suggesting non-Linux should use os.UserConfigDir or that build tags alone indicate correctness. That criterion can overvalue patches that still call the loader with an absent path, silently ignore missing explicit --config files, bypass or duplicate the loader's default/env/deprecation/validation pipeline, or add a new internal config-path API without fixing the caller's notion of whether a file was actually found. For this task, the better rubric should focus on the observable control flow: path resolution should return both the selected path and whether a config file should be loaded; buildConfig should use internal defaults directly when no implicit config exists; explicit paths and existing selected files should still be loaded and invalid/read errors should remain fatal; platform-specific default path should avoid assuming /etc on non-Linux, commonly by making the non-Linux packaged default path empty while retaining the existing user-config lookup. Avoid the tempting criterion that merely asks for build tags, runtime.GOOS checks, or a DefaultConfigPath helper. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence in determinePath/buildConfig/Load interactions, preservation of env/default behavior and warnings, and tests or validation that missing implicit config differs from malformed or explicitly requested config.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory introduces or plans a config fallback that treats cross-platform path selection as the main fix while failing to preserve the distinction between an explicitly requested config file, an existing discovered config file, a platform packaged default path, and no config file at all. This includes solutions that return only a path string with no found/should-load signal, call the Viper loader on an empty or absent implicit path, silently ignore missing explicit --config paths, or replace the Linux hardcoded path with another implicit non-Linux user-config path even though the caller already checks that location. The issue is most severe when the patch changes Load to ignore missing files for all callers or bypasses the normal default/env/warning/validation pipeline.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Conflated no-config fallback and path selection

metadata.repo_type: Go service with Cobra CLI and Viper config loading
visible_files_to_check: platform-specific default path files if added
key_evidence: whether path resolution returns a found/should-load boolean or equivalent
whether internal defaults are used only when no implicit config exists
whether explicit config paths still fail on missing or invalid files
whether non-Linux packaged default avoids assuming a Linux /etc path without duplicating the existing user config lookup

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory clearly separates explicit/config-found loading from no-config fallback, keeps invalid selected files fatal, and handles platform default paths without adding an inappropriate non-Linux implicit file assumption.
scale.2: Minor risk only: the trajectory recognizes the need to distinguish no config from explicit paths, but implementation details or tests for one branch are still incomplete.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory fixes either missing-file fallback or cross-platform path handling, but visible evidence is ambiguous about whether explicit missing paths, existing malformed files, or env/default processing are preserved.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory primarily changes the default path or ignores missing ReadInConfig errors while leaving only a path-string API or otherwise failing to show a reliable no-config sentinel and explicit-path behavior.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory makes all missing config files optional, bypasses or corrupts the normal config pipeline, adds an inappropriate non-Linux default path, or otherwise demonstrates that cross-platform path changes are being used as a substitute for correct startup fallback semantics.

experiences.title: Narrow timezone-preserving pivot criterion
experiences.description: Use when a Django/Python date-difference bug is traced to an internally constructed month/year pivot datetime that is later subtracted from an aware datetime.
experiences.context: Apply in trajectories for timezone-aware datetime arithmetic bugs where the task or investigation identifies a calendar month/year pivot created with datetime.datetime(...) from an input datetime and then used in subtraction. This is especially relevant after the agent has inspected the relevant utility, reproduced an offset-naive versus offset-aware TypeError, or attempted a patch around the pivot constructor. It is less useful during very early repository exploration, for timezone issues unrelated to an intermediate constructed datetime, for intervals that never enter the month/year pivot path, or for broad framework timezone policy changes where the required fix is not localized to preserving an operand's tzinfo.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases was not a generic 'handle timezones correctly' criterion; it was the narrower requirement that the internally constructed month/year pivot preserve the source datetime's timezone awareness before subtraction. This aligned well because the visible evidence repeatedly showed the same causal chain: aware input and aware current time, a naive pivot created by datetime.datetime(...), and a crash at now - pivot. A strong rubric should therefore check the actual implementation state: the pivot constructor includes the input datetime's tzinfo in a valid way, preferably as a keyword argument, and the surrounding month/year calculation remains otherwise unchanged. It should also give credit for reproducing the original TypeError and for validating that the long aware interval returns the expected month string while naive datetime behavior still works. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as requiring all datetime constructors in the file to use the current timezone, forcing timezone normalization between unrelated inputs, or rewarding broad rewrites just because tests pass. Also avoid judging only the agent's stated intent: visible bad sed edits, duplicated constructor arguments, placing tzinfo before year/month arguments, passing tzinfo as the microsecond positional argument, or checking out the file after applying the fix are important negative evidence even if the agent described the right idea.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the month/year pivot datetime used in the date-difference calculation preserves the input datetime's timezone awareness before being subtracted from the comparison datetime. Strong evidence includes inspecting the pivot construction, identifying it as the naive operand in the aware-naive subtraction, applying a syntactically valid constructor change that carries through the input tzinfo, and validating the reported long timezone-aware interval without disturbing existing naive or month-boundary behavior.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Timezone-preserving month/year pivot

primary_evidence: The agent locates the month/year pivot construction used before subtracting remaining time.
The agent identifies the pivot as naive when the input/current datetimes are aware.
The edited constructor preserves the source datetime tzinfo using a valid datetime.datetime argument form.
The trajectory includes validation of the reported one-month-or-longer aware interval and, ideally, a naive datetime sanity check.
negative_evidence: The constructor block is duplicated, malformed, or contains arguments in an invalid order.
tzinfo is passed as the seventh positional argument without an explicit microsecond, causing it to be interpreted incorrectly.
The fix is removed or left only in a temporary script rather than the target implementation.
The trajectory replaces localized pivot handling with broad timezone coercions that risk changing existing semantics.

scale.1: No visible progress toward identifying or changing the pivot timezone mismatch; the trajectory remains at exploration or unrelated timezone changes.
scale.2: The trajectory suspects timezone awareness but has not produced a valid localized pivot change, or the current edit is clearly malformed/invalid.
scale.3: The trajectory correctly identifies the pivot timezone problem or partially edits the constructor, but visible evidence is incomplete or leaves meaningful uncertainty about syntax, argument order, or behavior preservation.
scale.4: The trajectory shows a valid timezone-preserving pivot change and reproduces or validates the reported aware long-interval behavior, with limited evidence about surrounding regressions.
scale.5: The trajectory shows a clean localized pivot change preserving the input tzinfo, confirms the reported aware long-interval case, and provides visible evidence that naive datetime and existing month/year boundary behavior remain intact.

experiences.title: Rubric for Wrapped Method Ownership in Documentation Skipping
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Sphinx/Napoleon task concerns a decorated class initializer being skipped despite preserved docstring metadata, and the trajectory is inspecting or modifying member-ownership logic around wrapper globals, qualnames, and init-inclusion config.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Sphinx repository, especially the napoleon/autodoc skip-member path, when the visible issue is not missing docstring text but failure to classify a `functools.wraps`-decorated `__init__` as owned by its class. Strong retrieval cues include `napoleon_include_init_with_doc`, `_skip_member`, `cls_is_owner`, `obj.__qualname__`, `obj.__globals__`, `__wrapped__`/unwrap, external decorators, or tests showing a wrapper's globals lack the class. This is most useful after the agent has localized or begun patching ownership detection. It is less relevant for generic decorated-function signature issues, ordinary docstring parsing failures, or trajectories that have not yet reached the member-skipping/ownership mechanism.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged whether the trajectory addressed the semantic failure: a wrapped `__init__` can keep `__doc__`, `__name__`, and `__qualname__`, while the wrapper function's `__globals__` points to the decorator context and cannot resolve the owner class. A good criterion should therefore ask whether the agent makes class-ownership detection robust for `functools.wraps`-decorated initializers and still honors `napoleon_include_init_with_doc` and existing skip behavior. It should allow different sound implementation strategies, such as unwrapping before owner lookup or resolving the owner via module plus qualname, rather than requiring a single patch shape. Avoid tempting but weak criteria such as merely checking that the docstring is preserved, that a broad test suite passes, or that any decorated function is handled; the decisive evidence is whether `_skip_member` can return the include decision for a documented decorated `__init__` whose wrapper globals do not contain the class. Prioritize visible evidence from realistic reproductions with an external decorator, focused checks of the include flag, and preservation of ordinary undecorated, private/special, module, and nested-class semantics.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should fix the documentation member-skipping ownership check so a documented `__init__` wrapped with `functools.wraps` is recognized as a class-owned initializer and is included when the init-with-doc configuration is enabled. The evidence should show the agent understands that wrapper globals, not docstring loss, cause the failure; uses a robust owner-resolution approach such as unwrapping or module/qualname lookup; and avoids regressions to undecorated methods, nested class ownership, and private/special member skip semantics.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Wrapped Initializer Ownership Preservation

metadata.failure_mechanism: decorator wrapper preserves doc metadata but its globals may not contain the owning class
metadata.required_behavior: documented decorated initializer is force-included only when the relevant init-inclusion config is enabled
acceptable_fix_strategies: unwrap the decorated callable before class lookup
resolve the owner class from preserved module/qualname metadata without relying on wrapper globals
important_regression_boundaries: private and special member inclusion flags
nested or dotted class ownership where applicable
high_value_visible_evidence: focused reproduction using an external decorator or wrapper globals lacking the class
inspection of `_skip_member`/`cls_is_owner` decision path
focused tests or manual checks showing include decision with config enabled and default behavior otherwise

scale.1: The trajectory has not connected the bug to ownership detection, or focuses only on docstring parsing/preservation, generic autodoc behavior, or unrelated decorated-function signatures.
scale.2: The trajectory has found the relevant skip-member code or mentions wrapper metadata, but lacks a concrete plan or evidence for fixing class ownership when wrapper globals do not contain the class.
scale.3: The trajectory proposes or partially applies an ownership fix for decorated initializers, but evidence is limited, uses same-module decorators that may mask the failure, or does not address config-gated inclusion and existing skip semantics.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly modifies or plans robust owner resolution for `functools.wraps`-decorated `__init__`, validates the include decision with the init-with-doc flag enabled, and considers preserving normal/private/special behavior.
scale.5: The trajectory demonstrates a realistic external-wrapper failure mode, implements a robust owner-resolution fix without overfitting to one patch shape, verifies decorated and undecorated initializer behavior under the relevant config, and checks important regression boundaries such as nested classes and existing napoleon member-skipping tests.

experiences.title: PEP-257 Docstring Dedent Semantics
experiences.description: Use when a Django admindocs/docutils bug involves rendering failures caused by docstring text starting on the first line and the trajectory is modifying or validating docstring normalization logic.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django/Python codebase when the task identifies admindocs or docutils rendering errors caused by a docstring normalization routine treating the first line as part of the common indentation calculation. The criterion is most useful once the agent has found the admindocs utility or call sites that clean docstrings, has made or is about to make a patch, or is validating examples. It should be framed semantically enough to allow either a targeted fix in the existing trimming helper or replacement with standard PEP-257-style cleaning at all admindocs entry points. It is less useful during very early repository exploration before the relevant function/call sites are found, and a separate source-validity criterion should only be used near final submission rather than while the agent is still repairing a temporarily broken edit.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful rubric checked whether the trajectory corrected the actual normalization contract: the first docstring line must be handled specially so its column-0 text does not force the common indent to zero, while one-line docstrings, blank-only docstrings, and existing empty-first-line Django-style docstrings remain safe. This aligned with visible evidence such as a diff using non-empty lines after the first line for common-indent calculation, a fallback/default indent when there are no subsequent non-empty lines, or use of a standard clean-doc implementation at every admindocs path that feeds docstrings to parsing/rendering. A better rubric should focus on that semantic behavior, not require the exact one-line edit suggested in the issue and not over-credit unrelated activity such as installing docutils, running tests that are skipped, or merely locating the file. Also avoid making a temporary mid-edit syntax/source corruption criterion decisive unless the current cutoff is a final-review/submission stage; agents may recover from botched sed edits. Prioritize observable evidence from the current trajectory: the changed normalization code, whether all relevant admindocs call paths use it, manual examples showing first-line-text docstrings dedent subsequent lines, and regression/edge checks for single-line and empty-subsequent-line docstrings.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly converge on PEP-257-compatible docstring normalization for admindocs rendering: docstrings whose summary text begins on the first line must have indentation for subsequent non-empty lines computed independently of that first line, or be passed through an equivalent standard clean-doc routine, while preserving existing behavior for Django-style docstrings with an initial blank line and safely handling one-line, blank-only, or trailing-blank docstrings. Evidence may come from the patch, from inspection of all admindocs parsing/rendering call paths, and from targeted manual or automated checks of these cases.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: First-Line-Aware Docstring Normalization

metadata.target_symptom: admindocs/docutils rendering error for docstrings whose first line contains text
metadata.key_behavior: first line does not participate in common indentation measurement for later lines
acceptable_implementations: compute common indent from non-empty lines after the first line with an empty-sequence fallback
use a standard PEP-257/clean-doc implementation at all relevant admindocs docstring parsing/rendering entry points
edge_cases_to_check: first-line text followed by indented body lines
docstrings with no non-empty lines after the first
avoid_overweighting: dependency installation alone
test runs that skip the relevant docutils or admindocs checks
the exact suggested patch shape when an equivalent semantic implementation is present

scale.1: No visible progress on changing docstring normalization semantics, or changes are unrelated to the first-line indentation problem.
scale.2: Identifies the relevant docstring trimming/parsing code or reproduces the preserved-indentation symptom, but the patch is absent or still includes the first line in the common-indent calculation.
scale.3: Attempts to skip the first line or use an equivalent cleaning approach, but evidence is incomplete: edge cases such as single-line or empty-subsequent-line docstrings may still fail, or not all relevant admindocs call paths appear covered.
scale.4: Clearly implements first-line-aware normalization and shows targeted checks for the reported first-line-text case plus preservation of existing empty-first-line behavior, with only minor uncertainty about full call-path coverage or edge-case testing.
scale.5: Provides a robust semantic fix across the relevant admindocs parsing/rendering paths, safely handles empty/single-line/trailing-blank cases, preserves existing behavior, and validates with targeted examples or tests that exercise both the reported failure mode and compatibility cases.

experiences.title: Runtime-specific regression requires exact change-to-code-path tracing
experiences.description: Retrieve when a bug report explicitly ties behavior to a particular language/runtime version or linked changelog, especially in library compatibility issues where the local environment differs from the report.
experiences.context: Applies to Python/library maintenance tasks where the user reports a regression only on a specific CPython version and cites runtime release notes, while the trajectory is investigating proxy/auth/network behavior or another boundary delegated to stdlib/dependencies. It is most useful during diagnosis or final review before accepting a speculative patch. It is less useful when the task has no version-specific signal, when the trajectory has already isolated and tested the concrete compatibility invariant, or when the remaining issue is purely local refactoring unrelated to runtime/dependency behavior.
experiences.experience: The earlier rubrics correctly emphasized version-specific investigation because the visible trajectories often stayed on generic proxy-auth mechanics, installed or tested under mismatched local dependencies and Python versions, repeated irrelevant checks, or patched nearby code without tying the change to the reported CPython behavior. For similar cases, generate a rubric that rewards tracing the reported runtime change to the exact affected library boundary: which stdlib/dependency API changed, how the project uses it, what invariant is broken, and how the proposed fix preserves behavior across versions. The criterion should not merely demand searching for version guards or adding `sys.version_info` conditionals; compatibility fixes often should be version-agnostic. Also avoid rewarding superficial evidence such as confirming auth headers are constructed in isolation, testing only on the current interpreter, or adding proxy credentials to ordinary request headers where they could leak to the destination. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent noticed the environment mismatch, consulted or reconstructed the target-version behavior, mapped it to the URL/proxy normalization or CONNECT/auth transmission path, and planned or added a deterministic regression test using mocks/local simulation instead of relying on an unavailable external proxy.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a bug explicitly reported only on a specific runtime version with a linked changelog, the trajectory should identify the concrete runtime or dependency behavior change, connect it to the project code path that can drop or misroute authentication data, account for any mismatch between the reported stack and the local test environment, and validate the fix with a targeted simulation or regression test that preserves compatibility and credential-routing safety.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Exact runtime-change compatibility analysis

required_visible_evidence: acknowledges the specific reported runtime/dependency versions and any local mismatch
consults or reconstructs the relevant runtime/dependency behavior change rather than relying on generic proxy-auth assumptions
maps the change to the library boundary where URL/proxy/auth data is transformed or transmitted
uses a deterministic test, mock, or local simulation appropriate when the exact runtime or external service is unavailable
checks that proxy credentials remain available to the proxy path without being leaked to the destination request
anti_evidence: only checks the current interpreter version or installs unrelated latest dependencies
repeats generic proxy-header or tunneling checks without using the reported version change
patches an unrelated nearby path such as chunked upload or generic auth parsing without showing relevance to the user repro
suggests runtime version guards as the main fix without proving they are necessary
adds proxy authorization as an ordinary request header for tunneled requests without considering credential leakage
metadata.applicable_stage: diagnosis, patch planning, or final review for explicit runtime-version regressions

scale.1: No meaningful version-specific analysis; the trajectory ignores the reported runtime/changelog or only performs generic repository exploration.
scale.2: Mentions the runtime version but tests or reasons only under a mismatched local environment, with little connection to the affected code path.
scale.3: Investigates relevant proxy/auth or dependency code paths but does not clearly identify the concrete runtime behavior change or validate it.
scale.4: Clearly identifies a plausible runtime/dependency behavior change, maps it to the relevant project boundary, and proposes a targeted compatibility test or simulation.
scale.5: Strongly traces the exact reported behavior through the project and dependency/stdlib boundary, accounts for environment mismatch, and validates a credential-safe, cross-version fix with focused regression evidence.

experiences.title: Explicit None Return Annotation Is Not a Unit Target
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python decorator uses return annotations to drive runtime conversion/validation and the reported failure involves a function or constructor annotated `-> None` being treated like a convertible return value.
experiences.context: Applies in Python projects where annotations are inspected at runtime, especially Astropy-style unit decorators that validate arguments and convert returned quantities based on a return annotation. It is most useful after the trajectory has found the wrapper path that calls a conversion method for every non-empty return annotation, or when the task statement already supplies a traceback showing `.to(...)` or equivalent being called on `None`. The criterion is relevant for implementation or final-review stages where the agent is modifying the annotation/conversion guard. It is less useful for unrelated import/build compatibility problems, pure argument-validation bugs, decorators that do not perform return conversion, or very early exploration before the trajectory has connected the failure to return-annotation handling.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases focused on the semantic boundary between an explicit `-> None` annotation and a real unit/quantity return annotation. The observed failure was not that all annotated returns are bad; the existing decorator intentionally converts returned quantities for annotations like a target unit. The bug is that `None` is a valid Python return annotation for constructors and void functions, but it is not a unit target and should bypass conversion. A strong rubric should therefore reward evidence that the agent preserves three cases: no return annotation returns directly, explicit `None` return annotation returns directly, and unit-like return annotations still call the existing conversion path. It should also prioritize evidence that the agent identified the existing conversion guard and changed that guard or equivalent logic, rather than chasing environment import errors. Avoid a tempting but weaker criterion that merely checks whether the agent prevents an AttributeError by skipping conversion whenever the runtime return value is `None`; that may pass the reproducer but blurs the intended contract because the annotation value, not just the returned object, determines whether conversion is requested. Also avoid rewarding broad removal of return conversion or broad Python-version compatibility edits, since those do not preserve the decorator’s existing unit-return semantics.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the decorator treats an explicit `None` return annotation as a non-conversion annotation while preserving existing return conversion for real unit/quantity annotations. Strong evidence includes locating the wrapper logic that checks for a non-empty return annotation before calling a conversion method, recognizing that `-> None` produces an annotation value of `None` rather than an absent annotation, modifying the conversion condition so `None` annotations bypass conversion, and considering or adding regression coverage for a decorated constructor or void function plus an existing unit-return conversion case.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Preserve Unit Return Conversion While Skipping Explicit None Annotation

required_visible_evidence: The task or trajectory shows a decorated constructor or void function annotated `-> None` returning `None`.
The trajectory identifies a runtime annotation-based return conversion path that calls a method such as `.to(...)` on the returned value.
The proposed fix distinguishes explicit `None` return annotation from both absent annotation and real unit annotation.
The trajectory acknowledges that normal unit-return annotations must continue to convert returned quantities.
boundary_conditions: Do not count unrelated dependency, import, or Python-version compatibility work as satisfying the criterion.
Do not give full credit if the agent removes all return-annotation conversion.
Runtime-value-only checks are weaker than annotation-based handling unless the trajectory also preserves the intended annotation contract.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses return-annotation conversion; it focuses on unrelated setup/import issues or only argument validation.
scale.2: The trajectory notices that `None` lacks the conversion method but proposes a vague or overly broad workaround without preserving unit-return conversion semantics.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies the conversion call and plans or applies a fix that avoids converting `None` returns, but the evidence is ambiguous about distinguishing explicit `None` annotations from real unit annotations.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly changes or plans the return-conversion guard so explicit `None` annotations bypass conversion and real unit annotations still convert, with some validation reasoning or test inspection.
scale.5: The trajectory precisely preserves the annotation contract for absent annotation, explicit `None` annotation, and unit annotation; it targets the existing wrapper guard, avoids unrelated compatibility edits, and includes or plans focused regression coverage for both the `-> None` constructor/void case and existing unit-return conversion.

experiences.title: Do not stop at repository signature changes when identity must propagate through per-user callers
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go repository/API refactor requires explicit user identity for per-user state, especially when an intermediate wrapper or integration can still derive identity from context instead of using an existing userId argument.
experiences.context: This applies to Go codebases using repository interfaces plus request context identity, where a task asks for all per-user property reads/writes to require an explicit userId. The misleading pattern is generating a rubric that rewards only adding userId parameters to repository methods and SQL filters, while ignoring whether higher-level per-user features actually pass the intended userId through their wrappers. The original repository-signature criterion is still useful during early investigation or as one subcriterion, and context may still legitimately be passed for cancellation/transactions or to obtain the authenticated user at an HTTP boundary. It becomes insufficient at implementation/final-review stages when visible code shows feature methods already receive a userId or router/auth flows have a concrete user id, but the patch reintroduces implicit identity by extracting from context inside a helper such as a session-key wrapper.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics asked whether UserPropsRepository methods require explicit userId parameters and whether persistence scopes SQL by that userId. That is necessary, but it led to over-optimistic judgments because an implementation can satisfy the repository contract while leaving LastFM/per-user behavior ambiguous: an intermediate wrapper can call request.UserFrom(ctx) internally and pass that to the repository, so agent methods with explicit userId parameters still ignore their userId and may operate on the context user instead. A better rubric should check end-to-end identity propagation: repository methods accept userId, persistence uses only that parameter for user_props rows, wrapper methods also accept userId, and callers that already know the relevant user pass that value through rather than relying on context inside the wrapper. Avoid the tempting criterion that “all callers pass the authenticated user ID” if it accepts context lookup at any layer; prioritize visible evidence that the specific operation userId flows from public feature methods/auth router into the session-key/property wrapper and then into the repository, with context used only for non-identity concerns or at the outer authenticated boundary.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Identity re-derived in per-user wrapper instead of propagated
reference_golden_rubrics.description: After changing per-user repository methods to accept a userId, the trajectory still leaves an intermediate per-user feature layer deriving the user id from request/context internally, or fails to update feature methods that already receive a userId to pass that value through to property/session-key access. This is a flaw even if the repository interface and SQL filters now have userId parameters, because the operation may still use the context user rather than the explicit user for reads/writes.

look_for: Repository interface methods such as Put/Get/Delete/DefaultGet now include userId
Persistence implementation filters by the supplied userId
Intermediate helper methods for per-user state still accept only context or call request.UserFrom/context identity internally
Higher-level feature methods have a userId parameter but do not pass it to the helper/repository
Router/auth flows have a concrete uid/user.ID but helper calls omit it
do_not_require: Removing context from datastore/repository construction when context is still needed for non-identity behavior

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: explicit userId is propagated from each relevant caller or authenticated boundary through wrappers into repository calls, and wrappers do not re-resolve identity from context for repository scoping.
scale.2: Minor evidence: most paths propagate userId correctly, but one low-impact test/helper or unclear call path still appears to rely on context identity.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: repository signatures are updated, but at least one important per-user wrapper or caller path still obtains userId from context instead of accepting/passing the explicit operation userId.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the main integration path keeps wrapper methods context-only or ignores existing userId parameters in feature methods, so per-user state access remains context-dependent despite repository changes.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the patch primarily adds userId parameters at the repository/persistence layer while all or nearly all higher-level per-user reads/writes still rederive identity from context or omit explicit userId propagation, leaving the ambiguity essentially unresolved.

experiences.title: Behavior-Preserving Mixin Consolidation
experiences.description: Use when a Python refactor task asks to collapse a mixin into its owning model while preserving registry, changeset, helper, and routing/owner behavior.
experiences.context: Applies to Open Library-style Python model refactors where a model currently gains behavior from a separate mixin and the task explicitly requires the consolidated model to keep framework registrations, plugin call sites, and edge-case behavior. This is most useful after the trajectory has identified the mixin, the model class, imports/type annotations, registration points, and helper classes such as seed/change wrappers. It is especially decisive if the trajectory has begun editing or has run import/compile checks. It is less useful during very early repository exploration before the agent has seen the model/mixin boundary, and it should not be used to require a specific destination file or to require moving unrelated helper classes unless visible call sites prove those public import paths are being intentionally changed.
experiences.experience: For mixin-consolidation tasks, the useful criterion is not merely whether the mixin name disappears. A good rubric should judge whether the trajectory preserves behavior while eliminating the mixin dependency: the registered model must directly expose the former mixin methods, all production imports and type hints must resolve to the consolidated model, existing helper classes or public import paths must remain usable or be updated consistently, and explicit task contracts such as model registration, changeset registration, and owner resolution edge cases must be verified. The previous rubrics were directionally useful when they focused on complete consolidation, updated references, preserved registration, changeset availability, and owner resolution. They became too brittle when they prescribed relocating helper classes as a requirement or treated removal of the mixin/imports as sufficient. Future rubrics should prioritize observable evidence such as grep results for stale mixin references, inspection of registration setup, plugin call-site updates, import/compile/test results, and tests or reasoning for owner keys with letters, hyphens, and underscores. Avoid tempting proxy criteria like 'all methods copied into a particular file,' 'Seed must be moved,' or 'no ListMixin text remains' without also checking buildability and behavioral compatibility.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates a behavior-preserving consolidation of a list-related mixin into the actual registered List model: the List model no longer relies on the mixin for behavior, former mixin methods/properties remain available on List, production imports/type annotations/call sites are updated without introducing circular imports or broken public helper references, the list model and list changeset registrations are preserved, owner resolution through List is explicitly checked for person keys containing letters, hyphens, and underscores, and the agent validates the refactor with grep plus import/compile or targeted tests. The criterion should credit semantic preservation and validation over a particular file layout.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete behavior-preserving mixin consolidation

required_visible_evidence: identified all production references to the mixin and updated them or explained why they remain
confirmed the registered model directly exposes the former mixin behavior
preserved or consistently updated helper classes and public import paths used by other modules/tests
confirmed model registry and changeset registration still resolve correctly
checked owner-resolution edge cases required by the task
ran or planned concrete syntax/import/targeted-test validation
avoid_overprescription: do not require a specific destination module unless the task or visible design requires it
do not require moving helper classes solely because mixin methods reference them
do not treat stale-name grep cleanup as sufficient without behavioral validation

scale.1: No meaningful consolidation evidence: the trajectory only explores files or proposes broad changes without identifying all mixin/model references, registration obligations, or behavior that must be preserved.
scale.2: Weak progress: the trajectory finds the mixin and model and may plan or start renaming/removing imports, but does not show that former mixin behavior, helper dependencies, registrations, and plugin call sites will remain functional.
scale.3: Moderate progress: the trajectory partially moves or copies mixin methods and updates some references, but leaves important uncertainty such as unverified helper import paths, stale production references, missing registration/changeset checks, owner edge cases, or no build/test validation.
scale.4: Strong progress: the trajectory updates the model inheritance and most call sites, accounts for helper dependencies, checks for stale mixin references, and verifies syntax/imports or targeted behavior, but may still lack complete explicit coverage of all required edge cases or registrations.
scale.5: Excellent progress: the trajectory shows a complete, validated, behavior-preserving consolidation: all former mixin behavior is directly available on the registered List model, all production references and helper dependencies are consistent, list and changeset registrations are confirmed, owner resolution edge cases are tested or explicitly validated, and compile/import/targeted tests pass.

experiences.title: Do not overvalue config-only changes when a preference must control startup behavior
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go/viper configuration task adds a new setting for a runtime behavior such as version/update checking, especially when the trajectory searches for existing behavior and finds none.
experiences.context: This applies to repositories where configuration is loaded through structured config structs, YAML examples, and environment binding, but the task language says the setting lets users control application behavior at startup. A misleading rubric in this situation treats adding a metadata/config field, a default, and YAML documentation as nearly sufficient. That may be appropriate only when the task explicitly asks for schema support or storing a value for future use. It is not appropriate when the problem statement frames the option as enabling/disabling an actual startup check or other runtime side effect. If exploration shows no existing update/version-check implementation, the absence should not downgrade the need for behavior wiring; it is evidence that the agent may need to add the runtime consumer rather than stop at config parsing.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics focused on a metadata section, default values, YAML/env loading, and sometimes vaguely on wiring to any existing startup logic.
