This can mislead because an implementation can satisfy the visible config-shape checklist while still leaving users unable to control the actual version-check behavior. For these tasks, generate a criterion that distinguishes data-model support from end-to-end preference semantics: the trajectory should either locate and gate the existing runtime behavior with the loaded setting, or, if searches show none exists, recognize and implement the missing startup update-check path so the setting has an observable consumer. Avoid tempting criteria that say only 'wire any existing logic' or reward 'accessible throughout the application' without requiring a concrete read site. A better replacement criterion should prioritize visible evidence such as searches for startup/version-check call sites, modifications in the startup path that conditionally perform or skip the check based on loaded config, handling of the default behavior, and tests or examples proving an explicit false/disabled setting suppresses the runtime behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory is flawed if it treats a new metadata/version-check preference as a config-schema-only addition even though the task requires users to control startup update-check behavior. This is especially severe when the agent's own searches find no existing version/update-check call site and the subsequent plan or edits only add config structs, YAML defaults, and parsing, without adding or gating a runtime startup consumer for the setting.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Config-only preference without runtime consumer

metadata.environment: Go project using structured configuration and viper/YAML/env loading
task_markers: startup behavior or users controlling whether a check occurs
high_priority_evidence: search results for existing version/update-check logic
whether the loaded config value is read outside the config package
tests or examples for disabled preference suppressing behavior
do_not_overvalue: adding parse/env constants without a runtime read site

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory either finds an existing startup check and plans/edits it to respect the config, or explicitly adds a missing startup check path controlled by the loaded preference.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory emphasizes config structure but also has a concrete plan or partial edits showing where startup behavior will consume the setting.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory has only partial config work and ambiguous intent about runtime consumption, with no clear read site yet but not enough evidence that it will stop there.
scale.4: Clear evidence: after finding little or no existing update-check logic, the trajectory proceeds with config structs/defaults/YAML/parsing and does not identify any startup consumer or behavioral test.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory finalizes or validates a patch that only adds the metadata preference to config files/loading while searches showed no existing check to wire, leaving the setting unused for startup behavior.

experiences.title: Caller-Supplied SameSite and Secure Semantics for Cookie Deletion
experiences.description: Use when evaluating a Django-like cookie deletion fix where deleted cookies must retain SameSite semantics across later responses, especially for framework callers that know the cookie settings.
experiences.context: Apply in a Python/Django-style web framework task involving `HttpResponse.delete_cookie()` or equivalent Set-Cookie expiration behavior, where the issue report shows a cookie is set with `SameSite` but a later deletion response omits it. This is most useful after the trajectory has inspected both the generic response deletion API and caller sites such as message/session storage that set cookies with configured attributes. It is especially relevant when the trajectory has discovered that same-response set/delete tests are misleading because cookie morsels may retain attributes locally, while fresh-response deletion lacks access to prior browser cookie attributes. Do not apply as a broad generic criterion for all cookie attributes, and do not require caller updates before the agent has located relevant callers. If the task is only about deleting a cookie already present on the same response object, the caller-supplied cross-response requirement may be too strong.
experiences.experience: For this cluster, the most discriminative rubric is not simply “preserve all security attributes from the existing cookie.” That wording can over-credit patches that read attributes from the current response’s cookie jar, because the reported bug occurs on a later response where the server cannot infer the browser’s previously stored SameSite value. A better rubric should check whether the generic deletion API accepts and forwards an explicit SameSite value, whether framework callers that know the cookie configuration pass their configured SameSite value when deleting, and whether `SameSite=None` deletion headers are marked `Secure` so modern browsers do not ignore them. It should also ensure the fix keeps the existing deletion contract: empty value, expiration date, max-age zero, path/domain handling, and existing secure-prefix behavior. Avoid tempting but weak criteria such as passing only same-response manual tests, copying session cookie settings into the generic deletion method for all cookies, or preserving unrelated attributes like `httponly` without addressing the cross-response SameSite source. Prioritize visible evidence from the trajectory: recognition of fresh-response vs same-response behavior, an API path for caller-provided SameSite, updates to known cookie-setting callers, and validation or tests that inspect rendered deletion Set-Cookie headers including `SameSite=None; Secure`.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement SameSite-aware cookie deletion for the real cross-response scenario: the deletion API accepts an explicit SameSite value and forwards it through existing Set-Cookie serialization; callers that know the original cookie settings pass their configured SameSite value when deleting; deletion with `SameSite=None` also emits `Secure` for ordinary cookie names as well as secure-prefixed names; and the existing expiration, max-age, path, domain, and validation behavior is preserved without hardcoding session settings globally.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Cross-Response SameSite Deletion Contract

metadata.environment: Python Django-like web framework
metadata.task_type: HTTP response cookie deletion semantics
key_visible_evidence: The trajectory distinguishes fresh-response deletion from same-response set/delete morsel retention.
The generic delete-cookie method has a caller-supplied SameSite path rather than relying only on current response cookies.
Known framework callers that set cookies with configured SameSite values are considered for deletion updates.
SameSite=None deletion is paired with Secure so browser deletion is honored.
The implementation avoids globally applying session cookie settings inside the generic response method.
non_goals: Do not overvalue preservation of unrelated attributes if SameSite=None Secure handling or caller propagation is missing.
Do not treat same-response manual preservation as sufficient evidence for the reported later-response bug.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of a SameSite-aware deletion design; the trajectory only inspects code or relies on existing deletion behavior without a path to include SameSite in fresh deletion responses.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory focuses on preserving attributes from an existing current-response cookie or passes same-response checks, but does not address caller-supplied SameSite for later responses.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the deletion API forwards an explicit SameSite value or a key caller is updated, but the solution is incomplete because affected callers, fresh-response tests, or SameSite=None Secure behavior are missing.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory supports explicit SameSite deletion and updates relevant cookie-setting callers, while preserving existing expiration/path/domain behavior, but validation or edge-case handling for SameSite=None Secure is not fully demonstrated.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory clearly targets the fresh-response bug, implements explicit SameSite propagation through the deletion API and relevant callers, ensures SameSite=None deletion emits Secure in addition to prefix rules, avoids global session-setting leakage, and validates rendered deletion headers for the important cases.

experiences.title: Pre-Overwrite Version State for Upgrade Filtering
experiences.description: Use this when a task asks for configurable behavior based on patch/minor/major upgrades and the trajectory has found that startup state stores a previous version but later overwrites it before UI policy code runs.
experiences.context: Applies in Python application startup/configuration work, especially qutebrowser-like projects where a persisted state file records the last application version, exposes only a boolean version-changed flag, and a later startup/UI function decides whether to show an upgrade notification or changelog. This experience is most useful after the trajectory has inspected both the state-loading lifecycle and the notification-opening code, or after an implementation starts comparing old/current versions. It is less useful for purely declarative config-schema edits before the state lifecycle is known, for tasks where the previous version remains directly available at the decision point, or for unrelated changelog/docs-only changes.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on whether the implementation bases upgrade-type filtering on the actual pre-upgrade version rather than on a stale boolean or on a state field already rewritten to the current version. That criterion was discriminative because many trajectories added a string/enum setting and wrote plausible patch/minor/major comparison logic, but performed the comparison in the later UI path by reading the state’s current version after startup initialization had already overwritten the old value. Ad hoc tests that directly pass old/new version strings, syntax checks, YAML validation, or documentation updates are tempting but weak proxies; they do not prove integration with the real state lifecycle. A better rubric should reward preserving or computing the version-change classification at the state-loading point, exposing a structured result such as equal/patch/minor/major/unknown/downgrade, and having the notification policy consume that result according to the configured threshold. It should penalize implementations that only keep a boolean changed flag, re-read the updated state version later, ignore downgrade/missing/unparseable old versions, or validate only duplicated comparison logic outside the real startup path.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: State-Lifecycle-Aware Upgrade Classification
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should ensure patch/minor/major changelog filtering is driven by the real previous application version captured before persistent startup state is rewritten. Strong evidence includes modifying or planning the state-loading layer to preserve a structured version-change classification, using project-standard version parsing/comparison, treating no-change/new-install/missing or malformed old versions safely, and having the later changelog-opening policy apply the configured threshold to that preserved classification rather than re-reading an already-updated version field.

prioritized_visible_evidence: The trajectory recognizes that the persisted version is read during state initialization and then overwritten with the current version before later UI/changelog logic runs.
The implementation or plan changes the state/version-change owner to retain enough information to distinguish equal, patch, minor, major, and exceptional cases.
The changelog decision consumes the preserved classification and the user setting, instead of comparing the current version against a state value that may already be current.
Validation exercises the integrated startup/state path or relevant state unit tests, not only standalone version-comparison snippets.
common_false_positive_evidence: A new multi-value config setting exists but the state lifecycle still exposes only a boolean.
The UI/changelog function parses old_version from the same state section after initialization has overwritten it.
Manual tests pass by supplying old/new strings directly, bypassing persistent state loading.
Docs, syntax checks, or YAML schema checks pass without proving correct upgrade classification.

scale.1: No meaningful attention to how the previous version is obtained; the work only changes config/docs or keeps the original all-upgrades boolean behavior.
scale.2: Mentions or sketches version comparison, but relies on a generic changed flag or does not identify where the old version is lost in startup state handling.
scale.3: Recognizes that old/current comparison is needed and may add comparison logic, but still appears to read the old version from a location that is overwritten before the decision point or lacks integrated validation.
scale.4: Clearly preserves or exposes the pre-overwrite version/change classification and applies the setting to suppress patch upgrades while allowing configured minor/major behavior, with only minor edge-case or validation gaps.
scale.5: Fully integrates upgrade classification at the state-loading owner before overwrite, handles equal/new-install/missing/malformed/downgrade cases safely, maps all configured thresholds correctly, and validates through the real state-to-changelog decision path.

experiences.title: SymPy assumption fixes need API-path and special-value validation
experiences.description: Retrieve when a SymPy task changes logical relationships among assumptions, especially when the user-facing symptom is an `.is_*` property but the trajectory also investigates `ask(Q.*)` predicates.
experiences.context: Applies in the SymPy codebase when the task is about assumption implication propagation such as parity, integer/rational/algebraic, real/complex, finite/infinite, or similar predicates. It is most relevant after the trajectory has identified that old property accessors (`expr.is_*`) and newer predicate queries (`ask(Q.*)`) may use different inference paths, or after the agent has tried modifying one path without fixing the reproducer. It is especially important when special singleton values such as infinities, complex infinity, or NaN have visible three-valued assumption behavior. Do not apply this as a generic rubric for early repository exploration, for tasks that only touch concrete numeric handlers without symbolic assumption inference, or for non-SymPy projects where there is no visible dual assumptions architecture.
experiences.experience: Prior rubrics in this cluster often asked for understanding SymPy’s assumption rule system, correct old-vs-new targeting, consistency between `.is_*` and `ask(Q.*)`, and preservation of special values. That theme is useful, but only if the criterion requires observable implementation and validation evidence. It is too weak to reward merely finding `FactRules`, reading handlers, or stating that there are two systems; several trajectories had that understanding while still making no valid patch, looping on greps/stash checks, or changing only one ineffective path. A better rubric should focus on whether the agent demonstrates that the user-visible accessor is driven by the old assumption closure, that any new predicate facts are kept in sync through the generated-data workflow when touched, and that both APIs are re-run on the reported symbolic case. It should also require explicit safeguards for SymPy’s special values: broad rules such as old-style `real -> finite` or `complex -> finite` are tempting because of mathematical documentation, but they can conflict with existing infinity semantics; direct `even/odd/integer -> finite` changes can also have contrapositive effects on non-finite objects, so the trajectory must check whether those changes intentionally preserve or update `None` vs `False` behavior. Prioritize visible evidence such as passing reproducer output for `Symbol(..., even=True).is_finite`, corresponding `ask(Q.finite(...))` behavior, regenerated predicate facts when applicable, targeted tests or sanity checks for infinities/NaN/complex infinity, and absence of unresolved contradictions or repeated non-progress commands. Avoid a criterion that simply says “modify both assumption systems” without checking whether the semantic implication chosen is safe and validated.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show a safe, validated assumption-propagation fix for the reported symbolic property accessor, not just conceptual exploration. Strong evidence includes identifying the old `.is_*` assumption closure as necessary for the user-visible symptom, keeping newer `ask(Q.*)` predicate facts consistent if they are modified, regenerating generated predicate data through the documented workflow rather than hand-editing it, and validating both the reported accessor and corresponding predicate query. The trajectory should also account for SymPy’s three-valued assumptions on special non-finite values, avoiding broad finite implications that create contradictions or unintentionally collapse `None` into `False` without deliberate test updates.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Validated dual-path assumption propagation

required_visible_evidence: recognizes the distinction between old `.is_*` assumptions and newer `ask(Q.*)` predicates
targets the path that actually drives the reported accessor
updates or regenerates new predicate facts if that system is touched
runs the original symbolic reproducer after changes
checks special non-finite values and three-valued assumption behavior
unsafe_shortcuts_to_penalize: only editing predicate known facts while `.is_*` remains unchanged
adding broad old-style real/complex-to-finite rules without infinity validation
rewarding repeated searches or conceptual notes without a working validated change
ignoring generated-data workflow after changing new assumption facts

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of implementing or validating assumption propagation; the trajectory is limited to repository browsing, repeated greps, or an ineffective edit with the original accessor still unresolved.
scale.2: Some relevant investigation of assumption code paths, but the trajectory targets only one API path, makes a risky broad implication, or lacks any post-change reproducer showing the reported `.is_*` behavior fixed.
scale.3: Partial progress comparable to the parent trajectory: the agent understands old vs new assumptions and may fix or inspect one path, but evidence remains incomplete because `ask(Q.*)` consistency, generated facts, or special-value regressions are unresolved.
scale.4: Strong progress: the trajectory targets the correct old assumption mechanism, keeps the new predicate path in mind or updated when needed, reruns the reported symbolic case, and performs at least basic infinity/NaN sanity checks, though some edge-case or test-suite validation may still be incomplete.
scale.5: Complete visible evidence of a safe assumption fix: both the reported `.is_*` accessor and corresponding `ask(Q.*)` query behave correctly, generated predicate data is updated through the documented process if applicable, targeted regression tests are added or run, and special non-finite values retain deliberate three-valued behavior without contradictions.

experiences.title: Do not treat ECR CredentialFunc refresh as the whole feature
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a multi-component Go feature that adds provider-backed AWS ECR authentication for OCI/ORAS storage, especially when the trajectory focuses on token fetching or repeated discovery but has incomplete config/schema wiring, broken edits, or no end-to-end validation.
experiences.context: This warning applies in Go repositories where OCI registry authentication is configured through schemas, config structs, functional store options, and multiple store-construction paths. A rubric that checks only whether the agent discovered or implemented an AWS ECR CredentialFunc can be misleading when visible evidence shows the work is still exploratory, recent steps are repetitive searches, schema artifacts are stale, config shape may require static credentials for provider auth, call sites are not wired, exported APIs were broken, or builds/tests are failing. The original credential-refresh idea remains appropriate when the current review scope is specifically the isolated ECR provider and the trajectory already shows coherent config selection, store integration, backward-compatible static auth, schema updates, and validation.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked whether the trajectory used AWS SDK default credentials, called ECR GetAuthorizationToken, decoded the base64 username/password, and returned an ORAS CredentialFunc that refreshes per request. That is a necessary implementation detail for this task, but as a standalone criterion it over-emphasizes a small core and can over-credit trajectories that repeatedly investigate the same API, write a provider into a broken file, or pass an isolated package while leaving the feature unusable. For configuration-driven auth features, generate rubrics that prioritize end-to-end integration evidence: a selectable auth mode that does not force static username/password for ECR, synchronized schema artifacts and config decoding/validation, wiring through all relevant store creation paths, preservation of existing static auth and exported option/helper APIs, dependency changes kept buildable, and targeted validation covering config plus store behavior. Avoid the tempting criterion “has an ECR CredentialFunc that fetches fresh tokens” unless it is conditioned on the surrounding integration already being intact. Replacement criteria should look first for visible build/test results, absence of syntax/API regressions, complete schema/config propagation, and compatibility with existing static auth.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Provider-only ECR auth without end-to-end integration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for a configuration-driven AWS ECR OCI authentication feature when they focus mainly on token-refresh mechanics or API discovery while visible evidence shows the feature is not integrated or validated end to end. The flaw is present when the trajectory lacks coherent auth selection in config, leaves schema artifacts inconsistent, fails to wire provider auth through all relevant OCI store construction paths, breaks existing static authentication or exported APIs, introduces syntax/build errors, or keeps repeating discovery commands instead of converging on a buildable implementation. Do not apply this penalty merely because the agent has not yet implemented every detail during early exploration; apply it when the trajectory is being judged as implementation progress or final-review quality and the visible work would still be unusable despite having some ECR CredentialFunc/token-refresh logic.

metadata.task_type: multi_component_provider_backed_auth_feature
metadata.environment: Go project using OCI/ORAS registry clients, checked-in config schemas, Go config structs, and AWS SDK dependencies
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: presence of AWS ECR GetAuthorizationToken/base64 decoding/CredentialFunc alone
preferred_visible_evidence: auth mode is selectable and backward compatible with static credentials
schema and config structs are synchronized and allow provider auth without mandatory static secrets
all relevant store creation paths pass the selected auth option
existing exported helpers/options used by downstream packages remain available
build or targeted tests validate config decoding and OCI auth integration
recent steps show repair of concrete integration failures rather than repeated identical discovery commands

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory shows coherent provider-auth selection, config/schema propagation, store wiring, backward compatibility, and validation, or it is still clearly limited to early discovery without claiming implementation completeness.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the token provider is emphasized, but most integration surfaces are identified and there are no visible build-breaking or schema-shape problems.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: some ECR token-refresh logic or design exists, but at least one important integration surface such as schema synchronization, config decoding, store wiring, or compatibility validation is visibly incomplete.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory has provider/token code or repeated API investigation while multiple required integration pieces are stale, missing, malformed, or unvalidated, making the feature unlikely to work end to end.
scale.5: Severe evidence: recent work visibly breaks compilation or existing APIs, corrupts config/schema code, omits required wiring, or loops on redundant discovery, yet the main apparent progress is only the ECR CredentialFunc/token-refresh idea.

experiences.title: Do not let TLS credential validation mask broken server integration
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for a Go server task that adds HTTPS/TLS configuration and the trajectory already shows broad rewrites, partial startup edits, or narrow manual checks of missing cert/key behavior.
experiences.context: This applies in a Go service such as Flipt where HTTPS support spans Viper-backed config parsing, defaults, example configuration, HTTP REST/UI startup, gRPC/gateway wiring, CLI behavior, and build compatibility. A cert/key fail-fast check is a valid subrequirement, but it becomes misleading as a primary trajectory-quality rubric when visible evidence shows wholesale replacement of main startup files, compile errors, unverified diffs, unrelated edits, or tests that only exercise missing certificate paths. The original validation idea is still appropriate as a focused sub-rubric early in implementation or when the visible trajectory has already preserved existing server startup and is specifically validating HTTPS credential handling.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics focused on whether `protocol=https` fails fast when `cert_file` or `cert_key` is missing or nonexistent. That criterion is correct but too narrow for this task: an implementation can pass those manual checks while still breaking the command structure, default HTTP compatibility, listener selection, gRPC/gateway connectivity, examples/docs, or even compilation. For future rubric generation, avoid treating successful missing-certificate tests or clear validation errors as strong evidence of final patch correctness when the trajectory shows broad edits to startup/config code. Prefer a rubric that penalizes integration instability: preservation of the original CLI/config flow, minimal and coherent server startup changes, successful build after edits, protocol-aware port and scheme selection, unchanged HTTP defaults, and no corruption of unrelated startup logic. Visible replacement evidence should prioritize `git diff`/build output, whether errors were fixed without wholesale rewrites, whether both HTTP and HTTPS paths were exercised, and whether config examples/defaults were updated consistently. Avoid the tempting standalone criterion that only asks for fail-fast TLS credential validation unless the parent rubric is explicitly evaluating that one subrequirement.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Narrow TLS validation masking integration breakage
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that focus on adding or manually demonstrating HTTPS certificate/key validation while leaving visible evidence that the broader server integration is incomplete or unstable. This includes broad rewrites of central startup/config files without preserving original CLI and server flow, unresolved or recently introduced build errors, missing verification that the default HTTP path still works, protocol/port selection that is only partially wired, gateway or gRPC behavior ignored despite being part of the server architecture, or configuration examples/defaults left inconsistent. Do not apply this penalty merely because the agent has not yet tested every TLS edge case during early exploration; apply it when the trajectory is using cert validation as apparent completion evidence despite visible integration risk.

metadata.environment: Go service with Viper-style configuration, HTTP REST/UI server, gRPC or gateway startup, and YAML config examples
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: successful missing cert_file/cert_key validation or clear fail-fast error messages as a standalone proxy for HTTPS feature correctness
replacement_evidence: minimal preservation of original command/startup structure
correct protocol-aware listener and port selection
evidence that gateway/gRPC assumptions remain coherent

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory treats certificate validation as one subrequirement and also verifies or preserves build, startup flow, HTTP defaults, protocol/port behavior, and config consistency.
scale.2: Minor evidence: cert validation receives disproportionate attention, but the trajectory still shows some build or integration verification and no clear corruption of existing startup behavior.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory demonstrates cert/key validation but has weak or incomplete evidence for preserving default HTTP behavior, protocol-aware startup, or config examples.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory relies on cert validation checks while visible edits or outputs show broad startup/config rewrites, unresolved integration questions, missing example/default updates, or limited validation of only one path.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory presents cert validation as success despite visible compile errors, corrupted command/server structure, unrelated rewrites, or no credible verification that the server can build and run in both HTTP and HTTPS modes.

experiences.title: Do not treat a custom strength meter as proof of passphrase-validation correctness
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a TypeScript/React dialog task that requires password or passphrase strength, match, and submit gating, especially after the trajectory discovers existing shared validation components or field-validation infrastructure.
experiences.context: This warning applies in a Matrix-style React/TypeScript UI codebase where an export/security dialog must reject empty, weak, or mismatched passphrases and provide feedback. The misleading pattern is a rubric that rewards visible real-time strength UI, zxcvbn scoring, suggestions, or a disabled button without checking whether the implementation is wired into the project’s existing field-validation lifecycle. The original idea can still be appropriate when the repository has no reusable password/passphrase validation component, when the task explicitly mandates a custom visual strength meter, or when the trajectory is only being judged for early requirements discovery rather than implementation correctness. At final-review or late-implementation stages, the decisive evidence is not the mere presence of feedback text or a strength bar, but whether the same validation path that displays feedback also prevents export on submit.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked for real-time strength feedback, strength meters, zxcvbn labels, suggestions, and export-button gating. Those are plausible user-facing requirements, but they became misleading because many trajectories satisfied them with ad hoc local state and custom UI while missing the more important integration contract: the dialog should reuse or mirror the existing passphrase and confirmation validation components, run field validation before starting export, disallow empty values during validation, focus/show the first invalid field, and avoid bypasses from stale state or submit events. A better rubric should focus on visible evidence that the agent found and adopted the repository’s established validation pattern for passphrase and confirmation fields, including submit-time validation and localized feedback. Avoid making a custom strength meter, direct raw zxcvbn state, or a disabled Export button the main criterion; those are weak proxies and can overrate patches that look secure but do not compile cleanly, do not localize strings, bypass validation on submit, or diverge from the shared UI framework.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a React/TypeScript security dialog after the trajectory has discovered existing passphrase scoring and field-validation infrastructure, penalize implementations that build a standalone password-strength widget or local zxcvbn state but do not visibly integrate with the project’s shared passphrase/confirmation validation flow. The flaw is present when export prevention depends mainly on custom render-time state or button disabling, without submit-time validation of both fields, non-empty validation through the field framework, clear confirmation-field validation, and safe prevention of the export action when validation fails.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Ad hoc strength UI instead of integrated field validation

metadata.environment: React/TypeScript dialog with existing reusable password/passphrase validation components
prioritize_evidence: reuse of shared passphrase and confirmation validation components or equivalent field-validation hooks
submit handler validates all relevant fields before starting export
validation disallows empty values and rejects weak scores through the same path that displays feedback
mismatch feedback is tied to confirmation-field validation
export action cannot proceed through submit even if button state is stale
avoid_overvaluing: direct zxcvbn imports and local score state

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory clearly uses the established validation components or equivalent field-validation lifecycle and validates both passphrase fields before export.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory adds some custom feedback, but still shows a credible submit-time validation path using shared field validation for the important checks.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory mixes shared and custom validation, or blocks export in state/button logic while leaving submit-time validation or confirmation-field integration uncertain.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory primarily implements custom strength feedback and local score/match state, with little or no evidence that existing field validation is used before starting export.
scale.5: Most severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory relies entirely on ad hoc UI, strength bars, direct scoring, or disabled-button logic and visibly lacks integrated submit validation for empty, weak, and mismatched passphrases.

experiences.title: Unhealthy-path read-through TTL fallback for hot cache getters
experiences.description: Use when a Teleport/Go cache task asks for short-lived fallback caching during primary cache initialization or unhealthy states, and the trajectory is editing or planning edits around `lib/cache` read paths and high-frequency resource getters.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go codebase with a watch-backed primary cache where a central `read()` method returns local cache services when healthy and direct configured backend services when unhealthy or initializing. Retrieve this experience when the requested behavior is to reduce repeated backend reads for frequently requested resources such as certificate authorities, nodes, tokens, cluster configuration/name, proxies, or remote clusters using a short TTL. It is most useful once the trajectory has enough visible evidence to judge integration choices: added cache structs, wrapper services, getter changes, `read()` changes, or tests. It is less useful during very early repository exploration with no implementation direction, and it should not be applied to unrelated persistent-cache TTL, `PreferRecent`/`OnlyRecent` stale-cache policy work, or tasks where healthy primary-cache semantics are the main feature.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric pattern is to judge whether the implementation actually intercepts the unhealthy/initializing backend-read path with a short-lived read-through cache for the specific hot getters. In these cases, weak trajectories added TTL map fields, config knobs, or broad wrapper services but did not make repeated calls to `GetCertAuthority`, `GetCertAuthorities`, node getters, cluster config/name getters, token/proxy/remote-cluster getters, etc. reuse a recently loaded result while `readGuard.IsCacheRead()` is false. The best criterion should prioritize visible evidence that getters or a shared helper call a TTL/singleflight-style cache around the backend load function only when the primary cache is not being read, and that cache keys include the method and all request parameters that affect results. It should also check for a short default TTL such as the existing recent-cache TTL, preservation of healthy-cache behavior, and safety for mutable returned resource objects or slices, usually via cloning or otherwise avoiding shared mutable cached values. Avoid tempting but misleading criteria that merely require adding a `ttlmap` field, populating fallback data during healthy watch processing, replacing `read()` with generic local services, or tying the feature to `PreferRecent`/`OnlyRecent`; those proxies can exist without reducing backend amplification or can change cache semantics incorrectly. Visible evidence to prioritize includes: a reusable fallback function/cache with TTL and concurrent load coalescing; selected public getters using it only on the direct-backend path; cache keys covering flags/options such as CA type, name, namespace, list parameters, and secret-loading flags; no long persistent TTL; normal cache reads still going through existing local services and locks; and, ideally, tests or build feedback showing repeated unhealthy reads hit the backend once per TTL and reload after expiry.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Read-through TTL fallback on unhealthy hot getters
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly converge on a short-TTL, read-through fallback cache that is used only when the primary cache is initializing or unhealthy, and should wire it into the high-frequency getters that otherwise call backend services directly. Strong evidence includes a shared TTL helper or function cache that coalesces concurrent loads, selected getter integration for certificate authorities, nodes/server lists, cluster configuration/name, and similarly frequent resources, cache keys that include all request parameters affecting results, short default TTL reuse rather than long persistent-cache TTLs, preservation of healthy primary-cache behavior, and handling of mutable cached resources/slices through cloning or equivalent safety.

metadata.environment: Go Teleport-style lib/cache package with Cache.read(), readGuard.IsCacheRead(), Config backend services, and watch-backed local cache services
required_visible_evidence: fallback cache is consulted on the non-cache-read/unhealthy path, not on normal healthy local-cache reads
successful backend loads populate the fallback cache for repeat calls within TTL
hot public getters or a shared helper used by them are integrated, not just struct/config fields
TTL is short and distinct from long persistent cache TTL
cache keys include relevant method arguments and options
implementation avoids shared mutable cached return values where resources can be mutated by callers
anti_patterns: only adding TTL map fields or constants without getter/read-path use
requiring healthy watch processing to prepopulate fallback entries as the main strategy
confusing this feature with PreferRecent/OnlyRecent resource expiry
generic service-wrapper replacement that does not demonstrably populate and reuse backend results
using long persistent cache TTL for fallback entries

scale.1: No meaningful fallback read-through behavior is visible; changes are limited to exploration, constants, fields, or corrupted edits, and repeated unhealthy reads would still go directly to backend.
scale.2: A fallback cache structure or config is introduced, but integration is missing or largely speculative; getter/read-path use, population, TTL defaults, or parameterized keys are absent.
scale.3: Some unhealthy-path integration exists for one or a few getters, but coverage of the requested hot resources, cache key correctness, TTL choice, or preservation of healthy-cache semantics is incomplete or uncertain.
scale.4: Clear read-through fallback integration exists for most requested hot getters with short TTL and proper unhealthy-path gating, though tests, cloning/mutability handling, or some edge-case keys may still need refinement.
scale.5: The trajectory shows a complete, idiomatic short-TTL fallback implementation: shared helper with load coalescing/expiry, broad targeted getter coverage, correct parameterized keys, healthy-path preservation, safe returned values, and validation that repeated unhealthy reads are reduced and entries refresh after TTL.

experiences.title: UDL Parsing Requires Exact Token Boundary Semantics
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a parser fix for C++ user-defined literal expressions in Sphinx or a similar recursive-descent C/C++ parser, especially when the failure is leftover suffix text after a numeric/string/character literal.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python codebase implementing a hand-written C/C++ parser where a task asks to parse C++ user-defined literals such as a numeric literal immediately followed by an identifier-like suffix in declarations or expressions. It is most useful after the trajectory has located literal parsing, regex-based token matching, or parser-position evidence showing the base literal is consumed but the suffix remains. It is less useful during very early repository exploration, for tasks only about declaring literal operators such as operator"" suffix, or for fixes that do not touch expression/literal parsing. If the task examples use suffixes without a leading underscore, the criterion must not silently narrow acceptance to underscore-only suffixes merely because that is a common C++-standard rule.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster were those that targeted the concrete failure mode: the parser consumes the core literal and must then consume an adjacent UDL suffix without relying on a generic identifier regex whose leading word-boundary fails after digits. However, broad rubrics such as “support all UDLs” or “suffix starts with underscore” can be misleading here. Several trajectories looked strong because they added an AST wrapper and passed underscore-only ad-hoc tests, but they still missed the reported no-underscore examples, inserted whitespace in stringification, allowed whitespace before the suffix, left debug/broad expression-parser changes, or failed to distinguish built-in numeric suffixes from UDL suffixes. A better rubric should focus on observable token-boundary behavior: exact reported literals parse through the suffix; suffix matching is immediate and does not use an inappropriate word-boundary identifier matcher; built-in integer/float suffixes remain separated with word-boundary-aware logic; string/character/numeric literals preserve existing behavior; AST rendering does not add spaces; and validation uses complete declarations plus expression tests rather than fallback parsing or substring regex checks. Avoid rewarding unrelated parser rewrites, literal-operator declaration support, or manual tests that only cover `_suffix` forms when the task example uses `q_J`/`q_s`.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Exact UDL Token Semantics and Parser Preservation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement C++ user-defined literal expression parsing at the literal-token level, consuming an identifier-like suffix immediately following numeric, string, and character literals without requiring a leading word boundary or intervening whitespace. The implementation should satisfy the task’s concrete examples, including suffixes shaped like `q_J` and `q_s` when those appear in the problem statement, while preserving existing handling of ordinary literals and built-in integer/floating suffixes via word-boundary-aware suffix logic. It should integrate cleanly with the existing literal AST/stringification/signature conventions, avoid inserting spaces between literal and suffix, avoid broad unrelated expression-parser rewrites or leftover debug code, and validate with parser/declaration tests that ensure the full input is consumed without fallback.

metadata.environment: Python Sphinx C++ domain or similar recursive-descent C/C++ parser
key_visible_files: C++ domain parser literal parsing method
priority_evidence: base literal previously parsed while suffix remained unconsumed
suffix matcher works at the current parser position after digits/quotes, not only on sliced substrings
tests include the exact reported declaration/expression and assert full consumption
stringification/rendering preserves adjacent literal+suffix spelling
anti_evidence: only underscore-leading suffixes are tested when the report uses no-underscore suffixes
suffix parsing calls whitespace skipping before matching the suffix
generic identifier regex with leading word boundary is reused unchanged
broad binary-expression parser behavior is changed to make tests pass
debug prints or temporary test artifacts remain

scale.1: No meaningful UDL expression support is implemented or the parser remains broken/missing methods; evidence shows suffix text is still left unconsumed.
scale.2: A partial AST or suffix idea is present, but it relies on unsuitable identifier matching, supports only unrelated forms, corrupts existing parser structure, or lacks full-consumption validation.
scale.3: The trajectory is roughly at parent-level progress: it identifies the literal suffix boundary issue and attempts to consume suffixes, but important acceptance details remain uncertain, such as exact task suffix forms, whitespace adjacency, built-in suffix preservation, or clean parser integration.
scale.4: Strong evidence shows adjacent suffixes after the relevant literal types parse in complete expressions/declarations, with a dedicated no-leading-boundary matcher and no major parser regressions, though some secondary integration or regression coverage may still need review.
scale.5: The implementation and validation fully cover the reported declaration and representative numeric/string/character UDLs, preserve built-in literal suffix behavior and existing C/C++ parser tests, render literal+suffix without added whitespace, avoid unrelated parser rewrites/debug artifacts, and use full-consumption parser tests rather than fallback or substring-only checks.

experiences.title: End-to-End Seed Note Contract Beats Rendering-Only Checks
experiences.description: Use when evaluating an Open Library-style list feature that adds user-provided per-item Markdown notes to heterogeneous seeds; prefer a rubric that checks the whole storage/input/rendering contract instead of only safe Markdown rendering.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories modifying a list feature where items/seeds may be stored in multiple representations, such as Thing references versus subject strings, and the task requires optional public notes only for real Thing items. It is most useful once the agent has started changing model/normalization/API/templates or is near final review, because enough evidence exists to judge whether notes survive the full flow. It is less useful during initial repository exploration before any implementation choices are visible, or for tasks that only change display of already-sanitized content without adding new storage/input semantics.
experiences.experience: The recurring generated rubrics focused on safe Markdown rendering of public notes. That is an important requirement, but it is too narrow for this class of task: several trajectories visibly used a Markdown formatting helper yet still left the feature broken because note data was not consistently stored, parsed, associated with the correct seed, excluded from subject seeds, or resolved back into renderable item objects. A better rubric should treat safe rendering as one part of an end-to-end seed annotation contract. It should prioritize visible evidence that the agent understands the heterogeneous seed model: Thing seeds and subject string seeds must remain distinct; note metadata must travel through form or JSON input normalization, persistence, add/remove/deduplication, runtime seed wrappers, API output, and list templates without converting subject strings into note-bearing records. The rubric should also watch for common regressions visible in the trajectory: making optional note fields required for existing seed dicts, storing notes on transient resolved objects instead of persisted seed data, comparing whole dicts instead of seed keys, rendering notes outside the corresponding list item, adding note fields for subjects, using an unverified or nonexistent Markdown helper, or relying on broad sed edits that corrupt model/controller/template code. Avoid the tempting criterion 'uses format() or markdown() somewhere' as a standalone success signal; it can overrate patches with serious data-flow bugs. Prioritize inspected diffs, targeted tests/manual checks showing create/edit/API persistence and subject exclusion, and template evidence that user content is rendered through the project's safe Markdown/sanitization path beneath the matching item.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete per-seed note data-flow contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a coherent end-to-end implementation for optional public Markdown notes on Thing list items: note metadata is accepted and persisted with the individual Thing seed, preserved through create/edit/API add flows, exposed by the runtime seed wrapper without breaking existing item resolution, rendered beneath the corresponding list item through the project’s safe Markdown/sanitization pipeline, and explicitly excluded from subject string seeds. Strong evidence includes inspected changes or tests covering backward-compatible seed records without notes, dedupe/removal by seed key rather than by full metadata object, form/JSON field names that match the parser, API/list output carrying notes for Thing seeds, and subject pseudo/string seeds remaining bare strings with no note UI/rendering.

prioritize_evidence: seed identity and note metadata are handled separately
Thing seeds and subject string seeds remain distinct
input normalization preserves notes only for non-subject Thing seeds
stored seed representation survives create/edit/add/remove/API paths
runtime seed objects can still resolve title/type/url/cover while exposing note
safe Markdown rendering is used beneath the matching item
tests or manual validation cover persistence, subject exclusion, and backward compatibility
avoid_overweighting: presence of a Markdown helper call without persistence evidence
CSS or textarea additions without parser/storage support
manual scripts that do not exercise subject seeds or existing seed records
broad unverified text substitutions in Python or web templates

scale.1: Little or no evidence of an end-to-end note contract; changes are limited to superficial UI/rendering or corrupt existing seed handling.
scale.2: Some isolated pieces exist, such as a note field or display block, but note data is not demonstrably preserved through normalization/storage/runtime rendering, or subject-seed exclusion is missing.
scale.3: Comparable partial progress to the parent trajectory: several relevant files are touched, but there are unresolved gaps such as optional-field compatibility, dict/Thing resolution, add/remove behavior, form parsing, safe rendering placement, or lack of validation.
scale.4: Strong evidence of a mostly coherent flow across input, storage, runtime seed access, and safe display, with subject strings kept unchanged and only minor validation or edge-case uncertainty remaining.
scale.5: Clear, verified implementation of the full contract with focused tests or manual checks for create/edit/API persistence, key-based dedupe/removal, existing seeds without notes, subject exclusion, and XSS-safe Markdown rendering under the correct list item.

experiences.title: Do not over-credit nominal chunk-seek logic without playback-interface integration evidence
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for a TypeScript/React audio seekbar task where the trajectory discusses or partially implements global-to-chunk seeking for voice-broadcast playback, especially after broad file rewrites, unvalidated code, or only exploratory evidence.
experiences.context: This applies in a Matrix/React-style codebase with chunked voice-broadcast playback built on lower-level audio Playback objects and an existing seekbar/clock pattern. A rubric about cross-chunk seek synchronization is semantically relevant, but it becomes misleading when the visible trajectory only shows conceptual understanding, helper names such as currentTime/seekTo/getChunkAtTime, custom sliders, fake observables, manual timers, or type-only fixes without demonstrating that the model, hook, UI, and existing playback state contracts still work together. The original cross-chunk seeking idea remains appropriate when the trajectory exposes concrete, validated code that maps a broadcast timeline to chunk-local playback, uses the real playback clock/update source, preserves stopped/paused/playing/live behavior, and passes relevant checks. In early exploration or mid-implementation, absence of finished chunk mapping should not be judged as decisive failure, but apparent presence of chunk mapping should also not be treated as strong evidence of correctness unless the integration contract is visible.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster generated broad positive criteria such as “Cross-Chunk Seek Synchronization” or “Voice Broadcast Chunk-Aware Seeking.” Those criteria capture a necessary feature, but they invite over-optimistic judgments from superficial evidence: an agent can add a range input, expose currentTime/seekTo, or write code that finds a target chunk while still breaking imports, using inconsistent milliseconds-vs-seconds units, creating inert liveData objects, polling instead of subscribing to actual playback updates, failing to stop or switch the old chunk correctly, or altering legacy stopped/live start behavior. A better rubric should focus on the integration contract that makes the seekbar actually usable: the voice-broadcast playback layer must behave like the existing playback abstraction, derive current time and duration from the active underlying playback plus accumulated prior chunk lengths with consistent units, delegate seeking to the target chunk’s low-level skip operation, emit/subscribe to real time updates, reset state appropriately on stop, preserve existing state transitions, and show validation through relevant compile/tests or focused debugging. Avoid rewarding mere planned understanding, helper-method names, custom UI presence, snapshot updates, or generic typecheck success as evidence of synchronized seeking. Prioritize visible evidence from diffs, event subscriptions, unit conversions, state-flow handling, and validation output.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Nominal seekbar support without real playback synchronization contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear to add voice-broadcast seekbar or chunk-seeking support but do not provide visible evidence that the implementation is wired to the existing playback abstraction and state model. This includes code or plans that add helper methods, a custom slider, or global-to-chunk lookup while leaving current-time updates disconnected from the active audio playback clock, mixing milliseconds and seconds, using fake or non-updating observables, failing to switch/pause/stop the previous chunk when seeking, failing to reset position/state on stop, changing live-vs-stopped start semantics, or proceeding after broad overwrites without relevant validation. The issue is not the absence of a particular helper name; it is the mismatch between the seekbar UI/model API and the actual audio playback state.

key_visible_evidence: model exposes current time, duration, live update source, and seek behavior compatible with existing playback/seekbar expectations
global broadcast time is converted to target chunk plus local offset with consistent units
time updates come from underlying playback clock/live data or an equivalent real playback source
seek preserves or intentionally changes playing/paused/stopped/buffering state and handles old chunk cleanup
existing behavior for ended versus live broadcasts is preserved
relevant typecheck/tests or focused validation are run after edits
misleading_evidence_to_discount: presence of method names like seekTo/currentTime/getChunkAtTime alone
custom range input or CSS alone
manual intervals or newly constructed observables not fed by actual playback
snapshots or unrelated UI checks without model playback validation

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the visible trajectory shows a seekbar-compatible playback contract tied to real playback updates, coherent units, correct chunk switching, preserved state behavior, and relevant validation.
scale.2: Minor concern only: most integration evidence is present, but one secondary aspect such as styling, a narrow validation gap, or a small edge-case note remains unresolved.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory implements some real chunk-aware seeking or time tracking, but visible evidence is incomplete about live updates, unit consistency, state preservation, or validation.
scale.4: Clear concern: the trajectory mainly shows nominal helper methods or UI wiring while relying on questionable observables/timers, inconsistent units, unverified state transitions, or broad unreviewed rewrites.
scale.5: Severe concern: the implementation is visibly disconnected from the actual playback clock/state model, breaks or ignores existing playback semantics, lacks meaningful validation, or remains in a broken/debugging state despite apparent seekbar code.

experiences.title: Do not over-credit internal CORS wiring without schema and custom-config validation
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a Go/Viper configuration feature where the agent adds a new config-backed CORS/header option and appears to have wired defaults into runtime code, especially if tests are failing or schema/test fixtures were not fully updated.
experiences.context: This applies to trajectories in a Go service using centralized configuration, Viper-style defaults, generated or maintained configuration schemas, YAML/env loading tests, and HTTP middleware. The misleading pattern is that the agent adds an internal config field, includes the requested default headers, and changes middleware to read that field, so a rubric focused only on default Fern headers or basic configurability looks satisfied. That is insufficient when the task also promises user customization through public configuration: schemas/docs, config fixtures, default constructors, env/YAML loading behavior, and existing middleware options must remain consistent. A narrow default-header rubric may still be useful during early implementation or in a codebase with no public schema/test fixture layer, but at final-review stage it should not be the main success criterion if visible evidence shows failing config tests, omitted/corrupted schema edits, no custom non-default example, or regressions to unrelated CORS options.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics rewarded evidence such as adding X-Fern-* headers to a default list, adding an AllowedHeaders field, or updating tests for changed defaults. Those criteria are directionally correct but misleadingly optimistic for this task because they ignore the public configuration contract and validation surfaces. In these cases, visible trajectories often showed only partial internal wiring, failing TestLoad-style config tests, ad hoc env overrides for slices, malformed schema edits, missing schema sources, or no fixture proving that user-specified headers replace the defaults. A better rubric should focus on end-to-end configuration completeness: the runtime middleware uses configured headers while preserving unrelated CORS options; defaults are consistent across all default constructors and serialized default fixtures; public schemas/docs expose the new option without corrupting existing references; YAML and environment loading are validated; and at least one custom configuration example uses non-default headers to prove customization. Avoid the tempting criterion that 'Fern headers are present by default' or 'YAML works, ENV failure is just test infrastructure' is enough. Prefer visible evidence from successful targeted tests, schema validation, and coherent fixture updates over mere presence of the new header names in internal code.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for a config-backed CORS/header feature when they judge or implement completion based only on internal default header additions and middleware wiring, while leaving the public configuration contract incomplete or unverified. This flaw is present when visible evidence shows missing or malformed schema/docs for the new option, inconsistent defaults between config constructors and Viper-style defaults, failing config load/marshal tests, lack of a custom non-default allowed-header fixture, invalid or unproven env/YAML slice handling, or accidental removal of unrelated middleware options. Do not apply this criticism merely because the agent has not yet reached the schema/test phase during early exploration; apply it when the trajectory is presenting implementation completeness, running final tests, or making broad schema/test edits.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Incomplete public config contract for CORS header customization

metadata.task_type: Go configuration feature
visible_evidence_to_prioritize: runtime middleware uses the configured header list
default headers include existing headers and required new client headers
public configuration schema or documentation exposes the new option
schema edits preserve existing schema structure
default constructor and Viper/config-loader defaults agree
serialized default fixtures are updated
custom YAML/env fixture demonstrates non-default allowed headers
relevant config/schema tests pass or failures are accurately addressed
tempting_but_insufficient_evidence: new header names appear in one default list
a config struct field exists
middleware references the config field
failing environment tests are dismissed as harness incompatibility without proof
tests are updated only to expect defaults, not customization

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory verifies runtime wiring, defaults, schema/docs, fixtures, and relevant tests for both default Fern headers and custom user-specified headers.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: most public contract surfaces are addressed, but one low-risk validation artifact such as formatting, a narrow fixture, or a secondary schema representation remains unconfirmed.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: internal config and middleware are present, but public schema/test fixture coverage or custom non-default loading evidence is incomplete or only partially verified.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory relies on default header inclusion while config tests fail, schema/docs are missing or suspicious, env/YAML behavior is unproven, or custom allowed headers are not demonstrated.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: schema or fixtures are visibly corrupted, tests fail due to the new config field, unrelated CORS behavior is regressed, and the agent still treats the feature as essentially complete based on internal header additions.

experiences.title: Complete Early QtWebEngine Locale Workaround
experiences.description: Use when a trajectory is addressing a QtWebEngine/Chromium subprocess crash tied to a specific version and system locale, especially after it has inspected startup argument/environment handling or historical workaround commits.
experiences.context: Applies in a PyQt/qutebrowser-like codebase where the reported symptom is an external QtWebEngine/Chromium network-service or subprocess crash causing blank pages under certain locales. The useful stage is when the agent is choosing or implementing the workaround location: central Qt/Chromium startup argument generation is relevant, while tab rendering callbacks, profile HTTP-header configuration, or generic environment initialization are usually too late or too broad. Do not apply this as-is to ordinary Accept-Language header bugs, renderer crash UI handling, non-version-specific locale formatting bugs, or very early exploration where the agent has not yet connected the failure to QtWebEngine startup arguments.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful criterion is not merely whether the agent noticed a Qt version-specific bug. A good rubric should check whether the trajectory converges on the complete early-startup locale workaround contract: an opt-in/default-disabled setting, exact affected QtWebEngine version and platform guard, discovery of the current Qt locale, resolution to an available Chromium/QtWebEngine locale resource, and emission of a Chromium language switch before QtWebEngine subprocesses start. Rubrics that only reward identifying a version-specific workaround are too permissive: several trajectories knew the version boundary but pursued wrong fixes such as mutating LANG/LC_ALL globally, skipping Accept-Language headers, setting a guessed locales-path environment variable, or patching late WebEngine profile/interceptor code. The better rubric should prioritize visible evidence that the agent found the central startup-argument mechanism or historical implementation, verified the workaround was absent, added or planned the config gate, implemented locale resource existence checks and locale-name fallback mapping, wired the override into early QtWebEngine argument generation, and considered tests around disabled config, non-Linux, other versions, existing locale files, and missing locale directories. Avoid treating documentation/changelog additions, repeated grep searches, or a bare QTBUG reference as sufficient without the behavioral startup-argument path.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Early Version-Gated Locale Override Completeness
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the fix for a QtWebEngine locale-triggered network-service/subprocess crash is implemented or clearly planned as an early Chromium/QtWebEngine language override, not as late request/profile handling or a global locale mutation. Strong evidence includes using the project’s central QtWebEngine argument construction path, adding an opt-in/default-disabled workaround setting, guarding the behavior to the affected QtWebEngine version and relevant platform, obtaining the current Qt locale, locating available QtWebEngine/Chromium locale resources, avoiding overrides when the requested locale resource already exists, mapping unsupported locale names to available resource names with a safe fallback, yielding a language switch before WebEngine startup, and adding or restoring targeted tests for the guard conditions and resource-resolution behavior.

metadata.environment: Python/PyQt application using QtWebEngine/Chromium subprocesses
problem_signature: external network-service or subprocess crash log
prioritize_visible_evidence: central QtWebEngine startup argument or flag generation is identified
workaround is exact-version and platform guarded
workaround is config-gated and disabled by default when appropriate
current Qt locale is converted to an available Chromium/QtWebEngine locale resource
language override is emitted before QtWebEngine/profile initialization
tests or validation cover disabled setting, unaffected versions/platforms, existing resource files, missing resource directory, and fallback mapping
insufficient_or_wrong_proxies: only naming a QTBUG or saying version-specific workaround
guessing a QTWEBENGINE_LOCALES_PATH-style environment variable without version/resource behavior
patching tab render-process or request-interceptor code for a startup subprocess crash

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward an early locale workaround; the trajectory remains in repeated searches or focuses on unrelated tab/render/profile handling.
scale.2: Recognizes a locale/version relationship but proposes or implements a broad or late workaround such as global locale environment changes, Accept-Language suppression, or guessed resource-path variables without the required startup language override semantics.
scale.3: Identifies the correct early startup-argument layer and affected version, but the implementation or plan is incomplete, missing important guards, config gating, locale resource checks, fallback mapping, or validation.
scale.4: Shows strong implementation evidence for an early language override with most required pieces: exact version/platform guard, config setting, current Qt locale lookup, resource-directory checks, and wiring into QtWebEngine startup arguments, with only minor gaps in mapping, fallback behavior, or tests.
scale.5: Fully satisfies the workaround contract: opt-in/default-disabled setting, precise affected-version/platform guards, current locale resolution, available-resource detection, Chromium-compatible locale fallback mapping, safe fallback when needed, early language switch emission before WebEngine startup, and targeted tests/validation for both active and inactive paths.

experiences.title: Do Not Stop at Uploader Initialization When Task Lists Kube Exec Lifecycle Bugs
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Teleport Kubernetes exec/session-recording task names the missing uploader directory as the visible symptom but also explicitly calls out cluster session caching, audit context cancellation, response-error logging, or forwarder config cleanup.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go Teleport-style codebase where Kubernetes exec flows through a kube proxy/forwarder and session recording uses events/filesessions under a service startup path. It is most useful once the trajectory has already identified or implemented the obvious upload-directory/session-uploader initialization fix, or has inspected forwarder code showing cached cluster sessions and audit emission tied to request contexts. It is less useful for a task statement that only asks to create a missing directory, for very early repository exploration before the agent has found the session recording path, or for trajectories that are already actively modifying the forwarder/session lifecycle and audit semantics.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics were useful because they checked the part of the task that minimal patches tended to miss: the task was not only about creating the upload/streaming directory. The visible trajectory repeatedly showed the agent focusing on `initUploaderService`, `filesessions.NewUploader`, or `MkdirAll` near the async streamer, while leaving the Kubernetes forwarder behavior untouched. In this situation, a good rubric should ask whether the trajectory is still accounting for the listed lifecycle fixes: not caching request-scoped or remote-cluster state inside long-lived cluster sessions, emitting audit events with a context that survives client disconnect, preserving/logging exec response errors, and cleaning confusing forwarder config dependencies consistently. Avoid the tempting but too-narrow criterion that rewards only finding the missing directory or adding uploader initialization; that criterion cannot distinguish a partial symptom fix from a complete task-level fix when the prompt explicitly includes additional exec robustness requirements. Prioritize visible evidence such as searches/edits around cluster session cache construction, request context use in audit emission, exec stream/status error handling, and forwarder config field naming or dependency separation, rather than build success or the mere presence of an uploader call.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Covers Kubernetes Exec Lifecycle Semantics Beyond Upload Directory
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show concrete investigation or implementation of the Kubernetes exec/session lifecycle issues explicitly listed alongside the missing uploader symptom: separating cached reusable session credentials from request-specific or remote-cluster/tunnel state, avoiding request-context cancellation for audit event emission, logging or preserving exec response/status errors, and keeping forwarder configuration dependencies clearly named and consistently wired. Merely adding uploader initialization or creating the streaming upload directory is not enough for high credit when these broader requirements remain visible in the task.

required_visible_evidence: Inspection or edits of Kubernetes forwarder cluster session cache/auth context handling
Inspection or edits of audit event emission context used by exec/session end events
Inspection or edits of exec stream response/status error logging
Inspection or edits of forwarder configuration dependency names or wiring
Uploader/directory initialization is treated as one requirement rather than the whole task
common_partial_evidence: Only adds service startup uploader initialization
Only creates the async streaming directory before constructing a file streamer
Only validates package build/tests without addressing forwarder lifecycle semantics

scale.1: No visible attention to the non-uploader lifecycle issues; the trajectory only explores or patches the missing directory/uploader symptom.
scale.2: Mentions the broader lifecycle issues from the task but does not inspect the relevant forwarder/audit/cache code or plan concrete changes.
scale.3: Inspects some relevant forwarder code and recognizes at least one broader issue, but implementation or plan remains dominated by uploader/directory initialization.
scale.4: Shows concrete edits or a clear implementation plan for most broader exec lifecycle issues in addition to uploader initialization.
scale.5: Systematically addresses uploader initialization and the forwarder lifecycle contract: cached state boundaries, non-canceled audit contexts, response-error logging, and coherent config wiring are all visibly handled or validated.

experiences.title: Mocked import base-name preservation
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Sphinx/autodoc trajectory is fixing malformed inheritance documentation for classes whose external bases are supplied by autodoc-style mocked imports.
experiences.context: Applies in Python documentation tooling, especially Sphinx autodoc, when the task symptom is that a documented class inheriting from a mocked external class is present but its Bases/inheritance line renders a truncated dotted name such as a module prefix ending in a dot. The trajectory should have reached or be close to the mock-object construction and base-stringification path: autodoc collects bases, optionally exposes them to a bases-processing event, then converts each base/type-like object into a reST reference. This experience is most useful after the agent has inspected mock metadata such as display-name, module, name, qualname, marker attributes, and how mock instances/classes differ. It is less useful for unrelated autodoc discovery failures, downstream project configuration changes, generic Sphinx build dependency problems, or very early exploration where the agent has not yet connected the Bases output to mocked object metadata.
experiences.experience: For this cluster, useful rubrics were those that judged whether the trajectory understood the real invariant: mocked import objects need to preserve a full logical class name through introspection/stringification, not merely make the derived class discoverable. The visible evidence to prioritize is whether the agent traces the Bases rendering path to the type/reST formatter and the mock implementation, observes that mocked objects carry a full display name while normal formatting may combine module with an empty qualname/name, and validates both direct mocked bases and real/local subclasses. A better rubric should not only say 'handle mocked classes in restify'; that is sometimes a viable patch direction, but it can be too broad and can reward unsafe detection based on inherited marker attributes. The criterion should require a boundary: actual mock objects or mock-generated base metadata should render as the full external class path, while real Python classes that inherit from mocks must still render as themselves and normal class/type behavior must remain unchanged. Avoid tempting proxy criteria such as requiring the full downstream HTML build, rewarding repeated dependency installation attempts, or accepting a superficial change that sets a class-level qualname while instance initialization still overwrites the value seen by introspection.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Preserves full mocked base identity without misclassifying real subclasses
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate, from visible code inspection, experiments, or tests, that the fix preserves the complete dotted identity of bases supplied by autodoc-style mocked imports when generating inheritance/Bases documentation. Strong evidence includes tracing the base-rendering pipeline from collected bases to the type-to-reST formatter, identifying which mock metadata contains the full intended name versus which normal introspection attributes can be empty or inherited, and ensuring the implementation distinguishes actual mock objects/classes from real classes that merely inherit mock marker/display attributes. The trajectory should also guard normal behavior for builtins, ordinary classes, generics, and package-local subclasses.

metadata.environment: Python documentation generator with autodoc-style mocked imports and reST rendering of class bases
key_visible_evidence: connects malformed Bases output to base object stringification rather than class discovery
inspects mock metadata such as full display name, module, name, qualname, and mock marker attributes
recognizes instance-versus-class metadata differences in dynamically created mocks
tests or reasons about both mocked external bases and real/local subclasses inheriting from mocked bases
avoids broad inherited-marker detection that would render real subclasses as their mocked parent
non_goals: requiring a full downstream documentation build when focused mock/autodoc tests expose the issue
rewarding dependency-installation loops or unrelated Sphinx extension setup
