accepting only class-level qualname edits without checking the value actually seen by the renderer

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory links the malformed inheritance text to mocked import metadata or the base stringification path.
scale.2: Some awareness that mocked imports are involved, but investigation remains at configuration/discovery level or only checks simplified cases that do not exercise the malformed name.
scale.3: Identifies the autodoc Bases-to-stringification path and mock objects, but the proposed reasoning or patch does not clearly handle the instance/class metadata boundary or real subclasses inheriting mock attributes.
scale.4: Clearly diagnoses the full-name metadata loss and proposes or validates a fix using the correct mock display/name information, with some protection for ordinary classes and local subclasses.
scale.5: Provides decisive evidence that mocked external bases render with their full dotted class path while real subclasses and normal type rendering remain unchanged, using targeted tests or experiments that cover direct mocked objects, inherited bases, and non-mock classes.

experiences.title: Analogous Parser Pattern Beats Exhaustive Coordinate-Site Search
experiences.description: Use when a Python/Qt codebase task asks for centralizing parsing of coordinate strings into QPoint and the trajectory is still localizing where to implement or integrate the parser.
experiences.context: Applies in qutebrowser-like Python projects using PyQt/QPoint, command modules, utility modules, and tests, especially during exploration before or just after choosing an implementation location. The relevant visible evidence is whether the agent has found an existing analogous geometry parser or clear user-facing coordinate entry point, versus repeatedly grepping for comma-split/QPoint patterns without progress. Do not apply as an exhaustive-call-site criterion when searches show no obvious existing ad-hoc coordinate parser; in that situation, demanding discovery of every current parser can be too strict and may miss productive progress toward adding a central utility. It is also less relevant after a full patch is already visible; then rubrics should judge implementation and integration behavior directly.
experiences.experience: In these trajectories, rubrics that simply required identifying all existing coordinate-string parsing sites were only useful when the agent was clearly stuck in repeated broad searches; they correctly highlighted lack of localization. However, that criterion was too broad when the codebase did not visibly contain many existing ad-hoc QPoint parsers. A better rubric should reward the decisive exploration cue: finding the established nearby pattern for parsing geometry strings, such as an existing rectangle parser in a general utility module, and using it to infer the appropriate home, error style, and tests for a new point parser. It should also reward identifying a real user-facing integration surface, such as a command/filter that accepts an x,y value and calls a QPoint-based API, but it should not require proving every possible QPoint construction is user input. Avoid tempting proxies like counting grep commands, insisting on the command argument conversion pipeline without evidence it handles QPoint, or treating internal QPoint creation from structured session/UI data as affected parsing. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent distinguishes unrelated comma-splitting/color/config/session code from coordinate-string parsing, discovers an analogous utility parser and test style, and plans controlled ValueError-to-user-message handling at command boundaries.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should productively localize the coordinate-string parsing change by finding an analogous existing geometry/string parser and a plausible user-facing coordinate entry point, while filtering out unrelated QPoint constructions and comma-splitting. Strong evidence includes identifying the established utility module and parser conventions, recognizing that internal QPoint values from structured data are not user-provided coordinate strings, and connecting the new parser to command-facing error handling or tests.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Canonical Geometry Parser Localization

preferred_evidence: Finds an existing geometry parser or nearby utility pattern for parsing strings into Qt geometry objects
Identifies where a new point parser should live and what exception style it should use
Looks for actual user-facing coordinate inputs such as command/filter values passed to QPoint-consuming APIs
Separates unrelated color/config/version/session parsing from malformed coordinate-string handling
Stops or redirects unproductive repeated grep loops
avoid_as_primary_evidence: Exhaustive discovery of every QPoint construction when most are internal structured data
Assuming command argument conversion must be modified without evidence
Treating generic comma splitting as coordinate parsing

scale.1: No useful localization: the trajectory repeats broad searches or inspects unrelated comma-splitting/QPoint uses without identifying a parser pattern, utility location, or user-facing coordinate input.
scale.2: Weak localization: the trajectory finds some relevant QPoint or command infrastructure but still conflates internal structured data or unrelated parsing with user coordinate strings.
scale.3: Moderate progress: the trajectory has narrowed to likely utility/command areas and rejected some unrelated leads, but has not yet found a concrete analogous parser or integration point.
scale.4: Strong progress: the trajectory identifies an analogous string-to-Qt-geometry parser or established utility/test convention and can explain why it is the right model for a centralized point parser.
scale.5: Strongest progress: the trajectory finds the analogous parser pattern, chooses an appropriate shared location and error behavior, distinguishes unrelated sites, and identifies at least one real user-facing coordinate path or test surface to integrate or validate the parser.

experiences.title: Do not let deprecation warnings mask iterator behavior preservation
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating an API-migration task that replaces legacy constants with public enum-like state types while preserving compatibility and existing behavior, especially in Ansible `PlayIterator`-style state machines.
experiences.context: This applies in Python/Ansible executor code where state constants are being migrated to public namespaced types and the task also explicitly requires old class/instance access to keep working with deprecation notices. A deprecation-path rubric is valid only as one subcriterion after the trajectory shows the new state representation, compatibility access, and behavioral preservation are being handled. It is misleading as the dominant criterion when the visible trajectory contains wholesale rewrites, broken or repeated iterator tests, empty/no-op finalization, unresolved class-vs-instance access experiments, or added requirements not in the task such as module-level legacy names. The original idea remains appropriate when the trajectory is specifically implementing the compatibility shim and there is no visible evidence of state-machine regression.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics often judged the trajectory mainly on whether legacy `PlayIterator.ITERATING_*` / `FAILED_*` access emitted deprecation warnings. That requirement is real, but by itself it over-credits trajectories that break the iterator state machine, repeatedly inspect warning configuration without making progress, or leave failing tests unresolved. Some variants also invented stricter requirements such as module-level deprecated constants, a particular warning API, or stacklevel behavior, even though the task only requires old names through `PlayIterator` class and instances. For similar tasks, generate a rubric that treats deprecation as part of a broader migration contract: public integer-compatible run states and flag-compatible failure states, core executor/strategy code using the new public names, old class and instance names remaining compatible with warnings, readable string output, and unchanged task iteration/failure semantics. Avoid a standalone high-confidence criterion that says warning implementation is sufficient. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence such as minimal diffs to the sensitive state-machine methods, preservation of original numeric/bitwise values, updates to all internal consumers, successful targeted iterator tests, and no unresolved regression notes in the trajectory.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that focus on the legacy deprecation shim while leaving evidence that the iterator migration changes core task-selection behavior or compatibility scope is wrong. This includes wholesale rewrites of the iterator state machine, failing or unresolved play-iterator tests, repeated tasks/no progress in manual iterator smoke tests, use of deprecated aliases inside core paths causing noisy internal warnings, or adding non-requested module-level compatibility while missing class/instance compatibility. The issue is most severe when the trajectory has visible regression evidence and still treats deprecation warnings as the main success signal.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Deprecation shim over core state-machine correctness

metadata.task_type: state constant to public enum migration
metadata.environment: Python Ansible executor/strategy code
required_compatibility: old names accessible through PlayIterator class
old names accessible through PlayIterator instances
failure states preserve bitwise flag behavior
visible_evidence_to_prioritize: targeted iterator tests or smoke tests preserve task order
no broad rewrite of _get_next_task_from_state or equivalent state machine
core consumers use new public state types
HostState string output shows readable names
legacy access warns without being used internally
avoid_inventing: a mandatory warning mechanism not evidenced by the repository
stacklevel-only warning criteria as the main success proxy

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory balances compatibility warnings with a minimal enum migration and preserves iterator behavior, or it is still early exploration without misleading conclusions.
scale.2: Minor evidence: deprecation behavior is discussed disproportionately, but the trajectory still checks state values, core consumers, and behavior-preserving tests.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory implements or investigates warnings but has incomplete evidence for preserving state-machine behavior or class/instance compatibility.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory emphasizes warning implementation while visible tests, smoke checks, or diffs show likely iterator-order or state-transition regressions.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory gives high confidence based on deprecation warnings despite unresolved failing iterator tests, wholesale state-machine rewrites, repeated no-progress iterator output, empty/no-op finalization, or invented compatibility requirements that distract from the specified migration contract.

experiences.title: Canonical setting default as the primary contract
experiences.description: Use this when a Django task asks to change an upload/storage default and the trajectory has identified that existing storage code already applies a non-None permission setting after saving files.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django repository when the task is specifically about making uploaded files default to a stable mode such as `0o644`, and visible investigation shows a canonical plural setting (`FILE_UPLOAD_PERMISSIONS`) currently defaults to `None` while `FileSystemStorage` already resolves that setting and chmods final saved files when it is non-None. This is most useful once the agent has inspected the setting and storage save path or has begun editing. It is less useful for early repository exploration before the setting/storage relationship is known, for docs-only warning tasks, or for bugs where the storage save path lacks any existing permission-application mechanism and must be redesigned.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases should evaluate the central behavior contract: the agent should update Django’s existing canonical upload-permissions setting to the octal integer `0o644`, so final files saved through the storage layer get consistent permissions regardless of whether upload content came from memory or a temporary file. This criterion aligns with visible evidence such as grepping the current default, inspecting the storage property that falls back to the setting, seeing the post-save chmod when the mode is non-None, and verifying final saved file modes for both temporary-backed and memory-backed uploads. It should also mention preserving explicit user control: custom permission values and an explicit `None` should continue to mean what the existing storage API defines, rather than introducing a new singular setting or hardcoding permissions in unrelated paths. Avoid making documentation edits, release note formatting, package installation, or broad test-runner success the primary criterion for this task; those can be noisy and sometimes distract from the core patch. Also avoid over-penalizing solely because an agent experiments with raw temporary-file permissions: the rubric should prioritize the final saved file behavior through the storage contract, while treating unnecessary upload-handler/temp-file edits as a secondary risk rather than the main pass/fail signal unless they visibly break explicit overrides or security-sensitive documented behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that it is implementing the canonical Django upload-permissions default contract: use the existing `FILE_UPLOAD_PERMISSIONS` setting, change its default value to the octal integer `0o644`, rely on the existing storage permission mechanism so final saved files are normalized for both memory-backed and temporary-file-backed uploads, and preserve explicit `None` or custom permission overrides rather than creating a new setting or hardcoding permissions in unrelated upload paths.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Canonical upload permission default

metadata.primary_behavior: final files saved by FileSystemStorage receive consistent permissions by default
metadata.important_boundary: explicit None/custom permission settings remain supported
evidence_to_prioritize: visible discovery of the existing setting default
visible inspection of the storage fallback/chmod behavior
edit or planned edit to the canonical default rather than a new setting
validation or reasoning about both temporary-file and in-memory upload save paths
secondary_risks: unnecessary chmods on transient temporary upload files
tests that only inspect raw temporary-file permissions instead of final saved files

scale.1: No visible progress toward the canonical setting default; the trajectory focuses on unrelated docs, creates a new setting/name, or changes unrelated upload code without identifying the existing storage permission contract.
scale.2: Some relevant investigation of uploads or permissions is visible, but the trajectory has not clearly targeted the existing `FILE_UPLOAD_PERMISSIONS` default or is primarily reasoning from raw temporary-file permissions rather than final storage behavior.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies the existing setting and storage mechanism, but the implementation/plan is incomplete, ambiguous, or lacks evidence that explicit overrides and both upload paths remain within the existing contract.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly changes or plans to change the canonical default to `0o644` and explains that storage will apply it to final saved files, with only minor uncertainty around validation, docs, or override behavior.
scale.5: The trajectory strongly establishes the full contract: the canonical default is set to octal `0o644`, the existing storage chmod path is used for final files from both temporary and memory uploads, explicit `None` and custom values are preserved, and no unrelated setting or hardcoded permission path is introduced.

experiences.title: Topic Backlinks Must Surface Through the Existing Timeline UI
experiences.description: Use this when a NodeBB-style feature requires reverse topic links to appear in the topic timeline, and the trajectory has begun implementing storage/admin settings but display integration is uncertain.
experiences.context: Applies to Node.js/NodeBB-like forum codebases where topic pages are rendered from server-provided topic data plus Benchpress/theme templates or an existing topic-events/timeline renderer. The task explicitly requires a user-facing, localized, styled backlink such as “Referenced by” linking to the referencing post, gated by an admin setting. This criterion is most useful once the agent has enough evidence about topic rendering, events, templates, or controller data flow to judge whether backlinks will actually be visible. It is premature during pure repository exploration before any UI/rendering path has been identified. It is less useful for tasks that only require storing backlink metadata or exposing an API, or for products whose accepted UI is not timeline/event-based.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often checked for localization or generic template work. Those cues were only partially useful: adding translation strings or creating a standalone partial is not enough if the partial is never imported, if it edits only generated/build or node_modules theme files, or if the backend does not provide the data shape the template expects. The more discriminative rubric should focus on the complete presentation contract: referenced-topic backlinks must be surfaced in the actual topic timeline/rendering path, include a link to the referencing post, use localized text, and be hidden when the admin feature flag is disabled. In NodeBB-style code, strong evidence includes adding/using an existing topic event/timeline type or verified source template insertion, wiring topic data from the controller/topic assembly layer, and ensuring the rendered link has the correct href to the source post. Avoid rewarding broad proxies like “created a backlinks sorted set,” “added admin checkbox,” “added language keys,” or “created a partial” unless the trajectory also shows that these connect to the active topic UI. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent identified the real source of the topic timeline rather than editing build output or bundled theme copies blindly, and evidence that backend fields match the frontend template’s expected objects.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Timeline Backlink Presentation Contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that topic backlinks will be rendered in the actual user-facing topic timeline or equivalent existing topic event UI, not merely stored or exposed. Strong implementations identify the real topic rendering/event path, add localized “Referenced by” text, include a correct link to the referencing post, gate visibility on the admin setting, and ensure the backend supplies exactly the data fields consumed by the renderer/template. Evidence should come from visible edits or plans to the topic controller/topic data assembly, event/timeline definitions or verified source templates, and the matching localization/config paths.

metadata.environment: NodeBB-style Node.js forum with server-side topic data, admin settings, language JSON files, and Benchpress/theme topic rendering
required_visible_evidence: Backlinks are connected to the active topic timeline/event renderer or a verified source topic template
Rendered backlink text is localized
Rendered backlink links to the referencing post, not just the referencing topic
Visibility is controlled by the admin feature setting
Backend data shape matches the frontend/template fields used for display
red_flags: Only storage, parsing, or admin setting work is present
A partial/template is created but not imported or routed into the topic page
Only generated build files or node_modules theme copies are edited without confirming source-of-truth
Template references nested fields that the backend does not populate
Backlinks display even when the setting is disabled

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that backlinks will appear in the user-facing topic timeline; work is limited to exploration, storage, parsing, settings, or disconnected localization.
scale.2: Weak display evidence exists, such as adding language strings or drafting a partial, but it is not connected to the active topic rendering path or lacks the post-link/data contract.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory attempts to pass backlink data to a topic page and render it, but integration is incomplete, source-template choice is uncertain, feature gating/localization is partial, or backend fields may not match the template.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory identifies the active topic timeline/template path and wires localized, feature-gated backlink display with links to referencing posts, with only minor uncertainty or validation remaining.
scale.5: Complete evidence: backlinks are integrated through the established topic timeline/event or verified source template path, use localized text, link directly to referencing posts, obey the admin setting, and have a consistent backend/frontend data contract with validation or tests.

experiences.title: Separate Matcher API from Variable Interpolation
experiences.description: Use when a Go parse/interpolation package task asks for matcher-expression support, examples are one-argument matcher functions, and the existing code only has a Variable/Expression interpolation API.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go codebase where a package currently parses `{{...}}` expressions for trait/value interpolation and the task explicitly adds string matcher validation support. Strong retrieval cues include task wording about missing `Matcher`/matcher types, one-argument examples such as `regexp.match("pattern")` or `regexp.not_match("pattern")`, required support for literals/wildcards/regex, and a requirement that matcher use inside the existing `Variable()` interpolation path be rejected. This is most useful after the agent has inspected the parse package or visible tests and before or during implementation review. It is less applicable if the task truly asks to filter interpolated trait values, if matcher expressions intentionally include a variable argument, or if an existing matcher API already defines incompatible signatures that must be preserved.
experiences.experience: In this cluster, broad rubrics that merely asked for a regexp namespace transformer or `regexp.match`/`regexp.not_match` handling in the existing AST walker were not discriminative enough: agents often implemented two-argument regexp functions as interpolation transformers, added matchers to `Expression`, or changed `Interpolate` behavior, while missing the central contract. The useful criterion should focus on the semantic boundary visible in the task: matcher expressions validate an input string through a separate matcher abstraction, while `Variable()` remains for interpolation and must not accept matcher syntax. Prioritize evidence that the trajectory introduces a matcher interface/type and a matcher parsing entry point, handles one-argument regexp matcher functions, covers literal/wildcard/regex patterns, preserves existing interpolation behavior, and adds clear error paths for malformed templates, unsupported functions, invalid pattern arguments, and matcher misuse in `Variable()`. Avoid tempting but wrong criteria that reward copying predicate-package parsing, requiring curried function syntax, or treating regexp functions as value transformers over trait variables.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should recognize and implement matcher support as a separate string-validation API rather than as an extension of interpolation. Strong evidence includes defining a `Matcher`-style abstraction with a `Match` operation, adding a matcher parser entry point for literals, wildcard-style strings, regex patterns, and one-argument `regexp.match`/`regexp.not_match` expressions, compiling/validating regex patterns with clear trace-style errors, and ensuring the existing `Variable()`/`Expression.Interpolate()` path continues to parse only interpolation variables and rejects matcher functions instead of treating them as variable transforms.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Matcher/Interpolation Boundary Preservation

metadata.expected_boundary: Matcher expressions validate candidate strings independently; interpolation expressions expand variables from traits.
positive_evidence: Defines a matcher abstraction and concrete regexp/inverted matcher behavior.
Adds a matcher parsing function or equivalent API distinct from `Variable()`.
Parses one-argument matcher functions such as `regexp.match("pattern")` and `regexp.not_match("pattern")`.
Supports non-template literal, wildcard, and regex pattern matching semantics.
Rejects matcher functions in the interpolation parser with a clear error.
Maintains existing interpolation tests and behavior.
negative_evidence: Only adds regexp transformers to `Expression` or `Interpolate`.
Requires regexp matcher functions to take a trait variable argument.
Stores matchers on interpolation expressions and lets `Variable()` accept matcher syntax.
Omits literal/wildcard pattern support.
Relies on unrelated predicate-package APIs without matching the task’s matcher contract.

scale.1: No evidence of a separate matcher abstraction or parser; work remains exploratory or only searches for matcher references.
scale.2: Adds or plans regexp function names/types but primarily treats them as interpolation transformers or does not address `Variable()` rejection and literal/wildcard matching.
scale.3: Identifies the need for matcher support and some boundary with interpolation, but implementation or plan is incomplete, ambiguous on API shape, or only covers regexp functions.
scale.4: Clearly implements or plans a distinct matcher API with regexp match/not_match and preserves interpolation behavior, with only minor gaps in pattern variants or error coverage.
scale.5: Fully separates matcher parsing from interpolation, supports literal/wildcard/regex and one-argument regexp match/not_match semantics, validates malformed inputs clearly, rejects matcher misuse in `Variable()`, and verifies both new matcher behavior and existing interpolation regressions.

experiences.title: Bulk Update Must Preserve Plain F Expressions
experiences.description: Use this when evaluating Django ORM trajectories for a `bulk_update()` bug where plain `F('field')` assignments are being treated as literals rather than resolvable expressions.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django codebase when the task concerns `QuerySet.bulk_update()` storing the string representation of a plain `F(...)` assignment instead of resolving it to a column reference. The criterion is most useful once the trajectory has inspected or modified the CASE/WHEN construction that decides whether an assigned attribute is wrapped as a literal value or passed through as an ORM expression. It is also relevant when the trajectory has discovered that plain `F` objects are expression-like but do not subclass the nominal expression base class. It is less useful as a strict judgment during the first few exploratory steps before any code location or class hierarchy evidence is visible, and it should not be replaced by a requirement to have successfully run the full Django test suite, since test-runner setup failures can be unrelated. Do not apply this pattern to unrelated `bulk_update()` issues, ordinary literal update bugs, or cases that only involve combined expressions such as arithmetic `F()` expressions that already become expression subclasses.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic boundary between literal values and resolvable ORM expressions inside `bulk_update()`: plain `F('other_field')` must be passed through to the generated `When(..., then=...)` expression machinery instead of being wrapped in a literal `Value(...)`, while normal Python values must still be wrapped. This aligned well when the visible trajectory showed the agent identifying the too-narrow expression check, recognizing that plain `F` has `resolve_expression()` despite not being a nominal expression subclass, and applying or validating a minimal change that preserves expression-like objects. A better rubric should prioritize visible evidence that the agent handles the exact failing case: assigning a plain, uncombined `F()` to a model field, calling `bulk_update()`, and confirming the refreshed value or SQL uses the referenced column rather than the string `F(name)`. It should also credit preservation of ordinary literals and existing expression subclasses. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as requiring an official regression test before any implementation progress, treating `F('x') + 1` coverage as sufficient, or judging primarily on Django test-runner command success when the trajectory shows environmental configuration problems. Regression tests are valuable at final review, but for predicting patch correctness here the decisive evidence is whether the expression/literal detection logic no longer misclassifies plain `F()`.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that `bulk_update()` distinguishes ordinary literal field values from expression-like assigned values using the ORM expression protocol or an equivalently precise inclusion of plain `F()` objects. Strong evidence includes identifying that plain `F('field')` is resolvable but not a nominal expression subclass, changing the literal-wrapping decision so plain `F()` is passed through to CASE/WHEN SQL generation, and validating that a refreshed object receives the referenced column value rather than the string representation. The trajectory should also preserve wrapping for normal Python values and avoid relying solely on combined `F()` expressions as proof.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Plain F Expression Preservation

metadata.required_behavior: Plain uncombined F assignments in bulk_update are treated as resolvable ORM expressions, not literal values.
key_visible_evidence: Inspection of the bulk_update value-to-CASE/WHEN construction
Recognition that plain F exposes resolve_expression but is not covered by the old nominal expression check
A code change or design that prevents plain F from being wrapped as Value while leaving literals wrapped
Validation via refreshed database value or generated SQL for a plain F assignment
non_decisive_or_insufficient_evidence: Only testing F arithmetic or other combined expressions
Only attempting test-runner setup without addressing expression detection

scale.1: No visible progress on the expression/literal distinction; the trajectory does not identify why plain F is stored as a string or where bulk_update wraps values.
scale.2: Some relevant exploration, such as locating bulk_update or F, but no clear understanding that plain F is resolvable yet missed by the current expression check.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory diagnoses the narrow expression check or proposes including plain F, but has not clearly shown a robust implementation or validation of the plain uncombined F case.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory implements or clearly plans a targeted fix so plain F is not wrapped as a literal, with some validation or reasoning that ordinary literals and existing expressions still work.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory identifies the exact protocol/class-hierarchy issue, applies a minimal fix preserving expression-like values while wrapping literals, and validates the original plain F behavior plus representative literal/existing-expression cases.

experiences.title: Judge the Settled Sentinel Control Flow, Not Transient Edit Attempts
experiences.description: Use when intermediate failed edits or an temporarily unsafe sentinel initialization are being turned into a prediction that the eventual localized parser fix will remain broken.
experiences.context: During a localized parser repair, malformed shell edits and tentative initializations may appear before the agent restores the function and validates both branches. These are serious only when they remain in the visible settled patch or the agent claims completion without rerunning the reproducer. The criterion should follow correction evidence rather than freezing judgment at the first failed edit.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics correctly noticed unsafe empty-string and uninitialized-sentinel states but treated those temporary states as the whole trajectory. A better negative rubric asks whether the current implementation still lets the no-placeholder path reference or construct the sentinel, or whether the placeholder path's replacement and cleanup semantics have been damaged. Avoid rewarding an exact edit shape; use the latest code inspection and branch-specific executions.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Persisting Sentinel Branch Corruption
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize the current trajectory when the no-placeholder path still references an uninitialized or universally matching sentinel, when edits damage the placeholder replacement/cleanup branch, or when a claimed fix still fails either branch. Earlier malformed edits that were visibly reverted and revalidated should not count as an unresolved defect.

observable_evidence: latest function body rather than superseded edits
no-placeholder reproducer
placeholder replacement and cleanup checks
syntax/import validation after edits

scale.1: No visible evidence of unsafe sentinel control flow remaining in the current parser implementation; the available implementation and validation evidence is consistent with the required behavior.
scale.2: A minor or early-stage concern about unsafe sentinel control flow remaining in the current parser implementation is visible, but it is not confirmed and the trajectory is still actively resolving it.
scale.3: Evidence about unsafe sentinel control flow remaining in the current parser implementation is mixed or incomplete; the concern remains plausible but is not yet decisive.
scale.4: Clear visible evidence indicates unsafe sentinel control flow remaining in the current parser implementation, with no convincing correction or validation yet.
scale.5: The trajectory directly reproduces or validates unsafe sentinel control flow remaining in the current parser implementation, or claims completion while the contradiction remains unresolved.

experiences.title: Auth Method Registry Before New Service Surface
experiences.description: Use when a Go service adds a new authentication method and the trajectory is extrapolating from existing token/OIDC implementations; prioritize whether the agent identified the repository’s config/protobuf method registry contract before demanding a full new server or middleware path.
experiences.context: Applies in Go repositories with an existing authentication subsystem where available methods are represented through a central method enum, config structs, public method metadata, defaulting/cleanup behavior, generated protobuf artifacts, and config fixtures. It is especially relevant when the task asks to add a Kubernetes/service-account authentication method and the visible trajectory has inspected token/OIDC code, auth config, proto definitions, and registration wiring. Do not apply this as a blanket requirement when the codebase clearly requires every auth method to expose a distinct runtime service endpoint, when tests or documentation explicitly demand live token validation/TokenReview behavior, or when the agent is still doing only initial repository reconnaissance with no design or edits.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics often demanded a complete Kubernetes auth server, HTTP/gRPC service, middleware registration, Kubernetes API TokenReview validation, RBAC mapping, and tests. That can be a tempting proxy because existing token and OIDC methods have method-specific packages, but it is too broad when the visible architecture shows that authentication methods are also governed by a central config/protobuf method registry and public method listing. In these cases, the discriminative evidence is whether the agent follows the repository’s method declaration contract: add the new method enum and regenerated artifacts, add the method to the central auth configuration collection, implement the method info/defaulting hooks consistently with the generic method abstraction, preserve existing cleanup/default validation behavior, and add config examples/fixtures. A better rubric should not reward inventing new unauthenticated RPC endpoints or server registration unless the trajectory has concrete evidence that such a runtime endpoint is required. It should penalize plans or edits that add new services while leaving generated proto files stale, bypassing generic method defaults, breaking existing auth config validation, or omitting the method from the public/listed method metadata path.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Registry-Centric Auth Method Integration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the new authentication method is being integrated through the repository’s existing method registry contract before adding extra runtime surfaces. Strong evidence includes locating the central auth method enum and generated artifacts, updating or planning updates to generated code after proto changes, adding the new method to the central authentication methods configuration/listing, implementing method metadata/default hooks consistently with the existing generic auth-method abstraction, preserving cleanup/default validation behavior, and adding representative configuration fixtures or examples. The judge should prefer this evidence over speculative creation of a new server package, gateway route, or token-validation endpoint unless the visible code or task-specific tests clearly require such a service.

metadata.environment: Go repository with protobuf-generated auth APIs and centralized authentication configuration
key_visible_evidence: central enum or type that identifies auth methods
generated protobuf or API artifacts affected by enum changes
generic auth-method config wrapper or method-info provider pattern
public/listed authentication method metadata path
defaulting, cleanup, and validation behavior for enabled methods
configuration fixtures/examples for auth methods
avoid_as_primary_evidence: new auth server package without proof it is required
new gateway routes or RPC services invented from analogy alone
manual token/JWT/TokenReview validation when the visible integration contract is still incomplete
middleware registration before method metadata/config integration is correct

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent has identified the repository’s central auth method registry/config/proto contract; it focuses on unrelated files or guesses at a standalone implementation.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the agent notices existing auth methods or the proto enum but has not connected the new method to generated artifacts, central config/listing, defaults, or fixtures.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent identifies the enum and central config/listing path and plans or starts updates there, but leaves important registry-contract details uncertain, such as generated artifacts, default hooks, cleanup validation, or config examples.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory updates or clearly plans the enum/generated artifacts, central method configuration/listing, method metadata, and default/cleanup behavior consistently, with only minor omissions such as incomplete fixtures or formatting checks.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory fully follows the existing registry contract, keeps generated artifacts synchronized, preserves validation/default semantics, adds representative config coverage, and avoids inventing unnecessary service/middleware surfaces unless justified by visible repository requirements.

experiences.title: End-to-End Date Deprecation Plumbing, Not Alias Validation Alone
experiences.description: Retrieve when an Ansible/module-utils task adds date-based deprecation support and the trajectory is focused on deprecated_aliases schema or validation. The useful rubric should check whether date metadata is propagated through runtime warnings and display, not just whether version/date validation rules exist.
experiences.context: Applies in an Ansible-style Python repository when the task explicitly names module utilities, validate-modules/static validation, Display, and AnsibleModule behavior for supporting date-based deprecations. It is especially relevant once the trajectory has discovered deprecated_aliases handling, option deprecation metadata such as removed_in_version/removed_at_date, warning accumulation, and display formatting, or has started editing validation/schema code. It is less useful during the very earliest reconnaissance before the runtime warning/display path is visible, and it should not be reduced to a generic validation criterion when the task is only about static schema checks. Boundaries: date support must preserve version-based behavior, distinguish alias-entry keys such as version/date from option-level removal-date metadata, and treat DateTime/datetime objects as first-class date values rather than merely parsing or overloading strings.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics often asked only whether deprecated_aliases entries require exactly one of version/date and reject bad date types. That criterion is partially relevant because the task explicitly calls out those internal errors, but it is not discriminative by itself: trajectories can implement those checks while still failing the feature by storing dates in the old version field, validating strings instead of DateTime objects, not extending the deprecation helper signature, not preserving date in returned deprecation messages, not updating display formatting, or not supporting option-level removed_at_date. A better rubric should focus on end-to-end date deprecation plumbing across the runtime module path, warning/deprecation accumulation, output/display formatting, static validation, and parity paths when present. It should reward visible evidence that date is passed as a separate field/argument from the source spec through warning storage to user-facing messages, and that existing version-only behavior remains compatible. Avoid the tempting proxy of checking only schema changes, exact-one validation, or regex YYYY-MM-DD parsing; those may look aligned with the error strings but miss the core feature contract. Prioritize visible trajectory evidence such as inspected or edited runtime deprecate wrappers, warning accumulator payload shape, parameter deprecation listing, display formatter signature/message text, DateTime/datetime type checks, targeted tests showing date appears as date rather than version, and absence of unresolved broad-edit corruption or failing regression tests.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Date Deprecation Propagation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show progress toward implementing date-based deprecations as a first-class runtime and validation feature, not merely as deprecated_aliases schema validation. Strong evidence includes preserving version-based deprecations while adding a separate date path for alias and option deprecations; enforcing exactly one of version/date for deprecated alias entries with the specified internal-error semantics; validating date values as DateTime/datetime objects rather than accepting arbitrary strings or regex-only dates; extending runtime deprecation helpers and warning/deprecation storage to carry date separately from version; ensuring returned deprecation data and user-facing display formatting mention removal after a date; updating static validate-modules checks consistently; and considering parallel module utility implementations when the repository has them. The criterion should penalize implementations that overload the version field with dates, only patch schema/static validation, skip display/warning plumbing, leave date-based parameter deprecations unsupported, or introduce unresolved test failures/global warning-state regressions.

required_visible_evidence: runtime deprecation API or wrapper accepts and forwards a separate date value
warning/deprecation accumulator stores date separately from version while preserving existing version entries
display or user-facing formatter has date-specific message behavior
option-level removal date metadata is handled in the same path that currently handles removal version metadata
deprecated_aliases validation enforces missing/both/type errors with DateTime/datetime semantics
static validation/schema is updated without replacing runtime behavior
tests or manual checks demonstrate date-based deprecations in emitted output and unchanged version-based behavior
common_false_proxies: only adding optional date to schema
checking exactly-one version/date but still passing date as version
validating YYYY-MM-DD strings instead of DateTime/datetime objects
updating deprecated_aliases while ignoring option-level date deprecation
omitting display/warning formatter changes

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of date-based deprecation support beyond exploratory searches, or changes are absent/irrelevant.
scale.2: Only a narrow static/schema or alias-validation change is visible; date is not propagated through runtime warnings/display, or date is treated as a version/string substitute.
scale.3: Validation and some runtime handling are attempted, but important pieces such as separate date storage, display formatting, option-level date deprecations, compatibility, or tests remain missing or uncertain.
scale.4: Strong end-to-end implementation evidence covers validation, runtime propagation, warning storage, and at least some display/output behavior, with mostly preserved version compatibility and targeted tests.
scale.5: Comprehensive visible evidence shows first-class date deprecation support across validation, runtime module behavior, warning/deprecation payloads, user-facing display, option and alias deprecations, relevant parity paths, and regression tests confirming both date and version behavior.

experiences.title: Prefer SSH classification when prefixed metadata is already parsed downstream
experiences.description: Retrieve when a protocol multiplexer rejects an internal SSH metadata prefix, but the trajectory has found an existing downstream SSH connection wrapper that already parses that prefix and updates client metadata.
experiences.context: Applies in Go networking/multiplexer tasks where an incoming stream starts with an application-specific prefix plus JSON metadata before the real SSH stream. The key matching condition is visible trajectory evidence that protocol detection happens before SSH handling and currently only recognizes ordinary SSH bytes, while a later SSH-layer wrapper already knows how to consume the prefix, unmarshal the JSON payload, and update the remote/client address. In this situation, the most discriminative rubric is not generic JSON parsing in the multiplexer; it is whether the agent preserves the existing downstream parser by routing the prefixed stream as SSH without consuming the bytes. Do not apply this guidance if the trajectory has not found any existing downstream parser, if the accepted multiplexer connection itself must expose the parsed address before any SSH read occurs, or if the task explicitly requires the multiplexer layer—not the SSH server wrapper—to own payload parsing.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics often demanded that the multiplexer detect the prefix, parse the JSON payload, extract ClientAddr, and override RemoteAddr itself. That wording matched the task statement superficially but was too broad for trajectories that had already discovered an existing SSH-server connection wrapper parsing the same prefix and setting the client address. In those contexts, a better rubric should focus on the semantic boundary: the multiplexer’s job is to classify the prefixed stream as SSH using the shared prefix definition, peek enough bytes to avoid false positives, and leave the prefix/payload buffered for the existing SSH parser. The judge should prioritize visible evidence that the agent identified the pre-existing parser, avoided duplicating or consuming the handshake in the multiplexer, and kept normal SSH/TLS/HTTP/PROXY behavior intact. A tempting but wrong criterion is to require a new protocol enum, separate routing branch, or mux-level JSON/RemoteAddr override merely because the task mentions ClientAddr; that can break stream ownership, double-consume the payload, or bypass the established parser. If the visible trajectory instead shows no downstream parser or tests require RemoteAddr on the mux wrapper before SSH reads, then a parsing-and-RemoteAddr rubric may be appropriate, but it should explicitly account for preserving unread SSH bytes.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Classifies prefixed metadata streams as SSH without stealing downstream parsing
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should converge on a minimal, layer-correct fix: recognize the internal metadata prefix during protocol detection as an SSH connection, using the existing shared prefix constant or equivalent source of truth; peek enough bytes to confirm the full prefix while preserving all buffered bytes; route the connection through the normal SSH listener path; and rely on the already-identified SSH-layer wrapper to parse the JSON payload and update the remote/client address. Strong evidence includes explicit discussion that the prefix is not HAProxy PROXY protocol, that downstream SSH code already consumes the NUL-terminated JSON payload and handles ClientAddr, and that tests or reasoning cover both prefixed and ordinary SSH behavior without regressing other protocol classifications.

required_visible_evidence: The trajectory has identified an earlier protocol detector that rejects non-SSH initial bytes.
The trajectory has identified a later SSH-layer parser for the same prefix and JSON payload.
The intended implementation preserves buffered bytes rather than consuming the metadata in the detector.
avoid_overrequiring: Do not require mux-level JSON parsing when an existing SSH wrapper already owns that parsing.
Do not reward a distinct protocol path unless it is clearly routed back to SSH and preserves stream semantics.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent connects the prefix problem to SSH protocol classification; it may remain in unrelated files, confuse the prefix with another proxy protocol, or damage existing protocol handling.
scale.2: Some evidence of recognizing the prefix, but the plan or edits are incomplete, malformed, or ignore the existing downstream parser and stream-preservation concerns.
scale.3: Moderate progress: the agent identifies the multiplexer detector and the prefix, but its criterion or implementation still ambiguously mixes classification with mux-level payload parsing or lacks clear preservation of downstream parsing behavior.
scale.4: Strong progress: the agent plans or implements prefix recognition as SSH using careful peeking and normal SSH routing, while acknowledging existing downstream ClientAddr parsing and avoiding unnecessary duplicate parsing.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory cleanly implements or validates additive SSH classification for the full prefix, uses the shared prefix definition, preserves buffered bytes for the SSH wrapper, and checks prefixed SSH plus normal protocol regression cases.

experiences.title: Do not reward superficial interface satisfaction at legacy-to-modern adapter boundaries
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go trajectory fixes a runtime interface assertion failure on a wrapper/multiplexer type by adding the missing method, especially where old and new event/logging interfaces coexist.
experiences.context: Applies in Go codebases with structural interfaces and adapter or fan-out types, where a startup error says a concrete wrapper does not satisfy a newer interface while the wrapper was constructed from values typed as an older interface. The misleading case is a trajectory that identifies the missing method and adds it to the wrapper, but implements it by best-effort type assertions against children and silently ignores children that do not implement the newer interface. The original interface-completeness idea is still appropriate when the type is a leaf implementation or when all delegated dependencies are already guaranteed to satisfy the full contract. It is insufficient when construction sites accept legacy-only implementations, when an existing modern fan-out abstraction already exists, or when correctness requires changing constructors/callers so non-compliant children are rejected or adapted rather than skipped.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics rewarded the agent for noticing that the wrapper lacked the method required by the newer interface. That observation was useful but too shallow: merely adding the method can make the type assertion pass while dropping events for any legacy-only child logger. In this setting, a better rubric should evaluate whether the trajectory checks the whole configuration path: how the wrapper is constructed, which concrete child loggers are included, whether any child is legacy-only, whether an existing modern multiplexer/adapter should be reused, and whether constructor/caller signatures propagate errors when a child cannot satisfy the modern contract. Avoid the tempting criterion that 'the fix must add the missing method with the exact signature' as the main success signal. Instead prioritize visible evidence that the agent prevents silent partial fan-out, adapts legacy stdout/writer-style logs through a proper modern emitter, validates children before creating the composite, and updates service initialization to handle the new construction contract.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat a wrapper's interface assertion failure as solved merely by adding the missing method, while leaving the wrapper constructed from older-interface children and forwarding only to children that happen to satisfy the newer interface. This flaw is especially important when visible code shows a legacy/new API split, a composite log/emitter type, child implementations that may be legacy-only, or an existing modern fan-out abstraction. The key issue is silent loss of behavior after startup validation passes, not just compile-time method presence.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial Wrapper Interface Fix

observable_cues: runtime error from a failed type assertion to an interface
wrapper or multiplexer type constructed from values typed as an older interface
newer interface has a missing method with similar legacy counterpart
proposed method delegates via child type assertions and skips non-matching children
little or no inspection of construction sites, concrete child implementations, or existing modern adapter/fan-out types
better_evidence: verifies every child in the composite satisfies or is adapted to the newer contract
uses or mirrors the existing modern fan-out abstraction rather than best-effort skipping
changes constructor/caller error handling when non-compliant children are possible
preserves audit/logging behavior instead of only satisfying startup type checks

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory validates or adapts all delegated children, updates construction/caller paths as needed, and avoids silent skipping.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory initially focuses on the missing method but also investigates child implementations and construction paths before deciding on a complete adapter strategy.
scale.3: Equivalent mixed behavior: the trajectory identifies the missing method and some delegation pattern, but it is unclear whether non-compliant children are impossible or whether skipped children would lose required behavior.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory plans or implements the missing method with best-effort child type assertions and no visible guarantee that all wrapped children implement the newer interface.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory confidently treats method presence/type assertion satisfaction as the complete fix despite visible legacy-only child implementations or an existing modern multiplexer/adapter path that should be used.

experiences.title: End-to-End Trusted Proxy Login Bootstrap
experiences.description: Use when a web app task asks for reverse-proxy/header-based auto-login to avoid a second browser login, especially in a Go server plus client-side UI with existing token/session auth.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories implementing optional trusted reverse-proxy authentication where the task requires a configurable username header and proxy IP allowlist, and the app already has a normal login/token flow. It is most useful once the agent has inspected or edited config, auth middleware, route wiring, login bootstrap, or client auth storage. It may be premature during pure repository exploration, and it is less relevant for tasks that only ask to protect backend API endpoints or where existing server middleware automatically establishes the browser session before the UI login screen appears.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics correctly identified the high-level contract: only trusted proxy requests may map a header username to a Navidrome user and normal login must remain intact. However, broad wording can over-credit patches that merely add config fields or an API middleware. For this task, the discriminating evidence is whether the reverse-proxy-authenticated browser is actually bootstrapped into the same session/token state as a successful normal login before the UI prompts for credentials. A better rubric should require visible integration with the initial UI/app login path or equivalent client-visible token delivery, plus user lookup and token/session payload creation compatible with existing auth. It should also check that the proxy allowlist validates the actual connecting proxy address, not blindly trusts spoofable forwarding headers from the request being authenticated. Avoid making default-user or auto-create behavior the main criterion unless the trajectory explicitly commits to that design; mapping the configured header to an existing user is often the core safe behavior. Also avoid treating build success or adding a middleware before the API authenticator as sufficient: middleware order, request-vs-response header use, client storage/bootstrap, and fallbacks for untrusted/missing headers are the important observable cues.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Browser Session Bootstrap for Trusted Proxy Auth
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement reverse-proxy auto-login end to end: expose safe configuration for the username header and trusted proxy IP/CIDR allowlist; only trust the header when the actual peer/proxy address is allowed; resolve the header value to an existing Navidrome user; create the same token/session payload used by normal login, including any client-required API/subsystem tokens; deliver that payload through the initial UI/app bootstrap or an equivalent path so the browser avoids the login screen; and preserve normal login behavior when the feature is disabled, the proxy is untrusted, the header is absent, or the user is unknown.

required_evidence: configuration fields/defaults for header name and trusted proxy addresses with feature disabled or fail-closed unless explicitly configured
allowlist check based on direct peer/proxy address or a demonstrably trusted real-IP mechanism, not unauthenticated client-supplied forwarding headers alone
case-insensitive lookup or equivalent mapping of proxy username to an existing application user
reuse of existing auth token/session creation and user context semantics
client-visible bootstrap that prevents the browser login prompt, not only backend API request authentication
normal authentication path remains available for disabled, untrusted, missing-header, and unknown-user cases
common_false_positives: only adding config fields and defaults
only adding middleware to protected API routes
setting a response header without making the UI/client consume and persist the token
placing proxy auth after the auth middleware it is supposed to bypass
trusting X-Forwarded-For or X-Real-IP from arbitrary clients as the whitelist subject
breaking unrelated auth routes or subpackages while adding proxy support

scale.1: No meaningful proxy-login implementation is visible, or changes are broken/unrelated to the existing auth flow.
scale.2: Some configuration or partial middleware exists, but there is little evidence of safe allowlist enforcement, user mapping, or usable session/token integration.
scale.3: Implements a backend trusted-header path for existing users with some token/context integration, but the browser login bootstrap, middleware ordering, or security boundary remains incomplete or ambiguous.
scale.4: Strong implementation of configured header, trusted proxy allowlist, existing-user lookup, and existing token/session integration, with normal-login fallback; only minor uncertainty remains around client bootstrap details or edge-case validation.
scale.5: Complete visible end-to-end solution: safe opt-in config, fail-closed actual-proxy allowlist, existing-user mapping, normal-login-equivalent token/session payload, initial UI/client bootstrap that avoids the second login, preserved fallback behavior, and targeted validation of trusted/untrusted cases.

experiences.title: Atomic bytes-like handling for iterable buffer inputs
experiences.description: Use when a Django/Python HTTP response task concerns `memoryview` or another buffer-like object being converted incorrectly because response content logic stringifies it or treats it as a generic iterable.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django repository when the task asks for `HttpResponse(memoryview(...)).content` or equivalent binary response content to return the underlying bytes. It is most useful after the trajectory has located the response content conversion path, such as a shared bytes conversion helper and/or a content setter that consumes generic iterables. It remains relevant when visible evidence shows `memoryview` is iterable and may yield integers, causing outputs like concatenated decimal byte values, or falls through to `str(value).encode(...)`, causing object-representation bytes. Do not apply broadly to unrelated response bugs, header handling, charset-only issues, database retrieval code, or tasks where the object is genuinely intended to be streamed/iterated chunk by chunk. If the agent has only begun exploring and has not yet inspected content conversion or reproduced the type behavior, this criterion may be premature as a high-confidence judgment but can still guide what evidence to seek.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged whether the trajectory treated `memoryview` as atomic bytes-like response content. They were discriminative because the visible trajectory repeatedly exposed the real compatibility boundary: `memoryview` is not a `bytes` instance, is iterable, and either falls through to string conversion or is consumed as integers before byte conversion sees the original object. A strong rubric should therefore focus on observable semantic behavior: `HttpResponse(memoryview(b'...')).content` must equal the underlying bytes; conversion should use `bytes(value)` or equivalent; existing `str`, `bytes`, and legitimate iterable chunk behavior must not be broken; and the agent should recognize that changing only a fallback conversion helper may be insufficient if an earlier iterable branch consumes the object. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as merely adding a special case somewhere, only checking `make_bytes(memoryview)` directly, over-requiring unrelated support for every buffer type, or making streaming response behavior the main success condition unless the trajectory/task explicitly covers streaming. Prioritize evidence from reproduction output, inspection of the conversion helper and content setter, checks of `hasattr(memoryview, '__iter__')`/integer iteration, and validation through actual `HttpResponse` construction or content assignment rather than isolated helper calls.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Memoryview is handled as atomic bytes-like response content
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates progress toward making `HttpResponse` convert a `memoryview` to its underlying bytes rather than stringifying it or consuming it as an iterable of integer byte values, while preserving existing behavior for strings, bytes, and legitimate iterable response chunks. Strong evidence includes locating the shared response-byte conversion path, identifying any generic iterable branch that intercepts `memoryview`, using `bytes(value)` or an equivalent raw-byte conversion for `memoryview`, and validating through actual `HttpResponse(memoryview(...)).content` or content assignment rather than only through isolated helper calls.

metadata.environment: Python Django HTTP response implementation
key_observable_inputs: response conversion helper handles bytes/str and has a generic fallback
content setter or constructor may consume generic iterables
manual output shows object representation bytes or concatenated integer byte strings
metadata.desired_semantics: Treat `memoryview` as scalar bytes-like content and return the underlying bytes.
regression_boundaries: strings are still encoded with the response charset
lists/generators of valid chunks are still consumed as iterable content
avoid_overreach: do not require unrelated database-layer changes
do not treat streaming support as central unless explicitly investigated
do not accept helper-only validation if constructor/content assignment still iterates the memoryview

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses `memoryview` byte semantics; it may inspect unrelated files, focus on database behavior, or leave `memoryview` subject to stringification/generic fallback.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory suspects the bytes conversion helper or mentions converting `memoryview` to bytes, but has not accounted for actual `HttpResponse` construction/content assignment or the possibility that `memoryview` is consumed as an iterable.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory locates the relevant conversion path and proposes or applies raw-byte conversion for `memoryview`, but validation is incomplete or it remains unclear whether the generic iterable branch still intercepts `memoryview`.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory identifies both raw-byte conversion and atomic treatment relative to iterable handling, and shows `HttpResponse(memoryview(...)).content` producing the underlying bytes while checking existing bytes/string behavior.
scale.5: Very strong evidence: the trajectory clearly diagnoses the failure mode, implements or plans the fix at the correct response conversion boundary, prevents `memoryview` from being treated as integer-yielding iterable content where applicable, and validates memoryview construction/content assignment plus representative regressions for bytes, strings, and iterable chunks.

experiences.title: Role and Metadata Robustness as a Separate ansible-doc Criterion
experiences.description: Retrieve when an ansible-doc-style task includes both terminal formatting and explicit robustness requirements for role docs/listing, metadata-only roles, doc fragments, or resolved plugin identity.
experiences.context: Applies in an Ansible-like CLI documentation generator where the task is broader than visual styling: role listing/detail output must remain useful when role metadata or argument specs are absent, malformed, or metadata-only; summaries should use available Galaxy/metadata descriptions; documentation fragments may be specified as comma-separated strings; and plugin display should use resolved fully-qualified identity. This criterion is most useful after the trajectory has inspected or modified the documentation/role loading paths, run role-list/detail examples, or spent substantial effort on styling without addressing role/data robustness. It is less applicable for tasks limited only to cosmetic terminal output, for very early exploration before any implementation direction is visible, or when the trajectory is exclusively working on unrelated parser/display infrastructure with no evidence about docs/roles/fragment handling yet.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics were useful because they separated a critical acceptance area from the more obvious ANSI/color formatting work. In these trajectories, visible progress on colored section headers or option names did not imply correctness: the task also required role discovery/listing/detail behavior to survive metadata-only roles, missing or malformed argspecs, doc-fragment strings, and resolved plugin naming. A better rubric should focus on observable evidence that the agent has treated these as first-class data-loading and display contracts: it inspects role metadata and argspec loading separately, tests role listing and role detail commands against roles with only metadata and roles with argument specs, preserves continuation/error handling, parses comma-separated fragment declarations, and uses loader resolution context for displayed plugin names. It should not over-credit manual color smoke tests, raw ANSI helper additions, repeated greps for color constants, or partial role edits that still produce empty role output. Also avoid requiring one exact implementation shape; judge by the behavior the trajectory demonstrates or the code paths it plausibly updates and validates. Prioritize visible evidence such as role-list/doc commands showing actual rows/docs for metadata-only roles, explicit fallback from argspec descriptions to metadata summaries, safe handling of absent/malformed files without aborting the whole listing, fragment parsing that splits and trims string lists, and plugin identity derived from resolution context rather than the user-entered alias.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Role Metadata and Fragment Robustness
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should make clear progress toward robust documentation behavior beyond cosmetic terminal styling: role listing and role detail output should work for roles with argument specs, roles with only metadata, and roles with missing or malformed metadata/spec files; available metadata or Galaxy summaries should be surfaced rather than silently dropping the role; failures should be skipped or reported without aborting unrelated entries; comma-separated documentation-fragment declarations should be split and trimmed like list declarations; and displayed plugin identity should come from the resolved loader context. Credit only evidence visible in the trajectory, such as inspected/modified role loading and summary construction, fragment parsing or loader-context handling, and targeted role/list/detail validation. Do not treat colored headers, option styling, or generic plugin-doc smoke tests alone as satisfying this criterion.

metadata.environment: Ansible-like CLI documentation generator with text, JSON, plugin, and role documentation modes
observable_evidence: role listing/detail commands or tests for metadata-only and argspec-backed roles
fallback from missing argument specs to metadata or Galaxy summary fields
graceful continuation on missing or malformed role files
string documentation fragments split on commas and stripped
plugin names displayed from resolved loader context
machine-readable output paths not polluted with terminal styling
non_evidence: role commands that still show no role rows or docs
hard-coded behavior tied to a single fixture

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of role/data robustness work; trajectory is only exploring, repeating unrelated searches, or making cosmetic styling changes while role docs/listing, fragment strings, and resolved identity remain unaddressed.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the agent mentions role robustness or inspects relevant paths, but implements little or validates only plugin/color output; role commands may still be empty or untested.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory partially modifies or tests role metadata/argspec handling, but coverage is incomplete, fragile, or lacks proof for metadata-only roles, malformed/missing files, comma-separated fragments, or resolved identity.
scale.4: Strong evidence: role listing/detail behavior is deliberately implemented and validated for multiple role metadata/spec combinations, with graceful continuation and useful summaries; at least one of fragment parsing or resolved identity is also addressed.
scale.5: Comprehensive evidence: the trajectory covers role listing and detailed docs end-to-end for argspec-backed, metadata-only, missing, and malformed cases; preserves JSON/plain output boundaries; parses comma-separated fragments robustly; uses resolved plugin identity; and validates these behaviors with targeted commands or tests.

experiences.title: End-to-End Optional Config Versioning Contract
experiences.description: Use when a Go/Viper configuration-loading task adds a new optional top-level config version field that must be accepted, defaulted, schema-documented, and rejected when unsupported.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go repository where runtime configuration is loaded through a central loader and schema files are maintained separately for YAML/editor validation. The task explicitly requires an optional top-level version-like field, a supported-version set, backward compatibility when the field is absent, and a clear runtime error for unsupported values. This is most useful once the trajectory has identified the config struct/load path, schema files, or tests, and especially during implementation review. It is less applicable to purely documentation/schema-only tasks, to early repository exploration before the agent has enough evidence about the loading pipeline, or to unrelated config additions that do not require runtime validation/default semantics.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster treated the feature as an end-to-end loading contract, not merely as a schema edit. They asked whether the agent added a top-level scalar version field, ensured the loader reads it, defaulted missing configs to the supported version, rejected unsupported values with a clear error, kept JSON/CUE schemas consistent, and added tests for missing/valid/invalid cases. This focus is appropriate because visible trajectories repeatedly showed partial work that looked plausible—adding a struct field, editing schemas, or defining a validate method—but still left important gaps such as no tests, schema-only implementation, validation not wired into the actual load path, defaulting not represented in the loaded config, or syntax/control-flow damage from ad hoc edits. A better rubric should prioritize observable evidence that runtime loading enforces the contract after unmarshalling and before returning success, and that validation is actually reachable in the existing loader pattern. Avoid the tempting narrower criterion that only checks whether both schema files mention the new field; schema synchronization matters, but by itself it does not prove unsupported configs are rejected during loading or that old configs remain compatible. Also avoid rewarding a root validate method unless the trajectory shows it is invoked by the loader, since reflection-based loaders may only collect validators from sub-config fields. The strongest visible evidence includes: the agent understands the loader order, updates the root config model with the correct scalar shape, implements supported-version validation/defaulting in the actual load path, covers missing/supported/unsupported fixtures or test cases, keeps schemas aligned, and runs formatting/tests after edits.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Optional Config Versioning
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluate whether the trajectory is progressing toward a complete optional configuration versioning implementation: a top-level scalar version value is decoded by the runtime config loader, absent values remain backward compatible and become the supported default, unsupported present values are rejected with a clear load-time error, schema definitions are updated consistently, and tests exercise missing, supported, and unsupported versions. Give most credit for evidence that validation/defaulting is wired into the actual loading path and verified, not just for adding a field or editing schema text.

runtime_loader_contract: top-level scalar config field is added to the root config model
loader reads the field during normal config unmarshal/decode
missing field is accepted and represented as the supported default
unsupported present values fail during config loading with a clear error
validation is reachable in the existing loader flow
schema_contract: JSON schema includes the optional top-level version property
CUE or source schema includes the same optional version property
schemas constrain or document the currently supported value and default
verification_contract: tests or fixtures cover missing version
tests or fixtures cover supported version
tests or fixtures cover unsupported version
format/build/test commands are run or planned after edits
anti_patterns: schema-only update with no runtime validation
struct field only with no default/rejection behavior
validate method added but not invoked by the loader
nested config shape when the file format requires a scalar value
syntax/control-flow corruption from line-based edits

scale.1: The trajectory has not connected the task to the actual config loading path or schema/test locations, or is pursuing an incompatible config shape.
scale.2: The trajectory identifies some relevant files or adds only a superficial field/schema mention, but lacks evidence of load-time validation/defaulting and test coverage.
scale.3: The trajectory has a plausible partial implementation plan or edits for the root field plus either schema updates or validation, but key contract pieces are missing or validation reachability is uncertain.
scale.4: The trajectory shows strong implementation evidence for runtime read/default/reject behavior and schema synchronization, with at least planned or partial tests for the three required scenarios.
scale.5: The trajectory demonstrates a coherent, verified implementation: correct top-level scalar field, defaulting for absence, reachable unsupported-version rejection, synchronized schemas, targeted tests for missing/supported/unsupported versions, and successful formatting/build/test feedback.

experiences.title: Safe Identifier Handling in Sessions Refresh
