experiences.description: Use when a Matrix/React TypeScript task explicitly includes fragile sessions/devices loading around startup or auth changes, and the trajectory has inspected or edited the sessions device-refresh hook where user/device IDs may be null.
experiences.context: Applies in React/TypeScript Matrix client codebases with a My sessions/devices view backed by a hook or refresh function that calls MatrixClient device APIs and uses current user/device identifiers. It is most useful once the trajectory has visible evidence of the relevant refresh path, such as a device hook returning currentDeviceId/refreshDevices, calls to getUserId/getDeviceId, a throw on missing userId, or event handlers comparing updated users to a nullable userId. It may be premature during broad repository exploration before the sessions refresh code is located, and it is not sufficient as the only rubric for multi-part tasks that also require account-data pruning, voice-broadcast offline blocking, or chunk sequencing. Do not apply it to unrelated device deletion-only flows unless the sessions refresh robustness requirement is present.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics correctly targeted a discriminative subproblem: the task explicitly required the sessions/devices screen to refresh reliably when identifiers are temporarily missing. The visible cue was the sessions hook reading MatrixClient user/device IDs and using them in refresh logic, including paths that throw or compare against possibly missing values. This criterion aligned with poor trajectories because many agents either only noticed the issue, added superficial guards, or introduced unsafe fixes such as returning from a React hook before all hooks run, converting missing IDs to an empty string, or guarding only an event callback while leaving refreshDevices able to throw. A better rubric should not merely ask whether the agent “understands” safe identifiers; it should judge whether the trajectory is moving toward a valid React-safe implementation that preserves hook ordering and state shape, avoids throwing on absent user/device IDs, uses nullable/safe identifiers consistently in refresh and device-update callbacks, and keeps loading/error state coherent so a later refresh can succeed. Avoid the tempting proxy of crediting any client-info deletion or sign-out cleanup as a sessions-loading robustness fix; those address stale metadata, not missing-ID refresh failures. Prioritize evidence in visible commands/edits around the sessions hook: calls to getUserId/getDeviceId or safe alternatives, refreshDevices behavior on missing IDs, CryptoEvent.DevicesUpdated handling, currentDeviceId return typing/fallbacks, and whether any edit violates React hook rules or masks null IDs with bogus strings.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Robust Sessions Refresh Identifiers
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a concrete, React-safe plan or implementation for the sessions/devices refresh path to handle temporarily missing Matrix user/device identifiers without throwing or producing bogus session state. Strong evidence includes locating the device-refresh hook, recognizing nullable user/device IDs as the failure source, changing refresh and device-update callbacks to no-op or defer safely when IDs are absent, preserving hook ordering and return-shape/type correctness, and using real safe identifiers rather than empty-string placeholders. The criterion should be judged from visible trajectory evidence in the sessions/devices code, not from unrelated device deletion or voice-broadcast changes.

metadata.environment: React TypeScript Matrix client
metadata.relevant_area: sessions/devices view refresh hook or equivalent device-list loader
key_visible_evidence: refresh function behavior when userId/deviceId is null or undefined
current device ID returned to UI without fake empty identifier
device-updated event handler guards nullable userId before includes/comparison
React hook ordering preserved; no conditional early return before hooks
loading/error state remains coherent and later refresh can retry
avoid_credit_for: client-information account-data cleanup alone
voice-broadcast offline checks
guards in unrelated deletion flows that do not affect sessions refresh
masking missing identifiers with empty strings

scale.1: No visible progress on sessions refresh identifier safety, or the trajectory focuses only on unrelated cleanup/broadcast code while the refresh path can still throw on missing IDs.
scale.2: Weak progress: the trajectory identifies the relevant sessions hook or nullable identifier concern but has no concrete fix, or adds a narrow guard that leaves refreshDevices or returned identifiers unsafe.
scale.3: Moderate progress: the trajectory addresses one obvious missing-user/device path in the refresh logic while preserving most existing behavior, but evidence is incomplete around event callbacks, currentDeviceId handling, retry/loading state, or React hook safety.
scale.4: Strong progress: the trajectory implements or clearly plans consistent safe handling for missing user/device IDs across refresh and device-update paths, avoids throwing, and preserves hook structure and return types, with only minor uncertainty or validation gaps.
scale.5: Strongest progress: the trajectory fully and visibly hardens the sessions/devices refresh path using safe/null-aware identifiers, coherent loading/error retry semantics, guarded event handling, valid React hook ordering, and no bogus placeholder IDs, making the view reliable during startup/auth transitions.

experiences.title: Honor Explicit Timezone via Existing Resolution Helper
experiences.description: Use this when a Django ORM datetime function task asks an override to respect an explicit `tzinfo` argument, and the visible trajectory shows a shared timezone mixin/helper is being bypassed by direct current-timezone lookup.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django/Python codebase when the issue is narrowly about `TruncDate()` and `TruncTime()` or similar datetime expression subclasses that inherit timezone-handling behavior but override SQL generation. The criterion is most useful after the agent has inspected the datetime function implementation or applied a change, because the decisive evidence is whether both affected SQL-generation paths now route timezone resolution through the inherited helper. It is less applicable for unrelated timezone bugs, tasks requiring new timezone APIs, database-backend SQL changes, or trajectories that are still only exploring without visible evidence of how timezone names are computed.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic contract: an explicit `tzinfo` supplied to both date and time truncation/cast functions must override the global/current timezone, while the existing fallback behavior for no explicit timezone and disabled timezone support must remain intact. This was discriminative because the visible implementation already contained a helper on a timezone mixin that encodes exactly those branches, and the bug was caused by subclass `as_sql()` overrides bypassing it. A strong future rubric should therefore ask whether both affected override methods use the existing timezone-resolution path before passing the timezone name to backend date/time cast SQL. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as merely accepting a `tzinfo` parameter, adding ad hoc timezone conversion logic, changing only one of the two functions, or judging mainly by whether ad hoc tests ran successfully. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent identified the helper/mixin relationship, replaced direct current-timezone lookup in both affected SQL-generation paths, preserved backend cast calls and parameters, and understood fallback behavior rather than duplicating it manually.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Explicit tzinfo Routed Through Timezone Helper
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should make both affected datetime-to-date and datetime-to-time SQL conversion methods honor an explicitly supplied `tzinfo` by resolving the timezone through the existing mixin/helper method, rather than directly reading the current global timezone, while preserving the established behavior when no `tzinfo` is provided or timezone support is disabled.

metadata.environment: Django ORM datetime database functions in Python
metadata.target_behavior: explicit tzinfo overrides current/global timezone for both date and time conversion
metadata.expected_resolution_path: use inherited timezone-name helper that handles explicit tzinfo, current-timezone fallback, and disabled-timezone behavior
key_visible_evidence: agent inspects or describes the shared timezone helper/mixin
agent identifies both date and time conversion overrides as bypassing the helper
change routes both SQL conversion methods through the helper
backend date/time cast SQL calls and existing parameters are otherwise preserved
avoid_as_primary_evidence: only installing dependencies or attempting tests
only proving the constructor accepts tzinfo
manual timezone-name branching that duplicates helper behavior
fixing only one of the affected conversion methods

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses explicit `tzinfo`; it leaves direct current/global timezone lookup in the affected conversion path or pursues an unrelated timezone change.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the agent recognizes a timezone issue or changes timezone handling, but fixes only one affected path, relies on manual/ad hoc logic, or does not show that explicit `tzinfo` overrides the current timezone.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent identifies the helper/mixin and the bypass, and appears to route timezone resolution through it, but the visible work is incomplete, ambiguous for one affected method, or does not clearly preserve fallback behavior.
scale.4: Strong evidence: both affected date and time SQL conversion methods are visibly changed to use the existing timezone-resolution helper, with the surrounding backend cast behavior preserved; fallback behavior is at least implicitly maintained by using the helper.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory clearly diagnoses the helper bypass, updates both affected conversion methods to use the helper, explicitly notes preservation of current-timezone and disabled-timezone behavior, and provides relevant validation or inspection showing explicit `tzinfo` is the value used for SQL conversion.

experiences.title: Cond-Coupled Deadline Semantics for Resumable Connection Primitives
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go networking task asks for low-level buffering/deadline primitives for resilient or resumable connections and the trajectory is designing or implementing the deadline helper.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go codebase with connection-oriented utilities where the task requires a deadline helper that coordinates blocked readers/writers through a condition variable, alongside a byte staging buffer. It is most useful once the agent has inspected existing buffer/timeout code or started designing/adding a deadline primitive. It is also useful when the agent is repeatedly searching without implementing, because lack of any cond-coupled deadline design is decisive evidence of missing progress. Do not apply as the sole criterion for unrelated timeout wrappers, ordinary context deadlines, net.Conn SetDeadline passthroughs, or tasks where no shared condition-variable waiting is part of the requested contract. Be careful at very early reconnaissance: absence of code is weak evidence unless the trajectory is already stuck or choosing an incompatible standalone API.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster were useful because they targeted a semantic boundary that repeatedly separated plausible-looking work from correct connection-resumption primitives: the deadline helper must wake operations waiting on shared connection state, not merely expose an independent timer or channel API. The good part of those rubrics was emphasizing timeout/stop state, zero/past/future deadline transitions, and sync.Cond notification. The weaker versions were too prescriptive about a public Set/Clear/Wait API or a self-contained helper owning its own lock/condition; for this kind of task, the more important evidence is whether the deadline state is protected by the same lock as the connection/buffer state and broadcasts the caller-provided condition variable when a timeout occurs or when state changes require waiters to re-check. A better rubric should focus on cond-coupled deadline semantics: setting a future timer, clearing to a disabled non-timeout state, immediately timing out and broadcasting for past times, safely stopping/reusing an existing timer, marking timeout/stopped state under lock, and having the timer callback acquire the condition lock before updating state and broadcasting. Avoid rewarding tempting proxies such as the mere presence of a type named Deadline, use of time.After/time.Timer, exported Wait/WaitChan methods, tests that sleep, or no-op net.Conn deadline methods. Prioritize visible evidence in the trajectory: API shape that accepts or is paired with a sync.Cond/shared mutex, timer callback code that locks and broadcasts, explicit zero/past/future branches, safe replacement of existing timers without stale callbacks racing, and tests or reasoning that check wakeups and state transitions.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Shared-Condition Deadline Contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a deadline primitive suitable for connection-style blocking operations: deadline state is guarded by the same lock/condition variable used by waiting operations; setting a future deadline schedules a timer whose callback locks that condition, marks timeout, marks the timer stopped/reusable, and broadcasts; setting a zero deadline clears timeout without leaving waiters permanently blocked when state changes; setting a past deadline marks timeout immediately and broadcasts; replacing or stopping an existing timer handles Stop/Reset races so stale callbacks cannot later set timeout incorrectly. The criterion should judge semantic evidence rather than exact names or file placement.

required_visible_evidence: deadline state includes timeout and stopped/reusable timer state
deadline operations are tied to a sync.Cond or equivalent shared condition used by blocked operations
future, zero/cleared, and past deadline cases are handled distinctly
timer callback updates state while holding the condition lock and notifies waiters
existing timer replacement or cancellation is race-safe enough to prevent stale timeout transitions
common_false_positives: standalone Deadline type with Wait/WaitChan but no integration with shared connection condition state
sleep-based timer code that sets a boolean without condition-variable broadcast
no-op SetDeadline methods or context deadline checks unrelated to the helper
tests for time passing that do not verify wakeup/notification semantics

scale.1: No implemented or planned deadline helper, or only unrelated context/net.Conn deadline references with no condition-variable coordination.
scale.2: Mentions or sketches a deadline/timer helper but lacks clear shared-lock/sync.Cond integration or misses key zero/past/future behavior.
scale.3: Implements some deadline state and notification behavior, but the API is largely standalone or race-prone, with incomplete handling of clear/stop/replacement semantics.
scale.4: Shows a deadline helper paired with a condition variable, correct immediate and future timeout behavior, and broadcasts waiters, with only minor uncertainty around timer reuse or stale callback races.
scale.5: Clearly implements the cond-coupled deadline contract: lock-protected timeout/stopped state, zero clear, past immediate timeout, future timer callback that locks and broadcasts, and safe stop/reset/reuse behavior verified or reasoned about.

experiences.title: CUE/YAML Diagnostic Attribution, Not Surface Message Enrichment
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go CLI task asks to improve YAML validation diagnostics produced through CUE, especially when current output has generic messages, parent-node locations, or repeated line/column coordinates for distinct invalid keys.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories in a Go command-line repository where YAML files are validated against a CUE schema and the user-facing problem is diagnostic precision rather than simply accepting/rejecting input. It is most useful after the agent has inspected the validation/error-formatting path or reproduced failures involving multiple misspelled keys and at least one invalid value. The criterion is less useful for early repository navigation before any validation mechanism is identified, for tasks about changing schema validity rules rather than reporting, or for validators that do not expose structured source positions/messages. It should remain conditional on preserving both machine-readable JSON and text CLI behavior, because a patch that improves one local message can still be incomplete if it breaks output contracts or only handles one CUE error shape.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful rubric asked whether the trajectory would produce precise diagnostics: exact offending YAML field/value names and accurate file/line/column coordinates for each occurrence. That focus is correct because the decisive issue is mapping CUE validation failures back to the user's YAML source, not merely changing validation success/failure. However, future rubrics should be sharper than a broad “include the field path” criterion. They should reward evidence that the agent understands CUE error metadata boundaries: generic message APIs may omit the path; rendered/path metadata can identify the invalid field; position lists can contain both YAML and schema/parent locations; and the correct source position may differ between unknown-field errors and range/value errors. A tempting but weak proxy is accepting any patch that appends a path, iterates every input position, or hardcodes a single input-position index after one manual example. Another tempting proxy is focusing only on the command wrapper or only on text output. The better rubric should prioritize visible evidence that the agent reproduced duplicate coordinates with multiple invalid keys, inspected available CUE error path/position APIs, selected user-file coordinates robustly across unknown fields and invalid scalar values, verified distinct JSON/text output entries, preserved success/no-output and exit-code semantics, and removed scratch artifacts. It should penalize trajectories that keep generic `field not allowed`, duplicate parent coordinates, report schema/internal positions as user-file locations, emit multiple bogus errors for one validation failure, or rely on brittle one-case heuristics without validating both error types.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Robust YAML Validation Diagnostic Attribution
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show progress toward a validation-reporting fix that uses CUE/YAML error metadata to map each validation failure to the exact offending user YAML field or value, with accurate and non-duplicated file, line, and column coordinates, while preserving the existing JSON/text CLI output contract. Strong evidence includes reproducing multiple misspelled-key failures that originally share a parent location, identifying that generic CUE messages alone are insufficient, using path/rendered-error information to name the bad key or full path, choosing source positions in a way that handles both unknown-field and invalid-value errors, and validating both failure formats plus success behavior. The rubric should not give high credit for merely appending paths, blindly using all positions, hardcoding one position index for every error type, or changing validation/schema behavior instead of diagnostic attribution.

metadata.environment: Go CLI using CUE to validate YAML configuration and emit structured JSON/text diagnostics
primary_observable_evidence: manual or test reproduction with multiple invalid YAML keys showing whether coordinates are distinct
inspection or use of CUE error path/rendered message metadata instead of only generic message text
inspection or handling of multiple CUE source positions with attention to user YAML versus schema/parent locations
checks for both unknown fields and invalid scalar/range values
verification of JSON and text failure output plus success output semantics
common_false_positives: message-only improvement with unchanged repeated coordinates
coordinate-only change that still omits offending key names
emitting one error per raw position instead of one diagnostic per validation failure
hardcoded position selection demonstrated on only one error class
temporary repro/debug files or broken imports left in the patch

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent is addressing diagnostic attribution; it only navigates files, changes unrelated validation/schema behavior, or repeats failing commands without using the information.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the agent recognizes generic/repeated errors or adds superficial message/path text, but does not address accurate user-file coordinates across multiple errors or preserve output behavior.
scale.3: Moderate evidence comparable to the parent trajectory: the agent targets the validation error loop and improves either field naming or locations for a narrow example, but relies on a brittle heuristic, lacks coverage of both unknown-field and invalid-value cases, or does not verify both JSON and text formats.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the agent uses CUE error path and source-position metadata to produce field-specific messages and distinct user-file coordinates for repeated invalid keys, tests invalid values separately, and checks JSON/text outputs and success behavior, with only minor robustness or integration uncertainty remaining.
scale.5: Very strong evidence: the trajectory demonstrates a robust diagnostic contract across error types and formats, avoids schema/internal/parent locations, emits one clear diagnostic per failure, preserves CLI success/failure semantics, includes or updates relevant tests/repro cases, and leaves the workspace clean of debug artifacts.

experiences.title: Resolver-Level Upgrade Semantics for Installed Dependencies
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task adds an upgrade/update flag for package or collection installation where installed artifacts are currently skipped or preferred during dependency resolution.
experiences.context: Applies to Python CLI/package-management style tasks, especially Ansible Galaxy collection installation, where the visible trajectory has identified a flow from CLI parsing into an install function and then into a dependency resolver/provider. The key contextual cue is existing logic that filters already-installed requirements or passes installed artifacts as preferred candidates, plus task requirements to choose the latest compatible version, respect pre-release gating, update dependencies only as needed, and remain a no-op when already current. This guidance is most useful once the agent has inspected or begun editing install/resolution logic; it is less decisive during very early repository exploration and may be irrelevant for tasks that are purely documentation/help text or do not use a dependency resolver/preferred-candidate mechanism.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric pattern in these cases was to evaluate the actual upgrade semantics rather than superficial CLI plumbing. A trajectory that only adds `--upgrade`, threads a boolean into the install function, or stops filtering installed requirements is still likely incomplete if installed candidates remain blindly preferred, if all preferred candidates are removed causing unnecessary dependency reinstalls, or if the resolver/provider is not taught when an installed version should be kept versus replaced by a newer compatible candidate. A better criterion should focus on observable evidence that the upgrade flag is propagated through the whole resolution path and changes candidate ordering/selection at the resolver boundary: installed versions should satisfy constraints and be retained only when no newer compatible candidate exists; newer candidates should respect version constraints and pre-release settings; dependencies should be reconsidered only when resolution requires it; normal install and force behavior should not regress. Avoid tempting but weak criteria such as merely checking that the CLI option exists, that the code manually queries available versions somewhere, that tests were mechanically updated for a new parameter, or that all installed collections are removed from preferred candidates. Prioritize visible evidence in diffs or trajectory notes showing changes to install filtering, preferred-candidate construction, resolver builder signatures, provider candidate matching/order, and validation of no-op/pre-release/dependency behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Resolver-Aware Upgrade Behavior
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the new upgrade option is implemented as resolver-aware version selection, not merely as a CLI flag or forced reinstall. Strong evidence includes threading the option from collection-install CLI parsing through the install orchestration into dependency resolution/provider code; preserving pre-release gating through the existing pre-release flag; selecting the latest compatible candidate when an installed collection is older; keeping an installed candidate when it already satisfies constraints and no newer compatible version exists; and avoiding unnecessary dependency upgrades or reinstalls unless dependency constraints require them. The implementation should also preserve existing non-upgrade and force/force-with-dependencies semantics.

expected_visible_evidence: CLI option is collection-install scoped and read defensively where collection-only args may be absent
upgrade flag is passed from CLI to install function and onward to dependency-map/resolver construction
existing installed-requirement filtering is adjusted so upgrade can consider newer compatible versions
preferred installed candidates are not blindly selected ahead of newer compatible candidates during upgrade
resolver/provider candidate matching compares installed candidates against latest compatible matches before deciding to keep them
pre-release handling continues to depend on the existing pre-release option
dependency behavior is resolver-driven rather than unconditional reinstall of all installed dependencies
normal install without upgrade still skips already-satisfied installed collections
anti_patterns: only adding help text or a parsed flag
treating upgrade exactly like force
dropping all preferred installed candidates in a way that upgrades or reinstalls unrelated dependencies
checking only whether an installed version satisfies the requested constraint without checking whether a newer compatible version exists
manual version-query logic that bypasses existing resolver pre-release or dependency behavior

scale.1: No meaningful upgrade semantics are visible; the trajectory is limited to exploration, broken edits, or a CLI flag with no reliable propagation into install/resolution logic.
scale.2: Some plumbing or install-function changes are visible, but the resolver/provider still cannot reliably choose latest compatible versions or preserve no-op behavior.
scale.3: The trajectory changes installed filtering or preferred candidates and may pass an upgrade flag through part of the stack, but dependency handling, latest-versus-installed comparison, or pre-release preservation remains incomplete or ambiguous.
scale.4: The trajectory shows strong end-to-end handling through install and resolver layers, with mostly correct treatment of installed candidates, latest compatible versions, pre-release gating, and dependency constraints, though validation or edge cases may be incomplete.
scale.5: The trajectory provides complete resolver-aware upgrade support with clear propagation, correct candidate ordering/retention logic, preserved non-upgrade and force behavior, dependency upgrades only as required, pre-release correctness, and targeted validation of no-op and upgrade scenarios.

experiences.title: Do not canonize caller-side attr copying when the task points to a mutating widget contract
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django forms/widget bug is observed through a composite widget, but the issue statement explicitly identifies a lower-level widget mutating caller-provided attrs as the exceptional cause.
experiences.context: Applies in Django form rendering tasks involving mutable attrs dictionaries, CheckboxInput, and composite/repeated widgets such as SplitArrayWidget. The misleading pattern is a trajectory that reproduces the split-array rendering symptom and makes manual tests pass by copying attrs per child, while the task text itself emphasizes that CheckboxInput.get_context() is the only widget mutating attrs. In this setting, per-subwidget attr isolation may be a useful workaround or exploratory hypothesis, but it should not be treated as the definitive correctness criterion unless the visible project evidence clearly frames the composite widget as the intended compatibility boundary. The original idea remains appropriate when the task asks to harden a specific container widget against arbitrary child mutation, when child widget mutation is documented/intentional API, or when existing nearby framework patterns/tests specifically require defensive copying at the caller boundary.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics rewarded trajectories for ensuring each SplitArrayWidget subwidget receives an independent attrs dict and for preserving id suffixing. That criterion was tempting because it matches the observed symptom and makes ad hoc SplitArrayField(BooleanField) rendering tests pass. It is misleading here because it locks the judge onto a local workaround and ignores the stronger visible cue in the task: the underlying widget mutates an input attrs dict, and that mutation is called out as unique among widgets. A better rubric should ask whether the trajectory recognizes and preserves the broader widget contract that get_context/rendering should not mutate caller-supplied attrs, or at least explicitly justifies why a localized caller-side copy is the intended fix. Avoid generating a criterion that fully credits manual split-array success or MultiWidget-style copying alone. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence such as inspecting the mutating widget, preventing caller attrs from being modified when checked state is added, handling attrs=None safely, and validating both the original split-array symptom and direct non-mutation of the attrs object passed into the checkbox widget.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear to resolve the reported split-array checkbox symptom only by adding attrs copies in the composite/repeater widget, while leaving unaddressed the visibly identified lower-level behavior where the checkbox widget mutates the attrs dict supplied by its caller. This flaw is most relevant when the task statement explicitly names the child widget mutation as exceptional or contract-breaking. Do not apply this penalty merely because the trajectory initially investigates caller-side copying; apply it when the trajectory's implementation or stated plan treats that localized workaround as sufficient without checking or fixing the mutating source or providing project evidence that the source mutation must remain.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Over-localized workaround for a mutating widget contract

metadata.environment: Django forms/widgets rendering code
task_cues: Issue statement identifies a child widget's get_context() as mutating attrs
Mutation is described as unusual or unique among widgets
Observed failure occurs through a composite or repeated widget that reuses attrs
misleading_evidence: Manual split-array rendering now shows correct checked states
Implementation copies attrs per subwidget and preserves generated ids
Ad hoc tests cover only the composite widget symptom
preferred_evidence: Trajectory inspects or modifies the mutating checkbox widget behavior
Caller-provided attrs remain unchanged after checked state is computed
Validation includes both direct widget-context non-mutation and the split-array regression

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory addresses the lower-level attrs mutation contract or clearly justifies, with project evidence, why only caller-side isolation is intended.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory emphasizes composite-widget copying but also investigates the mutating child widget or plans a direct non-mutation test.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory makes the split-array symptom pass through caller-side copying and mentions the child mutation, but does not decide whether the child widget contract itself must change.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the planned or applied fix is only per-subwidget attrs copying, with validation limited to SplitArrayField rendering despite the task explicitly identifying the child widget mutation.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory treats caller-side copying as definitively correct, adds unrelated id/attrs behavior changes or overfits to the composite widget, and never tests or addresses whether the checkbox widget mutates caller-provided attrs.

experiences.title: Require Strategy-Integrated Handler Execution for Broad Ansible Handler Tasks
experiences.description: Retrieve when an Ansible-core task asks for predictable multi-host handler behavior under linear/serial execution, especially with conditional flushes, meta handlers, failed hosts, always/rescue blocks, or any_errors_fatal.
experiences.context: Applies to Ansible-core trajectories where the task is not merely to parse or validate handler syntax, but to make runtime handler execution predictable across hosts. The trajectory usually inspects or edits strategy execution, handler flushing, play iteration, notification state, meta task handling, or linear strategy failure propagation. This guidance is most useful once the agent has enough visible evidence to distinguish broad runtime semantics from narrow parser/meta-action fixes. It is less applicable for single-purpose tasks that only ask for YAML loading validation, documentation-only handler behavior, or early exploration before the agent has identified where handler execution is performed.
experiences.experience: For this task shape, a useful rubric should not reward isolated fixes such as removing a conditional warning from `meta: flush_handlers`, adding a raw-data parser check for `flush_handlers` as a handler, or adding ad hoc failed-host filters in one strategy. Those may be necessary sub-pieces, but the decisive issue is whether the trajectory is moving handler execution into the same scheduling/failure machinery as normal tasks so the selected strategy governs host ordering, serial batches, notification deduplication, failed-host filtering, and fatal-error propagation. Prior rubrics in this cluster were useful when they focused on observable runtime commitments: correct linear/serial ordering, no duplicate or skipped handlers, no leakage after always/rescue sections, consistent any_errors_fatal behavior, and the meta-handler boundary. The better criterion should prioritize visible evidence that the agent has designed or implemented handler execution as a dedicated strategy/iterator phase or equivalent integrated mechanism, plus tests/reproducers that exercise multi-host runtime ordering and failure behavior. Avoid the tempting proxy of counting touched files or accepting parser-only/ad hoc playbook-load tests as sufficient; also avoid requiring broad cross-strategy rewrites unless the task or trajectory explicitly shows multiple strategies are in scope. Strong evidence includes changes or plans that route handlers through the selected strategy's normal execution path, preserve per-host notification state and cleanup, explicitly handle failed hosts after always/rescue blocks, propagate handler failures under fatal-error settings, and validate conditional flush and meta-as-handler behavior with real multi-host execution scenarios.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Strategy-Integrated Multi-Host Handler Semantics
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show substantive progress toward making handler execution participate in the selected strategy's runtime scheduling and failure semantics, not just parser-level or single-branch meta fixes. Excellence requires visible implementation or a concrete, validated design for a dedicated handler execution phase or equivalent mechanism that preserves linear/serial host ordering, avoids duplicate/skipped notifications, filters failed hosts correctly after always/rescue sections, propagates handler failures under fatal-error settings, supports conditional handler flushes, and allows meta handlers while explicitly excluding recursive handler flushing.

multi-host or serial ordering and notification deduplication addressed
handler failure propagation and failed-host filtering addressed
conditional flush and meta-handler boundary addressed

avoid_as_sufficient: only editing conditional warnings for flush handlers
only adding parser checks for handler definitions
only adding ad hoc failed-host filters without ordering or scheduling changes

scale.1: No meaningful progress on runtime handler execution semantics; trajectory is stuck in repeated searches, parser-only checks, or unrelated edits.
scale.2: Addresses one narrow sub-feature such as conditional flush parsing/execution or handler validation, but leaves core multi-host strategy scheduling, ordering, and failure behavior essentially untouched.

experiences.title: Connection-Timezone Source for Non-TZ Datetime Lookups
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django-like ORM task concerns per-database TIME_ZONE handling for DateTimeField date/time extract, cast, truncation, or lookup behavior on backends that store naive datetimes.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django backend-operations setting where USE_TZ is enabled, some database backends do not store timezone-aware datetimes, and the visible task/trajectory distinguishes the database storage timezone from the current or explicit lookup timezone. It is especially relevant once the trajectory has inspected backend datetime SQL generation or SQLite-style registered datetime functions. Do not apply as a general timezone rubric for backends with native timezone storage, for read/write adaptation bugs that do not involve date/extract/trunc/cast lookup conversion, or when the task only asks for global application TIME_ZONE behavior. At very early exploration stages, use this as a directional progress criterion; near final review, require evidence that all affected backend paths and no-op same-timezone behavior are implemented consistently.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics were useful because they targeted the semantic contract that determines correctness here: datetime lookup operations must treat stored naive database values as being in the connection/database timezone, then convert to the current or explicit target timezone before applying date/time functions. This separated promising MySQL/Oracle edits from incomplete trajectories that kept searching, only replaced a hardcoded UTC source, omitted SQLite’s custom-function path, or failed to avoid unnecessary conversion when source and target timezones matched. A better rubric should be concrete about the observable implementation evidence: backend operations must obtain the source timezone from the connection-level database timezone API, preserve UTC fallback through that API when no database TIME_ZONE is set, and understand that the existing tzname argument is the destination/current timezone. For SQL backends, conversion should be emitted only when source and destination differ. For SQLite-like UDF backends, generated SQL, registered function arities, helper signatures, and parse/localization logic must all carry both target and database timezones so naive values are first interpreted in the database timezone. Avoid weak proxies such as merely mentioning connection.timezone_name, editing files for all named backends, running unrelated tests, or making a MySQL-only fix. Prioritize visible evidence from diffs or stated plans that covers all date/time cast, extract, truncation, and date lookup paths, the same-timezone no-op case, USE_TZ disabled behavior, and backend-specific safety such as timezone-name validation where interpolation is used.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Database-Source Timezone Conversion Contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show that datetime date/time lookup, cast, extract, and truncation paths on non-timezone-storing backends convert from the connection/database timezone to the current or explicit target timezone, using the connection timezone as the source, preserving the configured UTC fallback when no database TIME_ZONE is set, and skipping conversion entirely when source and target timezone names are equal. For backends implemented through registered datetime helper functions, the trajectory should update the SQL call sites, function registrations, helper signatures, and parsing logic together so stored naive values are interpreted in the database timezone before target conversion.

metadata.environment: Python Django-like ORM backend operations with USE_TZ and per-database TIME_ZONE settings

source timezone is obtained from the database connection timezone API
same source and target timezone bypasses SQL or helper conversion
SQLite-style custom datetime functions receive and use both target and source timezones consistently
USE_TZ disabled and unset database TIME_ZONE fallback behavior are preserved
avoid_as_proxy: only replacing a hardcoded UTC literal in one backend
only changing generated SQL without matching registered helper arity/signature changes
repetitive grepping or unrelated test-runner work

scale.2: Recognizes a hardcoded UTC/source-timezone problem or patches one backend, but omits major required backends, same-timezone no-op behavior, or the custom-function conversion path.
scale.3: Shows partial parent-level progress: uses the connection/database timezone as a source in some relevant paths, but the implementation or plan is incomplete across backends or lacks clear handling of equal timezones and helper-function consistency.
scale.4: Strongly addresses the contract across the affected backend paths, including connection source timezone and same-timezone bypass, with only minor uncertainty around validation, fallback behavior, or complete test coverage.

experiences.title: Proxy URL Auth Preservation over Broad Version Diagnosis
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a Requests proxy-auth regression tied to a Python version change and the visible trajectory is inspecting proxy URL parsing/normalization, especially interactions between Requests utilities and urllib3 parsing.
experiences.context: Applies in the Requests codebase for authenticated proxy failures such as HTTP 407 on Python 3.8.12/urllib3 1.26.x, when the trajectory has visible evidence around `select_proxy`, proxy URL normalization, `prepend_scheme_if_needed`, `get_auth_from_url`, `HTTPAdapter.proxy_manager_for`, or urllib3 `parse_url` behavior. It is strongest once the agent has observed that proxy credentials are embedded in the proxy URL and that one parser/normalizer may separate `auth` from `netloc`. It is less applicable for unrelated proxy failures without embedded credentials, for cases where the only evidence concerns runtime CONNECT wire transmission with no URL normalization path, or at a very early repository-navigation stage before any proxy URL parsing code has been inspected.
experiences.experience: Broad criteria that simply reward investigating the named Python version, `http.client`, or CONNECT tunneling are too generic here. They can identify the theme of the report but do not discriminate the key Requests-side failure mode. A better rubric should focus on whether the agent verifies preservation of `user:pass@` credentials while Requests normalizes proxy URLs before passing them to urllib3 and before constructing proxy auth headers. The decisive visible evidence is exploration or testing of how a proxy URL like `scheme://user:pass@host:port` flows through `prepend_scheme_if_needed`/parser output, including whether `auth` is dropped from `netloc`, and whether the normalized URL still contains credentials needed for `Proxy-Authorization`. Avoid rewarding fixes that add `Proxy-Authorization` directly to ordinary request headers or tunnel-origin headers without proving the credentials remain scoped to the proxy; that is a tempting but unsafe proxy-auth shortcut. Also avoid treating local installation of a different urllib3/Python version as sufficient validation. The rubric should prioritize targeted URL parsing comparisons, preservation of auth during normalization, and regression tests or small checks demonstrating that proxy-manager/header construction receives a credential-bearing proxy URL.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should identify and validate the proxy URL credential-preservation path: authenticated proxy URLs are selected, normalized with the scheme-prepending helper, parsed by urllib3-style parsing that may expose `auth` separately from `netloc`, and then used to construct proxy managers or `Proxy-Authorization` headers. Strong evidence includes checking parser outputs for `user:pass@host:port`, inspecting the normalization helper for whether it reconstructs `auth@netloc`, and aiming any fix/test at preserving embedded proxy credentials through normalization rather than injecting proxy credentials into normal destination request headers.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Authenticated Proxy URL Normalization

key_flow: proxy manager or proxy header creation
preferred_evidence: inspection of proxy URL normalization helper
comparison of parser fields for auth versus netloc
verification that normalized proxy URL preserves credentials
targeted regression check for credential-bearing proxy URLs
avoid_as_primary_evidence: generic Python version investigation only
repeated CONNECT tunnel routing checks
adding Proxy-Authorization directly to request headers without scoping analysis
validation only on mismatched local dependency versions

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent considered proxy URL credential preservation; the trajectory stays at generic version/debugging or repeats unrelated inspections.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the agent inspects proxy auth/header construction but does not trace whether URL normalization preserves embedded credentials.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent inspects both proxy auth extraction and URL parsing/normalization, but has not clearly identified the auth-versus-netloc preservation issue or a targeted validation path.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the agent recognizes that parser/normalizer behavior can drop `user:pass@` from the proxy URL and focuses the fix or tests on preserving credentials through the proxy manager/header flow.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the agent demonstrates the parser output and normalization failure on an authenticated proxy URL, scopes the solution to reconstruct/preserve auth in the normalized proxy URL, and plans or adds a local regression check without leaking proxy credentials to origin request headers.

experiences.title: Do not reward blanket pointer conversion for mixed NULL-scan bugs
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go database-scan bug involves nullable SQL columns, especially a mix of optional timestamps and scalar/string fields, and the trajectory is converting model fields to pointers across many layers.
experiences.context: Applies in Go repositories where model structs are scanned from SQL rows via struct tags/reflection and migrations reveal nullable columns. The misleading pattern is a rubric that treats converting every nullable DB-backed field to pointer types as the central or sufficient success condition. That idea is only appropriate for fields whose application semantics are genuinely optional, such as unset expiration/cache timestamps where nil can mean absent and existing code has a nullable timestamp convention. It is not appropriate for scalar fields where the application historically treats an empty string/zero value as absence and the schema accidentally allows NULL after an upgrade; those may be better fixed with migration/backfill/default handling while preserving value-typed models and API contracts. At implementation or final-review stages, unresolved build errors, corrupted sed edits, broad unrelated conversions, and unverified call-site changes should dominate the assessment over whether some model fields were changed to pointers.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often said that all nullable timestamp/string database fields must be converted to pointer types and all call sites nil-checked. That criterion is partly sound for optional timestamp fields, but it becomes misleading when it is generalized to every nullable column or used as a positive progress proxy despite visible compile failures. In the sampled trajectories, agents received high credit after changing model fields to pointers, yet the visible work often had unresolved Go build errors, risky whole-file rewrites, broken sed replacements, nil-dereference risks, changed public helper/API signatures unnecessarily, or over-converted unrelated nullable fields. A better rubric should require the trajectory to distinguish semantic nullability from legacy NULL cleanup: timestamps that truly represent absence should use a nullable representation with carefully updated comparisons, assignments, serialization, and persistence; non-optional strings or other scalar fields that merely contain NULL because of an upgrade should be handled by schema migration/backfill/defaults or another compatibility layer unless there is visible evidence that pointer semantics are intended. Avoid the tempting criterion 'all nullable DB columns must be pointer fields.' Prioritize visible evidence that the exact reported NULL-scan column and the named timestamp columns were traced through migrations and model tags, that the chosen fix preserves existing value/JSON/API contracts where appropriate, that all affected call sites compile and handle nil or default values safely, and that validation has no outstanding compiler errors or file corruption.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for overgeneralizing a NULL-scan fix into blanket pointer conversion without proving semantic nullability, preserving schema/API contracts, and reaching a compile-clean state. This flaw is present when the visible work converts every nullable SQL-mapped field to pointers, including scalar fields or unrelated models, while ignoring migration/backfill/default handling for legacy NULLs or leaving unresolved call-site/build errors.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Overgeneralized Nullable-Field Conversion

metadata.applicable_environment: Go SQL-backed application with model structs mapped to database columns and migrations defining nullability
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: Pointer conversion of nullable model fields as sufficient evidence of correctness
preferred_visible_evidence: schema and migration review distinguishes optional fields from accidental legacy NULLs
exact reported NULL-scan column is addressed
optional timestamps use nullable-safe reads, writes, comparisons, and serialization
non-optional scalar fields preserve existing empty/default semantics through migration/backfill/defaults or justified compatibility handling
no unresolved compiler errors, sed corruption, nil dereferences, or unnecessary public API signature changes remain

scale.1: No evidence of blanket conversion or contract breakage; the trajectory distinguishes optional nullable timestamps from scalar legacy NULL cleanup and keeps build/validation status clean or clearly pending without contradictory errors.
scale.2: Minor risk of overgeneralization, such as considering pointer conversion for scalar fields, but the trajectory still investigates schema semantics and has not introduced visible broken call sites or unrelated API changes.
scale.3: Moderate flaw: the trajectory has changed some fields to pointers and updated some call sites, but visible evidence is incomplete on whether scalar NULLs should instead be normalized, or validation/build status is not yet established.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory broadly converts nullable fields to pointers across models/layers, leaves visible compile errors or unsafe nil handling, or changes unrelated public/helper APIs without showing necessity.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory relies almost entirely on blanket pointer conversion, corrupts files or leaves unresolved build failures, ignores the exact reported scalar NULL-scan path or migration/default compatibility, and expands changes to unrelated fields or API contracts.

experiences.title: Teleport Cloud Identity Certificate Plumbing
experiences.description: Use when a Teleport task adds a new cloud impersonation identity analogous to AWS roles or Azure identities, and visible exploration shows role/API support may already exist while TLS certificate identity encoding is missing or being edited.
experiences.context: Applies in the Go Teleport repository for tasks about deriving temporary cloud credentials from Teleport identity, especially when the agent has inspected AWSRoleARN/AzureIdentity patterns in lib/tlsca/ca.go or found existing role/checker/request support for the new cloud identity. It is most useful after the trajectory has enough evidence about certificate identity propagation, or when the agent is choosing between cloud-client/token code and Teleport identity plumbing. It is less applicable if the task is narrowly about an already-authenticated resource-specific flow such as Cloud SQL database auth only, if certificate identity already carries the new cloud principal end-to-end, or if the trajectory is still at a very early repository-listing stage with no inspection of auth/tlsca/role paths.
experiences.experience: For Teleport cloud impersonation features, a strong rubric should not primarily ask for a new provider client, tbot destination, database schema field, or direct IAM Credentials API call. Those are tempting but can be the wrong layer: the central contract is that Teleport certificates must carry both the set of cloud identities the user is allowed to assume and the specific identity selected for an app/cloud route, just as AWS role ARNs and Azure identities do. Prior rubrics that focused on GenerateAccessToken, Cloud SQL auth, proto database metadata, or tbot config were too broad or pointed at secondary flows; they missed the observable architectural gap that identity information must survive certificate issue, encode/decode, audit/event conversion, and metadata extraction. A better criterion should prioritize evidence that the agent has found and updated the TLS identity model: adding GCP service account fields parallel to AWS/Azure, assigning distinct ASN.1 extension OIDs, encoding allowed accounts and selected route account in Subject ExtraNames, decoding them in FromSubject, and propagating them into event identity/user metadata. Visible evidence to value includes searches showing existing GCP role/checker/request fields, absence of GCP fields in tlsca identity code, and edits/tests around certificate extension round-tripping. Avoid treating low-level token generation or adding a Cloud SQL-specific service account field as sufficient unless the task and trajectory explicitly narrow the feature to that resource path.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Certificate-carried GCP service account identity
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should recognize and implement the Teleport identity propagation layer for GCP service account impersonation by extending the TLS certificate identity model in the same way existing AWS role ARN and Azure identity support is represented. Excellent progress includes adding fields for allowed GCP service accounts and the selected app/cloud route service account, assigning distinct certificate extension identifiers, encoding both values into certificate subject extra names, decoding them back into the identity, and preserving them in event identity and user metadata paths. The criterion should be judged from visible trajectory evidence such as inspected AWS/Azure certificate patterns, discovered existing GCP role/checker/request support, absence or presence of GCP fields in the TLS identity code, and concrete edits or tests for certificate round-trip behavior.

positive_evidence: mirrors AWSRoleARN/AzureIdentity certificate plumbing for GCP service accounts
distinguishes allowed service account list from selected route service account
adds round-trip encode/decode behavior rather than only cloud-client calls
preserves GCP service account information in audit/event metadata
do_not_overweight: new IAM Credentials client wrappers alone
Cloud SQL-only database service account fields
tbot configuration additions without certificate identity support
generic claims about token generation without Teleport identity propagation

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory identifies or edits Teleport certificate identity propagation for GCP service accounts; work is limited to unrelated exploration or provider/token/config layers.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory mentions AWS/Azure identity parity or GCP service accounts but does not locate the TLS certificate identity gap or proposes only secondary cloud-client/database/tbot changes.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory locates the relevant TLS identity area or notes that GCP service account role/request support must be carried in certificates, but implementation is incomplete or lacks encode/decode/event coverage.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory adds or plans concrete TLS identity fields and ASN.1 encode/decode support for allowed and selected GCP service accounts, with only minor omissions such as metadata propagation or tests.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory implements or clearly specifies the full certificate identity contract parallel to AWS/Azure, including allowed-account and selected-route fields, distinct extensions, Subject encoding, FromSubject decoding, event/user metadata propagation, and appropriate round-trip validation.

experiences.title: Redundant Database Alias Parameter Removal
experiences.description: Use when a Django/database-backend task asks to simplify an operation method by dropping an explicit database alias/using argument because the bound operation object can infer it from its connection.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django-style repository when the task is a narrow internal API simplification: a backend operation method currently accepts a redundant `using`/alias parameter, the method is bound to a connection object exposing an alias, and visible trajectory evidence includes locating the method implementation plus production call sites. It is most useful once the agent has begun editing or has enough grep/search evidence to judge whether the signature, internal alias use, and production callers are consistent. Do not apply as a broad requirement for unrelated database flush behavior, backend-specific SQL generation, or test-runner setup problems. If multiple backend overrides or third-party compatibility/deprecation concerns are visible, the rubric should be expanded to cover override compatibility rather than assuming one base implementation. Test call-site updates are useful supporting evidence, but should not be the central correctness gate when the task’s functional code change is limited to the implementation and production callers.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic contract of the API migration: remove the explicit alias parameter from the backend operation method, replace any use of the removed local parameter with the bound connection alias, and make production callers invoke the new one-argument API. This aligned because the decisive observable evidence was not whether the agent successfully ran Django’s test suite or updated every test file, but whether the edited code avoided an arity mismatch and preserved transaction routing through `self.connection.alias`. A better rubric should therefore prioritize: (1) the method signature no longer includes the redundant `using`/alias argument; (2) the transaction or equivalent internal routing uses the instance connection alias rather than an undefined removed variable or a caller-provided value; (3) production/internal non-test call sites no longer pass the alias; and (4) search evidence shows no remaining production references to the old call shape or unhandled overrides. Avoid the tempting overly broad criterion that demands all tests be edited or that penalizes failed ad hoc test-runner attempts; those are weaker proxies here and can under-rate otherwise correct trajectories. Also avoid accepting a superficial caller-only change if the implementation still references the removed variable, since that would produce a runtime failure.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a coherent one-argument API migration for the database flush execution operation: the implementation signature drops the explicit database alias/using parameter, the method obtains the correct alias from its bound connection object for transaction routing, and production call sites are updated to pass only the SQL statement list. Strong evidence includes repository search for definitions/callers/overrides, inspection or diff output confirming the new signature and `self.connection.alias`-style internal routing, and confirmation that no non-test production callers still use the old two-argument shape.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Bound Connection Alias API Migration

required_evidence: method signature changed from accepting an explicit alias/using argument to accepting only the SQL list besides self
internal transaction/routing code uses the operation object's bound connection alias
production callers invoke the method with only the SQL list
search or inspection accounts for remaining definitions, overrides, and non-test call sites
supporting_evidence: test callers updated to the new signature
lightweight signature or smoke validation succeeds
failed test-runner setup is distinguished from a patch failure
avoid_overweighting: ad hoc dependency installation or test-runner configuration failures
pure formatting differences
requiring test-only call-site edits as the main correctness gate when production code is otherwise coherent

scale.1: Little or no relevant migration evidence; the trajectory has not located the implementation/callers or proposes unrelated changes.
scale.2: Some relevant investigation or a partial edit is visible, but either the method still has the old signature, the implementation still depends on the removed alias variable, or production callers are not addressed.
scale.3: Equivalent parent-child behavior: the trajectory has identified the right implementation and at least one caller and may have begun the correct edits, but visible evidence is incomplete about either internal alias inference or remaining production call sites.
scale.4: Strong evidence of a coherent migration: the implementation signature and internal alias usage are corrected and the known production caller is updated, though validation/search for all overrides or residual references may be limited.
scale.5: Complete visible evidence: signature, internal bound-alias transaction routing, and all production call sites are updated; searches account for definitions/overrides and stale old-shape calls, with any test-runner issues clearly unrelated to the code change.

experiences.title: Default-setting change with preserved middleware semantics
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django-like task asks to make an existing security setting default to a specific value and the trajectory has found that middleware/check logic already supports that value.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django repository where the requested behavior is achieved primarily by changing a framework global default for an existing setting, and visible trajectory evidence shows the middleware already reads that setting, emits the relevant header when truthy, preserves preexisting response headers, and accepts the requested value as valid. This is most useful after the agent has inspected the setting definition and the consuming middleware/checks, or after it has made the default-setting edit. It is less applicable if the task asks for new header-generation logic, new validation values, a docs-only change, or a behavior change for explicit user overrides. It is also premature if the trajectory has not yet identified where the setting default is defined.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases evaluated the semantic contract: the framework default for `SECURE_REFERRER_POLICY` should become exactly `same-origin`, causing default `SecurityMiddleware` responses to emit `Referrer-Policy: same-origin`, while existing override behavior remains intact. This aligned well because the visible evidence repeatedly showed that the middleware and validation paths already supported the requested value; correctness depended on changing the default in the global settings rather than rewriting middleware or security checks. A better rubric should prioritize evidence that the agent found the current default, confirmed `same-origin` is already a valid policy, confirmed middleware uses the setting via existing truthy/setdefault behavior, and either changed only the default or preserved explicit `None`, other valid values, and preexisting response headers. Avoid making documentation updates, release-note edits, or removal/rewording of warnings the main criterion unless the task explicitly requires them; those can be distracting proxies and may even encourage unnecessary changes. Also avoid rewarding broad rewrites of check logic merely because the default is no longer `None`; explicit opt-out and invalid-value validation should continue to work unless the task states otherwise.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly move toward the minimal semantic change: make the default `SECURE_REFERRER_POLICY` value exactly `same-origin` so the existing security middleware emits `Referrer-Policy: same-origin` by default, while preserving existing behavior for explicit `None`, other valid policy values, invalid-value validation, and already-present response headers.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Exact secure default with preserved override contract

No unnecessary middleware/check rewrites that change the established validation or header-preservation contract
secondary_evidence: Manual or repository tests showing default header emission
Inspection confirming `same-origin` is already in the valid policy set
Checks that preexisting `Referrer-Policy` headers are preserved
avoid_as_primary_evidence: Documentation-only changes
Release-note edits
Deleting warnings or validation logic solely because the default changed

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory found or changed the setting default, or it pursues unrelated header/middleware behavior.
scale.2: The trajectory identifies relevant files or the setting but has not made or committed to the exact `same-origin` default, or risks changing unrelated behavior.
scale.3: The trajectory changes or plans to change the default to `same-origin`, but provides limited evidence about preserving explicit overrides, valid-value handling, or existing header behavior.
scale.4: The trajectory changes the default to `same-origin` and inspects or reasons correctly that existing middleware and validation support the new default without needing broad rewrites.
scale.5: The trajectory makes the minimal exact default change and provides strong visible evidence, through inspection or focused validation, that default responses emit `Referrer-Policy: same-origin` while explicit `None`, other valid policies, invalid values, and already-present headers retain their existing behavior.

experiences.title: Do not score enum-only WebSocket routing as a complete reliability fix
experiences.description: Retrieve when a TypeScript WebSocket handler task mentions ad-hoc message type strings together with ordering, delivery, or internal handler naming requirements. A constants/enum criterion alone can overvalue cosmetic routing changes and miss broken update semantics.
experiences.context: Applies to client/worker TypeScript code where incoming WebSocket messages are parsed from a stable wire format such as `type;payload` and routed to different update paths. The misleading case is a trajectory that discovers raw string comparisons and existing queues, then focuses on adding a WebSocket message-type enum/constant or handler map as the main rubric target. That idea is still appropriate as a small maintainability subcondition when the task explicitly complains about ad-hoc type strings, but it should not be used as the primary or standalone criterion when the same task also requires strict entity-update serialization, reliable unread-counter delivery, and compatible internal handler naming. Be especially cautious if the trajectory proposes new queues for non-entity payloads, casts unrelated payloads into entity-update queue types, or adds public wrapper methods instead of checking the existing callback contract.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics rewarded replacing string literals like `entityUpdate` and `unreadCounterUpdate` with centralized constants/enums. That was directionally relevant, but misleading: patches can satisfy it while leaving the actual reliability bug untouched, introducing invalid queues for counter/leader/phishing payloads, failing to await worker delivery, or changing internal API shape in a way that does not match the existing WebSocket callback usage. A better rubric should focus on the whole message-handling contract visible in the trajectory: preserve the existing wire format; route all known message types through one clear async handler; keep entity-update payloads flowing through the existing ordered entity-update queue without overlapping processing; deliver unread-counter payloads directly and consistently to the worker, returning/awaiting the promise rather than fire-and-forget; and make internal naming consistent at the actual WebSocket callback boundaries without unnecessary API expansion. Avoid the tempting criterion that “a centralized enum/constant for all message types” is enough. Replacement criteria should prioritize evidence of preserved payload types, correct per-message side effects, sequential entity processing, awaited counter delivery, and compatibility with existing tests/call sites.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat centralized WebSocket message-type constants as the primary fix while lacking evidence that the handler preserves the semantic delivery contract: entity-update messages must stay on the existing ordered entity-update path, unread-counter messages must be delivered to the worker as their native counter payload and awaited/returned consistently, other message types must keep their existing side effects, and internal handler naming changes must be wired through existing WebSocket callbacks without unnecessary public API expansion or incompatible test breakage.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Enum-only routing without delivery semantics

metadata.environment: TypeScript worker/client WebSocket message handler
metadata.misleading_positive_signal: Adds enum/constants or handler map for message type strings
required_visible_evidence: all known message types are routed in one clear handler without changing the wire format
