unread-counter payloads are delivered to the worker as counter data and the resulting promise is awaited or returned
phishing/leader status side effects remain direct and type-correct
handler naming/callback changes preserve existing call sites and do not expose unnecessary new API
avoid_rewarding: constants-only replacement
new EventQueue instances for non-entity payloads using unsafe casts
fire-and-forget worker counter updates
public wrapper methods that are not used by the WebSocket callback

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory evaluates or implements routing together with correct typed payload handling, existing ordered entity-update queuing, awaited/returned counter delivery, preserved side effects, and compatible callback naming.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: message-type constants are emphasized, but the trajectory also checks most semantic paths and does not propose unsafe queues or API changes.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory mainly focuses on constants/enums and only partially considers ordering or counter delivery, leaving important semantic behavior unverified.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory proposes or rewards enum/constant routing while ignoring awaited counter delivery, handler compatibility, or the existing ordered entity queue contract.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory treats enum/constant replacement as sufficient and proposes harmful changes such as casting counter/leader/phishing payloads into entity queues, adding unnecessary queues, or changing exposed handler APIs without preserving existing callback behavior.

experiences.title: Do not treat a hand-built XDG data path as sufficient for legacy tool-state migrations
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for XDG Base Directory compliance in a Python CLI/tool repository where a legacy hidden home directory stores persistent run state, especially if the trajectory is converging on manually joining XDG environment variables.
experiences.context: This applies to tasks asking to move a legacy dot-directory such as a per-user tool state directory into XDG-compliant locations, in a Python project with import-time path constants, packaging metadata, and persistent stats/cache-like files. The misleading case is a rubric that rewards only `PYLINTHOME` precedence plus `$XDG_DATA_HOME/<program>` or `~/.local/share/<program>` string construction and directory creation. That can overstate progress when the repository's intended fix should classify the stored artifacts correctly, use a platform/XDG helper library or project-approved abstraction, update dependency/tooling metadata, and handle users who already have the old directory. The original exact-path idea may still be appropriate when the task and code clearly require data files specifically under `$XDG_DATA_HOME`, the repository avoids external directory helpers, and there is no legacy migration or platform-abstraction concern. At early exploration stages, absence of these details may be inconclusive; near implementation or final-review stages, evidence of a hard-coded environment-variable path without considering artifact class, legacy-dir behavior, and packaging changes is a meaningful warning.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked whether the trajectory implemented `PYLINTHOME` override, then `$XDG_DATA_HOME/pylint` or `$HOME/.local/share/pylint`, stopped defaulting to `~/.pylint.d`, and created nested directories. That criterion is partly useful but too narrow and sometimes wrong as a predictor: it assumes the user-facing phrase 'data' fixes the exact target directory, and it treats a manually joined XDG path as sufficient. In a mature Python CLI, persistent `.stats` or comparison-state files may be treated as cache/state rather than user data, and maintainers may prefer a dependency such as a directory-helper package to encode platform-specific XDG behavior. A better rubric should focus on whether the agent investigated the stored artifact semantics, selected a project-appropriate XDG/platform directory abstraction rather than blindly concatenating `$XDG_DATA_HOME`, preserved explicit override and unresolved-home fallbacks, addressed the existing legacy dot-directory with a user-visible compatibility notice instead of silently ignoring it, and updated packaging/import tooling when adding a helper dependency. Avoid generating a tempting criterion that says '`$XDG_DATA_HOME/<program>` or `~/.local/share/<program>` is the correct destination' as the main pass condition unless visible evidence rules out cache/state classification and helper-library expectations. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence from code inspection and trajectory notes: what files are stored there, whether the agent distinguishes data/cache/config/state, whether it searches project dependency policy, whether it considers users with an existing legacy directory, and whether any new import is reflected in install and static-analysis configuration.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Hard-coded XDG data path treated as complete migration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: For an XDG-compliance change to a Python CLI/tool's legacy per-user persistent-state directory, penalize trajectories that converge on manual `$XDG_DATA_HOME/<program>` or `$HOME/.local/share/<program>` path construction as the complete solution while showing little or no evidence that they classified the stored artifacts correctly, considered a project-appropriate platform/XDG directory helper, handled an existing legacy dot-directory with user-visible compatibility behavior, and updated packaging/tooling metadata for any new helper dependency. This is especially important when the visible code stores generated stats/cache-like comparison files rather than user-authored configuration.

applies_when: Task requests XDG Base Directory compliance for a legacy hidden home directory
Repository is a Python CLI/tool with persistent generated run-state files
Trajectory edits an import-time path constant or home-directory default
Trajectory uses or plans to use raw environment-variable joins for the new location
visible_evidence_to_check: Agent identifies whether the legacy files are data, cache, config, or state
Agent considers platform/XDG helper libraries or existing project directory abstractions
Agent preserves explicit override behavior
Agent preserves special fallback behavior when the home directory cannot be resolved
Agent considers warning or compatibility behavior when the old legacy directory already exists
Agent updates dependency and tooling configuration if adding a new helper import
avoid_overrewarding: Passing temporary scripts that only validate those hard-coded paths
Updating help text without addressing dependency, artifact classification, or legacy-dir behavior

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory investigates artifact semantics, chooses a project-appropriate XDG/platform directory mechanism, preserves override and unresolved-home behavior, handles the legacy directory compatibly, and accounts for any dependency/tooling changes.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory initially mentions hard-coded XDG data paths but also investigates cache/state semantics or helper-library approaches and has not committed to the manual path as sufficient.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory implements or plans raw XDG data path construction and preserves basic override behavior, but only partially considers artifact class, platform abstraction, legacy-dir handling, or packaging metadata.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory treats `$XDG_DATA_HOME/<program>` or `~/.local/share/<program>` as the central correctness criterion, validates only that behavior, and omits legacy-directory compatibility or helper/dependency considerations.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory hard-codes XDG data paths as final, updates tests/documentation to match that assumption, ignores cache/state classification and existing legacy directories, and does not account for project-approved directory helpers or required packaging/tooling updates.

experiences.title: External Deserialization Exception Compatibility in Cache Recovery
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python trajectory is fixing crashes from corrupted serialized/cache data read through an external library, especially after the agent has found the cache-loading method and is inspecting the library’s actual exception hierarchy.
experiences.context: Applies in Python application repositories where startup or feature initialization reads a serialized cache file through a third-party deserializer, and the task asks for graceful recovery from corrupted cache data. It is most useful once the trajectory has visible evidence of the exact deserialization call site, existing partial exception handling, or investigation of the third-party package’s exception classes/version behavior. It is less useful during very early repository exploration before the cache read path is identified, for unrelated cache-miss/file-permission issues, or for tasks where the desired behavior is to fail fast rather than continue after corrupted optional state.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on localized graceful recovery at the cache deserialization boundary: catch the deserialization failure that actually escapes from the external library, notify/log an actionable error, and allow the application to continue without disturbing normal cache-miss or valid-cache behavior. A better rubric should be sharper than a generic 'handle corrupted cache' criterion: it should reward visible investigation of the library’s real exception API, including compatibility with older behavior where deserialization failures may have been represented as a generic ValueError/string, while preserving propagation of unrelated exceptions. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as merely catching Exception broadly, changing unrelated adblock/blocklist code, relying only on an ad hoc reproduction script without the project’s configured test fixtures, or treating any passing existing test run as sufficient. Prioritize evidence that the agent found the precise deserialize call, confirmed the thrown exception type/hierarchy, patched only the corrupted-cache path, kept the user-facing recovery message, and considered regression coverage for corrupted data.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a localized, compatibility-aware fix for corrupted optional cache deserialization: identify the cache-loading/deserialization call that can crash startup, determine the actual third-party deserialization exception type and any legacy wrapper behavior, handle only that expected corrupted-cache failure at the read boundary, report an actionable user/log message, continue initialization where possible, and preserve behavior for valid caches, absent caches, and unrelated exceptions.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Compatibility-Aware Corrupted Cache Deserialization Recovery

prioritize_visible_evidence: agent locates the specific cache read method and deserialize-from-file call
agent inspects or reproduces the third-party library's actual exception type/hierarchy
fix catches the explicit deserialization failure and, where relevant, legacy generic-wrapper behavior
fix reports a clear recovery/update message and does not abort application startup
fix avoids broad masking of unrelated failures and preserves existing cache-miss/update behavior
trajectory includes a targeted corrupted-cache check or a plan to add one using project fixtures
avoid_overrewarding: broad catch-all exception handling without justification
tests that only exercise valid cache behavior
standalone reproductions that fail before reaching the target deserialization path

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory found the cache deserialization path or understood the corrupted-cache crash mechanism.
scale.2: Finds a relevant cache-reading area or proposes generic error handling, but does not establish the actual exception type or may alter unrelated behavior.
scale.3: Shows moderate progress comparable to the parent trajectory: identifies the deserialize call and corrupted-cache failure, but the proposed criterion/fix is still somewhat broad, incomplete, or lacks compatibility/unrelated-exception boundaries.
scale.4: Strong evidence of a localized fix that catches the real deserialization failure, preserves normal cache behavior, emits an actionable message, and avoids most unrelated masking.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory verifies the external library exception hierarchy/version behavior, handles both current and legacy deserialization-error representations narrowly, preserves unrelated exception propagation and cache-miss/update semantics, and validates the corrupted-cache scenario with appropriate project test setup.

experiences.title: Semantic Parity Across Named Backends
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django/database task explicitly names multiple backend implementations for the same behavior and the trajectory is implementing or reviewing backend-specific fixes.
experiences.context: Applies in Django-style repository tasks where a bug report identifies the same contract across several database backends or adapters, especially non-timezone-aware backends with separate SQL/Python conversion mechanisms. It is most useful once the agent has begun editing backend code or is near final review, because visible diffs and inspections can show whether each named backend path was handled. It should not be applied rigidly when the task only gives one backend as an example, when a shared base-layer change demonstrably covers every named backend, or during very early exploration before the agent has selected an implementation strategy.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics correctly noticed that the task required more than a single-backend MySQL change: MySQL, SQLite, and Oracle each had distinct conversion paths, so trajectories that only investigated or patched one or two paths were visibly incomplete. However, a broad criterion like “multi-backend consistency” can be too weak: simply touching all named backend files or adding superficially similar code is not enough. The better rubric should require semantic parity across each backend-specific mechanism: stored naive values must be treated as coming from the database connection timezone, the lookup/current timezone must remain the target, conversion should be skipped when source and target are identical where that matters, and helper APIs must pass the necessary source and target information consistently. In UDF-based or adapter-style backends, prioritize evidence that SQL generation, registered function arity, and helper parameter order all agree; this is more discriminative than file coverage alone. Avoid tempting proxy criteria such as “all three backend files were modified” or “the hardcoded UTC string was replaced everywhere.” The visible evidence to prioritize is: which named backends were inspected/edited, whether the backend’s actual cast/extract/trunc lookup path was changed, whether source-vs-target timezone roles are explicit and ordered correctly, whether no-op same-timezone behavior is preserved, and whether focused tests or generated SQL checks exercise equal and different database/current timezone cases.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Backend-Specific Semantic Coverage
reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a task that names multiple database backends or adapters as affected by the same datetime/timezone lookup bug, the trajectory should demonstrate semantic coverage for every named backend, not merely edit multiple files. A strong trajectory identifies each backend’s actual date/time cast, extract, or truncation path; uses the database connection timezone as the source for stored naive values; keeps the active/current lookup timezone as the target; avoids unnecessary conversion when source and target match where the task requires it; and keeps backend-specific plumbing consistent, such as SQL generation matching registered helper signatures for Python-backed database functions. Evidence may include diffs, code inspections, generated SQL checks, or focused tests covering both same-timezone and different-timezone scenarios.

expected_visible_evidence: All explicitly named backends or adapters are accounted for, or a shared implementation is shown to cover them.
The trajectory distinguishes source database timezone from target/current lookup timezone.
Backend-specific conversion mechanisms are handled according to their actual implementation model.
Same-source-and-target timezone behavior is considered rather than always forcing conversion.
For helper-function based backends, generated SQL arguments, registered function arity, and helper parameter order are consistent.
anti_proxy: Do not give full credit solely because all named backend files were touched.
Do not give full credit solely because a hardcoded UTC literal was replaced.
Do not ignore a named backend unless the trajectory gives a code-based reason it is covered elsewhere or unaffected.
metadata.applicable_stage: Implementation review or late-stage trajectory assessment after backend code paths have been inspected or edited.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent is tracking all named backend implementations or the source-vs-target timezone contract; work is limited to generic searching, a single example backend, or unrelated tests.
scale.2: Weak evidence of multi-backend awareness, such as mentioning the named backends or patching one backend correctly, but other named backend paths are omitted or only superficially inspected.
scale.3: Comparable to the parent trajectory: the agent recognizes the multi-backend scope and has partial implementation or investigation, but visible evidence leaves important backend-specific mechanisms, same-timezone behavior, or helper API consistency unresolved.
scale.4: Strong evidence that each named backend path is addressed with the correct source database timezone and target lookup timezone distinction, with only minor uncertainty around validation, edge cases, or one backend-specific detail.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: every named backend’s actual conversion path is semantically handled, same-timezone no-op behavior is implemented where required, helper signatures and generated SQL are internally consistent, and focused validation or tests demonstrate same-timezone and different-timezone scenarios.

experiences.title: Do not let abstraction intent mask unstable integration
experiences.description: Retrieve when a React/TypeScript refactor task explicitly asks for decoupling or dependency injection, but the trajectory shows broad rewrites, partial migrations, failing validation, or only design-level progress.
experiences.context: This applies to UI/helper refactors in a TypeScript React monorepo where the requested change is to decouple modal-based verification from token creation through reusable injectable functions. The misleading pattern is a rubric that simply restates the desired abstraction, so a trajectory looks good after introducing a handler name or planning an extraction even though visible evidence shows parse/type errors, corrupted component structure, incomplete call-site migration, unvalidated edits, or unrelated UI regressions. The original abstraction-boundary idea is still useful at a stable implementation or final-review stage, where code is syntactically sound and the main risk is whether the API boundary is truly clean. During early exploration, absence of the handler is not itself a decisive flaw; rubrics should instead assess whether the agent has identified the helper, modal contract, status/polling behavior, and all consumers before editing.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked whether the verification flow was extracted into a reusable handler and decoupled from modal rendering. That is a real task requirement, but as a standalone criterion it is too easy to satisfy superficially: adding a VerificationHandler interface, default handler, or factory can coexist with broken TSX, failing type checks, missing consumers, duplicated modal logic moved elsewhere, or changed payment/component behavior. For similar trajectories, generate a rubric that evaluates behavior-preserving integration of the abstraction rather than the mere presence of abstraction terminology. The replacement criterion should prioritize visible evidence that the agent enumerated all direct and cross-container call sites, preserved existing verification polling/abort/resolve/reject semantics, kept the modal prop contract intact inside the default handler, migrated consumers without duplicating modal JSX, avoided unrelated full-file rewrites or UI changes, and ran relevant TypeScript/tests after edits. Avoid the tempting criterion that a handler is a pure/customizable function or that backward compatibility fallback exists; those details do not predict correctness when the visible trajectory already shows syntax churn, failing validation, or incomplete migration.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Abstraction-only progress despite unstable migration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat creation of a reusable verification abstraction as sufficient while visible evidence indicates the integration is incomplete or unstable: malformed TSX/brace structure, failing TypeScript or tests, broad heredoc/sed rewrites of large components, unrelated UI or payload changes, stale call sites still using the old modal-coupled API, missing cross-container consumers, or failure to preserve existing verification modal callbacks and polling/abort behavior. This rubric should not penalize early read-only exploration that has not attempted implementation; in that stage, judge whether the agent is gathering the necessary call-site and modal-contract evidence instead.

metadata.environment: React TSX components and TypeScript helper code in a monorepo
visible_evidence_to_check: validation output from TypeScript, tests, or lint
whether all discovered consumers are migrated consistently
whether edits are minimal and localized versus broad rewrites
whether existing modal callback, polling, abort, and payment payload semantics are preserved
whether the trajectory distinguishes design intent from validated implementation
do_not_overweight: presence of a VerificationHandler type or factory alone
comments claiming reusability
fallback compatibility branches without validation
planned future migration steps

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the abstraction work is integrated cleanly, call sites are accounted for, behavior-preserving details are visible, and validation is clean or not yet applicable because the agent is still only investigating.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the abstraction exists and most integration evidence is sound, but one visible item such as a not-yet-run validation command or a small unchecked consumer remains.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory has a plausible handler extraction but also visible incomplete migration, missing validation, or uncertainty about preserving modal/process behavior.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the agent has introduced abstraction code while TypeScript/tests fail, component structure is suspect, consumers are partially migrated, or unrelated behavior was changed.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory is dominated by broken broad rewrites, repeated syntax/brace/type errors, stale or corrupted call sites, and no reliable validation, while the only apparent progress is nominal abstraction terminology.

experiences.title: Do not equate NumPy copying with compatible coordinate snapshot semantics
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for Matplotlib-style annotation/coordinate aliasing fixes where the agent has found direct storage of a mutable coordinate pair and is tempted to patch it with `np.asarray(...).copy()` or `np.array(..., copy=True)`.
experiences.context: Applies in Python plotting/graphics codebases with public coordinate APIs that accept more than plain numeric ndarrays, such as two-element tuples/lists, unit-aware values, object-like coordinate elements, or coordinate helper objects whose reference coordinates are read later during rendering. The misleading situation is a trajectory that correctly identifies mutable aliasing in annotation coordinate storage and adds a defensive NumPy copy, but does not show that this preserves existing coordinate input semantics or covers other persistent coordinate-pair storage used by the same annotation rendering path. A broad defensive-copy rubric can still be appropriate when the API explicitly canonicalizes all accepted coordinates to ndarrays and no other coordinate pair is stored by reference, or at an early exploration stage where no implementation is being judged yet.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics rewarded the general idea that annotation `xy` should be copied so caller mutation cannot move the arrow. That idea is directionally correct but too broad for this task family: a visible patch such as assigning `np.asarray(xy).copy()` or `np.array(xy, copy=True)` can fix the simple ndarray reproduction while changing the public/internal representation for tuple, list, unitized, or object coordinate inputs, and it may skip other stored coordinate pairs used by offset/annotation transforms. A better rubric should focus on value-snapshot semantics that preserve coordinate API behavior: the implementation should detach from mutable containers by extracting exactly the two coordinate elements into a stable pair, retain element types/units rather than forcing ndarray conversion, preserve existing shape validation behavior, and inspect related annotation coordinate-storage paths that are consumed later during drawing. Avoid the tempting criterion 'any independent copy of `xy` is sufficient.' Prioritize visible evidence of compatible two-element unpacking or equivalent non-coercive copying, coverage of all later-read coordinate pair storage involved in the annotation path, and validation against the local checkout with both ndarray mutation and ordinary tuple/list or unit-like coordinate cases.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Array-coercive or incomplete coordinate snapshot
reference_golden_rubrics.description: For annotation-coordinate aliasing fixes in a Matplotlib-like plotting library, penalize trajectories whose implementation merely coerces the user-supplied coordinate pair to a NumPy array copy, or otherwise demonstrates only the simple ndarray mutation case, without visible evidence that accepted coordinate semantics are preserved and that all persistent coordinate-pair references used by annotation/offset rendering are detached from caller mutation.

metadata.environment: Python plotting library with annotation objects, arrows, coordinate transforms, and mutable array-like coordinate inputs
metadata.problem_signature: A mutable coordinate pair passed to an annotation API is stored and read later during drawing, so mutating the caller object changes the rendered annotation or arrow target
problematic_visible_patterns: Patch replaces direct coordinate storage with `np.asarray(coord).copy()` or `np.array(coord, copy=True)` for all inputs
Trajectory claims success based only on the reported ndarray reproduction or visual image generation
No evidence is shown for tuple/list, unit-aware, object-valued, or coordinate-helper reference semantics
Only the primary annotation target is inspected while related stored reference coordinates used by offset/transform helpers are ignored
preferred_visible_evidence: Coordinate pairs are detached by unpacking or an equivalent non-coercive value snapshot of exactly two elements
The stored representation remains a normal two-element coordinate iterable and preserves element types/units
Shape/length errors remain naturally checked rather than silently changing behavior through ndarray conversion
Related annotation/offset coordinate storage that is read during rendering is audited and fixed if it can retain caller mutable state
Validation imports the local checkout and covers both ndarray mutation and ordinary accepted coordinate inputs

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory uses a non-coercive two-element coordinate snapshot or otherwise clearly preserves accepted coordinate semantics, audits related stored coordinate references, and validates beyond the simple ndarray case.
scale.2: Minor concern: the trajectory mostly preserves coordinate semantics but validation is thin or related coordinate-storage paths are only partially discussed.
scale.3: Equivalent parent-child behavior: the trajectory identifies aliasing and proposes copying, but visible evidence is insufficient to tell whether the copy preserves coordinate semantics or covers all later-read coordinate references.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory implements or strongly commits to NumPy array coercion as the defensive copy and validates only that ndarray mutation no longer changes the simple annotation target.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory relies on array coercion, ignores compatibility for non-ndarray coordinate inputs and related offset/reference coordinate storage, and treats possibly non-local or purely visual validation as proof of correctness.

experiences.title: Do not treat timestamp sorting as a complete public-session fix
experiences.description: Retrieve this when a task concerns unreliable latest persisted-session retrieval on public pages in a TypeScript/React monorepo, and the trajectory focuses on localStorage ordering, shared auth helpers, or parse-error handling.
experiences.context: The misleading pattern is a trajectory that identifies persisted sessions, STORAGE_PREFIX keys, persistedAt ordering, or storage-access failure handling, then receives a rubric centered on sorting sessions or safely parsing localStorage. Those are useful subproblems, but for public-page initialization they are not sufficient if the visible call chain still obtains UID and localID through separate helpers or leaves the public session provider, auth context, telemetry, or user-facing localID consumers using stale/inconsistent identifiers. The original sorting/error-handling idea may still be appropriate when the task is explicitly scoped to a low-level storage API or a helper whose only contract is to return sessions in recency order. During early exploration, understanding storage layout can be a progress signal, but at implementation/final-review stage the rubric must require evidence that the selected latest session object is integrated into the public-page consumers that need its identifying fields.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often rewarded criteria such as “sort persisted sessions by persistedAt descending,” “handle corrupted storage,” or “demonstrate session storage comprehension.” These criteria were misleading when the trajectory patched only a shared storage/helper layer or duplicated defensive parsing while leaving the public-page flow split between separate UID and localID lookups. The semantic requirement is not merely choosing a recent timestamp; it is that public-page initialization consistently uses one latest valid persisted session, including its identifying fields, so resume-session calls, auth state, metrics/telemetry headers, and any public-session user localID all agree. A better rubric should focus on whether the agent traces and updates the application-level public-session consumer path and replaces split UID/localID retrieval with a unified persisted-session result. Avoid the tempting criterion that a sorted getPersistedSessions() or per-item JSON try/catch is enough. Prioritize visible evidence such as: the trajectory inspected public-session provider usages, recognized that UID and localID must come from the same selected session, planned or implemented consumer updates, preserved safe null/error reporting behavior, and avoided unrelated shared-only changes that no public-page code calls.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a public-page persisted-session bug, penalize a trajectory or patch that confines the fix to timestamp sorting, localStorage parsing, or a new shared/helper API while failing to integrate a single latest persisted session object through the public-page initialization path. The flaw is present when visible evidence shows public-page consumers still call separate UID/localID helpers, resume a session using an ID selected independently from the UID used for headers, fail to set authentication state from the selected persisted session, or leave telemetry/user-localID consumers on the old split lookup. This criterion should not penalize early investigation that merely studies storage ordering, nor a task explicitly scoped only to a storage helper with no public-page consumer contract.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Public-session identity integration gap

metadata.task_family: latest persisted session retrieval for public pages
metadata.environment: TypeScript/React monorepo with shared authentication storage and application-level public session consumers
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: sorted persistedAt order or safe localStorage parsing alone
replacement_evidence: public session provider or equivalent application consumer is inspected or modified
UID and localID are derived from the same latest valid persisted session object
resume-session calls, auth state, metrics/telemetry headers, and public user localID consumers remain consistent
storage failures or invalid session data still return no session with error reporting

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory either remains in early investigation without claiming a complete fix, or it clearly plans/implements a unified latest persisted-session object integrated into the public-page consumer path.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory emphasizes sorting or storage safety but also identifies the public-page consumers and the need to keep UID/localID consistent; integration is not yet fully visible.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory patches or plans a latest-session helper and considers at least one consumer, but visible evidence still leaves split UID/localID selection or unclear auth/telemetry/user-localID propagation.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory implements storage ordering, parse handling, or a shared helper and may run passing helper tests, but the public-page provider or related consumers still use the old separate lookup path.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory treats a storage-only or unrelated package change as the complete solution, ignores the public-page call chain entirely, or makes broad unrelated edits while leaving session identity integration unaddressed.

experiences.title: Do not reward label-decoding intent without visible local patch evidence
experiences.description: Retrieve when a scikit-learn trajectory for HistGradientBoosting early-stopping target encoding shows investigation, planned decoding, or tests against a different installed sklearn, but the current local source diff is not clearly verified or the agent may be drifting to unrelated files.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/scikit-learn source-tree tasks where the reported bug is a target-representation mismatch during scorer-based early stopping: classifier targets are internally encoded, while predictions/scorers operate on original class labels. The label-decoding idea is a valid semantic target when the trajectory is at final-review stage and the visible local diff shows the scorer path decoding both training-subset and validation targets while preserving loss/regressor behavior. It is misleading when the visible trajectory is still early exploration, only states the intended fix, relies on successful runs from a separately installed sklearn wheel, cannot import the local checkout, or later edits unrelated model-selection/build files. In those situations, a rubric that only asks for “decode labels before scoring” can over-credit understanding or stale summaries and miss whether the final patch is actually in the right local code path.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster correctly identified the central semantic fix: scorer-based early stopping for classifiers should pass targets in the same label space as predictions, without changing loss-based scoring or regressors. The problem was that the criterion was too solution-shaped and too broad for the visible stage of the trajectories. It gave partial or high credit to trajectories that merely reasoned about the fix, had unverified/truncated source edits, ran reproductions against an installed modern sklearn instead of the checkout under repair, or later drifted into unrelated files. For future rubric generation, keep the label-space criterion only when there is visible evidence of a current local edit in the early-stopping scorer path. Otherwise generate a stage-aware criterion that penalizes lack of verified local diff/current method inspection, reliance on the wrong installed package as validation, or unrelated final edits. Avoid the tempting criterion “agent understands it should decode y via classes_” as the main predictor; prioritize observable evidence: current diff or method body in the target scorer path, both train and validation scorer calls covered, loss/regressor paths left alone, and no unrelated changes replacing the intended fix.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for this scikit-learn early-stopping target-encoding bug when the visible work does not establish that the local source checkout currently contains the intended scorer-path fix, especially if the agent only describes the decoding idea, inspects truncated output, validates by running a separately installed sklearn version, cannot import/build the local package, or drifts into unrelated files instead of maintaining a focused change in the histogram gradient boosting early-stopping scorer logic.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Unverified or Drifted Local Early-Stopping Fix

coverage of both training-subset and validation scorer targets
explicit preservation of loss-based scoring and regressor behavior
awareness that installed sklearn runs do not validate the patched checkout
absence of unrelated file changes as the only final work
avoid_overcrediting: plans or comments that mention decoding without a verified local edit
successful reproducer output from a different installed sklearn package
stale earlier-summary claims not confirmed by recent diff
broad environment/build exploration with no source change

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory shows a current, focused local source change in the early-stopping scorer path or is still explicitly in early exploration without claiming validation; no unrelated drift is visible.
scale.2: Minor concern: the agent has a plausible local edit or clear plan but has not fully inspected the current diff/method body, while avoiding misleading validation claims and unrelated edits.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory mainly demonstrates understanding of the label-decoding fix or has truncated/unverified edit evidence, and validation is blocked or ambiguous.
scale.4: Clear concern: the agent treats runs against an installed sklearn or stale summaries as validation of the local patch, or recent steps fail to confirm that both scorer targets are fixed in the local checkout.

experiences.title: State Reconciliation Must Preserve Historical Child-Derived Timestamps
experiences.description: Use this when a Go backend task concerns a parent resource whose status is reconciled from ephemeral child/presence records, and the bug is that deleting all child records clears a previously valid timestamp while status should still change.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go service/repository when the task explicitly separates a persistent parent resource from transient connection/heartbeat records: absence of child records should drive an Offline/Unavailable status, but should not overwrite the parent’s stored last-observed heartbeat with zero or an older value. The rubric is most useful once the trajectory has either located the reconciliation/update function or begun editing the no-child-record branch. It is premature during pure repository exploration unless the agent has not yet found the reconciliation path. It is less relevant for tasks where the timestamp is intentionally a live-only field, where deleting child records should clear all derived fields, or where the issue is only display-layer formatting rather than persistence semantics.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases focused on the task’s semantic contract rather than on broad exploration: the agent must distinguish status derivation from heartbeat retention. A good patch should update the parent resource to Offline when no current child connection records exist, while preserving the already persisted heartbeat and continuing to update the heartbeat only when a newer child heartbeat is observed. It should also retain the compare-before-write behavior so the backend is not updated when neither status nor heartbeat meaningfully changes. This criterion is discriminative because visible trajectories often show agents finding the right function but then only adding comments, storing previous values without using them, making fragile line-range edits, or relying on build success while not proving the no-child branch preserves the timestamp. Do not replace this with a weaker criterion such as “located RemoteCluster and TunnelConnection definitions,” “compiled successfully,” or “mentions preserving heartbeat.” Prioritize visible evidence in the inspected diff and commands: the no-child/not-found branch, whether `SetLastHeartbeat` or equivalent is avoided there, whether the existing timestamp remains untouched, whether active-child logic only accepts newer heartbeats, whether backend writes are gated by status/newer-heartbeat changes, and whether the agent inspected the final diff or tested the relevant scenario.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Correct Parent Status and Timestamp Reconciliation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show concrete implementation progress toward the reconciliation contract: in the branch where no transient connection/heartbeat child records are found, the parent resource is marked Offline without clearing or replacing its persisted last heartbeat; in the branch where child records exist, the parent heartbeat is advanced only from a newer observed child heartbeat; and backend persistence remains conditional on an actual status change or newer heartbeat. The judgment should be based on visible code edits, inspected diffs, and relevant validation, not merely comments or exploration.

required_visible_evidence: The agent has identified the reconciliation/update path that mutates the parent resource from child connection records.
The no-child-record branch is inspected or edited.
The edit keeps Offline status behavior while leaving the existing parent heartbeat intact.
The active-child-record path does not regress newer-heartbeat-only behavior.
Backend update calls are guarded by meaningful status or heartbeat changes.
The agent verifies the resulting code structure with a diff, targeted file inspection, compilation, or a focused test.
common_false_positives: Only adding comments that say the heartbeat is preserved.
Saving previous heartbeat into a variable but never using it to prevent clearing.
Changing resource model getters/setters instead of the reconciliation logic.
Unconditionally writing the parent resource whenever child records are absent.
Treating an absent child record as a zero or newer heartbeat.
Corrupting the function with broad line-range edits and not repairing/validating the diff.

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward the reconciliation contract: the trajectory is only generic exploration, edits an unrelated area, corrupts the relevant function, or would still clear/overwrite the persisted heartbeat when child records are absent.
scale.2: Weak progress: the agent finds related resource definitions or mentions the correct behavior, but has not located or safely changed the reconciliation branch; any code change is comment-only, fragile, or lacks evidence that the heartbeat is preserved.
scale.3: Moderate progress: the agent locates the correct reconciliation path and attempts to keep the parent Offline while avoiding heartbeat clearing, but the implementation or validation is incomplete, overbroad, or does not clearly preserve write gating and newer-heartbeat semantics.
scale.4: Strong progress: the visible diff correctly handles the no-child branch by preserving the existing parent heartbeat and only writing on a status change, while leaving the active-child newer-heartbeat logic largely intact; the agent inspects the diff or performs some relevant validation.
scale.5: Strongest progress: the trajectory presents a clean, minimal, validated change in the reconciliation logic that preserves historical heartbeat on child removal, marks the parent Offline, advances heartbeat only on newer observations, avoids unnecessary backend writes, and includes or runs a focused test or equivalent scenario validation.

experiences.title: Do not reward superficial metadata validation when CLI defaults affect namespace semantics
experiences.description: Retrieve for export/import tasks that add serialized document version and namespace metadata, especially in a Go/Cobra CLI where a namespace flag has a default value and the document may also declare a namespace.
experiences.context: This applies when a trajectory is implementing YAML export/import metadata and validation, and visible code or plans show both a CLI namespace source and a document namespace source. The misleading rubric pattern is to judge success from merely adding `version`/`namespace` fields and a generic mismatch check. That is not enough when the CLI always supplies a default namespace: the implementation must distinguish an explicitly provided CLI namespace from an implicit default, otherwise a document-only namespace can be incorrectly rejected or ignored. The same caution applies to the document version contract: the chosen version literal and compatibility check should be tied to the repository’s expected export format, not an arbitrary new value. The original broad criterion may still be appropriate at an early exploration stage or when the task only requires metadata presence, but once implementation quality is being judged, it must include source-precedence and compatibility-boundary evidence.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked for version and namespace fields plus import-side validation. That criterion is necessary but too coarse: trajectories can appear to satisfy it while still using the wrong document-version contract, treating the default CLI namespace as if the user explicitly supplied it, accepting missing/unsupported versions inconsistently, or only updating happy-path fixtures. A better rubric should focus on the semantic contract visible in the trajectory: whether the CLI layer preserves whether the namespace flag was explicitly set, whether the importer resolves the effective namespace according to document-vs-CLI precedence before creating any resources, whether all created resources use that resolved namespace, whether unsupported versions fail clearly, and whether tests cover invalid version, namespace mismatch, and document-only namespace cases. Avoid the tempting criterion “has version and namespace validation logic” by itself; prioritize evidence of explicit namespace-source handling and negative compatibility tests.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a trajectory implementing serialized export/import metadata in a CLI with a default namespace flag, penalize superficial validation that does not distinguish an explicitly supplied CLI namespace from the flag’s default, chooses or validates a document version without evidence it matches the intended format contract, or lacks negative tests for unsupported versions and namespace conflicts. This flaw is judgeable from visible plans, diffs, or tests showing the importer compares any non-empty CLI namespace directly against the YAML namespace, uses an arbitrary version string, only updates happy-path fixtures, or fails to demonstrate document-only namespace import behavior.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial metadata validation misses CLI-default namespace semantics

metadata.environment: Go CLI using defaulted namespace flags and shared serialization structs
required_evidence: explicit handling of whether the CLI namespace was actually provided
resolved namespace used consistently for every imported resource
clear unsupported-version rejection tied to the intended document format
tests or visible checks for invalid version, namespace mismatch, and single-source namespace behavior
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: presence of version/namespace fields plus any generic mismatch check

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory explicitly distinguishes CLI default from user-provided namespace, resolves namespace precedence correctly, rejects unsupported versions, and includes or plans targeted negative tests.
scale.2: Minor risk: the trajectory mostly handles namespace precedence and version compatibility but leaves one edge case or test implicit rather than clearly demonstrated.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory adds metadata and generic validation, but visible evidence is ambiguous about CLI default-vs-explicit namespace handling or targeted invalid-version/mismatch tests.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory validates by comparing any non-empty CLI namespace to the document namespace, uses an unsupported/arbitrary version contract, or only updates happy-path fixtures without negative coverage.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory’s implemented or planned logic would reject document-only namespaces because of the CLI default, ignore the document namespace despite the task requirements, or silently accept unsupported versions while claiming validation is complete.

experiences.title: Do not reward extraction-only refactors without boundary and hygiene checks
experiences.description: Retrieve this when a TypeScript/React task asks to move inline DOM Selection/Range logic from a hook or component into a reusable utility.
experiences.context: In small frontend refactor tasks, a criterion that only checks whether inline range manipulation was moved into a helper can be misleading. The extraction idea is still appropriate when the trajectory clearly preserves the existing selection data contract, puts the helper in the feature-level shared utility area, keeps the change minimal, and shows compile/lint-safe code. It is not enough when the agent merely wraps the code in any function, places it in a hook-private helper or overly broad global utility, changes null/return behavior without need, adds unrelated selection APIs, or leaves visible style/type-quality issues. During early exploration, absence of the utility should not be penalized; this warning applies once the trajectory has begun or claims to have completed the refactor.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics asked for a reusable selection restoration utility and delegation from the hook. That was directionally correct but too broad: it allowed high confidence for patches that created a helper while ignoring whether the helper was actually in the intended shared boundary, whether the API stayed minimal and compatible with the saved anchor/focus-node contract, and whether the new file followed repository hygiene. For similar tasks, do not generate a criterion whose strongest evidence is only an import plus a call to a newly named helper. A better rubric should focus on the observable diff shape: the inline DOM Range/Selection block is removed from the hook, a small selection-specific utility is added in the feature's reusable utility area rather than a hook-only or unrelated global location, the hook passes the same saved selection object without changing save semantics, the helper does only the extracted restoration behavior, and visible validation or code review evidence does not show type/style problems such as invalid imports, unnecessary API expansion, or lint-visible whitespace. Avoid treating arbitrary helper names, broad utility modules, or extra generalized selection functions as proof of correctness unless the task or surrounding code clearly calls for that broader API.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear to satisfy a selection-restoration extraction task only superficially: the hook delegates to a helper, but visible evidence shows the helper is placed in a hook-private or unrelated global utility area instead of the feature's reusable utility boundary, changes the saved selection contract or null/return behavior without a task-driven reason, introduces unrelated selection/cursor helpers, leaves duplicated inline Range/Selection manipulation, or contains visible type/lint/style hygiene issues in the new utility. Apply this only after the agent has started editing or claimed completion, not during initial file discovery.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial or Misbounded Selection Utility Extraction

metadata.environment: TypeScript React frontend using browser DOM Selection and Range APIs
evidence_to_check: location and scope of the new utility module
whether hook-private inline range code was actually removed
whether the hook passes the same saved anchor/focus node and offset data
whether the helper performs only the requested restoration behavior
visible compile, type, lint, or diff-hygiene signals
avoid_using_as_sufficient_evidence: presence of any helper function with a selection-related name
a passing transpile step that does not run lint or full type/style checks
broad claims of reusability without checking module boundary

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the extraction is minimal, in an appropriate feature-level reusable utility location, preserves the saved selection contract, removes inline duplication, and shows no visible type/style hygiene concerns.
scale.2: Minor concern only: the main extraction boundary and behavior look correct, but there are small naming, documentation, or validation gaps that do not visibly change behavior or scope.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the helper exists and the hook delegates, but the trajectory leaves uncertainty or weak evidence about utility placement, API minimality, style hygiene, or preservation of the original selection contract.
scale.4: Clear concern: the trajectory places the helper in a hook-private or overly broad utility area, changes API/return/null behavior unnecessarily, leaves some duplicated range manipulation, or introduces visible style/type issues despite completing the extraction.
scale.5: Severe concern: the refactor is mostly superficial or risky, with misplaced utility boundaries, unrelated generalized APIs, contract drift, remaining inline duplication, or unresolved visible compile/type/lint problems in the modified selection code.

experiences.title: Do not treat lifecycle-table edits as complete release recognition
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go vulnerability scanner task combines OS EOL/lifecycle fixes with making a new distro release recognized for package or CVE metadata collection.
experiences.context: This applies in Vuls-like Go repositories where Ubuntu or another distro release is represented in multiple independent registries: lifecycle/EOL tables, vulnerability data source support maps, OVAL/kernel handling, and sometimes module or dictionary data source versions. The misleading case is a rubric that rewards adding correct support dates to the lifecycle map, or merely identifying scanner distribution parsing, while the task also says package/CVE metadata is omitted for the new release. A lifecycle-only criterion can still be appropriate as a subcriterion when the task is strictly about EOL reporting, or during early investigation before the agent has attempted a final patch, but it should not be the primary success criterion once the trajectory claims the release is recognized end-to-end.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics asked whether Ubuntu 20.04 extended support was set to April 2030 and Ubuntu 22.04 was added to the EOL table, sometimes with a generic mention of distribution detection. That was too narrow: the visible task language required the scanner to gather package and CVE metadata for Ubuntu 22.04, and the trajectories repeatedly exposed separate support gates such as private supported-version maps and OVAL release switches that can reject or skip a release even after EOL lookup succeeds. A better rubric should evaluate whether the agent traced and updated every visible release-support gate that affects metadata processing, and whether it validated those paths with package tests or targeted smoke checks. Avoid the tempting criterion that a correct lifecycle map alone means the release is recognized. Replacement criteria should prioritize evidence from greps/diffs/tests showing: the EOL behavior for the older LTS, the new release in vulnerability metadata support registries, the new release accepted by OVAL or equivalent enrichment code, no unsupported-release errors remaining, no malformed broad sed edits, and validation beyond a single lifecycle smoke test.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: When the task requires both lifecycle correctness and recognition of a new distro release for package/CVE metadata processing, penalize a trajectory that treats lifecycle-table updates or generic OS parsing as sufficient while leaving visible independent metadata support gates unhandled or unvalidated. This includes failing to investigate or update supported-release/codename registries, OVAL or equivalent release switches that return unsupported-release errors, data-source version compatibility where visible, or tests/smoke checks that exercise metadata collection for the new release. This flaw is especially severe when the trajectory claims completion after only EOL checks or when diffs show malformed edits or missing support-map changes.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Incomplete End-to-End Release Recognition

metadata.environment: Go vulnerability scanner with hardcoded distro lifecycle and vulnerability metadata support paths
task_signals: EOL or lifecycle support dates must be corrected
new distro release is not recognized
package or CVE metadata is omitted
visible_evidence_to_prioritize: diffs or planned edits touching all independent release support registries discovered in the trajectory
unsupported-release guards, supported-version maps, codename maps, or OVAL/kernel switches
tests or targeted commands for both EOL behavior and metadata enrichment support
git diff or formatting checks showing no corruption from broad text substitution
avoid_as_sufficient_evidence: only adding standard/extended support dates to a lifecycle map
only inspecting generic scanner OS parsing
only running a lifecycle smoke test
claiming unrelated test failures without checking the new metadata path

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory clearly identifies and handles all visible lifecycle and metadata support gates for the new release, with appropriate validation and clean diffs.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory covers lifecycle and most metadata gates, but one low-risk compatibility or validation detail remains only partially evidenced.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory updates lifecycle data and one metadata path, but leaves another visible support gate or unsupported-release path uninvestigated or untested.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory mostly focuses on lifecycle dates or generic detection while visible metadata support maps/switches remain missing, or validation exercises only EOL behavior.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory claims the release is recognized after lifecycle-only edits, ignores visible unsupported metadata paths, or introduces malformed broad edits while lacking meaningful validation.

experiences.title: Distinguish proxy resource-cache reuse from host certificate-cache sharing
experiences.description: Use when a Go reverse-tunnel refactor asks to remove a redundant single local-site slice and eliminate duplicate local-site cache/watchers by reusing the proxy/server cache.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go codebase where a reverse-tunnel server has exactly one local/in-cluster site but stores it as a slice, and the local-site constructor creates a separate caching access point or resource watcher even though the server already has a local/proxy access point. This is most useful once the trajectory has inspected or edited the server constructor and local-site constructor. It is less useful for unrelated remote-site cache creation, generic cleanup, or tasks where multiple local sites are intentionally supported. Be cautious when the trajectory focuses only on host certificate caching: that cache may be separate from the duplicated resource watcher/cache described by the task.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics often judged whether a certificateCache was shared at the server level. That is a tempting but usually wrong proxy for this task: the duplicated resource monitoring comes from the local-site constructing a new caching access point/resource cache, not merely from host certificate cache allocation. A better rubric should reward visible evidence that the local-site path stops calling the server's new caching-access-point factory for the local cluster and instead uses the existing server/proxy local access point, while preserving the separate remote-site cache behavior. It should also check that the singleton refactor is complete enough that the server stores one local site and direct local-site operations replace slice append/iteration/removal. Prioritize trajectory evidence such as: searches for all local-site slice references; constructor changes assigning one local site rather than appending; local-site constructor using server-owned local auth/access-point/peer-client dependencies; removal of now-unused local caching factory fields if they only served the duplicate local cache; and validation by gofmt/tests. Avoid criteria that consider adding a server-level certificateCache or passing certificateCache into the local-site constructor sufficient, especially if the code still calls the per-local-site caching access point factory.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Local site reuses existing proxy resource cache
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show that the local/in-cluster site no longer constructs its own resource caching access point or watcher. Strong evidence includes changing the local-site constructor to derive its client, peer client, and access point from the server's existing local/proxy dependencies; removing the local-site call to the new caching-access-point factory; and completing the single-local-site refactor so server code assigns and uses one local-site pointer instead of appending to and iterating/removing from a local-site slice. The criterion should not give high credit for only moving or sharing a host certificate cache while leaving the duplicate resource access-point cache construction in place.

required_visible_evidence: local-site constructor no longer calls the per-site caching access-point factory for the local cluster
local-site access point is sourced from the server/proxy local access point or equivalent existing proxy cache
server stores one local-site instance and local-site call sites are converted from slice semantics to direct singleton use
remote-site-specific cache behavior is not unnecessarily collapsed into the local-site change
anti_evidence: trajectory focuses only on certificateCache sharing
new local-site signature merely passes certificateCache while still building a new resource access point
remaining localSites slice append/iteration/removal references
broad sed edits leave damaged or unvalidated Go code

scale.1: No evidence that the local-site resource cache construction or localSites slice design is being corrected; the trajectory only explores unrelated files or repeats searches.
scale.2: Weak evidence: identifies the relevant local-site slice or cache issue, but proposed edits focus mainly on certificateCache sharing or leave the duplicate caching access-point call intact.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: partially converts the local-site slice to a singleton or partially changes cache use, but important references remain, the local-site constructor still has ambiguous/new cache construction, or validation is absent.
scale.4: Strong evidence: removes most singleton-slice uses and clearly redirects the local-site resource access point to the existing server/proxy cache, with only minor cleanup or validation gaps.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: fully converts local-site storage and all call sites to a singleton, removes local per-site resource cache construction and unused factory plumbing for that path, preserves remote-site behavior, and shows gofmt/tests or equivalent validation.

experiences.title: Do not use dead-code removal as the main success proxy for lint-complexity refactors
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python/Ruff task combines removal of apparently unused logic with reducing function complexity, especially when lint failures may be hidden by per-file ignores or config suppressions.
experiences.context: This warning applies in Python repositories using Ruff or similar static analysis where the task names both a dead/untested code path and concrete complexity violations such as C901, PLR0912, or PLR0915. The misleading case is a trajectory that successfully finds an unused helper/regex and removes it, but treats that as enough even though the main acceptance condition is making the target function compliant without relying on existing suppressions and preserving parsing/categorization behavior. The original dead-code-removal idea is still appropriate when the task is solely about removing unused code, or when visible evidence already shows the lint gate is independently clean after suppressions are removed and behavior is protected by relevant tests.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often rewarded locating and removing the unused Aspects/find_aspects logic. That criterion is not wrong, but it is too weak and can be misleading for a lint-complexity refactor: an agent can remove the dead branch while still leaving the per-file ignore in place, relying on a suppressed Ruff run, or performing a large helper extraction that has not been validated against the real complexity thresholds and subject semantics. A better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory recognizes that normal Ruff output may be suppressed, reproduces or accounts for the violations without the suppression, changes the implementation so the target function itself is under the configured complexity limits, removes the obsolete ignore entry when appropriate, and verifies behavior with existing subject-extraction tests. Avoid generating a criterion that treats “no test coverage for the dead code” or “grep found no external references” as sufficient evidence of task completion. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence of unsuppressed lint validation, removal or intentional handling of stale Ruff suppressions, and preservation of category-specific subject handling and normalization behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Dead-code-only completion proxy in a suppressed lint refactor
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat removal of an unused helper/regex path as the main evidence of success while failing to establish that the target complexity violations are fixed under the relevant Ruff configuration. This applies when the visible trajectory shows existing per-file ignores or other suppressions for the named rules, default Ruff runs with no diagnostics despite known suppressions, or a refactor that is validated only by tests/default lint rather than by an unsuppressed or suppression-removed complexity check. Also consider whether the trajectory protects subject extraction semantics, including independent category counts and post-processing behavior, instead of only proving that the unused path has no tests.

metadata.environment: Python project using Ruff with pyproject.toml per-file ignores
metadata.task_type: maintainability refactor with concrete complexity lint violations and an unused logic path
visible_evidence_to_check: per-file ignore or suppression for the target file and rules
attempts to reproduce complexity diagnostics with suppression removed, bypassed, or accounted for
post-refactor Ruff check for C901/PLR0912/PLR0915 under the intended configuration
removal or explicit justification of stale lint suppression
tests or reasoning covering subject category preservation
metadata.misleading_proxy: finding and removing unused Aspects/find_aspects logic alone

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory treats dead-code removal as one subtask, explicitly accounts for suppressed lint diagnostics, validates the real complexity rules after the change, and preserves behavior.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory emphasizes dead-code removal but also performs some unsuppressed lint or configuration validation and behavior checks.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory removes or plans to remove the unused path and runs tests/default Ruff, but only partially accounts for suppressions or does not clearly show the intended complexity gate is clean.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory centers success on unused Aspects removal and passing tests/default Ruff while visible per-file ignores or suppressions still undermine the lint evidence.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory removes the unused path and declares the task solved despite known suppressed complexity violations, no meaningful unsuppressed lint validation, and little or no attention to subject categorization semantics.

experiences.title: Judge Effective Platform-Gated Runtime Behavior
experiences.description: Use when a task adds a configuration value or feature that is valid generally but should only take effect on a specific backend, platform, or library-version combination with fallback behavior elsewhere.
experiences.context: Applies in a qutebrowser/PyQt-style codebase when the visible task requires adding a new config option whose runtime effect is supported only on QtWebEngine, a minimum Qt version, and non-macOS, while unsupported environments must retain existing non-overlay behavior. This is most useful once the trajectory has identified or edited the config schema, migration logic, stylesheet/runtime behavior, backend settings, startup argument handling, or platform/version helpers. In very early repository discovery, use it as a progress-oriented criterion rather than expecting complete implementation. Do not retrieve it for tasks that only add a static enum/documentation entry with no environment-dependent behavior, or for platform-neutral features where fallback semantics are not part of the requested contract.
experiences.experience: The prior platform-gating rubrics were useful because the decisive visible issue was not whether the agent mentioned Qt version or macOS, but whether the implementation made the new option effective only at the real runtime boundary and preserved old behavior elsewhere. Better rubrics should ask for coordinated evidence: the new config value is accepted and documented; the enablement mechanism is placed where the backend actually turns the feature on, such as startup/runtime feature configuration for the supported web engine rather than an unrelated setting; the availability check uses the project’s existing Qt-version and platform helpers; unsupported environments normalize the new value to an existing non-overlay behavior; and migrations/defaults remain valid under the new enum. Avoid rewarding tempting proxies such as comments saying the feature is gated, adding the enum alone, using a generic scrollbar visibility attribute as if it created overlay scrollbars, adding CSS that hides scrollbars or uses unsupported overlay styling, or rejecting the value entirely on unsupported backends instead of allowing it with fallback. Prioritize visible diffs, summaries, or tests showing that old values like always/never/when-searching still behave as before, WebKit/macOS/old-Qt paths do not accidentally enable the new effect, and old boolean configuration values are migrated to a valid value consistent with the new default and fallback contract.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Effective Support-Boundary Implementation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the new configuration value is both accepted and implemented at the correct runtime boundary, with the feature enabled only for the supported backend/version/platform combination and with unsupported environments falling back to existing non-overlay behavior. Strong evidence includes use of established project helpers for Qt-version and platform checks, backend-specific placement of the actual enablement mechanism, preservation of existing scrollbar visibility semantics for all preexisting values, and migration/default/documentation updates that keep old boolean values valid under the new option.

required_evidence: The new configuration value is added to the schema or equivalent validation source and described with its support and fallback semantics.
Runtime enablement occurs in the code path that can actually affect the supported backend, not merely in unrelated UI or generic visibility settings.
The implementation checks the minimum Qt version and excludes macOS using existing project utilities or clearly equivalent mechanisms.
Unsupported environments treat the new value as an existing non-overlay behavior instead of enabling the feature unconditionally or breaking validation.
Existing values and old boolean migration behavior remain valid and semantically consistent.
common_negative_evidence: Only documentation or enum metadata is changed.
The code hides scrollbars or toggles generic scrollbar visibility and calls that overlay support.
Platform/version checks appear only in comments or in a code path that does not control the feature.
The new value is disabled entirely on unsupported backends rather than accepted with fallback.
Migration changes map old values to a more restrictive or semantically different behavior without justification.

scale.1: No meaningful implementation evidence: the trajectory is still searching/repeating commands, or only identifies files without adding or planning the support boundary.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the new value is added to docs/schema or comments, but runtime behavior is missing, unconditional, or based on an unrelated scrollbar mechanism.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: some platform/version/backend checks or runtime edits are present, but the checks are not clearly at the effective boundary, fallback behavior is incomplete, or migration/default consistency is unresolved.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the implementation mostly gates the feature at the relevant runtime boundary and preserves unsupported fallback behavior, with only minor gaps such as incomplete docs, tests, or migration details.
scale.5: Complete evidence: schema/docs, runtime enablement, backend/version/platform gating, unsupported fallback, preserved old values, and boolean migration/default behavior are all visibly coordinated and validated or made readily testable.

experiences.title: End-to-End Multi-SAN Certificate Data Path
experiences.description: Use when a Go CLI certificate-signing task expands a single hostname field into multiple SANs while preserving a legacy single-name API field.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go codebase where a CLI command builds a certificate signing request, request types are protobuf-generated, and server-side certificate issuance maps request names into X.509 SANs. Retrieve this when the task or trajectory mentions comma-separated hostnames/IPs, Subject Alternative Names, a legacy singular server-name field, and a new repeated names field. It is most useful after the agent has located at least two layers of the data path, or during final review when judging whether edits are coherent. It is premature during pure repository discovery unless the rubric is framed as evidence of tracing the full path. Do not apply to unrelated certificate changes that do not cross CLI/API/server boundaries, and downweight generated-protobuf requirements if the project does not use checked-in generated code.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics correctly focused on the behavioral contract: comma-separated --host input must become a list of SANs, the first entry must remain the CommonName/legacy single-name value, and server-side certificate generation must include every name. This was useful because visible trajectories often showed whether the agent had traced the real data flow from CLI parsing, through the request type, into certificate generation. However, a more discriminative rubric should not stop at that high-level behavior. In this kind of task, correctness also depends on preserving wire/API compatibility and keeping generated protobuf code coherent. A patch that only changes flag help, adds a repeated field plus getter, or passes ServerNames in ordinary Go code while generated marshal/size/unmarshal code is stale or corrupted is not strong progress. Likewise, splitting the host string but leaving the legacy ServerName as the raw comma-separated input, omitting fallback for older clients that send only ServerName, or using ServerNames only on the server can break compatibility. The better criterion should reward evidence that the agent has implemented and validated the entire chain: parse and normalize the comma-separated list once in the database-signing CLI path; use the first non-empty value consistently for CommonName and legacy ServerName; populate the repeated field with all intended SAN entries; update the proto source and generated code by regeneration or exact, function-scoped manual edits; have the auth server merge/prefer repeated names while still honoring the legacy field; and verify via targeted tests/builds or careful inspection. Avoid tempting proxy criteria such as documentation updates, flag-description changes, or tests that only assert request fields without proving generated serialization and server SAN behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates end-to-end implementation of multi-SAN database certificate signing across CLI parsing, request schema/serialization, server certificate issuance, and compatibility.
