Strong evidence includes parsing comma-separated hostnames/IPs in the relevant database certificate CLI path; consistently using the first parsed entry as the CSR CommonName and legacy singular server-name field; populating a repeated server-names field with all entries; updating both protobuf source and checked-in generated code, including serialization/deserialization/size support or a successful regeneration path; server-side SAN assignment that includes all repeated names and still falls back to or merges the legacy singular field for older callers; and validation through focused tests, build output, or precise inspection that generated-code edits are not corrupting unrelated message types.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete Multi-SAN Signing Contract

required_visible_evidence: CLI request construction uses a parsed host list rather than the raw comma-separated string for all new behavior
First parsed host is used for CommonName and legacy singular server-name compatibility
All parsed hosts are sent through a repeated request field intended for SANs
Server certificate generation maps the full repeated list into certificate SAN inputs and preserves legacy fallback behavior
Protobuf source and generated Go bindings are consistent, including marshal, unmarshal, and size handling or successful regeneration
Validation or inspection addresses both single-host and multi-host behavior
common_failure_evidence: Only the proto field/getter is added while generated serialization is missing
Broad sed/script edits corrupt unrelated generated protobuf methods
ServerName remains the raw comma-separated string
Server ignores legacy ServerName when ServerNames is absent
Only flag help or superficial tests are updated
metadata.environment: Go CLI/server repository with checked-in protobuf-generated request types and X.509 certificate generation

scale.1: No substantive evidence of the multi-SAN data path being implemented; the trajectory is limited to exploration, superficial flag text, or a single isolated schema/code edit.
scale.2: Partial progress in one or two layers, such as adding a repeated field or splitting the CLI host string, but missing key compatibility behavior, server SAN mapping, or generated-code consistency.
scale.3: Moderate progress comparable to an in-progress parent trajectory: the agent has identified and partially edited the CLI/API/server path, but visible evidence still shows unresolved generated protobuf work, fragile manual edits, lack of validation, or an important compatibility gap.
scale.4: Strong evidence that the CLI, request construction, server SAN mapping, and legacy fallback are implemented coherently, with generated protobuf code mostly addressed and only minor robustness, documentation, or validation gaps remaining.
scale.5: Complete, validated end-to-end support: parsed multi-host input flows through compatible singular and repeated request fields into all certificate SANs; generated protobuf code is correctly regenerated or comprehensively patched; single-host/legacy behavior is preserved; and targeted tests or builds support the change.

experiences.title: Avoid over-crediting superficial pending-state UI fixes
experiences.description: Use this when a React/TypeScript UI task asks for async-action feedback and duplicate-submission prevention, and the trajectory adds loading state/spinners/disabled buttons in an existing settings flow.
experiences.context: This applies in Element/Matrix-style React TypeScript settings components where the bug is at an async UI submission boundary, such as a cryptographic reset button that invokes a long-running SDK call before showing auth prompts. The misleading pattern is generating only a broad positive rubric like “show progress, warn the user, and prevent duplicate submissions”; that can over-credit trajectories that merely add an `isLoading`/`isResetting` boolean and spinner while leaving visible integration problems: broken Compound component props, changed breadcrumb semantics, malformed or missing i18n strings, wrong spinner imports/API, omitted do-not-close guidance, unvalidated TypeScript errors, or unrelated snapshot/layout churn. The original idea is still appropriate as part of the acceptance criteria when the trajectory has already preserved existing UI contracts and validated the change. During early exploration, absence of the implementation should be treated as incomplete progress rather than as evidence that the final fix will be correct.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics correctly identified the core user-facing requirement—immediate pending feedback and a single reset flow—but they were too broad to discriminate correct patches from superficial ones. For this class of task, do not make the main judgeable criterion simply “has a loading state, spinner, disabled Continue, and duplicate guard.” That proxy is tempting but misleading because agents often add those tokens while breaking the surrounding panel or omitting a required visible warning. A better rubric should require the async boundary to be guarded before awaiting the long-running call, while also preserving the existing component API/layout and localized UX contract. Prioritize visible evidence such as: the original breadcrumb/pages/back behavior remains compatible; translations are valid and referenced keys exist; the progress UI includes explicit do-not-close/refresh guidance, not just a spinner; disabled/hidden controls actually cover repeated reset entry points; and focused tests or type checks do not show new errors in the edited component. Avoid rewarding mere presence of `useState`, `disabled`, or `InlineSpinner` unless the trajectory shows these are integrated without regressions.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial async-state fix with UI integration regressions
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear to address async reset feedback by adding loading state, spinners, or disabled buttons, but whose visible evidence shows the implementation is not safely integrated into the existing React/TypeScript settings panel. Examples include unresolved TypeScript/test errors in the edited component, malformed or missing i18n strings, incorrect imports or props for existing UI components, changed breadcrumb/page semantics unrelated to the bug, missing explicit guidance not to close or refresh during the reset, or a guard that does not clearly prevent repeated invocations before the awaited reset call.

metadata.environment: React/TypeScript web settings UI using localized strings and existing design-system components
metadata.high_risk_proxy_to_avoid: Counting `isResetting`, `disabled`, or spinner additions as sufficient without checking integration and validation
preferred_visible_evidence: state/guard is set before awaiting the async reset operation
existing component API and navigation/breadcrumb behavior are preserved
localized progress and do-not-close/refresh guidance are both present and valid
controls that could start or interrupt duplicate flows are disabled or hidden consistently
focused validation does not expose new errors in the modified component

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the pending-state/duplicate-submission fix is integrated cleanly, preserves surrounding UI contracts, includes valid localized guidance, and visible validation is clean or only has unrelated failures.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory has the right async guard and guidance but leaves small uncertainty about styling, snapshots, or validation without visible component breakage.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory adds loading/disabled behavior but has incomplete proof of duplicate-call prevention, incomplete do-not-close guidance, or unverified i18n/UI integration.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory relies on superficial loading-state additions while showing concrete integration problems such as wrong component props/imports, malformed/missing translation keys, changed existing breadcrumb semantics, or focused tests/type checks failing in the touched area.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory either produces no substantive patch despite claiming progress, or the patch both fails validation and breaks existing panel structure/navigation while only superficially adding spinner/disabled UI.

experiences.title: Exact Exported Config API Contract
experiences.description: Use when a Go configuration task explicitly reports undefined exported symbols for defaults and decode hooks, and the trajectory is deciding or editing the package API surface.
experiences.context: Applies in Go repositories where configuration loading uses mapstructure/Viper-style decode hooks and the task states that consumers need public symbols such as a default-config constructor and an exported decode-hook slice. It is most useful once the trajectory has found an existing private hook list, a test/helper or defaulting source for complete defaults, or a current diff touching the config package. It is less useful for unrelated schema-only failures, for very early repository exploration before the relevant config code has been inspected, or after the exports already compile and the remaining question is broader schema/model alignment.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics focused on whether the agent implemented the required public exports. That criterion is useful when the visible trajectory shows no edits, repeated searches despite the task naming the missing symbols, malformed attempts to append code, duplicate exported variables, unused imports, or a wrong export name/signature. In those situations, visible evidence about API absence or broken compilation is strongly diagnostic. However, the criterion should not be reduced to a superficial 'capitalized names exist' check: a better rubric should require the exported decode hooks to reuse the existing internal hook behavior, the default constructor to return a complete configuration from the existing default source, internal loading behavior to remain intact, and the package to compile. Avoid tempting proxies such as passing visible tests that do not reference the new API, repeatedly grepping for absent references, inventing a differently named function, duplicating hook lists in conflicting locations, or hand-writing incomplete defaults without validating against the package’s existing expected defaults.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Public Config Export Contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement the reported public configuration API exactly and safely: expose a public mapstructure decode-hook slice with the same hook behavior already used by the loader, provide the required public default-configuration constructor returning a complete default config from the package’s canonical default source, update or alias internal uses without changing load semantics, avoid duplicate declarations or malformed edits, and verify that the config package compiles/tests. The judgment should prioritize visible diff evidence and compile output over searches showing that visible tests do not yet reference the symbols.

required_exports: public decode hook slice with mapstructure-compatible element type
public default configuration constructor returning *Config or task-specified equivalent
evidence_to_check: existing private hook list is exported or safely aliased
loader composes the same base hooks plus any contextual internal hooks
default constructor covers all major config sections using existing defaults/test helper/defaulting source
no duplicate declarations, unused imports, or appended package/import fragments
targeted Go build or config package tests pass
avoid_as_sufficient: symbols exist with wrong name or incomplete contents
manual defaults omit sections needed for schema validation

scale.1: No implementation progress toward the required exports, or the trajectory only repeats searches/tests that do not exercise the reported public API.
scale.2: Recognizes the needed exports but has not edited safely, or proposes/starts changes with wrong names, incomplete defaults, or no evidence of preserving existing hook behavior.
scale.3: Equivalent parent-child behavior: identifies the correct API contract and may make partial edits, but there is not yet enough visible evidence that exports are complete, compile-safe, and behavior-preserving.
scale.4: Strong implementation evidence: the required public symbols are added with correct general shape, reuse existing hook behavior, include a reasonably complete default config, and internal loader behavior is preserved, with only minor validation gaps remaining.
scale.5: Complete, compile-verified implementation: exact required public exports exist, defaults are sourced or mirrored comprehensively from canonical package defaults, decode hooks remain compatible for external decoder composition, loader semantics are unchanged, formatting/build/tests confirm the package is sound, and no duplicate or malformed edits remain.

experiences.title: Exception-Specific HEAD-to-GET Fallback
experiences.description: Use when a Python HTTP/link-checking task asks for a narrow fallback behavior: an exception from an initial lightweight request should enter an existing retry path rather than broader broken/error handling.
experiences.context: Applies in repositories like Sphinx or similar Python projects where visible trajectory evidence shows an existing request flow that tries HEAD first, falls back to GET for selected HEAD failures, and then classifies the result after the GET/HEAD response. It is especially relevant when the task names a concrete exception such as `requests.exceptions.TooManyRedirects` and the code currently catches a neighboring exception such as `HTTPError`. The criterion is strongest after the agent has located the fallback code or begun editing imports/exception handlers. It is premature if the trajectory has only explored files without finding the request flow, and it is not the right primary criterion for tasks about changing global redirect limits, anchor checking, request-wrapper internals, or adding tests only.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases judged the core behavioral contract: a `TooManyRedirects` raised by the initial HEAD attempt must be handled at the same inner fallback point as existing HEAD failures, causing the existing GET request path to run. This aligned well because the decisive visible evidence was not generic progress or test activity, but whether the agent imported/referenced the specific exception and extended the precise `except` around the HEAD request without moving the behavior into the outer generic error handler. A better rubric should reward evidence that the existing GET fallback is reused, that existing `HTTPError` handling remains intact, and that failures from the subsequent GET are still allowed to propagate to the established broken-link/status handling. Avoid making test coverage the primary criterion for a minimal bugfix unless the task explicitly requires tests; absence of a new regression test may be useful secondary evidence but can incorrectly underrate an otherwise complete narrow patch. Also avoid broad criteria such as “handle redirects better” or “catch all request exceptions,” because the important boundary is exception-specific and location-specific: catch the named HEAD exception before it reaches the outer broken-link path, while preserving successful, redirected, anchored, and GET-failure semantics.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement the narrow fallback contract by handling the named redirect-loop exception at the existing initial-request fallback site, so that a HEAD failure due to too many redirects retries with the established GET flow rather than being classified as broken immediately. Strong evidence includes locating the HEAD-first/GET-fallback code, importing or otherwise correctly referencing the specific exception type, changing the inner HEAD exception handler to include it alongside the existing handled exception, and preserving the subsequent GET request, `raise_for_status`, redirect classification, anchor behavior, and outer error handling.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Specific HEAD Exception Enters Existing GET Fallback

prioritize_evidence: The agent identifies the existing HEAD-first request path and its GET fallback.
The named exception from the HTTP library is handled in the same inner fallback block as the existing HEAD failure exception.
The existing GET retry call and its error/status handling are reused rather than replaced or swallowed.
The outer generic broken-link handling is not used as the fix for the HEAD exception.
avoid_overweighting: Installing dependencies or attempting to run tests without completing the code change.
Adding a regression test as a substitute for the implementation.
Broadly catching all exceptions or changing global redirect behavior.
Editing unrelated request wrappers or link classification logic without evidence it is necessary.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory has found or changed the relevant HEAD-to-GET fallback path; it may only explore the repository or focus on unrelated redirect/test machinery.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory identifies the bug or imports/references the named exception, but has not yet connected it to the inner HEAD fallback handler or risks leaving the exception to the outer broken-link path.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory is positioned to make the correct change or partially modifies the fallback, but visible evidence is incomplete about preserving existing GET retry and error/status semantics.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory updates the inner HEAD fallback to catch the named exception and keeps the existing GET retry flow, with only minor uncertainty such as limited validation or incidental comment/test work.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory clearly implements the exact exception-specific inner fallback, preserves existing HTTPError, GET failure, redirect, and anchor behavior, and validates or reviews the focused change without introducing unrelated request-flow changes.

experiences.title: Do not let success logging eclipse required error-path coverage
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task combines observability on success with safety/error-normalization requirements for file I/O, and the trajectory visibly satisfies the logging part while only partially auditing read/seek failure paths.
experiences.context: Applies in Python parser-style code where the task explicitly requires both: converting file read/seek failures such as OSError and OverflowError into a domain parsing error, and emitting a debug log on successful parsing. A rubric about successful debug logging is valid only as a secondary criterion or when the trajectory already shows comprehensive handling of all relevant file operations. It is misleading as the main criterion when the visible work adds a success log and maybe handles one fallback read/seek path, but has not inventoried every direct read, seek, mmap/fallback, or helper-based structured read in the parser.
experiences.experience: The generated rubrics repeatedly focused on emitting a debug log with detected versions after successful ELF parsing. That is a real requirement, but it is not sufficient to predict correctness for a task whose primary reliability goal is safe handling of read and seek failures. In several trajectories, the agent added the success log and caught OverflowError in one fallback block while leaving other visible file operations unprotected, such as structured reads through a helper, seeks used while locating sections, direct reads of string tables/data, or mmap-related fallback paths. A better rubric should focus on whether the implementation systematically normalizes both OSError and OverflowError from all parser file operations into the parser’s domain error, with tests or reasoning that exercise seek and read failures on each path. Avoid the tempting criterion “successful parse logs detected versions” as the sole or dominant rubric unless the visible trajectory already demonstrates complete error-path coverage; treat logging as a small companion check. Prioritize evidence such as a complete inventory of file-operation sites, helper functions for safe read/seek or equivalent local wrapping, preservation of existing ParseError behavior, and targeted tests/mocks that force OSError and OverflowError from both read and seek operations.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The implementation is incomplete if it adds or verifies successful debug logging but does not comprehensively convert all relevant parser file read and seek failures into the parser-level error. This includes direct reads, direct seeks, structured-read helpers, mmap fallback reads/seeks, and any section/header traversal file operations visible in the trajectory. The flaw is especially concerning when only one fallback block is updated while other read/seek sites can still leak OSError or OverflowError.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Incomplete read/seek exception normalization

metadata.task_type: Python binary/file parser reliability change
metadata.acceptable_outcome: file-operation failures are converted to the parser's domain parse error without bypassing existing failure handling
metadata.logging_role: success debug logging is required but should not substitute for error-path coverage

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory shows a complete audit or helper-based approach covering read and seek failures for both OSError and OverflowError, with success logging handled separately.
scale.2: Minor evidence of incompleteness: most file-operation sites are covered, but one low-risk or indirectly covered site is not clearly justified or tested.
scale.3: Moderate issue: the trajectory handles some important read/seek paths and adds success logging, but coverage of other visible parser file operations is uncertain or untested.
scale.4: Clear issue: the implementation visibly updates only selected paths, such as a fallback read/seek block, while other direct reads or seeks remain able to leak OSError or OverflowError.
scale.5: Severe issue: the trajectory primarily or exclusively satisfies successful debug logging while leaving most required read/seek error handling unimplemented or unaudited.

experiences.title: Do not overgeneralize Etc/GMT fixes into universal offset formatting
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django timezone regression involves Trunc()/Extract(), `_get_timezone_name()`, and backend sign flipping for `Etc/GMT±N` zones, especially if a proposed rubric says all timezones or all backends must receive `+HH`/`-HH` offsets.
experiences.context: This applies in a Django/Python timezone-handling task where the visible trajectory has identified `TimezoneMixin.get_tzname()`, `django.utils.timezone._get_timezone_name()`, and backend `_prepare_tzname_delta()` methods. The misleading pattern is treating the `Etc/GMT-10` regression as a requirement to convert every pytz, zoneinfo, fixed-offset, UTC, or DST-aware named timezone into numeric offsets, or as a requirement to modify a backend helper without confirming that the patched value is what the ORM actually passes. The original idea remains useful only for the narrow class of fixed-offset-style names such as `Etc/GMT±N` and timezone objects whose `tzname(None)` already supplies an offset-like abbreviation; it should not be extended to ordinary named zones such as `America/New_York`, `US/Eastern`, `Europe/London`, or `Australia/Melbourne`, where database-side named-zone rules and DST behavior should be preserved.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often rewarded statements like “return `+HH`/`-HH` for all database backends” or “generate correct offset strings for any timezone using a reference datetime.” That criterion is misleading because the bug is not a general need to flatten all timezones into offsets. The narrow contract is that the value flowing from `TimezoneMixin` into backend datetime SQL must avoid passing the literal signed `Etc/GMT±N` name into sign-flipping code, while preserving normal timezone names. Rubrics should therefore prefer visible evidence that the active call path uses a simple timezone-name contract such as `tzinfo.tzname(None)` with fallback to `str(tzinfo)`, or an equivalently narrow special case for fixed-offset/Etc/GMT zones, plus checks that ordinary named zones remain names. Avoid rubrics that require date-dependent offset calculation for DST zones, demand exact formatting such as only `+HH`/`-HH` across all cases, or credit backend-only changes that expect tzinfo objects when the inspected ORM path passes strings. A better criterion should prioritize whether the patch is in the actual `TimezoneMixin`/timezone-name flow, whether `Etc/GMT-10` and `Etc/GMT+10` produce offset-like values for both pytz and zoneinfo, whether normal named zones fall back to their names, and whether tests or smoke checks exercise this distinction.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For Django Trunc()/Extract() timezone regressions involving `Etc/GMT±N`, penalize trajectories whose proposed fix or validation overgeneralizes the repair into universal numeric offset generation, date-dependent offset calculation for ordinary named zones, or backend-only handling that is not connected to the visible `TimezoneMixin` string-producing call path. The flaw is present when the trajectory treats `America/New_York`, `US/Eastern`, `Europe/London`, `Australia/Melbourne`, UTC names, or all database backends as requiring the same `+HH`/`-HH` conversion instead of preserving named-zone behavior while only correcting fixed-offset/Etc/GMT-style inputs.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Overbroad timezone offset conversion

preferred_visible_evidence: Etc/GMT-10 and Etc/GMT+10 become offset-like values before backend sign preparation
both pytz and zoneinfo variants are considered when available
ordinary named zones continue to be represented by their names
the changed code lies on the actual string-valued ORM/backend call path
tests or smoke checks distinguish fixed-offset-style zones from DST-aware named zones
misleading_evidence_to_avoid: requiring all timezones to become +HH/-HH offsets
using an arbitrary reference datetime for DST-aware named zones
claiming all database backends need the same offset format without inspecting their contracts
editing a backend branch that expects tzinfo objects when the visible caller passes strings

scale.1: No evidence of overbroad conversion: the trajectory keeps the repair narrow to fixed-offset/Etc/GMT-style names or `tzname(None)` fallback behavior and preserves ordinary named zones.
scale.2: Minor risk only: the trajectory discusses broad backend compatibility or fixed offsets loosely, but visible code or tests still preserve named zones and remain on the active call path.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory focuses on offset formatting for the reported zones but has ambiguous handling of normal named zones, exact offset formats, or the actual ORM/backend call path.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory proposes or implements numeric offset generation for many ordinary named or DST-aware zones, relies on arbitrary reference dates, or validates only helper behavior unrelated to what Trunc()/Extract() passes.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory fully reframes the task as converting all timezones/all backends to `+HH`/`-HH`, breaks or ignores named-zone semantics, and lacks evidence that the fix affects the actual TimezoneMixin-to-backend SQL path.

experiences.title: Central Call-Audio Mute Recovery at Playback Boundary
experiences.description: Use when a browser/TypeScript call-audio bug involves muted HTML media elements and the trajectory has found, or is close to finding, the centralized call sound playback method that calls play().
experiences.context: Applies in TypeScript/React browser applications where call cues such as ring, ringback, busy, or call-end sounds are played through HTMLMediaElement or DOM audio elements identified by stable IDs. The criterion is most useful once the trajectory has visible evidence of the actual call-sound playback boundary, such as an enum/list of call audio IDs, document.getElementById or equivalent media lookup, and an await audio.play() call. It is less useful during very early broad repository exploration before any call-audio path is identified, and it should not be generalized to unrelated notification sounds, voice-message playback, media recording, or user silence/mute policy unless the task explicitly includes those paths.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics correctly focused on the core behavioral contract: a call sound must not be allowed to remain muted at the moment playback is triggered. That was discriminative because the visible trajectories repeatedly showed agents searching for ring/ringback handling and sometimes identifying a centralized legacy call playback method with audio IDs and play() calls. However, a rubric that only says 'set muted=false somewhere' is too broad and can give credit to superficial or misplaced edits, such as modifying notification playback, looking for audio element creation in the host app, or adding an unmute outside the existing serialized play flow. A better rubric should require evidence that the agent has found the actual call-audio playback boundary, understands that the recovery belongs immediately before the media play() call and ordered with any existing play/pause promise sequencing, and avoids changing silence policy or unrelated audio systems. If the trajectory is only searching for where audio tags are created, judge that as weaker progress unless it connects back to the playback method that receives the media element at runtime. Prioritize visible evidence such as targeted searches for ring/ringback/call audio IDs, inspection of the central play method, recognition that the SDK may not define the DOM audio tags itself, and a planned or implemented recovery that conditionally or explicitly unmutes the target HTMLMediaElement right before play().

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the agent has identified the centralized call-sound playback boundary and is implementing mute-state recovery there: it should connect the call audio identifiers for ring/ringback and related call cues to the method that retrieves an HTML media element and calls play(), then ensure that this specific media element is unmuted immediately before playback within the existing sequencing/error-handling structure. Strong evidence includes distinguishing this call-audio path from unrelated notification or voice-message audio paths, avoiding changes to user silence policy, and recognizing that audio element creation may be outside the inspected package while recovery is still enforceable at playback time.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Playback-Boundary Mute Recovery for Call Cues

required_visible_evidence: Identifies the call-sound playback path rather than only generic audio utilities
Finds concrete call cue identifiers such as ring/ringback or an equivalent call-audio enum/list
Inspects the method or helper that obtains the HTML media element and invokes play()
Plans or applies unmuting of that element immediately before play(), preserving existing async play/pause ordering
Avoids treating unrelated notification sounds, voice-message playback, or silence controls as the primary fix
metadata.stage_notes: Early broad search may earn limited credit only if it is converging on call-audio playback. Once the playback method is visible, continued searches for host HTML definitions are less valuable than making the localized playback-boundary recovery.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of locating the call-sound playback path; the trajectory remains in unrelated audio, notification, UI, recording, or generic repository exploration.
scale.2: Some relevant searches mention call sounds, ring/ringback, or audio elements, but the trajectory has not connected them to the concrete playback method that calls play(), or it remains focused on finding audio tag creation with no recovery plan.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies the likely call-audio playback method and recognizes that muted elements need to be unmuted, but the plan or edit is vague, may be outside the serialized playback boundary, or does not clearly distinguish unrelated audio paths.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly targets the centralized call-sound play method, ties it to ring/ringback and related call audio IDs, and plans or implements unmuting the retrieved HTML media element immediately before play() while avoiding unrelated systems.
scale.5: The trajectory provides a precise, localized recovery at the call-audio playback boundary, preserves existing play/pause promise sequencing and error handling, distinguishes host-provided audio elements from SDK playback responsibility, and avoids unnecessary edits to notification audio, voice-message audio, or silence policy.

experiences.title: FreeBSD pkg info inventory is a separate acceptance path
experiences.description: Retrieve when a FreeBSD scanning task mentions both suppressing updatable counts and using pkg info to recognize installed vulnerable packages/CVEs, especially when the trajectory is focusing on summary-display logic.
experiences.context: Applies in Go vulnerability-scanner repositories with OS-family-specific scan code and model/report formatting, where the task explicitly states that FreeBSD should not show updatable package numbers and also that installed package inventory must come from pkg info semantics so audit-detected CVEs can be mapped to installed packages. This guidance is most useful after the trajectory has found or edited the updatable-count display decision but visible evidence still shows the FreeBSD package collection path relying on pkg version-style output, or the agent has not added/validated pkg info parsing. It is less useful if the task is only about report wording/display suppression, if FreeBSD package inventory is already demonstrably collected from pkg info and associated with audit results, or if the trajectory is still in very early repository exploration before either display or scanner paths have been located.
experiences.experience: The generated rubrics in these cases focused on FreeBSD installed-package discovery via pkg info and CVE association. That was a useful discriminator because the visible trajectories repeatedly found and patched the scan-summary decision for updatable counts, but did not complete the separate package-inventory requirement: the FreeBSD scanner path still visibly used pkg version-style collection, lacked a pkg info parser, or had not shown any merge/association logic ensuring audit-reported package names exist in the installed package map. A better rubric for similar trajectories should therefore check whether the agent treats the issue as two linked requirements: suppress irrelevant updatable counts in summaries and fix the underlying FreeBSD installed package inventory so vulnerable packages are present for CVE association. Avoid the tempting but too-narrow criterion that rewards only adding FreeBSD to an updatable-count switch or updating a display test; passing model/report tests does not establish that pkg audit CVEs can be matched to installed packages. Prioritize visible evidence such as commands still using pkg version for installed inventory, absence or presence of pkg info output parsing, whether parsed package names and versions handle hyphenated package names, whether audit results look up packages in the populated inventory, and whether any tests or inspection cover the pkg info-to-CVE-association path.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that FreeBSD package inventory is collected and parsed with pkg info-compatible semantics, not only that updatable package counts are hidden. Strong progress includes identifying the FreeBSD installed-package collection path, replacing or augmenting pkg version-based inventory with pkg info parsing, preserving any needed update-version information separately, and ensuring vulnerability audit results can find installed packages by name so CVEs are associated with the correct packages.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: FreeBSD pkg info inventory and CVE association

required_visible_evidence: FreeBSD-specific installed package collection path is inspected or modified
pkg info is used or a pkg info-compatible parser is introduced for installed package inventory
pkg version-style output is not the sole source of installed package presence
audit/CVE association is checked against the populated installed package map
display suppression is not treated as the only acceptance criterion
metadata.common_false_proxy: Only changing scan-summary updatable-count logic or its unit test while leaving FreeBSD installed package discovery unchanged

scale.1: No visible attention to FreeBSD installed-package inventory or CVE association; the work only explores or changes unrelated/report-only code.
scale.2: Acknowledges pkg info or FreeBSD package parsing but does not inspect or alter the installed-package collection path, or leaves pkg version-style inventory as the only mechanism.
scale.3: Inspects the relevant FreeBSD scanner path and recognizes the pkg info requirement, but implementation or validation of parsing and audit association is incomplete or speculative.
scale.4: Implements or clearly plans pkg info-compatible installed-package parsing and connects it to the package map used by vulnerability audit association, with some validation or reasoning about package names/versions.
scale.5: Fully addresses the FreeBSD inventory path with pkg info-compatible parsing, preserves any separate update-version data as needed, verifies audit-reported packages can be matched to installed packages, and treats summary updatable-count suppression as a separate but completed requirement.

experiences.title: Do not equate custom-widget config acceptance with complete statusbar support
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for a qutebrowser/PyQt statusbar customization task where the trajectory changes or plans config validation for custom text widgets.
experiences.context: This applies when the task is to let users mix custom text with existing statusbar widgets, and the visible trajectory focuses on the configuration schema, regexes, valid_values, or a new config type. A rubric that only asks whether custom values are accepted can be misleading once the trajectory has moved beyond early exploration, because the feature also depends on preserving existing widget validation/docs, rendering the custom text in the configured order, and cleaning up dynamic text widgets on redraw/config changes. The original config-validation idea is still appropriate when the visible work is specifically investigating a validation bug, such as adding a regex while leaving restrictive valid_values in place, but it should not be treated as the main success criterion for the whole feature.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics often rewarded trajectories for accepting custom statusbar values, using a prefix such as text:, or designing a custom config schema. That criterion is too narrow for this feature: a patch can pass smoke tests for config parsing while still silently accepting misspelled widget names, dropping predefined value documentation/completions, failing to display the literal custom text, leaking/duplicating TextBase widgets on redraw, or corrupting unrelated YAML via broad edits. Conversely, do not invent an overengineered requirement such as dict-based custom widgets with alignment/properties unless the task or trajectory has established that syntax. A better rubric should prioritize visible end-to-end integration evidence: a clear custom-text encoding that does not conflict with built-in widget names; validation that preserves existing predefined widget behavior and rejects unrelated invalid names; statusbar rendering that extracts and displays the custom text in list order; lifecycle cleanup for dynamically created text widgets during redraw/config changes; and targeted verification that the config YAML remains intact. Avoid using “configuration accepts custom strings” as a standalone positive criterion except as a narrow subcriterion during validation-focused debugging.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Config-only or schema-damaging custom statusbar implementation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for this statusbar custom-text feature when visible evidence shows they broaden or redesign configuration acceptance without completing safe end-to-end integration: they remove or bypass predefined widget validation/documentation instead of preserving it through a compatible custom item type; accept arbitrary strings or a separate unrelated setting that makes misspelled built-in widgets indistinguishable from custom text; add regexes that still conflict with existing valid-values validation; render custom text without tracking/removing dynamic widgets on subsequent redraws; fail to display the literal text after the custom-text marker; omit documentation for the user-facing custom-text syntax; or use broad YAML edits that visibly corrupt unrelated settings. This rubric should be applied after the trajectory has begun implementation or validation, not to a very early exploration step with no edits yet.

metadata.environment: qutebrowser-style Python/PyQt application with YAML-backed config schema and a config-driven statusbar layout
visible_evidence_to_check: config schema for statusbar widget list
validation interaction between predefined valid values and custom text syntax
statusbar redraw/rendering logic for configured widget segments
dynamic text widget cleanup on redraw or config changes
YAML diff/syntax integrity and documentation updates
metadata.avoid_as_sole_positive_proxy: custom values validate or a text: prefix is mentioned

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory preserves built-in widget validation/docs, defines a non-conflicting custom-text syntax, renders and cleans up dynamic text widgets, and keeps YAML/docs coherent.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory mostly integrates validation and rendering but has small unresolved documentation or verification gaps, with no sign of schema corruption or arbitrary invalid-widget acceptance.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory implements either validation or rendering well, but the other side is incomplete or unverified; lifecycle cleanup or preservation of predefined value metadata remains unclear.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory relies mainly on broadening config acceptance, regex-only validation, or a separate custom setting while leaving rendering, cleanup, invalid-name rejection, or predefined docs/completions substantially incomplete.
scale.5: Severe evidence: visible edits corrupt unrelated YAML/config entries, leave custom text rejected by conflicting validation, accept arbitrary invalid widget names, or repeatedly fail to verify/fix the config and redraw integration.

experiences.title: Do not reward superficial rename UI when data-owner integration and regression control are missing
experiences.description: Retrieve for React/TypeScript settings UI feature work that adds device/session renaming or similar persisted edits across current and list-detail views, especially after the agent has already found the SDK mutation API and is editing multiple components.
experiences.context: This warning applies when the visible trajectory contains or is about to contain implementation edits for a persisted UI rename flow in a component hierarchy with an existing data-fetching hook or parent refresh owner. A broad checklist of Rename button, input, Save/Cancel, spinner, error text, and visibility notice can be appropriate during early requirements discovery, but becomes misleading once the agent starts changing files: agents may satisfy that surface checklist while bypassing the existing device data lifecycle, failing to refresh or locally update the displayed name, placing controls outside the requested details context, or introducing unrelated regressions through full-file rewrites and fragile text substitutions. The original UI/UX checklist is still useful as a secondary acceptance check when the trajectory also shows safe integration with the existing parent-owned device state and preserves neighboring list/filter/sign-out/verification behavior.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often asked whether the trajectory implemented the complete rename UI/UX or showed multi-component planning. Those criteria were too broad and over-optimistic for later-stage trajectories because visible evidence of a dialog, buttons, spinner, direct SDK call, or callback plumbing did not prove the feature would work correctly. The more predictive rubric should focus on whether the mutation is integrated through the existing device data owner: the save operation should be exposed or coordinated from the component/hook that already owns device loading and refresh, passed to both current-session and other-session detail paths, and followed by a refresh or local state update so the renamed session is immediately reflected. It should also penalize evidence of risky implementation practices such as direct SDK calls from leaf UI without a refresh path, adding rename controls only to summary tiles rather than the detail view, making callback props required without updating all call sites/tests, corrupting JSX with repeated sed patches, or rewriting unrelated list/filter/date/verification behavior. Avoid generating a standalone criterion that merely checks for user-facing rename widgets and messages. Prioritize visible evidence from diffs, prop flow, hook ownership, build/typecheck results, and preservation of existing behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial rename UI without safe state integration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that add or plan visible rename controls for a persisted device/session name feature while lacking clear integration with the existing device data lifecycle or while destabilizing surrounding session-manager behavior. This applies once implementation work has begun in a React/TypeScript settings UI where current and other sessions are rendered through shared or parent-managed device data. Evidence of the flaw includes direct SDK mutation calls in leaf UI components with no parent refresh/local update path, callbacks added inconsistently through the hierarchy, rename controls placed only on summary rows instead of the session details context requested by the task, no visible handling for immediate display update after save, required prop changes not reflected in all call sites/tests, malformed JSX or failed patches from fragile text edits, or unrelated rewrites to filtering, sorting, date formatting, verification, or sign-out behavior. Do not penalize early exploration that has not yet edited code, or a design that uses either inline editing or a dialog, as long as it visibly preserves the existing data owner and refresh/update contract.

applies_when: Persisted rename/edit feature spanning current item and list/detail item views
Existing hook or parent component owns fetched device/session data and refresh behavior
Trajectory is in implementation or final-review stage, not pure exploration
flaw_signals: UI checklist is satisfied but save is implemented only inside a leaf component
No callback, refresh, optimistic update, or parent-owned save function is visibly wired after successful persistence
Current-session and other-session paths are wired differently or one path is missing
Full-file rewrites or sed edits alter unrelated session-list behavior
Visible syntax/type errors, malformed JSX, or unaddressed call-site/test breakage after adding props
acceptable_boundaries: Inline editor and modal dialog are both acceptable UX choices if integrated with the data lifecycle
A parent callback refresh approach and a locally optimistic update approach are both acceptable if the displayed name updates immediately
A broad UI checklist may be used as a secondary rubric after safe integration and regression preservation are established

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory clearly routes persistence through the existing data owner or refresh/update mechanism, covers both current and other session detail paths, and preserves neighboring behavior.
scale.2: Minor risk only: most integration is sound, but one visible edge such as a test/call-site update, immediate display update detail, or placement of the rename affordance remains slightly unclear.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory has plausible rename UI and API usage, but parent refresh/local update wiring or both-session coverage is incomplete or only implied, with limited evidence of regression checks.
scale.4: Clear flaw: implementation centers on surface UI/direct SDK calls or inconsistent callback plumbing, with no convincing immediate-update path and some unrelated component churn or call-site risk.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the rename UI is superficial and the trajectory visibly corrupts or rewrites surrounding session-manager code, leaves malformed/type-broken integration, omits refresh/update behavior, or breaks existing filtering/sign-out/verification/list behavior.

experiences.title: Replace-mode MutableMapping compatibility over dict-union patch shape
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python mapping-combination bug is caused by using dict-specific union semantics on a custom MutableMapping wrapper, especially in a replace/shallow-combine branch where right-hand values should override left-hand values.
experiences.context: Applies in an Ansible-like Python codebase when the task explicitly reports a TypeError from combining a plain dict with a dict-like MutableMapping wrapper in a replace-mode variable-combination utility. It is most useful once the trajectory has located the relevant combine branch, seen that inputs are validated as MutableMapping, or reproduced/confirmed that the `|` operator is the failing operation. It can still be used during early investigation if the agent has identified the target function and wrapper type, but the rubric should then judge diagnosis and planned semantic direction rather than completed implementation. Do not apply this as a generic mapping rubric when the failure is in recursive merge behavior, list merging, non-mapping validation, YAML/source display, or an unrelated operator-overload task. Also avoid requiring one exact implementation: either changing the combiner to use mapping-protocol operations or adding compatible union behavior to the wrapper may satisfy the visible contract if the public combine operation behaves correctly.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic boundary exposed by the task: replace mode promises to combine validated mutable mappings, but the implementation used dict-union behavior that does not necessarily work for custom MutableMapping subclasses. This was discriminative because trajectories that located the replace branch, identified the wrapper as dict-like rather than a dict subclass, reproduced the TypeError, and then used a mapping-compatible combination strategy were on the right path. A better rubric should not merely ask for a change in the named function or for tests to pass; it should ask whether the trajectory preserves the public contract: no TypeError for dict plus wrapper, right-hand precedence on conflicts, ordinary dict behavior unchanged, validation still present, and merge-mode behavior not accidentally altered. It should also check visible code hygiene after edits, because some trajectories used brittle sed replacements that temporarily duplicated or damaged the function; without verifying the final function structure or running a focused test, the same semantic intention can still leave a bad patch. Avoid the tempting but overly broad criterion that both merge and replace modes need new type-mismatch handling: the reported failure is specifically in the replace/shallow-combine path, while merge may already use generic mapping operations. Also avoid over-prescribing `{**a, **b}`, `copy().update()`, or wrapper `__or__` methods as the only acceptable patch shape; judge the observable behavior and preserved contracts instead.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a correct semantic fix for replace-mode combination of a plain dict with a custom MutableMapping wrapper: it identifies that dict-union is incompatible with the accepted mapping interface, implements or plans a mapping-compatible combination without weakening input validation, preserves right-hand key precedence, leaves recursive/merge behavior unchanged, and verifies the edited code is structurally clean with focused reproducer or unit-test evidence.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Replace-mode generic mapping contract

required_visible_evidence: The failing operation is isolated to a replace or shallow-combine branch using dict-union or similarly dict-specific behavior.
The wrapper type is recognized as a MutableMapping/dict-like object that may not implement dict union.
The proposed or applied fix combines through generic mapping protocol behavior or compatible operator overloads.
Conflict behavior is considered so the second operand overrides the first.
Existing validation and merge-mode behavior are not removed or broadened incorrectly.
The trajectory verifies the reproducer or relevant tests and checks that the edited function is not duplicated or syntactically corrupted.
acceptable_patch_shapes: Use mapping expansion or copy/update in the combiner.
Implement compatible union methods on the wrapper so the existing combiner operation works.
Any equivalent approach that satisfies the public mapping-combination contract.
non_goals: Rewriting unrelated recursive merge/list merge behavior.
Requiring a specific syntax when multiple mapping-compatible implementations are valid.
Treating temporary ad hoc scripts alone as sufficient without evidence of a coherent production-code edit.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory has isolated the replace-mode dict-union incompatibility or understood the custom mapping contract.
scale.2: Some investigation of the relevant function or wrapper exists, but the trajectory is still generic, may conflate merge and replace behavior, or has no plausible mapping-compatible fix direction.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies the failing replace-mode operation and proposes a plausible generic mapping combination, but evidence is incomplete on right-hand precedence, validation preservation, merge-mode safety, or code cleanliness.
scale.4: The trajectory applies or clearly plans a mapping-compatible fix, preserves second-operand precedence and ordinary dict behavior, avoids changing merge mode, and has some focused verification or inspection.
scale.5: The trajectory fully demonstrates the contract with a clean production edit or equivalent plan, confirms dict plus custom MutableMapping no longer raises, checks conflict precedence and merge-mode non-regression, preserves validation, and verifies the edited function structure/tests without relying on an exact patch shape.

experiences.title: Choices-Only AlterField Must Be a Schema No-op
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django migration/schema-editor task concerns SQLite emitting DDL for `AlterField` changes that only affect model metadata such as `choices`.
experiences.context: Applies in the Django codebase when the task or trajectory is about `AlterField`, SQLite table remakes, schema-editor no-op detection, or field deconstruction differences for `choices`. It is especially relevant once the trajectory has located `schema_editor.alter_field()`, `_field_should_be_altered()`, or evidence that `choices` appears in field deconstruction but does not affect the database column definition. It can still be useful early because the task statement itself specifies the semantic boundary. Do not apply this as a generic SQLite-performance criterion, to migration autodetector-only tasks, or to changes where the field alteration includes database-affecting attributes such as type, length, nullability, indexes, constraints, column name changes, or relation target changes.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged the core semantic contract: changing only `choices` must not trigger SQLite schema SQL/table remakes, while true schema changes must still execute normally. This aligned because the decisive visible evidence was not merely that the agent edited a plausible file, but that the trajectory identified the shared schema-alter comparison, recognized `choices` as Python/model metadata serialized by field deconstruction, and validated both the no-op cases and negative controls. A better rubric should focus on the no-op decision boundary: additions, removals, or modifications of `choices` on an otherwise identical field should be ignored by the database-alter predicate, without suppressing migration state serialization and without making all `AlterField` operations no-ops. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as “modify the SQLite backend,” “match PostgreSQL behavior” without explaining why, “run any migration tests,” or “add `choices` to some list” as the main judgment. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent traced `AlterField` to the schema editor, found the non-database attribute filtering/deconstruction comparison, demonstrated no SQL or `_field_should_be_altered() == False` for choices-only changes, and also showed schema-affecting changes still return true or emit SQL.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should establish and preserve the correct schema-alteration boundary for Django `AlterField`: changes limited to field `choices` are treated as non-database metadata and therefore produce no SQLite schema SQL/table remake, while database-affecting field differences continue to trigger normal alteration behavior. Strong evidence includes locating the shared schema-editor predicate used by SQLite, explaining that field deconstruction includes `choices` even though it does not affect the column definition, avoiding migration-autodetector suppression as the fix, and validating choices-only add/change/remove cases plus at least one real schema-change control.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Non-Database Field Metadata Alter No-op

metadata.backend_symptom: SQLite table remake or emitted schema SQL
metadata.key_boundary: choices-only changes no-op; database-affecting changes still alter
preferred_evidence: schema editor no-op predicate inspected
field deconstruction comparison understood
choices classified as non-database metadata
zero SQL or false alter predicate shown for choices-only cases
positive control for real schema changes retained

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses choices-only schema no-op behavior; it may only explore unrelated migration or SQLite code.
scale.2: Recognizes that SQLite emits unnecessary SQL for `choices`, but lacks a clear schema-editor boundary or risks suppressing migrations/alterations too broadly.
scale.3: Identifies the likely schema-alter decision path and treats `choices` as non-database metadata, but validation or preservation of real schema changes is incomplete.
scale.4: Clearly targets the schema-alter comparison so choices-only add/change/remove cases no-op on SQLite and includes evidence that real schema-affecting changes still alter.
scale.5: Fully demonstrates the intended boundary with code-level reasoning and focused validation: `choices` remains model-state metadata but is ignored for database DDL decisions, SQLite emits no SQL for choices-only changes, and schema-changing attributes still produce SQL.

experiences.title: Do not score in-progress multi-adapter work as final consistency failure
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Node.js database abstraction task spans multiple backend adapters and the trajectory is still exploring or actively editing, especially when only some adapters are patched in the visible cutoff.
experiences.context: This applies to tasks where the same public API is implemented separately for Redis, MongoDB, PostgreSQL, or similar adapters, and the agent has discovered that a change should be made across all of them. A final-review rubric about cross-backend consistency is appropriate only when the agent claims completion, is preparing the final patch, or has no visible plan to handle the remaining adapters. It is misleading during investigation or mid-edit stages to judge the trajectory primarily by whether every adapter is already changed in the current worktree, because temporary partial edits, malformed blocks, or missing later adapter patches may be normal intermediate states when the visible evidence still shows the agent understands the full scope and intends to continue.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics demanded that all database adapters already expose identical `sortedSetsCardSum(keys, min, max)` behavior and sometimes even identical delegation logic. That criterion is useful as a final patch property, but it becomes misleading at early or mid-implementation cutoffs: the visible trajectory often showed the agent had already found all backend implementations and relevant range-count primitives, yet had not finished applying or cleaning up every edit. A better rubric should distinguish stage and intent. During exploration or active editing, focus on whether the agent has identified the multi-backend scope, inspected backend-specific range-count semantics, preserved no-range behavior, and is avoiding inefficient per-key database calls where backend batching/querying exists. Avoid a tempting criterion that treats incomplete current coverage or temporary edit corruption as decisive unless the agent is claiming to be done or abandoning the other adapters. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence such as searches locating all adapter implementations, inspection of existing single-key range-count helpers, awareness of `-inf`/`+inf` or optional-bound semantics, use of backend-native batch/query approaches, and whether the agent plans to validate or repair malformed edits before finalizing.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Premature Multi-Backend Completion Assumption
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize only when the trajectory treats a multi-backend database API change as complete while visibly leaving required adapters unexamined or unmodified, using incompatible parameter semantics across adapters, or ignoring backend-specific efficient range-count mechanisms. Do not penalize merely because the visible cutoff is mid-edit and only one adapter is currently patched, if the agent has identified the other adapters, inspected relevant helper behavior, and has not claimed completion.

metadata.environment: Node.js project with separate database backend adapter files implementing the same sorted-set API
required_visible_evidence: Whether the agent has located all relevant backend implementations
Whether the agent has inspected existing range-count helpers or backend score-bound conventions
Whether the agent is still actively editing versus claiming completion
Whether unmodified adapters are being ignored or are planned next
Whether the proposed implementation preserves no-range behavior and uses backend-appropriate batching/querying
do_not_treat_as_failure_by_itself: Only one adapter has been edited so far during active implementation
Temporary malformed code appears while the agent is still inspecting or repairing it
Backend implementations use different internal mechanisms to provide the same public semantics

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the agent recognizes the multi-backend scope or is still in active exploration/editing with a plausible plan to update and validate remaining adapters.
scale.2: Minor concern: the agent has focused on one adapter for several steps but visible notes or searches still indicate awareness that other adapters must be handled.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the agent has patched one or two adapters and appears to be moving on without clearly inspecting all backend-specific range semantics, but has not explicitly claimed the work is complete.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the agent claims or implies completion after changing only a subset of required adapters, or applies inconsistent min/max/default behavior without noticing the mismatch.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the agent finalizes a patch that ignores entire required backends, uses incompatible public signatures or return semantics across adapters, or replaces efficient backend-native multi-key counting with unnecessarily inefficient or serial per-key calls despite visible better primitives.

experiences.title: Exact Config Export API and Validation Contract
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go configuration task explicitly names missing exported symbols for default config construction and mapstructure decode hooks, and the defaults must decode and pass a schema/CUE validation step.
experiences.context: Applies in Go repositories with a configuration package using Viper/mapstructure-style decoding, where the task states that tests fail to compile because exact exported identifiers such as a default configuration constructor and decode hook slice are missing, and where later validation of the decoded defaults against a schema is part of the acceptance path. This is most useful after the trajectory has found a private hook collection, existing default-loading/test-helper behavior, or schema assets. It is not enough for tasks that only require visible package tests to pass, only require internal loading behavior, or are still in early repository exploration before the agent has connected the named exports to the decode/validation workflow. At final-review or implementation stages, the criterion must not stop at “some default function exists”; it must check exact names/signatures and that the returned defaults and schema/serialization behavior support validation.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics correctly identified a strong cue: the task names missing public configuration entry points, and the visible trajectory repeatedly finds a private decode hook slice and no default config export. A rubric requiring those exports is useful when the agent has not edited code or is still searching, because absence of the exact symbols is decisive evidence of non-progress. However, a too-broad version is misleading: accepting a differently named function such as a generic Default(), or accepting a hand-written default struct without checking validation compatibility, can overrate a patch that still fails callers expecting the task’s exact API. A better rubric should focus on the full externally observable contract: exact exported identifier names and types, reuse of the existing decode hook behavior/order, a complete default config matching the package’s real default-loading semantics, and evidence that the decoded/marshaled defaults can satisfy the schema path including duration handling and optional/omitempty behavior. Avoid the tempting proxy of “visible tests pass” or “there is any public default constructor,” because hidden/updated tests may compile against exact exported names and then exercise schema validation not present in visible tests. Prioritize visible evidence such as greps showing missing/existing exact symbols, edits promoting or aliasing the private hook slice, implementation of the named default constructor, use of existing defaulters/test-helper defaults as the source of truth, and validation or reasoning that schema mismatches are addressed rather than ignored.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement the exact public configuration API named by the task and preserve the full decode-and-validate contract: a public default configuration function with the expected name/signature, a public mapstructure decode hook slice exposing the same hook behavior used internally, complete defaults derived from the package’s existing default semantics, and attention to schema/CUE compatibility for the serialized/decoded default configuration, including duration fields and optional nested fields.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Exact Exported Config Validation Contract

expected_public_api: public default configuration constructor with the exact task-specified name
public []mapstructure.DecodeHookFunc hook slice with the exact task-specified name
evidence_to_check: private decode hooks are exported or aliased without losing existing hooks/order
internal loading still uses compatible hooks
default constructor returns a complete configuration matching existing default loading behavior
duration, enum, and slice decoding remain supported
schema/CUE validation compatibility is considered beyond mere compilation
the implementation does not substitute a differently named constructor for the requested API
metadata.environment: Go configuration package using mapstructure/Viper and schema/CUE validation assets

scale.1: No concrete progress toward the exact exported API; trajectory only explores files, repeats searches/tests, or leaves the missing symbols unresolved.
scale.2: Partial recognition of the missing exports, but no reliable implementation plan or code; may identify private hooks or default helpers without adding exact public entry points.
scale.3: Implements or plans one part of the API, or adds broadly similar exports, but leaves uncertainty about exact names/signatures, hook compatibility, default completeness, or schema validation.
scale.4: Adds the exact public hook slice and default config constructor with largely complete defaults and preserved decode behavior, but validation compatibility or edge cases such as optional nested fields/duration serialization are not fully demonstrated.
scale.5: Clearly satisfies the exact named API, preserves existing decode hook semantics, derives complete defaults from existing loading/default behavior, and verifies or explicitly addresses schema/CUE validation compatibility for the decoded default configuration.

experiences.title: Don’t treat token-splitting compliance as end-to-end address input coverage
experiences.description: Retrieve when a mail/address parsing task involves UI autocomplete input paths plus recipient-object creation, and a tempting rubric only restates comma/semicolon splitting, trimming, bracket stripping, and `Name`/`Address` output.
experiences.context: This warning applies in a TypeScript/React monorepo where recipient input is handled through autocomplete components and shared recipient helpers. A broad parsing-contract rubric is misleading when the visible trajectory has found or edited only the low-level recipient parser or the paste/change splitter, because the user-facing behavior can also depend on the confirm/add path used on Enter, blur, or add-on-blur. The original broad contract is still appropriate when evaluating an isolated utility explicitly used by all entry paths, or when tests directly target only that utility. During early exploration, absence of the final integration edit should not be judged as a definite defect; instead, prefer criteria about locating all consumer paths before implementation.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics correctly summarized the requested normalization contract but were too broad to distinguish incomplete fixes. They rewarded evidence such as filtering empty tokens after `split(/[,;]/)` or modifying the single-token recipient parser for `<email>`, even though those changes can miss the actual UI path where a trimmed input string is validated and added as a single recipient on Enter/blur/add-on-blur. A better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory identifies and normalizes the user-facing recipient-add pipeline: the same separator/bracket/empty-token handling must be applied before both live paste/change additions and final add/blur additions, and validation should run per normalized recipient rather than on the unsplit combined string. Avoid the tempting criterion that “all split sites were filtered” or “`inputToRecipient` handles bracketed email” is sufficient. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent inspected the autocomplete handlers, understood how `hasEmailPasting`, add-on-blur/Enter handling, and recipient validation interact, and planned or implemented shared normalization across those paths with scenarios for leading/trailing separators and bracketed single emails.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear to satisfy the address parsing contract only by changing a token splitter or the single-recipient parser while leaving a visible user-facing add/confirm path able to treat a comma/semicolon-separated or bracketed input string as one unsplit recipient. This flaw is especially relevant when the trajectory has located autocomplete input handlers with separate paste/change and blur/Enter/add-recipient logic, but does not ensure normalized splitting, bracket removal, empty-token filtering, and per-token validation are applied consistently before recipients are added.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: UI add path bypasses normalized splitting

metadata.task_type: mail recipient address parsing in a React/TypeScript autocomplete UI
evidence_to_prioritize: inspection or edit of both live input/paste handler and final add/blur/Enter handler
normalization before recipient creation in every user entry path
per-token validation after splitting normalized input
manual or automated scenarios covering leading/trailing/consecutive separators and bracketed email input through the add path
tempting_proxy_to_avoid: only filtering empty tokens at existing split(/[,;]/) lines
only changing the single-token recipient parser
only claiming all comma/semicolon split sites were updated without checking add/confirm flow

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory clearly identifies all relevant autocomplete entry paths and applies or plans consistent normalization before adding recipients.
scale.2: Minor risk: the trajectory mostly covers the add pipeline but leaves some uncertainty about whether validation or one secondary entry path uses the normalized tokens.
scale.3: Moderate issue: the trajectory handles either the paste/change splitter or the single-token parser, but visible evidence is insufficient that the final add/blur/Enter path is normalized.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory edits filtering or bracket handling in one path while visible autocomplete add logic can still validate/add an unsplit combined string.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory explicitly treats splitter filtering or recipient-parser changes as complete despite visible separate add/confirm logic that remains unexamined or unchanged.

experiences.title: Reducer Mirrors State-Forward Clearing Semantics
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django migration optimizer task involves folding a model-option alteration into model creation, and the key correctness question is whether omitted option keys are treated as removals rather than preserved by a dict merge.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django repository when the trajectory has localized a squash/optimizer bug to reducing a CreateModel-like operation with an AlterModelOptions-like operation, especially after inspecting the alter operation’s state_forwards behavior or reproducing stale Meta options after optimization. This is most useful once the agent has enough evidence about the reducer and the operation’s canonical state transition; it is less useful during very early dependency/setup exploration before the relevant reducer semantics are known. Do not generalize it to unrelated migration operations unless their state_forwards logic also defines deletion semantics. Do not use it as a requirement that a regression test must be added when the current visible evidence is primarily about semantic code correctness.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged whether the optimizer reduction preserved the same state semantics as applying the operations sequentially: supplied model options are updated, omitted keys owned by the model-options operation are removed, and unrelated options are preserved. This aligned well because the decisive visible evidence was semantic: the agent compared the reducer’s plain dict merge with the alter operation’s state_forwards removal loop, reproduced stale ordering/permissions/verbose-name-style options, and patched the reducer to pop omitted alterable keys. A better rubric should focus on that reducer/state_forwards equivalence, including empty and partial option dictionaries. Avoid the tempting but weaker criterion of merely requiring a Django-native regression test; tests are valuable, but absence of an added test is not the core semantic correctness signal here. Also avoid overbroad criteria that reward changing adjacent reducer branches whose state_forwards behavior does not require deletion, or criteria that clear all options indiscriminately rather than only the operation-owned alterable option set. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent identified the canonical alterable-key list, handled omission as removal, preserved non-owned/custom options, and validated both empty-options and partial-update cases.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should make the CreateModel-plus-AlterModelOptions optimization semantically equivalent to applying AlterModelOptions.state_forwards: build the resulting model options from the original and supplied options, remove any omitted keys governed by the alter operation’s owned option-key set, correctly handle an empty options dictionary as clearing those owned options, and preserve unrelated or non-owned options. The judge should look for evidence from code inspection, patch intent, or reproductions that omission is treated as deletion for the alterable option set rather than as a no-op merge.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: State-Equivalent Model Option Reduction

required_visible_evidence: The trajectory identifies that the reducer’s plain option merge preserves stale model options.
The trajectory uses the alter operation’s state-forward behavior or owned option-key list as the semantic source of truth.
The proposed or applied change removes omitted owned option keys from the reduced CreateModel options.
The approach preserves unrelated/non-owned options instead of clearing the entire options dictionary blindly.
boundary_conditions: Do not require changes to adjacent option-operation reducers unless their own state-forward behavior has comparable deletion semantics.
Do not make the rubric primarily about adding tests when code-level semantic evidence is already visible.
Do not accept a fix that only handles the literal empty-options case while leaving partial-option omissions stale.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory understands or addresses the option-clearing semantics; it continues to rely on a plain merge or focuses only on unrelated setup.
scale.2: Weak evidence of the right area, such as locating the reducer or reproducing stale options, but no clear plan to mirror state-forward deletion semantics.
