scale.3: Moderate evidence equivalent to the parent trajectory: it identifies that omitted alterable options must be cleared and begins implementing or validating that idea, but may not fully cover partial updates or preservation of unrelated options.
scale.4: Strong evidence that the reducer is changed or planned to remove omitted owned option keys while updating supplied options, with some validation of empty or partial option cases.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory explicitly mirrors the alter operation’s state-forward semantics, handles empty and partial option dictionaries, preserves non-owned options, avoids unnecessary adjacent-branch changes, and validates the behavior with targeted reproduction or relevant tests.

experiences.title: Element-load freshness must integrate with existing retry and pending-action state
experiences.description: Use when a mail-style mailbox/list task explicitly involves backend-marked stale responses, failed fetch retries, and deferring reloads during item-modifying backend operations, and the trajectory has reached the element loading Redux/action/selectors pipeline.
experiences.context: Applies in a TypeScript/React/Redux mail app where mailbox or conversation list data is loaded through an elements domain such as actions/thunks, reducers, selectors, a query helper, and a hook that dispatches loads. It is especially relevant after the agent has inspected or edited files analogous to elementQuery, elementsActions, elementsReducers, elementsSelectors, elementsSlice, useElements, and mutation hooks. The criterion is less useful during very early repository exploration before the agent has found the loading pipeline, and it should not be applied to tasks that only require generic network retry behavior without a backend stale marker or list reload gating. Do not require a documented shared response interface when the codebase uses untyped API request builders; judge whether the implementation safely threads and handles the response freshness signal in the local loading flow.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics that asked only for generic controlled retries, exponential backoff, or proof that a specific API field exists were too easy to misapply. The important discriminator in these trajectories is whether the agent connects all three required freshness mechanisms to the existing list-loading state machine: backend operations increment/decrement a pending-action count around real async mutations; request eligibility and loading selectors use that pending state so reloads wait; and list API results carry a stale marker into the Redux flow so stale payloads are not committed and instead advance the existing bounded retry path. A better rubric should focus on visible edits or plans in the element query helper, load thunk/actions, fulfilled/retry reducers, slice wiring, selectors, useElements hook, and backend mutation hooks. Avoid rewarding broad claims like “implement exponential backoff” or “check Stale in queryElements” if the trajectory still lets loadFulfilled commit stale Elements, bypasses the existing retry count/max-retry semantics, omits reducer/slice wiring, or tracks only optimistic UI rollback rather than actual backend work. Prioritize concrete evidence: local response typing or mapping for the stale flag, a distinct retry-on-stale path before cache/page updates, bounded retry state updates using existing constants/selectors, pending backend action start/finish actions balanced in finally-style mutation flows, and loading/request selectors that reflect pending actions plus pending requests.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Freshness-aware element loading integration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show that mailbox element reload freshness is handled inside the existing elements loading state machine: backend item-modifying operations are tracked until their async work completes; request and loading selectors defer list loads while those operations are pending; list API responses expose the backend stale marker to the load result; stale responses are not committed to the element cache/page state; and stale or failed fetches trigger the existing bounded retry mechanism with reducer and slice wiring rather than an unrelated ad hoc retry loop.

relevant_areas: mailbox/useElements hook or equivalent load-dispatch hook
element query helper mapping conversation/message list responses
backend mutation hooks for label/move/delete/mark actions
strong_evidence: pending backend action counter or equivalent state is added and initialized
backend action started/finished actions are dispatched around real API mutations and balanced on success/failure
request eligibility/loading selectors consume pending backend action state
query results include the backend stale marker from the raw API response
fulfilled handling rejects or diverts stale results before updating pages/elements
retry and retry-on-stale actions/reducers are wired into the slice and respect existing max-retry semantics
anti_patterns: only adding exponential backoff without integrating existing retry state
checking a stale flag but still allowing fulfilled reducers to commit stale Elements
tracking optimistic UI rollback only rather than backend operation completion
rewriting large files without validating imports, reducer wiring, or TypeScript correctness
requiring shared API response interfaces when the local API layer is structurally typed or untyped

scale.1: The trajectory has not found the element loading pipeline or only discusses mailbox UI symptoms without identifying where requests, retries, or response commits occur.
scale.2: The trajectory mentions stale responses, retries, or pending mutations abstractly, but lacks concrete integration points or proposes a generic retry mechanism unrelated to existing selectors/reducers.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies the correct query/thunk/reducer/selector areas and may add a stale field or retry idea, but leaves major gaps such as stale payloads still being committed, retry reducers not wired, or pending backend actions not affecting request eligibility.
scale.4: The trajectory provides strong partial integration: stale results are carried and mostly prevented from committing, retries use existing state, or pending backend actions gate requests, but one required part is missing or insufficiently validated.
scale.5: The trajectory fully integrates freshness handling across query mapping, load actions, reducers, slice wiring, selectors/loading state, and backend mutation hooks, with stale responses retried instead of committed and reloads deferred until all backend item-modifying actions finish.

experiences.title: Stateful behavior contract after settings UI relocation
experiences.description: Retrieve when a React/TypeScript settings task requires moving a reusable settings section between tabs and also preserving feature-flag, displayed-value, and toggle failure semantics.
experiences.context: Applies to settings UI trajectories where the task is not just visual relocation: the section must be removed from one tab, added to another, gated by a feature flag, display a service/manager name correctly, and keep a stateful toggle consistent with persisted settings. It is especially useful once the trajectory has already found or edited the tab placement, because simple import/render movement becomes a weak proxy for correctness. It may be premature or too broad for tasks that only ask for navigation/placement changes, and it should not replace a syntax/regression criterion when the visible trajectory shows corrupted JSX, failing tests, or unrelated rewrites.
experiences.experience: In these cases, placement-only rubrics were tempting because the trajectory often showed visible removal from the old tab and addition to the new tab. That criterion can over-credit partial patches: a moved component may still fail the task if the reusable settings component was not inspected or updated for manager-name display, account-level provisioning updates, error logging, and rollback. Conversely, rubrics focused on feature-flag and provisioning-toggle behavior were useful when the visible trajectory showed only tab edits or exploratory greps and no concrete evidence of fixing the toggle contract. A better rubric should require end-to-end handling: the section is absent from the old settings tab, rendered in the intended settings tab without breaking existing sections, hidden when the relevant feature is disabled, and the underlying reusable component correctly reflects and persists the provisioning setting while reverting and logging on failure. Avoid judging by superficial proxies such as the presence of a new import, wrapping the component in an extra section, or a single grep showing no old-tab references. Prioritize visible evidence of: clean sibling placement in the tab render tree, no dangling references after removal, explicit feature-gate behavior that does not leave empty UI, inspection or modification of the reusable component’s toggle error path, preservation of the displayed manager name, and targeted validation/tests for both placement and toggle behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete relocation plus provisioning behavior
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the Integration Manager settings work as a complete feature after relocation, not merely that a component was moved. Strong evidence includes removing the section from the previous settings tab, adding it as a valid sibling in the intended settings tab without disrupting existing sections, ensuring the whole section is absent when the widgets feature is disabled, preserving correct display of the configured manager name, and verifying or implementing the provisioning toggle so it updates the persisted account-level setting, reflects success in the UI, logs failures, and restores the prior toggle state on failure.

expected_visible_evidence: old tab no longer imports, defines, or renders the Integration Manager settings section
new tab renders the reusable Integration Manager settings UI in a clean top-level placement that does not corrupt or nest unrelated settings sections
widgets feature-flag behavior is explicitly preserved so disabled widgets do not leave a visible empty section
the reusable settings component or its tests are inspected/changed for manager-name display and provisioning-toggle semantics
toggle failure path includes both error logging and rollback to the previous UI state
validation covers absence in the old tab, presence in the new tab, feature-disabled behavior, displayed manager name, and toggle success/failure behavior
metadata.common_false_positive: Only moving an import/render call between tabs, or adding a feature-flag check around the render, while leaving the displayed manager name and toggle failure behavior unverified.

scale.1: No visible progress beyond repository exploration or superficial tab-location guesses; no evidence of handling placement, feature flag, displayed name, or toggle behavior.
scale.2: Some placement work is visible, such as removing or adding the section in one tab, but the implementation is incomplete, unvalidated, or ignores feature flag and provisioning behavior.
scale.3: Relocation appears mostly addressed and basic feature gating may be present, but there is little or no concrete evidence that manager-name display and toggle success/failure semantics were inspected, fixed, or tested.
scale.4: Relocation and feature-gate behavior are implemented cleanly, and the trajectory shows meaningful attention to the reusable component’s manager-name and provisioning-toggle behavior, with partial validation.
scale.5: The trajectory provides strong evidence of a complete, validated fix: correct old/new tab placement, no broken surrounding settings UI, correct feature-flag visibility, correct manager-name display, persisted toggle updates, failure logging, rollback, and targeted tests or equivalent validation.

experiences.title: Protocol-faithful device enrollment with native test hooks
experiences.description: Use when a Go/Teleport-style OSS client task asks for missing device trust enrollment and the trajectory has found existing generated DeviceTrustService protos but no hand-written OSS enrollment/native implementation.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go repository where device trust protobuf/gRPC types already define an enrollment stream, the OSS implementation is mostly absent, and the task emphasizes client-side enrollment plus native extension points or simulation without enterprise/native dependencies. It is most useful once the trajectory has inspected the generated enrollment messages, existing client accessors for a DeviceTrustService client, and the empty or minimal device-trust package. Do not apply as a generic device/MFA rubric, to server-side admin token creation tasks, to CLI-only tasks unless the prompt explicitly demands a command, or before the agent has enough evidence about the protocol shape. Also avoid assuming broad multi-OS TPM/Secure Enclave support unless visible API comments or the task explicitly require it.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful criterion is not merely “add some device enrollment code.” The visible evidence that matters is whether the trajectory is converging on the existing DeviceTrustService enrollment contract and isolating native responsibilities behind hooks/fakes. Earlier rubrics correctly looked for a client-side enrollment ceremony, collected device data, signed challenges, and simulation hooks; this is useful because the task’s real gap is protocol orchestration plus native abstraction, not new schemas. However, the better rubric must avoid tempting but misleading requirements: do not require creating enrollment tokens from the client as part of enrollment, do not substitute AuthenticateDevice for the enrollment challenge response, do not insist on a tsh CLI command unless specified, and do not reward placeholder Linux/Windows/TPM implementations or ad hoc credential managers that ignore the proto-defined macOS enrollment stream. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent plans or implements a small reusable device-trust enrollment layer using the generated gRPC client, sends the init payload with the enrollment token and native-collected data, receives the macOS enrollment challenge, signs it via a native hook, sends the matching challenge response, handles success and unsupported OS errors deliberately, and provides fake native/device-service hooks so tests can run without enterprise server or OS-native dependencies.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Protocol-faithful enrollment ceremony with native isolation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show concrete progress toward an OSS client-side device trust enrollment layer that reuses the generated DeviceTrustService enrollment stream and separates native device operations from protocol orchestration. Strong evidence includes identifying the exact init/challenge/response/success sequence, using the existing generated device-trust client rather than inventing new APIs, collecting the proto-required device data through a native abstraction, signing the server enrollment challenge through an injectable hook, handling unsupported platforms explicitly, and adding or planning fake native/device-service test infrastructure so the flow can be validated without enterprise server support or OS-native dependencies. The criterion should not reward generic device/MFA code, placeholder multi-OS collectors, token administration, authentication-only challenge flows, or CLI wiring as substitutes for the enrollment ceremony.

expected_visible_evidence: existing generated DeviceTrustService enrollment stream is reused
client-side ceremony follows init, server challenge, signed challenge response, success
native operations are isolated behind injectable hooks or interfaces
test or fake environment can simulate service/native behavior without enterprise or OS-native dependencies
unsupported platforms are handled intentionally rather than faked with placeholders
avoid_as_primary_requirements: AuthenticateDevice flow as a substitute for enrollment
broad TPM/Secure Enclave support without task or proto evidence
ad hoc code in unrelated client packages that bypasses the device-trust abstraction

scale.1: No visible movement toward the enrollment ceremony or native abstraction; the trajectory is only exploring unrelated client/MFA code or repeating searches.
scale.2: Some relevant proto or client accessors are identified, but the plan remains generic or confuses enrollment with token creation, authentication, CLI work, or unrelated device concepts.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies the generated enrollment stream and native-data/signing needs, but has not yet committed to a protocol-faithful abstraction or isolated test strategy.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly designs or begins implementing the generated enrollment sequence with injectable native collection/signing hooks and avoids unrelated token/CLI/authentication detours.
scale.5: The trajectory provides strong, concrete evidence of a small reusable enrollment layer plus fake/native test hooks that can validate init, challenge signing, success handling, and unsupported-platform behavior without enterprise or OS-native dependencies.

experiences.title: Decimal conversion invalid-type coverage beyond the reported dict
experiences.description: Use when a Django model decimal-field conversion bug involves low-level decimal exceptions leaking instead of the field’s normal validation error, especially after the trajectory inspects or tests unsupported Python input types.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django/Python decimal environment when the task is about model DecimalField conversion semantics and the visible trajectory has located the model field conversion path that calls decimal.Decimal() inside a narrow exception handler. It is most useful once the agent has reproduced or reasoned about raw TypeError from dict input, or has begun broader invalid-type testing. The criterion is less useful during very early repository exploration before the relevant conversion method is found, and should not be generalized to form DecimalField unless the trajectory shows the form implementation has the same leak; in these cases forms often already normalize invalid values correctly.
experiences.experience: The previously useful rubrics focused on ensuring dictionary input raises Django ValidationError and preserving valid conversions. That is necessary but too narrow: a patch that only catches TypeError can satisfy the reported dict example while still leaking ValueError for other unsupported decimal.Decimal() inputs such as malformed sequence-like values. The better rubric should evaluate the model field’s invalid-value contract: all expected conversion failures from decimal.Decimal() for unsupported user/model values should flow through the existing ValidationError path with the field’s invalid message/code/params, while None, floats using the existing context path, ints, Decimals, and valid strings remain unchanged. Avoid a tempting proxy criterion that only checks the exact reported dict TypeError, or that rewards unrelated edits to the form field implementation. Prioritize visible evidence such as: inspection of the model conversion try/except around decimal.Decimal(), manual or test output showing dict TypeError and list/tuple ValueError behavior, a source change broadening the caught conversion exceptions to include both TypeError and ValueError in the model field, and validation that successful decimal conversions are preserved.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should fix the model decimal field conversion contract by routing unsupported decimal.Decimal() conversion failures, including the reported dictionary TypeError and sequence-related ValueError cases, into the field’s existing Django ValidationError path without changing successful conversions or making unrelated form-field changes.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete model decimal invalid-type validation contract

required_visible_evidence: The agent identifies the model field conversion method as the relevant target rather than the form field.
The agent recognizes that decimal.Decimal() can raise TypeError for dictionaries and ValueError for some other unsupported inputs.
The agent preserves the existing invalid ValidationError semantics instead of introducing a new exception type or message path.
The agent checks or reasons that valid strings, integers, floats, Decimal instances, and None still behave as before.
pitfalls_to_penalize: Only catching TypeError for the reported dictionary case while leaving ValueError leaks for other unsupported conversion inputs.
Changing the form DecimalField without evidence it is part of the bug.
Catching overly broad exceptions in a way that could mask unrelated implementation errors.
Altering float handling, None handling, or successful decimal conversion behavior.

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory has identified the model decimal conversion path or the ValidationError contract.
scale.2: Identifies the model conversion path or the dict TypeError symptom, but proposes only vague validation handling or focuses on the wrong component.
scale.3: Addresses the reported dictionary TypeError by routing it to ValidationError, but does not consider other decimal.Decimal() conversion exceptions such as ValueError or lacks preservation evidence for normal conversions.
scale.4: Clearly handles dictionary TypeError and recognizes additional unsupported-input failures, with strong evidence that normal conversions are preserved, but may lack focused regression-test evidence or has minor unrelated exploration.
scale.5: Fully demonstrates the model field fix for TypeError and ValueError conversion failures using the existing ValidationError semantics, preserves valid/None/float behavior, and avoids unnecessary form-field or broad exception changes.

experiences.title: Reverse-proxy auth must gate trusted headers on non-spoofable proxy source
experiences.description: Use this when a Go/HTTP web app task adds reverse-proxy/header-based auto-login with a configurable username header and proxy allowlist.
experiences.context: Applies to Navidrome-like Go HTTP server trajectories implementing authentication bypass from a reverse proxy, especially when the task explicitly says only whitelisted proxy IPs may forward identity headers. It is most useful once the agent has identified or edited auth middleware, route middleware order, config options, or helper code for IP extraction/allowlist matching. It is less useful for unrelated authentication changes, pure configuration-only work with no auth-bypass design yet, or deployments where the framework already has a separately audited trusted-proxy chain and the trajectory clearly uses that mechanism correctly.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases focused on the security boundary: a username header is only trustworthy if the request actually came from an allowed proxy. This was discriminative because many visible implementations added header auth and CIDR matching but derived the source IP from client-controlled forwarding headers such as X-Forwarded-For or X-Real-IP, allowing a direct client to spoof allowlist membership. A better rubric should ask whether the bypass decision is based on the immediate peer/proxy address or a clearly trusted, sanitized proxy-chain mechanism; whether an empty or malformed allowlist fails closed; whether exact IP and CIDR entries are parsed safely; and whether tests or code cover untrusted-source spoofing. Avoid a tempting but wrong criterion that rewards merely adding config fields, middleware, token creation, or support for forwarded headers. Also avoid treating successful builds/tests as enough unless the visible tests specifically exercise trusted versus untrusted proxy sources and spoofed forwarding headers.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For reverse-proxy/header-based authentication, the trajectory should show that the implementation only trusts the configured username header after verifying the non-spoofable requesting proxy source against an explicit IP/CIDR allowlist. Empty, missing, or malformed allowlist configuration should not permit bypass. Client-controlled forwarding headers must not be used as proof that the request came from an allowed proxy unless the trajectory demonstrates a trusted proxy-chain mechanism that sanitizes them before this decision. Evidence should come from visible middleware/helper code, route ordering, and targeted tests for trusted proxy, untrusted direct request, missing header, malformed allowlist, and spoofed X-Forwarded-For/X-Real-IP behavior.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Non-spoofable trusted proxy source validation

primary_evidence: source IP used for allowlist check
fail-closed behavior for empty/malformed allowlist
CIDR and exact IP parsing
tests rejecting spoofed forwarding headers from untrusted peers
avoid_rewarding: config fields without enforcement
middleware that trusts X-Forwarded-For or X-Real-IP directly
build success without security tests
token/context injection before proving proxy trust

scale.1: No meaningful proxy-source validation is visible, or the implementation trusts the configured username header globally.
scale.2: Some allowlist concept exists, but it is incomplete, defaults open, ignores CIDR/exact parsing errors unsafely, or is not clearly connected to the auth-bypass path.
scale.3: The trajectory is roughly equivalent to the parent state: it recognizes the need for a proxy allowlist but visible evidence is partial, untested, or ambiguous about whether the checked address is spoofable.
scale.4: Strong evidence shows fail-closed allowlist enforcement using the direct peer or a trusted proxy-chain source, with sensible exact IP/CIDR handling, though targeted spoofing tests or edge-case handling may still be incomplete.
scale.5: The trajectory clearly enforces the allowlist before reading/using the username header, bases the decision on a non-spoofable proxy source, fails closed on missing/malformed configuration, supports exact IP and CIDR entries, and includes targeted tests proving untrusted requests cannot spoof trust via forwarding headers.

experiences.title: Empty Category Unit Conversion Boundary
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Matplotlib trajectory is fixing false warnings/errors for empty inputs on string/category-unit axes and visible evidence includes converter classification logic or empty-data validation.
experiences.context: Applies in the Matplotlib Python codebase when the reported failure is that plotting or converting empty data after category/string units are installed emits a numeric-pass-through deprecation warning or becomes a conversion error under warnings-as-errors. It is most useful once the trajectory has inspected the unit conversion path, identified the category converter’s empty-sequence classification behavior, or applied/validated a localized fix. It can still be used early as a progress rubric, but should be scored weakly if the agent has only installed dependencies or reproduced import failures. Do not apply this criterion to unrelated plotting bugs, generic warning-message changes, broad exception handling changes, or trajectories working in the wrong checkout/subsystem without evidence tied to category unit conversion.
experiences.experience:
The useful rubrics in this cluster focused on the semantic boundary that empty sequences are not evidence of numeric data. They were useful because correct trajectories visibly traced the failure to the category unit conversion path, recognized the vacuous truth problem in an aggregate numeric-like check over empty values, and changed the behavior so empty lists/arrays create empty artists or empty converted arrays without the misleading deprecation warning. The same criterion also exposed bad trajectories: searching unrelated plotting areas, working in a stale checkout with no active category-unit diff, or validating an unrelated boolean-contour change provides no evidence for the reported bug even if commands run successfully.

When generating a rubric for similar situations, focus on whether the trajectory preserves the intended contract: empty data on category axes should be allowed without warning/error, ordinary categorical strings should still map normally, and real non-empty numeric values passed directly through the category converter should not silently lose the intended deprecation behavior. Prioritize visible evidence such as a localized guard that requires non-empty input before taking the numeric-pass-through warning path, warning-as-error reproduction of the original snippet, checks of direct empty unit conversion, and smoke tests for normal categorical values. If the trajectory notices related empty-sequence false positives in category metadata/logging, that is stronger evidence, but the core criterion should not require a particular patch shape.

Avoid tempting but weaker criteria: do not reward merely changing the warning text, globally suppressing deprecations, changing broad conversion error handling, or expecting numeric `plot([1, 2])` on an already categorical axis to necessarily emit the converter warning, because native numeric plotting may bypass the converter. Also avoid treating environment setup or a custom runner that executes zero tests as validation. The best rubric is a behavior-preservation criterion tied to empty category-unit conversion, not a generic test-count or warning-suppression criterion.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates a correct semantic fix for empty inputs in Matplotlib category/string unit conversion: empty lists or arrays on category-unit axes are not classified as numeric pass-throughs by an empty aggregate predicate, do not emit the misleading numeric-converter deprecation warning, and do not become conversion errors under warnings-as-errors. It also preserves normal categorical mapping and the intended behavior for non-empty numeric values when they are actually routed through the category converter. Strong evidence includes localized converter logic, active diffs in the relevant category unit code, validation of the original empty plotting snippet and direct empty unit conversion, and awareness that some numeric plotting paths may bypass converter warnings.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Preserve Empty Category Conversion Semantics

metadata.environment: Matplotlib Python source tree with string/category units and the units conversion framework
primary_visible_evidence: analysis of the category/string unit converter path reached by empty plot or convert calls
recognition that an all/aggregate numeric-like check over empty values is vacuously true
localized non-empty guard or equivalent behavior before the numeric-pass-through warning path
warning-as-error validation of empty plotting after category units
validation that direct empty unit conversion returns an empty result
checks that ordinary categorical values still convert and non-empty numeric converter input is not broadly suppressed
negative_evidence: global warning suppression
only changing error or warning text
modifying unrelated plotting subsystems
working in a checkout with no relevant active diff
assuming numeric plot calls must warn even when native numeric data may bypass category conversion

scale.1: No visible evidence that the trajectory addresses category/string unit conversion for empty inputs; work is unrelated, purely environment setup, or only changes generic warnings/errors.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory mentions empty category data or reproduces part of the failure, but has no localized semantic fix or validates only unrelated behavior.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies the category converter empty-input issue or proposes a non-empty guard, but validation is incomplete, the active diff is uncertain, or preservation of non-empty behavior is not checked.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory applies a localized fix preventing empty inputs from entering the numeric-deprecation path, validates the original empty plotting failure with warnings-as-errors, and checks normal categorical conversion.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: in addition to the level-4 evidence, the trajectory validates direct empty unit conversion, handles list and array empties, preserves intended non-empty numeric converter behavior without relying on misleading numeric plot expectations, and avoids broad suppression or unrelated edits.

experiences.title: Report-scoped WpVulnDB cache helper lifecycle
experiences.description: Use when a Go/Vuls WordPress WpVulnDB task asks only for the first-step helper that searches cache, especially after the trajectory has identified `wordpress.FillWordPress`, `report.WordPressOption`, and the existing changelog-oriented `cache` package.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories in the Vuls Go codebase where WordPress vulnerability enrichment is performed during reporting via `report/report.go` calling `wordpress.FillWordPress`, and the feature request is narrowly phrased as creating a helper function to look for cached WpVulnDB responses for repeated core versions, themes, and plugins. The criterion is most useful once the agent has enough visible evidence about the report-time call path and the three WpVulnDB API call sites. It is less appropriate for very early repository exploration before the call path is known, for tasks that explicitly request persistent BoltDB cache storage or cache invalidation, or for a different repository where WordPress vulnerability fetching is already owned by a persistent cache layer.
experiences.experience: In these cases, rubrics that only asked for “stable keys” or “reduced API calls” were directionally useful but too easy to satisfy with over-scoped BoltDB/interface changes that did not match the helper-only iteration or normal report workflow. A better rubric should focus on cache ownership and integration: the trajectory should move toward a small helper that searches a shared WpVulnDB cache carried through the report-time WordPress enrichment path, checks before each core/theme/plugin HTTP request, stores the fetched body after misses, and leaves the existing vulnerability conversion, version matching, and `ScannedCves` merge behavior intact. Do not reward merely adding methods to the global `cache.DB` interface, wrapping `httpRequest` globally, initializing cache only for `WordPressOnly`, or passing tests/build if the normal report loop will not share cache state across repeated WordPress resources. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent understands where repeated WpVulnDB calls happen, introduces or plans a report-scoped shared cache object passed into `WordPressOption`/`FillWordPress`, uses simple resource keys such as core version and plugin/theme names, distinguishes cache miss from cached empty response, and avoids unrelated rewrites of parsing or matching logic.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly converge on a narrow report-scoped WpVulnDB cache lookup helper: initialize a shared cache for the report run, pass it through the WordPress reporting option into `FillWordPress`, use a helper that returns cached body plus presence status, consult it before the core, theme, and plugin WpVulnDB `httpRequest` calls, store fetched responses back into the shared cache, and preserve the existing vulnerability parsing, matching, logging, and `ScannedCves` merge semantics.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Narrow report-time WpVulnDB search helper

metadata.task_scope: helper/search function for WpVulnDB cache, not broad persistent cache redesign
expected_call_path_evidence: FillWordPress makes separate core, theme, and plugin WpVulnDB requests
existing cache package is changelog/scan oriented
key_success_evidence: shared cache object lives across multiple FillWordPress calls in one report run
helper distinguishes found cached value from miss
cache is checked before HTTP and populated after miss
existing convert/match/ScannedCves behavior is left unchanged
common_false_proxies: only adding BoltDB methods to cache interface
only wrapping httpRequest with cache.DB lookups
only initializing cache for WordPressOnly scans
changing JSON parsing or vulnerability matching while adding cache

scale.1: No meaningful movement toward a WpVulnDB cache lookup helper; trajectory is only exploring unrelated files or proposes unrelated cache changes.
scale.2: Identifies some WpVulnDB call sites or existing cache infrastructure, but the planned/implemented approach is vague, not report-scoped, or risks using cache state that is absent in the normal WordPress reporting workflow.
scale.3: Shows parent-level progress: recognizes the core/theme/plugin requests and proposes a helper or cache keys, but integration with a shared report-run cache or preservation of existing vulnerability processing remains incomplete or ambiguous.
scale.4: Strong evidence of the correct design: a shared cache is passed through the WordPress report path, the helper checks before each WpVulnDB request and stores after misses, with only minor uncertainty about edge cases such as cached empty responses or exact key choice.
scale.5: Complete evidence of the intended helper-only implementation: report-run cache initialization and plumbing are present, a `searchCache`-style helper returns value plus hit status, all core/theme/plugin lookups use it before HTTP and update it after misses, cached empty responses are not confused with misses, and existing parsing/matching/ScannedCves behavior is preserved.

experiences.title: Preserve Exact Numeric Types Before Formatting
experiences.description: Use this when a formatting/filter bug is caused by converting an already-exact numeric value, such as a Decimal, through an imprecise representation before rounding or rendering.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Django-like template or formatting code when the task explicitly reports precision loss for Decimal or other exact numeric inputs, and the visible trajectory has located the input-normalization path or is editing it. It is especially relevant once the agent has observed that a parse failure or fallback path sends the exact value through binary float conversion. It is less useful for unrelated display-format bugs, localization-only issues, or very early exploration before the conversion mechanism is visible. At final-review stages, the criterion should judge the semantic conversion behavior more than whether the agent added a formal regression test, unless the task specifically requires test changes.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the core semantic contract: the formatting filter must build its internal Decimal from the original exact value, or from a precision-preserving string form, and must not route Decimal inputs through float. This aligned well because the visible trajectory repeatedly showed decisive evidence: the agent reproduced the precision loss, identified that repr-like conversion of Decimal was not directly parseable, found the fallback to float, and patched that conversion path while smoke-testing high-precision Decimal output and common formatting variants. A better rubric should ask whether the trajectory preserves exact Decimal digits while maintaining existing behavior for floats, strings, ints, rounding, and grouping/localization suffixes. Avoid making a project-native regression test the primary criterion in this situation: adding a test is valuable, but a code-only semantic fix can still address the task, and a test-focused rubric may understate a correct trajectory. Also avoid broad proxies such as “ran many tests” or “changed the filter file”; prioritize visible evidence that the lossy conversion path is removed or bypassed for exact numeric inputs and that fallback behavior remains available for non-Decimal inputs.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the formatting/filter implementation preserves exact Decimal precision by avoiding any Decimal-to-float conversion for Decimal inputs, using the original Decimal value or a precision-preserving textual representation before rounding and rendering, while keeping existing behavior for non-Decimal inputs and format options intact.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Exact Decimal Conversion Preservation

prioritize_evidence: The agent identifies a lossy conversion or fallback path involving binary float.
The proposed or applied edit bypasses that path for Decimal/exact numeric inputs.
The trajectory validates high-precision Decimal rendering with the requested number of places.
The trajectory considers preservation of existing behavior for other numeric/string inputs and formatting suffixes.
avoid_as_primary_evidence: Only adding a regression test without fixing the conversion path.
Only running broad test suites without inspecting the numeric conversion semantics.
Changing unrelated formatting or localization behavior as a proxy for precision preservation.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent understands or addresses the lossy exact-numeric conversion; the trajectory may focus on unrelated formatting behavior.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the agent reproduces the precision issue or mentions float precision loss, but has not located or changed the conversion path that causes Decimal inputs to lose digits.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent identifies the lossy conversion path and proposes a plausible precision-preserving approach, but implementation or validation is incomplete or does not clearly cover preservation of existing non-Decimal behavior.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the agent patches or clearly plans a patch so Decimal inputs avoid binary float conversion, and validates the reported high-precision case while showing awareness of non-Decimal compatibility.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory decisively removes or bypasses the lossy path for Decimal inputs, preserves fallback behavior for other inputs, and validates both the reported high-precision rendering and representative existing formatting behaviors such as rounding, strings/ints/floats, and grouping/localization options.

experiences.title: Do not reward task-restatement chain handling without a compatible report round-trip
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating pytest/xdist-style report serialization work where the agent identifies that chained exceptions live in a chain object and proposes serializing it, but visible evidence is mostly exploration, ad-hoc output, or partial edits to report JSON methods.
experiences.context: Applies in Python pytest-core environments where xdist transports TestReport/CollectReport data through JSON-like report serialization hooks, and the bug is loss of chained exception longrepr data. The tempting rubric idea—requiring full __cause__/__context__ chain serialization—is directionally correct, but it is too broad when the trajectory is early, when no durable source patch exists, when validation uses an incompatible globally installed pytest/xdist, or when the edit only adds a chain field without proving deserialization compatibility. The original idea remains appropriate only as a high-level acceptance goal after visible evidence shows both serialization and deserialization paths were patched in the checked-out source and validated by a source-level round-trip or regression test.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics often said the fix must serialize every chained exception, traceback, crash, and separator message. That criterion matches the user-facing requirement, but it overcredits trajectories that merely discover ExceptionChainRepr.chain or add superficial chain handling. In this repository, correctness depends on a compatible round-trip across the exact report serialization contract: preserving the existing longrepr payload shape for normal exceptions, adding structured chain data without discarding sections or outer repr fields, reconstructing the right pytest repr objects using the repository version’s constructor names, and exercising the pytest_report_to/from_serializable or _to_json/_from_json boundary. Avoid generating a rubric that treats “mentions/serializes ExceptionChainRepr.chain” or “manual xdist output seems to show chains” as sufficient. A better rubric should focus on visible implementation evidence: reusable serialization/deserialization helpers for traceback entries and crash objects, handling both chained and non-chained longreprs, preserving description strings and order, compatibility with the checked-out source rather than site-packages, and a source-level round-trip/regression test that fails if the chain collapses to the outermost exception.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear to address chained exception serialization only superficially: they identify or partially serialize the chain but lack visible evidence of a compatible round-trip through the repository's report serialization/deserialization path, or they rely on incompatible external pytest/xdist runs instead of source-level validation.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial or incompatible chained-longrepr round-trip

metadata.target_boundary: pytest report JSON serialization/deserialization used by distributed reporting
evidence_to_check: edits are in the checked-out report serialization source, not only installed site-packages or temporary reproducer files
both serialization and deserialization paths are updated
normal non-chained longrepr payloads remain backward-compatible
chain entries preserve traceback reprs, crash reprs, order, sections, and separator descriptions
deserialization constructs repr objects using APIs/constructor keywords appropriate to the checked-out pytest version
validation exercises _to_json/_from_json or report serialization hooks rather than relying only on truncated failing-test summaries

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory shows a coherent source-level round-trip implementation for chained and non-chained longreprs with compatible constructors and meaningful serialization validation.
scale.2: Minor concern: the trajectory mostly implements a compatible round-trip, but validation is limited or one compatibility detail is not yet explicitly checked.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory has the right design direction and partial source edits, but visible evidence does not establish that deserialization, non-chained compatibility, or version-specific APIs work correctly.
scale.4: Clear concern: the trajectory adds or discusses chain serialization while relying on ad-hoc/truncated xdist output, polluted installed packages, or unverified generated edits; important round-trip details remain unproven.
scale.5: Severe concern: there is no durable source patch, the patch is in the wrong environment/file, or the edit is incompatible with the repository's report repr APIs despite claiming to preserve full chained exceptions.

experiences.title: Do not reward assumption-system diagnosis as sufficient for a modulo/gcd exception leak
experiences.description: Retrieve when a SymPy substitution/assumptions bug is traced through hyperbolic realness checks into modulo and polynomial gcd machinery with Piecewise expressions, especially when candidate criteria focus on cache awareness, root-cause narration, or returning None from assumptions methods.
experiences.context: This applies in SymPy debugging trajectories where a harmless user operation such as subs triggers an assumptions query; the query computes a modulo of an imaginary part, the modulo simplifier calls polynomial gcd logic, and polynomial conversion rejects a Piecewise-containing expression. In that setting, identifying the hyperbolic assumption path or reproducing cache-sensitive behavior is useful exploration evidence but is not a reliable final-correctness criterion. The original idea may still be appropriate early in the investigation, before a patch is proposed, as a progress rubric for tracing the stack. It should not be used at final-review stage to approve patches that modify broad assumption predicates, allow Piecewise as a polynomial generator, or catch polynomial exceptions throughout polynomial APIs.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often rewarded broad statements like “handle Piecewise in the assumption system,” “respect three-valued assumptions logic,” “identify the symbolic root cause,” or “reproduce the cache-sensitive bug.” These criteria overpredict because an agent can correctly observe that a hyperbolic _eval_is_real path computes an im % pi check, yet still patch the wrong layer or make no patch at all. The durable semantic issue is narrower: a best-effort modulo simplification tries to extract a gcd through polynomial routines; if that gcd extraction cannot handle the operands, the modulo operation should abandon that simplification and continue without leaking the polynomial exception. A better rubric should focus on whether the patch localizes the recovery to the modulo/gcd simplification boundary and preserves normal polynomial error behavior elsewhere. Avoid the tempting criterion that the fix must return None from hyperbolic assumption methods whenever Piecewise appears; that can unnecessarily weaken assumptions and misses that other unary functions can trigger the same modulo path. Also avoid rewarding broad catches in polynomial constructors or factorization APIs, because those can mask legitimate polynomial errors. Prioritize visible evidence such as a traced call from an assumptions query into modulo, a patch that treats failed gcd extraction as “no simplifiable gcd” only in that modulo context, and tests showing both the substitution no longer raises and unrelated polynomial APIs still raise or behave as before.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that, after tracing a SymPy substitution failure through an assumptions-driven modulo computation into polynomial gcd/conversion with a Piecewise-containing operand, propose or implement the recovery at the wrong abstraction layer: broad changes to hyperbolic/assumption predicates, global polynomial exception handling, or weakening Piecewise polynomial-generator validation. The correct evidence to look for is a localized fallback around the modulo simplifier's gcd extraction so that an unsupported polynomial conversion merely skips gcd-based simplification for that modulo expression, while ordinary polynomial construction/factorization errors remain observable.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Mislocalized handling of polynomial errors escaping modulo simplification

metadata.environment: SymPy symbolic manipulation bug involving subs, assumptions, Piecewise, modulo, and polynomial gcd conversion
applies_when_visible_evidence_includes: the failure is reproduced only under specific assumptions/cache conditions
the traceback or instrumentation shows an assumptions query computing a modulo of an expression containing Piecewise
the modulo path calls gcd or polynomial conversion and receives a polynomial error about Piecewise generators
misleading_positive_signals_to_discount: the agent identifies the hyperbolic realness check but has not localized the patch to modulo simplification
the agent adds guards returning None from assumption methods solely because Piecewise is present
the agent catches PolynomialError broadly in polynomial APIs or changes generator validation semantics
the agent only demonstrates cache-aware reproduction without a patch
preferred_evidence: a patch catches the unsupported polynomial conversion only while extracting a gcd for modulo simplification
the fallback behaves like no gcd simplification was possible rather than changing the mathematical expression incorrectly
tests cover the original substitution and a representative polynomial API/error-preservation case

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory either remains in investigation without claiming a final fix, or the proposed fix is clearly localized to the modulo gcd-simplification fallback and preserves polynomial API semantics.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory emphasizes assumptions/cache diagnosis more than the modulo boundary, but still considers preserving polynomial exceptions and has not made a broad or weakening patch.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory correctly traces the assumptions-to-polys path but proposes an ambiguous fix in assumptions or polynomial conversion without showing that modulo gcd extraction is the only recovered context.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the patch or plan guards hyperbolic assumptions, changes Piecewise generator handling, or catches polynomial errors across multiple polynomial operations, with little evidence that unrelated polynomial behavior is preserved.
scale.5: Most severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory treats broad assumption weakening, global PolynomialError swallowing, cache reproduction, or root-cause narration as sufficient final correctness, and either makes no effective patch or masks legitimate polynomial errors outside the modulo simplification path.

experiences.title: Do not reward converter-copy fixes as complete DB-to-model mapping fixes
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go persistence task involves database wrapper structs with post-scan hooks plus a separate list/model converter, especially when play-count normalization and JSON field decoding are both part of the DB-to-model contract.
experiences.context: This warning applies in Go repository/persistence layers where rows are scanned into an intermediate database wrapper type, that wrapper has a post-scan or post-map hook for field conversions, and another helper converts a slice of wrappers into model values. A misleading rubric in this setting may overvalue broad checks like 'discs round-trip, play-count modes, no mutation, uniform batch conversion' when the trajectory is actually fixing only the batch converter by copying before normalization. The original idea of verifying discs, play-count modes, and consistency is still appropriate, but only if the criterion distinguishes where the mapping contract is implemented. During early exploration it is fine to reward locating the wrapper, hooks, and converter; during implementation or final review, the rubric should not treat discovery, ad-hoc scripts, deep-copying maps, or avoiding mutation of transient wrapper objects as sufficient evidence of correctness.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked for generic album mapping consistency and often included 'do not mutate source data' or 'avoid double-normalization' as if those were central acceptance criteria. That can mislead the judge because copying in the list converter may look careful while leaving the per-row scan mapping incomplete. In this pattern, the important semantic boundary is the database-row-to-model conversion hook: JSON fields and configuration-dependent derived fields should become correct as the row is scanned, and list conversion should mainly preserve already-mapped model values across Get/GetAll/Search-like paths. Source mutation of a freshly scanned wrapper is not automatically a defect; it may be the intended way to finalize model fields. Avoid tempting criteria that prioritize deep-copying Discs, handling unrelated nil/null cases, or inspecting unrelated album-construction helpers. A better rubric should prioritize visible evidence that the agent inspected the row scan/post-map lifecycle, moved or centralized play-count normalization at the row mapping boundary alongside discs parsing, simplified batch conversion to preserve all scanned fields, and verified both direct wrapper scan behavior and multi-album conversion under absolute and normalized modes.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: At an implementation or final-review stage, penalize a trajectory that treats copying or non-mutating logic inside the batch/list converter as a sufficient album DB-to-model mapping fix while leaving the row-level scan hook responsible only for JSON field parsing and not for configuration-dependent play-count normalization. This flaw is especially relevant when visible code shows a database wrapper with post-scan/post-map hooks and multiple read paths that convert scanned wrappers to models.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Misplaced mapping transformation in batch converter

Play-count normalization is implemented only in a later slice/model converter
The proposed fix focuses on copying before normalizing or avoiding double-normalization
Read paths share or depend on scanned wrapper values before list conversion
Tests or reasoning do not verify that a scanned single database row already maps to a fully correct model
preferred_evidence: The trajectory identifies the row scan hook as the correct DB-to-model boundary
Configuration-dependent play-count normalization is applied during row scanning when appropriate
Batch conversion preserves already-scanned model values uniformly across read paths
Discs JSON handling remains in the serialization/deserialization hook
Validation covers direct row scan and multi-row conversion in both play-count modes

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory clearly treats row scanning as the mapping boundary and uses batch conversion only to preserve scanned model values.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory mentions copying or mutation concerns, but still verifies or plans row-level scan mapping for play counts and serialized fields.
scale.3: Mixed evidence: the trajectory recognizes both the post-scan hook and converter, but it is unclear whether normalization will be centralized at scan time or left in the converter.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory proposes fixing play-count behavior mainly by copying in the converter while leaving the row scan hook unchanged or unexamined.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory concludes that converter immutability/deep-copy changes solve the task, ignores the row-level mapping hook, and validates only ad-hoc converter behavior rather than direct database-row scanning and all read paths.

experiences.title: Unregister Must Invalidate Cached Registry Lookups
experiences.description: Use when a Django/Python task concerns removing a registered lookup or registry entry while lookup resolution is cached, especially when registration already clears the same cache.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django codebase where the visible task and trajectory identify a class-level lookup/registry, a cached lookup-resolution method such as an LRU-cached merged lookup dictionary, and paired register/unregister operations. It is most useful once the agent has inspected or edited the relevant unregister path, so the trajectory can show whether cache invalidation was added after the registry mutation. It may be premature during initial repository exploration before the cache mechanism is visible, and it should not be used for unrelated test-runner setup issues, purely test-only refactors, or registry systems where removal is intentionally lazy or invalidated by a different observable mechanism.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases focused on the semantic invariant: when unregistering/removing a lookup from a cached class-level lookup registry, the same cache-clearing path used by registration must run after the removal so later lookup resolution cannot return stale entries. This aligned well because the visible trajectory often showed decisive evidence: the cached lookup method, the existing clear-cache helper, registration already calling it, and the edit adding that helper call in the unregister path while preserving lookup-name fallback and deletion behavior. A tempting but less reliable criterion is to require the agent to update the named schema regression test merely because the task text mentions minor test changes; in these trajectories that proxy under-credited correct core fixes, since the central correctness condition was the cache invalidation itself. A better generated rubric should prioritize observable implementation evidence over test-file churn: the unregister method should delete the registered lookup and then invalidate the cached lookup dictionaries through the established project helper, without changing unrelated lookup semantics, swallowing missing-key errors, or inventing a different cache-clearing mechanism.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates that unregistering a lookup from the class-level lookup registry invalidates cached lookup-resolution results using the same established cache-clearing mechanism as registration. Strong evidence includes identifying that lookup resolution is cached, observing that registration already clears cached lookups, and modifying or planning the unregister path so it removes the lookup under the correct lookup name and then clears the cached lookup dictionaries for affected classes/subclasses. The criterion should reward preserving existing deletion and lookup-name semantics and should not require unrelated test edits when the core cache-invalidation fix is already evident.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Symmetric Cache Invalidation on Lookup Removal

required_visible_evidence: A cached lookup-resolution method or cached lookup dictionary is identified.
Registration/addition already uses an established cache-clearing helper or equivalent invalidation path.
The unregister/removal path is shown to remove the lookup entry and then call the same cache invalidation path.
Existing lookup-name fallback and deletion behavior are preserved.
do_not_overweight: Whether a named regression test was edited if the task's functional change is already implemented.
Failed attempts to run the test suite caused by environment or settings issues.
Formatting-only differences such as an extra blank line around the added cache-clear call.

scale.1: No evidence that the agent connected unregister/removal to cached lookup invalidation; the trajectory either ignores the relevant unregister path or changes unrelated files.
scale.2: The agent locates the register/unregister code or cached lookup mechanism but does not implement or clearly propose invalidating caches after removal.
scale.3: The trajectory is comparable to the parent: it identifies the missing invalidation and may propose adding it, but evidence is incomplete, unverified, or ambiguous about preserving existing unregister semantics.
scale.4: The agent clearly adds or plans the established cache-clearing call in the unregister path after lookup removal and preserves lookup-name fallback/deletion semantics, with minor uncertainty such as limited validation.
scale.5: The trajectory decisively shows the correct unregister behavior: removal of the lookup under the existing semantics followed immediately by the project’s established cache invalidation for cached lookup dictionaries, with supporting inspection of the cached lookup mechanism and registration symmetry.

experiences.title: Do not over-credit cache migrations on authorization-boundary intent alone
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go/gRPC service bug asks to remove middleware-level caching because of authorization ordering, performance, and architecture concerns, and the trajectory has already found or started using a storage/data-access cache layer.
experiences.context: This warning applies to Flipt-like Go services where caching was implemented as a unary gRPC interceptor with request type switches and is also available as a storage.Store-style decorator. A rubric that asks only whether cached responses can no longer bypass authz is tempting and partially relevant, especially during early exploration or when the proposed fix merely reorders interceptors. However, once the trajectory visibly chooses the architectural migration path—removing cache interceptor registration and adding storage-level cache methods—the authorization-boundary criterion becomes too broad and can over-credit incomplete or broken work. At that stage, correctness depends on preserving cache semantics, invalidation, removal of middleware dependencies, and build validity, not just on the statement that storage is reached after authz.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded the agent for moving cache access below the authorization boundary or for avoiding middleware ordering. That is a sound necessary property, but it was misleading when used as the main or sole criterion: several trajectories had visible evidence of removing the interceptor registration or adding a storage GetFlag cache, yet lacked complete invalidation for all mutations that affect cached flag contents, left obsolete middleware code/type-switch helpers or broken imports, or had syntax/build failures from unsafe deletion. For this task shape, a better rubric should focus on whether the migration is behavior-preserving and mechanically safe: the gRPC response-cache interceptor is not registered in production; the storage cache covers the reads previously cached by middleware; cached flag data is invalidated on flag and variant changes; serialization/keying is appropriate for storage-layer values; stale middleware tests or dead code are handled deliberately; and the Go build/tests are validated. Avoid the tempting criterion “storage-layer caching inherently respects authorization” as a high-confidence success signal unless paired with visible evidence of complete storage-cache behavior and compilation. Prioritize concrete evidence from greps, edited storage cache methods, invalidation paths, gofmt/build/test output, and absence of production interceptor registration.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: In a Go/gRPC cache-migration trajectory, penalize evidence that the agent treats moving cache access below authorization as sufficient while leaving the storage-layer cache migration incomplete or mechanically unsafe. This flaw is present when the trajectory removes or stops registering the middleware cache but only adds a narrow read cache without invalidating cached flag data on all visible flag-affecting mutations, leaves obsolete middleware cache helpers/type switches/imports in an inconsistent state, relies on broad line deletions that introduce syntax errors, or lacks build/test validation after editing core middleware and storage cache code.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Incomplete or Unsafe Storage-Cache Migration

metadata.environment: Go service with gRPC unary interceptors, authorization middleware, and a storage-layer cache decorator
visible_evidence_to_check: production registration of the cache unary interceptor is removed or absent
storage-layer cache implements the read paths formerly cached by middleware
flag cache invalidation covers flag mutations and variant mutations that change flag contents
obsolete middleware cache helpers/imports/tests are removed or intentionally kept without production use
gofmt, go build, or targeted go tests are run after edits
no visible syntax errors, unused imports, or malformed Go blocks remain
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: crediting the trajectory mainly because storage-layer caching is after authz

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory shows a coherent storage-cache migration, appropriate invalidation for affected cached data, no production middleware cache registration, and successful formatting/build or targeted tests.
scale.2: Minor evidence of incompleteness: the architecture is mostly correct, but validation or cleanup evidence is thin, or one noncritical stale test/helper issue remains without signs of broken production code.
scale.3: Moderate flaw: the trajectory removes middleware registration and adds some storage caching, but visible evidence leaves important behavior uncertain, such as missing tests for invalidation or unclear handling of mutation paths.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory over-focuses on the auth boundary while visibly missing important storage-cache semantics, such as caching flags without invalidating on variant or flag changes, or leaving obsolete middleware cache code in a confusing/inconsistent state.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the migration is mechanically broken or largely incomplete, with syntax/build errors, malformed middleware deletion, remaining production middleware cache usage, or storage caching that can serve stale data after common mutations.

experiences.title: Check-mode commands must be non-mutating
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django-style management command option named `--check` is meant to report pending work via exit status without performing the work, especially when the bug is that it currently writes files unless combined with dry-run.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django/Python management-command task where the user explicitly contrasts `--check` behavior with other non-mutating check modes and the trajectory has located or edited the control flow that computes pending changes and then writes/updates generated migration artifacts. It is most useful once the visible trajectory shows either the write-before-exit bug, a patch moving the check guard before write/update helpers, or manual/test evidence about both exit status and filesystem effects. It is less applicable to unrelated migration-generation bugs, pure documentation/output wording tasks, or early exploration where the command’s mutating code path has not yet been identified. Do not require exact output text or help-text updates unless the task or trajectory makes those requirements explicit.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged the semantic contract of `--check`: pending changes should produce a nonzero exit and no file creation, update, deletion, or formatting side effect, while ordinary generation and no-change behavior remain intact. This aligned well because visible trajectory evidence repeatedly exposed the decisive control-flow boundary: whether the check condition is evaluated before any migration-writing or update helper is invoked, or otherwise guarantees a no-write path. A better rubric should focus on observable behavior and implementation placement, not merely on whether tests pass or whether the command exits with status 1. Also avoid overfitting to optional details such as an exact log message, a documentation/help-string edit, or making `--check` globally equivalent to dry-run; those can be acceptable or irrelevant depending on the task, but they are not the core correctness signal. Prioritize evidence such as: manual reproduction showing no generated migration file after `--check`; normal command still writes; no-change `--check` succeeds; update/delete paths are not reached under `--check`; and targeted regression tests assert both exit code and absence of filesystem changes.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Non-mutating check-mode migration detection
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the check-mode path detects pending migration work and reports it with a nonzero exit status before any migration artifact is created, updated, deleted, or formatted, while preserving successful no-change behavior and normal file-writing behavior when check mode is not requested. Strong evidence includes a control-flow change that short-circuits before write/update helpers or an equivalent no-write guarantee, plus validation that inspects both exit status and migration-file presence.

required_behavior: pending changes under check mode return a nonzero status
pending changes under check mode do not create new migration files
check mode does not update, delete, or otherwise mutate existing migration files
no pending changes under check mode remains successful
normal non-check generation still writes migrations
high_value_visible_evidence: guard or early exit before migration write/update calls
filesystem assertions after running check mode
comparison with other non-mutating check-mode commands
targeted regression test for no-write behavior
avoid_as_primary_signal: exit status alone
generic test-suite pass messages without filesystem assertion
exact log wording
optional help-text or documentation changes unless explicitly required

scale.1: No visible evidence that check mode avoids writes; the trajectory only preserves or discusses the existing write-then-exit behavior, or focuses solely on exit status.
scale.2: Some recognition that check mode should not write, but the implementation or validation is incomplete, ambiguous, or fails to cover the actual write/update path.
scale.3: Moderate evidence equivalent to the parent trajectory: the intended no-write guard is identified or partially implemented, but validation is limited or important paths such as normal generation/no-change/update behavior are not checked.
scale.4: Strong evidence that check mode exits nonzero before normal migration writing and that ordinary generation remains intact, with at least manual or targeted validation of no generated file.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory clearly guarantees check mode is non-mutating across create/update/delete paths, preserves no-change and non-check behavior, and includes or plans a focused regression test/assertion that verifies both exit code and filesystem non-mutation.

experiences.title: Preserve Nested Dependency Submatrices in Parallel Composition
experiences.description: Retrieve when a modeling/math library bug involves an output-input dependency or separability matrix for nested parallel compound expressions, especially where a nested submodel should be equivalent to the flattened expression.
experiences.context: Applies in Python scientific/modeling code where a public separability/dependency-matrix API analyzes compound model expression trees with parallel composition. The task or trajectory should show a nested parallel composition producing an all-coupled sub-block even though the same components are separable when flattened. This is most useful once the trajectory has inspected the operator-combination helper or has visible evidence that recursive analysis returns intermediate matrices which are then embedded into a larger block matrix. It is less applicable for unrelated environment setup, pure import/build failures, serial composition bugs, arithmetic-composition semantics, or cases where the nested component is genuinely nonseparable and should produce a dense block.
experiences.experience: The useful criterion in these cases is not merely 'handle nested CompoundModels recursively.' The discriminative issue is whether the parallel-composition path preserves an already-computed child dependency matrix when placing it into the larger output-input matrix. The best rubric should reward trajectories that identify the nested-vs-flattened equivalence invariant, inspect the matrix stacking logic for parallel composition, notice that an intermediate right-hand or child matrix can be replaced by an all-ones/all-true block, and implement or validate copying the existing submatrix into the correct block. Earlier rubrics that broadly required recursion through compound models or changes to serial composition were weaker because they could point to unnecessary changes; the visible evidence instead supports a narrower block-preservation criterion. Avoid criteria that overvalue dependency installation attempts, generic test running, changes to the individual leaf models, or blanket treatment of all nested models as atomic/nonseparable. Prioritize evidence such as: the user-provided nested expression should match the flattened expression; the lower-right block should remain diagonal for independent 1D components; the trajectory inspects the operator dispatcher and stacking helper; and any validation compares old all-coupled behavior against the expected block-diagonal matrix.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should preserve separability/dependency submatrices produced by nested parallel compound operands when embedding them into a larger dependency matrix. Strong evidence includes recognizing that the nested expression must be equivalent to the flattened expression, locating the parallel-composition matrix stacking logic, identifying that an intermediate child matrix is being replaced by a dense/all-true block rather than copied, and validating that the nested case keeps independent leaf outputs separated in the resulting block matrix.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Nested Parallel Submatrix Preservation

task_features: public API returns an output-input separability or dependency matrix
bug appears only when an equivalent compound expression is nested
parallel composition should place child dependency matrices in disjoint blocks
high_value_evidence: comparison between nested and flattened equivalent expressions
inspection of recursive expression-tree analysis and parallel stacking helper
recognition that an already-computed child matrix must be copied, not replaced by ones
validation of a block-diagonal or partially block-diagonal expected matrix
avoid_overgeneralizing_to: serial composition unless the trajectory shows the same matrix-preservation flaw there
environment setup progress without semantic diagnosis

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory understands nested parallel separability or dependency-matrix preservation; focus remains on unrelated setup, leaf models, or generic exploration.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory mentions nested compound handling or flattened-vs-nested mismatch but has not connected it to preserving a computed child dependency matrix in the parallel composition path.
scale.3: Moderate evidence equivalent to parent behavior: the trajectory identifies the relevant separability code and states that nested parallel compounds should preserve child dependencies, but the diagnosis remains broad or lacks a clear block-copy/all-coupled-block explanation.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory locates the parallel stacking logic, explains that an intermediate nested operand matrix is being expanded into a dense block, and proposes preserving the actual submatrix in the correct block.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory implements or clearly specifies the submatrix-preservation fix and validates the nested expression against the flattened equivalent or an explicit expected block matrix showing independent leaf components remain separated.

experiences.title: Do not reward annotation volume when dynamic seed behavior is unproven
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python/OpenLibrary-style task asks for List-model typing and seed cleanup, and the trajectory mainly adds TypedDicts, unions, return annotations, or broad rewrites around polymorphic seeds.
experiences.context: This applies in a dynamic Infogami/Thing-based Python 3.11 codebase where list seeds may be stored or passed as objects, {'key': ...} dictionaries, subject strings, and sometimes legacy non-string storage-like values.
