A rubric that only checks whether many annotations, TypedDicts, or type aliases were introduced is misleading when the visible trajectory shows wholesale rewrites, unresolved type-checker errors, failing or skipped plugin tests, manual AttributeErrors from seed/export paths, direct access to .key/.type on raw self.seeds, or unverified assumptions about where related interfaces such as user lookup, list input normalization, casts, and safe URL helpers live. The original idea remains useful only when judging a later, stable patch that already demonstrates behavior-preserving seed normalization, correct cross-module scope, and validation beyond syntax/focused smoke tests.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics praised comprehensive type annotation coverage: TypedDicts, union aliases, TypeGuard-style narrowing, explicit return types, and public-method annotation completeness. That criterion is too easy to satisfy superficially in this task. In these trajectories, adding many annotations often coincided with broad file replacement, new helper aliases that did not actually narrow runtime behavior, direct iteration over raw polymorphic seeds as if they were homogeneous objects, or ignoring related modules where list input normalization, casts, get_user-style typing, and URL-safety cleanup actually belonged. A better rubric should not ask whether annotations are numerous or comprehensive in isolation. It should ask whether the trajectory preserves the legacy seed contract while making it clearer: object/dict/string seeds are normalized at boundaries; subject strings keep the expected key/url behavior; dict seeds are resolved only where a site lookup is valid and with None-safe handling; export/list queries do not access object attributes on raw dict/string seeds; and any reported failing tests or mypy errors around these paths are investigated rather than waved away. Avoid the tempting criterion 'all public methods are annotated' or 'uses TypedDict/Union/TYPE_CHECKING broadly.' Prioritize visible evidence from targeted diffs, tests, manual reproductions, and failure traces showing that the annotation cleanup is behavior-preserving across List, Seed, plugin list input, user/cast helpers, and safe URL boundaries.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for this List-model typing task when the visible work emphasizes broad annotation coverage or full-file rewrites without preserving the dynamic seed/list behavior contract. This flaw is present if the agent adds TypedDicts, unions, return types, or type guards but leaves evidence that raw seeds are treated as a single homogeneous type, dict/string/object seed variants are not normalized safely, subject key/url normalization is changed or untested, export logic accesses .key or .type on raw polymorphic values, related list input/user/cast/url-safety modules are not considered despite task cues, or reported plugin/manual/type-check failures around these paths remain unresolved or dismissed without traceback-based triage.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Annotation-first refactor risks dynamic seed regressions

metadata.environment: Python 3.11 dynamic Infogami/Thing model code with OpenLibrary-style List and Seed objects
visible_evidence_to_check: diffs that add many annotations, type aliases, or full-file rewrites
seed handling code for object, dict-with-key, subject-string, and legacy non-string values
export/list query code that iterates raw stored seeds
plugin/list input normalization and related user/cast/url helper search
test, mypy, or manual reproduction outputs and whether failures are investigated
not_sufficient_evidence: presence of TypedDict or Union aliases alone
a few focused tests passing while seed/export/plugin failures remain visible

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory makes targeted typing changes, preserves all visible seed variants, handles related modules, and validates relevant behavior/failures.
scale.2: Minor evidence: annotations are somewhat coverage-driven, but the agent still checks key seed variants and no visible unresolved behavior issue remains.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory adds useful annotations but leaves some cross-module scope or seed-normalization behavior unverified, with limited validation.
scale.4: Clear evidence: broad annotation/rewrite work is paired with unresolved test, mypy, or manual failures around seed/export/list behavior, or direct unsafe assumptions about raw seed shapes.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory repeatedly rewrites code or adds extensive typing while visibly breaking polymorphic seed handling, dismissing relevant failures, or patching unrelated registration/setup code instead of addressing the behavioral contract.

experiences.title: Prefer Sentinel-Safe Conditional Semantics Over Test-Only Criteria
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task describes a localized framework bug caused by a sentinel value such as None reaching an existing conditional, especially when a neighboring branch already shows the intended guard pattern.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django-style codebase when the visible task and trajectory identify a narrow failure path: a public/helper method is intentionally called with a sentinel index for an empty/prototype object, and a conditional compares that sentinel to an integer or count. It is most useful after the agent has inspected the relevant method or reproduced the traceback, or when the task itself explicitly names the failing condition. It may be premature during pure repository exploration before the failing branch and intended semantics are known. It should not be used as the primary criterion when the bug is broad, requires redesign, or the main uncertainty is test infrastructure rather than the behavioral contract.
experiences.experience: For this cluster, rubrics that focused on adding a project-native regression test were too strict as a predictor of patch correctness: a minimal source fix can satisfy the requested behavior even without committing a new test. The useful rubrics instead evaluated the semantic boundary of the fix: the code must not compare a sentinel None index with an integer count, but it must still preserve the existing deletion-field behavior for the non-sentinel cases. A better rubric should ask whether the trajectory has identified the None-index call path, guarded only the unsafe comparison, preserved the short-circuit behavior when extra deletions are allowed, and preserved delete-field addition for indexed initial forms. Avoid the tempting generic criterion “follow the existing pattern” unless it is tied to the concrete contract being protected; consistency is useful evidence only because the neighboring branch demonstrates how this same sentinel should be handled. Prioritize visible evidence such as traceback lines, call-site inspection showing a None argument, source inspection of the conditional, and a patch/intended patch that adds an explicit non-None guard without changing unrelated formset construction or field ownership semantics.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate and implement the precise sentinel-safe conditional fix for a formset empty/prototype form path: the method that adds fields must not compare a None index to an integer initial-form count, while preserving the existing deletion-field behavior for both allowed extra deletion fields and indexed initial forms. Strong evidence includes identifying that the empty/prototype form passes None into the field-adding method, locating the deletion-field conditional that currently compares the index to the initial count, and changing or planning to change only that comparison so it is evaluated only when the index is not None unless the extra-deletion option already makes the comparison unnecessary.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: None-Safe Deletion Field Conditional

required_visible_evidence: A call path where an empty or prototype form invokes field addition with a None index.
A conditional that adds a deletion field using a disjunction involving an extra-deletion flag and an index/count comparison.
Recognition that the unsafe operation is the index/count comparison, not the empty-form construction itself.
A fix or patch plan that guards the comparison with a non-None check while leaving the extra-deletion short-circuit and indexed initial-form behavior intact.
anti_evidence: Changing broad formset construction or empty-form behavior instead of guarding the unsafe comparison.
Suppressing deletion fields whenever the index is None in a way that also breaks the extra-deletion-allowed case.
Requiring only a regression test without evaluating whether the source behavior is semantically correct.

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory has identified the None-index comparison or the deletion-field semantics; it may be exploring unrelated files or focusing only on environment/test setup.
scale.2: The trajectory notices a None-related failure or reproduces a traceback but has not isolated the exact conditional or may propose broad changes that risk altering formset behavior.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies the failing conditional and the need for a non-None guard, but evidence is incomplete about preserving extra-deletion and indexed initial-form behavior.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly targets the unsafe index/count comparison with a non-None guard and shows awareness that existing deletion-field behavior should remain unchanged for the main non-sentinel cases.
scale.5: The trajectory provides decisive evidence: it traces the None-index call path, applies or plans a minimal guard around only the unsafe comparison, preserves the extra-deletion short-circuit and initial-form index behavior, and validates the reported empty/prototype form scenario.

experiences.title: Reverse-proxy auth must pass pre-auth parameter gates
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go HTTP endpoint adds reverse-proxy authentication but the reported failure is a missing credential parameter emitted by middleware that runs before authentication.
experiences.context: Applies to Go/chi-style middleware stacks where an endpoint has independent authentication from the main API, an existing trusted reverse-proxy auth implementation elsewhere, and the task explicitly expects requests with a trusted user header to work without normal credential parameters. It is especially relevant after the trajectory has inspected middleware order or begun editing auth middleware. Do not apply as the primary criterion when there is no pre-auth required-parameter validation, when credential parsing occurs only inside the auth function, or during very early repository exploration before the agent has enough evidence about middleware order.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics often focused on whether the Subsonic authenticate middleware reads the reverse-proxy user header, validates proxy trust, and skips credential validation. That is necessary but not sufficiently discriminative in this situation: the visible task failure is `Missing required parameter "u"`, and the trajectory repeatedly shows a required-parameter middleware running before authentication. Patches that only add reverse-proxy logic inside authentication can still be blocked before auth is reached. A better rubric should explicitly evaluate whether the agent handles the pre-auth parameter gate: a trusted reverse-proxy header must be recognized before `u` is required, only non-auth parameters should remain required for that path, and absent/untrusted headers must still follow normal Subsonic credential requirements. The rubric should also prefer using the existing reverse-proxy trust helper or matching its semantics exactly, because config-only bypasses or duplicated IP checks can accept missing `u` in the wrong cases. Avoid the tempting broad criterion of “checks ReverseProxyWhitelist and header in authenticate”; prioritize visible evidence of middleware-order awareness, changes or tests covering the missing-`u` gate, correct username context setup, preservation of standard Subsonic auth, and negative validation for missing header or untrusted proxy.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Header-aware required-parameter gate
reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a reverse-proxy-auth task on an endpoint whose middleware validates required credential parameters before authentication, the trajectory should ensure the trusted reverse-proxy username is considered before the required-parameter check rejects missing `u`. A strong trajectory either reuses the existing reverse-proxy trust/header helper or exactly preserves its behavior, relaxes the `u` requirement only when a trusted configured header supplies a username, sets request username/user context consistently, skips Subsonic credential validation only on that trusted path, preserves normal password/token/JWT auth otherwise, and validates both the no-`u` trusted-header request and negative cases such as missing header or untrusted proxy.

metadata.environment: Go HTTP server with chained middleware and separate endpoint authentication
key_visible_evidence: middleware order shows required-parameter validation before endpoint authentication
reported failure is a missing credential parameter rather than bad credentials
trajectory edits or plans include the required-parameter middleware, not only the authenticate function
reverse-proxy trust semantics come from the existing implementation or are matched exactly
validation includes trusted-header request without credential params and fallback/negative cases
anti_patterns: only adding reverse-proxy lookup inside authentication after the required-parameter gate
relaxing required `u` whenever reverse-proxy config is set, even without a trusted header
requiring the header username to match a missing query username
duplicating whitelist logic without checking unix-socket and context-IP behavior
breaking existing Subsonic password, token, encoded password, or JWT auth while adding the bypass

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory recognizes the pre-auth required-parameter gate; it focuses only on generic header parsing or credential validation.
scale.2: Some reverse-proxy auth logic is proposed or implemented, but it is only inside the authenticate path and would still allow the earlier required-parameter check to reject missing `u`.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies the required-parameter ordering issue or partially relaxes `u`, but the relaxation is too broad, not tied to a trusted header, lacks context consistency, or has no meaningful negative validation.
scale.4: The trajectory addresses both the required-parameter gate and authentication path for trusted reverse-proxy headers, preserves normal auth in intent, and shows relevant validation, with only minor uncertainty such as duplicated trust logic or incomplete edge-case tests.
scale.5: The trajectory cleanly integrates the existing reverse-proxy trust/header semantics before required-parameter enforcement, bypasses credentials only for a trusted supplied username, preserves all standard auth modes and context behavior, and validates positive and negative `/rest/*` scenarios without relying on unrelated test pass signals.

experiences.title: Identity-Based Sentinel Checks for Equality-Hostile Patch Values
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python testing framework failure involves mock patch metadata, DEFAULT sentinels, and user-supplied `new` values such as NumPy arrays whose equality/truthiness is unsafe.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/pytest-like repositories when the visible issue or trajectory points to collection or fixture-argument inference inspecting mock patch decorators, especially a condition that checks whether a patch replacement value is a DEFAULT sentinel using list membership or equality. It is most useful once the trajectory has identified that explicit replacement values should not consume mock-injected arguments, while DEFAULT sentinel patchers should. It may be premature during generic dependency setup before the relevant mock-patching logic is located, and it is not the right criterion for unrelated NumPy truth-value bugs, general array comparison semantics, or patches that only alter test-running environment problems without touching sentinel detection.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic boundary between sentinel identity and arbitrary object equality. They were discriminative because the visible trajectory repeatedly showed the failing operation was equality-based membership against mock DEFAULT sentinels, and the successful direction was to compare against sentinel singleton objects by identity. A strong rubric should require that the agent preserve mock.patch semantics: explicit `new` values, including arrays or objects with overloaded equality, should not be counted as injected mock arguments and should not be compared via `==` or `in`; actual DEFAULT sentinel values from the supported mock modules should still be counted when appropriate. The criterion should prioritize visible evidence such as identifying membership/equality as the root cause, replacing it with identity-based sentinel checks, and validating both the array-like explicit replacement case and the DEFAULT case. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as merely “handle NumPy arrays,” special-casing NumPy, catching the ValueError, using `any()`/`all()` on array comparisons, or only proving collection no longer crashes without checking that DEFAULT patchers still consume arguments.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should resolve the mock patch argument-counting bug by treating DEFAULT values as singleton sentinels and comparing them by object identity rather than equality or container membership. It should preserve the intended distinction that patchers with explicit replacement values, including arrays or custom equality-hostile objects, do not inject mock arguments, while patchers whose replacement is the DEFAULT sentinel still do. Strong evidence includes locating the mock patch metadata inspection, explaining why equality invokes array-like truth-value behavior, implementing or proposing an identity-based sentinel test for all relevant mock implementations, and validating both the no-crash explicit-array case and the DEFAULT-counting case.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Sentinel Identity Preserves Mock Patch Semantics

key_evidence: Identifies equality or membership comparison against DEFAULT sentinels as the source of array truth-value errors
Uses identity semantics for sentinel detection instead of `==`, `in`, or array truth coercion
Maintains correct counting of patchers that actually inject mock arguments
Confirms explicit `new` values such as arrays are not counted and do not raise
not_required: Full test suite success when the repository test environment is incompatible
common_pitfalls: Special-casing NumPy arrays rather than fixing sentinel comparison semantics
Catching or suppressing the ValueError while leaving equality-based logic

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses sentinel comparison semantics; it may focus only on environment setup, generic NumPy handling, or unrelated collection logic.
scale.2: Recognizes that array-like `new` values cause a crash but proposes a NumPy-specific workaround, exception handling, or another approach that does not clearly preserve mock DEFAULT behavior.
scale.3: Identifies the mock DEFAULT comparison as relevant and partially moves toward safer logic, but evidence is incomplete about identity semantics, support for relevant sentinels, or preservation of argument counting.
scale.4: Clearly uses identity-based sentinel detection and avoids equality with arbitrary replacement values, with some validation or reasoning for both explicit replacements and DEFAULT patchers.
scale.5: Fully demonstrates the intended semantics: identity checks against the relevant DEFAULT sentinels, no equality or membership on arbitrary `new` objects, explicit array-like replacements return zero without raising, and DEFAULT patchers still count correctly.

experiences.title: Read-only --check semantics for CLI commands
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task asks for a management/CLI `--check` mode to match related commands by detecting pending work without performing the normal side effect.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django/Python CLI-management-command setting when the problem statement explicitly contrasts one command's `--check` behavior with peer commands and says the check should exit without creating files, applying changes, or otherwise performing the primary action. It is especially relevant once the trajectory has found the command control flow where pending work is detected and then write/apply/update helpers are invoked before the check exit. It can still be useful during early exploration if the task text itself makes the read-only contract explicit, but the rubric should be judged more cautiously until the trajectory has inspected the actual write path. Do not apply broadly to every flag named `--check`; it may be irrelevant when `--check` is only a validation toggle, when side effects are intentionally part of the check, or when the task is about output formatting/documentation rather than preventing persistent changes.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful rubric in these cases evaluated whether `--check` has consistent, read-only semantics across related commands. That was discriminative because the visible task contract was not merely 'return the right exit code'; it required detecting missing migrations while avoiding file generation, matching peer commands that exit before doing their normal action. The strongest observable evidence is control-flow ordering: after pending changes are detected, the trajectory should move the check-mode exit/return before any migration-writing, update, delete, apply, or optimization write helper is called, while leaving the no-change path successful and ordinary non-check behavior unchanged. Manual validation evidence should prioritize filesystem or persistent-state checks before and after running the command, plus coverage of alternate write paths such as update modes where applicable. A tempting but weaker criterion is to say '`--check` should imply `--dry-run`' or only require nonzero exit status; that can miss cases where dry-run has different logging/exit semantics, where update/delete helpers still run, or where a patch reports success but still performs side effects. A better generated rubric should phrase the requirement as a read-only check-mode short-circuit preserving exit-code semantics, not as generic cross-command consistency detached from the specific side-effect boundary.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates that the check-mode implementation detects pending work but prevents the command's normal persistent action from running. For this Django CLI task, excellent progress means the agent has identified the write/update side-effect path, compared the intended behavior with related check modes, and either implemented or is clearly steering toward a control-flow change that exits nonzero on detected pending changes before invoking file-writing or update/deletion helpers, while preserving successful no-change behavior and normal non-check operation.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Read-only check-mode short-circuit

task_cues: Problem statement says a `--check` flag should exit without making migrations or persistent changes.
Problem statement compares the command to related commands whose `--check` modes do not perform the primary action.
trajectory_evidence_to_prioritize: Inspection of the command branch where pending work is detected.
Recognition that existing behavior invokes write/update helpers before the check-mode exit.
Patch or plan that places the check-mode exit/return before all relevant persistent side-effect calls.
Validation that no files or persistent state are changed under `--check`, not just that the exit code is nonzero.
Preservation of normal behavior when `--check` is absent and success when no pending work exists.
anti_evidence: Only checking for nonzero exit status after pending work is detected.
Treating `--check` as a generic alias for `--dry-run` without verifying exit-code and side-effect differences.
Skipping alternate write paths such as update/delete modes when the command has them.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent understands or addresses the read-only side-effect boundary of check mode; focus is unrelated or only on locating files.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the agent mentions consistency or exit codes, but has not identified the actual persistent write/apply path or may conflate check mode with dry-run.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent identifies that check mode currently performs the primary action before exiting and proposes preventing side effects, but coverage of alternate write paths, no-change behavior, or validation is incomplete.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory shows a concrete control-flow change or precise plan to exit/return before the normal write/update action, with attention to preserving ordinary command behavior and nonzero status on pending changes.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: in addition to the correct short-circuit before all relevant persistent side-effect paths, the trajectory includes targeted validation or test planning/assertions that check mode leaves files/state unchanged, exits appropriately on pending work, succeeds with no work, and does not regress non-check execution.

experiences.title: Do not over-credit generic Windows case-preservation insight
experiences.description: Retrieve when a pytest/conftest Windows casing task involves `normcase`, `realpath`, `py.path.local`, or cache deduplication, and the trajectory has only identified or partially separated normalized paths from import paths.
experiences.context: This applies in Python/pytest-style repositories where a Windows case-insensitive but case-preserving filesystem regression is caused by using a lowercased/canonicalized path in conftest discovery or import-name derivation. The misleading rubric pattern is to reward the broad idea that imports should preserve original casing while normalized paths are used for cache keys. That idea is directionally useful, but it is not sufficient when multiple conftest-loading boundaries exist: parent-directory discovery, cut-directory comparisons, conftest module import/package detection, and duplicate-load cache identity. It may still be appropriate to mention case preservation as a component criterion when the trajectory also shows a coherent end-to-end treatment of those boundaries. It is not appropriate as the main success criterion at early investigation or after a partial edit that only changes one call site, changes the shared path helper globally, assumes `realpath()` restores actual Windows spelling, or relies on Linux lowercase-path simulations.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster generated criteria like “preserve original path casing for Python imports while using normalized paths for deduplication.” Those rubrics were too broad and tended to over-credit trajectories that had found `normcase` and conftest import code but had not proven the fix was complete. The important distinction is not merely whether the agent knows lowercasing is bad for imports; it is whether the proposed patch confines case-insensitive canonicalization to identity keys without feeding it into package discovery, parent traversal, or module import, and whether it preserves the prior duplicate-conftest behavior. A better rubric should focus on visible evidence that the agent has audited all conftest path-normalization call sites, avoided mutating the shared normalization helper in a way that drops deduplication semantics, used a case-preserving resolved identity for cache keys, kept package/import operations on the case-preserved filesystem path, and understood why Linux wrong-case experiments are not decisive for Windows. Avoid the tempting criterion that simply rewards “avoid `normcase()`” or “use original case for imports”; replacement criteria should prioritize complete boundary separation, cache-key consistency, and regression coverage for both mixed-case import success and duplicate-load prevention.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Incomplete separation of import paths from identity keys
reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a Windows conftest path-casing regression, penalize trajectories that treat the root cause as solved after only identifying lowercasing or preserving case at one import call site, without visible evidence that all conftest discovery/import boundaries are handled coherently. This flaw is present when the agent leaves canonicalized/lowercased paths in package discovery or parent traversal, modifies a shared path-normalization helper so duplicate-load semantics are weakened, assumes `realpath()` alone recovers Windows filesystem spelling, keys related caches inconsistently, ignores cut-directory comparison behavior, or validates primarily with Linux lowercase paths that do not model Windows case-insensitive lookup.

metadata.task_family: pytest conftest loading on Windows case-insensitive/case-preserving filesystems
evidence_to_check: whether normalized paths are restricted to cache or duplicate-detection identity
whether package discovery and module import use case-preserved paths
whether parent-directory conftest discovery avoids walking a lowercased path
whether cache keys remain consistent across conftest module and directory caches
whether previous duplicate-load behavior for symlinks or bad casing is preserved
whether validation acknowledges Linux cannot directly reproduce Windows casing lookup
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: agent merely states that `normcase` lowercases paths on Windows or that Python imports need original casing

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory visibly audits the relevant conftest-loading path boundaries, keeps import/package operations case-preserved, uses a consistent case-insensitive identity key only where needed, and accounts for duplicate-load behavior.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory has the right separation concept and most affected boundaries are considered, but one secondary cache or comparison path remains insufficiently justified.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory identifies the root cause and partially separates import paths from cache keys, but visible work covers only the main import call and leaves discovery traversal, cut-directory comparisons, or duplicate-load preservation uncertain.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory proposes a patch based mainly on avoiding lowercasing or using original paths, but does not audit multiple normalization call sites and risks inconsistent caches or lost duplicate prevention.
scale.5: Most severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory changes an unrelated area or globally alters/removes path normalization without preserving conftest discovery/import semantics, while relying on generic Windows casing statements or invalid Linux simulations as sufficient validation.

experiences.title: Zero-like Decimal Formatting Crash Contract
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python/Django numeric formatting bug involves Decimal/string zero values with stored fractional zeros and a precision argument of zero causing an invalid Decimal context or quantization precision.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django/Python codebase when the task reports that a formatting helper/filter crashes for inputs like a string zero with trailing decimal places or an equivalent Decimal value, especially with an explicit zero decimal-place argument. It is most useful once the trajectory has located the formatting implementation or reproduced/debugged the Decimal tuple/precision path. It is less useful for unrelated float formatting regressions, nonzero rounding-only changes, localization-only issues, or very early exploration before the agent has connected the crash to Decimal precision/integer-zero handling.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics were useful because they focused on the semantic contract visible in the trajectory: zero-valued Decimal-compatible inputs with trailing fractional zeros must not flow into Decimal.Context or quantize with an invalid precision, and the returned value should match normal zero-decimal formatting while preserving existing behavior. However, rubrics that require a specific implementation such as clamping the computed precision to at least one are too narrow: an equally valid fix may bypass quantization for integer-valued inputs when the requested precision is zero. A better rubric should judge whether the trajectory has identified the zero-like Decimal edge case and applied a narrow fix that prevents the crash for both string and Decimal inputs without disrupting rounding, sign handling, positive/negative precision, grouping, or localization suffix behavior. Avoid tempting proxies such as rewarding broad exception swallowing, special-casing only the literal string input, or requiring one exact patch shape. Prioritize visible evidence: reproduction of both reported inputs, Decimal tuple/precision diagnosis showing how a zero value with a negative exponent creates invalid precision, a targeted code change in the formatting path, and validation of nearby formatting cases.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a targeted fix for the numeric formatting crash where zero-valued string and Decimal inputs with trailing fractional zeros and a zero decimal-place argument previously produced an invalid Decimal context precision. Strong evidence includes reproducing both input forms, diagnosing the Decimal exponent/precision or integer-zero branch that causes the invalid precision, implementing a narrow change that either safely avoids the invalid quantization path or guarantees valid precision, and checking that normal formatting behavior for nonzero values, positive and negative precision arguments, signs, grouping/localization suffixes, and nearby zero cases remains intact.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Zero-like Decimal Precision Safety

metadata.environment: Python Django-style numeric formatting/filter code using Decimal quantization and localization-aware number formatting
key_inputs: string zero with trailing fractional zeros and precision 0
Decimal zero with trailing fractional zeros and precision 0
priority_evidence: reported crash reproduced or explicitly traced
Decimal tuple/exponent/precision cause identified
targeted formatting-path change prevents invalid Decimal context precision
validation covers both string and Decimal inputs plus nearby formatting cases
avoid: requiring a single implementation shape such as only max-clamping precision

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory has connected the crash to zero-like Decimal/string inputs or the Decimal precision path.
scale.2: Some investigation of the formatting function or reproduction attempts, but no clear diagnosis of why zero values with trailing fractional zeros create invalid precision and no targeted fix yet.
scale.3: Comparable parent-level progress: the trajectory has found the relevant formatting path and understands that Decimal precision can become invalid, but the proposed or applied fix is incomplete, too implementation-specific, or insufficiently validated across both reported input forms.
scale.4: Clear evidence of a targeted fix that prevents invalid Decimal precision for the reported zero string and Decimal cases, with basic validation of expected output and some nearby formatting behavior.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory precisely diagnoses the Decimal zero/exponent/precision edge case, applies a narrow robust fix without broad behavior changes, and validates both reported inputs plus representative nonzero, sign, positive/negative precision, and localization/grouping-related cases.

experiences.title: Django W042 inherited PK discriminator
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django model-check task concerns `models.W042` being raised for inherited primary keys, especially after the trajectory has inspected default primary-key checks or multi-table inheritance parent-link metadata.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django codebase when the issue is a false `models.W042` warning for models whose primary key comes from a concrete parent model. The strongest matching trajectories have located the W042/default-primary-key check and observed that multi-table inheritance creates an auto-created parent-link relation that becomes the child primary key. This guidance is less applicable to unrelated inheritance bugs, abstract/proxy-only inheritance issues, or tasks about changing `DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD` behavior globally. At very early exploration, the rubric can credit locating W042 and tracing inheritance setup; at implementation/final-review stages, it should require evidence of a clean condition that distinguishes inherited parent-link primary keys from genuinely implicit default primary keys, not just repeated failing test attempts or a vague inheritance explanation.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic boundary that made the bug real: `pk.auto_created` is not sufficient evidence that Django invented a default primary key, because a child model in multi-table inheritance can have an auto-created parent-link field as its primary key. A strong criterion should ask whether the trajectory identifies the parent-link marker on the primary key relation and uses it to suppress W042 only for inherited parent-link primary keys, while preserving W042 for standalone models with truly implicit default AutoField primary keys and preserving existing settings/AppConfig override behavior. The tempting but weaker criterion is a broad request to 'trace inheritance' or 'verify all inheritance patterns'; that may sound methodical but misses the decisive discriminator. Another tempting proxy to avoid is rewarding the agent merely for knowing the warning lives in model checks or for repeatedly running broken tests. Prioritize visible evidence such as inspection of the W042 condition, inspection or runtime metadata showing an inherited child primary key is both auto-created and a parent link, a proposed or applied guard excluding that parent-link case, and control validation or test intent showing ordinary auto-created primary keys still warn.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluate whether the trajectory correctly isolates the W042 false positive to Django treating an inherited multi-table parent-link primary key as a default auto-created primary key, and whether it moves toward a narrow fix that excludes only parent-link primary keys while preserving normal default-primary-key warnings and existing override behavior.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Parent-link primary key exception for default-PK warning

metadata.task_signal: models.W042 raised for child models inheriting a manually specified primary key
key_positive_evidence: Finds the warning condition that relies on primary-key auto-created metadata.
Traces multi-table inheritance primary-key setup or inspects child model metadata.
Recognizes that a child primary key can be an auto-created relation with a parent-link marker.
Proposes or applies a narrow exclusion for parent-link primary keys.
Preserves warnings for genuinely implicit default primary keys and preserves DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD/AppConfig override behavior.
key_negative_evidence: Treats all auto-created primary keys as equivalent.
Suppresses W042 for all inherited models or all auto-created primary keys.
Changes project settings/default auto-field configuration instead of the check logic.
Only repeats failing test commands without maintaining a clean implementation or clear validation path.

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward the discriminator: the trajectory has not located the W042/default-primary-key logic or incorrectly frames the issue as a settings/migration problem.
scale.2: Some relevant exploration, such as finding W042 or primary-key setup, but no clear recognition that inherited parent-link primary keys are auto-created yet semantically different from default implicit primary keys.
scale.3: Equivalent baseline progress: identifies that inherited primary keys need special handling, but the proposed fix or reasoning is broad, incomplete, or not clearly tied to the parent-link marker while preserving ordinary W042 behavior.
scale.4: Strong progress: identifies the parent-link primary-key metadata and proposes or implements a narrow guard so inherited parent-link primary keys do not warn, with at least some attention to preserving true implicit-primary-key warnings.
scale.5: Excellent progress: demonstrates the exact semantic distinction with code inspection or runtime metadata, keeps the implementation clean and narrow, preserves settings/AppConfig override behavior and normal W042 controls, and has a credible regression-test or validation plan for both inherited and ordinary auto-created primary keys.

experiences.title: Transparent Wrapper GROUP BY Delegation
experiences.description: Use when a Django ORM expression wrapper changes GROUP BY behavior compared with the wrapped expression, especially when constants are grouped only after being wrapped.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django source tree, primarily around ORM expression classes and `get_group_by_cols()` behavior, when the task or trajectory shows that a wrapper-like expression adds context such as an output field but should otherwise preserve the wrapped expression's SQL grouping semantics. It is most useful once the trajectory has inspected or reproduced the distinction between a bare constant expression and the same expression inside the wrapper, or has identified the base expression default that groups non-aggregate expressions by themselves. It is less applicable for unrelated SQL compiler bugs, backend-specific syntax workarounds, issues where the wrapped expression itself has wrong grouping behavior, or early exploration before the agent has found the expression classes and grouping API. During transient editing stages, judge the semantic direction and cleanliness separately: a temporary corrupted edit is a visible flaw, but the core criterion should remain about wrapper delegation rather than generic test-running progress.
experiences.experience: For this cluster, the useful rubric was the one requiring `ExpressionWrapper` to compute GROUP BY columns from its wrapped expression. This aligned with correct fixes because the observable root cause was that constants already know not to group themselves, while the wrapper inherited the default non-aggregate behavior and therefore grouped by the wrapper/literal. A good rubric should reward evidence that the agent found this semantic boundary: `Value.get_group_by_cols()` returns no columns, the base expression implementation returns the expression itself, and `ExpressionWrapper` is intended to be transparent except for context such as `output_field`. The preferred criterion should check for a clean delegation implementation on the wrapper, preserving constants as non-grouping while still allowing field, function, compound, and aggregate-containing expressions to contribute their normal grouping columns. It should also value validation by inspecting generated SQL or query group-by state for an annotate/values/aggregate query comparing wrapped and unwrapped constants. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as fixing PostgreSQL only, special-casing `Value` in query compilation, changing the constant expression class, merely installing dependencies or finding the test runner, or broadly demanding all tests pass without checking the wrapper semantics. Visible evidence to prioritize includes targeted inspection of expression grouping methods, a reproduction showing `GROUP BY ..., 3` only for the wrapped constant, a clean method added in the wrapper class rather than global or misplaced edits, forwarding/delegating the alias argument consistently, and regression checks that nonconstant wrapped expressions still group appropriately.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should identify that the wrapper is incorrectly using default expression GROUP BY behavior and should preserve the wrapped expression's own grouping contract. Strong evidence includes a clean implementation or well-supported plan for `ExpressionWrapper.get_group_by_cols()` to delegate to the inner expression, so wrapped constants contribute no GROUP BY columns while wrapped column-dependent, functional, compound, or aggregate expressions continue to contribute the columns their inner expressions require. The trajectory should avoid backend-specific hacks or changes to constant-expression behavior when the visible evidence shows the wrapper layer is the differentiator.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Wrapper Preserves Inner GROUP BY Contract

metadata.environment: Django ORM expression system
required_visible_evidence: Recognizes bare constants already omit themselves from GROUP BY
Recognizes the wrapper inherits default non-aggregate grouping unless overridden
Delegates wrapper group-by calculation to the wrapped/source expression
Checks that constants are omitted and nonconstant expressions still group normally
anti_patterns: PostgreSQL-only SQL string workaround
Special-casing constants in the SQL compiler instead of preserving expression contracts
Changing Value behavior despite bare Value already working
Misplaced broad sed edits that add methods outside the wrapper class

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory understands expression GROUP BY semantics or the wrapper-vs-bare expression distinction.
scale.2: Identifies the reported GROUP BY symptom but focuses on generic SQL/backend behavior, constants broadly, or test setup without locating the wrapper grouping contract.
scale.3: Finds relevant expression classes and suspects wrapper delegation, but the plan or edit is incomplete, unvalidated, misplaced, or does not address preservation of nonconstant grouping behavior.
scale.4: Implements or clearly plans a wrapper-level `get_group_by_cols()` delegation and validates that wrapped constants no longer appear in GROUP BY, with some attention to nonconstant expressions or clean placement.
scale.5: Cleanly implements wrapper-level delegation to the wrapped expression, preserves alias/source-expression semantics, validates the annotate/values/aggregate regression for wrapped constants, and confirms column-dependent or compound wrapped expressions still group as required.

experiences.title: Don’t reward generic criteria checklists without repo API and wire-format fit
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for a Go/Navidrome-style composable filtering API where the agent has found existing Squirrel filters, smart-playlist rules, or QueryOptions and may implement a broad but parallel criteria abstraction.
experiences.context: Applies to repository-specific API implementation tasks, especially in Go projects using Masterminds/squirrel and existing model/query conventions. The misleading pattern is a rubric that only asks whether the trajectory covers composability, JSON, SQL conversion, operators, and field mapping; such a checklist can overvalue a generic top-level package or builder that has those features but does not match the repository’s intended public API, package placement, JSON shape, or Squirrel integration contract. The original broad checklist can still be useful during very early exploration or for a greenfield library with no established patterns. Do not overcorrect by requiring reuse of smart-playlist internals when the task asks for a new general criteria API; smart-playlist code is mainly evidence for field names, operator semantics, and Squirrel conventions, not necessarily the API to extend directly.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded high-level feature coverage such as All/Any, Is/IsNot, text operators, JSON round-trips, SQL generation, and automatic field mapping. That criterion is too weak once the trajectory has enough visible repository evidence: agents can satisfy the words by inventing a separate package, a custom combinator/rules JSON schema, or an external field-mapper builder while missing the expected API contract. A better rubric should focus on whether the implementation fits the existing Go module structure and query pipeline: a criteria API exposed from the model-side namespace, expressions that naturally implement or wrap squirrel.Sqlizer/ToSql, JSON that preserves the intended All/Any expression structure rather than an arbitrary new schema, built-in mapping for the repository’s media-file fields, and operator SQL semantics compatible with existing Squirrel usage. Avoid the tempting criterion “implements all requested features” unless it is paired with compatibility evidence. Also avoid the opposite misleading criterion “must build on smart playlists rather than from scratch”; the visible smart-playlist code should inform behavior and field mapping, not force coupling if the new API is meant to be reusable. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible code evidence: package/import path choice, exported API shape, JSON tags/operator names, ToSql/Sqlizer behavior, field mapping coverage, and tests or examples that exercise the repository-facing API rather than only a self-contained custom builder.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Parallel criteria API incompatible with repository contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that implement or plan a generic criteria abstraction with the requested feature names but visibly diverge from the repository’s intended integration contract: e.g. placing the API as an unrelated top-level package or ad hoc model file instead of a model-side criteria namespace; exposing only a custom builder/combinator/rules schema rather than first-class All/Any expression structure; requiring callers to supply all mapping logic despite the task calling for automatic field mapping; returning raw SQL strings or custom wrappers where existing query code expects Squirrel-compatible Sqlizer behavior; or testing only the invented abstraction without demonstrating the repository-facing JSON and SQL contract. This rubric should not penalize merely creating new criteria types, nor should it require direct reuse of smart-playlist implementation, as long as the new API conforms to repository conventions and observable task semantics.

metadata.environment: Go repository using Masterminds/squirrel and existing model/query filtering conventions
visible_evidence_to_check: package/import path and whether the API is discoverable from the model-side criteria namespace
whether criteria expressions implement or delegate to squirrel.Sqlizer/ToSql
JSON wire shape for All/Any and operator expressions, not just any nested combinator format
presence of built-in media field-to-column mapping
operator SQL semantics for equality, negation, text matching, inclusive ranges, booleans, and temporal filters
tests/examples exercising repository-facing JSON and SQL output rather than only a standalone builder
do_not_require: integration into every existing API endpoint when the task only asks for a reusable criteria API

scale.1: No evidence of a parallel or incompatible API; the trajectory is still exploring, or the design/code visibly aligns with repository package, JSON, mapping, and Squirrel conventions.
scale.2: Minor risk only: the agent mentions a generic builder or extra helpers, but also preserves the expected repository-facing API and integration contract.
scale.3: Mixed evidence: the implementation covers many feature requirements but the visible API shape, package placement, JSON format, or mapping strategy is only partially aligned with repository conventions.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory creates a mostly standalone criteria system with custom schema or mapping expectations, even though it has found repository evidence for Squirrel filters, model query options, or smart-playlist field/operator semantics.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the implementation is essentially an isolated generic filtering library or incompatible model addition that satisfies a feature checklist but lacks the expected repository-facing package/API, All/Any JSON contract, automatic media field mapping, or Squirrel-compatible SQL behavior.

experiences.title: AST comparison rewrite for evaluate=False parser bugs
experiences.description: Use when a parsing task reports that an evaluation-suppression flag is ignored for relational/comparison syntax, especially after the trajectory has inspected the parser’s AST rewrite path.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/SymPy-like repository where expression parsing supports an `evaluate=False`-style option by rewriting Python AST nodes into library constructors, and the reported failure is that concrete comparisons such as `1 < 2` are returned as booleans instead of unevaluated relational objects. It is most useful once the trajectory has visible evidence that comparisons are represented as AST comparison nodes and that the existing evaluate-false transformer handles arithmetic/function calls but lacks comparison handling. It can also guide early exploration if the agent is searching parser internals, but should not be used as the main criterion for unrelated relational simplification bugs, tokenizer-only equality-sign conversion issues, general boolean logic parsing, or tasks where relationals already reach constructors and the problem is in the relational classes themselves. Do not make chained comparisons or boolean `and`/`or` support the central requirement unless the task explicitly demands them.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic contract: under `evaluate=False`, parsed comparison syntax must be converted to the corresponding relational constructor with `evaluate=False`, while normal evaluation remains unchanged. This aligned well because the visible trajectory repeatedly showed the decisive root cause: the parser’s evaluate-false path rewrites AST nodes, Python comparison syntax appears as `ast.Compare`, and no comparison visitor existed, so numeric comparisons escaped into normal truth evaluation. A strong rubric should therefore prioritize evidence that the agent maps the standard comparison operators (`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `==`, `!=`) to the library’s relational constructors, recursively preserves operands, passes the evaluation-suppression keyword, and validates both the original failing example and default/evaluate-true behavior. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as merely finding `parse_expr`, investigating token transformations like equals-sign conversion, checking the relational class constructors in isolation, or requiring broad boolean/chained-comparison rewrites beyond the task. At early trajectory cutoffs, judge progress by whether the agent has identified the AST comparison gap and constructor mapping plan; at implementation/review cutoffs, judge by concrete patch evidence and tests showing unevaluated relationals for standard operators without breaking ordinary evaluated parsing.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should diagnose and address the parser's evaluate-false comparison gap by handling Python comparison AST nodes in the evaluation-suppression path, converting standard relational operators into the corresponding symbolic relational constructors with `evaluate=False`, and validating that parsed numeric comparisons remain unevaluated while normal evaluated parsing behavior is preserved.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Evaluate-false comparison AST preservation

key_visible_evidence: Reproduces or cites that parsing a numeric comparison with evaluation disabled returns a boolean instead of an unevaluated relational
Identifies that Python comparison syntax is represented as an AST comparison node rather than a binary-operation node
Finds that the existing evaluate-false transformer handles arithmetic or calls but lacks comparison handling
Plans or implements a mapping from standard comparison AST operators to symbolic relational constructors with an evaluation-suppression keyword
Checks that evaluation-enabled/default parsing still returns normal booleans for concrete comparisons
non_requirements_unless_task_expands_sco: Changes to the relational constructor implementations themselves

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory connects the failure to comparison AST handling or evaluation-suppression propagation; it focuses on unrelated files, token transforms, or relational internals without a plausible parser fix.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory locates the parser or reproduces the symptom but has not identified that comparison syntax bypasses the evaluate-false AST rewrite path, or proposes only vague relational handling.
scale.3: Moderate evidence equivalent to parent progress: the trajectory identifies the missing comparison-node handling and the need to map comparison operators to symbolic relational constructors with evaluation disabled, but implementation or validation is incomplete.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory implements or clearly prepares a comparison-node rewrite for the standard relational operators with `evaluate=False`, and tests the original example plus several related operators or operands.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory cleanly implements the comparison rewrite in the existing evaluate-false parser architecture, covers the standard operators, preserves recursive operand handling and default evaluated behavior, and validates with focused examples and relevant parser tests.

experiences.title: Preserve Callable Constructor Arguments in Deconstruction
experiences.description: Use when a Django-like model field accepts a callable constructor argument that is evaluated for runtime behavior but must be serialized/deconstructed as the original callable for migrations or reconstruction.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django environment when the task is specifically about field deconstruction or migration serialization of a callable argument, especially where the trajectory has inspected the field constructor and deconstruct logic or reproduced that deconstruction returns an evaluated object. It is strongest at implementation/review stages where the visible trajectory includes a proposed code change or direct deconstruct() checks. It is less useful for unrelated runtime storage bugs, for tasks about callable upload paths that are already stored unchanged, or very early exploration where the agent has not yet connected constructor-time evaluation with deconstruction semantics.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster focused on the semantic contract: deconstruction must return the original callable reference, while runtime behavior must still use the evaluated Storage instance. This is discriminative because the visible trajectories repeatedly showed the key bug source: the constructor evaluates a callable storage argument and overwrites the only stored value, then deconstruct() serializes that evaluated object. A good criterion should therefore prioritize evidence that the agent preserves two representations: the original constructor callable for deconstruction/migration serialization, and the evaluated storage object for runtime file operations and validation. It should also check compatibility boundaries: omitted/default storage should not be serialized unnecessarily, explicit non-callable storage instances should behave as before, ImageField or subclasses that inherit FileField behavior should remain covered, and invalid callable return validation should not be bypassed. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as merely checking that kwargs['storage'] is callable, deferring callable evaluation entirely, requiring a specific private attribute name, or judging success only by broad test-suite attempts. The strongest visible evidence is identity-based reproduction or tests showing deconstruct() returns the same callable object that was passed in, plus edge-case checks for default storage, non-callable storage, callable returning default storage, runtime storage access, and migration serialization.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate or implement the deconstruction contract for callable storage-like constructor arguments: preserve the exact original callable reference for deconstruct()/migration serialization, while continuing to evaluate the callable during normal runtime initialization so the field uses a valid Storage instance. The evidence should also show that default storage omission, explicit non-callable storage instances, inherited image/file-field behavior, and validation of callable return values are not regressed.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Callable Argument Deconstruction Contract

metadata.expected_component: Django model field deconstruction for callable storage-like arguments
key_positive_evidence: Identifies that constructor-time callable evaluation overwrites the original argument before deconstruction
Stores or otherwise preserves the original callable separately from the evaluated runtime object
deconstruct() emits the original callable by object identity, not the evaluated Storage instance
Runtime field.storage or equivalent remains an evaluated Storage instance
Default/omitted storage and explicit non-callable storage semantics remain compatible
ImageField/subclass behavior is considered when it inherits the same deconstruction path
common_false_proxies_to_avoid: Only checking that the deconstructed value is callable rather than the same original callable
Solving by delaying all callable evaluation and breaking runtime behavior or validation
Requiring a particular private attribute name or exact patch shape
Treating unrelated test-runner setup failures as evidence against the semantic fix

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent understands or addresses callable storage deconstruction; focuses on unrelated files, runtime-only behavior, or generic testing.
scale.2: Recognizes that callable storage is involved or reproduces a deconstruction symptom, but does not clearly preserve the original callable separately from the evaluated runtime storage.
scale.3: Shows moderate progress equivalent to the parent trajectory: identifies the constructor/deconstruct interaction and proposes or partially implements preserving the original callable, but compatibility with runtime evaluation, defaults, or non-callable storage remains unclear.
scale.4: Strong evidence of a correct semantic fix: deconstruct() returns the original callable and runtime behavior still uses an evaluated Storage instance, with at least some checks for default or non-callable storage behavior.
scale.5: Comprehensive evidence: implementation or tests verify exact callable identity in deconstruction, runtime evaluated storage and validation are preserved, default/omitted and explicit storage semantics are maintained, inherited ImageField behavior is covered, and migration serialization or focused regression tests confirm the contract.

experiences.title: Model-aware comparison contracts for copied Django fields
experiences.description: Use when a Django task concerns equality, hashing, or ordering of model Field instances copied from abstract bases or otherwise sharing a creation counter across owning models.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django repository when the task or trajectory identifies Field comparison methods as the implementation point and the observed bug is that distinct fields with the same creation_counter collapse under equality/hash or lack deterministic ordering. It is most useful after the agent has inspected or edited the comparison methods, or has reproduction output showing two fields with the same counter but different owning models. It is less predictive during very early dependency/setup work before any comparison design is visible, and it should not be retrieved for unrelated model metadata issues or tasks that only require test-runner cleanup.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases checked the full semantic contract rather than just whether the reported example prints the desired equality result. A strong criterion should require equality and hashing to use both creation_counter and owning model identity so copied fields on different concrete models remain distinct in sets, while same retrieved field/same owning model behavior remains unchanged. It should also require less-than ordering to keep creation_counter as the primary key and use model information only as a tie-breaker for equal counters, because model-first ordering can reorder unrelated fields. The criterion should explicitly look for safe handling of fields that may not yet have a model attribute and for avoiding direct ordering of Django model classes, which can raise TypeError; deterministic model metadata or guarded fallback logic is preferable. Do not let broad passing test runs or a manual equality-only reproduction substitute for evidence that hash and ordering invariants are preserved. Conversely, if the trajectory has only installed dependencies or explored files, judge it as early progress toward this contract rather than as a completed fix.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates or implements a complete model-aware Field comparison contract: fields with the same creation_counter but different attached models compare unequal and hash distinctly; fields from the same model or the same inherited concrete object preserve previous equality/hash behavior; ordering remains primarily by creation_counter and only uses model identity as a tie-breaker for equal counters; and the implementation is safe for unattached fields and avoids directly ordering non-orderable model classes.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete model-aware Field comparison semantics

priority_evidence: Diff or inspected code changes Field equality, hashing, and less-than comparison rather than only one method.
Equality and hash use consistent identity components including owning model when available.
Less-than comparison checks creation_counter before any model tie-breaker.
The code guards missing model attributes or otherwise preserves behavior for unbound Field instances.
Validation includes the abstract-base sibling model case with set length/hash behavior and at least some edge cases for existing ordering or unbound/same-model behavior.
common_failure_modes: Only equality is changed while hash or ordering remains creation_counter-only.
Ordering compares model classes directly or orders by model before creation_counter.
Direct self.model access breaks unattached fields.
Manual tests only verify the original equality example and omit hash/set/order compatibility.

scale.1: No visible progress toward changing Field comparison semantics, or changes are unrelated to equality/hash/order behavior.
scale.2: Identifies the relevant comparison area or reproduces the same-counter/different-model collision, but has no credible implementation or only changes one method.
scale.3: Implements or plans model-aware comparison for the main reported equality case, but evidence is incomplete for hash consistency, ordering compatibility, or unattached fields.
scale.4: Updates equality, hash, and ordering with creation_counter-first behavior and validates the reported set/equality scenario, with only minor uncertainty about edge cases or deterministic model tie-breaking.
scale.5: Fully satisfies the contract with guarded model-aware equality/hash, creation_counter-primary ordering with a safe deterministic tie-breaker, preservation of same-model/unattached behavior, and visible validation of the reported regression plus relevant compatibility cases.

experiences.title: Nullable Read-Token Parameter Over Client Ownership Checks
experiences.description: Use when a TypeScript client task concerns an unnecessary request parameter for blob/archive read-token creation, and the trajectory has found a hard-coded token parameter plus generated request DTO metadata requiring it.
experiences.context: Applies in a TypeScript/web client codebase with generated entity/service request models and hand-written facades, especially when the task says a read-token request through an entity REST client should work without an archive/type discriminator for owned archives. The key visible stage is after the trajectory has identified the read-token service request construction, the generated request type/model field cardinality, and the EntityRestClient call that hard-codes an ArchiveDataType. This guidance is strongest when searches show no reliable client-side service or usage for loading archive ownership metadata. It is less applicable during very early repository exploration before the token path is found, and it should not be used if the task explicitly asks to implement authorization policy or the trajectory reveals an existing, reliable ownership-check API that the current code is expected to call.
experiences.experience: The earlier rubrics in this cluster tended to require ownership-based authorization logic, such as loading BlobArchiveRef._ownerGroup or using UserFacade.hasGroup before omitting archiveDataType. That is a tempting but misleading criterion when the visible trajectory shows no usable client-side ownership lookup and the reported failure is caused by the client/API shape requiring a parameter before the service can decide authorization. A better rubric should reward evidence that the agent is relaxing the read-token request contract in a coordinated, narrow way: the generated/request model can represent a missing/null archiveDataType, read-token facade method signatures accept that nullable value, and the EntityRestClient blob-element/archive read path stops passing a hard-coded data type and passes the nullable value instead. The criterion should also check preservation boundaries: write-token paths and unrelated blob-reference APIs should not be weakened, and ordinary callers that still know an ArchiveDataType should continue to pass it. Avoid rubrics that demand client-side ownership detection unless the trajectory has found an existing, authoritative source for ownership; otherwise that proxy encourages invasive changes and misses the actual compatibility contract. Prioritize visible evidence such as the hard-coded ArchiveDataType in EntityRestClient, BlobAccessTokenPostIn.archiveDataType being required in TypeRefs/TypeModels, read methods constructing createBlobAccessTokenPostIn, read cache keyed by archive id, and lack of BlobArchiveRef usages outside generated declarations.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Coordinated Nullable Read-Token Contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should move toward a narrow fix that allows blob read-token requests to carry a null or otherwise explicitly absent archiveDataType through the request model and read-token facade, and should update the EntityRestClient blob-element/archive read path to use that nullable value instead of a hard-coded ArchiveDataType. Strong evidence includes inspecting both generated request metadata/types and hand-written facade request construction, recognizing that ownership is likely enforced by the service rather than by unavailable client-side BlobArchiveRef lookups, preserving write-token behavior and unrelated blob reference operations, and avoiding broad/invented ownership checks in BlobFacade or AuthDataProvider.

required_visible_evidence: The trajectory identifies the EntityRestClient blob-element or archive read path that calls the blob access-token facade with a hard-coded ArchiveDataType.
The trajectory inspects the blob access-token request DTO/type/model and notices archiveDataType is currently required.
The trajectory inspects BlobAccessTokenFacade read-token construction and distinguishes read-token methods from write-token methods.
The trajectory observes little or no usable client-side ownership-loading path, such as no non-generated BlobArchiveRef service/usages.
preferred_fix_direction: Represent archiveDataType as nullable/optional in the read-token request contract, including generated model/type metadata where applicable.
Allow read-token facade methods to accept a nullable archiveDataType while retaining existing typed callers.
Change the EntityRestClient archive/blob-element read-token call to pass the nullable value rather than a hard-coded data type.
Do not require new client-side ownership checks unless an authoritative existing API is visible.
preservation_boundaries: Do not weaken write-token archiveDataType requirements or write-cache behavior.
Do not broaden the change to unrelated blob reference put/delete APIs without evidence they share the same read-token contract.
Do not add speculative AuthDataProvider/UserFacade ownership APIs solely to justify omitting the parameter.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory has found the read-token request path or the required archiveDataType contract; it remains on generic search or unrelated blob download/upload code.
scale.2: Some relevant files or methods are identified, but the trajectory either focuses mainly on speculative ownership detection or misses the need to change both request contract and EntityRestClient call site.
scale.3: The trajectory has found the hard-coded EntityRestClient call and required request field, and proposes making archiveDataType optional/null for read tokens, but has not clearly addressed generated model metadata, null-vs-undefined serialization, or preservation of write-token behavior.
scale.4: The trajectory shows a coherent narrow plan or implementation to make archiveDataType nullable for read-token requests, update the facade signatures/request construction, and change the EntityRestClient call away from the hard-coded data type, while avoiding client-side ownership invention.
scale.5: The trajectory fully coordinates the nullable read-token contract across generated/request metadata, TypeScript DTOs, read-token facade methods, and the EntityRestClient blob-element/archive path; it explicitly preserves write-token and unrelated APIs, explains why client-side ownership checks are not appropriate given visible code, and validates or plans validation for the affected read-token behavior.

experiences.title: Unused Explicit Array Arguments Must Retain Codegen Dimensions
experiences.description: Use when a SymPy/autowrap/codegen trajectory concerns array-like arguments supplied in a requested signature but absent from the expression body, especially C/Cython wrapper scalar-conversion errors.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/SymPy-style code generation environment where user-provided argument lists or argument sequences determine a generated low-level function signature. The key situation is an array-like argument, such as a matrix or indexed array object with shape information, being explicitly listed as an input even though the expression is constant or otherwise does not reference that argument. This guidance is most discriminative once the trajectory has inspected routine/signature construction, argument metadata, generated prototypes, or wrapper behavior. It can also be used earlier as a negative progress criterion if the agent has only explored unrelated code and has not connected the runtime scalar-conversion error to lost array metadata. It is less applicable when all array arguments appear in the expression, when the task is about numerical evaluation rather than signature generation, or when the backend does not use argument dimension metadata to decide pointer/array declarations.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster focused on whether explicit unused array arguments keep their array/pointer signature in code generation. They aligned well because the decisive visible evidence was not generic repository exploration or Cython wrapper debugging, but whether the trajectory identified and preserved dimension metadata when a requested argument is not found among expression-derived symbols. Strong evidence includes observations that constant expressions have no matrix/indexed atoms or free symbols, that generated routine arguments show missing or null dimensions, that generated C/Cython signatures treat a NumPy array as a scalar, and that the proposed edit creates input arguments with shape-derived dimension metadata in the argument-sequence fallback path. A weaker but still useful rubric only asks whether the agent located the codegen signature logic; that can be appropriate very early, but it is too broad once the agent has reached implementation. Avoid tempting criteria that focus on making the expression artificially depend on the array, changing the Cython wrapper’s scalar conversion behavior directly, merely adding the argument to a symbol set without dimensions, or validating only the case where the array appears in the expression. The better criterion should ask whether the trajectory preserves the user-requested signature contract for unused array-like inputs by carrying shape/dimension metadata through routine construction and into the generated prototype/wrapper.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that explicitly supplied array-like inputs remain array inputs in generated code even when they are absent from the expression body. Excellent progress identifies that expression-derived symbol/atom analysis misses unused arrays, traces the runtime scalar-conversion symptom to missing argument dimension metadata in routine/signature construction, and implements or plans a fix that creates input arguments with shape-derived dimensions for missing entries from the requested argument sequence while leaving ordinary scalar arguments unchanged.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Preserve Dimensions for Unused Explicit Array Inputs

prioritize_visible_evidence: The agent recognizes that the argument is present only in the user-supplied signature or argument sequence, not in expression free symbols or atoms.
The agent inspects routine argument metadata, generated prototypes, or wrapper declarations and connects missing dimensions to scalar declarations.
The proposed change derives dimensions from the original array-like argument shape when constructing a new input argument for a requested but otherwise absent argument.
Validation includes an unused array argument case and does not rely only on cases where the expression references the array.
avoid_overcrediting: Only locating autowrap or Cython wrapper files without identifying metadata loss.
Adding unused arguments to a symbol list but still creating scalar input arguments.
Changing the mathematical expression to reference the argument just to trigger existing array inference.
Testing only scalar arguments or array arguments that appear in the expression.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory understands the issue as lost array dimension metadata for explicit unused arguments; it focuses on unrelated files, dependency setup, or generic code exploration.
