scale.2: Some evidence of investigating autowrap or generated signatures, but the trajectory has not connected the unused explicit array argument to missing dimensions or pointer-vs-scalar declaration.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies the relevant codegen/signature path and suspects expression-derived array detection is insufficient, but the proposed fix or validation is incomplete or only generally described.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly targets argument-sequence handling and proposes preserving shape-derived dimensions for unused matrix/indexed-style arguments, with some validation or inspection of generated routine metadata.
scale.5: The trajectory directly fixes or specifies the fallback creation of requested-but-absent input arguments so array-like objects receive correct dimensions, preserves scalar behavior, and validates with an unused array argument case plus relevant generated-signature or wrapper evidence.

experiences.title: End-to-End Quoted Repoquery Contract
experiences.description: Use when a Go/Vuls-style scanner task concerns strict parsing of repoquery/yum/dnf package output, especially when the code both constructs the query format and parses stdout, and the problem statement mentions quoted fields, prompts, auxiliary output, and epoch-aware versions.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go repository where Amazon/RedHat-family scanner logic builds a repoquery command with a custom query format and then parses each output line into package records. It is most relevant once the trajectory has found both the command construction and the line parser, or when the task explicitly requires handling quoted fields. The criterion is less useful for an early repository-discovery stage before the agent has located the parser/command, or for systems where the output format cannot be controlled and the only feasible fix is defensive filtering of an external unquoted stream.
experiences.experience: The broad rubrics in these cases correctly focused on strict package-line parsing, prompt/auxiliary-output rejection, and epoch-aware version construction, but they were too easy to satisfy with incomplete fixes: hardcoded prompt whitelists, unquoted regex validation, or skipping all parser errors can appear aligned with the task while failing the actual contract. For this pattern, generate a rubric that explicitly evaluates the end-to-end output contract: the scanner should make repoquery emit unambiguous quoted fields for every relevant command branch, and the parser should consume exactly that quoted record format while preserving epoch semantics. Visible evidence to prioritize includes the agent inspecting and modifying the repoquery `--qf` format, recognizing that repository names or other fields may contain spaces, parsing quoted five-field records rather than arbitrary whitespace tokens, handling prompt text that may precede a record, and adding tests for quoted records plus prompts/extraneous lines. Avoid a rubric that rewards only prefix skip lists, numeric-epoch regexes over the old unquoted format, or passing existing tests without adding quoted/prompt coverage.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Quoted Repoquery Format and Parser Contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should move toward an end-to-end strict repoquery parsing fix: update every relevant updatable-package repoquery query-format branch to emit each field as a quoted token, parse only the resulting quoted five-field records, tolerate prompt text only by removing/ignoring it without treating it as package data, preserve epoch-aware version construction, and add or plan regression coverage for quoted fields, prompt/auxiliary output, repository names with spaces, and zero versus nonzero epoch behavior.

metadata.environment: Go scanner code for Amazon/RedHat-family repoquery output parsing

parser expects the quoted field contract rather than arbitrary whitespace-split rows

epoch zero remains plain version and nonzero epoch becomes epoch:version
tests or validation cover quoted records and prompt/extraneous output

only validating old unquoted whitespace-separated rows with a regex

experiences.title: Do not let OVAL spelling cleanup stand in for multi-issue Go task correctness
experiences.description: Retrieve this when a Go maintenance task combines a simple log-message spelling fix with independent API-visibility, documentation, and distro-integration requirements, especially if the trajectory visibly fixes `Unmarshall` but still has unresolved edits elsewhere.
experiences.context: In a Go repository with packages such as `oval`, `gost`, `scan`, `report`, `config`, and `models`, the task asks for several independent changes: correcting OVAL `Unmarshall` messages, unexporting a Debian helper consistently, adding meaningful Go doc comments, and adding Oracle Linux support to HTTP scanning. A rubric that only checks OVAL `Unmarshal` spelling can be appropriate as a narrow subcriterion when the task is exclusively about log wording or when a parent rubric already covers the other required behavioral/API changes. It is misleading as a primary or highly weighted criterion when the visible trajectory also includes risky identifier renames, switch-case edits, doc-comment placement issues, skipped tests, malformed sed edits, or uncertainty about where Oracle ViaHTTP handling belongs.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics often rewarded correcting `Failed to Unmarshall` to `Failed to Unmarshal`, sometimes alongside a single `DummyFileInfo` comment. That criterion is factually sound but too weak for this class of task: the spelling edit is a localized string replacement and can be completed while the patch still fails the requested behavior through malformed Go switch statements, missing or wrong Oracle HTTP dispatch, API rename fallout, ignored test failures, or non-godoc comments. Future rubric generation should not use the typo cleanup as the main predictor once the trajectory shows the spelling fix is already done. Instead, generate a criterion that checks integration completeness across the independent requirements and prioritizes visible evidence such as all renamed helper call sites/tests being addressed, Oracle being added to the actual `ViaHTTP` dispatch using the existing scanner type rather than unrelated OVAL/report mapping, doc comments being placed immediately before exported Go identifiers, and validation or inspection confirming sed edits did not corrupt syntax. Avoid the tempting criterion “all OVAL Unmarshall strings are fixed” unless it is explicitly scoped as a minor subcheck.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Typo-only progress masks incomplete integration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for multi-requirement Go maintenance tasks when they primarily demonstrate localized `Unmarshall`-to-`Unmarshal` cleanup but leave visible evidence that other requested API, documentation, or distro-integration changes are incomplete, syntactically risky, or unvalidated. This includes renaming an exported helper without checking all call sites/tests, adding documentation inline or after the declaration instead of as proper Go doc comments, editing unrelated OVAL/report family mapping instead of the actual HTTP scan dispatcher, corrupting switch cases with repeated sed insertions, or declaring success after tests/build output indicates unresolved failures.

metadata.task_shape: multi-part Go maintenance task with spelling, API visibility, doc comments, and distro support
preferred_evidence: all call sites/tests considered after unexporting an identifier
proper Go doc-comment placement for exported identifiers relevant to the task
Oracle support added in the actual ViaHTTP family dispatch using existing scanner structures
manual diff or validation confirms switch syntax and error semantics are intact

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory treats spelling as one minor part and visibly checks the other requested changes and syntax/validation.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory emphasizes spelling cleanup but also makes credible progress on the other requirements with no obvious broken edits.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: spelling is complete, but one other requirement is only partially checked or validation/call-site review is missing.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory rewards or declares success based on spelling/doc cleanup while visible unresolved issues remain in Oracle dispatch, helper rename consistency, doc-comment placement, or tests.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory has fixed the typo but contains obvious malformed edits, wrong-file Oracle handling, ignored compile/test failures, or missing required non-spelling changes while still treating the task as complete.

experiences.title: Mixed-Dimension Coordinate Distance Semantics
experiences.description: Use when a trajectory is fixing a coordinate-wise distance bug caused by truncating `zip` over points or vectors of unequal length, especially in SymPy geometry `Point.distance`.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python geometry/math library task where the problem statement or trajectory explicitly identifies Euclidean distance over points of different ambient dimensions as wrong because coordinate sequences are zipped and extra coordinates are ignored. The strongest fit is a SymPy-style `Point.distance` implementation that stores coordinates in `.args`, accepts another point or coordinate iterable, and should treat omitted trailing coordinates as zero for the reported mixed 2D/3D case. This criterion is most useful once the trajectory has located or edited the distance method, or has enough visible evidence of the truncating coordinate-pairing logic. It is less useful during very early repository exploration before the relevant method is found, and it should not be broadened to every `zip`-using point operation such as equality, midpoint, dot product, or addition unless the task or trajectory provides specific evidence that those operations share the same required mixed-dimensional semantics.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged the semantic contract rather than the exact implementation shape: `Point.distance` must compute over the maximum coordinate length, include coordinates present in either operand, and model missing coordinates as zero so the mixed 2D/3D example becomes `sqrt(5)` while same-dimensional and symbolic distances still behave normally. This aligned well because the visible trajectories repeatedly identified the concrete root cause (`zip` truncation) and either patched it with `zip_longest(..., fillvalue=0)` or equivalent padding logic. A better rubric should also require the actual edited file to contain valid, executable distance code; do not over-credit a standalone mock test or verbal claim if the repository code has malformed parentheses, a botched sed replacement, or an incomplete import/change. Avoid the tempting but overbroad criterion that all nearby point operations must be changed just because they use `zip`; equality may already guard on equal lengths, and midpoint/dot/addition may have separate API semantics. Prioritize visible evidence in this order: the located target method, replacement of truncating `zip` in Euclidean distance with zero-padding or `zip_longest`, preservation of non-Point iterable support where already present, same-dimensional regression safety, and inspection or tests confirming the patch in the real source is syntactically coherent.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should correctly repair the Euclidean distance calculation for unequal-dimensional points by replacing truncating coordinate pairing with a maximum-dimension computation that treats missing coordinates as zero. The evidence should show that the actual source implementation of the distance method includes all coordinates from both operands, preserves existing behavior for equal-dimensional and symbolic points, continues to handle supported point-like iterable inputs, and is syntactically valid in the edited file. Additional changes to related coordinate-wise methods should not substitute for, or distract from, a correct `distance` fix unless they are separately justified.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Zero-Padded Unequal-Dimension Distance

metadata.target_behavior: Euclidean distance over all coordinates present in either point
metadata.root_cause_to_address: plain zip truncates to the shorter coordinate sequence
metadata.expected_example: a 2D point compared with a 3D point should include the third coordinate as a difference from zero
preserve_behavior: documented point-like iterable inputs when already supported
implementation_evidence: uses zero-padding, index bounds, or zip_longest with fillvalue zero for distance
does not leave a malformed or partially edited return expression
does not rely solely on a standalone mock while the repository file remains broken
metadata.scope_boundary: Do not require changing every nearby zip-based point operation unless the task explicitly covers it.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the distance method’s truncating coordinate pairing is identified or changed, or the trajectory focuses on unrelated point classes/functions.
scale.2: The trajectory recognizes `zip` truncation or mentions zero-padding, but has not made a credible source change to the relevant Euclidean distance implementation, or the visible edit is clearly incomplete.
scale.3: The trajectory changes the relevant distance logic toward maximum-dimension zero-padding, but evidence is partial: validation is only conceptual, iterable/same-dimension behavior is uncertain, or the edited code has not been inspected closely.
scale.4: The trajectory provides strong evidence of a valid source-level distance fix that includes extra coordinates as zero-padded differences and preserves ordinary equal-dimensional behavior, with only minor gaps such as limited test execution due environment issues.
scale.5: The trajectory clearly implements a syntactically valid, localized Euclidean distance fix in the real source, demonstrates or tests the reported mixed-dimensional case and same-dimensional regressions, preserves supported input forms, and avoids unjustified broad changes to unrelated point operations.

experiences.title: End-to-End Watcher Metrics, Not Utility-Only Progress
experiences.description: Retrieve for Go/Prometheus observability tasks where a missing rolling numeric buffer is only one prerequisite and the real requirement is watcher event volume/size/top-resource visibility in monitoring output.
experiences.context: Applies in a Teleport-like Go repository when the task explicitly asks for watcher event observability: emitted event rates, byte rates, per-resource/top-event visibility, and a monitoring or TUI display, while also mentioning a missing circular float64/sliding-window utility. This criterion is most useful once the trajectory has moved past first-pass repository exploration or has begun editing utility, metrics, watcher, or monitoring code. It is less appropriate as a sole criterion during the first few exploratory steps, and it should not be retrieved for tasks that only require adding a standalone utility buffer with no watcher metrics/display requirement.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged whether the trajectory was converging on actual watcher event observability rather than stopping at a reusable float64 ring buffer, repeated greps, metric-name constants, or collector definitions. The decisive visible evidence was whether the agent identified and modified the real emitted-event path, measured serialized event size and resource labels there, registered scrapeable metrics, and connected the monitoring/top UI to those metrics so rates and top resources can be derived. A better rubric should be positive and end-to-end: reward utility buffer work only as supporting progress, and give much stronger credit for instrumentation at the actual watcher stream/emission boundary plus metrics registration and display consumption. Avoid an overly specific proxy such as “must wire the buffer into fanOutEvent” if the codebase has a later stream-send path where emitted event size/resource are available; instead phrase it as “actual watcher event emission path or equivalent.” Also avoid treating repeated searches, build confirmation, or standalone utility tests as sufficient for the observability task.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Watcher Event Observability
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show concrete progress toward complete watcher event observability: a fixed-size float64/circular buffer may be added as a prerequisite, but the central evidence is that watcher-emitted events are instrumented at the actual emission/streaming boundary or an equivalent path, event counts and serialized byte sizes are recorded with bounded resource labels, the Prometheus-style collectors/constants are registered consistently, and the monitoring/top UI or report generation consumes those metrics to derive events-per-second, bytes-per-second, and top resources. Standalone utility-buffer implementation, repeated searches, or metric definitions without emission updates should receive low credit.

required_visible_evidence: identifies actual watcher event emission/streaming path rather than only backend queue depth
records event count and byte size when events are emitted
derives bounded resource labels for top-resource reporting
registers metrics using existing repository conventions
updates monitoring/report/TUI consumption to compute rates and top resources
keeps utility circular buffer as supporting infrastructure, not the whole solution
common_insufficient_evidence: only adds a circular float64 buffer and tests
only defines collectors without incrementing/observing them
repeats greps after no relevant symbols are found
targets queue length/backlog metrics instead of emitted watcher events
does not validate build after risky metric or var-block edits

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward watcher observability is visible; the trajectory is stuck in repeated searches, generic exploration, or unrelated build checks.
scale.2: Some prerequisite or planning progress is visible, such as locating watcher/metrics files or adding a standalone numeric circular buffer, but there is no concrete instrumentation of emitted watcher events.
scale.3: Moderate progress: metric names, collectors, or likely emission points are identified or partially edited, but metrics are not clearly updated on actual watcher event emission and monitoring/report consumption is absent or unvalidated.
scale.4: Strong progress: watcher emitted events are instrumented for counts and byte sizes with resource labels and metrics are registered, but rate/top-resource reporting or validation remains incomplete.
scale.5: Complete end-to-end progress: utility support, emitted-event instrumentation, bounded resource labeling, metric registration, build/test validation, and monitoring/report/TUI rate/top-resource consumption are all visibly addressed.

experiences.title: Do Not Substitute Exact Test Placement for ORM-Fix Evidence
experiences.description: Use when a generated rubric makes a permanent framework-native regression test the dominant signal while the trajectory is still diagnosing or implementing a proxy-model query fix.
experiences.context: ORM defects involving proxy relations may be explored with small reproductions before a repository test is integrated. At an intermediate cutoff, this can provide stronger evidence about field selection and related-object loading than the location of the test file. Missing permanent coverage becomes important near completion, especially when the task explicitly requests it, but it should not erase visible evidence that the query path has been corrected.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics repeatedly scored the absence of a canonical test module rather than the proxy foreign-key behavior itself. Generate a conditional negative criterion around a query that still crashes, omits the related key, or is validated only by assertions unrelated to the reported interaction. Avoid requiring a particular test app or file as the definition of correctness.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Unresolved Proxy Relation Field-Selection Failure
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize a trajectory when its current implementation still makes the proxy-relation query crash or omit required related-object identity data, or when claimed validation never evaluates the relevant relation/field-selection combination. Do not infer failure solely from use of an ad hoc reproducer during active development.

observable_evidence: query shape exercised by visible checks
evaluation outcome and related-object fields
current ORM compiler or field-selection change
trajectory completion stage

scale.1: No visible evidence of the proxy relation and restricted-field query remaining behaviorally broken; the available implementation and validation evidence is consistent with the required behavior.
scale.2: A minor or early-stage concern about the proxy relation and restricted-field query remaining behaviorally broken is visible, but it is not confirmed and the trajectory is still actively resolving it.
scale.3: Evidence about the proxy relation and restricted-field query remaining behaviorally broken is mixed or incomplete; the concern remains plausible but is not yet decisive.
scale.4: Clear visible evidence indicates the proxy relation and restricted-field query remaining behaviorally broken, with no convincing correction or validation yet.
scale.5: The trajectory directly reproduces or validates the proxy relation and restricted-field query remaining behaviorally broken, or claims completion while the contradiction remains unresolved.

experiences.title: Do not make MIME-parser cleanup the main success proxy for format-support tasks
experiences.description: Retrieve when a browser/web-app task asks for new image format support plus MIME detection simplification, especially when the trajectory is working across shared MIME constants, extension lookup, preview eligibility, and browser capability checks.
experiences.context: This warning applies in TypeScript/browser monorepos where the task combines several requirements: adding a missing modern image MIME type, mapping extensions so files do not become generic octet-stream values, and enabling previews/thumbnails only for capable browsers such as Safari 17+ on Apple platforms. A rubric about simplifying MIME type detection can be useful only after the trajectory has visibly found the upload/file MIME parser and is changing real content-reading or fallback behavior. It becomes misleading when used as the dominant criterion before that parser has been found, when the agent is still exploring, or when the main correctness risk is actually missing format constants, extension mappings, preview-supported-image allowlisting, or overly broad browser gating. It is also insufficient when the trajectory is stuck in repeated searches or has made broad unvalidated rewrites: the mere claim that file-content MIME logic was removed does not establish end-to-end support.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics asked whether the trajectory simplified MIME type detection by prioritizing file type and extension over content analysis. That criterion is not generally wrong, but in this task shape it was too narrow and sometimes stage-inappropriate. It can understate promising work when the agent has identified the correct support pipeline but has not yet edited the parser, and it can overstate poor work when the agent only removes or claims to remove a content-reader while leaving the modern format unsupported or browser-gated incorrectly. A better rubric should focus on visible end-to-end evidence: the missing format is added to the MIME vocabulary, extension-based lookup covers that format so fallback to a generic MIME is avoided, supported-image or preview eligibility includes the new formats behind conservative Safari 17+ Apple-platform capability checks, and existing WebP/AVIF/text/video/PDF helper behavior is preserved. Avoid using repeated test searches, an input accept-list tweak, or a standalone parser cleanup as the main correctness signal. If a MIME parser simplification criterion is generated at all, make it secondary and conditional on the trajectory having located the parser and shown how the new extension mappings integrate with preview/thumbnail eligibility.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a task that adds browser-conditional HEIC/JXL-style image preview or thumbnail support, it is a flaw if the trajectory treats MIME parser simplification or removal of file-content reading as the primary evidence of success while lacking a coherent visible plan or edits for the full support path: adding the missing MIME type, adding extension lookup/fallback coverage for the new extension, gating preview-supported image formats by the intended browser and platform capability, and preserving existing MIME helper behavior. This should not penalize early exploration merely for not having changed the parser yet; it should penalize overfocus on parser cleanup when the trajectory has enough context to address the end-to-end support layers.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Parser-cleanup overfocus instead of end-to-end format support

stronger_evidence_to_prioritize: missing modern image MIME type is added to the shared MIME vocabulary
extension-based MIME lookup covers the new extension so it does not fall back to a generic MIME
preview or supported-image allowlist includes the new formats only behind the required browser/version/platform capability
existing image format support and exported helper behavior are preserved after edits
the agent inspects diffs or validates after broad rewrites
tempting_but_weak_evidence: only removing a content-reading helper from MIME detection
only adding an input accept-list entry
only checking Safari version without considering the intended platform/browser-name boundary
repeating no-result searches for tests without inspecting the actual modified behavior

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory addresses or explicitly plans the end-to-end MIME constant, extension lookup, and capability-gated preview path, with parser simplification treated as secondary if relevant.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory mentions parser simplification prominently, but also shows concrete progress on most of the required format-support and browser-gating layers.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: parser simplification is emphasized and at least one core layer, such as extension mapping or capability-gated preview support, remains unverified or only vaguely planned.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory mostly focuses on removing or finding MIME content-analysis logic while missing important visible work on the new format constant, extension fallback, or conditional preview support.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory assumes parser cleanup or repeated searches are sufficient, has no coherent end-to-end support path, or performs broad unvalidated rewrites that risk breaking existing MIME/image helper behavior.

experiences.title: Qt WebEngine file-picker MIME workaround must add suffixes, not just aliases
experiences.description: Use when a qutebrowser/Qt WebEngine task concerns missing files in upload dialogs under accepted MIME filters, especially JPEG/JPG under image-only accept rules, and the trajectory has located `chooseFiles`/`accepted_mimetypes` handling.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python qutebrowser-style Qt WebEngine environment where web content supplies accepted MIME/file-type entries to a `chooseFiles` override and the default Qt file picker is invoked with that iterable. The useful evidence is that JPG files disappear only when filters are restricted, affected Qt versions are called out, and the code currently passes `accepted_mimetypes` through to Qt with little or no preprocessing. This criterion is most relevant once the trajectory has found the file-picker integration point or is proposing a patch there. It is less applicable if the work is still broad repository exploration, if the reported path is an external/custom file selector that intentionally ignores Qt MIME filters, or if the task is about download/display MIME sniffing rather than upload file-dialog filtering.
experiences.experience: Earlier rubrics in this cluster often identified the right area (`accepted_mimetypes` in Qt WebEngine `chooseFiles`) but were too permissive or too focused on the tempting `image/jpg` versus `image/jpeg` alias story. That alias-only framing can approve patches that merely replace or append MIME aliases, which does not address the observed failure: Qt's file dialog needs missing filename suffixes/extensions made explicit when its MIME database/filter expansion is incomplete. A better rubric should ask whether the trajectory is converging on a version-scoped workaround that derives file suffixes from the upstream accepted entries, handles both concrete MIME types and wildcard MIME groups such as `image/*`, avoids duplicating suffixes already present, and passes the augmented accepted list into the Qt default dialog path. It should also check that version gating uses the relevant Qt runtime boundary for the upstream bug, and that the patch stays localized to WebEngine file selection rather than changing unrelated WebKit response handling, downloads, generic config placeholders, or external selector behavior. Visible evidence to prioritize includes: searches showing `accepted_mimetypes` is only used in WebEngine `chooseFiles`; recognition that `shared.choose_file` lacks MIME filtering and is not the primary reproduction path; inspection of existing MIME helpers or Python `mimetypes`; and plans/tests/logging around adding extensions such as `.jpg`/`.jpeg` from MIME entries before delegating to Qt. Avoid generating a rubric that treats simple MIME normalization (`image/jpg` ↔ `image/jpeg`) as sufficient unless the trajectory has evidence that the upstream accepted list itself contains the wrong alias and Qt would correctly expand it after normalization.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should identify the Qt WebEngine upload file-picker hook receiving `accepted_mimetypes` and pursue a narrow workaround for affected Qt versions that augments the accepted entries with explicit filename suffixes derived from MIME types and wildcard MIME groups before delegating to Qt's default dialog. Strong evidence includes handling `image/*` as well as `image/jpeg`, using Python or project MIME utilities to obtain all relevant extensions such as `.jpg` and `.jpeg`, subtracting suffixes already present, preserving existing file-selection modes, and avoiding unrelated changes to external selectors, downloads, or WebKit content MIME handling.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Suffix-expansion workaround for MIME-filtered Qt file dialogs

required_visible_evidence: Trajectory has located the WebEngine file-selection override or equivalent `chooseFiles` path.
Trajectory recognizes `accepted_mimetypes` is the data passed to Qt's default file picker.
Trajectory distinguishes adding explicit file suffix entries from merely normalizing MIME aliases.
Trajectory accounts for the affected Qt version range or runtime-version boundary.
Trajectory does not base the solution primarily on unrelated WebKit/download/external-selector code.
metadata.task_family: Qt WebEngine upload file picker MIME filtering bugs
metadata.common_false_proxy: Treating `image/jpg` and `image/jpeg` alias conversion alone as the complete fix.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory has found the WebEngine file-picker MIME path; it is exploring unrelated files or MIME handling for downloads/display.
scale.2: Finds some file-selection or MIME-related code but focuses on external selectors, WebKit response handling, or generic filter strings without connecting the issue to Qt's default dialog `accepted_mimetypes` path.
scale.3: Locates `chooseFiles` and `accepted_mimetypes` and proposes a plausible version-gated MIME workaround, but mainly discusses or implements MIME alias normalization rather than explicit suffix expansion.
scale.4: Clearly identifies that the Qt dialog needs missing extensions/suffixes added to the accepted list, plans to derive them from MIME entries, and keeps the change localized to WebEngine file selection with appropriate version gating, though wildcard handling or duplicate avoidance may be incomplete.
scale.5: Fully converges on a robust suffix-expansion workaround: handles concrete MIME types and wildcard groups like `image/*`, adds all missing known suffixes such as JPEG variants while preserving existing accepted entries, gates on the affected Qt runtime versions, and passes the augmented list to the default Qt file picker without unrelated behavioral changes.

experiences.title: Do not equate MultiOutput support with validation-layer estimators_ introspection
experiences.description: Retrieve when a scikit-learn task involves a meta-estimator missing a fitted attribute used by a generic utility, especially `MultiOutputClassifier` with `cross_val_predict(..., method='predict_proba')` and class-order enforcement.
experiences.context: In old scikit-learn-style code, the visible failure is that a generic cross-validation prediction helper expects a fitted classifier to expose `classes_`, while `MultiOutputClassifier` fits one classifier per output and initially exposes only `estimators_[i].classes_`. A tempting rubric says the solution must special-case `MultiOutputClassifier` inside the validation helper and read classes from `estimators_`. That can be appropriate only as a narrowly justified fallback that preserves existing `estimator.classes_` semantics and avoids broad heuristics. It is misleading when the codebase’s estimator API already expects fitted classifiers to publish `classes_`, when related multi-output estimators already set a list-of-classes attribute, or when other estimators such as ensembles also have `estimators_` for unrelated reasons.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics over-focused on accessing `estimators_[i].classes_` from the cross-validation/class-ordering code. This over-rewarded patches that used broad `hasattr(estimator, 'estimators_')` or class-name checks in a generic utility, even though `estimators_` is not a reliable signal for per-output wrappers and can break ensemble or multilabel classifiers whose own `classes_` is already correct. It also under-valued trajectories moving toward the cleaner API-level fix: make the multi-output classifier expose a fitted `classes_` attribute as a list of per-output class arrays, so the existing generic prediction-order code continues to work. When generating rubrics for this pattern, focus on whether the trajectory preserves the estimator interface contract and existing generic class-order enforcement, not merely whether it knows sub-estimators contain class labels. Avoid requiring modifications to the validation helper or requiring direct sub-estimator access as the only acceptable solution. Prefer visible evidence such as: inspection of the multi-output estimator’s fit behavior, recognition that cloned fold estimators must have `classes_` after fitting, comparison with related estimators that set per-output `classes_`, and awareness that generic `estimators_` detection is unsafe for ensembles.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that solve a missing fitted classifier attribute by adding broad or brittle `estimators_`-based special handling in a generic cross-validation/class-ordering path, instead of preserving the estimator API by ensuring the multi-output classifier exposes per-output `classes_` after fit. This flaw is especially concerning when the visible trajectory shows use of `hasattr(estimator, 'estimators_')`, class-name checks, or sub-estimator class extraction without demonstrating that other estimators with `estimators_` remain compatible.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Brittle meta-estimator introspection in generic validation code

metadata.environment: scikit-learn-style Python library; multi-output classifier meta-estimator; cross-validation prediction helper; probability or decision methods requiring class-column ordering
risk_signals: solution treats all `estimators_` containers as per-output classifiers
patch bypasses or rewrites existing class-order enforcement
trajectory ignores that the wrapper can expose `classes_` after fitting
better_evidence: fitted multi-output classifier publishes list-like per-output `classes_`
existing generic validation code can continue using `estimator.classes_`
trajectory distinguishes multi-output wrappers from ensembles
regression reasoning includes ordinary classifiers and multilabel ensemble classifiers

scale.1: No evidence of the brittle introspection flaw; the trajectory preserves the generic validation path and either adds the fitted `classes_` interface to the multi-output classifier or explicitly validates a very narrow fallback.
scale.2: Minor concern: the trajectory mentions sub-estimator classes but also recognizes that the wrapper should expose `classes_` or that broad `estimators_` checks are unsafe.
scale.3: Mixed behavior: the trajectory explores validation-layer sub-estimator access without yet committing, and has not shown whether it will preserve the estimator interface or avoid ensemble regressions.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory patches or plans to patch the generic validation/class-ordering helper using `estimators_` or class-name heuristics, with little evidence of compatibility checks for other estimators.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory implements broad `estimators_`-based class extraction or rewrites class-order handling in a way likely to mis-handle existing estimators that already expose correct `classes_`, while not addressing the missing fitted attribute on the multi-output classifier.

experiences.title: Do not over-credit generic simulation hooks for a missing protocol ceremony
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go/Teleport-style task asks for both a client-side enrollment/authentication flow and native hooks or fakes for isolated validation, especially where generated gRPC/protobuf APIs already exist but OSS workflow code is missing.
experiences.context: This applies to trajectories in a Go monorepo where the visible task requires an end-to-end client ceremony using existing generated Device Trust RPCs plus native collection/signing abstractions. A rubric that only asks for interfaces, callbacks, mocks, or a simulated authenticator is misleading when those hooks are disconnected from the actual streaming enrollment/authentication protocol, use invented data/certificate flows, return dummy signatures, or stop at NotImplemented during challenge handling. The original idea is still appropriate when narrowed to protocol-faithful native seams: hooks should replace OS-native operations and/or the server in tests while exercising the same generated messages and challenge-response order. During pure exploration with no edits, absence of hooks is not by itself a useful discriminator; evaluate whether the agent has identified the existing API contracts and the need for a reusable, testable ceremony instead.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked whether the trajectory provided native hooks, mocks, or simulation paths for isolated validation. That criterion reflects a real task requirement, but in this setting it became too broad: agents could score well by adding generic hook structs, simulated managers, fake signatures, or tests while still failing to implement the actual enrollment ceremony against the generated DeviceTrustService stream. A better rubric should focus on whether the native abstraction is wired into a protocol-correct client flow: sends the enrollment init with token/device data/public key material, receives the OS-specific challenge, signs it through the native hook, sends the generated challenge-response message, validates success, and offers a fake service/device implementation that exercises that same flow without an enterprise server. Avoid the tempting criterion that any interface, callback, mock client, or 'SimulateEnrollment' helper satisfies the native-hooks requirement. Prioritize visible evidence that the code uses existing generated message types and streaming clients, keeps OS-native data collection/signing behind narrow replaceable functions or interfaces, and avoids invented certificates, dummy signatures, unimplemented challenge branches, or simulations that bypass the real ceremony.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial native-hook simulation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear to satisfy the native-hooks requirement by adding generic interfaces, callbacks, mocks, or simulated authenticators, but the visible implementation does not exercise the actual generated enrollment/authentication ceremony. This flaw is present when the hooks are not used to collect protocol-required device data, prepare native enrollment init payloads, sign server challenges, and drive the same streaming request/response flow that a real client would use; or when simulation bypasses the service protocol with dummy devices, dummy signatures, invented certificates, or NotImplemented challenge handling.

metadata.environment: Go monorepo with generated devicetrust protobuf/gRPC client types and missing higher-level OSS client enrollment workflow
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: presence of hook structs, callbacks, mock implementations, or simulate methods alone
better_visible_evidence: uses existing generated DeviceTrustService client/message types rather than invented protocol types
implements the documented streaming enrollment order including init, challenge, signed challenge response, and success validation
routes OS-native operations such as device data collection, native enrollment init, credential access, and challenge signing through narrow replaceable seams
provides fakes or test environment that exercise the same generated RPC flow without a real enterprise server
does not leave challenge response as NotImplemented and does not use dummy signatures for the real path

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: native hooks or fakes, if present, are visibly wired into a protocol-correct generated RPC ceremony and the real path signs challenges through the abstraction.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory has mostly protocol-coupled hooks but some validation/test coverage or native seam boundaries are incomplete or only described.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory adds some useful native abstraction and partial stream handling, but simulation or tests bypass important parts of the actual challenge-response flow.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory adds generic hooks/mocks/simulation while the real enrollment flow is incomplete, uses dummy/generated data in place of native challenge signing, or does not complete the documented stream.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory relies almost entirely on disconnected simulation helpers, invented device/certificate behavior, dummy signatures, or NotImplemented challenge handling, with little or no protocol-faithful enrollment path.

experiences.title: Require a Runnable, Documented Backend Compose Example
experiences.description: Retrieve when a backend-support task explicitly asks for a Docker Compose or deployment example, especially after the trajectory has inspected existing examples or modified compose/docs files.
experiences.context: Applies in Go service repositories with SQL/database backend support where the task includes both code-level backend integration and a documented Docker Compose example. It is strongest once the trajectory has found repository conventions for examples, touched docker-compose files, or appears to be nearing finalization. It is less useful for tasks that do not request deployment documentation, or at very early exploration before the agent has had a chance to inspect examples/docs; in those cases, a core protocol/migration criterion may be more timely. Do not treat any compose-related edit as sufficient: the criterion should distinguish a runnable, project-conventional example from a commented stub, an unrelated modification to the default compose file, or an example using the wrong application environment variables.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics correctly targeted the deployment-example requirement because the task made it an explicit acceptance concern and the trajectories repeatedly showed visible evidence of missing, misplaced, or unusable compose documentation. The useful judgment cue was not merely whether a file containing 'cockroachdb' existed, but whether the repository gained a documented example that a user could run: a CockroachDB service, Flipt configured with the project’s actual configuration variable for the DB URL, a CockroachDB URL/protocol rather than silently falling back to Postgres, sensible service ordering/readiness or documented initialization assumptions, and placement following the repository’s existing examples pattern. A better rubric should focus on this end-to-end usability and documentation contract. Avoid tempting weak proxies such as rewarding a root docker-compose.yml rewrite, a commented-out sample, a copied Postgres example with renamed strings, or a compose file that starts CockroachDB but does not configure Flipt correctly. Also avoid over-weighting aesthetic details like image versions or logos unless they affect runnability. Prioritize visible trajectory evidence: inspection of existing example conventions, creation of a dedicated documented example, correct Flipt environment/config names, correct CockroachDB service and connection URL, dependency/readiness handling, and preservation of unrelated default compose behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Project-Conventional Runnable Compose Example
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should add a documented Docker Compose example for the new database backend that follows the repository's existing example conventions and is practically runnable: it starts the database service, configures the application with the correct backend URL using the application's real configuration environment variable names, handles or documents database readiness/initialization assumptions, avoids avoidable port/service conflicts, and does not replace an unrelated default compose file with a backend-specific sample unless that is the repository convention.

required_visible_evidence: The task explicitly requests a Docker Compose or documented deployment example for a new database backend.
The trajectory inspects or can infer the repository's existing example/documentation conventions.
The trajectory creates or updates a compose example with both the application service and the new database service.
The application service uses the repository's actual configuration environment variables and a backend-appropriate connection URL.
The example includes runnable instructions or documentation, not only an uncommented or commented service fragment.
common_failure_signals: Only a commented-out compose snippet is added.
The root/default compose file is repurposed in a way that removes or obscures the existing generic example.
The compose file uses generic or incorrect environment variable names instead of the project's real configuration keys.
The URL uses the old backend protocol or points to the wrong service.
No README/instructions or readiness/initialization guidance is provided.

scale.1: No meaningful compose/documentation work is visible, or only unrelated backend code changes are present despite the explicit example requirement.
scale.2: A minimal or partial compose-related edit is visible, but it is not a runnable documented example: for instance it is only a commented stub, is placed inconsistently with repository conventions, or lacks application configuration.
scale.3: The trajectory is roughly equivalent to the parent state: it may mention the need for an example or has begun one, but visible evidence does not yet show a complete, documented, project-conventional runnable setup.
scale.4: Clear progress toward a usable example is visible: a compose file includes the application and database services with mostly correct configuration, but may still have minor gaps such as weak readiness handling, sparse documentation, or questionable placement.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory adds a dedicated, documented, project-conventional Docker Compose example that can reasonably be run as-is, uses the correct application configuration variables and backend URL, includes database service setup and readiness/initialization guidance, and avoids unrelated compose regressions.

experiences.title: Holistic OS-backed scanner reversion, not textual fs eradication
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go directory-scanner task asks to revert from fs.FS/os.DirFS traversal to direct OS filesystem operations and the trajectory is editing traversal helpers, scanner call sites, or tests.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go codebase where a scanner currently passes an fs.FS/os.DirFS abstraction through directory-walking functions and the requested fix is to restore real OS path traversal. It is most useful after the agent has inspected or modified the walker, empty-folder check, audio-file loading, and caller wiring, or has build/test output showing signature mismatches. Do not apply as a blanket ban on every io/fs import or fs.DirEntry type: direct os.ReadDir still returns values compatible with fs.DirEntry, and tests may legitimately use fs.ReadDirFile/fstest-style helpers. It is also premature during initial exploration before the trajectory exposes the coupled call sites and helper signatures.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful rubric pattern is to judge whether the revert is coherent across the whole production scanner path, not whether one function was edited or whether all text containing `fs` disappeared. Earlier rubrics were helpful when they caught visible leftovers such as `rootFS := os.DirFS(...)`, calls still passing an fs.FS into the walker or empty-folder helper, `fs.ReadDir(os.DirFS(dirPath), ".")` in audio loading, stale tests that no longer compile against reverted signatures, or build errors from half-updated APIs. However, a stronger rubric should avoid the tempting but wrong criterion “no fs.FS imports or references anywhere”: the important boundary is removing the virtual filesystem abstraction from production traversal while preserving valid entry interfaces, error-tolerant reading, sorting, symlink handling, ignore-marker behavior, unreadable-directory handling, playlist/image/audio detection, and the scanner’s channel/error contract. Prioritize observable evidence such as diffs/greps of production call sites, function signatures, actual OS calls (`os.ReadDir`, `os.Stat`, `os.Open` or equivalent utilities), compile/test results after caller and test updates, and whether the agent reconciles old historical code with current model/helper APIs. Do not over-reward passing local scanner tests if the trajectory shows tests were rewritten to match a broken implementation or production behavior was narrowed.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Coherent OS-backed traversal revert
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a complete, production-safe revert from virtual fs.FS traversal to direct OS path traversal across the scanner workflow. Strong evidence includes removing os.DirFS/fs.FS parameters from the production walker and empty-folder path, updating the scanner caller to preserve the existing asynchronous results/error-channel behavior, using direct OS reads/stats/opens or an equivalent OS-backed readability utility for traversal and audio-file loading, preserving directory stats and behavior for audio/image/playlist detection, ignored directories, unreadable directories, symlinks, sorted traversal, and partial read/error reporting, and validating with build/tests after updating coupled tests or compatibility layers. The criterion should not require eliminating all io/fs types when they are only used as entry interfaces or test support.

visible_evidence: walker and helper signatures/calls no longer pass fs.FS or os.DirFS in production scanning
direct OS filesystem operations are used for traversal, stat, readability, and immediate audio-file listing
scanner caller preserves channel lifecycle and error propagation
directory behavior such as ignore markers, hidden-directory rules, unreadable-directory skipping, symlink-to-directory handling, sorted traversal, and media-type stats is retained
tests/build outputs show caller and tests are synchronized with the reverted contract
avoid_as_proxy: textual absence of every io/fs import
editing only the central walker while leaving caller/helper fs.FS usage
passing tests after weakening or corrupting test expectations

scale.1: The trajectory only identifies the fs.FS walker or makes isolated edits while leaving production call sites, helper signatures, or audio-file loading visibly tied to os.DirFS/fs.FS, with no meaningful validation.
scale.2: Some direct OS calls are introduced, but the production path remains inconsistent: stale fs.FS parameters or os.DirFS calls remain, helper bodies use mismatched paths, or compile errors from partial signature changes are visible.
scale.3: The parent-level behavior is roughly preserved: the main walker or caller is partly reverted and some validation occurs, but evidence is incomplete for coupled helpers, channel/error semantics, tests, or key traversal behaviors.
scale.4: Most production scanner paths are coherently OS-backed, caller signatures are aligned, build/tests are being used, and the trajectory explicitly preserves key directory behaviors, with only minor uncertainty around edge cases or tests.
scale.5: The trajectory provides decisive evidence of a holistic revert: all production traversal/caller/helper paths use real OS paths instead of fs.FS abstraction, behavior-preserving edge cases are maintained, tests/callers are synchronized without weakening coverage, and validation succeeds or remaining issues are clearly outside the reverted scanner path.

experiences.title: Do not treat rendered maxlength alone as enough for Django widget attr fixes
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for Django form regressions where a dynamic field property must be synchronized to `widget.attrs`, especially when the trajectory proposes `str(...)` coercion or a generic `widget_attrs()` refresh for `maxlength`.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django source-tree task involving `AuthenticationForm`, `UsernameField`, `CharField.widget_attrs()`, and the form/widget rendering lifecycle. The misleading rubric pattern is to reward any trajectory that makes rendered HTML contain `maxlength` and preserves visible browser-hint attrs, without checking the public `widget.attrs` contract and value fidelity. The original rendered-HTML criterion is still relevant when the trajectory has not reached implementation or when the task only asks for end-user markup; however, once the trajectory shows a concrete patch to `widget.attrs`, the rubric must distinguish direct synchronization of the widget attr to the computed max-length value from manual stringification or broad recomputation through `widget_attrs()`.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics correctly identified the main regression: `AuthenticationForm` sets `field.max_length` after widget initialization, so the username widget must receive `maxlength`. They were misleading because they stopped at “renders a `maxlength` HTML attribute matching the user model” and therefore over-rewarded patches that set `widget.attrs['maxlength'] = str(field.max_length)` or bulk-updated `widget.attrs` with `field.widget_attrs(widget)`. In this Django context, `widget.attrs` itself is observable and may be asserted directly, not merely the final serialized HTML. A better rubric should focus on whether the implementation synchronizes the username field and widget using a single computed max-length value, preserves the 254 fallback and existing label/widget behavior, and avoids unnecessary broad changes to `UsernameField` or generic widget attr refreshes. Avoid the tempting criterion “rendered HTML contains maxlength” as the sole success proxy; prioritize visible evidence in the trajectory such as the exact assignment to `widget.attrs`, the value type/fidelity relative to `field.max_length`, fallback handling, and whether tests or smoke checks inspect `widget.attrs` rather than only rendered markup.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a Django `AuthenticationForm` maxlength regression, penalize trajectories that implement or plan a widget fix by manually stringifying the computed max length, by bulk-refreshing all widget attrs through `widget_attrs()`, or by validating only rendered HTML while leaving the internal `widget.attrs['maxlength']` value contract ambiguous. This flaw is especially important once the visible trajectory has reached a concrete edit in `AuthenticationForm.__init__` after the dynamic `max_length` assignment.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Widget attrs value contract missed

metadata.environment: Django form/widget internals
visible_cues: patch assigns `widget.attrs['maxlength'] = str(...)`
patch uses `widget.attrs.update(field.widget_attrs(widget))` as the maxlength fix
checks only rendered HTML contains `maxlength`
no evidence that `widget.attrs['maxlength']` equals the computed field max_length value without unnecessary coercion
preferred_evidence: single computed username max-length value is used for both `field.max_length` and `widget.attrs['maxlength']`
fallback value remains 254 when the model username field has no max_length
existing widget attrs and label behavior remain unchanged
validation inspects `widget.attrs` or an equivalent direct form state in addition to rendered markup

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory either has not implemented the fix yet, or it clearly preserves direct value fidelity between the computed max length, `field.max_length`, and `widget.attrs['maxlength']`.
scale.2: Minor concern: the trajectory emphasizes rendered HTML more than internal widget state, but the visible implementation does not show string coercion, bulk attr refresh, or incompatible widget attr handling.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory has the right lifecycle diagnosis and likely restores rendered markup, but the intended patch or validation leaves the exact `widget.attrs['maxlength']` value contract unclear.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the visible patch sets `maxlength` with `str(...)` or uses a generic `widget_attrs()` update, and the trajectory validates mostly through rendered HTML or smoke output rather than direct widget attr fidelity.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory explicitly treats rendered HTML as the only acceptance criterion while committing a stringified or bulk-refreshed widget attr patch, making it likely to miss direct `widget.attrs` expectations and introduce unnecessary attr rewrites.

experiences.title: End-to-End Password Change Validation Contract
experiences.description: Use when a password-change security task spans a React/Admin-style UI, a Go REST update path, and user repository persistence with separate current/new password semantics.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories for a Go backend plus React Admin UI where user edits flow through a generic REST resource/repository, the model has or needs a transient current-password input alongside an existing new-password field, and the task requires different rules for self password changes versus administrator resets. It is most useful after the agent has identified the user edit form, the backend update hook, and the REST error behavior, or has begun editing those areas. It is less useful for unrelated authentication-only fixes, standalone API endpoints not used by the UI, systems with an already established password hashing/validation service unless that service is visible, or very early exploration before the update path and error contract are known.
experiences.experience: Prior rubrics that only checked whether the agent planned or implemented role-based current-password comparison were necessary but too broad: they over-credit implementations that compare the right stored password yet still fail the real UI/API contract. In this setting, a better rubric should evaluate the whole password-change validation contract: self-updates require both current and new password, incorrect current password is rejected on the currentPassword field, admins changing other users are exempt, transient currentPassword is not persisted as a database column, and the REST/UI layer can actually surface field-specific validation errors instead of generic 500/error strings. Avoid the tempting but wrong criterion that demands bcrypt/hash comparison when repository tests and login code visibly use plain password comparison; also avoid treating UI-only required fields as sufficient security. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent has inspected the generic REST controller's error mapping, the repository update/put split, the SQL argument mapping for request-only fields, and the React Admin form/save behavior. Good rubric wording should reward implementations that preserve create/admin-reset behavior while enforcing bidirectional current/new pairing and using a supported validation response shape.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete Password Change Validation Contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show progress toward an end-to-end password-change fix that enforces the correct self-versus-admin rules in the backend update path and integrates them with the UI/REST validation contract. Strong evidence includes adding a transient currentPassword input field, validating in the authenticated user update path rather than only in the UI, requiring new password and current password as a pair for self-updates, comparing the submitted current password against the logged-in user's stored password using the codebase's existing password semantics, exempting administrator resets of other users, preventing currentPassword from being persisted as a database column, and ensuring field-specific validation errors can be returned and consumed by the React Admin form.

expected_evidence: Identification or modification of the user REST update/repository path used by the UI
Role/self distinction based on logged-in actor versus target user
Both missing-current and missing-new password validation with field-specific errors
Admin reset of another account remains allowed without target current password
Transient currentPassword is excluded from SQL persistence
REST/UI error handling supports returning field errors rather than generic failures
UI collects currentPassword conditionally for self/non-admin password changes without forcing password changes on every profile edit
avoid_overcrediting: Only adding a currentPassword form field
Only comparing current password when new password is non-empty
Returning arbitrary errors through a REST controller that maps them to generic server errors
Persisting request-only fields
Introducing hashing requirements not supported by visible login/storage code

scale.1: No meaningful progress on the password-change contract; the trajectory remains in unrelated auth/Subsonic/UI exploration or proposes an inapplicable mechanism.
scale.2: Weak progress: identifies some relevant files or adds a current-password concept, but lacks backend enforcement or ignores self/admin distinctions, paired-field validation, or supported error handling.
scale.3: Moderate progress equivalent to the parent state: implements or plans the main self/admin current-password check but leaves important contract gaps such as missing-new validation, transient-field persistence, UI conditional behavior, or REST field-error propagation.
scale.4: Strong progress: addresses backend role-based validation and most paired-field/error-field requirements, with evidence of checking persistence and REST/UI integration, though one secondary integration detail may remain unresolved.
scale.5: Complete progress: visible trajectory covers the full end-to-end contract, including backend enforcement, admin reset exemption, bidirectional current/new validation, correct comparison semantics, non-persistence of currentPassword, supported field-specific REST errors, and conditional React Admin UI behavior.

experiences.title: Backend-Neutral In-Flight Posting Lock
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Node.js/NodeBB-like task is about duplicate topic creation from simultaneous same-user API requests and the trajectory is choosing or implementing a concurrency guard in the topic creation/write path.
experiences.context: Applies in a multi-backend forum codebase where topic creation flows through an API/write controller into a shared topic-posting routine, and the visible trajectory has found that concurrent authenticated creates need to be rejected while one request completes. The criterion is most useful once the agent has identified the creation path or started editing it. It is less useful for unrelated sequential duplicate-content prevention, for tasks where a single database backend is explicitly guaranteed, or for very early exploration before any route/model/database evidence has been gathered. If the trajectory only repeats searches for raw Redis/client support without implementing anything, the rubric should treat that as lack of progress rather than reward the lock idea alone.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics were useful when they checked for an actual in-flight per-user concurrency guard, because the bug is about overlapping requests, not ordinary duplicate title/content validation. However, rubrics that merely accepted any lock, especially a Redis SET NX lock or a content-hash idempotency key, were too broad: they could reward patches that were backend-specific, scoped too narrowly to only the topic-id allocation step, released before the full create request finished, or blocked only identical content while missing the project’s posting semantics. A better rubric should focus on observable evidence that the agent uses a project-idiomatic atomic database operation available through the shared database abstraction, keys the lock to the authenticated poster/session rather than globally, rejects contenders with the codebase’s normal client-error/localized-error path, and releases or deletes the lock in a finally block after the whole topic creation operation has completed or failed. Avoid making the criterion require Redis-specific primitives unless the trajectory has established Redis is the only supported backend. Also avoid rewarding repeated investigation or tests alone without a concrete guard spanning the critical section.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly converge on a backend-neutral, in-flight posting lock for the same authenticated actor around the full topic creation/write operation. Strong evidence includes use of the project database abstraction's atomic object-field increment/check or equivalent portable primitive, a per-user or per-session lock key, rejection of overlapping requests via the normal client-error/localized-error mechanism, and guaranteed cleanup in a finally block after the complete create operation, not merely after allocating a topic id. The rubric should not give full credit to Redis-only raw client calls, in-memory mutexes, content-hash duplicate checks, or locks that are released before post creation/hooks/response work finish.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Portable Full-Span User Posting Lock

required_evidence: lock is acquired atomically before the topic creation critical section
lock is scoped to the current posting actor rather than all users
contending overlapping requests are rejected as client-facing errors
cleanup is guaranteed on success and failure
implementation uses project-supported database abstractions or otherwise proves backend compatibility
failure_modes_to_penalize: raw Redis-only SET NX or db.client usage in a multi-backend path without abstraction
content-only or title-only duplicate detection instead of in-flight concurrency control
locking only a small substep such as id allocation
missing finally cleanup or leaving counters/locks behind
no implementation beyond repeated searches or design notes

scale.1: No concrete concurrency guard is implemented or the trajectory is stuck repeating investigation commands without changing the create path.
scale.2: The agent identifies the need for a per-user lock and relevant creation path, but has not implemented it or proposes a non-portable/raw-client approach without resolving compatibility.
scale.3: A lock-like mechanism is partially implemented, but it is too narrow, backend-specific, content-dedup oriented, or has uncertain cleanup/error semantics.
scale.4: A mostly correct in-flight per-user guard is implemented with atomic acquisition, contender rejection, and cleanup, with only minor uncertainty about exact placement or integration.
scale.5: The trajectory shows a project-idiomatic portable lock spanning the full create/write operation, correctly scoped to the actor, rejecting overlaps through normal client-error handling, and reliably cleaning up in all outcomes.

experiences.title: Avoid checklist rubrics when a backend feature is only superficially assembled
experiences.description: Retrieve this when a trajectory for a large Python/web.py backend feature has added schema/model/API/workflow hooks but shows blind appends, sed repairs, import-only checks, failing tests, or repetitive debugging. Broad feature-completeness rubrics can overvalue the mere presence of named components.
experiences.context: Applies in Open Library-style Python backend tasks involving SQL schema changes, core DB models, web.py delegate.page API handlers, account anonymization, and work-redirect integration. The misleading pattern is a trajectory that appears to cover all requested areas on paper—table, model, endpoints, Already Read validation, uniqueness, counts, anonymization, redirects—but visible evidence also shows unresolved behavioral failures, malformed edits, unverified SQL, failing targeted tests, or only py_compile/import smoke tests. The original idea of checking feature coverage is still useful at final-review time when the diff is stable and there is direct evidence that each endpoint and data workflow behaves correctly; it is not enough when the agent has only added matching symbols/classes or is still repairing generated code.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often restated the task as a checklist: require a Best Book Awards schema, CRUD/count APIs, Already Read validation, uniqueness, anonymization, and redirect support. That criterion is too broad and can be misleading because a trajectory may contain all those labels while still having broken SQL, incompatible query result handling, incorrect route/auth behavior, corrupted methods from sed insertions, unfinished update/count semantics, or failing tests. For similar trajectories, generate a rubric that penalizes treating surface coverage as completion without behavioral validation. Focus on visible evidence: whether targeted tests or manual DB/API checks exercise add/update/remove/count, not-read rejection, duplicate constraints, anonymization updates, and redirect updates; whether failures remain unresolved; whether schema syntax and DB helper conventions were verified; whether API responses match JSON expectations rather than redirects or HTTPError objects; and whether the agent inspected diffs after risky edits. Avoid tempting criteria that merely ask whether the implementation 'includes' the required files/classes or mentions the right validation hook.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Surface feature coverage without behavioral validation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for broad backend feature work where the agent has added apparent schema/model/API/workflow components but visible evidence shows they are not yet behaviorally validated or are still likely broken: unresolved targeted test failures, only import/compile smoke checks, DB schema/query errors, route/auth/count/update behavior not exercised, risky sed/appended edits with incomplete inspection, or repetitive debugging that does not advance the implementation. This is especially important when the task spans persistence, JSON APIs, eligibility validation, uniqueness, anonymization, and redirect maintenance.

metadata.environment: Python Open Library backend using web.py delegate.page APIs, core DB helper models, schema.sql, account anonymization, and work redirect maintenance
metadata.avoid_proxy: mere presence of files/classes/method names/endpoints matching the task checklist
prioritize_evidence: targeted tests or manual checks exercising CRUD/count behavior
explicit validation of Already Read rejection and authenticated success paths
verified uniqueness semantics, including topic/work conflicts as specified
schema and SQL query correctness under the repository DB conventions
clean diffs after sed/appended edits
verified anonymization and redirect update behavior

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory has stable implementation evidence and behavioral tests/checks for the major persistence, API, validation, uniqueness, anonymization, and redirect paths, with no unresolved relevant failures.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: most behavior is validated, but one secondary integration path or response detail remains only superficially checked.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory contains the main components and some checks, but important behavior such as counts, update/remove semantics, or workflow integration remains untested or partially failing.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the agent relies mainly on component presence, py_compile/import checks, or incomplete manual scripts while relevant tests fail, SQL/API behavior is uncertain, or sed/appended edits needed repairs.
scale.5: Most severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory is still broken or stalled, with unresolved syntax/SQL/test failures or repetitive non-progress, yet the apparent implementation only superficially matches the requested feature checklist.

experiences.title: Do not let the room-link label criterion overshadow external-link semantics
experiences.description: Retrieve when a React/TypeScript accessibility task names both a raw URL/share link needing a descriptive accessible name and a separate external-link cue/icon problem, especially when the trajectory has already located both render sites.
experiences.context: This applies in Element Web-like React/TSX UI accessibility fixes where the task has multiple acceptance requirements: one local link, such as a share/permalink URL, needs a descriptive title or aria-label, and another external link with a visual external-link icon must communicate new-tab behavior and avoid decorative/icon-only accessibility problems. A rubric about the share link’s accessible name is useful as a subcriterion when the task is limited to that link, or when judging only whether the trajectory has found and patched that specific issue. It becomes misleading as the main or only rubric once the visible task and trajectory show that the external-link implementation is equally central, because many trajectories can add a plausible label to the share URL while still leaving the external link inaccessible or structurally wrong.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics repeatedly focused on whether the Share dialog room permalink received a descriptive accessible name. That criterion is technically correct but too narrow for this task: the visible requirements also demand an accessible external-link cue and decorative icon handling. In the trajectories, agents often added an aria-label/title to the room link and then made weak or harmful external-link changes, such as leaving a separate icon-only anchor as an extra focusable duplicate, labeling both the text link and icon link with the same new-tab text, relying only on title text, or failing to remove/hide the decorative visual cue from assistive technology. A better rubric should focus on the external hosting/signup link structure and semantics: there should be a clear new-tab/external cue associated with the actual user-facing link, and the visual icon should not create an ambiguous or duplicate screen-reader target. Avoid the tempting criterion “room share link has aria-label/title” as the dominant signal when the task includes external-link cues; instead prioritize visible evidence that the agent handles the external link as an accessible whole, ideally with one coherent focusable link or an explicitly non-accessible decorative icon, while preserving href/target/rel behavior and localization conventions.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: External-link cue implemented as duplicate or inaccessible icon link
reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a React/TSX accessibility task that includes an external hosting/signup link with a visual external-link icon, penalize trajectories that appear to solve only the share/permalink accessible-name issue while leaving the external-link UI with an ambiguous duplicate focus target or without a coherent screen-reader cue that the real link opens in a new tab/window. This flaw is present when visible edits/plans keep a separate icon-only anchor pointing to the same URL without making it non-focusable/decorative, add the same aria-label/title to both the text link and icon link instead of consolidating the external-link affordance, rely solely on the icon or on an empty-alt image inside a focusable anchor, or omit a localized/new-tab cue on the actual link users activate. It is not present merely because the agent has not yet edited the file during early investigation, or when the trajectory shows a plan or implementation that makes the external icon decorative/non-announced and associates the new-tab cue with a single meaningful link while preserving target/rel security attributes.

metadata.environment: React TypeScript UI with localized JSX strings and external anchors using target="_blank" plus rel security attributes
visible_evidence_to_check: whether the external hosting/signup link remains split into a text anchor plus a separate icon-only anchor
whether the new-tab/external cue is attached to the meaningful link text or accessible name
whether the visual external-link icon is decorative or otherwise excluded from assistive technology
whether duplicate focusable anchors to the same URL are removed, consolidated, or clearly disambiguated
whether href, target, and rel behavior are preserved
metadata.do_not_use_as_primary_signal: presence of an aria-label/title on the room share URL alone

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory has not yet reached the external-link patch, or it clearly plans/implements a coherent accessible external link with no duplicate ambiguous icon-only target.
