scale.2: Minor concern: the trajectory mentions the external-link cue but has not yet shown enough code to confirm whether duplicate icon/link semantics will be handled.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory adds or plans a new-tab cue but leaves uncertainty about the separate visual icon anchor or decorative handling.
scale.4: Clear flaw: visible edits add labels/titles to existing anchors while keeping a separate icon-only or duplicate external-link anchor that remains focusable or ambiguously named.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory treats the task as solved after the share-link label and leaves the external link relying on a visual/icon-only cue, or creates multiple confusing focusable links to the same external URL without proper decorative hiding or consolidation.

experiences.title: Cross-layer limit alignment must be functional, not just literal
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task asks to keep an external service/runtime limit aligned with an application-side cap, especially for large Solr/query boolean-clause limits configured in YAML and enforced in Python backend code.
experiences.context: Applies in Python web repositories with Docker Compose or similar service configuration, where the task explicitly names both a service-level setting and a backend cap that must share a numeric value. It is especially useful once the trajectory has inspected at least one named file or query path and can show whether the service option, backend cap, and generated large query are connected. It is less appropriate for tasks that only require changing one configuration file, for very early trajectories with no file inspection, or for cases where the backend cap is intentionally outside the named module. Do not treat repeated unsuccessful greps as sufficient progress once the relevant files and missing setting have already been established.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics in this cluster focused on locating both configuration points and checking that they agree on the required value. That was useful because the visible trajectories repeatedly showed the agent stuck in duplicate searches, or making only the obvious service-side change, without demonstrating a complete cross-file alignment. However, a stronger rubric should not stop at the existence of matching literals. In this kind of task, an arbitrary new constant with the right number can be a tempting but weak proxy if it is not tied to the code path that builds or bounds the large query. The better criterion should reward evidence that the agent: preserves existing service options while adding the runtime limit in the named service configuration; identifies or creates the backend cap in the reading-log/search path; ensures the same value is used or documented as the controlling cap; and verifies the result with targeted inspection or tests. Avoid over-crediting repeated repository-wide greps, edits to similarly named but non-target config files, unrelated boolean-clause comments, or a standalone unused constant. Prioritize visible evidence such as targeted diffs/greps of the named config, inspection of the reading-log-to-query flow, confirmation that existing options remain intact, and a validation step showing both sides share the same limit.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates functional cross-layer alignment of the service-level boolean-clause limit and the application-side reading-log cap. It should show that the named service configuration includes the required Solr boolean-clause JVM/system property with value 30000 while preserving existing service options, and that the backend reading-log/search code defines or uses the same cap in the path that can generate large boolean queries. Strong evidence includes inspecting the relevant config and backend files after changes, avoiding unrelated config files or comments, and validating the aligned value with a targeted grep, diff review, or test. Merely adding a matching number in an unused location, or repeatedly searching after the missing setting is already known, is not enough.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Functional cross-layer limit alignment

metadata.required_service_evidence: Named service configuration contains the Solr boolean-clause limit option with value 30000 and keeps pre-existing options intact.
metadata.required_backend_evidence: Backend reading-log/search cap is present with the same value and is connected to the query/filter path rather than being an unused placeholder.
metadata.validation_evidence: Trajectory includes targeted post-change inspection, diff review, or tests confirming both sides remain aligned.
common_anti_patterns: Adding an unused backend constant with the right number
Editing a similarly named non-target compose/config file
Repeating the same unsuccessful searches instead of patching or inspecting the query path
Treating unrelated boolean-clause comments as the application cap

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of alignment work; the trajectory is mostly duplicate searches or unrelated exploration and has not established either the service setting or backend cap.
scale.2: Identifies one side of the alignment, such as the missing service option or absence of an obvious backend cap, but does not make or verify a coherent cross-file change.
scale.3: Shows partial alignment work, such as patching the service option or proposing a backend cap, but lacks evidence that both sides are verified, preserved, and connected to the actual reading-log/query path.
scale.4: Strongly demonstrates both values are present and equal, preserves existing configuration, and performs targeted verification, though the evidence that the backend cap is functionally used may be incomplete.
scale.5: Completely demonstrates functional alignment: the service option and backend cap share value 30000, existing config is preserved, the backend cap is in or used by the large-query path, irrelevant files are avoided, and targeted validation confirms the final state.

experiences.title: Django sequence escaping must use conditional per-item semantics
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django template-filter task asks for a sequence analogue of an existing escaping/safety filter, especially one intended to run before `join` with autoescape disabled.
experiences.context: Applies in Django template work where the agent is adding a built-in sequence filter analogous to an existing scalar filter such as `safe`/`escape`, and the visible trajectory has identified the default filter registry plus Django’s distinction between normal template escaping and force escaping. It is most useful once the agent is choosing or implementing the escaping helper, writing tests, or validating behavior. It is less applicable to unrelated HTML escaping utilities, non-template code, tasks where double-escaping is explicitly desired, or very early exploration before the agent has reached the semantic choice between conditional escaping and always-escape behavior.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases was not merely “add an `escapeseq` filter” or “run tests.” The decisive semantic boundary is that the sequence filter should mirror Django’s normal template `escape` behavior element-by-element: it should conditionally escape each item so already-safe values remain safe, while still making unsafe HTML-special-character strings safe for downstream sequence filters such as `join` when autoescape is off. A tempting but wrong criterion is to require or praise direct use of the low-level always-escaping helper just because its name matches the requested filter; that helper corresponds to force-escaping behavior and can double-escape safe/already-escaped values. Another weak proxy is generic validation of unsafe strings only, because tests that omit safe-string behavior can pass while preserving the wrong semantic choice. When generating rubrics here, prioritize visible evidence that the agent has recognized the existing scalar escape filter’s conditional behavior, applies that behavior per item without converting the whole sequence to a single string, registers the filter as a default template filter, and considers autoescape-off `join` plus safe-value preservation. Penalize trajectories that explicitly choose always-escape semantics or validate only raw HTML escaping while ignoring the safe-value boundary.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly converge on a registered Django default template filter for sequence escaping that applies Django’s normal conditional template escaping semantics to each individual sequence element, returns a sequence suitable for downstream filters such as `join`, works for the motivating autoescape-disabled rendering case, and preserves already-safe/HTML-aware values rather than force-escaping or double-escaping them.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Conditional per-item template escaping

required_visible_evidence: The agent identifies the new filter as the sequence analogue of Django’s normal template escape behavior, not force-escape behavior.
The intended implementation transforms each element independently and returns a sequence/list for later filters such as join.
The chosen helper or described semantics respect already-safe values via conditional escaping.
The filter is registered in the default template filter mechanism.
Validation or reasoning includes the autoescape-off join use case and, ideally, safe/already-escaped value behavior.
negative_visible_evidence: The agent chooses an always-escaping helper while claiming it is equivalent to normal template escape semantics.
The implementation would convert the entire input sequence to a string before escaping.
Tests or reasoning cover only unsafe raw strings and omit the safe-value/double-escaping boundary.
The filter is not registered for template use or is implemented only as an isolated helper.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of a registered per-sequence template filter, or the trajectory is still only exploring without committing to per-item escaping semantics.
scale.2: Some evidence of adding a sequence filter, but the plan or code is vague, may escape the whole sequence, lacks template registration, or ignores the autoescape-off join use case.
scale.3: Implements or plans a registered per-item sequence filter usable with join, but the escaping helper choice or safe-value behavior is ambiguous or unvalidated.
scale.4: Clearly implements or plans registered per-item conditional escaping for join/autoescape-off usage, with only minor gaps such as incomplete tests or limited discussion of safe values.
scale.5: Strong evidence of the full contract: registered default template filter, per-item conditional escaping, returned sequence for downstream filters, explicit autoescape-off join behavior, and validation or reasoning that already-safe values are not force-escaped.

experiences.title: First-Class Compatible Backend Requires Its Own Migration Driver
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task adds a new database backend that is wire-compatible with an existing backend but explicitly requires first-class migration support through a distinct migration driver.
experiences.context: Applies to Go database-backend feature work in repositories that centralize SQL URL parsing/opening and migrations, especially when the task names a backend such as CockroachDB that can reuse PostgreSQL runtime SQL behavior but must still be recognized as its own protocol and migration target. This is most useful after the trajectory has inspected or edited migration code, driver/protocol maps, or claims the backend is complete. It may be premature during pure repository exploration unless the agent has already formed an implementation plan. It is less relevant when the task only asks for a connection-string alias or when the project has no separate migration-driver layer.
experiences.experience: A useful rubric should distinguish runtime SQL-driver compatibility from migration-driver first-class support. In these cases, agents often added a new protocol enum, mapped the URL to the PostgreSQL-compatible SQL driver, updated store switches, copied migration files, or added Docker Compose examples, yet still routed migrations through the PostgreSQL golang-migrate driver or failed to wire migrations at all. That visible choice is a strong quality signal because the task explicitly asks for CockroachDB migration support, not just PostgreSQL impersonation. The better criterion should focus on evidence in the migration integration: a CockroachDB migration driver import/dependency, a CockroachDB switch branch using that driver, an appropriate CockroachDB migration source path and version handling, and validation that migrations resolve. Avoid the tempting but wrong criterion that CockroachDB migrations should simply use the PostgreSQL migration driver because the runtime wire protocol is compatible; PostgreSQL-compatible SQL opening is acceptable for application queries, but migration-driver identity is a separate contract.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Backend-Specific Migration Driver Integration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show that the new PostgreSQL-compatible backend is treated as a first-class migration target: the migration setup imports or otherwise depends on the backend-specific golang-migrate database driver, selects it in the migrator switch/dispatch for the new backend, resolves migrations from a backend-appropriate migration path or explicitly compatible migration assets, and preserves the repository's expected migration version semantics. Reusing PostgreSQL runtime SQL connection/store behavior may be correct, but routing migrations through the PostgreSQL migrate driver alone is insufficient when the task explicitly asks for the backend-specific migration driver.

prioritize_visible_evidence: migration file imports include the backend-specific golang-migrate database package
migrator switch/dispatch has a distinct branch for the new backend using that backend's WithInstance/config
migration source path and database instance name align with the new backend rather than silently substituting the old backend
expected migration version/count is intentionally set for the new backend's migration assets
build/test output or diff inspection confirms migration code compiles with any new dependency
do_not_overvalue: only mapping runtime SQL opens to the PostgreSQL driver
only adding store switch cases or Docker Compose examples
copying existing PostgreSQL migrations while still using the PostgreSQL migrate driver

scale.1: No meaningful migration integration for the new backend is visible, or the trajectory has not yet reached migration-related implementation.
scale.2: The trajectory mentions or partially edits migrations but only copies assets or aliases paths, with no distinct backend-specific migration driver wiring.
scale.3: Migration handling is partially addressed, but evidence suggests equivalent behavior to the parent state or ambiguous routing through an existing backend's migrator.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly adds a distinct backend branch and migration assets/path, but some details such as version handling, dependency updates, or validation remain uncertain.
scale.5: The trajectory clearly wires the backend-specific golang-migrate driver, uses an appropriate migration path/assets and version semantics, and provides visible validation or compile evidence for the migration changes.

experiences.title: Do not treat reducer-side status matching as sufficient for bypass-filter fixes
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for a TypeScript/Redux mail UI task where optimistic read/unread updates maintain a bypass list for filtered views, especially if the visible trajectory proposes pruning by comparing element unread state to the active filter.
experiences.context: This warning applies in a mail application with Redux-style element state, an optimistic mark-as-read/unread flow, and a `bypassFilter`/bypass-list mechanism used by selectors to keep items visible under Read/Unread filters. The misleading rubric pattern is to reward any implementation that removes an ID when `isUnread(element)` appears to match `filter.Unread`. That can be too shallow because the reducer may need to know the requested mark-as operation, not just inspect current element state, and it must avoid pruning unrelated bypass entries or treating non-read/unread filters as a Read filter. The original idea is still appropriate as a partial behavioral goal: the final behavior must remove stale bypass IDs when the item no longer needs to bypass. It is not appropriate as the sole criterion once the trajectory has reached implementation or final-review stage. In early exploration, a rubric may focus on finding the reducer, selector, caller, and filter semantics rather than requiring a complete patch.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked whether the trajectory implemented `bypassFilter` removal when an element's read/unread status matches the active filter. That criterion sounded aligned with the task, but it over-rewarded reducer-only patches that simply imported an unread helper, compared the updated element to `filter.Unread`, and filtered IDs out. The better signal is whether the trajectory establishes an action-intent-aware lifecycle: the optimistic mark-as caller/action contract should convey, or the agent should otherwise prove it already conveys, the requested read/unread operation; the reducer should gate add/remove decisions to the read/unread filter case; it should mutate only IDs affected by the current optimistic mark-as update using the same message/conversation ID mapping as the existing bypass logic; and it should preserve move/no-filter/unrelated bypass behavior. Avoid generating a tempting rubric that says `computes isUnread and removes when it matches the filter` is enough, or that rewards global cleanup of the entire bypass list under any active filter. A replacement criterion should prioritize visible evidence that the agent inspected both the selector and the optimistic mark-as dispatch path, updated or justified the action payload/type data needed to distinguish marking READ versus UNREAD, handled `Unread` undefined separately from `Unread: 0`, and validated the two task examples plus preservation of existing bypass additions.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for this bypass-list task when the proposed or applied fix only adds reducer-side pruning based on the element's derived unread state and the current filter, without establishing that the optimistic update carries enough mark-as intent to distinguish marking read from marking unread, and without limiting pruning to the current read/unread mark-as operation. This flaw is especially visible when the trajectory filters the whole bypass list, treats any non-empty filter as a Read/Unread filter, assumes truthiness of the unread flag instead of handling the undefined/zero/nonzero cases, or never inspects/updates the caller and action type that dispatch the optimistic mark-as update.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Missing action-intent-aware bypass lifecycle

metadata.environment: TypeScript React/Redux mail application with optimistic read/unread updates and selector-driven filtered element visibility
visible_positive_evidence: The trajectory inspects both the selector using the bypass list and the caller that dispatches optimistic mark-as updates.
The trajectory verifies whether the reducer receives the requested mark-as direction, or updates the action contract/type to provide it.
The reducer logic is explicitly gated to read/unread filters and handles no read/unread filter without unintended cleanup.
Only IDs affected by the current optimistic mark-as update are added or removed, preserving existing move and unrelated bypass behavior.
Reasoning or tests cover the examples: Unread filter plus marking unread removes, Read filter plus marking read removes, and opposite transitions still add/keep bypass.
visible_negative_evidence: The patch only imports an unread helper and compares element state to the active filter in the reducer.
The patch globally filters `bypassFilter` entries rather than considering only the affected optimistic update.
The patch treats `filter.Unread` truthiness or any active filter as sufficient to represent Read/Unread filtering.
The trajectory never examines the optimistic mark-as dispatch path or action payload/type.
Validation is limited to compilation or unrelated tests with no reasoning about the bypass truth table and no-filter behavior.

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory is action-intent-aware, handles read/unread filter boundaries, preserves unrelated bypass entries, and validates the relevant scenarios.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory mostly accounts for action intent and filter boundaries but leaves one edge case or validation gap ambiguous.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory recognizes add/remove behavior but it is unclear whether the reducer has sufficient mark-as intent or whether non-read/unread filters and unrelated entries are preserved.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory implements or plans a reducer-only status-vs-filter comparison without inspecting/updating the optimistic mark-as action contract or adequately gating the cleanup.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory globally prunes bypass entries, conflates unrelated filters with Read/Unread filtering, relies only on element unreadness, and provides no caller/action-contract reasoning or scenario validation.

experiences.title: Propagate Caller-Derived CLI Program Name to Early Parser
experiences.description: Use this when a Python CLI/management utility already derives a program name from an explicit argv but an argparse-like preliminary parser still defaults to global sys.argv.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django-style command-line framework where the task explicitly contrasts caller-provided argv with global sys.argv, and the visible trajectory has identified an initialization path that computes a reusable program name plus a later ArgumentParser/CommandParser construction whose usage string contains %(prog)s. It is especially relevant after the agent has located the target parser construction or has begun editing it. It is less useful for unrelated command parsing bugs, for tasks where no explicit argv contract exists, for code paths that should intentionally read sys.argv, or for a separate requirement to make argv[0] itself None-safe when no valid custom argv is supplied. Validation-focused criteria are useful only once the trajectory shows a runnable or designed regression scenario; they are premature when the agent is still locating files or is blocked by missing dependencies.
experiences.experience: In these cases, the most reliable rubric is a narrow implementation-contract criterion: the early parser used before command dispatch must receive the program name already computed from the utility's argv, rather than relying on the parser default based on global sys.argv. Rubrics that only demanded a full embedded-environment regression test were semantically relevant but often too harsh at early or dependency-blocked stages, because the visible trajectory could already contain decisive evidence of the correct one-line fix. A better rubric should reward editing the exact preliminary parser construction to pass the computed program name while preserving the existing usage string and option-parsing behavior. It may additionally value a regression check that creates divergence between global sys.argv[0] and the explicit argv[0], but testing should not replace the core implementation requirement. Avoid tempting wrong criteria such as requiring mutation of global sys.argv, accepting a hardcoded fallback program name, changing the computed argv-derived name in initialization, or treating argv=[None, ...] as the main scenario; the reported contract is that a valid explicit argv should avoid dependence on an invalid global sys.argv[0]. Visible evidence to prioritize includes: the agent locating the initialization-computed program-name field, identifying the early parser whose usage interpolates %(prog)s, modifying that parser construction with prog set to the computed field, preserving add_help/allow_abbrev/default option parsing, and optionally validating help/error output with mismatched explicit argv and global sys.argv.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should fix the command-line utility by passing the already-computed argv-derived program name into the preliminary argparse/CommandParser instance used for early option parsing, so %(prog)s no longer falls back to global sys.argv[0]. The evidence should show that the targeted early parser construction is updated with the computed program-name value, while retaining the existing usage template and parser options such as disabled automatic help, abbreviation behavior, and default-option parsing flow. Stronger evidence includes a regression check or clearly described scenario where global sys.argv[0] is invalid or different but a valid explicit argv is supplied and help/error usage reflects the explicit argv-derived program name.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Use Computed Program Name in Preliminary Parser

required_visible_evidence: Identification of a utility initialization path that computes a program name from an explicit argv
Identification of a later preliminary parser construction whose usage contains %(prog)s and lacks an explicit prog
Patch or concrete plan to pass the computed program-name field into that parser construction
Preservation of existing usage text and parser behavior for default option parsing
optional_strong_evidence: A regression scenario with global sys.argv[0] invalid or different from explicit argv[0]
Help, usage, or error output demonstrating the explicit argv-derived program name is used
anti_patterns: Mutating global sys.argv to work around the bug
Hardcoding a fallback program name instead of propagating the computed value
Changing argv initialization semantics without fixing the parser construction
Using argv[0] = None as the primary explicit-argv scenario when the intended explicit argv is valid

scale.1: No evidence that the agent has connected the parser's %(prog)s behavior to the already-computed argv-derived program name, or the trajectory pursues unrelated command parsing changes.
scale.2: The agent recognizes a sys.argv versus explicit argv issue but has not located the relevant preliminary parser construction or proposes only global sys.argv mutation, hardcoding, or broad initialization changes.
scale.3: The agent has located both the computed program-name value and the early parser construction, and its plan is directionally correct, but no visible patch or concrete edit yet proves the computed value is passed to the parser.
scale.4: The trajectory visibly updates the correct preliminary parser construction to pass the computed program-name value and preserves the existing usage/options behavior, but validation is absent, ad hoc, or blocked.
scale.5: The trajectory updates the correct parser construction, preserves existing parser semantics, and includes a focused regression check or convincing output showing that an explicit argv-derived program name is used even when global sys.argv[0] is invalid or different.

experiences.title: Auto-created M2M inline view/edit permission split
experiences.description: Use when a Django admin bug involves implicit ManyToMany through-model inlines being editable for view-only users, and the trajectory has reached permission-method analysis or implementation.
experiences.context: Applies in Django core/admin trajectories where the task concerns TabularInline/StackedInline over an auto-created ManyToManyField through model, especially after the agent has inspected inline permission methods, observed opts.auto_created handling, or reproduced that a user with only target-model view permission receives add/change/delete capability. The criterion is most useful once there is enough visible evidence to judge the intended permission contract or a proposed code change. It is less useful during very early repository exploration with no permission analysis yet, for explicit/custom through models with their own permissions, for ordinary ForeignKey inlines, or for unrelated admin rendering issues.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged the semantic boundary between read access and relationship mutation for implicit M2M inline models. The key evidence was not merely that the agent found admin inlines or ran tests, but that it identified the buggy delegation where add/change/delete for auto-created through models used view permission semantics. A strong rubric should require: mutation operations on the implicit through inline are not granted by target-model view permission alone; the inline can still be visible/read-only to users with view permission; users with target-model change permission retain the ability to modify the relationship; the permission check is mapped to the related target model because the auto-created through model has no independent permissions; and non-auto-created inline behavior is not broadened. Prefer judging visible artifacts such as inspection of the auto-created branch, a helper or equivalent logic to locate the non-parent target model, manual/test output for view-only versus change-permitted users, and regression tests in an existing Django admin inline test app. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria that only demand hiding UI controls, focus on test-runner setup, require permissions on the through model itself, make view permission disappear entirely, or require separate add/delete target permissions when the task evidence frames add/remove of the relationship as requiring change-level permission.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Implicit M2M inline permission contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate or implement the correct permission contract for Django admin inlines backed by an auto-created ManyToMany through model: view-only users may see the inline in read-only form but must not be able to add, change, or delete relationship rows; relationship mutation requires change permission on the related target model; view permission continues to allow view access, with change permission also sufficient for viewing. The evidence should show the agent is addressing the auto-created through-model permission methods rather than generic form rendering, and that permission checks are mapped to the target related model rather than to the through model itself.

applicability_signals: auto-created ManyToMany through model used as an admin inline
view-only staff user can add or remove inline relationships
trajectory inspects or edits inline add/change/delete/view permission methods
permission mapping must use the related target model
priority_evidence: add/change/delete no longer delegate to view permission for auto-created through models
target model is located from the through model by excluding the parent side of the relation
mutation checks require target-model change permission
view check still accepts target-model view or change permission
validation covers view-only denial of mutation and change-permitted edit access
anti_patterns: hiding the inline entirely for view-only users
checking permissions on the implicit through model
changing unrelated normal inline permission behavior
treating standalone reproduction setup success as sufficient correctness evidence

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory distinguishes view-only display from edit permissions for auto-created ManyToMany inline models.
scale.2: Identifies admin inline permissions or view-only behavior, but remains vague or risks solving it through generic UI hiding, through-model permissions, or unrelated admin changes.
scale.3: Recognizes that auto-created ManyToMany inline add/change/delete should not use view permission, but the visible plan or patch is incomplete, unvalidated, or unclear about preserving view-only read access.
scale.4: Clearly targets the auto-created through-model permission branch, maps checks to the related target model, prevents view-only mutation, and preserves view access, with some validation or test evidence.
scale.5: Fully captures the contract: target-model change permission gates add/change/delete relationship mutation, target-model view or change gates read-only visibility, non-auto-created behavior is preserved, and focused tests or manual permission-matrix evidence validate both view-only and change-permitted cases.

experiences.title: Do not overreward “already fixed” validation without checking for stale-task dead ends
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task says a feature is missing, but the trajectory has found the named API, behavior, and tests already present and passing, and the agent is considering no-op or duplicate work in that same area.
experiences.context: This warning applies in codebase-debugging trajectories, especially in Go repositories with existing tests, where the agent locates the component named by the task, confirms the described behavior already exists, and then a rubric is tempted to reward broad exploration or pre-existing-fix recognition. The misleading pattern is not the investigation itself; it is treating “the agent found existing code and tests” as strong evidence of final patch quality even when the trajectory has no failing reproduction, no concrete unmet caller/API requirement, repeated searches, scratch artifacts, or plans for redundant changes. A pre-existing-implementation criterion can still be useful when the task explicitly asks for verification, documentation, test-only coverage, or when the agent cleanly proves that no production change is needed and leaves the tree clean. It is much less appropriate when the visible cutoff shows uncertainty, duplicated commands, assumptions based on wording alone, or proposed edits that duplicate existing methods/tests or alter cache cleanup semantics already provided by a library callback.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics praised “problem identification,” “verification of an existing fix,” or “pre-existing solution recognition.” Those ideas were directionally reasonable early in exploration, but became misleading at the observed stage because the agent had already found the requested deletion method, existing tests, and library callback behavior; rewarding that alone did not distinguish a clean resolution from an unnecessary duplicate patch, a no-op with dirty artifacts, or a regression such as manually invoking cleanup that the LRU already performs. For similar cases, avoid a broad positive criterion that says the agent should simply verify the existing implementation. Instead generate a criterion that checks whether the agent handles the stale-task possibility safely: it should identify a concrete remaining requirement before editing, tie any new API/test to visible caller or acceptance evidence, verify current diffs/status, clean temporary files and dependency noise, and avoid contradicting confirmed library/source behavior. Tempting wrong criteria include rewarding systematic grepping, passing existing tests, or noticing that references are stored in fixed versus non-fixed containers as if those facts alone imply correctness. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence of a failing repro or unmet contract, source-backed understanding of callback/eviction behavior, a minimal non-duplicative patch plan, and a clean working tree.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories where, after finding that the task-described feature and its basic tests already exist and pass, the agent continues toward unsupported or redundant work instead of establishing a concrete remaining gap. This includes proposing or adding duplicate deletion APIs/tests, adding unrequested reference-classification helpers without caller or test evidence, reintroducing manual cleanup despite source evidence that the dependency already invokes cleanup callbacks, repeatedly running the same searches without new information, finalizing a no-op while leaving scratch or dependency-download artifacts, or treating passing baseline tests as sufficient without reconciling the task/code mismatch.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Unsupported redundant work after existing behavior is confirmed

retrieval_conditions: Task describes a missing feature or behavior.
Trajectory has located an existing implementation of that feature.
Existing targeted tests or manual checks appear to pass.
Agent has not yet shown a concrete failing scenario or unmet downstream contract.
avoid_proxy: Do not treat broad exploration quality or passing existing tests as sufficient evidence of a good final patch.
Do not reward adding APIs solely because the task wording mentions distinguishing categories when no caller, test, or interface requires the new API.
Do not reward manual cleanup calls when the trajectory has source evidence that a library callback already performs cleanup.
preferred_visible_evidence: A failing reproduction tied to the current baseline.
A specific caller or interface that cannot satisfy the task with the existing implementation.
A clean git status or explicit cleanup plan for exploratory artifacts.
A minimal patch plan that avoids duplicating existing methods/tests and respects confirmed dependency behavior.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the agent either finds a concrete unmet requirement before editing, or cleanly concludes the existing implementation satisfies the task while avoiding redundant changes and cleaning artifacts.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the agent briefly considers redundant work or relies on passing tests, but corrects course and seeks a concrete remaining gap or cleans up before patching.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent has confirmed existing behavior but remains uncertain, repeats some checks, or has an unsupported tentative patch idea without yet committing to it.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the agent proceeds toward duplicate APIs/tests, unnecessary cleanup logic, or no-op finalization despite passing baseline behavior and no visible failing requirement.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory strongly indicates an unnecessary or regressive patch, such as duplicating existing methods/tests, contradicting confirmed dependency callback semantics, leaving scratch/dependency artifacts, or looping on the same irrelevant checks while treating the stale-task conclusion as sufficient.

experiences.title: Prioritize Q-descriptor dispatch over broad VLA equality criteria
experiences.description: Use this when generating rubrics for FITS diff bugs involving variable-length array columns, especially when the reproducer uses a Q-prefixed VLA format and the visible code already has P-prefixed VLA special handling.
experiences.context: In Python/Astropy FITS diff trajectories, the misleading pattern is a rubric that either rewards general awareness of VLA comparison issues without requiring a visible applied change, or demands broad nested-array equality behavior such as shape, dtype, length, and every suffix family when the observable bug is narrower: Q-prefixed VLA columns bypass existing P-prefixed VLA comparison logic and fall into generic object-array comparison. A P/Q format-completeness criterion can be appropriate during implementation or final review if the trajectory has reached the comparison branch or is editing it. At early exploration stages, mere absence of a patch should be treated as incomplete progress rather than a decisive failure. General VLA element-comparison semantics are only the right focus if visible evidence shows Q and P descriptors are already routed into the VLA-specific comparison path and the remaining problem is the row-level equality operation itself.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often said the trajectory must handle all VLA formats, all suffixes, or compare nested VLA elements by shape/dtype/value. That was sometimes directionally useful, but it became misleading in two ways: it over-rewarded trajectories that only identified the P-versus-Q issue or repeatedly searched code without a visible patch, and it under-emphasized the actual failure mode when an agent changed row-level VLA comparison semantics while leaving Q-prefixed columns outside the VLA branch. For this task shape/length helper logic is not the main observable proxy; the key judgeable evidence is whether Q-prefixed variable-length FITS columns are detected as VLAs and routed through the same per-row comparison path as P-prefixed columns. A better rubric should focus on visible source or test evidence that the comparison dispatch recognizes both descriptor families, preserves existing P behavior and tolerance-aware row comparison, and preferably validates the user-style Q-prefixed self-comparison. Avoid tempting criteria that require enumerating every element suffix or adding a new comparison helper unless the trajectory has already established that descriptor routing is correct and row-level equality remains defective.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a FITS table diff bug where the reproducer uses a Q-prefixed variable-length array column and the existing code visibly special-cases only P-prefixed VLA formats, penalize trajectories that do not visibly make Q-prefixed columns enter the VLA-specific row-by-row comparison path. This flaw includes patches that only alter the nested array equality helper while leaving the VLA detection condition P-only, tests that cover only P-prefixed VLAs, or final-review trajectories that claim the issue is solved based solely on source inspection without a visible applied change. Do not penalize early exploratory trajectories as severely when they have only just located the relevant comparison logic and identified Q as the likely missing descriptor.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Q-prefixed VLA still bypasses VLA comparison

metadata.key_reproducer_signal: Q-prefixed variable-length array column compared to itself
metadata.primary_visible_evidence: comparison dispatch condition or equivalent parsed-format check treats both P and Q descriptors as VLAs
metadata.secondary_visible_evidence: regression test or manual validation using a Q-prefixed VLA self-comparison
metadata.stage_boundary: conceptual identification is progress during exploration but insufficient at implementation/final-review stages

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory visibly routes Q-prefixed and P-prefixed VLA columns through the VLA-specific row comparison path or otherwise demonstrates equivalent behavior with a Q-prefixed self-comparison.
scale.2: Minor evidence of risk: the trajectory likely handles Q-prefixed VLAs but uses a brittle or lightly justified check, lacks direct Q-prefixed validation, or leaves small uncertainty about preserving existing P-prefixed behavior.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies the P-versus-Q descriptor issue and the relevant comparison branch, but the visible cutoff does not show an applied change or validation yet.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory modifies VLA row comparison semantics, adds helper logic, or tests only P-prefixed VLAs while the visible dispatch still appears to recognize only P-prefixed formats.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory ignores the Q-prefixed descriptor failure mode, relies on generic object-array comparison for Q-prefixed VLA data, or claims a fix in unrelated code with no visible path for Q-prefixed columns to use VLA-specific comparison.

experiences.title: Do not over-credit broad metadata propagation without verified contract and regression evidence
experiences.description: Retrieve this when a task asks to thread new metadata through a backend/API/template/client pipeline, especially in a NodeBB-style privilege/admin UI refactor, and the candidate rubric would simply require “add the metadata and propagate it through layers.”
experiences.context: This warning applies to JavaScript/NodeBB trajectories where privilege or UI metadata must move from a server-side map through list/API payloads into templates and client-side filtering. The misleading pattern is a rubric that treats a broad checklist such as “add type fields, expose through list(), update templates, replace hardcoded indices” as enough to predict patch quality, even when the trajectory only contains exploration, unverified full-file rewrites, claims in summaries, or repetitive searches. The original propagation idea is still appropriate as a core requirement when visible evidence shows precise edits and a preserved end-to-end contract; it is not sufficient as the only criterion at a late stage or after risky rewrites. During early exploration, absence of implementation should not be judged as a definitive failure; during final-review or post-edit stages, the rubric should focus on whether the actual edited contract is coherent and non-regressive.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster generated a high-level “Privilege Type Metadata Propagation” criterion. That criterion matches the user-facing goal, but it is too coarse: it can over-credit trajectories that merely state or attempt propagation while damaging existing privilege behavior, omitting validation, or failing to prove that the rendered DOM/API contract actually carries type data for every privilege column. For similar tasks, avoid a tempting criterion that rewards the presence of `type` fields or changed filter buttons alone. A better rubric should ask for concrete visible evidence that the metadata remains aligned with privilege keys after hooks/dynamic additions, defaults missing types safely, is available to both header and body rendering, and preserves existing privilege-table behaviors such as checkbox state handling, group/user rows, confirmation flows, and API consumers. If the trajectory used full-file rewrites or broad copy-over patches, prioritize evidence of `git diff` review, targeted validation, and preservation of unrelated code over broad claims of completion. Do not require every possible documentation or route update unless the visible code path exposes the changed payload publicly, but do require the agent to identify and maintain the relevant API/template/client contract.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Unverified cross-layer metadata contract and regression risk
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for a metadata-through-UI refactor when visible evidence shows the agent is relying on broad propagation claims or risky edits rather than proving a coherent, non-regressive contract. This flaw is present when the trajectory adds or plans metadata fields but does not demonstrate that the type data stays aligned with privilege keys after hooks/dynamic additions, defaults missing types at the point of consumption, reaches both table headers and generated body cells, and preserves existing admin privilege table behavior. The flaw is especially severe after full-file rewrites, repetitive searches, or late-stage editing with no diff review, tests, lint/build, or manual contract checks.

default handling for missing type values at list/render time
header and body cells both carry type data used by filtering
existing checkbox/group/user privilege behavior is preserved
diff review and relevant validation commands are run or planned concretely

filter buttons renamed from index attributes to type attributes

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory either remains in early exploration without overclaiming implementation, or it shows precise edits plus concrete checks that the metadata contract is aligned and existing behavior is preserved.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory identifies the right layers and some contract risks, but validation or diff review is still incomplete; no obvious destructive edits or broken alignment are visible.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory makes or proposes broad propagation changes but only partially demonstrates key alignment, default handling, rendered cell metadata, or preservation of existing UI behavior.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory edits multiple backend/template/client files or claims completion while leaving visible gaps such as no body-cell type contract, unsafe default handling, continued index/core-size assumptions, or no review after large rewrites.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory performs broad/full-file rewrites or repetitive non-informative searches after editing, provides no meaningful diff/test validation, and the visible changes or summaries indicate a high risk of broken privilege behavior despite satisfying the superficial metadata-propagation checklist.

experiences.title: Do not reward superficial useState conversion during broad hook refactors
experiences.description: Retrieve when a React/TypeScript task asks both to extract business logic from a hook and to migrate a UI flag to state, and the trajectory already shows a `useState` conversion but the refactor is still unstable or behavior preservation is uncertain.
experiences.context: Applies in a React/TypeScript monorepo, especially hook refactors where a mutable local flag such as `canUndo` is only one part of a larger acceptance contract involving helper extraction, API calls, notifications, modals, authorization rules, and tests. The misleading case is a trajectory that visibly adds `useState` or removes `let canUndo`, causing a narrow rubric to look satisfied, while the same trajectory also shows incomplete rewrites, unresolved TypeScript errors, missing imports, dropped hook parameters, incorrect dependency injection, altered notification text, or no meaningful validation. The original state-migration idea remains appropriate when the task is primarily about UI reactivity, when the absence of state is still the main unresolved issue, or as one subcriterion after there is evidence that the broader refactor preserves the existing hook API and behavior.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster focused on whether the agent replaced a mutable `canUndo` variable with React `useState`. That criterion is directionally relevant but misleading as a dominant rubric for a broad move-to-folder refactor: agents can add `useState` while breaking compilation, dropping public hook arguments, misusing notification/API helpers, leaving helper files untracked or unvalidated, or changing business rules for spam, unauthorized moves, scheduled modals, and move-all suggestions. A better rubric should judge whether the trajectory preserves the complete move flow while extracting reusable helpers: the hook signature and returned modals remain compatible with callers; extracted helpers have correct imports/types and are actually part of the diff; scheduled-item handling updates undo eligibility without losing modal/focus behavior; spam action handling preserves API request semantics; notification and authorization text logic remains equivalent; and TypeScript plus focused tests or equivalent validation have been run and interpreted. Avoid the tempting criterion that merely checks for `useState`, absence of `let canUndo`, or a generic statement about UI reactivity. Prioritize visible evidence from diffs, compile/test output, API signature checks, and comparison against original behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize a trajectory that treats converting a UI flag such as scheduled-item undo eligibility to React state as sufficient while the broader hook refactor remains behaviorally or type-wise unsafe. This flaw is present when visible evidence shows a `useState` conversion or extracted helper names, but also shows unresolved TypeScript/import errors, a dropped or incompatible hook public API, incorrect API/request callback typing, missing event-manager or notification calls, helper files not fully integrated, changed notification/authorization/spam/scheduled behavior without justification, or validation that only checks the new helper superficially rather than the refactored hook flow.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial state migration masks broken refactor

metadata.environment: React TypeScript mail application hook refactor
metadata.avoid_proxy: Do not use the mere presence of useState or removal of a mutable local variable as sufficient evidence of correctness.
preferred_evidence: clean relevant TypeScript output or clearly separated baseline errors
preserved hook signature and caller compatibility
complete extracted helper integration with correct imports and API request semantics
unchanged notification, authorization, spam, scheduled-modal, move-all, optimistic update, and undo behavior
focused helper tests plus validation that the hook still compiles

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory either has not yet claimed the state conversion as a solution, or it shows the state migration together with preserved hook API, correct helper integration, and relevant validation.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory emphasizes `useState`, but visible code or tests still mostly preserve the broader move flow and only small validation gaps remain.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory adds state and helpers, but validation is incomplete and there are plausible unresolved integration risks such as dependency arrays, helper typing, or untested hook behavior.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory satisfies the superficial state-conversion cue while also showing compile errors, missing imports, dropped parameters, incorrect API/helper signatures, or altered business logic that has not been fixed.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory repeatedly relies on the `useState` conversion as proof of progress while the refactor is visibly broken or unvalidated, with multiple integration regressions such as incompatible hook API, missing core imports/calls, incorrect helper placement or untracked files, and no reliable TypeScript/test confirmation.

experiences.title: Do not treat a forceNewDatabase toggle as sufficient end-to-end offline reuse
experiences.description: Retrieve when a login/session fix involves returning database-key metadata and reusing offline storage, and a candidate rubric is tempted to check only whether cache initialization sets forceNewDatabase based on databaseKey.
experiences.context: Applies in TypeScript login/offline-storage flows where create-session spans a main controller, worker facade, credential persistence, and UI/relogin callers. The misleading pattern is a trajectory that discovers or edits the local cache-init condition, e.g. changing forceNewDatabase from true to databaseKey == null, while still lacking visible evidence that an existing stored database key is actually obtained, passed into session creation, returned to callers, and stored back consistently. The original forceNewDatabase criterion remains useful as a sub-check when the database-key data path is already clearly handled and the task is only about destructive cache initialization. It is not sufficient when the task also requires comprehensive session data or when relogin/persistent-session callers may still call createSession without the previous key.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded the local offline-storage condition: if a databaseKey is present, pass forceNewDatabase=false so the offline DB is reused. That criterion is semantically correct but misleading as the primary or only rubric for this task. Many trajectories can satisfy or attempt that line-level change while still breaking the actual contract: the worker result may not include the key, the main controller may return only a wrapper instead of the full session data callers need, persistent/relogin flows may generate or discard keys incorrectly, old stored keys may not be passed back into createSession, or broad call-site edits may introduce type/import regressions. A better rubric should focus on end-to-end database-key lifecycle evidence: key acquisition/generation at the appropriate layer, inclusion in the session result returned across the worker-main boundary, main-controller preservation of full session data needed for partial login and callers, persistent/relogin callers passing existing keys for reuse, callers unwrapping credentials only where needed, and validation through typecheck/tests. Avoid generating a criterion that implies correctness solely from the presence of `forceNewDatabase: databaseKey == null`; prioritize visible evidence that the same existing key flows from stored credentials into cache initialization and back into persisted credentials without API-shape or caller breakage.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial offline reuse without database-key lifecycle preservation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that focus on toggling destructive cache creation based on `databaseKey` but do not show an end-to-end, type-safe database-key lifecycle for session creation. This flaw is present when the visible work changes cache initialization to avoid forced recreation yet leaves evidence that existing stored keys are not fetched and supplied on persistent/relogin creation, worker/main session return data does not reliably carry the key, callers still treat the new return value as raw credentials or store the wrong key, external/temporary flows are modified without a clear key contract, or typecheck/caller audits remain unresolved. The issue is especially severe when the trajectory repeatedly uses broad replacements in nested TypeScript object literals and has unresolved compile/type symptoms around createSession return types.

primary_visible_signals: databaseKey included in worker session data and controller return
persistent/relogin callers pass existing stored databaseKey into createSession
credentials persistence stores returned databaseKey with credentials
call sites unwrap credentials only where appropriate
typecheck or targeted tests cover return-shape and cache-init behavior
metadata.tempting_but_insufficient_signal: Only changing forceNewDatabase from true to a databaseKey null check

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory shows an end-to-end key path from stored/generated key through session creation/cache initialization and back to persisted credentials, with caller/type validation.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the forceNewDatabase logic and most key propagation are handled, but one low-risk caller or validation detail remains only partially inspected.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the cache flag is addressed and some return-shape work is present, but the trajectory has incomplete caller updates or unclear preservation of existing keys in persistent/relogin flows.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory mainly implements the local forceNewDatabase condition while leaving key return/propagation/caller storage inconsistent or visibly type-risky.
scale.5: Most severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory treats the forceNewDatabase toggle as the fix despite missing or broken database-key data flow, broad unsafe edits, unresolved compile errors, or callers that still discard/pass null for keys needed to reuse offline storage.

experiences.title: Localized date-format token semantics over test-presence proxies
experiences.description: Use when a trajectory for a small formatting-token bug has identified the formatter implementation and the required behavior is an external compatibility contract, such as returning a fixed-width zero-padded year fragment.
experiences.context: Applies in Python web-framework/library tasks where the problem statement gives concrete formatting examples and compares behavior to established APIs, and the trajectory has visibly located the responsible date-format token implementation or reproduced the mismatch. It is especially relevant after localization or just before/after a one-line formatter edit. It is less applicable during pure repository exploration before the responsible code path is found, for broad date/time parsing or timezone issues, or when the task explicitly prioritizes adding tests rather than fixing a narrowly specified formatting semantic.
experiences.experience: In these cases, rubrics that focused on the exact semantic contract of the formatter were the most durable: the implementation must compute the trailing two year digits and zero-pad to width two for every valid year, while leaving unrelated format tokens alone. This aligns with visible evidence such as the agent finding the old string-slicing implementation, observing outputs like empty strings or one-digit strings for early years, and planning or applying a numeric modulo plus zero-padding fix. A weaker or misleading rubric is to require a permanent repository-native regression test as the main criterion; adding tests is good practice, but visible trajectories can still produce the correct minimal library fix without committing tests. Also avoid over-constraining the syntax to one formatting idiom, and avoid accepting padding that only works for short years but fails to truncate four-digit years. The better rubric should judge whether the trajectory has preserved the compatibility boundary: exactly two characters, last two digits, leading zero when needed, for both small and normal years, with no broad changes to unrelated date formatting behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should identify and fix the specific date-format token implementation so that the two-digit year token returns exactly the last two digits of the year, zero-padded to length two, matching the documented external formatter behavior for early years and ordinary years, without altering unrelated date or time format tokens.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Exact two-digit year formatter semantics

expected_visible_evidence: The agent locates the formatter code responsible for the two-digit year token.
The agent recognizes that slicing the string form of the full year drops required leading digits or zeros for years with fewer than four digits.
The proposed or applied fix uses modulo/truncation to obtain the last two year digits and pads the result to width two.
Validation or reasoning covers representative one-, two-, three-, and four-digit years, not only the originally reported example.
The trajectory does not make broad, unrelated changes to other date/time format behavior.
avoid_as_primary_requirement: Requiring committed regression tests when the task is a narrowly scoped implementation bug and tests were not explicitly requested.
Rewarding a padding-only expression that can emit more than two digits for normal four-digit years.
Treating dependency installation or test-run setup problems as evidence against the formatter semantics once the responsible code and behavior are clear.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory has found the responsible formatter logic or understood the required two-digit, zero-padded trailing-year behavior.
scale.2: The trajectory notices a date-formatting issue but gives only vague padding intent, lacks clear truncation to the last two digits, or risks changing unrelated formatting behavior.
scale.3: The trajectory localizes the formatter and states the need for a two-digit year, but evidence is incomplete about both zero-padding and truncating normal years to the last two digits.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly proposes or applies an equivalent last-two-digits plus zero-padding fix in the localized formatter, with some representative validation or reasoning and no unrelated changes.
scale.5: The trajectory fully demonstrates the compatibility contract across one-, two-, three-, and four-digit years, applies a minimal localized fix that always returns exactly two characters, and preserves unrelated formatter behavior.

experiences.title: Validate Monotonicity Only on Inferred Concat Dimensions
experiences.description: Retrieve when an xarray-style coordinate-combining bug involves identical/non-varying coordinate dimensions being rejected for non-monotonic order even though only varying coordinates should determine concatenation.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories working on a coordinate-based dataset combine operation where the task explicitly distinguishes dimensions that vary across input datasets from identical bystander coordinates. It is most useful once the agent has found the combine workflow or inferred-concat-dimension abstraction, or has reproduced a failure where an identical non-monotonic coordinate is rejected after combining along another dimension. It remains relevant during early diagnosis, implementation, and final review, but should be judged more strongly when the trajectory shows code or tests proving the validation scope. Do not apply this criterion to tasks whose intended behavior is to require all result coordinates to be monotonic, to bugs where the non-monotonic coordinate actually varies between datasets and determines order, or to unrelated dependency/test-suite failures in an old scientific Python environment.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic boundary between bystander coordinates and true concatenation dimensions: identical coordinates across all inputs should be ignored for ordering and therefore should not be subject to the final global monotonicity check, while dimensions used to infer concatenation must still be validated. This aligned well when the trajectory showed the agent locating the inference step that returns the varying concat dimensions, identifying a later validation loop over all result dimensions, and changing or planning to change that loop to use the inferred concat-dimension list. The strongest visible evidence is not merely that the MCVE stops raising, but that the implementation preserves the guard for impossible ordering along actual concat dimensions. A weaker but still relevant cue is early reasoning that identical coordinates are already excluded from concat inference and the bug is downstream validation scope. Avoid generating a primary rubric that simply demands a persistent regression test; tests are valuable supporting evidence, but a code-only patch can still be semantically correct. Also avoid the tempting overbroad criterion “allow non-monotonic coordinates” because that would reward disabling validation for genuinely varying concat dimensions. Prioritize evidence such as: comparison of identical coordinates during concat inference, use of an inferred concat-dimension collection for post-combine validation, MCVE success without relying on full dataset repr, targeted negative checks for invalid concat dimensions, and recognition that broad pytest or NumPy alias failures are environmental noise rather than combine-regression evidence.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that coordinate monotonicity validation in the coordinate-based combine path is scoped to dimensions that actually vary between input datasets and are used to infer concatenation order. Identical coordinate dimensions that are merely carried through the result may be non-monotonic and should not trigger the global monotonicity error, while invalid ordering on real concatenation dimensions must continue to raise. Strong evidence includes locating the inference/validation boundary, modifying or explicitly proposing validation over inferred concat dimensions rather than all result dimensions, and verifying both the reported bystander-coordinate success case and at least one true concat-dimension failure case.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Concat-Dimension-Scoped Monotonicity

agent scopes final monotonicity validation to inferred concat dimensions or an equivalent varying-coordinate set

non-monotonic or impossible ordering along an actual concat dimension is still expected to fail

test-only work without visible implementation behavior when the code fix is already assessable

scale.1: No visible recognition of the bystander-versus-concat-dimension distinction; the trajectory either does not address monotonicity scope or risks accepting/rejecting all coordinates indiscriminately.
scale.2: Mentions that identical coordinates should be ignored, but has not connected this to the existing concat-dimension inference or may weaken monotonicity validation too broadly.
scale.3: Correctly identifies that validation should exempt identical non-varying coordinates, but evidence is mostly diagnostic or lacks confirmation that true concat dimensions remain guarded.
scale.4: Shows a concrete implementation or precise plan to validate only inferred concat dimensions, with the reported identical non-monotonic coordinate case reproduced or manually checked.
scale.5: Provides clear implementation evidence plus targeted validation: the bystander non-monotonic coordinate case succeeds, actual concat-dimension ordering errors still raise, and unrelated environment/test noise is appropriately discounted.

experiences.title: Do not equate visible symlink preservation with safe extraction correctness
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for Python/Ansible tarfile or collection build/install fixes involving symlinks, especially after the agent has patched helper APIs or shown manual tar/install output.
experiences.context: Applies in an Ansible source tree, mainly `lib/ansible/galaxy/collection.py`, for tasks requiring internal symlinks to be preserved in collection archives while unsafe external or traversal links are prevented/materialized safely. The misleading situation is a trajectory that appears to satisfy the headline behavior—tar listings show `SYMTYPE`/`lrwx` entries and installed directories show symlinks—but the implementation has broad string-replacement edits, helper API changes, incomplete call-site updates, weak path containment checks, or visible test failures. A high-level symlink preservation rubric may still be useful during early exploration before code exists, but late-stage or final-review rubrics should not reward only manual build/install demonstrations.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often restated the task bullets: preserve internal symlinks in tar, materialize external symlinks, recreate symlinks on install, and return `TarInfo` plus a file object. That is a valid acceptance summary, but it becomes misleading when used as the main judge after implementation work because agents can show a tar listing and an `ls -la` install result while still leaving unsafe or broken extraction behavior. For this task family, the better rubric should focus on whether the patch integrates symlink support through the extraction helper contract safely and consistently: all callers must match the helper return shape, regular-file checksum/hash/JSON paths must keep working, `tar.extractfile()` returning `None` for symlinks must be handled, symlink targets must be resolved relative to the final symlink location and checked with a robust parent-boundary helper rather than raw prefix checks, and install should validate the actual tar member metadata before creating a filesystem symlink. Avoid the tempting criterion that manual evidence of `lrwx... -> target` in a tar or installed tree is sufficient. Prefer visible evidence such as robust containment helper logic, call-site audit after helper API changes, focused tests for malicious/out-of-destination symlink members and regular-file helper compatibility, and attention to failing unit tests rather than dismissing them wholesale as legacy expectations.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that implement or validate collection symlink preservation only at the superficial archive/install-output level while leaving safe extraction and helper API integration visibly incomplete. This includes creating symlinks directly from manifest fields without validating the actual tar member, using simple string-prefix checks for containment, failing to resolve relative link targets from the symlink's final parent directory, breaking `_tarfile_extract` or `_get_tar_file_member` callers after changing return values, leaking context managers, mishandling `None` file objects for symlink members, or proceeding despite focused unit tests showing helper/hash/JSON extraction regressions.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial symlink preservation with unsafe or inconsistent extraction integration

regular file checksum/hash/JSON extraction compatibility
symlink target containment validation relative to final link path
handling of tar symlink members whose extractfile result is None
tests or manual checks for malicious/out-of-destination symlink members
misleading_evidence_to_discount: tar listing alone shows lrwx/SYMTYPE entries
manual install listing alone shows symlinks

scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: symlink behavior is implemented and mostly integrated, but one safety or compatibility edge is only lightly addressed or not validated.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: visible code or reasoning covers archive/install preservation, but helper API compatibility or robust containment validation remains uncertain.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory relies on manual tar/install success while showing weak prefix-based validation, incomplete call-site updates, or unresolved helper-related test failures.
scale.5: Most severe evidence of the flaw: the implementation directly creates symlinks without safe tar-member validation, breaks existing helper consumers or regular-file extraction paths, and ignores visible failures/regressions.

experiences.title: Authoritative s390 sysinfo fallback for Ansible hardware facts
experiences.description: Retrieve this when an Ansible Linux setup/facts task targets IBM Z/s390 hardware facts that are `NA` because DMI sysfs and dmidecode are unavailable.
experiences.context: Applies in Ansible-style Linux hardware fact collection, especially when the trajectory has already localized the problem to setup/gather_facts hardware identity/DMI facts on s390 or s390x. The useful criterion is strongest once the agent is choosing or implementing the replacement data source. It is less useful during very early repository navigation, for unrelated s390 CPU or virtualization facts, or for platforms where normal DMI sysfs/dmidecode sources should remain authoritative. Do not apply it broadly to any architecture-specific fact change: the key boundary is IBM Z/s390 systems lacking DMI data and needing hardware identity facts from a stable platform file.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics were useful when they penalized trajectories that made no progress beyond repeated searches or failed syntax edits, but they were too permissive when they accepted any s390-looking source such as `/proc/cpuinfo`, `lscpu`, `/sys/firmware`, hard-coded IBM defaults, or guessed machine-code mappings. Those proxies can look plausible from visible fixtures, yet they do not reliably satisfy the task because CPU/virtualization data is not the same as the hardware identity data expected by setup facts. A better rubric for this context should require the trajectory to identify `/proc/sysinfo` as the s390 Linux hardware-information source, parse only relevant fields such as manufacturer/type/sequence code, map them into existing standard hardware fact keys, and integrate that collection without disrupting the existing DMI sysfs and dmidecode behavior for other Linux systems. Avoid criteria that reward merely passing `collected_facts` into the DMI routine, inventing default non-NA values, using `lscpu` output, or mapping CPU fixture fields to BIOS/product facts. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent names `/proc/sysinfo`, handles absence of that file by returning no override, preserves standard `NA` semantics for unavailable fields, updates the hardware fact merge path, and validates syntax or tests rather than continuing blind regex edits.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: s390 `/proc/sysinfo` hardware identity fallback
reference_golden_rubrics.description: For Ansible Linux setup hardware facts on IBM Z/s390, the trajectory should converge on a non-invasive fallback that reads `/proc/sysinfo` when present, extracts authoritative hardware identity fields, maps them to the existing standard fact schema, and merges them alongside the existing DMI facts without replacing or regressing the normal DMI sysfs/dmidecode paths. Strong evidence includes recognizing that `/proc/cpuinfo` and `lscpu` are CPU or virtualization-oriented sources, not sufficient replacements for hardware identity facts; avoiding fabricated IBM defaults or guessed model mappings; returning an empty/no-op result when `/proc/sysinfo` is absent; preserving `NA` for unavailable standard keys; and keeping the implementation syntactically valid and localized to Linux hardware fact collection.

required_visible_evidence: Identifies `/proc/sysinfo` as the s390 hardware identity source
Maps manufacturer/type/sequence-code style fields to existing hardware fact keys such as system vendor, product name, and product serial
Integrates the new facts into the Linux hardware fact merge path without requiring DMI sysfs or dmidecode
Leaves non-s390 DMI sysfs and dmidecode behavior unchanged
Avoids relying on `/proc/cpuinfo`, `lscpu`, hard-coded defaults, or guessed IBM model mappings as the primary fix
metadata.environment: Ansible Linux setup/gather_facts hardware collector on IBM Z/s390 or s390x

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward an s390 hardware identity fallback; the trajectory repeats searches, edits unrelated setup/virtualization code, or leaves no patch.
scale.2: Recognizes that DMI/dmidecode are unavailable on s390 but only proposes vague platform-specific probing or uses local non-s390 filesystem evidence without identifying a concrete reliable source.
scale.3: Adds or plans an s390-specific fallback but relies mainly on weak proxies such as `/proc/cpuinfo`, `lscpu`, hard-coded IBM values, or broad default non-NA replacements, while preserving some existing behavior.
scale.4: Identifies `/proc/sysinfo` and mostly maps relevant fields into standard hardware facts with localized, non-invasive integration, though validation, absence handling, or exact field coverage may be incomplete.
scale.5: Implements or clearly plans a clean `/proc/sysinfo` fallback that parses authoritative fields, preserves `NA` for unavailable values, no-ops when the file is absent, merges with hardware facts without disturbing DMI/dmidecode paths, and includes syntax/test or fixture-based validation.

experiences.title: Do not overvalue an already-satisfied subrequirement in broad feature work
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task has several required integration surfaces, but the trajectory has already made clear progress on one narrow requirement such as context propagation while other user-visible feature contracts remain unresolved.
experiences.context: Applies to Go service feature additions that require both internal interface plumbing and externally visible behavior/configuration, such as adding a new audit sink with configuration, schema/default support, server wiring, HTTP behavior, signing, retry/backoff, and tests.
