A context-propagation rubric is appropriate when the visible trajectory is still deciding whether to change the shared send interface, compile errors show stale SendAudits signatures, or the agent has not yet threaded caller context through exporter-to-sink calls. It becomes misleading at later stages when the trajectory already shows the Sink/EventExporter/exporter/sink method signatures mostly updated and tests or builds are now failing because of configuration defaults, schema coverage, webhook construction, retry semantics, or missing generated schema artifacts.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics asked judges to reward context.Context propagation through the audit pipeline. That criterion is semantically valid because the task explicitly requires SendAudits(ctx, events), but it was too narrow and often already visibly satisfied. It therefore overpredicted trajectories where the patch still lacked end-to-end webhook sink correctness: configuration and schema sources were inconsistent, config tests were being patched ad hoc, webhook files were missing or misplaced, retry/backoff behavior was unbounded or reused requests incorrectly, signing/header details were not verified, and full test runs still showed failures outside the context-plumbing area. For broad feature work, do not generate a primary rubric around a subrequirement that the trajectory has already substantially completed unless that subrequirement is the active blocker. Instead, focus on the highest-risk remaining integration contract visible in the trajectory: whether the new feature is exposed through all config/schema/default layers, validated when enabled, wired alongside existing sinks without replacement, implements the required HTTP JSON/signing/retry behavior, and passes relevant build/schema/config tests. Avoid the tempting criterion “all SendAudits methods accept context” when visible evidence shows the agent is now fighting schema/config/default/test failures; prioritize visible evidence from failed commands, unresolved TODOs, missing schema updates, inconsistent defaults, absent webhook package behavior, or broad rewrites that leave integration unverified.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat internal context propagation as sufficient while leaving the webhook audit sink incomplete as an end-to-end feature. This applies when visible steps or summaries show SendAudits/context signatures are already mostly updated, but the agent has not resolved user-facing configuration/schema/default consistency, validation for enabled webhook configuration, server wiring that appends the webhook sink alongside existing sinks, correct HTTP POST JSON behavior with the required signature header, bounded/cancellable retry/backoff behavior, and passing focused/full tests. The flaw is especially strong when current failures point to config/schema/build/test breakage or when the webhook implementation is missing, misplaced, uncompiled, or untested.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Incomplete End-to-End Webhook Sink Integration

preferred_evidence: recent test/build output showing config, schema, compile, or full-suite failures after context plumbing was added
visible missing or inconsistent config defaults, validation, schema definitions, or generated schema artifacts for the new webhook settings
server wiring that is absent, malformed, replaces existing sink behavior, or has not been verified by build/tests
webhook HTTP implementation lacking required JSON POST headers, HMAC signature header, bounded retry/backoff, response body handling, or context-aware cancellation
trajectory edits that patch tests/defaults ad hoc without proving the complete feature contract
metadata.do_not_use_as_primary_signal: mere presence of context.Context in the Sink interface, exporter interface, or sink method signatures when the remaining visible blockers concern configuration, schema, webhook behavior, or integration tests
metadata.applicability_boundary: If the trajectory is still before or during the interface migration and visible failures are specifically stale SendAudits signatures or missing ctx forwarding, a separate context-propagation rubric can still be appropriate.

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory addresses context propagation and also visibly covers configuration/schema/defaults, validation, multi-sink wiring, webhook HTTP/signing/retry behavior, and relevant tests or build results.
scale.2: Minor evidence: context propagation is emphasized, but only a small, clearly identified integration item remains and the trajectory is actively validating it.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: context propagation is mostly complete, while some important webhook integration surfaces such as schema/defaults, validation, or retry behavior remain only partially checked.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory celebrates or focuses on context plumbing despite visible unresolved config/schema/build/test failures or incomplete webhook behavior.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the patch/trajectory has context signatures but lacks a complete or compiling end-to-end webhook sink, has malformed wiring/configuration, missing schema exposure, absent/misplaced webhook implementation, or failing full validation.

experiences.title: Context-Scoped UserProps Integration Over Prefix Replacement
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go persistence task moves user-specific settings from globally prefixed property keys into a normalized user_props repository, especially Last.fm session keys.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go codebase with model repository interfaces, SQL persistence implementations, goose migrations, request context user identity, and Last.fm/session-key call sites that currently build keys like a property prefix plus user ID. It is most useful once the trajectory has found the old global PropertyRepository usage and is adding or reviewing the new user_props abstraction. Do not apply to ordinary global properties such as scanner timestamps or JWT secrets, and do not use it as the only criterion during very early exploration before the agent has examined the repository and auth/session-key code. If a task explicitly asks only for a schema migration without application call-site changes, this should be narrowed; otherwise it should cover schema, API shape, call-site semantics, and validation.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics often checked whether Last.fm session-key call sites were converted away from manually prefixed global property keys and whether old data was migrated. That catches an important symptom, but it can be too broad or misleading: simply changing calls to `UserProps(ctx).Get(userID, key)` or adding a migration is not enough if the repository is not actually user-scoped, if request-context ownership is bypassed, or if only the auth router is changed while other session-key consumers still pass explicit user IDs. A better rubric should focus on whether the new repository abstraction owns user scoping transparently: its public methods should operate on property keys/values for the current context user, the persistence layer should derive the user ID from authenticated request context and return an auth error when absent, and Last.fm helpers/routes/agent methods should use that context-scoped API without constructing or passing manual user-specific storage identifiers. It should also require the normalized table and DataStore wiring, and it may mention preserving existing data only as part of migration/compatibility if the visible trajectory has reached migration design. Avoid the tempting proxy of rewarding any occurrence of `UserPropsRepository` or any Last.fm test update; prioritize visible evidence in the interface signatures, persistence implementation, session key helper signatures, callback/user-context handling, and build/test results after all DataStore mocks are updated.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Context-scoped normalized user properties
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement user-specific properties as a normalized, context-scoped repository rather than as a thin wrapper around explicit user-ID arguments. Strong evidence includes a `user_props` schema keyed by user ID and property key; a DataStore-accessible repository whose public methods accept property key/value arguments without requiring callers to concatenate prefixes or pass storage user IDs; persistence code that obtains the current user from request context and rejects missing auth context; Last.fm session-key helpers and all session-key consumers updated to use that context-scoped repository with a stable property name; non-authenticated callback paths explicitly placing the relevant user into context before storing a key; existing global property usages left alone when they are not user-specific; mocks/tests updated with realistic read-after-write behavior; and successful formatting/build/test validation. Migration or backward-compatible handling of existing prefixed session-key rows should be considered additional strong evidence when the trajectory is modifying migrations or compatibility paths, but it should not substitute for the context-scoped API contract.

metadata.environment: Go repository with model.DataStore interfaces, SQL persistence repositories, goose migrations, request-context user identity, and Last.fm auth/session-key code
key_visible_evidence: UserPropsRepository method signatures are key/value scoped rather than requiring callers to build prefixed global IDs
persistence implementation derives user_id from request context and handles missing auth context
Last.fm sessionKeys helper no longer accepts or forwards a storage user ID where context should supply ownership
callback or unauthenticated routes attach the intended user to context before writing user props
all DataStore implementers and mocks are updated and tests/build are run
global non-user properties remain on the original PropertyRepository
avoid_scoring_as_sufficient: only replacing `Property` with `UserProps` while still passing explicit user IDs everywhere
only updating tests or one auth-router call site
only adding a user_props migration without application-layer conversion
unrelated rewrites to Resource dispatch or mocks that mask missing repository behavior

scale.1: No substantive evidence of a normalized user property abstraction; trajectory still relies on global PropertyRepository with manually prefixed user-specific keys or has only explored files.
scale.2: Some schema or interface work exists, but Last.fm/user-specific call sites still use prefixed global keys, or the new repository is not wired through DataStore and persistence/mocks.
scale.3: Moderate progress: a user_props table/repository is sketched and some call sites use it, but ownership is still caller-managed through explicit user-ID parameters, context/auth handling is missing, or important consumers/tests/mocks remain incomplete.
scale.4: Strong progress: schema, DataStore wiring, persistence, mocks, and main Last.fm storage/retrieval/deletion call sites are converted, with little or no manual prefixing left, but there are remaining concerns such as incomplete context handling, callback user setup, compatibility/migration review, or incomplete validation.
scale.5: Complete visible implementation of context-scoped normalized user properties: repository API hides user IDs and prefixing, persistence derives current user from context with proper auth errors, all Last.fm helpers/routes/agent consumers use the stable property key through that API, necessary migrations/compatibility are addressed for the stage, non-user global properties are untouched, mocks preserve read-after-write behavior, and build/tests pass.

experiences.title: R128 gain requires format-aware ReplayGain conversion
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go audio metadata scanner task asks to support R128 track/album gain tags alongside existing ReplayGain gain fields while preserving the app’s loudness reference.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories in a Go/Navidrome-like metadata scanner where raw tags are normalized through metadata accessors before being mapped into existing ReplayGain-style model fields. The task text or agent notes must explicitly require R128 gain tags such as track/album gain to be reported consistently with existing ReplayGain outputs. This guidance is most useful once the trajectory has located the ReplayGain gain accessors/parser or begun designing the patch. It is less applicable during very early repository exploration with no semantic decisions yet, to tasks that only expose raw tags without converting values, or to unrelated ReplayGain peak handling unless the task explicitly asks for R128 peaks.
experiences.experience: A strong rubric should not stop at checking that the agent adds the R128 tag names as fallbacks. In these cases, the decisive visible issue was whether the trajectory understood the R128 gain value contract: common Opus/R128 gain tags are fixed-point integer values using a different loudness reference, so they must be parsed separately from ordinary ReplayGain dB strings, converted to dB by dividing by 256, and shifted to the existing ReplayGain reference by adding 5 dB. The previous rubrics were useful when they emphasized R128-specific parsing/conversion, ReplayGain precedence, and safe invalid handling, because trajectories that merely reused the existing dB parser, treated R128 as a plain float/LUFS value, or only added variadic tag lookup would still leave inconsistent gain values. The better criterion should prioritize observable evidence in the agent’s plan, code, tests, or comments that it distinguishes ReplayGain string parsing from R128 integer parsing and covers both album and track gain. Avoid the tempting but weak criterion of “supports both tag names” or “uses getFirstTagValue with two names”; that proxy misses the semantic conversion. Also avoid requiring new model fields, scanner mapping changes, extractor-specific changes, or R128 peak support unless the trajectory has evidence those are necessary, because the core issue is normalization of gain values into the existing fields.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Format-aware R128 gain normalization
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly commit to implementing R128 track and album gain support in the metadata normalization layer by preserving existing ReplayGain behavior, using R128 only as an additional source/fallback for gain, parsing R128 values according to their fixed-point integer representation rather than as ordinary ReplayGain dB strings, converting them to the existing ReplayGain loudness reference by applying the appropriate scale and offset, and safely returning neutral values for missing or invalid inputs.

required_visible_evidence: Both track and album R128 gain tags are considered, not just one of them.
Existing ReplayGain gain tags keep their current parsing and precedence when present.
R128 gain parsing is separate from ReplayGain dB-string parsing.
The R128 conversion includes fixed-point scaling and the loudness-reference offset.
Invalid or missing R128 values do not throw errors or corrupt scan output.
warning_signs: The patch only passes multiple tag names to the old ReplayGain parser.
The trajectory describes R128 values as plain dB or directly equivalent to ReplayGain.
The implementation adds only a +5 offset without fixed-point scaling.
The work focuses on peaks, model fields, or scanner mapping while the gain conversion remains unresolved.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory distinguishes R128 gain semantics from existing ReplayGain parsing; it only explores files or mentions tag names.
scale.2: Recognizes the R128 track/album tag names but proposes or implements simple fallback through the existing dB parser with no correct R128 conversion.
scale.3: Partially addresses R128 semantics, such as preserving ReplayGain precedence or adding a reference-level offset, but omits fixed-point scaling, safe invalid handling, or one of track/album coverage.
scale.4: Strong evidence of a correct design: separate R128 parsing, ReplayGain precedence, track and album coverage, fixed-point scaling, reference offset, and safe defaults are all considered, though tests or integration details may be incomplete.
scale.5: Complete visible evidence of a robust fix: implementation and/or tests demonstrate correct R128 fixed-point parsing, conversion to the existing ReplayGain reference, fallback behavior for both track and album gain, preservation of existing ReplayGain outputs, and safe handling of invalid/missing inputs.

experiences.title: End-to-End Test Harness Support Triad
experiences.description: Use when a Go CLI/client/server task explicitly requires test-environment support across mockable login flows, dynamically assigned listener addresses, and non-exiting CLI errors.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories in a Go codebase with a CLI login client and server-side listener startup, where the task states that tests bind services to ':0', need to mock browser/SSO login, and need command failures as returned errors. The criterion is most useful once the agent has begun selecting or editing implementation seams; at very early exploration, judge only whether the agent has found the relevant seams, not whether the full fix is complete. It is less applicable if the task concerns only ordinary proxy parsing, only SSO protocol behavior, or only CLI UX without dynamic test listeners and programmatic test assertions.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful rubric is the three-part testability contract, but it must be framed as end-to-end implementation evidence rather than mere issue identification. A good rubric should require: a per-client or otherwise test-safe SSO override that bypasses the browser/redirect flow only when configured; propagation of actual listener addresses obtained after binding to ':0' into the addresses advertised to dependent clients; and systematic conversion of testable CLI command paths from process exits/fatal helpers to returned errors, with only the top-level process entrypoint allowed to exit. This criterion is discriminative because trajectories that only grep relevant files, modify client-side port parsing, or partially replace fatal calls often look related but still leave tests unable to connect to real random ports or catch failures. Avoid rewarding broad searches, repeated greps, a global mock hook that can break isolation, a client-only port fallback change when the server still advertises ':0', or a superficial removal of fatal calls without updating function signatures/callers and validating compilation. Prioritize visible evidence: edits at the SSO call boundary, listener-backed address propagation after net.Listen/imported listener creation, command dispatch and handlers returning errors consistently, absence of fatal exits in tested paths, and a build/test/gofmt check after structural refactors.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete Test-Environment Login and CLI Error Contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate an end-to-end fix for test-environment operation: it introduces a test-configurable SSO login override at the client login boundary while preserving normal browser/redirect behavior when unset; it ensures services that bind to dynamic ports advertise and pass along the actual bound listener addresses rather than configured ':0' values; and it refactors CLI command execution so testable command paths return errors instead of terminating the process, with validation that the refactor compiles.

high_priority_evidence: client login configuration or equivalent per-instance hook is checked before starting SSO redirect/browser flow
server/listener startup reads listener.Addr() or equivalent after binding and uses it for advertised auth/proxy/web/ssh/kube addresses
command dispatcher and handlers have error-returning signatures and replace fatal/os.Exit behavior in tested command paths
callers are updated consistently and build/gofmt/tests are attempted after signature changes
common_false_positives: only identifies relevant files without edits
only changes client-side address parsing while advertised server settings still contain ':0'
only changes one login handler while nested commands still exit
uses broad text replacement that leaves syntax errors or stale fatal behavior
adds a global mutable SSO hook without considering test isolation or configuration path

scale.1: No meaningful progress beyond generic repository exploration or repeated searches; the trajectory has not located the SSO seam, listener advertisement path, or CLI fatal-error paths.
scale.2: Some relevant seams are identified, such as the SSO redirect call or fatal-error helper, but there is no coherent plan or implementation covering all three required test-environment capabilities.
scale.3: The trajectory has a plausible plan or partial edits for one or two capabilities, but important gaps remain, such as dynamic address propagation only on the client side, SSO mocking not wired through configuration, or CLI errors still exiting in nested handlers.
scale.4: Strong implementation evidence covers all three capabilities, with appropriate seams chosen and most callers updated; only minor validation, naming, or edge-case cleanup appears unresolved.
scale.5: The trajectory shows a coherent, compilable end-to-end solution: configurable SSO mocking, actual post-bind listener address propagation to dependent clients, systematic CLI error returns with top-level-only exiting, and formatting/build or targeted test validation.

experiences.title: Stage-Aware Cross-Module Refactor Completeness
experiences.description: Use when a Python/PyQt task reports a helper moved between utility modules and runtime failures from stale qualified call sites, especially when the checkout may not match the bug report exactly.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories in a Python codebase where a function/helper is being moved from one module to another, affected UI or service call sites still reference the old module path, and investigation has visible grep/history/import evidence about the helper's current and intended owner. It is strongest after the agent has identified the relevant definition, all call sites, and module import relationships, or after edits are visible. It is less useful as a harsh early-progress criterion before the agent has had a chance to edit; at that stage, prefer judging whether the agent is reconciling the bug report with the actual checkout. Do not apply when the task is simply to add a missing wrapper/API for backward compatibility with no intended ownership change, or when no cross-module import/call-site migration is involved.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic contract of a cross-module refactor: the helper must live in the new, appropriate owner module, all stale qualified usages must be updated, required private helpers/imports must move with it, and the source module must not retain or reintroduce problematic dependencies that the refactor was meant to eliminate. This aligned well when the trajectory showed decisive evidence such as grep results for all occurrences, inspection of both modules' imports, awareness of circular-import rationale, and validation by import/compile/smoke tests. A better rubric should be stage-aware: early on, reward verifying the mismatch between the report and the checkout and locating the canonical refactor; during implementation/final review, require complete migration and validation. Avoid a tempting but weak criterion that only checks whether the agent noticed the bug report/code mismatch, or only whether call sites were changed; those proxies miss broken partial moves, missing typing/import dependencies, accidental line-range deletions, or circular compatibility shims. Also avoid over-penalizing a trajectory at an early cutoff just because call-site edits are not yet visible if the agent has already found the relevant usages and is preparing the correct move. Prioritize visible evidence from precise searches, module ownership reasoning, import dependency checks, cleanup of the old module, and validation commands; be cautious with imprecise substring greps when the new module name contains the old module name.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a moved-helper refactor causing stale module-qualified call sites, the trajectory should demonstrate complete, validated migration: it reconciles the bug report with the actual checkout, identifies the canonical new owner and any import/circular-dependency rationale, moves the full helper implementation plus private helper/dependency imports to the destination module, updates every affected call site to use the new module path with necessary imports, removes the obsolete implementation or dependency from the source module rather than adding a circular shim, and validates with precise searches plus import/compile or targeted smoke tests.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete Validated Helper Migration

required_visible_evidence: Search or inspection showing where the helper is currently defined and where it is intended to live
Repository-wide or otherwise systematic identification of all non-test call sites using the old qualified name
Reasoning about module ownership and circular-import or dependency implications
Edits or planned edits that move the helper and its private dependencies/imports together
Call-site updates to the new qualified name with needed destination-module imports
Cleanup of obsolete source-module implementation/imports where appropriate
Validation by precise grep, py_compile/import checks, targeted unit tests, or equivalent smoke tests
common_failure_modes: Only changing call sites while the destination module lacks the helper
Copying the helper without moving private helpers or typing/Qt imports
Leaving the old source module dependent on the destination in a way that preserves the circular import problem
Using an imprecise search that mistakes the new qualified name for the old one
Deleting code by line range without checking syntax around neighboring functions
metadata.stage_boundary: At investigation-only cutoffs, judge evidence of correct discovery and planned migration more than completed edits; at implementation or final-review cutoffs, require the actual migration and validation evidence.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent has identified the moved-helper contract, the actual current definition, or the stale call sites; it may blindly follow the report or propose an unrelated fix.
scale.2: Some relevant discovery is present, such as finding the helper or one call site, but the trajectory lacks systematic call-site coverage, destination-module dependency reasoning, or a coherent migration plan.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies the old and new module relationship and most affected usages, but implementation is not yet visible or remains partial, with unresolved dependency/import cleanup or validation.
scale.4: The trajectory shows a mostly complete migration plan or edits: destination helper and dependencies are handled, stale call sites are updated, and source cleanup is considered, with only minor validation/style gaps.
scale.5: The trajectory provides strong evidence of a complete and validated cross-module migration: all usages are found and updated, helper/private dependencies/imports are correctly moved, obsolete source code/dependencies are removed without circular shims, and precise searches plus compile/import or targeted smoke tests confirm the result.

experiences.title: Require upstream surd-domain validation, not just empty-helper guards
experiences.description: Use for SymPy/symbolic-denesting trajectories where an IndexError arises from an empty surd list in a low-level helper, but the caller may be invoking surd-splitting on expressions outside its mathematical domain.
experiences.context: Applies in Python symbolic algebra tasks involving square-root denesting or radical simplification, especially when the visible traceback reaches a helper that assumes a nonempty list after a caller filters terms into surds. The key matching evidence is that the agent has inspected a caller like a sqrt-matching routine, observed a broad predicate such as 'all term squares are rational', and found that complex or imaginary terms can satisfy it while not being valid positive-radicand surds. This guidance is most useful after the trajectory has enough code inspection to distinguish caller eligibility from helper robustness. It is less applicable to generic empty-list crashes where the helper is explicitly documented to accept empty input, or to early exploration before the agent has inspected the caller's domain checks.
experiences.experience: The tempting rubric in these cases is to require an empty-input guard in the low-level gcd/surd helper or a neutral return from the splitter. That criterion can look plausible because it prevents the immediate IndexError, and it may correctly flag trajectories that have made no implementation progress. However, it is not a reliable semantic criterion once the agent starts patching: a neutral empty-helper return can hide the crash while allowing the denesting algorithm to treat non-surd complex sums as valid radical matches. The better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory recognizes and fixes the upstream domain boundary: surd splitting should only be attempted for additive terms whose squared values are positive rationals/valid surd radicands, while expressions with imaginary or non-positive rational squares should be treated as non-denestable and returned unchanged. Prioritize visible evidence such as: inspection of the caller predicate that admits too many expressions; recognition that terms like imaginary components have rational but non-positive squares; comments or tests showing the splitter is intended for positive-rational surds; a change or planned change that narrows the caller's eligibility before invoking surd grouping; and validation that known denestable radicals still denest while non-denestable complex expressions no longer crash. Avoid rewarding mere direct helper tests, repeated public calls that simplify away the problematic structure, or a patch that only makes the empty helper return a default tuple.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Upstream surd-domain eligibility is corrected
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should identify and address the mathematical-domain error that lets the denesting matcher call surd-splitting on additive expressions whose term squares are rational but not positive-rational surd radicands. Strong evidence includes narrowing the caller-side condition before surd splitting, treating complex/non-positive-square sums as non-denestable so the public denesting API returns them unchanged, and preserving successful denesting for valid radical inputs. A low-level empty-input guard alone is insufficient unless paired with evidence that the upstream matcher no longer classifies invalid complex sums as surd-splittable.

metadata.visible_failure_shape: IndexError from helper called with an empty surd collection
metadata.semantic_boundary: surd splitting is valid for positive-rational radicand terms, not merely any terms whose squares are rational
preferred_evidence: caller predicate inspection
recognition of non-positive or imaginary square cases
caller-side domain narrowing or equivalent non-denestable fallback
tests for non-crash/unchanged behavior and preservation of valid denesting
avoid_as_primary_evidence: only adding an empty varargs/list guard to the helper
only checking that direct helper calls no longer raise
using an original reproducer that auto-simplifies before reaching the buggy path

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory distinguishes caller-domain validation from the low-level empty-list crash; it only repeats reproduction attempts or focuses on unrelated behavior.
scale.2: The trajectory notices the empty surd list or helper crash but frames the solution only as an empty-input guard, with no recognition that the caller is accepting invalid non-positive/complex terms.
scale.3: The trajectory partially recognizes that some non-surd expressions are being routed into surd splitting, but the proposed fix or tests still center on neutral helper returns rather than a clear upstream eligibility boundary.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly identifies that the matcher's eligibility predicate is too broad and proposes or implements narrowing before surd splitting, with some validation that non-denestable complex expressions pass through unchanged.
scale.5: The trajectory decisively fixes or plans the upstream domain check for positive-rational surd terms, avoids relying on helper defaults as the main solution, and validates both non-denestable complex/no-surd cases and existing valid denesting behavior.

experiences.title: Error-message contract over regression-test proxy
experiences.description: Use when a framework validation task asks to enrich an existing diagnostic message with the offending option value, and the trajectory has localized the message formatter and shown the value is already available.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django-like framework codebase during implementation or final review of an admin/system-check diagnostic change, especially when the task explicitly says an indexed option error such as readonly_fields[0] omits the bad field name while comparable option checks include it. The criterion is useful once the trajectory has found the relevant item-level validation path, identified the indexed label and offending value variables, or reproduced/computed the message. It is less useful for early exploration before the error site is known, for tasks that require changing validation semantics rather than only message content, or when the only visible issue is missing test-suite integration and the behavior contract is already unquestionably satisfied.
experiences.experience: The strongest rubric in these cases judged the actual diagnostic contract: invalid readonly_fields entries must report both the indexed option label and the offending field name/value, without changing what counts as valid. This aligned because the decisive visible evidence was whether the agent located the existing readonly_fields error construction, recognized that label only contains readonly_fields[index], compared nearby checks that say the option “refers to” a field value, and planned or applied a localized message interpolation using the existing field value. Rubrics that made a project-native regression test mandatory were weaker here: tests are desirable, but the core task acceptance is the emitted admin.E035 message content and unchanged validation behavior. A better rubric should focus on preserving the existing error id, indexed label, admin/model context, and accepted cases such as callables, admin attributes, model attributes, and real model fields. Avoid tempting proxies such as requiring a helper refactor, requiring exact test-run success in a difficult local Django test environment, or rewarding broad changes to admin checks. Prioritize visible evidence from code inspection, manual reproduction output, or patch intent showing the offending value appears in the invalid-readonly-field message while the validation branches remain intact.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly converge on a localized update to the readonly_fields invalid-item diagnostic so the admin check error includes both the indexed option label and the actual offending field name/value, using wording consistent with neighboring admin option checks, while preserving the existing error identity, admin/model context, and all existing valid readonly_fields acceptance semantics.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Readonly-field diagnostic includes offending value

metadata.environment: Django-style Python framework admin system checks
primary_visible_evidence: The trajectory identifies the readonly_fields item-level error construction as the relevant code path.
It distinguishes the indexed option label from the offending field value/name.
It compares or follows nearby admin check message style that includes referenced field values.
It preserves callable, admin-attribute, model-attribute, and valid model-field success cases.
It keeps the existing check identity and contextual class/model information.
avoid_as_mandatory: A regression test update as the sole or mandatory success criterion when the behavior contract is otherwise satisfied.
Broad refactors or helper reuse that are not required for the message-content change.
Changing validation semantics or error ids.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent has identified the readonly_fields diagnostic problem or the relevant message path.
scale.2: The agent understands that a readonly_fields message is missing information but has not shown how to include the offending value or risks changing unrelated validation behavior.
scale.3: The agent has localized the relevant check and intends to include the field value, but evidence is incomplete about preserving existing accepted cases, error identity, or established message style.
scale.4: The agent shows a localized change or strong plan that includes both the indexed label and offending value and preserves the existing validation branches and context, with some validation or comparison evidence.
scale.5: The agent clearly implements or verifies the exact behavior contract: invalid readonly_fields errors include both option index and bad value in consistent wording, existing valid cases still pass, and the error id/context remain unchanged.

experiences.title: Do not over-credit isolated severity-to-score conversion in end-to-end scoring bugs
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go CVE/CVSS task requires severity-only vulnerabilities to affect filtering, grouping, summaries, and reports, and the trajectory has only found or patched a severity conversion helper or one max-score path.
experiences.context: This applies in Go repositories where vulnerability severity labels must be converted into approximate numeric CVSS values and then consumed by multiple model and report paths. The misleading pattern is generating a broad positive rubric such as “severity-only CVEs get estimated scores everywhere” when the visible trajectory only shows exploration, a partial change to one score helper, or a broken intermediate file. The original idea is still useful when the trajectory visibly audits the actual downstream consumers, updates the shared scoring/display APIs they call, preserves numeric-score precedence and source ordering, and validates filtering/grouping/report behavior. It is less appropriate as a high-confidence criterion at early investigation stages or when there is no visible evidence beyond identifying an existing mapping function.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics correctly identified the task theme—severity labels like HIGH or CRITICAL need rough numeric CVSS scores—but they were misleading because they treated finding or adding conversion logic as equivalent to a complete fix. In this class of bug, correctness depends on propagation through all actual consumers: max score selection, threshold filtering, scored-vulnerability selection, severity bucket summaries including critical/high/medium/low boundaries, and report display/listing paths. A better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory has visible evidence that it traced and aligned those consumer paths, not merely that it reused a mapping helper or patched a single CVSS version helper. Avoid the tempting criterion “uses severityToScore mapping” as a standalone positive signal. Prioritize evidence such as: direct inspection or modification of the filter path that previously bypassed the aggregate score accessor; grouping code using the correct severity-aware score and preserving critical counts; report/list helpers showing severity-derived scores rather than dropping them; tests or repros covering severity-only CVEs at threshold boundaries; and absence of broken intermediate code or leftover temporary repro files.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Partial severity conversion without consumer propagation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for severity-only CVE scoring tasks when the visible work stops at identifying or adding a severity-to-score conversion in one helper, while leaving unclear or unchanged the downstream paths that actually drive filtering, severity grouping, summaries, max-score formatting, and report outputs. This flaw is especially clear if the trajectory changes only a CVSS2 or CVSS3 max helper, changes max-score selection without auditing direct version-specific callers, omits critical/high/medium/low bucket behavior, does not validate report/list display of calculated scores, or leaves the repository in a non-compiling/intermediate state.

metadata.environment: Go CVE/CVSS vulnerability model and reporting code
metadata.task_pattern: severity label present, numeric CVSS score missing, expected inclusion in filtering/grouping/reports
required_visible_evidence: severity-derived scores participate in the score accessor used by threshold filtering
severity grouping uses a severity-aware score and accounts for critical/high/medium/low thresholds
report/display helpers include severity-only entries instead of omitting or formatting them as unscored
max-score selection preserves real numeric-score precedence while still allowing calculated scores when no numeric score exists
focused validation covers severity-only CVEs passing a threshold and being counted in summaries
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: presence of a severity-to-score mapping helper or a single patched max-score function

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory visibly traces and aligns the shared scoring accessor, filter path, grouping buckets, and report/display consumers, with validation for severity-only CVEs.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory implements most consumer propagation but has small gaps in report formatting or test coverage while preserving compiling code and core filter/group behavior.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory adds severity conversion in a central helper and recognizes some consumers, but leaves at least one major path such as grouping, filtering, or report display unaudited or unvalidated.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory focuses on one CVSS version/helper or the mapping function and assumes downstream behavior will follow, with little visible work on direct consumers or boundary tests.
scale.5: Most severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory is only exploratory, produces no usable patch, corrupts/removes scoring functions, or leaves broken code while still appearing to satisfy a broad severity-conversion criterion.

experiences.title: End-to-End OCI Bundle Backend Completeness
experiences.description: Use when a Go storage-backend task asks for native OCI feature bundle consumption and caching, especially after the trajectory has identified existing config but no runtime/store implementation or has begun adding an OCI store/source.
experiences.context: Applies to Flipt-like Go codebases where storage backends are selected from configuration, filesystem-backed storage is built through a snapshot source abstraction, and the task requires adding OCI artifact consumption from both registries and local bundle layouts. It is most useful once visible evidence includes either implementation attempts or enough repository inspection to know the expected storage/config integration points. It is less useful as a narrow media-type-only rubric, for purely exploratory early steps with no edits, or for tasks limited to configuration parsing without bundle fetching/caching semantics.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in this cluster was the broad completeness check: OCI bundle support is not correct unless the trajectory converges on a real bundle store plus integration, not merely a new package, a switch case, or generic ORAS calls. The better criterion should require observable evidence for all required behavioral boundaries: remote registry and local bundle-directory references, digest-aware skip/caching behavior based on resolved artifact digests, validation of the Flipt-specific artifact/layer media types and json/yaml/yml encodings with clear errors, filesystem snapshot compatibility, and clean configuration/runtime wiring. A tempting but weaker criterion is to credit any media-type validation or any SnapshotSource skeleton; this can overrate trajectories that use wrong media type constants, invent unsupported config fields, leave compile/API mismatches, corrupt switch cases, or omit local references and digest matching. Prioritize visible evidence such as use of the repository’s existing config semantics, ORAS v2 APIs compatible with the current dependency, explicit If-No-Match/digest comparison flow, layer descriptor parsing that separates media type from encoding suffix, integration through the established filesystem snapshot pipeline, and build/test feedback. If only exploration is visible, the rubric should be scaled as planning/progress toward these components rather than judging final implementation quality.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete OCI Bundle Storage Semantics
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show credible progress toward a compile-ready OCI feature bundle backend that fits the existing storage architecture: a dedicated OCI fetching abstraction, a filesystem snapshot source wrapper, configuration/runtime integration for the OCI storage type, support for both remote registry references and local bundle-directory references, digest-aware fetch skipping or caching when the artifact digest is unchanged, and strict rejection of unexpected bundle media types or encoding suffixes with clear errors. Strong evidence includes preserving existing config reference semantics instead of inventing incompatible options, using dependency-compatible OCI/ORAS APIs, validating Flipt-specific artifact and namespace layer descriptors, accepting only json/yaml/yml or empty/default encodings, returning files/snapshots through the existing filesystem store pipeline, and running or responding to focused build/tests. Do not give high credit for a partial source skeleton, broad repository searches, generic tar extraction, wrong media type constants, broken switch-case insertion, or unresolved compile errors.

required_visible_evidence: OCI store/fetch abstraction using current OCI registry/content APIs
remote registry and local bundle-directory/reference handling
digest comparison or If-No-Match-style caching to avoid redundant fetches
descriptor media type and encoding validation with clear errors
filesystem snapshot source integration with existing storage pipeline
configuration and runtime storage-type wiring
compile/test validation or concrete fixes to observed integration errors
common_false_positives: only adding config fields
only adding a SnapshotSource shell
using generic container image layer media types instead of Flipt bundle media types
tracking a digest after fetching but still always downloading
manual switch/import edits that leave broken Go syntax or unresolved identifiers
adding new dependencies or APIs incompatible with the repository's Go version

scale.1: No meaningful OCI backend progress beyond exploration or repeated searches; no credible implementation path for fetching, caching, validation, and integration is visible.
scale.2: Some relevant architecture is identified or a small skeleton is started, but most required behaviors are missing, speculative, or disconnected from the existing storage/config pipeline.
scale.3: Moderate progress: the trajectory identifies the correct integration model and implements some components, but key pieces such as local references, digest-aware skipping, exact media/encoding validation, or compile-ready wiring remain incomplete.
scale.4: Strong progress: most core components are implemented in the existing architecture with plausible remote/local handling, digest matching, validation, and runtime integration, with only minor gaps or unverified edge cases remaining.
scale.5: Complete, coherent, and validated progress: the visible trajectory demonstrates a compile-ready OCI bundle backend with correct remote and local reference handling, digest-aware caching/skip semantics, Flipt-specific media type and encoding rejection, clean config/runtime integration, and focused tests or build results supporting the behavior.

experiences.title: Do not overvalue manual SVG-relative path math when a renderer already rewrites SVG links
experiences.description: Retrieve for Sphinx/Graphviz-style bugs where SVG resources are embedded via object tags and the trajectory focuses on computing links relative to _images or the SVG file location, especially while an existing SVG link post-processor is visible.
experiences.context: Applies in Python documentation-build systems like Sphinx when an extension generates Graphviz/DOT URLs for SVG output and then delegates rendering to a shared renderer that already rewrites relative SVG hrefs. The misleading case is a rubric that says the fix must manually compute final paths from the SVG asset directory to HTML targets; this can reward agents that understand the browser base-URI issue but violate the renderer contract, change generic Graphviz behavior, add skip flags, or produce no patch. The original path-base idea is still appropriate when there is no centralized SVG href rewriting layer, when the task is inside the renderer responsible for final SVG XML hrefs, or when visible evidence shows the existing post-processor is absent or bypassed by design.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked whether the agent computed links relative to the SVG file location or _images. That is too broad for this code path: inheritance-diagram URL generation supplies URLs to Graphviz, and Graphviz has a dedicated SVG relative-link fixer. A good trajectory should preserve that division of responsibility: remove or avoid the inheritance-layer hard-coded parent-directory adjustment that conflicts with the renderer, keep PNG/image-map document-relative behavior intact, ensure same-document anchors become usable SVG links rather than bare HTML-page fragments, and avoid modifying generic graphviz SVG rewriting without clear evidence it is the broken component. Do not generate a criterion that rewards any output-root/_images path algebra, changing image-directory variables, cache-key churn, or merely stating that object-embedded SVG links resolve relative to the SVG. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence that the agent traced resolved cross-reference values through the inheritance-diagram URL map into DOT and through the existing SVG post-processing step, verified generated SVG hrefs with a nested document and real resolved class/object targets, and considered non-local/external references where the graph node key may differ from the displayed reference title.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat the inheritance-diagram layer as responsible for manually computing final SVG-file-relative paths even though the visible codebase has a shared Graphviz SVG href rewriting step. This flaw is present when the agent proposes or edits code to convert resolved document-relative references into output-root or _images-relative paths, changes the generic SVG relative-path fixer without isolating the inheritance-diagram bug, adds options to skip the fixer, or relies only on conceptual discussion of object-tag base URI without a concrete patch and nested SVG href validation. Do not apply this criticism when the trajectory has shown that no renderer-level SVG href fixer exists, that the fixer is demonstrably the faulty component, or that the code under edit is itself the final SVG XML rewriting layer.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Manual path algebra bypasses renderer SVG-link contract

metadata.environment: Python Sphinx-style documentation builder using inheritance diagrams delegated to Graphviz SVG rendering
visible_evidence_to_check: existence of a renderer-level function that rewrites relative hrefs in generated SVG files
inheritance-diagram code building a map from resolved cross-reference nodes to Graphviz DOT URL attributes
whether edits preserve the expected document-relative URL contract before renderer post-processing
whether tests or manual builds inspect generated SVG hrefs for a nested source document with resolved targets
metadata.tempting_but_misleading_proxy: agent states or implements that links must be computed directly relative to _images/the SVG file location

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory respects the existing SVG href post-processing contract, avoids unnecessary generic Graphviz changes, and validates nested generated SVG hrefs with resolved targets.
scale.2: Minor concern: the trajectory discusses SVG-file-relative resolution broadly but also investigates the renderer contract and has not committed to manual path recomputation.
scale.3: Mixed behavior: the trajectory identifies the hard-coded parent-directory adjustment but is ambiguous about whether URLs should be document-relative input to the renderer or final SVG-relative output.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory implements or plans output-root/_images-relative path construction in the inheritance layer, or changes generic SVG path rewriting, without convincing evidence this matches the renderer contract.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory primarily rewards or implements manual SVG-relative path algebra, skip-fixer options, or generic graphviz rewrites, lacks nested SVG href validation with resolved references, and risks regressing PNG/image-map or unrelated Graphviz SVG behavior.

experiences.title: Protocol-scoped ORM filterability checks
experiences.description: Use when a Django ORM trajectory is fixing an attribute-name collision where an internal expression protocol flag such as `filterable` is accidentally read from ordinary filter RHS values or model instances.
experiences.context: Applies in Django ORM query-building tasks where the reported failure is a filter/query error caused by `check_filterable` or similar validation reading a user-defined model field/attribute named like an internal expression flag. The trajectory should have visible evidence that model instances can reach RHS validation unchanged, while real SQL expression objects use the flag to control WHERE-clause legality. This is most useful after the agent has inspected the relevant query construction path or begun patching it. It is less useful for unrelated queryset lookup bugs, for tasks about documenting reserved model field names, or at a very early stage before the agent has identified whether the value being checked is an expression, a model instance, or another arbitrary object.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful rubric in these cases judged whether the fix separated ordinary model values from Django expression objects before honoring `filterable=False`. That criterion is discriminative because the visible bug mechanism is not that related objects need different FK preparation; it is that a generic `getattr(value, 'filterable', True)` treats application data as if it were an ORM expression. A better rubric should reward evidence that the agent scopes the check to the expression protocol, preserves rejection of genuinely non-filterable expressions such as window expressions, and keeps recursive child-expression validation and code structure intact. It should not over-focus on a tempting but weaker proxy such as simply skipping anything with `_meta`, resolving all model instances to primary keys before validation, or checking only one concrete base class without considering Django’s expression protocol. It should also not ignore visible edit damage: if the trajectory shows a malformed or duplicated method after scripted edits, the semantic idea alone is not enough. Prioritize visible evidence such as: the agent traces RHS resolution and confirms model instances lack expression APIs; identifies `filterable` as an expression-level flag; changes validation so arbitrary model fields named `filterable` are not consulted; confirms a related-object filter with `filterable=False` works; confirms a non-filterable expression still raises; and runs or plans a focused regression test.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates a structurally sound fix for the Django ORM filterability collision by applying the `filterable` flag only to expression-like objects, not arbitrary RHS values or model instances, while preserving existing rejection and recursive validation for genuinely non-filterable SQL expressions.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Expression-protocol filterability boundary

expected_visible_evidence: The agent identifies that ordinary model instances can expose a user field or attribute named `filterable`.
The agent identifies that the internal `filterable` flag belongs to Django SQL expression objects and controls WHERE-clause eligibility.
The proposed code gates the `filterable=False` check on expression-like behavior, preferably the expression protocol such as `resolve_expression`, rather than reading the attribute from every value.
The existing recursion into source expressions is preserved where applicable.
Validation covers both sides of the boundary: a model instance with `filterable=False` is accepted as a related filter value, and a known non-filterable expression remains rejected.
The edited query-building code remains syntactically and structurally intact.
anti_patterns: Continuing to call `getattr(value, 'filterable', True)` on arbitrary RHS values.
Treating `filterable` as a reserved model field name instead of fixing the protocol collision.
Only special-casing the reported model or field while leaving the broader collision.
Breaking or duplicating the method during scripted edits.
Removing expression filterability enforcement entirely.
metadata.environment: Django ORM query construction and expression validation

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of the protocol boundary; the trajectory still treats arbitrary values as filterable/non-filterable based on a coincidental attribute, removes validation entirely, or leaves visibly broken code.
scale.2: Recognizes that model fields named `filterable` are involved, but proposes a narrow or unvalidated workaround that does not clearly preserve non-filterable expression behavior or code integrity.
scale.3: Maintains roughly the parent trajectory’s level of progress: identifies the model-vs-expression issue but has only partial implementation or partial validation, with unresolved uncertainty about expression handling or edit correctness.
scale.4: Strong evidence of a correct boundary: the patch avoids reading `filterable` from model instances or other plain RHS values, keeps non-filterable expressions rejected, preserves recursive checks, and passes focused ad hoc or targeted validation.
scale.5: Complete, robust evidence: the fix is scoped to Django’s expression protocol rather than arbitrary attributes, includes a focused regression test for a related-object RHS with a `filterable=False` model field, confirms existing non-filterable expression behavior, preserves surrounding query logic, and relevant Django tests pass.

experiences.title: End-to-End Propagator Support Must Match Available APIs
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go/OpenTelemetry task adds configurable context propagators and the trajectory is editing config, schema, or server initialization that currently hardcodes propagators.
experiences.context: Applies in Go repositories using OpenTelemetry where propagation is configured through application config and applied via global or server initialization, especially after the agent has found a hardcoded call such as a composite TraceContext/Baggage propagator and is adding a user-facing propagators list. It is most useful during mid-implementation or final-review stages, when visible edits or build output show whether declared propagator names, validation, dependencies, and runtime construction are consistent. Do not apply as a strict rule during early exploration before the implementation strategy is chosen. Do not assume only core propagators are valid if the trajectory visibly adds and imports the correct OpenTelemetry contrib propagator modules or an official auto-propagator mechanism; the key boundary is consistency between the supported config surface and actual available implementations.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on propagator configuration wiring and API compatibility: the new config field must not stop at structs/defaults/schema, but must actually replace the hardcoded OpenTelemetry propagator setup in server initialization, and every accepted propagator name must map to a real TextMapPropagator provided by current dependencies. This aligned well when trajectories exposed decisive evidence: the hardcoded SetTextMapPropagator call remained unchanged, the helper silently ignored unknown names, validation accepted names that were never built, or builds failed with undefined propagation.B3/Jaeger symbols. A better rubric should ask for end-to-end consistency across config defaults, validation/schema, dependency/import choices, and runtime construction. It should reward either a limited supported set that matches core APIs or a broader set backed by explicit dependencies and correct constructors. Avoid the tempting but wrong criterion that merely checks for a Propagators field or a sampler change; also avoid hardcoding a universal rule that B3/Jaeger are invalid, because they are valid if the implementation adds the proper contrib packages or official factory. Prioritize visible evidence such as go.mod changes, import paths, build/doc output for available propagator types, validation enum lists, schema enum lists, and the actual call passed to otel.SetTextMapPropagator.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Propagator Configuration End-to-End Consistency
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that configurable trace propagators are implemented consistently from user-facing configuration through validation and into actual OpenTelemetry runtime setup. The accepted propagator names in config/schema must exactly match implementations available through current or newly added dependencies, and server initialization must replace the prior hardcoded propagator list with a composite/factory built from the configured list while preserving sensible defaults.

evidence_to_check: Tracing configuration contains a propagators field with defaults preserving prior behavior.
Config validation and schema restrict values to the same supported set used at runtime.
Any non-core propagator names are backed by explicit module dependencies and correct imports/constructors.
The hardcoded OpenTelemetry propagator setup in server initialization is replaced by config-driven construction.
Build output or API inspection does not show undefined propagator symbols.
common_failure_modes: Adding a propagators config field but leaving otel.SetTextMapPropagator hardcoded.
Accepting B3, Jaeger, or other names in validation/schema without adding the packages that implement them.
Referencing nonexistent types from the core propagation package.
Silently ignoring unsupported configured names instead of rejecting them during config loading.
Letting schema/default names diverge from Go struct tags or runtime lookup names.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of propagator configuration reaching runtime; the hardcoded propagator setup remains or the implementation only adds unused config fields.
scale.2: Some config or default work is present, but runtime wiring is missing or supported names are not validated against actual implementations.
scale.3: Propagator configuration is partially wired to runtime with defaults, but there are unresolved consistency risks such as schema/name mismatches, silent fallback behavior, or unverified dependency support.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly wires configured propagators into OpenTelemetry setup and aligns validation with available implementations, with only minor gaps such as incomplete tests or documentation.
scale.5: The trajectory provides strong end-to-end evidence: config fields, defaults, schema, validation, dependencies/imports, and otel.SetTextMapPropagator construction all agree, unsupported values fail clearly, and build/API checks confirm all referenced propagators exist.

experiences.title: End-to-End Untrusted Contact Encryption Preference
experiences.description: Retrieve when a TypeScript/React mail/contact task introduces or mentions a new vCard-style encryption preference for WKD or otherwise untrusted external keys, especially when searches show no existing support and the symptoms span UI, persistence, contact-key model construction, and send-time preference extraction.
experiences.context: Applies in a monorepo-style frontend/shared-library environment where contact encryption preferences flow through contact settings UI, vCard custom-property parsing/serialization, public-key model construction, and mail-send encryption preference extraction. It is most useful once the trajectory has found that WKD/external API keys are treated differently from pinned keys, or that the named untrusted encryption flag is absent from existing types/constants/parsers. At early exploration stages, the criterion should reward identifying this multi-layer data flow rather than demanding a complete patch. At implementation/final-review stages, it should be strict about preserving separate semantics for pinned trusted keys versus untrusted/WKD keys. Do not apply this rubric to a narrow send-time-only encryption bug with no contact persistence/UI requirement, or to tasks where the relevant preference field already exists and only one consumer needs adjustment.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often checked that WKD contacts no longer hardcode encryption and that a user-visible toggle or existing encrypt flag is respected. That focus was directionally relevant because the visible trajectories repeatedly found a WKD branch forcing encryption and UI conditions hiding controls behind an API-key check. However, as a correctness predictor it was too weak when it treated “use model.encrypt” or “save x-pm-encrypt for WKD” as sufficient. The task’s discriminating boundary is that untrusted/WKD keys need their own persisted preference path, distinct from pinned-key x-pm-encrypt, and contacts with no valid keys must not acquire misleading disabled encryption state. A better rubric should require evidence that the agent is implementing the preference end to end: adding the new untrusted flag to vCard field allowlists/types/parsers, extracting it separately from the pinned-key flag, mapping pinned versus untrusted preferences into the public-key model with the right defaults, making send-time extraction consume that model instead of hardcoded values, exposing UI control only for the relevant external-contact cases, and saving the correct property depending on whether keys are pinned or untrusted. Avoid the tempting proxy criterion that rewards only a UI toggle, only changing hardcoded WKD booleans, or broadening existing x-pm-encrypt persistence to all external contacts; those partial changes can visibly leave the new flag unsupported, break internal/self-send behavior, or preserve the no-key false-state bug. Prioritize visible evidence such as searches showing the new flag is absent, edits or plans spanning schema/parser/model/UI/save/send layers, careful distinction of missing versus explicit false, preservation of internal/pinned behavior, and regression tests or at least targeted checks for WKD disable, legacy pinned default, untrusted persistence, and no-valid-key persistence.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Untrusted Encryption Preference Support
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the new untrusted/WKD encryption preference is handled as a first-class contact preference across the full data flow, not merely by changing one hardcoded send-time boolean or showing a UI toggle. Strong evidence includes adding or planning support for the untrusted vCard field in contact key-field allowlists, type definitions, boolean parsing, and key-property extraction; keeping pinned-key encryption preference separate from untrusted-key encryption preference; deriving the public-key model so legacy pinned keys and untrusted/WKD keys default to encryption enabled when the relevant flag is missing while explicit false disables encryption; making send-time WKD preference extraction consume the model’s encrypt/sign values rather than forcing true; updating contact settings UI and save logic so external WKD/untrusted-key contacts can toggle encryption and the correct preference property is saved only when a valid pinned or untrusted key source exists; preserving invalid/unusable key warnings; and avoiding broad edits that alter internal/self-send or unrelated branches.

preferred_visible_evidence: Searches or inspections establish whether the untrusted encryption field already exists.
The agent distinguishes pinned/trusted key preferences from untrusted/WKD key preferences.
The trajectory covers schema/type/parser/extractor/model/UI/save/send-preference layers, or explicitly plans them before editing.
Missing preference and explicit false are treated differently.
No-key external contacts are guarded against misleading saved encryption flags.
Edits are targeted and do not change internal or self-send encryption defaults accidentally.
Tests or test plans cover WKD explicit disable, legacy pinned default enable, untrusted field persistence, invalid WKD warnings, and no-valid-key persistence behavior.
anti_patterns: Only replacing hardcoded WKD encrypt/sign true with existing model fields.
Only exposing an encryption toggle for WKD contacts.
Saving the existing pinned-key encryption field for all external contacts, including untrusted-key or no-key contacts.
Using broad text substitutions that affect internal/self-send branches.
Treating absence of the new field in searches as proof no new parser/type/persistence work is needed.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of addressing WKD/untrusted contact encryption preference semantics; the trajectory is still generic exploration or changes unrelated encryption code.
scale.2: Weak partial evidence, such as identifying a hardcoded WKD encryption branch or hidden UI toggle, but no credible plan or edits for the new untrusted preference field, persistence, model mapping, and no-key behavior.
scale.3: Moderate progress equivalent to the parent trajectory: the agent addresses one or two visible symptoms, such as UI control or send-time hardcoding, but still conflates pinned and untrusted preferences or omits important layers like parsing/types/save logic.
scale.4: Strong evidence of an end-to-end approach: the trajectory distinguishes pinned versus untrusted flags, updates most relevant layers, respects explicit disable versus missing default, and avoids misleading no-key persistence, with only minor validation or edge-case gaps.
scale.5: Complete and carefully validated evidence: the trajectory implements or clearly prepares all necessary type/parser/field/model/UI/save/send extraction changes, preserves internal and pinned behavior, handles invalid/unusable WKD warnings and no-key contacts, and includes targeted regression coverage for the stated scenarios.

experiences.title: Do not treat hook extraction as sufficient in behavior-preserving UI refactors
experiences.description: Retrieve when a React/TypeScript task asks to refactor a class component into hooks while preserving existing rendering, async lookup, DOM utility, and public import behavior.
experiences.context: This warning applies to large behavior-preserving UI refactors where the task explicitly requests a hook extraction and named utility exports, but the visible trajectory shows wholesale rewrites, import/export churn, partial TypeScript or Jest validation, or failures around DOM traversal and special rendering paths. In this setting, a rubric that only checks whether a usePermalink-style hook exists and whether helper functions were exported can be misleading: those are structural requirements, but they do not demonstrate that the refactor is safe. The original idea is still appropriate as a low-level subcriterion when the trajectory is at design or early implementation stage, or when separate evidence already shows behavior parity and compile/test health. It should not be the dominant success criterion during final review or after unvalidated/broken rewrites.
experiences.experience: Several generated rubrics rewarded extraction of permalink logic into a hook and movement of room-notification helpers to named exports. That criterion matches part of the task, but it is too narrow for judging trajectory quality in a widely used component refactor. Visible evidence often showed agents creating a hook while breaking core behavior: async profile lookups mutated objects without reliably triggering re-render, unmount/staleness guards were incomplete, special @room pills were mishandled because they may have no URL/resourceId, parsePermalink nullability and in-message vs non-message parsing diverged from the original behavior, DOM pillification traversal was rewritten incorrectly, tests still failed, or public import compatibility was disrupted. A better rubric should prioritize behavior-preservation evidence around all legacy pill types, rendering modes, avatars/tooltips, click dispatch, room alias/user resolution, DOM text splitting, duplicate pillification, and local validation results. Avoid the tempting criterion that a hook file plus named utility exports implies correctness; instead, ask whether the extracted hook and component together preserve the old observable contract and whether any compiler/test output or code inspection reveals regressions.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Structural hook extraction masks behavior regressions
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Flag the trajectory when it focuses on creating a reusable permalink hook or named helper exports but lacks visible evidence that the refactored component preserves the original UI and utility contract. This includes trajectories with unvalidated wholesale rewrites, local TypeScript or Jest failures after the rewrite, changed public import/export shapes without updating all consumers, hook/component circular dependencies, parsePermalink or null-handling regressions, async profile lookup logic that mutates members without a state update or safe unmount/staleness guard, special @room rendering that requires a URL/resourceId, changed anchor-vs-span behavior for message contexts, missing avatars/tooltips/click dispatch behavior, or altered DOM pillification traversal/text splitting that can duplicate pills or crash on text nodes.

metadata.environment: React and TypeScript UI codebase with a widely used pill/mention component, a DOM pillification utility, permalink parsing helpers, and Jest/TypeScript validation available.
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: Presence of a usePermalink-style hook and named room notification helper exports as the main evidence of correctness.
preferred_visible_evidence: Component remains type-safe after refactor or local compiler errors are unrelated and clearly isolated
Relevant tests for DOM pillification and direct component consumers pass, or failures are investigated and fixed
All legacy pill types and rendering contexts are explicitly preserved
Public imports/exports remain compatible or all consumers are updated coherently
Async profile and room resolution behavior preserves re-render and unmount safety
DOM text-node splitting for @room is minimally changed and still handles repeated pillification

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory pairs hook extraction with clear behavior-preservation checks, compatible exports, and passing relevant validation.
scale.2: Minor risk only: hook extraction is emphasized, but the visible changes mostly preserve existing behavior and any missing validation or edge-case discussion is limited.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory has a hook and helper exports, but behavior parity is only partially demonstrated or some important consumer/edge-case checks are absent.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory rewards or proceeds with structural extraction despite visible risks such as unvalidated wholesale rewrites, import/export incompatibilities, async re-render issues, or altered pillification logic.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory has compiler/test failures or obvious behavioral regressions after the hook refactor, yet the main success evidence remains the mere existence of the hook or named utility exports.

experiences.title: Do not treat tag/digest XOR validation as sufficient for digest image support
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go task adds an alternative image identifier such as digest alongside tag and the trajectory has already found or edited validation logic. A validation-only rubric can overvalue partial fixes that still leave scanning, reporting, or model propagation assuming tag-only references.
experiences.context: This applies in Go container/image configuration tasks where image data flows from config loading into scan and report models, and where existing code constructs image references from separate name and tag fields. The misleading case is generating a rubric centered on enforcing exactly one of tag or digest after the trajectory already shows that validation is implemented or planned; that criterion is necessary but no longer discriminates correctness if downstream paths still use name:tag, fail to copy the digest into result models, or build unstable per-image/server/report identifiers. The original validation criterion remains appropriate when the trajectory has not yet addressed config validation at all, or when the task is explicitly limited to loader/config validation rather than end-to-end scan/report behavior. At early exploration with no edits, phrase such checks as planned requirements rather than as evidence of final patch quality.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics emphasized digest/tag mutual exclusivity and sometimes bundled it with generic full-reference formatting. That is semantically correct as a requirement, but it was a misleading primary criterion in trajectories where the agent had already implemented XOR validation while the risky work was elsewhere. For digest-image tasks, correctness depends on end-to-end propagation and every consumer that previously assumed tag-only data: config must expose the digest, validation must require exactly one identifier, scan result/model types must carry the digest, conversion code must copy it, scanner input must use name:tag or name@digest, and reporting/logging/pseudo-server names must no longer concatenate only the tag or accidentally drop required identifiers.
