Avoid the tempting criterion “validation enforces exactly one of tag or digest” as the main rubric once visible steps show it has been addressed. Instead, generate a criterion that prioritizes visible evidence from grep/diff/build review that all hardcoded name + ':' + tag or Image.Tag-only reference construction sites were audited and either centralized through a full-reference helper or updated consistently, with special attention to dataflow boundaries between config structs and report/model structs.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Incomplete downstream digest propagation despite valid config checks
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for digest-image support when they mainly implement tag/digest mutual-exclusion validation but leave visible downstream assumptions that only tag-based image references exist. This flaw is present if the trajectory or diff shows remaining or unreviewed hardcoded name:tag construction in scan/report/logging paths, fails to add/copy digest through both configuration and result-model image structures, changes only one of multiple image-reference construction sites, or alters per-image/report identifiers in a way that drops the digest, drops the image key/name, or preserves tag-only naming. Do not count ordinary field copying or image-presence checks as flaws by themselves; focus on reference construction and cross-layer propagation evidence.

metadata.task_family: Go container image configuration with tag-or-digest identifiers
necessary_but_insufficient_evidence: validation rejects neither tag nor digest
validation rejects both tag and digest
priority_evidence: digest field exists in both config-facing and report/result-facing image representations when both are used
conversion from config/server image data to scan result/model image data copies digest
scanner input/full image reference construction uses name:tag for tag and name@digest for digest
reporting, logging, UUID keys, and per-image pseudo-server names no longer rely solely on Image.Tag or name:tag format
repository-wide search for Image.Tag, Image.Name, or colon-based format strings has been used to audit remaining assumptions
build/gofmt or comparable compile validation after edits, especially when sed/manual replacements were used
do_not_overweight: XOR validation alone
adding a digest field only to the config struct
adding a helper that is not used at all reference construction sites

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory visibly audits downstream image-reference construction, propagates digest through relevant config/model boundaries, and uses consistent tag-or-digest formatting across scanning and reporting paths.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: validation and most propagation/reference sites are handled, but one low-risk log/report display site is not clearly audited or the trajectory lacks final grep/build confirmation.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: validation is implemented and some scan/report formatting is updated, but at least one important downstream path or model conversion remains unverified or likely still tag-only.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory relies on validation plus a partial helper or one scanner edit while visible report/model/pseudo-server/reference construction sites still use Image.Tag or name:tag assumptions.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory only adds digest validation or a field, with little or no downstream propagation, or introduces inconsistent formatting that drops required image identity information in scan/report workflows.

experiences.title: Fractional Size Parameters Must Be Normalized at Integer-Only Boundaries
experiences.description: Retrieve when a bug involves an API parameter that may be given as a fraction of the sample count but later reaches code that requires an integer count, especially after the trajectory has located the scale-by-sample-count path.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/scientific-library bug-fix tasks where a documented size/count parameter accepts either an absolute integer or a fractional float, validation intentionally allows fractions, and the failure occurs because the scaled fractional value remains a float when passed to an integer-only consumer such as a nearest-neighbor count or count-threshold routine. It is most useful once the trajectory has inspected the relevant implementation path or traceback and found the conversion point. It is less useful during pure repository exploration before the failing data flow is identified, for parameters that are genuinely continuous floats, for fixes that should reject fractional inputs rather than support them, or when the codebase specifies a different rounding/floor/ceil convention that must be followed instead of assuming one.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster focused on the semantic boundary between public fractional-parameter support and downstream integer-only APIs. A good criterion should check that the trajectory identifies the fractional branch where a value like a sample-size proportion is multiplied by the number of samples, recognizes that existing validation permits this input but does not coerce its type, and ensures the resulting sample count is explicitly converted to an integer before being used by downstream count-based code. The criterion should also value preserving the existing minimum-count rule and absolute-integer behavior, and optionally checking related call sites that perform the same fractional-size normalization. The previous rubrics were useful when they prioritized this visible data flow rather than generic testing or broad refactoring. However, avoid overfitting the rubric to a single textual patch shape: the important evidence is correct normalization using the task/codebase’s intended rounding or truncation convention, not blindly requiring one exact expression in all repositories. Also avoid rewarding unrelated build-debugging, dependency installation, or edits in unrelated modules as evidence of correctness. If local tests are blocked by compiled-extension or environment issues, source-level confirmation of the conversion and targeted logical/regression-test intent can still be meaningful evidence, while malformed sed edits, duplicate broken lines, or unrelated file changes should reduce confidence.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a trajectory fixing a fractional size/count parameter bug, assess whether it demonstrates the correct normalization boundary: it should trace the accepted fractional input through validation, find where it is scaled by the sample count, convert the scaled value into an integer count before any integer-only consumer receives it, preserve the documented lower bound and existing absolute-integer validation semantics, and avoid unrelated behavioral changes. Stronger evidence includes checking analogous fractional size parameters in the same algorithm and adding or attempting a focused regression test for the reported fractional-input scenario, while recognizing when full test execution is blocked by unrelated environment/build constraints.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Normalize Fractional Counts Before Integer Consumers

observable_evidence: The trajectory locates the size/count parameter branch that handles floats as fractions of the number of samples.
The trajectory recognizes that validation permits fractional values and that the downstream consumer requires an integer count.
The proposed or applied change casts the scaled count to an integer using the task/codebase's intended rounding, flooring, or minimum-count convention.
The change is placed before the integer-only API or count-threshold use, not by rejecting valid fractional inputs.
The trajectory avoids unrelated modules or broad refactors and preserves existing behavior for valid integer counts.
metadata.stage_guidance: Most discriminative after the implementation path has been inspected or edited; before that, judge only whether the investigation is converging on this data flow.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory identifies the fractional-size-to-integer-consumer data flow; it focuses on unrelated files, generic dependency/build issues, or rejects valid fractional inputs.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory finds the relevant area or repeats the error message but does not clearly explain that the scaled fractional value must be coerced before an integer-only consumer.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies the primary fractional conversion path and proposes or begins an integer conversion, but verification is incomplete, related analogous call sites are unexamined, or the edit may be only partially confirmed.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory correctly applies or plans an integer conversion at the primary scaled-fraction branch before the integer-only consumer, preserves validation and minimum-count semantics, and avoids unrelated behavioral changes.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: in addition to the primary fix, the trajectory checks analogous fractional size/count conversions in the same algorithm, confirms the diff is clean and syntactically correct, and adds or attempts a focused regression/logical test for fractional input while appropriately handling unrelated environment limitations.

experiences.title: Excluded Seed-Type Invariant for Item Notes
experiences.description: Use when a list-item annotation task explicitly limits notes to concrete Thing-like seeds while preserving a separate subject/string seed representation.
experiences.context: Applies in an Open Library-style Python/web.py list feature where list seeds have two semantic forms: resolvable Thing references such as works, editions, or authors, and subject-like string seeds that must remain plain strings. This is most useful after the trajectory has begun modifying seed normalization, model wrappers, edit forms, or list-view rendering for per-item notes. It is premature during pure exploration before any implementation evidence exists, and it is irrelevant for features where every seed type is supposed to accept notes or where there is no separate subject-string representation. This criterion is also not sufficient by itself: satisfying the exclusion invariant does not prove note persistence, safe rendering, or edit round-tripping are correct.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics focused on excluding subject/string seeds from public notes. That is a useful discriminating criterion in this task because the requirement creates a sharp boundary: notes belong only to Thing list items, while subject seeds must stay unchanged. The criterion should be generated when visible trajectory evidence shows the agent adding note fields or note preservation broadly across seed dictionaries, templates, or serialization paths. It is especially important if the edit UI appears to render a note textarea for every seed, if normalization preserves a note after converting a subject pseudo-key to a subject string, if the Seed wrapper exposes notes for values identified as subjects, or if the list view renders `seed.note` without ensuring the seed is a note-capable Thing. A better rubric should focus on the full invariant across input normalization, stored data shape, edit UI, model/API serialization, and display: subject/string seeds should remain strings, submitted notes for subject pseudo-keys should be discarded rather than attached, and view/edit code should not offer or render notes for subject rows. Avoid the tempting weaker proxy of checking only that notes are preserved for non-subject seed dicts, or that Markdown rendering exists somewhere; those can coexist with a violation of the excluded seed-type contract. Also avoid treating this as the only correctness criterion, since an implementation can respect subject exclusion while still breaking Thing-seed resolution, note round-tripping, safe Markdown placement, or list add/remove behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Preserves Subject-Seed Note Exclusion
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The implementation maintains the explicit boundary that only resolvable Thing-like list items may have public notes, while subject/string seeds remain unchanged and note-less. Judge visible trajectory evidence from the current work: normalization of submitted seeds should convert subject pseudo-keys or subject strings to the existing subject-string representation and drop any note value; persisted list seed data should not turn subject seeds into note-bearing dictionaries; edit UI generation should avoid note controls for subject seeds; model/API wrappers should not expose note data for subject-type seeds; and list views should not render public notes beneath subject entries. The strongest evidence shows this invariant handled consistently across input, storage, editing, serialization, and rendering.

metadata.task_boundary: Notes apply only to Thing-like seeds; subject/string seeds are explicitly excluded.
evidence_to_prioritize: Seed input normalization discards notes when the seed is or becomes a subject string.
Subject seeds remain represented as strings rather than note-bearing dictionaries.
Edit form logic conditionally omits note textareas for subject seeds.
Display/API logic does not render or serialize notes for subject-type seeds.
Thing-seed note support is implemented without broadening the subject-seed contract.
common_visible_risks: A note field is added unconditionally for every rendered seed.
Normalization preserves a note after converting a subject pseudo-key to a subject string.
View code checks only for a note attribute and renders it without excluding subject seeds.
Model changes treat all seed dictionaries as note-capable without guarding subject keys.

scale.1: The visible implementation actively violates the boundary, such as by accepting, storing, editing, or rendering notes for subject/string seeds.
scale.2: There is weak or inconsistent protection: one layer drops subject notes, but other visible layers still expose note fields, preserve note data, or render notes for subject seeds.
scale.3: The trajectory provides no clear net improvement over the parent on this invariant, or the evidence is too ambiguous to tell whether subject seeds can receive notes.
scale.4: The implementation clearly prevents subject notes in the main normalization/storage path and mostly avoids subject note rendering, with only minor unverified edges remaining.
scale.5: The implementation consistently preserves subject seeds as note-less strings across normalization, persistence, edit UI, model/API serialization, and list-view rendering while allowing notes only for Thing-like seeds.

experiences.title: Do not equate seed type aliases with behavior-safe list cleanup
experiences.description: Retrieve this when generating rubrics for Python dynamic-model cleanup tasks where polymorphic inputs are being typed, especially list seed handling with object, key-dict, and subject-string variants.
experiences.context: The misleading pattern is a rubric that rewards the presence of `TypedDict`, `Union`/type aliases, or nominal type guards for heterogeneous seed values as if that alone predicts a correct patch. In this Open Library-style Python codebase, list seeds flow through dynamic Infogami `Thing` objects, dictionaries, subject strings, web/API normalization, export, Solr query construction, and tests. A seed-typing rubric can still be useful when the task is narrowly about seed type definitions and the trajectory shows behavior-preserving normalization across all call sites. It is misleading when the task also asks for related-module annotations, casting safety, URL/user cleanup, and regression-free simplification, or when the trajectory only shows broad rewrites, imports/signature checks, or unresolved runtime/test failures.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster focused on whether the agent introduced `SeedDict`, `SeedSubjectString`, `SeedValue`, type guards, and annotations for `add_seed`, `remove_seed`, `get_seed`, and `Seed.__init__`. That criterion is incomplete: agents can add those names while still breaking existing behavior by treating dict seeds as objects, assuming subject seeds have object `.type.key`, changing stored seed representations, missing related web/API normalization, omitting requested return types in other modules, or dismissing failing list tests as pre-existing without evidence. A better rubric should focus on evidence that each accepted seed shape is normalized once and then safely handled in add/remove/has/get/export/query/presentation paths, that related modules mentioned by the task are inspected or updated, and that failing tests or manual repros are investigated to a concrete root cause. Avoid the tempting criterion “defines precise polymorphic seed types” as a standalone positive signal. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence from diffs, test output, and debugging: preservation of accepted inputs, no object-only attribute assumptions on strings/dicts, no unrelated registration/setup workarounds, and coverage of the broader cleanup scope beyond the central model file.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that present polymorphic seed typing as complete while visible evidence shows incomplete behavior-preserving normalization or incomplete task scope. This applies when the task requires typing and cleanup for a dynamic list model and related modules, and the agent mainly adds `TypedDict`/`Union` aliases or annotations without proving that object seeds, key-dict seeds, and subject-string seeds still work through add/remove/indexing, `Seed` wrapping, Solr query/export paths, and API/web normalization. It also applies when the trajectory shows unresolved runtime errors, failed list-related tests being dismissed without traceback/root-cause analysis, or unrelated setup/registration changes used as a workaround. Do not apply this penalty merely because the agent is still in early exploration before editing; apply it when the generated criterion would over-reward superficial type coverage despite visible missing validation or regressions.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial polymorphic seed typing masks behavior regressions

metadata.task_type: Python type-annotation and cleanup task for dynamic model code
metadata.avoid_proxy: presence of SeedDict/SeedValue/type aliases/type guards alone
prioritize_evidence: normalization handles object, key-dict, and subject-string seed variants consistently
seed paths avoid unsafe `.key` or `.type.key` assumptions on strings/dicts
related API/web/user/cast/URL cleanup scope is considered when requested
failing tests and manual repros are investigated rather than dismissed
patch avoids unrelated registration/setup workarounds

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory either remains in exploration or shows behavior-preserving seed normalization across variants, related-scope awareness, and credible validation.
scale.2: Minor evidence: type aliases or annotations are emphasized, but the trajectory also shows some checks of runtime seed behavior and no clear unresolved failures.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent adds seed typing and some normalization, but visible work is mostly central-model-only or lacks validation of one or more seed variants or related modules.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory over-relies on type definitions/signature checks while tests fail, runtime seed paths show attribute errors or ambiguous dict/string handling, or requested related cleanup is largely ignored.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the patch is a broad rewrite that breaks or leaves unresolved core seed behavior, dismisses failing tests without root cause, and/or adds unrelated workarounds while claiming polymorphic seed type safety is complete.

experiences.title: Printer dispatch support for unsupported indexed expressions
experiences.description: Use when a SymPy-style code-printer task reports unsupported-code comments for an expression type and asks for a small dispatch method that should render normal target-language syntax.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/SymPy printing subsystem when the task is specifically about `pycode`/`PythonCodePrinter` emitting `# Not supported` for `Indexed` and the trajectory has found the printer class, reproduced or discussed the unsupported fallback, or is editing the printer dispatch methods. The criterion is most decisive after implementation or validation evidence is visible, but it can still guide early exploration by checking whether the agent is moving toward the localized printer method. It is less applicable for tasks about tensor indexing semantics, code generation memory layout, C/JS-style flattened indexing, generic lambdify behavior, dependency installation, or broad refactors outside the Python code printer.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic output contract: add printer dispatch support for `Indexed` in the Python code printer so `pycode(IndexedBase('p')[0])` becomes plain subscription syntax with no unsupported-code comment, and so multiple, symbolic, or compound indices are joined as Python subscripts using the printer for each index. This aligned well because visible trajectories often showed the exact missing dispatch path, the unsupported fallback behavior, and later validation outputs such as `p[0]`, `p[0, 1]`, or `p[i + 1, 2*j]` without warning comments. A better rubric should not merely reward repository exploration, installing missing dependencies, or running existing tests; those are supporting evidence only. It also should not require copying C/JS printer implementations, because those flatten indices for memory layout and are a tempting but wrong proxy for Python subscription syntax. Avoid over-specifying optional extras such as adding an `IndexedBase` printer or changing lambdify internals when the task is satisfied by the localized `Indexed` printer method. Prioritize evidence that the method is placed on the relevant Python printer class, decomposes the expression into base and all indices, renders `base[index1, index2, ...]`, recursively prints index expressions, and eliminates the unsupported-code path.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement localized Python code-printer support for SymPy `Indexed` expressions by adding the appropriate dispatch method on the Python code printer. The implementation should render indexed expressions as normal Python subscription syntax, preserve all indices in order including multi-index, symbolic, and compound index expressions, use the printer's normal formatting for index expressions, and prevent the unsupported-code comment from appearing in `pycode` output. Strong evidence includes a clean edit in the printer class plus validation of the original reproducer and representative multi-index cases.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Localized Indexed subscription printing

metadata.target_component: Python code printer dispatch for Indexed expressions
important_evidence: method added to the Python printer dispatch class rather than unrelated lambdify or generic fallback code
indices are collected from the Indexed expression and printed with the printer
single-index and multi-index outputs are validated or directly visible
unsupported-code warning/comment is absent after the change
avoid_as_primary_evidence: dependency installation only
copying flattened-index behavior from non-Python printers
broad refactors unrelated to the missing dispatch method

scale.1: No evidence of moving toward printer support for `Indexed`; the trajectory is only generic exploration, dependency setup, or unrelated code changes.
scale.2: Identifies the unsupported `Indexed` printing issue or relevant files, but has not made a credible localized implementation and may be distracted by unrelated printer or lambdify changes.
scale.3: Has located the Python printer and is on the correct approach, or has a partial/uncertain edit, but lacks clear evidence that `Indexed` renders correctly without unsupported comments.
scale.4: Adds a plausible `Indexed` dispatch method in the Python printer that formats Python subscripts and prints indices appropriately, with at least basic validation of the original case.
scale.5: Cleanly implements the localized dispatch method and verifies no unsupported comments for the original case plus multi-index, symbolic, or compound index examples, without introducing unrelated printer semantics.

experiences.title: End-to-End Dynamic Registry Credential Wiring
experiences.description: Use when a Go/ORAS OCI-registry task requires replacing static username/password auth with provider-backed expiring-token auth such as AWS ECR via the AWS credentials chain.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories for a Go codebase using ORAS or a similar OCI registry client where investigation has exposed a static registry-auth path and the task asks for continuous pulls across expiring cloud registry tokens. It is most useful once the agent has identified the central registry client construction and config schema/structs, or has begun editing those areas. It is premature as a strict implementation criterion during very early file discovery, and it is not relevant for tasks that only require static credentials, a one-shot login command, unrelated AWS storage integration, or documentation-only changes.
experiences.experience: The useful criterion in these cases is not merely whether the agent mentions AWS ECR or researches ORAS credentials; it should require visible end-to-end implementation of dynamic provider-backed auth. Previous rubrics were directionally right when they emphasized an AWS SDK-backed ORAS credential callback, because static username/password changes do not solve token expiry. They were too broad when they gave credit for repeated API discovery, a nested config idea with no validation, or a naive token fetch that was not wired through all OCI store creation paths. A better rubric should focus on concrete evidence: a backwards-compatible config discriminator or provider mode for OCI authentication; schema and Go config structs kept in sync; a store option abstraction that can select static or AWS ECR auth and reject unsupported modes; an AWS ECR credential function using the AWS SDK default config/credential chain and ECR authorization-token API, returning registry username/password credentials and refreshing on demand or by expiration; ORAS auth client wiring at the central remote repository construction point; wiring through both runtime storage sync and bundle/CLI store construction; required dependency updates and validation/tests where the repo convention requires them. Avoid tempting proxies such as simply adding an `aws_ecr` field, fetching a token once at startup, using AWS access keys directly as registry credentials, changing only the polling loop, relying on nonexistent built-in ORAS ECR support, or rewarding repeated greps/go-doc commands as implementation progress.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete Dynamic ECR Auth Path
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate an end-to-end dynamic OCI registry authentication implementation for AWS ECR: user configuration can explicitly select AWS ECR while preserving existing static username/password behavior; config schema, decoded structs, validation/defaulting, and generated schema/test fixtures are kept consistent; the OCI store option model accepts a credential-function/provider abstraction rather than storing only static secrets; the AWS ECR provider loads AWS configuration through the default credentials chain, calls the ECR authorization-token API, decodes the Docker-style token into registry credentials, and refreshes credentials on demand or with expiration awareness; the central ORAS remote client uses this dynamic CredentialFunc for registry requests; both server-side OCI storage sync and bundle/CLI OCI operations pass the selected auth mode; dependency and build/test updates are present enough to make the code compile and validate.

metadata.applicability: Go OCI registry clients using ORAS or equivalent auth callbacks; tasks involving expiring provider-backed registry tokens such as AWS ECR.
required_visible_evidence: configuration mode or discriminator for static versus AWS ECR auth
schema and runtime config structs updated consistently
central store/client option abstraction supports dynamic credential functions
AWS SDK default credential chain plus ECR authorization-token retrieval
token decoded into registry username/password and refreshed beyond process startup
ORAS auth client receives the dynamic credential function
all relevant OCI store construction paths are wired
static auth remains backward compatible
dependency and validation/test updates are addressed
common_false_positives: only researching CredentialFunc or AWS docs
adding config fields without runtime wiring
fetching one ECR token once and treating it as static
using AWS access keys as registry username/password
wiring only CLI or only server storage
missing schema/dependency/build updates

scale.1: No substantive evidence of dynamic provider-backed registry auth; trajectory only repeats searches/docs or preserves static username/password behavior.
scale.2: Identifies the correct integration concept, such as ORAS CredentialFunc and AWS ECR token retrieval, but has little or no coherent code/config wiring.
scale.3: Partial implementation exists, but it is incomplete or fragile: for example only one consumer is wired, schema and structs diverge, the ECR token is fetched once without refresh semantics, dependencies are missing, or static auth compatibility is unclear.
scale.4: Strong implementation of the dynamic provider and central ORAS wiring with most configuration and consumer paths covered, but some validation, generated schema, tests, dependency hygiene, or edge-case refresh behavior remains incomplete.
scale.5: Complete, coherent, and build-ready end-to-end solution covering config/schema/defaults, AWS ECR credential provider with refresh behavior, central ORAS CredentialFunc integration, all OCI store creation paths, static-auth compatibility, dependencies, and tests/fixtures.

experiences.title: Composer Signature Pipeline Entry-Point Coverage
experiences.description: Use when a mail/composer task requires an existing signature-insertion pipeline to carry new user-specific signature content, especially in a TypeScript monorepo where early exploration may confuse settings UI or shared preview helpers with actual draft assembly.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories for webmail/composer fixes where the problem statement explicitly says to reuse the standard signature pipeline for new, reply, reply-all, and forward drafts, with sender-specific signatures, HTML/plain-text conversion, blank-line normalization, and optional product/referral footer behavior. It is most useful during exploration or early implementation review: visible evidence should show whether the agent has found the real draft-construction path and the signature rendering/update path, not merely generic editor components, settings toggles, API request helpers, or shared footer preview utilities. Do not apply as the main criterion for unrelated composer UI work, for tasks that intentionally add a new independent footer mechanism, or after the agent has already clearly identified all relevant entry points—in that later stage, use a narrower implementation-correctness rubric instead.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases asked whether the agent located and planned to integrate with the existing signature insertion pipeline across draft creation paths. That was discriminative because the visible trajectories repeatedly spent many steps in reusable components/settings folders, found only signature preview/toggle utilities or generic editor code, and had not yet identified the mail app draft assembly and sender-change/editor content paths. Such evidence predicts weak patches: agents that do not anchor on the real draft pipeline tend to pass referral/user settings ad hoc, misuse hooks, alter unrelated behavior, or miss plain-text, reply/forward, external composer, and sender-switch cases. A better rubric should focus on concrete discovery and coverage: has the trajectory found the draft builder for all compose actions, the helper that inserts/replaces signatures, the sender-selection path that changes signatures, the content conversion path, and any alternate composer path; and does it preserve the existing formatting/positioning semantics instead of appending referral links manually. Avoid tempting but weak criteria such as “found getProtonMailSignature,” “searched for composer files,” “modified a shared signature string,” or “added user settings somewhere”; those are insufficient unless tied to the actual pipeline that builds draft body HTML and updates it when sender/content mode changes. Prioritize visible evidence of exact integration points, call-chain understanding, and recognition that settings/preview components are not the draft insertion path.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates that the agent has identified the real mail draft-construction and signature-update pipeline and is using it as the basis for the referral-link signature fix. Strong evidence includes locating the draft builder used for new, reply, reply-all, and forward actions; tracing how the selected sender's configured signature is chosen before draft body assembly; finding the standard signature template/insert/change helper rather than creating a parallel append path; accounting for HTML cleanup, line-break and blank-line behavior, product footer ordering/settings, and plain-text-to-HTML conversion; and noticing alternate composer/content paths such as sender switching or external/reply composers. The criterion should reward understanding and planned integration with these existing pathways, not mere repository search or edits to preview/settings helpers.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Real Draft Signature Pipeline Located and Covered

required_visible_evidence: draft assembly entry point for multiple compose actions
standard signature insertion or replacement helper
sender-specific signature selection before insertion
HTML/plain-text formatting and blank-line behavior
recognition of non-draft settings or preview code as insufficient
anti_patterns: only finding settings toggles or signature previews
only inspecting generic editor components
adding a separate referral-link append mechanism
passing user/referral data through isolated call sites without tracing all compose paths

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent has found the actual draft construction or signature insertion path; exploration remains in unrelated settings, preview, generic editor, or low-level API code.
scale.2: Some relevant signature or composer concepts are found, but the trajectory has not connected them to the draft body assembly path used by compose actions.
scale.3: The trajectory has behavior comparable to the parent: it has partial leads toward draft/signature code but still lacks clear coverage of all compose actions and the standard insertion/update pipeline.
scale.4: The agent has located the main draft builder and standard signature helper and shows intent to reuse them, with some attention to sender selection and formatting, though one secondary path or conversion mode may still be uncertain.
scale.5: The agent clearly traces the full existing pipeline across compose actions, sender changes, content conversion, and alternate composer paths, and frames the fix as carrying referral-capable signature data through that pipeline without duplicating formatting logic.

experiences.title: Identity Tuple Hashability for Mutable Relation Options
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django-style relation/object identity tuple is used for equality or hashing and the reported failure is an unhashable mutable option, especially when the task names the standard hash-normalization utility.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Django repository trajectories where the visible task or investigation shows an object implements equality/hash via an `identity` tuple, one identity component can legally be a list or other mutable container, and the codebase already has a utility/pattern for normalizing such values before hashing. This is most useful once the agent has inspected the relation identity implementation or is at final-review with a visible diff. If the trajectory is still only resolving environment setup or has not yet located the identity tuple, use a scale that credits diagnosis but does not require completed implementation. Do not retrieve for unrelated many-to-many validation issues, database schema behavior, proxy-model check counts, or failures where the fix is to reject invalid user input rather than preserve valid list/tuple semantics.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases focused on the semantic invariant: every element placed in an identity tuple that feeds `__hash__` must itself be hashable, and mutable user-provided configuration must be converted with the project’s existing hash-normalization utility. This aligned well because the decisive visible evidence was a one-line change wrapping the mutable `through_fields` value at the point it is added to the relation identity, while preserving the surrounding identity components. A better rubric should judge whether the trajectory both identifies the identity/hash path and applies the standard utility to the specific mutable component, with secondary credit for validation that list-valued input hashes successfully and remains equivalent to tuple-valued input. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as merely running many-to-many/proxy tests, adding an ad hoc reproduction script, changing `__hash__`, rejecting lists, converting the public stored option in a constructor, or broadly altering relation equality. Test coverage is helpful evidence but should not replace checking the actual identity construction; conversely, a correct minimal code change can be strong even if no formal regression test has been added yet.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should preserve identity-based equality and hashing by normalizing the specific mutable relation option before it is included in the identity tuple. Strong evidence includes locating the relation identity property used by `__hash__`, observing the existing project pattern for `make_hashable()` on comparable identity members, changing only the mutable `through_fields` identity element to use that utility, preserving the other identity tuple elements and public relation behavior, and validating that list-valued input no longer raises `TypeError` while tuple or unset values retain equivalent semantics.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Hashable Relation Identity Construction

required_visible_evidence: The task or trajectory shows equality/hash depends on an identity tuple.
A mutable user-provided option such as list-valued relation field names is included in that identity tuple.
The repository has an existing hash-normalization utility or pattern for identity members.
The proposed or applied change normalizes the mutable identity member at identity construction rather than changing unrelated checks.
secondary_evidence: Focused reproduction demonstrates hashing fails before or would fail for list-valued input.
Validation demonstrates list-valued input hashes successfully after the change.
Validation or reasoning preserves equality/hash consistency between list and tuple representations.
Existing targeted tests for related relation/check behavior pass.
avoid_as_primary_evidence: Proxy model checks passing without inspecting the identity tuple.
Broad many-to-many test runs alone.
Rejecting list input as invalid.
Changing generic hash/equality behavior instead of normalizing the mutable identity component.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory connects the unhashable-list failure to identity tuple construction; proposed work is unrelated, such as changing proxy checks, many-to-many validation, or generic test setup only.
scale.2: The trajectory identifies that a mutable option may be causing hash failure or finds the relevant relation identity code, but no visible change applies the project’s normalization utility to the mutable identity component.
scale.3: The trajectory makes partial or uncertain progress equivalent to the parent behavior: it modifies the relevant identity/hash area or proposes normalization, but either the exact mutable component is not clearly handled, other identity semantics may be disturbed, or validation is absent.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly updates the relevant identity tuple construction to normalize the mutable relation option with the standard utility while preserving the other identity members, with some focused reasoning or reproduction showing the list hash failure is addressed.
scale.5: The trajectory provides the targeted normalization of the mutable identity component, preserves list/tuple/None behavior and identity equality semantics, avoids unrelated behavioral changes, and includes convincing visible validation such as successful hashing of list input plus consistency with tuple input or passing relevant targeted tests.

experiences.title: Avatar Color End-to-End Wiring Over Discovery
experiences.description: Use for NodeBB-like avatar background-color customization tasks once the trajectory has found the existing generated-avatar color field/palette or has begun edits; evaluate whether the user-selectable color is wired from UI selection through validated persistence to rendering fallback, not merely whether the codebase was understood.
experiences.context: Applies in a Node.js/NodeBB-style codebase where generated avatar icons already have a render-facing background color field, a username-derived default palette, account edit or picture-selection UI, and user/profile update flows. This guidance is most useful after the agent has located the existing avatar color generation/rendering path or is modifying profile/settings/client/template code. It is less appropriate for very early repository exploration before the render field or update path is known, and should be narrowed if the task is only to document an API or only to change rendering. If the feature request explicitly allows arbitrary CSS colors rather than available options, replace palette enforcement with safe CSS validation; otherwise prefer available-option validation.
experiences.experience: In these cases, rubrics that rewarded broad discovery or general understanding of the avatar color system were too permissive: an agent could correctly identify the palette, render helper, and profile update path but still produce an inaccessible, unpersisted, or unsafe implementation. Rubrics became more useful when they focused on concrete end-to-end evidence: a user-visible selector in the active account/avatar UI, client code that sends the selected value through the existing save/change flow, backend code that persists the selected value in the data model actually used by avatar rendering, validation against the existing available palette, and fallback to the username-derived color when no valid custom value exists. Avoid the tempting proxy criterion of “has found all relevant files” or “added a color field somewhere”; also avoid over-focusing on a template-only change unless the cutoff already shows backend persistence and rendering are complete. Prioritize visible trajectory evidence such as inspected diffs/commands showing the selector markup, submit handler payload, update controller/profile/settings persistence, user-data color resolution, whitelist/field inclusion, allowed-color source, and fallback behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Selectable Avatar Background Color
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate an implementation plan or edits that make avatar background color customization genuinely usable end to end: expose the existing allowed color choices to the account/avatar UI; let the user select one through a visible control; send that selected value through the existing authenticated profile or picture update flow; validate or clamp the value against the available palette; persist it in the same user data path used to produce rendered avatar icon data; render future avatars with the selected color while preserving the username-derived fallback for unset or invalid selections. Credit should depend on concrete wiring evidence, not on merely locating the color-generation code or adding an isolated field.

required_visible_evidence: existing generated-avatar background color field and username-derived palette have been identified
user-facing selector or equivalent UI is added in the active account/avatar customization surface
client submit/change handler includes the selected color in the existing update request or socket/API call
server-side update path persists the selected color for the target user with existing permission checks
server-side validation uses the available palette or an explicitly safe color contract
user data assembly prefers a valid persisted color and falls back to the deterministic default
rendering continues to consume the established avatar icon color field without breaking uploaded/default avatar behavior
common_false_positives: only discovering relevant files and functions
only adding translations or labels
only adding a backend field with no UI submission path
only adding a UI control with no persistence
accepting arbitrary unsanitized color strings when the task says available options
loading custom color through an unrelated setting branch that may not run

scale.1: No concrete implementation evidence beyond initial exploration, or changes are unrelated to the avatar icon color path.
scale.2: Identifies the existing avatar color field/palette and proposes changes, but lacks implemented UI, persistence, or render-resolution wiring.
scale.3: Implements some relevant pieces, such as backend storage or a UI control, but at least one essential link is missing or visibly fragile, so the selected color may not be selectable, saved, validated, or rendered reliably.
scale.4: Shows strong end-to-end wiring with UI, client submission, persistence, render-field resolution, and fallback behavior, with only minor uncertainty around theme coverage, documentation, or polish.
scale.5: Provides complete, coherent wiring across UI, client, authenticated backend persistence, palette exposure/validation, render data resolution, fallback behavior, and visible verification or tests that the selected color persists and appears on subsequent avatar renders.

experiences.title: End-to-End Reachability Population for Port Exposure Features
experiences.description: Retrieve when a scanning/reporting task asks to turn existing listening-port data into vulnerability exposure signals by probing endpoint reachability and surfacing the result in model, summary, and detail output.
experiences.context: Applies in Go scanner/reporting codebases where affected processes already have listening-port data and the requested feature requires a new structured port model plus active reachability probing. Most useful once the trajectory has moved beyond repository exploration into implementation or review, especially when visible edits touch the package/process model, lsof/listener parsing, scan workflow integration, and report/TUI formatting. It is less useful as the sole criterion for very early exploration with no edits, for tasks that only reformat already-computed exposure data, or when an obvious compile-time/file-corruption issue is the dominant observable blocker; in those cases pair it with build/integration integrity rather than replacing it.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged whether the trajectory implemented the core semantic contract: exposure is not just a new field or glyph, but a value computed by probing listening endpoints from the relevant host/network addresses and writing successful addresses into each affected process port. This aligned well because many trajectories added `ListenPort` structs or report formatting but either lacked reliable scanning, wired scanning at the wrong point, damaged scan flow, failed to expand wildcard listeners, mishandled IPv6 parsing, or produced nondeterministic/duplicated results. A better rubric should focus on end-to-end data flow: parse listener address/port without losing wildcard or bracketed IPv6 syntax; collect/de-duplicate affected-process ports; run bounded reachability checks after port data exists and before results are converted/rendered; expand `*` using configured IPv4 addresses; populate unique, deterministic success-address slices; and make both summary and detail views depend on that populated exposure state. Avoid the tempting weaker criterion of merely checking that model fields, helper names, or a `◉` string were added, since those can be present while no correct exposure computation exists. Also avoid judging generic network dialing in isolation without checking that it is integrated into the scanner lifecycle and updates the same package/process objects consumed by reports. Prioritize visible evidence from the trajectory such as changed listener parsing, scan workflow call sites, use of server address lists, timeout/de-dup/order handling, helper methods that inspect nested port-scan results, and report code that renders empty ports and scannable addresses from the model rather than hardcoded markers.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Port Exposure Computation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a coherent implementation of port exposure as computed state, not just display text. Strong evidence includes a structured listen-port model with address, port, and successful scan addresses; scanner-side parsing that preserves wildcard and bracketed IPv6 forms; reachability probing integrated after affected-process listen ports are collected and before scan results are rendered or converted; wildcard listeners expanded against configured IPv4 addresses; bounded connection attempts that record only successful target/source addresses; deterministic empty/non-nil slices, stable ordering, and de-duplication of both listen endpoints and success-address lists; package-level helpers that detect nested scan successes; and summary/detail output that derives the `◉` indicator and `addr:port(◉ Scannable: [...])` text from populated model data, including literal `Port: []` when no ports exist.

metadata.task_family: network exposure enrichment for vulnerability scan reports
primary_evidence: model field migration from raw port strings to structured listen-port objects
listener parsing handles IPv4, wildcard, and bracketed IPv6 without corrupting printable address
reachability probing is called in the scan lifecycle after affected-process ports are known
configured host/server IP address lists are used for wildcard expansion and scan targets
PortScanSuccessOn-like data is populated uniquely and deterministically
summary and detailed renderers consume the populated exposure state
anti_evidence: only adds display glyphs or helper names without a probe path
only changes reports while scan results never contain successful addresses
runs generic local dials disconnected from affected process ports or configured host addresses
uses map iteration or nil slices where deterministic empty ordered results are required
breaks existing scanner interfaces or leaves build-visible corruption while adding exposure code

scale.1: No meaningful exposure computation is visible: changes are absent, purely cosmetic, or limited to unrelated exploration; no credible path exists from collected listen ports to populated successful scan addresses.
scale.2: Weak progress: introduces some model or formatting pieces, but active probing is missing, not integrated with affected-process ports, or cannot populate success-address data consumed by reports.
scale.3: Moderate progress: implements parts of parsing, probing, or rendering, but has important gaps such as incomplete workflow integration, missing wildcard expansion, fragile IPv6 handling, nondeterministic/duplicated results, or summary/detail output not consistently derived from scan results.
scale.4: Strong progress: shows an end-to-end path from collected listener data through bounded reachability checks to model population and report rendering, with most required edge cases handled; only minor validation, placement, or determinism concerns remain.
scale.5: Complete, robust evidence: listener parsing, workflow integration, port probing, wildcard expansion, IPv6 bracket preservation, de-duplication, deterministic empty/ordered slices, package exposure helpers, and all required summary/detail outputs are implemented coherently and are visibly validated or structured to compile cleanly.

experiences.title: Sentinel index dtype capacity in NumPy-backed lookup arrays
experiences.description: Retrieve when a trajectory is addressing NumPy deprecation warnings or overflow errors caused by storing special lookup-table sentinel indices into narrow integer arrays, especially in colormap-style array indexing code.
experiences.context: Applies in Python scientific stack tasks, particularly NumPy 1.24+ compatibility work, where visible evidence shows an index array preserves an input dtype such as uint8/int8 and later receives reserved sentinel values outside that dtype's range before a lookup-table take/index operation. It is most useful once the trajectory has identified the assignment site and the reserved indices, or is already proposing a fix. It is less applicable to unrelated deprecations, byte-output/LUT-value conversion issues, backend/import failures, or cases where the real problem is constructing invalid narrow-dtype arrays before the library code runs. It should not be used to reward fixes that merely silence warnings, clamp sentinel values, or rely on old wraparound behavior, because those can destroy under/over/bad lookup semantics.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on whether the agent preserved the semantic role of the special lookup indices by widening the index array before sentinel assignment. That criterion aligned well because the decisive visible evidence was concrete: warnings/errors named values like 256, 257, and 258 being assigned into uint8; the code showed integer inputs bypassing the float path's cast to a wider integer type; and later lookup logic expected those sentinel values to remain valid indices into extra LUT rows. A better rubric should therefore ask whether the trajectory ensures the index array can represent all normal and special indices before assignment, and whether it preserves float scaling, integer-index behavior, masks/bad values, under/over handling, empty arrays, scalar/array shapes, and byte-output semantics. Avoid the tempting but wrong criterion of accepting clamping, modulo overflow, converting the LUT output to bytes, or treating the bug as only an empty-array special case. Prioritize observable evidence such as root-cause statements about dtype capacity, a patch or plan that widens integer index arrays before special-index writes, and validation with warnings-as-errors or stricter NumPy behavior on empty and non-empty narrow integer inputs plus representative float/masked/bytes paths.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should correctly fix the NumPy compatibility issue by ensuring the colormap/index array is converted to an integer dtype capable of representing reserved under/over/bad sentinel indices before those sentinels are assigned. A high-quality trajectory recognizes that the issue is the dtype capacity of the index array, not LUT byte conversion or warning suppression; preserves normal float scaling and integer lookup semantics; keeps masked/bad, under-range, over-range, empty-array, scalar/array shape, and bytes-output behavior intact; and validates with the reported narrow integer reproducer under warnings-as-errors or a stricter NumPy version, ideally with additional representative integer, float, masked, and bytes-output checks.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Widen index dtype before sentinel assignment

key_evidence: Reported warning/error involves assigning reserved indices outside a narrow integer dtype's range
Code path shows integer inputs retaining their original dtype while float inputs are cast wider
Reserved sentinels are required as lookup-table indices and must not be clamped or wrapped
Validation covers the reported narrow integer reproducer and checks no regression in related colormap paths
avoid_credit_for: Clamping sentinel values into the narrow dtype
Relying on overflow/wraparound casts
Only changing byte-output LUT conversion
Suppressing warnings without preserving lookup semantics

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory identifies or addresses out-of-range sentinel assignment into narrow integer index arrays.
scale.2: The trajectory notices a NumPy integer overflow/deprecation symptom but proposes an incomplete or risky fix such as warning suppression, clamping, byte-output changes, or handling only the exact empty input without preserving sentinel semantics.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies dtype capacity as the likely issue and moves toward widening integer index arrays, but evidence is partial: the fix location, semantic preservation, or validation of related paths remains uncertain.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly widens integer index arrays before sentinel assignment and validates the reported reproducer, with reasonable attention to preserving normal integer and float lookup behavior.
scale.5: The trajectory provides a robust sentinel-safe dtype fix before assignment, avoids clamping/wraparound, preserves float, integer, masked/bad, under/over, empty-array, scalar/array, and bytes-output semantics, and validates the reported case plus representative edge cases under warning/error-sensitive NumPy behavior.

experiences.title: Descriptor-Safe Admin Field Lookup
experiences.description: Use when a Django admin list_display validation task involves false admin.E108 errors caused by model fields whose class-level descriptors make hasattr()/getattr() unreliable, and the trajectory is evaluating or modifying the lookup logic.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django source checkout when the task or trajectory concerns ModelAdmin list_display checks, especially a regression where a valid model field is present in model metadata but class attribute access fails or returns misleading values. The criterion is most useful once the agent has located the admin list_display item validator or is proposing/testing a patch to its model-field resolution control flow. It is less useful for unrelated admin checks, for tasks only about test-runner setup, or for very early exploration before the trajectory has connected the bug to model metadata lookup versus descriptor/class attribute probing. Do not apply it as a generic Django admin quality rubric unless the visible evidence includes E108/E109 list_display semantics, _meta.get_field(), hasattr()/getattr() behavior, or descriptor edge cases.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged the semantic contract of list_display item resolution rather than superficial activity such as installing dependencies, running broad tests, or merely editing the right file. They were predictive because the decisive bug boundary is visible from the trajectory: a valid field can be found through model metadata even when class-level hasattr()/getattr() fails, so validation must not return E108 just because descriptor probing fails. A strong rubric should require the patch or plan to preserve the full decision table: callables and ModelAdmin attributes remain valid; model metadata lookup is attempted independently of class attribute accessibility; model attribute/method fallback is used only when metadata lookup fails; E108 is returned only when both model-field and model-attribute resolution fail; and ManyToManyField resolution still produces E109. It should also reward evidence that descriptor-returning-None behavior is not conflated with missing fields. Avoid a tempting but weaker criterion such as 'the agent reproduced the PositionField issue' or 'tests pass', because those can miss regressions where nonexistent fields stop raising E108 or ManyToMany fields stop raising E109. Also avoid rewarding patches that simply reorder or remove hasattr() without showing that both metadata and attribute fallback paths still exist. Prioritize visible evidence from code inspection, patch snippets, stated control flow, and focused tests covering a metadata-only field, missing name, ManyToMany field, callable/admin attribute, and descriptor/None edge cases.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the admin list_display item validator resolves model fields through metadata even when model class attribute access is false or unsafe, while preserving the surrounding validation contract: callable entries and admin attributes pass; a model field found through metadata passes unless it is a many-to-many field; model attribute/method fallback is attempted when metadata lookup fails; the missing-entry error is emitted only after both model-field and model-attribute resolution fail; and descriptor values such as None are not treated as lookup failure by sentinel conflation.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Descriptor-Safe list_display Resolution Contract

metadata.environment: Django admin system checks for ModelAdmin list_display validation
required_visible_evidence: recognizes class-level hasattr/getattr on model descriptors can be unreliable
attempts model metadata field lookup regardless of class attribute accessibility
preserves missing-entry E108 only after both metadata and model attribute lookup fail
preserves many-to-many E109 after successful field resolution
preserves valid callables and ModelAdmin attributes
common_failure_modes: keeps hasattr(model, item) as a gate before metadata lookup
accepts every missing model attribute without E108
drops or narrows the ManyToManyField E109 check
uses None as a missing-field sentinel and rejects descriptors returning None
tests only the happy descriptor case without missing-field or many-to-many coverage

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses descriptor-safe model field resolution; it relies on the existing class attribute/hasattr behavior or focuses only on environment/test setup.
scale.2: Weak evidence of the issue is present, such as mentioning descriptors or E108, but the proposed behavior is incomplete or risks accepting missing fields, skipping metadata lookup, or ignoring E109.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory attempts to change lookup order or reproduce the metadata-versus-hasattr problem, but does not clearly preserve all required outcomes for missing entries, many-to-many fields, and normal callable/admin attribute cases.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory implements or clearly plans metadata-first resolution with model attribute fallback and E108 only after both fail, while also preserving E109 and validating at least some important edge cases.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory fully demonstrates the descriptor-safe contract in code or precise plan, explicitly avoids the unsafe hasattr gate and None-sentinel conflation, and validates metadata-only fields, nonexistent names, many-to-many fields, callables/admin attributes, and descriptor edge cases.

experiences.title: Autodoc Mock Generic Subscription Name Normalization
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python documentation/mock-import bug involves generic typing objects, especially TypeVar, reaching dynamic mock name or subclass creation and causing string concatenation/type-name failures.
experiences.context: Applies in Python codebases with autodoc-style mocked imports or dynamic mock objects, when the task or trajectory visibly connects a generic typed class, TypeVar, or typing subscription to a mock object name-building path. It is most useful once the agent has located the dynamic mock factory or subscription/attribute access call path and can see non-string values being used as names. It is less useful for unrelated TypeVar rendering/documenter bugs, real import-resolution failures, or early exploration before the trajectory has tied the crash to mock subscription/name creation rather than general dependency setup.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic boundary that matters: generic subscription keys are not guaranteed to be strings, but mock subclass/display-name construction assumes strings. A good rubric should reward evidence that the agent identifies the mock generic-subscription path, normalizes non-string typing inputs before string concatenation or dynamic class creation, and preserves ordinary mocked attribute/name behavior. Visible evidence to prioritize includes finding the `module + '.' + name`-style failure, tracing calls from mock item access or dynamic subclass creation, reproducing the TypeError with `TypeVar('T')`, observing that `str(TypeVar)` is safe, applying a narrow normalization at the caller or helper that covers the failing path, and running focused checks such as a mocked object indexed by a TypeVar plus existing mock tests. Avoid generating a broad criterion about all generic/typehint rendering, dependency installation, or the external docs project build; those are tempting proxies but do not directly predict whether the mock crash is fixed. Also avoid over-constraining the exact patch location or exact display spelling unless visible tests require it: the judgeable requirement is that non-string generic names are converted safely and normal string-name behavior remains intact.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the agent is fixing the mock-object generic subscription/name path by safely converting TypeVar or other non-string typing objects into usable string names before they are used in display-name concatenation or dynamic class creation, while preserving existing behavior for normal string attribute access and validating the failing TypeVar scenario.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Type-Safe Generic Names in Mock Subclass Creation

required_visible_evidence: Identifies the dynamic mock subclass or display-name construction that assumes a string name
Connects TypeVar or generic subscription to the non-string name argument
Implements or plans a narrow normalization of non-string generic keys/names
Checks that normal string mock attributes still behave as before
Uses a focused TypeVar/mock subscription reproduction or regression test when feasible
avoid_as_primary_evidence: Only installing missing documentation/test dependencies
Only inspecting general TypeVar documenter/typehint rendering code
Only attempting the external project docs build without isolating the mock failure

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses non-string generic values in the mock name/subclass path.
scale.2: Recognizes TypeVar or generics are involved but does not clearly connect them to mock subscription/name construction or proposes only broad unrelated changes.
scale.3: Identifies the string-concatenation/name assumption and the need to handle TypeVar, but implementation or validation of the actual mock subscription path is incomplete.
scale.4: Clearly normalizes TypeVar or other non-string generic names in the relevant mock path and shows focused validation, with only minor uncertainty about coverage or regression testing.
scale.5: Precisely traces the generic subscription path, applies a minimal safe normalization before display-name/dynamic-class use, preserves ordinary mock behavior, and validates both the TypeVar failure case and existing mock behavior.

experiences.title: Import Cover Host Filtering at Record Preprocessing
experiences.description: Use when an Open Library book-import task concerns unsupported external cover URL hosts causing hangs, and the trajectory has exposed the import-to-coverstore path plus ambiguous or absent proxy allow-list config.
experiences.context: Applies in the Open Library Python codebase when `load()`/import records include a `cover` URL that is later sent to coverstore as `source_url`, and investigation shows coverstore eventually performs a remote request while proxy settings are only generic runtime environment configuration. This is most useful after the agent has found the shared import cover path in `openlibrary/catalog/add_book/__init__.py` and before or during patch review. It is less applicable for unrelated cover upload UI behavior, generic download timeout tasks, or very early trajectories that have not yet distinguished import-record cover handling from coverstore internals. Do not retrieve it for tasks where the repository already exposes a clear dedicated cover-host allow-list API with different semantics.
experiences.experience: The earlier rubrics correctly noticed that unsupported cover hosts must be skipped before any remote fetch, but they were too broad when they framed the required policy as `no_proxy_addresses` or a configurable wildcard allow-list. In these cases, visible evidence showed `no_proxy_addresses` only configures proxy environment variables and local config files did not define an actual cover-host policy. Patches that simply read `no_proxy_addresses`, fail open when it is absent, add arbitrary config entries, or validate only inside `add_cover()` can look superficially aligned while still missing the intended import behavior. A better rubric should focus on whether the agent filters the import record’s `cover` URL at the point where the edition/import data is normalized, removes or consumes the `cover` field regardless of whether it is used, parses the URL safely, and only lets known supported cover hosts proceed to `add_cover`/coverstore. It should reward exact, case-insensitive host comparison against a narrow supported-cover-host policy and preserving normal import without a cover for unsupported hosts. Avoid tempting proxy-centric criteria that accept suffix/wildcard matches, fail-open behavior, new dev config keys, extension validation, or merely adding request timeouts.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a fix strategy that filters imported cover URLs during the book import data-processing path before `add_cover` or coverstore download is invoked. Strong evidence includes identifying the `cover` field extraction in the import/load flow, introducing or using a narrow supported cover-host policy, parsing the URL host with standard URL parsing, comparing hosts case-insensitively without broad suffix or fail-open matching, removing/consuming the `cover` key from the edition/import dict even when unsupported, and allowing unsupported hosts to be ignored so the book import continues without attempting a network cover fetch.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Pre-fetch Import Cover Host Gate

key_evidence: import/load flow with a `cover` field is identified
guard occurs before invoking cover upload/fetch
allowed host policy is narrow and cover-specific
unsupported cover URL is skipped without blocking import
the cover field is removed or normalized from import data whether accepted or rejected
anti_patterns: using generic proxy/no_proxy configuration as if it were the cover allow-list without evidence
failing open when no allow-list config is present
adding arbitrary config hosts in dev YAML
only adding timeouts or file-extension validation
checking host only after coverstore has already been contacted

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory plans or implements host filtering for imported cover URLs before fetch/upload.
scale.2: Mentions skipping unsupported cover hosts but remains generic, proxy-centric, or focused on coverstore/download timeouts without tying the fix to import `cover` processing.
scale.3: Identifies the import-to-coverstore path and proposes host validation, but the planned or implemented policy is broad, fail-open, config-dependent without evidence, or placed in a less precise layer.
scale.4: Implements or clearly plans a pre-fetch guard in the import cover path with URL parsing and graceful skipping, though some details such as exact host policy or cover-field cleanup may be incomplete.
scale.5: Clearly filters the import record’s cover URL before `add_cover`/coverstore, uses a narrow case-insensitive allowed-host policy, consumes/removes the cover field consistently, skips unsupported hosts without network access, and preserves supported cover imports.

experiences.title: End-to-End Auditd Contract Over Exploration
experiences.description: Use when a Go service task asks for Linux auditd reporting of login/session/auth-failure activity with platform gating, exact disabled/status-error behavior, and stable audit payloads.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories for OS-level audit integration, especially in a large Go codebase where the agent is locating existing audit/event emitters or has begun adding auditd helpers, wrappers, or event hooks. The criterion is most useful after the task requirements are known and there is visible evidence about implementation choices: new platform-specific files, auditd status checks, message formatting, event conversion, service wiring, or build/test results. It is less useful as a sole criterion during the first few exploratory commands unless phrased to recognize that no implementation evidence exists yet. Do not apply it to generic application audit-log storage tasks that do not require Linux auditd, per-event availability checks, host-level payload semantics, and no effect on non-Linux systems.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful rubrics enumerated the real auditd acceptance contract instead of rewarding repository exploration. They were useful because the visible trajectories repeatedly showed decisive gaps: no code changes yet; utility code that only formatted strings or logged/TODOed instead of sending to auditd; wrappers not wired into the runtime emitter path; build errors; cached or missing auditd status checks; non-Linux stubs with the wrong semantics; and hooks for only one login path while session-end or invalid-auth coverage was still absent. A better rubric should require end-to-end evidence: a Linux-isolated auditd implementation, a safe non-Linux/no-disabled behavior, a status check before every attempted audit event, deterministic key=value formatting with omission of empty optional fields, and hooks at the actual host/session/auth failure points that produce the required audit records. Avoid the tempting proxy of giving credit merely for finding Teleport audit-event structs, adding a central emitter wrapper, passing a utility package build, or covering a single `UserLogin`-style event. Also avoid overfitting to web/SSO application-login events if the task is about host-level Linux audit records; prioritize evidence that the OS account, terminal, remote address, result, and session lifecycle are available at the hook point. The judge should prioritize compile/build evidence, exact error-string behavior, per-event status checking, deterministic payload construction, and complete coverage of the task-named event categories over broad claims in comments or tests that mock only formatting.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Linux Auditd Contract Compliance
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show an implementation path that satisfies the full auditd contract, not just discovery or partial formatting. Strong evidence includes platform-isolated Linux auditd code with non-Linux/no-disabled safety, a real auditd availability/enabled check performed before each relevant event, exact disabled/status-check error behavior, deterministic space-separated key=value payload construction with required fields and omission of an empty optional Teleport-user field, and wiring into the actual runtime paths for user login, session end, and invalid user/auth failure so exactly one auditd message is attempted for each required event without disrupting normal operation when auditd is unavailable.

metadata.task_family: Linux auditd / host audit integration in Go services
evidence_priorities: visible Linux vs non-Linux build-tag or equivalent platform isolation
real auditd status/enabled check before each send, not just once at startup or first use
exact or clearly preserved errors for disabled auditd and failed status checks
deterministic ordered payload fields and conditional omission of empty teleportUser
actual send path to auditd or a realistic auditd client abstraction, not only logging, TODOs, or tests
runtime hooks for all required event categories: login, session end, invalid user/auth failure
build/test evidence for touched packages and no interface-method assumptions contradicted by compiler output
common_false_positives: repository exploration that only locates existing application audit emitters
a formatter or test suite without a real status-gated send path
a generic emitter wrapper that is not wired into the service or does not filter/map required events correctly
coverage of only one login/auth path while session-end or invalid-auth hooks are missing
caching auditd status despite a requirement to check before every event
non-Linux stubs that return success in contexts where callers need to observe disabled/status errors

scale.1: No implementation evidence beyond exploration, or changes are unrelated to auditd reporting.
scale.2: Some auditd-related files, helpers, or payload formatting exist, but they are not wired into real event paths, do not build, or lack real status-gated sending.
scale.3: Partial implementation covers one or two required aspects, such as a formatter plus one login hook or a central wrapper, but important contract pieces remain missing or uncertain: per-event status checks, exact errors, platform behavior, real send path, or full event coverage.
scale.4: Strong implementation evidence covers platform isolation, deterministic formatting, status/error semantics, and most required event hooks, but has a significant remaining risk such as cached status, one missing event category/path, weak send mechanism, or incomplete build/test validation.
scale.5: Complete visible evidence shows a buildable, tested, platform-safe auditd integration that checks enabled status before every relevant event, returns the specified disabled/status-check errors, emits exactly one stable payload per login/session-end/invalid-auth event with correct optional fields, and does not affect non-Linux or auditd-disabled hosts.

experiences.title: Tuple Return Shape Migration Completeness
experiences.description: Use when a TypeScript/React task asks to replace ambiguous multi-value array/tuple returns from cached retrieval APIs with named-field objects.
experiences.context: Applies in codebases where a small set of store/hook-style functions return positional tuples such as links plus a status boolean, and the trajectory is searching for or modifying those APIs and their consumers.
