It is most useful once the agent has identified the exact tuple-returning functions or has begun changing signatures/returns/call sites. It is less useful for unrelated arrays that are semantically single values, for early repository browsing with no target function identified, or for temporary test-file syntax damage unless that syntax issue is the only remaining blocker and the core migration is already complete.
experiences.experience: For tuple-to-object refactor tasks, the discriminative rubric should focus on end-to-end API migration rather than a local edit or transient validation issue. Strong evidence includes: locating the actual cached retrieval helper and public getters returning a tuple; choosing descriptive field names that preserve the original semantics, such as a links array and an is-decrypting/loading boolean; updating TypeScript return annotations and return expressions consistently; converting every consumer from array destructuring or index access to object destructuring or property access, using aliases where existing local names differ; and updating direct return-shape test expectations when present. Earlier generated rubrics that asked only for clear return structure were directionally right but too broad unless they also required all callers and tests to be migrated. Rubrics that focused narrowly on repairing a malformed test edit were brittle when the visible core implementation already matched the task and the test file was not part of the final intended change. Avoid rewarding searches that merely find any `return [...]` array, because unrelated arrays may represent different semantics. Prioritize visible grep results, inspected signatures, changed call-site patterns, and validation evidence over style-only concerns such as whether the object type is inline or named.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete Named-Field Return Migration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates a complete migration of the affected cached retrieval API from positional tuple returns to a named object return shape. It should show evidence that the agent identified the actual tuple-returning cached retrieval helper/getters, preserved the original semantics with descriptive fields for the returned links and decryption/loading status, updated TypeScript signatures and return expressions consistently, and propagated the new access pattern to all visible consumers and direct tests without leaving legacy array destructuring or index access for the migrated API.

key_evidence: Identification of tuple-returning cached retrieval functions rather than unrelated array returns
Return object has semantically descriptive fields for both values
Function signatures and return expressions are changed consistently
Consumers use object destructuring, aliases, or property access instead of tuple destructuring/indexing
Tests or expectations that directly assert the return shape are updated when encountered
Validation or search evidence checks for missed legacy usages
avoid_as_primary_evidence: Generic repository exploration before locating the tuple API
Unrelated arrays used for string/name helpers or validation lists
Transient syntax errors in experimental test edits when the core migration evidence is otherwise decisive
Requiring a separate exported interface when an inline object type would satisfy the task

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent found the affected tuple-returning cached retrieval API; it is still browsing unrelated files or confusing unrelated array returns with the task.
scale.2: The agent has identified a likely tuple-returning cached retrieval function or the desired object shape, but has not yet shown a coherent implementation plan or call-site migration evidence.
scale.3: The trajectory shows partial migration, such as changing the helper return expression or signatures, but visible evidence is incomplete for public getters, consumers, tests, or remaining tuple destructuring/index access.
scale.4: The core API and most visible consumers are migrated to named fields, with semantics preserved and some search or validation evidence, but there may still be minor uncertainty about missed tests/call sites or cleanup.
scale.5: The trajectory provides strong end-to-end evidence: all affected cached retrieval functions return the named object shape, all visible call sites/tests use the new fields, legacy tuple accesses are searched for or eliminated, and relevant typecheck/tests or equivalent validation support the change.

experiences.title: Verify the Footnote’s Full-Details Path
experiences.description: Retrieve this when a CLI table-spoofing task requires truncating/annotating unbounded table fields and adding a footnote that points users to a command for full untruncated details.
experiences.context: Applies in Go CLI codebases with text/ASCII table output plus structured output modes, especially when the task names a full-details command and the trajectory has inspected command registration or searched for that command. It is most useful after the vulnerable list/table renderer and the relevant command hierarchy have been identified. It may be premature during very early file discovery, and it is less relevant for tasks that only require escaping newlines without truncation/annotation or where an existing verified detail command is already known and not being changed.
experiences.experience: Prior rubrics that required truncation, a marker, and a footnote captured an important requirement, but they were too easy to satisfy with superficial newline replacement plus a hardcoded message. In these trajectories, the decisive visible cue was repeated uncertainty or negative search results for the referenced request detail command, followed by plans or edits that either hardcoded the footnote anyway or added a detail command that reused the same truncated overview output. A better rubric should make the footnote contract end-to-end: the list view must safely shorten annotated reason fields, and the referenced path must actually exist or be added and must display the original full details. Avoid the tempting proxy of accepting any `[*]` suffix or any printed footnote. Prioritize evidence that the agent verified command wiring, handled both displayed reason fields, preserved full data in JSON/detail output, and did not point users to an unsupported or still-truncated retrieval path.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Truncation Footnote Contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show that annotated truncation in the list/table view is paired with an accurate, supported way to retrieve the untruncated reason text. Strong evidence includes verifying the CLI command structure before choosing footnote wording; adding or using a real request detail path if none exists; ensuring that detail/structured output preserves full request and resolve reasons rather than reusing the truncated list rendering; and applying the marker/footnote only in the table context where content is shortened or otherwise made safe.

metadata.environment: Go CLI with text table rendering and separate structured output mode
visible_cues: Task requires truncated reason fields with an annotation marker and a footnote for full details
Trajectory has inspected or searched command registration for the referenced detail command
Unbounded request/resolve reason fields are rendered in a table
There is risk of hardcoding a nonexistent command or routing detail output through the same truncated overview renderer
judge_priorities: Accuracy of referenced full-detail retrieval path
Table-only truncation/annotation of unsafe reason fields
Avoidance of unsupported hardcoded footnote text

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of this contract: the trajectory ignores the full-details path, hardcodes unverified guidance, or only discusses generic newline replacement without preserving any way to see full content.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory implements or plans truncation and a marker, but the footnote points to an unverified or absent command, or any added detail command appears to reuse the same truncated table output.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory has identified the command-structure issue and intends to resolve it, but wiring, detail rendering, or preservation of untruncated reasons remains incomplete or not yet verified.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory verifies or adds the referenced detail path and separates safe list rendering from full-detail output, with only minor uncertainty around marker conditions, exact wording, or edge-case sanitization.
scale.5: Complete evidence: the trajectory demonstrates a working end-to-end design where table output safely truncates/annotates all relevant reason fields, the footnote names a supported command, that command or structured output shows untruncated reasons, and machine-readable/full-detail behavior is preserved.

experiences.title: Do not equate arbitrary separator support with using the custom string in numeric contexts
experiences.description: Retrieve when a pretty-printer option is being opened from fixed aliases to arbitrary user strings and the implementation has distinct general-vs-numeric separator paths or comments warning that numbers need an explicit operator.
experiences.context: This applies in Python/SymPy-style printer tasks where a user asks for arbitrary LaTeX multiplication separators such as a thin space, and the visible code normalizes the public option into separate internal settings for ordinary factor separation and number/scientific-notation separation. The misleading case is a trajectory that correctly finds the fixed alias table and adds a fallback for arbitrary strings, but then assigns the same whitespace-like custom string to numeric multiplication as well, despite visible comments or existing logic indicating that numeric products need an explicit symbol to avoid ambiguous output. The original idea of allowing arbitrary strings remains appropriate for ordinary symbolic factors, and using the custom string for numeric contexts may be acceptable when the custom string is an explicit operator-like symbol, or when the codebase has no separate numeric separator contract.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics rewarded broad 'arbitrary mul_symbol support' and vague 'preserve number-separator behavior' language. That over-credits patches that accept `r'\,'` for simple products but silently regress the special numeric path by using a spacing-only separator for numbers or scientific notation. For this pattern, generate a sharper criterion around the visible split between general multiplication separators and numeric multiplication separators. A better rubric should require evidence that unknown/custom strings are accepted for normal factor separation while numeric/scientific notation still gets a visible multiplication operator when the custom string is blank or spacing-only. Avoid the tempting criterion that any arbitrary string should be used uniformly everywhere. Prioritize visible evidence such as: the code keeps separate derived settings for general and numeric separators; whitespace-like custom values are detected or otherwise routed to the existing explicit numeric separator; and tests or reasoning cover a numeric/scientific-notation example, not only `number * symbol` or purely symbolic products.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that implement arbitrary LaTeX multiplication separators by passing every unknown custom string directly into both the ordinary factor separator and the numeric/scientific-notation separator, when the visible printer design has a separate numeric separator path or comments indicating numbers require an explicit multiplication symbol. This flaw is especially relevant for spacing-only custom values such as thin spaces, empty strings, plain spaces, or LaTeX spacing commands, because they can make numeric products or scientific notation ambiguous even if simple symbolic products appear correct.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Spacing-only custom separator reused for numeric multiplication

metadata.visible_task_type: LaTeX or pretty-printer option accepts arbitrary multiplication separator strings
critical_code_evidence: public separator option is normalized into separate general and numeric/internal separator settings
existing logic maps the default or numeric case to an explicit operator-like separator
comments or tests mention avoiding ambiguous numeric output such as adjacent numbers or scientific notation
replacement_focus: custom separator accepted for ordinary symbolic factor separation
spacing-only custom separators do not replace the explicit numeric separator
numeric/scientific-notation behavior is tested or explicitly reasoned about
avoid_overcredit_for: using the custom string uniformly for all separator settings

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory preserves or explicitly accounts for the separate numeric separator behavior while allowing custom strings for ordinary multiplication.
scale.2: Minor concern only: the trajectory recognizes the separate numeric path but has not fully demonstrated tests for spacing-only custom values.
scale.3: Equivalent/unclear: the trajectory allows arbitrary separators but visible evidence is insufficient to determine whether numeric separator behavior is preserved or regressed.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory sets the numeric separator to the arbitrary custom string for all custom values and only validates ordinary symbolic products.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory knowingly observes the need for explicit numeric separators or existing special numeric logic, then replaces it with spacing-only custom separators and claims the patch is complete without numeric/scientific-notation coverage.

experiences.title: Authoritative Static KB Mapping Refresh
experiences.description: Retrieve this when a Windows scanner task is about stale static update metadata: KB/build-revision mappings in a Go scanner must be refreshed so unapplied and fully-patched decisions work for Windows 10/11 or Windows Server tracks.
experiences.context: Applies in Go repositories where Windows update detection is data-driven by a nested static map of OS family, version/build, and ordered KB/revision entries. It is most useful after the trajectory has already located the mapping structure and affected build sections, or when judging an attempted data update. It is less useful for early repository exploration before the agent has found the map, for algorithmic scanner bugs unrelated to stale KB data, or for tasks that explicitly require a different source of truth. Do not treat absence of a newer product build, broad KB prefix greps, or visible later commits as sufficient by itself; the criterion should be bounded to the task’s affected tracks and the repository’s mapping contract.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics were most helpful when they asked whether the trajectory identified the affected Windows tracks, used authoritative Microsoft update-history or an equivalent trustworthy upstream source, and planned to insert exact KB-to-build-revision pairs into the correct static mapping arrays. That evidence is discriminative because this class of bug is usually not in control flow: the scanner’s behavior depends directly on whether its ordered metadata contains the right revision thresholds and KB IDs. However, several rubrics were too broad when they rewarded merely noticing stale data, missing build numbers, or the existence of newer KB ranges. Those cues can coexist with no real progress, repeated no-op commands, fabricated revisions, unrelated edits, or over-broad updates outside the requested scope. A better rubric should require source-backed exactness: the agent should name the existing build/release keys being updated, extract concrete revision/KB pairs from the code comments’ official sources or a clearly relevant upstream data refresh, preserve the map’s syntax and ascending revision order, include both rollup and security-only lists where the existing track uses them, and validate that the Go package still builds or relevant KB-detection tests run. Avoid tempting proxy criteria such as 'mentions KB503/504', 'adds Windows 11 23H2 because it is absent', 'passes old tests only', or 'copies from any later commit'. Prioritize visible evidence of precise mapping coverage, bounded scope, correct data format, and post-edit validation.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should perform a bounded, source-backed refresh of the Windows scanner’s static KB/revision metadata: identify the affected existing Windows client/server tracks, obtain exact monthly cumulative/security KB IDs and associated build revisions from authoritative update-history sources or an explicitly relevant upstream data update, insert them into the correct nested mapping entries in the repository’s established format and order, avoid fabricated or unrelated build/version additions, and validate that the modified Go code compiles and the relevant KB-detection behavior is exercised.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Source-Backed KB/Revision Mapping Update

required_evidence: affected Windows tracks and build keys are identified from the existing mapping structure
official update-history pages or an equivalent relevant upstream data source are consulted for exact KB/revision pairs
new entries are added to the correct rollup or security-only collections using the repository's existing string conventions
entries remain chronologically or numerically ordered so revision comparisons behave correctly
scope excludes unsupported, guessed, unrelated, or merely trendy build/Kb additions unless the task explicitly requires them
post-edit validation includes gofmt/go test/build feedback or equivalent syntax verification
common_false_positives: only observes that mappings are stale or that KB numbers are old
repeats grep commands without extracting exact source-backed data
uses broad KB prefix searches that match unrelated older KB IDs
adds plausible-looking but unsupported revision numbers
focuses on absent new product builds when the task is a bounded metadata refresh
leaves the large composite literal syntactically broken

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward the static KB mapping refresh; the trajectory is unrelated, stuck in repeated searches, or does not locate the relevant metadata.
scale.2: Weak progress: the trajectory locates the Windows mapping or notices stale/missing KB coverage, but does not identify exact affected tracks or source-backed revision/KB pairs.
scale.3: Moderate progress equivalent to the parent state: the trajectory identifies likely affected build sections and understands that ordered data updates are needed, but exact authoritative entries, scope boundaries, or validation are still incomplete.
scale.4: Strong progress: the trajectory obtains credible exact KB/revision data for the main affected tracks and applies or plans a correctly scoped update in the proper map format, with only minor coverage or validation gaps.
scale.5: Complete progress: the trajectory source-verifies all required KB/revision additions for the affected tracks, updates the correct rollup/security-only mappings in order without unrelated changes, preserves Go syntax, and validates the scanner behavior with relevant tests or build checks.

experiences.title: Do not let typed platform-name extraction stand in for modal layout/message refactor
experiences.description: Retrieve when a React/TypeScript i18n task asks to fix subscription or in-app-purchase modal messaging, translation flexibility, and Prompt/layout coupling, and the trajectory mostly introduces typed platform/name helpers or preserves ttag interpolation.
experiences.context: Applies in a Proton-style monorepo using React, TypeScript, ttag, and shared modal components when the task explicitly combines two concerns: stringly typed platform/manager values and inflexible warning content/layout embedded in a generic Prompt-style modal. The misleading case is a trajectory that extracts Google/Apple display names into an enum/helper, adds translator comments, or keeps template-literal interpolation, but leaves the in-app-purchase warning as a computed single text string rendered inside the same generic Prompt with the same one-paragraph body and close-button structure. A typed helper can still be a useful subcriterion when the task only asks for stronger platform typing, or when visible edits already address structured modal content/layout; it should not be treated as sufficient evidence for a task whose main defect includes formatting and layout inflexibility.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics emphasized strongly typed platform handling and translation-safe interpolation. That criterion is only partially relevant here and becomes misleading because the existing code already used ttag template literals with interpolated dynamic values; simply moving platform labels into a typed map does not solve the reported formatting/layout problem. For this task shape, a better rubric should check whether the trajectory restructures the in-app-purchase modal content away from a single computed `userText` paragraph inside a generic Prompt, and whether it creates separate, complete translated message units that can support richer formatting, platform-specific instructions, and the admin/user variants. Avoid the tempting criterion “uses an External enum utility and ttag interpolation” as the primary success signal. Prioritize visible evidence such as replacing or bypassing the constrained Prompt shell where needed, splitting title/body/footer responsibilities, using React/ttag patterns that allow formatted inline elements, providing distinct Android/iOS user-facing guidance rather than only substituting a manager name, and updating tests to cover the new structured copy and layout behavior rather than only preserving old text snippets.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Typed-name refactor without structured modal messaging
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for an in-app-purchase subscription warning task when they mainly add a typed platform/display-name mapping or ttag interpolation comments but keep the warning implemented as one computed string rendered in the same generic Prompt-style modal. This is especially severe when the task text calls out inflexible layout or translation formatting and the visible code/plan does not introduce structured modal content, separate translated message blocks, or richer React-formatted copy for platform-specific and admin variants.

task_cues: task mentions subscription or in-app-purchase warning modal
task mentions Prompt or generic modal coupling
task mentions inflexible layout, formatting options, or translation handling
task also mentions stringly typed subscriptionManager/platform context
misleading_proxy_to_avoid: only extracting platform names into enum/helper
only adding translator comments
only preserving or using ttag template interpolation
tests that only assert old one-line text still appears
replacement_evidence_to_prioritize: modal content is no longer a single computed text paragraph constrained by Prompt
title, body lines, and footer/action are structured separately
translated messages are complete units and can include formatted React elements when needed
Android/iOS and admin/user variants are intentionally handled with appropriate copy/layout
tests or validation cover the new structured modal behavior

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory either has not reached implementation yet while still investigating both layout and typing, or it visibly restructures the modal content/layout and treats typed platform handling as a supporting detail.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory spends notable effort on typed platform helpers, but also contains a concrete plan or partial edits for structured modal content, richer formatting, or Prompt replacement/bypass.
scale.3: Moderate/equivalent: the trajectory recognizes both the platform-typing and layout/translation issues, but visible evidence is balanced or incomplete, so it is unclear whether the final implementation will move beyond helper extraction.
scale.4: Clear flaw: visible edits introduce typed platform/display-name utilities or translator comments while the modal still renders a single computed warning string inside the same Prompt-style wrapper with largely unchanged copy/layout.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory declares the task solved, validates only old behavior, or repeatedly focuses on enum/name extraction and ttag interpolation while ignoring the required structured message/layout refactor.

experiences.title: Do not treat missing-ISBN scoring as sufficient when the bug is a matching-path bypass
experiences.description: Retrieve for Python catalog/import matching tasks where sparse imported records can overwrite richer identifier-backed records, especially when the trajectory has found multiple matching stages and has not proven the threshold scorer is the failing path.
experiences.context: This warning applies in Open Library-style record import flows with layered matching: a fast identifier match, a permissive exact/sparse-field match, and a threshold-based bibliographic comparison. A misleading rubric in this setting rewards penalizing one-missing-ISBN cases inside the threshold scorer, even though visible evidence may show the actual risk is an earlier or alternate title/sparse-field path that bypasses threshold scoring. The missing-ISBN penalty idea may still be appropriate if the trajectory has reproduced that the threshold comparator itself returns true for sparse no-ISBN versus ISBN-backed candidates and no earlier path can return the bad match. It is not enough when the task statement or code-reading evidence points to quick/exact/title-only bypasses, or when a reproduction shows threshold comparison already rejects the sparse record.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics often asked for “ISBN precedence” or “penalize absent ISBN” in the scoring function. That criterion is tempting because the task mentions ISBN-backed promise items, but it can mislead evaluation: a patch can modify ISBN scoring while leaving a permissive matching stage that compares only incoming fields and skips missing existing fields, so sparse title-only records can still be selected before robust comparison. It can also overconstrain legitimate non-ISBN bibliographic matches. A better rubric should focus on whether the agent verifies the whole matching orchestration, identifies any path that returns a match without robust bibliographic scoring, and ensures title-derived candidate pools must pass threshold-style comparison before overwrite, while preserving true identifier-based quick matches. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence such as: reading the full match call chain; distinguishing identifier matches from title/sparse-field candidates; reproducing which helper returns the bad match; removing or guarding the permissive exact/sparse match path; and making existing candidate metadata, including authors reachable through related records or redirects, available to the threshold comparator. Avoid generating a rubric that treats an ISBN-missing penalty alone as the central correctness requirement unless the trajectory has clearly established the scorer itself is the defective path.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: In a record-import matching trajectory where the visible code shows multiple matching stages and a title/sparse-field candidate path can return a match before robust threshold comparison, penalize trajectories or patches that focus primarily on changing the ISBN-missing score inside the threshold comparator while leaving the permissive bypass path intact. This flaw is especially clear when the agent has seen that threshold matching already rejects a sparse no-ISBN case, or when the proposed fix does not ensure title-derived candidates are subjected to the robust bibliographic comparison before overwriting existing identifier-backed records.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Threshold Bypass Left Unaddressed

required_visible_evidence: The trajectory has identified layered import matching stages rather than a single scorer.
There is a non-identifier matching path that compares only a subset of fields or can match on title-derived candidates before threshold scoring.
The proposed direction or patch changes ISBN scoring or adds an ISBN guard inside the scorer without eliminating or guarding that bypass.
safe_boundaries: Do not apply this negative criterion when the trajectory proves the threshold comparator itself is the only path producing the bad match.
Do not penalize preserving fast matches based on strong identifiers such as matching ISBNs or explicit catalog keys.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory identifies the bypassing title/sparse-field path and plans or implements routing so non-identifier candidates must pass robust comparison while preserving strong identifier matches.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory discusses ISBN scoring but also investigates the full matching call chain and does not rely on the scorer change as the sole fix.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory has found both the scorer and the layered match flow but has not yet determined which path produces the bad match or how to prevent bypasses.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory asserts missing-ISBN scoring is the root cause and proposes or implements only a scorer-level penalty despite visible matching stages that can bypass threshold scoring.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory ignores or preserves a demonstrated title/sparse-field bypass, possibly after observing threshold comparison already rejects the sparse case, and treats an ISBN-missing penalty or blanket ISBN precedence rule as sufficient.

experiences.title: Conservative tri-valued zero checks for complex Add cancellation
experiences.description: Use this when a SymPy assumptions task involves `is_zero` returning a wrong definite `False` for an unevaluated complex/imaginary addition that simplifies to zero.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/SymPy core-assumption debugging where the visible trajectory has reproduced an `Add` expression whose `.is_zero` is `False` while simplification or expansion proves zero, especially after the agent inspects term assumptions showing individually nonzero imaginary addends that may cancel. It is most useful once the trajectory has located or is reasoning about the Add zero-check control flow. If the trajectory is only doing repository exploration, the criterion should stay at the contract level and not demand a specific branch. It is not a general instruction to force algebraic simplification inside assumptions, nor does it apply to unrelated numeric zero predicates or tasks that require proving every simplifiable zero as `True`.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster focused on SymPy’s tri-valued assumptions contract: `is_zero` may return `None` when undecidable, but must not return `False` unless nonzero is proven. They aligned well when the visible trajectory showed the decisive cue: an unevaluated complex Add has imaginary addends that are each nonzero, yet can cancel after expansion/simplification, and the current Add zero logic infers `False` from the classification rather than from a proof of nonzero. A better rubric should reward identifying and removing/guarding that unsound `False` path while preserving known `True` and known `False` cases such as already simplified zero and clearly nonzero sums. Avoid the tempting but weaker criterion that the fix should “consider algebraic simplification” or explicitly simplify the imaginary terms; that led to overcomplicated or regressive patches. Also avoid judging only whether the reported example changes result, because broad changes that return `None` for cases previously known nonzero can break assumptions. Prioritize visible evidence such as: reproduction of the wrong `False`; inspection of the Add args and their `is_real`, `is_imaginary`, and `is_zero` values; tracing that the zero-check reaches an imaginary-only/complex path where cancellation cannot be ruled out; a minimal conservative change that returns unknown rather than false in that situation; and validation that definitive zero/nonzero behavior remains intact.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should respect the conservative tri-valued semantics of symbolic zero assumptions for complex Add expressions: when an unevaluated sum contains imaginary or complex components that may cancel, it must avoid returning a definite `False` unless nonzero is actually proven. Strong evidence includes reproducing the reported wrong `False`, tracing the Add zero-check logic to the branch that treats imaginary components as nonzero despite possible cancellation, making or planning a minimal change that yields `None` for the undecidable case, and checking that clearly zero and clearly nonzero expressions still receive correct definite answers. The criterion should not reward fixes that rely on broad simplification inside the assumptions predicate or that sacrifice existing definite nonzero results.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Conservative complex Add zero-assumption semantics

metadata.environment: Python SymPy core assumptions
metadata.applicable_stage: After reproduction and localization to Add zero-check reasoning, or during final review of such a patch
priority_evidence: reported expression returns a wrong definite False before the fix
simplification or expansion demonstrates the expression can be zero
individual addends are classified as imaginary/nonzero but cancellation remains possible
the trajectory distinguishes returning None from proving True
validation includes preservation of definite zero and nonzero cases
avoid_evidence: treating all nonzero imaginary addends as proving a nonzero sum
accepting a change solely because the reproducer no longer returns False

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory reproduced or understood the complex Add `is_zero` contract violation; it may work in unrelated code or assume a definite false result is acceptable.
scale.2: The trajectory reproduces the symptom or mentions complex zero handling, but the proposed direction is vague, focuses on broad simplification, or does not address why a definite `False` is unsound.
scale.3: The trajectory localizes the issue to Add zero-assumption logic and recognizes that `None` is preferable to an incorrect `False`, but lacks clear evidence of preserving known definite cases or avoiding simplification-heavy fixes.
scale.4: The trajectory identifies the imaginary/complex cancellation path, proposes or applies a conservative unknown result where cancellation cannot be ruled out, and performs some checks for the original case and common definite cases.
scale.5: The trajectory gives decisive evidence of the unsound branch, makes a minimal conservative change that avoids false nonzero conclusions without adding broad simplification, and validates the original case plus representative known zero and known nonzero Add expressions.

experiences.title: Avoid broad config-loader rubrics that miss public key spelling and runtime effect
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a Go/Viper configuration task where an agent adds missing config fields and loader checks for DB pool/update-check options, especially if the exact YAML/env key names and default semantics are not already established in visible code.
experiences.context: This warning applies in Go projects using explicit Viper config constants, defaults, and YAML examples/tests. The misleading pattern is a trajectory that correctly finds the config structs and adds fields plus IsSet/Get* calls, but invents public key names, pluralizes/singularizes fields without evidence, omits documented examples/tests, changes unrelated defaults, or fails to make loaded DB pool values affect the startup database connection. A broad rubric like “load DB pool options and update-check flag while preserving defaults” may be a reasonable parent goal during early exploration, but after implementation evidence appears it is too weak unless it checks the exact externally visible schema, default preservation, and end-to-end use. Do not apply this warning to tasks where key spelling is private/internal or clearly dictated by existing generated schema; in those cases a generic loader-coverage criterion may be enough.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics rewarded the agent for adding database idle/open/lifetime fields and reading the update-check flag through the config loader. That high-level idea is correct, but it overstates progress when the agent has merely invented plausible names such as plural connection keys, added extra unsupported options, or only populated an in-memory Config without proving compatibility with the public config surface and startup behavior. For configuration bugs, the better rubric should focus on visible evidence that the agent established or updated the canonical user-facing keys consistently across constants, YAML examples/fixtures/tests, defaults, and runtime consumers. Avoid the tempting criterion “adds fields and viper.IsSet calls for all requested options” by itself. Prioritize evidence that explicit false booleans are handled with IsSet, durations use the project’s duration parsing convention, absent keys preserve existing defaults including nonzero defaults, no unrelated config defaults are changed, and DB pool limits are applied to the opened database connection in the normal startup path rather than only stored in the config object.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize an implementation trajectory for a public configuration-loader bug when it appears to add the requested DB pool/update-check fields but relies on unverified or inconsistent external key names, fails to preserve documented/default behavior, or stops at loading values without ensuring the normal startup database connection uses the pool settings. This is judgeable from visible trajectory evidence such as invented YAML/env constants, lack of fixture/test/default-example updates after implementation, unrelated default changes, or absence of calls applying pool values to the opened database handle.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Invented Config Surface or Non-End-to-End Pool Support

metadata.environment: Go project using Viper-style explicit config constants, YAML fixtures/default examples, and a startup path that opens a database connection
metadata.task_type: missing configuration options for database pool limits, connection lifetime, and update-check boolean
flaw_indicators: new public config keys are guessed without confirming or documenting canonical spelling
plural/singular or snake_case key choices are inconsistent across struct fields, constants, YAML examples, and tests
explicit false update-check value is not loaded via an IsSet-style guard
absent DB pool keys do not preserve existing defaults, including nonzero defaults
loaded DB pool values are never applied to the database connection used by normal startup
patch changes unrelated defaults or loader behavior while addressing the new options
manual ad hoc checks replace repository fixtures/tests for the public config contract
positive_evidence_to_prioritize: canonical key names are established or encoded consistently in constants, examples, fixtures, and assertions
tests cover explicit configured values and omitted-key default preservation
duration and boolean parsing follow existing loader conventions
startup applies idle/open/lifetime values to the opened SQL database handle
unrelated configuration sections retain previous behavior

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory verifies or encodes the canonical public keys consistently, preserves defaults, and connects loaded DB pool settings to runtime startup behavior.
scale.2: Minor concern only: the trajectory has mostly consistent keys and runtime application, but lacks one supporting artifact such as an example update or an explicit omitted-key test.
scale.3: Moderate risk: the trajectory loads plausible fields and handles the boolean, but key spelling/default preservation or runtime application remains insufficiently evidenced.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory implements fields and Viper reads using guessed or inconsistent public keys, misses fixture/default-test coverage, changes unrelated defaults, or does not apply pool settings at startup.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory mostly invents a new config surface or extra unsupported options, leaves the normal startup behavior unaffected, and/or regresses unrelated configuration behavior while appearing to satisfy the broad loader goal.

experiences.title: DynamoDB Date-Partition Migration Over Generic Event-Date Plumbing
experiences.description: Use when an event-search efficiency task in a Go audit/event subsystem exposes a DynamoDB backend whose existing time-search index partitions by namespace and ranges by timestamp, and the trajectory is deciding or implementing date attributes/indexes.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go repository with audit/event storage under lib/events-like backends, especially when visible exploration shows a DynamoDB event table with fields such as CreatedAt, EventNamespace, SessionID/EventIndex, a time-search GSI, and SearchEvents(fromUTC, toUTC, filter, limit). It is most useful after the trajectory has inspected or begun editing DynamoDB schema/query/migration code. It is less applicable during very early reconnaissance before any backend bottleneck has been identified, or when visible task/code evidence clearly requires a public event schema/API change across all backends rather than a storage-index migration. Do not retrieve this as an all-purpose rule for every date-field task; the key boundary is that the scalability problem is the storage backend’s partition/index design, not merely absence of a JSON/protobuf date property.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful signal is not whether the agent adds a `date` constant, protobuf field, or Firestore/filelog property. Those are tempting but weak proxies. In this setting, correct progress is visible when the trajectory treats the normalized date as a DynamoDB storage/indexing attribute used to avoid the hot namespace partition, backfills existing rows, and preserves timestamp-level search semantics. Previous rubrics that demanded automatic date population, backend persistence, and historical migration were directionally useful because they penalized superficial additions, but they were often too broad when they required all storage backends, public protobuf metadata, FileLog changes, or SearchSessionEvents changes without evidence those were the actual bottleneck. A better rubric should focus on DynamoDB: adding a UTC day string derived from CreatedAt/event time, using it as the partition key for a replacement time-search index while keeping CreatedAt as the range key, updating new writes, changing SearchEvents to query each day/date bucket and still apply the exact from/to timestamp bounds and ordering/limit contract, and adding startup/table migration/backfill for historical events and index transition. Prioritize visible evidence in the trajectory: inspection or edits to DynamoDB table schema/GSI definitions, write paths, SearchEvents query construction, helper functions for day iteration, table-status/index migration functions, and a backfill scan/update path. Penalize evidence that the agent only edits proto/generated files, generic EventFields constants, Firestore indexes, or creates a date-range index still partitioned by namespace, because that does not address the observed hot-partition efficiency problem and may break unrelated public schemas.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: DynamoDB Date-Partitioned Time Search Migration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show concrete progress toward a DynamoDB-centered storage/index migration for efficient event time search: derive a normalized UTC day string from each event's timestamp, persist it as a backend storage attribute on new DynamoDB events, replace or version the existing time-search GSI so the day/date attribute is the partition key and the original timestamp remains the range key, update SearchEvents to query the relevant day buckets across multi-day/month-boundary ranges while preserving exact from/to timestamp filtering, result ordering, filter behavior, and limit semantics, and provide a startup-compatible migration/backfill path for historical rows and old indexes. Credit should come from visible DynamoDB schema/query/migration work, not from merely adding public protobuf fields or generic date constants.

priority_files_or_areas: DynamoDB event backend storage struct and write paths
DynamoDB table attribute definitions and global secondary indexes
table/index status checks and startup migration code
positive_evidence: UTC YYYY-MM-DD or equivalent ISO day derived from the same event timestamp used for CreatedAt
new time-search index partitions by date/day rather than namespace to reduce hot partitions
timestamp remains available as the range key or post-filter so partial-day ranges are exact
multi-day range search loops over all days including month boundaries
migration/backfill updates existing events and manages old/new index transition
new writes populate the storage date attribute consistently
negative_evidence: only adds protobuf/API/EventFields date fields without DynamoDB index/query migration
adds Firestore/FileLog changes while DynamoDB hot partition remains unaddressed
creates a date index that still hashes on namespace and therefore does not fix partition hot spots
queries only date strings and loses exact timestamp filtering within boundary days
no historical data backfill or startup migration path
manual generated-code edits or broad sed changes that leave compilation/schema consistency doubtful

scale.1: No meaningful DynamoDB date-index progress is visible; the trajectory only explores, edits unrelated public schemas/constants, or makes malformed changes without addressing storage/query/migration.
scale.2: Some date attribute plumbing is visible, such as adding a storage field or write-time date, but there is little or no correct DynamoDB GSI/query design and no credible migration/backfill plan.
scale.3: Moderate progress: the trajectory identifies DynamoDB as relevant and partially updates storage/index or SearchEvents, but leaves important gaps such as namespace-based hot partitioning, exact timestamp bounds, multi-day iteration, or historical migration.
scale.4: Strong progress: DynamoDB write paths, a date-partitioned time-search index, and SearchEvents day-bucket querying are substantially addressed, with at least a plausible migration/backfill direction, though some validation, edge cases, or cleanup may remain.
scale.5: Complete visible solution direction: DynamoDB stores a UTC date derived from event time, uses a replacement/versioned date-partitioned GSI with timestamp range semantics, searches all relevant dates while preserving ordering/filter/limit and partial-day correctness, and includes robust startup migration/backfill/index-transition handling with validation or tests.

experiences.title: CycloneDX PURL ecosystem parsing must be applied at constructor call sites
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go SBOM/CycloneDX task involves malformed Package URLs because package names need ecosystem-specific namespace/name/subpath parsing before calling a package-url constructor.
experiences.context: Applies in Go repositories that build CycloneDX components locally with a package-url library and pass raw package names, empty namespace, or empty subpath into PURL constructors. It is most useful once the trajectory has located the SBOM generation path or is evaluating an attempted patch. It is less useful during very early repository exploration before any PURL construction site is visible, and it should not be reduced to checking whether an external scanner dependency has its own PURL parser if the local reporter also synthesizes PURLs.
experiences.experience: The earlier rubrics correctly emphasized that Maven, PyPI, Golang, npm, and Cocoapods each have different parsing rules, which is the central semantic requirement. However, a broad rubric about merely understanding those rules can overrate incomplete patches. For this task family, the discriminative evidence is whether the agent applies ecosystem parsing at every local CycloneDX PURL synthesis point that uses raw package names, maps scanner or dependency-graph ecosystem identifiers to valid package-url types, and passes namespace/name/subpath into the constructor fields rather than encoding subpath as an ordinary qualifier. The better rubric should reward visible evidence that Maven colon names become namespace/name, PyPI names are normalized lowercase with hyphens, Go module paths and npm scopes split on path boundaries, and Cocoapods submodules use the PURL subpath field. It should also check that existing qualifiers and vulnerability-reference maps remain keyed consistently, and that generated PURLs for both scanned libraries and dependency-graph packages are handled. Avoid a tempting but weak criterion that only asks whether the agent found Trivy's external parser or reused an existing PURL string; that does not fix local PURLs still synthesized from raw names. Also avoid rewarding a helper function in isolation if the constructor is still called with the original type string, empty subpath, or only one of the relevant component paths is updated.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete ecosystem-aware PURL synthesis
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show that the agent identifies local CycloneDX Package URL construction from raw package names and implements or plans a fix that converts ecosystem-specific package identifiers into valid package-url type, namespace, name, and subpath fields at all relevant SBOM component creation sites. Strong evidence includes handling Maven group/artifact names, PyPI lowercase hyphen normalization, Go module path splitting, npm scoped package splitting, and Cocoapods subpath separation; mapping scanner and dependency-graph ecosystem labels to package-url type constants; preserving existing qualifiers such as file path or repository metadata; preserving original-name lookup maps used for vulnerability references; and adding focused tests or static examples that assert the resulting PURL strings for the specified ecosystems.

prioritize_visible_evidence: local package-url constructor calls that previously used raw name and empty namespace/subpath are inspected or changed
ecosystem-specific parser returns namespace, normalized name, and subpath separately
PURL type mapping covers scanner language types and dependency graph ecosystem names
subpath is supplied as the constructor subpath field, not as a qualifier
tests or examples cover Maven, PyPI, Golang, npm scoped names, and Cocoapods
common_false_positives: only inspecting an external scanner PURL parser while leaving local SBOM construction unchanged
using an already stored PURL as a fallback without fixing synthesized PURLs
adding a parser helper but not applying it to all relevant SBOM package sources
normalizing name text while still passing invalid ecosystem type strings into the package-url constructor

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent has found local SBOM PURL construction or the required ecosystem parsing rules; work is limited to broad searches or unrelated files.
scale.2: The agent recognizes some ecosystem-specific parsing requirements or a likely raw-name constructor call, but has not connected them to a concrete local fix across the SBOM generation path.
scale.3: The agent identifies the main local constructor call and proposes or partially implements parsing for several ecosystems, but evidence is incomplete: some ecosystems, type mappings, subpath placement, dependency-graph PURLs, or preservation of existing qualifiers/maps are missing.
scale.4: The agent implements or clearly plans an ecosystem-aware helper applied to the main local SBOM PURL creation paths, with mostly correct type mapping and constructor-field usage, though validation or edge coverage may still be limited.
scale.5: The agent provides a complete, well-integrated fix or plan covering all specified ecosystems and all local SBOM PURL synthesis paths, uses correct package-url constructor fields and type mappings, preserves existing qualifiers/reference behavior, and includes focused validation for the expected PURL forms.

experiences.title: Recursive Container Printing Contract
experiences.description: Use when a Python repr-style printer handles some built-in containers recursively but leaves dict/set contents in raw string form, and the trajectory has evidence about missing or incorrect container-specific printer dispatch.
experiences.context: Applies to Python codebases with printer/serializer dispatch methods where the task asks that dictionaries and sets print their contained symbolic/custom objects the same way lists and tuples already do. It is especially relevant once the trajectory has located the printer implementation, observed existing list/tuple handling, reproduced raw dict/set output, or started adding container-specific methods. It remains useful at early stages as a target criterion if the visible investigation identifies missing dict/set dispatch, and at implementation stages as a semantic correctness criterion. Do not retrieve this for unrelated formatting tasks where normal str/repr output is intended, for tasks solely about deterministic ordering, or when the codebase uses a different serialization contract that does not require recursive printing of keys, values, and elements.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic contract: dict keys, dict values, and set elements must be recursively printed by the same repr-style printer used for list/tuple elements, while preserving valid Python container syntax. This aligned well because the visible trajectory repeatedly showed the root cause: list and tuple had dedicated printer methods using recursive printing, while dict and set had no equivalent and therefore fell back to raw Python string formatting. A better rubric should not merely ask whether `_print_dict` and `_print_set` names were added; it should judge whether the implementation formats dicts as `key: value` pairs using recursively printed key/value strings, formats sets as recursively printed elements, handles empty set as `set()` rather than `{}`, preserves empty dict as `{}`, and avoids artifacts such as tuple-pair dict output or quoted key-value strings. Do not overemphasize unrelated extras like frozenset support, full test-suite status in an environment with unrelated failures, or deterministic set ordering unless the task or tests explicitly require them. Prioritize visible evidence from reproduction output, inspected printer-dispatch code, inserted container methods, and post-change examples showing `Symbol(...)`-style recursive output inside dicts/sets.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate progress toward a repr-style printer fix for built-in dict and set containers by recursively applying the printer to set elements and to both dictionary keys and values, while emitting valid Python container syntax. Strong evidence includes locating the existing recursive list/tuple printer pattern, identifying missing dict/set dispatch or fallback string formatting, implementing container-specific handling that preserves `key: value` formatting, and validating representative non-empty and empty dict/set outputs without tuple-pair or quoted-string artifacts.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Recursive dict/set repr semantics

required_semantics: set elements are printed through the repr-style printer, not raw str output
dictionary keys and values are each printed through the repr-style printer
dictionary output uses key-colon-value syntax, not repr of item tuples
empty set is represented unambiguously as set()
high_value_visible_evidence: existing list/tuple recursive printing pattern is identified
absence or inadequacy of dict/set printer handling is identified
post-change examples show recursive symbolic/custom-object representations inside dicts and sets
edge-case checks cover empty containers or nested/mixed contents
avoid_as_primary_criteria: requiring deterministic set order without task evidence
treating unrelated test-suite failures as evidence against the container fix
crediting method-name insertion without validating output syntax

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses recursive dict/set printing; it remains focused on unrelated code, raw str output, or generic printer changes without connecting to container contents.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory identifies the printer area or missing dict/set handling, but has not shown a plausible implementation or may propose an approach that would still print raw contents or malformed dict syntax.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory has localized the issue and proposes or partially implements dict/set handling, but visible evidence is incomplete or shows remaining risks such as no empty-container handling, no validation, or uncertain key/value formatting.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory implements or clearly plans recursive set-element and dict key/value printing with valid syntax, handles empty dict/set, and validates the main reported examples, with only minor omissions such as limited tests or nonessential edge cases.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory cleanly follows the existing recursive container-printer pattern, correctly handles non-empty and empty dicts/sets, avoids tuple-pair and quoted-string artifacts, preserves list/tuple behavior, and validates representative nested or mixed cases while distinguishing unrelated test/environment failures.

experiences.title: Discriminate namespace packages from fileless regular packages
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python/Django task asks to stop treating missing `__file__` as sufficient evidence of a namespace package, especially in migration/package discovery code for frozen import environments.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories in a Python codebase where the requested behavior hinges on import-system package attributes: regular packages may lack `__file__`, while PEP-420 namespace packages are identified by a non-ordinary-list `__path__`. It is especially relevant once the agent has inspected or edited package discovery logic such as a migration loader after importing a migrations module. It is less useful for unrelated migration behavior, tasks that intentionally enable namespace packages, or stages where the agent has only installed dependencies without engaging the import-attribute distinction. Do not over-penalize incomplete repository test setup when the visible code and focused probes clearly exercise the predicate, but do penalize an inverted predicate even if the agent says the intent is correct.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic boundary that actually determines correctness: a missing `__file__` must no longer cause a regular package to be skipped if its `__path__` is an ordinary list, but true namespace packages with missing `__file__` and non-list `__path__` must still be rejected/ignored. This was discriminative because several trajectories had the exact easy-to-invert conditional; visible evidence such as `... is None and not isinstance(module.__path__, list)` plus manual checks for both frozen-style regular packages and namespace fixtures strongly indicated a sound patch, while `... and isinstance(module.__path__, list)` was the opposite behavior. A better rubric should ask the judge to inspect the implemented predicate and any focused validation for all three cases: normal package, fileless regular package with list `__path__`, and namespace package with non-list `__path__`. It should also check that existing handling of non-packages/import failures is not broadly rewritten. Avoid tempting but wrong criteria such as merely requiring any `__path__` check, requiring reference to CPython’s `_NamespacePath`, treating failed ad hoc pytest/Django commands as decisive, or rewarding tests that only prove namespace packages are still ignored without proving fileless regular packages are accepted.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate, through the visible code change and/or focused validation, that package discovery now treats missing `__file__` as insufficient by itself: regular migration packages with an ordinary list `__path__` are still searched when `__file__` is absent, while PEP-420 namespace packages with missing `__file__` and non-list `__path__` remain unmigrated/ignored. The implementation should use a portable list-vs-non-list `__path__` distinction rather than a CPython-specific namespace-path class, and should preserve existing behavior for module files and import errors.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Portable namespace-package predicate

expected_visible_evidence: Predicate combines missing __file__ with non-list __path__ for rejection
No reliance on CPython-specific namespace path class names
Evidence or reasoning covers both fileless regular packages and true namespace packages
Existing non-package/import-error handling is not intentionally weakened
common_failure_modes: Inverted condition that rejects list __path__ packages
Continuing to reject every module with missing __file__
Only validating namespace rejection without validating fileless regular-package acceptance
Broad rewrites of migration loading unrelated to the import-attribute boundary

scale.1: No meaningful progress on the import-attribute distinction, or the trajectory still treats missing __file__ alone as a reason to skip migration packages.
scale.2: Recognizes that __file__ is insufficient but implements or proposes an incomplete/ambiguous check that does not clearly accept fileless regular packages and reject namespace packages.
scale.3: Roughly equivalent parent-child behavior: the trajectory identifies the right boundary but visible code or validation is partial, unverified, or risks preserving an inverted/fragile condition.
scale.4: Strong evidence of the correct portable predicate and preservation of namespace rejection, with at least some focused reasoning or tests for fileless regular packages.
scale.5: Clear implementation of the correct predicate, explicit coverage of normal packages, fileless regular packages with list __path__, and namespace packages with non-list __path__, plus no visible regression to module-file/import-error handling.

experiences.title: Do not reward no-op completion from unresolved task/codebase mismatch
experiences.description: Retrieve when a SWE task describes reverting/removing an architecture, but the agent’s checked-out tree appears not to contain the named artifacts and the trajectory starts treating that absence as evidence the task is already complete.
experiences.context: This applies in repository-maintenance tasks, especially Go projects with git history/remotes visible, where the agent finds a detached or unexpected checkout, greps for task-named symbols, and discovers a historical commit that introduced or reverted the relevant behavior. The useful underlying idea is that agents should verify task assumptions before editing; it is appropriate as an early diagnostic criterion. It becomes misleading as a completion/correctness criterion when the agent has not resolved the base/target mismatch, has made no substantive patch, has not validated the expected behavior across affected call sites, and keeps inferring that absence of exact identifiers means no work is needed.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics emphasized “task completion recognition,” “correct state recognition,” or “task-state alignment verification,” often rewarding the agent for concluding that the current tree already satisfies the task. That criterion is too optimistic in trajectories where the visible evidence shows an unresolved mismatch rather than a proven no-op: clean working tree, repeated greps for exact identifiers, detached HEAD or branch-history confusion, historical commits matching the task, and no implementation. In such cases, a better rubric should judge whether the agent converts the mismatch into a concrete resolution path: identify the actual target base, inspect the relevant historical diff as a blueprint, stop unproductive graph walking, decide whether a patch is required in the checked-out tree, and validate with build/tests or focused comparisons. Avoid generating a rubric whose main success condition is “recognize the task is already done” based only on missing symbols like a removed interface or wrapper. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence of resolved target/base ambiguity, substantive code changes when required by the task, consistency across dependency injection/persistence call sites, and validation; if no code change is truly appropriate, the trajectory should show a conclusive, tested justification rather than repeated searches and speculation.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat a task/codebase mismatch as proof of completion without resolving whether the checked-out code is the actual target for the requested change. This flaw is present when the agent repeatedly notes that task-named artifacts are absent, explores git history or branches, but makes no substantive fix and does not establish a tested, actionable conclusion about whether the requested architecture change is required.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Unresolved mismatch mistaken for completion

visible_cues: clean working tree or no substantive diff
detached or unexpected HEAD/branch relative to task history
repeated grep/find checks for exact task identifiers
historical commits found that match the requested change
no clear decision to apply, adapt, or reject the historical change
no targeted build/test validation supporting a no-op conclusion
metadata.avoid_as_positive_proxy: absence of exact legacy symbols alone
metadata.better_evidence: resolved base/target ambiguity plus concrete patch or validated no-op rationale

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the agent either implements the requested change or gives a well-supported, validated reason that no code change is appropriate after resolving the target-base question.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the agent notices absent artifacts and briefly considers no-op completion, but continues toward resolving the mismatch with concrete file comparisons, validation, or a patch plan.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent performs useful verification but leaves the base/target ambiguity unresolved and has not yet produced or validated a fix.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the agent repeatedly relies on missing exact identifiers or current-branch greps to imply the task is already satisfied, while historical/task evidence suggests the situation is unresolved and no substantive patch exists.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory finalizes or effectively settles on a no-op or cosmetic-only change solely because the named artifacts are absent, after extensive unresolved branch/history exploration and without validation or a real implementation.

experiences.title: Do not equate “centralized resolver” with adding another shared switch
experiences.description: Retrieve when a TypeScript monorepo task asks to replace a local plan-to-addon resolver and normalize checkout planIDs, especially when the trajectory has found an existing resolver plus unresolved public-entrypoint/import concerns.
experiences.context: This applies to assistant upsell / Scribe addon work in a Proton-style monorepo where billing helpers, shared planID utilities, and component hooks are split across packages. The misleading pattern is a rubric that rewards any removal of a local switch or any new “centralized” function, even when the trajectory is creating a second mapping in a generic shared helper, importing through deep/internal paths, or ignoring the conditional planIDs contract. The original idea remains useful when the trajectory has not found an existing resolver and the task truly requires creating a new single source of truth, or when a later-stage patch already proves the resolver is exposed through the package’s intended public barrel and both single- and multi-user planIDs are built safely. Do not apply this warning to unrelated tasks where there is no existing domain resolver or no public-entrypoint requirement.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often said the trajectory must “use a centralized Scribe addon resolver” or “return unified planIDs.” Those criteria were too broad: they could over-credit a patch that simply moves the same switch statement into another shared file, uses addon-support boolean helpers as if they were a name resolver, defaults unknown plans to a Mail addon, or imports from an internal helper path. They also sometimes overreached by requiring the resolver to handle free-user or downgrade flows, even though free-user upsell can remain a dedicated Mail Plus + addon configuration and downgrade behavior may be out of scope. A better rubric should distinguish true source-of-truth adoption from superficial centralization: prioritize visible evidence that the agent reuses the already-discovered payments/subscription resolver, exposes it through the package’s public entrypoint, updates consumers away from deep selected-plan/helper imports, and constructs planIDs by first including the base plan/existing selected plan IDs and only adding a Scribe addon key if the resolver returns one. Avoid generating a criterion that says “create a resolver in shared planIDs” unless the trajectory has established that no suitable resolver exists and that shared planID helpers are the intended public API. Replacement criteria should focus on import/export boundaries, avoiding duplicate switch mappings, preserving existing addons and member/Scribe quantities, and conditional addon insertion rather than the mere presence of a function named like a resolver.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial resolver centralization
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize a trajectory when it treats centralization as moving or duplicating the plan-to-Scribe mapping instead of adopting the existing domain resolver through the intended public entrypoint, or when it normalizes planIDs without preserving the conditional addon contract. This flaw is especially clear if the trajectory has already found an existing resolver in subscription/payment code but proposes a second switch in generic planID utilities, imports the resolver through a deep/internal helper path, creates an unverified root shared barrel, defaults unsupported plans to a Scribe addon, or builds planIDs with a potentially undefined addon key. Do not penalize mere early investigation where the resolver/export boundary is still being discovered and no implementation choice has been made.

metadata.environment: TypeScript monorepo with component hooks, payment/subscription helpers, and shared planID utilities
metadata.applicability_stage: late planning or implementation after the trajectory has inspected assistant upsell code and resolver/import locations
primary_visible_evidence: whether an existing plan-to-Scribe resolver was found and reused rather than duplicated
whether the resolver is exposed/imported via the package's public barrel instead of a deep helper path
whether single-user planIDs include the base plan before conditionally adding the addon
whether multi-user planIDs preserve existing selected plan/addon entries and only overwrite/add the resolved Scribe addon when present
whether the trajectory avoids broad unrelated rewrites or test deletions to satisfy the rubric
tempting_but_misleading_evidence: local switch was removed but the same mapping was recreated elsewhere
a helper named like a resolver exists but is not the established source of truth
free-user or downgrade paths were forced through the resolver without task evidence
tests were changed to match a simplified implementation rather than validating the checkout contract

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory is still investigating without making a centralization decision, or it clearly plans/implements reuse of the existing resolver through a public entrypoint with conditional planIDs.
scale.2: Minor risk: the trajectory mentions centralization generally but has not yet resolved the public entrypoint or planIDs details; no duplicate resolver or unsafe planIDs construction is visible.
scale.3: Moderate risk: the trajectory removes or plans to remove the local resolver and use a shared function, but visible evidence is ambiguous about whether this is the existing source of truth, whether imports are public, or whether addon insertion is conditional.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory creates or proposes a second switch mapping, imports from an internal helper path, uses an inappropriate support-helper as a resolver, or builds planIDs with an unconditional addon key despite knowing the resolver may return no addon.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory combines duplicate resolver creation with broad unrelated rewrites, unverified root/public barrels, deletion or weakening of relevant tests, or behavioral changes to free/downgrade/member-count flows that are not supported by the task evidence.

experiences.title: Do not over-credit hand-rolled hostname suffix logic when a shared widening helper is expected
experiences.description: Retrieve this when evaluating a qutebrowser/Python host-blocking task where the agent implements parent-domain blocking by manually splitting host strings or adding a local helper, especially after only ad hoc validation or unchanged existing tests.
experiences.context: This applies in a Python/PyQt5 qutebrowser-style codebase where hosts-based blocking must check a request hostname and its parent-domain suffixes, with whitelist rules taking precedence. The misleading pattern is a trajectory that correctly identifies the host-blocking decision point and appears to implement the requested behavior locally, but does so by duplicating hostname-widening logic inside the blocker, adding unnecessary special cases, or relying on temporary scripts rather than integrating with existing URL/hostname utility conventions. A broad rubric about “blocks subdomains and respects whitelist” may still be appropriate during early exploration before code is written, or in a repository with no existing canonical hostname-widening behavior. At implementation or final-review stage, however, the criterion should distinguish local semantic sketches from repository-integrated solutions.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics focused almost entirely on the task-level behavior: derive parent-domain suffixes, check both block sets, and allow whitelisted URLs. That is a necessary behavior, but it was too broad and over-optimistic for trajectories where the visible evidence showed manual `host.split('.')` implementations, new private helpers in the blocker, extra public-suffix/IP/trailing-dot logic, temporary scripts, and no permanent regression tests. In this setting, the better rubric should ask whether the agent found or centralized an existing hostname-widening abstraction in the URL/config utility layer and then reused it from the host blocker, preserving existing callers rather than creating duplicate inconsistent logic. Avoid the tempting criterion “the trajectory has a suffix loop and ad hoc tests pass,” because that misses integration quality and maintainability. Prioritize visible evidence such as searches for existing widened-hostname utilities, changes that share a single helper between host blocking and other config URL matching code, use of repository fixtures/tests rather than standalone config mocks, and absence of unnecessary local special cases that diverge from established hostname normalization behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that implement parent-domain host blocking by hand-rolling hostname suffix generation inside the host blocker or adding local special-case logic, without investigating or reusing an existing repository-level hostname-widening utility and without integrating the behavior into the established URL/config utility path. This flaw is especially important when the visible trajectory shows ad hoc scripts or existing tests passing but no evidence that duplicate hostname-widening behavior was avoided.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Duplicate Local Hostname Widening Instead of Shared Utility Integration

metadata.environment: Python/PyQt5 qutebrowser-style host blocking and URL/config utilities
visible_evidence_to_check: manual host.split('.') suffix loops or private helper added only in the blocker
lack of search/use of existing hostname-widening utilities in URL/config code
temporary standalone scripts used as primary validation
no permanent regression tests or fixture-based validation for subdomain blocking and whitelist precedence
unnecessary special cases that may diverge from existing URL normalization semantics
not_a_flaw_when: the trajectory is still pre-implementation exploration
the repository has no existing hostname-widening abstraction
the agent explicitly centralizes the helper and updates existing callers to use the shared behavior

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory identifies/reuses or centralizes an existing hostname-widening abstraction, applies it from the host blocker, preserves existing utility callers, and validates with repository tests or planned regression tests.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory mostly follows shared-utility integration but has incomplete validation or only briefly relies on local logic before moving toward a common helper.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory implements correct-looking suffix semantics locally and may mention tests, but shows little or no investigation of existing utility behavior or duplicate logic risks.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory adds a private helper or manual suffix loop in the blocker, relies mainly on ad hoc scripts or unchanged tests, and does not address existing shared hostname-widening behavior.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory entrenches duplicated/manual hostname logic with extra divergent special cases, ignores visible utility/config matching code, and treats ad hoc validation as sufficient for final correctness.

experiences.title: Validate real external metadata import path, not provider/UI proxies
experiences.description: Use when an Open Library task asks for automated ingestion of a new external metadata source, especially Open Textbook Library, and the trajectory is exploring or implementing fetch/transform/batch-import behavior.
experiences.context: Applies in the Open Library Python codebase when the requested change is catalog import/ingestion from an external repository, not merely exposing read links or provider availability.
