The criterion is most useful once the trajectory has either investigated the source endpoint/schema or started writing importer code. At early exploration stages, judge whether the agent is moving toward the real external source contract rather than querying unrelated APIs. At implementation/final-review stages, judge whether a runnable import job exists and uses existing Open Library import queue patterns. Do not apply this as a requirement for tasks that only add provider buttons, search display fields, or UI templates, and do not require importapi web hooks or provider registration unless the task separately asks for those surfaces.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster focused on the semantic core of the task: an automated importer must fetch Open Textbook Library metadata from the actual external source, transform the source response into Open Library edition/import records, and enqueue those records through existing import infrastructure. This is discriminative because failed trajectories often showed observable proxies instead: repeated calls to Open Library’s own API, guessed Open Textbook Library endpoints with invented response shapes, provider/search plumbing without an importer, or tests built around fabricated metadata. A better rubric should therefore prioritize visible evidence of a validated source contract and an end-to-end import path: code or commands using the Open Textbook Library host and the JSON feed/pagination contract, mapping actual fields such as title, contributors/authors, ISBN10/ISBN13, language, description, subjects/call numbers, publishers, copyright year, source_records, and open_textbook_library identifiers, plus Batch-based ingestion with dry-run/limit behavior. Avoid tempting but weak criteria like “adds a provider class,” “registers an importapi hook,” “handles authentication,” or “adds rate limiting” unless the trajectory has shown those are needed; they can reward unrelated work or penalize the simpler established script-based import pattern. The strongest visible evidence is a new runnable importer following existing script conventions, dry-run output showing plausible Open Library records from real Open Textbook Library data, and syntax/test verification. The weakest evidence is generic planning, broad greps, or code that assumes unverified endpoints/field names.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a concrete, validated automated import path for Open Textbook Library metadata: it identifies the real external feed/API contract, implements a runnable importer using Open Library's existing batch import infrastructure, maps actual source fields into valid Open Library import records with stable source_records and open_textbook_library identifiers, supports bounded/dry-run execution, and verifies the importer with syntax checks, tests, or dry-run output. Provider/search/UI additions may be useful extras, but they do not satisfy this criterion without the actual fetch-transform-enqueue importer.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Validated external metadata batch importer

expected_visible_evidence: Uses the Open Textbook Library external host and a verified response format rather than Open Library's own APIs or guessed paths
Follows existing script/import-job conventions with configuration loading, Batch usage, and CLI entry point

Transforms actual source metadata into Open Library record keys including title, authors/contributors, identifiers, source_records, ISBNs, language, description, subjects/classifications, publishers, and publish date where present
Includes dry-run and limiting or pagination behavior suitable for safe automated import
Shows validation such as dry-run sample output, py_compile, or relevant tests
common_false_positives: Only adding a book provider class, provider templates, or worksearch fields
Querying openlibrary.org APIs instead of the external source
Using unverified endpoint names or response keys
Adding an importapi hook around invented metadata without proving the source fetch works

scale.1: No meaningful import progress: only generic exploration, repeated unrelated API calls, or UI/provider/search changes with no external metadata fetch and no import record construction.
scale.2: Weak progress: identifies some relevant import infrastructure or sketches an importer, but the source endpoint/schema is unverified, response fields are invented, or no Batch/import enqueue path is present.
scale.3: Moderate progress: has a plausible importer structure and some Open Library field mapping, but important parts remain uncertain or unvalidated, such as pagination, identifiers/source_records, actual OTL response keys, or runnable dry-run behavior.
scale.4: Strong progress: implements a runnable Batch-based importer using a credible Open Textbook Library endpoint, maps most important metadata fields, supports dry-run/limits or pagination, and shows some local verification.
scale.5: Strongest progress: provides an end-to-end validated importer following established Open Library script conventions, uses the real OTL feed/pagination contract, maps actual metadata comprehensively into valid import records with stable identifiers/source_records, safely enqueues via Batch, and demonstrates successful dry-run or tests.

experiences.title: Previous-reference expansion in production Solr update logs
experiences.description: Use when an Open Library Solr indexing task involves stale aggregate work documents after an edition’s work reference changes, especially when the trajectory has evidence about recent-change/change-set processing rather than only UI edit code.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Open Library-style codebase where Solr work documents aggregate related edition data and incremental indexing is driven from saved document/change-log records. Retrieve this when the task explicitly requires including both current and previous document keys, or when the trajectory has identified that a moved edition’s current document only points to the destination work while the source work key exists in previous document state or existing index state. The criterion is most useful once the agent has begun inspecting Solr updater/recent-change key selection; it is less useful as an early exploration rubric before any update pipeline has been found. It should not be reduced to finding a UI move handler or touching a dev-only edit hook, and it may be premature if the visible trajectory has not yet distinguished production asynchronous indexing from local/dev reindexing paths.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful idea is that stale Solr aggregate data is fixed by expanding the set of keys queued for the production incremental updater from both the new and old versions of changed documents. Earlier rubrics that merely said “reindex source and destination works” captured the semantic invariant, but were too broad: agents could satisfy the wording conceptually while patching a dev-only hook, touching the edit form, or querying current Solr state in a secondary updater path without fixing the log parser that actually schedules production updates. A better rubric should focus on visible evidence that the agent is using the change-set/recent-change payload containing current docs and previous docs, comparing or recursively extracting referenced keys from both, and queuing keys that disappeared or changed so removed edition-to-work associations cause the old work to be rebuilt. Avoid a tempting criterion that requires locating a named “move edition” function; in this codebase the move is usually just an edit to an edition’s `works` reference. Also avoid over-specifying a Solr lookup helper as mandatory when the task text points to previous document keys. Prioritize evidence such as inspection of the production updater’s save/save_many parsing, recognition that current changed keys alone miss nested previous work references, and tests or reasoning showing that a changed edition from work A to work B yields both A and B for indexing.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate progress toward fixing the production incremental Solr update path by deriving affected reindex keys from both current and previous saved document states. For an edition whose work association changes, it should recognize that the destination work is discoverable from the new document while the source work must be recovered from the previous document or removed nested references, and that those previous keys must be queued so stale aggregate work documents are rebuilt. Strong evidence includes inspecting the recent-change/change-set parser used by the asynchronous updater, handling both single-save and multi-save records, comparing or recursively extracting nested `key` references from old and new documents, and preserving unrelated update triggers. Weak evidence is only high-level awareness that both works need reindexing without connecting it to the production key-selection mechanism.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Production updater includes removed previous references

expected_visible_evidence: Identifies the asynchronous or production Solr key-selection path that consumes saved change records
Uses both current documents and previous documents from the change payload
Queues keys that were present before but are absent or changed afterward, including nested work references inside edition data
Keeps existing handling for normal changed document keys and non-edition update events
common_false_positives: Only patches a dev-only immediate Solr hook
Only touches the UI/edit save path by saving or touching the old work
Only reindexes the edition’s current work from the latest database document
Requires a named move-edition handler despite the move being a generic relationship edit

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory connects the stale Solr issue to previous document state or the production update-key pipeline.
scale.2: Mentions that both old and new works should be reindexed, but focuses on UI move code, dev-only hooks, or generic Solr updates without identifying how previous references enter the production queue.
scale.3: Understands that previous/source work keys are needed and inspects some update-key logic, but the proposed direction is incomplete, over-specific to current Solr lookup, or not clearly tied to the production recent-change/change-set parser.
scale.4: Clearly targets the production incremental updater and plans to use old and new document data to queue both current and removed referenced keys, with only minor gaps such as incomplete coverage of save variants or nested references.
scale.5: Provides strong, actionable evidence that the fix will expand production update keys from both current and previous document states, including removed nested references, while preserving existing update events and validating the edition-move case.

experiences.title: Do not treat generic placeholder centralization as sufficient when strict artwork semantics are required
experiences.description: Retrieve this when generating rubrics for Go/Navidrome-style artwork retrieval tasks that ask both for centralized placeholder fallback and for strict unavailable-artwork signaling at HTTP or internal callers.
experiences.context: This applies when the task explicitly separates two behaviors: a centralized fallback method that may return built-in placeholders, and strict retrieval paths that must continue to report artwork unavailability so callers can return 404 or avoid caching placeholders. The misleading pattern is a trajectory that adds a method such as GetOrPlaceholder and removes some reader-level placeholder calls, but also masks errors too broadly, routes strict HTTP/public/cache/internal callers through fallback, leaves empty-ID placeholder behavior inside a reader, or fails to introduce a consistent unavailable-artwork error boundary. The original centralization idea remains useful when the visible trajectory is only exploring scattered placeholder sources, or when a task only asks to consolidate UI fallback without requiring strict not-found behavior. It is not enough for final-review rubrics when caller-specific strict-vs-fallback semantics are visible in the task.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded broad signs of progress such as adding GetOrPlaceholder, removing fromAlbumPlaceholder/fromArtistPlaceholder from readers, and making endpoints use the new centralized method. That overstates trajectory quality because the hard contract is not merely where the placeholder code lives; it is whether unavailable artwork is represented consistently and only fallback-eligible callers receive placeholders. A better rubric should focus on visible evidence that strict retrieval still propagates a canonical unavailable-artwork error, fallback catches only that availability condition, invalid/empty IDs do not silently travel through reader-level placeholders, internal source/resize/cache paths use the strict API correctly, and HTTP handlers preserve the intended 404/debug behavior rather than universally serving placeholders. Avoid the tempting criterion 'HTTP endpoints should use GetOrPlaceholder' or 'all placeholder logic removed from readers means success' unless the task explicitly says every endpoint should receive fallback images. Replacement criteria should prioritize exact caller selection, error-type boundaries, and whether tests or diffs show broad error swallowing, optional interface/type-assertion shims, or retained placeholder readers in strict paths.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Fallback method masks strict unavailable-artwork contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for artwork fallback tasks when they conflate centralized placeholder fallback with strict retrieval semantics. The flaw is present if the trajectory switches strict HTTP/public/cache/internal callers to a fallback method despite a requirement to return not-found on unavailable artwork, catches broad errors such as all retrieval failures or generic not-found errors and substitutes placeholders, keeps empty/default ID placeholder behavior in a reader that can be reached by strict retrieval, or avoids a clear interface/error contract by using ad-hoc optional interfaces or type assertions. This criterion should be applied at implementation or final-review stages where edited files or stated plans reveal caller choices and error handling; it should not be applied as a failure during early exploration before the agent has chosen an API shape.

metadata.task_family: Go artwork retrieval with centralized placeholder fallback
evidence_to_check: Whether strict retrieval remains available and returns a consistent unavailable-artwork error
Whether fallback retrieval substitutes placeholders only for the intended availability error
Whether HTTP handlers that must return 404 continue to call strict retrieval and log appropriately
Whether placeholder behavior remains embedded in reader/default-ID paths reachable by strict retrieval
Whether internal source, resize, and cache-warming call sites use the intended strict or fallback API
avoid_using_as_positive_proxy: Presence of a GetOrPlaceholder method alone
Removal of some reader-level placeholder calls alone
Endpoint use of the fallback method without checking endpoint-specific requirements

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory clearly preserves strict retrieval for unavailable artwork, uses fallback only for intended callers, and maintains a narrow availability-error boundary.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the plan or diff is mostly correct but leaves one ambiguous caller or error condition without showing that it will preserve strict unavailable-artwork behavior.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory centralizes placeholders but has mixed or unclear strict-vs-fallback caller selection, such as changing some endpoints or internals without justifying their required behavior.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory routes an HTTP/public/cache/internal strict path through fallback, masks unavailable artwork with placeholders in default/empty reader paths, or catches overly broad errors for placeholder substitution.
scale.5: Most severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory makes fallback the default behavior for strict retrieval, removes 404/not-found handling from endpoints that require it, or rewrites tests/handlers to expect placeholders where the task requires explicit unavailability signaling.

experiences.title: Do not reduce multi-symptom FreeBSD package tasks to fast-mode summary suppression
experiences.description: Retrieve this when a Go vulnerability-scanner task mentions both hiding updatable package counts for FreeBSD and fixing FreeBSD installed-package discovery/CVE association, especially when the trajectory only edits scan-result summary display logic.
experiences.context: Applies in Go scanner/reporting codebases where OS-family-specific behavior spans both scan-result formatting and package inventory collection. The misleading pattern is a trajectory that finds the updatable-count summary helper and adds FreeBSD to a fast-scan suppression list, possibly with a test expectation update, while leaving the FreeBSD package enumeration path using the wrong command or parser. The original idea of checking summary suppression is still appropriate when the task is explicitly only about UI/report formatting or when the trajectory has already addressed FreeBSD installed-package parsing. It is not sufficient when the task text explicitly states that FreeBSD package lists must come from `pkg info`, that packages such as `python27` can be missed, or that detected CVEs fail to associate with installed packages.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics rewarded locating the scan-summary updatable-package display logic and suppressing FreeBSD counts in fast mode. That criterion is directionally relevant but misleadingly narrow for tasks whose problem statement has two coupled requirements: FreeBSD summaries should omit updatable counts, and FreeBSD package inventory must be parsed from the correct installed-package command so audit CVEs map to actual installed packages. A trajectory that only adds FreeBSD to a fast-mode switch can look correct under a summary-only rubric while still leaving deep/other mode display behavior and the package/CVE association bug unresolved. Future rubrics should avoid using 'FreeBSD is in the updatable-count suppression list' or 'the existing test expectation changed to false' as the main success proxy. Instead, prioritize visible evidence that the agent distinguishes display policy from package inventory correctness: it should inspect and modify the FreeBSD installed-package scan path to use/parse `pkg info`, preserve any needed new-version information separately, and add or discuss tests for parsing FreeBSD package names/versions and associating audit results with installed packages, in addition to suppressing updatable counts for the FreeBSD family wherever the summary decision is made.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Display-only FreeBSD fix misses package inventory contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for FreeBSD package-handling tasks when they only modify scan-result summary logic to hide updatable counts, especially only in a fast-scan branch, while showing no concrete plan or code change for retrieving/parsing the FreeBSD installed package list with `pkg info` and ensuring audit/CVE package names are present in the scanner's package inventory. This flaw is present when the trajectory treats updatable-count suppression as the whole task despite visible task language about `pkg info`, missed packages, and CVE association.

required_visible_task_cues: updatable package numbers should not be displayed
`pkg info` is required for installed packages or `pkg version -v` is insufficient
vulnerable packages may be reported missing or CVEs fail to associate
misleading_visible_agent_cues: edits only a scan-result formatting/display predicate
limits suppression to one scan mode when the task says FreeBSD generally
updates only an updatable-count expectation test
does not implement or test FreeBSD installed-package parsing from `pkg info`
replacement_focus: FreeBSD updatable-count suppression at the family policy level
FreeBSD installed package enumeration from `pkg info`
correct parsing of package name/version strings including names containing hyphens or digits
preservation or merging of any available updatable/new-version metadata without using it as the sole package inventory
tests or validation covering both summary output and package/CVE association

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory addresses both FreeBSD summary suppression and the installed-package parsing/CVE association path, or the visible task is purely about display formatting.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory starts with summary suppression but explicitly identifies the package-inventory requirement and is actively investigating or planning the `pkg info` parsing change.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory implements summary suppression and briefly inspects FreeBSD package scanning, but leaves package inventory handling unresolved at the cutoff.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory implements or plans only a FreeBSD addition to the updatable-count display logic and test expectations, despite visible task text requiring `pkg info` installed-package parsing.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory declares the issue fixed after a display-only fast-mode suppression change, runs unrelated or insufficient tests, and ignores the FreeBSD package enumeration/CVE association requirement entirely.

experiences.title: Prefer Observed Delegation-Contract Violations over Prescriptive Loader Shape
experiences.description: Use when a generated rubric insists on one finder-detection mechanism or complete loader-level testing despite direct evidence that the actual delegated call signature has been respected.
experiences.context: Import-loader repairs must preserve distinct contracts for native and collection-specific finders. The exact implementation can vary by supported runtime and repository conventions. A criterion should become strict when the visible current call passes an unsupported argument, damages adjacent fallback structure, or breaks one delegation path; it should not reject a working patch merely for using a different robust discriminator or lacking a specific permanent test at an intermediate cutoff.
experiences.experience: The previous rubric mixed the essential signature boundary with preferred implementation details. Replace it with a negative criterion that checks the current dispatch against signatures the trajectory actually inspected and whether both native and collection paths remain reachable. Avoid treating an unchosen detection idiom as a defect without evidence that it misclassifies a finder.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Finder Delegation Contract Mismatch
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize the current loader change when it visibly sends arguments unsupported by the delegated finder, routes a finder through the wrong path, corrupts fallback method structure, or fails a reproduced native/collection delegation check. Implementation style alone is not a violation unless visible evidence shows misclassification.

observable_evidence: inspected finder signatures
current dispatch arguments
native and collection-path executions
latest file structure and import validation

scale.1: No visible evidence of a visible finder delegation contract mismatch or damaged fallback path; the available implementation and validation evidence is consistent with the required behavior.
scale.2: A minor or early-stage concern about a visible finder delegation contract mismatch or damaged fallback path is visible, but it is not confirmed and the trajectory is still actively resolving it.
scale.3: Evidence about a visible finder delegation contract mismatch or damaged fallback path is mixed or incomplete; the concern remains plausible but is not yet decisive.
scale.4: Clear visible evidence indicates a visible finder delegation contract mismatch or damaged fallback path, with no convincing correction or validation yet.
scale.5: The trajectory directly reproduces or validates a visible finder delegation contract mismatch or damaged fallback path, or claims completion while the contradiction remains unresolved.

experiences.title: Do not equate GridSpec propagation with a correct subfigure-spacing fix
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a Matplotlib subfigure spacing trajectory where the agent traces wspace/hspace through GridSpec or proposes using GridSpec/SubplotSpec position helpers for SubFigure placement.
experiences.context: This applies in Matplotlib layout bugs involving Figure.subfigures, GridSpec spacing, SubFigure bounding boxes, constrained layout, and existing subfigure geometry tests. The misleading pattern is a rubric that rewards any evidence that wspace/hspace are passed to GridSpec or any fix that delegates SubFigure placement to GridSpec position calculations. That idea is useful during early investigation to locate the parameter flow, but it is not enough for final-patch quality once the trajectory shows implementation choices. GridSpec position helpers may also import figure subplot margins, rcParams defaults, and layout-engine behavior, so a broad SubFigure-level replacement can change default, add_subfigure, spanning, tightbbox, or constrained-layout semantics even though explicit spacing visibly changes.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked the judge to value 'GridSpec/SubFigure spacing parameter propagation' or 'delegating to GridSpec layout calculations.' That criterion can overvalue naive patches that make wspace/hspace affect bboxes by using get_position/get_grid_positions unconditionally, because those helpers also apply subplot parameters and default margins. It can also be too vague at early exploration stages, where merely finding that GridSpec stores wspace/hspace does not show the downstream layout contract is understood. A better rubric should focus on the compatibility boundary: explicit wspace/hspace passed through subfigures should affect subfigure spacing, while unspecified spacing should preserve the historical full-parent tiling unless a layout engine is responsible, and constrained-layout explicit-bbox updates should remain controlled by the layout engine. Avoid tempting criteria that require all add_subfigure calls or all SubFigure positioning to honor GridSpec spacing in the same way. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence such as guarded handling for explicit spacing, avoidance of unguarded get_position/get_grid_positions in the generic SubFigure transform path, preservation of width/height ratios and spanning behavior, and regression checks or reasoning around tightbbox/constrained-layout/default-margin tests.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat GridSpec position propagation as sufficient by broadly replacing generic SubFigure placement with GridSpec/SubplotSpec position calculations, without preserving the legacy default/no-layout-engine and constrained-layout boundaries. This flaw is especially present when the trajectory has already observed that these helpers include subplot margins, rcParams/default spacing, or cause tightbbox/spanning/constrained-layout regressions, yet the proposed direction still applies them unconditionally or requires add_subfigure behavior to change globally.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Overbroad GridSpec Position Delegation

metadata.repository_context: Matplotlib layout code involving Figure.subfigures, GridSpec spacing, SubFigure bbox/transform updates, and constrained layout
visible_warning_signs: Uses SubplotSpec.get_position or GridSpec.get_grid_positions as a generic replacement for manual SubFigure bbox computation
Does not distinguish explicit wspace/hspace from None/default spacing
Does not distinguish no layout engine from constrained-layout or other layout-engine control
Changes add_subfigure or all SubFigure placements rather than only the subfigures explicit-spacing case
Trajectory reports regressions in subfigure tightbbox, spanning, image comparison, or constrained-layout tests
preferred_evidence: Explicit spacing values alter subfigure bboxes
Default spacing and no-layout-engine behavior continue to tile the parent as before
Constrained-layout explicit bbox path remains owned by the layout engine
Width/height ratios and spanning subfigures remain compatible
Tests or numeric bbox checks cover both explicit-spacing behavior and default/constrained regression boundaries

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory clearly preserves default/constrained/add_subfigure behavior while making explicit subfigures spacing effective, or it is only investigating without endorsing a broad GridSpec-position fix.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory emphasizes GridSpec propagation but also recognizes default-margin or layout-engine risks and has not committed to an unguarded implementation.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory proposes or favors using GridSpec/SubplotSpec position helpers for spacing, with only partial or unclear safeguards for explicit spacing versus defaults and layout engines.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory applies or plans an unguarded generic SubFigure placement change using GridSpec position calculations, despite visible signs that defaults, margins, spanning, tightbbox, or constrained layout may be affected.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory has observed concrete regressions or documented that GridSpec position helpers import subplot defaults/margins, yet still treats the broad delegation as the correct fix or final criterion.

experiences.title: Do not reward no-op “already fixed” conclusions when the obvious branch is already present
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django/Python exception-chaining task appears already satisfied because current code contains the requested `__suppress_context__` logic and existing tests pass, but the agent has not produced or investigated a substantive repository change.
experiences.context: Applies in patch-generation trajectories for framework debugging tasks, especially Django technical error reporting / Python exception chaining, where the task description points to a simple semantic condition but repository inspection shows that exact condition is already present. In these cases, an agent may over-focus on git history, ad hoc repros, and existing regression tests, then conclude no changes are needed. The original idea of verifying an existing fix can still be appropriate for pure triage/support tasks or when the requested deliverable explicitly allows confirming no code change; it is not a good correctness criterion when the task is to produce a patch and visible evidence shows no diff or only redundant reapplication of code already in the checkout.
experiences.experience: The misleading rubrics in this cluster rewarded agents for identifying a pre-existing fix, validating current behavior, and avoiding redundant edits. That is tempting when the current helper already returns the explicit cause or suppresses implicit context for `raise ... from None`. However, for a patch-generation task, that evidence is insufficient and can actively mislead: passing the existing suppressed-context test only proves the already-present branch works, not that the trajectory has found the expected repository change. A better rubric should penalize premature no-op finalization and should focus on whether the agent reconciles the apparent pre-fixed semantic logic with the need for a concrete change, inspects how exception causes are reused while building traceback frame data, and considers structural improvements around separating cause selection and per-exception frame generation. Avoid generating a criterion whose main success signal is “the agent confirmed the bug is already fixed.” Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence such as a non-redundant patch, analysis of all call sites where the cause helper is used, preservation of explicit/implicit/suppressed chaining behavior, and validation that traceback frames carry cause metadata associated with the correct exception rather than merely observing that an existing regression test passes.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat the presence of an existing `__suppress_context__` branch and passing existing suppressed-context tests as sufficient evidence to finish with no meaningful patch, without investigating whether the traceback-frame construction itself still needs a repository change. This is especially severe when the agent repeatedly cites git history or ad hoc repros, produces no diff or a redundant diff, and does not analyze how exception-cause selection is shared between exception-chain traversal and frame metadata generation.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Premature no-op after apparent existing exception-chain fix

metadata.environment: Django-style framework repository; Python exception chaining; technical/debug traceback reporter
visible_failure_cues: current code already includes the simple suppress-context condition from the task text
agent concludes the issue is already fixed or no changes are needed
validation relies mainly on existing tests, git history, or ad hoc scripts
trajectory lacks a non-redundant patch or deeper analysis of traceback frame construction
replacement_focus: non-redundant code change in exception reporting path
separation or centralization of cause-selection logic so traversal and frame metadata remain consistent
preservation of explicit cause, implicit context, suppressed context, and cycle behavior
tests or reasoning that distinguish chain rendering from source-context text

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory either produces a substantive, relevant patch or clearly investigates beyond the already-present suppress-context branch before deciding next steps.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the agent notices the existing branch and leans toward no-op, but still inspects related frame-building paths or acknowledges that a patch may be required.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent validates the existing behavior and existing tests, with only superficial consideration of whether the task still requires a code change.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the agent repeatedly asserts the issue is already fixed and relies on history/tests while failing to inspect deeper traceback-frame responsibilities or produce a meaningful patch.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory is dominated by no-op verification or redundant reapplication of existing logic, treats that as final correctness, and ignores visible signs that the task still needs a repository-level change.

experiences.title: Do not reward arbitrary UTF-8 locale fallback when the task is about parseable command output
experiences.description: Retrieve this when an Ansible/module-utils locale fallback task asks for a reliable parsing locale after default locale initialization fails, and the trajectory is likely to implement an inline `locale -a` scan that picks any UTF-8 locale.
experiences.context: This applies in Python Ansible module utility code where `_check_locale` falls back after `locale.setlocale(..., '')` raises `locale.Error`, especially when the task motivation is parsing human-readable output from external tools. In this setting, simply avoiding plain `C` by selecting the first installed UTF-8 locale is not enough: a UTF-8 locale can still localize messages unpredictably, and ad hoc command execution may violate project portability conventions. The original UTF-8-discovery idea is still relevant as part of the solution, and a rubric about installed UTF-8 fallback can be appropriate for a task that only asks for Unicode-capable encoding. It is misleading when the task emphasizes reliable parseability, Ansible core compatibility, and system-command discovery semantics.
experiences.experience: The generated rubrics in this cluster mostly asked whether the trajectory queried installed locales, found a UTF-8-capable locale, updated environment variables, and used `C` only as a last resort. That criterion is too broad here and can over-credit patches that pick an arbitrary UTF-8 locale or implement the logic inline with non-portable subprocess APIs. For parseable output, the better evidence is whether the trajectory is converging on a stable, project-compatible locale-selection contract: prefer known parseable/non-localizing or expected-English locales in a deliberate order, include `C`/`POSIX` as defined final fallbacks, locate and invoke the `locale` command through the module’s command helpers, handle missing command/no output/nonzero status explicitly, and isolate the selection logic in reusable module utility code rather than burying ad hoc scanning in `_check_locale`. Avoid generating a rubric that treats “first UTF-8 locale from `locale -a`” as sufficient. A replacement criterion should prioritize visible evidence of a parseability-oriented preference list, robust error contract, Ansible-compatible command execution, and integration that sets locale plus `LANG`, `LC_ALL`, and `LC_MESSAGES` consistently.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: In an Ansible module utility locale fallback task motivated by reliable parsing of external command output, penalize trajectories that only implement ad hoc discovery of any UTF-8 locale from installed locale output. The flaw is present when the visible plan or patch picks the first/arbitrary UTF-8 locale, omits a deliberate parseable-locale preference order with `C`/`POSIX` fallback semantics, uses direct or Python-version-sensitive subprocess APIs instead of the module’s command/path helpers, or keeps the locale-selection policy embedded in `_check_locale` without a reusable helper/error contract.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Arbitrary UTF-8 Locale Is Not a Parseability Contract

evidence_to_check: whether the fallback chooses stable parseable locales by explicit preference rather than first UTF-8 match
whether installed-locale discovery uses project command/path helpers
whether command failure, missing locale tool, and empty output have a defined fallback/error path
whether locale and environment variables are updated together
whether reusable locale-selection logic is factored outside the caller when appropriate
metadata.avoid_as_primary_proxy: presence of `locale -a` scanning plus any UTF-8 match

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory clearly uses a parseability-oriented preference order, portable module command helpers, robust fallback/error handling, and consistent locale/environment updates.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory has the right parseable-locale preference concept and consistent integration, but one secondary portability or factoring concern is not yet resolved.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory discovers installed locales and avoids unconditional `C`, but the visible policy is still mostly generic UTF-8 selection rather than a reliable parseability contract.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory implements or plans first/arbitrary UTF-8 selection inline in `_check_locale`, with weak handling of command discovery/failure or project compatibility.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory strongly relies on ad hoc `locale -a` parsing or Python-version-specific subprocess calls, treats any UTF-8 locale as sufficient for parsing, and lacks a defined final fallback/error contract.

experiences.title: Django FK attname ordering vs related-model ordering
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django ORM task concerns `order_by()` on a related foreign-key `_id`/attname path that is being mistaken for ordering by the related object, especially with self-referential FKs and `Meta.ordering` causing wrong direction or extra joins.
experiences.context: Applies in Django ORM/query-compiler trajectories where the problem statement or reproduction shows `order_by('relation__fk_id')` producing SQL that joins to the related model and applies that model's default ordering, while an explicit target-field path or annotation orders directly by the FK column. It is most useful after the agent has either reproduced generated SQL or started inspecting ordering/path resolution internals. It is less useful for generic join optimization, unrelated queryset filtering bugs, database-backend-specific ordering behavior, or cases where the ordering target is intentionally the relation name rather than the concrete FK attname. In very early exploration, judge evidence of moving toward SQL compiler/path resolution rather than requiring a completed fix; near final review, require a concrete distinction between relation-name ordering and attname-column ordering.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic boundary that decides correctness: `relation__fk_id` must be treated as an explicit concrete FK column/attname ordering, not as `relation__fk` followed by related-model default ordering. This criterion aligned with patch quality because successful trajectories visibly reproduced the bad SQL, compared it with `relation__fk__id` or an `F()` annotation workaround, traced ordering through Django's SQL compiler/path-resolution logic, and identified that the default-ordering branch was firing because the FK field's attname was compared against the whole lookup path rather than the terminal lookup component. A better rubric should therefore reward evidence that the agent preserves explicit `order_by()` direction, avoids the unnecessary self-join for `_id` ordering, and keeps relation-name ordering behavior distinct. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as merely 'finds query.py', 'reduces joins', or 'handles self-referential foreign keys' without checking the attname-vs-relation distinction; those proxies can rate unfocused exploration too highly. Prioritize visible evidence from generated SQL, inspection of ordering-name resolution, and tests or reproductions covering both positive `_id` paths and the boundary case where ordering by the relation itself may still use related-model `Meta.ordering`.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the agent understands and is fixing the Django ORM ordering-name resolution boundary between ordering by a related FK's concrete attname, such as `relation__parent_id`, and ordering by the related object, such as `relation__parent`. Strong evidence includes reproducing the generated SQL symptom, recognizing that related-model `Meta.ordering` must not override an explicit `_id` order_by path, targeting the SQL ordering/path-resolution logic rather than only high-level QuerySet APIs, and preserving correct behavior for explicit descending order and relation-name ordering.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: FK attname ordering is not related-object ordering

key_evidence: Generated SQL for `_id` ordering is checked for direct FK-column ordering rather than ordering by a joined related-table primary key.
The agent distinguishes the terminal FK attname component from the full lookup string.
The agent notes that related-model default ordering may apply to relation-name ordering but should not apply to concrete attname ordering.
Validation covers both ascending and descending explicit order_by directions and watches for unnecessary joins.
boundaries: Do not require changing behavior for ordering by the relation name itself unless the task explicitly asks for it.
Do not treat repeated high-level grepping in QuerySet code as meaningful progress if it does not move toward SQL compiler/path resolution.
Do not reward a join-removal idea unless it also preserves explicit ordering direction and default-ordering semantics.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory understands the `_id` attname ordering issue; it stays in generic exploration or repeatedly inspects irrelevant high-level files without reproduction or path-resolution insight.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory recognizes the task involves Django `order_by()` and foreign keys, but does not clearly distinguish concrete FK attname ordering from related-object ordering or does not inspect the relevant ordering-resolution layer.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory reproduces or describes the wrong SQL and identifies that extra joins/default ordering are involved, but has not yet isolated the attname-vs-full-path/default-ordering condition or proposed a precise fix.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory traces the issue into SQL compiler/path-resolution logic and identifies that explicit `_id` ordering should bypass related-model default ordering while relation-name ordering remains distinct; it has a plausible narrow fix or focused validation plan.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory applies or clearly specifies a narrow fix that treats the terminal FK attname as a concrete column ordering, verifies generated SQL has no unnecessary related self-join and respects ASC/DESC, and checks boundary cases such as relation-name ordering and explicit target-field ordering.

experiences.title: GFK Prefetch UUID Key-Type Normalization
experiences.description: Use this when a Django ORM/contenttypes task involves `GenericForeignKey.prefetch_related()` failing for UUID primary keys stored through a string-like object-id field.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django source checkout when the issue is specifically about `GenericForeignKey` prefetch assignment for a target model with `UUIDField(primary_key=True)` and a source model whose GFK object-id column is a `CharField` or otherwise stores UUID text. It is most useful once the trajectory has inspected `GenericForeignKey.get_prefetch_queryset()`, Django field conversion methods, or has reproduced that direct GFK access can work while prefetched access returns `None`. It is less appropriate as a strict correctness criterion during very early repository exploration with no implementation evidence, and it should not be used for unrelated prefetch bugs, ordinary `ForeignKey` joins, ContentType registration failures in ad hoc scripts, or SQL-only filtering issues.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster focused on the semantic cause: prefetch assignment joins fetched related objects back to source instances using Python key equality, and UUID text from the GFK object-id field must be normalized to the same Python type as the related object's primary key. This aligned well when the visible trajectory showed the agent comparing the GFK source-side key with the related-object key, observing `str` versus `uuid.UUID`, and validating a fix on UUID plus non-UUID primary-key cases. A better rubric should not require one exact patch location or spell out only `to_python()` inside `gfk_key()`, because the same contract could be satisfied by improving the target field's preparation/conversion path. It should instead judge whether the trajectory implements compatible target-PK-aware normalization for the in-memory prefetch match and preserves existing integer/character primary-key behavior. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as merely 'handle UUID primary keys,' changing ContentType/model registration setup, or focusing only on whether the database `pk__in` query returns rows. Prioritize visible evidence: inspection of GFK prefetch key callables, demonstration that `UUIDField.get_prep_value()` and `to_python()` differ on string UUIDs, reproduction where prefetched GFK is `None`, and post-change validation that prefetched GFKs resolve for UUID targets without breaking other primary-key types or content-type grouping.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Target-PK-Compatible GFK Prefetch Matching
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should identify and address the Python-level key mismatch in Django `GenericForeignKey` prefetching when a string-like GFK object-id value refers to a UUID primary key. An excellent trajectory shows that the source-instance key and fetched-related-object key must compare equal after target primary-key conversion, implements a target-field-aware normalization so UUID text matches `uuid.UUID` primary keys, and checks that normal integer and character primary-key GFK prefetch behavior remains intact.

metadata.environment: Django ORM contenttypes / GenericForeignKey prefetch_related
metadata.issue_shape: UUID primary key target model; GFK object_id stored as text; prefetched relation resolves to None
priority_evidence: Inspection of GenericForeignKey prefetch key functions or equivalent prefetch assignment path
Recognition that the failure is Python key equality after fetching, not merely SQL lookup
Comparison of string UUID object_id values with uuid.UUID model primary keys
Use of target primary-key field conversion or equivalent normalization
Validation covering UUID and existing non-UUID primary-key cases
avoid_overfitting: Do not require only one exact file or method if the semantic conversion contract is satisfied
Do not treat ContentType setup errors in temporary scripts as the core bug
Do not accept a fix that only changes querying while leaving prefetch key comparison incompatible

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory understands or addresses GFK prefetch key normalization; it may only restate the task or inspect unrelated prefetch/ContentType code.
scale.2: Some relevant exploration of GenericForeignKey or UUID fields, but the trajectory has not clearly identified the source object-id versus related primary-key Python type mismatch or has no plausible normalization plan.
scale.3: Identifies that GFK prefetch matching likely involves inconsistent UUID/string values, but implementation or validation is partial, overly narrow, or not yet shown to preserve non-UUID cases.
scale.4: Clearly diagnoses the Python-level prefetch key mismatch and applies a plausible target-PK-aware conversion so string UUID object IDs can match UUID primary keys, with some reproduction or focused validation.
scale.5: Fully demonstrates the mismatch between source and related prefetch keys, implements robust normalization through the target primary-key conversion contract, and validates UUID, integer, and character primary-key GFK prefetch behavior without disrupting content-type grouping.

experiences.title: Empty-input identity semantics over test-maintenance proxies
experiences.description: Use when a symbolic/math API task changes zero-argument behavior from raising an error to returning operation-specific identity values, and the trajectory has visible evidence about the constructor guard, identity attributes, or runtime behavior.
experiences.context: Applies in Python symbolic/math library tasks where the requested change is a public behavior contract for empty inputs, such as extremum-like operations returning extended-real identity elements instead of raising. It is most useful once the trajectory has found the shared implementation path or has run direct calls showing the current exception and/or new return values. It remains applicable before patching if the task statement and inspected code make the expected identity values clear. It is less useful for unrelated validation-only stages, tasks where empty input should remain invalid, or cases where the operation has no well-defined identity; in those cases a rubric should not assume that removing an error is correct. If legacy tests fail because they assert the old error behavior, treat that as supporting evidence for an intentional behavior change, not as a mandatory requirement that the agent must edit tests.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged the central semantic contract: the public zero-argument calls must stop raising and must return the correct operation-specific identity values, while ordinary one- and multi-argument behavior remains intact. This aligned well because the visible trajectory repeatedly showed decisive evidence: the agent located an early no-argument guard that raised, found or inferred class-level identity values with opposite signed infinities for the two operations, changed only that empty-input path, and validated direct calls plus representative non-empty calls. A better future rubric should therefore focus on observable semantic outcomes and preservation boundaries: correct positive/negative infinity polarity, no exception for empty input, use of a per-operation identity or equivalent branching rather than one hardcoded value for both, and no disruption to existing simplification/argument handling. Avoid the tempting but weaker criterion that the agent must update repository tests whenever old tests fail; test updates can be useful, but the decisive patch-quality evidence here is the changed public behavior and non-regression of normal calls. Also avoid overemphasizing installation/path setup once the agent has enough code evidence; environment fixes matter only insofar as they enable validating the behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates that the empty-input behavior is implemented according to the operation's mathematical identity contract: the zero-argument minimum returns positive infinity, the zero-argument maximum returns negative infinity, neither raises the old argument error, and representative non-empty calls still simplify or evaluate as before. Strong evidence may come from inspecting the shared constructor/dispatcher and its per-operation identity values, applying a minimal change to the empty-input path, and running direct public API checks for both empty and non-empty cases.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Correct empty-input identity contract

key_visible_evidence: old zero-argument error path identified
operation-specific identity values identified or equivalent polarity handled
empty calls validated not to raise and to return the expected infinities
non-empty calls validated or reasoning shows unchanged handling
avoid_as_required: requiring legacy test files to be edited as a condition of semantic correctness
accepting a single hardcoded infinity for both operations
treating import/path setup failures as evidence about the API behavior

scale.1: No visible evidence that the agent understands or implements the empty-input identity behavior; it may leave the old exception, target unrelated code, or confuse which operation gets which infinity.
scale.2: Weak evidence of intent to change empty-input behavior, but the trajectory lacks a concrete implementation path, has unclear or incorrect signed-infinity polarity, or does not distinguish the two operations.
scale.3: Moderate evidence equivalent to the parent state: the agent has located the relevant error guard or identity concept and plans a plausible fix, but has not yet shown both correct empty-call results and preservation of non-empty behavior.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory changes or clearly plans the empty-input path using operation-specific identity semantics and validates or reasons through both expected zero-argument results, with some attention to ordinary non-empty calls.
scale.5: Very strong evidence: the trajectory makes a minimal, well-scoped change to the empty-input path, demonstrates the exact positive/negative infinity results for both public calls, and checks representative one- and multi-argument behavior remains unchanged while correctly interpreting legacy tests that assert the old exception.

experiences.title: Do not let correct 4xx/5xx logic mask the required metrics abstraction
experiences.description: Retrieve when an API error metrics task asks for grouped client/server/other failures in a TypeScript monorepo with an existing metrics package, and the trajectory is focusing on HTTP status categorization, new metric schemas, counters, or direct API-handler instrumentation.
experiences.context: The misleading rubric pattern is a narrow criterion that rewards whether status codes are categorized as 4xx client, 5xx server, and other/failure. That classification is relevant, but in this setting it is not enough to judge patch quality: the task may be better served by a small reusable observer/helper exported from the metrics package, leaving actual metric emission to callers, rather than adding a concrete metric registry entry, generated schema files, raw status-code labels, application-specific labels, or imports from shared API code back into the metrics package. The original categorization rubric can still be appropriate as a subcriterion once the trajectory has already chosen the correct abstraction and is only implementing the mapping behavior. It is misleading when used as the main rubric during exploration or implementation review, because an agent can implement plausible 4xx/5xx logic while breaking package boundaries, adding high-cardinality labels, editing generated files by hand, or not exposing the reusable API needed by consumers.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster mostly asked for correct HTTP status grouping. That was a tempting but incomplete proxy: many trajectories visibly explored or edited the metrics registry, generated schema declarations, shared API handlers, or application catch blocks, and their status mapping could look reasonable while the overall design diverged from the requested low-cardinality API-error observation utility. A better rubric should evaluate whether the trajectory is converging on a reusable metrics-package helper that accepts an arbitrary error plus a caller-supplied observer callback and emits only grouped categories such as client class, server class, or generic failure. It should also notice visible anti-patterns: adding raw status_code or application labels despite the request to avoid per-code metrics, creating a new concrete counter/schema when no source schema workflow is established, wiring metric emission into shared API handlers in a way that introduces package coupling or recursion risk, or scattering instrumentation in one application flow. Avoid generating a standalone criterion that only checks IANA/RFC status classification or insists on enumerating every official code; prioritize visible evidence about abstraction boundaries, exported API shape, low-cardinality labels, and fallback behavior for missing/non-HTTP errors.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat API error metrics primarily as a new concrete metric counter/schema or direct shared/application instrumentation, instead of providing a lightweight reusable observer abstraction in the metrics package. This applies when visible steps or diffs show manual creation of generated metric schema declarations, registration of a new singleton counter, raw status-code or application labels, imports from shared API handlers into the metrics package or vice versa, or scattered calls in specific application flows. The flaw is absent when the trajectory exposes a small helper from the metrics package that classifies an arbitrary API error into broad low-cardinality categories and delegates actual observation to a callback supplied by the caller.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Wrong abstraction for API error metrics

better_visible_evidence: A reusable helper is added in the metrics package rather than direct instrumentation in a single app or shared API catch path
The helper accepts an error-like value and an observer callback, so callers control how the metric is recorded
Only broad categories are emitted, such as 4xx/client class, 5xx/server class, and generic failure
Missing error/status, non-HTTP failures, and non-error HTTP classes fall back to the generic failure category
misleading_visible_evidence: New concrete metric schema/counter registration is added without evidence that this is the desired generated-schema workflow
Labels include raw status codes, endpoints, methods, or application names despite the task emphasizing grouped types
Shared API handlers import the metrics singleton, creating coupling or possible recursive metric reporting
Implementation is scattered in application-specific catch blocks rather than reusable for all consumers

scale.1: No evidence of the abstraction flaw: the trajectory clearly favors a reusable exported observer/helper with callback-based reporting and broad categories only.
scale.2: Minor concern: the trajectory discusses counters or schemas but still preserves a reusable helper boundary and avoids raw-code/application-specific labels.
scale.3: Mixed evidence: the trajectory has correct broad categorization logic but is ambiguous between a reusable helper and a concrete metric/instrumentation design.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory adds or plans a concrete metric registry entry, direct API-handler/app instrumentation, or extra labels while only partially preserving reusable categorization.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory centers on new generated schema/counter wiring or invasive shared/app changes, includes raw status/application/endpoint labels, and lacks a clean callback-based observer abstraction.

experiences.title: Avoid privilege-only rubrics when reorder semantics are the real unresolved bug
experiences.description: Retrieve for pinned-item or ordered-list tasks where the trajectory has already found an existing backend admin/mod privilege check, but the remaining failures involve payload shape, no-op handling for non-members, and sorted-set/list ordering semantics.
experiences.context: Applies in a Node.js/forum-style codebase where a reorder operation is exposed through a socket or similar client-callable entry point, stores pinned or prioritized items in an ordered collection such as a sorted set, and the task statement combines authorization, ignoring unpinned/non-member items, and correct relative ordering. This guidance is especially relevant once the trajectory visibly inspected the core reorder function, the socket/client caller, existing tests, and a category/topic admin-or-moderator helper, and there is visible evidence that privilege enforcement already exists in the backend before mutation. It is less applicable early in exploration before the privilege path is known, or when the inspected implementation genuinely lacks any server-side permission check; in those situations a privilege rubric may still be useful.
experiences.experience: In these cases, generated rubrics repeatedly emphasized adding or preserving privilege checks for the reorder operation. That criterion can be tempting because the task statement mentions unprivileged users, but it is often a poor discriminator once the visible code already performs a category admin/mod check in the core reorder path. Over-focusing on authorization can over-credit trajectories that keep searching controllers/routes, add unrelated API endpoints, or merely check that a socket has a uid, while missing the actual correctness boundary: the operation must validate the reorder payload, ignore or no-op when the requested item is not currently pinned/in the ordered set, and update the existing ordered set using the same score/index direction that readers and tests use. A better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory recognizes that the remaining work is ordered-list semantics, not just permission enforcement: it should prioritize evidence such as inspecting the client payload shape, understanding whether the API sends one moved item or a full array, checking numeric order validation, checking membership before mutation, reasoning about reverse-range/high-score-first behavior, and running the full relevant stateful test group rather than isolated tests. Avoid generating a broad criterion like “add privilege validation” when the trajectory has already observed an existing backend check; instead, generate a criterion that rewards preserving that check while solving no-op and relative-order behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Reorder Semantics Beyond Existing Authorization
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should recognize, after observing an existing backend admin/mod permission check, that correctness depends on the reorder contract and ordered-set mutation semantics: validate the incoming item/order payload, preserve server-side authorization, no-op for items that are not currently members of the pinned/ordered set, and update the relative order using score/index direction consistent with how the list is later read and displayed. It should avoid treating a redundant privilege check or a new unrelated route as the main fix when the visible implementation already gates mutation by moderator/admin status.

metadata.task_pattern: A reorder bug combines permission, non-member no-op behavior, and relative ordering of pinned/prioritized items.
visible_evidence_to_prioritize: Core reorder function already contains a backend admin/mod or equivalent privilege check before mutating state.
Client/socket caller and tests reveal the expected payload shape and ordering convention.
Ordered collection is read in a direction where score/index mapping matters, such as reverse sorted-set reads.
Existing or intended tests cover invalid data, unprivileged users, unpinned/non-member no-op, and multi-item relative ordering.
avoid_as_primary_signal: Merely adding a socket uid check.
Repeatedly searching for REST/controller endpoints after the socket-only path is established.
Adding a new API route unrelated to the observed caller.
Filtering unpinned items without proving the existing pinned order remains unchanged.
Assigning scores without checking the read direction of the ordered collection.

scale.1: The trajectory focuses almost entirely on finding or adding authorization checks, despite visible evidence that backend privilege enforcement already exists, and shows no meaningful reasoning about payload validation, non-member no-op behavior, or ordering direction.
scale.2: The trajectory mentions unpinned/non-member handling or ordering but still treats privilege validation as the central fix, with little evidence that it understands the ordered-set score/index convention or the actual client/socket payload contract.
scale.3: The trajectory has comparable behavior to its parent: it identifies the core reorder path and existing permission gate, and partially considers membership filtering or tests, but has not yet formed a clear plan for preserving no-op behavior and updating relative order consistently with the collection’s read direction.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly shifts beyond redundant privilege work: it uses visible client/test evidence to reason about payload shape, validates order input, checks current membership before mutation, and accounts for sorted-set/list direction when updating relative order.
scale.5: The trajectory decisively targets the true reorder semantics: it preserves the existing server-side admin/mod gate, validates a well-defined reorder payload, no-ops without changing scores for non-members, moves the requested pinned item within the current pinned list, rewrites scores/indexes consistently with display/read order, avoids unrelated endpoint work, and verifies the full relevant stateful test group.

experiences.title: Alias-binding import contract for migration serialization
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django migration-generation task involves generated migration code referencing a framework alias such as `models.Model` without a corresponding import, especially from serialized model bases.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Django repository trajectories where the agent is diagnosing migration writer/serializer import collection and the visible evidence shows generated migration text containing `models.Model` or another alias-qualified framework object. It is most useful after the agent has inspected serialization/import flow or reproduced generated migration output; it can still be a weaker early-stage criterion if the agent has found a serializer special case emitting the alias. Do not apply as a generic import-validity rubric when the generated expression does not actually use the alias, when default bases are omitted from output, or when the implementation changes the rendered expression to a fully qualified name with matching imports. Avoid using this criterion for unrelated migration failures where the issue is database state, app registry setup, or test-runner configuration rather than source-code import emission.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the exact contract between rendered migration source and collected imports: if serialization emits `models.Model`, the generated migration must bind the name `models`, preferably via `from django.db import models`, and the writer may then consolidate it with the migrations import. This aligned well because the decisive visible evidence was not merely that migrations should be valid Python; it was that the agent found a class/type serializer special case rendering `models.Model` while returning no import, reproduced a migration header lacking `models`, and then verified output containing a valid Django `models` import while preserving the original bases expression and app-local imports. A better rubric should prioritize that evidence: identification of the serializer import contract, use of an import that actually binds the alias used in generated code, and validation on the mixed-base/custom-field scenario where no other field serialization necessarily forces a `models` import. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as adding special handling only in the migration writer for `bases`, requiring `bases` to be expanded for formatting, accepting `import models` or `import django.db.models` even though they do not bind the `models` name used by `models.Model`, or judging primarily on whether the agent managed to run the full upstream test suite in a difficult environment. Regression tests or manual `makemigrations`/writer-output validation are valuable, but the core judgeable criterion is whether the trajectory makes every emitted alias resolvable without changing unrelated serialization semantics.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Serialized alias has matching import
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should ensure that whenever migration serialization emits a source expression using the `models` alias, such as `models.Model` in a non-default model bases tuple alongside an app-local mixin or custom class, the generated migration imports Django's models namespace in a way that binds that alias. Strong evidence includes locating the serializer/import contract that produced the alias without imports, rejecting imports that do not bind the emitted name, preserving existing serialization of custom fields and app-local bases, and validating generated migration output or an equivalent writer serialization result.

metadata.required_binding: from django.db import models or equivalent alias-binding import
metadata.representative_trigger: non-default serialized model bases containing both an app-local class and the framework base model
invalid_proxies_to_penalize: import django.db.models while still emitting models.Model
ad hoc writer insertion that ignores serializer import contracts

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory connects the emitted `models.Model` expression to a required import binding for `models`; it focuses on unrelated setup, broad migration validity, or formatting-only changes.
scale.2: Recognizes a missing import problem but proposes or accepts an import that may not bind the emitted alias, or does not distinguish alias resolution from generic Django import presence.
scale.3: Identifies that generated migration code using `models.Model` needs a corresponding Django models import, but provides limited evidence about the serializer/import source or validation of the mixed-bases scenario.
scale.4: Clearly traces the missing import to migration serialization/import collection, uses an alias-binding import such as `from django.db import models`, and validates generated output for a scenario where `models.Model` appears in bases.
scale.5: Fully establishes the serializer contract: the emitted `models.Model` string contributes a matching Django models import, invalid alternatives are rejected, existing app-local/custom-field serialization is preserved, import consolidation remains compatible, and the fixed output is validated as valid migration Python in the representative mixed-base case.

experiences.title: Do Not Require a Closed Form When Safe Unevaluated Semantics Are Correct
experiences.description: Use when rubric generation treats the absence of a preferred symbolic closed form as a correctness failure even though preserving an unevaluated product avoids a mathematically invalid transformation.
experiences.context: Computer-algebra evaluators may legitimately decline to simplify expressions outside a proven rule's domain. For a product over an additive non-polynomial term, mathematical correctness is more important than producing a particular special-function form. A stronger criterion is warranted only if the task explicitly requires that form or if finite substitution/evaluation remains wrong after the normal evaluation sequence.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics conflated useful simplification with correctness and penalized patches that safely stopped distributing a product across addition. Generate a negative rubric for provably invalid transformations or regressions to supported polynomial/rational products. Do not make a named closed form mandatory when leaving the expression unevaluated is an accepted conservative result.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Mathematically Invalid Additive-Product Transformation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize a symbolic product change when it distributes a product across additive terms, returns a result contradicted by finite numeric expansion, or disables previously valid polynomial/rational product rules. A conservative unevaluated result is not itself a defect unless visible requirements demand further evaluation.

observable_evidence: finite direct expansion versus evaluator result
scope of the changed Add rule
supported polynomial/rational regression checks
explicit task requirement for a closed form

scale.1: No visible evidence of a mathematically invalid product transformation or a regression outside the intended rule boundary; the available implementation and validation evidence is consistent with the required behavior.
scale.2: A minor or early-stage concern about a mathematically invalid product transformation or a regression outside the intended rule boundary is visible, but it is not confirmed and the trajectory is still actively resolving it.
scale.3: Evidence about a mathematically invalid product transformation or a regression outside the intended rule boundary is mixed or incomplete; the concern remains plausible but is not yet decisive.
scale.4: Clear visible evidence indicates a mathematically invalid product transformation or a regression outside the intended rule boundary, with no convincing correction or validation yet.
scale.5: The trajectory directly reproduces or validates a mathematically invalid product transformation or a regression outside the intended rule boundary, or claims completion while the contradiction remains unresolved.

experiences.title: Do not equate XML-removal grep results with a correct JSON migration
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for a legacy XML-to-JSON Solr/Worksearch refactor where the trajectory has found XML parsing and is replacing it with dict/list handling.
experiences.context: This applies in Python web-plugin code that manually builds Solr select requests and adapts Solr responses into template/API-facing objects. A rubric that merely asks whether lxml imports, XML() calls, XMLSyntaxError handling, or XML fixtures were removed can be misleading once the agent has begun editing: those removals are necessary but do not show that the new JSON path preserves the old search contract. The original XML-removal idea is still appropriate as a narrow negative check when production code still imports or invokes XML parsing for Solr query responses. It should not be the main success criterion after edits are underway, especially when visible evidence includes changes to run_solr_query, do_search, facet parsing, get_doc/document conversion, work_search, or tests.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded locating/removing all XML parsing and replacing it with JSON handling. That is correct only as a surface-level cleanup criterion. In these trajectories, the dangerous failure mode was superficial conversion: agents removed or commented out XML imports and rewrote .find/.attrib/.text access, but used the wrong response type between helper functions, double-parsed or failed to parse JSON, mishandled Solr JSON facet_fields as dicts instead of alternating value/count lists, changed boolean semantics such as string 'false' becoming truthy, returned raw docs where template-compatible storage objects were expected, or rewrote unrelated tests/query expectations. A better rubric should focus on the end-to-end JSON response contract: how requests force or preserve wt=json, what execute/run helpers return, how do_search handles None/error/HTML/JSON failures, how facets/spellcheck/docs/numFound are extracted from Solr JSON, and whether public/template/API output shapes remain compatible. Avoid generating a criterion that treats a clean grep for XML/lxml/etree or removal of XML test fixtures as strong evidence of correctness. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence of consistent data types across call boundaries, faithful handling of Solr JSON structures, preservation of existing field/boolean/author/facet behavior, and minimal test updates limited to the migrated format.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize a trajectory that performs a superficial XML-to-JSON migration in the Worksearch Solr response path without proving that the new JSON data contract is internally consistent and behavior-preserving. This flaw is present when visible edits or plans emphasize removing lxml/XML calls while leaving or introducing mismatches such as parsing an already-decoded object with json.loads, treating a Response/bytes/dict inconsistently between execute_solr_query, run_solr_query, do_search, and work_search, assuming the wrong Solr facet_fields or spellcheck shape, returning raw JSON docs where callers/templates expect converted storage objects, changing boolean/string semantics for fields like public_scan or has_fulltext, failing to preserve numFound/facet/doc/spellcheck/error outputs, or rewriting unrelated tests/query-parser behavior to make the migration appear green.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial JSON Migration Contract Breakage

metadata.task_type: legacy Solr XML response parsing removal
metadata.environment: Python Worksearch plugin using requests/web.storage and Solr JSON responses
primary_visible_evidence: edits to Solr request/response helper return types
edits to do_search/work_search JSON parsing
edits to facet, spellcheck, and document conversion logic
test changes beyond XML fixture conversion
metadata.avoid_proxy: absence of XML/lxml/etree grep hits alone
