scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory either has not edited the migration yet, or it explicitly keeps response types consistent and preserves Solr JSON extraction and caller-facing output contracts.
scale.2: Minor evidence: XML removal is emphasized, but the trajectory also checks most JSON contracts; only small uncertainties remain around an edge case such as error formatting or one optional field.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory replaces XML access with JSON access but leaves unclear or partially inconsistent assumptions about response type, facet/spellcheck shape, or converted document output.
scale.4: Clear evidence: visible edits introduce likely contract breaks such as double JSON parsing, wrong facet_fields representation, raw docs returned to template-facing code, or changed boolean semantics, even if XML imports/calls are removed.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory mainly proves removal of XML text/imports while multiple core contracts are broken or unvalidated, and it also changes unrelated tests or behavior to accommodate the refactor.

experiences.title: End-to-End Tri-State Option Semantics
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go SSH/CLI client task replaces a boolean forwarding option with explicit modes that must choose among multiple runtime resources, especially when parser, CLI flag, client config, web/default behavior, and session setup are all involved.
experiences.context: Apply in a Go client codebase where an existing boolean option currently means only enabled/disabled, but the requested behavior requires three user-visible values such as yes/local/no with distinct runtime effects. This is most useful once the trajectory has visible evidence of the parser/config path and the session/resource-selection path, or when edits have started in those areas. It is less useful for unrelated server-side authorization booleans, pure role/capability checks, or very early exploration before the agent has identified where the selected mode is consumed. At final-review stage, the criterion should be strict about end-to-end propagation and command-line compatibility; during early planning, it can reward correct identification of the semantic boundary.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics generally asked for ForwardAgent to support yes/local/no, defaults, validation, and session application. That is the right semantic target because the decisive visible issue is not merely accepting another string: the old boolean path loses the distinction between forwarding the system SSH agent, forwarding the internal client agent, and forwarding nothing. A better rubric should explicitly require the chosen mode to be represented and propagated all the way from configuration/CLI parsing into session creation, where it selects the correct agent object. It should also check the boundary cases that broad rubrics can miss: invalid errors must name the option and token, values must be normalized case-insensitively, normal CLI default must remain disabled, web-terminal/defaulted sessions that previously used the internal agent must map to local rather than yes, and OpenSSH-style command-line shorthand such as bare forwarding flags should not be accidentally broken by changing a boolean flag into a mandatory string flag unless the task explicitly allows that. Avoid tempting but weak criteria such as build success, adding local to an allowed-values map, changing a bool field to string, or adding tests only for parser acceptance. Also avoid focusing on role/server authorization booleans unless the user request is about authorization; in this pattern those booleans are separate from client-side resource selection. Prioritize visible evidence in diffs and trajectory notes: a durable mode/enum or normalized constants; parser validation with option-specific errors; CLI/config merge preserving precedence and defaults; session code selecting system-agent handle for yes, internal-agent handle for local, and no forwarding call for no; web/client defaults set intentionally; no stale boolean or legacy true branch remains; and targeted tests or inspections cover parsing, invalid values, defaults, and session selection.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Mode Propagation and Agent Selection
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the forwarding option is implemented as an explicit three-mode contract, not as a widened boolean. Excellent evidence shows case-insensitive parsing of exactly the supported values, option-specific invalid-value errors, preservation of CLI/config precedence and defaults, explicit web/internal default behavior, and session-time selection of the correct runtime agent for each mode with no stale boolean forwarding path.

required_visible_evidence: mode representation survives from parsed user input into client/session configuration
yes maps to the system SSH agent rather than the internal client agent
local maps to the internal client agent
no prevents agent forwarding calls
invalid-value handling names the forwarding option and includes the rejected token
normal CLI and web-terminal defaults are handled separately
command-line compatibility is considered, including OpenSSH-style shorthand when present
avoid_as_primary_evidence: generic build success
only adding a new accepted string to the parser
only changing a field type without showing session behavior
modifying unrelated server authorization booleans

scale.1: No visible progress toward preserving a three-mode forwarding decision; the trajectory remains focused on the old boolean behavior or unrelated authorization/config areas.
scale.2: Weak progress: accepts or mentions additional values, but the selected mode is not clearly propagated to the runtime session path or still collapses yes/local into a boolean.
scale.3: Moderate progress: parser/config and some defaults are addressed, and session selection is planned or partially edited, but important boundaries such as invalid errors, case normalization, CLI shorthand compatibility, web default, or stale boolean branches remain unresolved.
scale.4: Strong progress: the trajectory shows an explicit mode flowing through parser/CLI/client config into session creation, with correct yes/local/no agent behavior and distinct CLI/web defaults; only minor validation/test or compatibility details remain uncertain.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the implementation and validation plan cover exact values, case-insensitive parsing, clear invalid-token errors, CLI/config precedence and shorthand compatibility, CLI default no, web default local, correct session agent selection for all modes, no stale boolean forwarding logic, and targeted tests or inspections for these contracts.

experiences.title: Local proxy URL rewrite must be integrated at real service-URL consumers
experiences.description: Use when a task asks for environment-gated domain rewriting of runtime service URLs in a monorepo, especially when literal domain searches find few production references and the agent may be adding an isolated/shared helper without proving the affected URLs flow through it.
experiences.context: Applies in browser TypeScript monorepos with app-level and shared URL helpers, where the reported behavior is that URLs received or generated at runtime for one deployment domain must be rewritten only under a local/proxy host. The criterion is most useful after the trajectory has searched URL/config/app-link areas or started editing rewrite logic. It should emphasize finding the actual URL consumption paths for externally supplied service URLs, not just adding a generic helper. It may be premature during the very first repository-orientation steps, and it should not force app-specific consumers if the visible trajectory has strong evidence that all affected URLs are constructed by one central shared URL-generation API.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics were useful because they penalized trajectories that either made no implementation progress or added domain-rewrite code without evidence that the problematic service URLs would pass through it. In these cases, repeated searches showed that the problematic domain was not hardcoded in normal production code, which is a cue that the URLs are likely API/config/runtime values consumed at app call sites. A better rubric should therefore require both the exact rewrite contract and demonstrated integration at the affected runtime URL consumers, such as transfer/download/upload/share/public-link paths, with tests or reasoning showing those are the URLs observed by users. Avoid the tempting but weaker criterion “add a shared local SSO rewrite helper” or “patch app-link/static/API URL builders” unless the trajectory has shown the reported service URLs actually flow through those helpers. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent: stops repeating exhausted grep searches, traces runtime URL values to their use sites, wraps those URLs before fetch/navigation/display, preserves path/query/hash and the local port, gates on the current local proxy hostname, and leaves localhost/production/non-target domains unchanged.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the local-proxy domain rewrite is not merely implemented as an unused helper or placed in unrelated app-link/static URL code, but is applied where externally supplied service URLs are actually consumed by the application. Strong evidence includes tracing runtime service URLs from API/config responses to fetch/upload/download/share-link/public-link usage, adding a narrowly gated rewrite at those consumption points or a helper invoked by them, preserving subdomain, path, query, hash, protocol as appropriate, and replacing the target deployment-domain host/port with the corresponding current local-proxy host/port only when the current browser hostname is under the local proxy domain. It should also show non-local hosts and unrelated URLs remain unchanged.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Integrated runtime service-URL rewrite

required_evidence: current-environment gate based on browser hostname ending in the local proxy domain
target URL check for the deployment-domain suffix that needs rewriting
application of the rewrite at actual runtime service URL consumers, not only helper definition
preservation of URL path/search/hash and use of current local port
unchanged behavior for localhost, production domains, and unrelated target URLs
negative_cues: repeated literal-domain grep searches after they stop producing new implementation evidence
helper added but never invoked by the affected service URL paths
patching shared app navigation/static URL helpers without showing the reported URLs flow through them
rewriting based only on target URL without checking current environment

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward locating or implementing the rewrite; trajectory is still generic exploration or repeats exhausted searches with no new evidence.
scale.2: Identifies the basic domain-rewrite contract or likely helper area, but has not traced the affected runtime service URLs or made an integrated change.
scale.3: Adds or plans a plausible rewrite helper with the right local-environment and target-domain checks, but invocation sites are missing, speculative, or limited to unrelated URL builders.
scale.4: Traces likely runtime service URL consumers and integrates the rewrite into at least the main affected paths, with mostly correct gating and URL preservation, though some edge coverage or validation may be incomplete.
scale.5: Clearly identifies all relevant runtime service URL consumption paths, applies a narrowly scoped rewrite before those URLs are used, preserves subdomain/path/query/hash/current port, leaves all non-local or unrelated cases unchanged, and includes focused validation or tests for both rewritten and unchanged cases.

experiences.title: Do not equate stack dtype checks with fixing MultiIndex level materialization
experiences.description: Retrieve when an xarray/pandas stack-related dtype issue is being evaluated and the trajectory mostly inspects Dataset.stack, PandasMultiIndex metadata, or local reproductions rather than the path that materializes MultiIndex level values as coordinate arrays.
experiences.context: This warning applies in Python data-library tasks where a coordinate dtype changes after stacking into a pandas-backed MultiIndex. A generic dtype-preservation rubric is tempting because the issue statement itself says int32 should remain int32. It becomes misleading when the trajectory is still in exploration, has no task-specific patch, only verifies that the MVCE passes in the current dependency environment, inspects level dtype metadata such as stored level-coordinate dtypes, or makes unrelated dependency-compatibility edits. In that situation, passing local checks or finding dtype metadata does not prove the user-facing coordinate array conversion is fixed. The original dtype-preservation idea is still appropriate at final review if the trajectory has traced and changed the actual conversion boundary where MultiIndex level values become numpy-backed coordinate values, or has a regression test that exercises the reported user-facing `.values.dtype` behavior under compatible dependencies.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked broadly whether stack operations preserve coordinate dtypes or whether PandasMultiIndex tracks level dtypes. That criterion is semantically relevant but too broad: it can over-credit trajectories that merely inspect stack construction, confirm metadata is present, or observe the reproducer passing locally without producing a corrective patch. For this class of bug, the important evidence is not just MultiIndex creation or stored dtype metadata; it is whether the path that exposes a MultiIndex level as an array defaults to the original level dtype when materializing values. A better rubric should penalize treating local non-reproduction, factorization-code dtypes, or level metadata as sufficient, and should prioritize visible evidence that the agent identified the user-facing conversion boundary, avoided unrelated environment fixes, and either implemented a targeted dtype-preserving conversion or added a regression test for the exact stacked-coordinate dtype behavior. Avoid generating a criterion that rewards broad dtype-preservation verification alone when the trajectory has not connected that verification to the actual materialization path.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a stack/MultiIndex coordinate dtype bug, the trajectory has the flaw of relying on generic stack dtype preservation checks, level-coordinate metadata inspection, or passing local reproductions without identifying or fixing the array-materialization path that exposes MultiIndex level values as coordinate values. This flaw is especially evident if the agent repeatedly explores stack construction or pandas factorization, concludes the issue is already fixed because the MVCE passes in its environment, or makes unrelated dependency compatibility edits instead of a task-specific change.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Over-crediting metadata or local non-reproduction instead of level-value materialization

metadata.task_family: xarray Dataset.stack / pandas MultiIndex coordinate dtype preservation
misleading_proxies: local MVCE passes under a different dependency setup
stored level-coordinate dtype metadata appears correct
pandas factorization or MultiIndex levels preserve dtype internally
unrelated NumPy compatibility edits are made to run the environment
preferred_visible_evidence: trace reaches the conversion point where MultiIndex level values become numpy coordinate values
patch or proposed fix explicitly preserves the original dtype during materialization
regression test checks the reported stacked coordinate `.values.dtype` behavior
trajectory distinguishes stacked-dimension object dtype from level-coordinate dtype

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory connects the reported dtype change to the user-facing level-value materialization path and has a targeted fix or targeted regression evidence.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory includes some generic stack or metadata checks, but also shows progress toward the conversion boundary and avoids treating those checks as sufficient.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory understands dtype preservation is required but focuses mainly on stack construction or level metadata, with limited evidence of investigating materialized coordinate values.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory repeatedly verifies local dtype preservation or inspects metadata and does not produce a task-specific fix for the user-facing conversion path.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory effectively treats a passing local reproduction or unrelated compatibility edit as resolution, with no credible task-specific patch or investigation of how MultiIndex level values are materialized.

experiences.title: NodeBB backlinks require timeline-lifecycle integration
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a NodeBB-like forum feature that creates reverse references/backlinks between topics from links inside posts, especially after the trajectory has identified post creation/edit flows, topic rendering/timeline mechanisms, admin settings, and localization.
experiences.context: Applies to cross-cutting forum features where a post referencing another topic must cause visible state on the referenced topic, gated by an admin setting and shown as part of the topic timeline or native topic-event UI. It is most useful once the trajectory has moved beyond initial repository listing into design or implementation choices. It is less appropriate for very early exploration with no implementation direction, for repositories without a native timeline/event rendering concept, or for simple UI-only link-display tasks where no post lifecycle synchronization is required.
experiences.experience: The earlier rubrics were useful when they recognized that this feature cannot be judged by a single edit: it needs link detection, persistence, retrieval/display, settings, and localization. However, broad component checklists and detection/storage-only rubrics can over-credit patches that add a standalone backlink module, JSON sorted-set records, an admin checkbox, or an isolated template without being wired into the existing topic timeline and post lifecycle. A better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory is using the platform’s native topic event/timeline/rendering path, and whether backlinks are synchronized when posts are created and edited, de-duplicated, self-links ignored, hidden when the setting is disabled, localized, and linked to the exact source post. The criterion should prioritize visible evidence such as: consistent config key across defaults/admin/runtime checks; registration or direct invocation from real post lifecycle paths; reconciliation/removal of old backlinks on edits/deletes where applicable; existing topic-event/timeline data being populated rather than only editing generated build artifacts or one theme copy; valid localization/templates; and a source-post href. Avoid tempting but weak criteria such as requiring every language to be translated, rewarding edits to generated templates, or treating successful URL regex extraction as sufficient for the feature.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Native timeline-backed backlink lifecycle
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate an implementation plan or edits that integrate reverse topic backlinks through the forum's established post lifecycle and topic timeline/event rendering path, not merely through an ad hoc storage helper or isolated template. Strong evidence includes detecting internal topic URLs from saved post content, ignoring self-references and duplicates, validating referenced topics, recording enough source-post data to link back to the exact referencing post, reconciling backlinks when post content changes or is removed, gating creation or display with the same admin config key exposed in defaults and settings UI, adding base-locale labels, and rendering through source-controlled topic timeline/event UI rather than generated build output or a single unrelated theme copy.

required_evidence: internal topic URL extraction tied to real post create/edit lifecycle
stable backlink relation from referenced topic to source post
self-reference and duplicate handling
setting gate consistently used in admin UI, defaults, and runtime display
localized label for the timeline entry or section
rendering through native topic timeline/event/source template path
visible link to the referencing post
anti_evidence: only creates a standalone backlinks module without registering or invoking it
only edits generated build templates or one theme artifact
adds admin setting/localization but no backend synchronization
stores backlink data but never exposes it to topic rendering
parses links only from href HTML when the available content format is not confirmed
does not update or remove backlinks after post edits/deletes
uses inconsistent config keys across UI, defaults, and runtime checks
metadata.environment: Node.js/NodeBB-like forum with posts, topics, meta config, admin settings templates, language JSON, and topic timeline/event rendering

scale.1: No concrete evidence of backlink lifecycle integration; the trajectory is still generic exploration or only mentions the requirement.
scale.2: Implements or plans one isolated surface, such as a setting, a regex, or a storage helper, but lacks clear wiring to real post lifecycle and topic display.
scale.3: Covers several surfaces such as detection, storage, admin setting, or display, but relies on ad hoc rendering, inconsistent config, generated templates, or omits edit/delete reconciliation.
scale.4: Shows strong end-to-end wiring through real post lifecycle and topic rendering with setting gate, localization, and source-post links, with only minor uncertainty about edge cases or validation.
scale.5: Clearly follows the platform's native timeline/event/source-template path and fully synchronizes backlink creation, update, removal, de-duplication, config gating, localization, and exact source-post linking with validation evidence.

experiences.title: Do not reward deletion-only client-info cleanup when the requirement is refresh-wide pruning
experiences.description: Retrieve when a sessions/device-management task asks stale device client metadata to be removed after device-list changes or refreshes, and the trajectory is focusing on sign-out/delete-device paths.
experiences.context: In a TypeScript/React Matrix-client style codebase, client/device metadata may be stored as account-data keyed by device identifiers, while the sessions UI refreshes from an authoritative device list. A rubric that asks only whether deleted devices have their client-info account-data removed during an explicit delete/sign-out flow is misleading when the task says cleanup must happen after any successful device list refresh, including but not limited to sign-out. Deletion-path cleanup can still be a valid supplementary criterion if the task is specifically scoped to explicit device deletion or if the refresh path already delegates to that deletion path. It should not be the main criterion when device-list changes may happen outside the local delete operation, or when the visible trajectory has not connected cleanup to the successful refresh result used by the sessions view.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded locating or modifying delete/sign-out handlers to delete client-info account-data for the requested device IDs. That is too narrow for tasks framed around stale session metadata after device-list refresh: it can miss devices removed elsewhere, cleanup triggered by remote changes, and the actual display path that merges fetched devices with client-info metadata. A better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory uses the successfully fetched authoritative device list as the source of truth, compares it against existing client-info account-data events, and prunes metadata for identifiers absent from that list only after refresh succeeds. Avoid the tempting criterion “deleteDevices removes client information for deleted IDs” as the primary signal. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent inspected or modified the sessions refresh hook/list-loading path, accounted for missing user/device IDs without throwing, added or reused a maintainable client-info event-type/pruning helper, and avoided cleanup based on transient missing IDs or unauthoritative local deletion attempts.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a task requiring stale client-information metadata to be removed after any successful sessions/device-list refresh, penalize trajectories that treat explicit delete/sign-out cleanup as sufficient without tying pruning to the authoritative refreshed device list used by the sessions UI. This flaw is present when the agent only adds or plans cleanup in delete-device/sign-out handlers, device-update listeners, or per-device removal helpers, while lacking visible evidence that successful refresh results are used to identify all currently valid device IDs and prune account-data entries for absent devices. It is especially severe if cleanup can run from incomplete local state, ignores refresh failures or missing identifiers, or leaves the display path able to read stale client-info events for devices not returned by the refreshed list.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Deletion-only stale metadata cleanup

metadata.task_type: sessions/device metadata hygiene in a TypeScript React Matrix client
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: cleanup in explicit delete/sign-out handlers alone
better_visible_evidence: cleanup is integrated after successful device-list refresh or the refresh path explicitly invokes a pruning helper
the refreshed authoritative device IDs are compared with existing client-info account-data event keys
missing user/device IDs are handled safely without using empty or transient state as proof that all devices are gone
client-info event type construction remains centralized or otherwise maintainable for future pruning
metadata.boundary_where_deletion_cleanup_is_ok: when the task is scoped only to explicit local device deletion, or when refresh-wide pruning is already visibly handled elsewhere

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory clearly ties stale client-info pruning to successful authoritative device-list refresh and handles missing identifiers safely; deletion cleanup, if present, is only supplementary.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory discusses or edits delete/sign-out cleanup, but also shows a credible plan or partial implementation to prune using refreshed device-list results.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory recognizes stale client-info account-data and refresh requirements, but implementation/planning is ambiguous between refresh-wide pruning and delete-only cleanup.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory mainly implements or plans per-device cleanup in delete/sign-out flows or device-update listeners, with little or no integration into the sessions refresh result.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory explicitly treats deletion-path cleanup as satisfying the refresh-wide requirement, or performs pruning from incomplete/local state such that devices removed outside the local delete path can still leave stale client-info metadata or valid metadata could be removed during transient startup/auth states.

experiences.title: Class Objects Must Not Be Treated as Estimator Instances
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python estimator-cloning or parameter-introspection bug involves class/type objects being stored as parameter values and an API mistakenly calls instance methods on those classes.
experiences.context: Applies in Python ML/library codebases, especially scikit-learn-style estimator APIs, when the task and trajectory show a clone/copy routine that identifies estimators by the presence of an instance method such as `get_params`, recursively clones parameter values with an unsafe/deep-copy fallback, and fails because a parameter is an estimator class rather than an estimator instance. This is most useful once the trajectory has inspected the clone implementation or reproduced/reasoned about the unbound-method failure. It is premature during pure repository exploration, and it is not applicable to tasks where parameters are always instances, where classes are intentionally callable factories to instantiate, or where the bug concerns unrelated build/import failures rather than the clone contract.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these trajectories focused on the semantic boundary between estimator instances and estimator classes. A class may expose methods like `get_params`, but it is not an initialized estimator and should not be sent through the estimator-instance branch that calls instance introspection. The better criterion should reward evidence that the agent changes the clone decision point so class/type objects are routed through the non-estimator value path when recursively cloning parameters, while leaving normal estimator instance cloning, recursive container handling, constructor reconstruction, and post-construction sanity checks intact. Avoid over-weighting a requirement to add a project-native regression test when the task is a small core-library bug and the visible trajectory may be blocked by local build issues; tests are useful evidence but should not replace the behavioral contract. Also avoid a criterion that merely says to special-case class-valued parameters inside the parameter loop if the implementation then duplicates or breaks the existing clone loop, omits object construction, or bypasses sanity checks. Prioritize visible evidence such as identifying the exact `hasattr(..., 'get_params')` style estimator check, recognizing that class objects cause unbound instance-method calls, using an explicit type/class guard before calling instance methods, and preserving the existing clone algorithm around that guard.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should move toward a fix where class/type objects used as estimator parameter values are treated as ordinary non-estimator values during recursive cloning, so the clone routine does not call unbound estimator instance methods on classes. The evidence should also show that the existing behavior for estimator instances, supported containers, constructor-based reconstruction, unsafe fallback copying for non-estimator parameter values, and sanity checks remains intact.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Preserve Clone Semantics While Routing Classes Away from Instance Introspection

required_context: A clone/copy routine distinguishes estimators from non-estimators using an instance-introspection method such as get_params
The reported failure involves a class/type object stored as a parameter value
Recursive parameter cloning uses an unsafe mode or fallback path for non-estimator values
strong_positive_evidence: The agent identifies that classes can have estimator methods but are not estimator instances
The proposed or applied change checks for class/type objects before invoking instance methods
Class-valued parameters are preserved or safely copied as values rather than recursively cloned as estimator instances
Normal estimator instances and container recursion continue through the existing clone flow
Constructor reconstruction and post-construction parameter validation are not removed or bypassed
negative_evidence: The patch only special-cases one parameter name or one estimator class
The patch skips cloning broadly for all parameters or all objects with get_params
The patch removes the construction of the cloned estimator or its sanity check
The trajectory validates only against an installed external package instead of the edited source when local validation is possible

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent understands or addresses the class-versus-instance boundary; the trajectory focuses on unrelated build/import issues or generic cloning without identifying the unbound-method cause.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the agent mentions estimator classes or the failure mode but has not connected it to the clone decision point, or proposes a narrow workaround that risks bypassing normal clone behavior.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent identifies that class-valued parameters should avoid instance-method introspection, but the visible plan or edit is incomplete, lacks preservation of surrounding clone semantics, or depends mainly on ad hoc tests.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the agent targets the estimator-detection branch with a class/type guard and appears to preserve recursive parameter cloning, estimator reconstruction, container handling, and unsafe fallback semantics.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory clearly demonstrates the unbound-method failure, applies or plans a minimal class/type guard before instance introspection, verifies or reasons through class-valued parameters plus normal estimator instances/containers, and leaves the existing clone reconstruction and sanity checks intact.

experiences.title: Precise External Identifier Propagation at Library Conversion Boundaries
experiences.description: Use when a Go task asks to expose an external package identifier, such as Trivy PURL, in Vuls-style library scan output and the trajectory has started inspecting the model struct and Trivy-to-internal conversion adapters.
experiences.context: Applies to Go repositories that convert third-party scanner package/application results into internal scan-result models. The useful moment is after the trajectory has identified the internal library model and at least one conversion boundary that constructs library entries from external package objects. The criterion is especially relevant when the external identifier is nested or pointer-valued and must be stringified safely. It is premature during pure repository exploration with no identified model/converter path; in that stage, prefer a discovery-oriented rubric. It should not be broadened to every reporter, detector, vulnerability, or OS-package path unless the visible task and code show those paths are part of the missing library output contract.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics were useful when they focused on whether the agent preserved PURL through the internal Library model and the Trivy-to-library conversion path, because visible trajectories repeatedly showed the model lacked a PURL field and conversion code copied name/version/path/digest while dropping identifier metadata. However, rubrics became misleading when they rewarded broad 'all downstream outputs' changes or treated any PURL-looking field access as sufficient. A better rubric should require: adding an exposed PURL field to the library model; populating it only at library-package conversion boundaries relevant to LibraryScanners; deriving the value from the correct Trivy package identifier representation or Trivy helper; converting pointer/object PURL values to strings with nil/error handling; and preserving existing package classification and fields. Avoid tempting proxies such as direct `lib.PURL`/`p.PURL` access without verification, unguarded `.String()` on a nullable identifier, changes to vulnerability or OS-package logic just because they also mention packages, or SBOM/reporting rewrites that do not address the scan-result library model. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent has verified the external type shape, found every relevant library-entry construction site, and is not expanding the patch into unrelated conversion behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly plan a precise, compile-safe propagation of external package URL identifiers into the internal library scanner output: the library model exposes a PURL value; library-package conversion code assigns it from the external package identifier or canonical helper as a string with nil/error handling; all relevant library-package conversion paths visible in the trajectory are covered; and unrelated vulnerability, OS-package, detector, or reporter behavior is left unchanged unless explicitly required by the task.

experiences.title: End-to-End Quiet Disablement for Optional Telemetry State Failures
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go service task concerns optional telemetry using a local state directory/file and the user-visible bug is warning-level log noise in read-only or non-persistent environments.
experiences.context: Apply in Go codebases where telemetry is optional, persists local state under a configurable state directory, and errors from state-directory creation or state-file open/write are propagated to a startup/reporting loop that logs warnings. This is especially relevant once the trajectory has found both the telemetry state I/O path and the caller warning sites, or the task statement itself explicitly requires quiet disablement in read-only filesystems. Do not apply to critical application storage, database migration, or server startup failures where continuing silently would be unsafe. Do not over-apply to unrelated telemetry network/client failures unless the task also says those should be quiet. At very early exploration stages, this criterion can be used as a target only if the task statement already names read-only state-directory warnings; otherwise wait until the trajectory identifies the actual logging and I/O paths.
experiences.experience:
The prior rubrics in this cluster were useful because they captured the real acceptance contract: optional telemetry must stop producing warning-level noise when its local state storage is inaccessible, while the rest of the service continues. The decisive visible evidence is not merely that the agent found telemetry code, but whether it connects all parts of the failure chain: startup state-directory initialization, telemetry state-file open/read/write/truncate operations, and caller code that turns returned report errors into warnings. A strong rubric should reward an end-to-end quiet-disable/no-op design with debug-level diagnostics at most, covering both directory creation/access failures and existing non-writable directory or state-file failures. It should also reward preventing repeated periodic warnings once telemetry has become unusable.

Avoid tempting but weak proxy criteria such as “adds a writability probe,” “handles os.ErrPermission,” “changes one Warn to Debug,” or “passes existing telemetry tests.” Those changes can miss read-only filesystem errors, fail under root-based permission tests, leave other warning sites intact, or keep retrying/logging periodically. Also avoid requiring a specific refactor shape; a localized sentinel/no-op implementation or a reporter-runner refactor can be acceptable if the visible behavior satisfies the quiet optional-telemetry contract. Prioritize visible evidence that the trajectory identifies the warning call sites, understands that returned telemetry state errors trigger those warnings, handles read-only/non-writable errors from both initialization and report-time file I/O, and validates without relying on chmod-only reproduction as root.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Quiet Optional Telemetry Disablement
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should move toward an implementation where inaccessible or non-writable telemetry state storage disables or skips optional telemetry quietly, with debug-level logs at most, no warning-level propagation from startup or periodic reporting, no repeated warning spam, and no disruption to normal server operation. The criterion should consider both state-directory initialization failures and telemetry state-file open/write/truncate failures, while preserving warning/error behavior for unrelated critical application failures.

observable_evidence: The trajectory identifies that telemetry state is stored in a local configurable directory/file.
The trajectory identifies caller warning sites that log errors returned from telemetry startup or reporting.
The trajectory distinguishes optional telemetry state failures from critical server/storage failures.
The trajectory considers read-only filesystem errors and non-writable existing directories, not only missing directories.
The trajectory avoids relying solely on chmod-based reproduction when running as root.
metadata.scope: optional telemetry local state handling in read-only or no-persistence deployments
anti_patterns: only changing one warning log level while leaving report-time errors to warn elsewhere
only adding a temporary writability probe without handling actual open/write/truncate failures
only checking os.ErrPermission and missing read-only filesystem errors
continuing to retry indefinitely with warning-level logs
silencing unrelated critical startup or storage failures

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward quiet telemetry disablement; the trajectory has not connected state-directory/file failures to warning logs or normal operation requirements.
scale.2: Recognizes telemetry state access as relevant but focuses on a narrow or unreliable proxy, such as a single writability check, a single log-level change, or permission-only handling, without covering the full warning path.
scale.3: Matches parent-level behavior: identifies the main telemetry state I/O and warning propagation path and proposes partial quiet handling, but coverage of startup versus report-time failures, repeated warnings, or read-only error varieties remains incomplete.
scale.4: Strong progress: covers most state-directory creation/access and state-file open/write failures with debug-only handling or no-op disablement, and addresses caller warning propagation so normal operation continues.
scale.5: Complete end-to-end approach: optional telemetry is disabled or stopped quietly for inaccessible/non-writable state storage across initialization and periodic reporting; warning-level logs are eliminated for this expected environment; repeated retries/noise are prevented; unrelated critical failures remain observable; and validation strategy accounts for real read-only behavior rather than root-masked chmod tests.

experiences.title: Centralize Edition Normalization at the Matching Boundary
experiences.description: Retrieve when an OpenLibrary-style edition matching task involves raw versus expanded record shapes, derived title/ISBN fields, author enrichment, and threshold-based comparison semantics.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python catalog/import workflow where edition comparison is layered: a public matching wrapper converts stored edition objects, a lower-level threshold scorer assumes normalized record fields, and helper functions expand titles/ISBNs and enrich authors. This guidance is most useful once the trajectory has located these layers or begun editing them. It is less useful for unrelated search matchers, tasks limited only to null-safe utility cleanup, or very early exploration before the agent has identified which comparison entrypoint owns normalization. Do not require arbitrary plain-dict support for a wrapper whose visible contract expects stored edition objects unless the task explicitly changes that contract; instead, judge whether the intended comparison path no longer depends on callers manually pre-expanding records.
experiences.experience: The recurring rubrics correctly noticed that the task is not just about avoiding exceptions in preprocessing helpers: the decisive issue is whether edition comparison has a single reliable normalization boundary. However, broad criteria like “make preprocessing robust” can overcredit patches that only make `expand_record` or `add_db_name` tolerate missing fields while leaving the matcher dependent on pre-expanded inputs. A better rubric should explicitly ask whether the comparison flow passes raw candidate and existing records through expansion/enrichment before threshold scoring, preserves threshold scoring behavior rather than changing scores opportunistically, and validates the task scenarios through relevant tests or reproductions. Prioritize visible evidence such as: the agent distinguishes the public matching wrapper from the lower-level threshold scorer; recognizes direct indexing of derived fields as evidence that unexpanded inputs will break; updates the comparison entrypoint or call flow instead of adding ad hoc expansion in only one caller; keeps ISBN variant combination and title-derived fields intact; handles missing/None authors and missing author names without corrupting valid author/date enrichment; and tests author/contributor, ISBN, title-without-ISBN, and threshold cases using the correct object shapes. Avoid tempting but weak criteria that reward only helper null checks, demand that all wrappers accept two plain dicts, or expect minimal title-only records to match at a high threshold when the existing scoring contract would not support that.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that edition matching is made reliable by centralizing record normalization/enrichment at the comparison boundary: callers should not need to manually pre-expand records before threshold scoring, both candidate and stored-edition-derived records should receive the derived title fields, combined ISBN list, transferable bibliographic fields, and author `db_name` enrichment needed by the scorer, and the fix should preserve existing threshold semantics while covering missing/None author data, incomplete author dates, author/contributor comparisons, ISBN variants, missing ISBN/title scenarios, and threshold edge behavior with appropriate tests or score/debug evidence.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Matching-Boundary Normalization Contract

prioritized_visible_evidence: agent identifies that the scorer assumes expanded fields such as short title, normalized/full title variants, and ISBN list
agent avoids relying on callers to pre-expand records and updates the comparison boundary or call flow accordingly
agent preserves threshold scoring behavior and validates varying thresholds rather than merely forcing matches
agent keeps ISBN variant aggregation and transferred bibliographic fields intact
agent handles missing, None, or malformed author data without breaking valid author/date db-name enrichment
agent uses tests or reproductions that match the real wrapper/scorer input contracts
common_insufficient_evidence: only adding null checks in preprocessing helpers
only expanding one side or one caller while the core comparison can still receive unexpanded records
treating a wrapper that expects a stored edition object as if it must accept two arbitrary dictionaries without confirming that contract
changing match thresholds or scores to make minimal title-only examples pass without preserving existing semantics

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses normalization at the matching boundary; it may explore unrelated search modules, make only superficial null checks, or leave comparison dependent on pre-expanded records.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory locates some relevant helpers or fixes isolated missing-field crashes, but does not connect those fixes to the threshold comparison path or does not show how callers avoid manual expansion.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory understands the layered matching flow and attempts to expand or enrich records before comparison, but coverage is partial, one-sided, untested, or risks changing input contracts/threshold behavior incorrectly.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory updates the comparison path so raw candidate and stored-edition-derived records are normalized before threshold scoring, preserves derived field/ISBN/author enrichment semantics, and validates several task-specific scenarios.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory clearly centralizes normalization at the correct matching boundary, removes brittle call-site pre-expansion assumptions, robustly handles missing/None title and author data while preserving valid enrichment, maintains threshold semantics, and includes targeted tests or debug evidence for ISBN variants, title-without-ISBN behavior, author/contributor matching, and threshold edge cases using the real wrapper/scorer contracts.

experiences.title: Multi-axis min_count valid-count semantics
experiences.description: Retrieve when an xarray/nan-reduction task asks for `min_count` to work over multiple dimensions or tuple/list axes, especially when the agent is editing the nan-aware reduction helper that counts valid elements.
experiences.context: Applies in an older xarray-style Python/Numpy codebase where `sum(..., min_count=...)` or a shared nan reduction path fails for multiple dimensions because tuple/list axes are rejected or because single-axis size logic is used with a tuple axis. It is most useful once the trajectory has found the reduction helper, reproduced the multi-dimensional `ValueError`, or begun patching valid-count logic. It is less useful for unrelated aggregation tasks, reductions that do not accept `min_count`, pure documentation/signature changes, integer/non-skipna dispatch issues, or environment setup problems. Scalar full reductions, `prod`, `axis=None`, and dtype-specific behavior can be supporting evidence when the trajectory already touches those paths, but they should not replace the core criterion unless the task or visible tests explicitly require them.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics were useful because they judged the semantic heart of this task: supporting tuple/list reduction axes is not just removing an exception; the implementation must compute the number of candidate elements across all reduced dimensions and compare the non-null count against `min_count`. A strong rubric should look for visible evidence that the agent removes the multi-axis rejection, replaces single-axis indexing like `shape[axis]` with a product over the reduced axis sizes, subtracts the null count from `mask.sum(axis=axis)`, and preserves existing single-axis/no-`min_count` behavior. Validation evidence should prioritize the original multi-dim reproduction, a NaN case where valid count meets `min_count`, a case where valid count is below `min_count`, and a partial multi-axis reduction that leaves remaining dimensions. Avoid a weak criterion that only checks whether the `ValueError` disappeared, because that can pass while `min_count` nulling is wrong. Also avoid overbroad criteria that require changes to unrelated dispatch code, `mean`, integer paths, public docs, or every scalar/datetime edge case unless those are clearly part of the visible trajectory; those can make an otherwise correct localized fix look worse than it is. The best rubric is narrow but semantic: multi-axis valid-count arithmetic plus regression preservation.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Rewards trajectories that implement the correct `min_count` semantics for nan-aware reductions over multiple dimensions: tuple/list axes should no longer be rejected, the total reduced element count should be computed as the product of the sizes of all reduced axes, the valid count should be that total minus the null mask count over the same axes, and the result should be nulled only where valid count is below `min_count`, while preserving existing single-axis and no-`min_count` behavior. Evidence from focused tests or manual checks should cover the original multi-dimensional reduction and at least one threshold/NaN case; broader scalar or shared-operation coverage is a plus when relevant but not a substitute for the core arithmetic.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Correct multi-axis min_count counting

applies_when: task concerns xarray-style nan-aware reductions with `min_count`
failure involves tuple/list or multiple reduction dimensions
agent is inspecting or editing the helper that applies nulling after replacing NaNs
core_visible_evidence: multi-axis rejection is removed or bypassed appropriately
reduced-axis size is computed by taking the product of sizes for all axes
null mask count is subtracted from that total to get valid count
tests or scripts include original reproduction plus NaN/min_count threshold behavior
non_core_evidence: prod coverage when it shares the helper
scalar full-reduction checks when the edited branch affects scalar results
avoid_overweighting: dependency installation work
changes to unrelated reductions such as mean
integer dispatch or docs unless explicitly required
simply removing the error without validating min_count semantics

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses multi-axis `min_count` semantics; it may only set up the environment, inspect files, or make unrelated changes.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory identifies or removes the tuple/list-axis error, but does not show a correct valid-count formula or validation beyond the original no-NaN reproduction.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory implements or plans the product-of-reduced-axis-size idea, but validation is incomplete or it is unclear whether null counts, threshold comparisons, or single-axis behavior are preserved.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory visibly computes valid count as product of reduced-axis sizes minus `mask.sum(axis)`, removes the multi-axis rejection, and checks original, NaN, below-threshold, and single-axis cases.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: in addition to the correct core arithmetic and regression preservation, the trajectory validates remaining-dimension multi-axis reductions and any visibly affected shared/scalar paths without broad unrelated changes.

experiences.title: Avoid broad RFC-compliance rubrics when consistency and regression risk are the real discriminator
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task cites a standard but also requires matching existing app behavior, especially when the agent has only identified the standard violation or has begun editing a shared formatter/exporter.
experiences.context: Applies to TypeScript/ESM codebases where vCard/contact export or similar serialization logic has both protocol-format requirements and an existing UI/source-of-truth normalization path. The misleading pattern is a rubric that simply asks whether output is RFC-compliant or whether URL colons are unescaped and handles become URLs; that can over-credit trajectories that duplicate UI logic imperfectly, rewrite unrelated exporter behavior, leave no usable patch, or only perform investigation. The original RFC-compliance idea is still appropriate as a sub-check once there is visible evidence of a narrow, compiling implementation that preserves existing serialization behavior and tests the affected outputs.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster focused on “RFC 6350 compliance”: full URLs for social fields and unescaped URL scheme colons. That criterion matches the bug statement, but it is too broad and can be misleading at trajectory cutoffs where the agent has merely diagnosed the issue or has made large, risky edits. In these cases, the visible quality signal should be whether the agent anchors social URL normalization to the existing web-client behavior/source of truth, applies escaping changes narrowly enough not to corrupt other vCard fields, and preserves unrelated exporter formatting such as name, birthday, address, email, phone, note, organization, line endings, and folding. Avoid generating a rubric that treats recognizing the RFC rule or writing any local URL template as sufficient. A better rubric should prioritize visible evidence of a minimal patch: reuse or extract the existing social URL helper used by the viewer, route exported social URL content through that helper, stop escaping colons where URL values are serialized, avoid wholesale rewrites of the exporter, and add/update focused regression tests for both vanity handles and existing full URLs.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory shows a risky or incomplete vCard-export fix that is framed as standards compliance but lacks evidence of preserving existing app behavior: it duplicates or invents social URL normalization instead of reusing/extracting the web-client source of truth, changes unrelated vCard serialization logic, applies URL escaping changes without considering non-URL fields, or performs only investigation/test attempts without a coherent patch.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Overbroad RFC Compliance Masks Exporter Regression Risk

metadata.task_type: vCard/contact export serialization bug
metadata.repository_environment: TypeScript/ESM web client with contacts exporter, viewer, model utilities, and ospec-style tests
key_visible_evidence: Whether the agent found existing web-client social URL normalization
Whether the proposed/exporter code reuses or extracts that normalization instead of duplicating templates
Whether colon escaping changes are confined to URL serialization or otherwise justified by vCard rules
Whether unrelated contact fields and formatting are left intact
Whether focused tests cover vanity handles, existing URLs, and URL colon escaping
metadata.avoid_as_primary_proxy: Generic statements that the output is RFC-compliant or that URLs have unescaped colons

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory keeps the patch narrow, relies on the existing UI normalization source or explicitly extracts it, preserves unrelated vCard output, and adds or plans focused tests for URL normalization and escaping.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory mostly targets the right exporter path but duplicates a small amount of existing normalization logic or leaves some preservation/testing details implicit while avoiding unrelated rewrites.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory addresses handle-to-URL conversion and colon escaping, but does so with a local reimplementation or broad escaping change and has limited visible assurance that existing vCard fields remain unchanged.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory rewrites unrelated exporter sections, changes formatting for names/birthdays/emails/addresses/other fields, or relies on ad-hoc validation while claiming standards compliance.
scale.5: Most severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory has no coherent relevant patch, edits the wrong subsystem, introduces syntax/type errors, or repeatedly validates unsuccessfully while the rubric would still over-credit based on RFC-compliance intent.

experiences.title: Do not let an offline voice-broadcast guard stand in for multi-issue coverage
experiences.description: Retrieve when a TypeScript/React Matrix-client task combines voice-broadcast offline blocking with sessions hygiene, chunk sequencing, and safe device refresh, and the trajectory is already inspecting or adding a sync-state precondition.
experiences.context: This warning applies in multi-part Matrix client tasks where one visible requirement is to block starting/preparing a voice broadcast during a sync/connection error, but the task also requires stale client-information pruning after successful device-list refresh, robust missing user/device ID handling, and clear chunk sequence semantics. The offline guard is a valid criterion when the current stage is narrowly about locating the voice-broadcast precondition path or when the task only concerns offline start behavior. It becomes misleading as a primary or high-confidence rubric at implementation/final-review stages if visible trajectory evidence shows the agent already knows to add `client.getSyncState()` checks while harder requirements remain unresolved or are being addressed in overly narrow places such as explicit delete/sign-out handlers only.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked whether starting or preparing a voice broadcast checks sync state and shows a user-facing dialog. That criterion is semantically correct, but in this multi-requirement task it over-emphasizes the easiest visible fix: adding a sync-state check in the centralized voice-broadcast precondition utility. Patches can satisfy that guard and still be poor because stale client-information cleanup is not tied to every successful device-list refresh, session refresh may still rely on unsafe identifiers, or chunk sequencing may remain off by one or ambiguous. For similar trajectories, avoid generating a rubric that treats the offline guard as the main predictor once the trajectory has already identified the precondition hook or has begun implementing it. Instead, generate criteria focused on the unresolved integration contracts visible in the task: cleanup must compare current refreshed device IDs against identifiable client-information account-data and prune removed-device metadata after refresh, not only after local delete; missing user/device IDs must be handled without throwing or violating React hook rules; and chunk sequence state must represent the last assigned sequence with a documented first chunk and final last-sequence value. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence that the agent chooses the correct lifecycle hook and preserves existing APIs/types, rather than merely observing a `SyncState.Error` dialog branch.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: In a multi-requirement sessions and voice-broadcast task, the trajectory shows the agent focusing on or implementing the offline voice-broadcast sync-state guard while leaving the refresh-driven sessions hygiene contract unaddressed or addressing it only through explicit device deletion/sign-out callbacks. This flaw is present when visible evidence indicates stale client-information account-data is removed only for locally selected deleted devices, or through incidental listener/toast logic, rather than after a successful authoritative device-list refresh by comparing currently returned devices to existing identifiable client-information records. The flaw is stronger if the same trajectory also leaves unsafe missing user/device ID handling or chunk sequence off-by-one semantics unresolved.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Narrow offline guard masks missing refresh-driven session hygiene

metadata.task_type: TypeScript React Matrix client multi-part bug fix
primary_visible_cues: task requires cleanup after any successful device list refresh
trajectory or patch plans cleanup only in delete/sign-out flow
trajectory already identified centralized voice-broadcast precondition path
remaining requirements include safe IDs and chunk sequencing
metadata.avoid_as_replacement: Do not score the trajectory highly solely because it adds a SyncState.Error dialog before voice broadcast start.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory explicitly plans or implements refresh-driven pruning based on the authoritative refreshed device list, while treating the offline guard as only one requirement among several.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the agent discusses the correct refresh-driven cleanup point but temporarily inspects delete/sign-out or offline-guard code without committing to a narrow solution.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent implements or prioritizes the offline guard and mentions stale cleanup, but the visible plan is ambiguous about whether cleanup runs after every successful device refresh.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the agent adds or plans stale client-information removal only in explicit deletion/sign-out handling, or in an unrelated listener path, while treating the offline guard as substantially complete.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory strongly centers success on the sync-state broadcast dialog and implements narrow delete-only or fragile cleanup, with no visible refresh-driven pruning contract and unresolved safe-ID or chunk-sequence concerns.

experiences.title: Template Tag Keyword-Only Signature Semantics
experiences.description: Use when a Django template tag parsing task involves keyword-only arguments, defaults, duplicate keyword diagnostics, or shared simple_tag/inclusion_tag argument binding.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django codebase when the task and trajectory point to the shared template tag argument parser for simple_tag and inclusion_tag, especially after the agent has inspected signature metadata such as keyword-only parameter names and keyword-only defaults or has begun changing keyword validation logic. It is most useful once the trajectory contains evidence about how supplied keyword bits are classified as accepted, duplicate, missing, or unexpected. It may be premature during pure repository exploration with no parser understanding, and it should not be generalized to unrelated template rendering, dependency setup, or broad test-runner configuration issues unless they directly validate these argument-binding semantics.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases focused on the exact call-signature contract rather than on a vague claim that the agent should fix template tags. A strong criterion should check whether the trajectory distinguishes valid keyword-only names from required keyword-only names: keyword-only parameters with defaults must be valid when supplied, but optional when omitted; keyword-only parameters without defaults must still be required. It should also check duplicate handling order: a repeated recognized keyword should be reported as a multiple-values error, not misclassified as unexpected merely because the name was consumed from a remaining-arguments list. The criterion should include preservation of true unexpected-keyword rejection and compatibility with the shared simple_tag/inclusion_tag parser. Avoid the tempting narrower proxy of only requiring that keyword-only defaults be added to an `unhandled` list, because that can make optional defaults appear required or fail to consume required keyword-only arguments correctly. Also avoid scoring dependency installation or broad pytest attempts as core progress; prioritize visible evidence from parser logic, targeted reproductions, and edge cases covering supplied defaulted keyword-only args, omitted defaults, required keyword-only args, duplicates, and unexpected keywords.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate or implement the correct template-tag argument binding semantics for keyword-only parameters in the shared simple_tag/inclusion_tag parser: all keyword-only parameter names are accepted as known keyword names when supplied; keyword-only parameters with defaults remain optional when omitted; keyword-only parameters without defaults remain required; duplicate supplied keywords, including keyword-only ones, are detected before unexpected-keyword classification and raise the multiple-values TemplateSyntaxError; truly unexpected keywords remain rejected when no variable keyword parameter is present; and the change is validated or reasoned about against both simple tags and inclusion tags or their shared parsing path.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Correct Keyword-Only Argument Binding Semantics

key_visible_evidence: Identifies the shared parser used by simple_tag and inclusion_tag
Separates known keyword-only names from required keyword-only names
Checks supplied keyword-only arguments with defaults
Checks omitted keyword-only defaults
Checks required keyword-only arguments
Checks duplicate keyword error classification
Preserves rejection of truly unexpected keywords
metadata.common_false_positive: Only includes defaulted keyword-only names in a tracking list without preserving optional-default behavior or correct duplicate ordering

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory handles keyword-only argument semantics in the shared template tag parser.
scale.2: Recognizes the likely parser or defaulted keyword-only issue, but lacks a concrete semantic fix or ignores required/default/duplicate distinctions.
scale.3: Makes partial progress, such as accepting supplied keyword-only defaults, but visible evidence leaves important behavior uncertain or flawed, such as omitted defaults, required keyword-only args, duplicate diagnostics, or unexpected keywords.
scale.4: Shows strong evidence of the full semantic model for supplied defaults, omitted defaults, required keyword-only args, duplicate keyword diagnostics, and unexpected keyword rejection, with only limited validation or incomplete coverage of the shared simple_tag/inclusion_tag path.
scale.5: Clearly implements and validates the complete shared parser behavior for simple_tag and inclusion_tag, including supplied defaulted keyword-only args, omitted defaults, required keyword-only enforcement, duplicate multiple-values errors, true unexpected-keyword errors, and compatibility with existing positional, varargs, and varkw behavior.

experiences.title: Direct Delete Eligibility via Alias Initialization
experiences.description: Use when a Django ORM regression concerns simple bulk deletes generating a redundant self-subquery instead of direct DELETE SQL, especially after the trajectory has reached SQL delete compilation, alias maps/refcounts, or fast-delete paths.
experiences.context: Applies in Django ORM/database compiler tasks where the reported bad behavior is that an unfiltered single-table bulk delete, such as deleting all rows of a model, is compiled as DELETE ... WHERE pk IN (SELECT pk FROM the same table) instead of a direct DELETE FROM table. It is most useful once the trajectory has visible evidence from SQL compiler inspection or ad-hoc SQL generation showing alias_map/alias_refcount/base-table initialization controls whether the direct-delete branch is selected. It can also be used earlier as a directional rubric if the agent has found DeleteQuery/SQLDeleteCompiler and the direct-vs-subquery branch. Do not apply as the main criterion for unrelated explicit subquery predicates, genuine joined/multi-table deletes, cascade semantics, or tasks whose intended fix is specifically a backend-specific SQL syntax change rather than shared delete compiler eligibility.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged whether the agent was converging on the real semantic boundary: simple single-table deletes should be recognized as safe for direct DELETE SQL, while deletes with active joins or multiple aliases should keep the subquery path. The strongest visible evidence was not merely mentioning MySQL LOCK TABLES, but identifying that a fresh/all-row queryset may have an empty or zero-refcount base alias until compiler setup, causing the single-alias check to choose the fallback self-subquery. A good rubric should therefore reward trajectories that inspect generated SQL, alias_map/alias_refcount, base-table alias initialization, and the shared delete compiler branch, and that validate both the simple all-delete case and a complex joined case. A tempting but weaker criterion is to focus only on MySQL locking or self-referencing subqueries in the MySQL backend; that can encourage a backend-specific patch that does not fix the shared regression for Model.objects.all().delete(). Another tempting but incomplete criterion is simply 'remove subqueries from deletes'; the correct boundary is preserving subqueries when joins/multiple aliases make them necessary.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the delete SQL regression is caused by the compiler's direct-delete eligibility being evaluated before the simple query's base table alias is initialized/refcounted, and should move toward a shared ORM compiler fix that makes unfiltered single-table bulk deletes compile to direct DELETE FROM table without a self-select, while preserving the fallback subquery for joined or otherwise multi-alias deletes. Judge from visible evidence such as inspection of the direct-vs-subquery branch, alias_map/alias_refcount observations, generated SQL for an all-row delete, and checks that complex joined deletes are not incorrectly forced into the direct path.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Single-Table Delete Direct-Path Diagnosis

prioritize_evidence: inspection of shared ORM delete compiler direct-vs-subquery branch
alias_map/alias_refcount or base-table initialization observations for an all-row queryset
generated SQL showing direct DELETE for simple single-table delete
generated SQL or reasoning showing subquery fallback remains for joined or multi-alias deletes
avoid_overweighting: backend-only MySQL syntax changes without addressing shared compiler eligibility
blanket removal of subqueries from all delete operations
tests that only execute deletion without checking SQL shape

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory has connected the regression to delete SQL compilation or direct-vs-subquery eligibility; focus is on unrelated deletion/cascade behavior or generic database performance.
scale.2: Some recognition that simple deletes should avoid a self-subquery, but little or no investigation of the compiler branch, alias state, or preservation of complex delete behavior.
scale.3: Equivalent parent-child behavior: the trajectory has found the delete compiler and understands that simple single-table deletes should use direct DELETE, but has not yet clearly diagnosed alias initialization/refcounting or validated the complex-case boundary.
scale.4: Strong evidence that the trajectory has identified alias/refcount/base-table setup as the reason the simple delete is misclassified, and is moving toward a shared compiler fix while considering joined/multi-alias preservation.
scale.5: The trajectory has decisively reproduced the bad SQL, shown that initializing/refcounting the base alias makes the single-table delete eligible for direct DELETE, implemented or planned a minimal shared compiler change, and checked both simple all-row delete SQL and a joined/multi-alias case.

experiences.title: Propagate constraint column-rendering flags through nested Q trees
experiences.description: Use this when a Django ORM/schema task concerns CheckConstraint SQL for mixed OR/AND Q expressions and the trajectory has reached the Query/WhereNode column compilation path.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django codebase when the reported defect is table-qualified column names appearing inside table-level CHECK constraint expressions, especially with nested Q objects combining OR and AND, and the trajectory has visible evidence about the check-constraint compilation path, Col versus SimpleCol behavior, or recursive Q processing. It is most useful after the agent has inspected or modified the ORM query-building path, or has reproduced generated CHECK SQL. It is less useful for purely backend-specific DDL formatting work, flat non-nested check constraints, UniqueConstraint behavior, normal SELECT query aliasing bugs, or very early exploration before the trajectory has identified how constraint expressions are compiled.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic boundary that table-level CheckConstraint SQL must use simple, unqualified column references throughout the CHECK expression, while ordinary query SQL should still use table aliases. This aligned well when the visible trajectory showed the agent tracing CheckConstraint generation into the query builder, identifying that nested Q/Node recursion could drop the flag that selects SimpleCol, applying a minimal propagation fix, and validating the CHECK clause itself. A better rubric should explicitly judge whether the trajectory preserves the column-rendering context through recursive Q processing for nested OR/AND branches, not merely whether SQLite or Oracle SQL strings are post-processed. It should also require evidence that normal query compilation remains qualified, because forcing all columns to be unqualified globally would be a regression. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as checking only that migrations run, checking only for a hard-coded temporary table name, searching the entire ALTER TABLE statement for table names, or rewarding broad backend-specific quote stripping. Prioritize visible evidence from generated CHECK SQL, before/after reproduction of mixed nested Q cases, inspection of Col versus SimpleCol selection, and clean minimal changes in the recursive query-building path.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that CheckConstraint expressions built from nested Q trees preserve the constraint-specific simple-column rendering context through all recursive OR/AND branches, so every column inside the CHECK expression is unqualified, while ordinary query/filter SQL continues to use normal table-qualified aliases. Strong evidence includes tracing the constraint-to-query compilation path, identifying the dropped propagation of the simple-column flag in recursive Q handling, applying a narrow fix there rather than backend-specific SQL rewriting, and validating the CHECK clause for mixed nested OR/AND cases separately from the outer DDL statement.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Nested CheckConstraint simple-column propagation

required_visible_evidence: The trajectory connects CheckConstraint SQL generation to ORM Q/WhereNode compilation rather than only backend schema string templates.
The trajectory distinguishes unqualified constraint columns from normal table-qualified query columns.
The trajectory inspects or modifies recursive nested Q handling where context flags are passed to child nodes.
Validation inspects the CHECK expression itself for absence of qualified column references in mixed OR/AND cases.
common_false_positives: Only checking for one hard-coded staging table name while other table aliases remain in the CHECK expression.
Treating table names in the outer ALTER TABLE or CREATE TABLE clause as evidence of a bad CHECK expression.
Solving by stripping table names in a backend-specific schema editor instead of preserving the query compiler's simple-column context.
Ignoring whether normal SELECT/filter queries still render qualified columns.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses nested Q CheckConstraint column qualification; it focuses on unrelated files, generic migration behavior, or only flat constraints.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory recognizes that CHECK constraints should avoid qualified columns, but does not identify nested Q recursion or does not distinguish the CHECK expression from the surrounding DDL.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory traces the relevant constraint compilation path and understands Col versus SimpleCol behavior, but the fix or validation is incomplete, unverified, or risks affecting normal query aliasing.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory identifies recursive Q processing as the source of lost simple-column context, applies or plans a narrow propagation fix, and validates mixed OR/AND CHECK SQL uses unqualified columns.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: in addition to a narrow recursive propagation fix, the trajectory verifies several nested OR/AND CHECK cases by inspecting the CHECK clause itself and shows normal query SQL remains table-qualified, with no reliance on backend-specific string stripping.

experiences.title: Avoid completion or wrapper-only criteria during mid-refactor extraction
