experiences.description: Retrieve when a trajectory is extracting logic from an overloaded module into a new module, especially when the visible cutoff is early or mid-refactor and the agent is still moving functions, updating imports, or responding to tests.
experiences.context: This applies to behavior-preserving Python refactors where Qt argument/environment setup is being moved from an existing configuration initializer into a new module. A rubric requiring all moved functions, all call sites, and all old definitions to be finalized is appropriate only at final-review stage or after the agent explicitly claims the refactor is complete. During exploration or partial editing, the absence of an updated external call site or removed original function can simply indicate pending work. Conversely, a rubric praising backward-compatible wrappers is only appropriate when the task or visible tests require preserving the old import surface; wrappers do not by themselves show that the implementation was safely extracted, and they can coexist with broken imports, malformed code, duplicated logic, or accidental rewrites of unrelated initialization behavior.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often generated criteria such as “all call sites must be updated,” “all Qt logic must be moved out,” or “maintain wrappers so tests pass.” Those ideas are useful final-state checks, but they are misleading when the trajectory is still mid-edit: they can understate a trajectory that later performs the straightforward wiring, or overstate a trajectory that adds wrappers while corrupting non-Qt configuration initialization. For similar refactor tasks, avoid using a single broad completeness or backward-compatibility criterion as the main predictor unless the visible trajectory is clearly at final validation. A better rubric should prioritize visible evidence that the refactor is behavior-preserving and scoped: the new module contains the moved logic with its dependencies; startup still invokes environment setup at the same point in initialization; application argument construction is routed to the new module when finalized; and unrelated config initialization, backend selection, font-default update, late initialization, and error handling are not rewritten or damaged. The tempting wrong criterion is treating wrapper presence or immediate total call-site completion as decisive. Replacement criteria should focus on concrete hazards visible in commands, diffs, and test output: broad `sed` deletions leaving stray code, malformed indentation or invalid function placement, changed return types for existing helpers, missing new-file inclusion, broken imports, or tests failing in unrelated config initialization paths.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize a behavior-preserving extraction trajectory when the visible evidence shows the agent is damaging unrelated initialization behavior or creating structural breakage while moving Qt argument/environment logic. This includes wholesale rewrites of the original configuration initializer, malformed inserted functions or indentation, changed semantics of backend/config/font/late-init helpers, undefined references after deletion, broken imports caused by moving dependencies incorrectly, leftover fragments from range deletion, or tests failing in unrelated initialization paths. Do not treat the mere absence or presence of compatibility wrappers as decisive; judge whether the extracted logic is centralized without corrupting the surrounding startup contract.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Scoped behavior-preserving extraction

metadata.task_type: Python module extraction/refactor
visible_evidence_to_prioritize: diffs or commands showing broad rewrites/deletions outside the target logic
syntax or import errors after moving functions
changed return types or control flow in unrelated initialization helpers
test failures in unrelated configuration initialization behavior
stray leftover code or duplicated moved logic in the original module
metadata.stage_boundary: Apply strongly during mid-to-late refactor and final review; avoid using it to require final call-site completion during initial exploration.

scale.1: No evidence of unrelated initialization damage; edits appear scoped to moving the target logic and preserving existing startup order.
scale.2: Minor risk only, such as unverified import cleanup or optional wrapper decisions, with no visible semantic damage outside the moved logic.
scale.3: Moderate concern: some unrelated code was touched or tests/imports have not been checked, but there is not yet clear evidence of broken behavior.
scale.4: Clear evidence of a scoped-refactor violation, such as altered unrelated helper semantics, missing required imports, leftover fragments, or failing tests in non-target initialization paths.
scale.5: Severe structural breakage: malformed code, undefined functions, wholesale rewritten initializer behavior, or multiple unrelated startup responsibilities broken while attempting the extraction.

experiences.title: Legacy-to-Split Config Compatibility Beyond Watch Removal
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go service/cache task involves backward compatibility between older remotes that expose a monolithic configuration resource and newer code that consumes split configuration resources.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go codebase with remote-cluster caching/access-point logic and a resource migration from a legacy monolithic configuration object to newer split resources, especially when the task states that older remote versions do not expose or authorize the split resources but current consumers call split-resource getters. This is most useful once the trajectory has identified or edited cache watch policy, version-gated remote access-point selection, cache collection/event processing, or split config getters. It is less useful as a pass/fail rubric during very early repository exploration unless phrased to require concrete implementation evidence. It should not be retrieved for tasks that only remove an unsupported watch with no requirement that split-resource consumers continue to receive equivalent data, or for modern-only paths where legacy remotes are out of scope.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the missing second half of the compatibility fix: the agent often removed unsupported split-resource watches or changed version routing, but did not actually derive the newer split configuration objects from the older monolithic configuration data. That criterion aligned well because visible trajectory evidence showed the task explicitly required both avoiding RBAC/cache churn and keeping split-resource consumers working; the code investigation also surfaced consumers of split config getters and cache logic that could clear or ignore legacy embedded fields. A better rubric should require concrete normalization/wiring: old-remotes should not be asked to watch unsupported split resources, but their legacy configuration must be transformed and stored/served through the split-resource cache/getter paths before any legacy fields are dropped. Avoid tempting proxies such as successful builds, repeated greps for tests, changing only the old-remote watch list, widening a version threshold, adding unused helper methods, or returning defaults when split resources are missing. Those actions may reduce one symptom but do not prove that configured legacy audit/networking/session/auth values remain available to callers. Prioritize visible evidence that the trajectory implements derivation from the legacy object during initial fetch and watch-event processing or equivalent access-point serving, wires it into the old-remote/pre-migration path, preserves configured values rather than replacing them with defaults, and validates the compatibility behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show a compatibility fix for older remote clusters that both avoids watching unsupported split configuration resources and preserves split-resource access by deriving the newer audit/networking-related configuration resources from the legacy monolithic configuration. Strong evidence includes code or a clear patch plan that materializes derived split resources during cache fetch/event processing or access-point serving, wires that behavior only to the legacy/pre-migration remote path, avoids clearing or discarding embedded legacy fields before derivation, and ensures callers of split-resource getters receive the legacy-configured values rather than NotFound errors or generic defaults.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete Legacy-to-Split Configuration Normalization

metadata.environment: Go remote-cluster cache/access-point code with legacy monolithic configuration and newer split configuration resources
required_visible_evidence: older remote path avoids unsupported split-resource watches
legacy monolithic configuration is converted into split configuration resources
conversion is wired into cache fetch/event processing or equivalent access-point getter path
configured legacy values are preserved rather than replaced by defaults
split-resource consumers remain served without remote reads that trigger authorization failures
common_false_positives: only removing split-resource watch kinds
only changing remote version threshold
only adding helper methods without cache/access-point integration
returning default split configs on missing data
build success without compatibility validation

scale.1: No concrete evidence of legacy-to-split normalization; trajectory only explores files or changes unrelated code.
scale.2: Mentions normalization or removes unsupported split-resource watches, but does not implement a wired path that serves split-resource getters from legacy data.
scale.3: Partial compatibility evidence: some legacy data extraction or helper code exists, but it is not clearly connected to both initial cache population and update/event handling, or it risks dropping configured legacy values.
scale.4: Strong compatibility evidence: old remote cache policy avoids unsupported split watches and legacy configuration is derived into split resources for the main consumer path, with only minor gaps such as limited validation or incomplete edge-case coverage.
scale.5: Complete evidence: the pre-migration remote path is correctly version/capability gated, unsupported split watches are avoided, legacy configuration is converted into all required split resources before being cleared or stored, split-resource getters serve preserved configured values for both fetch and event/update paths, and focused validation or tests cover the compatibility scenario.

experiences.title: Do not let simple h/m/s example parsing stand in for the full CLI duration contract
experiences.description: Retrieve this when a qutebrowser-style command change adds unit-suffixed durations to an existing numeric CLI argument and the trajectory has implemented or planned a helper parser. Be careful if the agent only demonstrates the headline examples or adds extra ad-hoc units; that evidence can look strong while missing the actual command grammar and integration requirements.
experiences.context: This applies in a Python/qutebrowser command framework where function annotations determine CLI argument conversion, the existing command takes an integer millisecond delay, and the requested feature is to accept readable duration expressions while keeping bare numbers as milliseconds. The misleading pattern is a rubric that rewards any parser handling examples like 5s, 2m30s, 1h, and 90, or rewards support for unspecified extras such as ms suffixes and arbitrary unit ordering, without checking whether the chosen grammar matches the requested sleep-like/XhYmZs duration contract and whether the command receives the raw duration string before scheduling. The original parsing-correctness idea is still useful when the visible trajectory is specifically designing or testing the duration parser, but it should not be the only or primary final-review criterion once the implementation touches command annotations, command-error handling, timer interval use, and compatibility behavior. Direct experiments with qutebrowser's command metadata, such as observing decorator attributes after registration or manually constructing command objects, are also not conclusive unless the trajectory uses the real registry path.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often asked whether the new helper parses combined integer unit strings, treats bare integers as milliseconds, and rejects invalid formats. That is a necessary but weak proxy: an implementation can pass those examples while using an ad-hoc regex, accepting non-requested syntax, omitting sleep-like fractional components or spacing, or failing to integrate cleanly with the command layer. A better rubric should focus on the visible end-to-end contract: the CLI duration argument must no longer be pre-converted as an int, valid duration text must be converted to integer milliseconds before the existing timer interval is set, invalid duration text must become a user-facing command error, the trailing command must still be preserved by the existing splitting behavior, and the accepted grammar should match the task's stated units/format rather than broad invented extensions. Avoid generating a tempting criterion that treats support for ms suffixes, arbitrary unit order, or a few manual helper calls as proof of correctness. Prefer evidence from the actual function signature or converter choice, the parser's full-match grammar, examples/tests covering the specified forms and compatibility fallback, error wrapping at the command boundary, and preservation of the existing scheduling path.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a CLI command that previously accepted an integer millisecond delay and now must accept unit-suffixed durations, penalize trajectories whose visible implementation or plan only demonstrates ad-hoc parsing of the headline integer h/m/s examples while lacking evidence that the full command contract is satisfied. This includes leaving the command argument in a form that would still be pre-converted as an integer before unit text reaches the command, failing to convert parser failures into the command layer's user-facing error type, passing a raw string rather than converted milliseconds to the existing timer/scheduler, breaking the existing maxsplit/trailing-command behavior, or choosing a parser grammar that rewards unspecified extras while missing the task's sleep-like/XhYmZs duration syntax such as fractional h/m/s components when that convention is relied on.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Incomplete duration grammar or command-layer integration

metadata.environment: Python qutebrowser command framework with annotation-driven argument conversion and timer scheduling
visible_evidence_to_check: command parameter annotation or converter allows raw duration text to reach parsing
duration parser uses a full-match grammar aligned with the requested units/format rather than partial matching
bare digit-only input remains milliseconds
converted integer milliseconds are used for the existing timer interval
parser ValueError or equivalent is wrapped as a command-facing error
existing command splitting/deferred command string semantics are preserved
tests or manual checks cover both specified examples and grammar edge cases implied by the task
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: Treating support for 5s, 2m30s, 1h, bare integers, or an extra ms suffix as sufficient evidence of correctness

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory shows command-layer integration, compatible bare milliseconds, aligned full-match duration grammar, command-error wrapping, and preservation of existing scheduling/splitting behavior.
scale.2: Minor concern only: most integration and grammar evidence is present, with at most a small unvalidated edge case or missing test that does not contradict the visible design.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the parser handles the main examples, but evidence is incomplete for either command-framework integration, exact grammar boundaries, or error conversion.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory relies mainly on helper-level example parsing or invented syntax and omits important command-boundary behavior such as annotation changes, user-facing errors, or preservation of trailing command handling.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the visible implementation would not reliably accept unit-suffixed input through the actual CLI command, would pass the wrong type/value to the timer, or uses a partial/ad-hoc grammar that visibly rejects or misinterprets required duration forms while appearing to pass superficial examples.

experiences.title: Controller Runtime Bump Requires Ansible-Test/CI Matrix Coverage
experiences.description: Retrieve when an ansible-core task raises/drops a supported controller Python version, especially with ansible-test named as the component, and the trajectory is auditing or editing version references.
experiences.context: Applies in ansible-core-like repositories where the task is to raise the controller Python minimum and remove the old controller version from supported environments. It is most useful once the trajectory has enough visible evidence from greps, file inspection, or edits to judge whether the agent is treating the change as a coordinated support-matrix transition rather than only updating the obvious runtime/package files. It is less applicable during the first few exploratory commands before the agent has had a chance to search CI, docs, test matrices, packaging, and compatibility cleanup sites. It should not be used to penalize unchanged unrelated version examples, package/kernel sample data, vendored version-parser examples, or managed-node/module Python minima unless the task explicitly expands scope beyond controller support.
experiences.experience: For controller minimum-version bumps, the useful rubric is a breadth-and-boundary criterion: require evidence that the agent audited and updated every controller-facing support declaration, including runtime guard text/checks, packaging metadata/classifiers, ansible-test/CI supported-version matrices, developer docs, changelog/feature notice, and compatibility/TODO code that was explicitly waiting for the new minimum. The prior rubrics in this cluster were useful when they focused on ansible-test and CI/test-matrix coverage, because trajectories that only changed setup metadata and the CLI guard left visible old-version support advertised elsewhere. A better rubric should also reward careful classification of search hits: preserving target-side interpreter discovery and module-side minima when they are not controller support, and leaving unrelated version strings alone. Avoid the tempting wrong criterion of simply checking whether every textual occurrence of the old version disappeared; blind replacements can corrupt comments, deprecation metadata, or remove target compatibility outside scope. Prioritize visible evidence such as searches including hidden support surfaces like CI configuration, hacking/developer docs, packaging/release tooling, changelog fragments, ansible-test matrices/constraints, plus diffs that remove old controller-version entries there without damaging unrelated data.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Coordinated Controller Python Support Matrix Update
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a coordinated controller Python minimum-version transition: update the runtime controller guard and user-facing error, align package metadata and classifiers, audit and adjust ansible-test/CI/test-environment matrices and any controller-version constraints, update relevant developer docs and release/changelog notes, and remove or simplify compatibility code or TODOs that are explicitly obsolete under the new controller minimum. It should also show careful scope control by preserving managed-node/module Python support, target interpreter discovery, sample package versions, vendored parser examples, and behavioral comments that are not controller support declarations.

required_surfaces: runtime controller version guard and message
ansible-test or CI supported Python version matrices
compatibility code/TODOs explicitly tied to the new controller minimum
scope_boundaries: do not require changing managed-node/module-side Python minima unless explicitly in scope
do not require changing unrelated numeric examples, package/kernel versions, or vendored version-parser examples
do not reward blind textual replacement that leaves stale support matrices or introduces malformed code/comments
observable_evidence: broad searches include configuration, CI, docs, packaging, tests, and source code rather than only lib Python files
diffs remove old controller-version entries from supported test/CI matrices
diffs align runtime and package metadata with the new minimum
trajectory acknowledges controller-versus-target distinction

scale.1: Only changes or plans to change the obvious runtime guard or package metadata, with no visible audit of ansible-test/CI/docs/compatibility surfaces and no clear controller-versus-target distinction.
scale.2: Finds and edits a few controller-facing references such as the CLI guard and setup metadata, but misses or dismisses ansible-test/CI/test-matrix or documentation surfaces, or performs broad textual replacements without adequate scope classification.
scale.3: Comparable to the parent trajectory: identifies the main controller guard and packaging metadata and some compatibility comments, but evidence of ansible-test/CI matrix coverage, release/docs updates, and precise target-side preservation is incomplete or uncertain.
scale.4: Shows strong coverage of runtime, packaging, docs, ansible-test/CI matrices, and relevant compatibility cleanup, while explicitly avoiding unrelated examples and managed-node/module support changes; minor surfaces may remain unverified.
scale.5: Provides exhaustive, well-scoped evidence of the complete controller support transition across runtime, packaging, ansible-test/CI matrices, constraints, docs/changelog, and obsolete compatibility code, with validation or final greps confirming only irrelevant old-version references remain.

experiences.title: Default Runtime Workaround Over Optional Canvas Toggle
experiences.description: Retrieve when a QtWebEngine rendering bug is known to disappear only when accelerated 2D canvas is disabled, especially in qutebrowser-style config/startup-argument code.
experiences.context: Applies to Python/Qt browser codebases with separate QtWebEngine settings, config schema, and Chromium/Qt startup-argument generation, when the task asks to fix rendering glitches on affected systems and explicitly says disabling accelerated 2D canvas removes the artifacts. It is most useful once the trajectory has begun choosing an implementation path or editing config/startup files; during very early exploration it should be framed as a target rather than a harsh completion judgment. Do not apply this criterion to unrelated canvas-read privacy settings, WebKit-only changes, tasks that merely ask to expose a user preference without changing default behavior, or rendering issues not tied to accelerated 2D canvas.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on whether the trajectory would actually make the problematic QtWebEngine runtime behavior go away, not merely whether it found a canvas-related API or added a setting. The recurring visible flaw was adding a new Bool setting such as an accelerated-canvas content option with default enabled, or wiring a WebAttribute while leaving the feature on by default; that gives users an opt-in workaround but does not satisfy a task whose expected behavior is correct rendering for affected default setups. A stronger rubric should ask whether the agent disables accelerated 2D canvas by default for the affected QtWebEngine/Chromium versions or conditions, while preserving explicit override semantics and keeping the change backend-scoped. It should prioritize evidence in the trajectory such as startup argument generation for the accelerated-2D-canvas disabling switch, an auto/always/never-style configuration or equivalent conditional default, version/affected-backend handling, restart/startup semantics, and avoidance of WebKit or canvas-reading confusion. Avoid the tempting but weak criterion of rewarding any config key, documentation, test, or QWebEngineSettings enum mapping: those are only useful if they change the default runtime behavior under the reported conditions.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly converge on a QtWebEngine-specific accelerated 2D canvas workaround that changes default runtime behavior for affected setups: accelerated 2D canvas is disabled via the appropriate QtWebEngine/Chromium startup mechanism under the problematic versions/conditions, users retain an explicit override path, and unrelated canvas-reading/privacy settings or non-QtWebEngine backends are not conflated with the rendering workaround.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Effective Default Accelerated Canvas Mitigation

prioritize_visible_evidence: Use of the QtWebEngine/Chromium startup argument path or equivalent early runtime mechanism to disable accelerated 2D canvas
Default or auto behavior that disables the feature for affected QtWebEngine/Chromium versions or systems rather than leaving it enabled
Explicit override semantics such as always/auto/never or equivalent
QtWebEngine-only scoping and restart/startup semantics
Clear distinction from canvas-reading permission/privacy flags and WebKit-only code
common_insufficient_evidence: Only adding a Bool setting with default true
Only mapping a QWebEngineSettings accelerated-canvas attribute without ensuring affected default behavior changes
Only updating documentation or tests for an opt-in setting

scale.1: No meaningful accelerated 2D canvas mitigation is visible, or the trajectory focuses on unrelated rendering, WebKit, GPU, WebGL, or canvas-reading behavior.
scale.2: The trajectory identifies accelerated 2D canvas or adds an opt-in/user-facing setting, but the feature remains enabled by default for affected users or the implementation mechanism is not shown to affect startup/runtime behavior.
scale.3: The trajectory adds a plausible disabling path or config mapping, but default/affected-version behavior, backend scoping, or override semantics are incomplete or ambiguous.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly disables accelerated 2D canvas for affected QtWebEngine runtime conditions using an appropriate startup/runtime mechanism and preserves user override behavior, with only minor validation or documentation gaps.
scale.5: The trajectory fully implements the workaround with affected-version/default auto behavior, explicit always/never overrides, QtWebEngine-only scoping, restart/startup handling, and avoids all canvas-reading or non-WebEngine conflation.

experiences.title: Cross-Backend Database Helper Contract Parity
experiences.description: Use when a task adds a database-layer helper/API in a project with separate Redis, MongoDB, and PostgreSQL adapters and the visible trajectory has identified or edited per-backend sorted-set implementations.
experiences.context: Applies to Node.js/NodeBB-style repositories where database methods are attached separately in backend modules rather than through one shared implementation. Retrieve this experience when the task explicitly requires a uniform database helper contract across multiple storage backends, especially for sorted-set/member APIs returning value-score data. It is most useful once the trajectory has found the existing values-only helpers or score-aware range helpers in Redis, MongoDB, and PostgreSQL files, or has begun editing those files. It may be premature during generic repository exploration before backend structure is known, and it is insufficient by itself if the current trajectory mainly shows syntax corruption, misplaced methods outside module initialization, unrelated bootstrap rewrites, or test-harness issues; in those cases an additional rubric should target those concrete risks.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful rubric in these cases asked whether the new sorted-set-with-scores helpers were implemented consistently across all database adapters. That is the right high-signal criterion because the task is not merely to make one backend return scores: callers need one database-layer contract regardless of configured backend. A good rubric should therefore check for both helper names in every adapter, singular helpers delegating or matching plural behavior, plural results aligned to the input keys, arrays of `{ value, score }`, ascending score order, empty-array behavior for missing/empty inputs, and numeric score normalization. Prioritize visible evidence such as the agent locating `redis/sorted`, `mongo/sorted`, and `postgres/sorted` modules; reusing backend-native sorted retrieval (`ZRANGE ... WITHSCORES`, Mongo score sort/projection, SQL ordered by score or equivalent); converting Redis/Postgres string-like score values to numbers; and mapping grouped multi-key results back with `keys.map(... || [])`. Avoid replacing this with a narrower criterion like “uses WITHSCORES in Redis” or “adds tests,” because those can miss backend parity. Also avoid making the rubric so broad that it ignores placement and preservation: if edits touch schema/bootstrap files or use sed-heavy insertion, generate a separate criterion for not corrupting unrelated database initialization and for attaching methods inside the correct backend module scope.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Uniform Multi-Backend Sorted-Set With-Scores Contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the new sorted-set member-with-scores API is being added as a consistent database-layer contract across all configured storage adapters, not as a single-backend shortcut. Strong evidence includes implementing or clearly planning both the singular and plural helpers in each backend module; preserving existing values-only helpers; returning arrays of `{ value, score }` objects with numeric scores; sorting each key's members by ascending score; returning `[]` for empty input lists and missing/empty individual keys; and preserving plural result alignment with the input key order.

contract_elements: same method names/signatures in each backend
array of objects with value and numeric score
plural output aligned with input keys
empty arrays for empty input and missing/empty sets
visible_evidence: agent identifies existing values-only member helpers in all backends
agent uses backend-native score retrieval and score conversion utilities where applicable
agent groups multi-key query results by key and maps back to input key order
agent avoids a Redis-only or test-only implementation

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent recognizes the multi-backend contract; work is focused on unrelated files or only one backend without addressing return shape, ordering, or edge cases.
scale.2: Weak evidence of the desired API, such as identifying one relevant backend or mentioning scores, but no clear plan or implementation for all adapters and no attention to plural key alignment or numeric score normalization.
scale.3: Moderate evidence equivalent to the parent trajectory: the agent has found the relevant backend modules and understands that all adapters need matching helpers, but implementation is incomplete, unverified, or missing some contract details such as empty-key behavior or score conversion.
scale.4: Strong evidence that all three backend modules are being updated with the two helpers and that the implementation mostly preserves the required contract, including sorted score order, object shape, numeric scores, and input-key-aligned plural results.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory shows a complete, correctly scoped cross-backend implementation that mirrors existing helper conventions, preserves existing values-only behavior, handles all specified edge cases, normalizes scores consistently, and validates the behavior with appropriate database-layer tests or equivalent checks.

experiences.title: Do not treat Jinja AST extraction as sufficient for stylesheet dependency fixes
experiences.description: Retrieve when a qutebrowser/PyQt/Jinja2 task asks for detecting `conf.` dependencies in stylesheet templates and the trajectory mainly shows AST experiments or a helper implementation, with incomplete or unvalidated integration into config-change-driven stylesheet updates.
experiences.context: This applies in Python qutebrowser-style code where stylesheets are Jinja2 template strings rendered with a `conf` config namespace and updated via a `Config.changed` signal. A rubric that only asks whether the agent can parse Jinja2 and extract `conf.foo.bar` chains is misleading once the trajectory has moved beyond exploration into implementation or final review: many trajectories visibly extracted paths but still left update filtering unused, mismatched signal slot signatures, compared dependency names in the wrong format, over-broadened prefix matching, crashed Qt tests, or did not verify the observer lifecycle. The original idea can still be appropriate as an early-exploration/prototype criterion when no integration has begun, but it should not be the primary correctness criterion for a patch that is supposed to change stylesheet update behavior.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded “static Jinja2 template dependency extraction” too directly. That is necessary but not sufficient for this task. A trajectory can demonstrate nested `Getattr` parsing and still produce an incorrect patch if the extracted option names are not exactly comparable to `Config.changed` emissions, if the observer remains connected to the old unconditional slot, if a `pyqtSignal(str)` is connected to a no-argument slot or vice versa, if dependencies are only stored and never used, if deleted/update-disabled observer behavior is broken, or if focused stylesheet observer tests are failing or ignored. Avoid tempting criteria that require broad extras like template inheritance or dynamic constructs unless the visible codebase actually uses them in these stylesheet strings. A better rubric should focus on end-to-end dependency-aware update behavior: extracting full leaf option names without the `conf.` prefix, validating or otherwise handling only real config options, connecting a slot with the correct signal signature, updating only on exact relevant option changes, preserving initial rendering and `update=False`/deleted-object semantics, and using focused tests or credible manual fixture-equivalent checks rather than only standalone AST smoke tests.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: AST extraction without correct stylesheet observer integration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear to implement or plan Jinja2 `conf.` dependency extraction but lack visible evidence that the extracted dependencies are correctly integrated with stylesheet update registration. This flaw is present when the trajectory stores extracted paths without filtering updates, uses dependency names in a different format than emitted config option names, connects `Config.changed` to a slot with an incompatible signature, changes update filtering while focused stylesheet observer tests fail or crash unresolved, ignores `update=False` or deleted-object lifecycle behavior, or relies only on standalone AST/manual extraction experiments to declare success. Do not penalize early repository exploration where no implementation claim has been made yet; in that stage, AST understanding may be useful progress.

metadata.environment: Python qutebrowser-like project using PyQt signals, Jinja2 templates, and stylesheet observer registration
visible_evidence_to_check: dependency paths are leaf option names comparable to config change signal strings
stylesheet observer connects a `str`-accepting filtered slot when updates are enabled
initial render and no-update/deleted-object behavior are preserved
focused tests or credible fixture-equivalent checks cover relevant and irrelevant config changes
failing Qt/config stylesheet tests are not dismissed without diagnosis
tempting_but_insufficient_evidence: manual Jinja2 AST experiments returning dotted `conf` chains
a helper function added but unused or only stored on the observer
manual extraction tests without exercising config signal update behavior
claims that failures are environmental while focused observer tests still fail or abort

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory either remains in early exploration without claiming a fix, or shows extraction plus correct signal integration, matching option-name formats, preserved observer lifecycle semantics, and focused validation.
scale.2: Minor evidence: extraction and integration are mostly coherent, but validation is thin or one secondary concern such as caching/type annotations/test placement is not yet addressed.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory has a plausible extractor and some integration, but visible gaps remain in exact option matching, update filtering semantics, lifecycle behavior, or focused test coverage.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory mainly validates AST extraction while the observer integration is incomplete, untested, or visibly fragile, such as storing dependencies without using them or connecting an uncertain signal/slot path.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory declares success despite focused stylesheet/config tests failing or crashing, an empty or nonfunctional final diff, incompatible signal signatures, wrong dependency name format, or update filtering that would miss necessary stylesheet updates.

experiences.title: End-to-End Message-Scoped Assistant Asset Restoration
experiences.description: Retrieve when a mail/composer assistant task involves Markdown↔HTML conversion plus embedded link/image restoration that must be scoped by the originating message identity.
experiences.context: Applies in a TypeScript/React mail or composer assistant pipeline where generated/refined content is prepared, converted between HTML and Markdown, rendered or inserted back into an editor, and embedded links/images are temporarily replaced then restored. It is most useful once the trajectory is searching for or has found the actual app-level content helpers/components, especially when there is evidence of shared URL/image placeholder state or unscoped restore calls. For early exploration, judge concrete localization of the real app pipeline rather than generic LLM prompt/download/editor files. Do not apply as the main criterion for unrelated assistant model infrastructure, pure prompt formatting, generic sanitization, or formatting-only bugs with no message-scoped embedded asset restoration requirement.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful rubric theme was message identity propagation through the assistant content pipeline. It correctly penalizes trajectories that stay in generic packages, inspect prompt/model code, or fail to locate the real prepare/render/insert helpers because those trajectories lack the observable foundation for a correct fix. However, a broad rubric that merely asks whether the agent has found the conversion pipeline or mentions messageID can overcredit incomplete work: discovering global URL/image maps or adding a parameter is not enough if restoration still uses shared state, accepts optional empty identifiers, substitutes user/session IDs, or leaves render/insertion call paths unscoped. A better rubric should require end-to-end, same-identity scoping: the originating message identity is obtained from the composer/message model, is passed as a required value through input preparation, model-result parsing, rendering, and insertion paths, and is used by the link/image placeholder store so restoration only succeeds for placeholders belonging to that message. It should also look for rejection of unknown or cross-message placeholders while preserving link text, and for preservation of relevant anchor/image attributes when the task includes formatting requirements. Avoid tempting proxies such as assistantID, uid/session ID, generic sanitization changes, list-formatting fixes, or a single helper signature change. Prioritize visible evidence from the trajectory: actual app-level helper/component files found or edited, unscoped call sites identified and updated, absence of remaining restore/parse calls without message identity, replacement/restoration storage keyed by message identity rather than module-global placeholders alone, and tests or manual checks covering cross-message and hallucinated placeholder behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates an end-to-end fix strategy or implementation for message-scoped embedded link/image restoration in the assistant Markdown↔HTML content pipeline. It should show that the agent has identified the real app-level preparation, parsing, rendering, and insertion paths; threads the originating message identity through each of those paths as the scoping key; uses that identity in the placeholder replacement/restoration data model; and ensures restoration rejects unknown or cross-message placeholders while preserving user-visible text and required anchor/image attributes. Strong evidence includes updating or planning updates for all visible call sites rather than only one render path, avoiding optional empty fallbacks and unrelated identifiers, and adding or describing validation for multiple messages and hallucinated placeholders.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete Message-Scoped Restoration Pipeline

required_visible_evidence: actual assistant content conversion/render/insert pipeline has been located
originating message identity is available from the composer or message model
identity is propagated through preparation and parsing/restoration helpers
rendering and insertion call sites are both considered
link/image placeholder storage and restoration are keyed or checked by message identity
unknown or mismatched placeholders are dropped safely while preserving link text
anchor/image formatting attributes relevant to the task are preserved or explicitly addressed
anti_patterns: using user/session ID or assistant instance ID as a substitute for message identity
leaving restore/parse helpers callable without a message identity
only changing a helper signature without updating all downstream callers
continuing to rely on unscoped module-global placeholder maps
focusing only on generic LLM prompt formatting, sanitization, or list indentation

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward the real assistant content pipeline or message-scoped restoration; the trajectory remains in unrelated model, prompt, shared utility, or editor infrastructure.
scale.2: Some relevant search or partial localization is visible, but the trajectory has not identified the full prepare/render/insert pipeline or has not connected it to message identity and embedded asset restoration.
scale.3: The trajectory has found relevant conversion or URL/image restoration helpers and recognizes the need for message scoping, but evidence is limited to diagnosis or partial propagation and does not show all call paths or storage/restoration behavior handled.
scale.4: The trajectory shows a mostly complete approach: message identity is propagated through the main preparation and rendering/restoration paths, placeholder storage is scoped or checked, and most call sites are considered, with only minor uncertainty around validation or secondary insertion paths.
scale.5: The trajectory provides strong end-to-end evidence: all visible preparation, parsing, rendering, and insertion paths receive the required originating message identity; placeholder storage/restoration is message-scoped; hallucinated or cross-message placeholders are safely dropped while preserving text; required link/image attributes and formatting concerns are addressed; and validation covers multi-message and unknown-placeholder cases.

experiences.title: Don’t equate symbolic-index diagnosis with a safe matrix-entry fix
experiences.description: Retrieve when a symbolic algebra/SymPy trajectory has reproduced or diagnosed an identity-matrix nested-sum bug, especially when it has not yet made a clean targeted implementation or has only edited environment compatibility issues.
experiences.context: Applies to old SymPy-style tasks involving symbolic matrix expressions, special matrices such as identity matrices, symbolic element access, and finite sums. The misleading pattern is a trajectory that observes that an identity entry like I[i, j] becomes 0 before summation, or discusses KroneckerDelta/Piecewise semantics, but is still in reproduction/debugging, environment setup, or unsafe editing. In that stage, a rubric saying the trajectory must handle symbolic matrix summation can over-credit mere understanding and miss absence of a durable code change, missing validation, broad summation hacks, or source-file corruption. The original idea is appropriate only at implementation-review stage when visible evidence shows a targeted, runnable change to symbolic identity-entry behavior and checks that concrete indexing, diagonal sums, and total symbolic sums still work.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often asked for “symbolic matrix summation correctness” or “return KroneckerDelta for symbolic indices.” That captures an important root cause when the visible trajectory proves that symbolic identity element access is prematurely reduced to 0, but it is misleading as a standalone rubric during early exploration: many trajectories had only reproduced the bug, inspected summation code, or identified the bad equality comparison, while no safe patch or test existed. It also misses implementation-safety evidence: the better fix should target the special matrix element representation rather than apply broad generic summation changes, should distinguish known equal/known unequal indices from unknown symbolic equality, should import symbolic-delta utilities without circular imports, and should preserve concrete identity entries and diagonal behavior. Avoid generating a criterion that rewards merely mentioning KroneckerDelta or summation semantics. A replacement criterion should prioritize visible evidence that the agent has a clean worktree, a targeted special-matrix indexing edit, validation of I[0,0], I[0,1], I[i,i], I[i,j], and the nested total sum, plus a regression test or equivalent runnable script. If the trajectory is still blocked by Python-version import issues or has only environment edits, generate a progress/stage rubric about separating setup from the target bug rather than a final correctness rubric.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Over-crediting Diagnosis Without a Safe Symbolic-Entry Fix
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for an identity-matrix symbolic-summation bug when they only reproduce or diagnose that symbolic element access collapses to zero, or when they make broad/unsafe edits, without visible evidence of a clean targeted implementation that represents unknown symbolic index equality conditionally while preserving concrete identity entries and validating the nested total sum.

visible_problem_cues: identity-like matrix expression is recognized correctly for concrete entries
diagonal sum works but total nested sum returns zero
debug output shows symbolic entry access becomes a constant zero before summation
do_not_overweight: mere reproduction of the user example
generic inspection of summation internals
mentioning KroneckerDelta or Piecewise without a runnable targeted change
environment compatibility edits unrelated to the mathematical bug
required_safe_evidence: targeted edit to special matrix element access or equivalent representation layer
unknown symbolic equality is represented symbolically rather than as definitely false
known diagonal and off-diagonal concrete accesses remain correct
nested symbolic total sum is checked to evaluate to the matrix dimension
worktree remains intact and tests or reproduction scripts run

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory shows a clean targeted fix for symbolic identity element access, preserves concrete/diagonal behavior, and validates the nested sum with a runnable check or regression test.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory has a plausible targeted implementation but validation is incomplete, or it validates the reproduction without covering concrete indexing and diagonal behavior.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory has correctly reproduced and diagnosed the symbolic-index root cause but has not yet produced a durable targeted code change or regression test.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory focuses on generic summation changes, environment edits, or unconditional symbolic rewrites without demonstrating that the special matrix entry behavior is fixed safely.
scale.5: Most severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory leaves the repository unrunnable or visibly corrupts key source while attempting broad text replacements or circular imports, and no reliable target-bug fix is present.

experiences.title: Prioritize Primary HTTP Status Before Fragment Validation
experiences.description: Retrieve when a link-checking or validation task reports a secondary validation error, such as a missing fragment/anchor, even though the underlying HTTP request returned an error status.
experiences.context: Applies in Python documentation/link-checking codebases, especially Sphinx-like linkcheck builders, when the task concerns URLs with fragments and a configuration that enables anchor validation. The useful stage is after the trajectory has either located the HTTP request plus fragment-validation path or explicitly reasoned that an error response is being parsed before status handling. It remains applicable during diagnosis, implementation, and final review, but the strictness should change by stage: early trajectories may only show the correct causal hypothesis, while later trajectories must show a clean code change and validation. Do not apply this criterion to unrelated anchor parsing bugs where the base HTTP response is successful, to non-HTTP URI handling, or to fixes that intentionally change anchor matching rules rather than error precedence.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful rubric in these cases checked whether the agent understood and implemented the precedence rule: for a fragmented HTTP/HTTPS URL, the base response status must be checked and routed through the existing HTTP error path before scanning the response body for an anchor. This aligned well when the visible trajectory showed the agent locating the branch that performs a GET for anchor checking, recognizing that it skipped status validation, and planning or adding a status check before anchor parsing. A better rubric should not merely say “fix linkcheck” or “add tests”; it should focus on the observable ordering contract: fetch base URL, raise/report 4xx/5xx through existing HTTPError handling, then only run missing-anchor logic on successful responses. It should also include the preservation boundary: normal missing-anchor reports on successful pages, non-fragment links, and existing special HTTP handling should not be broken. A tempting but weaker criterion is to reward any reproduction of the bug or any mention of `raise_for_status` without checking placement and code integrity. In later-stage trajectories, prioritize evidence that the status check is inserted in the anchor GET path before anchor validation, that it is inside the existing exception-handling scope, and that the edited file remains syntactically coherent; visible duplicate or misindented status checks should lower confidence even if the semantic idea is correct.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For fragmented HTTP/HTTPS links when anchor checking is enabled, the trajectory should identify and preserve the required precedence: the response status from the base URL request is checked and reported through the existing HTTP error handling before any anchor lookup or missing-anchor error is produced. Strong evidence includes locating the anchor-specific GET path, placing status validation before anchor parsing within the existing exception-handling flow, preserving normal anchor-not-found behavior for successful responses, and avoiding syntax/indentation regressions or duplicated misplaced checks.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: HTTP Status Before Fragment Validation

required_visible_evidence: The trajectory connects the bug to fragmented URLs whose base request returns a 4xx/5xx response.
The trajectory identifies that anchor parsing currently happens before status validation in the anchor-checking request path.
The proposed or applied change checks the HTTP status before anchor lookup and reuses existing HTTP error reporting behavior.
The trajectory accounts for preserving normal missing-anchor behavior on successful responses and existing non-anchor/special-status behavior.
At implementation-review stage, the edited code remains syntactically valid and the status check is not duplicated or inserted into the wrong branch.
metadata.applicability_boundary: Use for linkcheck-style HTTP-plus-fragment validation bugs, not for pure anchor matching bugs on successful pages or unrelated request failures.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory distinguishes HTTP status errors from missing-anchor errors in the fragment-checking path.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory mentions HTTP errors or anchors but does not clearly identify that status must be checked before anchor lookup in the anchor request path.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory diagnoses the ordering problem or proposes status validation before anchor parsing, but implementation placement, preservation of existing behavior, or code integrity remains uncertain.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory locates the correct anchor-checking request path and applies or plans a status check before anchor validation while preserving existing HTTP error handling, with only minor validation gaps.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory cleanly implements status validation before anchor parsing in the correct branch, keeps existing error-handling semantics and normal anchor behavior intact, and validates both HTTP-error and successful-page missing-anchor scenarios without visible code-quality regressions.

experiences.title: Central lazy-string normalization before string-only lookups
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django formatting/i18n task involves lazy translation strings reaching an API that uses the value as a format-setting name or attribute name, especially after the trajectory has inspected or modified the central format lookup helper.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django repository where the task explicitly says a formatting helper should accept lazy string/proxy parameters and the visible trajectory has found the central lookup path, reproduced a `getattr()`/attribute-name TypeError, inspected Django lazy utilities such as `force_str()`/`Promise`, or patched the central helper. It is most useful during implementation or final-review stages, when there is visible evidence of where coercion is placed and whether normal format lookup/localization behavior is preserved. It is less applicable to unrelated lazy-return behavior, generic template-filter issues where the central helper is not involved, or very early exploration with no identified string-only operation; in those cases a narrower root-cause or test-discovery rubric may be better.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic boundary: a lazy string-like format argument must be resolved to an ordinary string inside the central format lookup API before it is passed to Python/string-only operations such as module/settings attribute lookup and before fallback logic depends on string identity. This was discriminative because the visible trajectories repeatedly showed the exact failure path, the candidate utility for resolving lazy objects, and manual checks comparing lazy and regular format names/custom literal formats. A better rubric should reward evidence that the agent fixes the lower-level API rather than only the date template filter, preserves existing localization and fallback behavior, and validates both named settings like date/time formats and literal custom format strings. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as merely adding any regression test, repeatedly grepping for tests, decorating the helper to keep laziness, changing only the caller, or requiring an exact patch shape. Also avoid making cache-key normalization the sole pass/fail signal: normalizing before cache creation is ideal and should be rewarded, but the core observable correctness cue is that lazy values are converted before the operations that reject non-`str` attribute names while ordinary string behavior remains unchanged. Prioritize visible diff/context showing the conversion is inside the central helper, after the function docstring/style-sensitive area, without removing localization conditionals or settings fallbacks, plus reproduction/validation outputs for lazy and regular inputs.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a central fix for lazy string format parameters by converting the lazy/proxy `format_type` to an ordinary string inside the format lookup helper before it is used in attribute lookup, settings lookup, ISO/fallback checks, and ideally cache-key construction, while preserving existing behavior for regular strings, named format settings, literal custom formats, localization language handling, and unknown-format fallback. Strong evidence includes locating the `getattr(..., format_type, ...)` failure, using an established Django string-coercion mechanism or equivalent `str()` conversion at the API boundary, and validating both direct helper calls and the template/date formatting path with lazy and non-lazy inputs.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Lazy format argument normalized at lookup boundary

required_visible_evidence: The trajectory identifies that a lazy/proxy format argument reaches a central format lookup helper and fails at a string-only operation such as `getattr()`.
The proposed or applied code converts the format argument to a real string in the central helper rather than only in one caller.
The code preserves localization conditionals, settings/module fallback, unknown literal format behavior, and ordinary string inputs.
Validation or reasoning covers lazy named formats and lazy literal/custom format strings, not only the single reported example.
preferred_but_not_absolute_evidence: Conversion occurs before cache-key construction so lazy and non-lazy equivalents share cache behavior.
An in-tree regression test is added or a suitable test location is identified, with ad hoc reproduction scripts not treated as final artifacts.
anti_patterns: Fixing only the template date filter while leaving other callers of the central helper exposed.
Using lazy-preserving decorators/utilities when the problem is a Python API requiring an actual string.
Breaking unrelated localization language selection or settings fallback while adding the coercion.
Relying on repeated test discovery commands as evidence of semantic progress.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent identified or addressed lazy format arguments reaching string-only lookup operations; changes, if any, are unrelated or only generic exploration.
scale.2: The trajectory recognizes the lazy/getattr failure or reproduces it, but has no central fix yet, or proposes a caller-only/lazy-preserving approach that would leave the core lookup API vulnerable.
scale.3: The trajectory has a plausible central coercion plan or partial patch, but placement or preservation is uncertain, validation is minimal, or there are visible risks such as disrupted localization/fallback logic or code inserted in a style-sensitive location.
scale.4: The trajectory applies a central conversion before the failing attribute/settings/fallback operations and shows lazy inputs no longer crash while regular strings still work; minor gaps may remain in cache normalization, in-tree regression coverage, cleanup, or breadth of validation.
scale.5: The trajectory cleanly normalizes lazy format arguments at the central lookup boundary before all relevant uses including cache behavior, preserves localization and fallback semantics, validates lazy and regular named/custom formats through direct and caller paths, and prepares or identifies appropriate regression coverage without leaving ad hoc artifacts.

experiences.title: IDN Punycode Must Be Wired Into the User-Facing Link Flow
experiences.description: Use this when a web/TypeScript monorepo task asks for IDN/Punycode URL safety and the trajectory has found generic URL helpers plus an existing component-level link click/display path. The useful rubric should judge whether the agent connects hostname punycode conversion to the actual link confirmation/rendering flow, not merely whether it adds a standalone URL helper.
experiences.context: Applies in frontend web applications, especially TypeScript monorepos with shared utility packages and component packages, where the bug is observed when users click or view links containing Unicode hostnames. Retrieve this experience once the trajectory has visible evidence of both generic URL utilities and the UI path that extracts, sanitizes, confirms, or displays external links. It is most useful after the agent has inspected relevant link handlers, confirmation UI, URL helper tests, or existing punycode-related code. It is less applicable for purely backend URL storage tasks, tasks that only require a library utility with no user-facing integration, or very early exploration before the relevant link entry point has been located.
experiences.experience: The earlier rubrics correctly emphasized the core invariant: convert only the hostname of an IDN URL to ASCII/Punycode while preserving protocol, path, query, fragment, auth, and port. However, in this setting that criterion is too generic by itself. A trajectory can satisfy it superficially by adding a helper in a shared URL file, while leaving the actual clicked/displayed link path unchanged, or by modifying unrelated helpers such as validation, prefixing, or search-param serialization. The better rubric should focus on whether the agent has identified the user-facing link extraction/confirmation/rendering flow and wired the punycode-normalized URL into that flow. Prioritize visible evidence such as: inspection of existing link-click code that already distinguishes raw href from browser-encoded href; recognition of browser compatibility comments around Punycode/IDN handling; a helper placed where the link UI can import it without unnecessary dependency churn; replacement of the displayed/confirmed link value with a hostname-only Punycode version; and focused tests or examples showing a Unicode hostname becomes an xn-- hostname while path/query/hash remain unchanged. Avoid tempting but weak criteria like “adds a toPunycode function somewhere,” “uses the native URL API,” or “covers all URL entry points” unless the trajectory also shows the function is used by the specific user-facing path described in the task. Also avoid rewarding broad edits to unrelated URL utilities, validators, or dependency manifests when the visible issue is in the link display/click confirmation path.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: User-Facing IDN Link Flow Integration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the IDN/Punycode fix is integrated into the actual user-facing link handling flow where external links are extracted, displayed, sanitized, confirmed, or opened. A strong solution does not stop at a standalone URL helper: it identifies the relevant component-level link path, normalizes only the hostname to ASCII/Punycode, preserves the rest of the URL, handles raw versus browser-encoded href values safely, and avoids unrelated changes to validators, search-param helpers, or generic URL prefix logic unless directly required by the link flow.

expected_visible_evidence: The agent inspects the UI link click/render/confirmation path, not only generic shared URL utilities.
The agent notices existing IDN or Punycode-related handling, browser compatibility comments, or raw-versus-encoded href extraction in that path.
The proposed or implemented conversion is actually used before displaying or confirming the external link shown to the user.
The conversion targets only the hostname/domain labels and preserves protocol, pathname, query string, fragment, port, and credentials when present.
Tests, examples, or reasoning cover a Unicode hostname becoming an xn-- hostname without punycoding path/query/fragment content.
anti_evidence: Only adds an unused helper in a generic shared URL file.
Changes unrelated URL utilities, validators, or query-string behavior without tying them to the displayed link path.
Relies on broad claims about all URL entry points without showing the concrete user-facing path from the task.
Punycode-converts entire URL strings, paths, query parameters, or fragments rather than just the hostname.
Ignores existing browser compatibility or raw href extraction behavior already present in the link handling code.
metadata.applicability_stage: Most judgeable after repository search has located both URL helpers and the component/link handling path; premature during the first few exploratory commands.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent has connected IDN/Punycode handling to the user-facing link flow; it only explores unrelated files or discusses generic URL conversion.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the agent identifies generic URL helpers or Punycode libraries and may propose hostname conversion, but has not inspected or planned integration with the actual link display/click/confirmation path.
scale.3: Moderate evidence comparable to the parent trajectory: the agent understands hostname-only Punycode conversion and has found some relevant link or URL files, but the plan or edits still center on an isolated helper or broad entry-point changes rather than clear wiring into the user-facing link flow.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the agent identifies the concrete link handling path and proposes or starts changes that feed a hostname-only Punycode URL into the displayed/confirmed link while preserving other URL parts and respecting existing raw/encoded href behavior.
scale.5: Very strong evidence: the trajectory clearly implements or plans a minimal integrated fix in the link display/click confirmation flow, reuses or places the helper at an appropriate component-accessible layer, preserves all non-host URL components, avoids unrelated utility regressions, and includes focused tests or explicit examples for Unicode-hostname IDN links.

experiences.title: Preserve weakref-backed grouping during serialization fixes
experiences.description: Use when a pickling failure has been localized to persistent weak-reference state inside a semantic grouping/cache structure that is part of the object graph being serialized.
experiences.context: Applies in Python library bug-fix trajectories, especially Matplotlib-like object graphs, after visible evidence shows: a user-facing object becomes unpickleable only after an API populates persistent metadata; that metadata is a weakref-backed grouping/disjoint-set/cache; and the state is later used to preserve behavior after draw/query/unpickle. It is most useful once the agent has inspected the weakref container or reproduced `cannot pickle weakref.ReferenceType`. It is premature during broad repository search, and it should not be used when weakrefs are purely disposable caches whose loss is explicitly acceptable, when no weakref container has been identified, or when the trajectory is mainly dealing with environment/import contamination rather than the patch design.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on custom serialization for weakref-based data structures: convert weak references to strong referents only for pickle state, then reconstruct weak references on unpickle while preserving the logical grouping relationships. This was discriminative because simply making `pickle.dumps(...)` stop raising is not enough; dropping or emptying the weakref mapping destroys the persistent alignment/group semantics that the original API established. A better rubric should therefore judge whether the agent’s planned or implemented fix preserves live memberships, sibling/group relationships, and post-unpickle operations such as join/query/iteration, not merely whether weakrefs are excluded from the pickle stream. Avoid the tempting broad criterion that says “remove/clean/avoid weakrefs before pickling” without requiring reconstruction of the same semantic state. Prioritize visible evidence such as inspection of the weakref-backed mapping, recognition that another owner in the pickled object graph keeps referents alive, tests or reasoning about unpickle behavior, and checks that the feature relying on the groups still works after serialization.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a pickling bug caused by a persistent weakref-backed grouping structure, the trajectory should favor a serialization design that stores live referents or equivalent logical group state during pickling and rebuilds the weakref-based internal representation during unpickling, while preserving the grouping semantics used by the feature after deserialization. Strong evidence includes identifying the exact weakref container reachable from the serialized object, explaining why raw weakrefs cannot be pickled, avoiding permanent strong-reference ownership changes, and validating or planning validation that pickling succeeds and grouped objects remain related/queryable after unpickle.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Serialization preserves weakref-backed semantic groups

required_visible_evidence: A weakref-backed mapping/group/cache has been identified as reachable from the serialized object
The weakrefs are persistent feature state rather than disposable temporary cache
The proposed fix converts weakrefs to picklable state and reconstructs weakrefs afterward
The trajectory considers preservation of group membership or feature behavior after unpickle
metadata.common_false_positive: A patch that empties, drops, or merely cleans the weakref mapping so pickling no longer raises, without preserving the established relationships

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent has connected the pickling failure to weakref-backed persistent state or considered preserving the feature’s logical relationships.
scale.2: The agent identifies weakrefs as unpickleable but only proposes removing, clearing, or avoiding them without a credible reconstruction plan.
scale.3: The agent proposes custom serialization for the weakref container, but preservation of group membership and post-unpickle behavior is only partially reasoned about or unvalidated.
scale.4: The agent clearly plans or implements conversion from weakrefs to picklable live referents/logical groups and reconstruction back to weakrefs, with attention to preserving membership semantics.
scale.5: The agent both implements or specifies the weakref-to-strong-state-to-weakref round trip and validates that serialization succeeds while grouping/query/feature behavior remains intact after unpickle.

experiences.title: Avoid full-RFC proxies for narrow i18n URL-prefix parsing bugs
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django i18n task concerns script+region locale prefixes in `i18n_patterns()` and the trajectory discusses RFC 5646/BCP 47, `get_language_from_path()`, `language_code_prefix_re`, `LocaleMiddleware`, or `LocalePrefixPattern`.
experiences.context: This applies in Django URL internationalization fixes where the reported failure is that configured language prefixes with both script and region subtags, such as language-script-region, are not extracted from request paths. The misleading pattern is generating a rubric that rewards broad RFC 5646 compliance, full BCP 47 parsing, generalized case normalization, or resolver-wide case-insensitive matching. Those ideas can be relevant for a task explicitly asking for a complete language-tag parser or Accept-Language validation, but they are not the right proxy when the visible investigation shows a localized mismatch between the URL-prefix regex and existing language validation. In this environment, URL prefix extraction is followed by supported-language validation and interacts with unprefixed default-language URL routing, so overly broad parsing can create regressions by treating ordinary dashed URL slugs as language prefixes or by changing resolver/activation behavior unnecessarily.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often required “RFC 5646 Language Tag Compliance” or praised “minimal scope” without checking whether the actual trajectory stayed within the narrow URL-prefix extraction contract. This over-rewards patches that parse many RFC-shaped subtags, add custom validators, alter locale casing utilities, or make `LocalePrefixPattern` match case-insensitively/all configured languages. Those changes can look standards-compliant while breaking Django’s existing routing assumptions: middleware first extracts a path prefix, validates it against configured languages, activates a canonical language, and the resolver then matches the active prefix. A better rubric should focus on whether the agent has identified the specific restrictive path-prefix regex and is preserving existing validation/routing boundaries. Prefer criteria that look for evidence that the fix accepts the reported script+region prefixes after supported-language validation, keeps unsupported or slug-like dashed paths from being consumed as language codes, and avoids broad resolver or locale-conversion changes unless the trajectory proves they are necessary. Avoid the tempting criterion “handles all valid RFC 5646 tags with full case-insensitive matching”; for this task it is too broad and can point the judge toward incorrect overgeneralized solutions.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Overbroad language-tag or resolver semantics
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat the issue as a requirement for complete RFC 5646/BCP 47 parsing or broad case-insensitive resolver behavior rather than a narrow URL-prefix extraction bug. The flaw is present when the visible work loosens language-prefix matching to arbitrary multiple subtags, adds custom full-tag validators, changes locale conversion/canonicalization, or modifies locale-prefix URL resolver matching without demonstrating that these changes are required and without checking existing routing behavior for ordinary dashed paths and unprefixed default-language URLs.

metadata.environment: Django i18n URL routing with LocaleMiddleware, i18n_patterns, path language extraction, and supported-language validation
visible_positive_evidence_to_prioritize: The trajectory identifies the restrictive URL path-prefix extraction regex as the root cause.
The proposed change is limited to extracting configured language-script-region prefixes before existing supported-language validation.
The trajectory checks both reported positive paths and negative/compatibility cases such as unsupported language prefixes or ordinary dashed URL slugs.
The trajectory avoids changing LocalePrefixPattern, activation/canonicalization, or locale conversion unless direct evidence shows the regex-only fix is insufficient.
visible_red_flags: The trajectory frames success as supporting all RFC 5646 variants/extensions/private-use forms.
The trajectory reuses a broad language-code regex for URL prefixes without considering dashed non-language URL components.
The trajectory changes resolver matching to accept all languages or ignore case globally.
The trajectory changes locale casing or language activation semantics to make a URL resolve.

scale.1: No evidence of overbroad language-tag or resolver changes; the trajectory stays focused on path-prefix extraction plus existing validation and considers compatibility boundaries.
scale.2: Minor overbroad wording or exploratory tests appear, but the implementation direction remains localized and compatibility checks are considered.
scale.3: The trajectory partly relies on broad RFC/case-insensitive reasoning or touches adjacent resolver/locale behavior, with limited evidence about dashed-path or existing i18n regression risks.
scale.4: Clear evidence that the proposed fix broadens parsing or resolver semantics beyond the reported script+region prefix issue and lacks meaningful compatibility validation.
scale.5: Severe overgeneralization: the trajectory implements or strongly commits to full RFC-style parsing, custom validation, locale canonicalization, or global case-insensitive/all-language resolver matching, with visible risk to existing URL routing behavior.

experiences.title: Do not equate local dense stripping with fixing EX-domain zero detection
experiences.description: Retrieve when a SymPy polynomial bug involves `domain='EX'`, a Poly that prints/as_exprs as zero but `Poly.is_zero` is false, and the trajectory is tempted to fix only `clear_denoms()` or dense-list canonicalization.
experiences.context: This applies in SymPy/polys trajectories where the visible symptom is an unstripped dense representation after `clear_denoms()`, but the coefficients are expression-domain objects whose mathematical zero-ness is only revealed by symbolic `.is_zero` rather than by ordinary equality/truthiness. A rubric about canonical zero representation can be appropriate if the investigation has already ruled out coefficient-domain truthiness/zero-predicate issues and the defect is purely that one dense algorithm returns an otherwise correctly recognized zero list unstripped. It is misleading when the trajectory’s evidence shows a mismatch such as `as_expr().is_zero` being true while `Poly.is_zero` is false, because that points to how EX coefficients report boolean zero-ness across all dense-polynomial algorithms, not just to one missing strip call in `clear_denoms()`.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics rewarded trajectories for making `clear_denoms()` return `DMP([])`/a stripped zero and for making downstream methods pass on the reproduced example. That criterion was too narrow: agents could add local `dup_strip`/`dmp_strip` calls after denominator clearing and make the visible reproduction pass while leaving the underlying expression-domain zero predicate inconsistent. In this class of bug, the better rubric should ask whether the agent investigates and fixes how EX-domain coefficient objects decide truthiness/zero-ness, especially because dense stripping helpers and zero tests depend on coefficient boolean evaluation. Avoid the tempting criterion “the trajectory should normalize the `clear_denoms` result to canonical DMP zero” as the main success signal unless the trajectory has visible evidence that coefficient truthiness is already correct.
