Prefer evidence that the agent follows the mismatch from `as_expr().is_zero` versus `Poly.is_zero` into domain-level zero detection, validates that a coefficient simplifying to zero is treated as false/zero by dense polynomial internals, and uses `clear_denoms()` only as a regression scenario rather than the sole patched site.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat the EX-domain zero-polynomial bug as only a missing post-processing strip in `clear_denoms()` or dense denominator-clearing code, without investigating whether expression-domain coefficients that simplify to zero evaluate as zero/false for the dense-polynomial invariants. This flaw is especially clear when the visible reproduction shows `as_expr().is_zero` true but `Poly.is_zero` false, and the proposed direction is to add local stripping or consumer-method special cases rather than correcting the coefficient-domain zero predicate used by stripping and zero tests.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Local clear_denoms stripping masks EX zero-predicate bug

metadata.environment: SymPy polynomial internals with dense polynomial lists and expression-domain coefficients
misleading_evidence: Reproduction becomes `DMP([])` after adding local strip calls
Downstream methods such as `terms_gcd` or `primitive` pass only for the reproduced `clear_denoms()` path
Trajectory focuses on dense-list canonicalization while ignoring why an EX coefficient that is mathematically zero was truthy/nonzero
preferred_evidence: Agent connects `as_expr().is_zero` versus `Poly.is_zero` mismatch to expression-domain coefficient zero detection
Agent inspects or reasons about coefficient truthiness used by dense stripping/zero predicates
Fix is domain-level or otherwise general enough that EX coefficients simplifying to zero are recognized as zero across polynomial operations
Regression covers the public `clear_denoms()` symptom and, if possible, a smaller check that EX zero coefficients are treated as zero by dense-polynomial normalization

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory identifies the coefficient-domain zero/truthiness issue and treats dense representation as a symptom, not the root cause.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory discusses stripping but also meaningfully investigates EX coefficient zero detection before deciding on a fix.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory fixes or plans to fix local `clear_denoms()` normalization and passes the reproduction, but leaves some uncertainty about whether EX zero truthiness was considered.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory explicitly concludes the bug is missing dense stripping in `clear_denoms()` and proposes local strip calls, despite visible `as_expr().is_zero` versus `Poly.is_zero` evidence.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory only patches local denominator-clearing or downstream consumers, relies on the reproduced example passing, and never examines the expression-domain zero predicate that dense polynomial normalization depends on.

experiences.title: Do not equate FortiSwitch no-fortios checks with complete Fortinet CPE correctness
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for SNMP-to-CPE conversion tasks involving Fortinet product lines, especially when the visible trajectory validates only a FortiSwitch example or focuses on avoiding `fortios` for FortiSwitch.
experiences.context: This applies in a Go repository with a `contrib/snmp2cpe` converter where `snmp.Result` fields such as `EntPhysicalName` and `EntPhysicalSoftwareRev` are mapped to CPE 2.3 strings. The misleading pattern is a rubric that rewards only discriminating FortiGate versus FortiSwitch, or only emitting three CPEs for `FS_108E`, while ignoring whether OS/firmware product names use the product family rather than the model, whether duplicate hardware CPEs are introduced, whether other recognizable Fortinet prefixes are covered, and whether existing vendor behavior is preserved. A narrower FortiSwitch-specific rubric can be appropriate during early diagnosis or for a task explicitly limited to one fixture, but final-review rubrics for this task family should not treat a single passing FortiSwitch ad-hoc run as sufficient evidence of a complete Fortinet conversion fix.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics often said the trajectory should emit FortiSwitch hardware/OS/firmware CPEs and never use `fortios` for FortiSwitch. That idea is directionally correct but too weak and sometimes misleading: several patches satisfied the visible no-`fortios` check while using the full model string such as `fortiswitch-108e` as the OS or firmware product, duplicating hardware CPEs from both physical name and software revision, or only adding `FGT_`/`FS_` branches rather than a reusable mapping for recognizable Fortinet product prefixes. A better rubric should distinguish hardware model CPEs from OS/firmware family CPEs: hardware should include the product family plus model, while OS and firmware should use the Fortinet product family name and the parsed version. It should also check that the implementation derives OS/firmware from the recognized hardware/product family, handles build and non-build version tokens, avoids extra CPEs, preserves existing FortiGate behavior, and does not rewrite unrelated vendor logic. Avoid the tempting criterion “FortiSwitch emits three CPEs and not fortios” unless it explicitly verifies product-family naming and regression scope. Prioritize visible evidence from inspected diffs, unit tests or ad-hoc outputs showing exact CPE strings, coverage beyond one hard-coded model, absence of duplicates, and unchanged existing tests.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Over-narrow or model-confused Fortinet CPE fix
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories whose Fortinet SNMP-to-CPE fix appears to satisfy the single FortiSwitch example but is semantically incomplete: it only distinguishes `FGT_` and `FS_`, uses the full hardware model as the OS/firmware product instead of the Fortinet product family, emits duplicate hardware CPEs from both physical name and software revision, mishandles `v<version>` versus `v<version>,build...` parsing, adds firmware to product lines that should keep existing behavior, lacks coverage for other recognizable Fortinet prefixes implied by the task, or rewrites unrelated vendor detection/conversion code. Judge this from visible diffs, tests, and command outputs; do not require a specific implementation shape, but require evidence that product-family mapping and regression boundaries are correct.

visible_evidence: Fortinet branch in CPE conversion logic
mapping from physical-name prefixes or software-revision product names to hardware product families
exact emitted CPE strings in tests or ad-hoc runs
existing FortiGate and other vendor test results
diff scope showing whether unrelated vendor behavior was changed

key_distinctions.hardware_cpe_product: product-family plus model, e.g. a switch hardware model
key_distinctions.os_cpe_product: product family, not full model, except FortiGate/FortiWiFi mapping to fortios

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory visibly implements or plans a product-family-based Fortinet mapping, preserves FortiGate behavior, avoids duplicate CPEs, handles relevant version formats, and keeps unrelated vendor logic stable.
scale.2: Minor concern: the trajectory focuses on FortiSwitch but still shows correct family-versus-model CPE naming and regression awareness, with only limited evidence about broader Fortinet prefixes.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory has the right no-`fortios` intent for FortiSwitch but visible evidence is limited to one ad-hoc case or does not clearly prove absence of duplicates, correct version normalization, or preservation of existing behavior.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the visible patch or outputs use model-specific OS/firmware products, duplicate hardware CPEs, rely on hard-coded `FGT_`/`FS_` handling without broader recognizable-prefix mapping, or validate only self-matching tests while ignoring existing regressions.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory treats a single FortiSwitch output as complete despite wrong CPE product semantics, broad unrelated rewrites, failing or unrun existing tests, and no credible evidence that Fortinet product-line mapping or compatibility boundaries are preserved.

experiences.title: Do not treat tag validation as sufficient proof of OCI copy correctness
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a Go/Cobra CLI task that adds OCI bundle copy support, especially where the trajectory visibly adds missing-tag checks or local-reference checks but has limited evidence about copied artifact metadata, digest consistency, list/fetch discoverability, or regressions to existing bundle behavior.
experiences.context: This applies in Flipt-like Go CLI repositories using ORAS/OCI layouts, where a new bundle copy command and store Copy method are being added. A tag-validation rubric is appropriate as a narrow subcriterion when the task explicitly requires missing source/destination tags to fail. It becomes misleading when used as the main or sole criterion after implementation work: visible tag checks, CLI help output, or manual missing-tag failures do not establish that the copied bundle is identical, that the returned digest matches the copied root descriptor/list output, that CreatedAt is read from the copied manifest annotations, or that fetch/list behavior remains correct. Be careful with unconditional local-scheme requirements too: they may be relevant for a user-facing local-copy command, but if the codebase is evolving a reusable store copy primitive used by push/pull-style commands, the more important evidence is correct target resolution and avoiding unintended remote behavior in the exposed local workflow.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often rewarded 'requires both references to include tags' or 'requires flipt:// local references' as if that predicted the whole patch. That is a necessary contract check, but it over-emphasizes an easy visible proxy and misses the recurring semantic failures: returning a digest computed from a modified manifest instead of the ORAS copy descriptor, parsing CreatedAt from descriptor annotations that may not contain the manifest annotations, failing to prove the destination appears consistently in list/fetch, or making unrelated CLI/config/storage changes while chasing manual validation. A better rubric should focus on end-to-end copy metadata consistency and artifact discoverability: the implementation should copy the rooted DAG to the destination target, fetch/read the copied destination manifest when metadata is needed, return destination repository/tag with the actual copied descriptor digest and manifest creation time, and verify missing-tag failures plus successful list/fetch behavior. Avoid generating a high-level success criterion that can be satisfied by tag checks alone; use tag validation only as one component unless the task is exclusively about validation.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear to add OCI bundle copy support but rely on superficial validation evidence while leaving copied artifact metadata or discoverability unproven or inconsistent. This includes implementations that validate source/destination tags yet return a digest derived by re-marshalling or mutating the manifest instead of the actual copied root descriptor, parse creation time from the wrong metadata source, omit verification that the destination can be listed and fetched with the expected repository/tag/digest/CreatedAt, or introduce unrelated CLI/config/storage changes that could regress existing bundle commands. The flaw is especially relevant when recent steps show only CLI help, missing-tag checks, or partial manual commands rather than a successful copy followed by consistent list/fetch evidence.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Tag checks mask copy metadata inconsistency

metadata.task_type: Go Cobra CLI plus internal OCI/ORAS store copy implementation
metadata.avoid_proxy: presence of copy command or missing-tag error checks alone
prioritize_evidence: destination list/fetch contains the copied bundle
returned digest matches the ORAS copy descriptor and list output
CreatedAt is read from copied manifest annotations
repository and tag are set from destination reference
existing bundle commands and config behavior are not unnecessarily altered

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: tag validation, copy operation, returned metadata, and list/fetch verification are all addressed consistently without unrelated regressions.
scale.2: Minor concern: tag validation is visible and copy seems plausible, but the trajectory has only weak or incomplete evidence for one metadata or discoverability aspect.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory emphasizes tag/local validation and adds a copy path, but does not clearly verify list/fetch behavior or exact digest/CreatedAt consistency.
scale.4: Clear flaw: implementation or manual evidence shows tag checks passing, but copied metadata is likely wrong or unverified, such as using descriptor annotations for CreatedAt or lacking destination list/fetch confirmation.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the patch visibly returns incorrect copy metadata, recomputes digest from a modified manifest, breaks or risks existing bundle/config behavior, and the trajectory still treats tag validation or CLI help as sufficient proof.

experiences.title: Do not reward secondary typing detours over preserving empty-tuple semantics
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Sphinx/Python annotation parsing task involves an empty tuple annotation such as `Tuple[()]`, and the trajectory emphasizes reproductions, test failures, or related `typing`/autodoc issues rather than verifying the rendered representation of the empty tuple.
experiences.context: This applies in Python/Sphinx-style codebases where annotations are parsed or unparsed from AST nodes and the reported crash is caused by separator-trimming logic on an empty `ast.Tuple`. A misleading rubric in this setting rewards creating a minimal repro, investigating test failures, or fixing a secondary runtime `typing` issue, even when the visible implementation evidence only shows a guarded `pop()` and validation output like `Tuple[]` with no parentheses. Those process behaviors can be useful early in exploration, and secondary-module fixes can matter if they are clearly required for the reported scenario and pass existing formatting tests. But at final-review or patch-quality stages, they are not a substitute for checking that the empty tuple syntax is represented as `()` and that parallel annotation-unparse paths remain consistent.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked whether the agent created a minimal test case, investigated failing tests, or systematically fixed related issues in `sphinx/util/typing.py`. Those criteria can overpredict quality here because the visible trajectory may show lots of debugging and even a no-crash direct check while still accepting an incorrect semantic output: rendering `Tuple[()]` as if the subscript contents were empty (`Tuple[]`) instead of preserving the explicit empty tuple `()`. They can also reward broad edits to runtime typing internals that are environment-specific and have visible regressions in existing formatting tests. For this kind of task, generate a rubric focused on the actual annotation contract: the fix must handle `ast.Tuple(elts=[])` by emitting or stringifying explicit `(` and `)` for the empty tuple, must keep non-empty tuple/list/subscript formatting intact, and should consider other AST unparse utilities if the repository has multiple annotation rendering paths. Avoid a tempting criterion that rewards merely guarding `result.pop()`, making a Sphinx build pass, or chasing unrelated `typing._special` failures without stable tests. Prioritize visible evidence such as inspected AST shape, expected node/string output containing `()`, regression tests that assert the rendered annotation rather than only absence of `IndexError`, and explicit cleanup or reversion of experimental secondary-module edits that break existing tests.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for an empty-tuple annotation parsing bug when the visible fix or validation only prevents the `pop from empty list` crash but treats the empty tuple as no rendered content, or when the agent is diverted into broad runtime typing changes while leaving the core AST rendering contract unverified. This flaw is indicated by evidence such as accepting `_parse_annotation("Tuple[()]")` output with only `Tuple`, `[`, and `]`; describing the empty tuple slice as producing an empty node list; adding only a guarded separator pop; omitting checks for explicit `(` and `)` in the output; not inspecting/updating parallel AST unparse/stringify paths used for annotations; or leaving secondary `typing` edits with failing existing tests.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Empty tuple semantics lost behind no-crash fix

metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: no IndexError or successful minimal build alone
preferred_visible_evidence: expected output for Tuple[()] includes explicit parentheses
regression test asserts rendered nodes/string, not only no exception
non-empty tuple formatting remains covered
parallel annotation unparse utilities are considered when present
experimental secondary typing changes are validated or reverted
metadata.stage_boundary: Most relevant once the agent has identified or edited the tuple-unparse branch; less applicable during the first few exploratory steps before any candidate fix exists.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory explicitly preserves `()` for empty tuple annotations, validates rendered output, and avoids or cleans up unrelated regressive typing changes.
scale.2: Minor concern: the agent focuses mostly on no-crash behavior but also mentions or begins verifying explicit empty-tuple rendering and has no clear regressive secondary edits.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory fixes the crash and tests some normal annotations, but visible evidence is ambiguous about whether `Tuple[()]` renders with `()` or whether all annotation rendering paths are covered.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the candidate fix is essentially a guarded `pop()` or equivalent, visible validation accepts `Tuple[]`/empty interior output, and regression tests check absence of exception more than semantic rendering.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory both loses the empty tuple representation and becomes dominated by broad unrelated `typing` changes or leaves existing formatting tests failing, with no reliable evidence that the reported annotation is rendered correctly.

experiences.title: Canonical renamed option plus versioned backend key
experiences.description: Use when a qutebrowser/QtWebEngine dark mode task requires a public config option rename while preserving old user configs and changing only the backend Chromium key by version.
experiences.context: Apply for trajectories working in a Python application with declarative config schema and a version-dispatched backend settings table, especially when a user-facing option is renamed from an old semantic name to a new canonical name while the underlying backend key also changes at a specific dependency version. This is most useful after the agent has inspected or begun editing the config schema, migration/rename mechanism, and per-version dark mode setting definitions. It is less useful during very early repository exploration before the agent has found the config schema or settings mapping, and it should not be generalized to tasks that only require adding a new independent option without backward compatibility or version-dependent backend translation.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases was not merely 'add a Qt 6.4 variant' or 'add a foreground option.' The discriminative issue is whether the implementation treats the new foreground threshold as the single canonical qutebrowser option across all supported QtWebEngine variants, while varying only the emitted Chromium key by version. A strong trajectory should show that pre-6.4 definitions read the new foreground option and emit the old TextBrightnessThreshold key, that 6.4+ definitions read the same foreground option and emit ForegroundBrightnessThreshold, and that the old text option is handled through the repository's config rename/migration mechanism rather than ad hoc runtime fallbacks. Be cautious of tempting but weaker proxies: keeping both old and new options as normal schema entries, mutating config during settings generation, reading the old renamed option at runtime, or adding a fallback that is masked by defaults can look compatible but often fails the intended contract. Prioritize visible evidence from schema snippets, migration investigation, settings-table definitions, version-dispatch smoke tests, and tests or inspections showing the same user option maps to different backend keys on either side of the version boundary.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Canonical foreground option with versioned Chromium key and migration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should establish that the foreground dark-mode threshold is represented as the canonical user-facing option in the config schema, that the old text threshold name is preserved through the project's rename or migration mechanism rather than as a competing runtime option, and that the per-version backend mapping reads this canonical option while emitting TextBrightnessThreshold before QtWebEngine 6.4 and ForegroundBrightnessThreshold for QtWebEngine 6.4 or newer. Evidence should include correct version dispatch, updated variant-indexed mappings beyond just the main settings table where applicable, and validation or tests covering both sides of the 6.4 boundary and the old-name compatibility path.

required_visible_evidence: new canonical foreground threshold option exists with the same integer bounds/restart/backend semantics as the old threshold option
old text threshold name is represented as a rename/migration/alias according to repository conventions, not left as an independent normal option that conflicts with the new option
settings definitions for versions before the backend rename read the canonical foreground option and emit TextBrightnessThreshold
settings definitions for QtWebEngine 6.4 and newer read the canonical foreground option and emit ForegroundBrightnessThreshold
version dispatch selects a distinct 6.4+ mapping without regressing existing 6.3 and older behavior
tests, smoke checks, or inspected output cover foreground threshold mapping on both pre-6.4 and 6.4+ versions
common_failure_evidence: only the 6.4+ variant uses the foreground option while older variants still read the old text option
compatibility is attempted by calling get on an old option after marking it renamed
fallback logic relies on defaults or mutates config state during settings generation
both old and new threshold options remain normal user-visible options without clear precedence
new variant is added without updating all variant-keyed mappings needed by settings generation

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent has connected the public option rename to the version-specific backend key change; changes, if any, are limited to exploration or unrelated dark mode files.
scale.2: Some partial evidence such as finding the dark mode settings table or adding a 6.4+ backend key, but the canonical foreground option, old-name compatibility, or pre-6.4 mapping is missing or unexamined.
scale.3: Moderate progress: the trajectory adds or plans a foreground option and a 6.4+ mapping, but visible evidence still suggests fragile compatibility, duplicated old/new options, or incomplete handling of older variants and repository migration conventions.
scale.4: Strong progress: the trajectory uses the foreground option as the intended canonical setting, adds a version boundary for 6.4+, and investigates the repository rename mechanism; only minor validation gaps or implementation details remain uncertain.
scale.5: Complete visible evidence: the canonical foreground option exists, the old text name is handled via the proper migration/rename mechanism, pre-6.4 emits TextBrightnessThreshold from the canonical option, 6.4+ emits ForegroundBrightnessThreshold from the same option, all relevant variant-indexed mappings are updated, and boundary/compatibility tests or inspected outputs support the behavior.

experiences.title: Oversize-aware semantics for bounded HTTP body helper
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go task introduces a reusable helper such as `utils.ReadAtMost` to limit HTTP request/response body reads, and the trajectory shows or plans the helper implementation.
experiences.context: Applies in Go repositories, especially Teleport-like codebases using `ioutil.ReadAll`, `io.LimitReader`, and `trace` errors, when the security task is to prevent resource exhaustion from unbounded HTTP request or response body reads. The criterion is most useful after the agent has written or described the bounded-read helper, or added tests for it. It is less useful before any helper semantics are visible, and it is not sufficient by itself when the trajectory also shows broken imports, corrupted functions, missing call-site coverage, or broad non-HTTP replacements. Do not apply this criterion to tasks that explicitly require silent truncation, streaming discard behavior, or limits on non-HTTP data where over-limit detection is not part of the contract.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful rubric checked whether `ReadAtMost` actually detects oversized input and returns an error instead of merely wrapping `ReadAll(LimitReader(...))`. This matters because a silent `LimitReader` cap can prevent unbounded allocation while still accepting truncated JSON/XML/error bodies, causing downstream parsing or misleading behavior rather than enforcing the maximum. The best rubric should focus on the helper’s boundary semantics: accepts empty/smaller/exact-limit inputs, rejects input beyond the limit with a clear limit error, and ideally has tests for those boundaries. Visible evidence to prioritize includes the implementation using `io.LimitedReader` state or reading/probing one extra byte, an exported limit error such as a `trace.LimitExceeded` style error, comments matching behavior, and tests that fail on oversized data rather than expecting truncated bytes. Avoid the tempting but weaker criterion of only checking that `ioutil.ReadAll(body)` call sites were mechanically replaced, that a max-size constant exists, or that `io.LimitReader` appears somewhere. Also avoid over-crediting this rubric when the trajectory shows compile-breaking edits or out-of-scope replacements; in that stage, pair it with separate criteria for build validity, preserving existing control flow/status checks, and targeting only HTTP request/response bodies.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Oversize-aware bounded read helper
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement `utils.ReadAtMost` so it enforces the configured maximum as a validation boundary, not just as a truncation wrapper: normal reads below the limit and at the exact limit should succeed, reads beyond the limit should return a clear error without unbounded allocation, and any tests or comments should reflect that contract.

expected_helper_behavior: reads from an io.Reader with bounded memory use
preserves full data for bodies smaller than the limit
handles exact-limit input according to the documented boundary
detects data beyond the allowed limit
returns a recognizable limit/validation error for oversized input
strong_visible_evidence: uses io.LimitedReader state, max-plus-one probing, or an equivalent extra-byte check
does not simply return ReadAll(LimitReader(reader, max)) with nil error on oversized input
has unit tests covering under-limit, exact-limit, over-limit, empty input, and invalid limits if applicable
callers propagate or wrap the limit error rather than parsing truncated bytes
weak_or_misleading_evidence: mechanical replacement of ReadAll calls without inspecting helper semantics
comments claiming over-limit errors while implementation silently truncates
tests that assert oversized input returns truncated data with no error
using a size constant alone without an oversize detection path

scale.1: No visible helper semantics, or the helper plainly performs an unbounded read or silently truncates oversized input while tests/comments do not catch it.
scale.2: A bounded read wrapper exists, but it uses `LimitReader` or similar only to cap bytes and provides little or no evidence that oversized input is detected as an error.
scale.3: The trajectory is comparable to the parent: it recognizes the need for a reusable helper and bounded body reads, but helper semantics are incomplete, untested, or ambiguous at the exact-limit/over-limit boundary.
scale.4: The helper clearly detects oversized input and returns an error while accepting normal inputs, though tests, error type, or boundary handling may still be incomplete.
scale.5: The helper has robust oversize detection without unbounded allocation, clear limit error behavior, correct exact-limit handling, and visible boundary tests that reject oversized input rather than expecting truncation.

experiences.title: Behavior-Preserving Scoped Selector Coverage
experiences.description: Use when a React/TypeScript UI task asks for broad POM or data-testid coverage across conversation/message views and the trajectory is adding or planning selector attributes across many component areas.
experiences.context: Applies in frontend React/TypeScript codebases where the requested change is to add stable UI test selectors to many interactive or content-bearing elements, especially headers, banners, attachments, recipients, dropdown triggers/menu items, and message/conversation containers. This guidance is most useful after the agent has inspected relevant UI components or begun editing selector attributes, because visible evidence can show whether coverage is systematic and whether edits preserve behavior. It is less useful during very early repository discovery before the agent has identified component surfaces, and it should not be applied as a simple count of added data-testid strings when the trajectory shows whole-file rewrites, broad sed replacements, unsupported props on custom components, malformed JSX, or unrelated behavioral changes.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics correctly emphasized that the task is not satisfied by adding a few isolated data-testid attributes: the agent must cover all task-relevant interactive/content-bearing surfaces with uniquely scoped names. This was discriminative when the visible trajectory showed only narrow edits to conversation banners or headers while attachments, recipients, dropdown menu items, message extras, and action buttons remained unaddressed. However, the same broad coverage rubric can be misleading if it rewards a large number of selector additions without checking whether they are placed on rendered DOM elements or supported forwarding components and whether existing behavior is preserved. A better rubric should combine coverage completeness with implementation safety: require evidence of an audit across the named UI surfaces, consistent project-style scoping, direct placement on actual rendered elements or explicitly forwarded props, and absence of collateral rewrites or syntax/type risks. Avoid the tempting proxy of 'many data-testid additions' or 'many files touched'; prioritize visible evidence such as targeted JSX patches, searches for existing naming conventions, careful handling of repeated/dynamic elements, preservation of original component logic, and validation or diff review after edits.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete and Safe Scoped Selector Implementation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show a systematic, behavior-preserving plan or implementation for adding stable, uniquely scoped data-testid attributes across the conversation and message view UI surfaces named by the task. Strong evidence includes auditing existing selector conventions; covering containers, headers, banners, unread/trash/error actions, attachments and attachment actions, sender/recipient details, dropdown triggers and menu items, message extras/banners, and body/footer areas as applicable; using consistent hierarchical names; placing attributes on real rendered DOM elements or components known to forward DOM props; avoiding duplicate or ambiguous IDs; and preserving original JSX, props, logic, imports, lockfiles, and behavior except for selector additions. The judge should penalize trajectories that only add a few selectors, pass data-testid to custom components without forwarding support, rely on CSS classes as substitutes, use broad or whole-file rewrites that risk corruption, or fail to review/validate modified TypeScript/JSX.

required_visible_evidence: Search or inspection of existing data-testid naming conventions
Coverage across all task-mentioned UI categories, not only one component family
Selector attributes added to rendered elements or confirmed prop-forwarding components
Consistent scoped naming that distinguishes repeated conversation/message elements and actions
No unrelated behavioral rewrites, malformed JSX, duplicate attributes, or unsupported prop additions
Diff review or validation when edits are broad or touch many TSX components
common_failure_signals: Only conversation banners or headers are edited while attachments, recipients, dropdowns, or extras are omitted
Large whole-file rewrites or blind sed replacements introduce unrelated code changes
data-testid is passed into local custom components without updating/confirming prop interfaces and forwarding
Counting many selector strings replaces checking whether they are stable, unique, and reachable in the DOM
No validation after syntax-risky JSX edits

scale.1: Little or no progress toward scoped selector coverage, or edits are mainly exploratory/isolated with most required UI surfaces unaddressed.
scale.2: Some relevant data-testid additions are visible, but coverage is narrow, naming is inconsistent or weakly scoped, or several named task areas remain clearly missing.
scale.3: Moderate progress comparable to the parent trajectory: multiple relevant areas are addressed, but evidence is incomplete or there are unresolved risks around unsupported props, duplicate/ambiguous IDs, or unvalidated JSX edits.
scale.4: Strong evidence of systematic selector coverage across most required conversation/message surfaces with consistent names and mostly safe placement, with only minor omissions or validation gaps.
scale.5: Comprehensive, behavior-preserving selector implementation or plan: all named interactive/content-bearing surfaces are covered with consistent unique scoping, attributes are reachable in rendered DOM, existing behavior is preserved, and the trajectory includes review or validation sufficient to catch JSX/type regressions.

experiences.title: Parsed version comparison alone is insufficient for needs_extensions
experiences.description: Use this when a trajectory fixes a minimum-version check by replacing string ordering with a version parser, especially in Sphinx-style extension validation code with existing missing, unknown, or nonstandard-version behavior.
experiences.context: Applies to Python repository tasks where a config value maps extension names to minimum required versions and the visible bug is lexicographic ordering such as accepting/rejecting `0.10` vs `0.6`. A rubric that only asks whether semantic version ordering was introduced can be misleading once the trajectory has already found the right comparison site and added `packaging.version.Version` or another parser. At that stage, the main correctness boundary is whether the old validation contract is preserved: missing extensions remain warnings if that was existing behavior, an explicitly unknown loaded version remains unsatisfied, too-old versions still raise the intended requirement error, and unparsable/nonstandard version strings do not crash or silently pass when the previous code would have compared them as strings. The original semantic-comparison rubric is still appropriate during early exploration or before any implementation exists, but it is too broad for final-review trajectories that show exception handling, fallback logic, or tests around special version values.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster correctly identified the central bug—raw string comparison must be replaced with version-aware ordering so values like `0.10.0` satisfy a `0.6.0` minimum. However, they over-emphasized that necessary condition and did not distinguish implementations that change surrounding failure behavior. In these trajectories, visible evidence such as `except Exception`, `except InvalidVersion`, comments saying unknown versions are skipped, or ad hoc tests claiming `unknown version` passes should trigger a more specific criterion. A better rubric should focus on the control-flow contract around version parsing: the intentional requirement error for too-old versions must not be swallowed by broad exception handling; `unknown version` must be treated as unable to satisfy a stated minimum rather than continued past; parser failures should be narrowly handled and should fall back to the prior string comparison behavior rather than silently accepting or crashing; and the chosen parser should match available project dependencies and avoid deprecated alternatives when the codebase already uses a modern parser. Avoid generating a tempting criterion that gives high credit merely for importing a version parser or demonstrating `Version('0.10') > Version('0.6')` in scratch tests. Prioritize visible implementation evidence in the edited validation function and tests that cover newer numeric versions, genuinely older versions, unknown versions, and unparsable versions.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory is flawed if, after introducing parsed/version-aware comparison for an extension minimum-version check, it visibly weakens the existing validation contract around special cases: unknown loaded versions are skipped or accepted, the intended too-old-version requirement error can be caught by broad parser exception handling, parser failures are not narrowly limited to invalid version inputs, or nonstandard version strings lose the previous fallback comparison behavior. This criterion should be applied at implementation/final-review stage, not during initial search before the agent has edited the version-checking logic.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Broken failure-path preservation around parsed version checks

metadata.environment: Python/Sphinx-style extension validation using a config mapping of extension names to minimum versions
primary_visible_evidence: edited minimum-version validation code
exception handling around version parser calls
handling of explicit unknown-version sentinel
fallback behavior for invalid or nonstandard version strings
tests or ad hoc checks for too-old, unknown, and invalid versions
avoid_overweighting: presence of a version parser import alone
scratch proof that numeric version ordering works for only the reported example
passing tests that do not exercise unknown or invalid-version paths

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory preserves the prior missing/unknown/too-old behavior, uses version-aware ordering for valid versions, and narrowly handles parser invalid-version failures with an appropriate fallback.
scale.2: Minor concern only: the main control flow appears safe, but visible tests or explanation omit one special case such as invalid-version fallback while not showing code that accepts it incorrectly.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory implements semantic comparison but the visible code or reasoning is ambiguous about whether unknown or unparsable versions still fail/fallback correctly.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory shows one broken failure path, such as continuing past an unknown loaded version, using broad exception handling that risks swallowing the intended requirement error, or omitting fallback for invalid version strings.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory both relies on parsed comparison and visibly changes multiple validation semantics, such as accepting unknown versions and catching all exceptions around the comparison/raise block, making too-old or unparsable versions likely to pass incorrectly.

experiences.title: Subsonic Share Endpoints Require Existing Share Service Integration
experiences.description: Use when evaluating a Go/Navidrome trajectory for adding missing Subsonic share endpoints, especially when endpoints are currently h501 stubs and the codebase already has core/public share infrastructure.
experiences.context: Applies to Navidrome-like Go repositories where Subsonic API routes are centralized in server/subsonic/api.go, responses are modeled in server/subsonic/responses, and share functionality already exists in model/core/persistence/public layers. This experience is most useful after the trajectory has either gathered enough evidence about the share architecture or started editing routes/handlers. It is also useful when the agent is stuck repeating greps that only rediscover h501 stubs. It is less useful for unrelated endpoint work, for projects without preexisting share service/public URL infrastructure, or at a very early exploration point where the agent has not yet inspected routing, response structs, and share service/repository boundaries.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics correctly looked for real Subsonic share endpoint work rather than accepting repeated searches or route-only changes, but they were too broad when they demanded all four get/create/update/delete endpoints as the central success condition. In this task family, the more discriminative criterion is whether the trajectory is converging on a thin Subsonic adapter over the existing share subsystem: replacing the relevant h501 stubs, adding Subsonic Shares/Share response payloads with correct XML/JSON tags, parsing the Subsonic parameters for creating/listing shares, using the existing core/rest share repository path, and generating public share URLs through the existing public share URL helper rather than inventing URLs. Visible warning signs include repeated identical greps with no implementation, adding CRUD methods to the model interface just to satisfy new handler code, direct ad hoc ShareRepository.Get/Save/Delete assumptions, hand-built /share or /public URLs from config, requiring non-Subsonic parameters like resourceType/resourceIds, or implementing update/delete while still missing the create/list behavior requested by the task. A better rubric should prioritize evidence that the agent has inspected and reused core/share.go, persistence rest interfaces, public share URL helpers, and Subsonic response conventions. Avoid using 'all four endpoints implemented' as the sole proxy: it can reward superficial or incompatible handlers and may overstate update/delete when the task wording emphasizes create and retrieve.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Existing Share Service Adapter
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show that the Subsonic share work is being implemented as a compatible adapter over the repository's existing share infrastructure: replacing h501 behavior for the required share endpoints, adding a Subsonic shares response shape, parsing expected create/list request parameters, saving/loading shares through the existing core/rest share path rather than widening model interfaces ad hoc, and returning public share URLs using existing public URL helpers. Judge from visible trajectory evidence such as inspected files, route edits, handler code, response structs, build/test results, and whether implementation choices align with existing service boundaries.

positive_evidence: share endpoints removed from h501 and registered with normal Subsonic handler wrappers
responses.Subsonic gains a shares payload with Share/Shares structs following existing XML/JSON conventions
create/list handlers use id, description, expires-style parameters consistent with Subsonic behavior
handlers use existing core share service or rest.Persistable/rest.Repository capabilities instead of inventing new repository interface methods
share responses include public URLs generated through existing public share URL logic
build or targeted tests validate route/handler/response compilation
negative_evidence: trajectory repeats grep/search commands after confirming only h501 stubs exist
route wiring is malformed or handlers remain unregistered
implementation adds Get/Save/Update/Delete to the model share interface solely for new handlers
handlers handcraft public URLs from config/request instead of using existing public share helpers
handlers require resourceType/resourceIds or other nonstandard parameters while ignoring repeated id parameters
response fields/tags do not match the repository's Subsonic response style
work focuses on update/delete breadth while create/list and public URL behavior remain incomplete

scale.1: No implementation progress beyond confirming h501 stubs or repeating searches; no route, response, or handler changes.
scale.2: Some planning or partial edits exist, but key integration points are missing, such as response structs, valid route registration, or use of existing share infrastructure.
scale.3: Comparable to the parent trajectory: identifies the missing routes and relevant files or makes partial implementation attempts, but still relies on uncertain repository assumptions, lacks public URL/service integration, or has unvalidated compile issues.
scale.4: Strong evidence of a working Subsonic adapter: routes, response structs, create/list handlers, existing share service/rest persistence, and public URL generation are mostly aligned, with only minor validation or polish gaps.
scale.5: Complete, validated implementation evidence: required share endpoints no longer return h501, handlers follow Subsonic parameter/response conventions, use existing core/public share infrastructure cleanly, avoid interface hacks, and build/tests or snapshots confirm XML/JSON behavior.

experiences.title: Do not treat an IfNoMatch call as sufficient OCI local-refresh evidence
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for a Go/Flipt storage task where a new OCI-backed filesystem source is being added and the trajectory visibly adds `IfNoMatch` or digest tracking in the new source. The warning is that source-level conditional fetch is only one subrequirement and can mask missing local OCI cache refresh, context-aware interface migration, and snapshot semantics.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go repository with filesystem storage sources, a lower-level OCI fetch package, and a `SnapshotSource`-style interface. The misleading case is a trajectory that appears to satisfy the task by tracking a digest and passing it to `Fetch(... IfNoMatch(...))` in a new OCI source, while other visible evidence shows unresolved integration problems: the local OCI target may still be cached across fetches, `Get` may not accept or propagate context as required by the interface, unchanged fetches may return nil/error instead of preserving the current snapshot, existing local/git/s3 sources or the store interface may not be updated consistently, or the server storage switch/imports are still corrupted. The original IfNoMatch idea remains appropriate as a narrow positive subcriterion only after the trajectory has also addressed the underlying local reread mechanism and source/store compatibility.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded the presence of `IfNoMatch` and digest tracking as though that predicted correctness. That criterion is directionally related to the requirement, but it is too shallow for this task: a call to `IfNoMatch` in the new source does not by itself guarantee that externally modified local OCI layouts are reread, especially when the lower-level OCI store keeps a persistent target/cache. It also does not catch broken `SnapshotSource` signatures, nil snapshots on unchanged content, bad subscription behavior, or mangled runtime wiring. A better rubric should focus on the full refresh contract visible in the trajectory: whether the lower-level local OCI fetch path recreates or reopens the local target on each fetch before resolving descriptors/files; whether the new OCI source caches both digest and last snapshot and returns the existing snapshot when the digest matches; whether `Get(ctx)` and `Subscribe(ctx, ch)` match the context-aware interface and are propagated through existing sources/store; and whether the storage type is wired without breaking local/object/database cases. Avoid generating a standalone positive rubric that only asks whether `IfNoMatch` is used. If a replacement criterion mentions `IfNoMatch`, make it conditional on the surrounding evidence that local target caching is handled and unchanged results preserve a usable snapshot.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory treats source-level digest tracking or an `IfNoMatch` option as the main OCI refresh solution while leaving visible gaps in the actual storage contract: no evidence that the lower-level local OCI fetch target is recreated/reopened to avoid stale cached local layout data; no consistent context-aware `Get(ctx)` interface across the store and existing filesystem sources; unchanged fetches return nil or an error instead of the prior snapshot; or the server storage switch/imports remain structurally broken. This flaw is especially important when the task requires local OCI sources to reflect external process changes automatically.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Source-level IfNoMatch masks incomplete OCI refresh contract

metadata.misleading_positive_proxy: new source calls Fetch with IfNoMatch or stores a digest
higher_priority_evidence: local OCI backend does not reuse a stale cached target for repeated fetches
SnapshotSource/Get signature is context-aware and consistent across store and existing sources
matched digest returns the current snapshot rather than nil/error for initial/store refresh paths
subscription sends only real updates while preserving current state
runtime storage switch wires OCI without corrupting neighboring storage cases

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory couples conditional fetch with a cache-aware local OCI reread path, preserves snapshots on matches, and keeps the context-aware source/store interface coherent.
scale.2: Minor concern: `IfNoMatch` is emphasized, but visible code or plans also mostly address local target refresh and interface compatibility, with only small unresolved details.
scale.3: Moderate concern: digest tracking is implemented, but the trajectory has incomplete or ambiguous evidence for local target recreation, prior-snapshot preservation, or context propagation.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory uses `IfNoMatch` in the new source but visibly leaves key contract gaps such as non-context `Get`, nil/error on matched digest, or no lower-level local OCI cache refresh.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory appears to rely almost entirely on `IfNoMatch` while runtime wiring or interface compatibility is broken and there is no credible mechanism for externally changed local OCI layouts to be reread.

experiences.title: Centralized Full Verification Status Card
experiences.description: Use when a React/TypeScript device-settings task asks to fix duplicated or missing verified/unverified session status copy between Current Session and Device Details.
experiences.context: Applies when the visible trajectory has identified a current-session view that builds verified/unverified status card props inline, a device-details view that lacks the full status header/description, an existing security-card presentation component, and device data that already includes verification state. It is most useful once the agent is designing or reviewing an implementation, not during very early repository exploration. Do not apply broadly to unrelated verification UIs, right-panel device trust displays, or short device-list labels such as plain “Verified”/“Unverified” unless the task explicitly requires changing those full header/description views too.
experiences.experience: For this task shape, the strongest rubric should not merely ask whether Device Details now shows some status text. It should require a single shared source for the full status card mapping: verified/unverified variation, localized heading, localized description, and the existing card presentation. Rubrics that focused on unified rendering/copy were useful because weak trajectories often added another hard-coded Device Details block while leaving the current-session inline mapping in place. However, a rubric saying only “reuse the security card” is too weak, because duplicated prop construction can still use the same card component. A rubric that demands every device-related component, including summary tiles, use the same full status component is too broad; tiles may intentionally use short labels. Also avoid making “no status appears twice when expanded” the central criterion: the task is about consistent required locations and shared implementation, not necessarily eliminating every visual occurrence in a composed current-session/detail view. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent removed or plans to remove inline verified/unverified copy from the current-session component, introduced a reusable status-card component/helper, rendered that same unit in Device Details near the details header before metadata, preserved localization and verification-state typing, and limited changes to the relevant settings-device UI.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Single Source for Full Device Verification Status
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement the full verified/unverified session status as one reusable, localized status-card source and use it in both the current-session view and the expanded device-details view. The shared unit should own the mapping from verification state to visual variation, heading, and description; the current-session view should stop constructing duplicate inline status props; Device Details should receive device data with verification state and render the same status card in a consistent, prominent location near the device heading before metadata. The implementation should preserve existing short summary labels and avoid unrelated verification UI rewrites.

metadata.environment: React/TypeScript settings-device UI
key_visible_evidence: current-session component originally has inline verified/unverified heading and description mapping
device-details component originally lacks the full verification status card
existing reusable security-card presentation component is available
device model includes nullable or boolean verification state
trajectory shows implementation or concrete plan for shared status-card source used by both relevant views
avoid_as_primary_criteria: only checking that Device Details contains any status text
only checking that the existing card component is used somewhere
requiring short DeviceTile summary labels to use the full header/description card
penalizing solely because composed current-session and details areas can each show a status card

scale.1: No meaningful implementation evidence beyond exploration, or the trajectory changes unrelated verification/device areas without addressing the current-session and device-details full status mismatch.
scale.2: Adds or plans to add status text/card to only one relevant view, or adds a new hard-coded Device Details block while leaving the current-session verified/unverified copy duplicated inline.
scale.3: Both Current Session and Device Details would show similar full status copy, but the mapping/presentation remains duplicated or ad hoc, placement is inconsistent, or verification-state typing/localization is only partially handled.
scale.4: Introduces a shared component/helper for the full status card and uses it in the main relevant views with localized verified/unverified headings and descriptions, but has minor omissions such as uncertain exact placement, incomplete validation/test updates, or small style/layout follow-through gaps.
scale.5: Clearly centralizes the full status-card mapping and presentation, replaces the current-session inline mapping with that shared unit, renders the same unit in Device Details near the header before metadata, handles verified and non-verified states consistently with localization, preserves unrelated short device-list status behavior, and validates or updates focused tests/snapshots/styles when the trajectory reveals they are affected.

experiences.title: Non-bookseller bypass for source-scoped year cutoffs
experiences.description: Retrieve when an import/validation task changes a formerly global publication-year cutoff so it applies only to a named source subset, especially when existing ISBN/source rules already identify that subset.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Open Library-style catalog import flow where records carry source identifiers such as source_records, publication-year validation currently uses a global minimum, and the task explicitly says only selected bookseller sources such as Amazon/BWB should be subject to the too-old cutoff while archival/other sources bypass it. This is most useful once the trajectory has found or edited the year helper, record validation call site, exception message, tests, or existing source-specific ISBN logic. It may be premature during very early repository exploration with no validation path found. Do not apply this criterion to tasks where non-selected sources are meant to retain a default minimum year, where the requirement is only to change a numeric threshold globally, or where the cutoff applies to all sources with different thresholds.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in this cluster is not merely “make validation source-aware.” The discriminating boundary is that non-Amazon/BWB records must not be rejected by the too-old publication-year rule at all. Several trajectories added a 1400 branch for Amazon/BWB but left the old 1500 check for IA, unknown, or no-source records; tests still passed when they only exercised the old helper behavior, but the implementation violated the task. A better rubric should require visible evidence that the helper/record validation returns no too-old rejection unless the record has one of the selected bookseller source prefixes, and that the 1400 threshold is only used inside that selected-source branch. It should also value reusing a public shared source constant for both ISBN requirements and year validation, because duplicating or renaming separate Amazon/BWB lists risks divergence. Avoid the tempting but wrong criterion that “Amazon/BWB use 1400 while all other sources use 1500,” and avoid over-crediting source extraction that checks only the first source_record if the existing pattern checks any source record. Prioritize visible evidence from code snippets, diffs, manual checks, and tests showing: Amazon/BWB 1399 rejected and 1400 accepted; IA/archival/other/no-source historical years accepted with respect to the too-old rule; future-year validation remains independent; the exception message reports the active 1400 threshold only when the cutoff actually applies; and ISBN source rules use the same centralized source set.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Selected-source-only too-old year validation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement and validate publication-year logic so the too-old cutoff is active only for records whose source identifiers are in the selected bookseller set, using a 1400 minimum there, while all other sources bypass the too-old minimum entirely. Strong evidence includes centralized public source constants shared with existing ISBN/source validation, record-level source detection that considers source_records consistently with existing source rules, record validation that raises the too-old error only for selected-source records below 1400, error text that reports the active 1400 threshold when raised, and tests or manual checks covering selected sources, archival sources, other/unknown sources, and future-year behavior.

required_semantics: Amazon/BWB or equivalent selected bookseller sources below 1400 are rejected by the too-old rule
Selected bookseller sources at or above 1400 are not rejected by the too-old rule
IA, archival, other, unknown, or absent source records are not rejected solely for being before 1400 or 1500
Future-year validation remains separate and still applies
The source set used for year validation is centralized and reused by related ISBN/source validation
high_value_visible_evidence: helper returns false/no error for non-selected sources regardless of historical year
record validation passes the whole record or all relevant source_records to the helper
tests include non-selected historical records that would have failed under the old global cutoff
tests include selected-source boundary cases around 1399 and 1400
error message derives from the active selected-source threshold rather than a stale global constant
metadata.common_wrong_proxy: A source-aware branch that gives Amazon/BWB a 1400 threshold but keeps the old 1500 cutoff for all other sources.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of source-scoped publication-year validation, or the trajectory preserves the old global cutoff for all records.
scale.2: Mentions or partially adds Amazon/BWB-specific thresholding, but visible logic still applies a default too-old cutoff to IA/other/non-selected sources or duplicates source rules without integration.
scale.3: Implements some source-aware behavior but evidence is incomplete: selected-source cutoff may work, yet non-selected bypass, shared constants, error messaging, or tests are missing or ambiguous.
scale.4: Clear implementation evidence that selected sources use a 1400 cutoff and non-selected sources bypass the too-old rule, with mostly centralized source rules and some relevant tests or manual checks.
scale.5: Strong end-to-end evidence: centralized shared source constants, robust source_records detection, selected-source 1399/1400 boundary behavior, IA/other/no-source historical bypass, preserved future-year validation, correct active-threshold message, and tests covering these boundaries.

experiences.title: Avoid overcrediting exact delimiter overfits in metadata parsers
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for Python/Open Library-style import tasks where a sample metadata string uses delimiters such as semicolons and colons, and the trajectory is likely to patch a shared parser by matching only the example format.
experiences.context: This warning applies when the visible task is about splitting imported bibliographic metadata into structured fields, especially IA publisher/place strings, and the trajectory has found a shared parser used by an import endpoint. The misleading rubric pattern is to require only that `Place ; Place ; Place : Publisher` become one publisher plus three places. That criterion is too narrow when the parser is shared and the input domain visibly includes IA metadata rather than a single hard-coded shape; an implementation can satisfy the reproduced example while still depending on exact spacing, only handling one pre-colon location segment, failing mixed semicolon/colon publisher-place fragments, or not proving endpoint-level assignment. The original exact-example criterion is still reasonable as one regression case when the trajectory is early in investigation or when the problem statement explicitly restricts the accepted input grammar to that one canonical format. It should not be the main correctness rubric once the trajectory is editing parser logic or claiming a final fix.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics correctly noticed the core symptom—semicolon-separated locations before a colon must not remain in `publishers`—but they turned the sample string into the whole contract. This led to judging a simple change like “split the pre-colon text on `;` after splitting on exact ` : `” as sufficient. For import metadata parsers, generate criteria that distinguish a robust parsing contract from an example-specific patch. A better rubric should look for visible evidence that the solution defines a general location/publisher parser for IA metadata, trims whitespace and surrounding punctuation, preserves publisher-only and single-location behavior, handles semicolon-separated parts in order, tolerates realistic colon/semicolon combinations rather than only exact spaced delimiters, and verifies that the import path writes the returned lists into the correct structured fields. Avoid a tempting criterion that says the trajectory is good merely because the exact reported string prints the expected tuple. Prioritize evidence from parser tests or endpoint-level checks covering the representative grammar and compatibility fallbacks, plus code structure that does not mutate the old helper in a brittle way.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Example-only delimiter parsing
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat the reported IA publisher string as the entire parsing contract: they only split the text before an exact colon delimiter on semicolons, or only demonstrate the single sample case, without visible evidence of a robust import parser that handles realistic semicolon/colon publisher-place metadata, trims tokens safely, preserves no-place and single-place fallbacks, and verifies the endpoint/import record receives separate publisher and place lists.

metadata.environment: Python bibliographic import code using a shared parser called by an IA import endpoint
metadata.misleading_positive_proxy: Exact sample string produces the expected publisher and place tuple
preferred_evidence: parser logic handles semicolon-separated ordered location segments and colon-separated publisher segments beyond one exact spacing pattern
tokens are stripped of whitespace and common surrounding punctuation without keeping empty values
publisher-only, single-place, and existing list/string inputs remain compatible where applicable
import-level construction assigns parsed locations to publish-place fields and parsed names to publisher fields
tests or live checks cover both the reported regression and compatibility cases
metadata.anti_pattern: Replacing one append with a simple pre-colon semicolon split and relying only on the reproduced example

scale.1: No evidence of the overfit: the trajectory designs or verifies a general parser and endpoint assignment while preserving compatibility cases.
scale.2: Minor risk: the trajectory emphasizes the sample string but also includes some broader trimming, fallback, or endpoint-level compatibility evidence.
scale.3: Moderate risk: the trajectory fixes the reported sample and a single existing case, but the visible code or tests still rely on exact delimiter spacing or do not exercise realistic semicolon/colon variants.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the implementation is a narrow pre-colon semicolon split with little or no endpoint-level verification and limited compatibility coverage.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory only hard-codes or demonstrates the exact reported string, ignores parser grammar/fallbacks, or risks misassigning publishers and places in the import path.

experiences.title: Do not treat legacy backend wiring as sufficient for an explicit exporter config contract
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go/Viper configuration task asks to add a user-facing exporter option, but the existing code uses an older or different key such as backend and the trajectory mostly extends that legacy path.
experiences.context: Applies in Go services with typed configuration, enum decode hooks, generated or static schemas, default YAML, and runtime exporter initialization. The misleading pattern is a trajectory that adds an OTLP enum/config struct/default endpoint and runtime exporter case under the existing backend field, sometimes with passing build/config tests, while the task explicitly says users configure tracing.exporter and validation should accept that key. The original idea of checking OTLP endpoint defaults and runtime initialization is still useful when the repository’s public contract truly remains backend or when the task explicitly allows either spelling; it is incomplete when the task names a new public key or when schema/deprecation/default config evidence suggests a naming migration is part of the fix.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics overemphasized endpoint defaulting, adding otlp to the enum map, and creating the OTLP gRPC exporter. Those are necessary but can be misleadingly optimistic when visible trajectory evidence shows the agent is preserving the old backend terminology despite an explicit exporter requirement. In this situation, a better rubric should focus on whether the user-facing configuration contract is wired end to end: the config struct tags/default keys, decode hooks, schema/default files, deprecation guidance, tests/fixtures, and runtime switch should all agree on accepting the requested exporter key and preserving the default exporter behavior. Avoid a tempting criterion that says “backend/exporter” interchangeably or accepts adding otlp to the existing backend enum as configuration completeness. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent investigated and updated all validation surfaces for the exact public config key requested, and penalize trajectories that only make legacy backend configs pass while leaving tracing.exporter unsupported or undocumented.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Legacy Key-Only OTLP Support
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for a tracing exporter task when visible evidence shows they add OTLP support only to the pre-existing backend field or enum while failing to wire the explicitly requested exporter configuration key through decoding, defaults, validation schema, and user-facing examples. This is especially severe when the agent notices the terminology mismatch but decides to preserve backend without verifying that tracing.exporter is accepted.

metadata.environment: Go service using Viper/mapstructure-style configuration, enum string decode hooks, static or generated config schema, and OpenTelemetry tracing exporters
failure_cues: OTLP is added to TracingBackend or a backend string map, but no corresponding exporter field/key/default/decode path is added
fixtures or schema examples continue to use tracing.backend while the task reproduction uses tracing.exporter
tests exercise only backend: otlp or enum stringification rather than loading exporter: otlp
trajectory treats backend/exporter as interchangeable without validating the user-facing key named in the task
metadata.boundary: Do not apply when the task explicitly allows the existing backend key as the public API or when the trajectory demonstrates compatibility for both names and updates validation/documentation consistently.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory clearly validates the requested exporter key end to end or explains that the repository intentionally aliases it to the existing key.
scale.2: Minor risk: the trajectory mostly updates the requested exporter path but leaves one non-critical user-facing surface, such as an example or comment, unclear.
scale.3: Moderate issue: OTLP config/runtime support is implemented, but visible tests or schema updates only partially demonstrate that the requested exporter key is accepted.
scale.4: Clear issue: the trajectory implements OTLP under the legacy backend key and updates some validation/tests there, while the requested exporter key remains unverified or likely unsupported.
scale.5: Severe issue: the trajectory explicitly chooses to keep only backend terminology, builds/tests only that path, and leaves schema/defaults/deprecation guidance or decode hooks inconsistent with the requested exporter configuration contract.

experiences.title: Delimiter-aware start-of-buffer rubout semantics
experiences.description: Use when a trajectory is fixing a readline-style backward word/filename deletion bug where the first character is left behind if no delimiter precedes the cursor.
experiences.context: Applies to qutebrowser/PyQt readline command trajectories after the agent has identified or edited the shared rubout/backward deletion helper and visible evidence includes delimiter-scanning logic, manual Qt/offscreen reproductions, or existing readline tests. The key semantic boundary is a deletion scan that can stop either because it found a delimiter or because it reached the beginning of the input. This guidance is most useful during implementation or final review, not during pure repository exploration before the relevant helper has been located. It may be irrelevant for tasks about unrelated cursor movement, command registration, prompt bindings, or deletion commands that do not use delimiter-bounded backward selection.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster focused on the exact behavioral contract: when no delimiter exists before the cursor, rubout must delete the entire preceding word/segment including character 0; when a delimiter is found, including at index 0, the delimiter must remain. This was discriminative because many trajectories recognized the off-by-one but some fixes used tempting proxies such as always dropping the `- 1`, checking only `target_position > 0`, or treating all `target_position == 0` cases alike. Those proxies can fix `hello| -> |` while breaking ` hello| ->  |` or `hello world| -> hello |`. A better rubric should require visible evidence that the trajectory distinguishes “reached start without finding a delimiter” from “found a delimiter at the start,” and that it validates both normal word delimiters and filename/path delimiters. Prioritize evidence from targeted examples such as no-delimiter single words, delimiter-prefixed inputs, internal-space inputs, and filename/path-component inputs. Avoid judging success from a generic statement that an off-by-one was fixed, from a single passing no-delimiter reproduction, or from tests whose expected filename behavior ignores that path separators are delimiters.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement and validate delimiter-bounded backward rubout semantics in the shared readline deletion helper: it must delete through the first character when the backward scan reaches the beginning without encountering a delimiter, but must preserve an actual delimiter boundary when one is encountered, including a delimiter at position 0. The evidence should cover both ordinary word delimiters and filename/path delimiters, and should not rely on a simplistic movement calculation that treats all start-of-buffer cases the same.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Delimiter-aware start boundary handling

required_behavior: No-delimiter input before the cursor is fully deleted, including character 0.
Delimiter-prefixed input keeps the leading delimiter and deletes only the following word/segment.
Input with an internal delimiter keeps text through the delimiter before the deleted segment.
Filename/path rubout respects path separators as delimiters rather than deleting across them.
visible_evidence: Reasoning or code distinguishes scan termination due to start-of-buffer from scan termination due to a found delimiter.
Targeted reproduction or tests include examples analogous to `hello|`, ` hello|`, `hello world|`, and single-component versus slash-separated filename inputs.
Patch is localized to shared rubout selection/movement arithmetic rather than unrelated command registration or prompt binding.
anti_patterns: Always removing the existing delimiter-exclusion offset.
Checking only whether the computed target position is greater than zero.
Treating any target position at zero as no delimiter found.
Using filename tests with expectations that ignore separator boundaries.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses the delimiter-bounded rubout helper or the start-of-buffer first-character bug.
scale.2: Identifies or partially changes the off-by-one behavior, but only demonstrates the no-delimiter case or uses a broad calculation likely to delete delimiters.
scale.3: Shows comparable parent-level behavior: recognizes the start-of-buffer issue and attempts a fix, but evidence is incomplete or ambiguous for delimiter-at-start/path-separator preservation.
scale.4: Strong evidence that the fix distinguishes no-delimiter start-of-buffer from found-delimiter cases and validates ordinary delimiter-present and delimiter-absent examples.
scale.5: Complete evidence that both normal and filename rubout paths share the corrected semantics, with targeted validation covering no delimiter, leading delimiter, internal delimiter, and path-separator cases, while avoiding unrelated behavior changes.

experiences.title: Explicit Widget Kwarg Precedence in Django Admin M2M Hooks
experiences.description: Use when a Django admin task concerns making a many-to-many formfield hook honor a caller-supplied widget like the corresponding foreign-key hook.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Django admin trajectories where the problem statement or investigation compares many-to-many and foreign-key formfield behavior, and visible code exploration shows admin-specific widget selection for many-to-many fields such as autocomplete, raw ID, or filtered select. The criterion is most useful once the agent has inspected the relevant admin hook or proposed a patch; it can still guide early evaluation if the agent has identified that explicit kwargs should take precedence over framework defaults. Do not apply it as the main rubric for unrelated widget customization issues, for generic form rendering bugs, or where the trajectory has not reached the admin formfield code path. Also avoid treating a plain many-to-many field with no admin widget configuration as sufficient evidence, because that case may already preserve a custom widget without exercising the reported bug.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged the semantic contract rather than superficial testing activity: an explicitly supplied `widget` kwarg must not be overwritten by many-to-many admin widget selection, while existing default widgets must still be chosen when no override is supplied. This aligned well because the decisive visible evidence was the agent comparing the many-to-many hook to the foreign-key hook, noticing the missing `widget`-presence guard, and either adding or planning a guard around the branches that assign autocomplete, raw-ID, and filter-horizontal/filter-vertical widgets. A better rubric should specifically require coverage of the configured admin branches that overwrite widgets; merely checking that a custom widget works for an unconfigured many-to-many field is a tempting but weak proxy because it does not reproduce the bug.
