Do not make the criterion primarily about installing dependencies, using a particular test runner, or matching an exact refactoring shape; per-branch guards and an outer guard can both satisfy the behavior if they preserve precedence and defaults. Prioritize visible evidence such as the diff around admin widget assignment, reproduction results showing custom widgets are preserved under admin options, and confirmation that default admin widgets remain intact when no widget kwarg is provided.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the many-to-many admin formfield path preserves an explicitly supplied `widget` kwarg across all admin-specific widget-selection branches, matching the foreign-key hook's precedence semantics, while leaving existing automatic widget selection unchanged when no custom widget is supplied.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Many-to-Many Admin Widget Kwarg Precedence

required_visible_evidence: The agent identifies that the foreign-key formfield path only assigns admin widgets when no explicit widget is present.
The agent identifies that many-to-many admin options such as autocomplete, raw ID, and filtered select can overwrite an explicit widget.
The proposed or applied change prevents admin widget assignment from replacing an existing widget kwarg.
The trajectory preserves default admin widget behavior for cases without an explicit widget.
non_sufficient_evidence: Only testing a plain many-to-many field with no admin widget configuration.
Only running broad tests without inspecting or changing widget precedence.
Changing unrelated formfield behavior or removing admin widget selection entirely.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory recognizes or addresses explicit widget precedence in the many-to-many admin formfield path.
scale.2: Weak evidence of investigating widget override behavior, but the trajectory only checks unconfigured fields or proposes a generic change that may not affect admin widget-selection branches.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies the mismatch with the foreign-key path and attempts to preserve explicit widgets, but coverage of all configured many-to-many widget branches or default behavior is incomplete.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory changes or clearly plans to guard many-to-many admin widget assignment when a widget kwarg exists and verifies at least one overwriting admin configuration plus default behavior.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory explicitly handles autocomplete, raw-ID, and filtered-select many-to-many branches, preserves custom widget kwargs in those cases, and confirms existing default widgets still appear when no override is supplied.

experiences.title: Do not equate missing BSD uptime with adding new collectors before validating sysctl parsing
experiences.description: Retrieve when an Ansible facts task involves BSD uptime, `kern.boottime`, and platform hardware collectors, especially when the trajectory has only grepped for missing `uptime` in one BSD file and has not validated the sysctl output/parsing path.
experiences.context: Applies in Ansible/Python fact-gathering fixes where BSD uptime is exposed through hardware facts and `sysctl` helpers. The misleading pattern is to generate a rubric requiring implementation of `uptime_seconds` for FreeBSD, NetBSD, DragonFly, or all BSD variants solely because some platform files lack a `get_uptime_facts()` method, while visible evidence also shows an existing BSD uptime implementation, a shared `get_sysctl` parser, and uncertainty about the actual `kern.boottime` output format. A direct collector-addition rubric can still be appropriate if the trajectory has confirmed the reported target platform truly has no uptime path and the shared sysctl parser already handles the relevant output format; it is not appropriate when the cutoff evidence points to an unverified sysctl parsing/format problem or when broadening to other BSD variants is speculative.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often rewarded adding `get_uptime_facts()` to FreeBSD or multiple BSD hardware collectors using `get_sysctl(['kern'])` and regex parsing of `kern.boottime`. That is tempting because greps show Linux/OpenBSD have uptime and FreeBSD/NetBSD often do not. The flaw is that this criterion can overvalue patches that add new platform code while missing the shared failure mode: BSD boot-time values may be structured or multiline, existing `get_sysctl` parsing may drop or misparse them, and an existing BSD implementation may need a safer direct `sysctl -n kern.boottime` call or parser hardening. Better rubrics should focus on visible evidence that the agent verified the actual boot-time source and its output shape, checked whether the shared sysctl helper can parse that output without silently failing, preserved existing hardware fact behavior, and avoided speculative expansion to unrelated BSD variants. Avoid criteria that require 'all BSD variants' or 'FreeBSD and NetBSD parity' unless the task and investigation explicitly establish those platforms as affected and supported by the same format.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Speculative BSD collector implementation without sysctl parser validation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that turn a BSD uptime facts issue into adding new `uptime_seconds` methods across FreeBSD/NetBSD/DragonFly or copying an existing BSD implementation without first validating the actual `kern.boottime` command output and whether the shared sysctl parsing helper preserves that value. This flaw is especially severe when visible evidence shows an existing BSD uptime path and a shared `get_sysctl` parser whose splitting/multiline behavior has not been tested.

metadata.environment: Ansible Python fact-gathering code under platform hardware collectors and shared sysctl utilities
metadata.misleading_proxy: absence of `uptime` grep hits in one BSD hardware file or presence of `kern.boottime` in another file
preferred_evidence: inspection or test of `kern.boottime` output format for the relevant BSD platform
assessment of whether shared sysctl parsing handles structured or multiline values
use of a guarded direct boot-time command or parser fix when bulk sysctl parsing is unreliable
limited scope matching the reported platform rather than speculative changes to unrelated BSD variants
preservation of existing CPU, memory, device, mount, and DMI fact behavior

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory validates the boot-time source/output and the sysctl parsing path before choosing a narrowly scoped implementation or parser fix.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory leans toward adding platform uptime code but also recognizes parser/output-format uncertainty and plans validation.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies BSD hardware collectors and `kern.boottime` but treats direct collector changes and parser validation as roughly interchangeable without resolving which is needed.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory proposes or implements direct FreeBSD/NetBSD/DragonFly uptime methods based mainly on grep comparisons, with little or no validation of `kern.boottime` parsing or shared helper behavior.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory broadly modifies unrelated BSD collectors or existing hardware fact logic while relying on unverified `kern.boottime` assumptions and ignoring signs that a shared sysctl parser or existing BSD uptime path is the relevant failure point.

experiences.title: Do not reward superficial header feature wiring without optional-room and true-toggle checks
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a React/TypeScript room-header UI change that adds avatar, topic preview, and click-to-room-summary behavior, especially after the trajectory has already found the header component, topic hook, avatar components, and right-panel store.
experiences.context: This warning applies in Element/Matrix-style React TypeScript code where the compact room header accepts an optional room and optional out-of-band room data, and the right panel is controlled by a phase-based store. The misleading pattern is a rubric that restates the visible feature request—avatar, name, optional topic, header click opens Room Summary—or prescribes only a store call sequence, then treats the presence of those elements as strong evidence. That is not enough once the trajectory shows implementation work, lint/test failures, or code snippets involving optional room handling, hooks, avatars, or right-panel state. A broad feature-completeness checklist can still be appropriate during very early exploration before any patch exists, and right-panel navigation remains a valid criterion when judged semantically. But after code is visible, the rubric should focus on the high-risk integration contracts rather than just whether an onClick, topic div, and avatar component were added.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often said the implementation must show avatar/name/topic and make the header click open Room Summary, or that the handler must call the right-panel store with the Room Summary phase when opening and toggle when closing. Those criteria are directionally related to the task but become misleading because flawed patches can satisfy them superficially while still breaking important visible contracts. In this setting, the better rubric should check whether the header still works when no room object is available but out-of-band data is present; whether any topic hook is called in a React-hooks-compliant way and either accepts an optional room or is guarded without conditional hook calls; whether avatar rendering has a no-room/OOB fallback instead of only rendering a room-dependent decorated avatar; and whether clicking truly toggles the right panel—closed opens to Room Summary, already open closes—rather than treating an open non-summary phase as another opportunity to navigate to Room Summary. Avoid the tempting criterion that merely requires `setCard(RoomSummary)` plus `togglePanel` or rewards any conditional topic/avatar markup. Prioritize visible evidence from prop types, hook signatures, lint/test output, existing avatar fallback patterns, and the exact branch conditions in the click handler.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize a room-header implementation that superficially adds avatar/topic/click behavior but violates the component’s optional-room/OOB contract, React hook rules, or true right-panel toggle semantics. This applies when the visible trajectory or patch shows the compact header taking an optional room and optional out-of-band data, using a topic hook or avatar component, and controlling a phase-based right panel. The flaw is present if the header cannot render safely without a room, lacks a fallback avatar/name path for OOB-only data, calls a hook conditionally or passes optional/null values via unsafe casts without updating the hook contract, or implements click handling so an already-open right panel on a non-summary phase is navigated to summary instead of being toggled closed. It also applies if validation output already exposes hook-rule, type, or render failures tied to these contracts.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial room-header wiring breaks integration contracts

evidence_to_check: header prop type allows missing room and optional out-of-band data
topic hook signature and call site are compatible with optional room without conditional hook calls or unsafe casts
avatar rendering includes a safe OOB/no-room fallback
click handler branches on open versus closed panel state, opening to summary only from closed and closing when already open
lint/type/test output for hook-rule, optional-room, or render failures
tempting_but_insufficient_evidence: presence of an onClick handler
presence of a topic preview div
presence of an avatar component
mention of Room Summary phase without checking branch semantics

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the visible implementation preserves optional-room/OOB rendering, uses hooks legally with compatible optional-room handling, renders an appropriate avatar fallback, and the click behavior is a true toggle that opens to summary only when closed.
scale.2: Minor evidence of risk: most contracts appear handled, but one detail is not fully visible or lightly questionable, such as incomplete validation around the OOB/no-room path.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the implementation covers the main visible features but has an ambiguous or partially incorrect integration detail, such as unclear open-on-non-summary behavior or insufficient evidence that the hook/avatar path works without a room.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the patch adds the requested UI but visibly uses conditional hooks, unsafe optional-room casts, missing OOB avatar fallback, or non-toggle right-panel branch logic.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: multiple integration contracts are broken or validation already shows related failures, even though avatar/topic/onClick elements are present.

experiences.title: Do not reward a dirty-flag fix that leaves UUID validity semantics unchecked
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go trajectory fixes idempotent config writes for UUID-bearing SAAS/config.toml flows by adding a changed/needsWrite guard, especially if the existing code validates UUIDs with ad hoc regex or string matching.
experiences.context: This applies to tasks where the desired behavior is conditional persistence: do not rewrite a configuration file when all stored identifiers are already valid, but do rewrite when identifiers are missing or invalid. The misleading pattern is a trajectory that correctly notices the unconditional write and adds a boolean guard, then appears to satisfy no-rewrite behavior for one happy-path UUID string while leaving the existing validity check unchanged. In Go code that handles UUIDs, a manual regexp such as an unanchored lowercase-only pattern can be both too permissive for malformed strings containing a UUID substring and too strict for valid UUID representations such as uppercase hex. A broad idempotence rubric may still be appropriate if the repository already uses a reliable UUID parser or the task is purely about avoiding writes after an independently correct validity decision; it is not enough when the visible code path also decides whether existing UUIDs are valid.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics focused on the high-level requirement: add or demonstrate idempotent SAAS UUID behavior so config.toml is not backed up or rewritten when existing UUIDs are valid, while scan results reuse those UUIDs and missing/invalid UUIDs still trigger persistence. That idea is directionally correct, but it can over-credit a superficial changed/configChanged flag. In these trajectories, the visible code still relied on a manual UUID regex/string match, so the central contract, 'already valid UUIDs are preserved and invalid ones regenerated,' was not actually secured. Future rubrics for this situation should not judge a dirty flag, passing package tests, or a one-off no-backup script as sufficient. A better rubric should explicitly inspect whether the validity predicate is exact and standards-compatible, preferably by using the project/library UUID parser or an anchored validation equivalent, and whether tests or reasoning cover both valid variants and malformed near-matches. Avoid the tempting criterion 'only write when changed' by itself; prioritize visible evidence that the agent distinguishes semantic UUID changes from scan-result propagation, preserves all valid existing IDs without regeneration, and persists only when a genuinely missing or invalid ID is detected.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that present idempotent config rewriting as solved by adding a changed/needsWrite guard while leaving UUID validity dependent on an ad hoc or visibly unsound check, such as an unanchored regexp MatchString, a lowercase-only UUID pattern, substring matching, or no evidence that valid UUID variants and malformed near-matches are handled correctly. This flaw is especially important when the task requires preserving valid existing host/container UUIDs without regeneration and regenerating only missing or invalid UUIDs.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Dirty Flag Without Sound UUID Validation

metadata.environment: Go project with SAAS/config.toml UUID persistence
visible_risk_cues: manual UUID regexp or string validation remains in the rewritten path
boolean changed/configChanged/needsWrite is introduced as the main fix
tests or manual checks cover only one lowercase UUID happy path
no visible use of a UUID parser or anchored exact validation
preferred_evidence: valid existing UUIDs are parsed with a standards-compatible UUID parser or exact anchored equivalent
invalid UUID strings, including strings containing valid UUID substrings, are regenerated and persisted
valid UUID representations are not unnecessarily regenerated
scan results are populated from existing UUIDs without marking the config dirty

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory uses a reliable UUID parser or exact anchored validation and separates validity checking from the write guard.
scale.2: Minor risk: the trajectory mostly addresses UUID validity but lacks explicit coverage of one edge case, while the implementation is not obviously substring- or lowercase-only dependent.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory adds conditional writing and mentions invalid UUID handling, but visible evidence is insufficient to tell whether validation is exact and standards-compatible.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory adds a dirty flag or no-rewrite guard while retaining a visibly weak manual validation check and does not test valid variants or malformed near-matches.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory relies entirely on a dirty flag plus an unsound UUID check, treats a single happy-path no-rewrite demonstration as proof, and provides no evidence that valid UUIDs are preserved or invalid near-matches are regenerated correctly.

experiences.title: Do not let identifier algorithm tests substitute for edition-record integration
experiences.description: Retrieve when an OpenLibrary identifier-normalization task asks that saved or processed edition records store canonical values, and the trajectory is mostly focused on a standalone parser/helper algorithm, MARC fixture updates, or example-output checks.
experiences.context: This applies in the OpenLibrary Python codebase for LCCN/ISBN-like identifier cleanup tasks where the user-facing failure is about edition records after create/edit/import/save. A criterion about exact LCCN parsing rules is useful only after the trajectory has also shown the normalization is wired into the relevant record ingestion/edit paths. It is misleading when the visible work only modifies `catalog/marc/parse.py`, updates MARC snapshot expectations, or demonstrates a helper on sample strings, because those cues can look strong while leaving non-MARC edition creation/edit flows unnormalized. Do not apply this warning to a very early discovery stage as a hard failure; at that stage it is better framed as a next-step risk. Also, if the task is explicitly limited to MARC parsing only, then a parser-focused algorithm rubric may be appropriate.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics asked judges to reward whether the LCCN normalization algorithm preserves prefixes, removes spaces/hyphens, pads serials, and strips suffixes. That criterion is necessary but incomplete for this task: several trajectories could satisfy the sample transformations inside MARC parsing or a local helper while missing the actual edition-record normalization contract. A better rubric should evaluate whether the agent has identified and integrated a reusable LCCN normalizer at the points where edition records and identifier lists are accepted or saved, analogous to existing ISBN cleanup, and whether it avoids merely changing MARC expected fixtures to match a narrow parser change. Avoid the tempting criterion “sample inputs normalize correctly” as the main signal once implementation is underway. Prioritize visible evidence such as a dedicated identifier utility, cleanup of `lccn` lists alongside other bibliographic IDs before matching/saving, handling of edit/API identifier assignment paths, and targeted tests that exercise record-level normalization rather than only parser snapshots.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Algorithm-only LCCN fix misses edition-record integration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for an edition-record LCCN normalization task when they demonstrate or implement correct-looking string transformations only in a narrow parser/helper/test fixture context, but the visible work does not wire normalization into the edition record creation/edit/import paths where `lccn` lists are saved or matched. This includes relying on MARC `010$a` parsing changes alone, updating MARC snapshot expectations without showing record-level cleanup, or adding a helper in an incidental module without using it where edition identifiers are accepted.

metadata.environment: OpenLibrary Python repository
metadata.task_type: identifier normalization for saved/processed edition records
misleading_positive_evidence: sample LCCN strings normalize correctly in a standalone script
MARC parser tests pass after updating expected fixture LCCNs
a helper exists but is only called from one ingestion path
preferred_evidence: normalization is centralized in an identifier utility
edition import/load cleanup normalizes `lccn` lists alongside other bibliographic identifiers before matching/saving
edit/API identifier assignment paths normalize LCCN values before storing them
tests cover record-level or identifier-assignment behavior, not only parser snapshots
metadata.stage_boundary: At early exploration, treat missing integration as an unresolved risk; at implementation or final-review stage, treat it as a substantive flaw.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory shows a reusable normalizer and applies it in the visible edition-record save/import/edit paths, with record-level validation or tests.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: integration appears mostly covered, but one secondary identifier path or test type remains ambiguous.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory has a plausible normalizer and one relevant integration point, but it is unclear whether other visible edition-record creation/edit paths normalize LCCNs.
scale.4: Clear evidence: work is concentrated in MARC parsing, helper examples, or fixture updates while the main edition-record cleanup path is not shown to normalize `lccn` values.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory treats passing algorithm examples or parser snapshots as complete, with no visible integration into saved edition-record identifier handling and possible broad fixture/test changes masking the gap.

experiences.title: PostgreSQL dbshell psql argument-order invariant
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django-style database shell task concerns PostgreSQL `psql` ignoring extra `dbshell` parameters because they are placed after the database name.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django repository where the task explicitly states that PostgreSQL `psql` requires command-line options or user-provided dbshell parameters before the positional database name. The trajectory should have reached the PostgreSQL dbshell/client argument construction code, or at least identified that backend-specific command construction is the likely repair site. This guidance is strongest once the agent has inspected or edited the argument list builder and there is visible evidence about where `parameters` and the database name are appended. It is less useful during very early repository exploration before PostgreSQL-specific code is found, and should not be generalized to other database backends whose CLIs may intentionally order database names and parameters differently.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic command-line contract: for PostgreSQL, generated `psql` arguments must keep the executable and connection flags first, then append user-supplied dbshell parameters, and leave the database name as the final positional argument when present. This was discriminative because the task is not about generic dbshell execution, subprocess handling, or installing/running tests; it is about one ordering invariant that determines whether `psql -c ... dbname` works instead of treating `-c` as an ignored extra argument. A better rubric should judge visible evidence that the agent located the PostgreSQL-specific command builder, recognized the existing `dbname`-before-`parameters` bug, changed only the ordering so parameters precede the database name, and preserved existing user/host/port/password/SSL/environment behavior. Manual or unit-test evidence should be valued when it directly prints or asserts the constructed argument list with parameters before the database name. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as requiring successful full test-suite execution in an environment with missing dependencies, rewarding only test updates, changing shared dbshell/base client behavior, or applying PostgreSQL ordering rules to MySQL/SQLite/Oracle clients.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluate whether the trajectory is converging on the PostgreSQL `psql` argument-order fix: user-provided dbshell parameters/options must be inserted before the optional database name, with the database name remaining the final positional argument, while existing connection flags and environment handling remain unchanged.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Preserve PostgreSQL psql argument ordering contract

required_visible_evidence: Identifies PostgreSQL-specific dbshell/client command construction as the relevant implementation area
Recognizes that placing the database name before additional parameters causes `psql` to ignore later options
Shows or describes an edit that appends user parameters before appending the database name
Preserves existing executable, user, host, port, password, SSL, and environment option behavior
Optionally validates with an argument-list assertion or printout demonstrating parameters before database name
non_requirements: Full test-suite success is not required when dependency or settings setup blocks execution
Other database backends need not be changed
Regression tests are helpful but should not substitute for the implementation ordering fix

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent has found the PostgreSQL command builder or understood the `psql` ordering requirement.
scale.2: The agent mentions PostgreSQL or dbshell parameters, but the visible plan or edits do not clearly ensure parameters appear before the database name.
scale.3: The agent has identified the correct ordering issue and likely target area, but the visible evidence is incomplete, unverified, or risks disturbing unrelated connection behavior.
scale.4: The agent visibly changes or plans the correct localized ordering so parameters precede the database name, with reasonable preservation of existing connection options.
scale.5: The agent makes the localized PostgreSQL ordering fix, preserves surrounding connection/environment semantics, and provides direct validation or test expectations showing generated `psql` args with parameters before the final database name.

experiences.title: Mutable State Isolation in Custom Deepcopy
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python/Django task reports that object copies share a mutable per-instance attribute, especially a dictionary populated in initialization and omitted from a custom __deepcopy__ method.
experiences.context: Applies in Python framework code where the task and trajectory identify a custom copy/deepcopy method that already handles some mutable attributes but omits another mutable mapping, causing copied instances or form instances to leak mutations. This is most relevant once the trajectory has inspected the target method, reproduced object-identity sharing, or begun editing the copy method. It is less appropriate as a strict success criterion during the first few exploratory steps before the target code is inspected, and it should not be used for unrelated validation bugs where no copy/deepcopy semantics or shared mutable state are involved. If the current visible state shows broad line-number edits, unreachable code after return, missing return statements, or damaged neighboring classes, the rubric should explicitly treat code preservation and importability as part of the criterion.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric pattern is to evaluate the semantic copy contract: the copied object must receive its own error-message mapping, while the existing widget and validator copy behavior and surrounding class hierarchy remain intact. In these trajectories, strong evidence included inspecting Field.__deepcopy__, confirming that error_messages is built as an instance dict, showing a reproduction where two copied fields/forms shared the same dictionary, and producing a clean diff that adds the copy before return in the base deepcopy method. Negative visible evidence included inserting the line after return, replacing every return result in the file, duplicating subclass changes unnecessarily, removing return result, or corrupting following field classes. A better rubric should avoid overfitting to an exact implementation such as requiring copy.deepcopy in all cases; the core requirement is independent mapping identity, with deepcopy acceptable when chosen and shallow dict copy potentially sufficient unless the task/visible tests specifically require nested mutable message values to be isolated. Also avoid requiring redundant edits in subclasses that already call super().__deepcopy__; focus on the base method and on preserving subclass-specific deepcopy behavior. Prioritize visible evidence from git diff, targeted code placement before return, object identity checks, mutation-leak tests across direct field copies and form instances, and confirmation that imports/syntax are not broken.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should make the custom deepcopy implementation isolate the mutable error-message mapping for copied form fields without disrupting existing copy semantics. A strong trajectory identifies the base deepcopy method as the right central fix, places the error-message copy before returning the copied object, preserves the existing widget deepcopy and validator-list copy behavior, avoids corrupting neighboring field classes or adding unnecessary broad subclass edits, and validates that mutating one copied field or form instance no longer changes another.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Deepcopy Mutable Mapping Isolation

metadata.environment: Python Django forms codebase
metadata.target_behavior: copied field instances must not share the same error_messages mapping

experiences.title: Do not equate custom command failures with splitting an existing command option
experiences.description: Retrieve when an Ansible-style connection/plugin task involves a configurable command variable whose value in the report contains spaces or fixed arguments, especially when the option is documented as a command/executable rather than an argv or shell command.
experiences.context: In Python/Ansible connection plugin work, a visible error like “command not found” for a configured value containing spaces can tempt a rubric to require shlex-splitting that existing variable. That idea may be appropriate only when the option is explicitly documented or tested as a shell-like command line. It is misleading when the codebase’s option contract treats the variable as the executable command and has separate internal handling for framework-added arguments such as delegation flags and principals. At early trajectory stages, identifying the argv construction bug is useful evidence, but by implementation-review time the rubric should distinguish between a quick tokenization patch and a contract-preserving design.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics rewarded trajectories for parsing `ansible_winrm_kinit_cmd` into executable-plus-args and preserving subprocess/pexpect behavior. This over-focused on the symptom: the report’s example put fixed arguments in a variable named and documented as the kinit command. A patch that simply applies `shlex.split` to the existing command option can appear correct in narrow tests, but it changes the meaning of a public configuration option and may mishandle executable paths or future argument semantics. For similar tasks, generate rubrics that prioritize visible evidence that the agent inspected the option documentation and public variable contract, preserved the command option as the executable selector, and introduced or used a dedicated argument mechanism with clear ordering relative to framework-added flags and the principal. Avoid the tempting criterion “must split the existing *_cmd string”; instead require evidence of a compatibility-aware argument API, updated option docs/tests, and correct behavior for default command, explicit extra args, delegation defaults, and password/principal handling without shell execution.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory is flawed if it treats a public command/executable option as a shell-like command line solely by applying tokenization to the existing option, without addressing the documented configuration contract or providing a dedicated way to pass extra kinit arguments. This is especially severe when the visible code documents the option as a command, appends framework-managed flags/principal internally, and the agent does not update option documentation or tests for the new argument semantics.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Tokenizing Command Option Instead of Preserving Config Contract

metadata.environment: Python Ansible-style connection plugin with documented plugin options and unit tests
visible_evidence_to_check: whether the option is documented as a command/executable versus a shell command line or argv list
whether the patch changes the existing command option from a single executable string into tokenized argv
whether a separate extra-arguments option or equivalent contract-preserving mechanism is added
whether framework-added flags such as delegation and the authentication principal have defined ordering and override behavior
whether documentation, changelog, and unit tests cover default command, custom command, explicit args, delegation, and both execution paths

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the agent preserves the command option’s executable semantics and handles extra arguments through a documented, tested mechanism.
scale.2: Minor concern: the agent discusses splitting but also investigates the option contract and appears likely to avoid changing the public command option semantics.
scale.3: Equivalent/unclear: the trajectory identifies argv construction and tests execution paths, but visible evidence is insufficient to tell whether it will preserve the public option contract or merely split the existing command string.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the agent implements or plans direct tokenization of the existing command option and only validates narrow executable-plus-args examples, with little or no contract/documentation consideration.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory finalizes direct tokenization of the public command option, omits a dedicated argument API and documentation, and fails to reason about compatibility boundaries such as paths with spaces, delegation flag behavior, or public option semantics.

experiences.title: Go Iterator Slice Refactor Contract
experiences.description: Use when a Go 1.23+ task asks to replace custom slice chunking utilities with iterator-based APIs and the trajectory is modifying both the utility package and downstream callers.
experiences.context: Applies in Go repositories targeting Go 1.23 or newer where the requested change is a multi-part API modernization: deleting legacy slice chunk helpers, adopting `iter.Seq`/standard iterator helpers, preserving chunk semantics at callers, and adding a typed slice-to-sequence mapping helper. This is most useful after the agent has begun implementation and there is visible evidence from diffs, greps, tests, or build attempts. It is less useful during very early exploration before any edits, and it should not be narrowed to only one subrequirement such as adding a mapper if broader caller migration or compilation status is still unresolved.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics were useful when they treated the task as an end-to-end modernization contract rather than a local utility edit: the agent needed to remove deprecated APIs, migrate every production and test caller, preserve batch sizes/order/error propagation, keep iterator APIs idiomatic, and add the requested typed mapping iterator. The visible trajectories often showed partial success, such as no remaining grep hits for removed symbols or a new `Values` helper, while also showing risky full-file rewrites, broken sed edits, missing imports, malformed function bodies, failing builds, or omission of the explicit mapping utility. A better rubric should therefore require both semantic API compliance and caller-level integration evidence. Avoid the tempting but weak criterion “does it use `iter.Seq` somewhere” or “does it add a mapping helper”; those can be true while the patch still breaks compilation, removes unrelated code, changes streaming behavior, or leaves tests/callers inconsistent. Prioritize visible evidence such as checked diffs of the utility API, grep results for deleted symbols, migration of all chunking call sites with preserved loop behavior, updated tests for new APIs, and successful targeted or full Go builds/tests.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete Iterator Chunking Migration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate an integrated Go iterator modernization: legacy chunking helpers are removed from the utility API, `CollectChunks` remains or becomes an idiomatic `iter.Seq`-based chunk producer with safe allocation and early-yield behavior, a generic typed slice-to-sequence mapping helper is added, all production and test usages of removed APIs are migrated without changing chunk order, batch sizes, side effects, or error propagation, and the edited code is inspected and validated with relevant grep/build/test evidence.

metadata.environment: Go 1.23+ with `iter.Seq` and standard library iterator helpers available
required_visible_evidence: utility diff removing legacy chunk helpers rather than retaining compatibility shims
iterator-based chunking implementation or direct standard library iterator use where appropriate
typed mapper from slice elements to mapped iterator values that stops when `yield` returns false
grep or equivalent evidence that removed API names no longer appear in production callers or stale tests
caller migrations preserve chunk sizes, ordering, variadic usage, SQL/metadata side effects, and callback-style error returns
tests updated or added for new iterator helpers and chunk edge cases
successful relevant Go build/test output or clear resolution of earlier compile/import/syntax failures
common_failure_modes: only adding a `Values` helper while omitting the requested mapping iterator
collecting an entire iterator before chunking when streaming behavior is expected
leaving stale tests or callers that reference deleted APIs
breaking large files with broad sed or heredoc rewrites
missing imports, unused imports, malformed braces, or missing returns after caller migration
converting callback-based chunk loops without preserving early error returns

scale.1: No meaningful implementation evidence beyond exploration, or edits visibly preserve/reintroduce the deprecated APIs without addressing callers.
scale.2: Some local utility changes or isolated caller edits are present, but major requirements are missing, such as stale removed-API references, no typed mapping iterator, uninspected destructive rewrites, or no validation after risky edits.
scale.3: Moderate progress: legacy APIs are mostly removed and several callers are migrated, but visible evidence still shows incomplete tests, questionable chunk/error semantics, missing mapper or allocation/streaming concerns, or unresolved build/import issues.
scale.4: Strong progress: utility API, mapper, and most/all callers are coherently migrated with preserved behavior, stale references are checked, and targeted validation is mostly successful, with only minor cleanup or broader test coverage remaining.
scale.5: Complete visible evidence: all deprecated APIs and stale tests/callers are gone, iterator helpers are idiomatic and safe, mapper behavior is covered, all call-site semantics are preserved, diffs are reviewable, and relevant Go builds/tests pass.

experiences.title: Do not accept blanket cache re-enablement for vaulted-only read regressions
experiences.description: Retrieve when a performance bug involves repeated decryption or reads of vaulted variable/config files and the visible trajectory focuses on a disabled file-cache flag.
experiences.context: Applies in Ansible-core-like Python codebases where a loader has a general file cache, some callers intentionally bypass it for freshness, and the task complaint is specifically about repeated reads/decryptions of vaulted variable files. The misleading pattern is a rubric that treats restoring the loader cache at the vars-file call site as sufficient, so a simple `cache=True` or omitted-cache-argument patch looks correct. That original idea is still appropriate when the task explicitly requires caching all files on that path and there is no visible freshness contract for non-vaulted files. It is not sufficient when the report is vaulted-file-specific, nearby callers deliberately use uncached reads, or the loader’s cache option is too coarse to express “cache only expensive encrypted content.”
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked whether the trajectory identified the play vars_files loading path and restored DataLoader caching while preserving `unsafe`, templating, path lookup, and error handling. That criterion is too broad: it can over-credit an agent that merely flips `cache=False` to `cache=True`, even though that enables caching for plain variable files as well as vaulted files and may violate freshness semantics that motivated uncached loading. A better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory distinguishes the expensive vaulted-file decryption case from ordinary file reads, preserves intentionally uncached non-vault paths, and looks for or introduces a selective cache mode rather than globally changing cache behavior. Avoid the tempting criterion “the cache flag is restored to true/default.” Prefer evidence such as: the agent inspects how the loader detects vaulted/encrypted content, reasons about cache population versus cache lookup, preserves callers that need fresh reads, updates any affected cache API call sites consistently, and validates both that repeated vaulted vars-file loads avoid repeated physical reads/decryptions and that unrelated plain or inventory/config reads are not newly made stale.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat a vaulted vars-file performance regression as a blanket cache-on change. This flaw is present when the agent proposes or applies a simple call-site change that enables the loader cache for all vars_files, without considering that the user-visible regression concerns vaulted/decryption-heavy files and without preserving freshness for non-vaulted or intentionally uncached paths. The flaw is especially strong if validation only checks that a file appears in the cache, rather than proving selective behavior for encrypted content and unchanged behavior for ordinary file reads.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Blanket cache restoration ignores vaulted-only boundary

metadata.task_type: Ansible core variable-file loading performance regression
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: cache flag changed to true/default at the vars_files load call
preferred_visible_evidence: reasoning distinguishes vaulted encrypted file loads from plain file loads
implementation or plan provides selective caching for vaulted content rather than all vars files
intentionally uncached inventory/config/freshness-sensitive paths remain uncached
tests or instrumentation count physical reads/decryptions for repeated vaulted loads and check non-vault behavior is not broadly cached

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory explicitly accounts for vaulted-only caching and preserves freshness-sensitive non-vault paths.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory mentions restoring caching but also raises the need to avoid broad caching or to preserve non-vault freshness.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies the disabled cache and vaulted performance issue but does not yet decide whether caching should be selective or global.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory proposes or applies a blanket cache-on change for vars_files and only lightly acknowledges other uncached paths or freshness concerns.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory finalizes a simple `cache=True`/default-cache call-site patch and validates only that files enter the cache, with no consideration of vaulted-only semantics or non-vault stale-read risk.

experiences.title: Do not require auto-name restoration when the reverse path is intentionally a no-op
experiences.description: Use this when evaluating Django migration `RenameIndex` fixes for unnamed indexes identified by `old_fields`, especially when the visible test/source says reversing is a no-op and then re-applies the forward operation.
experiences.context: In Django migration operation tasks involving `RenameIndex(..., old_fields=...)`, the tempting interpretation is that backward migration must physically restore the old auto-generated index name. That interpretation is misleading when the visible regression test or existing source comments show `database_backwards()` for unnamed indexes is expected to issue no queries and leave the new named index present, then verify that re-applying `database_forwards()` does not crash. A reversibility/restoration rubric can still be appropriate for explicitly named indexes, for migration operations whose tests require the old database object name after rollback, or when the task/test explicitly asserts the new name disappears on backward. It should not be used merely because the operation participates in a forward/backward/forward cycle.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics often demanded that `database_backwards()` compute and restore an auto-generated index name. That criterion led toward patches that changed the intended no-op reverse behavior, guessed backend naming details, or rewrote tests to expect the new index name to disappear. In this scenario, the better evidence is whether the trajectory recognizes that after a no-op reverse the physical index may already have the target `new_name`, so the forward path must avoid renaming an index to the same name. A replacement rubric should focus on an idempotence guard in the forward rename logic: after resolving the current index by fields/columns, if the discovered/current index name already equals the requested new name, the operation should return without invoking the schema editor rename. Avoid generating a criterion that says backward must be a true inverse or must restore an auto-generated name unless visible tests or source behavior require that. Prioritize visible evidence such as: preserving the no-op reverse assertion, adding or considering a re-apply-forward regression check, inspecting the column-based index lookup in the forward path, and preventing self-renames or duplicate target-name renames.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a Django `RenameIndex` unnamed-index task where visible evidence shows the backward operation is intentionally a no-op and the regression is a forward re-apply after that no-op, penalize trajectories that treat auto-generated-name restoration in the backward path as the required fix. This includes implementing or validating a backward rename to a computed auto-generated name, changing tests to expect the new named index to disappear after backward, or judging success primarily by backward/forward inverse symmetry instead of by preventing a forward self-rename when the current index already has the target name.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Misapplied backward restoration requirement

metadata.operation_pattern: RenameIndex with unnamed index specified by fields
metadata.misleading_visible_cue: task wording mentions backward/forward cycle or auto-generated name
metadata.decisive_visible_cue: source/test indicates reverse is a no-op and still asserts the new index name exists before re-applying forward
metadata.preferred_fix_evidence: forward path detects current index name equals target name and skips schema-editor rename
metadata.avoid_fix_evidence: backward path computes auto-generated name and renames the index back solely to make the operation symmetric

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory preserves the no-op reverse behavior or focuses on forward idempotence/self-rename avoidance.
scale.2: Minor risk: the trajectory discusses restoring an auto-generated name as a possibility but has not made it the main criterion or patch direction.
scale.3: Moderate flaw: the trajectory frames the issue as general bidirectional reversibility while also acknowledging the no-op reverse behavior or forward re-apply collision.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory’s main solution or rubric requires `database_backwards()` for unnamed indexes to restore a computed auto-generated name despite visible no-op expectations.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory implements or endorses a backward auto-name restoration patch, changes tests/expectations away from the no-op reverse behavior, and does not address the forward self-rename/idempotence condition.

experiences.title: Centralize FontFamilies Without Changing Singleton Web-Font Boundaries
experiences.description: Use when a qutebrowser/PyQt configuration task introduces a structured FontFamilies representation and the trajectory touches font parsing, default-family migration, Qt font conversion, or web font settings.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python qutebrowser-style config system where font family strings are parsed in more than one path: runtime font conversion, configuration migrations/default-family handling, and web font-family settings. It is especially relevant after the trajectory has identified existing Font, FontFamily, QtFont-like concepts, an existing comma-splitting helper, migration call sites, and Qt WebEngine/WebKit setters. The criterion is most useful at implementation or final-review stages, and can also evaluate whether an exploration has found the right integration boundaries. It is less applicable if the task is only to improve a local parser with no shared representation requirement, or if the trajectory has not yet inspected downstream consumers. Do not assume plural font-family values should be passed through every setting: in this environment, web font-family APIs visibly accept a single string per font enum, while QFont-style UI font conversion can consume an ordered family list.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful signal is not merely that an agent added a class named FontFamilies or made parser tests pass. Strong trajectories preserve the existing single-family config/API contracts while introducing one shared, lightweight representation/parsing path for the places that actually need ordered fallback families. Previous rubrics that broadly demanded 'update configdata.yml, websettings, all call sites' could be misleading: agents often changed singular web font settings from strings to lists, then had to join them back for Qt, introduced empty-string/none_ok regressions, or chased circular imports. A better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory has audited and respected the boundary between plural fallback-family parsing and singleton web-font application. It should reward visible evidence that the new representation is reused by migration/default-family handling and Qt font conversion, provides list iteration plus string serialization/first-family behavior needed by downstream Qt calls, preserves existing tests/compatibility for empty entries and quote stripping, and avoids breaking the config type registry or import topology. It should penalize visible evidence of a divergent second parser, removal of the old helper without updating tests/callers, unvalidated YAML type changes, list values being passed directly to WebEngine/WebKit setters, or repeated probing that has already confirmed the Qt API only accepts strings. Avoid the tempting wrong criterion that 'websettings must support multiple families' unless the trajectory has independently found a real multi-family web API; in these cases, the safer and more predictive criterion is whether the implementation centralizes parsing while keeping web settings serialized as the existing single-string boundary.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Shared FontFamilies Representation With Preserved API Boundaries
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a coherent FontFamilies design that centralizes CSS-like font-family parsing for ordered fallback lists while preserving existing singleton web-font and config compatibility boundaries. Excellent evidence includes a shared representation/parser used by both migration/default-family logic and Qt font conversion; stable behavior for comma-separated families, surrounding quotes, whitespace, empty segments, and serialization back to a comma-joined string; downstream Qt font conversion using the first family and full ordered list where the Qt API supports lists; and explicit recognition that web font-family setters accept one string per font enum rather than a Python list. The trajectory should avoid broad schema/API changes that force list values into singular web settings, avoid duplicating parsers, and keep import/type-registration behavior testable.

prioritize_visible_evidence: call-site audit distinguishes plural fallback-family consumers from singular web-font consumers
central FontFamilies-like object or parser replaces ad-hoc repeated parsing in migration/default-family and Qt font conversion paths
ordered iteration/list conversion and string serialization are both considered
empty values, quotes, whitespace, and existing parser tests or equivalent targeted checks are addressed
Qt WebEngine/WebKit single-string setter limitation is respected rather than worked around with nonexistent list APIs
config type/YAML/import changes are validated rather than assumed
common_false_proxies_to_avoid: class exists but is not used by migration or Qt font conversion
all FontFamily settings are mechanically renamed to FontFamilies
web settings are changed to accept lists only because the new parser returns a list
parser is made quote-aware but existing call sites/tests are broken or abandoned
circular import or config registry failures are dismissed as unrelated without validation

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of a shared FontFamilies representation or downstream audit; the trajectory only explores or repeats commands, or changes unrelated parsing without considering consumers.
scale.2: Some parser/class work is visible, but it is local or duplicative and does not clearly preserve migration, Qt font conversion, and web-font API boundaries.
scale.3: The trajectory is roughly on par with partial parent progress: it identifies the main parser and some call sites, but leaves major uncertainty about default-family/migration integration, serialization, web setter string contracts, or config validation.
scale.4: Strong evidence of a coherent shared representation and call-site plan/implementation, with most compatibility boundaries respected and targeted validation attempted; only minor gaps remain.
scale.5: Complete visible evidence that FontFamilies is the single shared representation for ordered fallback parsing, migration/default-family handling and Qt font conversion are updated coherently, string serialization and first-family behavior are handled, existing empty/quote/whitespace semantics are preserved with tests, and singular web-font settings are not incorrectly converted to list-valued APIs.

experiences.title: Cgroup CPU Auto-Detection Must Not Yield Zero Workers
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task concerns automatic parallel worker selection in Linux container/Kubernetes cgroups, especially a crash where fractional cgroup CPU quota or shares are truncated to 0 before being passed to multiprocessing.
experiences.context: Applies in Python CLI/tooling repositories where an automatic jobs/worker setting derives process count from cgroup CPU quota, period, or shares, and visible trajectory evidence shows the agent inspected the CPU detection path and recognized that integer truncation of fractional CPU capacity can produce 0. This is most useful after the agent has located the relevant resource-detection code or is proposing a patch; it is less useful during unrelated dependency setup or repository exploration. Do not apply it to bugs about explicit user-supplied positive worker counts, non-container CPU detection, scheduling affinity alone, or cases where the failure is caused by multiprocessing availability rather than a zero process count.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged the semantic invariant rather than the exact edit: automatic cgroup-derived CPU detection must never hand 0 to multiprocessing. They aligned because the visible task evidence named Kubernetes cgroup values such as an unlimited quota and very low CPU shares, and the trajectory repeatedly identified the truncating calculations that turn a fractional CPU allocation into 0. A strong rubric should therefore focus on whether the proposed fix covers the actual cgroup quota/share computation path, clamps or otherwise converts only computed zero/fractional CPU results to a valid positive worker count, and preserves normal positive counts and fallback behavior when cgroup data is absent. Avoid a tempting but weaker criterion that rewards merely installing dependencies, writing ad hoc tests, changing only a downstream `min()` call without preventing the cgroup helper from returning 0, or requiring one exact implementation style such as `max(1, ...)` versus a post-computation zero check. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent connected the reported cgroup values to the truncation, edited the CPU count derivation or its immediate return contract, and considered both the low shares path and fractional quota path without breaking positive values.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the automatic worker-count fix enforces a positive lower bound for CPU counts derived from Linux cgroup quota/period or CPU-share data, so fractional container CPU allocations cannot be truncated to 0 and passed to multiprocessing, while preserving valid positive counts and the normal non-cgroup fallback behavior.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Positive Lower Bound for Cgroup-Derived Worker Count

metadata.key_failure_mode: fractional cgroup CPU allocation is converted with integer truncation to zero
required_visible_evidence: agent identifies the cgroup quota/share CPU detection path as the source of the zero worker count
agent proposes or applies a change that prevents computed cgroup CPU values of 0 from being used as a process count
agent preserves valid positive cgroup-derived counts and fallback behavior when cgroup data is unavailable
acceptable_fix_shapes: clamp computed cgroup CPU counts to at least one
post-process a computed zero cgroup CPU result into one valid worker
fallback from invalid zero cgroup results to another positive CPU count source
non_evidence: dependency installation or unrelated test setup alone
generic multiprocessing changes that do not address cgroup-derived zero
changes that only handle positive explicit job counts

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory addresses the cgroup-derived zero CPU count; it remains focused on unrelated setup, generic multiprocessing behavior, or repository exploration.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory mentions zero workers or containers but does not clearly connect the failure to cgroup quota/share integer truncation or proposes an incomplete/unclear fix.
scale.3: Moderate evidence equivalent to the parent: the trajectory identifies the truncating cgroup CPU calculation and attempts to ensure the resulting worker count is positive, but validation or preservation of normal positive/fallback behavior is limited.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory clearly fixes the cgroup quota/share path so fractional allocations cannot produce zero and considers at least one reported Kubernetes-style case while maintaining normal positive counts.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory explicitly covers both low CPU-share and fractional quota/period cases, ensures multiprocessing receives at least one worker, preserves non-cgroup fallback and valid positive counts, and includes meaningful validation of those behaviors.

experiences.title: Do not reward read-only flag plumbing without explicit optional-boolean semantics
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for config/UI tasks that add an optional read-only flag whose absence has legacy/default meaning, especially in Go/Viper backend plus React/Redux UI flows.
experiences.context: In these trajectories, the tempting rubric restated the feature checklist: add a storage.readOnly flag, validate non-database use, expose it to the UI, and render a header badge/icon. That is too coarse when the task depends on distinguishing an absent config value from an explicit boolean value. A plain bool field, schema default, or UI initial default can erase that distinction and make validation/defaulting look superficially complete while still accepting or rejecting the wrong configurations. The original checklist remains useful only after the trajectory shows the agent has handled optional presence semantics, preserved existing backend behavior, and avoided broad unrelated rewrites; during early exploration or after broad file rewrites, the rubric should focus on these risk signals rather than only on whether the named feature areas were touched.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics overemphasized visible coverage of backend flag, schema, UI selector, and badge rendering. That made trajectories look strong even when they used a non-optional boolean, added defaults that made absence indistinguishable from explicit false, validated only one boolean value, rewrote schema/config files broadly, or omitted compatibility behavior for existing non-database storage. For similar tasks, generate a criterion that checks whether the implementation preserves tri-state intent: absent flag means legacy/default read-only behavior for non-database storage, explicit database configuration can control read-only, and explicit unsupported overrides on non-database backends produce the required validation error. Avoid the tempting criterion “adds a readOnly boolean and validates it only for database storage” unless the visible trajectory also demonstrates how user intent is preserved through decoding, schema defaults, metadata JSON, and UI state. A better rubric should prioritize evidence such as pointer/nullable/optional modeling, absence-aware validation, no schema default that masks absence, UI selectors reading the exposed config value without duplicating stale type inference except as fallback, targeted tests/fixtures for explicit and absent cases, and minimal changes that do not alter unrelated storage/auth/schema behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that claim read-only configuration support but model the new flag as an ordinary defaulted boolean or otherwise lose the distinction between an absent config field and an explicit user setting. This flaw is especially severe when validation only checks one boolean value, schema/default changes force a default value into decoded config, UI initial state makes the field required, or the agent relies on broad feature plumbing without tests covering absent versus explicit values for database and non-database storage.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Lost optional read-only intent

evidence_to_check: Whether the backend config representation can distinguish unset from explicit true/false
Whether schema/default changes avoid injecting a value that masks absence
Whether validation handles unsupported explicit non-database read-only overrides with the required error
Whether UI state consumes the exposed config value while preserving fallback behavior only when the field is absent
Whether tests or fixtures cover absent, explicit database, and explicit non-database cases
Whether unrelated storage/auth/schema behavior is left intact
metadata.common_false_positive: The trajectory touches StorageConfig, schema, UI types, Redux selectors, and Header badges, but uses a defaulted bool and therefore cannot implement the compatibility contract correctly.
metadata.stage_boundary: At early exploration, absence of these details is not yet a flaw; after code edits or implementation claims, the rubric should require visible evidence of absence-aware handling.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory explicitly preserves unset-versus-explicit semantics across backend decoding/schema/UI and includes or plans targeted validation coverage.
scale.2: Minor concern: the trajectory mentions optional/absent semantics but has not yet verified all layers, or one layer is still pending while the intended approach remains compatible.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory implements broad plumbing but leaves ambiguous whether absence can be distinguished from explicit values, with no targeted tests yet.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory adds a defaulted/non-optional boolean or schema/UI default that likely masks absence, while claiming validation/UI behavior is complete.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory combines lost optional semantics with incorrect validation, broad unrelated rewrites, or changes that break existing non-database storage behavior while still treating the checklist as complete.

experiences.title: Prioritize operation coalescing semantics over test-only gates
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django migration optimizer task asks for repeated field-alter operations to collapse, especially after the trajectory has inspected or edited operation-level reduce logic.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django repository when the issue is specifically that multiple consecutive field-alter migration operations on the same model field are not optimized away unless an add-field operation is present. It is most useful once the trajectory has identified the migration operation reduction mechanism, reproduced the standalone alter-chain behavior, or modified the field operation reduction method. The criterion is less applicable for unrelated migration optimizer bugs, tasks about documenting intended behavior instead of changing semantics, or very early exploration where no evidence exists about the reduction target. It should not be replaced by a requirement for adding an in-repository regression test when the visible task and repository acceptance can be satisfied by a minimal behavioral fix, though tests remain useful supporting evidence.
experiences.experience: For this cluster, rubrics that evaluated the semantic contract of same-field alter-operation coalescing were the discriminative ones: the visible successful trajectories found that the optimizer delegates to operation-specific reduce methods and added logic so an earlier field alteration is superseded by a later alteration on the same model and field. This aligns with the reported behavior because only the last field definition matters in a chain of consecutive alterations. A better rubric should therefore focus on whether the trajectory implements or is clearly moving toward that exact operation-level rule, with a same-field/model guard and without disturbing existing reductions for remove, rename, add, different fields/models, or barriers. Avoid the tempting but overly strict criterion that the trajectory must add a permanent project-native regression test; lack of such a test may be a quality concern, but in these cases it was not the decisive indicator of patch correctness. Also avoid broad optimizer rewrites or criteria that merely check for any reduction in list length, since the important boundary is reducing only same-target alter chains to the later operation while preserving unrelated operations. Prioritize visible evidence such as direct reproduction of the original alter-only case, inspection of the operation reduce contract, a localized change in the field-alter operation’s reduction logic, edge-case checks for different fields/models and rename/remove behavior, and clean diff review after any failed automated edits.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate or implement the core migration optimizer semantic: when a field-alter operation is followed by another field-alter operation targeting the same app/model/field, the earlier operation is replaced by the later operation, while existing behavior for add-field absorption, remove-field absorption, rename-field ordering, unrelated fields/models, and optimization barriers remains intact. Strong evidence includes locating the operation-specific reduction method, using the repository’s same-field predicate rather than ad hoc comparisons, returning the later operation as the replacement, and validating the original alter-only chain plus representative negative cases.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Same-target alter-chain coalescing

metadata.required_behavior: Consecutive alter operations on the same model field reduce to the final alter operation.
safety_boundaries: Do not reduce operations on different fields or models.
Do not break existing add-field plus alter-field optimization.
Do not break remove-field or rename-field reduction semantics.
Do not optimize across non-elidable or reference-blocking operations.
preferred_evidence: Inspection of operation-level reduce semantics.
Localized change in the field-alter operation reduction path.
Reproduction showing alter-only chains collapse from multiple operations to one.
Edge-case checks for different targets and existing reduction cases.
non_decisive_evidence: Presence or absence of a permanent regression test by itself.
Broad migration optimizer rewrites without same-field safeguards.
Ad hoc scripts that are left in the final patch.

scale.1: No visible evidence that the trajectory understands or targets same-field alter-operation coalescing; it focuses on unrelated files, generic optimizer changes, documentation only, or unguarded list shortening.
scale.2: Weak evidence of the intended behavior, such as reproducing the issue or mentioning that later alters should supersede earlier ones, but no credible localized implementation or safeguards are visible.
scale.3: Moderate evidence equivalent to the parent trajectory: it identifies the operation-level reduction location and attempts the same-field alter-to-alter rule, but implementation cleanliness, placement, or preservation of related behaviors remains uncertain.
scale.4: Strong evidence: a localized reduction rule keeps the later same-field alter operation, uses the existing same-target predicate, and visible checks or reasoning cover different fields/models and at least one existing related reduction behavior.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory cleanly implements the exact same-target alter-chain coalescing rule, preserves add/remove/rename/barrier semantics, verifies the original reproduction and representative edge cases with repository-appropriate tests or reliable scripts, and reviews the final diff for accidental edits.

experiences.title: Do not treat ICX command-string snippets as sufficient for a new Ansible module
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for a task that adds a new Ansible network module, especially an ICX logging module, and the visible trajectory shows command syntax checks or tests but the full module state model, option schema, parsing, and idempotent diff behavior remain uncertain.
experiences.context: This applies in the legacy Ansible network-module environment under the ICX platform namespace, where a new module must parse running configuration, map module parameters and aggregate entries into desired objects, compute minimal commands for present/absent states, and follow existing ICX module conventions. The misleading pattern is to generate a high-level criterion that only asks whether exact ICX CLI strings are produced, such as the IPv6 host form with the literal ipv6 token or specific no logging forms. Those strings are necessary, but they can be present in isolated command-generation branches or self-written tests while the module is still incorrect because of incompatible option names/types, missing required conditions, broken aggregate handling, parser/type normalization bugs, non-idempotent comparisons, or missing ICX test-harness/runtime conventions. A command-syntax rubric is still appropriate when the current work is narrowly changing command rendering after the surrounding parser/schema/diff framework is already established, or as an early low-confidence understanding check. It should not be the main correctness rubric for a whole new module once implementation exists or tests are being adjusted.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics emphasized ICX-specific CLI syntax fidelity: ensuring IPv6 hosts use logging host ipv6 <addr>, facility clearing uses no logging facility, console/global/buffered disabling use the required no forms, and aggregate entries produce proper commands. That guidance is correct as a necessary compatibility requirement, but it is misleading as a standalone judge for a newly added Ansible module. In these trajectories, the visible evidence often included some correct command strings and passing local tests, yet the implementation still had deeper risks: the public argument spec did not consistently match the expected API, facility and persistence semantics were modeled inconsistently, parsed values were compared against parameter values without normalization, aggregate entries could inherit or drop fields incorrectly, tests were sometimes rewritten to fit fixture contents rather than validate behavior, and module setup did not always follow existing ICX conventions. A better rubric should focus on end-to-end declarative module behavior: whether the module exposes the expected parameters and aggregate suboptions, parses all relevant running-config forms into normalized objects, detects IPv6 and negated buffered/facility/global lines from current config, generates only necessary commands for present and absent states, preserves check mode and load_config behavior, and uses tests or manual checks that cover both already-present and differing configurations. Avoid the tempting criterion that merely scans for the right CLI string literals or a small set of passing syntax tests. Prioritize visible evidence from argument_spec, map_params/map_config/map_obj comparison logic, type normalization, state-specific command generation, fixture alignment, and full relevant unit-test output.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory is likely overvalued if it demonstrates or tests a few exact ICX logging command strings but does not provide visible evidence that the new Ansible module implements the full declarative contract: compatible option schema and aggregate suboptions, required parameter validation, normalized parsing of running logging configuration, idempotent comparison for present and absent states, correct handling of IPv4/IPv6 hosts, global facility, console, buffered, persistence/RFC5424/global logging, check mode/load_config behavior, and tests that validate both no-change and change scenarios without rewriting expectations around fixture accidents.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Command-string compliance without end-to-end state-model correctness

metadata.task_type: new logging module
visible_evidence_to_prioritize: argument_spec and aggregate options match the requested public API
running configuration parser covers all relevant logging line forms and normalizes types
parameter-to-object mapping handles host, buffered, facility, persistence/RFC5424, console, and global logging consistently
object comparison generates minimal commands for present and absent states
IPv6 host detection is integrated into both parsing and command rendering
check mode and load_config usage follow existing ICX module conventions
tests cover idempotent no-change, updates, removals, IPv4/IPv6, aggregate, and fixture-differing cases
metadata.tempting_but_insufficient_proxy: presence of exact ICX CLI string literals or passing tests that only assert those literals

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory verifies command syntax only as part of a broader review of schema, parser, normalized diffing, idempotency, aggregate behavior, and ICX module runtime conventions.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: command strings receive some emphasis, but the trajectory also checks most surrounding module-contract behavior and only small edge cases remain unexamined.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory has correct-looking command rendering and some tests, but visible evidence for parser normalization, aggregate inheritance, or idempotent present/absent comparisons is incomplete.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory relies heavily on command-string snippets or self-written tests while option schema compatibility, fixture alignment, state comparison, or ICX module conventions remain visibly uncertain or inconsistent.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory treats exact CLI literals or passing narrow tests as sufficient despite visible broken or unverified argument spec, parser, aggregate handling, type normalization, idempotency, or module execution behavior.

experiences.title: Command Module Contract for New Ansible Network Platforms
experiences.description: Use when evaluating an Ansible network-platform support task where the requested behavior includes running CLI commands with conditional wait/retry semantics, and the trajectory is adding platform plugins, docs, or preparing a patch.
experiences.context: Applies in an Ansible-style repository where network platform support is split across platform-specific cliconf plugins, terminal plugins, module_utils helpers, modules under network platform directories, and platform documentation. Retrieve this when the task asks for a new `ansible_network_os` platform to be recognized and explicitly expects command execution, `wait_for` conditions, retries, intervals, or command-output-driven logic.
