It is most useful after the agent has moved beyond initial exploration and is creating or finalizing files. It is especially applicable when the visible work only adds cliconf/terminal handlers or docs that reference a platform command module. Do not apply as the main criterion during very early repository exploration before implementation choices are visible, for tasks that only ask for loader recognition or terminal prompt handling, or in repositories whose convention is a generic command module rather than per-platform command modules.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on whether the new network platform had a real command-execution module with Ansible network command semantics, not merely whether platform plugins existed. This was discriminative because adding `cliconf` and `terminal` files can make `ansible_network_os` load, but it does not satisfy tasks that promise users a platform-specific command module with `commands`, `wait_for`, `match`, `retries`, `interval`, and normal `stdout`/`stdout_lines` results. A better rubric should require visible evidence that the agent created and wired the platform command module and supporting helper layer, adapted an existing network command-module pattern, and ensured those files are included in the submitted diff or patch. It should also check that command parsing handles string/list/dict forms and that waiting logic records failed conditions. Avoid the tempting but weaker criterion of rewarding syntax/import success, docs/index updates, terminal prompt regexes, or basic cliconf delegation as sufficient platform support. Also avoid requiring a new connection plugin when the visible codebase shows `network_cli` dynamically loads platform-specific terminal and cliconf plugins by `ansible_network_os`. Prioritize evidence such as module and module_utils files for the platform, a `run_commands` helper wired through the connection/cliconf layer, command-module options matching existing platform modules, wait/retry loop behavior, result formatting, and the final patch/diff actually containing those files rather than only creating untracked local files.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a new Ansible network platform whose requirements include command execution and conditional wait/retry behavior, the trajectory should implement and include in the submitted changes a platform-specific command module and supporting network helper layer. The implementation should follow existing Ansible network command-module conventions: accept normal command inputs, execute through the platform connection/cliconf path, expose `wait_for`, `match`, `retries`, and `interval`, report failed conditions, and return standard `stdout` and `stdout_lines` structures. Plugin recognition, terminal handling, docs, and syntax checks are helpful but are not sufficient without this command-execution contract.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Platform Command Module Wait/Retry Contract

required_visible_evidence: platform-specific command module or equivalent canonical command executor
supporting helper layer that obtains the network connection and runs commands
wait_for/match/retries/interval behavior modeled on existing network modules
standard command result fields such as stdout and stdout_lines
submitted diff or patch includes the command module and helper files
insufficient_evidence: only cliconf and terminal plugins
only documentation or platform index updates
docs referencing a command module that is not implemented
syntax/import checks without functional command semantics
new files created locally but absent from the generated patch

scale.1: No visible command module or helper-layer work; trajectory only explores the repo or adds unrelated platform recognition pieces.
scale.2: Acknowledges or references a needed command module, or documentation mentions one, but no included implementation is visible.
scale.3: Creates a partial command module or helper, but it is incomplete, not clearly wired through the network connection, lacks wait/retry semantics, or is not included in the patch being prepared.
scale.4: Implements and includes a mostly complete platform command module and helper with command execution plus most wait_for, match, retry, interval, and output behavior, with only minor omissions or weak validation.
scale.5: Fully implements and includes the platform command module and helper following existing Ansible network conventions, with robust command input handling, connection/cliconf wiring, wait_for/match/retries/interval logic, failed-condition reporting, and standard stdout/stdout_lines results.

experiences.title: Do not equate MultiValueField required-subfield bugs with clean() fixes only
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django forms task involves MultiValueField/MultiWidget required subfields and the trajectory is focusing on server-side clean()/is_valid behavior without checking rendered required attributes or widget attribute propagation.
experiences.context: This applies in Django form-validation/rendering issues where requiredness can be enforced in more than one layer: server-side field cleaning and client-side/rendered widget attributes. The misleading pattern is a trajectory that reproduces the issue with standalone is_valid() scripts, patches the composite field's cleaning shortcut, and runs validation-oriented tests, but never inspects how required attributes are assigned to MultiWidget subwidgets during form rendering. A clean()-semantics rubric may still be appropriate when the task or existing tests clearly establish a backend validation contract and the agent has ruled out rendering/attribute behavior. It is risky when the task mentions MultiWidget, require_all_fields=False, and child required flags, because the correct behavior may involve propagating required attributes to only the required subwidgets rather than changing all-empty server validation semantics.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics rewarded the agent for making an optional MultiValueField with require_all_fields=False reject an all-empty submitted list whenever any child field is required. That is a plausible reading of the reproducer, but it becomes misleading when the trajectory has not verified that the failing contract is server-side cleaning rather than rendered required-attribute assignment. In these cases, the agents could pass scratch is_valid() reproductions and local edge cases while working in the wrong layer. A better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory investigates both sides of the Django forms contract: how MultiValueField.clean() behaves and how MultiWidget subwidgets receive required attributes when require_all_fields=False. Avoid the tempting criterion that simply treats 'all-empty submitted subvalues must be invalid in clean()' as sufficient. Prefer visible evidence such as inspecting form rendering/attribute-building code, checking rendered HTML or widget attrs for required only on required child widgets, adding an official regression test for subwidget required attributes, and ensuring existing optional/partial MultiValueField validation behavior is not altered unnecessarily.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Wrong-layer MultiValueField requiredness fix
reference_golden_rubrics.description: In a Django forms trajectory for a MultiValueField/MultiWidget required-subfield issue, the agent assumes the fix belongs only in server-side composite-field cleaning and validates only with is_valid()/clean() scripts, while failing to investigate or test how required attributes are propagated to individual subwidgets during rendering when require_all_fields=False. This is especially concerning if the proposed work changes all-empty validation semantics but shows no rendered-form or widget-attribute evidence.

metadata.environment: Django forms with MultiValueField and MultiWidget
metadata.misleading_proxy: standalone is_valid()/clean() reproductions and patches to composite field empty-value handling
better_visible_evidence: inspection of bound-field or widget attribute construction for required attributes
rendered form or widget attrs showing required only on child fields marked required
regression coverage for require_all_fields=False subwidget required attributes
confirmation that existing optional and partial MultiValueField validation behavior is preserved
metadata.boundary: Do not apply this negative rubric when the visible task and tests clearly establish a purely server-side validation bug and the trajectory has reasonably ruled out rendering/required-attribute behavior.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory investigates rendering/attribute propagation as well as validation, and its tests or reasoning target required attributes on individual subwidgets.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory initially focuses on clean()/is_valid() but also begins checking widget rendering or required-attribute behavior before committing to a fix.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory is mostly validation-focused, with only superficial mention of widgets or rendering and no decisive rendered-attribute test.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory patches or plans to patch composite-field cleaning based on is_valid()/clean() scripts, runs validation tests, and does not inspect the rendering/required-attribute path.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory confidently finalizes a clean()/empty-value semantics change, claims the issue is solved from scratch validation scripts alone, and has no visible consideration of subwidget required attributes or rendered form behavior.

experiences.title: Scoped Middleware Routing for Public Endpoint Fixes
experiences.description: Use when a Go/chi API task requires making one endpoint public while the surrounding router currently applies authentication globally.
experiences.context: Applies in Go web-server repositories using chi-style routers where endpoint access is controlled by middleware order or route groups, especially when the task asks to move a single static/capability endpoint out of authentication. Retrieve this when the trajectory has inspected or edited route registration and middleware setup, or has encountered chi middleware-ordering failures. It is less useful for tasks about handler response content, datastore behavior, or unrelated auth mechanisms. At very early exploration stages, do not over-credit merely finding the endpoint; the decisive evidence is a concrete route structure or validated plan that avoids global route-before-Use problems.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in this cluster should not merely ask whether the endpoint was placed before the authentication middleware. In chi, registering a route and then calling Use on the same mux can panic, so a superficially public route can still be structurally invalid. A strong criterion should require scoped routing: common non-auth middleware may remain outside, the intended endpoint must be registered outside the auth/last-access chain, and the rest of the API must remain under an authenticated group or subrouter. It should also penalize path-specific bypasses inside the authentication middleware, duplicate registrations, malformed route groups from scripted edits, or exposing unrelated protected endpoints. Prioritize visible evidence such as the order of r.Use and h/hr calls, use of r.Group or subrouters to contain authenticate and last-access middleware, grep/diff evidence that the endpoint is registered only once, and build/test output showing no chi middleware-ordering panic. Avoid a tempting but weak criterion that rewards generic task completion, early discovery of the route, or manual curl verification without checking whether the router structure preserves auth boundaries and compiles.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates a correct scoped-routing solution for making the specified capability endpoint unauthenticated while preserving authentication for the rest of the API. Evidence should show the public endpoint registered outside the authentication and authenticated-user-dependent middleware chain, protected endpoints enclosed in an authenticated group or subrouter, no route registered on a chi mux before later Use calls on that same mux, no duplicate endpoint registration, and validation by build/tests or equivalent inspection.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Correct Public/Protected Route Scoping

must_check: public endpoint registration is outside authenticate middleware
other API endpoints remain protected by authenticate
middleware ordering is valid for chi
no duplicate or malformed route group remains
compilation or targeted tests confirm router construction
anti_patterns: adding a route before later root Use calls on the same mux
hard-coded path bypass inside authentication middleware
removing authentication globally
crediting endpoint discovery without a viable route change

scale.1: No concrete route change or plan; trajectory only explores files or makes unrelated edits.
scale.2: Identifies the endpoint/auth middleware and proposes moving it, but lacks a valid scoped-routing design or risks exposing other routes.
scale.3: Registers or plans the endpoint outside auth, but leaves uncertainty about chi middleware ordering, duplicate registrations, or preservation of protected routes.
scale.4: Uses route grouping/subrouter structure that appears to make only the intended endpoint public and keep others authenticated, with minor validation gaps.
scale.5: Clearly implements or plans valid chi middleware scoping, keeps common middleware appropriate, protects all other endpoints, avoids duplicates/path hacks, and validates with build/tests or equivalent router-construction evidence.

experiences.title: Do not overcredit a surface-level filesystem contract restatement
experiences.description: Use this when a Go audit/logfile sink task asks for directory creation, append/create behavior, JSONL output, clean close, and explicit stat/mkdir/open errors, but the visible trajectory mostly inspects code or adds direct filesystem calls/manual checks.
experiences.context: Applies in Go repository trajectories around a logfile-backed audit sink where the task includes multiple behavioral obligations and failure-mode obligations. The misleading pattern is a rubric that simply restates the full runtime contract and then treats discovery of the target file, use of filepath/os.MkdirAll/os.OpenFile, or ad-hoc manual scripts as strong evidence. That can miss whether the implementation actually distinguishes directory check, directory creation, and open failures in a testable way, and whether validation is committed rather than temporary. The original broad contract rubric can still be appropriate at a final-review stage if the trajectory shows concrete code or tests covering each required behavior and failure mode; it is too optimistic during early exploration or after a minimal direct-MkdirAll edit with only manual local verification.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics asked whether the logfile sink creates parent directories, opens/appends the file, returns clear errors, writes newline-delimited JSON, and closes cleanly. That criterion is semantically relevant, but as generated it was too broad and easy to satisfy superficially: the existing code already used JSON encoding and close behavior, and a direct parent-directory creation call can appear to solve the main repro while leaving the explicit directory-check/create/open error contract weak or untestable. A better rubric should focus on visible evidence that the agent separates filesystem operations enough to observe and report check, create, and open failures distinctly, and that validation is encoded in committed package tests or an equivalent testable seam rather than only in throwaway scripts under temporary paths. Avoid a tempting criterion that gives high confidence merely because the agent imported filepath, called MkdirAll, ran a manual program, or restated that json.Encoder writes newlines. Prioritize evidence such as: a parent-directory stat/check before conditional creation; creation only for missing directories; contextual wrapping for non-existence, non-directory, creation, and open errors; preservation of append/create flags; committed tests using temporary directories or injected filesystem behavior to cover missing parent, existing file append, JSON-lines output, close, and failure cases; and cleanup of ad-hoc main programs.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear to satisfy the logfile sink task only by adding a direct directory-creation call or by manually exercising a happy path, without visible evidence that directory check, directory creation, and file open failures are distinguishable and testable. This flaw is especially important when the task explicitly asks for clear errors from each filesystem operation and verification of newline-delimited output.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Surface-Level Filesystem Fix Without Testable Failure Modes

metadata.environment: Go audit/logfile sink implementation
risk_signals: adds direct os.MkdirAll before os.OpenFile with little or no separate stat/check handling
manual test programs are created instead of committed package tests
manual validation depends on mutable /tmp state or deletes conflicting paths rather than testing the conflict behavior
rubric evidence relies on existing json.Encoder or Close implementation rather than newly verified JSONL/close behavior
no seam or test strategy exists for forcing stat, mkdir, and open errors independently
preferred_evidence: conditional parent-directory check with contextual errors for non-missing stat failures
directory creation only for missing parents with contextual creation errors
file open/create/append failure remains separately wrapped
committed tests or equivalent visible validation cover missing parent creation, existing file append, JSON line count/trailing newline, close behavior, and representative filesystem failures
temporary ad-hoc programs are removed before finalization

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory includes a testable implementation and committed validation for distinct check/create/open errors plus the JSONL, append/create, and close behaviors.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: most behavior and failure modes are covered, but one less central validation detail is only inspected manually or inferred from existing code.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory implements directory creation and preserves basic open/write/close behavior, but failure-mode separation or committed tests are incomplete.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory mainly adds direct MkdirAll/OpenFile logic and relies on manual happy-path scripts, with little proof of distinct error handling or durable validation.
scale.5: Most severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory only identifies the target or restates the contract, or adds a superficial filesystem change that can mask errors, leaves temporary artifacts, and provides no reliable validation of required failure modes or JSONL output.

experiences.title: Delay Macro-Renderer Judgment Until Concrete Parsing Behavior Is Visible
experiences.description: Use when generated rubrics demand the complete final macro handler during exploration rather than judging the first visible parsing implementation and its boundary cases.
experiences.context: Documentation-renderer tasks often begin with locating generic token-processing code because literal searches for the requested macro names can fail. Before an implementation exists, absence of the handlers is stage information, not evidence that the final patch will be wrong. Once replacement expressions are visible, the criterion should focus on exact output and avoiding false matches in ordinary parenthesized text.
experiences.experience: The previous criteria were task checklists applied too early, causing correct exploration to look like failure. A better negative rubric activates when visible regexes or handlers produce wrong link/reference/rule text, consume ordinary tokens, or fail multi-token input, especially if the agent claims completion. Avoid predicting failure solely from the handler not yet being written.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Overbroad or Incorrect Documentation-Macro Parsing
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize a visible renderer implementation when its macro matching produces incorrect output, consumes ordinary parenthesized words, or fails representative multi-token lines, or when completion is claimed without exercising those boundaries. Do not penalize an exploration-stage trajectory solely because concrete handlers are not yet present.

observable_evidence: current replacement expressions
representative link/reference/rule outputs
ordinary parenthesized non-match
multi-token rendering check
completion claim

scale.1: No visible evidence of an implemented macro parser visibly misrendering required tokens or matching unrelated text; the available implementation and validation evidence is consistent with the required behavior.
scale.2: A minor or early-stage concern about an implemented macro parser visibly misrendering required tokens or matching unrelated text is visible, but it is not confirmed and the trajectory is still actively resolving it.
scale.3: Evidence about an implemented macro parser visibly misrendering required tokens or matching unrelated text is mixed or incomplete; the concern remains plausible but is not yet decisive.
scale.4: Clear visible evidence indicates an implemented macro parser visibly misrendering required tokens or matching unrelated text, with no convincing correction or validation yet.
scale.5: The trajectory directly reproduces or validates an implemented macro parser visibly misrendering required tokens or matching unrelated text, or claims completion while the contradiction remains unresolved.

experiences.title: Verify actual optional-config defaulting, not just acceptance
experiences.description: Use when a Go/Viper-style configuration loader task adds an optional top-level version field with supported-version validation and defaulting semantics.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories for configuration-loading changes where the task requires an optional root-level config key, a supported value such as "1.0", backwards compatibility for configs omitting the key, and rejection of unsupported values during loading. It is especially relevant when the loader discovers validators/defaulters by reflecting over nested config fields, because a root-level validation method may not run automatically. This criterion is most useful once the agent has begun editing loader code, schemas, or tests. It is less useful during pure repository exploration, and it should not give credit merely because an app starts with a missing field or because an external schema was edited.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics correctly targeted the task contract, but several were too broad and could over-credit partial work. The discriminating evidence is not just that a `version` property exists or that configs without the field still load; the key is whether loading produces the intended semantic state: absent version becomes the supported version, explicit supported version is retained, unsupported version fails in the runtime load path, and schema/editor validation matches the same contract. In this code pattern, a common trap is adding `validate()` to the root config while the loader only collects validators from child fields, so the validation/defaulting never runs unless the root is explicitly included or the logic is called after unmarshal. Another tempting but weak proxy is a CLI/manual run that proceeds past config loading with no version; that proves compatibility, not default assignment. A better rubric should require visible code or tests showing actual assignment/defaulting in the loaded config object, unsupported-version rejection after unmarshalling, root-level validation invocation, synchronized schema updates, and regression tests/fixtures for missing, valid, and invalid versions. Avoid criteria that reward schema-only changes, nested object modeling for a scalar field, or passing the existing test suite without any version-specific assertion.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should provide concrete evidence that optional top-level configuration versioning is implemented end-to-end: the loader reads a scalar root `version` value, defaults an omitted value to the supported version in the resulting loaded configuration state, accepts the supported explicit value, rejects unsupported values during the normal config load path with a clear version-related error, ensures any root-level validation/defaulting is actually invoked despite reflection-based nested validator collection, keeps machine-readable schemas consistent with the same optional/enumerated/defaulted contract, and adds or updates tests/fixtures that directly exercise missing, valid, and invalid version cases.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-end optional config version contract

prioritize_evidence: loader code after unmarshal or root validation path that assigns/defaults the missing version or otherwise proves the loaded object has the supported version
runtime rejection path for unsupported versions, not just schema rejection
explicit inclusion/call of root-level validation when validator discovery only visits child fields
schema changes that add an optional top-level scalar version with supported values and default
tests or fixtures asserting missing version, explicit supported version, and unsupported version behavior
avoid_credit_for: schema-only edits
successful load/startup with missing version but no assertion that the loaded config version is defaulted
a root validate method that is never registered or called
a nested config object for a scalar top-level version key
manual smoke tests that do not inspect the loaded version value or invalid-version error
metadata.environment: Go project using Viper/mapstructure-style config loading with reflection-based defaulter/validator discovery and separate schema files

scale.1: No concrete implementation evidence for version loading/defaulting/validation, or current edits leave the loader syntactically broken.
scale.2: Only superficial or partial evidence, such as adding a schema property or struct field, with no reliable runtime validation/defaulting path.
scale.3: Some runtime support exists, but one major semantic piece is missing or unproven, such as root validation not being invoked, missing version merely being accepted rather than defaulted, or no invalid-version test.
scale.4: Strong implementation evidence covers root field loading, supported/unsupported runtime validation, and either defaulting or schema synchronization, but lacks complete tests or has minor consistency gaps.
scale.5: Complete visible evidence covers runtime loading, actual missing-version default assignment, supported and unsupported cases, root validation invocation, synchronized schemas, and direct tests/fixtures for the full contract.

experiences.title: Do not treat visible multi-select UI pieces as sufficient without lifecycle integration
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a React/TypeScript device/session-management task where existing selectable-row and selected-count header primitives are being wired for bulk sign-out.
experiences.context: This applies to implementation-stage trajectories in a Matrix/Element-style React settings UI where the active session list is rendered by a filtered device list inside a parent session manager, and sign-out uses an existing asynchronous/interactive-auth deletion flow. A broad checklist of checkboxes, selected count, bulk sign-out, cancel, and filter clearing is useful during early planning, but it becomes misleading once code edits exist: patches can visibly add all those elements while keeping selection state in the wrong layer, clearing it at the wrong time, breaking existing prop contracts, or bypassing the existing success callback. The original broad idea may still be appropriate for a first-pass scope-understanding rubric, or for a purely local UI mock with no asynchronous owner flow; it should not be the main correctness proxy for a real session sign-out integration.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded trajectories for implementing the obvious surface area: SelectableDeviceTile checkboxes, a selected-count header, Sign out/Cancel actions, selected ID state, and clearing on filter changes. Those criteria describe necessary user-visible behavior, but they overcredit patches that bolt local UI into the list without proving the state is coordinated with the parent session manager and existing sign-out lifecycle. In this codebase, the critical evidence is whether selected IDs are owned or exposed at the level that already owns sign-out and filter navigation, whether bulk sign-out reuses the existing multi-device deletion/interactive-auth path, whether selection is cleared after the sign-out flow actually succeeds rather than immediately after starting it, and whether filter changes/security-card navigation reliably clear selection. A better rubric should also watch for preservation of existing component contracts and tests: do not rewrite unrelated security-card copy, change exported component shape or prop signatures gratuitously, remove filter controls unexpectedly, alter pusher/notification handling, or break expand/detail click behavior while adding row selection. Avoid the tempting criterion that a patch is likely correct merely because it imports the selectable tile and displays bulk buttons; prioritize visible evidence of lifecycle-safe state flow, success-callback cleanup, filter-reset integration, and minimal, type-safe changes around existing components.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that implement only the surface multi-selection UI for device/session sign-out while lacking visible evidence that selection state and cleanup are integrated with the existing parent sign-out/filter lifecycle. This flaw is present when selected device IDs are kept only in the list with no way for the existing asynchronous sign-out success callback to clear them, when the UI clears selection immediately after invoking sign-out regardless of auth success/failure, when filter/security-recommendation navigation is not wired to clear selection, or when the patch breaks existing component contracts while adding the UI.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Surface-only multi-select without sign-out lifecycle integration

metadata.environment: React/TypeScript settings UI for device/session management
visible_evidence_to_check: location and ownership of selected device IDs relative to the component that owns sign-out and filter navigation
reuse of existing multi-device sign-out/deletion helper or callback
selection cleanup tied to successful sign-out completion rather than only button click
selection clearing on filter changes or security recommendation navigation
preservation of existing props, exports, pusher/notification handling, row expansion behavior, and localized strings
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: crediting checkboxes, selected-count text, and bulk buttons as sufficient by themselves

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory clearly coordinates selected IDs with the existing sign-out owner/lifecycle, clears selection on successful completion and filter changes, and preserves existing component contracts.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: most lifecycle integration is present, but one cleanup path or contract-preservation detail is only weakly evidenced.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the UI pieces are present, but selection ownership or cleanup timing is ambiguous, with limited evidence that the existing asynchronous sign-out flow can clear state correctly.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory adds checkboxes/header/actions but keeps selection local or clears it immediately after invoking sign-out, and does not show reliable integration with parent filter/sign-out lifecycle.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the patch is primarily surface UI, bypasses or misuses the existing sign-out flow, lacks reliable success/failure cleanup and filter reset behavior, and also changes unrelated behavior or breaks existing component contracts.

experiences.title: Do not equate queued display text with method-preserving warning/deprecation proxying
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating an Ansible-style forked-worker display fix where warnings/deprecations are deduplicated per process and worker output is routed through a final queue.
experiences.context: This applies to Python multiprocessing/fork code with a Display-like singleton, per-process warning/deprecation deduplication state, and an existing worker-to-main queue. A broad criterion such as “identical warnings/deprecations from workers are globally deduplicated” is useful only as an end-to-end behavior check after a complete implementation is visible. It is misleading during code review if it rewards merely sending formatted warning/deprecation text through the existing display queue, adding ad hoc message types without preserving full method arguments, or demonstrating conceptual understanding without a main-process dispatch path. The original idea remains appropriate when paired with evidence that the queued payload preserves the original display method identity and arguments and that the main process invokes the corresponding Display method before any worker-local formatting, config gating, or deduplication can occur.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often asked only whether worker warnings/deprecations were routed to the main process and globally deduplicated. That over-rewarded trajectories that understood the per-process _warns/_deprecations problem or queued messages, but still lost semantics: formatted DisplaySend payloads were handled by display.display() so warning/deprecation dedup was never run in the main process; custom warning/deprecation payloads sometimes dropped arguments such as formatting flags or deprecation metadata; some fixes performed deprecation config checks or formatting in the worker before proxying; and some patches changed the public display signature or tests instead of preserving existing behavior. A better rubric should focus on method-preserving proxy semantics: when a worker has the final queue set, display, warning, and deprecated should enqueue the original method name plus complete args/kwargs before local method logic executes, and the main queue consumer should dispatch to the same Display method so existing main-process formatting, config checks, and dedup dictionaries remain authoritative. Avoid the tempting criterion “uses _final_q/send_display for warnings/deprecations” unless the queued payload is shown to make the main process call warning()/deprecated(), not merely display already-formatted text. Replacement evidence should prioritize visible code paths for worker-side early proxying, queue payload structure, main-process dispatch, preservation of all method parameters, and validation that non-worker Display behavior and existing tests are not altered by test-only resets or signature hacks.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Formatted-output proxy loses method semantics
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize fixes for forked-worker display deduplication when the visible trajectory or patch routes warning/deprecation output as already-formatted display text, performs warning/deprecation formatting/config checks/deduplication in the worker before queueing, omits original method arguments from the queued payload, or changes public display/test behavior instead of making the main process invoke the original Display method. The flaw is absent only when worker-side proxying occurs before method-specific logic, the queue preserves method identity and complete args/kwargs for display/warning/deprecated, and the main queue consumer dispatches to the corresponding main-process method so existing main-process deduplication and formatting remain authoritative.

metadata.environment: Python forked-worker application with Display singleton, per-process warning/deprecation dedup state, and a final queue consumed by the main process
required_visible_evidence: worker-side branch when final queue is set occurs before warning/deprecation local formatting, config gating, or dedup state updates
queue payload records which Display method was called, not just the rendered message text
payload preserves all positional and keyword arguments needed by warning/deprecated/display
main-process queue consumer invokes the same Display method rather than always calling the low-level display method
non-worker behavior and existing Display method signatures/tests are preserved without test-only production APIs
misleading_proxy_evidence: send_display is called with formatted warning/deprecation strings
new WarningSend/DeprecatedSend payloads drop deprecation metadata or formatting flags
deprecated returns early in the worker based on warning configuration before proxying
deduplication is moved into low-level display using extra message_type keywords
trajectory only states conceptual understanding without showing consumer dispatch code

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: worker proxying preserves method identity and all arguments before local semantics, and main dispatch calls the corresponding Display methods while preserving existing non-worker behavior.
scale.2: Minor risk only: the design is method-preserving and main-dispatched, but one edge such as validation coverage or argument preservation is not fully demonstrated in the visible trajectory.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory identifies the need for main-process deduplication and has some queue routing, but visible evidence is incomplete about whether worker-local formatting/config checks are bypassed or whether all arguments are preserved.
scale.4: Clear flaw: warnings/deprecations are queued separately or through send_display, but the code either sends formatted text, drops method arguments, or lacks a main-process dispatch to warning()/deprecated().
scale.5: Severe flaw: the patch only changes local worker dedup/formatting or low-level display behavior, performs semantic checks in workers before queueing, changes public Display APIs/tests, or shows only conceptual understanding with no reliable end-to-end method-preserving proxy path.

experiences.title: End-to-End Default Config Schema Compatibility
experiences.description: Use when a Go configuration task requires exported default configuration and mapstructure decode hooks so hidden or added tests can decode defaults and validate them against a CUE/config schema.
experiences.context: Applies in Go repositories with an internal configuration package using Viper/mapstructure defaults plus a separate CUE or schema validation path, especially when the task explicitly says tests fail on missing exported identifiers but the expected behavior includes successful decoding and schema validation. This is most useful once the trajectory has moved beyond initial repository inspection into implementation planning, patching, or final review. It is less useful for tasks that only ask for a compile-time API export without schema semantics, for very early exploration before the agent has inspected config structs/defaulting/schema files, or when the schema validation path is not part of the acceptance behavior.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful criterion was not merely whether the agent noticed the missing exported names. It was whether the trajectory provided evidence that the exported defaults and decode hooks actually form a schema-valid default configuration. In these situations, agents often fixate on grepping for visible tests, renaming a private decode hook slice, or copying an existing test helper into production. Those are necessary but weak signals: they can satisfy symbol lookup while still leaving duration fields, omitted zero nested structs, storage/experimental/auth/database fields, mapstructure tags, or CUE schema definitions incompatible with the serialized default config. A better rubric should ask for end-to-end compatibility evidence: the exported hook list preserves the existing duration/enum/slice conversions used by normal loading; DefaultConfig returns the same fully defaulted shape users/tests expect; and the agent has either run or added a validation path that marshals/decodes the exported default config and checks it against the relevant CUE/config schema. Prioritize visible evidence such as schema inspection, changes that align Go structs/tags/default values with schema-accepted fields and duration formats, targeted tests or commands exercising exported DefaultConfig plus DecodeHooks, and avoidance of divergent duplicate hook lists. Avoid the tempting narrower criterion that says copying the visible defaultConfig helper or exporting DecodeHooks is sufficient; in this task family, final correctness depends on the decoded default config crossing the schema boundary successfully.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the new public configuration API is not only present but schema-compatible: the exported decode hooks preserve the package's existing mapstructure conversions, the exported default configuration represents the complete post-default configuration shape, and the agent validates or reasons concretely that this decoded/defaulted output is accepted by the CUE/config schema, including duration fields, optional nested structs, and mapstructure/json field names.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Exported Defaults Validate Against Schema

required_visible_evidence: public DefaultConfig and DecodeHooks are implemented or explicitly planned with exact names
DecodeHooks reuse or preserve existing duration, enum, and string/slice conversion behavior
DefaultConfig is checked against the same defaults produced by the normal loading path or canonical test helper
schema compatibility is addressed directly, not inferred from compile success alone
validation evidence includes a targeted test/command or concrete inspection of fields that the schema may reject
metadata.common_false_positive: The trajectory only exports symbols or copies defaults but never checks whether the serialized/decoded default config passes the CUE/config schema.

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward exported defaults/hooks or schema compatibility; the trajectory is mostly redundant searching or unrelated build checks.
scale.2: Recognizes missing exported API names but provides little or no implementation or schema-validation reasoning.
scale.3: Implements or plans DefaultConfig and DecodeHooks, but evidence is limited to compile/build success or copying existing defaults, with no convincing check of CUE/schema compatibility.
scale.4: Exports the API while preserving existing decode behavior and compares defaults to the normal loading/test default shape; also inspects likely schema compatibility issues such as durations and optional nested fields.
scale.5: Provides strong end-to-end evidence: exported defaults are decoded with exported hooks and validated against the relevant CUE/config schema through a targeted test/command or equivalent concrete verification, with any schema/model mismatches corrected.

experiences.title: Do not score renewal-toggle tasks on modal copy alone
experiences.description: Retrieve when a React/TypeScript subscription auto-pay task asks for a confirmation modal plus hook extraction, especially after the agent has started editing a toggle/hook implementation.
experiences.context: Applies in monorepo React/TypeScript UI code where a subscription renewal/auto-pay toggle is being refactored into a hook and a modal flow. The misleading pattern is generating a rubric that only checks the high-level confirmation condition and required modal text, then treats the trajectory as promising even when the visible work shows risky hook placement, imports/exports, modal API misuse, stale async state, or missing integration with the actual toggle component. The original modal-copy criterion is still appropriate as one subcriterion when the implementation is otherwise integrated and buildable, or when the task is specifically about content/UX text. During early repository exploration with no edits, avoid implementation-completeness rubrics and instead evaluate whether the agent is locating the real shared payments component and relevant modal/API patterns.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics repeatedly required: show the modal only when disabling auto-pay, use VPN/non-VPN text, proceed directly when enabling, and expose the modal through a hook. That criterion is semantically relevant but too narrow for judging trajectory quality once code is being written. It misses common visible failure modes: creating a hook but not exporting/importing it consistently, moving it to an unexpected package path, using modal components with the wrong props or lifecycle, comparing enum values with magic numbers, calling the API for enabling through a confirm handler before pending state is set, not closing the modal on cancel, or failing to update the original toggle component at all. A better rubric should be stage-aware: before edits, reward accurate localization of the existing renewal toggle, API, enum, modal utility, and tests; after edits, focus on whether the extracted hook is actually buildable and preserves the renewal state machine and side effects. Avoid the tempting wrong criterion that the presence of the required sentence and a conditional modal is enough. Prioritize visible evidence from the changed code: imports/exports compile, the UI renders the hook-provided modal, the toggle is bound to `RenewState`-based state, the API call receives the intended next state on both disable-confirm and direct-enable paths, cancel performs no API/state mutation, modal close/resolve handlers are wired to the chosen modal API, and existing notifications/event-manager behavior is preserved.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a React/TypeScript subscription auto-pay refactor after the agent has begun editing the toggle or hook, penalize implementations that appear to satisfy the modal copy/branching requirement but show visible integration or state-machine defects: inconsistent hook file location/import/export, use of an incompatible modal API or missing close/resolve behavior, enum comparisons replaced with magic numbers, direct-enable paths that call the confirm/API logic before the intended next renewal state is available, cancel paths that can still mutate state or leave the modal stuck, missing render of the hook-provided modal in the UI component, or loss of existing API/event-manager/notification side effects. Do not apply this as a failure criterion when the trajectory is still pure repository exploration with no attempted implementation.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Fragile renewal hook and modal integration

metadata.environment: React TypeScript monorepo subscription/payments UI
visible_evidence: changed hook or toggle component
imports/exports for the new hook
modal component usage and handlers
renewal state transition code
API/event-manager/notification side effects
metadata.do_not_use_when: no implementation exists yet; use a localization/exploration rubric instead

scale.1: No evidence of integration or state-machine flaws: the hook and component are consistently wired, use the project modal API correctly, preserve side effects, and handle disable-confirm, cancel, and direct-enable paths with the intended renewal state.
scale.2: Minor concerns only, such as slightly awkward naming or placement, but the visible code still appears buildable and the modal/state/API paths are coherent.
scale.3: Moderate risk: the modal text/branching is present, but there is incomplete evidence that imports/exports, modal close handling, or one transition path is correctly wired.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the code likely misuses the modal API, omits rendering/exporting the hook, mishandles cancel/enable behavior, or risks sending the wrong renewal state despite containing the required modal copy.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the implementation is visibly unbuildable or the renewal flow is fundamentally broken, such as missing the UI integration entirely, using stale pending state for API calls, or allowing cancel/enabling paths to mutate state incorrectly.

experiences.title: Underlying-module redirect propagation is necessary but not sufficient
experiences.description: Retrieve when an Ansible task concerns module_defaults through wrapper action plugins and the trajectory fix/rubric focuses mainly on passing the underlying module's loader redirect_list to get_action_args_with_defaults.
experiences.context: Applies in Ansible-style codebases where action plugins such as fact gathering, package, or service wrappers dynamically execute another module, and the task requires module_defaults to work across short names, FQCNs, and ansible.legacy aliases. The tempting criterion—checking that the action plugin resolves the underlying module and passes its redirect_list—is relevant when evaluating one necessary part of the fix. It becomes misleading if used as the main or complete success criterion, especially after the trajectory has already identified or implemented that local change, because the task also depends on alias lookup semantics in the shared module_defaults merger and on gather_facts-specific state handling. The original idea is still appropriate as a subcriterion for action-plugin argument construction, but not as a standalone rubric for final patch correctness.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics rewarded trajectories for recognizing or implementing that gather_facts/package/service should pass the actually executed module's redirect_list to get_action_args_with_defaults instead of the wrapper task's redirect list. That is a valid necessary behavior, but it overstates correctness for this task. A patch that only changes the action plugins can still miss module_defaults defined under the short module name when the executed name is ansible.legacy.* or otherwise alias-resolved, because the shared default-merging helper may need to translate or consider alias forms consistently. It can also miss gather_facts requirements such as copying configured facts modules before replacing smart mode so global/config state is not mutated. When generating rubrics for this situation, avoid a single broad criterion saying redirect list propagation proves consistency across FQCN/short/legacy names. Instead, split the evaluation: one criterion for using the loaded underlying module's redirect context in each wrapper, another for the shared module_defaults lookup handling legacy/short-name equivalence, and another for gather_facts preserving smart/config behavior. Prioritize visible evidence such as edits to the common defaults merger, explicit handling of ansible.legacy-to-short-name defaults, non-mutating copies of configuration lists, and targeted tests or debugging of alias/FQCN cases, rather than repeated reasoning or local synthetic checks that only exercise redirect-list passing.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Overclaiming redirect-list propagation as complete defaults support
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat passing the underlying module's loader redirect_list from wrapper action plugins to get_action_args_with_defaults as sufficient for the whole task, while lacking visible work on the shared module_defaults alias-matching semantics and gather_facts-specific non-mutation requirement. This flaw is especially important when the task explicitly requires equivalent behavior for short names, FQCNs, and ansible.legacy aliases.

metadata.environment: Ansible action plugins and module_defaults resolution
metadata.misleading_proxy: Only checking that gather_facts/package/service call module_loader.find_plugin_with_context for the underlying module and pass context.redirect_list
better_evidence: The common defaults-merging logic is inspected or changed so ansible.legacy alias execution can also apply defaults keyed by the corresponding short module name when appropriate
Action plugins use the redirect context of the actually selected underlying module, not the wrapper action's stored redirect list
gather_facts copies configured facts module lists before replacing smart mode or otherwise avoids mutating shared configuration
The trajectory validates or reasons about FQCN, short-name, and ansible.legacy cases separately, rather than only synthetic redirect-list merging

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory treats redirect-list propagation as one subproblem and also addresses or plans to verify shared alias/default lookup and gather_facts non-mutation behavior.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory emphasizes action-plugin redirect-list propagation but still acknowledges other required alias or gather_facts behaviors as unresolved.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory implements or plans only the action-plugin redirect-list change and gives limited attention to shared defaults-merging alias semantics or gather_facts config mutation.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory claims consistency across short/FQCN/ansible.legacy names based mainly on passing the underlying redirect_list, with no visible inspection or modification of the common defaults lookup and no gather_facts smart-mode non-mutation handling.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory repeatedly or confidently concludes the fix is complete from redirect-list propagation alone despite failing/unfinished validation, absent code edits, or visible tests indicating unresolved gather_facts/alias behavior.

experiences.title: Optional Room Safety Over Blanket Feature Guarding
experiences.description: Retrieve when a React/TypeScript UI task involves an optional room-like prop plus a server feature-support flag, and the trajectory is evaluating guards around notification state, event listeners, rendering, and panel-opening actions.
experiences.context: Applies in a web React/TypeScript component where the task reports crashes from both an unsupported notification capability and a missing optional entity prop. The visible trajectory should show evidence such as an optional prop declaration, direct property reads on that prop, child components or store/hook calls that require a real entity, and a feature-support branch that selects between modern and fallback notification behavior. This is most useful at patch-review or late implementation stages when the agent has inspected the relevant component and dependencies. Do not apply as a blanket rule when the codebase has no legacy/fallback behavior for the feature, when the unsupported flag truly means the whole feature is unavailable, or when the trajectory has not yet identified any concrete room-dependent dereference sites.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this pattern often asked only whether all thread-related code was guarded by the feature-support check. That criterion is too broad and can be misleading: a support flag may distinguish modern notification support from a legacy notification-state path, not necessarily whether the whole threads UI should disappear. It can also overvalue patches that hide or no-op thread actions while still leaving missing-room crashes in render paths, child button props, or store calls. A better rubric should require a complete audit of every runtime path that can dereference the optional room: constructor initialization, notification color getters/update callbacks, lifecycle listener registration, right-panel toggle arguments, and child components/hooks/stores that assume a real room. It should also require nullable/default-safe handling of thread notification state and respect the observed feature-support boundary: guard unsupported notification accesses/actions as required by the task, but do not treat `supportsThreadNotifications` as a substitute for missing-room safety or as proof that unrelated UI rewrites are correct. Avoid using passing typecheck or a narrow targeted test as the sole proxy if the visible diff still renders children with an undefined room or shows file corruption from broad edits. Prioritize concrete visible evidence: optional prop types, dependency methods that dereference the prop, diff hunks adding early returns or conditional rendering before room-dependent children, safe defaults such as no notification color when state is absent, and clean validation after the final diff.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Comprehensive Optional Entity and Feature-Support Safety
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the component safely handles both a missing optional room-like prop and an unsupported notification capability across all relevant runtime paths. Strong evidence includes identifying that the prop is optional, identifying downstream calls that require a real room, ensuring render paths do not pass an absent room into child components or stores that dereference it, making notification state nullable or default-safe, guarding lifecycle subscriptions and property reads, and handling thread/panel actions according to the actual support semantics visible in the codebase rather than blindly disabling or enabling all thread behavior. The judgment should be based on inspected code and final diff evidence, with validation only strengthening an already complete semantic fix.

prioritize_evidence: optional prop declaration or visible possibility of null/undefined input
direct property reads or store/hook calls requiring a real room
render-level guards or conditional child rendering before room-dependent code
nullable/default-safe notification state handling
feature-support branch used consistently with observed legacy versus modern behavior
clean final diff and validation after the last edit
avoid_as_primary_proxy: blanket requirement that every thread-related path be gated by the support flag
narrow tests passing while render still passes undefined room to unsafe children
intentions or comments without corresponding code changes
large unrelated rewrites or syntactically corrupted files

scale.1: No concrete evidence that missing-room or unsupported-notification crash paths were identified or addressed.
scale.2: Some direct property accesses are guarded, but major runtime paths such as child rendering, store calls, lifecycle callbacks, or nullable notification state remain unaddressed.
scale.3: Comparable to the parent trajectory: partial guards or investigation exist, but the evidence does not establish complete safety across both missing-room and unsupported-notification scenarios.
scale.4: Strong evidence of a broad audit and coherent fixes for most room-dependent and notification-dependent paths, with only minor uncertainty about an edge path or validation coverage.
scale.5: Clear final evidence that all room-dependent render/callback/lifecycle/store paths are safe, thread notification state has safe defaults, feature-support behavior matches the codebase semantics and task constraints, the diff is coherent and minimal, and validation was run after the final edits.

experiences.title: End-to-End Package Identity Alignment
experiences.description: Use when a package lookup bug involves multiple Red Hat RPM architectures or versions and the trajectory exposes a mismatch between RPM-derived identifiers, fully qualified package strings, and a name-keyed package collection.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go scanner/package-management codebase where Red Hat RPM queries return name, epoch, version, release, and architecture; package records include architecture; lookup paths use a fully qualified package identifier; and the main package collection is visibly keyed or updated by package name. This criterion is most useful after the agent has inspected both the identifier formatting and the storage/update paths. It is premature during initial exploration before the map keying and lookup call sites are known. It should not be used as a rigid requirement to globally change all package-map keys if the visible codebase has a deliberate name-keyed contract and many consumers index by package name; in that boundary, an equally valid fix may instead align owner-package lookup to the existing name-keyed storage while preserving correct Red Hat behavior.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster correctly noticed that merely appending architecture to a fully qualified package string is not enough when installed packages are stored and written back under package names: same-name RPM variants can be overwritten or later looked up using an identifier that the map cannot represent. This made the criterion discriminative for trajectories that only changed string formatting, repeatedly inspected the same snippets, or edited unrelated Debian architecture handling while leaving Red Hat package association inconsistent. However, the tempting wording 'must change the data structure to FQPN keys or a nested map' is too narrow. In this kind of repository, broad key changes can break report, vulnerability, Debian, and other name-based consumers. A better rubric should ask whether the trajectory establishes one coherent package identity contract across RPM query output, parsing, lookup, existence checks, and write-back: either preserve all Red Hat variants with a fully audited unique-key strategy, or intentionally convert process-owner results to package names when updating a name-keyed collection. The judge should prioritize visible evidence that the agent has audited all producers and consumers of the package identifier, handled both running-process and need-restart association paths, avoided unverified or corrupted edits, and added targeted duplicate-architecture/version tests. Avoid giving credit for passing broad tests alone when no test exercises duplicate same-name RPM packages, and avoid penalizing a name-preserving design solely because it did not globally re-key the package map.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate an end-to-end identity strategy for Red Hat package ownership lookup under duplicate package names. Excellent progress means the agent recognizes that RPM owner queries, parsed package records, fully qualified package strings, package-map keys, existence checks, and write-back sites must all agree. The solution direction may either preserve multiple architecture/version variants with a carefully audited unique key, or keep the existing package-name map contract and change Red Hat owner lookup to return/update by compatible package names. It should explicitly avoid a superficial fix that only changes the formatted fully qualified package string while leaving name-key overwrite or lookup mismatches unresolved, and it should account for compatibility with non-Red-Hat/name-keyed consumers.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Coherent Package Identity Contract

required_visible_evidence: RPM query output includes architecture/version information and package records parse it
The package collection or update sites are keyed by package name
Lookup or association paths use fully qualified identifiers or compare against formatted package identity
The agent audits both lookup producers and package update/write-back consumers
acceptable_solution_families: Audited variant-preserving keying or data structure that keeps duplicate same-name packages addressable
Targeted Red Hat owner-package lookup that returns package names compatible with the existing name-keyed collection
common_failure_modes: Only appending architecture to a formatted identifier
Changing global package keys without auditing name-based consumers
Editing Debian architecture handling for a Red Hat-specific lookup issue
Relying on generic passing tests without duplicate same-name package coverage

scale.1: No meaningful recognition of the package identity mismatch; changes are absent, unrelated, or only repeated inspection with no plan.
scale.2: Notices one surface symptom such as missing architecture in a formatted package string, but does not address package-map keying, lookup producers, and write-back consumers together.
scale.3: Recognizes both formatted identifier mismatch and name-key collision risk, but the implementation or plan remains incomplete, unverified, or likely to break existing name-based consumers.
scale.4: Provides a coherent targeted strategy for Red Hat package association, auditing the relevant parse, lookup, existence-check, and update paths while preserving or explicitly adapting the package-map identity contract.
scale.5: Fully aligns package identity end to end, including running-process and restart-needed association paths, compatibility with name-keyed/non-Red-Hat consumers, safe editing, and focused tests or reproductions for duplicate same-name architecture/version packages.

experiences.title: Expose Existing Internal Command Options Through the Shared CLI Path
experiences.description: Use this when a Django-style management command task asks to make an existing internal/stealth option available from the command line, especially when execution logic already consumes the option.
experiences.context: Apply in a Python/Django-like management command framework after the trajectory has identified or edited the shared command parser, the existing execution-time option key, and the programmatic command invocation path. The criterion is most useful once there is visible evidence of parser wiring, execution semantics, or compatibility checks. It is premature during repository discovery before the agent has found the parser/execution flow. It may not apply to a brand-new option with no existing execution hook, to a command-specific flag that belongs only in one command, or to a task that intentionally changes broader behavior such as migration checks rather than only automatic system checks.
experiences.experience: For these cases, the useful rubrics focused on whether `--skip-checks` is wired into the common management-command CLI as the existing `skip_checks` option and whether that value flows into the already-present system-check bypass. That was more discriminative than merely checking that help output contains the flag. A better rubric should reward evidence that the agent uses the shared parser rather than per-command hacks, uses a boolean CLI action that produces the same option key consumed by execution, preserves default CLI behavior when the flag is absent, skips only automatic system checks when present, and does not regress programmatic invocation behavior such as omitted versus explicit `skip_checks` values. It should also value validation on a command that actually runs automatic checks, preferably by mocking/registering a check failure; testing only the `check` command, commands that opt out of automatic checks, or `--help` output is a weak proxy. Avoid an overly rigid criterion that requires keeping an option in a stealth-options list unchanged, because once it is parser-defined, compatibility depends on the programmatic invocation path and defaults, not the exact list membership. Also avoid making exact help ordering or patch shape the main criterion unless the trajectory has explicit evidence that the project enforces common-option help ordering. Prioritize visible evidence of semantic wiring, backward compatibility, adjacent parser syntax remaining intact, and meaningful behavioral validation.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Shared CLI Wiring Preserves Existing Skip-Check Semantics
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the new `--skip-checks` command-line flag is added through the shared management-command parser, maps to the existing `skip_checks` option consumed by command execution, defaults to normal system-check execution when absent, skips only automatic system checks when present, and preserves existing programmatic invocation semantics for omitted and explicit `skip_checks` values.

required_visible_evidence: The option is added in the shared/common parser path rather than duplicated in individual commands.
The CLI action stores a boolean value under the same option key already used by the execution path.
The existing execution guard for automatic system checks is reused rather than replaced with a separate code path.
Programmatic command invocation remains compatible for omitted `skip_checks` and explicit true/false values.
Adjacent common options and parser syntax are not corrupted by the edit.
strong_validation_evidence: Parser/help or parse-result evidence shows the flag is accepted and defaults correctly.
Behavioral validation uses a command that normally performs automatic system checks and shows checks are bypassed only when the flag is supplied.
Validation does not rely solely on `--help`, on a command that implements checks manually, or on commands that opt out of automatic system checks.
boundary_conditions: Do not require a specific internal list membership if parser-defined options already participate in programmatic validation.
Treat help ordering or conditional display for commands that do not run checks as secondary unless project conventions or tests make it explicit.
Do not credit changes that skip migration checks or other unrelated validations unless the task explicitly requests that behavior.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the CLI flag is connected to the existing management-command option or execution path; changes may be absent, per-command only, or syntactically broken.
scale.2: Weak evidence of parser exposure, such as a tentative flag insertion or help-output check, but unclear mapping to the existing option key, no behavioral validation, or visible risk of breaking adjacent parser/programmatic behavior.
scale.3: Moderate evidence equivalent to the parent state: the flag is plausibly added to the shared parser and maps to `skip_checks`, but validation is limited or compatibility with programmatic invocation and automatic-check semantics remains only partially examined.
scale.4: Strong evidence that the shared parser wiring, default false CLI behavior, execution-time skip behavior, and programmatic compatibility have been considered or tested, with no visible parser corruption or unrelated behavior changes.
scale.5: Complete evidence: the shared CLI flag is cleanly wired to the existing execution option, automatic system checks run by default and are skipped only when requested, programmatic invocation semantics are preserved, unrelated checks are unaffected, and focused tests or equivalent behavioral validation cover both parser acceptance and real check bypass.

experiences.title: Scheme-aware OCI repository validation as a behavioral criterion
experiences.description: Use this when a Go/Viper configuration task explicitly requires OCI storage configs to reject unsupported repository URL schemes with clear errors, and the trajectory has reached config-validation implementation or review.
experiences.context: Applies to backend configuration fixes where an OCI-like storage backend has a repository/reference field, optional URL schemes, schema/default parsing, and runtime store wiring. The criterion is most useful once the trajectory has inspected or edited the config validation path and reference parsing behavior, especially when examples include unsupported schemes such as `unknown://registry/repo:tag`. It is less useful during pure exploration with no implementation evidence, and it is not sufficient by itself when the task also requires schema support, default values, authentication, poll interval, or backend wiring. Do not apply it as a broad requirement to reject every bare or scheme-less reference unless the visible design says those forms are invalid; some backends intentionally default scheme-less references or support local references.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics were useful because the task made invalid OCI repository references a first-class acceptance requirement, and the visible trajectories repeatedly exposed the key decision point: config validation was using or considering a generic registry parser while the backend had its own scheme policy. A good rubric should judge the observable behavior: unsupported schemes are rejected during configuration loading with an actionable message, while supported forms remain accepted and the remaining reference is still structurally validated. The rubric should not overfit to a specific implementation such as requiring one exact parser function; an equivalent explicit scheme check plus registry/reference validation can be correct. It should also avoid the tempting but wrong proxy of requiring rejection of bare registry-looking strings in all cases, because the backend may intentionally allow scheme-less or local/default references. Prioritize concrete evidence visible in the trajectory: edits in the config validation path rather than only runtime parsing, a test fixture or command using the unsupported-scheme example, preservation of supported `http`, `https`, and local/default semantics if documented, clear wrapped error text naming the invalid scheme or allowed schemes, and no test changes that simply replace the failing case with an unrelated malformed value. If the trajectory is mainly adding server wiring or parsing fields without touching validation, this criterion should score low even if those other changes are useful.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate scheme-aware OCI repository validation at configuration-load time: missing repositories are rejected, unsupported URL schemes such as `unknown://...` fail with a clear actionable error, supported schemes and documented scheme-less/local forms are not accidentally rejected, and the underlying repository/reference is still structurally validated. Strong evidence includes concrete code or tests in the config validation path, not merely runtime parsing or stated intent.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Config-time OCI reference validation

required_visible_evidence: configuration validation path for the OCI repository field is inspected or modified
unsupported scheme examples are considered, preferably matching the task's `unknown://registry/repo:tag` style
error messaging is clear about invalid/unsupported schemes or allowed schemes
valid supported reference forms remain accepted according to the backend's documented semantics
avoid_overfitting_to: one exact parser function or package when equivalent behavior is implemented
rejecting all bare or scheme-less references without confirming they are invalid
runtime-only parsing that does not produce configuration-load validation errors

scale.1: No visible evidence that OCI repository validation is addressed, or the trajectory only explores unrelated files.
scale.2: Mentions invalid repository validation or inspects parsers, but makes no concrete config-validation change or test plan.
scale.3: Adds partial validation or relies on an existing/generic parser, but scheme handling, supported-form compatibility, or clear error behavior remains uncertain.
scale.4: Implements or tests config-time rejection of unsupported schemes with reasonably clear errors while preserving expected valid references, though coverage or wording may be incomplete.
scale.5: Provides clear, behavior-focused config validation with tests or fixtures for unsupported schemes, missing repositories, and valid supported references, with actionable errors and no unsupported narrowing of accepted OCI reference forms.

experiences.title: Do not let SQL Server error classifiers substitute for end-to-end diagnostic integration
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go/Teleport-style connection diagnostic task asks for a new database protocol and the visible trajectory is focusing on protocol-specific error categorization. The warning is especially relevant if the agent has not yet proven that the new pinger is registered, uses the correct driver path, compiles, and preserves existing database diagnostic contracts.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go backend repository where database connection diagnostics already use a protocol-specific pinger/factory pattern. The misleading rubric pattern is to judge mostly on whether SQL Server connection-refused/auth/invalid-database errors are categorized, even though the visible trajectory may still be missing the protocol dispatch wiring, may have corrupted a switch while editing, may be using an invalid driver API/name, or may be modifying unrelated database validation, RBAC, or common server error pipelines. Error categorization remains a useful criterion only after there is visible evidence that the new protocol pinger is actually reachable through the existing diagnostic flow and builds against the repository's SQL Server driver.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics overemphasized SQL Server error-code/message classification, and in one case even required integration with a common database error conversion pipeline. That led judgments to overvalue patches that had elaborate classifiers but were not wired into the diagnostic factory, used the wrong driver interface or driver name, failed to compile, or changed unrelated shared behavior such as database-name validation, role matching, or server-side error conversion. For connection-diagnostic feature tasks, generate a rubric that first checks the end-to-end diagnostic path: a protocol-specific SQL Server pinger exists, it is selected by the existing database tester for the SQL Server protocol, it uses the repository's registered SQL Server database/sql driver correctly, it validates the same request fields expected by the diagnostic flow unless the task explicitly changes that contract, and build/test evidence covers the touched packages. Avoid a tempting criterion that treats broad SQL Server error-code mapping as the main signal, or that requires common server error handling changes not used by the diagnostic pinger flow. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence of factory registration, correct driver/API usage, preservation of existing shared contracts, successful compilation after edits, and only then lightweight classifiers for the requested failure categories.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear to implement SQL Server diagnostic support mainly by adding error-category predicates or broad error-code mappings while lacking reliable evidence that the new protocol is actually reachable through the existing database connection diagnostic path. This includes missing or malformed protocol dispatch wiring, use of an unregistered or nonexistent SQL Server driver/API, compile errors after edits, wholesale rewrites or corrupted switch statements in the diagnostic package, or unrelated changes to shared validation/RBAC/common database error conversion that are not required for the connection diagnostic pinger.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Classifier-only or miswired SQL Server diagnostic implementation

metadata.environment: Go backend repository with protocol-specific database connection diagnostic pingers
prioritize_evidence: new SQL Server pinger is registered in the existing database diagnostic factory
