pinger uses the repository-supported SQL Server database/sql driver and connection string/API correctly
existing request validation and role/RBAC behavior are not changed unless explicitly justified by the task
build or focused tests are rerun after the final relevant edits
error classification exists for the requested categories after the pinger is reachable
avoid_overweighting: large lists of SQL Server error numbers without integration evidence
changes to common database server error conversion as a substitute for diagnostic pinger classification
tests that exercise only classifier helpers while the diagnostic factory is not wired

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory shows a minimal, compiled pinger integrated into the existing diagnostic factory, with requested classifiers and no unrelated shared-behavior changes.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: integration and driver usage are mostly correct, but classifier work is somewhat overemphasized or validation/build evidence is incomplete.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: classifier implementation is present, but visible evidence of factory wiring, driver correctness, or post-edit compilation is partial or uncertain.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory spends effort on SQL Server error mapping while missing or corrupting key diagnostic integration, using questionable driver APIs, or changing unrelated shared contracts.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the implementation is primarily classifier/error-pipeline work and the new SQL Server diagnostic path is not reliably reachable or buildable, or the agent introduced broad unrelated changes that risk regressions.

experiences.title: Avoid factory-only rubrics for new ModelForm Meta options
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django ModelForm task says a behavior should be specified through `Meta`, but the trajectory focuses on making a factory inherit an existing base-form value or avoiding a default `None` overwrite.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django forms/model-forms environment when the task is not merely about one factory keyword default, but about making a `ModelForm` `Meta` option participate in field construction. The misleading case is a trajectory that changes only dynamic factory class attributes so `modelform_factory(model, form=BaseForm)` appears to preserve `BaseForm.Meta.formfield_callback`, often validated with ad hoc tests where the base form also has a class-level callback or only the factory form is inspected. The original inheritance/precedence idea may still be appropriate if the codebase already parses the current form class's own `Meta` option into the normal form options object and the only visible bug is a factory passing an unwanted default value. It is not sufficient when direct `ModelForm` creation with a callback defined only in `Meta` would still bypass that callback.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked whether `modelform_factory()` preserves a base form's `Meta.formfield_callback` when no explicit callback is supplied and allows explicit overrides. That criterion is directionally relevant but too narrow: it can rate a factory-only patch highly even when the underlying ModelForm option plumbing still does not read the current class's own `Meta.formfield_callback` during model-field-to-form-field construction. For tasks phrased as allowing a `ModelForm` Meta option, generate a rubric that distinguishes visible `Meta` inheritance from actual callback use in the metaclass/options field-building path. The better rubric should look for evidence that the callback is stored/read as a normal Meta option and passed into field generation for both direct forms and factory-created forms. Avoid the tempting criterion that checking `FactoryForm.Meta.formfield_callback` or factory field `required` flags alone proves correctness; those can pass due to inherited attributes or duplicated class attrs while direct Meta-only forms remain wrong. Prioritize visible evidence such as tests or reasoning covering a form with callback defined only inside `Meta` and no class-level callback, plus confirmation that explicit factory callbacks still flow through the same option path rather than special-case inheritance hacks.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory is flawed if it treats the issue as only a `modelform_factory()` default-argument inheritance problem and does not show that a callback declared solely on a ModelForm's own `Meta` is consumed by the normal form field construction path. This includes patches or plans that only omit/conditionally set a generated class attribute, manually copy a parent `Meta` callback in the factory, or validate only factory-created forms, without evidence that direct Meta-only forms and factory-created forms both invoke the callback when fields are built.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Factory-only Meta callback fix

metadata.environment: Django ModelForm and model form factory code
metadata.risk_signal: trajectory focuses on generated factory class attributes or inherited parent Meta values
required_visible_evidence: the normal ModelForm options/metaclass path reads the current class's Meta callback
field construction receives that callback
tests or reasoning include a callback defined only in Meta, not also as a class attribute
factory explicit callback behavior remains covered
misleading_evidence_to_discount: a base form that also defines a class-level callback

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory explicitly integrates the Meta callback into the standard ModelForm option/field-building path and covers direct Meta-only and factory-created forms.
scale.2: Minor concern: the trajectory mostly uses the standard option path but has limited test evidence for direct Meta-only forms or explicit factory callback behavior.
scale.3: Mixed evidence: the trajectory recognizes both factory inheritance and direct Meta semantics but implementation or tests still rely partly on special-case factory handling.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory changes only factory class-attribute handling or parent-Meta copying and validates factory behavior, with no convincing direct Meta-only coverage.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory explicitly assumes preserving `FactoryForm.Meta.formfield_callback` or avoiding `None` in factory attrs is sufficient, while leaving the general ModelForm Meta option ignored during field generation.

experiences.title: Do not let generic resilient-parsing rubrics mask XAttr API/typing compatibility
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a TypeScript Drive/XAttr refactor where the agent is changing extended-attribute helper signatures, parser typing, encryption/decryption wrappers, and call sites. Be careful if a proposed rubric focuses only on malformed-input parsing or broadly demands every helper use an options object.
experiences.context: Applies in a TypeScript monorepo with Drive extended-attribute utilities that serialize/encrypt structured metadata and parse decrypted JSON. The misleading pattern is a trajectory that adds try/catch parsing, neutral fallback objects, or broad new option interfaces, but also rewrites unrelated helper behavior, changes public parse/decrypt return contracts, leaves type errors, corrupts call sites, or over-scopes the object-parameter migration. A resilient-parsing rubric is still appropriate when the visible work is specifically on parser helpers and preserves existing valid-input shapes, but it should not be the dominant correctness proxy for a refactor whose success depends on localized signature migration, strict partial-input typing, and unchanged encryption/decryption semantics.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often generated criteria such as “parsing must tolerate empty/invalid input, normalize known fields, ignore unknowns, and leave missing values unset,” or “all creation/parsing helpers must accept a single options object.” Those criteria are tempting because they restate the task, but they become misleading when judged from trajectories that show partial rewrites: an agent can satisfy the visible parsing checklist while breaking decryption return shape, changing the parse API from a serialized string to an options object, making folder helpers incompatible unnecessarily, introducing TypeScript errors, or failing to update the actual upload/folder call sites safely. Conversely, demanding that parsing itself or every creation/encryption helper adopt an options object can under-credit a compatible solution that only migrates the brittle multi-argument file-creation path and strengthens parsing through typed partial input while preserving existing parser and decryption contracts. For similar tasks, generate rubrics that prioritize integration-safe refactoring evidence: the object parameter should be applied to the helper(s) that actually had multiple optional positional values; exported wrapper signatures and all source call sites should remain consistent; parser hardening should be expressed through strict partial/unknown-safe types and existing field-normalization helpers rather than a wholesale behavior rewrite; valid serialized metadata shapes and decrypted result structures should be preserved; and TypeScript/Jest validation or visible correction of compiler errors should matter. Avoid a standalone “resilient parsing exists” criterion unless it also checks that parser API and downstream consumers are not changed incompatibly.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat the XAttr task as a broad parsing rewrite or universal options-object migration while failing to preserve existing public contracts and type safety. Evidence of this flaw includes changing the parser to require an options object instead of the existing serialized-input API, changing decryption to return only parsed attributes instead of the existing verified-result shape, making formerly stable folder helpers incompatible without a demonstrated need, adding neutral fallback logic that drops valid partial metadata semantics, retaining `any`-style parser inputs instead of a typed partial metadata model, corrupting multiline call sites during migration, or showing unresolved TypeScript errors after signature changes. Do not apply this penalty merely because the agent has not yet edited every call site during early exploration; apply it when the visible implementation direction or validation output shows contract breakage or over-scoped API changes.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Contract-breaking XAttr refactor overreach

metadata.environment: TypeScript Drive application in a monorepo
key_evidence: helper signature migration scope
parser input and output contract
decryption wrapper return shape
source call-site updates
strict partial metadata typing
validation/typecheck results
metadata.avoid_proxy: presence of try/catch or neutral parsing fallback alone

scale.1: No evidence of overreach: visible changes preserve parser/decryption contracts, apply object parameters only where needed, keep call sites consistent, and use stricter partial metadata typing.
scale.2: Minor risk only: implementation direction is mostly compatible, with small unresolved questions about call-site coverage or parser typing but no clear contract breakage.
scale.3: Mixed evidence: the agent improves parsing or signatures but also shows ambiguous API changes, incomplete call-site search, or limited validation, making compatibility uncertain.
scale.4: Clear flaw: visible edits or compiler output show incompatible helper/parser/decryption signatures, broken call sites, or broad rewrites that are not required for the refactor.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory has wholesale rewritten XAttr behavior, changed multiple public contracts, corrupted source files or tests, and lacks successful validation despite appearing to satisfy a generic parsing checklist.

experiences.title: Django Meta.ordering Lookup-vs-Transform Validation
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django trajectory is investigating models.E015 from Meta.ordering paths with double-underscore suffixes, especially when a valid ORM lookup such as isnull is rejected by system checks while runtime order_by is reported to work.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django repository during model system-check or Meta.ordering validation work, after the trajectory has visible evidence that the error is raised by ordering validation and that the problematic suffix is a registered Lookup rather than a Transform. Strong matching cues include: the agent locates models.E015 in model ordering validation, observes the validation walking related-field parts split on LOOKUP_SEP, sees it checking get_transform() on the previous field, and confirms APIs such as get_lookup()/get_transform() or a registered lookup like isnull. This guidance is most useful once the agent has moved beyond repository discovery and has identified the lookup/transform distinction. It is less applicable for unrelated admin checks, actual QuerySet execution failures, unregistered transform registration issues, or broad ORM query compiler bugs; in those cases, requiring a model-check-only lookup fix may be premature or too narrow.
experiences.experience: A useful rubric for these trajectories should focus on the semantic mismatch between Django’s model ordering check and ORM lookup resolution: valid registered lookups in ordering paths must be accepted in the same place transforms are accepted, while nonexistent fields or nonexistent lookups must still raise the existing validation error. The previous useful rubrics aligned because they asked whether the agent understood that isnull/exact-style suffixes are Lookups, not Transforms, and whether the validation should consult get_lookup() in addition to get_transform() rather than bypassing validation. A better criterion should also reward preserving the existing related-field traversal, pk handling, and transform behavior. Avoid tempting but misleading criteria that demand changes to the query execution layer, focus on registering Lower or other transforms by default, or broadly accept any unresolved double-underscore component. Prioritize visible evidence that the trajectory: locates the system-check validation path, compares get_lookup() and get_transform(), identifies the reported suffix as a registered lookup, plans or applies a narrow validation change, and considers a regression check that valid lookups pass while invalid lookup names still fail.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a narrow, correct understanding that the Meta.ordering system check is rejecting a valid registered lookup because it only accepts transforms after related-field traversal. Strong evidence includes locating the models.E015 ordering validation, identifying the previous field object used when a path part cannot be resolved as a field, recognizing that the problematic suffix is resolved by get_lookup() rather than get_transform(), and preserving rejection of genuinely nonexistent fields or lookup names. The criterion should not require query compiler changes when the reported failure is the system check, and should not conflate the issue with default transform registration.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Accept registered lookups in ordering validation

metadata.environment: Django model system checks for Meta.ordering
metadata.target_layer: model ordering validation, not general query execution
key_observable_evidence: models.E015 is traced to ordering validation
related ordering paths are split on the double-underscore lookup separator
current validation accepts get_transform() but not get_lookup()
the reported suffix is a registered Lookup such as isnull
invalid fields or invalid lookup names remain rejected
avoid_as_primary_criterion: requiring sql/query.py or order_by execution changes without separate evidence
treating transform registration, such as Lower on CharField, as the core bug

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory distinguishes fields, transforms, and lookups in Meta.ordering validation.
scale.2: Some recognition that ordering validation is involved, but the trajectory does not identify registered lookups as the missing accepted case.
scale.3: Identifies the relevant validation area and lookup/transform distinction, but the proposed direction is incomplete, overly broad, or lacks attention to preserving invalid lookup rejection.
scale.4: Clearly identifies that registered lookups should be accepted alongside transforms in the ordering check and keeps the change scoped to validation.
scale.5: Precisely targets the existing transform-only validation gap, uses the registered lookup API, preserves existing traversal and error behavior, and seeks regression evidence for both valid lookup acceptance and invalid lookup rejection.

experiences.title: Bounded HTTP body reads require over-limit rejection, not truncation
experiences.description: Use this when a Go trajectory is adding a reusable limited-read helper and replacing unbounded HTTP request/response body reads such as ioutil.ReadAll(r.Body) or ioutil.ReadAll(resp.Body).
experiences.context: Applies to Go codebases where the task is specifically about preventing resource exhaustion from internal HTTP request or response body reads. The visible trajectory should show evidence such as searching for ReadAll on Body, adding a utils-style ReadAtMost helper, adding fixed HTTP body size constants, or editing handlers/clients that read r.Body, resp.Body, response.Body, or failed HTTP upgrade bodies. The criterion is especially important once implementation details are visible, because simply wrapping a body in io.LimitReader can silently accept truncated input. Boundaries: do not apply this as a blanket requirement to unrelated file reads, embedded asset reads, SSH stderr reads, event stream uploads, or other non-HTTP readers unless the task explicitly broadens scope. In very early exploration before any helper design or call-site edits, the rubric should be framed as expected direction rather than final correctness. If the task only asks for a local handler change rather than a reusable helper, narrow the call-site coverage requirement accordingly.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged the semantic contract of bounded HTTP reads, not just the presence of a new helper or mechanical replacement of ioutil.ReadAll. The decisive visible evidence is whether ReadAtMost detects when more data than the maximum exists and returns an error so callers reject the body; an implementation like ioutil.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(r, max)) or io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(r, max)) is a tempting but wrong proxy because it bounds allocation while silently truncating and processing partial JSON/metadata/error bodies. A strong rubric should also require the fixed maximum to be applied to the relevant HTTP request and response body reads discovered in the trajectory, with request/response constants or similarly clear limits, while preserving existing status-code checks, parsing, defers, file writes, and error-message behavior. Avoid rewarding broad, mechanical ReadAll replacement: changing non-HTTP reads, response-drain paths, embedded assets, or stream uploads can introduce regressions and does not directly satisfy the security requirement. Prioritize visible evidence in this order: helper over-limit behavior including exact-limit handling; use at HTTP Body call sites; preservation of surrounding semantics and compileable imports; focused scope rather than indiscriminate replacements.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Correct bounded HTTP body read contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement and integrate a reusable bounded-read helper for HTTP request/response bodies that enforces a fixed maximum without unbounded allocation, returns an error when the input exceeds the maximum instead of silently truncating, allows bodies at or below the limit, and applies the helper only to relevant internal HTTP body reads while preserving existing control flow and error handling.

required_visible_evidence: A ReadAtMost-like helper is added or planned with a clear maximum-size parameter.
The helper reads in a way that can detect over-limit input, such as reading/probing beyond the limit or inspecting a limited reader state, and returns a typed or wrapped error on excess.
Exactly-at-limit and below-limit inputs remain acceptable.
Relevant HTTP request/response body reads using r.Body, resp.Body, response.Body, or failed HTTP response bodies are converted to the helper with a fixed maximum.
Existing HTTP status checks, JSON/XML parsing, response body closing, file writes, and error-message construction are preserved.
Unrelated non-HTTP reads are not mechanically capped without justification.
common_negative_evidence: ReadAtMost is implemented as ReadAll(LimitReader(..., max)) without over-limit detection.
Oversized bodies would be processed as truncated data.
Only one obvious HTTP body read is changed while other discovered vulnerable HTTP body reads remain unbounded.
Mechanical replacements affect file reads, embedded assets, SSH stderr, event streams, or response-draining semantics unrelated to the HTTP-body exhaustion risk.
Manual edits leave malformed imports, duplicate imports, missing status checks, or broken function structure.
metadata.environment: Go repository using io/io/ioutil, net/http request and response bodies, shared utility package, and trace-style error wrapping.

scale.1: No meaningful bounded HTTP body read solution is visible, or the trajectory only explores files without identifying the vulnerable HTTP body reads or helper contract.
scale.2: A helper or some replacements are proposed, but the helper merely limits allocation by truncating input or the trajectory shows broad mechanical edits with little attention to HTTP-body scope or surrounding behavior.
scale.3: Some relevant HTTP body reads are converted and a fixed maximum is introduced, but over-limit rejection, exact-limit behavior, call-site coverage, or preservation of nearby status/error logic remains uncertain or incomplete.
scale.4: The helper clearly rejects over-limit input and most relevant HTTP request/response body reads are converted with fixed limits, with only minor unresolved coverage, import, test, or formatting concerns.
scale.5: The trajectory shows a complete, focused implementation: over-limit bodies produce an error, exact-limit bodies succeed, all identified relevant internal HTTP request/response reads use the helper with appropriate fixed limits, unrelated reads are left alone, surrounding semantics are preserved, and validation or tests support the behavior.

experiences.title: Firestore binary values require full legacy read fallback
experiences.description: Use when a Go Firestore backend task changes stored item values from strings to native bytes while preserving compatibility with existing string-valued documents.
experiences.context: Applies in Go repositories using the Firestore client to persist backend/key-value records where the public item value type is []byte but the Firestore document model currently stores the value field as string. The task must explicitly require both native binary writes and backward-compatible reads of existing string-encoded documents. This criterion is most discriminative after the trajectory has identified or edited the Firestore record struct and read/write paths. It is less appropriate for unrelated Firestore event schemas, key/document-ID encoding, tasks without a legacy-data requirement, or very early exploration where the agent has not yet reached implementation planning.
experiences.experience: Generate a rubric that checks the migration contract end to end, not just a type change. The useful criterion in these cases is that new writes stop converting backend values to string and store the same Firestore value field as native bytes, while every read path that deserializes records can still accept old documents whose value field is a Firestore string. This is predictive because partial fixes commonly changed record.Value to []byte but left DataTo calls that would fail on legacy strings, missed range/watch/lease/CAS paths, or kept writing a string field alongside a new bytes field. Prefer evidence visible in the trajectory: confirmation that backend.Item.Value is []byte; Firestore SDK support for []byte as bytes/blob; removal of string(item.Value) and string(replaceWith.Value) from writes; binary-safe comparison with bytes.Equal; a centralized snapshot-to-record helper, legacy record fallback, or equivalent type-discrimination logic used by Get, GetRange, CompareAndSwap, KeepAlive, and watch/event conversion paths. Avoid tempting but wrong proxies: requiring base64 decoding for legacy values when the legacy format was direct string(item.Value); accepting a new value_bytes field while still populating the old string value field with binary data; relying on unsupported custom unmarshal interfaces unless the trajectory verifies the SDK honors them; or treating a successful package build as sufficient without visible legacy read coverage.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly converge on a complete Firestore value migration: backend values are written as native []byte/blob values in the existing value field, legacy string-valued documents are converted back to []byte on read, and the compatibility logic is applied consistently across all record deserialization and comparison paths.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete binary value migration with legacy reads

required_visible_evidence: The backend item value type is recognized as []byte and Firestore []byte/blob support is used for new writes.
Write paths no longer convert item values or replacement values through string before storing them.
Read deserialization handles both Firestore bytes and legacy string values for the value field.
Compatibility decoding is used by single get, range/list, compare-and-swap, lease/keepalive, and watcher/change paths where applicable.
Binary equality uses byte-wise comparison rather than string comparison.
common_failure_patterns: Only changing the record field to []byte while leaving legacy DataTo failures unhandled.
Adding a separate bytes field while still writing arbitrary binary into the old string field.
Assuming legacy strings are base64-encoded without evidence.
Relying on unsupported Firestore custom unmarshal hooks.
Leaving any string(item.Value) or string(replaceWith.Value) conversion in Firestore value writes.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that Firestore value storage/read logic is being changed for binary data or legacy compatibility.
scale.2: Identifies the string-vs-[]byte problem or changes one write/type location, but lacks a credible legacy read strategy or misses major paths.
scale.3: Makes partial binary-write changes and discusses or sketches legacy fallback, but coverage of all deserialization paths or binary-safe comparison remains uncertain.
scale.4: Implements native []byte writes and a plausible legacy string fallback used in most relevant read paths, with only minor uncertainty or cleanup remaining.
scale.5: Provides a coherent, centralized migration: native []byte writes, exact legacy string-to-byte fallback, all read/watch/CAS/lease paths updated, no lingering value stringification, and binary-safe comparisons.

experiences.title: Propagate owner configuration when wrapping caller data into a context object
experiences.description: Retrieve when a framework convenience API is reported to ignore an instance-level option because it constructs a default context/options object internally, especially when explicit caller-supplied context objects must remain authoritative.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django template-engine task where the visible issue states that a render helper creates a Context without the Engine's autoescape setting. The trajectory is useful to judge once it has inspected the render helper and the Context constructor, identified the non-Context wrapping branch, or applied/verified a localized change. The criterion is strongest after the trajectory shows code or tests distinguishing plain dict/None contexts from already-created Context objects. It is less applicable during very early repository exploration with no evidence about the wrapping path, and it should not be used for unrelated escaping behavior such as template literals, filters, backend wrappers that already propagate settings, or global changes to Context/Template rendering.
experiences.experience: The successful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic bridge between an owner object's configuration and the new context object created inside a convenience method: when the method wraps a plain mapping, it must pass the owner's autoescape value; when the caller passes a Context, the method must not rewrap or override it. This was discriminative because the visible trajectories repeatedly showed the actual bug site, the Context default that caused the option to be ignored, and manual tests using variable HTML through a real template name. A better rubric should therefore ask whether the trajectory preserves the two branches: propagate the engine option only in the newly-created context branch, and leave explicit contexts unchanged. Avoid weaker or misleading criteria such as merely checking that escaping was tested somewhere, that raw template strings were rendered, that pytest was installed, or that broad template tests were attempted. Prioritize visible evidence of: locating the internal Context construction, confirming the constructor default, applying a narrow localized change, testing variable output with autoescape disabled and enabled using a valid loader/template name, and optionally verifying explicit Context objects keep their own autoescape setting.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the render convenience method propagates the engine-level autoescape option when it creates a new rendering Context from a plain mapping or None, while preserving the existing branch where caller-supplied Context instances are rendered unchanged and control their own autoescape behavior. Strong evidence includes locating the exact internal Context creation responsible for the ignored option, confirming Context defaults to autoescape enabled unless told otherwise, making a narrow change at that creation point rather than altering global escaping behavior, and validating with a real template name/loader and unsafe variable value for both disabled and enabled autoescape.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Owner autoescape propagation into newly-created contexts

key_evidence: The trajectory identifies that the convenience render method loads/selects a template and then wraps non-Context inputs in a new Context.
The trajectory observes that Context has an autoescape parameter with a default that differs from an engine configured with autoescape disabled.
The trajectory's implementation or plan passes the engine's autoescape setting into the newly-created Context only for plain mapping/None inputs.
The trajectory preserves the existing behavior for caller-supplied Context objects rather than rewrapping or overriding them.
Validation, if present, uses HTML-like data in a template variable through a valid template name/loader, not literal template HTML or a raw template source passed as the template name.
common_false_proxies: Testing literal template markup instead of variable escaping.
Changing Context defaults globally or template rendering internals.
Focusing on backend render paths that already propagate the setting.
Treating failed broad test-runner setup as evidence for or against the semantic fix.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory identified or addressed the internal context-wrapping path that ignores the owner autoescape option.
scale.2: The trajectory recognizes an autoescape problem but focuses on broad escaping behavior, invalid reproductions, or global changes without clearly connecting the owner option to newly-created contexts.
scale.3: The trajectory locates the render helper and Context default and proposes or partially applies propagating the owner autoescape value, but evidence is incomplete about preserving explicit Context objects or validating the correct path.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly applies or plans a narrow propagation of the owner autoescape setting when creating a new Context and avoids changing the existing Context branch, with reasonable targeted validation of disabled and enabled escaping.
scale.5: The trajectory provides decisive evidence: it identifies the exact wrapping/default mismatch, implements the narrow propagation only for newly-created contexts, preserves caller-supplied Context semantics, and validates with real template-name rendering of unsafe variable data for both autoescape states and, ideally, explicit Context override behavior.

experiences.title: Distinguish Transient Editing Errors from Runtime-Independent Identifier Semantics
experiences.description: Use when a rubric generator overreacts to a corrected syntax/editing mistake or to unavailable legacy-runtime execution instead of inspecting the final identifier predicate's explicit semantics.
experiences.context: Cross-version compatibility work may be developed on only one available runtime. A sound visible implementation can still establish ASCII shape and an explicit reserved-name policy without executing every interpreter version. Conversely, relying on runtime-dependent keyword tables is a real concern when no explicit compatibility handling is present. Judge the latest code and stated invariant, not superseded import placement.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics mixed temporary syntax failures, uncertain assumptions about keyword tables, and the actual semantic contract. Generate a negative criterion that checks whether the current predicate explicitly enforces the same ASCII and reserved-name behavior on all supported runtimes. Avoid treating lack of a local legacy interpreter as proof of incompatibility when the code makes the invariant explicit and current tests cover representative inputs.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Runtime-Dependent Identifier Acceptance
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize the current identifier predicate when accepted character classes or reserved names visibly depend on interpreter-specific behavior, or when the latest module is syntactically invalid. Corrected intermediate edits and unavailable legacy-runtime execution are not defects if the final logic explicitly enforces the shared invariant.

observable_evidence: latest import and function structure
explicit ASCII character policy
explicit reserved-name handling
representative Unicode and reserved-name checks

scale.1: No visible evidence of runtime-dependent identifier semantics or a syntax error remaining in the current implementation; the available implementation and validation evidence is consistent with the required behavior.
scale.2: A minor or early-stage concern about runtime-dependent identifier semantics or a syntax error remaining in the current implementation is visible, but it is not confirmed and the trajectory is still actively resolving it.
scale.3: Evidence about runtime-dependent identifier semantics or a syntax error remaining in the current implementation is mixed or incomplete; the concern remains plausible but is not yet decisive.
scale.4: Clear visible evidence indicates runtime-dependent identifier semantics or a syntax error remaining in the current implementation, with no convincing correction or validation yet.
scale.5: The trajectory directly reproduces or validates runtime-dependent identifier semantics or a syntax error remaining in the current implementation, or claims completion while the contradiction remains unresolved.

experiences.title: Text-wrapper mode metadata must match write contract
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python file/capture wrapper delegates `.mode` from an underlying binary stream but publicly behaves like a text stream, especially when third-party code chooses bytes vs strings based on `'b' in mode`.
experiences.context: Applies in Python library maintenance tasks where the visible trajectory has identified a wrapper around a binary buffer/file whose public API accepts text and rejects bytes, while delegated metadata such as `.mode` still advertises binary mode. It is especially relevant in pytest-style capture code where `safe_text_dupfile` or equivalent opens an underlying fd in binary mode and returns a text-like wrapper. This criterion is useful once the agent has inspected the wrapper class, its `write()` behavior, and the delegation path for `.mode`. It is less useful if the task is still broad repository exploration with no wrapper/metadata mismatch identified, if the stream is genuinely binary and should accept bytes, or if the bug concerns capture lifecycle rather than advertised text-vs-binary semantics.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases focused on the semantic contract: the wrapper should explicitly expose a text-mode `.mode` value with the binary flag removed, while preserving the remaining mode information such as read/write/append/update flags and leaving the text-only write behavior intact. This aligned well because the visible evidence repeatedly showed the root cause: `write()` accepts strings and rejects bytes, while `__getattr__` leaks the wrapped binary buffer's mode, causing consumers to choose byte writes. A better rubric should judge whether the trajectory is converging on an explicit wrapper-level metadata override rather than changing the underlying fd opening strategy or making `write()` accept bytes. It should also value evidence that neighboring wrapper behavior, such as other delegated attributes and existing properties, remains undisturbed. Avoid a tempting but weaker criterion that requires reproducing the full third-party application or the entire capture pipeline; direct focused evidence from the wrapper and a real binary-mode file is often sufficient. Also avoid over-crediting tests built on objects without a real `.mode`, because they may not exercise the reported mismatch.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate or implement a narrow fix that makes the text-like file wrapper's advertised `.mode` consistent with its public write contract: `.mode` is provided by the wrapper itself, removes the binary marker from the underlying stream's mode, preserves other meaningful mode characters, and does not alter the intended behavior that text writes are encoded while bytes are rejected on Python 3. The judgment should prioritize visible inspection of the wrapper's `write()` method, the delegation path that previously exposed binary metadata, and validation using a buffer/file object that actually reports a binary mode.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Wrapper mode matches text-write contract

required_visible_evidence: The agent has identified a text-like wrapper around an underlying binary stream.
The wrapper's write behavior is understood as accepting strings and rejecting bytes.
The agent recognizes that delegated `.mode` metadata can mislead external callers into writing bytes.
The proposed or applied fix exposes a wrapper-level `.mode` without the binary flag while preserving other mode flags.
negative_indicators: Changing the wrapper to accept bytes instead of fixing misleading metadata.
Removing binary mode from the internal fd/buffer creation without considering why the internal binary buffer is used.
Breaking existing properties or generic delegation while adding the mode override.
Relying only on a mock object without a meaningful `.mode` attribute.

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory addresses the wrapper's advertised mode or understands the text-vs-binary metadata mismatch.
scale.2: The trajectory vaguely notices a mode or bytes/string issue but focuses on broad reproduction, dependency setup, or unrelated capture behavior without a concrete wrapper-level contract fix.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies that binary `.mode` is misleading for a text-like wrapper, but the proposed fix is incomplete, unvalidated, or risks changing write semantics or other delegated behavior.
scale.4: The trajectory proposes or applies an explicit `.mode` override that removes `b` and preserves text-only writes, with some focused validation or inspection of the relevant wrapper behavior.
scale.5: The trajectory cleanly implements or clearly plans the narrow wrapper-level `.mode` override, preserves other mode flags and existing properties/delegation, rejects changing byte-write semantics, and validates with a realistic binary-mode underlying stream or an equivalent targeted regression.

experiences.title: Preserve constructor callables in deconstruction despite evaluated defaults
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django-style field deconstruction/migration task involves a callable constructor argument that is evaluated at initialization and may return the same object as a default value.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Django repository work where the bug concerns migration serialization/deconstruction of a field option, especially when initialization stores both the original user-supplied callable and an evaluated runtime value. The useful stage is after the trajectory has found the field initialization/deconstruction code or is reviewing a proposed fix/validation. It is less useful during very early repository exploration before the agent has inspected the relevant constructor/deconstruct logic. It should not be applied to tasks about runtime file storage behavior only, or to cases where the constructor option is never evaluated before serialization. If the visible trajectory shows accidental method corruption or unrelated edits, this semantic criterion should be paired with a separate structural-integrity criterion rather than assuming the final patch will remain clean.
experiences.experience: The generated rubrics in these cases were useful because they targeted the exact semantic contract rather than superficial test activity: deconstruction must serialize the original callable supplied by the user, not decide solely from the evaluated storage object. This distinction is decisive when a callable returns the default storage object, because comparing only the evaluated value makes the deconstructed kwargs look like the field used an implicit default and omits the user’s callable. A strong rubric should therefore ask whether the trajectory preserves callable identity in the serialized kwargs whenever a callable storage argument was supplied, while still preserving legacy behavior for non-callable defaults and non-default storage instances. Prioritize visible evidence such as: the agent identifies the constructor-vs-runtime value distinction; the proposed code uses the stored callable/original argument before or independently of the default-value comparison; validation covers callable returning default, callable returning non-default, direct default/no storage, and direct non-default storage; subclasses relying on the same deconstruct path are considered if relevant. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as rewarding any successful test command, checking only existing callable-storage tests that return custom storage, or requiring broad migration test-suite success in a fragile environment. Also avoid a too-broad criterion like “include storage whenever storage is callable” unless it explicitly protects direct default omission and direct non-default inclusion. When current visible diffs show method-body corruption, misplaced subclass logic, or collateral changes, the semantic rubric should score low for current trajectory quality even if earlier notes show understanding, because the visible source no longer satisfies the deconstruction contract.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates that field deconstruction serializes the original user-supplied storage callable whenever the field was initialized with a callable, including when that callable evaluates to the default storage object, while preserving existing behavior for omitted/default non-callable storage and direct non-default storage. Judge from visible trajectory evidence: diagnosis of the original callable versus evaluated runtime storage distinction, an implementation or patch plan that consults the preserved callable before relying on the evaluated default comparison, and validation or reasoning covering the important callable/default and non-callable/default boundaries.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Callable constructor argument preserved across default comparison

metadata.task_family: Django model field deconstruction and migration serialization
key_contract: A callable constructor argument is serialized by its original callable identity.
A callable that evaluates to the default storage is still serialized as the callable.
No storage or direct default storage remains omitted from deconstruction.
Direct non-default storage remains serialized as the storage object.
Subclasses using the same deconstruction path are not regressed.
priority_evidence: The trajectory identifies that the runtime storage value is already evaluated.
The visible implementation prioritizes the saved callable/original argument over comparison to the default storage object.
Manual or automated checks inspect deconstructed kwargs for callable-returning-default and direct-default cases.
The final visible diff does not corrupt unrelated deconstruct methods or remove existing kwargs such as upload path and max length handling.
avoid_as_primary_evidence: Repeated test-runner setup attempts without semantic validation.
Only testing callable storage that returns a custom/non-default storage.
Only checking that evaluated storage is or is not the default object.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses callable storage deconstruction, or the visible change still bases serialization solely on the evaluated storage/default comparison or corrupts the deconstruct method.
scale.2: The trajectory mentions callable storage or migration serialization but lacks a clear fix for callable-returning-default behavior, or validates only unrelated/default/custom cases.
scale.3: The trajectory recognizes the original-callable versus evaluated-storage distinction and proposes a plausible direction, but visible implementation or validation is incomplete, ambiguous, or missing important boundary cases.
scale.4: The trajectory shows a mostly correct implementation that serializes the preserved callable before relying on default comparison and includes evidence for callable-returning-default behavior, with minor gaps such as limited subclass or direct-storage validation.
scale.5: The trajectory clearly implements and validates the full deconstruction contract: callable returning default is serialized as the original callable, callable returning non-default is serialized as the callable, direct/no default storage is omitted, direct non-default storage is included, and related inherited deconstruction behavior remains intact.

experiences.title: Separate Forced Encryption Value from Change Permission
experiences.description: Retrieve when an Element Web / Matrix React task adds a `.well-known` E2EE force-disable option and the trajectory has reached room-creation encryption defaults, UI toggles, or existing server force-enable handling.
experiences.context: Apply in TypeScript/React Element Web-style codebases where room creation has both a default encryption helper and a create-room UI with a boolean like `canChangeEncryption`, especially when existing server capability logic can force encryption enabled while the new `.well-known` key must force encryption disabled. The criterion is most useful once the trajectory has found or edited the room creation option builder and the UI state controlling encryption. It is less useful during very early search before the submit-path fallback is visible, and it should not be generalized to unrelated settings-only E2EE tasks or repositories without an existing forced-enable path.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful judgment is not simply whether the agent added `force_disable` to the well-known type or hid an encryption toggle. Those are necessary but not decisive. The decisive visible risk is that existing room creation code often treats “the user cannot change encryption” as synonymous with “encryption must be enabled,” for example by sending encryption enabled whenever the toggle is disabled. A correct rubric should therefore focus on whether the trajectory separates two concepts: permission to change the encryption setting, and the forced encryption value. The better criterion should reward evidence that the agent preserves server force-enable behavior, gives `.well-known force_disable` a forced false value, updates initial state/defaults accordingly, and ensures the create-room submission sends the forced value rather than reusing an old safety fallback that always enables encryption. UI suppression should be included as a consequence of that policy, but a rubric that only asks for hiding/disabling UI or for updating every consumer of the default helper is too broad and can miss the main correctness boundary. Avoid demanding matrix-js-sdk changes unless the visible code shows the SDK owns the relevant well-known parsing; in these cases the visible evidence supported local well-known handling. Prioritize evidence such as: an explicit helper or policy object returning both allow-change and forced-value information; conflict/precedence handling between server-forced enable and well-known forced disable; initialization of the encrypted state from the forced value; removal or bypassing of any fallback that passes encryption enabled solely because controls are disabled; and minimal, compile-safe integration with the create-room UI.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Explicit Forced Encryption Value Policy
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should establish a clear room-creation encryption policy that distinguishes whether the user may change encryption from what encryption value is forced. For a `.well-known` E2EE `force_disable: true` setting, the policy should force new room creation to request encryption disabled, hide or prevent the enable option in the creation UI, and avoid reusing existing forced-enable fallbacks that set encryption enabled whenever controls are disabled. It should also preserve existing server-forced-enable behavior and make any precedence between forced enable and forced disable deliberate and visible.

metadata.environment: Element Web / Matrix React TypeScript room creation and E2EE well-known handling
visible_evidence_to_prioritize: The trajectory has found the existing default-encryption helper and the create-room UI state for encryption.
The trajectory notices any existing fallback that enables encryption when the user cannot change the setting.
The trajectory plans or implements separate forced-value handling instead of using a single can-change boolean for both force-enable and force-disable.
The trajectory wires the forced false value into room creation submission, not only into UI messaging.
common_false_proxies_to_avoid: Only adding the new well-known field to a type/interface.
Only making the default encryption helper return false.
Only disabling or hiding the toggle while leaving room submission to send encryption enabled.
Broadly editing all consumers of the default helper without addressing the create-room forced-value fallback.
Assuming SDK force-enable helpers automatically cover the new well-known force-disable behavior.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of a forced-disable policy beyond perhaps superficial searching or unrelated E2EE edits.
scale.2: Adds or plans the well-known field or default-helper behavior, but does not address UI state or the room creation submission path.
scale.3: Recognizes the UI must hide or disable encryption and may set a can-change flag for force-disable, but still leaves ambiguous whether disabled controls mean forced enabled or forced disabled.
scale.4: Clearly separates force-disable from default-disable and updates UI/default state, with evidence that room creation will not intentionally enable encryption under force-disable, though conflict handling or integration may be incomplete.
scale.5: Fully models both permission-to-change and forced encryption value, preserves existing force-enable behavior with deliberate precedence, forces the encrypted state false for well-known force-disable, and ensures the final room creation options use that forced value rather than an old always-enable fallback.

experiences.title: Literalize Dynamic Prefixes in Regex-Based Field Matching
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django/admin-style task involves a configurable formset or field-name prefix being interpolated into a regex used to select POST keys.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Django repository trajectories where the task or exploration identifies a regex assembled from a formset prefix to match submitted field names such as prefix-row-primary-key, and the prefix is documented or inferred to be customizable and not regex-safe. This is most useful once the agent has located the regex construction or is editing the helper that scans POST keys; at earlier exploration stages, it can judge whether the agent is converging on the correct vulnerable interpolation. It may be irrelevant if the dynamic value is not used in a regex, if the value is already constrained to regex-safe identifiers, or if the agent is working on unrelated formset prefix generation rather than the regex consumer.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases focused on the semantic contract: the prefix must be treated as literal text when building the regex that recognizes list-editable primary-key POST fields. This aligned well because visible trajectory evidence often showed the agent locating the unsafe formatted regex, applying `re.escape()` to the prefix, and testing examples like a dot or brackets in the prefix that otherwise overmatch or fail to match. A better rubric should emphasize escaping only the dynamic literal portion while preserving the intended regex structure for row numbers and field-name delimiters. It should accept escaping the primary-key name as an additional conservative step if normal matching semantics remain intact, but it should not make that the central requirement because the reported unbounded input is the prefix. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as merely grepping for other regexes, running broad test suites, or changing formset default-prefix behavior; those are secondary validation steps and do not prove the bug is fixed. Prioritize visible evidence of: identifying the POST-key matching regex, applying literal escaping to the prefix before regex compilation, preserving matches for intended `prefix-index-pk` keys, and excluding regex-expanded false positives such as a `.` in the prefix matching arbitrary characters.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should repair the regex-based POST field matching by escaping the configurable formset prefix as literal text before compiling or using the pattern, while preserving the intended match shape for submitted primary-key fields. Strong evidence includes locating the helper that scans POST keys, changing the pattern construction to use literal escaping for the prefix rather than altering formset prefix generation, and validating with examples where regex metacharacters in the prefix no longer cause missed matches or false matches.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Literal Escaping of Configurable Regex Prefix

required_evidence: The agent identifies a regex built from a dynamic formset or field prefix.
The agent treats the prefix as literal regex text, typically with `re.escape(prefix)` or an equivalent escaping step.
The intended numeric row-index matching and primary-key field suffix matching remain intact.
Validation or reasoning distinguishes correct literal-prefix matches from regex-metacharacter false positives.
acceptable_variations: Escaping additional dynamic field-name components is acceptable if it does not change the intended POST-key matching behavior.
Manual focused regex tests are useful evidence even if full framework tests are not yet running.
non_goals: Changing default formset prefixes instead of fixing the regex consumer.
Escaping the entire regex string so that row-index matching no longer works.
Relying only on broad grep or test-run attempts without addressing the unsafe interpolation.

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory identifies or fixes the dynamic prefix interpolation in the regex; it may pursue unrelated admin or formset changes.
scale.2: The trajectory notices a regex or prefix issue but proposes vague sanitization, unrelated tests, or changes to prefix sources without clearly making the regex treat the prefix literally.
scale.3: The trajectory is roughly on track by locating the vulnerable regex or planning to escape the prefix, but has not yet shown a concrete correct edit or convincing validation that intended matching is preserved.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly applies literal escaping to the dynamic prefix in the regex construction and preserves the intended field-name pattern, with some reasoning or limited testing for metacharacter prefixes.
scale.5: The trajectory both applies the focused literal-prefix escaping fix and demonstrates the semantic boundary with examples or tests showing intended prefixed primary-key fields match while regex-expanded false positives are excluded, without introducing broad unrelated behavior changes.

experiences.title: Use bound listener addresses for dynamic ports
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go server/client CLI task involves services configured with `:0` or `127.0.0.1:0` and the trajectory is tracing how service listener addresses are advertised to clients through ping/discovery settings.
experiences.context: Applies to Teleport-like Go codebases where tests start auth/proxy/web/SSH services on dynamic local ports and clients learn connection targets from service startup metadata, web ping/discovery responses, or proxy settings. This criterion is most useful after the agent has located listener creation, service advertisement, and client ping/apply-settings paths, or claims to have fixed dynamic-port behavior. It is less useful as the sole criterion when the trajectory is only addressing independent SSO mocking or CLI error-return refactors, and it may be premature during very early repository exploration before any listener or advertised-setting flow is visible.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric pattern is to judge whether the agent recognizes that configured addresses containing `:0` are not usable after binding; the real port only exists on the bound listener. A strong trajectory should update or plan updates at the service/listener boundary so advertised proxy/auth settings and ping responses contain `listener.Addr()` or an equivalent registered-listener address, then rely on the client to consume those advertised settings. The previous rubrics were directionally useful because missing this propagation left clients with unusable `:0` addresses. However, broader wording can over-credit shallow client-side changes: modifying address parsing, default-port fallback, or client `applyProxySettings` alone cannot recover the random port if the server still advertises the configured `:0`. Also avoid confusing the local SSO callback bind address with the auth/proxy service listener addresses. Prioritize visible evidence that the trajectory traces and changes the full flow: service binds to dynamic port, captures actual listener address, inserts it into advertised proxy/auth settings or ping/discovery configuration, and preserves public-address/default behavior for non-dynamic cases.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that dynamic service binds are handled by propagating the actual bound listener addresses, not the configured `:0` addresses, into the settings returned to clients. Strong evidence includes locating the service startup/listener registration path, using the listener's actual address or an existing registered-listener helper after binding, wiring those real addresses into advertised proxy/auth settings and ping/discovery responses, and ensuring the client-side address application consumes those values without replacing them with defaults incorrectly. It should distinguish this from unrelated SSO mocking and CLI error-return work.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Actual listener address propagation

required_visible_evidence: The trajectory identifies where services bind/listen on configured addresses that may include port 0.
The trajectory identifies where connection settings are advertised to clients through ping/discovery/proxy settings.
The trajectory proposes or implements using actual bound listener addresses after listen succeeds.
The trajectory checks that clients receive real host:port values rather than configured `:0` values.
anti_evidence: Only client-side parsing/default-port logic is changed while server-advertised settings still originate from configured `:0` addresses.
The work repeatedly searches irrelevant packages without reaching the service advertisement source.
The trajectory addresses only mocked SSO or CLI fatal exits and leaves dynamic listener propagation untouched.
The trajectory treats the SSO callback listener bind address as the same problem as auth/proxy service listener propagation.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the dynamic-port propagation path has been identified; the trajectory ignores `:0` listener advertisement or works only on unrelated SSO/CLI issues.
scale.2: The trajectory recognizes that configured `:0` addresses are problematic but only performs exploration or suggests client-side parsing/default changes without a concrete service-side propagation plan.
scale.3: The trajectory locates both client consumption and some service advertisement code, but the implementation or plan is partial, still risks advertising configured `:0`, or covers only one endpoint while other required auth/proxy endpoints remain unresolved.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly implements or plans service-side replacement of configured dynamic addresses with actual bound listener addresses for the main advertised endpoints, with minor uncertainty about secondary endpoints, validation, or edge-case preservation.
scale.5: The trajectory fully traces and fixes the dynamic-address flow end to end: after binding, actual listener addresses are propagated into all relevant advertised settings and ping/discovery responses, clients consume those real addresses, public-address/default behavior is preserved, and visible validation or code inspection shows no remaining `:0` leakage for the tested paths.

experiences.title: Require End-to-End Delivery for Multi-Part Observability Tasks
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go observability task explicitly requires both a missing utility component and watcher/event metrics visualization, especially after the trajectory has mostly repeated searches or only addressed one component.
experiences.context: Applies to SWE-agent trajectories in a Go monorepo where the task combines a foundational utility needed for rolling/sliding numeric calculations with user-facing observability requirements such as emitted event counts, byte sizes, per-resource frequency, and monitoring or TUI display. It is most useful after the agent has already inspected likely utility, watcher/fanout, metrics, and UI/reporting areas, or when the visible trajectory shows clean builds and repeated greps with no implementation. It also applies to partial patches that add only a standalone numeric buffer without wiring watcher metrics or display. It is less appropriate during the first few exploratory steps before the agent has had a chance to locate relevant packages, or for tasks whose only acceptance criterion is fixing a directly visible undefined symbol rather than delivering metrics collection and visualization.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics were useful when they judged concrete progress toward all named deliverables instead of accepting investigation as success. In these trajectories, the observable evidence was repeated searching for circular/float64/rolling symbols, successful builds after fixing the Go PATH, clean working trees, and little or no code touching watcher event emission, metric registration, report generation, or TUI rendering. A better rubric should therefore require an end-to-end implementation: a fixed-size numeric buffer in the utilities area, instrumentation at a real watcher event emission/fanout point where event size and resource identity are available, registered metrics with appropriate labels, rate/top-resource aggregation using prior samples or rolling buffers, and monitoring/TUI integration that displays events/sec, bytes/sec, and top resources. Avoid the tempting but weak criterion that rewards merely locating or confirming the absence of a missing symbol; in this scenario the described build failure may not be reproducible in the visible tree, and hidden expectations are about implementing the requested capability. Also avoid over-constraining exact type names or API shapes for the buffer unless visible tests or compile errors establish them. Prioritize visible evidence of edits across the utility, metrics instrumentation, and reporting/UI paths, plus validation commands that compile or test the touched packages.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Watcher Observability Implementation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show concrete implementation progress across all major requirements of the observability task: a fixed-size float64 rolling/circular buffer in the utilities package, watcher event instrumentation at a code path that actually emits or fans out events, registered metrics capturing both event count/frequency and event byte size with resource-aware labeling, aggregation/reporting logic that can compute events-per-second, bytes-per-second, and top resources from current and previous or rolling samples, and monitoring/TUI integration that exposes these values to users. Strong evidence includes edits in the relevant utility, watcher/event emission, metrics definition/registration, report generation, and display layers, with targeted build or test validation. Weak evidence includes only grep searches, only confirming that no existing symbol is present, or adding an isolated buffer that is not consumed by watcher metrics.

required_evidence: utility-level fixed-size float64 buffer or equivalent rolling numeric sample structure
instrumentation at a real watcher event emission or fanout path where event size and resource identity are known
metric definitions and collector registration following project conventions
rate and top-resource calculation from metric samples or rolling buffers
monitoring/TUI/report integration that displays watcher event rates, byte rates, and top resources
targeted validation such as package tests or builds for touched utility, metrics, watcher, and UI/reporting code
anti_patterns: repeated broad searches for missing symbols without code changes
treating a successful baseline build as resolving the requested missing component
implementing only a standalone buffer with no watcher metrics integration
rewarding exact inferred symbol names when the visible trajectory has not established them
metadata.applicability_stage: post-initial exploration, implementation review, or partial-patch assessment

scale.1: No implementation evidence: the trajectory is limited to searches, build attempts, or inspection, with no code changes toward the buffer, watcher metrics, or display requirements.
scale.2: Weak progress: the trajectory identifies likely packages or adds only one isolated piece, such as a standalone numeric buffer, but does not wire watcher event metrics or user-visible reporting.
scale.3: Moderate progress: the trajectory implements some meaningful pieces, such as a utility buffer and partial metric definitions or instrumentation, but lacks complete rate/top-resource calculation or monitoring/TUI display.
scale.4: Strong progress: the trajectory wires most of the end-to-end path, including utility support, watcher event metrics, registration, and report/display integration, with only minor gaps or limited validation remaining.
scale.5: Complete progress: the trajectory clearly implements and validates the full feature across utility buffer, watcher event size/count/resource instrumentation, registered metrics, rolling or sample-delta rate calculations, top-resource reporting, and monitoring/TUI visualization.

experiences.title: Do not equate FontFamilies with changing web font settings or full CSS parsing
experiences.description: Retrieve when a qutebrowser font-family task asks for a structured FontFamilies representation and the trajectory is exploring configtypes/configutils/configfiles/websettings. Avoid rubrics that reward broad parser rewrites or switching singular web font settings to list-valued config types without evidence that those API boundaries are required.
experiences.context: Applies in the qutebrowser/PyQt configuration system where existing font handling includes Font, FontFamily, QtFont, configutils.parse_font_families, configfiles migrations, fonts.default_family, and web settings using Qt setFontFamily(str). The misleading pattern is generating criteria such as “replace FontFamily for web font settings,” “implement full CSS font-family parsing including escaped quotes/quoted commas,” or “round-trip through a new config type” when the visible codebase shows the existing parser already handles the example-style quoted comma-separated list and the main need is to centralize representation consistently across existing multi-family paths. Such criteria can still be appropriate if the task or trajectory explicitly establishes that web font-family settings must become multi-family list settings, that Qt’s web API can accept multiple families, or that the bug is specifically about stricter CSS grammar such as commas inside quoted names or escaped quotes.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often rewarded a new FontFamilies config type with richer CSS-like parsing, serialization, and replacement of FontFamily in fonts.web.family.*. That is misleading for this qutebrowser task because the stronger visible acceptance proxy is not broad parser sophistication or schema replacement of singular web settings. The safer criterion should focus on whether the agent identifies the existing shared parser and converts it into a structured low-level FontFamilies representation used by the existing multi-family consumers: QtFont family parsing, default_family string construction/fallback behavior, and config migration storage. Avoid tempting criteria that require replacing FontFamily web settings or modifying websettings.set_font_family to pass lists, because Qt web settings visibly use setFontFamily(str) and changing those settings can break API semantics. Also avoid requiring support for CSS features not evidenced by existing tests or task examples; preserving current split/strip/quote-trim behavior may be the intended compatibility boundary. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence that the class lives in a low-dependency utility location, exposes iteration/list conversion plus primary-family/string behavior, is used consistently by QtFont and migrations, preserves Unset/None/default_family behavior, and does not introduce unnecessary config schema or Qt API changes.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat the FontFamilies work primarily as a web-setting schema conversion or full parser rewrite while neglecting the existing multi-family integration points. This flaw is present when the visible trajectory or planned patch changes singular web font-family settings to list-valued FontFamilies, alters websettings to pass or join lists for Qt setFontFamily, or adds elaborate CSS parsing/round-trip behavior, but does not show a coherent low-level FontFamilies representation used by QtFont, default-family handling, and font migrations while preserving existing simple parsing compatibility.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Overbroad FontFamilies scope breaks integration boundaries

watch_for: fonts.web.family.* changed from singular FontFamily to list-valued FontFamilies without explicit API justification
websettings.set_font_family changed to accept lists despite Qt setFontFamily expecting a string
parser rewritten for unsupported CSS features while existing migration/QtFont/default_family paths remain inconsistent
configutils.parse_font_families removed or moved without preserving stable import/use sites
better_evidence: FontFamilies representation in a utility layer or otherwise import-safe location
QtFont._parse_families returns/uses the structured representation
default_family construction uses the representation to preserve fallback list string semantics
config migration uses the representation and stores a list
QFont.setFamilies receives list(families) and older fallback uses str(families)

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory respects singular web setting boundaries and focuses on centralizing the existing multi-family representation across QtFont/default_family/migration paths.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory briefly considers web setting or parser expansion but also recognizes API boundaries and prioritizes existing multi-family integration.
scale.3: Mixed behavior: the trajectory includes some correct centralization work but also makes or plans unnecessary web schema/API changes or unsupported parser changes.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory mainly implements FontFamilies as a config type for web settings or rewrites parsing while leaving key existing multi-family consumers or migrations insufficiently integrated.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory changes web font-family settings and Qt web application logic to list semantics, over-specifies parser behavior, and misses or breaks QtFont/default_family/migration consistency.

experiences.title: Do not score YAML attachment work on round-trip conversion alone
experiences.description: Retrieve this when generating rubrics for Go CLI YAML import/export tasks that convert internally stored JSON-string attachment fields to YAML-native structures and back.
experiences.context: This applies in a Go codebase using gopkg.in/yaml.v2 where import/export is implemented through shared YAML document structs and storage/RPC still expect JSON strings. The misleading pattern is a trajectory that correctly identifies the JSON-string-to-YAML-native conversion but then makes broad edits to CLI import/export files, shared structs, or storage validation; a rubric that only asks whether export→import preserves attachment structure can overvalue such work. The original round-trip idea is still useful as a subcriterion for helper behavior or early design, but it is not enough for final-review quality. Also avoid interpreting task wording about flags, variants, segments, rules, constraints, and distributions as requiring attachment conversion on every entity when visible API/proto evidence shows attachments only exist on variants; the other entities mainly need their existing import/export traversal preserved.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked for bidirectional serialization consistency: parse stored JSON strings into native YAML on export, accept YAML structures on import, and preserve semantic equivalence. That is a real requirement, but it became misleading because it ignored regressions visible in the trajectory: broad rewrites of import/export files, removed or changed existing export header/file behavior, duplicated or moved shared document types without verifying compilation, weakened storage JSON validation, missing yaml.v2 map-key normalization, missing nil/empty or legacy JSON-string handling, and reliance on scratch round-trip experiments instead of repository-level build/tests. A better rubric should focus on whether the conversion is localized at the YAML boundary while preserving the existing CLI import/export contract. Avoid the tempting criterion that 'round-trip conversion passes' is sufficient, and avoid requiring attachment handling for entity types that have no attachment field. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence such as: the variant attachment YAML field can decode maps/lists/scalars; yaml.v2 map[interface{}]interface{} values are normalized before json.Marshal; missing/null/empty attachment cases do not become JSON null or quoted empty strings unintentionally; legacy raw JSON string imports are either explicitly preserved or deliberately validated; storage/RPC validation is not loosened to accept invalid JSON; existing flag/segment/rule/distribution import/export order, file output, comments/headers, and writer closing behavior remain intact; and build/tests or targeted import/export fixtures were run after edits.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a trajectory attempting YAML-native import/export of an internally JSON-string attachment field, penalize evidence that the agent treats attachment round-trip conversion as complete while failing to preserve the surrounding import/export contract. This includes broad rewrites or shared-type moves that introduce compile risk, removing existing export file/header/comment behavior, changing unrelated entity traversal or creation order, weakening storage/API JSON validation instead of converting at the YAML boundary, omitting yaml.v2 map-key normalization before JSON marshaling, mishandling nil/empty/missing attachments, or ignoring legacy JSON-string attachment imports without an explicit compatibility decision.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Conversion-only implementation that regresses import/export contract

metadata.environment: Go CLI import/export using gopkg.in/yaml.v2 with storage/RPC attachment fields still typed as JSON strings
check_visible_evidence: attachment conversion is localized to YAML import/export boundary
existing export file output/header/comment behavior is preserved
existing flag, variant, segment, constraint, rule, and distribution traversal is unchanged except for variant attachment conversion
yaml.v2 map[interface{}]interface{} values are normalized before json.Marshal
missing, null, empty, structured, scalar, list, and legacy JSON-string attachment cases are considered
storage/API validation is not loosened to accept invalid JSON
repository build or relevant tests/fixtures are run after edits
metadata.avoid_overbroad_requirement: Do not demand attachment conversion for entities with no attachment field; require their existing import/export behavior to remain consistent.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory keeps conversion localized, preserves existing CLI behavior and validation, handles yaml.v2 and empty/legacy cases, and verifies with build/tests or targeted fixtures.
