scale.5: Complete, validated refactor: all relevant testable CLI command paths return errors instead of exiting, top-level process-exit behavior is preserved only at the executable boundary, related subcommands are included, success/error returns are consistent, and build/tests/gofmt confirm the change.

experiences.title: Prioritize Algebraic Soundness over a Preferred q-Product Representation
experiences.description: Use when a criterion marks a conservative symbolic product result as wrong merely because it does not produce the preferred special-function representation.
experiences.context: Symbolic evaluators should simplify only when an identity is valid over the expression class and bounds. Preventing a false closed form can be a complete correctness fix even if the result remains unevaluated. Requiring a q-product representation is appropriate only when the task explicitly makes evaluability after substitution part of the contract or visible project tests establish that expectation.
experiences.experience: The previous rubric demanded both removal of the bad additive split and a particular q-product output, which made safe conservative fixes look incorrect. Replace it with a negative rubric that compares the produced expression against direct finite products and checks that established rational/polynomial cases still simplify. Avoid equating 'unevaluated' with 'mathematically wrong.'

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Incorrect q-Geometric Product Evaluation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize the evaluator when it returns a symbolic expression contradicted by direct finite expansion, continues to split additive product terms, or regresses established supported product classes. Leaving an unsupported expression unevaluated is acceptable unless visible requirements specifically require a substitutable closed form.

observable_evidence: direct finite-product comparisons
current additive-product branch
regression checks for supported product classes
explicit evaluability requirement

scale.1: No visible evidence of a mathematically incorrect symbolic product result or an overbroad evaluator regression; the available implementation and validation evidence is consistent with the required behavior.
scale.2: A minor or early-stage concern about a mathematically incorrect symbolic product result or an overbroad evaluator regression is visible, but it is not confirmed and the trajectory is still actively resolving it.
scale.3: Evidence about a mathematically incorrect symbolic product result or an overbroad evaluator regression is mixed or incomplete; the concern remains plausible but is not yet decisive.
scale.4: Clear visible evidence indicates a mathematically incorrect symbolic product result or an overbroad evaluator regression, with no convincing correction or validation yet.
scale.5: The trajectory directly reproduces or validates a mathematically incorrect symbolic product result or an overbroad evaluator regression, or claims completion while the contradiction remains unresolved.

experiences.title: Do not let “cyclic import elimination” mask broken or incomplete refactors
experiences.description: Retrieve this when evaluating a Python modularization/refactor task where the task mentions cyclic imports and the agent is moving shared utilities/state into a new module.
experiences.context: This warning applies in Python refactor trajectories like the OpenLibrary Solr utility split, especially when the agent creates a new utility module, changes imports, or claims cyclic imports are resolved. The original cyclic-import criterion is relevant only if there is visible evidence that the new module is included in the final diff, imports are redirected to functions that actually live there, import direction avoids the old cycle, and behavior-preserving validation is clean. It is misleading when the trajectory is still in exploration, mid-edit, has syntax/test failures, uses broad rewrites or sed deletions, leaves a new file untracked, changes public APIs/tests just to fit the refactor, or imports mutable module state by value in a way that may become stale.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded or penalized the trajectory mainly on whether shared Solr utilities were moved to a dedicated module to eliminate cyclic imports. That idea is directionally correct for this task, but it is too broad and can overpredict quality: a trajectory can appear to break an import cycle while leaving the new module untracked, creating missing imports, deleting or corrupting large parts of the original module, changing helper signatures/semantics, or failing the existing test suite. A better rubric should focus on behavior-preserving extraction with concrete evidence: the new utility module is tracked and importable; moved symbols are removed or re-exported deliberately; downstream imports are updated only for actually moved utility/config/state helpers; core indexing/update logic remains in its original module unless intentionally migrated; mutable shared state is accessed through a single authoritative module or safe getters/setters; and syntax/import/test validation covers the touched modules. Avoid generating a criterion that simply asks whether cyclic imports were eliminated or whether imports now point at a utility module. Prioritize visible evidence from git status/diff, grep of import sites and duplicate definitions, py_compile/import smoke tests, targeted pytest results, and any signs of destructive editing or API drift.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Incomplete or behavior-breaking utility extraction
reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a Python refactor that moves shared Solr-style utility/config/state logic into a new module, this flaw is present when the trajectory treats import-cycle removal as sufficient while visible evidence shows the extraction is incomplete or unsafe: the new module is untracked or absent from the diff despite imports to it; changed imports reference symbols not present in the new module; moved helpers are copied with altered signatures or behavior; large source files are rewritten or range-deleted leaving dangling code; tests are modified to accommodate the refactor rather than preserving public behavior; mutable shared state is imported by value and later reassigned; or syntax/import/unit tests are failing or not rerun after risky edits.

evidence_to_check: git status/diff includes the new utility module when other files import it
grep/import checks show all redirected imports correspond to real exported symbols
core domain logic remains intact unless intentionally and safely migrated
duplicate definitions or compatibility re-exports are deliberate rather than accidental
shared mutable state has a single authoritative owner or safe accessors
py_compile, import smoke tests, and targeted unit tests pass after the final edits
trajectory avoids broad destructive rewrites or leaves no dangling fragments after them
metadata.applies_when: The task is a modularization/refactor motivated by cyclic imports or shared utility extraction in a Python codebase.
metadata.does_not_apply_when: The task is only asking for import-graph analysis with no code movement, or the trajectory is still in early read-only exploration with no claimed implementation.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the utility module is tracked and importable, imports are consistent, behavior-preserving validation passes, and state/API compatibility has been considered.
scale.2: Minor concern only: the extraction mostly looks consistent, but one low-risk validation or compatibility check is missing.
scale.3: Moderate concern: imports and module creation are partially correct, but there is unresolved uncertainty about duplicate definitions, mutable state ownership, or whether all downstream imports/tests were validated.
scale.4: Clear flaw: visible syntax/test/import failures, stale or inconsistent imports, altered helper behavior, or risky rewrites remain despite apparent cyclic-import cleanup.
scale.5: Severe flaw: files import a new utility module that is absent or untracked, the main module is corrupted/truncated, tests are failing broadly, or the refactor achieves apparent import redirection while breaking core behavior.

experiences.title: Do not let correct min/max rescale mask missing smoothing and integration contracts
experiences.description: Retrieve when a TypeScript utility task asks for both numeric resampling and rescaling, and the trajectory visibly implements a standard min/max linear mapping while other required behavior remains unresolved.
experiences.context: In a TypeScript/React repository with array utilities, a rubric that only checks linear rescale formula correctness can be misleading when the task also requires a deterministic smoothing resample and possibly adoption by existing consumers. This warning applies especially after the agent adds an exported rescale-like function in an array utility module but has not established exact exported names, the intended downsampling/upsampling algorithm, consumer updates, tests covering exact expected arrays, or preservation of existing utility behavior. The original rescale idea is still appropriate as a narrow sub-rubric when the trajectory is specifically focused on the rescale helper, when naming/export expectations are already satisfied, and when the sibling smoothing and integration requirements are covered by separate criteria.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded trajectories for computing input min/max and mapping values into an inclusive target range. That criterion is usually a necessary part of the task, but it over-emphasizes an easy subproblem: many trajectories can implement the rescale formula while still using the wrong public name, implementing smoothing as simple interpolation rather than the repository’s expected smoothing/downsampling behavior, omitting consumer updates that should use the new utilities, adding self-confirming tests with invented expected values, or even rewriting unrelated array helpers. For future rubric generation, avoid making min/max rescale correctness the main predictor when the visible task is multi-part. Prefer a criterion that evaluates whether the trajectory has aligned the whole numeric-array contract with the existing codebase: exact exports/imports, deterministic smoothing behavior for downsampling and upsampling, reuse or consistency with existing numeric helpers, integration points that previously resampled/clamped waveform-like arrays, and non-regression of existing array utilities. If a rescale-specific rubric is still generated, pair it with a stronger rubric for smoothing/integration and make clear that passing the formula alone is insufficient.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Over-narrow rescale-only progress on a multi-part numeric utility task
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear to satisfy only the linear min/max rescale subproblem while leaving visible evidence that the smoothing resample contract, public API naming, consumer adoption, tests with exact expected outputs, or existing utility behavior are incomplete or misaligned. This applies when the task requires both smoothing resample and rescale utilities, and the trajectory’s strongest evidence is a standard formula such as mapping `(value - oldMin) / (oldMax - oldMin)` into `[newMin, newMax]` without comparable evidence for the other required semantics.

visible_task_features: adds both smoothing resample and linear rescale utilities
existing array utilities and numeric percentage helpers are present
existing source may contain consumers of fast resampling or clamping that should be considered
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: correct-looking min/max linear rescale formula by itself
replacement_evidence: correct exported public names and imports consistent with project style
smoothing resample behavior explicitly handles downsampling, upsampling, and identity according to repository expectations rather than merely interpolating
consumer code that needs smoother/rescaled arrays is updated when visible and relevant
tests or validation cover exact outputs for both new utilities without deleting or weakening existing tests
patch avoids broad rewrites or regressions in unrelated array helpers

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory treats rescale as one subcomponent and also investigates or implements smoothing semantics, API naming, integration, tests, and non-regression concerns.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: rescale receives disproportionate attention, but the trajectory still has concrete plans or partial work addressing smoothing behavior and public API compatibility.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory implements or validates a min/max rescale and mentions smoothing, but the smoothing algorithm, exact exports, or integration evidence remains largely assumption-based.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory’s main accomplishment is a correct-looking rescale formula while smoothing is a generic interpolation, tests are absent or self-invented, or expected public names/integration are not checked.
scale.5: Most severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory relies on rescale correctness to justify completion while omitting or misnaming the required smoothing/rescale APIs, failing to update relevant consumers, corrupting tests or unrelated helpers, or otherwise leaving the multi-part contract visibly unsatisfied.

experiences.title: Zero Threshold Requires Core Similarity Short-Circuit
experiences.description: Retrieve when a linter/checker task says a numeric threshold value of 0 should disable a duplicate/similarity check, and the trajectory has identified that the option flows into a shared similarity-computation engine.
experiences.context: Applies in Python linter/checker repositories like Pylint when the reported bug is that a numeric option such as a minimum duplicate-line threshold is interpreted as an extremely permissive threshold instead of a disable sentinel. The useful evidence is visible when the trajectory has found that the option is parsed correctly, stored on the checker/engine, and then used by hashing/comparison logic where 0 makes every positive match eligible. This guidance is most useful after the agent has inspected the relevant checker implementation or is about to patch it. It is less useful during very early repository exploration, for tasks where 0 is documented as a valid low threshold rather than a disable value, or where the bug is only option parsing/config loading rather than computation semantics.
experiences.experience: For this cluster, broad rubrics saying only “min-similarity-lines=0 disables duplicate-code” were directionally correct but too weak, because an agent can satisfy that wording by adding an early return only in one reporting wrapper while leaving the shared similarity engine’s main computation path unchanged. Rubrics that demanded guards in a specific wrapper such as the linter close/report method were also misleading when the visible trajectory showed a separate shared/standalone engine entrypoint. A better rubric should focus on the semantic boundary: zero must be treated as a sentinel before the duplicate/similarity algorithm hashes, iterates, or reports matches, preferably at the shared computation entrypoint used by the checker modes rather than by changing the threshold comparison or default value. The rubric should also insist that normal positive thresholds continue to use the existing algorithm unchanged. Avoid tempting proxy criteria such as repeatedly constructing single-file duplicate examples, requiring multi-file reproduction as the main success condition, changing the option parser/default, or extending the requirement to negative values unless the task explicitly asks for non-positive values. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent found the option flow into the similarity engine, recognized why the existing comparison/hash logic makes 0 pathological, and placed an explicit guard before similarity computation/display in the shared path.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Core zero-threshold disable guard
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly plan an explicit special case where the duplicate/similarity checker treats the configured minimum-line threshold of exactly 0 as disabled before entering the shared similarity computation/reporting path. The fix should bypass hashing, pairwise comparison, and duplicate-message generation for the zero value, while preserving existing behavior for positive threshold values and without relying only on a wrapper-specific reporting guard, parser/default changes, or ad hoc reproduction attempts.

metadata.task_cue: numeric duplicate/similarity threshold value 0 is requested to disable the check
implementation_cues: the option already reaches the checker or similarity engine as an integer threshold
the algorithm uses the threshold in hashing or a comparison that makes 0 match nearly any positive commonality
there is a shared engine entrypoint or computation path used before duplicate results are displayed/reported
preferred_evidence: explicit guard for threshold == 0 before similarity computation starts
no duplicate-code messages or duplicate statistics are produced through that path when disabled
positive threshold behavior remains delegated to the existing algorithm
anti_patterns: only changing the threshold comparison so 0 becomes a low threshold
only modifying option parsing or the default value
guarding only one linter-report wrapper when a shared engine path remains active
requiring negative values to disable the check without task support
treating lack of R0801 in small same-file manual examples as sufficient validation

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory recognizes 0 as a disable sentinel; it treats the issue as ordinary threshold tuning, parser/default configuration, or unrelated duplicate-code behavior.
scale.2: Weak evidence of the desired semantics, such as mentioning that 0 should suppress reports, but no clear plan to bypass the underlying similarity computation path.
scale.3: Moderate evidence equivalent to the parent trajectory: the agent has identified the relevant threshold flow and problematic comparison/hash behavior, but the planned or implemented guard may target only a wrapper path or remain ambiguous.
scale.4: Strong evidence that the fix will explicitly short-circuit duplicate/similarity computation when the threshold is 0 and preserve positive-threshold behavior, though validation or coverage of all visible entrypoints may be incomplete.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory places the zero-threshold guard at the shared computation entrypoint before hashing/comparison/reporting, avoids unsupported behavior changes, preserves positive thresholds, and validates or plans regression coverage against the real checker mode.

experiences.title: Do not reward tracing testability before integration is coherent
experiences.description: Use this when generating rubrics for Go refactors that move OpenTelemetry tracing/exporter setup out of a gRPC server constructor. A broad positive criterion about “isolated testability” can be misleading if the visible trajectory shows broken wiring, duplicated old exporter logic, failing builds/tests, or untracked/new-package integration gaps.
experiences.context: Applies in Go repositories where a task asks to decouple tracing initialization from server startup, especially when the agent is editing a large constructor such as a gRPC server setup and creating a new tracing/telemetry package. The original idea—requiring tracing provider/resource/exporter construction to be independently callable and testable—is valid when the trajectory has a coherent extracted API and stable server wiring. It becomes misleading when used alone at mid-refactor or final-review stages where visible evidence includes compile errors, damaged surrounding server code, broad line-number sed deletions, old exporter helpers reintroduced into the server for tests, package-name/import collisions, missing or untracked new files, or tests that pass only after compatibility shims that preserve the old coupling.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often generated a positive criterion like “the refactor should enable isolated testing of tracing configuration without starting the gRPC server.” That is directionally aligned with the task, but it over-rewards superficial extraction: simply creating a new package or making a function callable does not mean the patch is correct. In this task family, the more predictive evidence is whether the server still builds and preserves lifecycle behavior while the exporter/resource logic is actually removed from the server file. A better rubric should focus on integration coherence: the gRPC constructor should delegate provider/resource/exporter creation to the extracted component, keep analytics/audit span processor registration working on the same provider, preserve global provider/propagator setup and shutdown ordering, remove stale imports/helpers from the server, and validate with relevant Go build/test commands. Avoid the tempting criterion that treats “new tracing package exists” or “isolated tests could be written” as sufficient. Also avoid rewarding compatibility wrappers that duplicate the old exporter switch in the server just to satisfy existing private tests, because that undermines the decoupling goal. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence from diffs, compiler/test output, grep results for leftover exporter logic in the server file, and whether new files are actually included in the working tree/diff.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial tracing extraction with broken or coupled integration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for a Go OpenTelemetry tracing refactor when the visible evidence shows that the agent has created or discussed an extracted tracing/telemetry component but has not maintained a coherent, buildable server integration. This includes any of: compiler/test failures after edits; broad sed/manual edits that corrupt unrelated gRPC server code; stale or missing imports after moving tracing logic; the server still containing duplicated exporter selection/resource construction logic except for a tiny temporary wrapper explicitly being removed or tests being migrated; analytics/audit span processors no longer registering on the same provider; provider/exporter/global propagator shutdown behavior becoming unclear or double-registered; package-name collisions such as confusing an internal otel package with OpenTelemetry’s global otel package; or a new tracing package that is untracked/not included in the diff. The flaw is absent only when the trajectory shows a clean extracted API, minimal server delegation, preserved lifecycle behavior, and successful relevant Go build/tests or a clearly justified inability to run them.

metadata.task_type: OpenTelemetry tracing decoupling from gRPC server startup
primary_visible_evidence: go build/go test output
diff or grep showing whether exporter/resource logic remains in server startup
imports and package aliases in server file
server shutdown/global provider wiring
whether new tracing package files are included
presence of compatibility wrappers duplicating old logic
do_not_reward_on: new package exists but server does not compile
isolated helper exists but old exporter switch is duplicated in server
tests pass only after brittle dummy globals or wrappers that preserve coupling
new file is untracked or absent from diff
manual edits visibly corrupt unrelated server/cache/database code

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the visible trajectory shows a clean extraction boundary, server code delegates tracing construction/exporter selection, lifecycle behavior is preserved, stale logic/imports are removed, and relevant builds/tests pass or are credibly blocked by environment only.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: extraction is mostly coherent but there are small unresolved cleanup issues such as a questionable temporary wrapper, missing test migration plan, or limited validation while no build-breaking evidence is visible.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the agent has a plausible extracted component but integration is incomplete or uncertain, with visible unresolved call-site/import/test issues or leftover server coupling that may still be fixed.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: build/test failures, duplicated exporter logic in the server, corrupted imports, missing lifecycle wiring, or brittle compatibility shims are visible despite claims of decoupling.
scale.5: Most severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory visibly leaves the repository unbuildable or structurally corrupted, removes/omits required new files, or effectively abandons the refactor while still satisfying only the superficial notion that tracing was made independently callable.

experiences.title: Cross-Layer Limit Alignment Requires Semantic Use
experiences.description: Use when a task asks to keep a numeric limit synchronized between infrastructure configuration and application code, especially when one side is a Solr/JVM option and the other is a backend cap for generated queries.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python web application with Docker Compose/Solr configuration when the problem statement names two locations that must share the same numeric cap, such as a Solr `SOLR_OPTS` system property and a backend reading-log/query cap. It is most useful after the trajectory has inspected the named config/code files or begun editing them. It is less useful for unrelated single-file configuration tasks, for purely exploratory trajectories before either location has been identified, or when the backend value is already visibly enforced and the only requested change is documentation or formatting.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics correctly noticed that the task is about keeping values aligned across files, and this was useful because the visible trajectories repeatedly found one missing Solr option and failed to establish a real backend-side cap. However, a broad “values are equal across files” criterion is too weak: it can give undue credit for appending the Solr option or adding an unused Python constant while never proving that the application actually enforces that cap in the reading-log/query path. The better rubric should require cross-layer alignment plus semantic usage: the Solr runtime option must be present under the existing `SOLR_OPTS` without dropping other options, the backend cap must be defined at the intended value, and the trajectory should show that the cap is used or at least intentionally placed in the code path that builds/limits the large boolean query. Avoid the tempting proxy of counting any matching `30000` constant as sufficient. Prioritize visible evidence such as targeted inspection of the Solr service environment, identification of the backend query/filter construction path, preservation of existing config values, exact numeric agreement, comments or naming that make future drift less likely, and verification commands showing both sides after edits.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a task requiring a Solr boolean-clause limit to stay aligned with an application reading-log filter cap, the trajectory should demonstrate more than numeric duplication. It should identify the Solr service configuration, add or verify the exact `-Dsolr.max.booleanClauses=30000` property inside the existing `SOLR_OPTS` while preserving other JVM options, identify or introduce the backend cap in the intended reading-log/bookshelf code area, and show that the backend cap is meaningfully tied to the query/filter behavior that can generate many boolean clauses rather than being an unused decorative constant. Strong evidence includes targeted before/after verification of both locations and comments or naming that make the cross-file dependency explicit.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Semantic Cross-Layer Limit Alignment

metadata.task_type: configuration_and_backend_limit_alignment
required_visible_evidence: Solr runtime option is present under the existing SOLR_OPTS configuration with value 30000
Backend reading-log/filter cap is defined with the same value
Backend cap is connected to the code path that limits or constructs large query/filter inputs
Existing Solr options are preserved
Trajectory verifies both aligned values after changes
metadata.common_false_positive: Adding a matching numeric constant in application code without using it or proving it is the actual backend cap

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward alignment: the trajectory repeats searches, does not edit or verify either side, or confuses unrelated SQL pagination/test-data values with the requested cap.
scale.2: Finds one relevant location or confirms one missing value, but does not make a correct aligned change or continues redundant exploration without establishing the backend cap.
scale.3: Partially aligns the visible numeric values, such as adding the Solr option or a backend constant, but lacks evidence that both sides are verified and that the backend value is semantically used in the relevant query/filter path.
scale.4: Sets both the Solr option and backend cap to the same intended value, preserves existing configuration, and provides some verification, but the connection between the backend cap and the actual large-query behavior is only partially demonstrated.
scale.5: Fully satisfies cross-layer alignment: exact Solr option is correctly placed under SOLR_OPTS, backend cap is defined and used in the relevant reading-log/query limiting path, existing behavior is preserved, the dependency is documented or clearly named, and both values are explicitly verified after the edit.

experiences.title: Do not reward speculative resource-glob fixes when the visible repros pass
experiences.description: Retrieve this when a qutebrowser/Python resource-handling task mentions globbing, package formats, or caching, but the trajectory shows the agent’s own checks already pass for the stated README/unrelated-extension, explicit subdirectory, zipfile/pathlib, or preload-cache scenarios.
experiences.context: Applies in Python repositories using pathlib/importlib_resources/zipfile.Path-style resource traversal, especially qutebrowser.utils.resources. The misleading pattern is a rubric that demands broad fixes such as recursive parent-directory globbing, hidden-file exclusion, read_file_binary cache population, or generic dual-backend consistency solely because the task description mentions globbing/caching. These criteria become unreliable when visible tests or ad-hoc repros show the existing implementation already filters README/unrelatedhtml, finds files when the subdirectory is explicitly globbed, and uses cache after preload. The original globbing/backend/cache ideas can still be appropriate if the trajectory has concrete failing evidence for that exact behavior, a failing test being added for it, or code inspection showing the helper’s documented contract requires it. At final-review stage, absence of a focused patch or repeated test-output probing should not be judged positively just because the agent discussed both pathlib and zipfile.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics overpredicted by treating the task prose as a checklist of speculative implementation requirements: recursively glob from a parent directory, exclude hidden files, cache direct reads and binary reads, or merely handle both filesystem and zip backends. In the visible trajectories, agents often disproved or failed to reproduce those issues, yet the rubric still rewarded progress toward unnecessary or harmful edits. A better rubric should focus on whether the agent ties any resource change to visible evidence: failing tests/repros for the exact contract, preservation of existing helper semantics, correct startup/preload call-site behavior, and direct unit coverage in the repository’s test conventions. Avoid tempting criteria that add unmentioned behaviors such as hidden-file filtering or recursive globbing from a parent directory unless the trajectory shows that is the intended contract. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent inspected current tests and call sites, distinguished explicit subdirectory globbing from recursive parent globbing, verified preload cache behavior by patching the loader after preload, and avoided unvalidated edits when existing behavior already satisfies the repro.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that proceed with speculative resource-globbing or cache edits after their own visible investigation shows the stated behaviors already pass, or that define correctness by unsupported requirements such as recursive parent globbing, hidden-file exclusion, or direct/binary-read cache population without a failing test, documented contract, or call-site need. This is especially severe when the agent repeatedly probes broad test output or backend APIs but does not connect the patch to the actual resource preload API/call-site behavior and repository test coverage.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Speculative Resource Contract Expansion

misleading_evidence: existing or ad-hoc tests pass for README/unrelated extension filtering
preload followed by read_file uses cache when loader is patched after preload
agent changes behavior based only on hypothesized hidden files, directories, recursion, or binary cache needs
replacement_focus: visible failing reproducer for the exact resource contract
inspection of startup/preload call sites
preservation of helper semantics across pathlib and zipfile
direct tests matching repository conventions rather than temporary scripts

scale.2: Minor speculation appears in discussion, but the agent still verifies current behavior and has not committed to unsupported globbing or caching changes.
scale.3: The trajectory gives similar weight to supported and unsupported resource concerns, making the direction ambiguous; some checks pass but the agent has not clearly narrowed the actual contract.
scale.4: Clear speculative implementation direction is visible, such as proposing recursive globbing, hidden-file filtering, direct read cache population, or binary cache changes despite passing repros or no failing test for those behaviors.
scale.5: The trajectory strongly centers or implements unsupported resource behavior while ignoring passed repros, existing tests, or actual preload/call-site contracts, and validation consists mainly of repeated broad test probing or temporary scripts rather than targeted repository tests.

experiences.title: Do not equate alias propagation with complete colormap-name fix
experiences.description: Retrieve this when a Matplotlib trajectory fixes colormap registration/pyplot alias lookup for a registered name that differs from `Colormap.name`, especially after discovering equality-based registry tests or `Colormap.__eq__` name sensitivity.
experiences.context: This applies in a Python/Matplotlib codebase where colormaps are stored in a registry, copied on registration/retrieval, and may be registered under an explicit public key different from the colormap object's internal `.name`. A rubric that only checks whether `plt.set_cmap('registered_name')` or registry lookup uses the alias can be misleading once the trajectory has visible evidence that renaming the stored copy changes equality behavior, existing tests compare a registered alias to the original colormap, or `Colormap.__eq__` includes `.name`. The alias-propagation idea is still appropriate during early diagnosis or as one subcriterion when the trajectory has not yet reached compatibility validation; it becomes insufficient at implementation/final-review stage if the agent has observed equality failures, modified only pyplot state, or dismissed existing compatibility tests as obsolete without addressing the semantic equality contract.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded preserving the registered colormap name in `pyplot.set_cmap` or making the registered copy's `.name` match the registry key. Those are useful symptoms of the bug, but they overstate patch quality when used alone. In this task, a fix also has to preserve existing colormap value/equality semantics: registering an alias should make string/default-cmap lookup work, while two colormaps with identical LUTs and behavior should not become unequal merely because one is stored under a different public key. Avoid generating a criterion that treats a passing manual `imshow` reproduction or `rcParams['image.cmap'] == registered_name` as decisive. Also avoid accepting a registry rename patch if the trajectory shows `test_register_cmap` or equality checks failing due to `Colormap.__eq__` comparing `.name`. A better rubric should prioritize visible evidence that the agent noticed and resolved the interaction between alias renaming and equality/data comparison, kept registry-copy isolation, preserved deprecated and modern registration APIs, and did not replace a central registry invariant with a pyplot-only workaround.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that address registered colormap alias lookup only at the pyplot/default-cmap surface or by renaming the registered copy, but fail to account for the visible compatibility interaction with colormap equality when the registration name differs from the original `Colormap.name`. This flaw is present when the trajectory has inspected or encountered evidence that `Colormap.__eq__` compares names, an existing registration test asserts equality between an aliased registered colormap and the source colormap, or retrieved aliases have identical LUT/color behavior but compare unequal, yet the agent leaves equality name-sensitive, dismisses the test as merely old behavior, or relies only on manual `imshow`/rcParams success.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Alias Lookup Fix Ignores Equality Compatibility

manual reproduction passes but existing registration/equality compatibility remains unresolved
not_a_flaw_when: the trajectory is still in early exploration before implementing or validating a fix
the agent explicitly updates equality semantics or otherwise preserves data-based colormap equality while making alias lookup work
the task/codebase has no equality contract or tests involving aliased registered colormaps

scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory focuses mostly on alias lookup and manual pyplot reproduction, but has not yet encountered equality-related evidence or still plans broader compatibility validation.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory implements a plausible alias/name propagation fix and runs manual tests, but visible validation does not cover equality or registry compatibility despite nearby evidence that colormap names and equality may interact.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory observes an equality-based registration failure or inspects name-sensitive `Colormap.__eq__`, yet treats pyplot success or registered-copy renaming as sufficient without resolving the equality contract.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory explicitly dismisses equality failures as obsolete, edits tests to match the incomplete behavior, or leaves a pyplot-only/registry-only workaround that makes the reported example pass while aliased colormaps with identical data still compare unequal.

experiences.title: Do not credit API parity from three added handlers alone
experiences.description: Use when a NodeBB/Express-style task migrates socket-only group invitation behavior to authenticated HTTP write APIs and the trajectory has added API/controller/route stubs but has not proven route contract, schema/docs, and socket/client migration parity.
experiences.context: This applies in Node.js/Express applications with layered write APIs: route modules, thin write controllers, reusable API/business methods, OpenAPI or route-schema validation, and existing socket handlers that define the old behavior. The misleading pattern is a rubric that rewards “issue/accept/reject endpoints with auth” after seeing three methods and three routes, even though visible evidence may show a mismatched endpoint shape, ignored path parameters, missing schema documentation, incomplete validation, or no deprecation/removal of the socket/web-client path. A broad endpoint-completeness rubric is still appropriate once the trajectory has inspected the repository’s existing route scaffold and documentation conventions and has evidence that the new HTTP contract matches them. An auth-only rubric is appropriate only when route shape and documentation are already settled. A socket-deprecation criterion is appropriate after API parity is otherwise demonstrated, not as the main criterion during early implementation scaffolding.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics often asked whether all three invitation operations were implemented with authentication and authorization. That idea is useful but too generic here: it can over-credit surface-level additions in the API, controller, and route layers while missing the contract details that determine whether external clients can actually use the feature. Avoid a tempting criterion that merely counts added issue/accept/reject functions, route registrations, or owner/invited-user checks. A better rubric should focus on visible end-to-end parity evidence: the HTTP paths and methods align with the repository’s existing scaffold and public API contract, the controller passes the same target-user parameters that the route exposes, API methods do not silently ignore those parameters, owner/invitee/rescind semantics match the old socket behavior, route-schema/OpenAPI documentation is added for every mounted endpoint, and the old socket/client flow is removed or redirected only after the API path reaches parity. If the cutoff only shows partial edits or inconclusive tests, generate a conditional or negative criterion about unresolved API contract/migration parity rather than a broad positive completeness criterion.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat group invitation API support as complete based only on added issue/accept/reject methods or routes, while visible evidence shows unresolved contract or migration parity: route paths do not match the repository’s established per-invitation target-user contract, controllers ignore or replace route parameters with body/current-user-only data without justification, mounted routes lack corresponding public API schema documentation, authorization does not cover both invitee and owner/rescind semantics where required, or the socket/web-client invitation path remains unaddressed after API parity is claimed.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Surface Endpoint Additions Without Contract and Migration Parity

API-layer permission checks and use of existing group invitation primitives
public API schema or OpenAPI updates for mounted routes
evidence of socket/client deprecation, removal, or redirection after API parity
targeted route/schema or behavior validation rather than syntax checks alone

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory verifies route contract, parameter flow, schema/docs, permission parity, and migration/deprecation boundaries, or it has not yet claimed completeness.
scale.2: Minor evidence: most API layers are aligned, but one secondary parity item such as documentation validation or socket cleanup remains explicitly noted as pending.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: handlers and routes exist, but route shape or parameter semantics are not reconciled with the existing API contract, and validation is incomplete.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the implementation visibly uses a divergent route/body/current-user contract or ignores target-user parameters, and also lacks schema/docs or migration evidence.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory claims or implies completion while only surface handlers/routes were added, with multiple unresolved issues in route contract, parameter forwarding, schema documentation, permissions, tests, and socket/client deprecation.

experiences.title: Index-adapter dtype preservation for copy regressions
experiences.description: Retrieve when an xarray copy regression involves unicode dimension/index coordinates changing from fixed-width NumPy string dtype to object, especially where Dataset/DataArray copy paths delegate to IndexVariable or pandas-index adapter copy behavior.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/xarray trajectories for a reported regression where copying Dataset/DataArray objects or using Python copy/deepcopy changes only index-backed unicode coordinates from '<U*' to object while ordinary coordinates/data variables keep their dtype. It is most useful once the trajectory has either reproduced the dtype change, inspected Dataset/DataArray copy delegation into variable/coordinate copies, or identified that dimension coordinates are represented by an IndexVariable backed by a pandas index adapter. It can also be used as a target criterion early in the task because the user-visible contract is explicit, but should not be treated as satisfied until visible evidence shows the index-copy path preserves the adapter/logical dtype across the named APIs. Do not apply this pattern to generic string dtype issues that do not involve index-backed coordinates, to unrelated NumPy-version compatibility errors, or to broad copy/refactor work where dtype preservation is not the reported contract.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic contract: copying must preserve the logical NumPy unicode dtype of xarray IndexVariable coordinates across all reported copy APIs, without altering non-index variable semantics. This was discriminative because the visible trajectories repeatedly showed the key mechanism: pandas stores string indexes as object, while xarray preserves '<U*' separately in an index adapter; reconstructing the adapter from a copied pandas Index without carrying the saved dtype causes the regression. A strong rubric should therefore reward evidence that the agent localizes the problem to IndexVariable/index-adapter copying, preserves the adapter/logical dtype when deep-copying or rewrapping the pandas index, and validates Dataset.copy(deep=True), DataArray.copy with relevant deep settings, copy.copy, and copy.deepcopy. It should also check that ordinary coordinates and data variables are not changed. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as merely replacing removed NumPy aliases, modifying generic Variable.copy behavior, only proving Dataset.copy shallow behavior, or relying on pandas Index dtype itself to represent unicode. Prioritize visible reproduction output, internal inspection showing index-backed vs non-index variables, a patch that carries adapter dtype through the copy path, and tests or scripts covering the exact reported copy surfaces.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Preserves logical unicode dtype in index copy paths
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the agent understands and fixes the xarray index-coordinate copy path so fixed-width NumPy unicode dtypes on IndexVariable/dimension coordinates remain '<U*' rather than becoming object after Dataset/DataArray copy operations and Python shallow/deep copy helpers. Strong evidence includes localizing the issue to index-backed coordinate copying rather than generic data-variable copying, recognizing that the wrapped pandas index may have object dtype while the adapter stores the logical xarray dtype, preserving that adapter/logical dtype when copying or rewrapping the index, and validating that non-index coordinates/data variables keep their existing semantics.

trajectory identifies Dataset/DataArray copy methods delegate to variable/coordinate copy logic
trajectory distinguishes IndexVariable/PandasIndexAdapter-backed coordinates from normal Variable data
patch carries the adapter/logical dtype through index copying or provides an equivalent adapter copy method
validation covers Dataset deep copy, DataArray copy variants, copy.copy, and copy.deepcopy where reported
non-index coordinate and data-variable dtype behavior remains unchanged
common_false_proxies_to_avoid: treating a NumPy alias compatibility workaround as the regression fix
changing generic Variable.copy without evidence the bug is there
checking only Dataset.copy() shallow behavior
assuming pandas Index dtype alone can preserve fixed-width unicode strings

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses unicode IndexVariable dtype preservation; it may only explore files, handle dependency/import issues, or make unrelated dtype changes.
scale.2: Some relevant exploration or reproduction exists, but the trajectory has not localized the cast to index-backed coordinate copying or does not cover the reported copy APIs.
scale.3: The trajectory reaches behavior comparable to the parent state: it identifies the copy delegation/index-coordinate area and may reproduce the dtype cast, but the fix or validation is still partial or conflates the issue with unrelated compatibility changes.
scale.4: Strong evidence shows localization to IndexVariable/index-adapter copying and a plausible dtype-preserving fix, with validation for several reported copy paths and no obvious change to non-index variable semantics.

experiences.title: Judge Scalar-Point Dispatch by Current Expressions, Not the First Incomplete Hook
experiences.description: Use when an early reverse-operator attempt or downstream workaround is treated as the final state despite later dispatch-priority corrections and direct expression checks.
experiences.context: Operator dispatch in symbolic geometry can require both a reverse method and priority integration. An intermediate hook that works only when called directly is not enough, but it also does not establish that the final patch will fail. The criterion should inspect the latest scalar-left expression across relevant scalar and point forms and reject downstream addition hacks that merely hide an unevaluated multiplication.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics accurately identified the desired behavior but often scored a transient partial implementation. Generate a negative criterion around observable dispatch failure: scalar-left multiplication still returns an unevaluated product, dimensions are mishandled, or addition is special-cased instead of fixing multiplication. Use the latest direct executions as primary evidence and do not require a particular operator mechanism.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Unresolved Scalar-Left Point Dispatch
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize the current geometry change when direct scalar-left multiplication still yields an unevaluated symbolic product, disagrees with scalar-right coordinate scaling, breaks dimensional behavior, or is hidden by a downstream arithmetic special case. Superseded partial hooks do not count once direct current checks demonstrate correct dispatch.

observable_evidence: latest direct scalar-left and scalar-right expressions
result type and coordinates
numeric and symbolic scalar checks
two- and higher-dimensional point checks
downstream workaround presence

scale.2: A minor or early-stage concern about scalar-left point multiplication remaining unresolved or being masked downstream is visible, but it is not confirmed and the trajectory is still actively resolving it.
scale.3: Evidence about scalar-left point multiplication remaining unresolved or being masked downstream is mixed or incomplete; the concern remains plausible but is not yet decisive.

experiences.title: Do not treat PRAGMA table-name quoting as the whole SQLite identifier fix
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for Django SQLite `check_constraints()` bugs involving reserved-word table names and raw SQL interpolation, especially when the trajectory is editing PRAGMA foreign-key checks or nearby fallback SQL.
experiences.context: Applies in Django backend tasks where SQLite raw SQL in `DatabaseWrapper.check_constraints()` must handle SQL keyword identifiers during fixture loading or constraint checking. The misleading rubric pattern is to reward broad or vague 'quote table identifiers everywhere' progress, or to require/credit edits to every nearby table-name interpolation, without checking the exact affected SQL surfaces. The original idea remains valid when a task truly concerns unquoted identifiers in raw SQL, but it must be scoped to identifier positions that are actually unquoted and affected. In this code path, the PRAGMA branch includes both table-name PRAGMA calls and a follow-up `SELECT` using dynamic column and table identifiers; the fallback branch may already have literal identifier quoting in its SQL template, so wrapping names again can be harmful unless the template is changed coherently.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics often said the trajectory should quote SQLite table identifiers in `PRAGMA foreign_key_check()` and `PRAGMA foreign_key_list()`, sometimes expanding this to 'all dynamic SQL' or fallback paths. That is directionally correct but misleadingly incomplete: visible progress that quotes only `table_name` can still leave dynamic `primary_key_column_name` and `column_name` unquoted in the same offending-row `SELECT`, so reserved or unusual column names remain vulnerable to syntax errors. Conversely, a rubric that demands quoting every nearby fallback table interpolation can over-credit or encourage changes to SQL templates that already quote identifiers with backticks; passing backend-quoted names into already-quoted placeholders can produce invalid identifiers. A better rubric should focus on the exact SQL construction boundary: use the backend identifier quoting API for every dynamic identifier in the PRAGMA-supported `check_constraints()` path, including `foreign_key_check(table)`, `foreign_key_list(table)`, and the rowid lookup `SELECT` table and column identifiers, while preserving raw names for introspection and error messages. Avoid the tempting criterion 'quote all table names/fallback SQL/DDL/DML everywhere' unless the trajectory has shown those specific templates are unquoted and affected. Prioritize visible evidence from diffs or inspected snippets showing which identifiers are interpolated into SQL, whether the SQL template already contains quotes, and whether tests exercise reserved table names plus the violation-reporting query path.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for this SQLite reserved-identifier task when their proposed `check_constraints()` fix is incomplete or overbroad at SQL identifier boundaries: they quote table names in the PRAGMA calls but leave dynamic column identifiers unquoted in the subsequent row lookup `SELECT`, or they modify the fallback/manual constraint-check SQL by combining backend-quoted identifiers with templates that already contain identifier quotes, risking double-quoting or misquoting. This flaw is judgeable from visible diffs, snippets, or summaries that show the PRAGMA branch, the rowid lookup query, and any fallback template edits.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Incomplete or double-applied SQLite identifier quoting

Whether any fallback/manual-check SQL template already contains identifier delimiters before quoted names are inserted

scale.2: Minor concern only: the trajectory identifies the row lookup and fallback quoting boundaries but has not yet fully shown the exact final diff; no visible double-quoting or missed column identifiers are present.
scale.3: Mixed evidence: PRAGMA table names are quoted and the agent is aware of identifier boundaries, but the visible work is ambiguous about whether dynamic row lookup columns are quoted or whether fallback edits are coherent.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the visible patch or plan quotes PRAGMA table names but leaves `SELECT` column identifiers raw, or edits fallback SQL without accounting for existing identifier delimiters.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory strongly centers on broad 'quote all table names' changes, leaves multiple dynamic identifiers unquoted in the violation-reporting query, and/or visibly creates double-quoted or misquoted fallback SQL while treating passing superficial reserved-table tests as sufficient.

experiences.title: Initial-Aware Required Attribute in Base File Widgets
experiences.description: Use when a Django-like forms widget task asks for file inputs to omit the HTML required attribute when an existing initial file is present, especially when the behavior already exists on a clearable subclass and should apply to the base file input.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Django form widget trajectories where the agent has localized the issue to the file input widget hierarchy and the required attribute is controlled by a method like use_required_attribute(initial). It is most useful during implementation or final-review stages when visible evidence includes inspected class relationships, a candidate edit, behavior checks, or tests for plain and clearable file inputs. It may be premature if the trajectory has only explored the repository without identifying the widget method, and it is not the right criterion for unrelated upload validation, file storage, template-only rendering changes, or server-side required-field validation.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic contract: the base file input widget must make required-attribute emission depend on whether initial file data exists, while preserving the normal superclass hidden-widget behavior and preserving the existing clearable file input behavior. This aligned well because the decisive observable evidence was whether the trajectory found that the plain file input inherited a default required-attribute decision, saw that the clearable subclass already used an initial-aware check, and then added the same initial-aware logic at the base file input level without damaging neighboring methods. A better rubric should not make cleanup of the subclass override mandatory: removing a now-redundant clearable override is tidy and matches the requested move, but leaving an equivalent override can still preserve behavior. Likewise, do not overfocus on dependency installation, pytest availability, template changes, or adding unrelated helper methods. Prioritize visible behavior and code integrity: plain file input returns false for truthy initial data, true for absent initial data when otherwise required, clearable file input still behaves the same through inheritance or equivalent logic, superclass hidden-widget semantics are retained, and existing file input data/omission methods are not corrupted by broad text edits.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly converge on an initial-aware required-attribute decision in the base file input widget: the base file input suppresses the HTML required attribute when initial file data is present, still allows required output when no initial data is present and the superclass permits it, and preserves the clearable file input's existing behavior either by inheritance or an equivalent override. The visible evidence should also show that neighboring file input behavior, such as reading uploaded files and detecting omitted file data, remains intact and that no unrelated widget required-attribute methods were accidentally removed or corrupted.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Base File Input Required-Attribute Semantics

experiences.title: Declarative DISTINCT Opt-In for Django Aggregates
experiences.description: Use when a Django ORM task asks to add aggregate-level `distinct=True` support for built-in aggregates and the trajectory has inspected or modified the aggregate class capability mechanism.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django source tree when the task concerns aggregate constructor support for `distinct=True`, especially for `Avg` and `Sum`, and visible trajectory evidence shows the base aggregate class rejects distinct unless a subclass opts in, with `Count` as an existing precedent. This criterion is useful during investigation, implementation, or final review: early stages can be judged on whether the agent found the opt-in mechanism and target classes; later stages can be judged on whether the attributes were actually added. It is less relevant for tasks about `QuerySet.distinct()`, PostgreSQL `DISTINCT ON`, custom SQL compilation, contrib-only aggregate classes, or broader aggregate semantic changes. Do not apply it as a hard requirement for `Min` and `Max`; those are optional in this task family and should only be treated as acceptable if they do not disturb existing behavior.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic contract: Django already has aggregate DISTINCT rendering and constructor validation, so the correct fix is to mark the relevant built-in aggregate classes as allowing distinct rather than rewriting SQL generation. They aligned well because the trajectories repeatedly showed decisive evidence: inspection of the aggregate base class, discovery that `allow_distinct` defaults to false, recognition that `Count` sets it to true, and edits adding the same opt-in to `Avg` and `Sum`. A better rubric should make `Avg` and `Sum` the mandatory targets, allow but not require `Min` and `Max`, and explicitly require preserving existing aggregate behavior. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as merely running ad hoc tests, installing dependencies, changing query-level distinct behavior, or adding custom SQL/compiler code. Prioritize visible evidence of the class-level opt-in mechanism, correct target selection, absence of unrelated aggregate rewrites, and validation or inspection showing `distinct=True` no longer hits the existing TypeError path.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should correctly support aggregate-level `distinct=True` for Django's `Avg` and `Sum` by using the existing aggregate opt-in capability, with optional non-disruptive extension to `Min` and `Max`. Strong evidence includes identifying that the base aggregate constructor rejects distinct unless a subclass enables it, using the existing `Count` pattern as precedent, adding the capability to the mandatory aggregate classes, and avoiding unnecessary SQL rendering or constructor rewrites.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Existing Aggregate DISTINCT Opt-In

metadata.required_mechanism: class-level opt-in to existing aggregate distinct support
key_visible_evidence: base aggregate class has a distinct-allowance guard
Count already opts into distinct support
Avg and Sum are edited or clearly planned to opt in
unrelated aggregate semantics are left unchanged

scale.1: No evidence that the agent found the aggregate-level distinct guard or the correct built-in aggregate targets.
scale.2: The agent recognizes a DISTINCT-related aggregate issue but focuses on query-level distinct behavior, tests only, or speculative SQL changes rather than the existing opt-in mechanism.
scale.3: The agent identifies the `allow_distinct`-style mechanism or the `Count` precedent and plans to apply it, but has not yet shown complete mandatory target coverage or has ambiguous implementation evidence.
scale.4: The agent has applied or clearly verified the class-level opt-in for both `Avg` and `Sum`, with little or no unrelated behavior change; optional `Min`/`Max` handling is acceptable if non-disruptive.
scale.5: The agent fully implements the existing opt-in mechanism for `Avg` and `Sum`, optionally and safely includes `Min`/`Max`, preserves existing aggregate SQL/constructor behavior, and provides relevant inspection or validation that `distinct=True` is accepted through the built-in path.

experiences.title: CLI testability requires end-to-end error propagation, not just fatal-call discovery
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go CLI task explicitly says automated tests must assert command failures and the trajectory has found process-exiting paths such as FatalError/os.Exit in command handlers.
experiences.context: Applies to Go CLI repositories where command handlers currently have void signatures or call fatal-exit helpers, and the task requires tests to invoke commands without terminating the process. It is especially relevant after the trajectory has inspected the command dispatch layer and found direct fatal calls in individual handlers or subcommand files. It is less useful when the task is only about backend connection behavior, SSO mocking, or dynamic listener addresses and has no requirement to make command errors observable. During very early exploration, the criterion should reward locating the fatal boundary and handler signatures, but it should not treat a grep list alone as implementation progress. During patch review, it should require that errors travel from leaf command logic through dispatch to a test-callable entrypoint, with normal CLI behavior preserved only at the outermost executable boundary.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics correctly targeted the task’s CLI-testability requirement: tests cannot assert failures while tsh command handlers call utils.FatalError or os.Exit. However, the useful version of this criterion must be narrower and more end-to-end than “find all FatalError calls” or “convert onLogin.” A trajectory can look promising after grepping FatalError sites or converting one handler, yet still be incorrect if the central Run/dispatch function swallows the returned error, if main rather than a testable entrypoint remains the only place errors are handled, if subcommands in companion files still fatal-exit, or if helper functions keep terminating the process. Generate this rubric when the visible evidence includes process-exiting CLI helpers, void command-handler signatures, and a task demand for programmatic assertion. The rubric should prioritize evidence of a coherent propagation design: command handlers return error, nested helpers return/wrap errors instead of exiting, dispatch captures and returns the selected command’s error, tests can call a non-exiting entrypoint, and the production main still formats/fatals only at the outer boundary. Avoid the tempting but weak criterion of merely changing the shared FatalError implementation globally, cataloging fatal sites without changing call paths, or adding a local err variable in dispatch without returning or handling it.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-end CLI error propagation for testable commands
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a concrete plan or implementation that moves command failures out of process-exiting helpers and into returned errors all the way through the CLI command stack. Strong evidence includes identifying the non-testable fatal boundary, changing relevant command handlers and subcommand helpers from void/fatal behavior to error returns, propagating wrapped errors through the central command dispatcher or Run-like entrypoint, preserving user-facing fatal formatting only in the executable main boundary, and covering more than a single login path when the task mentions many commands. The criterion should not give high credit for only grepping FatalError/os.Exit, only converting one handler while dispatch ignores the returned error, or modifying a shared fatal helper in a way that leaves command call sites non-observable or breaks unrelated CLIs.

required_visible_evidence: process-exiting helper or os.Exit call sites have been located in CLI command code
command handler signatures or helper APIs are being changed to return error
central command dispatch returns or propagates the selected command error to a test-callable entrypoint
production main/outer boundary remains responsible for printing/fatal behavior
multiple relevant command families are considered when the task says many commands are affected
common_false_positives: a grep list of fatal calls with no refactor plan
one handler returns error but the dispatcher drops it
global FatalError behavior is changed instead of command errors being propagated
SSO mocking or dynamic address work is used as a substitute for CLI error-return work

scale.1: No visible attention to process-exiting CLI behavior despite task requirements, or changes continue to rely on fatal exits in command paths.
scale.2: Recognizes FatalError/os.Exit call sites or mentions testability, but only catalogs them or proposes a vague conversion without tracing dispatch and handler return paths.
scale.3: Identifies the key fatal boundary and sketches conversion of relevant handlers to return errors, but implementation is partial, limited to one path, or does not yet show the central entrypoint returning errors to tests.
scale.4: Shows a coherent refactor where major affected handlers/helpers return wrapped errors and dispatch propagates them, with only minor gaps in command coverage or validation.
scale.5: Fully establishes an end-to-end non-exiting command execution path for tests across the relevant CLI commands, while preserving normal CLI fatal formatting at the outer executable boundary and avoiding swallowed errors.

experiences.title: Contenteditable Placeholder Must Be Driven by Real Empty State
experiences.description: Use this when evaluating placeholder support for a React/TypeScript contenteditable composer with separate rich-text and plain-text modes sharing an editor view.
experiences.context: Applies in a TS/React UI codebase where a WYSIWYG/message composer is built from a top-level send wrapper, separate rich-text and plain-text composer components, and a shared contenteditable editor component styled via project CSS/PCSS. Retrieve this once the trajectory has identified or begun editing the composer stack, especially when the task requires placeholder text to appear only while empty, hide on user input, and reappear after clearing. Do not apply as a generic native input placeholder criterion, to unrelated form controls, or at a very early exploration point where the agent has not yet exposed how content state and clear/send behavior are represented. It is also less useful if the editor library visibly provides a built-in placeholder API with documented lifecycle semantics.
experiences.experience: The earlier rubrics correctly targeted the high-level behavior—placeholder visible while empty, hidden with content, restored after clearing, and supported in both rich and plain modes—but that wording can be too easy for a judge to satisfy from superficial evidence such as adding a placeholder prop, data attributes, CSS, and passing type checks. For contenteditable composers, the discriminative evidence is whether placeholder visibility is derived from the actual content state for each mode and rendered as non-editable visual decoration. A better rubric should check that the supplied placeholder is threaded from the existing caller into the WYSIWYG send path, then conditionally passed to the shared editor only when that mode’s real content is empty: rich text should use the WYSIWYG hook/library content state, while plain text should use the same input/paste/clear path that owns the contenteditable ref, including initial content and programmatic clears. The shared editor should preserve the forwarded ref and existing accessibility/listbox attributes, and render the placeholder via a pseudo-element/CSS variable or equivalent non-content decoration on the actual editable element. Avoid tempting weaker criteria such as “adds placeholder prop everywhere,” “adds data-placeholder plus CSS,” “compiles,” or “hides on focus”; these miss failures where the placeholder disappears merely because the editor is focused, never reappears after a clear, is based on stale wrapper state, conflicts with existing event handlers, uses a CSS selector that cannot match the edited element, or injects placeholder text into the editable DOM.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Real Empty-State Placeholder Lifecycle
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement contenteditable placeholder support by wiring the existing placeholder text into the WYSIWYG composer stack, deriving visibility from the actual content state for both rich-text and plain-text modes, and rendering the placeholder as non-editable visual decoration on the shared editor without disturbing refs, accessibility attributes, input handlers, send/clear behavior, or existing composer functionality.

required_visible_evidence: placeholder prop is accepted by the WYSIWYG send path and propagated to both rich-text and plain-text composer variants
rich-text mode computes placeholder visibility from the editor library or hook content value rather than from focus alone or a static initial boolean
plain-text mode tracks content through its existing input/paste and clear/send mechanisms, including initial content and programmatic clearing
the shared contenteditable editor keeps its forwarded ref on the editable element and preserves role/aria/listbox/dir/disabled attributes
placeholder rendering is visual-only, such as a pseudo-element or CSS variable/class, and does not insert placeholder text into message content
CSS is added in the stylesheet that actually styles the shared editor element and uses selectors/classes/variables that match the rendered markup
common_flaws_to_penalize: only adding placeholder props or data attributes without reliable empty-state updates
hiding the placeholder on focus even while the composer is empty
tracking plain-text emptiness in a wrapper state that is not updated by clear/send
adding an onInput handler to the shared editor that conflicts with mode-specific handlers
moving or wrapping the forwarded ref so editor hooks/tests no longer target the contenteditable element
editing unrelated message display or edit-composer code when the task is send-composer placeholder support

scale.1: No substantive placeholder lifecycle implementation is visible, or changes are unrelated to the WYSIWYG contenteditable composer.
scale.2: Some placeholder text or props are added, but support is limited to one mode, not connected to real content emptiness, or likely rendered in the editable content.
scale.3: The implementation propagates placeholder text and attempts shared editor styling, but empty-state handling is incomplete for either rich or plain mode, clear/send behavior, initial content, refs, or matching CSS selectors.
scale.4: Strong evidence shows placeholder text is propagated and visually rendered only when empty for both modes, with mostly correct state handling and preserved editor behavior, though one edge case or validation point remains uncertain.
scale.5: Clear evidence shows end-to-end placeholder support for both rich and plain contenteditable composers: real content state controls visibility, initial content and clearing are handled, rendering is visual-only, refs/accessibility/input handlers are preserved, and relevant checks or tests validate the behavior.

experiences.title: Hook Contract Over Existing Admin Inline Loop
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django admin task asks for a new overridable hook that selects inline classes dynamically while reusing the existing inline instance creation and permission logic.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django repository when the user request is specifically to add a ModelAdmin-style `get_*` hook for inline selection based on `request` and/or `obj`, and the visible trajectory has located or edited the admin inline construction path. It is especially useful after the agent has inspected `ModelAdmin.inlines`, `get_inline_instances()`, nearby getter-hook conventions, or has already changed the loop that reads inline classes. It may be premature during pure repository exploration before the relevant admin code is found. It should not be applied as-is to tasks about validating inline declarations, changing permission semantics, adding tests/docs only, or redesigning inline instance construction rather than exposing a selection hook.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged the semantic API contract rather than superficial formatting: add a `ModelAdmin.get_inlines(request, obj=None)`-style method, make its default preserve existing behavior by returning the configured inline classes, and have `get_inline_instances()` obtain inline classes through that hook while leaving instantiation and permission filtering intact. This aligned well because the visible trajectories repeatedly showed the decisive evidence: the agent found the existing `self.inlines` loop, added the hook with `request` and optional `obj`, and changed only the loop source to `self.get_inlines(request, obj)`. A better rubric should prioritize whether subclasses can vary inline classes using the same request/object without copying the inline instance loop. Avoid tempting but less reliable criteria such as requiring a specific insertion location, exact docstring wording, successful ad hoc scripts in an underconfigured environment, or adding checks-framework validation of the hook return value; those can be useful project polish but are not the core contract for this task and may unfairly penalize a correct minimal patch. If the trajectory instead alters permission checks, duplicates the whole loop in a new method, ignores `obj`, or leaves `get_inline_instances()` reading the static attribute directly, the rubric should treat that as failing the essential behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement the inline-selection hook contract: introduce an overridable `ModelAdmin.get_inlines(request, obj=None)`-style method that preserves the existing default inline configuration, and route `get_inline_instances(request, obj=None)` through that hook with the same request/object so dynamic inline class choices still reuse the existing inline instantiation and permission-handling path.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Dynamic Inline Hook Contract

prioritize_evidence: A new ModelAdmin getter hook for inline classes is added with request and object parameters.
The default implementation returns the existing inline class configuration rather than changing default behavior.
The existing inline instance builder iterates over the hook result using the same request and object.
Existing permission checks, max_num handling, and inline instantiation are left substantially unchanged.
avoid_overweighting: Exact docstring wording or method placement when the hook is discoverable and functional.
Ad hoc test failures caused by missing local dependencies.
Unrequested validation/checks-framework changes unless the task explicitly asks for them.

scale.1: No meaningful hook contract evidence: the trajectory does not add a usable inline-selection hook or leaves inline instance construction tied only to the static inline attribute.
scale.2: Weak evidence: a hook is discussed or partially added, but it has the wrong signature, does not preserve default behavior, or is not actually used by inline instance construction.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: a hook defaulting to configured inlines exists or is planned, but integration with the existing instance/permission loop is uncertain, incomplete, or not verified in the visible trajectory.
