scale.4: Strong evidence: the hook has the right request/object contract and `get_inline_instances()` clearly delegates inline class selection to it, with only minor style, placement, or validation uncertainty.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the visible trajectory clearly adds the hook with default backward-compatible behavior, passes request/object into it from the existing inline instance loop, preserves permission and instantiation behavior, and avoids unnecessary redesign or duplication.

experiences.title: Test Generated-Page Resolution Instead of Demanding One Toctree Implementation
experiences.description: Use when generated criteria prescribe hardcoded builder/domain machinery rather than checking whether special generated pages resolve correctly without suppressing real missing-document diagnostics.
experiences.context: Documentation builders may represent generated index and search pages differently from source documents, and correct integration depends on builder and configuration. During exploration, recognizing that distinction is meaningful progress. A negative judgment becomes warranted when the current implementation merely silences warnings, creates empty or wrong links, maps an index to the wrong target, or accepts arbitrary missing documents.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics bundled warning suppression, target mapping, builder availability, titles, and exact internal representation into a positive checklist. Generate a narrower negative criterion based on observable end behavior: generated entries must resolve to usable targets while ordinary missing entries still warn. Avoid rejecting a different internal approach when builds and rendered navigation establish the contract.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Warning-Only Generated-Page Whitelisting
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize a toctree change when it only suppresses diagnostics but leaves generated-page links empty or misdirected, exposes pages unavailable for the active builder/configuration, or also suppresses genuine missing-document warnings. Different internal representations are acceptable when rendered navigation and diagnostics demonstrate correct behavior.

observable_evidence: builder output warnings
rendered navigation targets
generated-page availability under active configuration
ordinary missing-document control case
index target mapping

scale.1: No visible evidence of generated-page support merely hiding warnings without correct, bounded link resolution; the available implementation and validation evidence is consistent with the required behavior.
scale.2: A minor or early-stage concern about generated-page support merely hiding warnings without correct, bounded link resolution is visible, but it is not confirmed and the trajectory is still actively resolving it.
scale.3: Evidence about generated-page support merely hiding warnings without correct, bounded link resolution is mixed or incomplete; the concern remains plausible but is not yet decisive.
scale.4: Clear visible evidence indicates generated-page support merely hiding warnings without correct, bounded link resolution, with no convincing correction or validation yet.
scale.5: The trajectory directly reproduces or validates generated-page support merely hiding warnings without correct, bounded link resolution, or claims completion while the contradiction remains unresolved.

experiences.title: Return-contract fixes must include callers and follow-up data flow
experiences.description: Use when a Python async polymorphic method is being changed from returning a single accumulator object to returning a tuple with an auxiliary list, especially in Solr/updater-style code with batch dispatchers.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python codebase where a task reports that updater methods return only an update/request accumulator but callers should be able to unpack `(request, new_keys)`. The visible trajectory has identified the updater hierarchy, concrete implementations, a helper delegated by one implementation, and an internal batch driver that currently adds the bare return value into an accumulator. This criterion is most useful once the agent has enough evidence to modify or explicitly plan modifications to the interface and consumers. It is less useful during very early repository discovery, and it should not require finding an existing visible unpacking caller because the contract may be enforced by tests or external callers.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric pattern is to evaluate whether the trajectory treats the issue as a return-contract migration, not just a local return-statement tweak. A good fix should make each relevant implementation return a two-element tuple whose first element preserves the previous update request contents and whose second element is always a list of follow-up keys, often empty. It should also update the abstract/base annotation, delegated helper paths or recursive calls, and any internal batch dispatcher that previously did arithmetic or accumulation on the bare return value. The judge should prioritize visible evidence that the agent has found and reconciled both sides of the contract: method implementations and callers. Previous rubrics that only asked for understanding of the tuple shape were too weak when the trajectory repeatedly grepped without editing or deciding how callers would remain compatible. Conversely, do not overconstrain the exact storage mechanism for follow-up keys; retaining an existing `keys` field can be acceptable if the returned list and batch processing remain semantically consistent. Avoid using “found an in-repo unpacking call site” as the success criterion, because the absence of such a call does not negate the requested public API change. Also avoid a criterion that only names the two classes from the bug report while ignoring the shared hierarchy and batch updater, since changing return types without updating consumers can break the main workflow.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete tuple return contract migration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show concrete implementation progress, or an immediately actionable plan, for migrating the updater interface from a bare update request return value to a tuple `(update_request, follow_up_keys)`. Excellent evidence includes updating relevant concrete updater methods and the shared/base signature, ensuring delegated or recursive updater paths return the same tuple shape, returning an empty list where no follow-up keys are produced, preserving the original add/delete update-request contents, and modifying the batch dispatcher or other consumers that previously accumulated the bare return value so they unpack the tuple and handle the follow-up keys without breaking the public batch-update return type.

metadata.expected_contract: two-element tuple: update accumulator object plus list of follow-up keys
implementation_scope: all concrete implementations participating in the polymorphic dispatch
delegated helper or recursive update paths
batch dispatcher/call sites that previously used the bare accumulator
key_judging_evidence: actual code edits or precise patch plan, not repeated searches alone
first tuple element preserves prior update request behavior
second tuple element is always a list, even when empty
new/follow-up keys continue to be queued or exposed consistently
avoid_overconstraint: do not require a visible existing unpacking caller
do not mandate a specific internal storage refactor if the contract and follow-up-key behavior are correct

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward the tuple contract; the trajectory is still repeating searches or only restating the problem without identifying necessary implementation and caller changes.
scale.2: Recognizes that updater methods should return a tuple, but focuses only on one or two local return statements or annotations and does not address consumers, delegated paths, or follow-up key handling.
scale.3: Identifies the relevant updater methods and the internal caller that assumes a bare accumulator, with a plausible plan to update both, but has not yet implemented enough to show the contract is consistently enforced.
scale.4: Implements or clearly prepares a mostly complete migration: relevant methods return `(update_request, list)`, callers unpack before accumulation, and prior update contents are preserved, with only minor uncertainty around tests or exact follow-up key propagation.
scale.5: Fully implements the contract across the hierarchy and consumers: all dispatched updater paths return the tuple consistently, empty follow-up lists are explicit where appropriate, generated keys are exposed/queued correctly, batch update behavior remains compatible, and tests or test updates verify tuple unpacking and existing update semantics.

experiences.title: Passing local test is not enough to dismiss a branch-lag hierarchy task
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task reports an outdated test reference or renamed/refactored base class, but the active checkout still has the old hierarchy and the targeted test currently passes.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/pytest repository tasks where visible investigation shows a mismatch between the task’s described API or class hierarchy and the checked-out commit, especially when git history or another branch shows the described newer design. The misleading pattern is to treat the mismatch as proof that no change should be made, because the local test passes or the new symbol is absent. The original idea of checking task-state alignment is still useful when there is no corroborating evidence that the requested semantic change belongs in this codebase, or when the agent is about to blindly reference a non-existent symbol in tests without updating the implementation. It is not sufficient when the task, history, or branch comparison indicates that the code under test should be migrated so the test exercises the real common abstraction rather than an obsolete one.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics rewarded recognizing that the task description appeared to describe a different or future code state and avoiding unnecessary changes. That criterion can be correct during early investigation, but it becomes misleading here because visible evidence also showed the intended semantic direction: the test should cover all actual strategy implementations through the current common base, and the module may need to introduce or restore that common base rather than leave the old passing test untouched. A passing targeted test in the lagging checkout only shows the old test still matches the old hierarchy; it does not prove the issue is invalid. A better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory distinguishes a blind test-only symbol replacement from a coherent hierarchy update: identifying the intended common strategy abstraction, ensuring concrete/reachable strategies inherit from it or are otherwise collected by the test, preserving behavior of read/write methods, and validating that the test now covers the relevant strategy classes. Avoid generating a criterion that simply praises 'avoid changes when task state differs' if the agent has found branch/history evidence of a real migration or under-coverage. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence such as class declarations, subclass collection results, strategy selection mappings, history/branch comparisons, and whether the planned patch aligns implementation and tests rather than doing nothing.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that conclude the task should be dismissed or left unchanged solely because the checked-out test currently passes or the described base class is absent, despite visible evidence that the intended fix is to align the implementation/test hierarchy around the correct common strategy abstraction. This includes treating branch/version discrepancy as a reason for no-op without proposing a coherent migration, or planning only a brittle test reference change that would point at a non-existent symbol without updating the module hierarchy.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: No-op dismissal of intended hierarchy migration

visible_cues: task describes an obsolete subclass root or renamed common base
local targeted test passes under the old hierarchy
current checkout lacks the described new base class or abstraction
git history or another branch shows the intended newer hierarchy
agent has not connected the test’s coverage requirement to the implementation hierarchy
better_focus: identify the common abstraction that should own shared strategy behavior
ensure concrete or reachable strategy classes are covered by the test’s class collection
avoid a test-only reference to a symbol absent from the implementation
avoid doing nothing when evidence supports a real hierarchy update

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory treats local pass/branch mismatch as investigative context only and still pursues a coherent implementation/test alignment for the requested hierarchy.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory notes the local pass and mismatch but also recognizes that the task may require migration and continues gathering evidence toward a real hierarchy-aligned fix.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory is ambivalent, repeatedly emphasizing that the local checkout is old or passing while only weakly considering how to update the hierarchy or test coverage.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory frames the task as likely invalid or unnecessary because the local test passes, or proposes avoiding changes, despite having visible evidence of a newer intended hierarchy.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory commits to no-op dismissal or an incompatible test-only change, using task-state mismatch as the main justification and ignoring the need to align the implementation and test around the actual common strategy abstraction.

experiences.title: Method-as-property index formatting contract
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Sphinx/Python-domain task concerns `py:method` used with a property-like option and the trajectory is inspecting or modifying index-entry text generation.
experiences.context: Applies in a Sphinx documentation-codebase setting, especially the Python domain, when the reported behavior is that an index entry for `py:method` with `:property:` is formatted like a callable method with `()`, while property entries should be formatted without call parentheses. It is most useful once the trajectory has visible evidence about directive index text generation, such as locating the method directive's property option branch, comparing it to dedicated property directive behavior, building a minimal reproducer, or updating related tests. It may be premature during pure repository discovery with no contact with Python-domain directive/index logic. It may be irrelevant if the task is about visible signature rendering, object inventory registration, cross-reference resolution, or changing the dedicated `py:property` directive rather than the index text of method directives in property mode.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the narrow semantic contract: a method directive marked as a property should register property-style index text without `()`, while ordinary methods, classmethods, and staticmethods should keep callable-style parentheses. This aligned well because visible trajectory evidence repeatedly showed the agent finding a property-specific branch in the method directive index formatter, observing or reasoning that it currently emits `name() (... property)`, and comparing it to the dedicated property directive or generated index output. A better rubric should evaluate whether the trajectory is converging on that precise formatting contract and preserving the non-property method cases, not whether the agent simply installed dependencies, successfully ran a full Sphinx build, or broadly searched for the word `property`. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as requiring a particular test command, rewarding broad dependency-chasing, changing all index entries to remove parentheses, or modifying signature display instead of registered index text. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent has identified the index-entry generation path for method directives with the property option, has proposed or made a minimal no-parentheses change only for that property mode, and has validated or planned validation against both property and non-property method examples.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a Sphinx Python-domain issue where `py:method` with `:property:` produces an index entry with method-call parentheses, the trajectory should identify the method directive's property-mode index-text generation as the target, make or plan a minimal change so that property-mode method entries omit `()`, and preserve callable parentheses for ordinary methods, classmethods, and staticmethods. Strong evidence includes comparison with dedicated property directive output or generated index entries and updating or planning a focused regression check for the property-mode method index text.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Property-mode method index text preserves property semantics

metadata.target_behavior: method directive with property option indexes like a property, without call parentheses
metadata.preservation_boundary: non-property method-like directives retain callable parentheses
priority_evidence: located method directive index-entry formatting for property mode
contrasted property-mode method output with dedicated property directive output
minimal formatting change or patch plan limited to property-mode index text
focused validation of property-mode and non-property method index entries
avoid_evidence: changes to signature display instead of index text
removing parentheses from all method index entries

scale.1: No visible evidence that the trajectory has connected the bug to Python-domain method directive index-entry formatting; work remains generic exploration, dependency setup, or unrelated property handling.
scale.2: Some evidence of searching around Python-domain property handling, but the trajectory has not isolated the property-mode method index text or may be targeting broad/signature behavior instead.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies that the method directive's property option affects index text and recognizes that property entries should omit parentheses, but has not yet clearly preserved other method formats or validated the distinction.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly targets the property-mode method index text and proposes or applies a minimal no-parentheses change while explicitly preserving ordinary/class/static method parentheses.
scale.5: The trajectory applies the narrow property-mode index-text fix, compares it against dedicated property behavior or generated index output, and includes focused validation or test updates showing property-mode entries omit `()` while other method-like entries still include them.

experiences.title: Default ordering is suppressed for grouped ORM queries
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a Django ORM trajectory about an ordering/introspection bug where aggregate annotations create GROUP BY and model Meta.ordering no longer appears in the emitted ORDER BY.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django repository when the task concerns QuerySet ordering semantics, especially an `.ordered`-style property that should reflect whether SQL will actually contain ORDER BY. The relevant visible situation is: the agent has identified aggregate `annotate()` or `values().annotate()` as creating grouped queries; model default ordering remains recorded in query metadata; final SQL for grouped queries omits default Meta ordering; explicit `order_by()` may still be preserved. This criterion is most useful once the trajectory has enough evidence from ORM query/compiler inspection, reproduction output, or a proposed patch to distinguish default ordering from explicit ordering. It is less useful for unrelated SQL ordering bugs, non-grouped querysets, backend-specific ordering behavior without Django ORM grouping semantics, or very early exploration where the agent has not yet connected annotation, grouping, and default ordering.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster focused on the semantic boundary that determines correctness: GROUP BY suppresses default model ordering, but not necessarily explicit ordering. This made the criterion discriminative because visible trajectories either showed the agent discovering that `default_ordering`/Meta ordering can remain true while grouped SQL lacks ORDER BY, or showed the agent stuck repeating greps without reaching that compiler/property mismatch. A better rubric should reward evidence that the agent will make the public ordering property mirror emitted SQL: first honor explicit ordering, then treat default Meta ordering as effective only when the query is not grouped. It should also reward validating both sides of the boundary: normal default-ordered querysets remain ordered, grouped aggregate querysets with only default ordering become unordered, and grouped querysets with explicit `order_by()` remain ordered. Avoid a tempting but weaker criterion such as generic 'understands Django query compilation' or 'checks default_ordering'; that proxy misses the bug because the metadata flag can persist even when SQL ordering is removed. Also avoid a blanket 'GROUP BY queries are unordered' criterion, because explicit ordering can still produce ORDER BY. Prioritize visible evidence such as inspecting the ordering property, tracing aggregate annotations to grouped query state, finding compiler behavior that drops default Meta ordering for grouping, reproducing SQL/`.ordered` mismatch, and proposing a targeted property-level condition rather than mutating unrelated query state.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the agent understands and preserves the key Django ORM boundary: explicit ordering makes a queryset ordered, but default model ordering should not make a grouped aggregate queryset report ordered when the SQL compiler omits ORDER BY. Strong evidence includes tracing aggregate annotation to grouped query state, recognizing that default ordering metadata may remain true despite no emitted ORDER BY, and shaping or validating a fix so the ordering introspection property reflects actual SQL ordering without breaking normal default ordering or explicit `order_by()` behavior.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Grouped query default-ordering boundary

metadata.environment: Django ORM
metadata.issue_type: public queryset ordering introspection diverges from generated SQL
prioritized_evidence: aggregate annotation or values-annotation creates grouped query state
model default ordering remains in metadata but grouped SQL omits ORDER BY
explicit order_by or extra ordering remains a separate ordered case
proposed fix or tests distinguish default ordering from explicit ordering
avoid_as_primary_evidence: checking only the default_ordering flag
generic compiler exploration without the grouping/default-ordering boundary
assuming every GROUP BY query is unordered

scale.1: No evidence that the agent connects grouped aggregate queries with suppression of default model ordering; trajectory may only repeat searches or discuss ordering metadata generically.
scale.2: Weak evidence of the issue area, such as locating annotation or ordering code, but no clear recognition that default ordering metadata can remain true while grouped SQL has no ORDER BY.
scale.3: Moderate evidence equivalent to the parent trajectory: the agent identifies relevant ordering and grouping code, but has not yet clearly formulated the explicit-vs-default ordering boundary or a targeted fix.
scale.4: Clear evidence that the agent understands GROUP BY suppresses default Meta ordering and that the ordering property should account for grouped query state while preserving explicit ordering.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the agent has traced or reproduced the compiler/property mismatch, proposed or implemented a targeted property-level change, and validated normal default ordering, grouped default-ordering-only queries, and grouped explicit-ordering queries.

experiences.title: Do not credit broad privacy-state checklists without evidence of the exact analytics lifecycle contract
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a TypeScript analytics/privacy fix involving PostHog-style initialization, DNT, anonymity modes, and event tracking, especially if the trajectory has only inspected files, made partial boolean-based edits, changed API/return/error semantics, or become stuck on tests.
experiences.context: This warning applies in frontend TypeScript/Jest code where an analytics module must coordinate runtime config, Do Not Track, anonymous vs pseudonymous behavior, identification, capture, and URL redaction. A generic rubric about enforcing a privacy/anonymity state machine is relevant only when the visible trajectory contains concrete design or patch evidence for the module's exact lifecycle semantics. It becomes misleading when it merely checks that the agent mentioned DNT, anonymous mode, pre-init guards, or tests, because partial fixes can still preserve the single boolean model, disable analytics under DNT instead of forcing anonymous mode, introduce incompatible throwing/boolean return APIs, update redaction per event instead of from the active state, or confuse missing configuration with not-yet-initialized behavior. If the trajectory is still exploratory, a state-machine rubric should be framed as planning/diagnosis evidence, not as implementation correctness. If the trajectory is stuck repeatedly grepping test setup, a test-infrastructure rubric is too generic unless the task is actually about test harness configuration.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often generated broad criteria such as 'Privacy Mode State Machine Enforcement,' 'Privacy-Compliant Analytics Behavior,' or 'Test Infrastructure Completeness.' The privacy idea was directionally correct for the task, but the wording was too coarse: it let a judge give credit for superficial fixes that touched DNT, identifyUser, or pre-init guards while missing the core contract. The better rubric should require visible evidence that the agent has modeled the active anonymity mode explicitly and consistently, separated analytics being enabled by valid config from initialization completion, and preserved the intended caller-facing behavior rather than inventing return values or exceptions. It should also distinguish DNT-forced anonymous operation from disabling initialization entirely. Avoid tempting criteria that simply ask whether all privacy buzzwords are mentioned, whether a single typo was fixed, or whether tests/mocks were investigated. A replacement criterion should prioritize concrete evidence in the trajectory: planned or applied changes to the internal privacy state representation; how init handles valid vs absent config; how DNT affects the active mode while still allowing configured initialization; how capture behaves when disabled vs called before init completes; how identify and redaction read the active mode; and whether public/test-facing API semantics are kept or deliberately updated with matching tests.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that address the analytics privacy task only through superficial checks or ad hoc edits, without establishing the exact lifecycle contract: an explicit active anonymity state, DNT forcing that state to anonymous rather than disabling configured analytics, a separate notion of analytics enabled by valid configuration versus initialization completion, and consistent use of that state for identification, capture, and URL redaction. This flaw is especially severe when the trajectory keeps a single boolean as the central model, changes public methods to return booleans or throw errors without evidence that callers/tests expect that contract, treats missing config and pre-init calls identically, passes per-event anonymity overrides that can diverge from the active mode, or spends repeated steps on test setup searches without returning to the implementation contract.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial privacy-state implementation

visible_evidence_to_check: Whether the trajectory proposes or implements an explicit active anonymity mode rather than relying only on a boolean flag
Whether DNT is described or implemented as forcing anonymous mode while still allowing initialization when valid config exists
Whether valid/absent config controls an enabled state distinct from initialization completion
Whether capture, identify, and redaction consistently consult the active mode
Whether public API return/throw/async behavior is preserved or updated with justified caller/test changes
Whether test investigation is productive and tied to the task contract rather than repetitive environment searching
do_not_overvalue: Mere mention of DNT, anonymous mode, pre-init guards, or location redaction
Adding generic throws/boolean returns without compatibility analysis
Repeated grep commands for test setup with no implementation progress

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory clearly identifies or implements the exact analytics lifecycle contract with explicit active anonymity, DNT-forced anonymous mode, enabled-vs-initialized separation, consistent redaction/identify/capture behavior, and compatible API/test handling.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory has the right lifecycle model but leaves one boundary partially under-specified, such as caller compatibility or a specific disabled-vs-pre-init behavior.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory covers several required privacy behaviors but still relies on a boolean or mixes enabled, initialized, and anonymity concepts in a way that could produce incorrect edge-case behavior.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory makes ad hoc fixes for DNT, identify, or tracking while preserving the wrong state model, changing API semantics without justification, or failing to distinguish configured-disabled from not-yet-initialized analytics.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory largely ignores the lifecycle contract, disables analytics under DNT instead of forcing anonymous mode, invents incompatible return/throw behavior, or becomes stuck on repetitive test infrastructure searches without meaningful implementation progress.

experiences.title: Task-Specific Operation Absorption Semantics
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django migration optimizer task asks for an existing CreateModel absorption pattern to be extended to another state-only model operation.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django-like repository where migration optimization is implemented through operation reduce() methods, especially when the task explicitly compares an existing CreateModel + metadata-operation reduction with a requested analogous reduction for another model-state operation. Most useful once the trajectory has inspected or edited the model operation reduction code, or has enough visible evidence about the target operation’s state-only semantics. It is less useful for unrelated optimizer architecture work, database-affecting schema operations that cannot be folded into CreateModel, or very early exploration before the agent has identified the relevant operation classes and attributes. At early edit stages, the criterion should distinguish a correct semantic branch from a brittle or malformed insertion that has not been inspected or compiled.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged the exact semantic contract of the requested optimization rather than generic progress. They focused on whether the agent put the change in the operation-level reduction for CreateModel, guarded it to the same model, and returned a replacement CreateModel preserving unchanged constructor data while taking the new managers list from the later AlterModelManagers operation. This aligned well because the task’s correctness depended on a narrow absorption rule, not on changing the optimizer loop or adding broad migration behavior. A better rubric should prioritize visible evidence such as: the agent identified the existing CreateModel + AlterModelOptions pattern; confirmed AlterModelManagers stores a complete managers list and is state-only; inserted a syntactically valid branch in CreateModel.reduce before other option reductions; used operation.managers as a replacement, not a merge; preserved fields, options, bases, and name; and retained the lowercase same-model guard. Do not make the main criterion about installing dependencies, running pytest, or adding regression tests, because those are supporting evidence but not the core fix. Also avoid rewarding a mere sed insertion or planned patch unless the visible code placement is correct and the nested return structure remains intact.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show that the requested migration optimization is implemented as a same-model absorption rule in CreateModel's reduction logic: when a following AlterModelManagers targets the created model, the result is a single CreateModel that keeps the original name, fields, options, and bases while replacing managers with the managers from the AlterModelManagers operation. The judgment should emphasize semantic correctness and valid placement in the existing reduction chain over incidental test-running or environment setup.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Correct CreateModel Absorption of Manager Alteration

metadata.target_layer: operation reduce method for the model creation operation
supporting_evidence: uses the existing model-options absorption pattern as precedent
recognizes the manager alteration as state-only
inspects or validates that the inserted branch is syntactically well placed

scale.1: No visible evidence that the agent identified the correct reduction location or the manager absorption semantics.
scale.2: The agent has found relevant migration optimizer files or proposed a vague analogous change, but has not established the same-model guard, attribute preservation, or use of the later managers list.
scale.3: The trajectory is comparable to the parent state: it identifies CreateModel.reduce() and the AlterModelOptions precedent, and may attempt an AlterModelManagers branch, but code placement or validation is incomplete or uncertain.
scale.4: Strong evidence shows a correctly placed same-model branch in CreateModel.reduce() returning a replacement CreateModel with preserved fields/options/bases/name and managers from the later operation, with minor gaps such as limited testing.
scale.5: The trajectory clearly implements the correct same-model absorption rule, verifies the edited structure or behavior, and avoids regressions such as changing unrelated models, merging managers incorrectly, or modifying the optimizer architecture unnecessarily.

experiences.title: gRPC Response Cache Must Be Fully Rehomed to Storage Cache
experiences.description: Use when a Go/gRPC task reports cache middleware causing auth-order bypass or type-switch overhead, and the trajectory has found both a response-caching unary interceptor and an existing storage-layer cache wrapper.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go server codebase where caching currently exists in a gRPC unary middleware that can return cached responses before later authorization checks, while a storage/data-access cache decorator is already wired when caching is enabled. Retrieve this when the trajectory has visible evidence of interceptor registration, middleware request type switches/cache key helpers, and storage cache coverage or gaps. It is most useful after initial repository exploration or during implementation review. It is premature during the first few exploratory commands before the agent has located the registration and storage cache layer. It should not be used for unrelated cache TTL/key bugs, pure middleware-ordering fixes, or systems where no data-access cache layer exists.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the architectural boundary: the fix is not just to reorder interceptors or optimize the type switch, but to remove the gRPC response cache path and preserve needed caching inside the storage layer. They aligned with visible evidence because partial attempts often removed only the interceptor registration, left the CacheUnaryInterceptor/function/helpers/tests behind, or added GetFlag caching without mutation invalidation or without compiling. A better rubric should require evidence that the agent has identified the old middleware cache scope, removed its production use and supporting response-cache code, and extended the existing storage cache wrapper for the operations previously protected by middleware caching, especially flag retrieval plus evaluation data paths. It should also check that cached flag data is invalidated when flags or their variants change, since stale flag/variant data is an observable risk when moving GetFlag into storage. Avoid tempting but wrong criteria: do not reward merely keeping cache after auth in the chain; do not require authorization context in storage cache keys when the storage cache is reached only after auth decisions; do not demand caching every storage method or broad list/get operations just because a storage cache exists; and do not treat deletion of the middleware registration alone as complete. Prioritize visible trajectory evidence such as grep results showing CacheUnaryInterceptor definition/registration, inspection of storagecache.NewStore wiring, discovery that storage cache already covers evaluation rules/rollouts but not flags, planned or actual removal of cache-only imports/key helpers/type switches, added storage GetFlag cache with compatible keying/serialization, mutation invalidation for flag-affecting writes, and gofmt/build/test validation after structural edits.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show a complete middleware-to-storage cache migration plan or implementation: it identifies the gRPC response cache interceptor and its registration as the authorization-order risk, removes or plans to remove the interceptor and cache-only middleware helpers/type switches from production code, confirms the existing storage cache wrapper is already wired when caching is enabled, extends that storage layer to cover missing flag retrieval while preserving existing evaluation rules/rollouts caching, and accounts for invalidating cached flag data when flags or variants are created, updated, or deleted. Strong evidence also includes cleaning stale imports/tests and running formatting/build or targeted tests after structural changes.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete Storage-Layer Cache Migration

key_visible_evidence: CacheUnaryInterceptor definition and server-chain registration are located
storage cache decorator and its server wiring are located
storage cache coverage gap for flag retrieval is identified
middleware cache request type switches/key helpers are removed or explicitly scheduled for removal
storage GetFlag caching and flag-affecting mutation invalidation are implemented or planned
format/build/test validation is considered after edits
avoid_as_primary_evidence: only reordering cache after auth middleware
only deleting the registration while leaving middleware cache code intact
requiring auth context in storage cache keys
adding broad unrelated storage caching without matching the old cache semantics

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of the migration boundary; the trajectory treats the problem as generic caching or middleware ordering and has not located both the gRPC cache and storage cache layer.
scale.2: Some evidence of the problematic gRPC cache or its registration, but little or no recognition that caching must be rehomed to an existing storage/data-access wrapper.
scale.3: Recognizes that the gRPC cache should be removed and storage cache used, but coverage is incomplete or vague, such as missing the flag retrieval gap, mutation invalidation, or remaining middleware cache helpers/tests.
scale.4: Clear evidence of removing the gRPC response cache path and adding the missing storage-layer cache behavior for flags/evaluation data, with mostly correct invalidation and cleanup considerations, though validation or edge cleanup may still be incomplete.
scale.5: Compelling evidence of a complete, build-conscious migration: production registration and middleware response-cache code are removed, storage cache covers the previous necessary cacheable data paths, flag/variant mutations invalidate stale flag cache, stale imports/tests are handled, and formatting/build or targeted tests are run or explicitly planned.

experiences.title: Do not treat a streaming builder race fix as the whole token-usage contract
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go AI/chat task requires Chat.Complete or an agent loop to return accurate token counts, and the trajectory is focused mainly on streaming delta accumulation or synchronization.
experiences.context: In Go codebases with layered chat/agent flows, a streaming race around a completion string builder can be a real subproblem, but it is not enough when the task explicitly asks callers to receive token counts for prompt and completion across multi-step execution. The warning applies when visible work mostly uncomments or synchronizes completion.WriteString, adds a done channel/wait group/mutex, or extracts TokensUsed from response structs, while the API return contract, accumulated per-call counter lifecycle, call-site updates, and streaming completion timing remain incomplete or unverified. A narrow streaming-race rubric may still be appropriate as a secondary criterion after the trajectory already shows a coherent explicit token-count API, all call sites/tests are updated, and the remaining risk is specifically whether streamed deltas are safely counted.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics rewarded fixing the streaming token-counting race condition. That criterion is partially valid because streamed deltas must be collected without data races, and counting an empty completion string is a real bug. It became misleading because agents could satisfy that local criterion while leaving the main contract broken: Chat.Complete or Agent.PlanAndExecute still may not return token counts, counts may remain coupled to concrete response structs, callers such as assistant/web layers may not be updated, streaming usage may be read before the stream is fully consumed, tests may not compile after signature changes, or usage reporting/rate limiting may still use stale token data. Avoid a rubric that only asks for a mutex, wait group, done channel, or the original TODO to be fixed. Also avoid requiring provider streaming usage data unless the visible dependency/API actually exposes it; in this setting streaming counts are locally computed from prompts and concatenated deltas. A better rubric should prioritize visible end-to-end evidence: an explicit token count returned from both chat and agent layers, a per-operation accumulator that adds prompt and completion counts for every model call, safe handling of streamed deltas until all output has been forwarded/consumed, updated downstream call sites and tests for the new signature, and validation that affected packages compile.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Over-narrow streaming-only token fix
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for token-usage tasks when the visible solution mainly changes streaming delta accumulation or synchronization but does not establish the end-to-end token-count contract required by the task. This flaw is present if Chat.Complete and the underlying agent do not visibly return an explicit token count to callers, token accounting remains tied only to concrete response objects, accumulated counts are not clearly maintained across all planning/tool steps, downstream callers/tests are not updated for signature changes, or streaming token reporting can occur before streamed output is fully consumed. Do not count mere use of a mutex/wait group/done channel as sufficient unless the trajectory also shows the API, accumulator, call-site, and validation pieces.

metadata.environment: Go repository with lib/ai chat and model agent layers using streaming OpenAI chat completions
task_contract: Chat completion returns assistant response or action plus token count
Token count includes prompt and completion tokens
Counts accumulate across multi-step agent execution
Affected callers and tests compile after API changes
misleading_proxy_to_avoid: uncommenting completion.WriteString
adding mutex/wait group/done channel around a strings.Builder
extracting TokensUsed only from response structs
passing a narrow streaming-token test while changed signatures still break other callers
preferred_visible_evidence: explicit token-count return from chat and agent APIs
single per-completion accumulator updated once per model request
safe streamed-delta collection through stream completion or stream consumption
updated assistant/web/test call sites
successful targeted build or tests for affected packages

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory addresses both explicit token-count returns and safe accumulated streaming/multi-step accounting, with affected callers/tests considered.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory emphasizes streaming synchronization but also has a mostly coherent explicit token-count API and call-site plan, with only small verification gaps.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory fixes or plans the streaming accumulator but only partially updates the token-count API or caller propagation, leaving important contract pieces uncertain.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory primarily implements a local streaming builder/race change while missing explicit token return propagation, multi-step accumulator semantics, or necessary caller/test updates.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory treats the streaming race fix as the solution despite broken or absent API changes, uncompilable signature mismatches, missing call-site updates, or token reporting that cannot be accurate for streamed/multi-step completions.

experiences.title: End-to-End Config Flag Semantics Over UI Badge Presence
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task adds an explicit backend configuration flag that also drives frontend read-only/status display, especially in Go/Viper config plus React/Redux UI flows.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories for full-stack configuration features where the issue requires both runtime config parsing/validation and visible UI status. The relevant environment includes Go config structs with JSON/mapstructure tags and validation hooks, schema files, a metadata/config endpoint, and TypeScript Redux selectors/components. This guidance is most important after the agent has begun editing config and UI files or is near final review. It is less useful during very early repository exploration before any proposed implementation exists, and a narrow UI-rendering criterion may be appropriate only when the task is explicitly limited to visual header rendering rather than config semantics.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics often emphasized whether the header shows a storage icon and Read-Only badge. That can be a necessary sub-requirement, but it is not discriminative for this kind of task by itself: several trajectories visibly added badges and icons while still leaving the feature semantically broken through incorrect config validation, inability to distinguish an absent flag from an explicit value, schema damage, missing tests, or regressions in existing storage behavior. A better rubric should evaluate the end-to-end contract: the config flag is modeled with the right tags and optional/absence semantics, validation rejects unsupported explicit settings with the exact required error without breaking existing storage backends, the metadata shape matches the UI type, Redux derives read-only from the config field with the required fallback for non-database storage, and the header rendering consumes that state. Avoid the tempting proxy of rewarding superficial SVG/icon additions or a badge label alone. Prioritize visible evidence such as targeted config tests/fixtures, passing existing storage-load tests after changes, preservation of unrelated object/git/local validation, selectors using the config object rather than stale inferred state, and review of generated/schema files for minimal valid changes.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Storage Read-Only Contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the storage read-only feature is implemented as a coherent backend-to-frontend contract, not merely as a visual badge. Strong evidence includes a storage configuration field with correct JSON/mapstructure naming and absence semantics, validation that rejects explicitly configured read-only mode on unsupported storage backends with the required error while preserving existing storage validation behavior, schema/config recognition where applicable, UI metadata types and selectors that consume config.storage.readOnly with the required fallback for non-database storage when absent, and header rendering that uses this derived state to show storage/read-only status with backend-specific visual context.

prioritize_evidence: config struct field and tags match the API/UI property expected by the task
validation distinguishes absent flag from explicit flag value when the task requires fallback behavior
unsupported storage combinations produce the exact required error without introducing unrelated validation regressions
existing storage config tests continue to pass and new focused read-only tests or fixtures are added
Redux/UI selectors derive read-only from configuration rather than only from storage type
header display consumes the selector/config state and covers database, local, git, and object backends
avoid_overweighting: presence of SVG icons or a Read-Only label alone
manual no-op or unmatched tests
passing a narrow test while existing storage-load tests fail
large schema or file rewrites that are not reviewed for unrelated regressions

scale.1: No meaningful implementation of the config-to-UI contract is visible, or the work is limited to superficial UI edits while config parsing/validation remains unaddressed.
scale.2: Some pieces are present, such as a field or badge, but key semantics are missing: validation is incomplete, UI still relies primarily on storage-type inference, or schema/types do not align.
scale.3: Roughly equivalent partial progress: backend and UI are both touched, but evidence is mixed or unvalidated, with possible absence-semantics problems, missing focused tests, or unresolved existing test failures.
scale.4: Strong progress: the config field, validation, UI selector/defaulting, and header display are mostly coherent, with visible effort to preserve existing storage behavior and run relevant tests, though minor gaps may remain.
scale.5: Complete, well-validated end-to-end implementation: correct optional config semantics and exact validation error, no unrelated storage regressions, schema/API/UI types aligned, selectors use the config source of truth with required fallback, header shows the required storage/read-only context, and relevant existing plus focused tests pass.

experiences.title: Do not equate Redis option breadth with correct public config support
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go/Viper-backed Redis cache task asks for TLS and connection tuning via configuration, especially when the trajectory adds many internal go-redis option fields and passes build/tests but may not have validated the public config schema, names, defaults, and fixture parsing.
experiences.context: This applies in Go repositories where Redis cache behavior is configured through application config structs, defaults, schemas, and YAML/env parsing before being wired into github.com/redis/go-redis/v9 Options. A misleading rubric in this setting rewards exposing or wiring a broad set of plausible TLS/pool/timeout fields, even when the task-visible contract is really about operator-facing config compatibility: stable field names, schema updates, default preservation, and parsing examples/tests. The original wiring-completeness idea is still useful after the public config surface is established and the trajectory is specifically editing the Redis client construction; it should not be the only or primary criterion when schema/testdata/config naming is still unsettled, or when the implementation invents extra options such as skip-verify, max lifetime, max idle conns, or separate read/write/pool timeouts not clearly requested.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked whether all TLS and connection tuning parameters were exposed and wired to go-redis, often listing many fields such as TLSSkipVerify, MaxIdleConns, ConnMaxLifetime, DialTimeout, ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout, and PoolTimeout. That criterion over-rewards broad internal option coverage: an implementation can appear complete while using non-contract config names, omitting CUE/JSON schema updates, failing to update Redis config fixtures, changing defaults away from existing behavior, or adding insecure/unrequested TLS knobs. A better rubric should focus on whether the trajectory preserves and validates the operator-facing configuration contract end to end: new Redis settings must be named consistently across struct tags, defaults, schemas, env/YAML loading, and examples/tests; defaults must keep non-TLS and untuned Redis deployments working; TLS must only be enabled when the explicit config flag is set; and the chosen timeout/idle fields must map to the exact go-redis/v9 option names. Avoid the tempting criterion that more granular go-redis options equals better completeness. Prioritize visible evidence such as schema edits, config testdata updates, passing config/schema tests, explicit default alignment, and confirmation of the library option names over mere presence of many fields in a struct or client literal.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat Redis TLS/tuning as solved by adding many internal go-redis option fields without establishing a consistent public configuration contract. This flaw is present when the visible work invents or renames operator-facing keys inconsistently across struct tags/defaults/schema/testdata, omits schema or config fixture coverage, changes defaults in a way that may alter existing non-TLS Redis behavior, or wires TLS/timeouts using unverified or version-incompatible go-redis option names. The criterion should be judged from visible trajectory evidence such as edits to config structs/defaults, schema artifacts, YAML/env testdata, config tests, and Redis client construction.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Public Redis config contract neglected

required_visible_evidence: Redis config struct/default/schema/testdata or config-loading changes
Redis client construction using go-redis/v9 Options
Evidence of whether config/schema tests were updated or run
Evidence of exact option-name verification for the installed go-redis version
do_not_reward_alone: A long list of new Redis fields in the config struct
A client literal containing many pool and timeout options
Build success without config schema or parsing validation
Docker-dependent Redis tests failing only because Docker is unavailable

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory keeps a consistent public config surface across defaults, schema, testdata, and client wiring, preserves non-TLS defaults, and verifies go-redis option names.
scale.2: Minor evidence: most public config surfaces are aligned, but one low-risk artifact such as an example fixture or targeted config test is missing while the trajectory clearly plans or notes it.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: Redis client wiring is mostly plausible, but schema/testdata/default alignment is incomplete or only partially validated, leaving uncertainty about whether operators can actually configure the feature.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory mainly adds internal fields/options while omitting schema or config fixture updates, using inconsistent public key names, or changing defaults without compatibility reasoning.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory exposes a broad but inconsistent or invalid config API, uses wrong go-redis option names or TLS semantics, and relies on build or non-relevant tests while leaving schema/config parsing broken or unvalidated.

experiences.title: Do not treat token lookup alone as an end-to-end token-only invitation fix
experiences.description: Use this when generating rubrics for Node.js/NodeBB-like invitation registration bugs where email-keyed invitation storage is being changed to allow registration with only a token.
experiences.context: In this environment, invitation registration spans a client registration form, server registration validation, invitation persistence, post-create group joining, inviter reference cleanup, and optional email-confirmation behavior. A rubric that only asks whether the trajectory found or implemented token-only verification can be misleading, especially during early exploration or partial backend edits: the agent may identify the `!token || !email` guard or add a token-to-email lookup, yet still leave the user-facing registration form without token propagation, keep group/cleanup logic tied to email, lose inviter metadata, fail to expire/delete all invitation references, or silently reintroduce email as required by filling `userData.email` from the invite. The original idea is still appropriate as a subcriterion when the visible work is specifically limited to validation lookup design, but it should not be used as the main correctness predictor once the task requires full registration behavior and metadata association.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded broad progress such as “implement token-only verification,” “add a token-to-email lookup,” or “preserve groups/inviter metadata.” That wording was too easy to satisfy from exploration notes or an isolated backend change and overestimated trajectories that never completed a coherent end-to-end flow. For this task family, the better rubric should focus on whether the visible trajectory has evidence of a complete token-centric invitation path: invitation links/forms submit the token without requiring email, verification can validate directly from token-indexed invitation data, post-registration group joining and inviter tracking consume token-associated metadata rather than depending on request email, cleanup removes both token and reference records consistently, and existing email+token behavior/error semantics are not broken. Avoid the tempting criterion that a scan, reverse lookup, or relaxed `!email` check is enough. Prioritize visible evidence from diffs/tests that the request can arrive without email and still carries the token through creation, metadata application, and cleanup.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that present an incomplete token-only invitation fix by changing only invitation verification or token lookup while leaving other parts of the registration flow email-dependent. This flaw is present when the visible work lacks end-to-end evidence that a registration request with no email can receive the token from the client, validate the invitation, apply invite metadata such as groups and inviter references, and clean up invitation records without reconstructing or requiring the invited email as the registration email. Also count as flawed if the implementation adds token-indexed data but omits expiration/deletion symmetry or stores insufficient metadata for post-registration behavior.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Backend-only token lookup leaves invitation flow email-dependent

metadata.environment: Node.js/NodeBB-like registration and invitation system
evidence_to_check: client or form handling passes invitation token when email is absent
server validation accepts token-only without assigning the invited email as the required registration email
invitation storage or lookup by token contains enough metadata for groups and inviter tracking
post-registration group join and cleanup use token-associated metadata
token and reference records have matching expiration and deletion behavior
existing invalid/missing invitation errors remain preserved
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: relaxing the email check or adding token-to-email lookup alone

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the visible trajectory accounts for token propagation, token-based validation, metadata application, cleanup, and compatibility/error behavior.
scale.2: Minor evidence of incompleteness, such as one unverified edge around cleanup or tests, but the main end-to-end token-only flow is addressed.
scale.3: Mixed evidence: token-only validation is implemented or planned and some metadata handling is considered, but one major path such as client token submission, post-registration groups, or cleanup remains unclear.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory focuses on backend verification or lookup while leaving group joining, inviter metadata, cleanup, or registration form behavior tied to email.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the implementation merely relaxes the email guard, scans for a token, or fills in the invited email, with no credible end-to-end token-only registration path and likely broken metadata or cleanup.

experiences.title: Do not reward nominal refactor scaffolding without behavior-preserving integration
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for a large Python refactor task that names desired architecture elements, especially when the visible trajectory shows only exploration, broad rewrites, class scaffolding, or partial test repair.
experiences.context: This applies to Open Library-style Solr update pipeline refactors in Python where the task explicitly asks for a unified state object and dedicated updater classes. A misleading criterion merely checks that named classes such as a state object and work/author/edition updaters exist, or that the agent has understood the old monolithic structure. That idea is only useful as a small subcriterion after there is visible evidence of a coherent implementation. It should not be the primary rubric during early repository inspection, after repeated failed heredocs/partial rewrites, when tests are still failing, or when broad edits may have damaged legacy behavior. In these situations, the visible risk is not absence of class names; it is whether the refactor preserves Solr request serialization, public API compatibility, update orchestration semantics, and locked-down document-building behavior.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics restated the task-specific architecture request: introduce a unified update state, add dedicated updater classes, and make update_keys aggregate their results. This is directionally related to the issue, but it becomes misleading when used as the main success predictor. In several trajectories, the agent either only inspected files, produced partial or failed edits, or added classes with the expected names while leaving behavior broken or unvalidated. A better rubric should focus on behavior-preserving integration: whether the new state object is the real request representation used by solr_update/update_keys, whether updater classes preserve existing work, edition, and author semantics, whether public imports and CLI callers remain compatible or are deliberately migrated, and whether targeted tests or import checks demonstrate no regressions. Avoid the tempting criterion that class names or architectural intent alone are enough. Prioritize visible evidence such as passing targeted Solr tests, successful import/compile checks, reviewed diffs around request serialization and update_keys, and explicit handling of redirects, orphan editions/synthetic works, author stats, output modes, commits, and document fields.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize a trajectory for treating the requested refactor as satisfied by adding or planning named architecture elements without visible evidence that the new pipeline preserves the legacy Solr update contract. This flaw is present when the agent mainly introduces SolrUpdateState/updater scaffolding or delegates to a new module, but does not demonstrate that request serialization, update_keys orchestration, work/edition/author edge cases, public imports, output modes, commits, and document-building behavior remain intact. The flaw is especially severe if the trajectory shows broad manual rewrites, failed syntax/import/test collection, unresolved failing targeted tests, or ad hoc fixes to regressions caused by the refactor.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Nominal architecture without behavioral preservation

metadata.repository_context: Python Open Library Solr update refactor involving a large update_work module, Solr request serialization, update_keys orchestration, and tests under openlibrary/tests/solr.
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: Presence of named classes/state objects or high-level architecture understanding by itself.
preferred_visible_evidence: Targeted Solr tests or equivalent behavior checks pass after the refactor
Public imports and CLI/batch callers remain compatible or are explicitly migrated
Solr request JSON generation and retry/error behavior remain covered
update_keys still handles works, editions, authors, redirects, deletions, commits, output modes, and synthetic work cases
Document-building fields remain preserved rather than rewritten wholesale

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory ties the new architecture to concrete behavior preservation, validates targeted tests/imports, and reviews high-risk update paths.
scale.2: Minor evidence: named architecture is emphasized, but the trajectory also includes some meaningful compatibility checks or targeted validation.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory has partial scaffolding plus limited validation, but important update paths or public API compatibility remain unexamined.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory mostly adds/plans state/updater classes or delegates to new code while tests, imports, serialization, or edge-case behavior are missing or unresolved.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: broad or partial rewrites introduce syntax/import/test failures or known behavior regressions, yet the trajectory still appears to rely on the presence of the requested class names as proof of completion.

experiences.title: Descriptor detection alone is not enough for class-property autodoc fixes
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for Sphinx autodoc trajectories involving `@classmethod @property` members, especially when the agent focuses on raw descriptor detection, `__func__` unwrapping, or Python-version descriptor behavior.
experiences.context: Applies in the Sphinx autodoc/autosummary environment for a bug where class members decorated as `@classmethod` over `@property` are omitted or documented with the wrong docstring. A common misleading rubric rewards the agent for noticing that the raw class dictionary contains `classmethod(<property ...>)` and that the wrapped property is reachable through `.__func__`. That observation is useful during early investigation and can be a valid progress criterion before edits exist. It becomes insufficient or misleading at implementation/final-review stages, because successful documentation requires the full autodoc pipeline to preserve the raw descriptor, select the property documenter, import/replace the object with the underlying property for documentation, retrieve the original property docstring using the correct class/member context, emit the class-property marker in the directive, and avoid unrelated compatibility edits. The original detection-focused idea may still apply when the visible trajectory has only explored root cause; it should not be used as a primary correctness predictor once the agent has edited helper predicates, documenter logic, or version checks without demonstrating end-to-end generated documentation.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often asked whether the trajectory detected `classmethod` or `staticmethod` wrapping a `property` and extracted metadata from `.__func__`/`fget`. That criterion was too narrow: agents could satisfy it while still leaving autodoc to call normal `getattr()`, use the returned value’s docstring, fail to set a classmethod/property directive option, omit inherited-docstring lookup through the owning class and member name, or make broad helper/version changes unrelated to the reported behavior. For this task shape, avoid a tempting criterion that treats `inspect.isproperty(classmethod_obj)` or generic descriptor unwrapping as the fix. Also avoid rewarding Python version checks or `staticmethod` expansion unless the trajectory ties them to the requested behavior and tests. A better rubric should focus on the end-to-end autodoc contract visible in the trajectory: raw descriptor preservation from the defining class, classification as a property only for `classmethod` wrapping a property, replacement with the underlying property object during import/documentation, correct docstring/abstract/type-hint handling from the property/fget, emission and domain support for a class-property marker, and validation through actual autodoc output or targeted regression tests showing the expected docstring rather than the return value’s docstring.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Incomplete end-to-end class-property autodoc handling
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that stop at or primarily implement descriptor predicate changes for `@classmethod @property` members without showing that the complete autodoc path documents the original property correctly. This flaw is present when visible evidence shows the agent only expands property/classmethod detection, unwraps `.__func__` locally, or patches unrelated Python-version compatibility, while lacking evidence that class member discovery avoids evaluated `getattr()`, the selected documenter imports the underlying property object, the original docstring is retrieved using the actual owning class and member name, class-property directive metadata is emitted and understood by the Python domain, and an output/regression test confirms the documented text is the property getter’s docstring rather than the returned object’s docstring.

metadata.environment: Sphinx autodoc/autosummary; Python descriptor behavior for classmethod wrapping property
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: Recognizing `classmethod.__func__` as a property, broadening `isproperty`, or adding version checks without end-to-end autodoc validation
preferred_visible_evidence: raw class-dictionary descriptor or defining-class MRO lookup is used instead of evaluated attribute access
property documenter handles import/object replacement and records classmethod status
docstring lookup uses the owning class and member name and reaches the underlying property/getter
generated directive/domain output can represent a class property, including abstract variants when relevant
targeted test or documentation build confirms the class property appears with the intended docstring

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory demonstrates an end-to-end fix or test covering descriptor preservation, property documenter import/unwrapping, docstring retrieval, class-property directive output, and generated documentation content.
scale.2: Minor evidence of incompleteness: most end-to-end pieces are addressed, but one secondary aspect such as directive display or abstract/property metadata remains only lightly evidenced.
scale.3: Moderate incompleteness: the trajectory handles detection and some documenter logic, but visible evidence is missing for either correct docstring retrieval, class-property directive support, or an actual autodoc output/regression test.
scale.4: Clear incompleteness: the trajectory mainly changes helper predicates or local unwrapping logic and does not show that member discovery/import avoids evaluated attribute access or that generated documentation uses the original property docstring.
scale.5: Most severe incompleteness: the trajectory rewards or implements unrelated version/staticmethod/helper changes, or the visible output still shows the returned object’s docstring/metadata instead of the class-property getter’s documentation.

experiences.title: QtWebEngine locale crash requires a gated --lang/pak startup workaround
experiences.description: Retrieve when a qutebrowser/QtWebEngine task involves blank pages or Chromium network-service crashes that depend on QtWebEngine version and system locale, especially around startup initialization.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python qutebrowser codebase where the reported failure is QtWebEngine/Chromium-level, locale-dependent, and occurs before pages render. The strongest visible cues are: the exact crash log is absent from application sources, WebEngine tab/render-process handlers look unrelated, `qutebrowser/config/qtargs.py` or equivalent startup Chromium-argument code is identified, and investigation mentions locale resources or Chromium `--lang` handling. This guidance is most useful once the trajectory has moved beyond broad grep exploration or is beginning to choose a fix location. It is less useful for page-specific localization bugs, HTTP Accept-Language header bugs, renderer termination UI handling, or tasks where the engine crash is not tied to startup locale resource resolution.
experiences.experience: The earlier rubrics were useful only when they steered evaluation toward early QtWebEngine startup argument handling rather than tab-level crash handling. However, broad wording such as “force a safe locale,” “set LC_ALL=C,” “set QTWEBENGINE_LOCALE,” or “change QWebEngineProfile/Accept-Language” is too permissive and can rate plausible but wrong patches highly. For this failure class, the better criterion should reward evidence that the agent understands the workaround as a Chromium language/resource selection problem: add a version- and platform-gated QtWebEngine startup argument, compute a safe `--lang` only when the current locale’s QtWebEngine `.pak` resource is missing, use Chromium-like fallback mapping, and avoid globally mutating process locale or disabling language headers. It should also reward making the workaround user-controllable/documented when the project’s existing workaround settings indicate risky upstream-version workarounds should not silently affect all users. Prioritize visible evidence such as locating `qtargs.py`, using existing QtWebEngine version utilities, obtaining `QLocale().bcp47Name()`, checking the `qtwebengine_locales` path via Qt library info, and emitting a `--lang=` argument before WebEngine initialization. Penalize repeated searches with no new information, profile-level Accept-Language changes, broad environment changes like `LANG`/`LC_ALL`, fake or unverified Qt bug/environment variables, and un-gated behavior across versions/platforms.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should converge on a startup-level QtWebEngine locale workaround: identify that the network-service crash is external to qutebrowser and happens before page/profile behavior, place the fix in the existing QtWebEngine/Chromium argument construction path, gate it narrowly to the affected QtWebEngine version and relevant platform, make it opt-in or otherwise consistent with existing risky-workaround settings, inspect QtWebEngine locale `.pak` availability, and generate a `--lang` override using Chromium-compatible locale fallback only when needed. Strong evidence includes avoiding global `LANG`/`LC_ALL` mutation, avoiding Accept-Language/profile-only changes, using existing version/config/logging utilities, and adding tests or documentation for the version/platform/config/locale-resource cases.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Gated QtWebEngine language resource workaround

key_evidence: crash log absent from application sources, implying QtWebEngine/Chromium origin
fix location is startup QtWebEngine argument handling rather than tab/render handlers
uses exact affected WebEngine version and platform gating
checks QtWebEngine locale resource files before overriding language
emits Chromium `--lang` override rather than changing global process locale or HTTP headers
matches project convention for optional/documented upstream workarounds
common_false_positives: setting `LC_ALL`, `LANG`, or Python locale globally
inventing unsupported QtWebEngine locale environment variables
removing or skipping Accept-Language headers
changing QWebEngineProfile language settings only
handling renderer termination instead of startup network-service crash
applying workaround unconditionally to all versions or platforms

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward the startup locale-resource cause; focuses on generic renderer crashes, tab UI, repeated broad searches, or unrelated locale code.
scale.2: Recognizes the issue is likely QtWebEngine/Chromium and locale/version specific, but only proposes broad or risky fixes such as global locale environment changes, profile Accept-Language changes, or unsupported environment variables.
scale.3: Identifies early QtWebEngine startup/argument handling and version gating as relevant, but lacks the locale `.pak` resource check, Chromium `--lang` fallback logic, or project-appropriate opt-in/documentation boundaries.
scale.4: Clearly targets QtWebEngine startup arguments with a narrowly gated `--lang` workaround and avoids global locale/header changes, but is incomplete in fallback mapping, resource-path handling, tests, or user-facing configuration/documentation.
scale.5: Fully articulates or implements the robust workaround: opt-in/project-consistent setting, exact affected version and platform gating, QtWebEngine locale `.pak` path lookup, Chromium-compatible fallback mapping, conditional `--lang` emission before WebEngine initialization, logging, and validation/documentation for affected and unaffected cases.

experiences.title: Optional argument behavior across delegated public APIs
experiences.description: Use when a Django-style change makes an argument optional for a helper that is also exposed through a template filter or wrapper, and correctness depends on both no-argument behavior and preserving existing escaped output.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django repository when the task asks to make an existing argument optional for `json_script`-like functionality that has two public entry points: a core utility and a delegated template filter/wrapper. It is most useful once the trajectory has identified the implementation and wrapper locations, or has begun editing/verifying behavior.
