It is less decisive at the very first exploration step before the relevant API surfaces are known, and it should not be used for unrelated documentation-only changes or tasks where there is only one callable surface and no compatibility-sensitive escaping/rendering behavior.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases focused on the semantic contract rather than superficial activity: the argument must be optional at every public entry point, the no-argument call must render a script tag without an `id` attribute, and existing explicit-id output plus JSON escaping must remain unchanged. This aligned well because visible trajectory evidence often showed whether the agent edited only the core helper or also the template wrapper, whether smoke tests exercised both `json_script(value)` and template usage without an argument, and whether explicit-id output still matched the old shape. A better rubric should prioritize observable evidence such as changed function signatures in both layers, conditional rendering that removes the entire `id` attribute when no id is supplied, preservation of the JSON serialization/escaping pipeline, and validation of both id-present and id-omitted calls. Avoid tempting weaker criteria such as merely adding a default parameter in one file, passing only pre-existing tests that exercise explicit IDs, updating docs without behavior, or producing `id=""` for an omitted argument. Also avoid over-penalizing normal environment/test-runner struggles if the trajectory has reliable targeted smoke checks and preserves the compatibility/security contract.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate implementation of the optional `element_id` contract across all public access paths: the core JSON-script helper and its template filter/wrapper both accept an omitted argument; the omitted/default case renders a `<script type="application/json">...` tag with no `id` attribute; explicit IDs continue to render the same id-bearing tag as before; and the existing JSON serialization plus escaping of HTML-sensitive characters is preserved and validated.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete optional-ID contract preservation

preferred_visible_evidence: signature/default updates in both layers
conditional tag formatting rather than always interpolating an id
manual or official checks for both no-id and explicit-id usages

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the optional argument behavior is implemented; the trajectory only explores or changes unrelated files.
scale.2: Weak evidence: identifies the relevant API or changes only one layer, but no clear no-argument rendering behavior or compatibility preservation is shown.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: implements optional behavior for the main callable or wrapper and has some validation, but coverage of the second public surface or preservation of escaping/id behavior remains incomplete.
scale.4: Strong evidence: both public surfaces accept the omitted argument, no-id output and explicit-id output are manually or officially checked, and existing escaping logic appears preserved.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory clearly updates both layers, conditionally omits the entire id attribute only for the absent/default case, preserves the prior serialization/escaping path, and validates utility plus template usage with and without an ID.

experiences.title: Avoid schema-only tag/digest rubrics when downstream image identity is in scope
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task adds digest support as an alternative to image tags and the trajectory has moved beyond config validation into scan/report/result workflows.
experiences.context: In a Go codebase where configured container images flow from config loading into scanning, result models, reporting, and server/API detection, a rubric that only checks adding a Digest field and exact-one-of Tag/Digest validation is misleading once the trajectory has inspected or edited downstream reference construction. That validation criterion is still useful at an early stage focused only on config parsing, or as one subcriterion among several. It should not be the main predictor when the task explicitly requires full image-name construction/logging and reporting/scanning consistency, especially if visible searches show remaining name:tag assumptions or edits around per-image scan identity generation.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics rewarded “digest field plus XOR validation” as if it were sufficient. That criterion is necessary but too narrow for this task family: many trajectories visibly satisfy config validation while still leaving downstream paths tag-shaped, dropping Digest from result propagation, constructing inconsistent report/UUID names, updating only logs, or damaging the per-image scanning loop/server-name identity. A better rubric should focus on end-to-end propagation and reference semantics: the configured image and result image structures carry digest; validation requires name plus exactly one identifier; the scanner/extractor target uses name:tag or name@digest; reporting keys and logs are consistent; and per-image scan identity no longer depends on a tag-only format or malformed ad hoc string replacement. Avoid the tempting criterion that gives high confidence just because `IsValidImage` rejects both/neither or because a helper for tag/digest formatting exists. Prioritize visible evidence from grep/search results and diffs showing all hard-coded `Name + ':' + Tag` or `%s:%s` image-reference sites were addressed, result-model copying includes digest, server/API image iteration remains syntactically valid, and any helper is used in the actual scan/report paths rather than only in logging.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Downstream image-reference handling remains tag-shaped or inconsistent
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that add digest schema/validation but do not visibly complete the end-to-end image-reference migration across scanning, result propagation, reporting, and server/API image detection. This flaw is present when the visible trajectory leaves hard-coded tag-only image construction, fails to copy digest into the persisted/result image model, updates only a log rather than the actual scanner/report identity path, introduces a helper that returns a tag/digest fragment but is not used consistently, or corrupts surrounding Go control flow while editing these downstream sites.

metadata.environment: Go project with config-loaded container image definitions feeding scan, model, report, and server/API workflows
required_visible_evidence: Searches or diffs around image struct definitions and validation
Searches or diffs around scanner image-reference construction
Searches or diffs around result model population
Searches or diffs around reporting/UUID or display-name construction
Searches or diffs around server/API image iteration or logging where configured images are copied for scanning
Build/gofmt evidence when broad sed or line-range edits touched Go control flow
avoid_overcredit_for: Only updating logging while actual scan/report identity remains tag-only
Adding a formatter helper without proving all downstream construction sites use it correctly

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory visibly handles digest through config validation, scan target construction, result-model propagation, reporting identity, and server/API image iteration without tag-only leftovers or syntax damage.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: most downstream paths are addressed, but one low-impact display/logging site or formatting cleanup remains uncertain while core scanning and reporting appear digest-aware.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: config validation and some downstream paths are updated, but visible searches/diffs show at least one important scan, report, result-copy, or server/API identity path is incomplete or inconsistently formatted.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory mainly implements schema/XOR validation and one or two obvious reference sites, while multiple downstream assumptions remain tag-only, digest is not reliably propagated, or server/API image identity is changed incorrectly.
scale.5: Severe evidence: despite adding digest/validation, the visible edits leave actual scanning/reporting unusable for digest images, introduce undefined helpers or malformed Go control flow, or fail to address the core downstream image-reference construction paths.

experiences.title: Interpreter Option Propagation in Reloader Child Commands
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python web framework or tool reloader loses CPython `-X` behavior because the child process command is reconstructed without `sys._xoptions`.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django-like repository when the task describes autoreload/restart subprocesses losing interpreter-level options such as `-X utf8`, and the visible trajectory has located the child command construction path or probed `sys._xoptions`. It is most useful once the agent is choosing or editing the command reconstruction logic, or reviewing a proposed fix. It is less useful for unrelated encoding bugs, request handling bugs, or very early exploration before the trajectory has connected the symptom to process spawning. If the trajectory is only at a testing-planning stage, do not make test additions the primary correctness signal; tests are supportive but not the semantic fix.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases judged whether the agent preserved active CPython `-X` options in the autoreloader child command. This aligned well because the observable decisive evidence was the agent identifying the subprocess argument builder, reading existing warning-option preservation, probing `sys._xoptions`, and adding equivalent `-X` interpreter flags before the script/module arguments. A better rubric should focus on semantic propagation: using `sys._xoptions` rather than parsing app args, serializing flag-style entries as `-Xname` and valued entries as `-Xname=value`, placing them among interpreter options, and not disrupting existing warning, script, module, or platform-specific invocation behavior. A tempting but weaker criterion is to require new regression tests as the main signal; visible tests are good corroboration, especially for boolean and valued options, but absence of added tests does not by itself indicate the implementation is wrong. Also avoid rubrics that treat the Windows encoding symptom as a file-opening issue or runserver option parsing issue; the key evidence is faithful interpreter command reconstruction for the reloader child.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the autoreloader child-process command preserves CPython implementation `-X` options by deriving them from `sys._xoptions`, converting each active option back into a valid interpreter flag, and inserting those flags before the child script or module invocation while retaining existing warning-option and launch-mode behavior.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: CPython X-Option Child Command Preservation

required_visible_evidence: The trajectory connects the symptom to a reloader or restart subprocess losing interpreter options, not to application-level encoding or file I/O.
The trajectory identifies the child command reconstruction code path used by the reloader.
The trajectory uses `sys._xoptions` as the source of active `-X` options.
The trajectory handles both `True`/flag-style options and non-true valued options.
The trajectory keeps generated `-X` flags as interpreter arguments before script/module/application arguments.
The trajectory avoids breaking existing warning-option preservation and script/module/entrypoint behavior.
supporting_evidence: Manual or unit-level checks of reconstructed child arguments with examples such as `utf8`, multiple options, and a valued option.
Awareness that the behavior is CPython-specific or guarded/limited to environments where `sys._xoptions` is available.
anti_patterns: Treating added tests as a substitute for implementing option propagation.
Parsing Django/manage.py arguments to recover `-X` options.
Changing application file-opening behavior to mask the encoding symptom.
Appending `-X` options after the script or module name where they would become application arguments.

scale.1: No evidence that the trajectory addresses interpreter option propagation in the reloader child command; it focuses on unrelated encoding, app configuration, or generic restart behavior.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory suspects autoreload or mentions `-X`/`sys._xoptions`, but has not connected it to the child command builder or has no credible serialization plan.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies the child argument reconstruction path and proposes adding `sys._xoptions`, but handling of valued options, argument placement, or existing launch modes is incomplete or unverified.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory implements or clearly plans conversion of `sys._xoptions` into `-Xname` and `-Xname=value` flags before script/module arguments, with attention to existing warning and launch behavior.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: in addition to correct propagation semantics, the trajectory validates boolean, multiple, and valued `-X` options across relevant invocation modes and preserves existing reloader command behavior, including CPython-specific compatibility boundaries.

experiences.title: Stage-Aware Coordinate Parser Adoption
experiences.description: Use when a Python/PyQt application task asks for robust parsing of user-entered "x,y" coordinate strings into point objects, especially when the trajectory is searching QPoint/comma-split code or adding a shared parser.
experiences.context: Applies in a qutebrowser-like Python/PyQt5 codebase where user-facing commands or settings may accept coordinate strings and internal code uses QPoint for scroll, element, or geometry positions. The criterion is most useful once the trajectory has visible evidence about parser placement, validation behavior, tests, or command/error integration. During very early exploration, do not require full call-site replacement yet; instead distinguish productive localization from repeated uninformative greps. Do not apply this criterion to internal structured QPoint construction from saved numeric x/y fields, UI placement enum settings, color parsing, or generic comma splitting unless the trajectory connects them to user-entered coordinate strings.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics correctly captured that the core solution needs a centralized coordinate parser with robust errors, and this was especially discriminative when the trajectory had either made no concrete progress or had visibly implemented and tested a parser. However, broad wording such as “identify all coordinate parsing locations and replace all ad-hoc parsing” can be premature in early search stages and can underrate useful progress when no existing ad-hoc parser is found. A better rubric should be stage-aware: reward evidence of a reusable parser modeled after existing parse helpers, accepting signed integer x,y strings, rejecting malformed input without partial matches, converting point-constructor overflow into a clean parsing error, and adding repository tests rather than relying only on manual scripts. At later stages, also require visible adoption at the actual user-facing coordinate entry point, with utility errors converted into the project’s command/message error mechanism and documentation updated if command syntax changes. Avoid tempting but weak proxies: counting QPoint hits, treating any comma split as coordinate parsing, adding an unintegrated helper with no caller, creating a new coordinate command unrelated to the task, relying on manual test files left at repo root, or trusting a regex using prefix matching that accepts extra coordinates. Prioritize visible evidence in the trajectory: concrete diffs or file edits, parser semantics, pytest coverage for valid/invalid/overflow cases, integration with a user-facing coordinate command or feature, cleanup of temporary scripts, and confirmation that changes remain in the working tree.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Robust Shared Point Parsing and User-Facing Adoption
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show durable progress toward a shared coordinate-string parser for user input: a reusable utility returning a PyQt point object; strict, whole-string parsing of signed integer x,y input; clear ValueError-style failures for malformed strings and overflow; repository tests covering valid, invalid, negative, extra-field, and overflow cases; and, once implementation has begun, use of the parser at the relevant user-facing coordinate entry point with errors surfaced through the project’s normal command/message mechanism and any affected help text kept consistent.

metadata.environment: Python/PyQt5 application with QPoint-based internals and command-style user input
strong_evidence: shared parser placed near existing parsing utilities
parser returns a point object rather than tuples or raw strings
strict x,y validation with negative coordinates and no partial-prefix acceptance
malformed and overflow inputs become clear non-crashing parse errors
repository tests are added and run
actual user-facing coordinate command or feature calls the parser and reports errors cleanly
temporary manual test scripts are removed
weak_or_irrelevant_evidence: repeated grep output with no new localization
internal QPoint use from structured numeric state
unrelated comma splitting such as colors, URLs, or flags
an unintegrated parser with no user-facing adoption at final-review stage

scale.1: No meaningful parser progress is visible: the trajectory is only broad or repeated searching, confuses unrelated QPoint/comma-split code with user coordinate parsing, or has no edits/tests.
scale.2: Some localization or design progress is visible, or a parser is sketched, but it lacks strict validation, has no repository tests, or is not tied to any plausible user-facing coordinate input.
scale.3: A reusable parser is implemented with basic signed x,y handling and some validation/tests, but important robustness or integration evidence is missing, such as overflow handling, whole-string rejection of extra fields, cleanup of manual scripts, or user-facing error adaptation.
scale.4: The parser is robustly implemented and covered by repository tests, and there is clear evidence of integration with at least one relevant user-facing coordinate path, though documentation, exhaustive adoption checks, or final verification may still be incomplete.
scale.5: The trajectory demonstrates a complete, durable fix: robust shared parser, comprehensive repository tests, clean user-facing integration and error reporting, updated command/help documentation where needed, no unrelated coordinate changes, no leftover temporary scripts, and successful validation of the affected tests.

experiences.title: Optional SQL Keyword Separator in Aggregate Rendering
experiences.description: Use when a Django ORM aggregate bug is explicitly caused by a missing separator between an optional SQL keyword such as DISTINCT and the compiled aggregate expression, especially Count(Case(...), distinct=True).
experiences.context: Applies in a Django source-tree trajectory where the task reports malformed aggregate SQL like COUNT(DISTINCTCASE WHEN ...), and visible work has inspected or changed ORM aggregate rendering, Aggregate/Func templates, Count distinct handling, or manual queryset SQL output. This is most useful after the agent has enough evidence to judge the SQL-construction path, such as seeing that a template concatenates a distinct placeholder directly with expressions or that generated SQL changes to COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN ...). It should not be retrieved for unrelated DISTINCT ON/query-level distinct issues, backend-specific SQL grammar bugs, generic test-runner setup problems, or tasks where the failing behavior is not an optional keyword being concatenated with an expression. It is also not the right primary criterion when the only remaining question is repository hygiene or whether scratch files were removed.
experiences.experience: In these cases, rubrics that directly evaluated the aggregate DISTINCT spacing contract were useful because the visible trajectory could show the exact root cause and exact behavioral repair: the aggregate template placed the optional distinct token immediately before the compiled expression, so the non-empty distinct token needed to carry its own separator or otherwise be conditionally separated. Strong evidence included code inspection of aggregate template interpolation, a patch that emits DISTINCT followed by whitespace only when distinct is enabled, manual SQL showing COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN ...) instead of COUNT(DISTINCTCASE WHEN ...), and checks that non-distinct aggregates still render normally such as COUNT(*) rather than COUNT( *). The better rubric should focus on this semantic SQL-rendering contract and compatibility boundary, including filtered aggregate fallback paths when visible. Avoid making a committed regression test the main correctness criterion for this class of trajectory: tests are valuable, but in these examples a test-focused rubric under-rated trajectories that had already made the decisive implementation fix and verified the rendered SQL. Also avoid rewarding an unconditional template-space change unless the trajectory demonstrates it does not alter non-distinct formatting; that approach is a tempting but risky proxy.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should correctly repair Django aggregate SQL rendering so an enabled DISTINCT modifier is separated from the following compiled aggregate expression, especially for conditional expressions that begin with CASE/WHEN, while preserving existing formatting and behavior when distinct is disabled. Strong evidence includes identifying the aggregate template/context interpolation path, applying a conditional separator such as making the distinct token render as 'DISTINCT ' only when active or an equivalent safe mechanism, demonstrating generated SQL like COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN ...), and checking that non-distinct aggregates and filter/fallback aggregate paths are not regressed.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Aggregate DISTINCT Separator Contract

metadata.environment: Django ORM aggregate SQL generation in a source checkout
primary_visible_evidence: inspection of aggregate template/context interpolation where the distinct token is adjacent to expressions
implementation adds a separator only when distinct is enabled
manual or test output shows COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN ...) rather than COUNT(DISTINCTCASE WHEN ...)
preservation_checks: distinct=False aggregate SQL remains unchanged, especially COUNT(*)-style output
simple distinct field counts still render valid SQL
filtered aggregate SQL or CASE fallback remains compatible when examined
avoid_as_primary_signal: requiring a committed regression test when the implementation and SQL evidence are already decisive
unconditional template spacing that can produce altered non-distinct SQL
backend-specific fixes for a backend-independent string-rendering bug

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory identified or addressed the missing separator between DISTINCT and the aggregate expression.
scale.2: Some recognition that DISTINCT and CASE are concatenated, but no safe implementation path or preservation of non-distinct aggregate formatting is shown.
scale.3: Equivalent to the parent trajectory: partial diagnosis or partial patch evidence exists, but validation of the exact rendered SQL or non-distinct preservation is incomplete.
scale.4: Clear diagnosis and a plausible conditional separator fix are visible, with generated SQL or focused checks showing DISTINCT is separated from CASE and no obvious non-distinct regression.
scale.5: Decisive evidence of the correct rendering contract: the aggregate interpolation path is understood, the fix conditionally emits a separator only with DISTINCT, SQL output verifies COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN ...), and related non-distinct/simple/filter cases are considered or tested.

experiences.title: Do not equate pointer-return fixes with pointer-receiver convention
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go task mentions a helper’s pointer return, value receiver, copied struct with map fields, and family-specific filtering before downstream calls. The misleading pattern is generating a rubric that rewards generic receiver-style consistency instead of the semantic data-flow contract.
experiences.context: Applies in Go repositories where a model helper conditionally filters package maps based on an OS family and callers pass either values or pointers to downstream lookup functions. A rubric about pointer/value consistency can be useful if the task is explicitly about in-place mutation or API-wide receiver conventions. It becomes misleading when the visible code shows a value receiver used as a copy-transform helper: returning a pointer may be needed for caller ergonomics, but using a pointer receiver would change or obscure the intended non-mutating copy semantics. At early investigation stages, merely finding pointer-receiver methods elsewhere is weak evidence; at implementation/review stages, the decisive evidence is whether the returned object, its package maps, and all call sites preserve the intended filtering behavior for each family.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics overemphasized that mutating or modified-copy methods should use pointer receivers to match other methods. That criterion is wrong for copy-transform helpers on structs containing maps: a value receiver can intentionally create an isolated returned result while leaving the original receiver untouched, and a pointer return can still be appropriate so pointer-taking call sites receive the filtered copy. A better rubric should focus on the observable semantic contract: for the special family, both binary and source package maps are filtered using the existing package classifier; for other families, package sets are preserved; returned pointer/value usage is coherent at all call sites; and downstream vulnerability lookups actually use the filtered result without accidentally querying unsupported packages or mutating the original. Avoid rewarding trajectories just because they grep receiver conventions, convert the receiver to `*T`, or update `&result` call sites mechanically. Prefer evidence that the agent inspected all callers, understood map aliasing, considered centralizing the filter before shared lookup paths, and planned or added tests covering family branches, package and source-package filtering, and original-versus-returned object behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat a family-specific package-filtering helper primarily as a generic pointer-receiver consistency issue, especially when they infer that a value receiver should become a pointer receiver solely because the method returns a modified result or because other methods on the type mutate in place. This flaw is present when the trajectory does not verify the helper's copy-transform contract, map aliasing behavior, both package collections, and the downstream call sites that must consume the filtered result.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Receiver-style overfit instead of filtering data-flow contract

visible_cues: task mentions pointer return and package exclusion for a family-specific helper
target struct contains map fields such as package maps
helper currently uses a value receiver and returns a modified result
callers pass returned results to functions expecting pointers
trajectory focuses on grepping pointer receivers or matching receiver conventions
better_evidence: analysis of whether the original result should remain unmodified
analysis of both binary and source package filtering
inspection of all call sites and downstream query functions
tests or test plan for special-family filtering and non-special-family preservation
verification that returned pointer/value semantics do not cause unsupported packages to be queried

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory treats pointer return/receiver choice as subordinate to the family-specific filtering contract and call-site data flow.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory mentions receiver consistency but also checks package filtering, map aliasing, and relevant callers.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory balances receiver-style discussion with some semantic checks, but leaves important caller or filtering behavior unverified.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory mainly argues for pointer receiver or pointer return based on convention and only superficially inspects package filtering or call sites.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory repeatedly focuses on pointer-receiver conventions or mechanically changes receiver/call-site types while ignoring whether the filtered result is correctly produced and consumed for each family.

experiences.title: Minimum Dependency Floor Enforcement
experiences.description: Use when a task asks to drop support for versions below a new dependency/library minimum and the trajectory has found the canonical runtime/version guard plus old current documentation or tests.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django/Python-style repository, or similar framework backend, when the requested change is primarily to raise a supported dependency floor such as a database/library version. The visible trajectory should show evidence of locating the existing minimum-version enforcement point, the old threshold/error message, and possibly current docs or tests mentioning the old floor. This is most useful during implementation or final-review stages after the agent has enough evidence about where the support policy is enforced. It is less applicable when the task is actually to implement new feature behavior enabled by the newer version, when no canonical version guard exists, or when the trajectory is still only broad-searching without identifying the support-floor mechanism. Historical release notes and unrelated feature-specific version gates should be treated cautiously rather than as automatic edit targets.
experiences.experience: For support-drop tasks, the strongest rubric should judge whether the agent raised the actual runtime/enforcement floor and kept visible current-facing statements consistent. In these cases, the useful rubrics focused on changing the canonical SQLite backend guard from the old tuple/string to the new minimum and updating current user-facing text/tests when the trajectory found them. Rubrics that instead demanded cleanup of expression-index/JSON feature gates were misleading: the task rationale mentioned features available in the new version, but the observed code did not contain obsolete below-new-floor gates that needed removal, and unrelated higher-version feature checks remained valid. A better rubric should prioritize visible evidence that the agent: found the authoritative version check; changed both the numeric comparison and user-facing exception text to the new minimum; searched for stale old-minimum references; updated current docs/tests if present; and avoided broad, collateral edits to historical release notes or unrelated backend feature behavior. Do not make documentation-only consistency the main criterion if the runtime guard has not been addressed, and do not require rewriting old release history unless the project convention or visible task context clearly calls for a new current release note. If the trajectory shows accidental broad substitutions or malformed files, a separate collateral-regression rubric may be warranted, but the core support-floor rubric remains about the canonical guard and current consistency.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement the support-floor change at the authoritative runtime/version enforcement point by raising the old minimum to the requested new minimum, keeping the associated error/message behavior consistent, and updating any current tests or user-facing support documentation it has identified, while avoiding unrelated feature-gate changes or blind rewrites of historical references.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Canonical Minimum Version Floor Update

prioritize_evidence: Agent identifies the existing minimum-version guard or equivalent canonical enforcement mechanism.
Numeric comparison or version predicate is updated from the old floor to the requested new floor.
Exception, warning, or user-facing message names the same new minimum.
Current documentation/tests mentioning the old supported floor are searched and updated when relevant.
Historical release notes or unrelated feature-specific version checks are not treated as mandatory global replacements.
avoid_as_primary_criterion: Requiring cleanup of feature gates merely because the task rationale mentions features enabled by the new version.
Rewarding documentation updates without runtime enforcement.
Penalizing retained historical release-note facts unless the trajectory is explicitly adding or editing current release notes.
Treating all occurrences of an old version number as stale without checking context.

scale.1: No visible progress on the authoritative support-floor enforcement; the agent only explores unrelated files, updates rationale/docs without touching the runtime guard, or changes feature behavior unrelated to the requested minimum.
scale.2: Some relevant investigation or partial edits are visible, but the canonical guard, threshold, or message remains missing/inconsistent, or current references to the old minimum are not checked despite being identified.
scale.3: Comparable to the parent trajectory: the agent has identified the right enforcement point and may have made partial consistent edits, but evidence is incomplete, validation/search is limited, or current docs/tests consistency is uncertain.
scale.4: Strong evidence that the canonical version guard and error/message were updated to the new minimum, with targeted searches or edits for current docs/tests and no obvious unrelated feature-gate changes.
scale.5: Complete visible support-floor update: authoritative guard, message, relevant tests, and current user-facing documentation are consistent with the new minimum; stale current references are checked; historical or unrelated version references are deliberately preserved or excluded; and validation or focused inspection shows no collateral corruption.

experiences.title: Do not treat add_book ISBN extraction as sufficient for promise-item augmentation
experiences.description: Retrieve this when an Open Library promise-item import task mentions incomplete records, ASIN/ISBN-10 metadata augmentation, staged import_item/BookWorm data, and especially enrichment before validation.
experiences.context: In the Open Library Python import pipeline, it is tempting to focus on the visible ASIN-only hook in catalog/add_book and generate a rubric requiring a new ISBN-10 extractor plus another call to the existing supplement function. That can be a useful exploratory milestone when the trajectory is only locating the current narrow behavior. It becomes misleading as a correctness rubric when the task’s observable requirements involve incomplete promise records being accepted/enriched before import API validation and when metadata must be made available by staging/fetching BookWorm data upstream. In that situation, a local add_book-only criterion can overvalue patches that simply pass an ISBN-10 to the old supplement hook while leaving validation, placeholder handling, and promise batch staging unchanged. The original idea may still apply in a narrower codebase where staged metadata already exists for every identifier and the only missing behavior is a local identifier-selection branch at the existing augmentation call site.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked the judge to reward identifying or implementing ISBN-10 extraction in promise records and calling the existing add_book supplement path with ASIN/ISBN-10 identifiers. That criterion is not inherently useless, but in this task it is an over-narrow proxy: it ignores whether incomplete promise records are staged for metadata lookup in the first place, whether import API parsing/validation permits strong-identifier-only records to reach supplementation, and whether placeholder fields such as unknown authors or publish dates are handled consistently. A better rubric should focus on visible evidence that the agent traced and modified the full promise import pipeline: batch staging/fetching for incomplete records using ISBN-10 or ASIN, pre-validation supplementation or validation schema changes for records with strong identifiers, preservation of non-overwrite semantics, and avoidance of relying solely on the existing load-time non-ISBN ASIN hook. Avoid a tempting criterion that says the fix is to add a `get_isbn10` helper and call `supplement_rec_with_import_item_metadata` from `load`; that may produce plausible-looking code but misses the upstream contract. Replacement criteria should prioritize evidence that the agent inspected promise batch imports, import API parse/validation, import_item identifier/source formats, placeholder cleanup, and tests covering minimal promise records through the real import path.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Over-narrow add_book-only augmentation plan
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that frame the promise-item metadata fix primarily as adding ISBN-10 extraction and another local supplement call in the catalog add-book loader, without visible evidence of addressing the upstream promise import pipeline: staging incomplete records for metadata lookup, import API validation/parsing before load, placeholder-field handling, and the actual import_item identifier/source contract. This flaw is especially severe when the task states enrichment must happen before validation or when minimal records may contain only a strong identifier plus sparse metadata.

metadata.environment: Open Library Python codebase
relevant_pipeline_areas: promise batch import staging or BookWorm/Amazon metadata fetch
import API parse_data and validator schemas
import_item staged/pending lookup and identifier source formats
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: new ISBN-10 helper plus add_book supplement call as the main success condition
better_visible_evidence: agent traces how incomplete promise records are staged before load
agent checks validation behavior for records missing authors or publish_date but having ASIN/ISBN-10
agent ensures supplementation occurs before the relevant validation boundary
agent preserves existing populated fields and handles placeholder unknown values appropriately
agent adds or plans tests for minimal promise records through the real import path

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory treats local add-book ISBN extraction as at most one small part of the solution and explicitly investigates/addresses upstream staging, validation, and placeholder handling.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory begins with the add-book hook but also raises unresolved questions about staging, validation order, and import_item identifier formats before committing to a patch direction.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory mostly focuses on add-book identifier selection while only briefly mentioning validation or staging, leaving unclear whether minimal promise records can reach or benefit from supplementation.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory proposes or implements a local ISBN-10 helper and supplement call as the primary fix, with little or no investigation of promise batch staging, import API validators, or pre-validation behavior.
scale.5: Most severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory confidently changes only the add-book load-time supplement path, possibly altering import_item sources or identifier extraction ad hoc, while ignoring that incomplete promise records must be staged/fetched and accepted by upstream parsing/validation before that path can solve the task.

experiences.title: Semantic Unicode Combining-Mark Contract Over Test Presence
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task concerns accent stripping or Unicode normalization where already-decomposed text can still contain combining marks, especially after the trajectory identifies an unsafe normalization-equality shortcut.
experiences.context: Applies in Python text-processing/codebase repair trajectories, such as scikit-learn feature extraction utilities, when the visible problem is that precomposed accented characters and decomposed base-plus-combining-mark strings should produce the same accent-stripped output. It is most useful once the agent has inspected or reproduced the relevant helper and observed logic like normalizing to NFKD followed by an early return when the normalized string equals the input. It remains applicable even if normal package tests cannot run because compiled extension imports fail, as long as the pure Unicode behavior can be reasoned about or tested in isolation. Do not apply this as a generic Unicode criterion for unrelated normalization-format preservation tasks, for tasks where combining marks are meant to be retained, or as a primary criterion before the trajectory has enough evidence about the failing normalization path. Also avoid using it to require a repository regression test as the main success signal when the trajectory already shows a clear source-level semantic fix; tests are helpful supporting evidence but not the core discriminator here.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in this cluster judged whether the trajectory fixed the actual Unicode contract: after decomposition, combining diacritical marks must be removed even if the input was already in decomposed/NFKD form. This aligned well because the visible bug source was an optimization that confused `normalized == input` with `input has no accents`; already-normalized strings may still contain combining marks. A better rubric should focus on eliminating or bypassing that unsafe assumption while preserving existing behavior for composed accents and unaccented text. Acceptable implementations include always filtering combining marks after NFKD normalization, or using a safe fast path that only returns early for strictly ASCII-compatible input before normalizing/filtering non-ASCII text. The tempting wrong criterion is to require only that a project-native regression test be added, or to insist on one exact implementation shape such as unconditional filtering for every input; those are weaker than judging the semantic contract and can misclassify trajectories that fix behavior without adding tests or that use a valid ASCII fast path. Prioritize visible evidence such as: the agent identifies the `normalized == s` early return as unsafe, changes the target helper so decomposed base-plus-combining accents are filtered, validates both precomposed and decomposed examples to the same unaccented result, and checks plain ASCII/unaccented text remains unchanged.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the accent-stripping helper no longer treats NFKD-normalization equality as proof that no accents remain. Strong trajectories either modify the implementation or present a concrete planned patch so that non-ASCII text is normalized/decomposed and Unicode combining marks are removed even when the original input was already decomposed, while preserving established behavior for precomposed accented characters and unaccented/ASCII text. Standalone Unicode tests or manual reproductions are acceptable supporting evidence when full package tests are blocked by unrelated build issues.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Already-Decomposed Combining Marks Are Stripped

metadata.key_behavior: precomposed accented input and decomposed base-plus-combining-mark input both yield the same unaccented output
metadata.unsafe_pattern_to_remove: early return based only on NFKD-normalized string equaling the input
metadata.acceptable_fast_path: returning early only for strictly ASCII-compatible text before handling non-ASCII through normalization and combining-mark filtering
metadata.non_primary_evidence: repository regression tests are valuable but should not replace judging the implementation contract

scale.1: No visible evidence that the trajectory understands or addresses already-decomposed combining marks; it may only explore files or remain blocked by imports/builds.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory mentions Unicode normalization or tests composed accents, but does not identify the unsafe early return or ensure decomposed combining marks are removed.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory correctly diagnoses that already-NFKD strings can contain combining marks and proposes a plausible fix, but source edits or validation are incomplete, uncertain, or potentially limited to one example.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory edits or clearly plans the helper so non-ASCII input is normalized and combining marks are filtered, and validates both composed and decomposed accented inputs while preserving simple unaccented text.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory cleanly removes the unsafe normalization-equality shortcut or replaces it with a safe ASCII-only fast path, confirms precomposed and already-decomposed accented cases converge to the same unaccented output, checks representative existing/plain-text behavior, and avoids corrupting surrounding code.

experiences.title: ConnState TLS Auth Metrics Require Post-Handshake Lifecycle Tracking
experiences.description: Use when evaluating a Go net/http ingress metrics fix where authenticated connection counts should depend on TLS client certificate presence rather than all HTTP connections.
experiences.context: Applies in Go services using an http.Server ConnState callback to update accepted/active/authenticated ingress metrics, especially when the task mentions optional TLS client certificates and unauthenticated HTTPS connections being miscounted. The criterion is most useful once the trajectory has identified or edited the HTTP ConnState reporter and is reasoning about TLS peer certificates, close events, or metric gauges. It is less appropriate as a sole criterion during very early repository exploration, and it should not be applied to unrelated protocol-specific callers that invoke generic authenticated metrics only after SSH/database/application authentication has already succeeded.
experiences.experience: The recurring trap is generating a rubric that only asks whether the patch checks PeerCertificates before calling the authenticated increment. That is too weak: several trajectories added a *tls.Conn or ConnectionState().PeerCertificates check but still failed because they inspected TLS state at http.StateNew before the handshake/client-cert state is reliably available, unconditionally decremented authenticated gauges on close, double-counted or failed to track connections across repeated ConnState transitions, or changed unrelated metric definitions/generic reporter behavior. A better rubric should judge the full HTTP connection lifecycle: authenticated metrics should be recorded only after TLS state is available, only once per connection, only for connections with peer/client certificates, and closed/hijacked handling should decrement authenticated-active only for connections previously counted. It should also preserve non-HTTP reporter semantics and existing Prometheus metric labels/names. Prioritize visible evidence such as use of StateActive or another post-handshake point, a per-connection tracker keyed safely to the underlying TLS connection, unwrapping connection wrappers when the codebase already has NetConn-style wrappers, guarded close handling, tests or explicit validation for no-client-cert cases, and no broad rewrites of metric collectors. Avoid treating a plain `conn.(*tls.Conn)` + `len(PeerCertificates)>0` check at StateNew, passing only a plain HTTP test, or a successful build as sufficient evidence of correctness.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement HTTP ingress authenticated metrics using the correct net/http connection lifecycle: determine client-certificate authentication only after TLS handshake state is available, count each TLS connection at most once, leave plain/no-client-cert connections out of authenticated metrics, and decrement authenticated-active metrics only for connections that were previously authenticated, while preserving existing generic reporter methods and metric definitions.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Post-handshake TLS auth metric lifecycle

required_evidence: HTTP ConnState reporter is the scoped implementation target
TLS peer/client certificate presence is checked from connection state after handshake availability, not blindly at initial accept
per-connection tracking prevents repeated StateActive double-counting and enables symmetric close handling
close/hijack paths do not decrement authenticated gauges for unauthenticated connections
generic non-HTTP authenticated metric callers and Prometheus collector names/labels are not broadly rewritten
avoid_overcrediting: bare PeerCertificates check at StateNew
only updating plain HTTP expectations
unconditional AuthenticatedConnectionClosed after conditional ConnectionAuthenticated
global TLS checks inside generic ConnectionAuthenticated
large unrelated rewrites of metric collector definitions

scale.1: No meaningful HTTP ConnState auth-metric fix is visible, or the trajectory changes unrelated reporter behavior without addressing TLS client certificate semantics.
scale.2: Identifies the unconditional authenticated count or adds a superficial peer-certificate check, but does not address ConnState timing, repeated lifecycle events, or guarded close behavior.
scale.3: Scopes the fix to the HTTP ConnState reporter and distinguishes no-cert connections from client-cert TLS connections, but has incomplete evidence for post-handshake timing, once-per-connection tracking, or symmetric close handling.
scale.4: Implements or clearly plans post-handshake certificate checking with guarded authenticated close behavior and preserves generic reporter semantics, with only minor uncertainty around wrapper handling or complete test coverage.
scale.5: Fully handles the HTTP lifecycle: post-handshake TLS detection, safe unwrapping/keying of TLS connections, once-per-connection tracking, symmetric close/hijack cleanup, preserved metrics/API behavior, and validation for unauthenticated and authenticated TLS cases.

experiences.title: Do not reward a bare WordPress core-name substitution
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a Go/Vuls trajectory for WordPress core CVE attribution plus CVE-collection-level filtering, especially if the visible work focuses on changing the WPScan core call to pass "core" or models.WPCore.
experiences.context: In this Go codebase, WordPress CVEs flow from a WPScan detector through conversion into VulnInfo/WpPackageFixStats and later through ScanResult/VulnInfos filtering. A misleading rubric arises when it treats the fix as simply tagging core CVEs as the "core" component or passing "core" as the WPScan package name. That idea is only safe if the trajectory also shows how the WPScan core endpoint/version key, response conversion, installed-version matching, and reporting attribution remain correct. The original attribution criterion can still be useful as one subcheck once there is visible end-to-end evidence that core is represented as core in stored fix stats/output while the version-derived API lookup and filter semantics are preserved. It should not be the primary or sole rubric when the task also requires collection-level filters, or when the trajectory has only exploration/partial edits without tests or compile validation.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster rewarded trajectories for identifying that WordPress core should be attributed as "core" and for changing the detector call to pass "core"/models.WPCore. That is a tempting but unreliable proxy: in this WPScan flow, the normalized WordPress version is also part of the core lookup/conversion path, and the package name argument may propagate through multiple layers. A superficial substitution can look correct while failing to preserve response parsing, fixed-version matching, existing detector behavior, or the requested VulnInfos-level filtering. A better rubric should ask for visible evidence that the agent separated API lookup identity from component attribution, verified where WpPackageFixStats.Name or equivalent output labels are produced, preserved plugin/theme behavior, moved or delegated filters to the CVE collection with compatible ScanResult wrappers, and validated with gofmt/build/tests or direct model-level tests. Avoid generating a criterion that equates correctness with 'passes core as package name' or 'sets Type=core' unless the trajectory also demonstrates the surrounding dataflow and filtering contract.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial core attribution proxy
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat WordPress core CVE attribution as a one-line replacement of the WPScan package-name argument with "core"/models.WPCore or as a simple Type=core label, without visible evidence that the core version key used for WPScan lookup/conversion is preserved, WpPackageFixStats or equivalent stored attribution resolves to the core component in reports, plugin/theme behavior is unaffected, and the required CVE-collection-level filters are implemented with compatible semantics.

metadata.environment: Go project with WordPress WPScan detector, models.VulnInfos CVE map, models.ScanResult wrappers, and WordPress package/fix-status attribution
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: Changing the core WPScan call to pass a literal core name or checking only for a core label
better_visible_evidence: The trajectory traces how the core endpoint version key differs from stored component attribution
The conversion/storage path for WordPress fix stats is updated or verified end-to-end
Core fixed-version matching and plugin/theme matching remain compatible
Filtering logic is available on the CVE collection and ScanResult compatibility is preserved where needed
The agent runs or plans targeted model/detector tests plus formatting/build validation

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory explicitly separates WPScan version lookup from core attribution, preserves matching/reporting behavior, completes collection-level filters, and validates the changes.
scale.2: Minor concern: the trajectory mostly shows end-to-end attribution and filtering evidence, but validation or one compatibility detail is weak.
scale.3: Mixed evidence: the trajectory changes core attribution and some filters, but it is unclear whether version-key conversion, reporting attribution, or existing filter semantics are preserved.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory mainly relies on changing the core package-name argument or setting a core label, with little evidence about the conversion/reporting path or collection-level filtering contract.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory explicitly equates the fix with a bare core-name substitution and omits or disrupts the requested filtering refactor, compatibility wrappers, or validation.

experiences.title: Do not let Safari gating substitute for MIME identification fixes
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for browser-specific modern image support tasks where the prompt mentions both capability-gated preview/thumbnail support and MIME detection/defaulting problems such as `application/octet-stream`.
experiences.context: Applies in TypeScript/JavaScript frontend monorepos with shared MIME helpers, Drive/upload code, and preview/thumbnail feature gates. The misleading pattern is a rubric that focuses almost entirely on adding HEIC/JXL Safari 17+ capability detection or supported-image list entries, even though the task also requires MIME recognition through extension/type-based upload parsing. This can overvalue trajectories that add runtime browser checks and constants but leave the upload MIME path unable to classify files correctly, and it can undervalue early exploration before implementation has begun. The original browser-capability idea remains appropriate as a subcriterion when the MIME identification layer is already verified or when the task is solely about gating existing MIME types; at final-review stages for this kind of task, it should not be the sole or dominant criterion.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked whether the trajectory implemented browser capability detection for HEIC/JXL on macOS/iOS Safari 17+. That is a real requirement, but it is misleading as a standalone completion proxy for tasks whose stated symptoms include unknown MIME types and `application/octet-stream` fallbacks. A better rubric should evaluate the end-to-end contract: modern image MIME constants and extension mappings are present, upload MIME parsing prioritizes reliable file type/extension detection before defaulting, and preview/thumbnail support is gated by accurate Safari 17+ platform detection. Avoid the tempting criterion that merely rewards the presence of helper functions named like HEIC/JXL support checks, accepted-input additions, or supported-image array entries. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence that the trajectory inspected and modified the MIME identification path, accounted for extension lookup behavior and default fallbacks, integrated capability checks into preview support, and avoided unrelated regressions to existing image-format support.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for modern image preview/thumbnail support that treat browser capability gating or supported-image list updates as sufficient while failing to address the MIME identification path that maps file names/types to correct modern image MIME values before falling back to a generic default. This flaw is especially important when the task text explicitly mentions defaulting to `application/octet-stream`, extension-based detection, or upload MIME parsing. Do not apply this as a failure to very early exploration that has not yet claimed a solution; apply it when the trajectory is planning, implementing, validating, or finalizing a patch.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Browser-gating-only modern image fix

preview or thumbnail generation depends on supported image checks

required_evidence: format constants or equivalent MIME definitions

upload/file MIME parser fallback order that does not prematurely return a generic default
runtime capability gate for the limited browser/platform support
integration with supported-image or preview/thumbnail availability logic
flaw_cues: only appends formats to supported-image lists or accept attributes
does not inspect the upload/file MIME parser despite MIME defaulting being part of the task
claims completion after browser gating while extension/default behavior remains unresolved
modifies unrelated existing format detection without justification
metadata.stage_boundary: Use for implementation or final-review trajectories; for early repository exploration, prefer a discovery/progress rubric instead of treating missing implementation as a defect.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory either is still early exploration without claiming a fix, or it explicitly addresses both MIME identification/defaulting and browser-gated preview support.
scale.2: Minor evidence: browser gating is emphasized, but the trajectory recognizes the MIME parser or extension-mapping layer and has a plausible plan to address it.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: constants or browser-gated supported-image logic are implemented, while MIME parser/default behavior is only partially investigated or left ambiguous.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory implements browser detection and supported-image entries but omits the MIME identification/defaulting work even though the task calls it out.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory finalizes or validates a browser-gating-only patch, claims the task is complete, and provides no meaningful handling of extension-based MIME recognition or generic-default fallback behavior.

experiences.title: Semantic Target Discovery When Named Helper Is Absent
experiences.description: Retrieve when a bug report names a helper or parser, but trajectory evidence shows exact-symbol searches fail and the agent is still trying to identify where the behavior is exposed or should be implemented.
experiences.context: Applies in Python repositories, especially command/config/utility-heavy projects, during early discovery or stalled exploration. The task describes concrete parsing semantics, but the named helper is not found by direct search; visible evidence includes repeated greps for the helper name, noisy broad searches, unrelated duration/time hits, and no confirmed implementation or call site. The criterion is most useful before or during initial patch planning, when correctness depends on finding the semantic integration point rather than only writing a standalone helper. It is less useful once the agent has already located a real existing parser and is editing validation logic, or when the remaining risk is detailed edge-case behavior/tests rather than target discovery.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics were useful because they judged a decisive failure mode: the agent kept searching for a literal helper name that was absent, repeated low-value grep patterns, and never established the user-facing code path that would exercise duration strings. In this situation, a patch that merely adds a parser in a plausible utility module can still be incomplete if no command/config argument or caller is converted to use it. A better rubric should not require finding an exact pre-existing function named in the report; instead it should reward semantic target discovery: proving the helper is absent, identifying the command/config/argument conversion point that currently accepts raw milliseconds or validates timeouts, and deciding whether a new shared helper plus integration is needed. Avoid the tempting but too-narrow criterion 'locate parse_duration exactly'; when exact search has already failed, the observable evidence to prioritize is whether the agent follows behavior-oriented leads such as millisecond documentation, timeout/duration options, command argument annotations, tests/imports, and concrete valid/invalid example strings, rather than repeating broad h/m/s or parse/time greps.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate semantic discovery of the duration parsing target when the named helper is not present: it should confirm the exact symbol is absent, stop repeating unproductive broad searches, inspect likely user-facing command/config argument paths or tests that currently deal in millisecond durations, and articulate where a new parser must be added and integrated so the reported inputs can actually reach the corrected behavior.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Semantic Parser Target and Integration Discovery

required_visible_evidence: Direct searches for the named parser/helper return no matches or no relevant implementation.
The agent distinguishes unrelated duration/time mentions from actual user-input parsing.
The agent searches or inspects behavior-bearing surfaces such as command argument definitions, config schemas/types, tests, or documented millisecond timeout entries.
The agent forms a concrete plan for both adding/fixing the parser and wiring it into the entry point that currently accepts raw duration values.
anti_evidence: Repeating identical exact-name or broad unit-letter searches after they have failed.
Treating a formatting helper, elapsed-time logging, timer usage, or unrelated config parser as the target without call-path evidence.
Adding a standalone parser without identifying any caller or user-facing path that will use it.

scale.1: No meaningful target discovery: the agent only performs exact-name or noisy broad searches, finds no parser, and has no plausible integration point or next plan.
scale.2: Weak discovery: the agent confirms the named helper is absent and inspects a few plausible files, but mostly follows unrelated duration/time hits or repeats searches without narrowing toward a user-facing caller.
scale.3: Moderate discovery: the agent recognizes the helper may need to be created and distinguishes some unrelated hits, but has not yet inspected or identified the concrete command/config/test path where duration strings should be accepted.
scale.4: Strong discovery: the agent uses behavior-oriented searches and inspects likely command/config/test surfaces, identifying a plausible raw-millisecond or timeout entry point where a new duration parser should be integrated.
scale.5: Complete discovery: the agent clearly establishes the named helper is absent, identifies the precise semantic entry point and expected interface/error contract from visible code/tests, and lays out a patch plan covering both parser implementation and integration into the caller.

experiences.title: End-to-End Per-Package Scanner Metadata Flow
experiences.description: Use when a Go scanner task adds a per-package field for Red Hat/Fedora RPM data that must appear in scan-result JSON and affect downstream vulnerability/OVAL matching.
experiences.context: Applies to Vuls-like Go repositories where package data is collected by OS-family scanner commands, parsed into a shared Package model, serialized in scan results, and later consumed by matching logic. The visible trajectory should already identify Red Hat/Fedora RPM query/parsing paths, the Package model, and OVAL/request matching as relevant. This is most useful once the agent has moved beyond initial repository orientation or is editing/querying scanner paths. It is less appropriate for a very first exploratory step with no identified files, or for unrelated UI/reporting-only changes. Be careful when old RPM, OpenSUSE, Amazon Linux, or non-modular systems are in scope: the criterion should require backward-compatible/version-gated handling rather than blindly appending a new RPM tag everywhere.
experiences.experience: For per-package modularity-label tasks, a useful rubric should judge the complete data pipeline, not just whether the agent has discovered the RPM tag or added a model field. The previous rubrics were useful when they emphasized that enabled DNF module lists are only global state and cannot substitute for per-installed-package labels. However, rubrics that only asked for tag discovery or only checked rpmQa parsing were too narrow: a patch can still be incomplete if the field is not serialized with the requested JSON key, not populated on all relevant scanner paths, not preserved through scanner/base conversion, or not passed into OVAL request matching. The better criterion should prioritize visible evidence of: a Package field with the requested scan-result JSON name; RPM queryformat support for MODULARITYLABEL only on compatible Red Hat/Fedora/Amazon versions while preserving older paths; parsers that tolerate both labeled and unlabeled output and normalize empty/(none) labels; consistency for file-owner/package-owner queries; propagation from scanned packages into OVAL request construction; and matching logic that compares the installed package label’s name:stream against OVAL modular labels before falling back to enabled-module state. Avoid tempting proxies such as repeated greps for DNF module commands, relying solely on EnabledDnfModules, adding a field with the wrong camelCase JSON tag, or making parsers accept arbitrary extra fields without validating the expected layout.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete Per-Package Modularity Label Pipeline
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly converge on an end-to-end per-package modularitylabel solution: add the field to the package scan model with the requested JSON key; collect it from RPM package metadata on supported Red Hat/Fedora-family versions using the modularity label query tag; update installed-package, repoquery, and file-owner parsing paths to remain backward-compatible for packages or systems without labels; preserve the field through scanner result conversion; and pass it into OVAL request/matching logic so modular and non-modular packages with the same name are distinguished by the installed package’s label rather than only by globally enabled DNF modules.

required_visible_evidence: Package model or equivalent scan-result model gains a ModularityLabel-like field with JSON key matching the requested lowercase modularitylabel output.
RPM queryformat changes use a modularity-label tag for compatible Red Hat/Fedora-family package scans while retaining old query formats for unsupported/older distributions.
Parsers accept the prior field count and the new labeled field count, populate the package field, and handle empty or '(none)' modularity labels without breaking non-modular packages.
All relevant package collection paths that feed the same parser are considered, including normal installed package scans, repoquery variants, and file-owner rpm -qf queries when applicable.
OVAL request construction receives the scanned package’s modularity label, and matching compares package label name:stream against OVAL modular labels before falling back to enabled-module lists.
The trajectory avoids treating dnf module list or EnabledDnfModules as a per-package source of truth.
common_failure_signals: Only repeated searches for DNF/RPM modularity information with no implementation progress.
Only adds a Package field but never populates it from scanner output.
Blindly appends MODULARITYLABEL to every RPM query format, including older or unrelated RPM-family paths, without version/family compatibility.
Changes query output but leaves strict old parser field counts or corrupts parser syntax.
Uses the wrong JSON spelling, such as modularityLabel, when the requested scan-result field is modularitylabel.
Does not propagate the field to OVAL matching, leaving behavior dependent on global enabled modules.

scale.1: No meaningful per-package pipeline progress is visible; the trajectory is only exploring or repeating searches, or relies solely on global enabled DNF modules.
scale.2: A small piece is present, such as adding a model field or identifying a possible RPM tag, but scanner population, parser compatibility, or downstream use is mostly absent.
scale.3: The trajectory addresses the main scanner query and parser path or the model plus partial OVAL wiring, but misses important compatibility boundaries, relevant collection paths, JSON naming, or matching semantics.
scale.4: Strong end-to-end implementation evidence is visible across model, scanner query/parsing, and OVAL request propagation, with only minor uncertainty around tests or one secondary path.
scale.5: The trajectory shows a robust, version-aware, tested or verified end-to-end solution covering model serialization, supported RPM query paths, backward-compatible parsing, scanner result conversion, and OVAL modular/non-modular matching semantics.

experiences.title: Option-Specific Reporting Independence
experiences.description: Use when a pytest reporting bug is caused by an option intended for one marker type accidentally bypassing report normalization for another marker type.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/pytest source-tree task where the user reports that enabling an xfail-related option changes short-summary location reporting for mark-based skips. The trajectory should have visible evidence from the task statement or code inspection that the relevant runtest report hook handles xfail/runxfail and skip-location rewriting in the same control-flow chain. This criterion is most useful once the agent has inspected the report hook, formed or applied a control-flow fix, or is validating behavior. It is less useful for unrelated skip execution bugs, collection-time skip behavior, pure xfail status bugs, environment setup work with no semantic diagnosis yet, or cases where the issue concerns explicit runtime `pytest.skip()` rather than mark-based `skip`/`skipif` location normalization.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic boundary: `--runxfail` should disable or alter only xfail handling, while the skip/skipif report-location adjustment must still run for skipped reports. That was the discriminative point because the visible trajectories repeatedly identified an `elif runxfail: pass`-style branch before skip-location rewriting, and the correct solution is to make the skip-location normalization independent of that xfail-only branch. A good rubric should therefore judge whether the trajectory preserves test-item locations for mark-based skips under `-rs --runxfail` and avoids broad rewrites that change xfail/runxfail semantics. It should also credit checking both `skip` and `skipif` and, where visible, preserving ordinary xfail outcomes. Avoid tempting but weak criteria such as rewarding dependency installation attempts, trusting ad hoc runs that accidentally use an installed pytest instead of the modified source, or broadly requiring all skip mechanisms to change. Prioritize visible evidence from code inspection of the report hook, the branch relationship between runxfail and skip-location adjustment, diffs that separate xfail handling from skip reporting, and validation output that demonstrates the reported path points to the test item rather than internal skipping machinery.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the agent understands and addresses the control-flow boundary between xfail/runxfail handling and mark-based skip location reporting: enabling the xfail-running option must not prevent skipped reports produced by `skip` or `skipif` marks from having their short-summary location rewritten to the test item. Strong evidence includes identifying the report hook branch that causes the bypass, applying or planning a minimal change that lets skip-location normalization run independently of the xfail-only option, and avoiding regressions to ordinary xfail/runxfail behavior.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Runxfail Does Not Bypass Skip Location Normalization

metadata.primary_behavior: mark-based skip and skipif short-summary locations remain at the test item with the xfail-running option enabled
key_visible_evidence: inspection of the runtest report hook where xfail/runxfail and skip-location handling share an if/elif chain
recognition that the xfail-running option should not suppress skip report normalization
patch or plan that makes skip-location adjustment independent of the runxfail branch
validation or intended regression coverage for both skip and skipif under short-summary reporting
avoid_as_primary_evidence: successful runs using an unrelated installed pytest version
dependency installation progress without semantic code change
tests of explicit runtime skip calls only
broad xfail rewrites not tied to skip location reporting

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory distinguishes xfail/runxfail behavior from mark-based skip location reporting, or it focuses only on setup/dependencies without diagnosing the reporting control flow.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory repeats the desired skip location behavior but has not identified how the xfail-running option bypasses skip-location normalization or risks changing unrelated skip/xfail behavior.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies the relevant report hook and the likely runxfail branch interaction, but the proposed fix or validation remains incomplete or relies on questionable execution evidence.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory clearly separates xfail/runxfail handling from skip-location normalization and proposes or applies a minimal control-flow fix so mark-based skip reports still point to the test item under the option.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: in addition to the minimal semantic fix, the trajectory visibly considers both skip and skipif, checks or preserves xfail/runxfail semantics, and treats environment/test results cautiously when they may not exercise the modified source.

experiences.title: Do not reward helper extraction without behavioral wiring
experiences.description: Retrieve when a TypeScript/React mail-hook task asks to extract embedded business logic into reusable helpers while also fixing a stateful UI bug, especially around undo eligibility for scheduled items.
experiences.context: This applies to trajectories in a React/TypeScript mail application where an action hook mixes notification text, move authorization, spam-unsubscribe prompting, scheduled-item modal handling, optimistic move/undo orchestration, and UI notification rendering. The misleading pattern is generating a broad positive rubric that rewards creating helper functions or making them 'pure' even when the visible trajectory has not shown that the hook still compiles, preserves its public API, wires the helpers back correctly, and fixes the scheduled-only Trash undo state. Extraction remains an appropriate criterion when the trajectory has moved relevant logic to reusable modules and also shows correct integration with React state and existing side effects. It is less appropriate during early code-reading only, where the absence of extracted helpers is not yet evidence of poor final quality, and it is insufficient during implementation review, where superficial extraction can mask regressions.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster emphasized extracting move notifications, unauthorized-move validation, spam prompting, and scheduled-item handling into pure reusable helpers. That idea is directionally relevant to the task, but it became misleading because helper existence alone was treated as strong progress. In this task, some extracted logic legitimately needs injected side-effect dependencies such as API calls, modal callbacks, focus restoration, and persisted spam settings, so requiring or rewarding 'pure side-effect-free' helpers is too broad. A better rubric should focus on whether the refactor preserves the original hook behavior while decoupling testable decision logic: the hook should keep the same callable shape for existing consumers, use React state for undo eligibility, pass the state setter into scheduled-item handling, and render the undo action based on that state rather than a mutable local or stale closure. It should also preserve special cases such as scheduled-only moves to Trash showing the scheduled modal and disabling undo, mixed scheduled/non-scheduled moves keeping undo available, spam unsubscribe prompting and remembered spam action updates, authorized-message filtering, destination-label normalization, notification text variants, move-all suggestions, focus restoration, and backend/undo orchestration. Avoid the tempting criterion 'helpers were created and imported' as a standalone success signal.
