scale.1: No visible evidence that the endpoint reads an override query parameter or passes any override flag to the backend loader.
scale.2: Some override plumbing exists, but it uses the wrong public parameter spelling, relies on underscore attribute access for a hyphenated key, or does not clearly connect the endpoint to the loader.
scale.3: The behavior is roughly equivalent to the parent trajectory: partial or ambiguous query parsing/propagation exists, with unresolved evidence about exact key handling or default behavior.
scale.4: Clear evidence that the endpoint reads `override-validation`, defaults to normal validation otherwise, and passes the flag to the backend loader, though minor ambiguity remains around exact true-value handling or endpoint scope.
scale.5: Strong, unambiguous evidence that the targeted import POST endpoint reads exactly `override-validation=true`, enables override only for that explicit request, preserves default validation for all other requests, and passes the computed flag into the central backend load/validation path without unnecessary unrelated changes.

experiences.title: Preserve File-Selection Contract While Extracting Stateless Workaround
experiences.description: Retrieve when a task asks to move a class/static MIME-suffix or file-selection workaround to module scope, especially in a Python/Qt browser-style codebase where a file chooser override passes accepted MIME types/suffixes to a superclass.
experiences.context: Applies when the visible task and trajectory involve refactoring an existing stateless MIME/suffix workaround out of a class method into a module-level helper, and the relevant consumer is a file-selection override that may call a superclass with accepted MIME types/suffixes. It is most useful once the trajectory has either found the existing helper and chooser path or is at risk of editing similarly named but unrelated download/MIME suffix code. It is less useful for unrelated MIME sniffing/download filename fixes, for tasks that merely add new MIME mappings without changing ownership, or very early exploration before any plausible file-selection target has been identified.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic contract of the refactor, not just on moving text. A good criterion should reward evidence that the agent found the existing static/class workaround and its file-selection consumer, extracted the same stateless logic to a module-level helper, updated the chooser to call that helper directly, and preserved the chooser's superclass passthrough behavior with the original accepted entries plus only the extra workaround suffixes. It should also flag trajectories that chase unrelated download filename suffix logic or make broad behavioral changes to window/page handling, because those are visible signs the agent has lost the narrow target. Avoid making the rubric primarily about test edits, exact helper placement within the module, formatting, or whether a temporary compatibility wrapper remains; those are weaker proxies than whether consumers use the module helper and the file-selection call contract remains intact. Prioritize visible evidence such as grep results for the existing helper and chooser override, planned or applied replacement of self/class calls with module-level calls, preservation of the helper's version gate and suffix-difference behavior, a merged accepted list passed once to the superclass in default/unsupported paths, and absence of unrelated refactors.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a narrow, behavior-preserving extraction of the existing MIME-suffix workaround from class/static ownership to a pure module-level helper, and should keep the file-selection override's passthrough contract intact. Strong evidence includes locating the current static/class helper and chooser override, preserving the helper's stateless inputs and return value of only additional suffixes, replacing chooser calls to the class/static method with the module-level helper, merging original accepted MIME/suffix entries with extras without introducing duplicates or order-sensitive assumptions, and making exactly the expected superclass chooser call with that merged list for passthrough paths. The trajectory should avoid confusing this code with unrelated download filename suffix handling or broad WebEngine/WebView behavior changes.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Narrow Module Helper Extraction With Chooser Passthrough Preservation

required_visible_evidence: Existing class/static MIME-suffix workaround and file-selection override are identified or edited
New or planned module-level helper is stateless and preserves original workaround behavior
File-selection code consumes the module-level helper rather than class/static logic
Original accepted entries and extra suffixes are combined before superclass passthrough
No unrelated download/window/page-control refactor is introduced

stage_boundaries.exploration: Look for accurate localization of the helper and chooser path, and lack of drift into unrelated MIME/download code.
stage_boundaries.implementation: Look for direct module-level helper use and preservation of chooser behavior.
stage_boundaries.review: Look for exact passthrough call shape, merged accepted list semantics, and absence of broad unrelated changes.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence of the correct helper/chooser target; trajectory is focused on unrelated MIME/download/suffix code or broad unrelated refactors.
scale.2: Some file-selection or MIME exploration is visible, but the existing workaround or its consumer is not clearly localized, or planned edits risk changing unrelated behavior.
scale.3: The target helper and chooser path are identified and the intended extraction is plausible, but evidence is incomplete on preserving helper semantics or superclass passthrough behavior.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly extracts or plans to extract the stateless helper to module scope and updates the chooser to use it while mostly preserving merge and passthrough behavior.
scale.5: The trajectory gives strong, concrete evidence of a narrow refactor: same helper semantics at module scope, chooser calls the module helper, original and extra suffixes are combined appropriately, exactly the expected superclass passthrough is preserved, and no unrelated behavior is changed.

experiences.title: Do not credit superficial dict conversion as a complete ordered-mapping fix
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python trajectory is refactoring a list-backed configuration/value container into an ordered mapping keyed by patterns or scopes, especially when the repo supports Python versions without guaranteed dict order or existing tests inspect repr/iteration/private storage.
experiences.context: This warning applies to qutebrowser-like Python configuration code where the visible task asks for an ordered mapping, stable repr/iteration, duplicate replacement by key, and preservation of lookup/fallback behavior. A broad high-level criterion such as “uses an ordered mapping keyed by pattern and iterates over mapping values” can be useful during early exploration, but it becomes misleading at implementation/final-review time if it does not distinguish a repository-compatible ordered map from a plain dict, does not check all list-semantics call sites, or treats failing focused tests as merely obsolete. The original idea remains appropriate as a top-level semantic goal when the trajectory has not edited code yet or is only locating relevant methods; once edits exist, the rubric must look for compatibility, public representation details, and validation evidence.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics mostly restated the task goal: convert storage to an ordered mapping keyed by pattern, use mapping values for repr/iteration, and replace duplicate patterns. That over-credited trajectories that made a superficial dict-backed conversion but missed important visible constraints: the project declared support for older Python versions where plain dict insertion order is not guaranteed; existing tests exposed repr/iteration assumptions and sometimes failed; some patches preserved a list-like private property just to satisfy old tests rather than making the real storage model coherent; several trajectories did not audit every reverse-iteration, fallback, clear/remove, constructor, and exact-pattern lookup path; and validation was often incomplete or dismissed. Future rubrics should not use “has mapping semantics” alone as a success proxy. Prefer a criterion that checks whether the agent chose an explicitly ordered mapping when required by project compatibility, initialized it through the same duplicate-removal/replacement path, updated repr/iteration to expose the intended mapped values without relying on stale list internals, preserved global/None fallback and last-matching scoped lookup behavior, and responded to focused test failures by fixing implementation/tests rather than calling them expected. Avoid the tempting criterion that any assignment like `storage[pattern] = ScopedValue(...)` plus `.values()` iteration is enough. Prioritize visible evidence from setup/version requirements, the actual edited methods, focused test output, diff inspection, and whether private/internal compatibility hacks or brittle file rewrites remain.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial ordered-mapping refactor misses repository constraints
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that claim or appear to complete a list-to-mapping refactor for scoped configuration values while visible evidence shows the implementation is only superficially keyed by pattern and does not satisfy repository-compatible ordered semantics or public behavior. This includes using a plain dict despite a stated Python compatibility range where insertion order is not guaranteed, leaving old list-style private storage assumptions or compatibility shims in place instead of a coherent mapping, failing to update repr/iteration to reflect the intended mapped values, not auditing reverse iteration and fallback/exact-pattern lookup paths, dismissing focused test failures as expected without a corrective plan, or using brittle whole-class/file rewrites that cause syntax/corruption risk.

metadata.applicable_task_shape: Python data/container refactor from list of scoped values to ordered mapping keyed by pattern/scope
environment_cues: setup or project metadata declares Python versions older than guaranteed dict insertion order
existing tests or code inspect repr, iteration, or private storage
evidence_to_check: explicit ordered mapping choice or justified compatibility-safe alternative
all former list operations converted consistently
constructor, add, remove, clear, repr, iter, fallback, URL/pattern lookup behavior addressed
focused tests run and failures investigated rather than dismissed
no private list-compatibility shim used as a substitute for the requested storage model

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory either has not reached implementation yet, or it explicitly accounts for compatibility-safe ordered storage, audits all relevant methods, and validates/fixes repr/iteration/lookup behavior.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory identifies the ordered-mapping goal and most affected methods, but leaves one low-risk detail uncertain, such as test updates or type annotations, while not contradicting compatibility constraints.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory implements a keyed mapping and value iteration, but visible evidence is incomplete on compatibility, repr/public representation, or focused test failures; correctness is plausible but under-justified.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory uses a plain dict or stale private-storage compatibility approach despite visible constraints, leaves some list semantics unaudited, or treats a failing focused test as expected without fixing the behavior.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory performs a brittle or incoherent rewrite, corrupts syntax or class structure, edits the wrong area, or combines incompatible storage choices with unaddressed test failures while claiming the ordered-mapping refactor is complete.

experiences.title: Preserve pandas dtypes at value-preserving selector boundaries
experiences.description: Use this when a scikit-learn task concerns `set_output(transform='pandas')` losing input DataFrame dtypes for transformers that merely select or pass through existing columns, especially feature selectors with `float16`, categorical, nullable, or extension dtypes.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/scikit-learn repository when the visible task and trajectory involve pandas output wrapping, original DataFrame dtypes, and value-preserving transformers such as feature selectors or column subsetters. It is most useful once the trajectory has moved beyond pure environment setup into locating the wrapping/validation/selection paths or proposing code changes. It should not be applied as a blanket requirement for transformers that compute new values, scale/encode/generate features, or legitimately coerce numeric output. It is also not enough to check that the agent mentions pandas dtypes in general; the key boundary is whether the output columns still correspond to unmodified input columns and can therefore retain their original pandas dtypes safely.
experiences.experience: Prior rubrics in this cluster often asked broadly for dtype preservation through `_wrap_in_pandas_container`, `_wrap_data_with_container`, or a new `set_output`/global configuration option. That wording can be misleading: it may overvalue broad `astype(original_input.dtypes)` plumbing or public API churn, and undervalue a minimal fix that preserves the original pandas object through the value-preserving selection path. A better rubric should focus on the semantic mechanism visible in the trajectory: the agent should recognize that selected columns lose dtypes because pandas input is converted to a NumPy array during validation/selection, and that safe preservation requires keeping DataFrame inputs as DataFrames when pandas output is requested, then using pandas-aware column selection or a strictly column-aligned dtype restoration. The criterion should reward evidence that the agent distinguishes selectors/pass-through transformers from value-changing transformers, aligns any dtype mapping only to output columns that match original input columns, and avoids casting generated or transformed data back to original dtypes. Avoid the tempting but weaker criterion “adds a dtypes argument/config flag and calls astype,” because that can break shape/column alignment, categorical values, existing APIs, or value-changing transformers. Prioritize visible evidence such as: investigation of feature selector/validation flow, identification of ndarray coercion as the dtype-loss point, use of DataFrame-preserving validation or pandas-safe indexing for selected columns, tests or reasoning covering `float16` and categorical columns, and an explicit non-goal/counterexample for scalers or other value-modifying transformers.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Value-preserving DataFrame dtype preservation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a semantically safe plan or implementation for preserving pandas input dtypes only when transformer output consists of unmodified input columns. Strong evidence includes identifying that dtype loss occurs when a DataFrame is coerced to an ndarray before column selection, preserving the DataFrame through validation/selection when pandas output is configured, or applying dtype restoration only to output columns that exactly correspond to original input columns. The trajectory should also preserve existing default/pandas output behavior for value-changing transformers and avoid broad casts or API changes that would force original dtypes onto transformed/generated data.

key_visible_evidence: original task shows `set_output(transform='pandas')` losing `float16` and categorical dtypes after feature selection
trajectory inspects pandas output wrapping, transformer validation, or selector column-selection paths
trajectory reasons about original input dtypes, output column alignment, and value-preserving versus value-changing transformers
preferred_focus: preserve DataFrame inputs through value-preserving selection when pandas output is requested
use pandas-aware column selection or strictly filtered dtype mapping
test or reason about mixed numpy and pandas extension dtypes
avoid_as_primary_signal: unconditional `astype(original_input.dtypes)` on all pandas outputs
new public config/API parameters without proving value-preserving alignment
using installed newer package behavior as validation of local source changes

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses the dtype-loss mechanism for value-preserving pandas outputs; it remains in unrelated setup, generic reproduction, or makes changes unrelated to DataFrame dtype preservation.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory mentions preserving pandas dtypes or adding dtype plumbing, but does not connect the issue to unmodified selected columns, DataFrame-to-ndarray coercion, or safe output-column alignment.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies relevant wrapping or selection code and proposes preserving original dtypes for matching output columns, but the approach is incomplete or risks blanket casting, API incompatibility, or applying preservation to value-changing transformers.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory distinguishes value-preserving selectors from value-changing transformers, aligns dtype preservation to selected original columns, and proposes or implements a DataFrame-preserving/pandas-aware selection path or a tightly filtered dtype restoration with appropriate tests or reasoning.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory clearly fixes or plans the root dtype-loss path by avoiding unnecessary ndarray coercion for pandas-output selectors and using pandas-aware column selection, while preserving existing behavior for generated/transformed outputs, sparse/default outputs, and covering mixed `float16`/categorical or extension dtype regression cases.

experiences.title: Do not overvalue a standalone shortcut manager without safe integration
experiences.description: Retrieve when a keyboard-shortcut task asks for centralized, exact, platform-aware handling in a React/TypeScript app, and the trajectory has created or discussed a central matcher/registry but integration across existing handlers is incomplete, broad, or unstable.
experiences.context: This warning applies to trajectories in which the visible work emphasizes a new keyboard shortcut manager, matcher, registry, or Cmd/Ctrl abstraction, especially after exploration of fragmented handlers in a Matrix-style React/TypeScript client. The misleading case is treating the existence of a central module, isolated tests, or a platform-aware modifier helper as enough evidence of likely correctness while the trajectory shows unchanged call sites, partially applied imports, overwritten TSX files, failed lint/builds, missing action mappings, or lost existing behavior. The original centralization criterion can still be appropriate when the trajectory also shows coherent migration of runtime handlers, preservation of existing action side effects and event propagation semantics, lifecycle-safe registration, and successful validation. At early exploration stage, central design is only weak progress; at implementation/final-review stage, visible integration and validation matter more than architectural intent.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster often asked whether the agent created a centralized shortcut registry, platform-aware Cmd/Ctrl normalization, or reusable exact matcher. That idea is directionally useful for this task, but it becomes misleading when generated as the primary criterion after the trajectory already shows fragile or incomplete migration. A new module that matches key/modifier sets in isolation does not prove the patch fixes the product behavior: existing global, room, composer, and call handlers may still be hardcoded; large sed/cat rewrites may corrupt imports or remove dynamic component setup; registered shortcuts may lack handlers or dispatch the wrong actions; singleton/global registration may duplicate handlers across mounts; and validation may only cover ad hoc scripts rather than the integrated app. Better rubrics should focus on whether the central matching API is actually wired into the visible runtime shortcut entry points without regressing existing shortcuts, whether exact modifier and Shift/case rules are enforced at those call sites, whether platform-specific behavior is resolved consistently, whether extension/override behavior is represented by data/actions rather than hardcoded descriptions, and whether build/type/lint or focused integration tests support the changed files. Avoid the tempting criterion that simply rewards a named central manager, registry, or CmdOrCtrl helper. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence of coherent integration, preserved side effects and preventDefault/stopPropagation behavior, scoped registration/unregistration, unchanged shortcut documentation semantics, and clean validation after edits.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for a keyboard-shortcut centralization task when they primarily add or test a standalone shortcut matcher/manager or platform modifier abstraction, but visible evidence shows the runtime integration is incomplete or unsafe: important existing keydown call sites are not migrated, existing shortcut actions or focus/propagation behavior are not preserved, shortcut definitions are converted without executable handlers, component lifecycle scoping/unregistration is absent for global registrations, broad text replacements corrupt imports or unrelated component code, or build/type/lint/integration validation is failing or missing after the edits. This rubric should not penalize early exploration that has not claimed implementation completeness, nor a stable final integration that both centralizes matching and validates preserved behavior across the affected shortcut contexts.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Standalone Matcher Over Integration Evidence

metadata.task_type: keyboard shortcut centralization in React/TypeScript UI
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: presence of a central manager, registry, or CmdOrCtrl helper by itself
preferred_visible_evidence: runtime handlers call the central matcher for the relevant shortcut contexts
existing dispatched actions and preventDefault/stopPropagation/focus behavior are preserved
exact modifier matching including Shift and extra modifiers is validated at integrated call sites
platform Cmd/Ctrl behavior is resolved consistently without duplicating ad hoc checks
registration supports extension/override without duplicate global handlers or lifecycle leaks
changed files pass appropriate type, lint, build, or focused tests

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory either remains in investigation without overclaiming implementation, or shows a coherent centralized matcher integrated into the relevant runtime handlers with preserved behavior and clean validation.
scale.2: Minor evidence: a central matcher is emphasized and integration evidence is thin, but the trajectory has not yet made risky broad edits or there is a clear plan to validate and migrate remaining call sites.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory adds a plausible matcher or platform abstraction and some integration, but leaves important handlers hardcoded, relies mostly on isolated/ad hoc tests, or lacks clear evidence that existing shortcut side effects and exact modifier behavior are preserved.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory overfocuses on the new manager while visible edits show incomplete migration, missing handlers/action mappings, lifecycle risks, or failed/missing validation in changed UI files.
scale.5: Severe evidence: broad rewrites or sed-generated patches corrupt existing components, remove required imports or behavior, fail build/type/lint checks, or register shortcuts globally without safe dispatch/scoping, while the only strong positive evidence is a standalone matcher or Cmd/Ctrl abstraction.

experiences.title: Do not equate a standalone rate iterator with a usable benchmark generator feature
experiences.description: Retrieve when a benchmark-generator task is being evaluated in a Go codebase with existing benchmark execution and CLI/user-facing paths, and the trajectory is focusing on a small Next/HasNext-style iterator over request rates.
experiences.context: Apply when the task asks to automate progressive benchmark configurations for users, the repository already has benchmark execution/configuration code and often a command-line entry point, and the visible trajectory only adds or plans an isolated client-package generator with rate-sequence tests. In this setting, linear sequence correctness is a necessary sub-behavior but not enough to judge the trajectory as on track. The original idea remains appropriate as a narrow subcriterion if the task explicitly requests only a library iterator over an existing config type, or after the trajectory has already shown a coherent integration point, validation contract, and preservation of existing benchmark behavior. At early exploration, absence of integration is not yet decisive; at implementation/final-review stages, lack of integration or arbitrary API choices become important.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster praised or required details such as a constructor, Next(), HasNext(), Reset(), and inclusive linear rate progression. That can be misleading because an agent may satisfy those local mechanics while missing the feature’s actual user value: making progressive benchmark runs/configurations usable through the existing benchmark subsystem, with a design consistent with the repository and without regressing current benchmark execution. Avoid generating a rubric that mandates a particular iterator API shape unless the task or repository conventions visibly require it; a different interface, runner, or config object may be the better design. A better rubric should prioritize visible evidence that the agent has identified the existing benchmark execution path, designed a generator/config abstraction that composes with it, validates invalid bounds/steps to avoid hangs, preserves existing single-benchmark behavior, and adds tests or examples covering both generation and consumption. Also watch for tempting but harmful edits to unrelated benchmark scheduling/execution internals made merely to support the generator.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Isolated generator without benchmark-system integration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a task requesting progressive benchmark generation in a codebase with an existing benchmark runner or CLI, penalize trajectories that treat a standalone rate-sequence iterator as the whole feature. The flaw is present when the visible work only creates a local generator returning benchmark configs and tests the numeric rate sequence, while failing to show a coherent integration with the existing benchmark execution/user-facing path, failing to define validation for invalid step/bounds, or modifying existing benchmark execution behavior unnecessarily.

metadata.task_type: benchmark generator / progressive request-rate configuration
metadata.environment: Go repository with existing benchmark config, benchmark runner, and possible CLI command
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: Next/HasNext/Reset API existence or rate sequence tests alone
preferred_evidence: agent identifies existing benchmark execution and CLI or public API entry points
generator/config abstraction composes with existing benchmark runner rather than living as unused code
invalid step and bound cases are validated or safely rejected
existing single benchmark behavior is preserved
tests or examples cover both generated rates and their use in running/producing benchmark configurations

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory connects the generator to the existing benchmark subsystem or clearly scopes the work to a library-only API, with validation and no unrelated benchmark regressions.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory implements local rate generation but also investigates integration points and appears likely to wire the abstraction into existing benchmark usage.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory has a correct rate sequence generator and tests, but integration with benchmark execution or user-facing use remains only speculative.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory focuses on a standalone generator/API and local tests while ignoring existing benchmark runner/CLI paths or validation needed to make the feature usable.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory both relies on an isolated generator as the whole solution and introduces unrelated changes or likely regressions in existing benchmark execution, command handling, or build structure.

experiences.title: Local Wrapper Ownership for Dependency-Backed PURL Construction
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go SBOM/PURL task exposes both an external PURL helper and local CycloneDX code that directly constructs PackageURLs with raw package names and empty namespace/subpath fields.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go repository using CycloneDX/package-url libraries and an external scanner dependency when the trajectory has found an external PURL generator but also visible local reporter code calling a PackageURL constructor directly. It is especially relevant after code search has identified direct local call sites for language package components, ecosystem/type fields, and raw package names, while no local parser or vendored dependency source is available. Do not apply as a generic external-dependency rubric when the only observable code path is truly inside vendored/upstream code, or before the agent has inspected whether local wrapper/reporting code reconstructs URLs independently. Also avoid using it for unrelated OS package PURL generation unless the task explicitly targets those PURL formats.
experiences.experience: The useful lesson is not simply “inspect or patch the external dependency.” In these trajectories, the agent repeatedly noticed an external scanner PURL package, but the decisive visible evidence was that the SBOM reporter locally rebuilt PURLs with raw names and empty namespace/subpath arguments. A better rubric should reward recognizing the ownership boundary: external scanner PURLs may exist, but local CycloneDX component generation and dependency-graph generation still need an adapter/parser that maps repository ecosystem types to package-url types and applies the task’s ecosystem-specific split/normalization rules before calling the constructor. The rubric should prioritize evidence that the agent stops repeating broad dependency searches, inspects the direct constructor call sites, and plans or implements local parsing for Maven, PyPI, Go modules, npm scoped names, and Cocoapods subpaths while preserving existing qualifiers and lookup keys. Avoid a tempting wrong criterion that demands locating the exact upstream dependency parser or vendoring/upgrading it; that can mislead when the visible bug is local misuse of a general-purpose constructor. Also avoid accepting partial fixes that merely fall back to a preexisting stored PURL, only change the type string, or encode subpath as a qualifier instead of passing it as the PackageURL subpath.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Local PURL Construction Boundary
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should identify that the actionable fix belongs in the local SBOM PackageURL construction path, not primarily in the external scanner dependency, when local reporter code directly calls a PackageURL constructor with raw package names and empty namespace/subpath. Strong evidence includes locating the library and dependency-graph component builders, mapping scanner or manifest ecosystem names to package-url ecosystem types, applying the required package-name parsing rules for the affected ecosystems, preserving existing qualifiers and vulnerability-reference map keys, and avoiding repeated unproductive searches for unavailable dependency source.

visible_cues: external scanner PURL helper is present but not sufficient for all SBOM reporter output
local reporter calls PackageURL constructor with empty namespace and subpath
package type/ecosystem is available from local model fields or manifest helpers
task lists concrete ecosystem-specific namespace/name/subpath rules
vendor or module source may be unavailable, making local wrapper behavior the practical boundary
avoid_rewarding: repeated broad searches for a local parser after direct constructor call sites are known
assuming the fix must be upstream without checking local wrapper usage
using an existing stored PURL as the only fix when other local construction paths remain raw
placing subpath in qualifiers rather than the constructor subpath argument
changing only ecosystem/type strings without parsing package names

scale.1: The trajectory remains focused on finding or patching an external dependency, repeats broad searches, or has not inspected the local PackageURL construction sites despite visible evidence they exist.
scale.2: The trajectory notices both external and local PURL code but treats the issue mainly as an external dependency problem or proposes only a vague wrapper/upgrade strategy without concrete local parsing responsibilities.
scale.3: The trajectory localizes the likely bug to local SBOM PackageURL construction and recognizes empty namespace/subpath/raw-name usage, but has not yet covered all affected ecosystems or related construction paths.
scale.4: The trajectory plans or implements a local parsing/mapping helper at the reporter construction boundary for most required ecosystems, while preserving existing qualifiers and references, with only minor omissions or uncertain validation.
scale.5: The trajectory clearly owns the fix in local SBOM PURL construction, covers library and manifest-derived package paths, maps ecosystem/type values correctly, applies all specified parsing/normalization and subpath rules, preserves existing qualifiers/reference lookup behavior, and avoids unnecessary dependency vendoring or upstream changes.

experiences.title: Mixed Numeric MOD Type-Inference Alignment
experiences.description: Use when a Django ORM expression task concerns `output_field` inference for an existing arithmetic operator, especially `%`/MOD with mixed numeric operand types.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django codebase where arithmetic expressions are constructed successfully but `CombinedExpression` output-field resolution fails for mixed numeric operands because an operator is missing from a table-driven type-combination registry. This is most relevant once the trajectory has inspected or modified the expression type-inference matrix, reproduced a `FieldError` or resolver `None` for Decimal/Integer MOD, or compared MOD against ADD/SUB/MUL/DIV behavior. It is less useful before the agent has identified whether the problem is operator construction, SQL generation, or type inference. Do not apply it to backend-specific SQL modulo behavior, unrelated math functions, non-numeric expression types, or tasks where the desired fix is explicitly a caller-side `output_field` workaround.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases focused on the semantic contract: MOD must participate in the same mixed numeric type-resolution rules as other arithmetic operators. That criterion was discriminative because the observable successful trajectory evidence was not merely that tests were attempted, but that the agent found the centralized combinator/type matrix, observed MOD already worked for same-type operands while missing from mixed numeric connectors, and updated only that mixed numeric operator set so Decimal/Integer resolves to Decimal in both operand orders. A stronger version should also check that Integer/Float follows existing Float promotion, same-type MOD remains intact, and unsupported combinations such as Decimal/Float are not accidentally broadened if the surrounding arithmetic rules do not support them. Avoid generating a rubric that primarily rewards full Django test-suite invocation, since local test setup often fails for environmental reasons and is less semantically decisive here. Also avoid rewarding broad search-and-replace edits, backend SQL changes, or special-casing `CombinedExpression` when the visible design is registry-based. Prioritize evidence from: targeted inspection of the arithmetic connector registry, before/after resolver or query-expression output-field checks, careful cleanup of duplicate/malformed connector entries after sed edits, and validation of both operand orders.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should correctly align MOD with existing mixed numeric arithmetic type inference by adding the MOD connector to the mixed numeric expression-combination rules, so DecimalField with IntegerField resolves to DecimalField in both operand orders and related Integer/Float promotion remains consistent, without changing unrelated operator semantics or broadening unsupported numeric combinations.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: MOD Mixed Numeric Type Resolution

required_visible_evidence: Recognizes the failure as expression output-field/type inference rather than SQL execution or Python operator construction.
Identifies a table or registry of connector/type/result combinations where same-type numeric MOD exists but mixed numeric MOD is absent.
Targets the mixed numeric connector set so Decimal/Integer and Integer/Decimal MOD resolve to DecimalField.
Checks or preserves existing same-type MOD behavior and related Integer/Float promotion, and avoids unintended duplicate or malformed connector entries.
anti_evidence: Adds caller-side explicit output_field workarounds instead of fixing inference.
Changes backend SQL modulo generation without evidence that SQL execution is the failing layer.
Introduces broad special-case logic despite an existing table-driven type-resolution mechanism.
Uses imprecise global edits that duplicate MOD in unrelated connector groups or damage the registry syntax.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses mixed numeric MOD output-field inference; it focuses on unrelated SQL, tests, or caller workarounds.
scale.2: Identifies MOD or expression output_field generally but does not locate the mixed numeric type-resolution mechanism or proposes an overbroad/special-case fix.
scale.3: Locates the relevant type-combination rules and suspects MOD is missing for mixed numeric operands, but the edit is absent, unverified, or visibly risky/malformed.
scale.4: Implements or clearly plans the correct registry-level MOD addition for mixed Decimal/Integer inference and performs some targeted validation, with only minor uncertainty about cleanup or coverage.
scale.5: Cleanly updates the mixed numeric connector rules for MOD, verifies Decimal/Integer in both orders and related preserved behavior, and shows no evidence of unrelated semantic changes, duplicate entries, or syntax damage.

experiences.title: Qualified Paths for Nested Classmethod Serialization
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Django migration serialization task concerns a classmethod or callable default defined on a nested class, especially when the trajectory has inspected callable serialization and Python name/qualname behavior.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django codebase where migration files serialize callable references such as Field.default values. The useful stage is after the trajectory has either found the migration callable serializer branch for bound classmethods or has reproduced that a nested classmethod is emitted without its containing class. It is strongest when visible evidence includes Python introspection showing simple class names omit outer classes, serializer output before/after, or checks for top-level functions/classmethods and deeper nesting. It may be premature if the agent is only exploring repository structure with no evidence about callable serialization, and it may be irrelevant for bugs in model field defaults, database backends, enum value behavior, static methods, or serialization of classes themselves rather than classmethods bound to nested classes.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics were useful because they judged the exact semantic contract that determines correctness here: a bound classmethod used in a migration must serialize to an importable dotted path containing the module, every containing class, the nested class, and the method name. The discriminative evidence was not merely that the agent edited a migration file or ran many tests; it was that the trajectory identified the bound-classmethod serialization path, recognized that the owner class's simple name drops lexical nesting, and changed/validated the class component so nested paths such as Outer.Inner.method are preserved while top-level functions and classmethods still serialize normally. A better rubric for similar cases should focus on observable proof of this qualified-path behavior and compatibility boundary: before/after serializer output, use of the class's qualified name for the bound owner, preservation of the existing module import set, and sanity checks for non-nested and deeper-nested cases. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as requiring ArrayField-specific handling, TextChoices-specific handling, broad migration autodetector changes, dependency installation progress, or simply running unrelated Django tests. Those may support confidence but do not establish the core serialization contract.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that migration serialization of a classmethod bound to a nested class emits the full importable qualified path including all containing classes, while preserving existing callable serialization behavior for ordinary functions, top-level classmethods, deeper nesting, and module imports. Strong evidence includes identifying the bound-classmethod serializer branch, explaining why the owner class's simple name is insufficient for nested classes, applying a targeted change to use the owner class's qualified path, and validating serializer output for nested and non-nested cases.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Nested Classmethod Qualified Serialization

metadata.core_contract: Bound classmethods on nested classes serialize as module.Outer.Inner.method rather than module.Inner.method.
preferred_visible_evidence: Inspection of the callable or function serializer branch that handles methods whose __self__ is a class
Python introspection or reasoning showing __name__ omits outer classes while __qualname__ preserves them
A targeted source change in the classmethod serialization path rather than ArrayField-, enum-, or database-specific code
Serializer output before and after showing the containing class path appears in the serialized value
Checks that ordinary functions, top-level classmethods, deeper nested classmethods, and imports remain compatible
avoid_as_primary_evidence: Installing missing dependencies
Running unrelated test suites without checking serialized output
Changing migration autodetection or field default evaluation instead of callable reference serialization
Only proving TextChoices or ArrayField behavior without addressing the generic nested classmethod path

scale.1: No visible evidence that the trajectory understands or addresses nested classmethod serialization; it focuses on unrelated field, enum, database, or test-environment issues.
scale.2: Some recognition that migrations serialize callable defaults, but no clear identification of the bound-classmethod path or the missing containing-class qualification.
scale.3: Identifies that nested class names are being lost in migration serialization and may propose qualified names, but validation or compatibility evidence for non-nested callables is limited.
scale.4: Clearly targets the bound-classmethod serializer path, uses the owner class's qualified path, and shows serializer output now includes the containing class for a nested classmethod.
scale.5: Provides decisive evidence for the full contract: targeted qualified-path fix, before/after nested classmethod serialization, preservation of module imports, and sanity checks for ordinary functions, top-level classmethods, and deeper nested classmethods.

experiences.title: Do not reward generic CA-list mitigation without server-side ClientCAs compatibility
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating Teleport/Go Kubernetes proxy mTLS fixes for oversized acceptable-CA lists caused by many trusted clusters, especially when the trajectory discusses `ClientCAs`, `RootCAs`, SNI cluster filtering, or manual certificate verification.
experiences.context: This warning applies in Go TLS server code where the failure is caused by the server advertising too many acceptable client CA subject names in the mTLS CertificateRequest. A tempting but misleading rubric is to reward any mention of TLS 64KB limits, SNI filtering, CA reduction, or alternative verification. That over-credits trajectories that edit client-side `RootCAs`, CSR/kubeconfig paths, CA storage, or simply return an error when the list is too large. The original idea remains useful when the trajectory has actually located the server-side per-connection TLS config that assigns `tls.Config.ClientCAs`, distinguishes it from client `RootCAs`, and proposes a bounded advertised CA pool while preserving client certificate authentication. SNI-based filtering can be part of a correct solution, but it is not sufficient by itself unless no-SNI/legacy fallback behavior and server certificate naming support for encoded SNI are also handled.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked for broad TLS handshake size compliance, SNI-based CA filtering, or switching to `VerifyPeerCertificate`. Those ideas are directionally related but too broad: they can rate wrong-path changes as promising, such as trimming the upstream client trust pool, modifying kubeconfig context handling, failing early with a nicer error, globally changing CA storage/helpers, or removing `ClientCAs` without proving mTLS still requests and verifies client certs. A better rubric should focus on visible evidence that the trajectory targets the Kubernetes proxy's server-side acceptable-CA advertisement: it should identify the `ClientCAs` pool used in the per-client TLS config, compute or otherwise bound the serialized subject-name size, and only when oversized replace the advertised pool with a small safe pool such as the current/local cluster CA while preserving normal SNI narrowing and client certificate validation. Avoid making `VerifyPeerCertificate`, compression, or target-cluster filtering a required or sufficient criterion unless the visible trajectory also proves compatibility with Go TLS `ClientAuth`, Teleport auth middleware expectations, no-SNI clients, and encoded-SNI server certificate names. Prioritize evidence from `ClientCAs.Subjects()` sizing, fallback pool selection, preserved authentication semantics, and tests or reasoning covering both many-trusted-cluster and ordinary/SNI cases.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Overbroad CA-size fix misses server-side ClientCAs semantics
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories or patches that treat the large trusted-cluster mTLS failure as solved merely by reducing some CA list, adding a generic TLS limit check, returning an error, or switching verification mechanisms, without visible evidence that the server-side acceptable client CA list advertised by the Kubernetes proxy is bounded and that client certificate authentication remains compatible.

evidence_needed.server_side_path: The trajectory identifies the TLS server per-client config path that assigns `tls.Config.ClientCAs`, rather than only client-side `RootCAs` or CSR/kubeconfig code.
evidence_needed.size_accounting: The fix accounts for the serialized acceptable-CA subject list size, including per-subject length overhead or an equivalent bound against the TLS 2^16-1 limit.
evidence_needed.fallback_semantics: When the all-trusted-cluster pool is too large, the advertised CA pool is replaced with a bounded safe pool, such as the current/local cluster CA, rather than failing the handshake or advertising no CAs without a proven verification strategy.
evidence_needed.authentication_preserved: The solution preserves mTLS client certificate request and validation behavior, including Teleport identity/middleware expectations.
evidence_needed.compatibility: The reasoning or tests cover both SNI/cluster-name narrowing and no-SNI or legacy fallback behavior; if relying on encoded SNI, server certificate DNS-name support is addressed.
evidence_needed.wrong_path_exclusions: Changes limited to upstream client `RootCAs`, kubeconfig generation, CSR response CA bundles, or trusted-cluster CA persistence are not treated as sufficient for this failure.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory clearly targets the server-side `ClientCAs` advertisement, bounds the subject list only when necessary, uses a safe fallback pool, and preserves client certificate authentication and SNI/no-SNI compatibility.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory is on the correct server-side path and proposes a bounded fallback, but leaves small gaps such as limited tests or incomplete discussion of encoded-SNI certificate naming.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory understands the `ClientCAs` size issue but frames the fix too generically, or proposes filtering/manual verification without enough visible evidence that legacy fallback and mTLS validation semantics are preserved.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory edits or evaluates the wrong CA path, such as client `RootCAs`, CSR response bundles, kubeconfig handling, or global CA helpers, or it simply errors out when the pool is too large.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory ignores the server-side acceptable-CA mechanism, removes or weakens client certificate authentication/trust semantics, or treats conceptual awareness of the TLS limit as sufficient without an actionable compatible fix.

experiences.title: AST default alignment for positional-only signatures
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a trajectory for a Python/Sphinx-style signature parsing bug where defaults on parameters before the PEP 570 `/` marker disappear.
experiences.context: Applies in Python documentation or signature-inspection codebases where a directive or parser turns a textual function signature into parameter objects using Python AST semantics. It is especially relevant once the visible trajectory has found positional-only handling, inspected the intermediate signature object, or observed `posonlyargs`, regular positional args, and a shared defaults list. It is less useful for unrelated rendering-only bugs, parsers that do not use Python AST/default-list semantics, or very early exploration before the agent has identified the signature-construction layer; at that stage a broader reproduction/localization rubric may be more appropriate.
experiences.experience: The useful criterion in these cases is not merely that the final rendered documentation should show a missing default. The discriminative evidence is whether the agent recognizes the underlying semantic contract: Python AST stores defaults for the suffix of the combined positional parameter list, consisting of positional-only parameters followed by positional-or-keyword parameters. A strong trajectory should therefore map defaults from the right across that combined list, assign empty defaults to leading positional parameters with no default, preserve defaults for ordinary positional parameters, and leave slash placement, keyword-only arguments, varargs, annotations, and no-default signatures intact. Avoid generating a rubric that only rewards editing the visible renderer or the slash insertion code, because the missing default may originate earlier in the conversion to parameter objects. Also avoid a misleading criterion that assigns defaults to positional-only parameters from the start of the defaults list without accounting for right alignment; that shifts defaults in mixed signatures. Prioritize visible evidence such as AST inspection, direct checks of the intermediate signature parameters, tests using mixed signatures like a positional-only default followed by a normal default, and end-to-end rendering/build confirmation.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate or implement the correct Python AST default-mapping rule for signatures with positional-only parameters: defaults apply to the trailing parameters of the combined positional-only plus positional-or-keyword parameter sequence. Excellent progress includes locating the signature-construction layer rather than only the final renderer, verifying the AST representation or intermediate parameter defaults, applying a right-aligned mapping that preserves both positional-only and normal positional defaults, and validating slash rendering plus representative edge cases.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Right-aligned positional default mapping

key_evidence: Identifies that positional-only and positional-or-keyword parameters share one defaults sequence
Maps defaults to the suffix of the combined positional parameter list
Preserves the `/` separator and existing behavior for ordinary positional, keyword-only, varargs, annotations, and no-default cases
Uses direct intermediate-signature checks and/or rendered-output checks for a mixed positional-only/default signature
common_false_positives: Only changes display formatting without fixing parameter default construction
Assigns defaults to positional-only parameters from the beginning of the defaults sequence without right alignment
Fixes the reported example while shifting defaults for later normal positional parameters

scale.1: No visible evidence that the trajectory understands or addresses how defaults for positional-only parameters are represented; it may only inspect unrelated rendering or generic parsing code.
scale.2: Recognizes that defaults before `/` are lost, but proposes only a superficial rendering fix or handles the single example without reasoning about shared positional default alignment.
scale.3: Locates the signature-construction path and partially accounts for positional-only defaults, but evidence is incomplete or risks shifting defaults for mixed positional-only and normal positional parameters.
scale.4: Clearly identifies that defaults are right-aligned across the combined positional-only and positional-or-keyword list, and implements or plans a fix preserving normal defaults and slash behavior with some validation.
scale.5: Fully demonstrates the AST/default alignment rule, applies a robust combined-list mapping, preserves surrounding signature semantics, and validates with intermediate parameter checks plus representative rendered or regression cases.

experiences.title: Check instance actor identity beyond WebFinger response
experiences.description: Use when a NodeBB/ActivityPub task asks for WebFinger discovery of the instance actor and also requires the application actor identity to use the domain as its preferred username.
experiences.context: Applies in a NodeBB JavaScript/Express ActivityPub implementation where the agent has located or edited the WebFinger controller for `acct:` resources and the task explicitly couples WebFinger instance discovery with the ActivityPub application/instance actor’s `preferredUsername`. This is most useful once the trajectory has moved from exploration into implementation or final validation, especially if the visible work only changes the well-known/WebFinger response. It is less decisive during early repository exploration before the agent has inspected the application actor representation or before any patch direction is visible; at that stage, absence of a preferred-username change may be premature rather than a defect.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics correctly targeted a common incompleteness: agents often added a special WebFinger branch for `acct:domain@domain` but left the ActivityPub application actor still advertising the site title or another non-domain value as `preferredUsername`. That omission makes the WebFinger account identity inconsistent with the actor object it resolves to. The rubric was useful when the visible trajectory showed a near-complete WebFinger-only implementation, passing existing user WebFinger tests, or repeated claims that the fix was done without any evidence of updating the application actor representation. It was too harsh when applied during an earlier exploration stage where the agent had only just discovered the application actor route/controller and had not yet had a chance to patch it. A better rubric should require evidence that the trajectory either located and updated the application/instance actor JSON representation so `preferredUsername` comes from the configured hostname/domain, or at least explicitly plans and verifies that change before finalizing. Avoid replacing this with a broader criterion like “returns valid WebFinger aliases and links” or “uses the correct instance actor URL”; those can pass while the actor object remains inconsistent. Also avoid focusing only on whether the WebFinger controller compares the localpart to host versus hostname, because that is only one part of the contract. Prioritize visible evidence such as: an inspected application actor endpoint, a code edit or test assertion for its `preferredUsername`, use of the configured parsed hostname rather than forum title/name, and preservation of normal user WebFinger behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the instance actor WebFinger work is paired with a consistent ActivityPub application actor identity: the application/instance actor representation should expose the configured server hostname/domain as `preferredUsername`, while the WebFinger instance response resolves to that same actor and regular user WebFinger behavior remains separate. Strong evidence includes locating the application actor endpoint, modifying or verifying its actor JSON identity, and avoiding reliance on the site title or user-slug lookup for the instance actor.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Consistent instance actor preferred username

required_visible_evidence: WebFinger instance actor handling is being implemented or reviewed
Application/instance actor representation is inspected or modified
Preferred username is derived from configured hostname/domain rather than display title
User WebFinger branch remains distinct from instance actor branch
metadata.stage_boundary: Most discriminative after implementation begins or before final submission; weaker during initial exploration

scale.1: No visible evidence that the application/instance actor preferred username is considered; work focuses only on user or WebFinger response shape.
scale.2: Mentions instance actor identity but does not inspect or update the actor representation, or continues to use a display name/title as preferred username.
scale.3: Acknowledges the need for consistency between WebFinger and the application actor but has only partial or uncertain evidence of where/how `preferredUsername` will be set.
scale.4: Clearly locates the application actor representation and updates or plans a concrete update so `preferredUsername` uses the configured domain/hostname, while preserving user WebFinger behavior.
scale.5: Fully implements and/or validates the consistent instance actor identity: WebFinger instance discovery points to the application actor, the actor’s `preferredUsername` is the configured hostname/domain, and normal user WebFinger behavior is kept intact.

experiences.title: Include-Task Keyword Allowlist as a Necessary Subcriterion
experiences.description: Retrieve when an Ansible-like task asks for an existing task keyword to work in include-style tasks and the trajectory exposes a separate include-task validation/allowlist path.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Ansible-style CLI/playbook codebase where the task statement explicitly says an include-style task ignores or rejects a keyword, and visible exploration shows include tasks have their own keyword validation separate from the general task attribute model. This is most useful once the trajectory has inspected or edited that include validation path, or when the agent is at final-review stage and must ensure every independent acceptance item was covered. It should not be used as the sole correctness signal for multi-part tasks that also require CLI parser options, option naming compatibility, or task-dictionary propagation. It is also premature during early exploration before the agent has begun implementation, and irrelevant if include-style tasks share the normal task keyword loader with no separate validation boundary.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics focused on whether include-style task validation recognizes `timeout`. That is a useful necessary criterion because the existing task keyword machinery and executor support do not automatically make include tasks accept the keyword when a separate include-keyword allowlist rejects unknown keys. Visible evidence that supports this criterion includes the task statement naming include-style rejection, trajectory notes locating a distinct include validation list, a clean edit adding the keyword to that validation path, and ideally a targeted check that an include task containing the keyword is accepted. However, this subcriterion is not sufficient for the whole task: trajectories can satisfy it while still failing due to broken parser edits, conflating connection timeout with task timeout, placing timeout on the play instead of the task, omitting console extra-vars, or never producing a final patch. Conversely, absence of the edit at an intermediate cutoff may be weak evidence if the agent has clearly identified it as a remaining TODO. A better rubric should frame this as coverage of one independent acceptance requirement, not as proof that the CLI feature is complete. Avoid tempting proxies such as finding executor timeout support, searching only the generic task class, adding a changelog, or reusing an existing connection `--timeout`; prioritize the visible include-validation boundary and whether the new task keyword is admitted there without broad, unrelated rewrites.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Include-Style Keyword Validation Coverage
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should ensure that include-style task validation accepts the requested task keyword through the include-specific allowlist or equivalent validation mechanism, so tasks using that keyword are not rejected or silently ignored. Strong evidence is a clean, localized change to the include validation boundary plus a targeted inspection or test showing the keyword is now accepted. This criterion evaluates only the include-task acceptance requirement and should not be treated as evidence that CLI option exposure or task execution propagation is complete.

metadata.task_requirement: include-style tasks must accept the requested existing task keyword
metadata.validation_boundary: include-specific keyword validation or allowlist separate from general task attributes
preferred_visible_evidence: trajectory identifies the separate include validation path
keyword is added to the include validation mechanism or equivalent
change is localized and does not bypass validation broadly
optional targeted check demonstrates an include task with the keyword is accepted
non_sufficient_evidence: generic task attributes define the keyword
CLI parser option was added without include validation

scale.1: No visible evidence that the trajectory recognized or addressed the include-specific validation requirement; it assumes general task keyword support or CLI changes are enough.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory mentions include-style rejection or searches nearby code, but has not found or changed the actual include validation boundary.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies the include-specific validation mechanism and may plan or partially attempt a change, but the visible state is incomplete, unverified, or possibly syntactically/structurally damaged.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory cleanly updates the include-specific validation mechanism so the requested keyword is accepted, with no obvious broad bypass or unrelated rewrite, but lacks a direct acceptance check.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the trajectory cleanly updates the include-specific validation mechanism and verifies through a targeted inspection or test that include-style tasks containing the requested keyword are accepted while normal validation behavior remains intact.

experiences.title: Do not equate XHR Accept-Language preservation with blindly skipping the header
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating qutebrowser/QtWebEngine trajectories for the XHR `Accept-Language` override bug, especially when the agent proposes only expanding an existing XHR `Accept` skip condition or checking for an already-present request header.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/qutebrowser codebase where configured request headers are produced by shared header-building logic, applied by a QtWebEngine request interceptor, and the global Accept-Language value is also configured at the browser profile level. The misleading pattern is a trajectory that correctly finds the interceptor and existing XHR `Accept` special case, then treats the task as simply adding `Accept-Language` to that same unconditional XHR skip or as preserving only when an existing header is visible. That is incomplete because the task distinguishes the global fallback setting from URL/per-domain overrides: the global fallback should not clobber JavaScript XHR headers, but more specific configured overrides may still intentionally take precedence, and normal non-XHR behavior must remain intact. The original root-cause localization rubric can still be useful during early exploration, or in projects without a separate profile-level/global fallback versus URL-specific override mechanism, but it should not be used as a final-quality criterion once the trajectory has reached implementation design.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics rewarded the coarse semantic goal: find the request-interception path and prevent `content.headers.accept_language` from overwriting JavaScript-specified XHR headers. That sounds aligned with the issue, but it over-credits a tempting patch that just adds `Accept-Language` to an existing XHR `Accept` skip condition. In this environment, the important visible evidence is whether the agent has understood the layered configuration contract: global Accept-Language is a fallback/profile-level value, while per-domain or URL-specific header values are still applied through the interceptor. A better rubric should focus on preserving that distinction, not merely on whether the agent mentions XHR custom header preservation. Avoid generating criteria that say the trajectory should “skip Accept-Language for all XHR requests” or “only skip when an existing header is detected” unless the visible codebase truly lacks fallback/per-domain semantics. Prefer criteria that look for evidence the agent inspected both the header-building function and the WebEngine/profile setting path, reasoned about fallback versus URL-specific overrides, and implemented or planned a change that suppresses only the global fallback injection for XHR while keeping non-XHR and URL-specific override behavior intact.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that reduce the Accept-Language/XHR fix to a blanket interceptor skip or an ad hoc existing-header check without accounting for the codebase's separate global fallback/profile-level Accept-Language handling and URL-specific override behavior. This flaw is present when the visible trajectory proposes or implements skipping configured `Accept-Language` for every XHR request, or preserving it only based on currently visible request headers, while failing to reason about preserving more specific configured overrides and normal non-XHR header application.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Overbroad XHR Header Skip Ignores Fallback Semantics

metadata.environment: Python qutebrowser with QtWebEngine request interception and configurable Accept-Language headers
key_visible_evidence: Agent has found the interceptor loop applying shared/custom headers
Agent has found or reused the existing XHR Accept-header special case
Agent has not distinguished global fallback Accept-Language from URL/per-domain override values
Agent has not considered that the global value may already be set via the WebEngine profile
better_focus: Suppress only global fallback Accept-Language injection for XHR interceptor-applied headers
Preserve URL-specific/per-domain overrides where the configuration contract intends them to win
Use tests or reasoning that exercise fallback versus override cases, not only generic XHR detection

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory explicitly distinguishes global fallback/profile-level Accept-Language from URL-specific overrides and preserves non-XHR behavior.
scale.2: Minor risk: the trajectory mentions preserving normal requests but only partially discusses fallback versus override semantics.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory finds the right interceptor path and XHR issue but leaves the global fallback versus URL-specific override distinction unclear.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory proposes a blanket XHR `Accept-Language` skip or existing-header-only guard without addressing profile-level fallback handling or per-domain overrides.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory implements or strongly commits to an overbroad skip that would discard intended configured overrides or otherwise changes unrelated header behavior, while treating passing unrelated tests as sufficient validation.

experiences.title: Figure-Like Parent Abstraction for SubFigure Legends
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Matplotlib trajectory addresses a `SubFigure.legend()` failure caused by legend parent validation accepting `Figure` but not `SubFigure`, especially after the class hierarchy shows a shared figure-like base class.
experiences.context: Applies to Matplotlib source tasks where a public figure-like API on a subfigure is rejected by a constructor or validator that currently accepts axes and full figures only. The useful stage is after the trajectory has either inspected the legend parent-validation code or confirmed that `Figure` and `SubFigure` share a common base such as `FigureBase`; it can also apply once a minimal reproduction reaches the reported TypeError. It is less useful before any code localization, when the trajectory is only resolving import/build dependencies, or for bugs about legend placement, rendering, handle/label collection, backend behavior, or visual baseline differences rather than parent type acceptance.
experiences.experience: For this pattern, the useful rubric is not a generic 'add a test' or 'make the legend work' criterion. The discriminative criterion is whether the trajectory preserves the existing axes-vs-figure legend split while broadening the figure-like parent check from the concrete full-figure class to the shared figure/subfigure abstraction. The strongest visible evidence is: the agent identifies the failing parent validation, confirms that subfigures are not instances of the concrete figure class but do inherit the shared figure-like base, edits the figure-like branch rather than adding unrelated logic, keeps axes handling separate, and validates that `subfig.legend()` no longer raises while ordinary figure and axes legends still work. A native regression test is valuable when added, but should not be the primary criterion here because the minimal source change itself is sufficient to resolve the reported failure and trajectories may be constrained by Matplotlib build/test setup. Avoid criteria that over-prioritize environment setup, docstring/error-message wording, modifying `SubFigure.legend()` directly, special-casing only `SubFigure` when a shared base exists, or changing handle/label discovery.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should correctly resolve the subfigure legend failure by treating subfigures as valid figure-like legend parents through the shared figure/subfigure base abstraction. A strong trajectory localizes the TypeError to legend parent validation, preserves the existing axes-specific path, routes full figures and subfigures through the non-axes figure-like path with the correct figure assignment, and uses visible reproduction or targeted checks to show that subfigure, figure, and axes legends remain functional.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Shared Figure-Like Parent Support

required_visible_evidence: The trajectory identifies that the failure occurs in legend parent validation rather than in legend handle collection, rendering, or backend setup.
The trajectory observes or uses the class relationship that subfigures and full figures share a figure-like base class.
The implementation plan or edit broadens the concrete figure parent check to that shared base class.
The axes-specific branch remains distinct and existing axes/full-figure legend behavior is not intentionally changed.
Validation, if available, exercises the reported subfigure legend call and preferably also checks ordinary figure and axes legends.
common_false_proxies_to_avoid: Demanding a project-native test as the decisive success condition when the source fix is already clear and manually validated.
Rewarding time spent on Matplotlib import/build dependency issues without progress on the parent validation logic.
Accepting a direct subfigure-only special case when the visible hierarchy supports a shared abstraction.
Focusing on error-message or documentation wording as the main correctness signal.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory has localized the bug to legend parent validation or identified the figure/subfigure inheritance relationship.
scale.2: The trajectory suspects the parent-type issue or mentions subfigure support, but has not connected the fix to the shared figure-like base or risks changing unrelated legend behavior.
scale.3: The trajectory has identified the concrete parent check and the shared base-class approach, but has not yet clearly applied it or shown preservation of the axes/full-figure paths.
scale.4: The trajectory applies or is poised to apply the shared-base parent check while preserving the existing axes and figure-like branches; validation may be limited but the semantic fix is clear.
scale.5: The trajectory implements the shared-base parent support, leaves axes and full-figure behavior intact, and provides visible validation that the reported subfigure legend call works, with additional checks for ordinary figure and axes legends or equivalent confidence.

experiences.title: Do not reward nominal model-store-utils scaffolding when integration semantics are the real risk
experiences.description: Retrieve when a TypeScript/React refactor task explicitly asks for a model, store, utility, and event emitter architecture, and the trajectory has begun adding those named pieces. Avoid generating a broad rubric that merely checks for their existence.
experiences.context: This applies in Matrix React SDK-style feature refactors where the task statement already names desired artifacts such as a recording model, centralized recordings store, start utility, and TypedEventEmitter notifications. In these cases, trajectories often create plausible files/classes/events and export them, but the visible risk is whether the new architecture preserves the existing UI and Matrix event behavior, compiles, and is correctly wired into the existing start/display/stop flows. A broad pattern-adherence rubric may still be appropriate very early, before implementation exists, or as a low-weight scaffolding check. Once code has been written or integration points are being edited, the rubric should not treat the mere presence of model/store/utils/EventEmitter as strong evidence of quality.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics rewarded adoption of the model-store-utils pattern: a VoiceBroadcastRecording class, VoiceBroadcastRecordingsStore, start utility, and TypedEventEmitter events. That criterion is not wrong as a design direction, but it becomes misleading when the task itself already prescribes those names and the trajectory visibly creates superficial scaffolding. It misses higher-risk evidence: broken imports from line-based edits, utilities whose signature does not match the existing caller, stores using incorrect SDK event APIs, public type regressions, unvalidated compile errors, and failure to preserve the existing Matrix state-event semantics. A better rubric should focus on whether the newly introduced modules are behaviorally integrated and compatible: the existing start button should call the utility with the right dependencies, the utility should send the same voice broadcast info state event and update the store only when the event is observed, the display component should subscribe to store/model updates without breaking stop behavior, public exports and event content types should remain backward compatible, and validation output should not show errors in the touched files. Avoid the tempting criterion 'does it have a model, store, utility, and TypedEventEmitter?' as the main success proxy. Prioritize visible evidence from diffs, import blocks, call signatures, Matrix event content/state key handling, store listener lifecycle, and TypeScript/lint/test output.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that add the requested model/store/utility/EventEmitter scaffolding for a voice broadcast refactor but leave the new architecture behaviorally incompatible with the existing application flow. Evidence includes: the existing composer/start UI is not wired to the new utility, the utility signature or dependencies do not match the caller, Matrix state-event content/state key/chunk length/relation typing is changed without justification, the store listens to incorrect SDK events or cannot map observed state events to recordings, display/stop components are rewritten in ways that break existing behavior, public exports become incompatible, or validation shows errors in touched files. Do not count the mere existence of named classes or event enums as sufficient when these integration risks are visible.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Nominal architecture without compatible integration

metadata.task_family: TypeScript React Matrix SDK feature refactor
visible_evidence_to_check: existing start handler replacement and utility call signature
state event content and state key preservation
