store listener API and lifecycle correctness
model/store/display component interaction
barrel exports and public type compatibility
validation output for touched files
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: presence of named model/store/utils/TypedEventEmitter artifacts alone

scale.1: No visible evidence of this flaw: scaffolding is integrated with existing start/display/stop flows, public contracts are preserved, and touched-file validation is clean or convincingly addressed.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: named architecture exists and mostly integrates, but there are small unresolved compatibility or validation concerns that appear localized.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: model/store/utils are present, but important integration details such as caller signature, store updates, or public exports are incomplete or uncertain from the visible trajectory.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory mainly adds scaffolding while leaving existing UI flow unwired, changing event semantics/types, or showing compile/API errors in touched files.
scale.5: Severe evidence: superficial model/store/utils additions coexist with broken imports, incompatible utility calls, incorrect SDK event usage, behavior regressions in existing components, and unresolved validation failures.

experiences.title: Argparse required-group kwargs must be routed through parser validation
experiences.description: Use when a Django-style programmatic command API converts keyword options into argparse input and the reported bug involves members of a required mutually exclusive group not satisfying the group.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Django management-command work where `call_command()` or a similar wrapper builds an argparse parser, maps keyword options to argparse destinations, and selectively synthesizes command-line arguments before `parse_args()`. The key visible task cue is that individual actions in `add_mutually_exclusive_group(required=True)` have `required=False`, while the group itself is required. This criterion is most useful after the agent has inspected the parser/action handling or has begun patching the kwarg-to-parse_args bridge. It is less useful during very early file-location exploration, and it should not be expanded into a blanket requirement for subparser recursion, non-required mutually exclusive groups, or custom conflict handling unless the trajectory itself modifies or tests those behaviors.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster were useful when they judged the central semantic contract: kwargs whose argparse destination belongs to a required mutually exclusive group must be represented in the synthetic parse input so argparse can satisfy the required-group constraint, while ordinary required-option handling and missing-group errors continue to behave normally. They were strongest when they looked for visible evidence that the agent inspected `parser._mutually_exclusive_groups`/`group._group_actions`, understood that member actions are not individually required, and verified both the original kwarg success and the no-member failure. They became less reliable when they over-weighted tempting but task-adjacent concerns such as exhaustive subparser recursion, accepting option-string alias kwargs for every nested parser, or manually reimplementing mutual-exclusion errors. A better rubric should prioritize whether the patch extends the existing required-kwarg forwarding path to include actions in required mutually exclusive groups, without bypassing `parse_args()` or silently marking each member as individually required. If the trajectory shows conflicting kwargs in the same group being silently accepted, that is a meaningful warning, but it should be framed as preservation of argparse validation rather than as a standalone implementation mandate; judge it most strongly when the agent’s code explicitly chooses only one supplied group member, deletes others, or otherwise prevents argparse from seeing conflicts. Avoid rewarding broad private-API scans or unrelated test runs as proxies for correctness; prioritize the concrete code path that builds `parse_args`, the use of normalized destinations versus raw keyword names where visible, and targeted reproduction of provided member, missing member, and existing required-option behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the command wrapper fixes required mutually exclusive argparse groups by identifying actions that belong to required groups and forwarding supplied keyword values for those actions through the existing parser-validation path. Strong evidence includes inspecting argparse group internals, adding only the required-group membership condition to the required-kwarg parse input logic, using the same option string/destination mapping conventions already used by the wrapper, and validating that a single provided group member succeeds while an omitted required group still raises the parser’s required-group error. The rubric should also notice whether the agent preserves existing behavior for ordinary required options and avoids bypassing argparse with manual defaults or ad hoc success conditions.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Required group action forwarding

primary_visible_evidence: The task describes a required mutually exclusive argparse group whose member actions are not individually required.
The trajectory inspects or uses group-level argparse metadata such as required groups and their member actions.
The patch affects the synthetic parse argument construction rather than command execution or parser creation.
Validation includes at least the original kwarg case and the missing-required-group case.
secondary_evidence: Alias-to-destination normalization is considered when the trajectory exposes custom dest names.
Existing required-option tests or equivalent checks still pass.
Conflict behavior is preserved by allowing argparse to validate supplied group members rather than by silently choosing or deleting options.
do_not_overrequire: Subparser recursion unless the agent changes or relies on subparser behavior.
Manual reproduction artifacts as a substitute for the core code-path evidence.
Custom reimplementation of argparse error messages.

scale.1: No substantive evidence that the agent understands or addresses required mutually exclusive groups; the patch or plan remains focused only on individually required actions, unrelated files, or command execution after parsing.
scale.2: The agent identifies mutually exclusive groups but proposes or applies a weak fix that bypasses parser validation, marks group members as individually required, handles only an ad hoc command path, or lacks evidence that supplied group-member kwargs are added to parse input.
scale.3: The trajectory reaches behavior comparable to the parent state: it recognizes required group membership and has partial code or tests for the original kwarg case, but evidence is incomplete or there are unresolved concerns about destination mapping, missing-group behavior, or preserving existing required-option parsing.
scale.4: Strong evidence shows the fix extends the existing required-kwarg parse_args construction to include supplied actions from required mutually exclusive groups, with targeted checks that one provided member succeeds, missing members still error, and ordinary required options remain functional.
scale.5: The trajectory provides the strongest visible assurance: the implementation is minimal and integrated with existing parser action/destination mapping, relies on argparse for validation rather than manual shortcuts, covers the original case plus missing-required and existing required-option regressions, and addresses any exposed alias or conflict concerns without broad unrelated behavioral changes.

experiences.title: Integrated no_log Key Sanitization Over Isolated Helper Stubs
experiences.description: Use when an Ansible-style no_log task asks for narrow mapping-key sanitization, ignore-list support, and raw string redaction; especially after the trajectory has found remove_values/heuristic_log_sanitize and is deciding whether to patch existing redaction or add new helpers.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Ansible-like repositories where no_log values are collected centrally and existing utilities such as remove_values or heuristic_log_sanitize already redact values broadly. The criterion is most useful once the agent has enough evidence to know the relevant module_utils file and likely return/logging call sites, or after it starts implementing. It is less useful during the first few exploratory commands before relevant functions are located. Do not apply it to tasks that only require a standalone library helper with no existing serialization/logging path, or to pure string-sanitization bugs where mapping-key behavior and integration are not part of the task.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics often restated the visible task contract or rewarded creation of sanitize_keys/sanitize_string alone. That can be misleading here: several trajectories added plausible helper functions, or a separate raw string redactor, but left them unexported, unused by the actual module return path, placed in an unexpected module, based on fixed default sensitive-token lists instead of collected no_log values, or achieved ignore-list behavior by mutating remove_values in a way that risks existing tests and output semantics. A better rubric should focus on the discriminating evidence visible in the trajectory: whether the agent separates key-only sanitization from broad value redaction, preserves existing remove_values/heuristic behavior except where intentionally narrowing key mutation, implements exact ignore-key and sentinel rules using the runtime no_log set, and wires the sanitizer into the concrete logging/serialization/return path that can expose sensitive values in keys. Avoid making the separate string helper the main success criterion when key-sanitizer integration is still missing; it is secondary evidence. Also avoid rewarding repeated git-history searches or isolated ad-hoc scripts as implementation progress unless they lead to an actual patch and targeted tests.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: End-to-End Narrow no_log Key Sanitization
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show progress toward a complete, integrated no_log key-sanitization fix: a dedicated mapping-key sanitizer that uses the collected no_log strings, preserves non-mapping inputs and non-key values except for recursively reaching nested mappings, applies exact ignore-key checks before masking, replaces exact sensitive-key matches with the existing sentinel, masks sensitive substrings in key names with ********, and is wired into the relevant module return/logging/serialization path with an appropriate ignore-key set. It should avoid broad, risky changes to existing value redaction or heuristic log sanitization unless explicitly preserving compatibility, and should include or plan focused tests for pass-through, recursive keys, ignore keys, sentinel behavior, and integration.

metadata.environment: Python Ansible-style repository with lib/ansible/module_utils/basic.py, common no_log value collection, and unit tests under test/units/module_utils
prioritize_visible_evidence: actual code edits or concrete patch plan in the located no_log utilities and relevant call site
dedicated key sanitizer rather than only modifying raw string/value redaction
use of runtime no_log strings rather than hard-coded sensitive-token defaults
exact-key ignore-list handling and existing sentinel spelling
preservation of existing remove_values and heuristic_log_sanitize contracts
focused tests or manual checks covering contract and integration
deprioritize_visible_evidence: repeated repository searches after target functions are already found
standalone helper in a new module that is not imported or called
raw string redaction helper without mapping-key integration
passing isolated ad-hoc tests while broader existing tests or call-site behavior are unexamined

scale.1: No meaningful implementation progress: the agent is still repeating searches or ad-hoc reproduction, or only discusses the desired behavior without editing or identifying a concrete integration path.
scale.2: Weak progress: a helper or test sketch exists, but it is isolated, unimported, uses hard-coded sensitive defaults, lacks ignore/sentinel semantics, or only implements raw string redaction while mapping-key sanitization remains absent.
scale.3: Moderate progress: the helper covers some key-sanitization contract details, but integration into the actual no_log output/logging path is missing or the approach risks changing existing value-redaction behavior broadly.
scale.4: Strong progress: a dedicated key sanitizer with no_log-string matching, exact ignore keys, sentinel behavior, and compatibility-conscious implementation is present, with focused tests or manual validation; only minor integration, placement, or coverage gaps remain.
scale.5: Strongest progress: the trajectory demonstrates an end-to-end fix that separates key sanitization from value/string redaction, preserves existing redaction contracts, wires the sanitizer into the relevant return/logging/serialization path with an appropriate ignore list, and validates the contract with focused tests.

experiences.title: Do not reward collapsing complementary records as deduplication
experiences.description: Retrieve when a bug report complains about duplicate aggregated records, but the visible code/model shows multiple heterogeneous records under the same key because different input maps or phases populate different fields.
experiences.context: Applies in Go conversion/parser tasks like a Trivy-to-Vuls converter where output is an aggregation such as a map from source to a slice of content records, and the trajectory has identified separate append paths for severity data and CVSS score/vector data. The misleading case is generating a rubric that demands exactly one object per source and merging all fields into that object, even though visible tests/model structure may treat severity-only and CVSS-only content as distinct record shapes and only repeated severities or repeated identical CVSS records are true duplicates. The original one-object-per-source idea may still be appropriate when the visible data contract, tests, or schema explicitly requires a single homogeneous record per key and there is no evidence that different records under the key encode different semantic categories.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster asked whether the agent consolidated all same-source CveContent records into a single object, merging VendorSeverity severities with CVSS scores/vectors. That is tempting because the issue text says duplicate objects and one entry per source, and agents often validate by counting source keys. However, this criterion can over-reward over-consolidation: a patch may replace a source slice with a singleton, overwrite existing records across repeated vulnerabilities, or merge severity-only and CVSS-only records that the converter/model keeps as different content forms. A better rubric should distinguish true duplicates from complementary records. It should prioritize visible evidence that the agent preserves all non-duplicate CVSS score/vector records, consolidates multiple severity strings for the same source without losing or repeating severities, skips exact duplicate CVSS entries caused by repeated package detections, and keeps unrelated package/library conversion behavior intact. Avoid generating a broad criterion that treats every same-source record as a duplicate or judges success by array length alone; require field-level preservation and narrow converter changes instead.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that implement or strongly commit to over-consolidating heterogeneous CVE content records: treating any repeated source key as a duplicate, replacing the source's content slice with a single record after processing both severity and CVSS inputs, or updating expectations merely to remove separate CVSS/severity records. This flaw is present when the visible code/model shows different input maps or conversion paths populate different fields, but the proposed fix collapses them without proving that complementary CVSS scores/vectors, references, dates, and existing package/library conversion behavior are preserved. The correct direction is narrower: consolidate repeated severity values deterministically and avoid exact duplicate CVSS records while preserving distinct non-duplicate content data.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Over-collapsing heterogeneous CVE content

evidence_to_check: Whether the aggregation value type is a slice or otherwise permits multiple records per source
Whether separate conversion paths populate severity fields versus CVSS score/vector fields
Whether the agent's patch uses source-only maps or singleton assignment that overwrites existing content
Whether validation only counts source occurrences instead of inspecting preserved fields
Whether unrelated package/library conversion logic is changed while fixing CVE content duplication
preferred_positive_evidence: Deduplicates identical repeated records caused by repeated vulnerability/package occurrences
Combines multiple severity values without duplicates and with deterministic ordering
Preserves CVSS2/CVSS3 scores and vectors as distinct content when they are not exact duplicates
Keeps the change scoped to CVE content aggregation

scale.1: No evidence of over-consolidation; the trajectory distinguishes duplicate repeated data from complementary severity/CVSS records and preserves unrelated conversion behavior.
scale.2: Minor risk only; the agent discusses one-per-source language but also inspects field preservation and has not implemented source-only overwrites.
scale.3: Moderate concern; the plan or partial patch deduplicates by source but contains some safeguards for preserving severity and CVSS fields.
scale.4: Clear flaw; the patch or plan replaces each source with a singleton merged record or removes separate records without adequate field-level preservation.
scale.5: Severe flaw; the patch collapses all same-source records, overwrites prior content across repeated CVE occurrences, validates only by counts, or also disrupts unrelated package/library conversion logic.

experiences.title: ValidationError interpolation requires both placeholder and params
experiences.description: Use this when a Django/form-validation task asks that an invalid submitted value appear in an error, and the trajectory has identified a target field/class plus analogous code that already passes `ValidationError.params`.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django-style repository where form field validation raises structured `ValidationError`s with message templates, codes, and params. The matching situation is a task about an invalid-choice error omitting the rejected value, with visible evidence that the target implementation has a default error message lacking or using a `%(value)s` placeholder and a raise site that currently omits `params`, while a sibling/generic field demonstrates the intended contract. This is most useful after the trajectory has located the target class and invalid-choice raise path, or after edits/tests are visible. It is less useful as a harsh current-progress criterion during very early exploration or while the agent is only installing dependencies, because the agent may still recover later. Do not apply it to unrelated validation bugs where the issue is lookup logic, choice rendering, database setup, or a different error code.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics focused on the right semantic contract: invalid-choice errors must carry the rejected value through the structured `ValidationError.params` and the default/custom message path must be able to interpolate that value, without changing valid, empty, queryset, model-instance, or sibling-field behavior. This was useful because visible evidence such as inspecting the target `to_python()`/validation method, comparing it with `ChoiceField` or `ModelMultipleChoiceField`, seeing `params=None` in a repro, or seeing a patch add `params={'value': ...}` directly predicts whether the final behavior will satisfy the task. A better rubric should judge concrete implementation evidence, not just the agent’s stated plan: look for the actual target raise site being changed, the invalid value passed under the expected params key, the error code preserved, and message interpolation enabled where applicable. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as only changing the human-readable message, only installing dependencies or running an ad hoc script, editing unrelated `invalid_choice` raise sites, modifying the already-correct sibling field, or updating tests to expect new strings without fixing structured params. Also avoid over-penalizing temporary broken edits at a mid-trajectory cutoff if the agent has recognized the two-part contract and is still actively correcting the patch; phrase the rubric as current evidence of completion rather than a prediction that recovery is impossible.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates that the target model-backed choice validation path will raise its invalid-choice `ValidationError` with the rejected submitted/lookup value in structured params, while preserving the existing error code and normal validation behavior. Strong evidence includes identifying the exact invalid-choice raise site in the target class, comparing with an analogous field that already passes `params`, applying a patch at that raise site, enabling message interpolation for the default/custom invalid-choice message where needed, and verifying both `ValidationError.params` and rendered/interpolated messages for invalid inputs. The criterion should not give substantial credit for changing only tests, only editing a message string, changing unrelated invalid-choice paths, or merely planning the fix without visible implementation.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Structured invalid-choice value propagation

key_evidence: target invalid-choice raise site is modified
params include the rejected value under a value-like key
invalid_choice code is preserved
default or custom message can interpolate the value
valid, empty, queryset lookup, and sibling-field behavior are not broadened or broken
anti_evidence: only dependency installation or repro setup is visible
only message text changes without params
unrelated invalid_choice site is edited
already-correct sibling field is modified instead of the target path
tests are rewritten without implementation support

scale.1: No visible evidence that the target invalid-choice raise path or message/params contract has been understood or changed.
scale.2: The trajectory has found relevant files or stated the intended behavior, but has not implemented the params propagation at the target raise site.
scale.3: The trajectory is comparable to the parent state: it has identified the two-part contract or made partial edits, but evidence is incomplete, possibly only a message change or an unverified/in-progress patch.
scale.4: Clear implementation evidence shows the target invalid-choice `ValidationError` now receives params containing the rejected value, with the error code preserved; message interpolation or behavior preservation is at least partly checked.
scale.5: Strong end-to-end evidence shows the correct target raise site passes the rejected value in params, the invalid-choice message interpolates it for default/custom messages, and tests or focused repros confirm invalid cases while preserving valid/empty/queryset and sibling-field behavior.

experiences.title: OPeNDAP `_Unsigned=false` Signed-Byte Decode Semantics
experiences.description: Retrieve when an xarray trajectory is addressing pydap/OPeNDAP unsigned byte data marked with `_Unsigned=False` and must judge whether the implementation fixes decode-time signedness interpretation rather than unrelated backend or encode behavior.
experiences.context: Applies to Python/xarray CF decoding work where the task explicitly contrasts the existing netCDF `_Unsigned=True` signed-to-unsigned convention with the OPeNDAP/THREDDS `_Unsigned=False` unsigned-to-signed convention. The most useful stage is after the agent has inspected or modified the unsigned-integer variable coder, or has produced manual evidence using small integer arrays. It is less useful for unrelated pydap connectivity issues, general warning cleanup, or tasks focused only on serialization/encoding. At very early exploration, treat locating the coder and reproducing `uint8` values staying unsigned as partial progress; at final-review stage, require evidence that the actual decode branch handles the new case without disturbing existing `_Unsigned=True` behavior.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful rubric in these cases judged the core semantic contract: unsigned integer arrays carrying an explicit false `_Unsigned` marker must be decoded as same-width signed integers, e.g. high byte values map to negative signed values, while the existing signed-with-true path remains intact. This was discriminative because trajectories that implemented or validated that exact decode branch were on the right path, whereas broader proxies such as running backend tests, installing dependencies, testing network OPeNDAP access, or experimenting with encode roundtrips did not by themselves establish correctness. A better rubric should be precise about decode-time behavior, dtype width preservation, metadata movement/fill-value conversion, and using the repository’s existing lazy conversion pattern. Avoid a tempting but wrong criterion that rewards any symmetric-looking change: broad encode modifications, converting unsigned data for `_Unsigned=True`, or replacing established lazy conversion helpers with unverified alternatives can introduce regressions even if the new `uint8` example appears conceptually addressed. Prioritize visible evidence such as a branch conditioned on unsigned integer dtype plus false `_Unsigned`, construction of the matching signed dtype from itemsize, lazy elementwise conversion, `_FillValue` conversion to the target dtype, preservation of the warning for genuinely non-integer data, and manual or formal tests showing `uint8 [128, 255]` becomes `int8 [-128, -1]` while signed `_Unsigned=True` still becomes unsigned.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Decode unsigned `_Unsigned=false` data as signed
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should specifically implement and validate decode-time handling for the OPeNDAP/THREDDS convention where unsigned integer data with `_Unsigned` explicitly false is interpreted as the same-width signed dtype. Strong evidence includes a localized change in the unsigned-integer CF decoder that detects unsigned integer dtype and false `_Unsigned`, converts through the existing lazy elementwise conversion style to the corresponding signed dtype, converts `_FillValue` to that target dtype when present, preserves existing `_Unsigned=true` signed-to-unsigned behavior, and leaves warnings for genuinely non-integer `_Unsigned` data.

required_visible_evidence: decode path, not only encode or backend path, is modified or targeted
condition distinguishes unsigned integer dtype with false `_Unsigned`
target dtype is same itemsize signed integer
conversion preserves lazy-array compatibility using the established pattern
`_FillValue` is converted consistently when present
existing signed integer plus true `_Unsigned` behavior remains covered
manual or formal tests check both dtype and values such as 128 to -128 and 255 to -1
avoid_rewarding: network-only OPeNDAP reproduction without coder fix
encode-only symmetry changes
conversion of unsigned data for `_Unsigned=true`
generic warning suppression without signed dtype conversion
test commands that select no relevant tests

scale.1: No visible evidence that the trajectory identifies the unsigned `_Unsigned=false` decode contract; work is unrelated, backend-only, or only suppresses warnings.
scale.2: The trajectory recognizes the signed-byte problem or locates the unsigned-integer decoder, but has not implemented the unsigned-dtype plus false-attribute conversion or validates only unrelated behavior.
scale.3: The trajectory adds or proposes the correct high-level branch for unsigned data with false `_Unsigned`, but evidence is incomplete: dtype width, lazy conversion, fill-value handling, or preservation of existing `_Unsigned=true` behavior is uncertain.
scale.4: The trajectory implements the localized decode branch with same-width signed conversion and shows manual evidence for representative byte values while mostly preserving existing behavior; minor concerns remain about formal tests or exact helper compatibility.
scale.5: The trajectory cleanly implements the decode-only semantic fix using the established lazy conversion pattern, handles `_FillValue`, preserves existing signed-to-unsigned and non-integer warning behavior, and validates with relevant tests or clear manual checks for byte values and other integer widths.

experiences.title: Do not reward emitter compatibility that silently drops legacy audit backends
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a Go/Teleport-style fix for an interface mismatch between a composite legacy audit-log wrapper and a newer emitter interface, especially when the trajectory proposes adding a forwarding method that type-asserts children and skips non-matching backends.
experiences.context: Applies in Go repositories with transitional legacy/new audit APIs, where startup fails because a composite audit log type satisfies an older broad logging interface but not a newer emitter interface. The misleading rubric pattern is to treat adding the missing emitter method to the composite wrapper as sufficient if it forwards to children that already implement the new interface. That can be appropriate only after the trajectory has shown that every child reachable from the failing service configuration either already implements the new emitter interface or is explicitly adapted/validated. It is not sufficient when visible investigation shows some configured audit-log implementations, such as writer/stdout-style logs, implement only the legacy interface; in that situation a wrapper method that uses `if child implements Emitter { emit }` can make startup pass while silently losing audit events.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics correctly identified that the composite audit log must satisfy the new emitter contract, but they were too permissive because they rewarded forwarding only to “compatible” children. In this task shape, the important correctness boundary is not just whether the wrapper type passes the service-layer type assertion; it is whether all configured external audit destinations remain active under the new structured event path. A tempting but wrong criterion is: “MultiLog should implement EmitAuditEvent and forward to underlying emitters while aggregating errors.” That criterion overvalues a patch that silently skips non-emitter children. A better rubric should require visible evidence that non-emitter legacy audit logs are not ignored: either the construction path rejects them with a clear error before startup proceeds, or the service constructs/adapts those backends into real emitters, and the composite uses a fan-out over a complete emitter list with aggregate error handling. Prioritize evidence from the service configuration factory, concrete backend constructors, and wrapper construction semantics over mere presence of an `EmitAuditEvent` method on the composite type.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Silent Legacy Backend Drop in Emitter Wrapper
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that resolve a composite audit-log/new-emitter interface mismatch only by adding an emitter method that type-asserts each child and skips children that do not implement the new emitter interface, without also adapting or rejecting legacy-only audit backends reachable from the failing service configuration. This is especially severe when the trajectory has observed that some service-created audit destinations implement the legacy audit-log interface but not the new emitter interface.

metadata.environment: Go service with legacy audit-log interface and newer emitter interface
visible_evidence_to_check: Composite wrapper stores children typed as the legacy audit-log interface
Service startup later requires the composite or external log to satisfy the newer emitter interface
At least one reachable child/backend constructor appears legacy-only or was not verified as an emitter
Proposed implementation uses a conditional type assertion and does nothing for non-emitter children
No constructor-time validation, adapter, or service wiring change ensures all destinations receive new-format events
acceptable_alternatives: Validate all children as emitters when constructing the composite and return a clear error for any non-emitter
Introduce an adapter for legacy-only writer/stdout-style destinations so they implement the new emitter contract
Reuse an existing multi-emitter fan-out over a complete list of emitters while preserving legacy audit-log behavior for other methods

scale.1: No evidence of silent skipping: the trajectory verifies or ensures every configured child is an emitter, adapts legacy-only destinations, or fails clearly before constructing the composite.
scale.2: Minor concern only: the trajectory notes the non-emitter-child risk and appears to be checking concrete backends, but the final strategy is not yet fully visible.
scale.3: Equivalent/indeterminate: the trajectory adds or plans emitter compatibility but has not shown whether child backends can be skipped or whether all configured children implement the new interface.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory proposes or implements conditional forwarding to only children that satisfy the new emitter interface, with no visible handling for legacy-only children.
scale.5: Most severe flaw: the trajectory has visible evidence that a reachable configured backend is legacy-only, yet still implements the composite emitter by silently ignoring non-emitter children, making startup compatibility likely while dropping audit events for that destination.

experiences.title: Lifecycle-Aware Tracing Refactor Beyond OTLP Transport
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go/OpenTelemetry task asks for new OTLP HTTP/HTTPS export support and also explicitly requires tracing setup refactoring for modularity, shutdown, extensibility, or concurrency safety.
experiences.context: Applies to trajectories in a Go service where tracing exporter construction is currently embedded in server startup and the task combines transport support with lifecycle/refactor requirements. The criterion is most useful once the agent has inspected or edited the tracing initialization path, because visible evidence can show whether it is merely adding config/imports/switch cases or actually improving exporter/provider lifecycle. It is less relevant for tasks that only request adding a new exporter protocol, for codebases where tracing construction is already isolated and concurrency-safe, or at very early discovery stages before the agent has reached the tracing implementation; in those cases, use it as a progress signal rather than a final-completeness judgment.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric in these cases looked past superficial OTLP HTTP/HTTPS support and evaluated the architectural refactor promised by the task. The repeated failure mode was adding an HTTP exporter dependency, protocol/config fields, and inline switch branches inside the server startup code while leaving exporter creation tightly coupled, omitting a reusable construction abstraction, and failing to add explicit exporter shutdown or concurrency-safe initialization. A better rubric should ask whether the trajectory moves tracing exporter creation into a dedicated helper/factory, returns or registers lifecycle cleanup for created exporters in addition to provider shutdown, preserves existing exporters through the same path, and uses a concurrency guard or equivalent design if tracing resources are shared or initialized once. Do not substitute easier proxies such as successful builds, schema/config updates, new enum values, or use of the HTTP exporter package; those show transport progress but not the requested robustness. Prioritize visible evidence such as extracted exporter-construction logic, centralized protocol selection, shutdown callback registration tied to the server lifecycle, safe one-time initialization or locking, and reduced branching in the main server setup.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Modular and Safe Tracing Lifecycle
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluate whether the trajectory addresses the requested tracing refactor in addition to adding OTLP HTTP/HTTPS transport. Strong evidence includes isolating tracing exporter construction from the main server startup path, making protocol/exporter selection extensible, preserving existing Jaeger/Zipkin/OTLP gRPC behavior through the same abstraction, registering cleanup for any exporter/provider resources with the server shutdown mechanism, and using a concurrency-safe initialization pattern where tracing exporter/provider state is shared or cached. Weak evidence includes only adding config fields, dependency imports, or inline HTTP/HTTPS switch cases without improving lifecycle or coupling.

required_visible_evidence: Tracing exporter creation is extracted or centralized rather than expanded inline in server startup
The new OTLP HTTP/HTTPS path and existing exporters share a maintainable selection mechanism
Created tracing resources have explicit shutdown/cleanup registered with the server lifecycle
Initialization is safe under repeated or concurrent server construction when shared state is introduced
Existing tracing behavior remains compatible while adding the new protocol support
common_false_positives: Build passes after adding an HTTP exporter dependency
Configuration accepts a new protocol value but startup code remains tightly coupled
HTTP and HTTPS branches are added inline without lifecycle cleanup
Tests cover config loading but not tracing construction or shutdown behavior

scale.1: No visible progress on tracing refactoring; the trajectory is only exploring, broken, or unrelated to tracing lifecycle.
scale.2: Adds or plans OTLP HTTP/HTTPS support but keeps exporter creation inline and shows no meaningful shutdown or concurrency-safety improvements.
scale.3: Shows partial refactor intent, such as drafting a helper or identifying shutdown concerns, but the implementation remains incomplete, unvalidated, or does not clearly preserve existing exporters through the new path.
scale.4: Clearly centralizes exporter creation and preserves existing/new exporters, with visible cleanup handling, but has minor gaps in validation, extensibility, or concurrency-safety evidence.
scale.5: Fully addresses the lifecycle refactor: exporter creation is modular and extensible, existing and new protocols share the abstraction, exporter/provider cleanup is registered with server shutdown, and initialization is demonstrably safe for repeated or concurrent use.

experiences.title: Printer output contract beats test-only criteria
experiences.description: Use when a SymPy code-printer task asks for a specific rendered form for unsupported or fallback-rendered symbolic functions, especially when the trajectory has found the printer dispatch path and is implementing support.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/SymPy repository when the user request is about `pycode`/`PythonCodePrinter` rendering `Min` and `Max` as Python built-ins, and the visible trajectory shows the agent inspecting `sympy/printing`, finding the relevant printer class or known-function mapping, observing no direct Min/Max support, or seeing fallback `Piecewise`/ternary output. This is most useful once the trajectory has moved from exploration into implementation or validation. It is less applicable if the task is about NumPy/SciPy/C/C++ printers, if the desired output is intentionally a conditional/Piecewise expression, if the agent is only doing very early repository exploration, or if the current issue is primarily about adding project tests after an already correct implementation.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged whether the trajectory implemented the actual rendering contract: SymPy `Min` must print as Python `min(...)`, `Max` as `max(...)`, and each argument must be passed through the existing printer so nested expressions keep normal formatting. This aligned well because the decisive visible evidence was not merely that the agent ran a repro or added a test, but that it identified the Python printer dispatch mechanism and changed it so the user-facing `pycode` output becomes the requested built-in call rather than unsupported output or fallback ternary/Piecewise rendering. A better rubric should allow either idiomatic mechanism in this printer architecture, such as adding entries to the known-function mapping or defining direct `_print_Min`/`_print_Max` methods, as long as the observable result and recursive argument handling are correct. Avoid overprioritizing regression-test coverage as the main criterion for this cluster: tests are valuable, but several successful trajectories did not add formal tests, while the implementation contract was decisive. Also avoid overconstraining the exact insertion location or exact patch shape; focus on whether the change affects the plain Python code printer used by `pycode`, not unrelated printers or temporary scripts. Prioritize visible evidence such as grep results showing missing direct support, recognition of fallback rewrite behavior, edits to the plain Python printer or its known-function table, manual outputs like `min(a, b)`/`max(a, b)`, and use of `self._print`/existing printer machinery for all arguments.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement plain SymPy Python code-printer support for `Min` and `Max` so user-facing `pycode` renders them as Python built-ins `min(...)` and `max(...)`, respectively. The criterion should credit either a direct printer-dispatch method or an appropriate known-function mapping, provided the change applies to the plain Python printer used by `pycode`, handles all variadic arguments, and prints each argument through the existing printer machinery so nested expressions and function names retain normal formatting. It should not require a particular patch shape, nor should it treat fallback conditional/Piecewise output or edits only to unrelated printers as sufficient.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Plain Python printer Min/Max built-in rendering

important_evidence: agent identifies the plain Python code printer or known-function dispatch path
agent observes missing direct Min/Max handling or fallback conditional rendering
agent edits the dispatch/mapping used by pycode rather than only unrelated printers
agent preserves recursive printing of every argument
manual or formal checks show min(a, b) and max(a, b) style output
non_decisive_evidence: test-only activity before a printer change

scale.1: No visible progress toward changing the plain Python printer behavior for `Min` or `Max`; the trajectory only explores files, handles environment setup, or works on unrelated printer components.
scale.2: Some relevant investigation occurs, such as locating the printer or reproducing current output, but there is no clear implementation plan or edit that would make `pycode` emit Python built-in `min`/`max` calls.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies the correct printer path and proposes or begins a plausible implementation, but visible evidence is incomplete, only one of `Min`/`Max` is addressed, recursive argument printing is unclear, or the change may not affect the plain `pycode` API.
scale.4: The trajectory makes a clear implementation in the plain Python printer path for both `Min` and `Max`, using built-in names and existing argument printing, though validation may be limited or placement details may still need confirmation.
scale.5: The trajectory clearly implements both `Min` and `Max` for the plain `pycode` path, preserves variadic and recursive argument printing, avoids unrelated printer changes, and validates representative outputs such as symbolic, nested, or multi-argument cases.

experiences.title: Omitted Secondary Artwork Selection Requirement
experiences.description: Retrieve this when an artwork/media retrieval task explicitly includes both media-file embedded-art fallback behavior and deterministic album-image selection, and the trajectory is mostly implementing media-file dispatch while leaving album external-image ordering unexamined or unchanged.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go media-server-style codebase where artwork IDs or routes distinguish media-file artwork from album artwork, and album artwork is chosen from multiple external image files through an ordered list of candidate names/formats. The task text must explicitly require canonical album-image selection, such as preferring front-cover artwork and higher-quality formats, not merely embedded media-file cover extraction. This is most useful after the agent has inspected or edited the artwork retrieval path and there is visible evidence of the album fallback candidate order. It is less useful during very early exploration before the retrieval source order is visible, or in tasks whose only requirement is routing media-file artwork IDs with no multi-image album selection contract.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics in this cluster focused on canonical album image selection. That was useful because the trajectories repeatedly pursued the obvious media-file artwork bug but did not address a separate acceptance requirement: when album fallback has multiple image files, selection must be deterministic and prefer the canonical front image and better formats. Visible evidence included unchanged or copied album fallback lists that still searched generic names before front-cover names, plus tests that validated embedded-media-file retrieval but did not validate the multi-image album-selection contract. A better rubric should explicitly reward implementations that inspect and update the album fallback ordering wherever album artwork is selected, including fallback paths reached from media-file artwork, and that add or preserve tests for conflicting album images. Avoid the tempting proxy of judging only whether the agent branches on media-file artwork IDs or extracts embedded tags; those changes can pass local core tests while still failing the stated album-selection requirement. Prioritize observable evidence in the trajectory: the task’s explicit front/format priority clause, the ordered candidate list for external album artwork, whether fallback code reuses a single album-selection helper instead of duplicating stale order, and whether tests cover cases with multiple candidate images where the canonical front/high-quality choice should win.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should preserve the media-file embedded-art fix while also satisfying the explicit album fallback selection contract: when album artwork can be resolved from multiple external image candidates, the implementation should use a deterministic priority that selects canonical front-cover artwork ahead of less-specific names and prefers higher-quality formats such as PNG over JPEG/WebP when equivalent candidates exist. This criterion should be judged from visible trajectory evidence such as inspected source-order logic, edited candidate ordering or shared album-selection helper usage, and tests or reasoning that cover conflicting album image candidates in both direct album retrieval and media-file fallback paths.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Canonical Album Fallback Selection

required_visible_evidence: The task explicitly mentions canonical front-cover or format-priority selection among multiple album images.
The trajectory exposes ordered album-art candidate logic or fallback extraction order.
The trajectory is at an implementation or review stage where omissions in album fallback selection can be assessed.
do_not_substitute_with: Only checking that media-file artwork IDs are parsed or branched on.
Only checking that embedded tag extraction works.
Only relying on passing tests that do not include multiple competing album image candidates.

scale.1: No visible attention to the album multi-image ordering requirement; the trajectory only handles media-file artwork or leaves stale generic-before-front ordering unchanged.
scale.2: Mentions album fallback or image quality but provides no concrete ordering change or evidence that conflicting album image candidates are handled correctly.
scale.3: Maintains roughly equivalent behavior to the parent trajectory: some album fallback exists, but the canonical front/format-priority requirement is ambiguous, duplicated, or not validated.
scale.4: Clearly updates or centralizes album image selection so canonical front and higher-quality formats are preferred in at least the main album retrieval path, with some consideration of fallback reuse.
scale.5: Fully satisfies the album-selection contract across direct album retrieval and media-file fallback paths, avoids duplicated stale ordering, and includes or describes targeted validation with multiple competing album image candidates.

experiences.title: Alias-aware description-mode autodoc typehints
experiences.description: Use this when a Sphinx autodoc task reports that configured type aliases work in signatures but are expanded when type hints are moved into description/field-list output.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Sphinx autodoc codebase when the issue is specifically about `autodoc_type_aliases` being ignored under `autodoc_typehints='description'`, especially with postponed annotations or aliases that otherwise expand to `typing` expressions. It is most useful once the trajectory has found the split between normal signature rendering and description-mode annotation recording. It is less useful for unrelated typing stringification bugs, non-autodoc rendering paths, tasks about aliases in normal signatures only, or very early exploration before the agent has identified where description-mode type hints are collected.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful rubric judged whether the trajectory propagated the configured alias map into the description-mode typehint recording path, not merely whether aliases worked somewhere in autodoc. This aligned well because normal signature rendering already used alias-aware signature inspection, while description-mode output depended on a separate annotation-recording hook that was inspecting and stringifying annotations without the alias map. A strong rubric should therefore prioritize visible evidence that the agent compared the two flows, changed the description-mode annotation extraction to use the same alias-aware inspection configuration, and validated both parameter and return type descriptions render the alias rather than the expanded `Dict[...]`-style form. Do not reward fixes that only change global stringification helpers, only test non-description signature output, or rely on broad unrelated test failures/passes. Also avoid accepting manual-build claims unless the visible output or test assertions actually target the intended object and check alias-vs-expanded rendering. If a trajectory has convincing analysis but no persisted relevant code change yet, the criterion should score partial progress rather than full completion.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that Sphinx autodoc's description-mode typehint path records parameter and return annotations using the configured type-alias mapping before stringification, matching the behavior of normal signature rendering. Strong evidence includes identifying the separate description-mode annotation recording/merging flow, applying the alias configuration to the signature/annotation inspection step used by that flow, and validating that generated description fields show the configured alias for both arguments and return values instead of the underlying expanded typing expression. The criterion should not be satisfied by changes limited to normal signature rendering, broad typing formatter changes without config context, or tests that do not combine description-mode typehints with configured aliases.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Alias-Aware Description Typehint Recording

metadata.required_behavior: configured aliases are preserved when type hints are rendered in description fields
key_visible_evidence: separate normal-signature and description-mode typehint paths are recognized
description-mode annotation inspection receives the autodoc alias mapping
both parameter and return type descriptions are checked for alias output
expanded typing forms are treated as the regression symptom
common_false_positives: only verifying signature-mode alias rendering
changing generic typing stringification without passing configuration
manual output from an invalid or mis-targeted reproducer
unrelated file edits or broad test results that do not exercise the reported mode

scale.1: No visible evidence that the trajectory addresses alias handling in description-mode autodoc typehints; work is unrelated or focused only on generic typing/signature behavior.
scale.2: The trajectory notices aliases or description-mode typehints but has not identified the missing propagation point or proposes a vague/global formatting change.
scale.3: The trajectory identifies that the description-mode annotation recording path must use the alias configuration, but the implementation or validation is incomplete, unverified, or covers only parameters/signatures.
scale.4: The trajectory implements the minimal alias-propagation change in the description-mode recording flow and provides some targeted validation that aliases appear instead of expanded typing forms.
scale.5: The trajectory clearly implements the alias-aware description-mode recording behavior, validates both parameter and return type description output under combined `autodoc_typehints='description'` and alias configuration, and avoids unrelated changes or misleading test evidence.

experiences.title: Strict HTTP contracts when adding centralized fallback
experiences.description: Use this when a Go service task adds a centralized placeholder/fallback API but also explicitly requires HTTP artwork/image routes to keep not-found behavior for unavailable resources.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go web-service/codebase with a layered artwork/image service, reader/source implementations, and HTTP handlers. The task must visibly distinguish two contracts: a non-strict API that may return a placeholder and a strict retrieval path that must signal unavailable artwork. Retrieve this once the trajectory has identified or edited service callers/HTTP handlers, or when the agent plans which callers should use the fallback method. It is less useful during very early file discovery before any caller/API-boundary evidence exists, and it should not be applied as a blanket rule that every HTTP endpoint must avoid placeholders if the task or existing API contract clearly designates a particular endpoint as a placeholder-serving route.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics in this cluster focused on HTTP endpoint error handling. That was useful because the failures were not merely in adding a fallback method; they were visible in the agent treating fallback as a universal replacement for strict retrieval at HTTP boundaries. Observable bad evidence included changing image handlers to call a placeholder-returning method, adding type assertions to use fallback from handlers, deleting or bypassing not-found/unavailable branches, sending placeholder bytes where the requirement says to return 404, and even modifying tests to expect no endpoint error for missing artwork. A better rubric should evaluate whether the agent preserves the semantic boundary: readers should not own placeholder fallback, the central service may expose a fallback method, but HTTP routes that are supposed to report unavailable artwork must still receive/handle a strict unavailable error and respond with 404 plus the required debug-level logging before streaming a body. Avoid the tempting but overbroad criterion “all callers should use the new fallback method” or “all HTTP endpoints should use strict retrieval”; the useful check is caller-contract alignment. Prioritize visible evidence in planned or actual handler edits: which service method is invoked, whether unavailable/not-found errors remain distinguishable, whether fallback masks those errors, whether logging level/message matches the unavailable-artwork case, and whether tests/mocks are updated to preserve rather than erase the endpoint contract.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory preserves the strict HTTP not-found contract while introducing centralized placeholder fallback. Handler-level evidence should show that routes required to signal unavailable artwork do not blindly switch to the placeholder-returning API; instead they call a strict retrieval path or otherwise receive a distinguishable unavailable-artwork error, return a 404 response, and log the unavailable condition at the required debug level before writing image content. The fallback method may be used by callers whose contract is to display a placeholder, but it must not mask unavailability for strict HTTP routes.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Preserves strict HTTP unavailability behavior

applicability: task separates placeholder fallback from strict retrieval
trajectory has inspected or edited service callers/handlers
prioritize_visible_evidence: handler method calls to strict versus fallback retrieval APIs
presence of explicit unavailable/not-found error handling
404 response path before any image body is streamed
debug-level logging for unavailable artwork where required
tests or mocks that preserve endpoint error semantics rather than expecting placeholder success for unavailable artwork
common_failure_signals: HTTP handler switched wholesale to placeholder-returning method
not-found/unavailable branches removed or made unreachable
fallback method returns placeholders for all errors, including unknown errors
tests rewritten to accept placeholder responses from strict endpoints

scale.1: No evidence that HTTP unavailable-artwork behavior is preserved; fallback is likely applied universally or endpoint handling is not considered.
scale.2: A fallback API is added, but HTTP handlers appear to call it blindly or not-found/unavailable handling is removed, weakened, or untested.
scale.3: Some strict endpoint handling remains, but the boundary is incomplete: one route may mask unavailability, logging/status behavior is ambiguous, or errors are not clearly distinguishable.
scale.4: Most handler edits preserve strict retrieval and 404 behavior, with only minor uncertainty around logging level, exact unavailable error classification, or endpoint-specific fallback exceptions.
scale.5: Clear, consistent separation of contracts: centralized placeholder fallback exists for appropriate callers, strict HTTP routes retain distinguishable unavailable errors, return 404, debug-log the unavailable case, and tests/mocks reinforce that behavior.

experiences.title: Do not let semantic diagnosis substitute for an applied autodoc fix
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating Sphinx autodoc trajectories for an empty `__all__` bug, especially when the agent has identified the `None` versus empty-sequence distinction but may not yet have made or validated the relevant source change.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Sphinx `sphinx.ext.autodoc` tasks where the bug is caused by conflating a missing sentinel value with an explicitly empty container, such as treating `__all__ = []` like absent `__all__`. The semantic criterion that empty `__all__` should suppress automatic members is useful at implementation or final-review stages only if the trajectory shows a concrete change in the autodoc member-selection path and some direct validation. It is misleading at early exploration stages when the agent has merely inspected files, created a reproducer, or reasoned about `bool([])` without editing the repository. It is also insufficient if the visible trajectory drifts into unrelated Sphinx subsystems, dependency churn, or ad-hoc scripts that do not exercise the actual `automodule :members:` path.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster correctly named the desired contract: missing `__all__` should keep normal autodoc member discovery, an empty `__all__` should document no implicit members, and a non-empty `__all__` should filter to listed members. The misleading part was wording the rubric as if stating that contract or confirming `inspect.getall()` behavior were enough evidence of trajectory quality. For this kind of one-line sentinel bug, a better rubric should be stage-sensitive: before an edit, reward only localization of the exact branch and a plausible plan; after an edit, require visible evidence that the falsy check in the actual autodoc member-selection code was changed to a sentinel check and that validation covers empty, missing, and non-empty `__all__` through the autodoc pathway or existing test helpers. Avoid a tempting broad criterion like “understands Python `__all__` semantics” because it can score highly from commentary alone. Prioritize visible evidence from the repository diff, the specific code path used by `.. automodule::` with `:members:`, targeted autodoc tests or reliable doctree/build assertions, and absence of unrelated subsystem modifications.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for an empty-`__all__` autodoc task when they overclaim success from semantic reasoning alone or lack visible committable evidence in the actual autodoc member-selection path. This flaw is present when the agent identifies that empty containers are falsy, or even creates ad-hoc repro files, but has not applied a relevant repository change, has not verified the changed path with `automodule :members:` behavior or existing autodoc test helpers, or has drifted into unrelated Sphinx components. Do not apply this penalty merely because a focused regression test has not yet been added if the trajectory already shows the correct source edit and reliable targeted validation; in that case the original empty-versus-missing semantic rubric remains appropriate.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Semantic Diagnosis Without Autodoc Implementation Evidence

observable_evidence_to_prioritize: repository diff touches the autodoc module-member selection logic rather than unrelated builders/extensions
the condition distinguishes the absence sentinel from an explicit empty sequence
validation exercises `.. automodule::` with `:members:` or equivalent autodoc test helper behavior
checks include empty `__all__`, absent `__all__`, and preferably non-empty `__all__`
temporary repro or dependency-install work is not treated as proof unless tied to the actual changed code path
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: crediting comments, hypotheses, or direct `bool([])` demonstrations as if they prove the final autodoc behavior

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory shows a relevant source edit in autodoc member selection and credible validation of the empty-versus-missing behavior, with no unrelated patch drift.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the trajectory has the relevant edit but validation is mostly indirect, incomplete, or noisy while still tied to the autodoc path.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory correctly localizes the issue and proposes the sentinel change, but the visible cutoff lacks a confirmed repository edit or only uses simplified scripts rather than the actual autodoc behavior.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the trajectory mainly contains semantic reasoning, file inspection, or temporary repro setup and treats that as near-complete despite no demonstrated source change or reliable validation.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory is off-target, modifies or investigates unrelated Sphinx subsystems, or claims the empty-`__all__` issue is fixed without visible evidence in the autodoc member-selection path.

experiences.title: Delegating shadowed stream methods in IO wrappers
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python project bug involves a wrapper around stdout/stderr or another file-like stream where a method such as flush() is expected to reach the wrapped object, and the trajectory has evidence that inheritance from an IO base class may shadow __getattr__ delegation.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Django-like codebases at the diagnosis or implementation-review stage, especially when the reported behavior is delayed or missing progressive output despite explicit flush() calls. The key visible conditions are: command output is routed through a wrapper object; the wrapper stores an underlying stream and delegates missing attributes; the wrapper subclasses an IO base class that already defines flush(); and the affected command already calls flush() at the right user-visible point, such as after writing a partial progress line without a newline. This is less useful before the agent has inspected the wrapper/inheritance path, and it should not be applied to unrelated buffering problems where the command never calls flush(), the underlying stream itself is unflushable by design, or the fix belongs in command progress logic rather than the wrapper interface.
experiences.experience: The useful criterion in these cases focused on the semantic contract of the output wrapper: calling flush() on management command stdout/stderr must explicitly invoke the wrapped stream's flush(), because inherited IOBase/TextIOBase methods are found before __getattr__ and therefore do not delegate. This aligned well when the trajectory showed concrete evidence such as locating the wrapper class, observing no explicit flush() method, finding existing command-level flush() calls, inspecting the MRO or TextIOBase methods, and using a fake or buffered stream to prove the underlying flush was not called. A strong rubric should reward recognizing and fixing the wrapper-level delegation boundary while preserving existing write, ending, styling, and isatty behavior. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as merely checking that output appears in StringIO, adding extra flush calls inside the affected command, changing newline behavior, or treating hasattr(wrapper, 'flush') as proof of correctness. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent understands why __getattr__ is bypassed for inherited methods and that the intended patch is a narrow explicit delegating method on the wrapper, preferably guarded or otherwise compatible with wrapped streams that may not expose every stream method.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should identify that a file-like output wrapper's inherited IOBase/TextIOBase flush() shadows __getattr__ delegation, and should implement or plan a narrow wrapper-level flush() that calls the underlying stdout/stderr stream's flush() so progress text written without a newline is emitted immediately, while preserving existing write, ending, styling, and other stream behavior.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Explicit flush delegation for stream wrappers

required_visible_evidence: The trajectory locates the output wrapper used for command stdout/stderr or equivalent stream abstraction.
The trajectory observes that the affected command already calls flush() after partial progress output.
The trajectory explains that inherited IOBase/TextIOBase flush() prevents __getattr__ from delegating to the wrapped stream.
The proposed or applied change is an explicit flush() method on the wrapper that invokes the wrapped stream's flush().
The trajectory avoids modifying unrelated command progress formatting or write/style behavior.
strong_validation_evidence: A fake stream records that its flush() method is called through the wrapper.
A buffered file or similar real buffered target shows data becomes visible only after wrapper.flush().
The agent distinguishes meaningful flush-delegation tests from StringIO content visibility or terminal print observations.
common_false_proxies: hasattr(wrapper, 'flush') is treated as sufficient evidence.
StringIO.getvalue() before and after flush is treated as proof of delegation.
The agent adds more flush calls in the command even though existing calls are already present.
The patch changes newline, styling, or output formatting semantics.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory connects the buffering symptom to wrapper-level flush delegation; it focuses on unrelated output logic or only performs broad exploration.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory notices flush calls or the output wrapper but does not explain inherited-method shadowing or proposes an uncertain/generic buffering change.
scale.3: Moderate evidence equivalent to the parent: the trajectory has found the wrapper and affected flush calls and suspects delegation, but has not clearly shown why __getattr__ is bypassed or has not yet committed to a narrow wrapper-level fix.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory explicitly identifies inherited IOBase/TextIOBase flush() as shadowing delegation and proposes or applies an explicit wrapper.flush() calling the wrapped stream, with minimal risk to existing output behavior.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: in addition to the correct narrow delegating fix, the trajectory validates with an observable underlying flush call or buffered-stream behavior and explicitly avoids misleading tests or unrelated formatting changes.

experiences.title: Startup-Time .pak-Aware Locale Override
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating a qutebrowser/PyQt QtWebEngine task that adds a disabled workaround for a version-specific locale parsing failure involving Chromium locale .pak files.
experiences.context: Applies to Python/qutebrowser trajectories where the task requires a new `qt.workarounds.*` setting for QtWebEngine 5.15.3 locale failures on Linux, and the agent is choosing or implementing the workaround mechanism. It is most useful once the trajectory has moved beyond simple repository discovery into implementation planning, repeated searches, or code edits. It is less applicable to generic locale, HTTP Accept-Language, spellcheck-language, or documentation-only tasks, and it should not be used as a strict final-code criterion during very early exploration unless the visible trajectory is already stuck repeating unproductive searches or committing to a wrong mechanism.
experiences.experience: For this task family, the discriminating rubric should focus on whether the agent implements a startup-time Chromium/QtWebEngine locale override that is aware of installed locale `.pak` files. Earlier rubrics that only checked broad gating such as Linux + QtWebEngine 5.15.3 + setting enabled were too weak: several bad implementations had those guards but still changed the wrong thing. Likewise, a rubric that accepts generic environment changes, changing `LC_ALL`/`LANG`, setting a made-up QtWebEngine locale environment variable, or modifying `QWebEngineProfile.setHttpAcceptLanguage` misses the central bug: Chromium subprocess locale resource selection must be influenced before WebEngine startup. A better rubric should require visible evidence that the agent places logic in the QtWebEngine startup argument/environment assembly path, derives the current Qt/Chromium locale, locates the QtWebEngine locale resource directory, skips the workaround when the exact locale `.pak` already exists, maps unsupported regional locales to Chromium-compatible pak names, emits a `--lang`-style override only when needed, and logs/debug-continues when locale resources are unavailable. It should also require the new config setting to be disabled by default and scoped to the WebEngine backend. Avoid rewarding mere planning, repeated greps, config-only edits, or profile/header-language changes as substantial progress.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show that the locale workaround is implemented as a narrow, startup-time QtWebEngine/Chromium locale-resource override rather than as generic process locale or HTTP language changes. Strong evidence includes adding the disabled WebEngine-scoped config option, integrating helper logic where QtWebEngine startup arguments are assembled, checking the exact affected WebEngine version and Linux platform, inspecting the QtWebEngine locale `.pak` directory, skipping unchanged behavior when the current locale pak exists, mapping regional locale names to compatible Chromium pak names before emitting a language override, and logging/continuing if required locale resources are missing.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: QtWebEngine Locale Resource Override Correctness

prioritize_visible_evidence: startup argument or early initialization path for QtWebEngine/Chromium
exact QtWebEngine version and Linux guards
config flag guard
locale .pak path existence checks
Chromium-compatible locale name mapping
debug logging and continued startup when resources are missing
anti_evidence: only adding the config setting
only planning without implementation
changing HTTP Accept-Language or profile language APIs
overriding global LC_ALL or LANG
setting an unverified locale environment variable without .pak checks
unconditional locale override even when the current locale pak exists

scale.1: No meaningful implementation evidence, or the visible work is limited to repeated searches/config edits while the actual workaround mechanism is absent.
scale.2: Some relevant progress such as adding the setting or identifying startup files, but no credible startup-time locale-resource override is implemented.
scale.3: Implements or plans a guarded workaround for the right platform/version/setting, but the mechanism is incomplete or likely wrong, such as generic environment mutation, profile/header language changes, or no `.pak` availability logic.
scale.4: Shows a mostly correct startup-time QtWebEngine/Chromium language override with narrow guards and some locale resource checks, but misses an important edge case such as skipping when the current pak exists, robust fallback/logging, or Chromium-compatible regional locale mapping.
scale.5: Clearly implements the full `.pak`-aware startup override: disabled WebEngine-scoped setting, exact Linux/WebEngine-version/config guards, current-locale pak existence check, compatible pak-name mapping, conditional language override only when needed, and clear debug logging with continued operation on missing resources.

experiences.title: Do not treat an unused responsive-state hook as complete behavior
experiences.description: Retrieve when a TypeScript/React task asks for reactive window-width access through UI state and the trajectory mainly adds a generic hook or helper around an existing store event.
experiences.context: Applies in React codebases where a singleton UI state store already tracks window dimensions and emits resize events, and the agent proposes a new component-facing hook such as a window-width/window-dimensions API. This criterion is misleading when the visible trajectory stops at creating the helper, only tests the helper in isolation, or repeatedly validates import/export conventions without showing that any real component can or will use it. The original hook-focused idea may still be appropriate when the task is explicitly limited to adding a reusable API/library surface and no existing consumer behavior is implicated; in that narrower case, initialization from the store and resize subscription are central.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics praised trajectories for exposing `UIStore` window width reactively via a hook and subscribing to resize events. That is a useful implementation detail, but it over-credits patches that add an unused helper while leaving the user-visible responsive behavior unchanged. For tasks framed as enabling components to react to window width, a better rubric should look for evidence that the new API is actually consumable in the relevant UI path: a component imports it or otherwise subscribes through the new access layer, width-dependent rendering is updated at the intended responsive breakpoint, and validation covers the component behavior after resizing. Avoid the tempting criterion that a standalone hook with `useEventEmitterState` is sufficient by itself. Prioritize visible evidence of end-to-end integration, discoverable import/API shape, cleanup-safe subscription logic, and a focused test or scenario demonstrating that a component rerenders or changes behavior when UI-store width changes.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Unused reactive-width helper without component integration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for a responsive UI-state task when they only add or discuss a standalone window-width/window-dimensions hook around an existing UI store resize event, but provide no visible evidence that the affected component path imports the API, uses it to drive width-dependent rendering, or verifies the resize-driven behavior. This flaw is most relevant when the task motivation is that components cannot react correctly, not merely that a utility function is missing.

metadata.environment: TypeScript React application with singleton EventEmitter-style UI state store and hooks directory
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: existence of a hook that reads UIStore windowWidth and subscribes to a resize event
replacement_evidence: a real component or documented consumer uses the new API
the width value affects the intended responsive rendering condition
resize/update behavior is covered by a component-level or end-to-end test
the API remains importable/discoverable according to project conventions
metadata.boundary: If the issue explicitly asks only for a reusable API and names no consumer behavior, the absence of a component import is a weaker concern; then judge hook correctness, cleanup, and accessibility of the API instead.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory either integrates the width API into the relevant responsive UI behavior or clearly establishes that only a standalone reusable API is required and validates it appropriately.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory adds a correct-looking API and mentions likely consumers or import conventions, but component integration or behavior validation is still pending at the cutoff.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory implements a reactive hook and perhaps isolated tests, but does not show any real component consuming it or any user-visible resize behavior changing.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory focuses almost entirely on hook creation/typechecking while ignoring visible existing components or responsive behavior that should use the width value.
