scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory either produces no effective patch or repeatedly loops on exploration/validation, and the only proposed solution is an unused helper with no path to the component behavior the task is meant to enable.

experiences.title: Do not treat escape-only or broad regex parsing as sufficient for regex CSV options
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Python/Pylint-style config option is both comma-separated and regex-valued, and the reported failure is a valid regex quantifier such as `{1,3}` being split before compilation.
experiences.context: This applies in Pylint-like configuration parsing where an option is declared as a comma-separated list of regular expressions and the traceback shows the generic CSV splitter feeding fragments into regex compilation. The misleading case is generating a rubric that rewards any escaping/quoting mechanism, alternative delimiter, or full regex nesting parser as the main success signal. That can accept fixes that leave the reported unescaped quantifier example broken, change semantics for ordinary comma-separated regex lists, or modify broad CSV/path parsing without proving the actual option path is fixed. Escaping or full delimiter-aware parsing may be appropriate when the task explicitly asks for a new escaped syntax for all CSV options, documents that users must escape literal commas, or provides examples of literal commas outside regex quantifiers; otherwise the key contract is direct preservation of commas that are part of regex quantifier syntax while retaining existing list splitting.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics in this cluster said the fix must provide comma escaping/quoting or parse regex syntax including braces, brackets, groups, and escaped characters. The useful idea was preserving regex commas while keeping comma-separated lists, but the criterion was too broad and sometimes implementation-biased. It over-rewarded trajectories that only experimented with temporary scripts, changed generic CSV splitting, added escape-only behavior, or built complex parenthesis/bracket parsers without demonstrating that the actual regexp-list configuration transformer accepts the reported unescaped `{m,n}` pattern. A better rubric should focus on visible evidence that the solution is wired into the real regex-list option parsing path, keeps list/tuple inputs and normal `foo,bar`-style multiple regex values working, preserves commas inside brace quantifiers without requiring users to rewrite the reported config, and maintains invalid-regex error behavior. Avoid the tempting criterion “supports escaping commas” as sufficient unless the trajectory also shows the original unescaped valid regex is accepted or the task explicitly narrows acceptance to a documented escape mechanism.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a comma-separated regex configuration option whose reported reproducer is an unescaped quantifier comma, penalize trajectories that treat escape-only support, broad generic CSV changes, or ad hoc regex-syntax parsing as sufficient without visible proof that the actual regexp-list option path preserves commas inside brace quantifiers directly and still separates ordinary multiple regex values. This flaw is especially important when the agent edits unrelated CSV/path parsing, changes existing tests to fit the new behavior, or validates only helper scripts rather than the config transformer or option-level behavior.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Insufficient or overbroad regex CSV fix

required_visible_evidence: the real regex-list configuration transformer or option path is identified and updated
an unescaped regex quantifier containing a comma is accepted as one regex
ordinary comma-separated multiple regex patterns are still split
invalid regex fragments still surface a clear configuration error
misleading_proxies_to_avoid: escape-only comma support as the sole success signal
temporary helper-script outputs without integration evidence
broad changes to all CSV options or regex-path options without justification
parsing all parentheses/brackets/groups as list-protecting syntax without compatibility checks

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory targets the actual regex-list config path and visibly preserves unescaped quantifier commas while retaining normal list splitting and error handling.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the approach is mostly targeted but has incomplete visible validation, such as testing the helper but not the option path, while still addressing unescaped quantifier commas.
scale.3: Moderate evidence of the flaw: the trajectory recognizes the root cause but relies on broad or partially integrated parsing changes, with unclear preservation of existing comma-separated regex behavior.
scale.4: Clear evidence of the flaw: the solution emphasizes escaping, quoting, or broad regex nesting behavior and lacks proof that the reported unescaped quantifier case works through the real config option.
scale.5: Severe evidence of the flaw: the trajectory leaves the reported unescaped valid regex unsupported, changes generic CSV semantics or tests to accommodate the workaround, and validates only unrelated or temporary code.

experiences.title: Do not equate DTO int32 edits with a complete Go type migration
experiences.description: Retrieve when generating rubrics for Go API schema fixes that change exported response DTO integer fields from `int` to `int32`, especially when the trajectory has only inspected or edited the response struct file.
experiences.context: This applies in Go repositories where XML/JSON response structs define an external API schema and are populated from internal model or handler code using platform-native `int` values. The necessary response-struct type change is a good rubric component, but it is misleading as a standalone success criterion once edits have begun, because Go does not implicitly assign `int` values into `int32` fields. The original coverage criterion remains appropriate during inventory/planning or as one subcondition of a final-review rubric, but it should not be used to infer correctness when the trajectory has not shown compile-safe updates at all response construction boundaries, has visible build errors, or incorrectly claims the compiler will convert automatically.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics rewarded broad statements such as "all Subsonic response integer fields must use int32" or "identify every affected response type." Those criteria were directionally correct but too coarse: they overvalued trajectories that changed only the DTO declarations, grepped for no remaining `int` in the response file, or listed the affected structs, while leaving downstream assignments from `int` model fields unresolved. In Go, a correct schema migration must preserve internal/domain types unless intentionally in scope, convert values explicitly at the API response boundary, and validate with a package build or tests that include the handlers constructing the responses. Avoid a tempting rubric that treats response-file grep results, response-package-only tests, or exhaustive type inventory as sufficient evidence. A better rubric should prioritize visible evidence that the agent: (1) changed the externally serialized response fields to `int32` while preserving wider semantic types such as timestamps/sizes, (2) followed compiler errors or searched constructor sites to add explicit `int32(...)` conversions in handlers/helpers/builders, (3) avoided unnecessary migration of internal error codes, constants, model structs, or unrelated tests merely to chase types, and (4) ran a build/test target broad enough to cover the response package plus its population sites. If the cutoff is still early exploration with no edits, phrase the rubric as a planning/progress criterion rather than a final correctness requirement.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat changing API response struct fields from `int` to `int32` as complete without addressing the Go assignment fallout at response-construction boundaries. This flaw is present when the visible trajectory has edited or claims completion of DTO type changes but lacks explicit conversions from internal `int` sources, ignores or leaves compiler errors about assigning `int` to `int32`, validates only the isolated DTO package while handlers/builders remain uncompiled, or unnecessarily changes internal model/helper/error-code types instead of casting when populating the response. Do not apply this as a severe flaw to pure discovery-stage trajectories that have not yet made type edits and are still mapping the affected structs.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Incomplete compile-safe response-boundary migration

metadata.environment: Go API server with XML/JSON response DTOs populated from internal model/handler code
metadata.trigger_stage: after response DTO integer field types have been edited or the agent claims the migration is complete
key_visible_evidence: DTO fields changed from int to int32
assignments or struct literals populate those fields from int-valued model/helper variables
compiler errors or lack of broad build/test coverage
claims that Go will automatically convert int to int32
unnecessary changes to internal-only types instead of response-boundary casts
metadata.boundary: Do not penalize early inventory-only work for not yet adding conversions; do not require changing internal domain model types unless the task explicitly scopes them as serialized API DTOs.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory either remains in justified exploration, or it edits DTOs and also shows response-boundary conversions plus build/test coverage broad enough to include constructors.
scale.2: Minor evidence: DTO changes are made and some conversion sites are addressed, but validation scope is only partially shown or a small number of likely constructor sites remain unchecked.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory correctly identifies/edits many response fields but relies mainly on response-file grep or response-package tests, with incomplete visible handling of downstream assignments.
scale.4: Clear evidence: compile errors or obvious constructor assignments from `int` sources are visible and only partially fixed, or the agent claims completion before running a relevant package build.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory changes only the DTO declarations or overbroad internal types, explicitly assumes implicit `int` to `int32` conversion, ignores visible build failures, and presents the migration as complete.

experiences.title: Iterator Contract for Paginator-Like Containers
experiences.description: Use when a Python task explicitly asks to make a container/paginator object iterable by adding `__iter__`, and the visible trajectory has identified the target class plus existing page-range and page-construction APIs.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/Django-style codebase when the problem statement is narrow: implement normal iteration over an existing paginator-like class. The trajectory should show evidence such as locating the class, inspecting the existing `page_range`/range API and `page()`/page-construction method, or testing that direct iteration currently fails while manual iteration through page numbers works. This criterion is most useful once the agent is at implementation or review stage; it may be premature during pure repository exploration before the target class and existing APIs are visible. It is less applicable if the task asks for a broader redesign of pagination, iteration over raw objects rather than pages, async iteration, custom sequence behavior, or changes to page numbering/validation semantics.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the actual semantic contract: `__iter__` must be added to the paginator class and each fresh iteration must yield the existing `Page` objects produced by calling the existing page-construction method for every number in the existing page-range property. This aligned well because the task itself supplied the intended implementation and the trajectory exposed decisive evidence: manual loops over `page_range` plus `page()` worked, direct iteration failed before the change, and successful edits inserted a generator method without changing surrounding pagination behavior. A better rubric should judge whether the implementation preserves existing pagination semantics, including empty paginator, orphan handling, single-page cases, and repeated iteration, by delegating to `page_range` and `page()` rather than reimplementing slicing or validation. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as requiring a particular insertion line, docstring wording, full test-suite execution, adding new tests, comparing `Page` objects by equality, or merely checking that some `__iter__` method exists. Also avoid rewarding implementations that return page numbers, raw object lists, a one-time stored iterator, or modify `page_range`/`page()` to make tests pass.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement the Python iterator protocol on the paginator-like class by adding `__iter__` as a fresh generator that loops over the existing page-number range and yields the existing page object for each page number, while leaving existing page-count, range, validation, orphan, and empty-page behavior unchanged.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Paginator Iterator Delegates to Existing Page Semantics

required_visible_evidence: The target class has been identified as the paginator-like class requested by the task.
The class already exposes an existing page-number range API and an existing method that constructs/returns page objects.
The proposed or applied implementation adds `__iter__` to that class, not to the page class or an unrelated helper.
`__iter__` iterates over the existing page-number range and yields the result of the existing page-construction method for each number.
The trajectory does not show semantic changes to page numbering, validation, slicing, orphan handling, or empty-page behavior.
anti_patterns: Yielding raw items, object-list slices, or page numbers instead of page objects.
Returning a list rather than providing a normal reusable iteration protocol.
Using a stored one-shot iterator that would break repeated iteration.
Reimplementing pagination calculations inside `__iter__` instead of delegating to existing APIs.
Changing existing `page_range`, `page()`, validation, or page-count behavior to support iteration.
metadata.stage_notes: Before any implementation is visible, judge mostly on whether the agent has identified the correct contract and target APIs. After an edit is visible, prioritize the actual method body and absence of collateral semantic changes over test-run completeness.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory is implementing the requested iterator contract, or it targets the wrong class/API.
scale.2: Some recognition that the paginator should be iterable, but the visible plan or code is incomplete, ambiguous, or likely to yield the wrong type of value.
scale.3: The trajectory is approximately on track relative to the parent state, but the implementation evidence is partial or does not yet clearly prove delegation to the existing page-range and page-construction APIs.
scale.4: Clear evidence of an added `__iter__` on the correct class that loops through the existing page range and yields pages, with little sign of collateral behavior changes.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the correct generator-style `__iter__` is visible, it delegates exactly to the existing page-range and page-construction behavior, repeated/edge-case iteration is considered or tested, and no unrelated pagination semantics are changed.

experiences.title: End-to-End MARC 041$a Language Import
experiences.description: Retrieve when evaluating an Open Library MARC parsing trajectory for a task about importing all languages from 041$a, including obsolete concatenated 3-letter codes and interaction with 008 language fallback.
experiences.context: Applies in the Python Open Library MARC parser environment when the task and trajectory visibly involve MARC 041 language fields, 008 fixed-field language handling, field materialization through a wanted-tag list, and fixtures showing values such as concatenated 3-character language codes. It is most useful after the agent has inspected or modified the language reader and the main edition-building path, because the discriminating evidence is whether the full importer can see 041 and use it despite 008. It is less useful for early repository exploration with no parser evidence, for unrelated language-code normalization tasks, or for tasks that explicitly ask to import every MARC21 041 subfield rather than the 041$a text-language behavior described here.
experiences.experience: For this cluster, the useful rubric is not merely 'split concatenated codes.' A strong criterion should require the whole 041$a import path to work: the 041 tag must be included in the set of fields built for normal edition parsing; the 041$a reader must split obsolete concatenated values into ordered 3-character codes, map/filter them consistently with existing language handling, and reject or avoid malformed/non-language values; and the edition builder must consult 041$a even when 008 already supplies a single language, while still preserving a sane 008 fallback when 041$a is absent. Rubrics that focused on this full path aligned with visible success evidence such as direct 041 inspection showing raw concatenated values, `get_fields('041')` being empty after the normal build because the tag was omitted, and full `read_edition` checks changing from single 008 languages to all 041$a languages. Avoid the tempting but overbroad proxy criterion that the fix should import all possible 041 subfields such as original-language subfields, or blindly merge every 008 and 041 code; the task evidence is specifically about 041$a language(s) of the item, and over-expanding to other subfields can create extra languages not requested. Also avoid trusting stale fixture tests that still expect one language; prioritize visible manual validation of the full binary/XML edition output for the named records over helper-only tests.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete 041$a Import Pipeline
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate an end-to-end fix for MARC 041$a language import: the normal edition parser must materialize the 041 tag before helper readers run; the language reader must process all relevant 041$a values, including repeated values and obsolete concatenated strings made of consecutive 3-character MARC language codes, preserving order while applying existing language-code mapping and filtering non-linguistic codes; and the edition-building logic must use 041$a languages even when 008 contains only a single language, while retaining 008 as a fallback when 041$a has no usable languages. Evidence should come from full importer behavior on the provided binary/XML examples, not only direct helper output or passing stale fixture expectations.

required_visible_evidence: 041 is included in the field materialization path used by the main edition parser
041$a concatenated examples are split into ordered 3-character language codes
existing language normalization and zxx/non-language filtering are preserved
the full edition parser returns all 041$a languages for records whose 008 has only one language
008 still supplies a language when 041$a is absent or unusable
avoid_overbroad_evidence: importing original-language or other non-$a 041 subfields without task support
validating only the helper function while the main parser cannot see 041
treating unchanged legacy fixture expectations as proof of correctness

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that 041$a is parsed or used by the main edition importer.
scale.2: Only partial helper-level parsing is attempted, such as splitting concatenated values, but the main edition parser still cannot see or use 041$a reliably.
scale.3: Some parent-equivalent progress: 041$a parsing or field inclusion is addressed, but the trajectory has not shown the full interaction with 008 and normal edition output.
scale.4: Strong evidence that 041 is materialized, concatenated 041$a values are split and normalized, and full edition output includes multiple 041$a languages for key examples, with minor uncertainty around edge cases.
scale.5: Complete evidence of the full pipeline: 041 is built, 041$a values are parsed robustly and narrowly, 008 fallback/precedence is handled correctly, and binary/XML full-edition validations demonstrate the expected multi-language results without importing unrelated 041 subfields.

experiences.title: Literal Wildcard Escaping in Author Lookup Queries
experiences.description: Retrieve when an author-import or catalog-matching task explicitly mentions names containing asterisks/special characters and the trajectory has reached the search-query construction or matching-normalization code.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python catalog/import codebase where author lookup builds fuzzy search query dictionaries using operators such as `name~`, `alternate_names~`, or surname fallback patterns, and user-provided author names may contain `*`. It is most useful once the trajectory has inspected the lookup routine, backend/mock search semantics, or existing tests showing wildcard behavior. It is not sufficient as the only rubric when the same task also requires year-based birth/death-date lookup or honorific edge-case fixes; in those cases generate additional criteria. It may be premature during broad code discovery before the agent has found where author search queries are built. It should not be generalized to broad punctuation stripping in unrelated title/book normalization paths unless the trajectory shows those paths are part of author lookup.
experiences.experience: The useful rubric pattern is to check whether the agent treats an asterisk in an imported author name as literal input when constructing author-search queries. In these cases, a visible decisive cue was whether the trajectory identified that fuzzy search operators interpret `*` as a wildcard and then escaped input-derived asterisks in all relevant author-name query fields, including exact-name, alternate-name, and surname fallback searches. A better rubric should focus on query-boundary behavior: user-supplied special characters must not silently broaden matches, while any wildcard syntax deliberately inserted by the lookup routine itself may remain intentional. Avoid tempting but weaker criteria such as merely saying “handle special characters,” adding generic regex escaping without understanding the backend query language, preserving legacy user-supplied wildcard behavior without reconciling it with the task, or stripping asterisks in shared normalization used by unrelated matching features. Also avoid overvaluing ad hoc scripts or passing existing tests when no regression test or query evidence demonstrates literal-asterisk behavior. Prioritize visible evidence such as inspection of the lookup query dictionaries, understanding of the `~` operator/mock search wildcard semantics, changes applied at the author-search input boundary, and tests or mocks showing that names containing `*` neither match unintended authors nor fail to find literal-name records.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should ensure that special characters supplied as part of an author name, especially `*`, are handled safely at the author lookup query boundary. Strong evidence includes identifying that fuzzy author search treats `*` as wildcard syntax, escaping or otherwise literalizing input-derived asterisks before using the name in exact-name, alternate-name, and surname-based lookup queries, and preserving only wildcard syntax that the lookup algorithm intentionally adds itself. The trajectory should validate this with targeted tests or mock-query observations demonstrating that an author name containing `*` does not broaden to unrelated authors and can still participate in normal author matching.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Literal Input Wildcards in Author Lookup

evidence_to_prioritize: The trajectory inspects the author lookup query construction rather than only generic name normalization.
It recognizes that the fuzzy search operator interprets asterisks as wildcards.
It applies escaping or literal handling to user-provided author-name values used in all relevant author-search query fields.
It keeps algorithm-added wildcard patterns distinct from user-supplied literal characters.
It adds or runs targeted validation for literal asterisk behavior in author lookup.
common_false_proxies: Only changing broad normalization shared with unrelated matching paths.
Escaping with a generic regex/SQL helper without matching the repository search semantics.
Checking only the surname fallback query while leaving exact-name or alternate-name queries unsafe.
Relying solely on existing tests that exercise wildcard compatibility rather than literal-character safety.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory addresses literal asterisks or wildcard interpretation in author lookup queries.
scale.2: Mentions special characters or asterisks but only investigates them superficially, or changes an unrelated normalization path without showing author-search query safety.
scale.3: Equivalent parent-child behavior: recognizes that asterisks can affect author search and begins a plausible fix, but coverage is partial, backend semantics are uncertain, or validation does not prove literal-name behavior.
scale.4: Strong evidence that input-derived asterisks are escaped or literalized in the main author lookup queries, with some validation, though one secondary lookup path or compatibility boundary may remain under-specified.
scale.5: Complete evidence that the trajectory handles literal asterisks consistently across exact-name, alternate-name, and surname-based author lookup paths, distinguishes user input from intentional search wildcards, and validates both non-broadening and successful literal-name matching.

experiences.title: Assumption-preserving proxy symbol replacement
experiences.description: Use when a symbolic-math task reports that replacing symbols with dummy/proxy symbols loses assumptions such as finiteness, integrality, or rationality.
experiences.context: Applies in a Python/SymPy-like environment where a function intentionally replaces symbols whose positivity/sign is unknown with positive dummy symbols, and the visible trajectory has already connected the bug to the dummy construction dropping source assumptions. It is most useful once the agent has reproduced the assumption loss or is editing the replacement construction. It is less useful for unrelated simplification behavior, for tasks not involving symbol/proxy construction, or at a very early stage where the agent has not yet identified whether assumptions are actually lost during replacement versus inferred elsewhere.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases judged whether the trajectory preserved semantic assumptions when constructing replacement symbols, not merely whether the agent touched the right file or ran existing tests. The recurring decisive evidence was: the agent reproduced that a finite symbol becomes a positive dummy with unknown finiteness; located the replacement creation that used only a positivity assumption; changed replacement construction so the new dummy receives the original symbol's compatible assumptions while still being positive; and checked that existing mapping/replacement behavior remains intact. A better rubric should explicitly reward preserving constructor-level assumptions such as finite, integer, rational, prime, even, and odd for symbols that are actually replaced, while avoiding contradictory or duplicate sign-related assumptions when forcing positivity. Prefer evidence that the agent understands the boundary: symbols already known positive or non-positive should not be incorrectly replaced, and expression/iterable cases should preserve the assumptions of the generated replacement symbols. Avoid a tempting but weaker criterion that only asks for `finite=True` in one smoke test, or that rewards an arbitrary whitelist without checking conflict handling and existing `posify` semantics.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a semantically correct fix for symbol replacement that creates positive dummy/proxy symbols while preserving the original symbol's compatible assumptions, especially finiteness, and should validate that the change does not break replacement mappings or the rule that only symbols with unknown positivity are replaced.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Preserve compatible assumptions during positive dummy replacement

metadata.target_behavior: replacement symbols retain compatible assumptions from the original symbol while gaining positive=True
key_evidence: reproduces or references the finite-assumption loss
identifies dummy/proxy construction with only positive=True as the assumption-loss point
passes original compatible assumptions into the replacement constructor or otherwise preserves them robustly
avoids duplicate or contradictory positivity/sign assumptions
checks direct symbol replacement and at least one broader expression or iterable/mapping behavior
important_boundaries: symbols already known positive or known non-positive should keep existing behavior
compound expression assumptions should not be confused with assumptions of the generated replacement symbols
existing tests passing alone is insufficient without assumption-specific validation

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory preserves assumptions during replacement; it may only locate the function or run unrelated tests.
scale.2: Some evidence of the issue or target location, but the proposed direction still creates replacements with only positivity or lacks a concrete preservation mechanism.
scale.3: Moderate progress: identifies the replacement constructor and attempts to carry assumptions, but validation or conflict-boundary reasoning is incomplete.
scale.4: Strong progress: implements or clearly plans preservation of finite and related assumptions while forcing positivity, with checks for direct symbols and existing replacement behavior.
scale.5: Excellent progress: robustly preserves compatible original assumptions for replaced symbols, handles positivity/sign conflicts or duplicate assumption keys, maintains mapping and non-replacement semantics, and validates finite plus related assumptions across direct and expression/iterable cases.

experiences.title: Minimal distro dispatch wiring for ViaHTTP support
experiences.description: Retrieve when a Go scanning task says a distro is skipped in ViaHTTP/server-mode scans and the trajectory has found an existing distro scanner plus a family-dispatch switch.
experiences.context: Applies in a Go codebase with distro-specific scanner types and a ViaHTTP-like entry point that chooses an OS implementation from request/header family metadata. It is most useful once the trajectory has located the dispatch logic, the distro family constant, and evidence that the target distro can reuse an existing RedHat-like/base scanner path. It is also useful during final review if the agent is editing the dispatch file. It should not be the only criterion for multi-part tasks that also require unrelated renames, typo fixes, comments, or test updates. It is premature if the agent is still doing broad repository exploration and has not found the dispatch switch. It is the wrong focus if the agent is only changing OVAL/report/package-version comparison code while the user complaint is that HTTP scans are skipped before a scanner is selected.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics that simply asked for Oracle Linux ViaHTTP support captured an important requirement, but they were too broad when they did not distinguish the actual scan dispatch point from other HTTP/OVAL paths. The useful signal is not merely seeing the target distro name added somewhere in OVAL or version-comparison logic; it is seeing the agent minimally extend the existing ViaHTTP family switch so the target distro instantiates the already-existing compatible scanner/base implementation. A stronger rubric should also penalize destructive edits, such as rewriting a large server API file, removing existing functions/comments, or leaving malformed switch cases after sed replacements. Avoid rewarding broad mechanical additions of the distro constant to every RedHat-related case, because some branches have different semantics and the task’s skipped-scan symptom is specifically solved by dispatch wiring. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent found the family constant, found the existing target scanner type, followed the established CentOS/Amazon/RedHat-style construction, preserved all existing cases and behavior, and verified the file was not malformed.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Minimal compatible ViaHTTP distro dispatch
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should solve the missing distro support by minimally extending the ViaHTTP/server-mode OS-family dispatch to recognize the target distro family and instantiate the existing compatible scanner implementation using the same base pattern as analogous supported distros, while preserving the rest of the dispatch function and surrounding server API behavior. Strong evidence includes locating the dispatch switch, confirming the target family constant exists, confirming an existing scanner type/base exists, adding only the necessary dispatch branch, and avoiding unrelated or destructive rewrites. Do not give high credit for changes confined to OVAL/report HTTP fetching or package version comparison if the visible skipped-scan path still lacks distro dispatch.

required_visible_evidence: The trajectory identifies the ViaHTTP/server-mode function that switches on OS family metadata.
The trajectory identifies the target distro family constant and an existing scanner implementation or compatible base path.
The proposed/edit diff adds the target distro to that dispatch path using the established construction pattern for similar distros.
Existing dispatch cases and unrelated server API functions are preserved.
common_false_positives: Only adding the distro to OVAL affected-package/version-comparison logic.
Broad sed replacements that duplicate the distro in unrelated switch cases.
Rewriting or truncating the server API file while adding the branch.
Claiming support based only on finding the distro scanner without wiring it into ViaHTTP dispatch.

scale.1: No evidence that the agent found or modified the ViaHTTP/server-mode dispatch; changes, if any, are in unrelated OVAL/report/version-comparison paths or the trajectory is still broad exploration.
scale.2: The agent has identified the missing distro and perhaps the family constant or existing scanner, but has not yet connected it to the ViaHTTP dispatch or is pursuing an ambiguous/wrong path.
scale.3: The agent has located the correct dispatch area and intends to add the target distro, but the visible implementation is incomplete, unverified, or mixed with risky broad edits.
scale.4: The agent adds the target distro to the correct dispatch switch using the established compatible scanner/base pattern, with only minor uncertainty about formatting or validation.
scale.5: The agent cleanly and minimally wires the target distro into ViaHTTP dispatch, preserves all existing behavior, avoids unrelated switch-case pollution, and validates or clearly inspects the resulting code.

experiences.title: Do not credit default-blind deprecation checks as explicit-key handling
experiences.description: Retrieve for Go/Viper configuration tasks where warnings must be separated from config data and deprecated options should warn only when explicitly present, especially when the option also has defaults.
experiences.context: This applies when a trajectory is working in a Go configuration loader using Viper, defaults, env binding, and a deprecator-style warning mechanism. The misleading pattern is a rubric that rewards general understanding of the existing deprecation mechanism, adding a deprecator method, or returning a warnings slice, while not distinguishing explicit user-provided keys from values introduced by defaults. It is especially risky when the deprecated option is defaulted by the loader, because checks against the post-default Viper state can report false presence. The original idea remains appropriate when the trajectory has not yet reached implementation and the rubric is only about exploratory knowledge, or when the implementation demonstrably checks raw config/source presence before defaults and validates both present and absent cases.
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics often said the trajectory should understand the deprecation pattern, separate warnings from Config, or ensure ui.enabled warns only when explicitly present. Those criteria were too broad or used the wrong proxy: a trajectory can inspect the right files and add a deprecator while still using Viper state that includes defaults, such as IsSet/GetBool/AllKeys after defaults, causing warnings for keys that users did not configure. A better rubric should focus on source-aware explicitness and validation evidence: whether deprecation detection runs before defaults or consults raw config-file presence, whether absent/default-only configs are tested to produce no warning, whether explicit configs produce one warning, and whether refactoring warnings out of config data does not leave compatibility-breaking compile/test failures. Avoid generating criteria that name `viper.IsSet()` as sufficient in a defaulted-key context, or that gives high confidence for mere exploration of deprecations.go/Config.Warnings without evidence of correct default-boundary handling.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Default-derived deprecation false positives
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for configuration deprecation refactors when they implement or endorse deprecated-key detection using post-default/post-unmarshal configuration state rather than explicit source presence, or when they lack validation that absent/default-only configurations do not emit the new warning. This flaw is present if the agent relies on Viper APIs or loaded config values that include defaults for an option that itself has a default, collects deprecations only after defaults have been applied, or updates tests to ignore warnings instead of asserting the explicit-present versus absent/default-only behavior.

metadata.environment: Go configuration loader using Viper defaults and a deprecator warning pattern
metadata.risk_condition: deprecated option also has a default value or can be set by defaults/env binding
misleading_evidence: uses viper.IsSet/GetBool or all loaded settings without proving defaults are excluded
collects deprecations after running setDefaults for the deprecated key
manual test only covers explicit key present, not key absent
test updates remove or ignore warning assertions
preferred_evidence: checks raw config-file/source presence before defaults or uses an API proven to mean in-file presence
has tests for explicit deprecated key present and key absent/default-only
warnings are returned/handled separately from config data without leaving Config warning fields as the primary contract
updated callers and tests compile under the new load contract

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory explicitly distinguishes user-supplied keys from defaults and validates both warning and no-warning cases.
scale.2: Minor risk only: the trajectory states the explicitness requirement but has not yet implemented enough code to reveal whether defaults will contaminate detection.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory separates warnings or adds a deprecator, but validation of absent/default-only configs is missing or ambiguous.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory uses post-default Viper/config state as the presence check for a defaulted deprecated key, or tests show warnings for absent/default-only configs.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory doubles down on default-blind detection, rewrites tests to avoid checking warnings, or introduces compile/interface breakage while attempting to track explicit keys.

experiences.title: Expression-local EmptyResultSet handling for negated EXISTS
experiences.description: Use when a Django ORM task/trajectory involves an `Exists` subquery built from an empty queryset whose `EmptyResultSet` escapes and incorrectly affects the outer query, especially under `~Exists(...)` combined with other filters.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django ORM SQL-compilation debugging trajectory where visible evidence shows an empty inner queryset represented by an impossible WHERE node, `Exists`/`Subquery` compilation, and an outer filter that also contains unrelated predicates. It is most useful after the agent has located `Exists`/subquery compilation or reproduced that SQL stringification raises `EmptyResultSet`. It is less useful during very early repository exploration with no evidence of the ORM compilation path, and it should not be broadened into a generic rule that all empty querysets should stop raising or that `NothingNode` should be changed globally.
experiences.experience: A useful rubric in these cases should evaluate whether the trajectory preserves the semantic boundary between an empty inner subquery and an empty outer query. The important observable cue is that the empty queryset belongs inside an `EXISTS` expression, while the outer query still has sibling predicates that must remain compilable. Good rubrics should reward identifying that `EmptyResultSet` must be contained or translated at the `Exists` expression boundary, with `~Exists(empty)` acting as a true/no-op condition in an AND filter and `Exists(empty)` acting as false if represented directly. They should also check for correct negation handling exactly once; a common flawed patch sets a true constant for negated EXISTS and then falls through to an existing `NOT ...` wrapper, reversing the result. Avoid a tempting but weaker criterion that merely says the agent found `NothingNode`, modified `Query.exists()`, or returned any boolean-looking SQL constant. Also avoid requiring a broad global change to empty-queryset behavior, because top-level empty querysets should still be allowed to signal an empty result. Prioritize visible evidence such as reproduction of the failing outer WHERE, inspection of the inner empty subquery, awareness of the later negation step, and validation that unrelated outer filters remain present/effective.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the empty queryset is expression-local to an `Exists` subquery and should not make the whole outer query empty. A strong trajectory identifies the `EmptyResultSet` propagation path from the inner impossible subquery, handles it at the `Exists`/subquery expression boundary or an equivalently narrow point, preserves sibling outer predicates, and treats negation correctly without double-negating a constant fallback.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Preserve outer WHERE semantics for empty EXISTS

key_visible_evidence: empty inner queryset represented by an impossible condition that raises during compilation
outer WHERE still contains other predicates besides the Exists condition
Exists has a negation flag or later NOT-wrapping step
agent distinguishes expression-local emptiness from top-level empty queryset behavior
avoid_overgeneralizing_to: global changes to empty queryset or impossible-node semantics
criteria based only on locating files or adding any constant SQL
annotation or complex-expression requirements unless explicitly investigated

scale.1: No meaningful recognition that the empty result belongs to an inner Exists subquery; treats the whole query as legitimately empty or focuses only on unrelated exploration.
scale.2: Mentions Exists or empty querysets but does not connect the inner EmptyResultSet propagation to loss of the outer WHERE or sibling predicates.
scale.3: Recognizes that Exists over an empty queryset needs special handling and states the basic true/false semantics, but leaves the fix location, outer predicate preservation, or negation flow ambiguous.
scale.4: Clearly targets a narrow expression-level handling of the inner EmptyResultSet, preserves unrelated outer filters, and accounts for `Exists(empty)` versus `~Exists(empty)` semantics.
scale.5: Provides decisive evidence through inspection or validation that the empty subquery no longer collapses the outer query, sibling predicates remain effective, and negation is applied exactly once without changing global empty-queryset behavior.

experiences.title: Stage-Aware Issue Reproduction as a Validation Signal
experiences.description: Use when a bug report includes a concrete failing scenario and the trajectory is far enough along that a targeted reproduction or regression test should be visible, especially after edits or before final validation.
experiences.context: Applies in framework/library bug-fix tasks where the problem statement gives observable actual vs expected behavior, such as an ORM query result, rendered documentation output, migration recorder state, form choices, or introspection signature. This criterion is most useful once the agent has located the relevant subsystem, created or modified a candidate fix, or begun validation. It is less useful as a strict negative during the first few exploratory steps, when the agent is only locating files and reading code, or when the task is purely refactoring without a concrete runtime failure. In early exploration, lack of reproduction should be treated as limited evidence rather than a decisive flaw.
experiences.experience: The recurring rubric asked whether the agent first established a reproducible bug. This was useful when the visible trajectory contained task-specific reproduction evidence: a minimal script, focused test, or documented command showing the exact bad behavior and then confirming the intended behavior after the patch. It aligned well when the agent reproduced duplicate form options, stale migration application rows, incorrect manager method signatures, or missing autodoc members, because those observations directly exercised the user-visible contract. It was less discriminative when generated too early, before the agent had any reasonable chance to run a reproduction, because some later-correct fixes began with code inspection only. A better rubric should be stage-aware and concrete: ask whether the agent has established or is actively preserving a targeted failing scenario matching the reported bug, not merely whether it has run any tests or listed files. Avoid the tempting generic criterion “must run the full test suite” or “must reproduce before reading code”; the important evidence is a minimal, issue-specific before/after check or a regression test that would fail for the reported behavior and pass after the candidate fix. Prioritize visible evidence such as exact commands, scripts, assertions, rendered output checks, query results, exception messages, or targeted test names that correspond to the original report.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory establishes a targeted, reproducible check for the reported bug at an appropriate stage: it uses the concrete scenario from the task or an equivalent minimal regression, observes the original failure or clearly explains how the check would fail, and uses the same check or a focused test to validate the candidate behavior after changes. The reproduction should exercise the user-visible contract of the bug rather than unrelated code paths or only broad test-suite execution.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Targeted Bug Reproduction and Validation

required_evidence: A minimal script, focused test, or command tied to the task's actual/expected behavior
Observed failure output, duplicate/missing result, exception, wrong signature, wrong state, or equivalent concrete symptom
After a patch, a rerun or planned regression assertion showing the corrected behavior
Use of project-appropriate test runner or clear explanation when a generic runner is unsuitable
metadata.stage_boundary: Judge strongly only after the agent has located relevant code, attempted a fix, or entered validation; judge weakly during initial repository exploration.

scale.1: No meaningful task-specific reproduction or validation is visible despite the trajectory being at a stage where validation would be expected; commands, if any, are unrelated or only exploratory.
scale.2: Some attempt is made to run code or tests, but it does not closely match the reported bug, does not demonstrate the failing symptom, or fails due avoidable setup issues without a corrected follow-up.
scale.3: The trajectory has partial reproduction evidence or a plausible targeted test plan, but either the original failure or the post-fix validation is missing, incomplete, or only indirectly connected to the task.
scale.4: The trajectory clearly reproduces the reported behavior or adds a focused regression check and validates the candidate fix with relevant output, though coverage may be limited or not integrated into the official test suite.
scale.5: The trajectory provides a precise minimal reproduction or regression test matching the issue, observes the failure mode, validates the corrected behavior after the patch, and uses appropriate project-specific test commands or explains any unrelated test failures.

experiences.title: Stale Git Ref Polling Requires Fetch-Path and Base-Ref Boundaries
experiences.description: Use when a Git-backed polling/cache bug involves deleted remote refs retained in a local snapshot/reference cache, especially after the trajectory has inspected the polling update, fetch, and cache-reference flow.
experiences.context: Applies in Go or similar backend storage code where polling enumerates cached Git refs, fetches them from a remote, and rebuilds snapshots. The task explicitly says deleted non-primary refs should not block valid refs, while the configured startup/base ref must not be automatically removed. This experience is most useful once the trajectory has found that cached refs feed an all-at-once fetch or update loop, or when the agent is proposing cache eviction/removal. It is less useful during very early repository exploration before the update/fetch/cache control flow is visible, and it should not be reduced to a generic 'continue on error' criterion when the failure can occur before per-ref resolution.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics correctly focused on stale cached Git refs not disrupting polling, but they were often too broad: they credited merely detecting a resolve error, removing something from cache, or continuing the loop. In this scenario, visible code showed that cached refs are passed into a batch fetch before the per-ref resolve/build loop, so a deleted remote ref can fail the whole fetch before any resolve-time eviction runs. A stronger rubric should require evidence that the trajectory handles stale refs at the actual failure boundary: failed remote fetch/listing/pruning or filtering of remote refs, followed by processing remaining valid refs. It should also require preservation of the configured base/fixed ref and cache semantics, because the task excludes automatic primary-ref removal. Avoid the tempting proxy criterion 'calls Remove on any resolve error'; that can miss fetch failures, delete refs for transient errors, remove fixed refs if implemented carelessly, and still return an error that makes the poll tick unsuccessful. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent has identified the batch fetch over cached refs, distinguishes dynamic cached refs from fixed/base refs, uses remote-ref existence or a conservative missing-ref signal rather than arbitrary errors, removes only stale non-primary refs through a safe cache API, and continues/retries updates for valid refs.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Fetch-Aware Stale Ref Cleanup with Base-Ref Protection
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluate whether the trajectory is moving toward a fix that handles deleted cached Git refs at the polling fetch/update boundary, not just in a later resolve loop. Strong evidence includes recognizing that polling fetches all cached refs together, that one missing remote ref can poison the whole cycle, and that stale non-primary refs must be removed or filtered while valid refs still fetch/resolve/build. The trajectory should preserve the configured base/fixed ref, use cache deletion/removal semantics that do not corrupt shared snapshots, and avoid treating every resolve or transient Git error as proof that a ref should be removed.

evidence_to_prioritize: Agent identifies cached references being supplied to polling fetch/update as a batch or all-at-once set.
Agent accounts for missing-ref errors that arise during remote fetch/listing/pruning, before per-ref resolve may run.
Agent distinguishes configured primary/base/fixed references from extra/dynamic cached references.
Agent proposes or implements cache removal that preserves shared snapshot ownership and does not remove fixed refs.
Agent ensures remaining valid refs continue to be processed or retried after stale refs are removed or filtered.
evidence_to_downweight: Only adding a cache Remove method without wiring it into polling.
Removing refs on any resolve error without confirming the ref is missing remotely.
Handling only the per-ref resolve loop while leaving batch fetch failure unchanged.
Deleting fixed/base refs despite the task boundary.
Repeated exploration or grep loops with no plan for fetch/cache behavior.
metadata.applicable_stage: After the trajectory has inspected or modified the Git polling update/fetch path and the reference cache behavior.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory understands cached refs are involved in polling failures; it remains at generic repository exploration or unrelated files.
scale.2: Recognizes stale refs or cache involvement, but only proposes broad error skipping or cache removal without identifying the batch fetch/update failure path or base-ref boundary.
scale.3: Finds the polling update loop and cache references and proposes removing stale refs, but handles only per-ref resolve errors or lacks a safe distinction between missing remote refs, transient errors, and fixed/base refs.
scale.4: Clearly targets the fetch/update path where cached refs can fail as a group, plans to remove or filter only missing non-primary refs, and continues processing valid refs, though validation or cache ownership details may still be incomplete.
scale.5: Provides a coherent, fetch-aware design or implementation: verifies remote ref existence or uses conservative missing-ref handling, prunes/filters/removes only stale dynamic refs, preserves base/fixed refs and shared cache snapshots, and keeps polling/updating valid refs despite stale entries.

experiences.title: Task-Relevant Objective Verification After Risky Edits
experiences.description: Retrieve when an agent has already made code changes—especially broad refactors, API migrations, generated rewrites, or fragile search/replace edits—and the next useful rubric should judge whether it ran meaningful pass/fail validation and corrected failures before stopping.
experiences.context: Applies in software-repair trajectories across Go, Python, TypeScript/React, and similar repositories when visible work has moved beyond exploration into implementation or final review. It is most relevant after multi-file edits, removed/renamed APIs, import/type-sensitive changes, parser/formatter behavior changes, build-system/version updates, or any trajectory with failed sed/script edits, wholesale rewrites, or suspicious diffs. It is less applicable during pure investigation before a patch exists, and it should not replace a semantic task-specific rubric when the visible patch is small and clearly addresses the issue. The criterion should distinguish strong task-relevant validation from weak proxies: grep-only cleanup, syntax-only checks, or a narrow compile of one file may be useful evidence but should not be treated as proof that behavior, integration, or tests are correct.
experiences.experience: The recurring useful rubric in these cases asked whether the agent ran objective validation, read the result, and iterated on failures instead of declaring completion from inspection alone. This is valuable when the trajectory shows risky edits because lack of validation leaves obvious observable hazards: stale imports, malformed loops, untested API signature changes, untouched call sites, accidental broad diffs, or failed commands that were not followed by a corrective run. A better rubric should focus on task-relevant pass/fail evidence: unit tests, targeted integration tests, typecheck/build, lint/format, or an executable reproduction that encodes the reported behavior. It should also require the agent to inspect failures and either fix them or justify why they are unrelated. The tempting but weaker criterion to avoid is merely checking that the agent grepped for old names, ran a syntax/YAML compile, or produced an ad-hoc script without integrating the finding; those are partial signals only. Conversely, do not over-apply this as a universal demand to run the entire suite in early exploration or when no implementation has been attempted. Prioritize visible command output, exit status, whether the check matches the bug/refactor contract, and whether subsequent edits respond to the observed result.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Task-Relevant Objective Verification and Iteration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show that after making implementation changes, the agent ran at least one meaningful objective check with a clear pass/fail result that is relevant to the task, read the output, and used failures to drive further corrections before considering the work complete. Strong evidence includes targeted unit or integration tests for the reported behavior, build/typecheck/lint/format checks after risky edits, or an executable reproduction of the issue. Weak evidence includes grep-only searches, syntax-only checks that do not cover the changed behavior, or failed validation whose output is ignored.

prioritize_evidence: test/build/typecheck/lint/reproduction commands run after edits
observed pass/fail output or exit status
corrections made in response to failed checks
validation scope matches the task behavior and changed files
weak_or_insufficient_evidence: only running syntax checks when behavioral/integration risk remains
failed validation followed by stopping or unrelated edits
metadata.applicability_boundary: Use mainly after code changes or near final review; do not penalize pure investigation stages as strongly.

scale.1: No objective validation is run after implementation changes, or prior failed commands/checks are ignored while the agent continues toward completion.
scale.2: Only weak or indirect checks are run, such as grep, snippet inspection, or a narrow syntax check, with substantial unvalidated behavioral/build risk remaining.
scale.3: Some relevant objective validation is run and read, but coverage is partial, failures are not fully resolved, or the check does not exercise the main task contract.
scale.4: A targeted task-relevant check is run after the edits, its result is inspected, and visible failures lead to concrete corrective edits or a credible unrelated-failure assessment.
scale.5: The agent runs strong validation appropriate to the change set, such as targeted behavioral tests plus build/typecheck/format where relevant, resolves or convincingly isolates all failures, and leaves clear evidence that the changed behavior and integration points pass.

experiences.title: Dtype-Sensitive Contour Defaults Require Pre-Coercion and All Callers
experiences.description: Use when a plotting/array API enhancement depends on detecting boolean input dtype before numeric coercion and the agent is modifying shared contour level-selection logic.
experiences.context: Applies in Matplotlib-like Python plotting code where contour level defaults are chosen in a shared helper after Z data may already be converted to float, and where multiple public signatures or subclasses may call that helper. This is most useful once the trajectory has identified the contour argument parser and level-processing helper, or is reviewing an implementation diff. It is less useful during very early repository exploration before the relevant data-flow is known. Do not over-apply to tasks where the API has only one input path, where dtype is not erased before default selection, or where there is no evidence that filled/triangulated/alternate contour implementations share the changed helper.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics correctly focused on the task’s semantic contract: boolean contour inputs without explicit levels should default to the meaningful 0.5 boundary while explicit levels and non-boolean arrays remain unchanged. However, the broader versions were not discriminative enough because patches can appear to satisfy the simple `contour(bool_Z)` case while still being incomplete. The better rubric should focus on observable data-flow completeness: the implementation must preserve or pass the original Z dtype before float conversion, apply the bool default only after confirming no user levels were supplied, handle every supported Z input signature that goes through the same level helper, update all callers when the helper signature changes, and avoid breaking filled-contour validation if the shared path also serves filled contours. A tempting but weak criterion is merely checking for `np.issubdtype(..., bool)` or a smoke test that prints `[0.5]`; this can be misleading if tests import an installed package, if dtype has already been coerced to float, or if only the simplest call form is covered. Prioritize visible evidence such as diffs that remove forced dtype conversion before level selection or explicitly capture pre-coercion dtype, all call sites updated consistently, explicit-level precedence preserved, non-bool binary arrays left on the normal locator path, and validation run against the local checkout rather than a site-packages installation.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete Pre-Coercion Bool-Dtype Propagation for Contour Levels
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show an implementation or plan that preserves the original Z input dtype before any float conversion and uses that dtype in the centralized contour level-default logic. The bool special case should apply only when the user did not provide levels, should set line-contour defaults to a single 0.5 boundary, should keep filled-contour behavior valid if the same path is shared, should leave explicit levels and non-boolean 0/1 data on existing behavior, and should update every contour input path or subclass caller affected by any changed helper signature. Validation evidence should distinguish local source behavior from an installed package and should cover simple Z input plus alternate supported signatures such as explicit coordinates or other contour implementations when present.

expected_evidence: Original Z dtype is captured before float or masked-float coercion, or coercion is delayed until after dtype-sensitive default selection.
Default-level logic checks for omitted user levels before applying the boolean special case.
Non-boolean binary-valued arrays continue to use the normal automatic locator/default path.
All call signatures and shared helper callers are updated consistently when the level-processing API changes.
Filled contour paths are either intentionally handled with a valid multi-level default or explicitly shown not to be affected.
Tests or manual checks verify the edited checkout, not only a separately installed plotting package.
red_flags: The bool check uses a dtype after the data has already been converted to float.
Only the one-argument contour form is handled while coordinate/Z or alternate contour implementations still lose dtype information.
A shared helper signature is changed without updating every caller.
The patch sets a single level for filled contours despite existing validation requiring at least two levels.
Validation relies on site-packages behavior from a newer installed version.

scale.1: No credible progress toward dtype-sensitive contour default handling; evidence is limited to exploration or installed-package behavior.
scale.2: Adds or proposes a boolean check, but it is placed after dtype coercion, ignores explicit-level precedence, or only covers an unverified simple path.
scale.3: Covers the main line-contour simple Z path and preserves explicit/non-bool behavior, but evidence is incomplete for alternate signatures, shared callers, or local validation.
scale.4: Correctly propagates pre-coercion dtype through the main contour paths, preserves explicit and non-bool behavior, and accounts for filled-contour validity, with mostly consistent caller updates.
scale.5: Fully implements and validates pre-coercion bool-dtype propagation across all supported contour input paths and shared callers, preserves existing semantics for explicit and non-bool inputs, handles filled contours safely, and verifies behavior against the local source.

experiences.title: Exact Numeric Resampling Contract Over Generic Interpolation
experiences.description: Retrieve when a JS/TS task asks for deterministic numeric array resampling/rescaling with exact-output behavior, especially where an existing rough resample helper already exists and the agent is implementing or drafting new utilities.
experiences.context: Applies in JavaScript/TypeScript utility modules when the task requests new numeric array helpers that must be deterministic, shape-preserving, and exact enough for tests. It is most useful after the trajectory has inspected the existing array utility code, found related helpers, or begun editing/drafting the resample/rescale implementation. At very early exploration, use this only as a forward-looking progress criterion. Do not apply rigidly to open-ended visualization, signal-processing, or interpolation tasks where any standard interpolation method is acceptable, where public API names are explicitly different, or where exact expected outputs are not part of the task contract.
experiences.experience: The previous rubrics focused on whether the agent implemented a deterministic smoothing resample that returns the requested length for downsampling, upsampling, identity, and boundary cases. That was useful because the decisive observable flaw in many trajectories was not simply lack of code, but an underspecified or self-invented interpolation that looked plausible while failing the exact contract. However, a better rubric should be narrower and more concrete: it should require conformance to the repository’s expected public utility API, preservation of existing rough resampling behavior, deterministic exact-length behavior for all length relationships, real smoothing behavior for downsampling rather than merely endpoint interpolation or duplication, and a linear rescale based on the input’s actual min/max. Avoid the tempting proxy of rewarding ad-hoc tests, self-asserted “shape preservation,” or generic linear interpolation just because sample outputs look reasonable. Prioritize visible evidence such as: the agent compared against existing array helpers; chose export names and placement consistent with the utility module and consumers; handled identity, empty/zero-length, single-point, upsample, and downsample cases intentionally; used existing scalar mapping helpers or the equivalent min/max formula for rescale; ran relevant tests/lint; and did not rewrite unrelated array utilities while trying to fix the new functions.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Exact Deterministic Numeric Utility Contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should show that the new numeric array utilities are being implemented as stable public exports in the existing utility area, with exact deterministic behavior rather than merely plausible interpolation. Strong evidence includes preserving the existing fast/rough resample helper, adding a separate smoothing resample whose output length is exactly the requested length for downsampling, upsampling, identity, and boundary cases, applying intentional smoothing or repository-consistent helper composition for downsampling, and adding a linear rescale that maps the input array's actual minimum and maximum to the requested inclusive range. The trajectory should also avoid collateral rewrites of unrelated utilities and should validate behavior with exact-output tests or equivalent checks rather than relying only on self-authored smoke tests.

metadata.environment: JavaScript/TypeScript repository with existing utility module and Jest/lint-style validation
priority_evidence: new helpers are exported from the established utility location using names consistent with task/repository conventions
identity, upsample, downsample, empty or zero-target, and single-value cases are explicitly handled or safely covered
downsampling is not accepted solely because it linearly interpolates endpoints; it must satisfy the task's deterministic smoothing contract
linear rescale uses actual input min/max and requested inclusive output bounds
existing array utilities are preserved except for minimal compatible refactoring
validation targets exact outputs and relevant regressions
avoid_as_proxy: inventing alternate public API names without evidence consumers/tests expect them
rewriting unrelated helpers while fixing the new utility

scale.1: No meaningful implementation or plan for the requested deterministic numeric utilities is visible, or the trajectory only explores files without identifying the exact resample/rescale contract.
scale.2: The trajectory attempts a new resample or rescale but uses generic interpolation or duplication with unclear public API names, missing edge cases, little relation to existing helpers, or no exact-output validation.
scale.3: The trajectory implements deterministic resample/rescale behavior that roughly returns requested lengths and maps min/max values, but it remains underspecified for exact smoothing semantics, boundary cases, public API compatibility, or regression safety.
scale.4: The trajectory strongly aligns with the required contract: helpers are placed and exported consistently, most length and rescale cases are handled, existing utilities are preserved, and relevant exact-output tests or checks are run, with only minor uncertainty about exact smoothing expectations.
scale.5: The trajectory provides a contract-conforming implementation with repository-consistent public exports, exact deterministic behavior for downsampling/upsampling/identity and boundary cases, correct min/max linear rescale, no unrelated utility regressions, and convincing exact-output validation plus lint/test hygiene.

experiences.title: Squashed Migration Unapply Recorder Bookkeeping
experiences.description: Use when a Django migration task concerns unapplying squashed/replacement migrations and the trajectory has inspected executor recorder logic, Migration.replaces, or applied migration rows.
experiences.context: Applies in a Django codebase during a migration-executor bug fix where a squashed migration has a replacement list and the problem is that reversing/unapplying it leaves stale applied records. The criterion is most useful once the trajectory has enough visible evidence about MigrationExecutor unapply behavior, MigrationRecorder record deletion, or a reproduction showing both the squash and replaced migrations recorded. It is less useful or premature during pure environment setup, generic test-runner debugging, or unrelated migration graph/loader issues. Do not apply it as a blanket requirement to change migration planning: an empty plan from a stale executor/loader in an ad-hoc reproduction is not by itself evidence that the planner is the production bug.
experiences.experience: The useful rubrics in these cases focused on the semantic invariant: unapplying a squashed/replacement migration must remove the recorder row for the squashed migration itself while preserving the existing removal of each replaced migration row and preserving normal non-squashed behavior. This aligned with strong visible evidence when the trajectory inspected the unapply branch and saw that the replaces path deleted only replaced migration keys, or when manual recorder output showed the squash row remaining after unapply. A better rubric should reward a minimal, localized understanding of recorder bookkeeping in the unapply path and, if tests are discussed, direct recorder-state assertions after applying and unapplying with replaced migration files still available. Avoid the tempting but weaker proxy of requiring broad changes to graph planning, loader applied-state refreshing, or check_replacements solely because an ad-hoc script reused a stale executor and produced an empty plan. Also avoid the inverted criterion that only replaced migrations should be marked unapplied; the task explicitly requires the squash/replacement record to be removed too. Prioritize visible evidence such as: recognition of Migration.replaces semantics, comparison of apply/check replacement bookkeeping with unapply bookkeeping, identification of record_unapplied calls for both categories of migration records, and validation that the migration recorder no longer contains the squash key after reverse execution.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate a correct, localized understanding that the unapply path for squashed/replacement migrations must update recorder state for both the replacement migration itself and all migrations it replaces. Strong evidence includes inspecting the executor's unapply recorder branch, identifying that the replaces branch currently omits the replacement migration's own row, proposing or applying a minimal recorder deletion for the replacement key in addition to the existing replaced-key deletions, preserving ordinary non-replacement migration behavior, and validating or planning a regression assertion against applied migration records rather than only table/schema existence. The trajectory should not treat stale loader state or ad-hoc empty migration plans as sufficient reason for broad planner/loader changes unless independently confirmed in the normal fresh-loader execution path.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Correct Squash Unapply Recorder Invariant

metadata.task_signal: squashed or replacement migration with a replaces list remains recorded as applied after unapply
key_visible_evidence: Migration.replaces is present on the squashed migration
unapply recorder logic is inspected or modified
record_unapplied behavior is understood as deleting migration rows
recorder state is checked for both replacement and replaced migration keys
avoid_overweighting: plain test-runner configuration failures
stale executor loader applied_migrations from reused ad-hoc scripts
unconfirmed migration_plan rewrites

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the trajectory understands squashed migration recorder semantics; it focuses only on environment setup, unrelated files, or generic migration behavior.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the trajectory mentions squashed migrations or replacement files but does not identify that the unapply recorder state must include the squash/replacement migration's own row.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory identifies the relevant executor/recorder area and the need to remove the squash record, but has incomplete validation or mixes this with speculative planner/loader changes.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the trajectory clearly identifies the replaces-branch omission, proposes or makes a minimal recorder update that removes both replaced and replacement records, and preserves non-squashed behavior.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: in addition to the minimal correct recorder change, the trajectory uses or plans a focused regression check of applied migration records after unapplying a squashed migration with replaced files present, and avoids broad planner/loader changes based on stale ad-hoc state.

experiences.title: CONTINUE Escaping Must Remain Raw Until One Final Parse
experiences.description: Use when an Astropy FITS Card trajectory has localized a length-dependent doubled-quote round-trip bug to long string CONTINUE-card parsing and is inspecting `_split`, regex string/comment matching, or quote unescaping.
experiences.context: Applies in Python/Astropy FITS Card tasks where string values containing doubled single quotes round-trip correctly on short cards but fail when serialization crosses the 80-character FITS card boundary and uses CONTINUE cards. The visible trajectory should show concrete evidence such as card images split into a first quoted chunk plus CONTINUE chunks, regex captures for quoted strings, or discussion of `_split` reconstructing a synthetic value/comment string before a later parser unescapes FITS quotes. This guidance is most useful after the agent has moved beyond initial file discovery and has enough evidence to distinguish raw FITS escaping from Python string values. It is less applicable for unrelated FITS verification/reformatting issues, for purely short-card quote parsing bugs, or at a very early stage before the trajectory has identified whether CONTINUE-card reconstruction is involved.
experiences.experience: The useful criterion in this cluster is not merely that the agent reproduced the issue or noticed CONTINUE cards. Reproduction alone can look strong while the patch still changes the wrong layer. The discriminative issue is whether the agent preserves the FITS-escaped representation while recombining CONTINUE fragments and allows quote unescaping to happen exactly once at the normal value-parse stage. Rubrics that focus only on broad recombination, avoiding split quote runs, continuation-marker ordering, or verification side effects are too coarse or can reward plausible but incorrect fixes. A better rubric should ask whether the trajectory/patch avoids per-fragment conversion of doubled FITS quotes to Python quotes inside CONTINUE reconstruction, strips only the continuation marker from the raw captured fragment, rebuilds a syntactically valid quoted value/comment string for the downstream parser, and prevents partial string/comment regex matches from silently ignoring leftover quote characters. Visible evidence to prioritize includes raw card images, subcard value/comment fragments, regex `strg` groups, whether `.replace("''", "'")` is removed or deferred in the long-card reconstruction path, whether string/comment matching is full-string rather than partial, and regression checks for both trailing and embedded doubled quotes across boundary lengths. Avoid making the rubric about adding boundary-splitting heuristics, special-casing `''''` as empty, reformatting CONTINUE cards via verification, or simply passing the original reproducer without preserving general FITS quote semantics.
