reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates that a correct fix for long FITS string values keeps CONTINUE-card fragments in FITS-escaped form during reconstruction, removes only syntactic continuation markers, uses a full string/comment match so trailing quote/comment text cannot be ignored, and relies on the normal final parse to unescape doubled single quotes exactly once. Strong evidence includes inspecting raw multi-card images and subcard regex captures, identifying double-unescaping as the corruption mechanism, avoiding ad hoc special cases for null-looking quote runs, and validating boundary-length round trips for doubled quotes at the end and in the middle of long values.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Raw Escaping Preserved Through CONTINUE Reconstruction

key_visible_evidence: raw multi-80-character FITS card images or CONTINUE subcards are inspected
the long-card reconstruction path is distinguished from normal short-card parsing
doubled FITS quotes are not converted to Python quotes per CONTINUE fragment
continuation ampersands are stripped without altering quote escape pairs
string/comment regex matching is required to consume the relevant fragment fully
round-trip checks cover boundary lengths and both trailing and embedded doubled quotes
common_false_positives: only reproducing the reported failure
special-casing a CONTINUE fragment that looks like a null string
re-escaping already-unescaped fragments without proving the escape layer
blaming verification/reformatting without evidence it is in the failing parse path
testing only one failing length or only comment-free happy paths

scale.1: No visible evidence that the agent understands the CONTINUE reconstruction escape layer; the trajectory focuses on unrelated parsing, verification, or reproduction only.
scale.2: Some evidence that CONTINUE cards or quote escaping are relevant, but the proposed reasoning still unescapes fragments prematurely, special-cases quote runs, or lacks raw subcard evidence.
scale.3: Moderate evidence equivalent to the parent trajectory: the agent has identified long-card CONTINUE behavior and quote collapse, but has not clearly ensured exactly one final unescape and full string/comment matching.
scale.4: Strong evidence that the agent is preserving raw escaped fragments through reconstruction, stripping only continuation markers, and validating multiple boundary cases, with only minor uncertainty around comments or regex completeness.
scale.5: Complete visible evidence of the correct semantic contract: raw FITS escaping is preserved through CONTINUE recombination, matching is full-fragment, unescaping occurs exactly once downstream, and regression checks cover trailing/embedded doubled quotes across boundary lengths plus relevant comments.

experiences.title: Adaptive Localization After Failed Name Search
experiences.description: Use when a trajectory is still trying to find an absent or renamed target helper and visible evidence shows whether the agent pivots from failed exact-name greps to higher-signal localization strategies.
experiences.context: Applies in Python repository debugging tasks during the discovery/localization stage, especially when the task names a function/helper but exact searches return no matches. It is most useful after several failed searches or candidate inspections make localization the main blocker. The criterion should not be retrieved for final-review trajectories where the target code has already been found and edited, for the first one or two exploratory commands before a pivot is reasonably expected, or for tasks where the relevant file/function is already obvious from the prompt or stack trace.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics focused on search strategy and target-code discovery. They were useful because the visible trajectories showed a decisive blocker: the agent repeatedly issued the same or near-identical low-signal greps, kept inspecting unrelated duration/time hits, and made no edits or tests. In this situation, final patch quality is strongly constrained by whether the agent can escape the localization loop. A better rubric should evaluate adaptive, hypothesis-driven localization: after exact-name searches fail, the agent should search for concrete reproduction literals and unit syntax, inspect tests/docs/config/command call sites, trace likely user-facing entry points and argument parsing, broaden beyond only Python definitions when appropriate, and explicitly consider that the helper may need to be introduced rather than modified. Avoid a tempting but wrong rubric about the exact parser semantics or expected millisecond calculations when no implementation has been located yet; that is premature and may not distinguish the visible failure mode. Also avoid crediting sheer search volume: many greps are not progress if they repeat the same pattern or ignore earlier no-match results. Prioritize observable evidence such as changed search terms/scopes, use of example literals from the bug report, reading of relevant candidate call sites or tests, clear elimination of dead ends, and movement toward a concrete implementation location.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: After failed exact-name or obvious keyword searches for the reported helper, the agent adaptively localizes the relevant code by changing strategy rather than repeating low-signal commands. Strong evidence includes searching for concrete valid/invalid example literals from the task, inspecting tests and user-facing call sites that would consume the duration string, following config/type/import/command mappings, broadening file scopes when appropriate, and deciding whether a missing helper should be added in a logical module. The rubric should reward efficient narrowing toward an implementation location and penalize repetitive greps with unchanged results.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Adaptive Target Localization

metadata.trigger: named target helper or parser is not found by initial exact searches
positive_evidence: searches for concrete reproduction literals or syntax examples
inspection of tests, docs, configuration schemas, command definitions, or call sites
explicit pivot after no-match results
clear reasoning about whether the helper is absent and where it should be introduced
negative_evidence: repeating identical or near-identical grep commands
continuing broad time/duration searches after they produce unrelated hits
no code edits, tests, or concrete localization progress after many steps

scale.1: No meaningful adaptation: the agent repeats failed exact-name or broad keyword searches, re-reads unrelated hits, and does not establish any plausible target location.
scale.2: Weak adaptation: the agent tries a few nearby terms or obvious files but mostly continues low-signal searches and does not use task examples, tests, or call-site tracing.
scale.3: Moderate behavior: the agent explores some plausible modules or schemas and eliminates a few dead ends, but localization remains incomplete and pivots are inconsistent or not very targeted.
scale.4: Strong behavior: the agent reacts to failed searches with concrete new hypotheses, uses tests/examples/call sites/config or docs to narrow the search, and identifies one or more credible implementation locations.
scale.5: Excellent behavior: the agent efficiently confirms whether the named helper exists, traces the feature through high-signal entry points, identifies the correct place to modify or add code, and begins or plans validation around the reported behavior.

experiences.title: Backend-driven batch migration for legacy Drive shares
experiences.description: Retrieve this when a Proton Drive task asks for migrating legacy address-encrypted shares to link/node-key encryption and the trajectory is evaluating where/how migration should be implemented.
experiences.context: Applies in a TypeScript/React Proton Drive monorepo where share metadata, link private keys, session keys, and shared API route builders are visible. It is most useful once the agent has moved beyond generic exploration into design or implementation of migration endpoints and app integration. The key boundary is that the task is not simply to tweak passphrase decryption fallback or shared-link URL legacy handling; it requires a background/share-action migration workflow that cooperates with backend migration endpoints. In very early exploration, a broader discovery rubric may be acceptable, but at implementation review the criterion should distinguish real batch migration integration from superficial per-share endpoint calls, local re-encryption attempts, feature-flag scaffolding, or unrelated locked-volume/mail migration patterns.
experiences.experience: The earlier rubrics often checked only the task-level requirements: identify legacy shares, call a migration endpoint, handle non-decryptable session keys, and tolerate 404s. That broad criterion is adequate when the trajectory has no code because absence of any migration work is decisive, but it can over-credit wrong implementations that invent a per-share `migrate` or `update` route, use `possibleKeyPackets` as the only detector, or try to locally rewrite share passphrases without matching the backend contract. For this Drive migration problem, a better rubric should focus on observable evidence of a backend-driven batch flow: adding migration API descriptors for listing unmigrated shares and posting a batch migration payload; triggering migration during Drive startup or share-action initialization without blocking normal loading; deriving a node/link-key encrypted session-key packet from each readable share using existing share session-key and link private-key helpers; explicitly collecting shares whose session keys cannot be decrypted as unreadable rather than crashing or silently dropping them; posting both migrated packets and unreadable IDs; and making 404/unavailable migration endpoints non-fatal via request silence or local catch. Avoid rewarding code that only adds a `POST drive/shares/{id}/migrate`, only checks `PossibleKeyPackets`, mutates share metadata locally, rewrites crypto fallback behavior, or mounts a feature-flagged container with TODO/no-op migration. Visible evidence to prioritize includes route URLs/payloads, where the migration is invoked, use of existing link/share key helpers, per-share error isolation, and 404 handling in the actual migration request path.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete backend-driven legacy share migration flow
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should implement or clearly converge on a real Drive legacy-share migration workflow that uses backend migration endpoints to list unmigrated shares and submit a batch payload, integrates that workflow into normal Drive initialization/share actions, derives link/node-key encrypted session-key packets from existing share session keys and link private keys, records non-decryptable shares as unreadable instead of aborting, and handles unavailable migration endpoints such as 404 responses without breaking startup or share access. The judge should not give high credit for merely detecting legacy-looking metadata, inventing a per-share migration/update endpoint, locally re-encrypting share passphrases, or adding unrelated migration scaffolding without the batch API/payload/error contract.

required_evidence: shared Drive API route builders for both listing unmigrated shares and posting migration results
batch migration request payload includes encrypted session-key packets associated with share IDs and a way to report unreadable share IDs
migration is invoked from an app startup or share-actions path after normal share loading rather than only from ad hoc key lookup
implementation uses existing share session-key retrieval and link private-key/encryption helpers to compute the migration packet
session-key decryption failures are caught per share and converted into unreadable-share reporting
404 or unavailable migration endpoints are silenced or caught so the migration exits gracefully
anti_patterns: only adding a per-share migrate URL under the normal share resource
treating PossibleKeyPackets alone as a complete migration mechanism
attempting to update share passphrase/key fields directly without the migration endpoint contract
feature-flag or container scaffolding with TODO/no-op migration
changing core decryption fallback in a way that risks normal share access

scale.1: No concrete migration implementation or the work is unrelated to Drive share encryption migration.
scale.2: Mentions or partially detects legacy shares, but lacks a real backend migration API flow or uses an invented per-share/local re-encryption approach.
scale.3: Implements some migration plumbing, such as a trigger or endpoint helper, but misses major contract pieces like batch payloads, encrypted session-key packet generation, unreadable-share reporting, or non-fatal 404 handling.
scale.4: Shows a mostly correct batch migration design with appropriate endpoints, startup/share-action trigger, packet generation, and graceful per-share failure handling, but has minor integration, typing, or completeness gaps.
scale.5: Fully implements the batch migration workflow with correct route descriptors, trigger point, link-key packet generation, unreadable-share reporting, and robust 404/unavailable endpoint handling while preserving existing share access behavior.

experiences.title: Validate the Missing Update Workflow Contract, Not Just a PUT Handler
experiences.description: Use when an Open Library bookshelves/check-ins task asks for update-request validation and date normalization, and the trajectory has found only the existing create check-in handler plus low-level event persistence helpers, with no current update route.
experiences.context: Applies in Python web.py/Infogami delegate-page codebases where feature code is split between an HTTP handler layer and a core persistence layer. The key visible situation is: the task describes updating existing bookshelf/check-in events; the agent has found an existing create/check-in route, a date formatting helper, event table update helpers, and repeated searches showing no existing PUT/PATCH/update handler. This guidance is most useful at late discovery or early implementation planning, when the agent must decide what update workflow to add. It is less useful if the codebase already has a clearly identified update endpoint with tests, or if the task only concerns the create/check-in POST path rather than updating existing events.
experiences.experience: The prior rubrics were useful because they penalized trajectories that had not yet connected request validation to an actual event update workflow. However, their wording was too narrow when it required a PUT/PATCH method on the existing work-id check-in endpoint. The stronger criterion should focus on the semantic contract visible from the task and investigation: an update request must identify an existing event, reject empty/no-op updates, normalize dates through a shared formatter, verify that the event belongs to the addressed user/patron before updating, and call persistence through an event-level update API. Do not generate a rubric that treats “found or added a PUT/PATCH handler” as sufficient or mandatory; in this codebase the correct workflow may be a new user-scoped delegate route using POST-style JSON rather than PUT on the existing creation route. Also avoid rewarding repeated greps for endpoints after the trajectory has already established that none exists. Prioritize observable evidence that the agent recognizes the create route is not the update route, plans or implements a separate user/event-scoped update handler, adds/selects by event id for ownership checks, combines date/data updates without no-ops, serializes payload data consistently, and preserves/reuses canonical year/month/day formatting.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory should demonstrate that the agent is implementing the bookshelf check-in event update workflow according to the request contract, rather than merely modifying the existing create-check-in path or searching indefinitely for a PUT/PATCH endpoint. Strong evidence includes recognizing that no current HTTP update handler exists, adding or planning an appropriate user/patron-scoped event update handler, requiring an event id in the request body, rejecting requests with neither date content nor data payload, looking up the event by id, verifying the event belongs to the addressed/current user before updating, normalizing supplied year/month/day through a shared canonical formatter, and routing date/data changes through persistence helpers that can update only the supplied fields and report the update result.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Event Update Workflow Contract

required_visible_evidence: distinguishes create-check-in validation from update-request validation
does not assume the existing work-id creation route is automatically the update route
requires event identifier and at least one of date or data content
checks event existence and user ownership before mutation
uses canonical partial-date formatting with zero-padded month/day
integrates with persistence through event-id-based select/update behavior
avoid_overfitting_to: rewarding endpoint discovery alone after absence is established
treating a work id as a substitute for an event id
updating date and data through unrelated one-off SQL inside the handler without an event-level contract

scale.1: No meaningful progress toward an event update workflow; the trajectory only searches, edits unrelated files, or focuses solely on create-check-in validation/date formatting.
scale.2: Weak progress: identifies relevant handler and persistence helpers or proposes an update endpoint, but does not define the request contract around event id, non-empty update content, ownership, and normalized dates.
scale.3: Moderate progress: recognizes an update handler is missing and includes some validation such as event id plus date/data presence, but may attach it to the wrong existing route, omit ownership checks, or call separate persistence helpers without a coherent event-level update flow.
scale.4: Strong progress: implements or clearly plans a dedicated update workflow with event-id validation, no-op rejection, date normalization, and persistence integration, with only minor uncertainty about route shape or response details.
scale.5: Complete progress: establishes the correct user/event-scoped update contract end to end, including event lookup, ownership rejection, shared canonical date formatting, optional date/data updates without no-ops, consistent payload handling, and tests or explicit verification for invalid missing-id/empty-update cases.

experiences.title: Do not treat generic per-thread DB cleanup as sufficient when Django live-server connection overrides are involved
experiences.description: Retrieve this when generating rubrics for Django LiveServerTestCase / ThreadedWSGIServer bugs involving thread-local database connections, teardown races, and LiveServerThread connection sharing.
experiences.context: Applies in Django test-server code where LiveServerTestCase uses ThreadedWSGIServer/socketserver.ThreadingMixIn and database connections are thread-local. The misleading pattern is to generate a broad criterion such as “close database connections after each request thread,” especially when it accepts close_old_connections(), request_finished-style cleanup, or a simple process_request_thread finally block as enough. That idea can still be appropriate for a generic threaded server leak with no shared parent-thread connections and where the cleanup API force-closes all resources. It is not discriminative enough for Django live-server regressions that also involve LiveServerThread connections_override, in-memory SQLite/shared wrappers, and the difference between close_old_connections() and connections.close_all().
experiences.experience: Previous rubrics focused on the visible task wording and rewarded trajectories for adding any request-thread cleanup. This overstates progress because Django’s normal close_old_connections() only closes obsolete or unusable connections, not necessarily healthy open connections that block test database teardown. A simple close_all() in process_request_thread is also incomplete if it ignores LiveServerThread’s connection override mechanism or closes shared wrappers from the wrong thread context. For this class of task, generate a stricter rubric that checks whether the agent preserves Django live-server connection semantics: request-worker threads must inherit any supplied connection overrides before handling the request, cleanup must forcibly close the current thread’s initialized connections at the appropriate socketserver request-close point, and the solution must not merely add cleanup to a broad ServerHandler path or weaken/skip existing tests. Avoid the tempting criterion “calls close_old_connections/request_finished after each threaded request.” Prioritize visible evidence in the trajectory: inspection of ThreadingMixIn lifecycle, recognition that connections are thread-local, distinction between close_old_connections and close_all, handling of connections_override/inc_thread_sharing behavior, and behavioral validation with Django’s servers live-thread tests rather than introspection-only scripts.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Generic cleanup without live-server connection override semantics
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that propose or implement only a generic per-request/thread database cleanup for Django ThreadedWSGIServer while omitting the LiveServerThread connection-sharing contract. This flaw is present when the visible trajectory relies on close_old_connections(), request_finished-style cleanup, ServerHandler.close(), or a simple process_request_thread finally block, without evidence that worker threads receive any parent-provided connection overrides before request handling and without a forced close_all-style cleanup in the current request thread at the socketserver request close lifecycle. Also penalize changes that mask existing live-server connection tests, skip assertions, or validate only by introspecting that a method exists.

metadata.environment: Django LiveServerTestCase / LiveServerThread using ThreadedWSGIServer and socketserver.ThreadingMixIn
key_visible_evidence: Whether the trajectory distinguishes close_old_connections from forced connection closing
Whether it accounts for thread-local django.db.connections
Whether it preserves connections_override/shared connection behavior
Whether cleanup is attached to the request thread lifecycle rather than only the main/live-server thread or a broad WSGI handler path
Whether tests are run through Django's supported servers test harness instead of introspection-only scripts

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory explicitly handles thread-local connections, parent-provided connection overrides, and forced per-request cleanup in the correct request-thread lifecycle without weakening tests.
scale.2: Minor concern: the trajectory identifies the right lifecycle and forced cleanup need, but has not yet fully shown how connection overrides or existing live-server tests will be preserved.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the trajectory has a plausible request-thread cleanup plan, but it treats generic close_all or similar cleanup as sufficient and only partially investigates connection_override or shared-connection behavior.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory implements or endorses close_old_connections(), ServerHandler-level cleanup, or a simple process_request_thread cleanup without accounting for LiveServerThread connection overrides and thread-local wrapper ownership.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the trajectory both uses an incomplete generic cleanup approach and ignores or suppresses failing live-server connection tests, such as by weakening assertions or relying solely on method-presence/introspection validation.

experiences.title: Retrieve Protocol Reliability for Repeated or State-Disrupting Tool Errors
experiences.description: Retrieve when the visible trajectory contains malformed actions, empty assistant turns, fake tool syntax, invalid parameters, or repeated action-schema failures that may impede execution.
experiences.context: This guidance is useful once there is enough tool activity to distinguish a persistent protocol problem from an isolated formatting slip. A single malformed call that is immediately corrected with no state impact should reduce confidence only slightly. Repeated errors, unexecuted planned actions, or malformed editing commands that corrupt state make protocol reliability highly discriminative.
experiences.experience: The source rubric is useful because executable progress depends on actions reaching tools with valid structure and parameters. Apply it to the continuity of the workflow: whether calls execute, whether the agent recognizes format errors, and whether recovery restores state. Avoid treating every shell command that returns nonzero as a protocol violation or making one promptly repaired serialization lapse dominate otherwise reliable behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Sustained Executable Tool Protocol
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Assess whether the trajectory consistently emits executable, schema-valid tool actions with appropriate parameters and recovers promptly and safely from isolated format mistakes. Repeated malformed actions, fake tool markup, empty action turns, or unexecuted plans should sharply lower the rating.

observable_evidence: tool parser or action-format results
validity of required fields and parameter types
repetition versus immediate correction
workspace impact and recovery
planned actions actually executed

scale.1: The trajectory shows pervasive or unrecovered violations of executable tool-protocol compliance and safe recovery that prevent reliable progress.
scale.2: The trajectory shows repeated weaknesses in executable tool-protocol compliance and safe recovery; recovery is partial or costly.
scale.3: The evidence for executable tool-protocol compliance and safe recovery is mixed: ordinary work proceeds, but notable avoidable violations remain.
scale.4: The trajectory demonstrates strong executable tool-protocol compliance and safe recovery, with at most an isolated and promptly corrected lapse.
scale.5: The trajectory demonstrates consistently excellent executable tool-protocol compliance and safe recovery throughout the visible work.

experiences.title: Task-Critical Truncation Recovery Gate
experiences.description: Retrieve this when recent tool output is visibly truncated and the agent’s next reasoning or edits may depend on omitted code, not merely because any command output was shortened.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE-agent trajectories across Python, Go, TypeScript, or similar repositories when observations contain explicit truncation markers such as omitted middle sections from `cat`, broad `grep`, `ls`, or full-file reads, and the agent is using that output to decide where or how to patch. It is most relevant after locating a likely file/function but before or during edits, where omitted surrounding code could contain required control flow, compatibility branches, helper APIs, tests, or existing patterns. It is less useful for harmless initial exploration, truncated directory listings, broad searches that are immediately followed by targeted range reads, or failures whose visible evidence is mainly semantic incompleteness, missing tests, API-contract misunderstanding, environment setup, or repetitive non-truncated commands.
experiences.experience: The source rubric judged whether the agent reacted to truncated output by narrowing the next inspection instead of confidently inventing missing content. This is a good retrieval target only when the omitted content is plausibly task-critical and the agent is about to rely on it. A strong trajectory explicitly follows truncation with focused `grep -n`, `sed -n` ranges, `head`/`tail`, symbol-specific searches, or smaller file reads, then bases claims only on visible lines. A weak trajectory reads a large file, receives a truncated observation, then asserts details about unseen branches, copies or rewrites a file, or patches around a function without confirming nearby behavior. However, do not use mere presence of narrowed commands as a general correctness proxy: an agent can recover from truncation well while still missing the required semantic boundary, compatibility behavior, or backend/frontend contract. Also avoid penalizing truncation when the visible snippet already contains the entire simple change needed and the omitted region is unrelated. Prioritize evidence that the agent’s claim or edit depends on hidden lines: whether it cites unseen code, whether it inspected the exact function body and call sites after truncation, whether it checked analogous implementations without assuming equivalence, and whether unresolved questions from the omitted output remain before patching.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Recovers Task-Critical Omitted Context Before Editing
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluate whether, after receiving visibly truncated tool output for files, functions, search results, or tests relevant to the task, the agent narrows its subsequent inspection enough to ground its reasoning and edits in observed code. Give credit when the agent uses targeted range reads, symbol searches, focused greps, smaller commands, or call-site/test inspection before making claims about omitted behavior. Withhold credit when the agent confidently infers unseen implementation details, edits based on a truncated full-file read, repeats broad commands without exposing the missing region, or treats unrelated visible snippets as sufficient despite clear unresolved hidden context.

required_visible_evidence: A recent observation includes explicit truncation or omitted output from a command touching potentially relevant code.
The agent's next reasoning or edit could depend on the omitted portion.
Subsequent commands either narrow to the omitted relevant area or fail to do so.
do_not_apply_when: The truncation is only from initial repository listing or broad discovery and no task-specific decision depends on hidden content.
The agent has already inspected the full relevant function or a precise range containing the needed behavior.
The main issue is semantic design, test coverage, dependency setup, or repeated untruncated commands rather than missing omitted context.

scale.1: The agent relies on truncated or omitted output to make specific claims or edits, with no targeted follow-up to inspect the missing relevant code.
scale.2: The agent performs minimal or poorly targeted follow-up after truncation, but important omitted regions that could affect the patch remain uninspected before reasoning or editing.
scale.3: The agent partially narrows after truncation and inspects some relevant lines, but still leaves plausible task-critical omitted context unresolved or makes some assumptions beyond visible evidence.
scale.4: The agent responds to truncation with focused searches or range reads covering the likely relevant function, branch, or call sites before editing, with only minor remaining uncertainty.
scale.5: The agent systematically converts truncated output into precise inspections of all task-critical omitted areas, grounds claims only in visible evidence, and avoids editing until the relevant context is recovered.

experiences.title: Retrieve Efficiency Guidance Only When a Repetition Pattern Is Observable
experiences.description: Retrieve for sufficiently developed trajectories that show repeated identical reads, broad whole-file dumps, noisy polling, or many low-information commands where targeted batching was available.
experiences.context: Some exploration is necessary in an unfamiliar repository, and one broad read or a few nearby inspections should not trigger a strong efficiency judgment. This guidance becomes useful when the visible history contains a sustained repetition loop or avoidable output bloat. It is less relevant for short trajectories and for distinct checks that each resolve a new uncertainty.
experiences.experience: The source rubric is discriminative when it measures information gained per action rather than raw step count. Reward targeted searches, bounded range reads, batched independent checks, and adaptation after each result. Penalize exact or near-identical commands that add no information, repeated self-inflicted debugging, and large reads where a precise query was already available. Do not confuse deliberate validation across different boundaries with redundancy.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Targeted Non-Redundant Tool Use
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Assess whether repository exploration and validation use bounded, information-seeking actions, batch compatible work, and adapt to prior results without repeated low-value reads or excessive output. Judge redundancy by duplicated information rather than by tool-call count alone.

observable_evidence: repeated identical or near-identical commands
scope and truncation of file reads
new information gained after each action
batching opportunities
distinction between exploration and repeated self-inflicted recovery

scale.1: The trajectory shows pervasive or unrecovered violations of targeted, non-redundant, information-efficient tool use that prevent reliable progress.
scale.2: The trajectory shows repeated weaknesses in targeted, non-redundant, information-efficient tool use; recovery is partial or costly.
scale.3: The evidence for targeted, non-redundant, information-efficient tool use is mixed: ordinary work proceeds, but notable avoidable violations remain.
scale.4: The trajectory demonstrates strong targeted, non-redundant, information-efficient tool use, with at most an isolated and promptly corrected lapse.
scale.5: The trajectory demonstrates consistently excellent targeted, non-redundant, information-efficient tool use throughout the visible work.

experiences.title: Scoped Edit Coherence After Implementation Starts
experiences.description: Retrieve when the task appears localized or mechanically scoped and the visible trajectory already includes source edits, especially if there are signs of brittle sed/script edits, repeated same-file surgery, unrelated file churn, or a need to distinguish a clean targeted patch from edit thrash.
experiences.context: Apply in SWE-agent trajectories for coding tasks in typical repository environments after the agent has begun modifying files or is near final review. This is most useful when the requested change should be narrow or systematic: a one-line propagation bug, a small template/filter fix, a local UI markup adjustment, or a command rename where all touched files should follow an obvious mapping. It is also useful when the recent steps show high-risk editing behavior such as repeated line-number sed operations, deletion/reinsertion of method blocks, accidental duplicate replacements, broad generated rewrites, or untracked environment workaround edits mixed with the task patch. Do not retrieve as a primary criterion during pure discovery before edits exist. Do not treat it as sufficient for semantic correctness when the hard part is an algorithmic boundary, compatibility contract, or domain-specific behavior; in those cases pair it with a rubric about the actual semantic invariant. For explicitly broad refactors, use this only to flag incoherent wholesale deletion or circular-import risk, not to penalize legitimate multi-file consolidation.
experiences.experience: The useful judgment is not simply whether the diff is small; it is whether the visible editing process and resulting direction remain coherent, scoped, and reviewable for the stated task. This rubric correctly helps when the agent repeatedly edits the same block with brittle commands, leaves evidence of syntax damage, changes unrelated runtime-compatibility files, updates tests/config to match an incomplete implementation, or performs automated broad replacements without checking all affected registrations/references. It should reward trajectories where the agent identifies the narrow source of the bug, makes a targeted change, inspects the diff, and runs focused validation without hiding failures through unrelated test/config churn. Avoid the tempting wrong criterion of equating 'minimal' with 'correct': a one-line change can still miss a required edge case, and a no-op or unsubmitted change can look tidy but not solve the task. Prioritize visible evidence such as git diff scope, whether modified files map directly to the requested behavior, whether repeated sed/script edits caused malformed code or duplicate decorators, whether old aliases/tests/docs are changed consistently rather than opportunistically, whether temporary environment fixes are kept out of the task patch, and whether the agent verifies the exact edited behavior after the final edit.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Coherent Scoped Patch Discipline
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Assess whether, relative to the parent trajectory state, the agent's visible implementation work is a coherent, scoped, and reviewable response to the task rather than brittle edit thrash or unrelated churn. Strong evidence includes a small or systematically bounded set of file edits that directly correspond to the requested behavior, careful inspection after modifying risky regions, preservation of existing behavior unless intentionally changed, no unrelated environment/workaround files in the patch, and focused validation of the changed behavior. Weak evidence includes repeated same-file line-number surgery, accidental deletion/reinsertion of methods, broad automated replacements without checking all affected call sites, unrelated formatting/config/test changes, or claims of completion without inspecting the final diff and validating the last edit.

best_for: patches where diff scope and edit process are visible
visible_evidence_to_check: recent edit commands and whether they are brittle or repeated
git diff or inspected file excerpts after edits
number and relevance of changed files
presence of unrelated environment, formatting, config, or test-only churn
whether focused validation was rerun after the final source edit
not_sufficient_for: completion/submission status without visible final diff
broad refactors where many files are inherently in scope

scale.1: The visible work is incoherent or high-risk: repeated blind edits to the same file, malformed or partially deleted code, unrelated file churn, test/config changes that could mask failures, or no reliable inspection of the final edited state.
scale.2: Some task-relevant edits exist, but the process shows notable instability such as brittle sed replacements, accidental broad changes, inconsistent alias/reference updates, or unresolved uncertainty about whether the edited code is syntactically and behaviorally intact.
scale.3: The child trajectory is roughly equivalent to the parent in edit discipline: edits are plausibly scoped but not yet well-validated, or there is limited evidence of final diff inspection and no clear signs of severe thrash.
scale.4: The implementation is mostly coherent and scoped: touched files align with the task, risky edits are inspected, unrelated churn is avoided, and focused checks or reproductions support the final edited behavior.
scale.5: The work is highly disciplined: the agent makes the minimal or systematically complete task-relevant changes, preserves compatibility and existing behavior, keeps temporary/environment work out of the patch, inspects the final diff, and validates the exact acceptance scenario after the final edit.

experiences.title: Do not treat code-context browsing as evidence of semantic completion
experiences.description: Retrieve this warning when an agent has already inspected nearby or upstream code, but the task requires preserving a behavioral contract, compatibility boundary, public API, migration semantics, or storage/deletion invariant that must be implemented and validated rather than merely localized.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE trajectories across Python/TypeScript web frameworks, ORMs, parsers, storage layers, and database code where the visible steps show substantial file/function inspection around the suspected error site, but the remaining challenge is choosing the correct abstraction boundary and proving the required behavior. Misleading cases include agents that inspect adjacent methods, grep related symbols, or debug line indexes, then make a local/obvious patch without demonstrating the task-level contract: non-destructive load behavior, major/minor version compatibility, preservation of public exception context, grouped query semantics, header/read/write invariants, or regression compatibility. The original surrounding-code rubric can still be appropriate early in localization, especially when the agent is about to patch only the stack-trace line without checking callers/callees. It becomes weak or misleading after localization is already done, during patch-review or final-quality prediction, unless the trajectory also shows contract-specific reasoning and validation.
experiences.experience: The previous rubric rewarded looking beyond the immediate failing line. That is sound as an early debugging heuristic, but it overstates progress when the trajectory already contains code browsing and the real risk is a semantically wrong or incomplete fix. A better rubric should focus on whether the agent connected the inspected context to the task’s invariant: what state must not be overwritten, which version boundary is compatible, which public attribute/API must be preserved across re-raises, which related queries can safely be combined, which writer/reader line indexes remain valid, or which collection behavior must remain non-regressed. Avoid the tempting criterion that repeated greps, sed output, commit-history inspection, or surrounding-class inspection alone indicates correctness. Prioritize visible evidence that the agent: identifies the owner layer for the behavior, states the compatibility/edge cases, updates all affected call paths or APIs, adds or runs targeted regression checks, and avoids broad local changes that merely silence the observed symptom.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories where the agent has localized and inspected relevant surrounding code but continues to rely on that inspection as the main justification for a patch, without visibly satisfying the task-level behavioral contract or validating compatibility-sensitive cases. This is especially relevant when the task describes preservation, migration, non-destructive loading, public error context, database version semantics, query grouping, or format read/write invariants, and the recent trajectory shows an obvious local edit, repeated source browsing, or ad hoc reproduction attempts rather than a contract-aware implementation plan and regression validation.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Context inspection without contract validation

visible_evidence_to_check: agent has already inspected nearby/upstream code or related classes
task requires a semantic invariant beyond fixing the immediate stack-trace line
patch plan or edits are localized to the first suspicious site without addressing all ownership/call-path boundaries
no targeted test or reproduction validates the stated invariant and compatibility cases
recent steps show repetitive greps/debug prints or environment setup instead of closing the semantic gap
metadata.source_rubric_boundary: Surrounding-code inspection remains useful only as an early localization rubric, not as a strong predictor once the unresolved question is semantic correctness.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory both inspected context and tied the patch to the required invariant with targeted validation or clear coverage of affected call paths.
scale.2: Minor evidence: some contract reasoning is present, but one secondary compatibility or validation point remains weak.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent inspected the right area and made plausible local changes, but validation and ownership-boundary reasoning are incomplete.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory mostly consists of browsing or local symptom fixing, with little proof that the task-level invariant, public API, or compatibility behavior is preserved.
scale.5: Severe evidence: despite extensive surrounding-code inspection, the agent repeats searches or makes a narrow/fragile patch that ignores explicit preservation, migration, public-context, grouping, or read/write requirements and lacks meaningful regression validation.

experiences.title: Do not use common-cause triage as a proxy for contract-correct fixes
experiences.description: Retrieve this warning when a trajectory is already past initial triage on a library/framework bug and the task hinges on preserving a specific user-visible API/data contract across an abstraction boundary.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE-agent evaluations for framework/library repositories such as Python ORMs, plotting/printing libraries, data-array libraries, Go converters/services, or similar systems where the issue statement names an exact semantic contract: user-provided names must not collide with internal keywords, registered identifiers must remain usable, coordinate/package metadata must be preserved, listen addresses must not be advertised as routable addresses, or supported expressions must be rewritten rather than rejected. In these settings, a broad 'check common causes first' rubric can be misleading after the agent has already found plausible code paths or reproduced the issue, because correctness depends on mapping the exact data flow and preserving compatibility behavior. The source rubric may still be appropriate during very early exploration when the agent has no concrete hypothesis and is deciding whether to inspect obvious configuration, dependency, environment, or call-stack causes before exotic explanations.
experiences.experience: The previous rubric rewarded evidence that the agent pursued common or obvious causes first. That can be reasonable for early diagnosis, but it overpredicts quality when the visible task already exposes a precise contract violation and the trajectory shows only plausible searching, repeated greps, environment setup, or a superficially common fix. In these cases, the common explanation was often not enough: rejecting a supported operation instead of rewriting it, guessing a routable address instead of using the connection peer, changing registry/default lookup behavior instead of preserving the registered name on the copied object, or repeatedly searching external types without implementing field mapping all miss the actual contract. A better rubric should focus on whether the agent identifies the boundary where user data is confused with internal control state, traces the relevant value through the implementation, and proposes a minimal compatibility-preserving change with regression coverage. Avoid the tempting criterion that a common-looking root cause, a nearby call stack, or many searches in likely files is strong evidence of eventual correctness. Replacement criteria should prioritize visible evidence such as: the agent distinguishes user-facing fields/names from internal API parameters, preserves existing valid behavior for genuine internal constructs, maps all required metadata fields rather than only the obvious ones, chooses support/wrapping over rejection when the issue asks for supported behavior, stops unproductive repeated commands, and patches/tests the component actually responsible for the contract.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Plausible common-cause diagnosis substitutes for contract tracing
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories where the agent treats a plausible common cause or obvious nearby code path as sufficient, without verifying the exact user-visible contract that the task requires. This is especially important for library/framework bugs involving name collisions, metadata preservation, registry aliases, address advertisement, converter field mapping, or query/expression rewriting. The flaw is present when the visible steps emphasize generic searches, repeated greps, environment setup, or a locally plausible patch, but do not demonstrate that the fix preserves the required external semantics and existing valid behavior.

visible_evidence_to_prioritize: exact data/control-flow from user input to failing behavior
distinction between user data fields/names and internal control parameters
minimal patch at the responsible abstraction boundary
regression test covering the named contract and compatibility boundary
avoidance of repeated uninformative searches or wrong-component edits
tempting_but_weak_evidence: agent inspected common files or call stack locations
agent found a plausible common cause
agent reproduced only an environment/dependency issue
agent made a broad rejection or fallback instead of preserving supported behavior

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the agent traces the exact contract violation, distinguishes internal and user-facing semantics, and plans or makes a targeted compatibility-preserving fix with relevant regression coverage.
scale.2: Minor evidence of the flaw: the agent starts from common causes but also validates the semantic boundary and avoids broad or rejecting fixes.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent has a plausible common-cause hypothesis and relevant files, but visible evidence only partially checks whether the external contract and existing behavior are preserved.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the agent relies mainly on a common-looking diagnosis or nearby code path and proposes/leans toward a fix that may reject supported behavior, drop metadata, guess values, or patch the wrong abstraction boundary.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory consists mostly of repeated searches, environment churn, or a superficial common-cause patch, with no demonstrated tracing of the required contract and no meaningful regression evidence.

experiences.title: Do not use methodical debugging as a proxy for semantic patch correctness
experiences.description: Retrieve this warning when an agent is tracing a complex framework bug step-by-step, but the key evaluation question is whether the eventual fix matches the observed API/semantic contract rather than whether the debugging process is orderly.
experiences.context: Applies in Python framework/library bug fixes such as Django ORM, Matplotlib axes/autoscale, or SymPy polynomial internals where the trajectory shows reproduction, code inspection, tracing, and one-at-a-time hypotheses, but the candidate direction may still target an intermediate symptom instead of the contract-breaking boundary. The source rubric may still be appropriate early in an investigation when the main visible risk is shotgun-editing many unrelated areas without isolating failures. It is misleading as a final-review or late-debugging criterion when the agent has already narrowed to a plausible subsystem and correctness depends on preserving a specific behavior: per-parent slicing semantics, shared-axis unit propagation, queryset immutability/select-list invariants, lazy related-object normalization, or algebraic factor preservation.
experiences.experience: The previous rubric judged whether the agent tested hypotheses one at a time and avoided shotgun debugging. That is useful process guidance, but in these cases it often over-rewarded trajectories that were orderly yet still wrong: the agent traced a real symptom, then patched a nearby mechanism without proving that the patch satisfied the user-visible invariant. A better rubric should focus on validated root-cause-to-fix alignment. Avoid the tempting criterion “the agent is being systematic, so the patch is likely correct.” Instead, prioritize visible evidence that the agent identified the exact semantic boundary from the task, explained why the proposed code change enforces that boundary, and either ran or planned a regression check matching the original scenario. Penalize trajectories where tests still fail, no patch exists, broad edits are made after a failed hypothesis, or the agent repeatedly inspects/traces the same area while missing visible evidence that the issue lies in a different layer.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: At late debugging or patch-review stage, the trajectory shows orderly hypothesis testing or extensive tracing but lacks evidence that the proposed fix addresses the task's required semantic invariant. This includes cases where the agent patches an intermediate symptom, broadens behavior in a core helper, changes documented/intentional behavior, leaves a reproduced failure unresolved, omits a regression scenario matching the report, or fails to connect the patch to the visible contract such as preserving existing limits/state, keeping queryset clones independent, retaining all algebraic factors, converting lazy related values at the correct layer, or implementing efficient per-parent slicing rather than merely avoiding an exception.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Orderly tracing without semantic fix validation

metadata.retrieval_stage: late investigation, patch proposal, or final review
visible_positive_evidence_to_require: the original failure has been reproduced or a close regression test is described
the agent states the user-visible invariant that must be preserved
the proposed change is tied to the correct abstraction boundary rather than only the stacktrace leaf
the trajectory checks that existing related behavior remains intact
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: methodical one-hypothesis-at-a-time debugging style by itself

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory connects the patch to the exact semantic contract and validates or clearly plans a matching regression check.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the debugging process is orderly and mostly aligned, but validation of the full reported contract is incomplete.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent identifies a plausible local mechanism but only partially connects it to the user-visible invariant or leaves important compatibility boundaries untested.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the agent follows a methodical trace yet patches a symptom or nearby helper without showing that the original scenario and related behaviors are fixed.
scale.5: Severe evidence: despite extensive step-by-step debugging, the trajectory has no viable patch or continues after failed tests/repeated inspection toward a direction contradicted by visible evidence of the required abstraction boundary.

experiences.title: Breadth recognition is weak evidence when the task is already broad or still unresolved
experiences.description: Retrieve this warning before using a “broader issue” rubric on trajectories for multi-component bugs, broad task statements, or early discovery loops where the agent has only named related areas without implementing and validating the required behavioral contract.
experiences.context: This applies in SWE-agent evaluations across Python, Go, TypeScript, and similar repositories when the original issue already names several affected systems, sources, backends, or edge cases, or when the recent trajectory is still searching, repeating greps, inspecting dependencies, or making unrelated environment-compatibility edits. In these situations, noticing that the bug may affect related functionality is not a reliable sign of patch quality: the decisive evidence is whether the agent has found the actual owner path and closed the specific boundary conditions. The source rubric can still apply when the task starts from a narrow symptom and the trajectory has concrete implementation evidence that the same root cause affects a small, well-justified sibling case, such as adding a parallel printer handler or fixing multiple methods sharing the same raw-subexpression-printing defect.
experiences.experience: The previous rubric rewarded agents for considering whether a symptom was part of a broader issue. That is sound only when breadth follows from a demonstrated common root cause and is accompanied by targeted code changes/tests. It is misleading when the task itself is broad, when the agent merely repeats broad searches, or when the real failure depends on a precise compatibility or boundary contract. In the sampled trajectories, broad recognition overestimated progress for cases where the agent had no patch, searched irrelevant areas, added unrelated compatibility fixes, or proposed a broad-looking change while missing a required dependency update, same-timezone no-op, TLS handshake size owner behavior, or multiple explicitly listed acceptance contracts. A better rubric should focus on contract closure: has the trajectory identified the actual code path that owns the failing behavior, implemented the required source/backends/environment boundaries, preserved negative cases, and validated with targeted tests or repros? Avoid the tempting criterion “the agent considered related functionality” unless there is visible evidence that the related functionality shares the same root cause and that the patch covers it without widening behavior incorrectly.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories on broad or multi-component bug reports when the agent receives credit mainly for recognizing related functionality but has not visibly closed the concrete behavioral contract. This includes cases where recent steps contain only discovery or repeated searches; the proposed direction names multiple affected components without proving the owner path; edits address adjacent compatibility/environment issues rather than the reported behavior; or the implementation covers a broad surface while missing required boundaries such as source-specific parsing, dependency/API support, no-op conditions, preservation of unaffected environments, or targeted regression coverage.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Broad-scope recognition without contract implementation

primary_visible_evidence: original issue already enumerates multiple affected components, sources, backends, or edge cases
recent trajectory is mostly search, inspection, or repeated commands rather than implementation
agent states a broad hypothesis but lacks owner-path confirmation
edits or plan omit required boundary behavior or compatibility prerequisite
tests, if any, do not exercise the mandatory source/environment/negative cases
do_not_trigger_when: the issue begins as a narrow symptom
the agent demonstrates a common root cause shared by a closely related sibling case
the implementation and tests cover both the original symptom and the justified sibling without unrelated widening

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: breadth, if mentioned, is tied to a concrete root cause, implemented behavior, and relevant validation.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the agent mentions related areas somewhat speculatively, but the main owner path and key boundary behavior are still being addressed.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory recognizes broad scope and has partial implementation or plans, but visible evidence leaves important acceptance boundaries, negative cases, or dependency compatibility unproven.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the agent relies on broad recognition while missing a required owner path, no-op/negative condition, data-source conversion, dependency support, or targeted regression test.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory is mostly broad searching or unrelated edits, has no meaningful implementation for the reported contract, or treats an already broad task as solved merely by naming its breadth.

experiences.title: Branch-Sensitive Fix Review
experiences.description: Retrieve when the candidate fix changes a conditional, version gate, feature flag, or empty/non-empty case split and correctness depends on preserving both the newly fixed path and the previously working path.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE-agent repair trajectories for Python, Go, or similar codebases at the implementation or final-review stage, after the agent has identified or edited a concrete conditional decision point. It is most useful when the task statement itself contrasts two semantic branches, such as flag enabled vs disabled, old vs new backend version, explicit vs implicit value, empty vs non-empty suffix, authentication vs non-authentication error, or annotated None vs unit-valued return. Do not retrieve it as the main rubric during early exploration before a branch has been selected, for purely unconditional refactors, or when visible evidence shows the conditional is only one small part of a broader contract such as response formatting, schema migration, or end-to-end error propagation.
experiences.experience: The source rubric judged whether a conditional fix was checked on both sides rather than only on the originally broken path. This is discriminative when the patch’s main risk is a branch boundary: adding a separator only for non-empty suffixes, preserving ordinary skip behavior while changing xfail control flow, mapping a setting differently by backend version, or skipping return-unit conversion only for None. In those situations, visible evidence that the agent reasoned about or tested both true and false paths strongly predicts a safer patch. However, the criterion can be misleading if the agent merely adds a plausible conditional without validating the unaffected branch, or if the task requires additional downstream behavior beyond the conditional. A better retrieved rubric should focus on explicit branch coverage: identify the exact predicate, enumerate the semantic cases it separates, and look for tests/static reasoning showing the new branch works while legacy/default/opposite branches remain unchanged. Avoid the tempting proxy of rewarding the presence of an if-statement or a single reproduction passing; prioritize evidence such as paired examples, version/flag matrices, empty and non-empty inputs, auth and non-auth errors, or before/after behavior for both sides of the condition.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Both Branches of the Changed Predicate Are Accounted For
reference_golden_rubrics.description: When the repair introduces or modifies a conditional, version gate, flag check, or empty/non-empty split, the trajectory should make clear that the agent has validated or convincingly reasoned about every semantic branch affected by that predicate. Strong evidence includes naming the predicate, explaining what behavior belongs on each side, and using tests, focused scripts, or code inspection to show that the originally broken path is fixed without regressing the opposite or legacy path. The criterion should be applied only when the visible trajectory contains a concrete conditional decision relevant to the bug.

required_visible_evidence: A concrete changed or proposed conditional, branch, version gate, feature flag, or empty/non-empty split.
Identification of at least two semantic cases separated by the predicate.
Validation or explicit reasoning for both the newly fixed case and the previously working/default/opposite case.
do_not_reward_for: Only adding an if-statement without checking the opposite branch.
Ignoring broader non-conditional requirements when the task demands them.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent considered the opposite branch; the trajectory focuses only on the failing case or simply adds a conditional.
scale.2: Weak branch awareness: the agent mentions another branch but does not inspect, reason through, or validate its behavior.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent’s conditional is plausible and one branch is validated, with limited but incomplete reasoning about the other branch.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the agent explicitly describes both semantic branches and validates or statically checks that both produce the intended behavior.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the agent enumerates all relevant branch combinations, including legacy/default and edge cases, and validates them with targeted tests or precise code-level reasoning while noting any broader requirements outside the conditional.

experiences.title: Do not reward explicit checklist recognition as implicit-requirement discovery
experiences.description: Retrieve this warning when a task already spells out nuanced acceptance criteria and the trajectory merely identifies or restates them without visible evidence of a contract-compatible implementation.
experiences.context: Applies across SWE repair/addition tasks in Python, Go, TypeScript, Ansible modules, web APIs, and server configuration code where the prompt explicitly names requirements such as idempotency, lifecycle cleanup, accessibility labels, ordered message routing, validation states, reverse-proxy URL behavior, check mode, or preview/no-write behavior. In these cases, a rubric about identifying implicit requirements can be misleading because recognizing broad concerns is not the main risk; the important question is whether the agent connected the stated behavior to the existing API, persistence, configuration, UI, or test contracts. The source rubric can still be appropriate when the user request is underspecified and the code context strongly implies an unstated constraint, such as concurrency safety, backwards compatibility, security validation, or idempotency that the prompt did not mention.
experiences.experience: The previous rubric judged whether the agent identified implicit requirements. That can be useful for vague tasks, but it over-credits trajectories where the requirements are already explicit and the agent only repeats them, explores around them, or implements a superficial parallel path. A better rubric should focus on whether the visible trajectory shows contract-preserving execution: locating the existing side-effect boundary, reusing the normal processing pipeline instead of duplicating it, preserving documented option names and defaults, integrating with established helpers or module bases, handling all stated states/backends/endpoints, and validating with targeted tests or realistic command-generation checks. Avoid the tempting criterion that the agent mentioned hidden concerns like idempotency, lifecycle management, accessibility, or preview semantics; in these tasks those are not hidden. Prioritize evidence that the patch plan or edits are anchored to existing interfaces, data model semantics, side-effect controls, and observable outputs required by the task.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Explicit requirement checklist without contract integration
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for tasks with detailed stated acceptance criteria when the agent mainly restates or recognizes those criteria, or makes broad speculative edits, without visible evidence that the implementation is integrated through the repository's existing contracts. This includes adding a separate preview or validation path instead of reusing the normal pipeline with side effects disabled, adding lifecycle cancellation without proving the polling loop and close contract are coordinated, changing configuration semantics without preserving existing path/host behavior, implementing module options or API calls with names/endpoints that are not verified against nearby patterns, or stopping at exploration/repeated searches while claiming requirement understanding.

applicable_when: The prompt already enumerates specific behavioral requirements or acceptance criteria.
The trajectory contains requirement summaries, exploratory searches, or superficial edits but little evidence of tracing the real contract boundary.
Correctness depends on compatibility with existing APIs, config semantics, persistence/write boundaries, UI accessibility semantics, or module option conventions.
prioritize_visible_evidence: Edits reuse the existing normal execution path with a save/check/preview flag rather than duplicating behavior.
The agent verifies exact option names, defaults, endpoint paths, helper locations, and return fields from adjacent code.
The trajectory covers all explicitly named states/backends/entity types and side-effect boundaries.
Validation or tests target the stated behavior rather than only syntax, imports, or isolated helper output.
avoid_overcrediting: Mentioning idempotency, lifecycle cleanup, accessibility, validation, or preview behavior when those requirements are already in the task.
Assuming a new helper or config knob is correct without checking existing compatibility semantics.
Treating broad exploration or repeated unsuccessful searches as implementation progress.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory ties stated requirements to the existing contracts and validates the side-effect or compatibility boundary.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the agent recognizes explicit requirements and mostly follows existing contracts, but one boundary or verification step is weak.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent understands the task but implementation evidence is partial, with some speculative helpers or unverified interface assumptions.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the agent restates explicit requirements or makes broad edits while missing important existing API, persistence, config, lifecycle, or validation contracts.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory is mostly exploration/repetition or a disconnected implementation path that does not demonstrate integration with the required repository contracts.

experiences.title: Do not let generic error-style idioms substitute for protocol or feature contracts
experiences.description: Retrieve this warning when a trajectory uses normal language error mechanisms but the task’s acceptance depends on specific API contracts, state propagation, status codes, context preservation, generated interfaces, polling semantics, or integration ordering.
experiences.context: This applies across Go, Python, and JavaScript/Node repositories when the visible work already uses exceptions, returned errors, wrapping, or framework response helpers in a broadly idiomatic way, yet the task requires a precise behavioral contract: e.g. a named public interface must exist, an HTTP endpoint must return a specific status/body shape, an exception must preserve a public source object, a health/readiness state must update from component heartbeats, an OCI source must satisfy a context-aware interface, or telemetry must actually emit/persist the required anonymous event. The source rubric may still be appropriate when the trajectory visibly introduces ad-hoc error signaling, stringly status checks, swallowed exceptions, panics instead of returned errors, or non-framework response handling that directly threatens correctness. It is misleading when the main observable risk is not error-handling style but whether the patch implements the domain semantics and compatibility boundaries demanded by the task.
experiences.experience: The previous rubric rewarded idiomatic error handling: using Go error returns/wrapping, Python exceptions, or Express response helpers instead of ad-hoc mechanisms. That judgment can be locally true while still overpredicting patch quality because many trajectories failed despite idiomatic-looking errors: they added partial APIs without the required public types or generated stubs, placed interceptors after options were already built, returned a syntactically valid but contractually wrong HTTP status, lost required YAML object context through lazy evaluation recursion, polled the wrong health signal, or built a source that did not satisfy the context-aware interface. A better rubric should focus on the explicit external contract named in the task and on visible evidence that the implementation is wired end-to-end and validated. Avoid the tempting criterion “uses idiomatic errors/status helpers” as a substitute for checking the required semantics. Replacement criteria should prioritize: named API/interface compatibility, preservation of specified metadata or source context through catch/reraise paths, exact status/code/body requirements, correct event or polling source, correct initialization/order of middleware or services, generated artifacts when proto/API files change, and tests/builds that exercise the new contract rather than only unrelated or preexisting paths.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories where the implementation relies on generally idiomatic error returns, exceptions, or response helpers but lacks visible evidence that the task-specific behavioral contract is implemented end-to-end. This includes using normal error propagation while omitting required public symbols or generated API artifacts, returning the wrong specified HTTP/status/error payload, failing to preserve required error context metadata, wiring middleware or services in an order that prevents the new behavior from running, polling a generic or wrong health signal instead of the component signal named by the design, or implementing only a partial adapter that does not match the repository interface. The flaw is strongest when the recent trajectory shows repeated syntax/placement struggles, no focused tests for the new contract, or validation limited to builds/unrelated tests.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Idiomatic errors masking missing contract semantics

better_evidence_to_prioritize: Exact task-required API/interface symbols or generated stubs are present and used by callers
Specified status codes, machine-readable error codes, response fields, or public exception attributes are explicitly implemented
Errors preserve required metadata/source objects across catch, wrap, warning, and re-raise paths without triggering lazy evaluation or recursion
New services, interceptors, sources, or monitors are wired before dependent options are constructed and are registered in the actual runtime path
Polling/subscription logic uses the intended signal and interface signature, including context-aware operations when required
Focused tests or manual validation exercise the new behavior, not only preexisting tests or unrelated build success
metadata.misleading_proxy_to_avoid: Counting language-idiomatic error handling as strong evidence when the visible task is about a precise protocol, integration, or compatibility contract.

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory demonstrates the task-specific contract end-to-end and error handling supports that contract.
scale.2: Minor evidence: errors are idiomatic and most contract elements are addressed, but one edge of status/context/wiring validation is weak.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: implementation has idiomatic errors but only partial visible proof of the required external behavior or integration.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the patch uses normal error mechanisms while missing a key required API/status/context/wiring/polling/interface contract.
scale.5: Most severe evidence: the trajectory is dominated by generic error-style changes or build-only validation while the core requested contract is absent, wrongly wired, or contradicted by visible code.

experiences.title: Do not treat any cleanup primitive as lifecycle correctness
experiences.description: Retrieve this warning when a task mentions cleanup, shutdown, stale data, locks, polling goroutines, terminal state, or resource leaks, but the visible trajectory shows only generic cleanup reasoning such as adding Close, finally, delete/pop, or restore without proving the task-specific lifecycle contract.
experiences.context: Applies in Go, Python, and Node.js SWE tasks where lifecycle language is present but the real requirement is semantic: retaining process records for a grace period, restoring terminal state across interrupts and process exit, rejecting concurrent requests with the right scope and response behavior, or stopping backend polling goroutines without changing unrelated storage semantics. The original Reliable Resource Cleanup rubric can still apply when the main visible risk is a concrete low-level resource leak such as file handles, network clients, contexts, timers, goroutines, terminal modes, or exporter/processors that have a clearly identified owner and shutdown path. It is misleading when the trajectory has not yet implemented code, when cleanup is only incidental to a broader protocol/configuration feature, or when the agent equates deletion/Close/finally with correctness without checking owner behavior, retention requirements, compatibility, or tests.
experiences.experience: The previous rubric judged whether the agent handled cleanup using context managers, try/finally, RAII, or Close-like methods. That is sometimes correct, for example when a password prompt leaves the terminal in no-echo mode or polling goroutines need a cancellable owner. However, it becomes over-optimistic when the task uses words like cleanup or shutdown but correctness depends on a more specific lifecycle boundary. A future rubric should not reward the mere presence of `finally`, `Close()`, `delete`, `pop`, or terminal restore calls. Instead, it should ask whether the agent identified the resource/data owner, when the lifecycle begins and ends, what state must remain observable, and whether cleanup is triggered on every required path such as interrupt, successful completion, failed validation, concurrent overlap, or application shutdown. Avoid the tempting criterion 'adds cleanup to prevent leaks' when visible evidence shows broad rewrites, premature deletion of user-visible data, missing dependency/configuration compatibility, lock cleanup without correct rejection semantics, or cancellation added without preserving existing behavior. Replacement criteria should prioritize task-specific evidence: correct scope of locks or cancellation, preservation of existing public behavior, delayed/tombstoned data retention when required, signal/exit handling for global terminal readers, and tests or code paths that exercise the problematic lifecycle transition.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that rely on superficial cleanup constructs while failing to demonstrate the task-specific lifecycle contract. This applies when the visible task is about stale user-visible records, terminal restoration, concurrent request exclusion, polling goroutine shutdown, or telemetry/exporter shutdown, and the agent adds or plans cleanup primitives without showing that the cleanup is owned by the right component, occurs at the right time, preserves required observable state, and covers required error/interrupt/success paths. Do not apply this as a penalty when the trajectory has only just begun investigation and has not proposed a cleanup-based solution yet, or when the visible implementation explicitly ties cleanup to the correct owner and lifecycle boundary.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Superficial cleanup instead of semantic lifecycle ownership

evidence_to_prioritize: task-visible lifecycle boundary and owner
whether cleanup triggers on success, failure, interrupt, and shutdown paths relevant to the task
whether user-visible data retention or compatibility behavior is preserved
whether lock/cancel/Close logic is scoped to the correct user, request, backend, or singleton
whether tests or reasoning exercise the lifecycle transition rather than only syntax/build success
