misleading_evidence_to_downweight: generic restore/cancel calls without signal or owner integration
large lifecycle rewrites that alter unrelated semantics

scale.1: No evidence of superficial cleanup: the trajectory either has not proposed a cleanup solution yet or clearly reasons about the correct lifecycle owner and required observable behavior.
scale.2: Minor risk: cleanup primitives are mentioned, but the agent also investigates the relevant owner, timing, and compatibility boundaries.
scale.3: Moderate concern: the solution adds a plausible cleanup mechanism but leaves unclear whether it covers all required paths or preserves existing behavior.
scale.4: Clear flaw: the trajectory treats adding delete/finally/Close/cancel/restore as sufficient while missing an important lifecycle path, retention rule, scope boundary, or public behavior requirement.
scale.5: Severe flaw: the cleanup-focused approach directly conflicts with the task contract or introduces broad unrelated rewrites, such as deleting data that should remain visible for a grace period, closing a global reader at the wrong point, breaking existing storage semantics, or cleaning a lock while not enforcing the required concurrent rejection behavior.

experiences.title: Contract-Level Validation at Exposed Boundaries
experiences.description: Retrieve this when a task centers on rejecting malformed, missing, unsafe, or no-op inputs at an externally reachable boundary such as an HTTP API, config loader, protocol parser, or security-sensitive form.
experiences.context: Apply in web/API, CLI config, UI form, and protocol-parser environments when the problem statement explicitly names required fields, malformed input behavior, normalization rules, or boundary-safety requirements, and the trajectory shows the agent editing or planning validation in the reachable entrypoint before downstream processing. This is most useful at implementation or review time, after the boundary and expected contract are visible. Do not apply as the main criterion for broad feature work where persistence, routing, ownership, selection semantics, redirects, or aggregation are equally central unless those pieces are already addressed. Also avoid applying it when the agent has only added generic guard clauses without confirming the exact public route/config schema/protocol offsets/form component is wired into the real workflow.
experiences.experience: The previous rubric judged whether inputs were validated at public API boundaries rather than assuming correct callers. That is directionally correct for tasks about invalid request data, weak passphrases, incomplete auth configuration, packet offset bounds, or update bodies with missing identifiers. However, it can be misleading if it rewards any added validation. In the observed pattern, incomplete patches often added some checks but missed the full contract: required fields were only partly covered, valid default bodies were not handled, wrong field names or routes were introduced, existing validation components were bypassed, ownership/authentication constraints were ignored, or broader feature behavior such as persistence and selection remained broken. A better rubric should focus on complete contract-level validation at the actual exposed boundary: all specified missing/malformed/no-op cases are rejected before side effects or unsafe slicing; valid inputs still flow through unchanged; errors match the established API/config style; normalization is deterministic; and the trajectory includes evidence that the agent verified both invalid and valid cases through the real entrypoint. Avoid the tempting proxy of 'the patch added an if-statement near an API method' or 'the agent mentioned validation'; prioritize visible evidence that the exact external contract is enforced end-to-end.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Complete Boundary Contract Validation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates that the agent is enforcing the specified input contract at the actual externally reachable boundary, before unsafe operations or downstream side effects. It should cover every required missing, malformed, weak, out-of-range, no-op, or normalization case named by the task; preserve valid behavior; use established error/feedback conventions; and verify the checks through the real route/config loader/form/parser rather than an unconnected helper or invented endpoint.

prioritize_evidence: Identification of the real public entrypoint or parser/config/form boundary that receives untrusted input
Validation occurs before downstream calls, database writes, export/encryption, protocol slicing, or other side effects
All task-specified required fields and invalid cases are covered, not just one example
Valid inputs are still accepted and normalized according to the expected format
Error responses or feedback follow existing project conventions and include required context when applicable
Trajectory includes tests, fixtures, or manual checks for both failing invalid inputs and successful valid inputs through the actual workflow
do_not_reward_as_sufficient: Generic guard clauses that cover only missing truthy values
Validation added to an unused helper, wrong route, wrong config key, or non-public code path
Inventing unrelated endpoints or behavior instead of enforcing the existing contract
Ignoring authentication, ownership, routing, persistence, or selection requirements that are part of the same public contract
Only checking start offsets or single fields when the task names multiple boundary ranges or required fields
applicable_boundaries: Security-sensitive form submission and field validation
Update endpoints that must reject missing identifiers or empty update bodies

scale.1: Little or no evidence that validation is being added at the real exposed boundary; changes are exploratory, unrelated, or only assume well-formed callers.
scale.2: Some validation is added, but it is partial, generic, or may be in the wrong layer; important required fields, malformed cases, valid-flow preservation, or integration evidence are missing.
scale.3: Validation is comparable to the parent trajectory: it targets a plausible boundary and covers several obvious invalid cases, but completeness across the task contract or proof through the actual workflow remains uncertain.
scale.4: Strong evidence that validation is placed at the correct boundary, covers most named invalid cases, uses established errors/feedback, and preserves normal valid behavior, with some verification.
scale.5: Complete evidence that the real public contract is enforced end-to-end: every specified invalid/no-op/normalization case is handled before side effects or unsafe access, valid cases are verified, and the implementation is integrated into the existing route/config/form/parser without unrelated behavior.

experiences.title: Do not let concurrency-shaped evidence replace the feature contract
experiences.description: Retrieve this warning when a task mentions concurrency, async, streaming, load, forks, or shutdown, but the visible trajectory mainly needs validation against a specific behavioral/API/lifecycle contract rather than generic thread-safety hygiene.
experiences.context: Applies in Go, TypeScript/JavaScript, and Python repositories where problem statements include concurrent requests, streaming, forked workers, large-scale load, initialization/shutdown, or async races. The misleading pattern is that a trajectory adds or discusses a lock, queue, goroutine-safe primitive, snapshot timing change, sync.Once, or stream write fix, and the broad concurrency rubric would reward that evidence even though the patch has not shown the task-specific contract is satisfied. It is especially risky during early exploration with no patch, or final review of partial patches that address only a generic race/deadlock symptom. The original safe-concurrency rubric can still apply when the patch genuinely introduces shared mutable state, goroutines, multiprocessing queues, cursor buffers, locks, or async callbacks and the central acceptance risk is race freedom, deadlock avoidance, correct blocking behavior, and resource cleanup. It should not be the primary rubric when visible evidence shows the harder question is protocol compatibility, API return-shape propagation, authoritative state snapshots, user-facing error mapping, lifecycle ownership, or the correct root cause under load.
experiences.experience: The previous rubric judged whether the agent considered safe idiomatic concurrency: guarding shared state, avoiding blocking in async contexts, and using standard synchronization primitives. That is sound as a secondary safety check, but it becomes misleading when selected solely because the task text contains words like concurrent, streaming, forked, under load, or shutdown. In these cases it can overvalue superficial fixes such as adding a lock around one internal call, adding a queue without integrating parent-side handling and shutdown behavior, moving an async snapshot earlier without using the authoritative data source, or fixing one stream builder race while leaving the public token-count contract unchanged. A better rubric should focus on the observable behavioral contract: the correct scope and owner of a concurrency guard, whether all relevant call paths and response/error mappings are covered, whether protocol selection and dependencies are actually wired, whether streaming/multi-step accounting is propagated through public APIs, whether forked output is proxied without removing necessary shutdown defenses, or whether investigation identified the real bottleneck rather than assuming contention. Avoid the tempting criterion “the patch uses a lock/queue/sync primitive, so it is concurrency-safe.” Prioritize visible evidence that the agent traced the full call path from external symptom to authoritative state change, preserved lifecycle cleanup and backward compatibility, updated all public callers/tests/config/dependencies as needed, and validated the acceptance behavior under the scenario described.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that treat a concurrency-related symptom as solved merely by adding or discussing a synchronization primitive, queue, async ordering tweak, or stream write change, while visible evidence shows the task-specific behavioral contract remains unaddressed or unverified. This includes patches that guard the wrong owner or call path, use an unstable or overly narrow lock key, release before the full externally visible operation completes, introduce user-facing errors without proper mapping, omit required dependency/config/API propagation, remove existing shutdown safeguards without replacement, or focus on a suspected race/load issue without identifying the actual bottleneck. Do not apply this penalty when the trajectory is still in early repository exploration and no implementation judgment is being made, or when the visible patch fully covers the external contract and the remaining concern is only conventional race/deadlock hygiene.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Concurrency primitive without contract coverage

primary_evidence: task acceptance criteria require a specific externally visible behavior beyond generic thread safety
trajectory evidence centers on a lock, queue, sync.Once, goroutine/channel, async snapshot, stream write, or shutdown tweak
visible edits or plan do not demonstrate coverage of all relevant call paths, APIs, lifecycle cleanup, configuration/dependencies, or user-visible responses
avoid_as_proxy: partial cleanup in a finally/defer block without proving operation scope
early exploration commands that have not yet produced a patch
replacement_focus: external behavior under the described concurrent/async/load scenario
correct owner and duration of locks or lifecycle hooks
authoritative data source and snapshot timing
public API and caller propagation
dependency/configuration compatibility
preservation of shutdown and cleanup guarantees

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory either has not yet made an implementation claim, or the patch visibly satisfies the task-specific contract and any concurrency primitive is correctly scoped and integrated.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the trajectory emphasizes generic concurrency safety, but also investigates most relevant call paths and has a plausible plan to verify the external behavior.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the patch adds a plausible lock/queue/async/sync mechanism, but coverage of key API, lifecycle, response, dependency, or authoritative-state requirements is incomplete or unverified.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the implementation relies on a superficial concurrency mechanism while visibly missing an important contract boundary such as the correct owner, full operation duration, caller propagation, protocol wiring, or shutdown behavior.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory confidently treats the concurrency-shaped change as sufficient despite strong visible signs that it targets the wrong root cause or leaves the main acceptance behavior impossible, broken, or untested.

experiences.title: Behavior Preservation for Refactor-Only Changes
experiences.description: Retrieve this when the task is explicitly a refactor, API cleanup, or maintainability change where existing runtime behavior should remain stable except for narrowly requested contract changes.
experiences.context: Applies in Python, Go, or TypeScript repositories when the visible task language emphasizes simplification, replacing an implementation with an equivalent abstraction, reducing redundancy, or improving maintainability, and the trajectory has already made concrete code edits. It is most useful at implementation-review stage, when visible evidence includes changed signatures, updated callers, altered helper boundaries, rewritten traversal/cache logic, or return-shape refactors. Do not use it as the primary criterion when the task mainly requires a new public component, new validation behavior, static-analysis configuration work, or an explicitly accepted output change; in those cases, behavior preservation is secondary to satisfying the new contract. It is also premature during early exploration before the agent has made or proposed edits.
experiences.experience: The prior rubric judged whether a refactor avoided unintended observable behavior changes. That judgment is useful when the requested change is structurally motivated but downstream behavior must remain the same: for example, preserving selected database aliases after an API simplification, preserving externally visible paths while changing filesystem abstraction, preserving cache contents while removing pointer indirection, or preserving all consumers when changing tuple-like returns to named objects. It becomes misleading when used alone for tasks whose correctness depends on a specific new structural requirement, such as reusing an existing cache rather than merely avoiding behavior changes, moving configuration into a public component, or meeting lint/complexity thresholds. A better retrieved rubric should combine behavior preservation with exact refactor intent: verify both that the new abstraction/signature/data shape is actually adopted and that existing outputs, side effects, ordering, error handling, filtering, and public contracts are unchanged unless the task explicitly names a behavior change. Avoid the tempting proxy of rewarding broad rewrites, passing superficial smoke checks, or changing all visible call sites without checking semantic equivalence. Prioritize visible evidence such as exhaustive caller searches, tests or direct checks for old behavior, audits of boundary semantics like path relativity vs display paths, cache ownership, status filtering, return field names, and absence of unrelated logic rewrites.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Exact Refactor Intent with Observable Behavior Preservation
reference_golden_rubrics.description: For refactor-only or maintainability tasks, the trajectory should show that the agent implemented the requested structural change while preserving the prior observable contract everywhere not explicitly changed by the task. Strong evidence includes updating all affected producers and consumers, retaining side effects and data semantics, checking edge cases where the new abstraction could subtly change behavior, and avoiding unrelated rewrites.

applicable_task_types: implementation replacement with equivalent library or abstraction
prioritized_visible_evidence: all call sites or consumers audited and updated
old observable outputs or side effects explicitly compared against new behavior
task-specific invariants preserved except explicitly requested changes
no unrelated algorithmic rewrites or deleted behavior
validation attempts target both new structure and old behavior
non_applicable_or_secondary_when: task primarily introduces new validation/public component behavior
task explicitly accepts an output change
agent is still only exploring files
success depends mainly on lint/configuration thresholds rather than runtime equivalence

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the requested refactor was implemented or that existing behavior was considered; edits are absent, speculative, or clearly unrelated.
scale.2: Some structural edits are visible, but the trajectory does not audit important consumers or semantic invariants, making behavior preservation uncertain.
scale.3: The trajectory implements part of the refactor and updates obvious consumers, but validation is incomplete or misses plausible behavior-changing boundaries.
scale.4: The trajectory strongly preserves existing behavior while adopting the requested refactor, with caller audits and targeted checks for key semantics; only minor validation gaps remain.
scale.5: The trajectory fully implements the requested structural change, exhaustively updates affected consumers, explicitly verifies old observable behavior and new contract boundaries, and avoids unrelated functional rewrites.

experiences.title: End-to-End Error Classification Contract
experiences.description: Retrieve this when the task is explicitly about changing, preserving, or refactoring exception/error handling semantics, especially expected error classes, access-denied vs internal-error classification, or user-facing failure messages.
experiences.context: Applies in Python, Go, JavaScript, or similar service/library code when the issue statement names an actual vs expected exception, error type, status classification, or fallback behavior, and the trajectory is inspecting or editing catch/wrap/return/logging paths. It is especially relevant after the agent has found the local code that converts low-level errors into project-specific errors. It may be insufficient if the user-visible behavior also depends on a downstream response writer, serializer, API adapter, or client-facing error body that the agent has not inspected. It is less relevant for pure feature extraction or cleanup refactors unless the extraction changes error propagation, logging, or return-on-failure behavior.
experiences.experience: The prior rubric judged whether error handling semantics were preserved through a change. This is useful when the visible defect is a wrong error boundary: for example, a low-level parsing/encoding failure should become a project-specific invalid-input exception, or an auth failure should remain access-denied while unrelated setup failures retain their original type. However, a better retrieval target should not stop at the nearest local catch block. It should evaluate the complete user-visible error contract: which underlying errors are detected, which are converted, which are wrapped unchanged, what message/status/body reaches callers, and whether existing legitimate denial or placeholder behavior is preserved. Avoid the tempting proxy that any added catch, any project-specific wrapper, or any non-access-denied return is correct. Also avoid over-rewarding patches that only fix an internal return type while ignoring the framework layer that formats the response, or patches that replace structured typed errors with string matching. Prioritize visible evidence from the task’s expected/actual error class or message, the agent’s inspection of typed error predicates and wrapping conventions, downstream response serialization/writing paths, and tests or reproductions that assert the externally observed exception/status/message rather than only local control flow.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: User-Visible Error Semantics Preserved
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Assess whether the agent’s approach preserves the intended end-to-end error contract while fixing the reported failure. A strong solution identifies the exact boundary where errors are converted or masked, uses structured exception/error types or project-provided predicates instead of brittle string checks, keeps expected authorization/validation failures mapped to the documented project-level error, leaves unrelated internal/setup failures wrapped or propagated with their original classification, and accounts for any downstream layer that formats errors into API responses or template/filter errors. Evidence should come from the visible task statement, inspected code paths, proposed edits, and validation commands that exercise the user-facing behavior.

apply_when: Task describes actual vs expected exception, error type, status code, or failure message
Trajectory inspects catch, wrap, return, logging, or response-formatting code
Patch plan changes how errors are classified, converted, propagated, or displayed
prioritize_evidence: Exact expected user-facing exception/status/message from the issue statement
Typed error predicates, exception classes, or structured error objects used by the project
Whether downstream handlers preserve or reformat the classification correctly
Regression checks covering both the reported failure and existing valid failure paths
avoid_as_proxy: Local wrapping change without checking final caller-visible response
String matching when structured error types are available
Treating every failure as validation/auth denial
Treating any undefined/internal error as acceptable without preserving framework error conventions

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent identified or preserved the relevant error contract; proposed work ignores the stated expected error type/message or changes unrelated code.
scale.2: Weak evidence: the agent notices an error-handling site but uses a broad or brittle conversion, or validates only that an error occurs without checking the required class/status/message.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent fixes a plausible local conversion/wrapping issue and preserves some existing behavior, but has not accounted for downstream formatting or all important error categories.
scale.4: Strong evidence: the agent distinguishes expected validation/auth failures from internal/unexpected failures using project conventions and checks the reported user-visible behavior.
scale.5: Strongest evidence: the agent verifies the complete path from underlying failure through conversion/wrapping to the final caller/API/template response, preserves existing legitimate error semantics, and adds or runs targeted regression coverage for both changed and unchanged failure modes.

experiences.title: Don’t treat explicit performance tasks as speculative micro-optimization
experiences.description: Retrieve this warning when the task itself names a concrete performance regression, no-op overhead, cache gap, or measured bottleneck; avoid using a generic anti-micro-optimization rubric as the main correctness signal.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE-agent evaluations for Python/Django, Go services, browser/config tooling, security scanners, or automation engines where the original issue is explicitly about performance and often also states required behavior such as ordering, cache consistency, filtering, signal registration, or preserving explicit user actions. The misleading case is when a rubric that says to avoid speculative performance work is retrieved for an agent that is supposed to implement a small or localized optimization backed by the issue report or by traced code evidence. The source rubric can still apply when the agent invents unrelated performance refactors, rewrites broad subsystems without evidence, benchmarks toy code unrelated to the production path, or optimizes a non-critical path while ignoring the reported bug.
experiences.experience: The previous rubric judged whether the agent avoided speculative performance refactoring and targeted verified bottlenecks. That is useful only as a guardrail against side quests. It is misleading as a primary criterion when the task is itself a performance bug or feature request with concrete evidence, because it may under-credit valid small optimizations or over-credit any benchmark-driven change that does not satisfy the real API/behavioral contract. A better rubric should ask whether the agent targets the named hot path and preserves the visible semantics: e.g. no-op hooks are skipped only when truly no-op, caches include correct serialization/invalidation/order boundaries, narrowed queries still fetch fields required for cascades/signals, data-structure changes preserve iteration and equality behavior, and multi-part requests do not drop non-performance requirements such as inactive filtering or rescue/failure state. Avoid the tempting criterion “micro-optimization is bad unless extensively benchmarked” or “a benchmark plus a faster structure means correctness.” Prioritize visible evidence from the task text, traced call path, existing comments/tests, edge conditions, and validation runs that exercise both performance motivation and functional compatibility.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Performance fix ignores the stated semantic contract
reference_golden_rubrics.description: For tasks where the original request explicitly identifies a performance regression, no-op overhead, cache gap, or inefficient hot path, penalize trajectories that treat performance evidence as sufficient while failing to preserve the task’s visible behavioral requirements. This includes partial fixes that address only a named micro-optimization while missing another stated correctness requirement; cache or data-structure changes that do not preserve ordering, invalidation, serialization, or lookup semantics; query narrowing that ignores fields needed for lifecycle hooks, cascades, or signals; and removal of implicit/no-op work without respecting explicit user actions or pending state. Do not penalize a localized micro-optimization merely because it is small when the issue report supplies concrete motivation and the implementation is behavior-preserving.

task_conditions: Original task explicitly frames performance as the bug or feature request
Task names a concrete bottleneck, no-op path, regression, cache miss, unnecessary query, signal, or pointer/data-structure overhead
Task also states compatibility requirements such as ordering, explicit operations, filtering, invalidation, cascade/signal behavior, or preserving existing API output
visible_evidence_to_check: Agent traces the reported hot path rather than optimizing unrelated code
Patch scope is limited to the named path or justified integration points
Implementation preserves non-performance semantics visible in the issue and code comments
Tests or manual validation cover both the optimized/no-op case and the behavior-preserving edge case
Agent avoids broad rewrites or unrelated cleanups that change parsing, conversion, output, or lifecycle behavior
avoid_using_as_proxy: Use of a theoretically faster data structure alone
Removal of a loop, signal, query, or placeholder alone
Generic concern that all micro-optimizations are speculative

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory targets the reported performance path and visibly preserves the stated behavioral/compatibility requirements.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the optimization is on target, but validation of one secondary compatibility boundary is thin or only reasoned about.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory addresses the bottleneck but leaves important stated behavior, ordering, invalidation, filtering, or edge-case preservation uncertain.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the trajectory implements a performance change while missing a visible non-performance requirement or likely altering existing semantics.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory performs broad or unrelated performance refactoring, relies on speculative evidence, or breaks/omits central behavior required by the task.

experiences.title: End-to-End Return Contract Compatibility
experiences.description: Retrieve when the task or trajectory centers on changing, clarifying, or preserving a function’s return structure and there is visible evidence of callers unpacking, destructuring, indexing, or type-checking that return value.
experiences.context: Applies across Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, Go, and similar codebases when the issue explicitly mentions inconsistent return types, ambiguous tuple/array returns, scalar-versus-array behavior, missing companion return values, or callers failing because they expect a particular structure. It is most useful once the agent has inspected both the producer function and at least some direct call sites/tests. It is less decisive when the reported bug has multiple independent requirements, such as cache lifecycle, configuration, CLI/chart wiring, or parsing heuristics, and the trajectory only addresses a narrow return-type symptom. It is also premature during very early exploration before caller expectations are known.
experiences.experience: The prior rubric judged whether returned values and output types match what callers expect. This is highly useful when the visible trajectory shows a return-contract task: for example, a function currently returns a bare object but callers need to unpack an object plus related keys, or cached-link helpers return positional arrays that should become named fields. In those settings, a strong patch must update the producer signature, all concrete implementations, internal aggregation logic, tests, and every destructuring/indexing caller consistently. The same criterion can be misleading if the agent fixes only a local return shape while ignoring other required behavior, or if it changes the return type to allow partial/optional values that downstream code cannot safely consume. A better rubric should focus on end-to-end compatibility: does the new return value preserve the semantic data callers need, does every caller consume the new shape correctly, and are old scalar/single-value paths still supported where required? Avoid the tempting wrong criterion of rewarding any return-type cleanup or more descriptive structure in isolation. Prioritize visible evidence such as function annotations/docstrings, direct call-site destructuring/indexing, test assertions about returned structures, aggregation operators combining returned values, and downstream code that assumes non-null fields or specific object methods.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Producer-Caller Return Contract Coherence
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluate whether the agent’s trajectory demonstrates a coherent end-to-end return contract change or preservation: the producing function(s) return the exact structure required by the task, all polymorphic implementations or helper variants follow the same contract, and all visible callers/tests are updated or verified to consume that structure without positional ambiguity, unpacking errors, missing fields, or optional values that downstream code cannot handle.

required_visible_evidence: The task or inspected code identifies an expected return structure, such as tuple/object fields, named properties, list output, scalar-versus-array behavior, or non-null fields.
The agent inspects or reasons about both the return-producing function and representative callers/tests.
The planned or implemented change accounts for call-site destructuring, indexing, aggregation, type annotations, and backwards-compatible paths where applicable.
common_failure_modes: Only the producer return statement is changed while callers still unpack/index the old shape.
Only tests or one caller are updated while other visible consumers remain incompatible.
The patch introduces partial or nullable return fields without adapting downstream code that requires concrete values.
The patch fixes a return-contract symptom but ignores other independent requirements in the task.

scale.1: No meaningful evidence that the agent has identified the expected return contract or caller expectations; work is unrelated or only exploratory.
scale.2: The agent notices a return type issue but examines only the producer or only one caller, with no clear plan for all consumers or compatibility boundaries.
scale.3: The agent identifies the intended return structure and at least one relevant caller, but the trajectory leaves some implementations, aggregators, tests, or backwards-compatible paths unresolved.
scale.4: The agent shows strong evidence of updating or planning updates across producers and most visible consumers, preserving the needed semantic data and avoiding obvious unpacking/indexing/type mismatches.
scale.5: The trajectory fully aligns the return contract end-to-end: all relevant implementations share the same structure, all visible callers/tests consume named or otherwise correct fields, aggregation and batch/single paths are handled, and downstream non-null/type assumptions remain valid.

experiences.title: Evidence grounding is not task completion evidence
experiences.description: Retrieve this warning when a trajectory contains many verified code observations, greps, experiments, or cautious claims, but the task requires an end-to-end behavior change whose implementation and validation are not yet clearly covered.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE-agent code repair trajectories across Python, Go, TypeScript, or similar repositories where the agent is investigating behavior, configuration loading, migrations, UI/runtime settings, cache semantics, URL handling, notification state, or other multi-layer features. The misleading case is a trajectory that is mostly truthful and code-grounded, or avoids hallucinating unseen APIs, yet still has no semantic patch, a no-op/comment-only change, a patch limited to one layer while required runtime/application paths are untouched, repeated redundant probing, missing compatibility boundaries, or no regression validation of the user-visible contract. The source rubric can still be appropriate when the main risk is unsupported speculation, such as asserting an unseen function exists, assuming library behavior without checking, or changing code based on unverified configuration/system behavior. It should not be used as the primary success predictor once the visible task demands concrete behavior across call sites, data flow, compatibility gates, and tests.
experiences.experience: The previous rubric judged whether the agent’s behavior claims were supported by visible code evidence. That is a sound hygiene criterion, but it over-credits trajectories where accurate investigation does not close the task. A future rubric generator should not treat verified observations, successful greps, version checks, or cautious statements as strong evidence that the final repair will be correct. In these cases, the important question is whether the agent has connected the user-visible requirement to the owning implementation path and changed all necessary integration points: parsing/loading plus runtime use, per-scope state plus aggregation, static startup flags plus dynamic settings, migration semantics plus cross-cluster mappings, or nested data structure preservation plus regression coverage. Avoid the tempting criterion “the agent only made evidence-grounded claims” as a standalone positive rubric for behavior-change tasks. Prefer criteria that prioritize visible evidence of contract closure: an explicit requirement-to-code mapping, edits at the component that actually enforces the behavior, preservation of compatibility/default behavior, tests or reproducer validation for the reported scenario, and avoidance of no-op or merely cosmetic changes. At early exploration stages, evidence grounding can be a process-quality note, but it should remain subordinate to rubrics about forward progress, non-redundant investigation, and whether the planned patch addresses all required user-facing effects.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Verified investigation without end-to-end task closure
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories for behavior-change tasks when the visible evidence shows accurate code inspection or experiments but does not show that the required user-visible contract is implemented through the actual owning path. This includes no patch after extended investigation, repeated redundant lookups, comment-only or cosmetic changes, changing only configuration structs without applying the values at runtime, handling only the global case when scoped behavior is requested, adding a compatibility gate without using the correct runtime API, or validating only an intermediate representation rather than the externally relevant behavior. Do not apply this as a failure solely because the trajectory is in a short early exploration phase with a clear next step; apply it when the agent’s apparent confidence or chosen direction rests mainly on verified observations rather than concrete coverage of the task contract.

misleading_proxy_to_avoid: many greps or file inspections
accurate statements about current code
small experiments confirming library/API behavior
targeted tests that do not exercise the reported end-to-end scenario
absence of hallucinated claims
replacement_evidence_to_prioritize: explicit mapping from each requirement to an implementation point
edits in the code path that enforces the behavior at runtime
coverage of all required scopes or compatibility cases
preservation of existing defaults and backward compatibility
regression validation using the user-reported scenario or an equivalent focused test
metadata.stage_boundary: Use lightly during initial exploration; use strongly when the trajectory has settled on a fix, claims the issue is understood, or spends many steps without moving from observation to contract-covering implementation.

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: the trajectory connects verified observations to concrete implementation changes and validation that cover the task’s user-visible contract.
scale.2: Minor evidence: investigation is evidence-grounded and mostly on path, but one secondary integration point, compatibility note, or validation detail remains unresolved.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory has useful verified facts or a plausible partial edit, but coverage of an important required path or scope is still uncertain.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the agent relies on verified observations while omitting a major required behavior path, runtime application point, scoped case, or regression check.
scale.5: Severe evidence: after substantial work the trajectory has no semantic patch, a no-op/cosmetic patch, repetitive probing, or a fix direction visibly disconnected from the end-to-end behavior requested.

experiences.title: Contract-Level Behavioral Test Evidence
experiences.description: Retrieve this when an agent claims validation through added tests, changed expected outputs, or ad hoc scripts for a behavior-specific bug or feature; judge whether those tests assert the actual user-visible contract rather than merely exercising code paths.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE-agent trajectories across Python, Go, and TypeScript repositories after the agent has identified a fix and is using tests or manual scripts as confidence evidence. It is most relevant for tasks involving parsing metadata, fallback ordering, event-driven UI updates, set/membership semantics, deterministic selection, or API parameter precedence, where a patch can look plausible while missing a boundary condition. It is less decisive during early exploration, when no implementation exists yet, or for very small localized source fixes whose correctness is directly visible from the changed line and no durable test has been added. Do not retrieve it merely because no formal test was run; absence of tests alone is not a reliable flaw for simple one-line compatibility fixes. Do retrieve it when tests are present but may be superficial, omitted from the submitted diff, only check that code runs, or update expectations to match an incorrect intermediate representation.
experiences.experience: The prior rubric judged whether validation was meaningful. It was useful when visible test activity revealed whether the agent understood the behavioral contract: strong evidence came from tests that exercised the exact reported scenario, asserted the final observable result, and included important branches such as missing data, fallback paths, resize/update events, explicit override versus default behavior, or deterministic ordering. It correctly flagged trajectories where the agent relied on smoke scripts, repeated commands, changed expected values without checking the real semantic object, or added tests that did not cover the required fallback/edge case. However, it can be misleading if used as a blanket requirement: a tiny, obvious formatting or parameter-default fix may be correct even with weak or no committed tests. A better retrieved rubric should focus on the quality and relevance of the validation evidence, not on the mere presence, count, or passing status of tests. Avoid the tempting criterion “tests pass, therefore patch is good” or “no tests, therefore patch is bad.” Prioritize visible evidence that tests would fail on the original bug, assert the user-facing contract exactly, cover the boundary cases named in the task, and are actually part of the patch or otherwise reproducible from the trajectory.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluate whether the agent's validation evidence demonstrates the intended behavioral contract, not just code execution. High-quality evidence includes committed or clearly described tests/manual checks that reproduce the reported issue, assert the exact user-visible expected result, cover named edge cases and fallback/update paths, and would distinguish the proposed fix from common wrong implementations. This rubric should be applied relative to the current trajectory: look only at visible task requirements, test diffs, commands run, outputs observed, and whether validation artifacts are included or durable.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Meaningful Contract Validation

prioritize_evidence: tests or scripts reproduce the specific reported behavior
assertions check exact semantic outputs or state changes, not merely absence of crashes
coverage includes task-specified boundaries such as fallback order, missing data, update events, deterministic selection, membership semantics, or explicit override behavior
validation artifacts are committed or clearly part of the final patch when appropriate
test output confirms the relevant tests actually ran rather than being skipped or unmatched
deprioritize_evidence: test count or broad suite pass status without relevant assertions
manual scripts that only print values or check a superficial substring
updated expected values that mirror the implementation without checking the requested behavior
absence of tests for a trivial source-level fix whose correctness is directly inspectable
metadata.applicability_stage: post-implementation or final-review stage, especially when the agent cites validation as confidence

scale.1: No meaningful behavioral validation is visible, or the agent only ran commands that do not exercise the reported scenario; any tests are absent, skipped, unrelated, or merely confirm the code imports/runs.
scale.2: Weak validation exists but is superficial: it checks a narrow implementation detail, printed output, or a happy path while omitting the core behavior or task-specified boundaries.
scale.3: Validation is comparable to the parent trajectory: some relevant behavior is exercised, but important edge cases, fallback/update semantics, or exact assertions are incomplete or not clearly committed.
scale.4: Strong validation directly covers the reported scenario and at least one important boundary condition, with assertions on observable behavior and evidence that the relevant tests ran.
scale.5: Excellent validation would fail on the original bug and distinguishes the fix from likely wrong implementations; it asserts the exact user contract, includes all task-critical branches, is durable in the patch, and the trajectory shows the targeted tests actually executed.

experiences.title: Do not let broad cross-file activity substitute for acceptance-contract evidence
experiences.description: Retrieve this warning when a task spans many components and the trajectory shows broad searches, multi-file edits, or integration commentary, but the visible evidence does not yet prove the concrete behavioral contract required by the task.
experiences.context: Applies in software repositories where the task is inherently cross-cutting—UI terminology, API endpoint creation, version-support drops, dynamic service addresses, storage-unit centralization, onboarding/setup flows, generated RPC surfaces, or CLI testability. In these cases, a generic holistic-review rubric can be misleading because an agent may inspect or edit many related files while still missing the decisive contract: generated artifacts, actual listener addresses, source/localization synchronization, CI/test matrix updates, error-returning CLI paths, semantic boundary between user-facing text and protocol identifiers, or centralized constants. The source rubric can still be appropriate during final integration review when there is already a concrete patch and the main remaining question is whether the modified components interoperate. It should not be used as a high-confidence proxy during reconnaissance, no-op conclusions, repetitive search loops, or scattershot broad edits without visible acceptance-level closure.
experiences.experience: The previous rubric judged whether the agent reviewed the change holistically across components. That is a useful secondary check, but it became misleading when broad exploration or multi-file editing was treated as evidence of correctness. In the sampled trajectories, agents often touched or inspected many files yet left the core contract unresolved: no patch after investigation, incomplete generated-code/API wiring, changed comments that were historically false, omitted CI or changelog updates, over-edited localization files, failed to distinguish protocol/internal identifiers from user-facing strings, or repeated the same search without progressing. A better rubric should focus on whether the visible trajectory has closed the task-specific behavioral requirements and respected domain boundaries. Avoid the tempting criterion “the agent looked at all relevant components” or “the patch spans many components.” Prioritize evidence such as: exact acceptance cases identified and implemented, required generated files or configuration matrices updated, user-facing strings changed in source and canonical localization files together, dynamic runtime values propagated instead of configured placeholders, no-op conclusions justified by definitive repository state, and validation or targeted greps/tests showing the critical contract rather than only broad coverage.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories that appear cross-component or comprehensive but lack visible evidence that the task's concrete acceptance contract has been implemented and validated. This applies especially when the agent relies on broad grep results, file lists, or many edits while missing required artifacts, generated code, runtime propagation, source/localization synchronization, CI/config updates, or protocol-versus-user-facing boundaries. Do not penalize merely for working across many files if the trajectory also shows the decisive contract being satisfied with targeted validation.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Cross-component activity without contract closure

preferred_visible_evidence: explicit acceptance cases mapped to implementation
critical generated/configuration/test artifacts updated when required
semantic boundaries preserved, such as protocol identifiers versus user-facing labels
runtime values or API responses verified at the actual integration point
targeted validation demonstrating the requested behavior rather than only absence of search hits
typical_failure_stage: no-op conclusion despite remaining task-specific work

scale.1: No evidence of this flaw: the trajectory ties each major task requirement to concrete code changes and targeted validation, with broad component review used only to confirm integration.
scale.2: Minor evidence: the agent performs broad review and may leave a small validation or ancillary artifact ambiguous, but the main behavioral contract is visibly addressed.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the trajectory covers many related components but only partially demonstrates the decisive contract, leaving important requirements or boundary checks unresolved.
scale.4: Clear evidence: the agent relies heavily on cross-file exploration or multi-file edits while missing a central acceptance requirement, generated/configuration artifact, runtime propagation path, or semantic boundary.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory is mostly broad search, repetitive investigation, no-op reasoning, or scattershot edits, with little or no visible implementation of the task's core behavioral contract.

experiences.title: Do not reward read-only exploration after the key contract is already known
experiences.description: Use this warning when a trajectory contains many safe read commands, but the task’s success depends on applying a specific integration contract, lifecycle transition, owner/container boundary, or compatibility case rather than merely avoiding premature writes.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE-agent code-repair trajectories across TypeScript/React, Go, Python, and similar repositories where the recent evidence is mostly grep/cat/sed or file inspection. The misleading case is when normal or repetitive read-before-write behavior looks disciplined even though the agent has already identified the relevant files/APIs, is looping on similar searches, has not made task-specific progress, or is about to implement from a superficial understanding. The original read-before-write rubric may still be appropriate very early in exploration, especially when the agent is considering broad or destructive edits before locating the relevant component, tests, or API contract. It is not a strong correctness signal once the visible trajectory already contains enough file-local context and the remaining risk is semantic integration.
experiences.experience: The previous rubric judged the presence of non-destructive exploration before writes. That is useful as a safety/process check, but it overemphasizes command hygiene in tasks where correctness hinges on domain behavior: using the existing service instead of bypassing it, clearing owned state rather than only stopping an object, updating the right lifecycle entry point, preserving compatibility fallbacks, or applying a state/filter contract with the action’s intent. A better rubric should ask whether the agent has converted exploration into task-specific evidence and implementation choices. Avoid the tempting criterion of counting grep/cat/sed commands as positive progress. Prioritize visible evidence such as: the agent inspected the exact owner API or reusable service named by the discovered code path; stopped repeating identical searches after finding the relevant facts; planned or made edits at the lifecycle boundary where the bug occurs; accounted for compatibility or parent/owner context mentioned in the task; and added or targeted tests for the described behavior.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Exploration without contract-level follow-through
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Penalize trajectories where the visible evidence is dominated by generic or repetitive read-only exploration after the relevant files or APIs have already been identified, and there is little evidence that the agent is applying the task-specific contract, owner/lifecycle boundary, state transition, compatibility case, or existing service semantics needed for a correct patch.

observable_cues: earlier summary or recent reads already name the likely target files/functions
recent steps repeat similar grep/cat/sed searches without new information
agent inspects broad docs or unrelated files instead of the known domain service, lifecycle owner, or tests
no edit or plan addresses the specific state/contract boundary described by the task
implementation confidence would rest mainly on having read files rather than on satisfying the behavior contract
metadata.source_rubric_boundary: Read-before-write remains useful only as an early safety criterion before localization or before potentially destructive edits; it should not be used as a high-confidence correctness criterion after localization.
replacement_evidence_priority: inspection of the exact existing abstraction responsible for the behavior
clear mapping from task scenario to the call path being changed
handling of owner/container or lifecycle redirection when mentioned by the task
compatibility with multiple representations or versions when the task names them
tests or test-oriented reasoning that exercise the described regression

scale.1: No evidence of the flaw: exploration is brief, non-repetitive, and directly feeds a task-specific implementation or test plan.
scale.2: Minor evidence: some extra reading occurs, but the agent still clearly identifies the relevant contract and next implementation step.
scale.3: Moderate evidence: the agent has localized the area but remains partly focused on generic searches or superficial facts, with only partial attention to the needed behavior contract.
scale.4: Clear evidence: after finding the relevant files/APIs, the agent keeps reading or plans edits without addressing the owner/lifecycle/state/compatibility requirement central to the task.
scale.5: Severe evidence: the trajectory is largely read-only or repetitive despite known targets, or any proposed implementation would bypass the established abstraction or miss the key contract described by the task.

experiences.title: Recovering After Botched Partial Edits
experiences.description: Retrieve this when the trajectory shows a multi-step code-editing workflow has failed partway through, especially after malformed patches, broad sed replacements, duplicated blocks, deleted lines, or uncertain file state.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE-agent style repository repair sessions where the agent is modifying source files through shell commands and a recent edit attempt has visibly gone wrong or become uncertain. Strong matches include observations of duplicated code, missing functions, malformed syntax, failed patch application, repeated line-number deletions, or a checkout/revert followed by a new attempt. The criterion is most useful during recovery or final-review stages, when the next important question is whether the agent inspected the actual file/diff and restored a coherent baseline before continuing. It is less useful during early exploration before any destructive edit, and it should not be treated as a complete semantic-correctness rubric for issues that require broad coverage across multiple implementations, storage backends, interfaces, or call sites.
experiences.experience: The retrieved rubric judged whether the agent reassessed state after a partial workflow failure before continuing. This is discriminative when the visible trajectory contains failed edits: agents that stop, inspect numbered context or git diff, restore damaged files, and then apply a narrow patch are much more likely to leave a coherent change than agents that keep deleting or inserting by stale line numbers. The rubric can be wrong if used as a proxy for full task completeness: a clean recovery process may still miss a second affected subsystem, and a messy intermediate trajectory may later converge on a tiny correct change. A better rubric should focus on observable recovery evidence after the failure: explicit inspection of the damaged region, `git diff` or equivalent state review, restoring from version control when corruption is suspected, replacing blind sed loops with a precise patch, and running at least a targeted validation. Avoid the tempting wrong criterion of rewarding the agent merely for identifying the intended fix or for saying it will verify; prioritize whether it actually confirmed the current file state before making further edits.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: After a visible partial-edit failure or uncertain modification state, the agent should explicitly reassess the repository state before continuing: inspect the affected code and diff, restore or clean up corrupted edits when needed, then apply a precise minimal change and validate it. This rubric is about recovery discipline after a failed workflow, not about whether the chosen semantic fix covers every required subsystem.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: State Reassessment After Failed Edit Workflow

required_visible_evidence: A prior command or edit produced malformed, duplicated, misplaced, or uncertain code state.
The agent inspects the affected region, full diff, or repository status after the failure.
If corruption is plausible, the agent restores or deliberately cleans the file before applying the next edit.
Subsequent edits are targeted rather than repeated blind line-number operations.
The agent performs or plans a validation that checks the repaired state.
not_applicable_when: No partial workflow failure or destructive edit has occurred yet.
The main uncertainty is semantic coverage across multiple independent components rather than file-state recovery.
The trajectory is still pure exploration with no modified state to reassess.

scale.1: No meaningful reassessment after a failed or uncertain edit; the agent continues with blind deletions, insertions, or assumptions about file state.
scale.2: Weak reassessment; the agent briefly views truncated context or repeats the same fragile edit pattern without confirming the complete affected state.
scale.3: Moderate behavior; the agent recognizes something went wrong and partially inspects or restores state, but validation or cleanup remains incomplete.
scale.4: Strong behavior; the agent inspects the relevant code/diff, corrects or restores damaged state, and switches to a more controlled edit approach.
scale.5: Excellent behavior; the agent clearly diagnoses the failed workflow, restores a coherent baseline if needed, applies a minimal precise patch, verifies the resulting diff/context, and runs targeted validation.

experiences.title: Persisted Tool-Side Effects in Patch Hygiene
experiences.description: Retrieve when the trajectory includes side-effectful commands or environment workarounds, especially near finalization, and the key question is whether the agent contained or cleaned up unrelated file/environment mutations before relying on validation.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE-agent-style Unix `/testbed` repository work where the agent uses bash tools that can mutate state: broad `sed` edits, `git checkout`/restore, package installs, editable installs, source builds, manual copying into build trees or `site-packages`, lockfile-generating package-manager commands, or temporary import/build hacks. It is most useful after implementation or during final review, when visible evidence such as `git diff`, `git diff --stat`, `git status`, cleanup commands, or validation commands can show whether the intended patch is isolated. It is less useful for read-only exploration, early failed dependency installation attempts, or tasks where the visible working-tree diff is already clearly limited to the intended source change. Do not apply it as a broad penalty for failed builds, dependency installs, or untracked scratch scripts unless those side effects contaminate the repository, global package environment, or the evidence used to validate the fix.
experiences.experience: The source rubric judged whether the agent understood what its tool calls changed. That criterion is useful when the trajectory shows risky mutations whose persistence can make a patch unreliable: broad text replacements that may corrupt imports, manual build-tree or installed-package edits, package-manager actions that unexpectedly rewrite lockfiles, checkout/revert commands that may discard work, or tests run against an installed package rather than the modified checkout. In those situations, a strong rubric should reward explicit containment: inspecting `git diff`/`git status`, reverting unrelated hacks, keeping only task-relevant files, avoiding validation against a copied or globally patched dependency, and explaining which side effects are safe or temporary. It should down-rank trajectories that leave unrelated lockfile/source changes, copy repository files into external package directories, or treat passing tests in an unmodified/contaminated environment as proof. However, the tempting wrong criterion is to penalize every `pip install`, failed build, temporary reproducer, or repeated import failure as inherently bad; many correct patches arise despite environment setup failures if the agent keeps the source diff clean and reasons from targeted code inspection. Prioritize visible evidence of persistent repository/global mutations and cleanup behavior over the mere presence of side-effectful commands.

reference_golden_rubrics.title: Contains and Audits Tool-Induced Side Effects
reference_golden_rubrics.description: Evaluate whether the agent recognizes, audits, and contains side effects from mutating tool calls before relying on validation or finalizing code. Strong evidence includes checking the working tree after risky commands, reverting unrelated environment/debug edits, avoiding or explicitly isolating global package/build-tree modifications, ensuring tests exercise the modified checkout rather than an installed or copied package, and keeping the intended source change separate from generated lockfiles, temporary scripts, or dependency-install artifacts. The criterion should focus on persistent or validation-contaminating side effects visible in the trajectory, not on harmless dependency installation attempts or failed builds by themselves.

side_effect_evidence: broad source-editing commands such as sed/perl scripts
package-manager or build commands that may alter lockfiles or generated files
manual copying into build directories, site-packages, or installed dependencies
git diff, git diff --stat, git status, git checkout, git restore, or cleanup commands
validation commands whose import path or target package may not be the modified checkout
metadata.stage: Most applicable after risky tool use during implementation, validation, or final cleanup.

scale.1: No meaningful side-effect awareness: the agent uses risky mutating tools, leaves unrelated or global changes unexamined, or validates against a contaminated/unmodified environment with no cleanup evidence.
scale.2: Weak awareness: the agent notices some environment or repository side effects but continues with questionable validation or leaves unclear/unresolved unrelated changes.
scale.3: Moderate awareness: behavior is roughly parent-equivalent; the agent performs some inspection or cleanup, but evidence is incomplete about whether all persistent side effects are isolated from the intended patch.
scale.4: Strong awareness: the agent checks diffs/status after risky operations, reverts or avoids unrelated mutations, and distinguishes source changes from temporary environment workarounds before validating.
scale.5: Excellent awareness: the agent proactively contains all risky tool effects, keeps the working tree narrowly scoped, avoids global/package contamination, validates against the modified checkout or clearly explains why validation is limited, and documents/reverts temporary artifacts.

experiences.title: Validate Imported Tool Provenance Before Trusting Reproductions
experiences.description: Retrieve when an agent’s validation depends on command output from an installed package, test runner, or generated artifact that may not come from the edited checkout, especially after dependency/install problems or contradictory observations.
experiences.context: Applies in SWE trajectories across Python/JS repositories where the agent runs reproductions, pytest/build commands, or ad-hoc scripts and the output could be from a globally installed or cached version rather than the local source under repair. Strong matching cues include: failed editable installs, installing a newer package from PyPI, manual outputs contradicting visible local source, repeated greps or reruns that add no new evidence, or explicit need to print module paths/versions/working directories. The criterion is most useful during validation and final-review stages, after the agent has begun using tool output to justify a patch. It is less useful during very early code navigation with no execution evidence, or when the task can be judged directly from a small source edit and no suspect tool output is being used as proof.
experiences.experience: The original rubric judged whether the agent validated tool outputs instead of blindly trusting them. It is useful when command output is plausibly from the wrong environment or contradicts inspected source: a good trajectory should identify the mismatch, verify provenance such as imported file/version or test harness source, and avoid treating external or stale output as proof. However, avoid using a broad 'many commands were run' or 'some validation passed' proxy; repeated searches, passing tests from an unrelated installed package, or manual HTML/image output from the wrong source do not establish correctness. A better rubric should focus on whether the agent reconciles contradictions and bases confidence on evidence tied to the modified checkout. Also avoid over-penalizing mere dependency/setup failures if the final reasoning and patch do not actually rely on those invalid outputs. Prioritize visible evidence such as printed module paths, notes that installed packages mask the bug, rerunning with the repo’s own test harness, discarding contradictory external results, and ensuring explicit user-supplied behavior is not overridden while validating the intended case.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: The trajectory demonstrates that runtime or tool outputs used to justify the fix are tied to the local checkout and are reconciled with source-code observations. Strong evidence includes checking imported module paths or package versions after installing dependencies, recognizing when a global/newer package or stale build is being exercised, rerunning or planning validation through the repository’s own test harness, and not relying on contradictory outputs until their provenance is explained. The rubric should reward provenance-aware validation, not merely the presence of many commands or passing output.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Local-Provenance Tool Validation

required_evidence: Tool output is used or considered as support for the patch.
There is a plausible risk of wrong-version, wrong-path, cached, or externally installed code being exercised.
The agent either verifies or fails to verify that the output corresponds to the edited local source.
high_value_cues: printed module __file__, version, working directory, PYTHONPATH, or test harness provenance
explicitly identifies contradictions between command output and inspected source
uses in-repository regression tests or pytester/build fixtures instead of global binaries
does not claim proof from output known or suspected to be external
anti_cues: repeated greps or reruns with identical output treated as progress
passing results from a newly installed upstream package used to validate local edits
manual artifact inspection without confirming it was generated from modified code
ignoring a contradiction between runtime behavior and local source

scale.1: Tool outputs are absent, irrelevant, or clearly not used as evidence; no meaningful provenance issue is visible.
scale.2: Some tool output is gathered, but there is little sign the agent checks whether it comes from the local checkout despite mild environment uncertainty.
scale.3: The agent notices or partially investigates provenance concerns, but the trajectory remains mixed: some conclusions may still rely on unverified or contradictory outputs.
scale.4: The agent clearly verifies key tool-output provenance or explicitly discounts suspect outputs, and bases validation mainly on local-source-aware evidence.
scale.5: The agent systematically reconciles all important contradictory outputs, confirms local import/test provenance, reruns or designs validation through the repo’s own harness, and avoids using any external/stale output as proof of correctness.

experiences.title: Exact Failure-Mode Contract Coverage
experiences.description: Retrieve when the task is explicitly about invalid input, corrupted state, cancellation/timeout, auth rejection, or other failure handling where correctness depends on mapping a specific error source to a specific exception, status code, JSON body, or user-facing message.
experiences.context: Applies in Python or Go web/API/CLI/server codebases when the problem statement names concrete failure modes and expected error behavior, such as converting a low-level exception into a framework validation error, returning a protocol-specific status code, rejecting invalid credentials, or emitting structured failure output. It is most useful after the trajectory has identified the relevant error-producing call path and is editing the handler/interceptor/parser/converter responsible for error classification. It is less useful as a standalone criterion when the agent is still only exploring, when the patch only adds broad catch-all handling without proving the exact reported exception source, or when the real issue may involve another layer such as middleware ordering, response formatting, repository contracts, or compatibility across dependency versions.
experiences.experience: The source rubric judged whether error conditions and failure modes were explicitly covered. That is valuable for tasks whose requested behavior is itself an error-path contract, but it should not be retrieved as a generic 'has tests for errors' signal. It aligns best when visible evidence shows the agent has traced the exact failing input or exception type, implemented the required conversion at the layer where the failure actually escapes, and preserved unrelated errors instead of swallowing or reclassifying them. A better rubric should focus on whether every failure mode named in the task is handled with the specified observable response and whether the patch prevents downstream processing on failure. Avoid the tempting proxy of rewarding any added error test, broad exception catch, or passing package test; those can miss important origin paths, existing pass-through behavior, end-to-end response serialization, or dependency-version differences. Prioritize visible evidence such as reproduction of the specific invalid value/corrupted file/auth failure/timeout, inspection of the exception hierarchy or error contract, assertions on the exact status/code/message/body, and checks that unrelated errors and normal paths remain unchanged.

reference_golden_rubrics.description: For a task centered on failure handling, the trajectory should demonstrate that the patch handles the exact reported failure sources at the correct boundary and produces the specified observable error contract. Strong evidence includes tracing the failure to the concrete throwing/returning operation, distinguishing expected failure classes from unrelated errors, preventing protected or downstream work after rejection, preserving existing successful and unrelated-error behavior, and adding or running focused validation that checks the exact exception/status/code/message/structured body required by the task.
reference_golden_rubrics.title: Exact Failure-Mode Contract Implementation

task_signals: problem statement names invalid input, corrupted data, cancellation, timeout, auth failure, removed command, or structured error output
expected behavior specifies an exception class, protocol status, error code, JSON fields, or user-facing guidance
required_evidence: agent identifies the actual call path where the reported failure escapes
patch maps only the intended failure class/source to the required response
patch does not mask unrelated errors or regress existing pass-through behavior
validation or tests assert the exact observable failure contract, not just that some error occurred
boundaries: do not over-reward broad catch-all handlers without source-specific reasoning
do not treat package tests passing as sufficient if the named failure mode is untested
do not ignore other layers that can reclassify or reformat the error before it reaches users

scale.1: No visible evidence that the exact reported failure mode is understood or handled; the patch is unrelated, only explores files, or relies on generic success-path behavior.
scale.2: Some error-handling code is touched, but it is broad, speculative, or at an uncertain layer; the exact required status/exception/body is not validated and unrelated errors may be swallowed or misclassified.
scale.3: The trajectory addresses the likely failure path and expected error response, but coverage is partial: one named failure source is handled while other described origins, compatibility boundaries, or response-format details remain unverified.
scale.4: The exact reported failure source is traced and handled at the right boundary with the required observable response; focused validation checks the main error contract and the patch appears to preserve normal behavior.
scale.5: All named failure modes are explicitly handled and validated with precise assertions on status/code/exception/message/structured output, downstream processing is prevented where required, unrelated errors remain distinguishable, and compatibility or layering issues are considered.
